machine_text: I have read the paper "Bridge Text and Knowledge by Learning Multi-Prototype Entity Mention Embedding" with great interest. The proposed method is interesting and seems promising. However, there are several issues that should be addressed before publication. 1. It is not clear how the knowledge extraction phase is performed. How do you evaluate the knowledge gained? Did you compare the knowledge acquired with any external knowledge source? 2. In the training phase, you only report training loss but not the validation set loss. You should also report the F1 score on the validation set. Did the model overfit on the training set or not? 3. The length of the short poem used for poem pairs is short. Usually, poems are much longer than 30 lines. In this case, you may want to consider using a sequence of poems instead of a single poem. 4. In the evaluation, you report an F1 score for the first poem in the pair but not for the second. That makes it hard to compare with other results. I suggest adding an F1 score for the second poem in the pair as well. In addition, it would be nice to compare your result with other results on the same dataset. 5. Your code and data are not made publicly available. This prevents other researchers from verifying and improving upon your work. I suggest making the code and dataset publicly available. In the meantime, these issues should be addressed so that the work can be published. 1. Knowledge extraction phase In the Knowledge extraction phase, the multiple loss functions are applied to identify the contribution of each component. The general F1 score is used to measure the effectiveness of knowledge extraction. However, there is no clear definition of the knowledge acquired by the model. To illustrate the knowledge acquired by the model, a comparison with knowledge from external sources can be used. For example, if you expect the model to acquire knowledge about the period of poetry, you can compare the knowledge acquired with poems written in a certain period. 2. Evaluation metrics F1 score is used to measure the effectiveness of knowledge extraction. However, this metric does not distinguish whether the model has correctly identified the knowledge or simply a large portion of the input is comprised of knowledge. In contrast, if a specific knowledge type, such as Parnassus, is used to calculate the precision, and if the sum of precision and the model’s predicted F1 is used to calculate the F1 score, this metric will better reflect the contribution of the model. 3. Overfitting Model performance overfitting depends on the validation set. The validation set must be used to calculate the loss during the training process, and the performance is reported based on this data. 4. Length of poem In the model training phase, although the length of the poem used for poem pairs is short, the model can achieve good performance, so I recommend extending the length of poem pairs. 5. Comparison with other results It is better to compare the model performance with other results on the same dataset to show the improvement of the model. 6. Code and dataset made available To further improve the research directions of the paper, the code and dataset are made available to other researchers for research purposes.

The Bridge Text and Knowledge (BTK) model introduces a simple method for including language knowledge in neural named-entity se- quencing systems. In particular, BTK provides a method for entity types to learn to embed multiple plausible hidden representations of language knowl- edge in its input text, which the model then uses to predict missing entity mentions in new pieces of text. BTK uses an entity type embedding that is trained on entity types and associated types of knowledge that is hard-coded into the model, such as the relation type of “d” to days, and the name of streets and buildings. BTK has a number of interesting properties, but has several clear weaknesses. Most importantly, BTK does not learn any entity types from data, so it is only able to encode a limited amount of knowledge. BTK also does not have an auxiliary task to encourage the model to generate new plausible entities, so it is prone to generate incorrect entities in new contexts. The model has many interesting properties, in that it is very simple, and effective at incorporating limited amounts of hardcoded knowledge to se- quencing tasks. This allows it to be easily adaptable to specific tasks without the need for re-training, which provides speed in deployment. In addition, BTK’s entity types provide a lot of expressivity for a limited amount of parameters. To encourage the model to generate plausible but incorrect entities, BTK combines with the CopyQA model to provide a method to fine-tune the copy quality of the generated entities. The combination of these two methods allows the model to produce useful outputs even without any training data, which is an attractive property. Overall, BTK is an interesting model that shows how to make simple and effective use of limited knowledge. It provides a starting point for more principled ways of incorporating knowledge in neural se- quencing models. This paper addresses a number of problems with the BTK model, and addresses them in a creative and effective way. The main problem with the BTK model is that it only uses a limited set of hardcoded entity types, which limits the amount of knowledge that the model can learn from data. This is a critical problem, because the model is only able to encode a limited amount of knowledge. The BTK model also does not have an auxiliary task to encourage the model to generate new plausible entities. The model has the strong ability to reproduce its previous generated outputs, which could be a design flaw, as the model does not have an ability to explore new modes of generating entities. The model presented in this paper addresses these issues. The model uses a method for learning entity types from data that can then be used to encode knowledge. This makes the model more flexible, and allows it to encode more knowledge. In addition, the model generates a new auxiliary task to encourage the model to generate plausible but incorrect entities. This allows the model to generate entities in a more general way, with the hope that the generated entities can provide useful background knowledge. Overall, this is an interesting and useful method for incorporating knowledge in neural se- quencing models. The model described in this paper addresses several problems with the BTK model. First, it allows the model to learn new entity types from data. This provides the model with more flexibility, and makes the model more able to encode knowledge. In addition, the model generates a new auxiliary task to encourage the model to generate plausible but incorrect entities. This allows the model to generate entities in a more general way, with the hope that the generated entities can provide useful background knowledge. Overall, this is an interesting and useful method for incorporating knowledge in neural se- quencing models.

human_text:
- Strengths:
* Outperforms ALIGN in supervised entity linking task which suggests that the
proposed framework improves representations of text and knowledge that are
learned jointly.
* Direct comparison with closely related approach using very similar input
data.
* Analysis of the smoothing parameter provides useful analysis since impact of
popularity is a persistent issue in entity linking.

- Weaknesses:
* Comparison with ALIGN could be better. ALIGN used content window size 10 vs
this paper's 5, vector dimension of 500 vs this paper's 200. Also its not clear
to me whether N(e_j) includes only entities that link to e_j. The graph is
directed and consists of wikipedia outlinks, but is adjacency defined as it
would be for an undirected graph? For ALIGN, the context of an entity is the
set of entities that link to that entity. If N(e_j) is different, we cannot
tell how much impact this change has on the learned vectors, and this could
contribute to the difference in scores on the entity similarity task. 
* It is sometimes difficult to follow whether "mention" means a string type, or
a particular mention in a particular document. The phrase "mention embedding"
is used, but it appears that embeddings are only learned for mention senses.
* It is difficult to determine the impact of sense disambiguation order without
comparison to other unsupervised entity linking methods. 

- General Discussion:

This paper addresses the problem of disambiguating/linking textual entity
mentions into a given background knowledge base (in this case, English
Wikipedia).  (Its title and introduction are a little overblown/misleading,
since there is a lot more to bridging text and knowledge than the EDL task, but
EDL is a core part of the overall task nonetheless.)  The method is to perform
this bridging via an intermediate layer of representation, namely mention
senses, thus following two steps: (1) mention to mention sense, and (2) mention
sense to entity.  Various embedding representations are learned for the words,
the mention senses, and the entities, which are then jointly trained to
maximize a single overall objective function that maximizes all three types of
embedding equally.  

Technically the approach is fairly clear and conforms to the current deep
processing fashion and known best practices regarding embeddings; while one can
suggest all kinds of alternatives, it’s not clear they would make a material
difference.  Rather, my comments focus on the basic approach.  It is not
explained, however, exactly why a two-step process, involving the mention
senses, is better than a simple direct one-step mapping from word mentions to
their entities.  (This is the approach of Yamada et al., in what is called here
the ALIGN algorithm.)  Table 2 shows that the two-step MPME (and even its
simplification SPME) do better.  By why, exactly?  What is the exact
difference, and additional information, that the mention senses have compare4ed
to the entities?  To understand, please check if the following is correct (and
perhaps update the paper to make it exactly clear what is going on).  

For entities: their profiles consist of neighboring entities in a relatedness
graph.                    This graph is built (I assume) by looking at word-level
relatedness of
the entity definitions (pages in Wikipedia).  The profiles are (extended
skip-gram-based) embeddings.  

For words: their profiles are the standard distributional semantics approach,
without sense disambiguation.  

For mention senses: their profiles are the standard distributional semantics
approach, but WITH sense disambiguation.  Sense disambiguation is performed
using a sense-based profile (‘language model’) from local context words and
neighboring mentions, as mentioned briefly just before Section 4, but without
details.  This is a problem point in the approach.  How exactly are the senses
created and differentiated?  Who defines how many senses a mention string can
have?  If this is done by looking at the knowledge base, then we get a
bijective mapping between mention senses and entities -– that is, there is
exactly one entity for each mention sense (even if there may be more entities).
 In that case, are the sense collection’s definitional profiles built
starting with entity text as ‘seed words’?                    If so, what
information
is used
at the mention sense level that is NOT used at the entity level?  Just and
exactly the words in the texts that reliably associate with the mention sense,
but that do NOT occur in the equivalent entity webpage in Wikipedia?  How many
such words are there, on average, for a mention sense?                    That is,
how
powerful/necessary is it to keep this extra differentiation information in a
separate space (the mention sense space) as opposed to just loading these
additional words into the Entity space (by adding these words into the
Wikipedia entity pages)?  

If the above understanding is essentially correct, please update Section 5 of
the paper to say so, for (to me) it is the main new information in the paper.  

It is not true, as the paper says in Section 6, that “…this is the first
work to deal with mention ambiguity in the integration of text and knowledge
representations, so there is no exact baselines for comparison”.  The TAC KBP
evaluations for the past two years have hosted EDL tasks, involving eight or
nine systems, all performing exactly this task, albeit against Freebase, which
is considerably larger and more noisy than Wikipedia.  Please see
http://nlp.cs.rpi.edu/kbp/2016/ .  

On a positive note: I really liked the idea of the smoothing parameter in
Section 6.4.2.

Post-response: I have read the authors' responses.  I am not really satisfied
with their reply about the KBP evaluation not being relevant, but that they are
interested in the goodness of the embeddings instead.  In fact, the only way to
evaluate such 'goodness' is through an application.  No-one really cares how
conceptually elegant an embedding is, the question is: does it perform better?

- Strengths:
Good ideas, simple neural learning, interesting performance (altough not
striking) and finally large set of applications.

- Weaknesses: amount of novel content. Clarity in some sections. 

The paper presents a neural learning method for entity disambiguation and
linking. It introduces a good idea to integrate entity, mention and sense
modeling within the smame neural language modeling technique. The simple
training procedure connected with the modeling allows to support a large set of
application.

The paper is clear formally, but the discussion is not always at the same level
of the technical ideas.

The empirical evaluation is good although not striking improvements of the
performance are reported. Although it seems an extension of (Yamada et al.,
CoNLL 2016), it adds novel ideas and it is of a releant interest.

The weaker points of the paper are:

- The prose is not always clear. I found Section 3 not as clear. Some details
of Figure 2 are not explained and the terminology is somehow redundant: for
example, why do you refer to the dictionary of mentions? or the dictionary of
entity-mention pairs? are these different from text anchors and types for
annotated text anchors?
- Tha paper is quite close in nature to Yamada et al., 2016) and the authors
should at least outline the differences.

One general observation on the current version is:
The paper tests the Multiple Embedding model against entity
linking/disambiguation tasks. However, word embeddings are not only used to
model such tasks, but also some processes not directly depending on entities of
the KB, e.g. parsing, coreference or semantic role labeling. 
The authors should show that the word embeddings provided by the proposed MPME
method are not weaker wrt to simpler wordspaces in such other semantic tasks,
i.e. those involving directly entity mentions.

machine_text: This paper is interesting and novel in the field of NLP. It builds on prior work on monotonic attention for sequence-to-sequence generation tasks by adding a new purpose to the attention mechanism: learning the inflectional forms of words. Although similar work has been done in the generation of serial verb forms (e.g., the popular poem generator), this is the first work I know of that generates inflectional forms in the sense of part of speech tags (i.e., -ing, -ed, and -ible). This is a wide and important task, given that many NLP applications require the ability to generate sentences with proper grammar. The authors present an encoder-decoder model with a hard monotonic attention that seems to work well on the task. I would suggest adding a baseline to compare against (e.g., a simple encoder-decoder model with average attention), and results of generated samples with different model parameters. The samples generated by the model seem of very good quality for a machine learning model. I do have some concerns about the methodology and presentation of the results. The code and data are not publicly available, which is not standard practice for such a paper. In the code section, the models are trained on the siamese mating network, which is not open-source. The code for the generation part also has some inefficiencies: for example, splitting the duration and noise variables into their respective integer and fractional parts is not necessary given that they are fed into a deque object, which already handles such formatting for you. Additionally, in the results section, the authors report the results of a K-Means clustering on the generated samples, but do not provide the input to the cluster analysis, making it difficult to evaluate the efficacy of the results. I still found the paper to be very interesting and valuable, and the results impressive for a machine learning model, despite these issues.

This paper presents a novel approach to morphological inflection generation with hard monotonic attention. The proposed approach relies on a novel concatenated bi-LSTM-CRF architecture which integrates knowledge of word meaning and a wide range of dependencies between the morphosyntactic features and the surface form. The main idea of the proposed method is to force the model to learn to attend to the most important informations about the word meaning. The knowledge about the meaning is encoded in the form of hard monotonic tags. The model is trained to predict these tags from the generated word forms. The approach is evaluated on the widely used WSJ task 3 data set. The experiments show that the proposed approach significantly outperforms the state of the art. Problem addressed by the paper: Morphological inflection generation is a well known problem in NLP. The state of the art models use CRF with rich features. Despite the success of the state of the art models, they still fail to generate rich and diverse outputs. The main reason for this shortcoming is the limitations of the traditional feature based machine learning approaches. These approaches train the models by feeding them with lots of hand-crafted features that are easy to compute, but suffer from domain specific projections. In contrast, the meaning of a word or a phrase has to be understood by humans before it can be modeled and used by the machine. This human factor makes the problem much harder than it looks. Generally, the paper is very easy to understand and the results are very interesting. The main idea of using hard monotonic attention to generate morphological inflection is effective and the obtained results surpass most of the previously achieved results. The only issue I can see is that the paper only contains the result of the three datasets presented in the preliminary results section, and does not show the comparison results on other datasets. I think this is a very important piece of information to show the generalizability of the approach. I have provided a few suggestions to extend this paper as follows. 1. Add results of other datasets on the paper. 2. Since the paper only presents the comparison results of the three datasets presented in the preliminary results section, I think it is better to analyze the generated samples and the corresponding analysis should be added as a separate section. Overall, the paper is interesting and it would be helpful to the research community. I believe the paper can be improved by incorporating the comparison results on other datasets and analyzing the generated samples by the model. above = second review = preliminary results = main content In this paper, we present a morphological inflection generation model employing a hard monotonic attention, inspired by the nearly-monotonic alignment commonly found between the characters in a word and the characters in its inflection. We evaluate the model on three previously studied morphological inflection generation datasets and show that it provides state of the art results in various setups compared to previous neural and non-neural approaches. Finally we present an analysis of the continuous representations learned by both the hard and soft (Bahdanau, 2014) attention models for the task, shedding some light on the features such models extract.

This paper addresses the problem of Morphological Inflection Generation which employs a hard attention mechanism, based on the nearly-monotonic alignment commonly found between the characters in a word and the characters in its inflection. The model was evaluated on three previously studied morphological inflection generation datasets and shown to provide state of the art results in various setups compared to previous neural and non-neural approaches. Finally we present an analysis of the continuous representations learned by both the hard and soft attention models for the task, shedding some light on the features such models extract. strengths: This work is a pioneering effort on Morphological Inflection Generation, using a hard attention mechanism which is widely employed in NMT but seldom explored in MLM. In addition, the paper presents a systematic study on both the hard and soft attention models for the task. Through detailed experiments, we find that: 1) The hard attention model gives superior performance over the soft one in general. 2) A joint training with both hard and soft attentions yields the best results. weaknesses: The evaluation is conducted on three previously studied datasets, the generalization capability of the model needs to be further evaluated on more comprehensive corpus. Overall, this is an exciting and promising start to a new direction for Morphological Inflection Generation, we believe this work will inspire more researchers to explore the potential of hard attention for different NLP tasks. I recommend this work be accepted for publication in the Journal of Machine Learning Proceedings.
human_text:
- Strengths:
The idea of hard monotonic attention is new and substantially different from
others.

- Weaknesses:
The experiment results on morphological inflection generation is somewhat
mixed. The proposed model is effective if the amount of training data is small
(such as CELEX). It is also effective if the alignment is mostly monotonic and
less context sensitive (such as Russian, German and Spanish).

- General Discussion:

The authors proposed a novel neural model for morphological inflection
generation which uses "hard attention", character alignments separately
obtained by using a Bayesian method for transliteration. It is substantially
different from the previous state of the art neural model for the task which
uses "soft attention", where character alignment and conversion are solved
jointly in the probabilistic model.

The idea is novel and sound. The paper is clearly written. The experiment is
comprehensive. The only concern is that the proposed method is not necessarily
the state of the art in all conditions. It is suitable for the task with mostly
monotonic alignment and with less context sensitive phenomena. The paper would
be more convincing if it describe the practical merits of the proposed method,
such as the ease of implementation and computational cost.

- Strengths: A new encoder-decoder model is proposed that explicitly takes 
into account monotonicity.

- Weaknesses: Maybe the model is just an ordinary BiRNN with alignments
de-coupled.
Only evaluated on morphology, no other monotone Seq2Seq tasks.

- General Discussion:

The authors propose a novel encoder-decoder neural network architecture with
"hard monotonic attention". They evaluate it on three morphology datasets.

This paper is a tough one. One the one hand it is well-written, mostly very
clear and also presents a novel idea, namely including monotonicity in
morphology tasks. 

The reason for including such monotonicity is pretty obvious: Unlike machine
translation, many seq2seq tasks are monotone, and therefore general
encoder-decoder models should not be used in the first place. That they still
perform reasonably well should be considered a strong argument for neural
techniques, in general. The idea of this paper is now to explicity enforce a
monotonic output character generation. They do this by decoupling alignment and
transduction and first aligning input-output sequences monotonically and
then training to generate outputs in agreement with the monotone alignments.
However, the authors are unclear on this point. I have a few questions:

1) How do your alignments look like? On the one hand, the alignments seem to
be of the kind 1-to-many (as in the running example, Fig.1), that is, 1 input
character can be aligned with zero, 1, or several output characters. However,
this seems to contrast with the description given in lines 311-312 where the
authors speak of several input characters aligned to 1 output character. That
is, do you use 1-to-many, many-to-1 or many-to-many alignments?

2) Actually, there is a quite simple approach to monotone Seq2Seq. In a first
stage, align input and output characters monotonically with a 1-to-many
constraint (one can use any monotone aligner, such as the toolkit of
Jiampojamarn and Kondrak). Then one trains a standard sequence tagger(!) to
predict exactly these 1-to-many alignments. For example, flog->fliege (your
example on l.613): First align as in "f-l-o-g / f-l-ie-ge". Now use any tagger
(could use an LSTM, if you like) to predict "f-l-ie-ge" (sequence of length 4)
from "f-l-o-g" (sequence of length 4). Such an approach may have been suggested
in multiple papers, one reference could be [*, Section 4.2] below. 
My two questions here are: 

2a) How does your approach differ from this rather simple idea?

2b) Why did you not include it as a baseline?

Further issues:

3) It's really a pitty that you only tested on morphology, because there are
many other interesting monotonic seq2seq tasks, and you could have shown your
system's superiority by evaluating on these, given that you explicitly model
monotonicity (cf. also [*]).

4) You perform "on par or better" (l.791). There seems to be a general
cognitive bias among NLP researchers to map instances where they perform worse
to
"on par" and all the rest to "better". I think this wording should be
corrected, but otherwise I'm fine with the experimental results.

5) You say little about your linguistic features: From Fig. 1, I infer that
they include POS, etc. 

5a) Where did you take these features from?

5b) Is it possible that these are responsible for your better performance in
some cases, rather than the monotonicity constraints?

Minor points:

6) Equation (3): please re-write $NN$ as $\text{NN}$ or similar

7) l.231 "Where" should be lower case

8) l.237 and many more: $x_1\ldots x_n$. As far as I know, the math community
recommends to write $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ but $x_1\cdots x_n$. That is, dots should
be on the same level as surrounding symbols.

9) Figure 1: is it really necessary to use cyrillic font? I can't even address
your example here, because I don't have your fonts.

10) l.437: should be "these"

Secondly, the paper adopts the hard example mining method to generate the labels for weakly labeled data. The authors present a novel approach to cross-lingual named entity recognition (NER) via a two-stage approach that exploits both lexical and syntax information. First, they train an entity name token detector, which maps each input word to its corresponding entity name entity representation. Then, given a weakly labeled training set, they learn a cross-lingual representation for NER by projecting the source entity name representations into the space of the annotation language (i.e., target NER tags). This approach is evaluated on the cross-lingual wikipedia edition and shows competitive results to the state of the art on this task. This approach addresses the NER problem through two main insights. First, the authors show that entity name representations contain valuable entity name information, thus allowing to recover some part of the target NER annotation labels. Second, they observe that due to the shallow linguistic similarity between languages, projecting entity name representations of one language into the space of the other language usually results in low-ranked representations. This suggests that an aligned high-dimensional space offers a good basis for cross-lingual projection, as opposed to the original source and target spaces. The main drawback of this method is that it requires the construction of a projected space in which to perform the projection. This projection is learned from a weakly labeled dataset and is therefore limited in its application to new languages for which no labeled training data is available. The approach is evaluated on a set of 11 languages with in-domain data (e.g., WIKI8CHN) and out-of-domain data (e.g., Wikipedia Parallel Dataset) and generally performs competitively to state of the art methods. In addition, the authors provide an ablation study showing that the proposed approach is able to leverage both lexical and syntactic annotations to improve the NER performance.

The paper “Weakly Supervised Cross-Lingual Named Entity Recognition via Effective Annotation and Representation Projection” presents two weakly supervised approaches for cross-lingual NER with no human annotation in a target language. The first approach is to create automatically labeled NER data for a target language via annotation projection on comparable corpora, where we develop a heuristic scheme that effectively selects good-quality projection-labeled data from noisy data. The second approach is to project distributed representations of words (word embeddings) from a target language to a source language, so that the source-language NER system can be applied to the target language without re-training. We also design two co-decoding schemes that effectively combine the outputs of the two projection-based approaches. We evaluate the performance of the proposed approaches on both in-house and open NER data for several target languages. The results show that the combined systems outperform three other weakly supervised approaches on the CoNLL data. I have several questions about this paper: 1. It would be better if the authors describe what " weakly supervised" means in the introduction. 2. In the first approach, the authors use an annotation projection approach to create automatically labeled NER data for a target language, but the projection-labeling procedure is not described in detail. How do we know the projection-labeling procedure is effective? It would be good to have a validation set to check if the resulting model works well on unseen data that was used for projection. If the model does not perform well on the validation set, we might need to try a different projection method or even change to a different approach. 3. I think the second approach, the projection of distributed representations of word (word embeddings) from a target language to a source language, is promising. But, this approach also needs validation. It would be good to have a validation set to check if the resulting model works well on unseen data that was used for projection. If the model does not perform well on the validation set, we might need to try a different projection method or even change to a different approach. 4. In the last two approaches, the authors combine the outputs of two projection-based approaches. However, there could be many ways to combine these approaches. For example, we can take the intersection of the two projection-based results, or we can take the union of the two projection-based results. What is the best way? It would be good to test multiple combinations. 5. The last part of the results compares the proposed approach to state-of-the-art approaches that use human-labeled data for CoNLL-2018, and the proposed approach shows promise. But, I think the best way to compare these methods is to compare them on the same corpus, such as English CoNLL-2016, since these approaches all require training on large amounts of data. It would be good to include such a comparison. 6. Finally, I believe there could be many potential uses for an annotation projection method. For example, a company or institute could build projection models for different languages, and people in different locations could use these models to perform cross-language tasks (e.g., name entity recognition) without having to label these tasks directly on the projection data. It would be good to discuss other potential applications. This paper presents several weakly supervised methods for developing NERs. The

know how to tune the parameters for a new data set or a new language pair. 

Another contribution of the paper is the combination of the outputs of the two

authors try anything in this direction.

It would be good to know a bit more about the types of texts that are in the

This paper describes a model for cross-lingual named entity recognition (NER).
The authors employ conditional random fields, maximum entropy Markov, and
neural network-based NER methods. In addition, authors propose two methods to
combine the output of those methods (probability-based and ranking-based), and
a method to select the best training instances from cross-lingual comparable
corpora. The cross-lingual projection is done using a variant of Mikolov’s
proposal. In general, the paper is easy to follow, well-structured, and the
English quality is also correct. The results of the combined annotations are
interesting.

Detailed comments:

I was wondering which is the motivation behind proposing a Continuous
Bag-of-word (CBOW) model variation. You don’t give much details about this
(or the parameters employed). Was the original model (or the Continuous
Skip-gram model) offering low results? I suggest to include also the results
with the CBOW model, so readers can analyse the improvements of your approach.
Since you use a decay factor for the surrounding embeddings, I suggest to take
a look to the exponential decay used in [1].

Similarly to the previous comment, I would like to look at the differences
between the original Mikolov’s cross-lingual projections and your frequency
weighted projections. These contributions are more valuable if readers can see
that your method is really superior.

“the proposed data selection scheme is very effective in selecting

Have you conducted a test of statistical significance? I would like to know if

I miss a related work section. Your introduction includes part of that

This paper discusses a multigraph based model for overlapping entity recognition. This is an interesting problem because current methods either require substantial entity identification prior to identifying overlapping entities or construct a single graph without leveraging the relationship between different entities. The model proposed in this paper builds multiple relation graphs, one for each distinct entity type, and uses a multigraph label propagation algorithm to combine node labels. The method is evaluated on overlapping entity recognition on two datasets. Compared to the state of the art, the model significantly outperforms the method requiring pre-identification of entities. frame of reference: problem statement, objective, approaches to address problem, limitations of current approaches, approach proposed in the paper, comparison with state of the art The problem of overlapping entity recognition has not been fully addressed by previous work. Many existing systems require the identification of entities before performing overlapping entity recognition. These methods require the pre-identification of entities with specific labels. These pre-defined entity labels, however, may not reflect the real-world semantics of the entities and do not utilize the relationship between different entities. Some other approaches construct a single graph without leveraging the relationship between different entities. The proposed approach leverages multiple relation graphs, one for each distinct entity type, to perform overlapping entity recognition. For example, a forum thread and a video are from different entities but they have similar semantic relations. By building multiple relation graphs, the approach can better model the real-world relationships among entities. The approach is evaluated on two publicly available datasets. The results show that the approach outperforms state of the art methods that require prior identification of entities. Limitations of the approach and directions for future work are also discussed.

First of all, we would like to thank the authors for sharing their work and for their thoughtful review. We have evaluated our model against previous models on the standard overlapping and non-overlapping entity recognition datasets and found that our model outperforms the previous models in most of the cases. Below is a detailed comparison between our model and the previous models. Differential feature learning: Our model adopts multigraphs as the basic structural form of data, and it differs from previous methods which only utilize simple graphs. With the help of multigraphic structure, our model can learn different representations for nodes that are connected and those that are not, which helps model the relationship between entities. Better regularization: As the model utilizes multigraphs as its basic structure, it naturally takes into account the relationships among different entities during training and thus obtains better generalization ability. Our model is different from previous work as we use multigraphs as the basic structure of our data. We would like to thank the authors for their detailed response and for clarifying this point for us. We believe that our model could have a broader application scope and could be applied in other contexts besides overlapping entity recognition and thus we have briefly discussed the implications of the differences in the end of the paper. Overall, we believe that our model is more suitable for different application scenarios as it utilizes multigraphs as the basic structural form of data and learns better representations for entities that are connected. The rest of the paper remains largely the same.

In this paper, the author propose a new model for predicting overlapping entities based on multigraphs, as opposed to simple graphs commonly used in graphical models for structured predictions. Through experiments in standard datasets containing overlapping and non-overlapping entities, we demonstrate that the model outperform previous models. We also present some analysis on the differences between the model and the previous models and discuss the possible implications of the differences. This is the first structured prediction model utilizing multigraphs to predict overlapping structures. Social Networks Overlapping entities may appear in the form of person/place/organization names, county and city names, and email and mobile phone addresses. While previous works have attempted to tackle this problem by handcrafted features and features learning from other NLP tasks, this paper applies graph-based approaches that are more general and powerful to the overlapping entity task. The contribution of this paper is three-fold: 1) it is the first work that applies multigraph, an extended form of graph, to the overlapping entity task; 2) it proposes a new encoder that combines both the relationship encoder and the bilinear interaction encoder; 3) it presents an analysis on the differences between the model and the previous models and discusses the possible implications of the differences. abnormalities The first work that applies multigraph, an extended form of graph, to the overlapping entity task. The paper suggests an approach based on multigraphs (several edges may link two

The problem itself could be rather interesting especially for crossing entities
to decide which one might actually be mentioned in some text. The technique

Weaknesses:
The problem itself is not really well motivated. Why is it important to detect

As for the empirical evaluation, the achieved results are better than some
previous approaches but not really by a large margin. I would not really call

effect size? Does it really matter to some user that there is some improvement
of two percentage points in F_1? What is the actual effect one can observe? How
many "important" entities are discovered, that have not been discovered by
previous methods? Furthermore, what performance would some simplistic
dictionary-based method achieve that could also be used to find overlapping
things? And in a similar direction: what would some commercial system like
Google's NLP cloud that should also be able to detect and link entities would
have achieved on the datasets. Just to put the results also into contrast of
existing "commercial" systems.

As for the result discussion, I would have liked to see some more emphasis on
actual crossing entities. How is the performance there? This in my opinion is
the more interesting subset of overlapping entities than the nested ones. How
many more crossing entities are detected than were possible before? Which ones
were missed and maybe why? Is the performance improvement due to better nested
detection only or also detecting crossing entities? Some general error
discussion comparing errors made by the suggested system and previous ones
would also strengthen that part.

General Discussion:
I like the problems related to named entity recognition and see a point for
recognizing crossing entities. However, why is one interested in nested
entities? The paper at hand does not really motivate the scenario and also
sheds no light on that point in the evaluation. Discussing errors and maybe
advantages with some example cases and an emphasis on the results on crossing
entities compared to other approaches would possibly have convinced me more.
So, I am only lukewarm about the paper with maybe a slight tendency to
rejection. It just seems yet another try without really emphasizing the in my
opinion important question of crossing entities.

machine_text: The knowledge base question answering (KQA) task is an important task in natural language processing (NLP). Recently, neural approaches have achieved impressive results on large KQA benchmark datasets like Quaero and Heatlie. A strong baseline of KQA is formed with the interaction of pre-trained BERT model and external knowledge base (KB) facts. However, there are several limitations of this approach. First, the interaction of BERT and KB is not end-to-end trainable, and requires additional label indicating whether the input question and the facts can match. Second, the matching score between question and fact in the KB is only a ranking score, but not a probability score, which limits the detection of correct relations between questions and facts. Third, BERT model simply understands the semantic relatedness between questions and facts, but lacks the specific knowledge about the types of relations between them. To address these limitations, in this paper, we propose a novel end-to-end trainable framework BERT QA (BERT for QA). It directly takes the input facts and question as input, and outputs matching probability and relation types between them. We also extract important hidden representation from BERT using pre-training and fine-tuning methods. Several pre-trained and fine-tuned representations are introduced in our framework, which can capture different semantic relatedness between question and facts. Extensive experiments on two large KQA datasets show that our approach achieves superior performance compared with the state-of-the-art approaches.

The paper addressed a very important problem in the field of knowledge base question answering (KBC) - detecting relations between factual statements. As one of the first steps in downstream question answering evaluation, this is really important for ensuring that the answer is not simply based on unrelated facts but instead refers to some actual, real-life relationship between the facts mentioned in the answer, as opposed to just being an expression of a co-location relationship between the facts mentioned. The authors propose a neural approach to relation detection that is based on neural chainQuery learning, which allows the model to detect different types of relationships between two entities. They also provide a thorough evaluation of the approach, showing that it outperforms the state-of-the-art by a significant margin. This is an important step in the right direction, towards KBC systems that can answer questions about actual, not merely possible, relationships between entities. Still, there is still a long way to go, as this approach relies on detection of long distance relationships between entities, which means that not every relationship of interest will be detected. E.g. the authors point out that the model does not detect explicit relationships between entities, such as "Gandalf is a wizard" ( Gandalf is a fictional character, and "wizard" is an entity). However, by and large, this is still an interesting and substantial improvement over existing solutions, and the paper presents a good starting point for further research in this area.

This is an interesting paper, and I have some constructive comments as follows. First, the title of the paper is a bit misleading. From the method proposed, it seems that the relation detection is based on the neural networks, but I didn't find the detection results are fed back to the input of the neural network. I think the title should be changed to "Neural relation detection via residual learning", or something similar. Second, the time complexity of the paper is 0(N), where N is the length of the input sequence. As a result, it is not suitable for the scenarios where the input sequence is very long, such as the OpenQA benchmark. I suggest the authors try the following items to improve the paper. 1. Use a CRF layer on top of the LSTM unit to deal with the additional sequential labeling task. 2. For the labeled data, we can apply the transfer learning from other relation detection tasks, such as entailment detection, question type classification etc. 3. The results are not shown for the OpenQA evaluation, which limits the application of the method. Overall, this is an interesting paper, and I have some constructive comments to help you improve the quality of your paper. Thanks for your attention and assistance. We have investigated and analyzed your suggestions and modified the paper. Please find it below. 1. Title: changed to “Neural relation detection via deep learning for knowledge base question answering” 2. Time complexity: changed to “Time Complexity: 0(N), where N is the length of the input sequence” 3. Section 2: Using the proposed method, we achieve state-of-the-art performance on both the SimpleQuestions and WebQSP evaluation sets. 4. Neural relation detection for Knowledge Base Question Answering addresses a challenging problem and makes an excellent contribution to the field Strengths - employs novel, effective solutions to relation detection - uses a hierarchical LSTM architecture - improves the performance of our KBQA system by incorporating relation detection - experiments with different levels of abstraction (i.e. token and phrase levels) for relation detection Limitations - does not perform relation specific token embeddings, which limits its ability to capture fine-grained semantics - does not perform multiple instance learning which could further improve its overall performance - does not consider spatial proximity which is critical for identifying complex relations such as causation, reasonable, etc. Our approach uses deep residual LSTMs to encode question and relation name and compare them at different levels of abstraction. In addition, we propose a simple KBQA system that integrates entity linking and our relation detection model to make the two components enhance each other. On simple question QA task, our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance by applying different level fusion of relation name. As for the web-scale questions QA task, our approach helps our KBQA system achieve new state-of-the-art performance even on single relation QA task. Further analysis also shows that our approach helps improving answer-specific ranking. In summary, our proposed approach not only achieves outstanding relation detection performance, but also helps our KBQA system achieve new state-of-the-art performance on simple question QA task and web-scale question QA task.

The introduction clearly explains the problem statement and the role of the proposed solution in the grand scheme of things. The scope of the work is accurately presented from an industry point of view. The technique description is clear and straight forward. The Results section is concise and clear. The technique has been evaluated on three real world datasets and the experimental results are clearly presented. The limitations of the technique have been discussed in the concluding part of the paper. Overall, the paper is well articulated, and I recommend for acceptance with some minor edits print "Time Expression Analysis and Recognition using Syntactic Token types and General Heuristic rules" print "Agenda Setting and Time Expression Analysis" The problem statement The proposed solution Industry relevance Scope of the work Technique description Evaluation methodology Results Discussions Conclusion Overall the work is well recommended for acceptance Insurance - Time expression analysis and recognition Using syntactic token types and general heuristic rules Agenda setting and Time expression analysis The problem statement Businesses in India rely heavily on time information for decision making. As more and more businesses migrate to the cloud, the ability to access time sensitive information becomes critical. The problem of incorrect time synchronization and incorrect or incomplete timezone data costs Indian businesses millions of US dollars a year. For example, Indian office times typically use Eastern Standard Time (EST) which is 5 hours behind UTC. Indian enterprises often use Gujrat Daylight Time (GST) which is 6 hours ahead of UTC. As more Indian businesses are moving towards cloud based storage, the timezone mapping between the cloud service and end users becomes a crucial concern. An Indian business representative may believe they are showing their working hours from 9AM-5PM when in fact they are showing 9PM-5PM in EST, that is a difference of 10 hours. Additionally, incorrect time synchronization and timezone data in regulations can result in regulatory risk. For example, a price forecast for a major produce in India for an upcoming quarter might increase if the regulator changes their timezone and the forecasting team in India assumes they are in CST when in fact they are in IST. The industry provides tens of thousands of dollars per year in error cost. Indian enterprises rely on having access to accurate time information in order to manage business critical time information. Agenda Setting and Time Expression Analysis Time expression analysis uses formal grammars to describe time expressions. Temporal Adverbs, Temporal Adverbials, and Time Expressions are the three main categories of time expressions. The syntactic token types are The Japanese calendar system, the Hebrew calendar system, Indian calendar system, and British Summer Time. The general heuristic rules are always use 24 hour format, add an apostrophe for prefixes like ago, years, and months, and subtract one from the time to get minutes. The time expression grammar is defined using a combination of Formal Languages and Transformations. There are two types of transformations. The first type of transformation is based on mathematical laws and includes addition, subtraction, and multiplication. For example, "3 hours and 30 minutes" can be calculated as "30 minutes x 3 = 90 minutes", and "90 minutes + 30 minutes = 120 minutes". The second type of transformation is based on the order of operations. The order of operations for time expressions is generally from most to least specific. Time expressions are formed from Time Expression Building Blocks. The Time Expression Building Blocks are Temporal Adverbs Temporal Adverbials Time Expressions An example Time Expression is "3 hours and 30 minutes". The Time Expression can be decomposed to "3 hours" + "30 minutes". The Time Expression Analysis component of the work predicts the time expression using a combination of machine learning and heuristics. The Time Expression can be calculated using a combination of the Time Expression Building Blocks as shown above. However, Time Expressions may also be mispredicted if the heuristic calculation does not accurately reflect the correct time expression.

The main contribution of this paper is a novel type-based approach, named SynTime, to recognize time expressions. The paper firstly analyzes the time expressions from four datasets and finds that only a small group of words are used to express time information. Based on the findings, we propose a type-based approach to recognize time expressions. Specifically, we define three main syntactic token types, namely time token, modifier, and numeral, to group time-related regular expressions over tokens. On the types we design general heuristic rules to recognize time expressions. In recognition, SynTime first identifies the time tokens from raw text, then searches their surroundings for modifiers and numerals to form time segments, and finally merges the time segments to time expressions. SynTime runs in real time, and can be easily expanded by simply adding keywords for the text of different types and of different domains. The results on benchmark datasets and tweets data show that SynTime outperforms state-of-the-art methods. The main limitations of this paper are: first, it only recognizes time expressions with a few specific expressions like "5pm", "8:30am", "12d 6h", "2 weeks", "last Wednesday" which limits its application in some real-world scenarios; second, it uses regular expressions to define time token, modifier, and numeral. As a light-weight rule-based tagger, SynTime is limited by the expressive power of regular expressions, and it needs to define many rules to recognize different time expressions; third, the proposed heuristic rules are defined for all time expressions without specific rules for different time units, e.g., seconds, minutes, hours. For example, "5pm" and "5:pm" have the same time token and different time expressions, while the SynTime cannot tell them apart.

This paper describes a rule based approach to time expression extraction. Its
key insights are time expressions typically are short and contain at least 1
time token. It first recognizes the time token through a combination of
dictionary lookup, regular expression match with POS tagging information. It
then expands the time segment from either direction of the time token until it
reaches based on a set of heuristic rules. Finally, it merges the time segments
into a single time expression based on another set of rules. Evaluation of this
approach with both rule based & ML based systems on 3 data sets show
significant improvements.

 There are some underspecification in the paper that makes it difficult to

Firstly, thanks for sharing this paper. I find this paper very interesting and inspiring. However, I have some concerns about this paper, which need to be improved for this paper to be better. Firstly, the used datasets and evaluation metrics are not suitable for the evalution of this paper. In this paper, two datasets are used for the evaluation, including MLDialog and Guess.us, however, the used datasets and evaluation metrics are not suitable for the evaluation of this paper. MLDialog and Guess.us are two widely used datasets for the evaluation of dialogue systems, however, the labels in MLDialog and Guess.us are domain-specific and not suitable for the evaluation of dialogue state tracking. For example, the labels in MLDialog are Show Room and Game Show room, while the labels in Guess.us are game type and user interface type. Therefore, for this paper to be better, I would recommend using another two widely used datasets for the evaluation, including the ICM and DSTC2. Secondly, the evaluated results of this paper are not very convincing. The NBT approach is proposed to overcome the problem that the previous dialogue state tracking approaches rely on hand-crafted semantic lexicons to a large extent. In order to show the superiority of NBT, the evaluated results of NBT are presented in the last part of this paper. However, there is no comparative evaluation between NBT and the baseline approaches, such as the UCFIRST, PLM and MLP. Thus, the evaluated results of this paper are not very convincing. Moreover, NBT is evaluated on two datasets, MLDialog and Guess.us. However, MLDialog and Guess.us are not suitable for the evaluation of dialogue state tracking. For example, MLDialog is a data set of customer service domain, and Guess.us is a data set of game domain. Thus, the evaluated results of NBT on MLDialog and Guess.us are also not very convincing. In summary, this paper needs to be improved by comparing with baseline approaches on ICM and DSTC2 and evaluating on MLDialog, Guess.us and ICM, DSTC2. Nevertheless, this paper is still valuable and inspiring. Once these issues are fixed, I will recommend to accept this paper for publication in the Conference.

The Neural Belief Tracking (NBT) framework proposed in this paper addresses the problems of previous belief trackers by relying on pre-trained word vectors. Instead of hand-crafted lexicons, NBT models reason over pre-trained word vectors, learning to compose them into distributed representations of user utterances and dialogue context. We conduct experiments on two public datasets, and the results show that NBT significantly outperforms previous belief trackers. The main contributions of this paper are as follows: 1. a novel neural belief tracker is proposed which relies on representation learning to overcome the shortcomings of previous belief trackers; 2. a new public dataset is created to evaluate belief trackers, which can be accessed at https://github.com/xiaolong1566/NBT-Dataset. Some of the advantages of using representation learning for belief tracking are as follows: 1. The requirement of lexicon in previous belief trackers limits the application of belief trackers to smaller domains, where the necessary lexicon can be compiled; 2. Most previous belief trackers only use a small number of pre-defined lexicon categories, which may not fully capture the variations in users' language; 3. The modeling of dialogue language from a distributed semantic representation allows NBT to generalize beyond the specific labeled data used to train it. For example, NBT outperformed prior work when no labeled data were available for training, indicating that NBT has greater generalizability. One of the main contributions of this work is to release a new public dataset for belief tracking, referred to as NBT-Dataset. This dataset is created based on the CHAQ-10 corpus, which is widely used in prior work. However, compared with other similar datasets, NBT-Dataset has the following three main differences: 1. it allows for self-taught pre-training of word vectors on out-of-domain data; 2. it includes more fine-grained annotation of dialogue acts and relaxed coreference resolution; 3. it includes dialogue data in multiple languages, including English, Spanish and Chinese. This dataset is suitable for research using both supervised and unsupervised learning techniques for belief tracking, and can be downloaded from https://github.com/xiaolong1566/NBT-Dataset. In summary, this paper makes the following significant contributions: 1. It advances the state of the art in belief tracking by developing a representation learning approach; 2. It creates the NBT-Dataset, a public dataset for belief tracking, which is suitable for research using both supervised and unsupervised learning techniques for belief tracking; 3. It makes the pre-trained word vector technology available to the dialogue community, making it easier to integrate into existing belief tracking systems. deliver the details especially to readers who are not familiar with this area.

First of all, more formal definition of DST needs to be given at the beginning
of this paper.
It is not clear enough and could be more confusing after coupling with SLU.
My suggestion is to provide a general architecture of dialogue system described
in Section 1 rather than Section 2, followed by the problem definition of DST
focusing on its relationships to other components including ASR, SLU, and
policy learning.

And it would also help to improve the readability if all the notations used
throughout the paper are defined in an earlier section.
Some symbols (e.g. t_q, t_s, t_v) are used much earlier than their
descriptions.

Below are other comments or questions:

- Would it be possible to perform the separate SLU with this model? If no, the
term 'joint' could be misleading that this model is able to handle both tasks.

- Could you please provide some statistics about how many errors were corrected
from the original DSTC2 dataset?
If it is not very huge, the experiment could include the comparisons also with
other published work including DSTC2 entries using the same dataset.

- What do you think about using RNNs or LSTMs to learn the sequential aspects
in learning utterance representations?
Considering the recent successes of these recurrent networks in SLU problems,
it could be effective to DST as well.

- Some more details about the semantic dictionary used with the baseline would
help to imply the cost for building this kind of resources manually.

- It would be great if you could give some samples which were not correctly
predicted by the baseline but solved with your proposed models.

machine_text: In this paper the author attempts to address the long standing goal of using structured outputs from knowledge graphs to improve the quality of neural network prediction. This approach has been challenging in the past because the graph structure doesn’t explicitly capture the underlying relationship between the entities in the knowledge graph. This relationship is essential in guiding the way in which knowledge can be leveraged to produce better quality predictions. The proposed model centers around the use of knowledge-guided attention mechanisms to enable the neural network to learn this relationship. The model consists of two components, an encoder-decoder architecture that builds on BERT and knowledge graph embeddings, and an attention mechanism that is conditioned on the enriched intermediate representation. The model was evaluated on the benchmark dataset for this problem (MNLI) and was shown to improve upon the current state of the art performance (BLEU 92.3) by a large margin (43.2). Manish Chandakya (ManishN23 on Kaggle) esk I have several comments and suggestions for the author to enhance the paper. 1. The introduction is well written, but I would recommend the authors to go into more detail in the background section, for example, how previous approaches attempt to address the limitations of using structured outputs from knowledge graphs. Also, I think it would be helpful to summarize the key insights from the previous approaches, and how the proposed approach differs from them. 2. The description of the problem statement is missing in the abstract. I would recommend the author to include the objective of the paper, e.g., to address the quality problem of neural network predictions. Also, the targeted problem could be described in the abstract. 3. The main advantage of the proposed approach is that it improves the quality of neural network predictions. I think it would be helpful to mention some of the use cases where this quality improvement is crucial.

This paper presents Knowledge-Guided Structural Attention Networks (KGSANs), an end-to-end framework for automatically learning structural attention from unstructured text. To this end, the paper develops three main contributions. First, it introduces a relational concept map, based on topic models, which encapsulates domain knowledge and acts as a substrate for constructing teacher signals. Second, it presents a principled approach for learning structural attention from these teacher signals in a Bayesian neural network framework. Third, it defines a new task to evaluate structural attention, shown to be effective for improving unsupervised text understanding. Experiments on two benchmark datasets validate the efficacy of KGSANs for this task. ML1 ML2 ML3 Performs well on the question/problem described. However, I have a few concerns about the approach/technology presented. First, the KM used as a teacher signal is a shallow representation of the domain knowledge and likely does not contain any temporal or sequencing information. For example, it is unclear if the concepts surface in order of relatedness or prioritized by a human editor. This is a critical information for deriving structural attention. Second, the Bayesian NNs used to learn structural attention are unlikely to converge to global optima. Typically, simpler, local optima are good enough for model applications like generating clickable headlines or summarizations. However, for the task of deriving structural attention, we expect the global optimum. In order to find the global optimum, a generative model such as Variational Autoencoder would be necessary, which is not explored in this paper. In summary, though the KM serves as a good starting point for creating structural attention, the approach taken in this paper does not fulfill its promise of deriving structural attention from KM.

This paper introduces a knowledge-guided structural attention networks (K-SAN), a generalization of RNN to additionally incorporate non-flat network topologies guided by prior knowledge. The experiments on the benchmark ATIS data show that the proposed K-SAN architecture can effectively extract salient knowledge from substructures with an attention mechanism, and outperform the state-of-the-art neural network based frameworks. Natural language understanding (NLU) is a core component of a dialogue system. Recently, recurrent neural networks (RNN) obtained strong results on NLU due to their superior ability of preserving sequential information over time. Traditionally, the NLU module tags semantic slots for utterances considering their flat structures, as the underlying RNN structure is a linear chain. However, natural language exhibits linguistic properties that provide rich, structured information for better understanding. This paper introduces a novel model, knowledge-guided structural attention networks (K-SAN), a generalization of RNN to additionally incorporate non-flat network topologies guided by prior knowledge. There are two characteristics: 1) important substructures can be captured from small training data, allowing the model to generalize to previously unseen test data; 2) the model automatically figures out the salient substructures that are essential to predict the semantic tags of the given sentences, so that the understanding performance can be improved. The experiments on the benchmark ATIS data show that the proposed K-SAN architecture can effectively extract salient knowledge from text with an attention mechanism, and outperform the state-of-the-art neural network based frameworks. Overall this paper presents a promising direction to extract structured information from text for improving natural language understanding systems. I have some minor concerns that might affect the readability of the paper. For example, in section 2.2 the authors introduce prior knowledge and demonstrate the improvements on the airline booking domain. It is unclear how these knowledge about airline flights work for other domains. For example, in Table 1 the authors show the improvements using flight information, but the flight information is only relevant to the ATIS domain. How can we generalize this to other domains? Can the authors expand the Introduction to include how to generalize knowledge to other domains? The paper also lacks motivation and explanation for why knowledge-guided attention is better than traditional attention for NLU. Also the analysis on how the proposed method improves upon the state of the art is lacking. These are some minor concerns that would help improve the readability of this paper. This paper addresses how to effectively use prior knowledge, namely the linguistic substructures, for understanding and prediction. The paper introduces a novel knowledge-guided structural attention networks (K-SAN) for a dialogue system. The K-SAN can 1) capture the important substructures from small training data, and 2) automatically figure out the substructures that are essential to predict the semantic tags of the given sentences, through an attention mechanism. The experiments show that the K-SAN outperforms the state-of-the-art neural network based frameworks. As for strengths, the introduction of attention mechanism into K-SAN is innovative and effective, as it can select the important substructures from the input features and feed them to the next layers for better prediction. The easy-to-apply knowledge representation of substructures is another merit. On the other hand, we can also find some drawbacks. For example, there is no benchmarking on other data sets, and it would be better to perform in-language understanding task rather than other language understanding tasks such as ATIS and SSP. Overall, this paper makes a meaningful attempt to harness prior knowledge for understanding, and the attention mechanism is applied for the first time in K-SAN for better performance. The contributions can be generalized to other NLP tasks that leverage linguistic substructures. My own opinions, this paper seems good and promising, despite the drawbacks above. I recommend the editor to consider my suggestions as well as other expert opinions during the reviewing process.
human_text:
This paper proposes a neural network architecture that represent structural
linguistic knowledge in a memory network for sequence tagging tasks (in
particular, slot-filling of the natural language understanding unit in
conversation systems). Substructures (e.g. a node in the parse tree) is encoded
as a vector (a memory slot) and a weighted sum of the substructure embeddings
are fed in a RNN at each time step as additional context for labeling.

-----Strengths-----

I think the main contribution of this paper is a simple way to "flatten"
structured information to an array of vectors (the memory), which is then
connected to the tagger as additional knowledge. The idea is similar to
structured / syntax-based attention (i.e. attention over nodes from treeLSTM);
related work includes Zhao et al on textual entailment, Liu et al. on natural
language inference, and Eriguchi et al. for machine translation. The proposed
substructure encoder is similar to DCNN (Ma et al.): each node is embedded from
a sequence of ancestor words. The architecture does not look entirely novel,
but I kind of like the simple and practical approach compared to prior work.

-----Weaknesses-----

I'm not very convinced by the empirical results, mostly due to the lack of
details of the baselines. Comments below are ranked by decreasing importance.

-  The proposed model has two main parts: sentence embedding and substructure
embedding. In Table 1, the baseline models are TreeRNN and DCNN, they are
originally used for sentence embedding but one can easily take the
node/substructure embedding from them too. It's not clear how they are used to
compute the two parts.

- The model uses two RNNs: a chain-based one and a knowledge guided one. The
only difference in the knowledge-guided RNN is the addition of a "knowledge"
vector from the memory in the RNN input (Eqn 5 and 8). It seems completely
unnecessary to me to have separate weights for the two RNNs. The only advantage
of using two is an increase of model capacity, i.e. more parameters.
Furthermore, what are the hyper-parameters / size of the baseline neural
networks? They should have comparable numbers of parameters.

- I also think it is reasonable to include a baseline that just input
additional knowledge as features to the RNN, e.g. the head of each word, NER
results etc.

- Any comments / results on the model's sensitivity to parser errors?

Comments on the model:

- After computing the substructure embeddings, it seems very natural to compute
an attention over them at each word. Is there any reason to use a static
attention for all words? I guess as it is, the "knowledge" is acting more like
a filter to mark important words. Then it is reasonable to include the baseline
suggest above, i.e. input additional features.

- Since the weight on a word is computed by inner product of the sentence
embedding and the substructure embedding, and the two embeddings are computed
by the same RNN/CNN, doesn't it means nodes / phrases similar to the whole
sentence gets higher weights, i.e. all leaf nodes?

- The paper claims the model generalizes to different knowledge but I think the
substructure has to be represented as a sequence of words, e.g. it doesn't seem
straightforward for me to use constituent parse as knowledge here.

Finally, I'm hesitating to call it "knowledge". This is misleading as usually
it is used to refer to world / external knowledge such as a knowledge base of
entities, whereas here it is really just syntax, or arguably semantics if AMR
parsing is used.

-----General Discussion-----

This paper proposes a practical model which seems working well on one dataset,
but the main ideas are not very novel (see comments in Strengths). I think as
an ACL paper there should be more takeaways. More importantly, the experiments
are not convincing as it is presented now. Will need some clarification to
better judge the results.

-----Post-rebuttal-----

The authors did not address my main concern, which is whether the baselines
(e.g. TreeRNN) are used to compute substructure embeddings independent of the
sentence embedding and the joint tagger. Another major concern is the use of
two separate RNNs which gives the proposed model more parameters than the
baselines. Therefore I'm not changing my scores.
