machine_text: In this paper, the authors apply induced segmentation to Topical Coherence in LDA-based models. Induced segmentation, which is a new technique for aggregating similar documents in a corpus, is used to create topical segments from a corpus of unstructured text. The authors apply this technique to induce topics from a LDA model and show that the resulting topics have better topical coherence. The results support the hypothesis that induced segmentation can be used to enhance the topical coherence of LDA-based models. massages review. This paper provides a useful theoretical contribution to the field of LDA and shows potential for practical applications in the future. As a review, I suggest a few additional edits to further strengthen the logic and the usefulness to future readers. The induced segmentation approach does not provide a clear motivation or explanation of why it should improve coherence. The authors speculate that because induced segmentation creates coherent groups of similar documents, it may improve LDA model coherence. I would like to see the authors provide a more concrete rationale and explanation of this theory. For example, I might imagine that inducing similar topics within a document might reinforce the topic assignments, but it’s not clear why this would improve coherence. The authors might provide a stronger rationale for this improvement if they discussed other theoretical models that may motivate this approach, or they could provide a more general discussion of how induced segmentation could improve coherence in other models. The authors also speculate that the induced segmentation may improve LDA’s ability to identify topics that are cohesive. I might imagine that a cohesive topic would need to be built from individual keywords or phrases that are semantically related. Because induced segmentation creates groups of similar documents, this approach may also provide a better mechanism to identify and group these semantically-related phrases. This approach could be a strong candidate for enhancing LDA’s topic coherence. The authors should discuss this idea more fully, and they could provide a stronger evaluation of the technique to demonstrate that it is indeed improving LDA’s topic cohesion. The authors demonstrate that induced segmentation can improve coherence, but they only use three iterations and a small dataset to evaluate the quality of the induced segmentation. The authors should either describe how much longer iterations might improve the quality of the segmentation or provide an evaluation of the induced segmentation at a higher number of iterations. Additionally, the authors only use 800 documents and 50 topics to evaluate the induced segmentation. Although this evaluation is certainly not thorough, it is appropriate for showing initial improvements. I would like to see the authors provide a more exhaustive evaluation of the induced segmentation, such as using a wider range of segment sizes, a larger number of iterations, and a larger number of documents. The improved quality of the segmentation might lead to more stable results and more significant improvements.

The paper entitled “Topical Coherence in LDA-based Models through Induced Segmentation” by Dehghan et al. addresses the problem of Coherence Garners and introduces a new paradigm: Induced Segmentation. In induced segmentation, instead of generating a single continuous segment for a document, the model generates a label for each document section and then combines the labels to form a final segmentation. The induced segmentation model is shown to outperform existing methods on the Automatic Post-processing of LDA-generated Documents data set. One strength of this paper is its exploration of an unexamined scenario for the Automatic Post-processing of LDA-generated Documents data set: the case of coherent segmentation into two clearly-differentiated segments. The paper analyzes this scenario, concludes that it is not addressed by existing methods, and describes the induced segmentation approach to this scenario. A second strength of this paper is the definition of the induced segmentation problem, its solution, and comparison to other existing solutions. The evaluation of the induced segmentation approach on coherent segmentation into two clearly-differentiated segments is carried out in an rigorous and objective way. A separate coherence assessment metric is defined and used in the empirical comparison of induced segmentation to existing methods. The paper also contains a useful discussion of the limitations of the induced segmentation model and ways to improve it. was written to address the problem of coherence garners, i.e., sometimes coherence assessments give higher scores to documents with coherent, unidimensional segmentation into clearly-differentiated segments than to documents with non-coherent, multi-segmented (i.e., multi-dimensional) segmentation. The paper does this by inducing segmentation into clearly-differentiated segments. One strength of this approach is its exploration of the case of coherent segmentation into clearly-differentiated segments. The paper analyzes this scenario, concludes that it is not addressed by existing methods, and describes the induced segmentation approach to this scenario.

Overall, I think this paper makes some interesting and important contributions to the field of topic models. In particular, this work extends LDA in a meaningful way by encouraging the model to produce segments that are coherent both within documents and across topics. I have some minor comments and suggestions for improvement, which I comment on below. Comments - Although the authors note that their model is naturally superset of other LDA-based models, they perform no additional experimentation validating this claim. In particular, it would be interesting to see if the addition of the induced segmentation mechanism has an impact on perplexity on the six datasets they evaluate on. - Please define the terms "segment" and "topic" throughout the paper. This is especially important in the first paragraph of the "Introduction" section, where the terms are used interchangeably multiple times without further explanation. This may have been done with intend, but unless the reader is clear on the difference between the two, the model may not seem very interesting. - "The rationale behind this approach is that the coherence between topics is a global property, defined only at the level of the universe of discourse, i.e. the set of all possible topics, and that individual segments may depart from this idealogy in various ways." The "this approach" being referred to here could be made clearer. - Figure 1 in the main text shows a difference between the induced segmentation approach and prior work (Plan et al. 2014) in terms of how topic modeling is performed within each generated segment. It would be good to expand on the similarities and differences between the two models elsewhere in the main text. - In Figure 1, it is not entirely clear how the topics in the induced segmentation model relate to the topics in the prior work. In particular, is each segment tied to a single topic, or can a single segment contain multiple topics? If the later, does each topic in the prior model correspond to a single topic in the induced segmentation model, or is it a finer-grained classification? - In the main text, it seems as if induced segmentation is first introduced in Plan et al. 2014. This is not strictly true. The work of Plan et al. 2014 was in fact in response to an earlier paper by Hatzivakos et al. (2013), which described an algorithm for inducing topics from text.

This paper addresses the problem of generating topically coherent segments within documents, for example, abstracts of research papers. In particular, it approaches this problem by jointly segmenting documents and assigning topics to their words, binding the topics associated to the words of a segment. This paper shows that the proposed model naturally encompasses other state-of-the-art LDA-based models designed for similar tasks, such as LASLDA and SDPLDA. Furthermore, our experiments, conducted on six different publicly available datasets, show the effectiveness of the proposed model in terms of perplexity, which is a commonly used metric in NLP, as well as Normalized Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI), which captures the coherence between the generated topics, and the Micro F1 measure for text classification, which is a standard text classification metric. moed: The main content of the paper is: - this model promotes topic coherence between segments by binding the topics associated to the words in a segment - the model relies on both document and segment specific topic distributions so as to capture fine grained differences in topic assignments - the paper shows that the proposed model naturally encompasses other state-of-the-art LDA-based models designed for similar tasks The model promotes topic coherence by binding the topics associated to the words in a segment. This is achieved by maximizing the following objective: p(z_{d}|z_{s},I) = \prod p(z_{d}^{(z_{s},I)} | z_{s}^{(z_{s},I)} ) p(z_{s}|I), where $z_{d}$ and $z_{s}$ are the hidden variables for document and segment, respectively, $I$ are the model parameters, $p(z_{d}^{(z_{s},I)} | z_{s}^{(z_{s},I)} )$ is the conditional probability, that given the previous segment is $z_{s}^{(z_{s},I)}$ and current segment is $z_{s}$, the words in the current document are assigned to topic $z_{d}$, and $p(z_{s}|I)$ is the prior probability for a segment given the model parameters $I$. The model relies on both document and segment specific topic distributions so as to capture fine grained differences in topic assignments. This is achieved by factorizing the above conditional probability into: p(z_{d}^{(z_{s},I)} | z_{s}^{(z_{s},I)} ) = \prod_k \phi_k(z_{d}^{(z_{s},I)}, \theta_k), where $\phi$ is the coefficient vector for the topic mixture component, and $\theta$ is the vector of associated topic proportions. The paper shows that the proposed model naturally encompasses other state-of-the-art LDA-based models designed for similar tasks. The model was implemented by replacing the conventional LDA topic modeling assumption with the proposed model. Experimental results indicate that the proposed model achieves better text classification and automatic evaluation metrics, such as perplexity, PMI, and Micro F1, compared to the state-of-the-art LDA-based models.

machine_text: Overall, I enjoy the premise of this paper, with the premise of a city changing its signs to emphasize its most iconic aspects in response to what locals want. The results, while initially amusing, appear to be less so over time as people get used to the altered street names. While some examples are humorous, such as evoking an autumnal feeling with "Fallowfield" for a street named Blackley Avenue, I am less convinced that "Harlow Carr" is a particularly interesting addition to the rich palette of local place names. I do not doubt that Harlow Carr is a lovely part of town, but the addition of this name to a street sign is unlikely to excite passersby to take a second look, unlike more evocative and original examples such as "London Road" or "Vegas Highway". For these reasons, I recommend performing a more extensive checker, with some samples of impressive additions such as this, and save this for later when the novelty has worn off and the new names have started to feel like they might actually be useful rather than just amusing. The writing is clear and concise, laying out the background information and the rationale for the changes ahead of time, so the reader can decide for themselves whether these changes are worth taking notice of. The change in naming scheme does seem to increase the frequency of the more notable examples, with names such as Blackley Avenue or Vegas Highway appearing to have especially memorable first letters. There may even be a case to be made for studying these in-road names to evaluate whether a shift to these more evocative names might increase the city's name recognition, although I would need to see clearer evidence that the change is significantly increasing the number of visitors to the city, rather than just increasing the length of time that particular visitors spend in the city. My biggest issue is that the change is entirely nonsensical. "Harlow Carr" is certainly a lovely place, but to assert that a place of such resonance warrants a place name on street signs throughout the city, let alone for high-traffic areas such as the center of the city, is fanciful. I do not doubt that the officials responsible for this change are intelligent and well-intentioned, but this kind of reverse-engineering of the existing street name and Situationist-style change metonymy seems destined to fail. I'm also concerned that, aside from the few examples I already mentioned that are almost humorous in their dullness, the authors have not provided any kind of counter-example of a more evocative naming change that has been deemed worthy of maintenance, or even any further examples at all of the more conventional forms of the city's name, leaving the reader with the impression that the entire city is a sea of generic, unimaginative "London Road". All of this leaves me with a distinctly underwhelming response. I recommend that the authors make a stronger case for the rationale for the changes, perhaps by tracking the frequency of street name changes in the past and identifying what factors influence those changes (especially in the area that the authors have focused on, namely streets in the city center), and then present that case alongside a more conservative update with a more measured response from me, such as "Vancouver Welcomes You! Change only occurs when this area is in flux, such as when there is a major sporting event, or a change in government, and this change metonymy worked well for Sin City, but this model does not appear to work for quaint little Harlow Carr. This is a useful area to do research, but the change should be less abrupt in nature, and perhaps focus on a single theme rather than switching to a completely different model mid-stream." I also strongly urge the authors to provide an update to this report after a period of a few years, at which point we can see how the new names have played out and determine whether the city's name-recognition problem is, in fact, a problem at all. Finally, I would like to suggest that, in the spirit of the original report, the authors collect some of the more entertaining updates and include them as an appendix. "Vancouver Welcomes You! The paper "Vancouver Welcomes You" by Jon AllSET is a great example of a clear, concise marketing message. This is especially true considering the topic of the paper--the city of Vancouver, British Columbia. Specifically, this paper is a metonymy for the city. A metonymy is a phrase, phrase, or phrase that is substituted for something else that it represents, most commonly in address or telephone numbers. In this case, the paper is written as a short phrase, rather than a full address or phone number. This approach is very successful in communicating the city of Vancouver's welcoming attitude. It is brief and to the point. There are some clear strengths here. For one, this is a very well-known marketing message. Many other companies have used this approach or something similar. It will be easy for the target audience to recognize this marketing message. There are also some clear weaknesses. First, the writer did not consider cultural or political sensitivity in this phrase. For example, when writing to a group of people who are not from North America, it may be unclear to the reader that Vancouver is a city. The address might appear to be a country. Second, the reader may interpret the phrase as a value statement. The writer may intend it as a statement of fact, but the statement may be perceived as value-laden. Overall, this is a very successful marketing message. It is succinct and to the point, which is crucial in a world where attention is scarce. At the same time, it has some cultural and political sensitivities.

Minimalist Neural Approach combined with a novel predicate window method can achieve competitive results on the SemEval 2007 task on Metonymy Resolution. We also present a novel Wikipedia-based MR dataset called RelocaR, which is tailored towards locations as well as improving previous deficiencies in annotation guidelines. The main contributions of this paper are: 1. Minimalist approach: We present a minimalist neural approach for MR that only uses word representations, a few linear transformations and a softmax layer. We do not use pretrained word embeddings or other lexical resources, resulting in a highly feasible and efficient approach for metonymy resolution. 2. New predicate window method: Instead of searching for the best window in a large feature space, we introduce a new predicate window method that optimises a predicate in the existing window search space. This method decreases the number of iterations and search space while improving the precision. 3. RelocaR: Our proposed MR dataset, RelocaR, significantly improves the annotated benchmark from the original one released for the 2013 and 2014 Metonymy Resolution Shared Task. We added several rules to the guidelines to address the problems of over-annotation in the original annotations. The baseline system for the evaluation task uses a feature engineered with handcrafted rules followed by a genetic algorithm. The proposed minimalist approach outperforms the baseline by 8.5% F1-score, showing the effectiveness of the proposed approach. We also present an approach that combines this minimalist approach with a predicate window method, reducing the F1-score to be beaten by 9%. In contrast to the baseline, which performs worse with new approaches, our results are promising and worth investigating more thoroughly in the future. Finally, we evaluate an ensemble of the baseline model, the minimalist approach without predicate window and the minimalist approach with predicate window. The model with predicate window achieved the best result on the validation set with F1-score of 78.1%, which is 11.4% above the second best result and 17% above the baseline result. The results indicate that the predicate window approach could be a good candidate to improve the performance of the minimalist approach on the baseline system, especially for the metonymic variants that have fewer words associated. We hope that this paper will give a good starting point for further work on neural approaches for MR, especially in neural architecture design, reusing knowledge from other NLP tasks, better evaluation measures, and better coverage of NER and GPT in the annotation guidelines. We also provide code for replicating the experiments, as well as the full dataset of Wikipedia pages with the region names replaced by metonymy candidates. machine_text: This paper presents a novel tagging scheme to jointly extract entities and relations from unstructured textual data. It first segments the input text into spans corresponding to entities and associated relations using a specific string matching algorithm. Next, using the segmentation information, it applies multiple partitioning and hashing algorithms to construct a set of logical groups of tags, called semantic frames. Using a non-negative matrix factorization approach, it further reduces the number of tags in each semantic frame to a smaller set of key tags. To retrieve similar documents, the proposed scheme uses the hashing technique to index the semantic frames and associated tags, thus enabling fast search with low false positive rate. Using this scheme, the authors have applied it to a real world dataset and shown the effectiveness of the approach. However, there are some areas that the authors could consider for improvement. In the semantic frame construction step, the authors could consider incorporating more semantic information into the frame formation. For example, they could consider using additional metadata associated with the text span, such as part of speech tags, to further enrich the semantic content of the frame. Also, instead of using a non-negative matrix factorization approach, the authors could have used a generative probabilistic model to reduce the tag space. For example, they could have used a soft-assignment approach such as latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA) to perform this task. Besides these suggestions, I believe this is an interesting and useful approach to automatically extract entities and associated relations from textual data, and the paper is well-crafted with detailed explanations of the approach and validation on the real world dataset. I recommend the authors to accept this paper for publication in the abovementioned journal.

The paper "Joint Extraction of Entities and Relations Based on a Novel Tagging Scheme" addresses a problem in natural language processing, named joint extraction of entities and relations, with a novel tagging scheme. The main contributions of this work include: (1) a tagging scheme that reduces the search space and allows trained models to achieve better performance; (2) a new entity-relation annotation schema that combines multiple fields in one relation; and (3) the incorporation of relational facts and characteristics into entity-relation graphs for improved relation classification. The experiments conducted on a large scale dataset show the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed model. Strengths The proposed tagging scheme is simple and easy to implement. It can be easily adapted to other NLP tasks by adding a few constraints. The experiments on a large scale dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed model. The proposed annotation schema can effectively represent complex relations. For example, it is effective in capturing triplets (entity1, relation, entity2) and (relation, entity1, entity2) at the same time. Relational facts and characteristics are successfully incorporated into relation classification. It yields significant improvements on DBpedia 2014, Freebase 2016 and DBpedia 2017 snapshot datasets. Weaknesses The proposed model only extracts the entities and relations based on the tags of the input sentence. There is no external knowledge used, which limits the application of the model. Conclusion The proposed joint extraction of entities and relations based on a tagging scheme is simple and effective, and has the potential to be applied to other NLP tasks.

This paper presents an empirical study to identify a latent dimension of
sentiment in word embeddings.

# Strengths

 S1) Tackles a challenging problem of unsupervised sentiment analysis.

is not applied to any test case. The ideas on which it is based are explained
in an "intuitive" manner and not thoroughly justified.

experiments being carried out, comparison with other methods (for example, the

2008) - http://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/4906796/) and the
application of the knowledge obtained to a real sentiment analysis scenario. At

machine_text: In this thoughtful, well-crafted paper, Roman Shustikov and colleagues provide a very nice survey of word2vec, word embedding methods in general, and evaluation. My main takeaway is that there is more to evaluating word embeddings than the simple task of evaluating the word embedding representation of a given word against a fixed list of OOV (out-of-vocabulary) words. For example, a critical question is whether the embeddings capture semantic information, which leads to a second and related question of whether the embeddings are data-efficient: do the embeddings capture semantic information with fewer parameters than if one needed to separately train a larger lookup table? The answer to this second question can have a large impact on the viability of word embeddings for real-world applications (e.g., large model sizes make the embeddings difficult to deploy). The authors do an excellent job of reviewing word embedding methods, the evaluation space, and the related work on data-efficiency. A relevant evaluation of word embeddings should focus on data efficiency and simple supervised tasks. A more complete picture can be obtained by including the results for the Cosine similarity based evaluation as well as the result for a simple supervised task of Assessing the parity of the number of women and men in official positions. For the selected word embeddings these results are as below: * DistilBERT: Supervised tasksperform about the same for small data sizes but drop quickly for larger sizes. Results for Cosine similarity based evaluation are close to the ideal score of 1, except for some layers in the first tokenization scheme. * GPT-2: Supervised task scores are much lower than the Cosine similarity based evaluation. Results are affected by both data size and parameter count, although the latter has smaller impact. * BERT: Supervised task scores are close to the ideal score of 1 for all data sizes and parameter counts. * XLNet-Large: Supervised task scores are close to the ideal score of 1 for all data sizes and parameter counts, except the first tokenization scheme where the score is lower for larger sizes. * RoBERTa-Large: Supervised task scores are similar to BERT but drop for larger sizes. Results for the first tokenization scheme are lower for larger sizes. * DBLP-Large: Supervised task scores are low for small data sizes and drop quickly for larger sizes. Reasons for the differences between the supervised task score and the ideal score of 1 can be, among others, the size of the available training dataset, the simplicity of the task or the size of the model. We provide a more comprehensive evaluation with results for a supervised task of Assessing the parity of the number of women and men in official positions. The model output is given for different sizes of the available training dataset as well as the complexity of the task. The task is to predict if the number of women and men is equal or not. The results show that in most cases the size of the data does not affect the model's performance, only the first tokenization scheme of BERT has this property. When the data size increases from 50k to 500k, the model has problems to predict correctly in some cases. Also, the bigger the parameter count the model has, the better the performance.
human_text:
This paper proposes a framework for evaluation of word embeddings based on data
efficiency and simple supervised tasks. The main motivation is that word
embeddings are generally used in a transfer learning setting, where evaluation
is done based on how faster is to train a target model. The approach uses a set
of simple tasks evaluated in a supervised fashion, including common benchmarks
such as word similarity and word analogy. Experiments on a broad set of
embeddings show that ranks tend to be task-specific and change according to the
amount of training data used.

Strengths

- The transfer learning / data efficiency motivation is an interesting one, as
it directly relates to the idea of using embeddings as a simple
"semi-supervised" approach.

Weaknesses

- A good evaluation approach would be one that propagates to end tasks.
Specifically, if the approach gives some rank R for a set of embeddings, I
would like it to follow the same rank for an end task like text classification,
parsing or machine translation. However, the approach is not assessed in this
way so it is difficult to trust the technique is actually more useful than what
is traditionally done.
- The discussion about injective embeddings seems completely out-of-topic and
does not seem to add to the paper's understanding.
- The experimental section is very confusing. Section 3.7 points out that the
analysis results in answers to questions as "is it worth fitting syntax
specific embeddings even when supervised datset is large?" but I fail to
understand where in the evaluation the conclusion was made.
- Still in Section 3.7, the manuscript says "This hints, that purely
unsupervised large scale pretraining might not be suitable for NLP
applications". This is a very bold assumption and I again fail to understand
how this can be concluded from the proposed evaluation approach.
- All embeddings were obtained as off-the-shelf pretrained ones so there is no
control over which corpora they were trained on. This limits the validity of
the evaluation shown in the paper.
- The manuscript needs proofreading, especially in terms of citing figures in
the right places (why Figure 1, which is on page 3, is only cited in page 6?).

General Discussion

I think the paper starts with a very interesting motivation but it does not
properly evaluate if their approach is good or not. As mentioned above, for any
intrinsic evaluation approach I expect to see some study if the conclusions
propagate to end tasks and this is not done in the paper. The lack of clarity
and proofreading in the manuscript also hinders the understanding. In the
future, I think the paper would vastly benefit from some extrinsic studies and
a more controlled experimental setting (using the same corpora to train all
embeddings, for instance). But in the current state I do not think it is a good
addition to the conference.

- Strengths:

This paper proposed an interesting and important metric for evaluating the
quality of word embeddings, which is the "data efficiency" when it is used in
other supervised tasks.

Another interesting point in the paper is that the authors separated out three
questions: 1) whether supervised task offers more insights to evaluate
embedding quality; 2) How stable is the ranking vs labeled data set size; 3)
The benefit to linear vs non-linear models.

Overall, the authors presented comprehensive experiments to answer those
questions, and the results see quite interesting to know for the research
community.

- Weaknesses:

The overall result is not very useful for ML practioners in this field, because
it merely confirms what has been known or suspected, i.e. it depends on the
task at hand, the labeled data set size, the type of the model, etc. So, the
result in this paper is not very actionable. The reviewer noted that this
comprehensive analysis deepens the understanding of this topic.

- General Discussion:

The paper's presentation can be improved. Specifically: 

1) The order of the figures/tables in the paper should match the order they are
mentioned in the papers. Right now their order seems quite random.

2) Several typos (L250, 579, etc). Please use a spell checker.

3) Equation 1 is not very useful, and its exposition looks strange. It can be
removed, and leave just the text explanations.

4) L164 mentions the "Appendix", but it is not available in the paper.

5) Missing citation for the public skip-gram data set in L425.

6) The claim in L591-593 is too strong. It must be explained more clearly, i.e.
when it is useful and when it is not.

7) The observation in L642-645 is very interesting and important. It will be
good to follow up on this and provide concrete evidence or example from some
embedding. Some visualization may help too.

8) In L672 should provide examples of such "specialized word embeddings" and
how they are different than the general purpose embedding.

9) Figuer 3 is too small to read.

machine_text: This is an interesting research paper, though I have some concerns. The notion of vector additivity, or the "naive" expectation that a bag of terms should add up to the total like vector spaces, is a key part of this paper. However, there are a few issues with this argument in the paper. First, it's not clear that the Boltzman Sampling procedure used to generate the skip-gram word vector adds up to a legitimate probability distribution (with sufficient over-dispersion to cancel out). The claim that it does is based on a previous paper that assumes a logarithmic reference function for a hardplus function, but there is no evidence that the Boltzman Sampling procedure has such a property. Second, even if one accepts the Boltzman Sampler procedure as a legitimate probability distribution, there is a key disagreement between the authors' results and the assumptions of the model. The model assumes that each word has a vector, but the paper only shows how to compute the average of all the words' vectors. The result is a valid skip-gram model, but it's not clear how to get a vector for each word in the vocabulary. Overall, this is an interesting idea, but the models assumptions do not hold in the Boltzmann Sampler implementation, and the result is a very different model than the one described in the paper. Overall, I recommend trying to salvage the ideas in the paper, but starting with a different model.

The authors analyze the Skip-gram model for word representation, which is a state of the art neural network based model that treats each word as a vector and these vectors are learned based on the context words associated with it. The model and the implementation is publicly available as part of the TensorFlow ecosystem. The authors focus on the case when the common words are assigned lower vectors than the rare words. The intuition is that lower frequency words might not have received sufficient training examples to acquire a big vector representation, and these are captured in the model via the lower cost defaults. The article makes the following observations. First, the vector addition is not commutative, which means the order in which the vectors are added is important and not simply a matter of semantics. Second, the uniform distribution is nondffective in the sense that if the same percentage of each word is used as the learning rate, then the average of the vectors would be proportional to the sum of the individual word vectors, but the resulting vector would have smaller magnitude. The article makes the case that this behavior can be explained by the power law distributions that occur frequently in nature and these are captured by the parameter gamma in the power law model. The article then proceeds to solve the problem using a three-step approach. First, the problem is reformulated as one of constrained least squares. Second, the problem is regularized by replacing the logarithmic function with a smooth quadratic function. Third, the problem is solved using alternating updates. The article makes the case that the proposed approach can be applied to other situations where vector addition does not result in vector addition, but rather the average of the two vectors. The algorithm is evaluated on several large vocabulary tasks, showing that the proposed approach is generally better than existing methods that modify the model to fit the data better. This article makes a case for considering the problem from a different perspective. While the solution is mathematically sound, it is essentially performing gradient descent on a smooth but unimodal objective function, with alternating updates, which is guaranteed to yield a local maximum. Thus, though this method might achieve a local optimum, it might not be the global optimum. As an example, the code for this article is made available on GitHub in case the method needs to be implemented for other problems as well. The article is quite good at explaining theSkip-gram model and how it is used, but this particular paper addresses the problem of how to interpret the resulting word vector and it is not clear how this problem has to do with the Skip-gram model at all. The word vector addition is not commutative, so the order in which the vectors are added matters. Thus, if Alice is given as a word in a text, then the vector addition may not be the same as if the text was given to Bob. The vector addition is not uniform, so the total sum of the vectors might not be proportional to the total number of vectors. For example, consider two vectors, (1, 2) and (2, 1), which adds to (1 + 2, 2 + 1) = (3, 5). However, if (1 : 3) is split into thirds, (1 : 3, 1 : 3), then the sum of these vectors is (1 : 3) + (3 : 1) + (3 : 1) = 1, which has smaller magnitude. The uniform distribution is not neutral, so if the same percentage of each word is used as the learning rate, then the average of the vectors would be proportional to the sum of the individual word vectors, but the resulting vector would have smaller magnitude. The formula used for this average is (1 + 1 + 1 + 1) / 4 = 4 / 4 = 1. In fact, in this case, the square root is an even faster converging average. The article makes the case that these are counterintuitive. The counterintuitive nature of the vector addition or uniform distribution, however, is not a problem. The surprising nature of these results is counterintuitive, and it is the business of science to find counterintuitive results. I have carefully read the paper "Skip-gram - Zipf + Uniform = Vector Additivity" by Lee, Dang, and Daxani, and I have the following comments. First, the proposed method works for many distributions. It is also possible that the method can be extended to non-power law distributions. In fact, the article proposes that "a linear combination of two power law random variables with different exponents is another power law random variable with a different exponent." Second, the example used in the article that the order of addition makes a difference is very important. However, this case also needs to be considered for symmetric problems. In particular, for the equation x + y = z, if x = z and y

Generally speaking, the main idea of the paper is correct. However, there are several issues that need to be addressed. First, there is no error checking on the proposed model. In particular, the assumption that symbol frequencies sum to 1 is often not satisfied in practice. This could lead to numerical issues. For example, in the uniform case, if the last symbol has a frequency of 1, the total must be 1, which is not allowed by the model. Second, in the paper there is no discussion on how to select the learning rate in the optimization process. In practice, this needs to be determined by trial and error. Third, the paper only considers the Skip-gram model with the negative sampling technique. In fact, this model is only one of the possible implementations of the Skip-gram model. For example, there are other parameters that are also very important, such as the number of iterations and the size of the context window. How to determine these parameters is not discussed in the paper. Fourth, there is a lack of experimental results. For example, in the evaluation part of the paper, different datasets are used for testing, which is not very convincing. In sum, the quality of the proposed model depends heavily on the selected parameter values, and a more systematic study of parameter selection is needed. Overall, the paper provides a general theoretical framework for understanding additive compositionality, and theoreticians in this field may find this work useful. However, for applied use cases where the parameters need to be carefully selected, there are many implementation issues to be considered. Overall, the paper is an important step toward explaining compositionality in word vectors, but it still has some problems to be further addressed.

The paper “Write Once, Variate” provides a theoretical justification for the presence of additive compositionality in word vectors learned using the Skip-Gram model. The theoretical work establishes a connection between the Skip-Gram model and the Sufficient Dimensionality Reduction (SDR) framework of Globerson and Tishby: the parameters of SDR models can be obtained from those of Skip-Gram models simply by adding information on symbol frequencies. The work shows that Additive Compositionality holds in an even stricter sense (small distance rather than small angle) under certain assumptions on the process generating the corpus. When these assumptions do not hold, this work describes the correct non-linear composition operator. It also shows that vector calculus can be used to solve word analogies. Finally, it establishes a connection between the Skip-Gram model and the Sufficient Dimensionality Reduction (SDR) framework of Globerson and Tishby: the parameters of SDR models can be obtained from those of Skip-Gram models simply by adding information on symbol frequencies. The work is quite interesting and could have great implications in future studies about the nature of compositionality in word vectors. The main strength of the paper is that it derives the additive compositionality (i.e., vector addition) result from a more general “sufficient dimensionality reduction” result, and at the same time shows that vector calculus solves word analogies because the sufficient dimensionality reduction result also implies a general form of non-linear compositionality. However, I also have some concerns about the generality of the sufficient dimensionality reduction result, as it is not clear to me how the assumptions underlying this general result would hold for real word corpora. First, it seems that in order to apply this general result it is typically required that for each word there is at least one word in the corpus that generates the same semantic space, whereas in practice word vectors are obtained from a large collection of texts, and it is not clear how one could guarantee that all words in the corpus will map to a single semantic space. Second, it is not clear to me how one would formally verify the statistical independence assumption underlying this general result, as this assumption is usually difficult to verify in practice and relies on a large corpus of high-quality sample data. Third, even if we assume that all these conditions are met, how one would formally show that the total variation of word distributions in a specific semantic space was sufficiently small (i.e., the “distance” used in the general sufficient dimensionality result) to imply a small angle between two words' composition vectors? I think the theoretical work in this paper would be of more interest to readers in computational linguistics than in numerical analysis, and it would be of interest to clarify the applicability of the general sufficient dimensionality result to real word corpora. One of the interesting observations in this paper is that although word2vec represents each word with a low-dimensional vector, these vectors are surprisingly good in capturing compositional semantics (i.e., the meanings of words can be determined by looking at the meanings of their component parts), and this capacity is a desirable property for a model of semantic representation, as most compositional semantics can be expressed using word combination with a controlled form (e.g., "fly" + "fly" = "fly" + "drone" = "drone"). This observation is consistent with a general viewpoint of computational linguists that the human mind can also be seen as a distributed representation model (as opposed to a tree or regex-based approach), and human beings can exploit certain syntactic regularities in languages to compute the meanings of words and phrase from the meanings of their component parts. The work by Peters and Schäfer (http://homepage.diva-portal.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/05/suzuki.pdf) is another work that demonstrated the ability of neural network models to model compositional semantics by investigating the connection between the restricted Boltzmann machines used in the word2vec model and the methods in statistical physics of quantum statistical mechanics. human_text:
This paper delves into the mathematical properties of the skip-gram model,
explaining the reason for its success on the analogy task and for the general
superiority of additive composition models. It also establishes a link between
skip-gram and Sufficient Dimensionality Reduction.

I liked the focus of this paper on explaining the properties of skip-gram, and
generally found it inspiring to read. I very much appreciate the effort to
understand the assumptions of the model, and the way it affects (or is affected
by) the composition operations that it is used to perform. In that respect, I
think it is a very worthwhile read for the community.

My main criticism is however that the paper is linguistically rather naive. The
authors' use of 'compositionality' (as an operation that takes a set of words
and returns another with the same meaning) is extremely strange. Two words can
of course be composed and produce a vector that is a) far away from both; b)
does not correspond to any other concept in the space; c) still has meaning
(productivity wouldn't exist otherwise!) Compositionality in linguistic terms
simply refers to the process of combining linguistic constituents to produce
higher-level constructs. It does not assume any further constraint, apart from
some vague (and debatable) notion of semantic transparency. The paper's
implication (l254) that composition takes place over sets is also wrong:
ordering matters hugely (e.g. 'sugar cane' is not 'cane sugar'). This is a
well-known shortcoming of additive composition. 

Another important aspect is that there are pragmatic factors that make humans
prefer certain phrases to single words in particular contexts (and the
opposite), naturally changing the underlying distribution of words in a large
corpus. For instance, talking of a 'male royalty' rather than a 'king' or
'prince' usually has implications with regard to the intent of the speaker
(here, perhaps highlighting a gender difference). This means that the equation
in l258 (or for that matter the KL-divergence modification) does not hold, not
because of noise in the data, but because of fundamental linguistic processes.
This point may be addressed by the section on SDR, but I am not completely sure
(see my comments below).

In a nutshell, I think the way that the authors present composition is flawed,
but the paper convinces me that this is indeed what happens in skip-gram, and I
think this is an interesting contribution. 

The part about Sufficient Dimensionality Reduction seems a little disconnected
from the previous argument as it stands. I'm afraid I wasn't able to fully
follow the argument, and I would be grateful for some clarification in the
authors' response. If I understand it well, the argument is that skip-gram
produces a model where a word's neighbours follow some exponential
parametrisation of a categorical distribution, but it is unclear whether this
actually reflects the distribution of the corpus (as opposed to what happens
in, say, a pure count-based model). The fact that skip-gram performs well
despite not reflecting the data is that it implements some form of SDR, which
does not need to make any assumption about the underlying form of the data. But
then, is it fair to say that the resulting representations are optimised for
tasks where geometrical regularities are important, regardless of the actual
pattern of the data? I.e. there some kind of denoising going on?

Minor comments:

- The abstract is unusually long and could, I think, be shortened.

- para starting l71: I think it would be misconstrued to see circularity here.
Firth observed that co-occurrence effects were correlated with similarity
judgements, but those judgements are the very cognitive processes that we are
trying to model with statistical methods. Co-occurrence effects and vector
space word representations are in some sense 'the same thing', modelling an
underlying linguistic process we do not have direct observations for. So
pair-wise similarity is not there to break any circularity, it is there because
it better models the kind of judgements humans known to make.

- l296: I think 'paraphrase' would be a better word than 'synonym' here, given
that we are comparing a set of words with a unique lexical item.

- para starting l322: this is interesting, and actually, a lot of the zipfian
distribution (the long tail) is fairly uniform.

- l336: it is probably worth pointing out that the analogy relation does not
hold so well in practice and requires to 'ignore' the first returned neighbour
of the analogy computation (which is usually one of the observed terms).

- para starting l343: I don't find it so intuitive to say that 'man' would be a
synonym/paraphrase of anything involving 'woman'. The subtraction involved in
the analogy computation is precisely not a straightforward composition
operation, as it involves an implicit negation. 

- A last, tiny general comment. It is usual to write p(w|c) to mean the
probability of a word given a context, but in the paper 'w' is actually the
context and 'c' the target word. It makes reading a little bit harder...
Perhaps change the notation?

Literature:

The claim that Arora (2016) is the only work to try and understand vector
composition is a bit strong. For instance, see the work by Paperno & Baroni on
explaining the success of addition as a composition method over PMI-weighted
vectors:

D. Paperno and M. Baroni. 2016. When the whole is less than the sum of its
parts: How composition affects PMI values in distributional semantic vectors.
Computational Linguistics 42(2): 345-350.

***
I thank the authors for their response and hope to see this paper accepted.

machine_text: I have reviewed the paper of Learning Discourse-level Diversity for Neural Dialog Models using Conditional Variational Autoencoders. The motivation and problem statement is well articulated. The pros and cons of related work are clearly presented. The insights about challenges in the domain are helpful. The insights about proposed approach are also interesting. I have a few queries and suggestions as follows: 1. In the paper "Learning Discourse-level Diversity for Neural Dialog Models" authors have used generative models. Why not use discriminative models to analyze the diversity of responses produced by the models? 2. In the "Experiments" section, authors have mentioned the dataset, hyperparameter values and have shown the baseline results. However, I feel there could have been a graph/chart showing how the results changed with change in parameters. 3. The overall "cleanliness" of the responses produced by the model would have been better if the model could have a few rounds of refinement with some expert (human) review? 4. In the "Related Work" section, the Linguistic Inquiry Word Count (LIWC) tool has been mentioned. As the authors are from UIUC, I wonder if LIWC-based ablation study has been performed to understand if the diversity could have been improved by altering the model architecture? *These comments are made only for improving the quality of the paper. This does not affect the scientific significance of the work. I hope the above comments have added value to the paper. Thank you for sharing the paper.

This paper addresses the problem of how to best train a model to learn discourse-level diversity, i.e. the ability to generalize to unseen contexts and roles. The authors present a novel method to train a model using a combination of conditional variational autoencoders and multitask learning. The model uses a reference speaker that indicates the expected kind of discourse from which samples can be drawn. For example, a statement like "Just kidding, I totally messed up that project" would be associated with the "moral" class. The model is trained to identify the "moral" class for the entire dialog, regardless of the actual statements made by the reference speaker. This leads to a model that is able to generalize to new contexts and speakers based on its exposure to different types of discourse. The authors perform a series of experiments using synthetic data as well as a real-world dataset and show that the proposed approach outperforms several baselines. One strength of this approach is that it is able to make use of a relatively small amount of annotated data. This makes it possible to train on data from diverse speakers, even when that data is somewhat noisy. For example, in the synthetic data experiments, the authors generated a training set with 20 different teachers, each with 10 different lessons, resulting in a total of 1000 example dialogs. Because the model was able to observe all the different teachers and different lessons, it was able to learn to generalize to new contexts and individuals based on its observations. One drawback of the model is that the diversity of the generated content needs to be limited in order for the model to be able to correctly classify the samples. For example, the reference speaker should make it clear which kinds of statements should be included in each class. The model is therefore not able to discover the kind of diversity on its own. Another limitation is that the performance on certain kinds of diversity (e.g. multi-gender dialog) might be restricted by the reference speaker. In contrast, a system using the same model but no references (i.e. relying on the model to determine the kind of diversity on its own) would presumably perform worse on such kinds of diversity. This approach could be improved in a number of ways. For example, the assumption that the reference speaker always remains the same for a dialog could be relaxed. It would also be interesting to use the same model for multiple types of diversity and compare these results to see if the model can discover multiple levels of diversity by itself.

First, the responses are often generic because they rely on various crude heuristics to copy words from a pretrained word embedding. While recent advances in neural conversation models have greatly improved the quality of generated responses, they are still highly constrained and lack natural language expressiveness. Second, the generation mechanism often lacks discourse level coherence because the models only depend on the decoder to copy words from a fixed set of examples. We believe that the first problem is caused by a lack of modeling the relation between the input (i.e. a user’s turn) and the output (i.e. a response) and the second problem is caused by a lack of diversity in the generation process. To address these issues, we argue that neural conversation models should be trained to capture the discourse-level diversity in the encoder. - Strength and weakness One strength of this work is that it focuses on capturing discourse-level diversity in the encoder. The weakness is that this work only compares its model with other baseline approaches but doesn’t demonstrate the superiority of its proposed methods. human_text:
Review, ACL 2017, paper 256:

This paper extends the line of work which models generation in dialogue as a
sequence to sequence generation problem, where the past N-1 utterances (the
‘dialogue context’) are encoded into a context vector (plus potential
other, hand-crafted features), which is then decoded into a response: the Nth
turn in the dialogue. As it stands, such models tend to suffer from lack of
diversity, specificity and local coherence in the kinds of response they tend
to produce when trained over large dialogue datasets containing many topics
(e.g. Cornell, Opensubtitles, Ubuntu, etc.). Rather than attempting to produce
diverse responses using the decoder, e.g. through word-by-word beam search
(which has been shown not to work very well, even lose crucial information
about grammar and valid sequences), or via a different objective function (such
as in Li et. al.’s work) the authors introduce a latent variable, z, over
which a probability distribution is induced as part of the network. At
prediction time, after encoding utterances 1 to k, a context z is sampled, and
the decoder is greedily used to generate a response from this. The evaluation
shows small improvements in BLEU scores over a vanilla seq2seq model that does
not involve learning a probability distribution over contexts and sampling from
this.

The paper is certainly impressive from a technical point of view, i.e. in the
application of deep learning methods, specifically conditioned variational auto
encoders, to the problem of response generation, and its attendant difficulties
in training such models. Their use of Information-Retrieval techniques to get
more than one reference response is also interesting. 

I have some conceptual comments on the introduction and the motivations behind
the work, some on the model architecture, and the evaluation which I write
below in turn:

Comments on the introduction and motivations…. 

The authors seem not fully aware of the long history of this field, and its
various facets, whether from a theoretical perspective, or from an applied one.

1. “[the dialogue manager] typically takes a new utterance and the dialogue
context as input, and generates discourse level decisions.” 

        This is not accurate. Traditionally at least, the job of the dialogue
manager is to select actions (dialogue acts) in a particular dialogue context.
The                    action chosen is then passed to a separate generation
module
for
realisation. Dialogue management is usually done in the context of task-based
systems which are goal driven. The dialogue manager is to choose actions which
are optimal in some sense, e.g. reach a goal (e.g. book a restaurant) in as few
steps as possible. See publications from Lemon & Pietquin, 2012, Rieser, Keizer
and colleagues, and various publications from Steve Young, Milica Gasic and
colleagues for an overview of the large literature on Reinforcement Learning
and MDP models for task-based dialogue systems.

2. The authors need to make a clear distinction between task-based,
goal-oriented dialogue, and chatbots/social bots, the latter being usually no
more than a language model, albeit a sophisticated one (though see Wen et. al.
2016). What is required from these two types of system is usually distinct.
Whereas the former is required to complete a task, the latter is, perhaps only
required to keep the user engaged. Indeed the data-driven methods that have
been used to build such systems are usually very different. 
3. The authors refer to ‘open-domain’ conversation. I would suggest that
there is no such thing as open-domain conversation - conversation is always in
the context of some activity and for doing/achieving something specific in the
world. And it is this overarching goal, the overarching activity, this
overarching genre, which determines the outward shape of dialogues and
determines what sorts of dialogue structure are coherent. Coherence itself is
activity/context-specific. Indeed a human is not capable of open-domain
dialogue: if they are faced with a conversational topic or genre that they have
never participated in, they would embarrass themselves with utterances that
would look incoherent and out of place to others already familiar with it.
(think of a random person on the street trying to follow the conversations at
some coffee break at ACL). This is the fundamental problem I see with systems
that attempt to use data from an EXTREMELY DIVERSE, open-ended set of
conversational genres (e.g. movie subtitles) in order to train one model,
mushing everything together so that what emerges at the other end is just very
good grammatical structure. Or very generic responses. 

Comments on the model architecture:

Rather than generate from a single encoded context, the authors induce a
distribution over possible contexts, sample from this, and generate greedily
with the decoder. It seems to me that this general model is counter intuitive,
and goes against evidence from the Linguistic/Psycholinguistic literature on
dialogue: this literature shows that people tend to resolve potential problems
in understanding and acceptance very locally - i.e. make sure they agree on
what the context of the conversation is - and only then move on with the rest
of the conversation, so that at any given point, there is little uncertainty
about the current context of the conversation. The massive diversity one sees
results from the diversity in what the conversation is actually trying to
achieve (see above), diversity in topics and contexts etc, so that in a given,
fixed context, there is a multitude of possible next actions, all coherent, but
leading the conversation down a different path.

It therefore seems strange to me at least to shift the burden of explaining
diversity and coherence in follow-up actions to that of the
linguistic/verbal/surface contexts in which they are uttered, though of course,
uncertainty here can also arise as a result of mismatches in vocabulary,
grammars, concepts, people’s backgrounds etc. But this probably wouldn’t
explain much of the variation in follow-up response. 

In fact, at least as far as task-based Dialogue systems are concerned, the
challenge is to capture synonymy of contexts, i.e. dialogues that are distinct
on the surface, but lead to the same or similar context, either in virtue of
interactional and syntactic equivalence relations, or synonymy relations that
might hold in a particular domain between words or sequences of words (e.g.
“what is your destination?” = “where would you like to go?” in a flight
booking domain). See e.g. Bordes & Weston, 2016; and Kalatzis, Eshghi & Lemon,
2016 - the latter use a grammar to cluster semantically similar dialogues.

Comments on the evaluation:

The authors seek to show that their model can generate more coherent, and more
diverse responses. The evaluation method, though very interesting, seems to
address coherence but not diversity, despite what they say in section 5.2:

The precision and recall metrics measure distance between ground truth
utterances and the ones the model generates, but not that between the generated
utterances themselves (unless I’m misunderstanding the evaluation method).
See e.g. Li et al. who measure diversity by counting the number distinct
n-grams in the generated responses.

Furthermore, I’m not sure that the increase in BLEU scores are meaningful:
they are very small. In the qualitative assessment of the generated responses,
one certainly sees more diversity, and more contentful utterances in the
examples provided. But I can’t see how frequent such cases in fact are.

Also, it would have made for a stronger, more meaningful paper if the authors
had compared their results with other work, (e.g. Li et. al) that use very
different methods to promote diversity (e.g. by using a different objective
function). The authors in fact do not mention this, or characterise it
properly, despite actually referring to Li et. al. 2015.

This paper presents a neural sequence-to-sequence model for encoding dialog
contexts followed by decoding system responses in open-domain conversations.
The authors introduced conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) which is a
deep neural network-based generative model to learn the latent variables for
describing responses conditioning dialog contexts and dialog acts.
The proposed models achieved better performances than the baseline based on RNN
encoder-decoder without latent variables in both quantitative and qualitative
evaluations.

This paper is well written with clear descriptions, theoretically sound ideas,
reasonable comparisons, and also detailed analysis.
I have just a few minor comments as follows:

- Would it be possible to provide statistical significance of the results from
the proposed models compared to the baseline in quantitative evaluation? The
differences don't seem that much for some metrics.

- Considering the importance of dialog act in kgCVAE model, the DA tagging
performances should affect the quality of the final results. Would it be there
any possibility to achieve further improvement by using better DA tagger?
Recently, deep learning models have achieved better performances than SVM also
in DA tagging.

- What do you think about doing human evaluation as a part of qualitative
analysis? It could be costly, but worth a try to analyze the results in more
pragmatic perspective.

- As a future direction, it could be also interesting if kgCVAE model is
applied to more task-oriented human-machine conversations which usually have
much richer linguistic features available than open conversation.

- In Table 1, 'BLUE-1 recall' needs to be corrected to 'BLEU-1 recall'.

human_text:
26: An End-to-End Model for Question Answering over Knowledge Base with
Cross-Attention Combining Global Knowledge

This paper presents an approach for factoid question answering over a knowledge
graph (Freebase), by using a neural model that attempts to learn a semantic
correlation/correspondence between various "aspects" of the candidate answer
(e.g., answer type, relation to question entity, answer semantic, etc.) and a
subset of words of the question. A separate correspondence component is learned
for each "aspect" of the candidate answers. The two key contributions of this
work are: (1) the creation of separate components to capture different aspects
of the candidate answer, rather than relying on a single semantic
representation, and (2) incorporating global context (from the KB) of the
candidate answers.

The most interesting aspect of this work, in my opinion, is the separation of
candidate answer representation into distinct aspects, which gives us (the
neural model developer) a little more control over guiding the NN models
towards information that would be more beneficial in its decision making. It
sort of harkens to the more traditional algorithms that rely on feature
engineering. But in this case the "feature engineering" (i.e., aspects) is more
subtle, and less onerous. I encourage the authors to continue refining this
system along these lines.

While the high-level idea is fairly clear to a reasonably informed reader, the
devil in the details would make it hard for some audience to immediately grasp
key insights from this work. Some parts of the paper could benefit from more
explanation... Specifically:

(1) Context aspect of candidate answers (e_c) is not clearly explained in the
paper. Therefore, the last two sentences of Section 3.2.2 seem unclear.

(2) Mention of OOV in the abstract and introduction need more explanation. As
such, I think the current exposition in the paper assumes a deep understanding
of prior work by the reader.

(3) The experiments conducted in this paper restrict comparison to IR-based
system -- and the reasoning behind this decision is reasonable. But it is not
clear then why the work of Yang et al. (2014) -- which is described to be
SP-based -- is part of the comparison. While, I am all for including more
systems in the comparison, there seem to be some inconsistencies in what should
and should not be compared. Additionally, I see not harm in also mentioning the
comparable performance numbers for the best SP-based systems.

I observe in the paper that the embeddings are learned entirely from the
training data. I wonder how much impact the random initialization of these
embeddings has on the end performance. It would be interesting to determine
(and list) the variance if any. Additionally, if we were to start with
pre-trained embeddings (e.g., from word2vec) instead of the randomly
initialized ones, would that have any impact?

As I read the paper, one possible direction of future work that occurred to me
was to possibly include structured queries (from SP-based methods) as part of
the cross-attention mechanism. In other words, in addition to using the various
aspects of the candidate answers as features, one could include structured
queries that generate the produce that candidate answer as an additional aspect
of the candidate answer. An attention mechanism could then also focus on
various parts of the structured query, and its (semantic) matches to the input
question as an additional signal for the NN model. Just a thought.

Some notes regarding the positioning of the paper:

I hesitate to call the model proposed here "attention" models, because (per my
admittedly limited understanding) attention mechanisms apply to
"encoder-decoder" situations, where semantics expressed in one structured form
(e.g., image, sentence in one language, natural language question, etc.) are
encoded into an abstract representation, and then generated into another
structured form (e.g., caption, sentence in another language, structured query,
etc.). The attention mechanism allows the "encoder" to jump around and attend
to different parts of the input (instead of sequentially) as the output is
being generated by the decoder. This paper does not appear to fit this notion,
and may be confusing to a broader audience.

------

Thank you for clarifications in the author response.

- Strengths:
This paper contributes to the field of knowledge base-based question answering
(KB-QA), which is to tackle the problem of retrieving results from a structured
KB based on a natural language question. KB-QA is an important and challenging
task.

The authors clearly identify the contributions and the novelty of their work,
provide a good overview of the previous work and performance comparison of
their approach to the related methods.

Previous approaches to NN-based KB-QA represent questions and answers as fixed
length vectors, merely as a bag of words, which limits the expressiveness of
the models. And previous work also don’t leverage unsupervised training over
KG, which potentially can help a trained model to generalize.
This paper makes two major innovative points on the Question Answering problem.

1) The backbone of the architecture of the proposed approach is a
cross-attention based neural network, where attention is used for capture
different parts of questions and answer aspects. The cross-attention model
contains two parts, benefiting each other. The A-Q attention part tries to
dynamically capture different aspects of the question, thus leading to
different embedding representations of the question. And the Q-A attention part
also offer different attention weight of the question towards the answer
aspects when computing their Q-A similarity score. 
2) Answer embeddings are not only learnt on the QA task but also modeled using
TransE which allows to integrate more prior knowledge on the KB side. 
Experimental results are obtained on Web questions and the proposed approach
exhibits better behavior than state-of-the-art end-to-end methods. The two
contributions were made particularly clear by ablation experiment. Both the
cross-attention mechanism and global information improve QA performance by
large margins.

The paper contains a lot of contents. The proposed framework is quite
impressive and novel compared with the previous works.

- Weaknesses:
The paper is well-structured, the language is clear and correct. Some minor
typos are provided below.
1. Page 5, column 1, line 421:                                       re-read               
   
 
reread
2. Page 5, column 2, line 454: pairs be    pairs to be

- General Discussion:
In Equation 2: the four aspects of candidate answer aspects share the same W
and b. How about using separate W and b for each aspect? 
I would suggest considering giving a name to your approach instead of "our
approach", something like ANN or CA-LSTM…(yet something different from Table
2).  

In general, I think it is a good idea to capture the different aspects for
question answer similarity, and cross-attention based NN model is a novel
solution for the above task. The experimental results also demonstrate the
effectiveness of the authors’ approach. Although the overall performance is
weaker than SP-based methods or some other integrated systems, I think this
paper is a good attempt in end-to-end KB-QA area and should be encouraged.

My only suggestion is to expand the description of the auxiliary task a bit more, in order to make it easier for other readers to reproduce the experiment. Currently, the paper only presents the baseline results using only the main task data as input. In order for the results to be more reproducible, it would be good to also show the results of training the model on the same data but with the auxiliary task information as input. For example, using unsupervised pre-training and then fine-tuning the pre-trained model on the main task data. It would also be good to mention what type of auxiliary task(s) was used in this example (if you didn't include this in the text already). Also, it would be good to mention the type of neural network architecture used in the experiment (if you didn't include this in the text already). Overall, the paper is very interesting and I'm sure the results will be useful to many people in the NLP field. I recommend accepting this peer review and looking into the suggestions above to make the paper easier to reproduce. Many thanks! Best, Dora ----- Thanks a lot for the feedback, Dora! We have updated the paper to include the missing parts, and these changes have led to +1 improvement in the area under the precision-recall curve (AULPR). Please see the "Reviewer's Report" section below for the updated results. Regarding the suggestion to demonstrate the results of unsupervised pre-training followed by fine-tuning on the main task data, we actually tried that and it actually hurt the performance, which we explain in the "Discussion" section. Finally, we have included the details of the network architecture in the "Hyper-parameters" section. Reviewer's Report +1 improvement in the area under the precision-recall curve (AULPR) The original model only uses the original training set without any auxiliary tasks, and the area under the precision-recall curve (AULPR) score is 0.724. The author improved the model by using the auxiliary task information as the input of a BiGRU encoder, and a customized fully connected layer to do classification. The new model uses the same word embedding and LSTMs as the original model. Using the exact same training hyper parameters, the new model only gets an AULPR of 0.733. The author says that using auxiliary task information to improve classification accuracy of a main task is very compelling. To evaluate if the improved model is better than the original model, I first created a new test set by splitting the original test set into training and development sets. The model is then trained on the original training set and the development set, and the performance is compared on the test set. New model only gets a AULPR score of 0.733, which is +1 improvement over the original model. This is a very convincing result. -- Dora Original: + Improving sentiment classification with task-specific data Sentiment classification is an important and widely used problem in Natural Language Processing. Most existing works treat sentiment classification as a simple classification task and adopt Bidirectional Gated Recurrent Unit (BiGRU) as the basic model architecture. The prediction result is obtained by taking the last hidden state of the BiGRU for classification. In this work, I borrow the idea of using auxiliary task data to pre-train a model and make use of external information to construct task-specific features to improve the sentiment classification performance. The improved model consists of a BiGRU encoder and a customized fully connected layer, in which the customized fully connected layer takes both the original features and the task-specific features into consideration and makes the final classification decision. The model is pre-trained on a public text classification dataset that only contains the main task’s training set. Compared with the baseline model which only uses the main task’s training set for training, the improved model improves the sentiment classification AULPR from 0.724 to 0.733. Improved model only gets a BiGRU encoder, but it improves the sentiment classification performance by using the auxiliary task information as the input of the BiGRU encoder.

This paper attempts to improve the accuracy of sentiment classification by using task-specific data. The first step is to find out what the current status of the system is using baseline metrics. Then a dataset is created based on similar concepts in the target domain and the performance is evaluated against this dataset. This process is repeated until performance improvement stagnates. At that point, the author delves into the latent characteristics of the learned embedding by using the target task’s loss function and checks for redundant features in the model. Finally, the author dives into the latent characteristics of the learned embedding by using the target task’s loss function and checks for redundant features in the model. Offer specific criticism on the paper's premise. Often times customizing a dataset to a particular domain will remove knowledge of broader domains which could adversely affect generalizability of the models trained on such datasets. Similarly, performing model customization for a single metric (e.g. MSE) may not help when a more complex model with more parameters would have given better performance. Furthermore, custom dictionaries require re-tokenizing and indexing, which adds noise to the process and can add overhead.

Overall, I think the paper is very useful and addresses an important problem in sentiment analysis, which is task-specific data is often scarce. The idea is simple and practical and has broad applications. Below I provide some suggestions to improve the paper: 1. The introduction may want to spend more time to introduce this problem and show some examples of failure using generic embeddings on task-specific data. 2. The method proposed in Section 4.1 may be able to deal with other tasks that have similar problems. For example, in Section 4.1 the authors show that using a corpus to train word embeddings could lead to task-specific data leaking into the embeddings. This problem could also occur in semisupervised learning, where the labels of some samples are missing. Maybe another method could be introduced to show the difference between these two problems. 3. It would be good to include an empirical comparison of the proposed method to other methods for using task-specific data for improving word embeddings. 4. Some parts of the results may be confusing to some readers. For example, in some cases a sentence could be considered task-specific but it may still have a neutral sentiment. In such cases, the method may not work well because it is not able to distinguish the nuance between the sentiment classes. In such case, presenting the results with examples may help the readers to understand the method better. I believe the paper is worth publishing but it would be good to address these suggestions before publication. I have no further comments. Some sentences in the results appear to be confusing to me. In most cases, a sentence is considered task-specific if the word “task” is present in the sentence. However, this is not always the case for sentiment classification. Consider the following two sentences: 1. The score of the German reunification is a task that is very challenging to evaluate. 2. The reunification of Germany was a positive development and a milestone on the road to European unification. In case 1, the sentiment of this sentence is negative because the evaluation of the score is a challenging task. However, the method considers this sentence to be task-specific because the word “task” is present in the sentence. However, in case 2 the same sentence is neutral because the task of reunifying Germany was just a positive development. In my opinion, the use of word embeddings should not rely on the presence of the word “task” in a sentence to define its sentiment.
