The A* CCG parser is a state-of-the-art parser for achieving robust semantic parsing on a large corpus of natural language text. It can be used for downstream applications such as machine translation, question answering, and summarization. In this paper, the authors present a technique for efficiently implementing the A* algorithm on top of a dependency factored model. They demonstrate that the algorithm achieves comparable performance to the state of the art on standard benchmark datasets. This is a novel and very interesting contribution, however it lacks some technical detail regarding specific algorithmic techniques. Most importantly, this is not an algorithm for a natural language processing task, but rather a model for efficiently applying the A* algorithm to a semantic parsing task. Henceforth the paper would be stronger if it could describe how the dependency factored model differs from other approaches to semantic parsing and why it makes the A* algorithm applicable. For example, it would be nice to know whether there are other approaches to parsing that can also be factored in this way, and whether it is necessary to do so in order to apply the A* algorithm. The introduction could also do a better job of setting the scene and explaining the problem statement. tirespitorywould be stronger if it could describe how the dependency factored model differs from other approaches to semantic parsing and why it makes the A* algorithm applicable. For example, it would be nice to know whether there are other approaches to parsing that can also be factored in this way, and whether it is necessary to do so in order to apply the A* algorithm.

The paper is helpful for me to understand the model design and parameter learning approach, especially the factorized model design which is not clear for me before. The results also confirm the effectiveness of the model. However, there are some unclear points in the paper for me, which I hope the author can address. 1. What does "lexicalized dependency representation" mean? What kind of dependencies are we talking about? 2. Could you give some statistics about the parameters in your model? e.g. in what percentage of cases each parameter was updated during training? 3. What did you mean by "pre-computation of all probabilities", and how exactly is it performed? 4. Could you provide some discussion about the difference between this model and the previous models you compared with? Otherwise, congratulations for the great results! ---------------------- Zhe Liu Geometric parsing group Harbin Institute of Technology China Reference: [1] Gaddy, Carson, and Zhi-Hong Wang. "A Structured Attender for Compositional Parsing." In Proceedings of the North American Chapter of the International Speech Communication Association. 2015. [2] Liu, Zhe. Here are answers to your questions: 1. lexicalized dependency representation, we mean different types of dependency relation. This process requires modeling the problem as a search problem on a tree structure, and the syntax and semantics of the target language. In this paper, we present a new A* CG parsing model in which the probability of a tree is decomposed into factors of CG categories and dependency factors both defined on bi-directional LSTMs. Our factored model allows the precomputation of all probabilities and runs very efficiently, while modeling sentence structures explicitly via dependencies. Our model achieves the state-of-the-art results on English and Japanese CCG parsing. -- Zhe Liu A* CCG Parsing with a Supertag and Dependency Factored Model

A* CCG parsing is known to be challenging because CCG parser has to be able to locate multiple triggers on any given sentence. This paper tackles this problem with a novel factored model that explicitly models dependencies using LSTMs, allowing the CCG parser to precompute and be able to efficiently evaluate the overall parse probability. The model also factors categories, allowing the parser to do incremental update of the categories during parsing, reducing the risk of falling into local optima. The model is shown to achieve state-of-the-art results on both English and Japanese CCG parsing. I think the model has potential benefits over other methods that do not explicitly model dependencies and rely on heuristics or approximate methods for some components, for example the use of causative dependencies for wh- questions. I also think there is need for pre-training on larger datasets, to further reduce the risk of falling into local optima. Strengths: - use of LSTMs for dependency modeling, allows efficient evaluation of the overall parse probability - explicit modeling of dependencies allows the model to do incremental update of the dependencies during parsing - use of factored CCG categories allows the model to do incremental update of categories during parsing Weaknesses: - pre-training on larger datasets is needed for further reduction of the risk of falling into local optima - the use of causative dependencies for wh- questions could be a limitation Overall this is an interesting model that utilize the advantages of using LSTMs for dependency modeling and explicit modeling of CCG categories. I think this is worth exploring and could lead to further improvements in CCG parsing.

machine_text: Overall, this paper is well-written, though there are several aspects that could be expanded on to make the paper stronger. Firstly, the authors should consider the possibility that the ghostwritten rap lyrics were not wholly genuine, and that the artist was using a trick to try to get around intellectual property restrictions. The lyrics describe features of the neighbourhood the artist grew up in, and it seems unlikely that any local would not know about the existence of thesong's subject matter. The lyrics also contain a reference to a friend of the artist who is still alive, suggesting that the lyrics were not fully fabricated. The lyrics were also likely written quite a long time ago (12 years at the time of writing), and much has changed in the area over that time. The authors should consider the possibility that the artist was not actually involved in the composition of the lyrics, and that they are written in such a way as to give the appearance of a genuine rap song. The authenticity of the rap lyrics could be tested by the authors either by speaking to people who live in the area (and checking if they know anything about the subject matter), or by consulting academic resources about the area at the time the lyrics were written (for example, the Rap Map Project). The authors could also investigate whether the song was ever commercially successful, as this would suggest that the song could have sold commercially at some point, even if the artists didn't actually write them. The second aspect that could be expanded on is the idea of genre. The paper talks about how rap genre has changed over the past few decades, and that this has an impact on how much influence the producer has on the final song. However, there is actually a third aspect to genre that might have an impact on the paper's central idea: the "grain" of the lyric. This is a more general category of rap genre, which determines the style of the delivery of the lyrics. This could be thought of as analogous to the "energy" of a jazz musician, who can choose to play the melody or jump around within a given theme. The grain could be thought of as akin to the idea of a "flow" in traditional jazz. Most rap music has a lot of variety within it, and is usually not highly repetitive. Thus, even if a given rap lyric was written by a single person, that person could vary their phrasing and delivery of the lyrics in such a way that makes the song look like it is produced by multiple rappers. In this case, the idea of the producer having less influence over the final song would be even more strongly supported by the data. The final point to make about the paper is that I think the title is very misleading. The paper doesn't look at whether the generated lyrics are actually any good or not, but rather at whether they are commercially successful. The paper does not show that the generated rap lyrics are any good at all, and it's not clear that the ability to generate successful rap lyrics would even be a transferable skill to generating good songs of some other genre.

This paper addresses an important problem in the study of creativity: how to evaluate the originality of texts generated in a non-standard way, as in the case of rap lyrics written in someone else’s name. The paper develops a methodology that compares the style, structures, and topics of the generated texts to those of similar ones written by a reference writer. The method is illustrated with a case study on rappers who hire writers to write their lyrics in a more creative, art-like style. The strengths of this paper include the novelty of the proposed methodology, and the usefulness of the case study for testing the method’s utility. The weakness is that the paper does not present any new interesting findings on the topic of creative language generation, apart from the method’s usefulness. This paper contributes to the evaluation of creative activities by providing a methodology to assess the originality of texts generated in a non-standard way. To illustrate the methodology, I apply it to a case study on rappers who hire writers to write their lyrics in a more creative, art-like style, which is called “ghostwriting”. The case study is useful in at least two ways. First, it is novel since it is the first time that such a methodology is applied to ghostwriting. Second, it can be applied to other creative activities, such as songwriting. The method proposed is useful because it provides quantitative and qualitative measures of the originality of the texts. The strength of the paper is the novelty of the methodology, as it has not been applied to ghostwriting before. Another strength is the usefulness of the case study for testing the method’s utility, and the usefulness of the topic for researchers in the field of creativity and talent management. Finally, the paper is easy to read and provides a good introduction to a topic of growing interest in the scientific community.

The evaluation methodology developed in the paper is novel and compelling, and could easily be used to evaluate other creative language generation tasks. My favorite part of the paper is the introduction of an annotated corpus of rapl lyric for 13 artists, which could be used in the future to train and test models. I also think the described evaluation metric of "stylistic similarity" is very good. I don't have much criticism for the paper, and I think it makes a nice introduction to a topic that has only recently become popular. Fully Accepted Manuscript of "Evaluating Creative Language Generation: The Case of Rap Lyric Ghostwriting" Date: Tue, 29 Jun 2023 PDP: 1 week SCORE: 5/10 The author(s) have addressed all comments from the reviewers. All comments from the editors are provided below. This paper presents an evaluation methodology for evaluating the performance of creative language generation tasks. The evaluation focuses on the evaluation of generated text on three criteria: content, style, and creativity. The generated text must be similar to the style of the ground truth text, but distinct in its content. We develop a corpus of rap lyrics used by 13 different artists, with similarity annotations for content and style. We apply this to evaluate a system for rap lyric generation, using an attention-based model that has recently shown strong results on this domain. Our evaluation shows that the evaluated system struggles with the content and creativity criteria, and that it is only able to achieve low similarity in the style criteria. This suggests that it is difficult to produce text that is both similar to the ground truth and at the same time truly unique. We also evaluate some human-generated examples, and find that while the generated text is similar to the ground truth, it does not reflect the creativity and style we expect from a good rap lyric. The latter result suggests that it may not be possible to automatically measure creativity in this application, but it would be interesting to use such an evaluation to help find skilled examples for the community to review. This paper presents an interesting evaluation method for creative language generation, and I have no major concerns with the evaluation itself. The evaluation methodology seems straightforward and effective, and could be used for evaluating other such tasks. The corpus of 13 artists' raps is also interesting, and could be used for training and testing models in this domain.

human_text:
This paper presents evaluation metrics for lyrics generation exploring the need
for the lyrics to be original,but in a similar style to an artist whilst being
fluent and co-herent. The paper is well written and the motivation for the
metrics are well explained.  

The authors describe both hand annotated metrics (fluency, co-herence and
match) and an automatic metric for ‘Similarity'. Whilst the metric for
Similarity is unique and interesting the paper does not give any evidence of
this as an effective automatic metric as correlations between this metric and
the others are low, (which they say that they should be used separately). The
authors claim it can be used to meaningfully analyse system performance but we
have to take their word for it as again there is no correlation with any
hand-annotated performance metric.  Getting worse scores than a baseline system
isn’t evidence that the metric captures quality (e.g. you could have a very
strong baseline).

Some missing references, e.g. recent work looking at automating co-herence,
e.g. using mutual information density (e.g. Li et al. 2015). In addition, some
reference to style matching from the NLG community are missing (e.g. Dethlefs
et al. 2014 and the style matching work by Pennebaker).

This paper studies how to properly evaluate systems that produce ghostwriting
of rap lyrics.
The authors present manual evaluation along three key aspects: fluency,
coherence, and style matching.
They also introduce automatic metrics that consider uniqueness via maximum
training similarity, and stylistic similarity via rhyme density.

I can find some interesting analysis and discussion in the paper.
The way for manually evaluating style matching especially makes sense to me.

There also exist a few important concerns for me.

I am not convinced about the appropriateness of only doing fluency/coherence
ratings at line level.
The authors mention that they are following Wu (2014), but I find that work
actually studying a different setting of hip hop lyrical challenges and
responses, which should be treated at line level in nature.
While in this work, a full verse consists of multiple lines that normally
should be topically and structurally coherent.
Currently I cannot see any reason why not to evaluate fluency/coherence for a
verse as a whole.

Also, I do not reckon that one should count so much on automatic metrics, if
the main goal is to ``generate similar yet unique lyrics''.
For uniqueness evaluation, the calculations are performed on verse level.
However, many rappers may only produce lyrics within only a few specific topics
or themes.
If a system can only extract lines from different verses, presumably we might
also get a fluent, coherent verse with low verse level similarity score, but we
can hardly claim that the system ``generalizes'' well.
For stylistic similarity with the specified artist, I do not think rhyme
density can say it all, as it is position independent and therefore may not be
enough to reflect the full information of style of an artist.

It does not seem that the automatic metrics have been verified to be well
correlated with corresponding real manual ratings on uniqueness or stylistic
matching.
I also wonder if one needs to evaluate semantic information commonly expressed
by a specified rapper as well, other than only caring about rhythm.

Meanwhile, I understand the motivation for this study is the lack of *sound*
evaluation methodology.
However, I still find one statement particularly weird:
``our methodology produces a continuous numeric score for the whole verse,
enabling better comparison.''
Is enabling comparisons really more important than making slightly vague but
more reliable, more convincing judgements?

Minor issue:
Incorrect quotation marks in Line 389

This paper proposes to present a more comprehensive evaluation methodology for
the assessment of automatically generated rap lyrics (as being similar to a
target artist).  While the assessment of the generation of creative work is
very challenging and of great interest to the community, this effort falls
short of its claims of a comprehensive solution to this problem.

All assessment of this nature ultimately falls to a subjective measure -- can
the generated sample convince an expert that the generated sample was produced
by the true artist rather than an automated preocess?  This is essentially a
more specific version of a Turing Test.   The effort to automate some parts of
the evaluation to aid in optimization and to understand how humans assess
artistic similarity is valuable.  However, the specific findings reported in
this work do not encourage a belief that these have been reliably identified.

Specifically -- Consider the central question: Was a sample generated by a
target artist?        The human annotators who were asked this were not able to
consistently respond to this question.        This means either 1) the annotators did
not have sufficient expertise to perform the task, or 2) the task was too
challenging, or some combination of the two.  

The proposed automatic measures also failed to show a reliable agreement to
human raters performing the same task.        This dramatically limits their efficacy
in providing a proxy for human assessment.   The low interannotator agreement
may be "expected" because the task is subjective, but the idea of decomposing
the evaluation into fluency and coherence components is meant to make it more
tractable, and thereby improve the consistency of rater scores.  A low IAA for
an evaluation metric is a cause for concern and limits its viability as a
general purpose tool.  

Specific questions/comments:

* Why is a line-by-line level evaluation prefered to a verse level analysis. 
Specifically for "coherence", a line by line analysis limits the scope of
coherence to consequtive lines.

* Style matching -- This term assumes that these 13 artists each have a
distinct style, and always operate in that style. I would argue that some of
these artists (kanye west, eminem, jay z, drake, tupac and notorious big) have
produced work in multiple styles.  A more accurate term for this might be
"artist matching".

* In Section 4.2 The central automated component of the evaluation is low
tf*idf with existing verses, and similar rhyme density.  Given the limitations
of rhyme density -- how well does this work.  Even with the manual intervention
described?

* In Section 6.2 -- This description should include how many judges were used
in this study? In how many cases did the judges already know the verse they
were judging?  In this case the test will not assess how easy it is to match
style, but rather, the judges recall and rap knowledge.

The model is trained on a corpus of categorized news articles and is tested on novel samples with similar categories. The model uses a bidirectional RNN to encode the input text, resulting in sequence of hidden vectors, one vector for each timestep in the RNN. These vectors are used in a fully connected layer to compute document representations. The model is trained with stochastic gradient descent using categorical cross entropy as the loss function. The code for the model and experiments is available on GitHub at the following address: <URL to access model code>. The model is shown to be effective on two standard text categorization benchmarks, achieving state-of-the-art results on both the News corpus and the Newscorpus. I have several comments and suggestions that could enhance the transparency and understanding of the model and evaluation. 1. The authors should state the batch size used for training the model. It is not clear from the description if the model was trained on a single GPU or not. 2. In the preprocessing step, the stopwords are removed from the raw text. The paper Neural Discourse Structure for Text Categorization describes a neural network based approach for identifying the structural relations in text. The system first tokenize the input text and then using Recursive Neural Forest to identify the discourse structure. The approach is shown to outperform other state of the art techniques on standard benchmark datasets such as ISCST, TAC KBP, MLP, etc. The approach presented in the paper has several limitations. The most important one is the lack of general applicability to a wider range of NLP tasks. The approach works very well on problem where a discourse structure can be clearly defined. For example, movie review for a movie can have a clear beginning, central idea, ending and hence a clear discourse structure. However, the approach has limitations in cases where the structural relations are not as evident, for example, generic sentences with no clear component headers (i.e., beginning, central idea, ending) or when there are multiple valid discourse structures for a given text. I also think that the author could have shown the code and parameters used to train the model, this will allow other users to reproduce the model or extend it to a different use case I also think that the results presented in the paper lack concrete examples of how the model identify each structural relation. For example, I wasn't able to find examples of how the approach identify beginning of text or a central idea. I also noticed that the approach presented in the paper uses a single hidden layer neural network. The approach could be improved by using a deep neural network or Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network. LSTMs have been shown to perform very well on sequence modeling tasks like text classification. I also think that the paper could have been strengthened by including more experiments. For example, how does the approach perform on other language other than English. Overall, this is an interesting paper that describes a novel approach to identifying discourse structure in text, and although there are a few suggestions above to strengthen the paper, the work presented is of interest to anyone interested in NLP and text categorization

First, although RST is a popular theory for discourse analysis, it's not a fully automatic method, so this is not a fully automatic approach. It's unclear how well this approach will generalize to other text and how well it will perform on other tasks. Second, it's not clear how the choice of RST versus some other discourse analysis approach would impact the results. For example, an argument that some other approach would be more automatic than RST and therefore might yield better results. Third, it's not clear how the approach would perform if data that conforms to RST's assumptions were available, e.g., from a tool that converted the input text to RST. These limitations make it difficult to assess the approach's full potential, but it's a promising approach that could be improved on these points. In terms of applicability, the paper does not discuss the choice of text representation or indicate whether it is designed to capture discourse or any other useful aspects of text. Nor does it discuss the design of the attention mechanism. Consequently, these choices might limit the approach's utility. In general, it's helpful to provide a clearer rationale for selecting RST and for using a recursive neural network and an attention mechanism. While these choices are typical in NDS, it would be helpful to state explicitly why these choices were made and to discuss the consequences and benefits of these choices. The remainder of the paper has good practice and coverage of the approach. The details of the implementation are comprehensive. Overall, this is an interesting and well-documented contribution.

The paper Neural Discourse Structure for Text Categorization, its main content is as below: We show that discourse structure, as defined by Rhetorical Structure Theory and provided by an existing discourse parser, benefits text categorization. Our approach uses a recursive neural network and a newly proposed attention mechanism to compute a representation of the text that focuses on salient content, from the perspective of both RST and the task. Experiments consider variants of the approach and illustrate its strengths and weaknesses. The main idea of this paper is that discourse structure, as defined by Rhetorical Structure Theory (RST) and provided by an existing discourse parser, benefits text categorization. We present a neural network model that computes a representation of the text that focuses on salient content from the perspective of both RST and the task. We perform experiments considering variants of the approach and illustrate its strengths and weaknesses. First, we show that a standard classifier performs well on the new task with the provided RST-based discourse parsing as gold standard. We experiment with multiple combinations of pre-trained word embeddings and bi-directional LSTM RNNs and obtain the best performance with a combination of fastText and Bidirectional LSTM (17 million parameters). Second, we present a neural network model that uses an attention mechanism to compute a representation of the text that focuses on salient content from the perspective of both RST and the task. The model is similar to the state-of-the-art models for machine comprehension, though it computes a representation of the text that focuses on salient content from the perspective of both RST and the task. We apply the model to the Document Component of the TAC-KDD dataset, which does not have gold standard discourse parsing. We perform experiments with variants of the model and illustrate its strengths and weaknesses. Overall, we show that a standard classifier performs well on the new task with the provided RST-based discourse parsing as gold standard. We present a neural network model that uses an attention mechanism to compute a representation of the text that focuses on salient content from the perspective of both RST and the task. The model is similar to the state-of-the-art models for machine comprehension, though it computes a representation of the text that focuses on salient content from the perspective of both RST and the task.
human_text:
This paper proposed to explore discourse structure, as defined by Rhetorical
Structure Theory (RST) to improve text categorization. A RNN with attention
mechanism is employed to compute a representation of text. The experiments on
various of dataset shows the effectiveness of the proposed method. Below are my
comments:

(1) From Table 2, it shows that “UNLABELED” model performs better on four
out of five datasets than the “FULL” model. The authors should explain more
about this, because intuitively, incorporating additional relation labels
should bring some benefits. Is the performance of relation labelling so bad and
it hurts the performance instead?

(2) The paper also transforms the RST tree into a dependency structure as a
pre-process step. Instead of transforming, how about keep the original tree
structure and train a hierarchical model on that?

(3) For the experimental datasets, instead of comparing with only one dataset
with each of the previous work, the authors may want to run experiments on more
common datasets used by previous work.

- Strengths:

The main strength of this paper is the incorporation of discourse structure in
the DNN's attention model, which allows the model to learn the weights given to
different EDUs.

Also the paper is very clear, and provides a good explanation of both RST and
how it is used in the model.
Finally, the evaluation experiments are conducted thoroughly with strong,
state-of-the-art baselines.

- Weaknesses:

The main weakness of the paper is that the results do not strongly support the
main claim that discourse structure can help text classification. Even the
UNLABELED variant, which performs best and does outperform the state of the
art, only provides minimal gains (and hurts in the legal/bills domain). The
approach (particularly the FULL variant) seems to be too data greedy but no
real solution is provided to address this beyond the simpler UNLABELED and ROOT
variants.

- General Discussion:

In general, this paper feels like a good first shot at incorporating discourse
structure into DNN-based classification, but does not fully convince that
RST-style structure will significantly boost performance on most tasks (given
that it is also very costly to build a RST parser for a new domain, as would be
needed in the legal/bill domains described in this paper). I wish the authors
had explored or at least mentioned next steps in making this approach work, in
particular in the face of data sparsity. For example, how about defining
(task-independent) discourse embeddings? Would it be possible to use a DNN for
discourse parsing that could be incorporated in the main task DNN and optimized
jointly  end-to-end? Again, this is good work, I just wish the authors had
pushed it a little further given the mixed results.

The article would benefit from adding a few case studies and using more empirical evidence to support some of the claims. For example, it would be helpful to include a quantitative comparison to a baseline model. I also think it would be useful to show example of how to use the model by showing some examples of financial disclosures and the associated sentiments.

Paper Abstract Predicting volatility is an important task for financial professionals. Accurate predictions can lead to better risk management practices that can prevent volatility-related losses. Given that financial professionals are often required to provide reasons for predictions, this open-source challenge aims to demonstrate an alternative way to predict volatility that is more accessible. In this paper, we propose a new method for predicting volatility usingSentiment-based financial disclosure forecasts generated using automated IR technology. Our approach is to train a neural network to map financial statement text to aSentiment value, and use this to predict future financial statements. By applying techniques from Natural Language Processing (NLP), we find that sentiment levels related to uncertain statements are correlated with periods of higher volatility. We then build a classifier using features derived from both the financial statement text and sentiment, and test it on a proprietary dataset. The classifier demonstrates promising results relative to the existing state-of-the-art on this dataset.' Paper Strengths We present a framework for predicting volatility that is more accessible to non-financial professionals, and that does not require manually curated data. We propose a novel combination of two different technologies for the prediction problem: an automated (and therefore highly scalable) implementation of financial disclosure forecasting, and deep neural networks for predicting volatility. We evaluate our framework on a proprietary dataset and demonstrate that it is able to achieve promising results, comparable to the state-of-the-art. Paper Weaknesses We assume that the forecasting method is accurate, which is a common assumption in the finance industry but may not be true for a generic framework like this. Our framework focuses only on publicly available data, and therefore cannot capturePrivate corporate information, which likely contributes significantly to volatility.

The paper "Volatility Prediction Using Financial Disclosures Sentiments with Word Embedding-based IR Models" has addressed the subject of volatility prediction using the sentiment analysis methods. The author studied the use of related terms based on word embedding approach to IR models for forecasting volatility. The author studied the difference in the use of related terms between different financial sectors and found that the use of related terms in REIT sector was the most different from other sectors. The author also compared the use of fusion methods for combining text and market data, and found that the combination of LLR and opinion-based features using weighted vector sum is the best choice. The paper is well written with clear abstract, detailed description of the methods and results. The use of related terms based on word embedding approach to IR models for forecasting volatility is an interesting idea, which has not been studied before. The comparison of the use of related terms between different financial sectors is also interesting. However, I have some concerns about the objective of the paper. The abstract mentions that "This paper addresses the essence of volatility prediction in financial markets" but I think that the paper's main target is limited to the application of the disclosed financial data to predict the volatility. The title of the paper suggests that "the IR Term Weighting Models that are effectively extended by related terms using word embeddings" is the main contribution of the paper. However, I think that the main contribution should be the fusion methods that were studied in the paper, because the model that uses word embedding-based IR models was not designed to be the fusion model. The fusion methods should be studied independently of the IR models. Although I have some concerns about the main target of the paper, I think that the related subject of the "usage of disclosed financial data to predict volatility" should be the future research direction of the researchers. Nevertheless, I think that the topic is very promising, and the paper shows that the word embedding-based IR model with related term extension can be a good approach to the topic. The results showing that the REIT sector related terms perform best and that fusion of LLR and opinion-based features using weighted vector sum is the best fusion method are interesting. I think that the topic will be widely studied in the next papers, and the proposed fusion method will be compared with other methods using different financial sectors. I have following suggestions about the improvement of the paper: 1. More examples of word embeddings and their usage would be helpful for readers who are not familiar with this kind of data. For example, the usage of word2vec or GloVe would be good for non-financial examples. 2. The description of the related terms and the explanation of the results about their differences between financial sectors would be helpful for readers who are not familiar with this kind of data. For example, the explanation of the results of Reuters RDSM and the description of the differences between REIT and non-REIT sectors could be helpful. The improvement of the first point and the explanation of the results of the second point could be done through adding some new figures and/or adding some text into the existing "Related Works" section. Overall, the paper is very well written, and the fusion methods proposed in the paper could be a useful base for future research. I congratulate the author for this good work and wish him good luck for his further research. I hope you will find these comments useful and I appreciate the opportunity to review this paper.

At first I thought the introduction would be more like a literature review, but apart from that I have nothing to criticise. Well written and presented. I recommend to accept the paper. Gravner Jens. This paper presents a new algorithm for learning bilingual word embeddings that rely on mimicking the loss function of a state-of-the-art transformer-based single-task model, but instead using a zero-shot multitask setup, where we use no training data of the other language but only assume a small amount of data of each language is available. This can be an attractive setup for many language pairs for which huge amounts of parallel data is not available (e.g., Italian-English) or too expensive to acquire (e.g., bilingually recorded TV show transcripts). The proposed model, named XMERT, uses the transfer learning mechanism to capture useful information from the auxiliary task, which in this case is a language model (LM) trained on the large amount of data of each language present in the dataset. Extensive experiments show that the proposed model obtains improvements over the strong SOTA model, while using a much simpler setup and using very little data of the other language (less than 1K parallel sentence pairs for English-Japanese). I think this paper has an excellent idea, and presents it in a very well-crafted way. The model presented in this paper can be viewed as an adaptation of the multi-task, transfer learning setup to the task of bilingual word embeddings. Instead of sharing a common task-specific neural network among different language pairs, this model uses a shared code and has a language-specific output layer. The output layers of the different encoders are then used as the inputs of a soft sharing mechanism that adapts the common code to the specific languages in the dataset. This model uses the strengths of the shared code, which are guaranteed to be language-independent, while avoiding the weaknesses of the large amount of data assumption. The model is also simple, since it uses very little data of the other language (only a small amount of extra data is used for the LM, which can also be transferred from a different task). The evaluation of the proposed model is carried out on two datasets, with the same setup as the SOTA model. In all cases, the paper reports large improvements over the strong SOTA model, and in some cases (particularly for the smaller French-English dataset) the improvement is extremely significant. I recommend publication of this paper, even though I have some minor comments to address. First, there is some redundancy in the XMERT name and the "zero shot multitask" description. I suggest name one of these XM (pronounced "X-mer", as in "cross-mod") and leave the other name as is. Second, it would be good to provide a bit more discussion of how the language model (LM) is trained on the small amount of data of the other language (ELM). The language model is shown to have near-optimal performance when the only available training data for the other language is a small amount of data (e.g., 1K parallel sentence pairs). How is the small amount of data from the other language generated? Is it some kind of crowdsourced/bootstrapped dataset, or did the authors find a way to use large amounts of data from other domains (e.g., BooksCorpus) to train the language model? Or is it simply not possible to train a good language model on so little data? I've added a paragraph to the Discussion addressing these points. Finally, in the last paragraph of the Results, the authors mention that the small amount of data from the other language did not help when combined with the shared code part of the model. This is actually quite surprising, and I don't think this would be obvious to a reader without being told in the text that the XM model was also tested with a shared code setup. I suggest adding an extra paragraph to this section to clarify this. I've updated the Results section to mention the shared code setup. Finally, I also suggest including an additional small table that presents the results on the two small datasets. The table can be limited to just the top few methods, as there are only two entries. I've added this table. Overall, I think this is a very nice paper and I look forward to reading the source code to this model when it's published. I appreciate the feedback, and thank you again for recommending this paper for publication. ---!downs jdb_commenter: approve: true commenter: author date: 2020-05-20 17:04:28.000000000 +0000 UTC publication: None text: "XMERT: Multi-task Transfer for Bilingual Word Embeddings Without Parallel Data" uid: "Fz8Hd5Uxp9s" usage:

This paper Learning bilingual word embeddings with (almost) no bilingual data, its main content is as below: Most methods to learn bilingual word embeddings rely on large parallel corpora, which is difficult to obtain for most language pairs. This has motivated an active research line to relax this requirement, with methods that use document-aligned corpora or bilingual dictionaries of a few thousand words instead. In this work, we further reduce the need of bilingual resources using a very simple self-learning approach that can be combined with any dictionary-based mapping technique. Our method exploits the structural similarity of embedding spaces, and works with as little bilingual evidence as a 25 word dictionary or even an automatically generated list of numerals, obtaining results comparable to those of systems that use richer resources. Problem and Question: The bilingual word embeddings learning problem is difficult due to the lack of bilingual data. This paper uses a very simple method that only needs a 25-word bilingual dictionary to learn effective word embeddings for English and Spanish. Does this method achieve the same result as other more complex methods that use large bilingual corpora? The paper provides a simple and clear way to integrate this method into existing models with few bilingual resources. This is very useful for the reduction of the dependence on large bilingual data in the bilingual word embeddings learning problem. Strengths and weaknesses: The main advantage of the proposed method is that it uses a 25-word bilingual dictionary, which is much simpler than other more complex methods. Therefore, this method could be easily integrated into other models using less bilingual data. For example, you can build a model with less biometric data by using this method, which can be used to reduce the cost of user attribution and the risk of training error. However, the method also has some limitations. In the paper, it’s shown that using this method to learn word embeddings for Spanish and English, the result is comparable to other more complex methods that use large bilingual data. This means that the method can also be a shortcoming. Even though the method can be easily integrated into other models with less bilingual data, the method can only learn a locally similar mapping and does not reflect the global structural similarity of the two languages, so the learned embeddings lack semantic consistency.
human_text:
- Strengths:

The paper presents an iterative method to induce bilingual word embeddings
using large monolingual corpora starting with very few (or automatically
obtainable numeral) mappings between two languages. Compared to
state-of-the-art using larger bilingual dictionaries or parallel/comparable
corpora, the results obtained with the presented method that relies on very
little or no manually prepared input are exciting and impressive.

- Weaknesses:

I would have liked to see a discussion on the errors of the method, and
possibly a discussion on how the method could be adjusted to deal with them.

- General Discussion:

Does the frequency of the seeds in the monolingual corpora matter?

It would be interesting to see the partial (in the sense of after n number of
iterations) evolution of the mapping between words in the two languages for a
few words. 

What happens with different translations of the same word (like different
senses)?

One big difference between German and English is the prevalence of compounds in
German. What happens to these compounds? What are they mapped onto? Would a
preprocessing step of splitting the compounds help? (using maybe only
corpus-internal unigram information)

What would be the upper bound for such an approach? An analysis of errors --
e.g. words very far from their counterpart in the other language -- would be
very interesting. It would also be interesting to see a discussion of where
these errors come from, and if they could be addressed with the presented
approach.

This work proposes a self-learning bootstrapping approach to learning bilingual
word embeddings, which achieves competitive results in tasks of bilingual
lexicon induction and cross-lingual word similarity although it requires a
minimal amount of bilingual supervision: the method leads to competitive
performance even when the seed dictionary is extremely small (25 dictionary
items!) or is constructed without any language pair specific information (e.g.,
relying on numerals shared between languages). 

The paper is very well-written, admirably even so. I find this work 'eclectic'
in a sense that its original contribution is not a breakthrough finding (it is
more a 'short paper idea' in my opinion), but it connects the dots from prior
work drawing inspiration and modelling components from a variety of previous
papers on the subject, including the pre-embedding work on
self-learning/bootstrapping (which is not fully recognized in the current
version of the paper). I liked the paper in general, but there are few other
research questions that could/should have been pursued in this work. These,
along with only a partial recognition of related work and a lack of comparisons
with several other relevant baselines, are my main concern regarding this
paper, and they should be fixed in the updated version(s).

*Self-learning/bootstrapping of bilingual vector spaces: While this work is one
of the first to tackle this very limited setup for learning cross-lingual
embeddings (although not the first one, see Miceli Barone and more works
below), this is the first truly bootstrapping/self-learning approach to
learning cross-lingual embeddings. However, this idea of bootstrapping
bilingual vector spaces is not new at all (it is just reapplied to learning
embeddings), and there is a body of work which used exactly the same idea with
traditional 'count-based' bilingual vector spaces. I suggest the authors to
check the work of Peirsman and Pado (NAACL 2010) or Vulic and Moens (EMNLP
2013), and recognize the fact that their proposed bootstrapping approach is not
so novel in this domain. There is also related work of Ellen Riloff's group on
bootstrapping semantic lexicons in monolingual settings.

*Relation to Artetxe et al.: I might be missing something here, but it seems
that the proposed bootstrapping algorithm is in fact only an iterative approach
which repeatedly utilises the previously proposed model/formulation of Artetxe
et al. The only difference is the reparametrization (line 296-305). It is not
clear to me whether the bootstrapping approach draws its performance from this
reparametrization (and whether it would work with the previous
parametrization), or the performance is a product of both the algorithm and
this new parametrization. Perhaps a more explicit statement in the text is
needed to fully understand what is going on here.

*Comparison with prior work: Several very relevant papers have not been
mentioned nor discussed in the current version of the paper. For instance, the
recent work of Duong et al. (EMNLP 2016) on 'learning crosslingual word
embeddings without bilingual corpora' seems very related to this work (as the
basic word overlap between the two titles reveals!), and should be at least
discussed if not compared to. Another work which also relies on mappings with
seed lexicons and also partially analyzes the setting with only a few hundred
seed lexicon pairs is the work of Vulic and Korhonen (ACL 2016) 'on the role of
seed lexicons in learning bilingual word embeddings': these two papers might
also help the authors to provide more details for the future work section
(e.g., the selection of reliable translation pairs might boost the performance
further during the iterative process). Another very relevant work has appeared
only recently: Smith et al. (ICLR 2017) discuss 'offline bilingual word
vectors, orthogonal transformations and the inverted softmax'. This paper also
discusses learning bilingual embeddings in very limited settings (e.g., by
relying only on shared words and cognates between two languages in a pair). As
a side note, it would be interesting to report results obtained using only
shared words between the languages (such words definitely exist for all three
language pairs used in the experiments). This would also enable a direct
comparison with the work of Smith et al. (ICLR 2017) which rely on this setup.

*Seed dictionary size and bilingual lexicon induction: It seems that the
proposed algorithm (as discussed in Section 5) is almost invariant to the
starting seed lexicon, yielding very similar final BLI scores regardless of the
starting point. While a very intriguing finding per se, this also seems to
suggest an utter limitation of the current 'offline' approaches: they seem to
have hit the ceiling with the setup discussed in the paper; Vulic and Korhonen
(ACL 2016) showed that we cannot really improve the results by simply
collecting more seed lexicon pairs, and this work suggests that any number of
starting pairs (from 25 to 5k) is good enough to reach this near-optimal
performance, which is also very similar to the numbers reported by Dinu et al.
(arXiv 2015) or Lazaridou et al. (ACL 2015). I would like to see more
discussion on how to break this ceiling and further improve BLI results with
such 'offline' methods. Smith et al. (ICLR 2017) seem to report higher numbers
on the same dataset, so again it would be very interesting to link this work to
the work of Smith et al.

In other words, the authors state that in future work they plan to fine-tune
the method so that it can learn without any bilingual evidence. This is an
admirable 'philosophically-driven' feat, but from a more pragmatic point of
view, it seems more pragmatic to detect how we can go over the plateau/ceiling
which seems to be hit with these linear mapping approaches regardless of the
number of used seed lexicon pairs (Figure 2).

*Convergence criterion/training efficiency: The convergence criterion, although
crucial for the entire algorithm, both in terms of efficiency and efficacy, is
mentioned only as a side note, and it is not entirely clear how the whole
procedure terminates. I suspect that the authors use the vanishing variation in
crosslingual word similarity performance as the criterion to stop the
procedure, but that makes the method applicable only to languages which have a
cross-lingual word similarity dataset. I might be missing here given the
current description in the paper, but I do not fully understand how the
procedure stops for Finnish, given that there is no crosslingual word
similarity dataset for English-Finnish.

*Minor:
- There is a Finnish 'Web as a Corpus' (WaC) corpus (lines 414-416):
https://www.clarin.si/repository/xmlui/handle/11356/1074
- Since the authors claim that the method could work with a seed dictionary
containing only shared numerals, it would be very interesting to include an
additional language pair which does not share the alphabet (e.g.,
English-Russian, English-Bulgarian or even something more distant such as
Arabic and/or Hindi).

*After the response: I would like to thank the authors for investing their time
into their response which helped me clarify some doubts and points raised in my
initial review. I hope that they would indeed clarify these points in the final
version, if given the opportunity.

The paper presents a self-learning framework for learning of bilingual word
embeddings. The method uses two embeddings (in source and target languages) and
a seed lexicon. On each step of the mapping learning a new bilingual lexicon is
induced. Then the learning step is repeated using the new lexicon for learning
of new mapping. The process stops when a convergence criterion is met.

One of the strengths is that the seed lexicon is directly encoded in the
learning process as a binary matrix. Then the self-learning framework solves a
global optimization problem in which the seed lexicon is not explicitly
involved. Its role is to establish the initial mapping between the two
embeddings. This guarantees the convergence. The initial seed lexicon could be
quite small (25 correspondences).

The small size of the seed lexicon is appealing for mappings between languages
for which there are not large bilingual lexicons.

It will be good to evaluate the framework with respect to the quality of the
two word embeddings. If we have languages (or at least one of the languages)
with scarce language resources then the word embeddings for both languages
could differ in their structure and coverage. I think it could be simulated on
the basis of the available data via training the corresponding word embeddings
on different subcorpora for each language.

machine_text: Overall, I found the paper interesting, though a bit rough around the edges. Let me start by saying that I really enjoyed reading this work, and found it well written and well structured. The topic is interesting, and the author presents the material clearly. That said, there are a number of issues that I think might trip up some readers. First, there is some sloppy writing. I ran across some sentences that weren't clear, or that needed some clarification, or that were just written poorly. These could be from not having someone else look over the work, or they might be the result of not writing as well as I think the author does, and so I've marked these places with " FP ". Second, there is some mathiness in the work. The author uses math words and phrases pretty much everywhere, without clearly indicating what they are getting at, or explaining what the reader needs to know. Again, this is a case where another reader might not pick up on these issues, so I've marked the places where this happens with " MP ". I think these are the main points I found as I read the paper, and if the author is willing, I would be happy to provide a revised review. MY REVIEW I really enjoyed reading this work, and it was well written and presented. Though the topic is interesting, the topic itself is not yet developed in a clear way, as there are several terms, concepts, and ideas that are not explained sufficiently. I would be happy to help the author clarify these aspects of the work in a revised draft. I do have some suggestions for improvement, though. The paper has a number of different topics and sections. The first major topic is about how we can represent language as a string of characters rather than as a sequence of phonemes, syllables, and other forms. This raises the question of what representations are available to us, and what they can and can't do. The author does a good job of reviewing some of the more popular representations, and also explaining how character-based models have a hard time capturing things like accent and phrasal timing. A separate section of the paper deals with the nature of language. Here, the author talks about how the meaning of a word is related to the meanings of its component morphemes, and how this means that dictionaries don't really capture word forms. In the third major section of the paper, the author goes on to argue that one thing that could help capture the morphemes of words would be to use neural networks that can read and write sequences of characters. The author describes a system for doing this, and the result is that the model now also learns the meaning of words from a limited amount of text that has been manually tagged with its intended word-form and part-of-speech. In the final section, the author goes back to the original problem of capturing word forms. In this part of the paper, the author tries to figure out what has happened to the meaning of words during the process of converting them to characters. He does this by comparing the representations of words that have been generated by the model with the dictionaries found in the original training set, and showing that often words that have been generated have multiple potential meanings and dictionaries. The author shows that this result seems to hold generally, even when the word forms are no longer attached to the word's meanings. In general, I think this is an interesting paper that is worth thinking about. I agree that in some ways, dictionaries don't really capture word forms, though I think that having a computer that can write characters might actually help with that problem. This paper does a good job of presenting the various factors which might impact the ability of a model to capture the morphology of words, with particular focus on comparing word segments, characters and n-grams as basic units of representation. It also includes a helpful analysis of the impact of encoding regularities across a range of typological features, which should be of interest to a broad audience. However, I was missing some key motivating examples from various typological groups to help me understand the impact of these factors beyond the studies presented. For instance, I might have expected a difference in the performance between word segments and n-grams in typologically derived languages with agglutinative morphology, or between word segments and characters in typologically derived languages with e.g. Latin roots, or between non-compositional and compositional encodings. The current presentation of these factors seems to assume a priori that all typological groups share the same core concepts of word-like chunks, and that these are best captured by contiguous character n-grams. I think the message would be stronger if some comparative examples were added to help the reader see the extent to which these factors do or do not interact in unexpected ways with different typological frameworks. More generally, I think the choice of examples is sometimes a bit misleading or limited in its ability to generalize the impact of these factors beyond the example which is being used to explain a point. For instance, the `long form`/`short form` example is presented as if it would always be the case that long forms are always derived from previously existing short forms by adding an inflectional morpheme (e.g. turning verb toar into French vider), which might not always be true (for instance the German long form for cancer, Krebs, does not derive from its short form, Krebses, through a process of inflectional derivation). In this specific case, however, there is enough detailed discussion and explicit mention of factors which might impact the generalizability of the example that the discrepancy is not a major concern. Overall, I think the paper would benefit from adding a bit more speculation or qualitative claims about how the various factors compare and interacting with each other, and how the combination of factors could lead to differences in the generalizability of results across typological frameworks. For example, there are claims that characters are always superior to word segment and combination of both, but the text presents no evidence to support this except for a single case study, and it is unclear if the results could be generalizable beyond the data set used. Overall, however, I still believe the paper makes a compelling case that representations based on composing character n-grams together with character bi-LSTMs outperforms all others, with some additional support from a thorough analysis of the impact of the morphological typology of the language modeled. Overall, I think this paper is an important addition to the literature on this topic, and it provides a valuable resource for anyone interested in this topic area.

In this paper, the authors systematically vary the representation of words from characters to subword units (word segments, characters, and n-grams of characters) to examine their effectiveness in language modeling. Specifically, they compare the effectiveness of combining these representation in a composition way and in different morphological typologies. Their results show that the effectiveness of the character-level model was overshadowed by the word segment and n-gram models, and the character trigram model composed with Bi-LSTMs outperforms other models. However, they also find that none of these word representations can capture the predictive accuracy of a morphological analyzer. issues addressed The effectiveness of character-level models was overshadowed by word segment and n-gram models, and the character trigram model composed with Bi-LSTMs outperforms other models. - Strengths:
i. Motivation is well described.
ii. Provides detailed comparisons with various models across diverse languages

- Weaknesses:
i.          The conclusion is biased by the selected languages. 
ii.           The experiments do not cover the claim of this paper completely.

- General Discussion:
This paper issues a simple but fundamental question about word representation:
what subunit of a word is suitable to represent morphologies and how to compose
the units. To answer this question, this paper applied word representations
with various subunits (characters, character-trigram, and morphs) and
composition functions (LSTM, CNN, and a simple addition) to the language
modeling task to find the best combination. In addition, this paper evaluated
the task for more than 10 languages. This is because languages are
typologically diverse and the results can be different according to the word
representation and composition function. From their experimental results, this
paper concluded that character-level representations are more effective, but
they are still imperfective in comparing them with a model with explicit
knowledge of morphology. Another conclusion is that character-trigrams show
reliable perplexity in the majority of the languages. 

However, this paper leaves some issues behind.
-         First of all, there could be some selection bias of the experimental
languages. This paper chose ten languages in four categories (up to three
languages per a category). But, one basic question with the languages is “how
can it be claimed that the languages are representatives of each category?”
All the languages in the same category have the same tendency of word
representation and composition function? How can it be proved? For instance,
even in this paper, two languages belonging to the same typology
(agglutinative) show different results. Therefore, at least to me, it seems to
be better to focus on the languages tested in this paper instead of drawing a
general conclusions about all languages. 
-         There is some gap between the claim and the experiments. Is the
language modeling the best task to prove the claim of this paper? Isn’t there
any chance that the claim of this paper breaks in other tasks? Further
explanation on this issue is needed.
-         In Section 5.2, this paper evaluated the proposed method only for
Arabic. Is there any reason why the experiment is performed only for Arabic?
There are plenty of languages with automatic morphological analyzers such as
Japanese and Turkish.
-         This paper considers only character-trigram among various n-grams. Is
there any good reason to choose only character-trigram? Is it always better
than character-bigram or character-fourgram? In general, language modeling with
n-grams is affected by corpus size and some other factors. 

Minor typos: 
- There is a missing reference in Introduction. (88 line in Page 1)
- root-and-patter -> root-and-pattern (524 line in Page 6)

tldr: The authors compare a wide variety of approaches towards sub-word
modelling in language modelling, and show that modelling morphology gives the
best results over modelling pure characters. Further, the authors do some
precision experiments to show that the biggest benefit towards sub-word
modelling is gained after words typically exhibiting rich morphology (nouns and
verbs). The paper is comprehensive and the experiments justify the core claims
of the paper. 

- Strengths:

1) A comprehensive overview of different approaches and architectures towards
sub-word level modelling, with numerous experiments designed to support the
core claim that the best results come from modelling morphemes.

2) The authors introduce a novel form of sub-word modelling based on character
tri-grams and show it outperforms traditional approaches on a wide variety of
languages.

3) Splitting the languages examined by typology and examining the effects of
the models on various typologies is a welcome introduction of linguistics into
the world of language modelling.

4) The analysis of perplexity reduction after various classes of words in
Russian and Czech is particularly illuminating, showing how character-level and
morpheme-level models handle rare words much more gracefully. In light of these
results, could the authors say something about how much language modelling
requires understanding of semantics, and how much it requires just knowing
various morphosyntactic effects?

- Weaknesses:

1) The character tri-gram LSTM seems a little unmotivated. Did the authors try
other character n-grams as well? As a reviewer, I can guess that character
tri-grams roughly correspond to morphemes, especially in Semitic languages, but
what made the authors report results for 3-grams as opposed to 2- or 4-? In
addition, there are roughly 26^3=17576 possible distinct trigrams in the Latin
lower-case alphabet, which is enough to almost constitute a word embedding
table. Did the authors only consider observed trigrams? How many distinct
observed trigrams were there?

2) I don't think you can meaningfully claim to be examining the effectiveness
of character-level models on root-and-pattern morphology if your dataset is
unvocalised and thus doesn't have the 'pattern' bit of 'root-and-pattern'. I
appreciate that finding transcribed Arabic and Hebrew with vowels may be
challenging, but it's half of the typology.

3) Reduplication seems to be a different kind of phenomenon to the other three,
which are more strictly morphological typologies. Indonesian and Malay also
exhibit various word affixes, which can be used on top of reduplication, which
is a more lexical process. I'm not sure splitting it out from the other
linguistic typologies is justified.

- General Discussion:

1) The paper was structured very clearly and was very easy to read.

2) I'm a bit puzzled about why the authors chose to use 200 dimensional
character embeddings. Once the dimensionality of the embedding is greater than
the size of the vocabulary (here the number of characters in the alphabet),
surely you're not getting anything extra?

-------------------------------

Having read the author response, my opinions have altered little. I still think
the same strengths and weakness that I have already discussed hold.

This paper tackles the problem of understanding whether current language and vision (LaVi) models truly grasp the interaction between the two modalities. To this end, we propose an extension of the MS-COCO dataset, FOIL-COCO, that associates images with both correct and `foil' captions, that is, descriptions of the image that are highly similar to the original ones, but contain one single mistake (`foil word'). We show that current LaVi models fall into the traps of this data and perform badly on three tasks: a) caption classification (correct vs. foil); b) foil word detection; c) foil word correction. Humans, in contrast, have near-perfect performance on those tasks. We demonstrate that merely utilising language cues is not enough to model FOIL-COCO and that it challenges the state-of-the-art by requiring a fine-grained understanding of the relation between text and image. We make the FOIL-COCO dataset publicly available to facilitate future research. We find that current language and vision models are vulnerable to descriptions that contain mistakes with high confidence. This implies that a model's ability to understand images and text are tightly coupled, which may also explain some of the recent failures of current models in challenging benchmark metrics such as SemanticFC, SPIN2, etc. The main strength of this paper is the introduction of a highly flexible new dataset that captures the nuances of creating high-quality captions that describe an image, but that still contain mistakes. To our knowledge, FOIL-COCO is the first such dataset, and we make it available to the research community for the first time. We show that current language and vision models are vulnerable to descriptions that contain mistakes with high confidence. This implies that a model's ability to understand texts is tightly coupled, which may also explain some of the recent failures of current models in challenging benchmark metrics such as SemanticFC, SPIN2, etc. The main weakness of this paper is that we do not really provide much evidence that current language and vision models truly fail to understand the relationship between image and text. In particular, it is not clear to what extent existing approaches for generating "fooling" captions could be adapted to attack a specific model. Therefore, it would be desirable for a more extensive evaluation to be performed on this dataset. Overall, this paper makes three key contributions: - it introduces the FOIL-COCO dataset, the first of its kind that captures the nuances of creating high-quality captions that describe an image, but that still contain mistakes - it shows that current language and vision models are vulnerable to descriptions that contain mistakes with high confidence - it provides the first real, quantitative assessment of the relationship between image and text in language and vision models, opening the door for future work to investigate to what extent existing approaches for generating "fooling" captions could be adapted to attack a specific model.

In this work, the authors extend MS-COCO by adding an incorrect
caption to each existing caption, with only one word of difference.
The authors demonstrate that two state-of-the-art methods (one for VQA
and one for captioning) perform extremely poorly at a) determining if
a caption is fake, b) determining which word in a fake caption is
wrong, and c) selecting a replacement word for a given fake word.

This work builds upon a wealth of literature regarding the
underperformance of vision/language models relative to their apparent
capacities. I think this work makes concrete some of the big,
fundamental questions in this area: are vision/language models doing
"interesting" things, or not? The authors consider a nice mix of tasks
and models to shed light on the "broken-ness" of these settings, and
perform some insightful analyses of factors associated with model
failure (e.g., Figure 3).

My biggest concerns with the paper are similarity to Ding et al. That
being said, I do think the authors make some really good points; Ding
et al. generate similar captions, but the ones here differ by only one
word and *still* break the models -- I think that's a justifiably
fundamental difference. That observation demonstrates that Ding et
al.'s engineering is not a requirement, as this simple approach still
breaks things catastrophically.

Another concern is the use of NeuralTalk to select the "hardest"
foils.              While a clever idea, I am worried that the use of this model
creates a risk of self-reinforcement bias, i.e., NeuralTalk's biases
are now fundamentally "baked-in" to FOIL-COCO. 

I think the results section could be a bit longer, relative to the
rest of the paper (e.g. I would've liked more than one paragraph -- I
liked this part!)

Overall, I do like this paper, as it nicely builds upon some results
that highlight defficiencies in vision/language integration. In the
end, the Ding et al. similarity is not a "game-breaker," I think -- if
anything, this work shows that vision/language models are so easy to
fool, Ding et al.'s method is not even required.

Small things:

I would've liked to have seen another baseline that simply
concatenates BoW + extracted CNN features and trains a softmax
classifier over them. The "blind" model is a nice touch, but what
about a "dumb" vision+langauge baseline? I bet that would do close to
as well as the LSTM/Co-attention. That could've made the point of the
paper even stronger.

machine_text: This is an excellent paper! It nicely bridges the fields of NLP and MM and shows that a very useful tool in the MM arsenal can be developed using techniques from NLP. The technique developed for this paper could easily be applied to a wide range of MM tasks. The contributions of this paper are: 1. A technique for extracting all arguments from a text. The system first identifies entities that likely correspond to person names and locations and then uses those entities to find all phrases that probably denote arguments. 2. A new technique for using Pointer Networks for argument extraction. The existing technique for Pointer Networks is to use them to map words to concepts. The approach taken here is to use the Pointer Networks to map arguments to sentences. The approach shows promise and could easily be extended to other tasks, e.g. task-specific tuning of the parameters of the Pointer Networks or adding several other networks that are specialized for different subtasks, e.g. entity recognition, argument category identification, argument textual pattern matching. I have just a few suggestions for improvement: 1. The evaluation section of the paper lacks important information. The paper presents results for the SST2 and the argument extraction setup, but there is no description of the system that was used for this task. Was this system built from scratch or based on some other system? If it was based on some other system, what was the system and how was it configured? 2. In the same section there is a statement that 'the quality measure for ArgMax was the arguable text fraction'. What is arguable text fraction? Is this an official evaluation metric or just a placeholder for something else? 3. The second part of the section presents the results for the SST2 system. It would be good to have a table with a more detailed presentation of the results for other datasets and different arguments extraction setups. 4. The results for the AQUA system seem very promising but are not very clear. The result text is in Russian and I had a hard time understanding what exactly are the numbers (and where can I find them?). All in all, an excellent paper!
