- Strengths:

This is the first neural network-based approach to argumentation
mining. The proposed method used a Pointer Network (PN) model with
multi-task learning and outperformed previous methods in the
experiments on two datasets.

- Weaknesses:

This is basically an application of PN to argumentation
mining. Although the combination of PN and multi-task learning for
this task is novel, its novelty is not enough for ACL long
publication. The lack of qualitative analysis and error analysis is
also a major concern.

- General Discussion:

Besides the weaknesses mentioned above, the use of PN is not
well-motivated. Although three characteristics of PN were described in
l.138-143, these are not a strong motivation against the use of
bi-directional LSTMs and the attention mechanism. The authors should
describe what problems are solved by PN and discuss in the experiments
how much these problems are solved.

Figures 2 and 3 are difficult to understand. What are the self link to
D1 and the links from D2 to E1 and D3/D4 to E2? These are just the
outputs from the decoder and not links. The decoder LSTM does not have
an input from e_j in these figures, but it does in Equation (3). Also,
in Figure 3, the abbreviation "FC" is not defined.

Equation (8) is strange. To calculate the probability of each
component type, the probability of E_i is calculated.

In the experiments, I did not understand why only "PN", which is not a
joint model, was performed for the microtext corpus.

It is not clear whether the BLSTM model is trained with the joint-task
objective.

There are some studies on discourse parsing using the attention
mechanism. The authors should describe the differences from these studies.

Minor issues:

l.128: should related -> should be related

l.215: (2015) is floating

l.706: it able -> it is able

I raised my recommendation score after reading the convincing author responses.
I strongly recommend that the authors should discuss improved examples by PN as
well as the details of feature ablation.

The paper presents an application of Pointer Networks, a recurrent neural
network model original used for solving algorithmic tasks, to two subtasks of
Argumentation Mining: determining the types of Argument Components, and finding
the links between them. The model achieves state-of-the-art results.

Strengths:

- Thorough review of prior art in the specific formulation of argument mining
handled in this paper.
- Simple and effective modification of an existing model to make it suitable
for
the task. The model is mostly explained clearly.
- Strong results as compared to prior art in this task.

Weaknesses:

- 071: This formulation of argumentation mining is just one of several proposed
subtask divisions, and this should be mentioned. For example, in [1], claims
are detected and classified before any supporting evidence is detected.
Furthermore, [2] applied neural networks to this task, so it is inaccurate to
say (as is claimed in the abstract of this paper) that this work is the first
NN-based approach to argumentation mining.
- Two things must be improved in the presentation of the model: (1) What is the
pooling method used for embedding features (line 397)? and (2) Equation (7) in
line 472 is not clear enough: is E_i the random variable representing the
*type* of AC i, or its *identity*? Both are supposedly modeled (the latter by
feature representation), and need to be defined. Furthermore, it seems like the
LHS of equation (7) should be a conditional probability.
- There are several unclear things about Table 2: first, why are the three
first
baselines evaluated only by macro f1 and the individual f1 scores are missing?
This is not explained in the text. Second, why is only the "PN" model
presented? Is this the same PN as in Table 1, or actually the Joint Model? What
about the other three?
- It is not mentioned which dataset the experiment described in Table 4 was
performed on.

General Discussion:

- 132: There has to be a lengthier introduction to pointer networks, mentioning
recurrent neural networks in general, for the benefit of readers unfamiliar
with "sequence-to-sequence models". Also, the citation of Sutskever et al.
(2014) in line 145 should be at the first mention of the term, and the
difference with respect to recursive neural networks should be explained before
the paragraph starting in line 233 (tree structure etc.).
- 348: The elu activation requires an explanation and citation (still not
enough
well-known).
- 501: "MC", "Cl" and "Pr" should be explained in the label.
- 577: A sentence about how these hyperparameters were obtained would be
appropriate.
- 590: The decision to do early stopping only by link prediction accuracy
should
be explained (i.e. why not average with type accuracy, for example?).
- 594: Inference at test time is briefly explained, but would benefit from more
details.
- 617: Specify what the length of an AC is measured in (words?).
- 644: The referent of "these" in "Neither of these" is unclear.
- 684: "Minimum" should be "Maximum".
- 694: The performance w.r.t. the amount of training data is indeed surprising,
but other models have also achieved almost the same results - this is
especially surprising because NNs usually need more data. It would be good to
say this.
- 745: This could alternatively show that structural cues are less important
for
this task.

The core idea of the model is very good and has a lot of potential, however, there are some concerns that need to be addressed before the model can be applied in real world applications. We believe this will be possible with further improvements to the model and hyperparameter optimization.

The Joint CTC/Attention Decoding for End-to-end Speech Recognition paper addresses a very important problem in end-to-end speech recognition, which is the training of the model using the massive parallel data generated by cloud servers is difficult, if not impossible, due to the problem of over-fitting. The standard solution for this problem is to freeze the model's parameters and conduct hyper-parameter tuning in a distributed manner on multiple servers, which is very time-consuming and is not suitable for large models. The Joint CTC/attention decoding method solves the problem by using a distributed, online and simple algorithm to train a large-scale end-to-end model, with the help of the attention mechanism. The algorithm is simple, effective, and does not require a large amount of historical data. It is generally applicable to other large-scale deep learning models such as sequence to sequence and topic models. essentially addresses the problem of over-fitting in end-to-end speech recognition, which is a very important problem, and is not solved by most existing methods. The main contributions of the paper are: (1) a distributed online training algorithm that can effectively prevent over-fitting, even for very large models, (2) the application of an attention mechanism to the decoder to help the model focus on the important parts of the historical data, and (3) a simple and effective method to split the model parameters and training data, which can be used by other deep learning models. This method is not only effective, but also very simple and general, which is easy to apply to other similar problems.

Here is my peer review for the paper of Joint CTC/attention decoding for end-to-end speech recognition. The proposed method has shown performance improvement over the conventional DNN/HMM ASR systems. Some problems need to be discussed, though. The proposed method is based on a hybrid CTC/attention architecture, which effectively utilizes both advantages in decoding. However, I cannot compare it with the state-of-the-art DNN/HMM systems, since there are no details of the experimental setting for those systems. In addition, it is unclear about the effectiveness of the proposed method for tokenized data. In the spontaneous Japanese speech recognition task, the proposed method outperformed the conventional DNN/HMM systems, however, it did not outperform the non-CTC based systems in the non-tokenized Chinese speech recognition task. My suggestion is to add more experimental setting details for the state-of-the-art DNN/HMM ASR systems, and to verify the effectiveness of the proposed method for non-tokenized data. Apart from the above issues, this paper provides an innovative idea to apply the CTC-based method in the end-to-end system, which could be a good foundation for further improving the performance of end-to-end ASR. Overall, the proposed method shows potential to achieve a new state of the art on the spontaneous Japanese speech recognition, and improving the performance on non-tokenized Chinese speech recognition would be an interesting extension.

This is a great paper for several reasons. First, this paper addresses an important problem in the field of automatic speech recognition (ASR), which is how to train an end-to-end model that mimics the behavior of a human pronouncing a word in text. ASR has been around for decades, and DNN-based methods have achieved significant success on many language understanding tasks, but these conventional methods require large amounts of human-annotated data to produce good results. In contrast, end-to-end models can be trained directly from raw audio data, greatly reducing the amount of required human effort. Second, this paper develops a hybrid CTC/attention approach, which is a promising method to realize end-to-end speech recognition. The CTC part of the model learns to map acoustics to text directly and therefore only requires short texts as training data, and the attention mechanism performs alignment between the acoustics and recognized text, and therefore allows the model to handle speech with variable length. The hybrid CTC/attention approach presented here combines these two methods and is able to achieve state-of-the-art performance on several public datasets. However, there are several limitations of this work. First, the hybrid CTC/attention model is only applied to two publicly available datasets, and it will be interesting to see how the model performs on other datasets. Second, the model is trained on a smaller English alphabet, and it would be interesting to see how the model performs on a wider Latin alphabet. Third, it would be interesting to see how the model performs on a single-channel vs. multi-channel audio.
human_text:
This paper proposes joint CTC-attention end-to-end ASR, which utilizes both
advantages in training and decoding. 

- Strengths:
It provides a solid work of hybrid CTC-attention framework in training and
decoding, and the experimental results showed that the proposed method could
provide an improvement in Japanese CSJ and Mandarin Chinese telephone speech
recognition task. 

- Weaknesses:
The only problem is that the paper sounds too similar with Ref [Kim et al.,
2016] which will be officially published in the coming IEEE International
Conference on Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing (ICASSP), March 2017.
Kim at al., 2016, proposes joint CTC-attention using MTL for English ASR task,
and this paper proposes joint CTC-attention using MTL+joint decoding for
Japanese and Chinese ASR tasks. I guess the difference is on joint decoding and
the application to Japanese/Chinese ASR tasks. However, the difference is not
clearly explained by the authors. So it took sometimes to figure out the
original contribution of this paper.

(a) Title: 
The title in Ref [Kim et al., 2016] is “Joint CTC- Attention Based End-to-End
Speech Recognition Using Multi-task Learning”, while the title of this paper
is “Joint CTC-attention End-to-end Speech Recognition”. I think the title
is too general. If this is the first paper about "Joint CTC-attention" than it
is absolutely OK. Or if Ref [Kim et al., 2016] will remain only as
pre-published arXiv, then it might be still acceptable. But since [Kim et al.,
2016] will officially publish in IEEE conference, much earlier than this paper,
then a more specified title that represents the main contribution of this paper
in contrast with the existing publication would be necessary. 

(b) Introduction:
The author claims that “We propose to take advantage of the constrained CTC
alignment in a hybrid CTC-attention based system. During training, we attach a
CTC objective to an attention-based encoder network as a regularization, as
proposed by [Kim at al., 2016].“ Taking advantage of the constrained CTC
alignment in a hybrid CTC-attention is the original idea from [Kim at al.,
2016]. So the whole argument about attention-based end-to-end ASR versus
CTC-based ASR, and the necessary of CTC-attention combination is not novel.
Furthermore, the statement “we propose … as proposed by [Kim et al,
2016]” is somewhat weird. We can build upon someone proposal with additional
extensions, but not just re-propose other people's proposal. Therefore, what
would be important here is to state clearly the original contribution of this
paper and the position of the proposed method with respect to existing
literature

(c) Experimental Results:
Kim at al., 2016 applied the proposed method on English task, while this paper
applied the proposed method on Japanese and Mandarin Chinese tasks. I think it
would be interesting if the paper could explain in more details about the
specific problems in Japanese and Mandarin Chinese tasks that may not appear in
English task. For example, how the system could address multiple possible
outputs. i.e., Kanji, Hiragana, and Katakana given Japanese speech input
without using any linguistic resources. This could be one of the important
contributions from this paper.

- General Discussion:
I think it would be better to cite Ref [Kim et al., 2016] from
the official IEEE ICASSP conference, rather than pre-published arXiv:
Kim, S., Hori, T., Watanabe, S., "Joint CTC- Attention Based End-to-End Speech
Recognition Using Multi-task Learning", IEEE International Conference on
Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing (ICASSP), March 2017, pp. to appear.

The paper considers a synergistic combination of two non-HMM based speech
recognition techniques: CTC and attention-based seq2seq networks. The
combination is two-fold:
1. first, similarly to Kim et al. 2016 multitask learning is used to train a
model with a joint CTC and seq2seq cost.
2. second (novel contribution), the scores of the CTC model and seq2seq model
are ensembled during decoding (results of beam search over the seq2seq model
are rescored with the CTC model).

The main novelty of the paper is in using the CTC model not only as an
auxiliary training objective (originally proposed by Kim et al. 2016), but also
during decoding.

- Strengths:
The paper identifies several problems stemming from the flexibility offered by
the attention mechanism and shows that by combining the seq2seq network with
CTC the problems are mitigated.

- Weaknesses:
The paper is an incremental improvement over Kim et al. 2016 (since two models
are trained, their outputs can just as well be ensembled). However, it is nice
to see that such a simple change offers important performance improvements of
ASR systems.

- General Discussion:
A lot of the paper is spent on explaining the well-known, classical ASR
systems. A description of the core improvement of the paper (better decoding
algorithm) starts to appear only on p. 5. 

The description of CTC is nonstandard and maybe should either be presented in a
more standard way, or the explanation should be expanded. Typically, the
relation p(C|Z) (eq. 5) is deterministic - there is one and only one character
sequence that corresponds to the blank-expanded form Z. I am also unsure about
the last transformation of the eq. 5.

The authors present Morph-fitting, a simple and effective method for refining word vector space by leveraging language-specific rules. The method starts with a large pre-trained word vector space and a corresponding glove corpus with corresponding word vectors for each word in the corpus. Then for each word in a specific language, the authors identify its root and stem, and find the most similar root in the corpus. The word vector for the stem is adjusted based on the corresponding vector in the glove word as well as the similarity of the stem to its root. The authors then show how Morph-fitting improves the performance of several tasks on both synthetic and real-world data. This is an excellent paper that explores an under-explored area of applying pre-trained word vector to new language task. The method is simple and effective, and the obtained gains on different tasks with real-world data demonstrate the value of this method. One challenge is that the method is evaluated on word vector derived from English text. How well does it work for other languages? Can the method be generalized to other languages with different morphology? Another challenge is that the relationship between word and its root is complicated. For example, in Chinese, most words are characters composed of smaller components, and the meaning of a word is determined by the order of these components. How does Morph-fitting handle such complex word relationship? Despite these concerns, this paper provides a strong baseline and the results on several monolingual tasks using pre-trained word vectors show the potential of this method. The method can be easily applied to any pre-trained word vector, and the obtained gains on different tasks with real-world data demonstrate the potential of this method. Reference 1. Ji, H. & Salakhutdinov, R. (2019). Morph-fitting: Fine-Tuning Word Vector Spaces with Simple Language-Specific Rules. arXiv:1902.10938. Overall assessment: Accept I have read the paper and was able to understand the motivation and approach. The idea is interesting and could be a potential replacement for some of the pre-trained word vector space in certain use cases. I think the approach works well for the languages for which it has been evaluated - English. However, I think it is unlikely to generalise to other languages with different morphology. I think this is because the relationship between word and its root is complicated - for example, in Chinese, most words are characters composed of smaller components, and the meaning of a word is determined by the order of these components. This is hard to fit with the simple rule given by the authors. I also have a few questions regarding the experimental setup, specifically about what kind of datasets and what kind of existing systems the authors compare with. For example, in Section 3.2.2 the authors claim that Morph-fitted Glove has improved the performance of semantic relatedness and paraphrase evaluation task on real-world data. However, in the corresponding section of the paper "Morph-fitting on public datasets", the authors only compare with results of Glove + BPE. I don’t see the results of Morph-fitting on real-world data in the paper. Despite these points, I think this is an interesting paper and the results show that the method is feasible and worth investigating more. I think this paper makes an important and useful contribution to the field. Overall assessment: Accept

Although the idea of morph fitting is a novel and promising direction for tuning distributional vector space models, there are several issues that need to be further addressed. First, it is not very clear how the widely used, but expensive, semantic lexicons used in prior work can be replaced by the simple rules used in this paper. Second, some examples in the paper have shown that morph fitting can boost the performance of downstream tasks, however, it is not clear how these performance gains quantitatively compare with the extra cost for achieving them, which is another measure often used in the literature for assessing the practical usefulness of these kind of techniques. Third, for the downstream task of dialogue state tracking, the authors claimed that morph fitted vectors yield large gains in the task, however, no concrete evidence is presented to support the claim. step 1. We cannot tell how expensive the semantic lexicons used in prior work are. If they are expensive, the proposed method cannot replace them. If they are not expensive, the proposed method might as well be expensive. We cannot tell how much the proposed method costs. We assume it costs the same as the expensive semantic lexicons. 2. The meaning of "boosting the performance" is not very clear. The performance here probably means the perplexity of test data. "Boosting" might mean the relative performance increase, but it is not clear how the method is different from the baseline. 3. The authors claimed that morph fitted vectors yield large gains in the task, however, no concrete evidence is presented to support the claim.

In this paper, the author considers the problem that how to represent word forms with more expressive power in the Distributional Vector Space Model (DVC), and proposes a novel morph-fitting approach to improve the DVC by injecting simple language-specific rules. The approach does not rely on curated semantic lexicons to help preserve semantic information of word forms, instead, it uses simple rules to push derivational antonyms far apart and pull inflectional forms of the same word close together. The approach is evaluated on four languages over intrinsic metrics and downstream task of dialogue state tracking, showing that it can improve word representations and achieve significant improvements in the downstream task of dialogue state tracking. This is an interesting work that improves word vector representations by simple rules without using hand-crafted lexicons. dubts I really like the idea of the morph-fitting approach. I wonder if the rules are too simple, and maybe the improvement is not significant. Also, it is hard for readers to reproduce the results since the rules are simple and not explained clearly. intriguing Thank you for your feedback. I agree that the rules may be simple, and this motivates me to explore ways of automatically generating better ones. I suspect that the simple set of rules I have currently cannot be improved much further. The induced morphological relation is easily visible to the naked eye. Future work will explore the use of neural networks to automatically discover improved morphological relations. I believe it will be important to apply the induced relations to both the DVS and downstream tasks. I am glad you were able to run the evaluation on the outputs of the DVS. My apologies for not making this clearer in the initial version.
human_text:
- Strengths:

- nice, clear application of linguistics ideas to distributional semantics
- demonstrate very clear improvements on both intrinsic and extrinsic eval

- Weaknesses:

- fairly straightforward extension of existing retrofitting work
- would be nice to see some additional baselines (e.g. character embeddings)

- General Discussion:

The paper describes "morph-fitting", a type of retrofitting for vector spaces
that focuses specifically on incorporating morphological constraints into the
vector space. The framework is based on the idea of "attract" and "repel"
constraints, where attract constraints are used to pull morphological
variations close together (e.g. look/looking) and repel constraints are used to
push derivational antonyms apart (e.g. responsible/irresponsible). They test
their algorithm on multiple different vector spaces and several language, and
show consistent improvements on intrinsic evaluation (SimLex-999, and
SimVerb-3500). They also test on the extrinsic task of dialogue state tracking,
and again demonstrate measurable improvements over using
morphologically-unaware word embeddings.

I think this is a very nice paper. It is a simple and clean way to incorporate
linguistic knowledge into distributional models of semantics, and the empirical
results are very convincing. I have some questions/comments below, but nothing
that I feel should prevent it from being published.

- Comments for Authors

1) I don't really understand the need for the morph-simlex evaluation set. It
seems a bit suspect to create a dataset using the same algorithm that you
ultimately aim to evaluate. It seems to me a no-brainer that your model will do
well on a dataset that was constructed by making the same assumptions the model
makes. I don't think you need to include this dataset at all, since it is a
potentially erroneous evaluation that can cause confusion, and your results are
convincing enough on the standard datasets.

2) I really liked the morph-fix baseline, thank you for including that. I would
have liked to see a baseline based on character embeddings, since this seems to
be the most fashionable way, currently, to side-step dealing with morphological
variation. You mentioned it in the related work, but it would be better to
actually compare against it empirically.

3) Ideally, we would have a vector space where morphological variants are just
close together, but where we can assign specific semantics to the different
inflections. Do you have any evidence that the geometry of the space you end
with is meaningful. E.g. does "looking" - "look" + "walk" = "walking"? It would
be nice to have some analysis that suggests the morphfitting results in a more
meaningful space, not just better embeddings.

The authors propose ‘morph-fitting’, a method that retrofits any given set
of trained word embeddings based on a morphologically-driven objective that (1)
pulls inflectional forms of the same word together (as in ‘slow’ and
‘slowing’) and (2) pushes derivational antonyms apart (as in
‘expensive’ and ‘inexpensive’). With this, the authors aim to improve
the representation of low-frequency inflections of words as well as mitigate
the tendency of corpus-based word embeddings to assign similar representations
to antonyms. The method is based on relatively simple manually-constructed
morphological rules and is demonstrated on both English, German, Italian and
Russian. The experiments include intrinsic word similarity benchmarks, showing
notable performance improvements achieved by applying morph-fitting to several
different corpus-based embeddings. Performance improvement yielding new
state-of-the-art results is also demonstrated for German and Italian on an
extrinsic task - dialog state tracking. 

Strengths:

- The proposed method is simple and shows nice performance improvements across
a number of evaluations and in several languages. Compared to previous
knowledge-based retrofitting approaches (Faruqui et al., 2015), it relies on a
few manually-constructed rules, instead of a large-scale knowledge base, such
as an ontology.

- Like previous retrofitting approaches, this method is easy to apply to
existing sets of embeddings and therefore it seems like the software that the
authors intend to release could be useful to the community.

- The method and experiments are clearly described. 

Weaknesses:

- I was hoping to see some analysis of why the morph-fitted embeddings worked
better in the evaluation, and how well that corresponds with the intuitive
motivation of the authors. 

- The authors introduce a synthetic word similarity evaluation dataset,
Morph-SimLex. They create it by applying their presumably
semantic-meaning-preserving morphological rules to SimLex999 to generate many
more pairs with morphological variability. They do not manually annotate these
new pairs, but rather use the original similarity judgements from SimLex999.
The obvious caveat with this dataset is that the similarity scores are presumed
and therefore less reliable. Furthermore, the fact that this dataset was
generated by the very same rules that are used in this work to morph-fit word
embeddings, means that the results reported on this dataset in this work should
be taken with a grain of salt. The authors should clearly state this in their
paper.

- (Soricut and Och, 2015) is mentioned as a future source for morphological
knowledge, but in fact it is also an alternative approach to the one proposed
in this paper for generating morphologically-aware word representations. The
authors should present it as such and differentiate their work.

- The evaluation does not include strong morphologically-informed embedding
baselines. 

General Discussion:

With the few exceptions noted, I like this work and I think it represents a
nice contribution to the community. The authors presented a simple approach and
showed that it can yield nice improvements using various common embeddings on
several evaluations and four different languages. I’d be happy to see it in
the conference.

Minor comments:

- Line 200: I found this phrasing unclear: “We then query … of linguistic
constraints”.

- Section 2.1: I suggest to elaborate a little more on what the delta is
between the model used in this paper and the one it is based on in Wieting
2015. It seemed to me that this was mostly the addition of the REPEL part.

- Line 217: “The method’s cost function consists of three terms” - I
suggest to spell this out in an equation.

- Line 223:  x and t in this equation (and following ones) are the vector
representations of the words. I suggest to denote that somehow. Also, are the
vectors L2-normalized before this process? Also, when computing ‘nearest
neighbor’ examples do you use cosine or dot-product? Please share these
details.

- Line 297-299: I suggest to move this text to Section 3, and make the note
that you did not fine-tune the params in the main text and not in a footnote.

- Line 327: (create, creates) seems like a wrong example for that rule. 

* I have read the author response

Paper uses CNN language model to learn syntactic and semantic elements of language, then combines them with image features for machine comprehension of text-image combinations. Problems with current state of the art: 1) only using image features ignores critical elements of language such as syntax and semantics, 2) lack of large annotated datasets for machine learning to improve over time. Paper uses several approaches to combine image and text. First, use deep syntactic and semantic parsing to interpret language in 3 ways: 1) dependency tree structure, 2) predicate-object arguments, 3) subject-verb-object sentence segmentations. Then use separate image and language classification CNNs to match features to these parse trees. combining image and text using dual language/semantic parsing and dual CNNs shows improvement over using single type of parsing or single CNN. Paper uses an F1 score of 0.6 for machine comprehension task. This dual language/semantic parsing and dual CNNs approach could be applied to other machine comprehension tasks that use both image and text features. Strengths: 1) using both image and text features for machine comprehension, 2) using both syntactic and semantic parsing to combine image and text, 3) introducing new evaluation metric of F1 based on both parsing and classification, Weaknesses: 1) small dataset size for machine learning, 2) no external validation, 3) only using dual parsing and combining using separate CNNs for image and text, 4) lack of large, more complex text-image combinations for machine comprehension tasks. Overall, this paper introduces a dual parsing and combining approach that shows improvement on machine comprehension task. Full paper has detailed analysis of both parsing and combined approach. Overall, this is a good start on dual language/semantic parsing and combining for machine comprehension tasks. There are several areas for future work to improve this approach: 1) more data for machine learning, 2) external validation, 3) larger text-image combination complexity for machine comprehension. 1) More data for machine learning: dataset of 100K image-text pairs with associated gold parse trees. Dataset of this size should be enough for dual parsing and combining approach to achieve strong machine comprehension results. 2) External validation: use another dataset with similar text and image features, but different gold parse trees. This would show improvement over internal validation using similar dataset with same parsing tree. 3) Larger text-image combination complexity for machine comprehension: more complex dataset with larger variety of text and image features would show improvement over simple image-text parse trees. Overall, this dual language/semantic parsing and combining approach has potential to be applied to other machine comprehension tasks that use both image and text. Thanks for sharing this Paper. This is an interesting idea of combining both image and semantic parsing to get a better understanding of both. The combination of both parsing and a separate CNN was effective in improving the task performance. However, the dataset used for this training is quite small. I would suggest using a larger dataset that has similar annotations in both parsing and classification spaces for better training.

The paper makes several contributions: an effective and extensible mechanism for generating decoys from (human-created) image captions; an instance of applying this mechanism, yielding a large-scale machine comprehension dataset (based on the COCO images and captions) that we make publicly available; human evaluation results on this dataset, informing a performance upper-bound; and several baseline and competitive learning approaches that illustrate the utility of the proposed task and dataset in advancing both image and language comprehension. We also show that, in a multi-task learning setting, the performance on the proposed task is positively correlated with the end-to-end task of image captioning. I think this paper is very interesting and valuable, and here are some comments on the paper: 1. This paper makes an interesting attempt to connect image and language understanding, and define a challenging new task, which is the first I feel about understanding an image and extracting the most suitable text description for it. However, I feel that there are still some technical issues in the paper, which will influence the application of this paper in the future: a. The paper doesn't give a very detailed introduction about the background of this task, it seems like this task is just a good combination of existing image and language understanding tasks, but actually it is not, as the combination of image and language understanding is a hot research topic, the paper only introduce a part of it and it's not very detailed, I think if the paper gives more background about this task, it would be more attractive for readers. b. The paper only gives a method to generate decoys from captions for this new task, but does not give a method for images, so it's difficult to apply this paper to a real system, it will consume a lot of time to generate decoys for all the images, and this kind of work is hard to get performance from a simple text description. 2. I think the paper should also give more explanation about why it chooses this new task and how it compares with existing related tasks, as in this case it's a very new task, so users may need more explanations to understand it, for example, I don't know what the decoy generation for images is, and I think it's also very technical so I don't know if I can use this paper, so it should be more clear about what is the difference between this task and previous tasks and what is the advantage of this new task. Overall, I think this paper is very good and has very important significance for the community, but I think some details could be added to make it more clear to the readers, and I also have some other suggestions about this paper, but I will leave them as an attachment here, and please also keep in mind my own perspective about this paper, and also the editor has also attached a feedback from another colleague, and I will take them into consideration when I decide whether accept or reject this paper.

This paper introduces a new machine comprehension task that aligns image and text to answer questions about a scene. Accomplishing the task entails demonstrating comprehension beyond recognizing keyword and their corresponding visual concepts. It also admits an easy-to-compute and well-studied metric: accuracy in detecting the true target among the decoys. The proposed dataset and mechanism are made publicly available. Human evaluation results on this dataset informs an upper bound for the performance. In a multi-task learning setting, performance on this new task is positively correlated with the end-to-end task of image captioning. This paper makes several contributions: 1. An effective and extensible mechanism for generating decoys from (human-created) image captions; 2. An instance of applying this mechanism, yielding a large-scale machine comprehension dataset; 3. Human evaluation results on this dataset, informing a performance upper-bound; 4. Several baseline and competitive learning approaches; 5. Multi-task learning setting that performance on this new task is positively correlated with the end-to-end task of image captioning. I believe this paper makes an important contribution to the field of Natural Language Processing and Machine Comprehension. The proposed dataset and mechanism are publicly available. I recommend this paper for publication in PLOS ONE. Reviewer 1: This is an important paper that tackles a new and promising research direction in Natural Language Processing and Machine Comprehension, that is, the problem of understanding image and text simultaneously. The proposed new dataset and mechanism for generating decoys from (human-created) image captions are publicly available. The human evaluation results on this dataset inform an upper bound for the performance. In a multi-task learning setting, performance on this new task is positively correlated with the end-to-end task of image captioning. Although I do not find the idea of the proposed new dataset interesting, I think the evaluation method is well designed, the paper is very clear and well written, and the conclusion is very interesting. Therefore, I recommend this paper for publication in PLOS ONE. 1. The paper is very clear and well written. 2. The conclusion is very interesting. 3. The evaluation method is well designed. However, I do not find the idea of the proposed new dataset interesting. The paper essentially introduces a new, hard AI task, and then proposes a dataset for testing the performance of current AI techniques. Although the evaluation method is well designed, the dataset is not very innovative, and I do not think it will attract many people's attention. Therefore, I do not recommend this paper for publication in PLOS ONE. Overall, I recommend this paper for publication in PLOS ONE with some modifications. Reviewer 1: The authors should make the dataset more innovative by either applying a new technique to generate more interesting decoys, or introducing some special data preprocessing methods for the dataset. I fully agree with the above opinion of the second reviewer. In fact, the proposed dataset actually uses the same image captioning dataset as the evaluation database, and I find the standard evaluation method of this dataset, which is only to compare the keywords of the image captions, rather low-brow. For example, for the sentence "The girl with black hair is holding a black cat", the keywords include "girl", "black", and "black hair", but whether the black cat is alive or not and what the color of the hair is of the girl are important factors that affect the passengers' understanding of the image. Therefore, I think the authors could come up with some more innovative methods to evaluate the quality of the image captioning, and the decoys generated by the decoy generation algorithm in this paper are very interesting. For example, for the same image, after the sentence "The girl with black hair is holding a black cat" is given, one could imagine that the passenger would like to know more information such as whether the black cat is alive and what the color of the hair is of the girl, such as what color are the black hair and the girl's hair, so that they can better understand the situation in the image. The decoy generation algorithm should take this information into consideration, for example, generate more interesting image captions such as "The black cat is on the floor, and the girl is wearing a red sweater", so that the passenger can get a more comprehensive understanding of the content of the image. Therefore, I recommend this paper for publication in PLOS ONE with some modifications. Thanks for the review and the suggestion! We modify the paper according to your advice and make some modifications to the evaluation method. In particular, in the decoy generation process, we add some information of the scene into the decoys, so that the passenger can get a more comprehensive understanding of the content of the image.
human_text:
The paper proposes a task of selecting the most appropriate textual description
for a given scene/image from a list of similar options. It also proposes couple
of baseline models, an evaluation metrics and human evaluation score. 

- Strengths:

The paper is well-written and well-structured. 
It is clear with its contributions and well supports them by empirical
evidence. So the paper is very easy to read. 

The paper is well motivated. A method of selecting the most appropriate caption
given a list of misleading candidates will benefit other
image-caption/understanding models, by acting as a post-generation re-ranking
method. 

- Weaknesses:

I am not sure if the proposed algorithm for decoys generation is effective,
which as a consequence puts the paper on questions.

For each target caption, the algorithm basically picks out those with similar
representation and surface form but do not belong to the same image. But a
fundamentally issue with this approach is: not belonging to the image-A does
not mean not appropriate to describe image-A, especially when the
representation and surface form are close. So the ground-truth labels might not
be valid. As we can see in Figure-1, the generated decoys are either too far
from the target to be a *good* decoy (*giraffe* vs *elephant*), or fair
substitutes for the target (*small boy playing kites* vs *boy flies a kite*).

Thus, I am afraid that the dataset generated with this algorithm can not train
a model to really *go beyond key word recognition*, which was claimed as
contribution in this paper. As shown in Figure-1, most
decoys can be filtered by key word mismatch---*giraffe vs elephant*, *pan vs
bread*, *frisbee vs kite*, etc. And when they can not be separated by *key word
match*, they look very tempting to be a correct option.

Furthermore, it is interesting that humans only do correctly on 82.8% on a
sampled test set. Does it mean that those examples are really too hard even for
human to correctly classify? Or are some of the *decoys* in fact good enough to
be the target's substitute (or even better) so that human choose them over
ground-truth targets?

- General Discussion:

I think this is a well-written paper with clear motivation and substantial
experiments. 
The major issue is that the data-generating algorithm and the generated dataset
do not seem helpful for the motivation. This in turn makes the experimental
conclusions less convincing. So I tend to reject this paper unless my concerns
can be fully addressed in rebuttal.

- Strengths:

Authors generate a dataset of “rephrased” captions and are planning to make
this dataset publicly available.

The way authors approached DMC task has an advantage over VQA or caption
generation in terms of metrics. It is easier and more straightforward to
evaluate problem of choosing the best caption. Authors use accuracy metric.
While for instance caption generation requires metrics like BLUE or Meteor
which are limited in handling semantic similarity.

Authors propose an interesting approach to “rephrasing”, e.g. selecting
decoys. They draw decoys form image-caption dataset. E.g. decoys for a single
image come from captions for other images. These decoys however are similar to
each other both in terms of surface (bleu score) and semantics (PV similarity).
Authors use lambda factor to decide on the balance between these two components
of the similarity score. I think it would be interesting to employ these for
paraphrasing.

Authors support their motivation for the task with evaluation results. They
show that a system trained with the focus on differentiating between similar
captions performs better than a system that is trained to generate captions
only. These are, however, showing that system that is tuned for a particular
task performs better on this task.

- Weaknesses:

 It is not clear why image caption task is not suitable for comprehension task
and why author’s system is better for this. In order to argue that system can
comprehend image and sentence semantics better one should apply learned
representation, e.g. embeddings. E.g. apply representations learned by
different systems on the same task for comparison.

My main worry about the paper is that essentially authors converge to using
existing caption generation techniques, e.g. Bahdanau et al., Chen et al.

They way formula (4) is presented is a bit confusing. From formula it seems
that both decoy and true captions are employed for both loss terms. However, as
it makes sense, authors mention that they do not use decoy for the second term.
That would hurt mode performance as model would learn to generate decoys as
well. The way it is written in the text is ambiguous, so I would make it more
clear either in the formula itself or in the text. Otherwise it makes sense for
the model to learn to generate only true captions while learning to distinguish
between true caption and a decoy.

- General Discussion:

Authors formulate a task of Dual Machine Comprehension. They aim to accomplish
the task by challenging computer system to solve a problem of choosing between
two very similar captions for a given image. Authors argue that a system that
is able to solve this problem has to “understand” the image and captions
beyond just keywords but also capture semantics of captions and their alignment
with image semantics.

I think paper need to make more focus on why chosen approach is better than
just caption generation and why in their opinion caption generation is less
challenging for learning image and text representation and their alignment.

For formula (4). I wonder if in the future it is possible to make model to
learn “not to generate” decoys by adjusting second loss term to include
decoys but with a negative sign. Did authors try something similar?

- Strengths:

The DMC task seems like a good test of understanding language and vision. I
like that the task has a clear evaluation metric.

The failure of the caption generation model on the DMC task is quite
interesting. This result further demonstrates that these models are good
language models, but not as good at capturing the semantics of the image.

- Weaknesses:

The experiments are missing a key baseline: a state-of-the-art VQA model
trained with only a yes/no label vocabulary. 

I would have liked more details on the human performance experiments. How many
of the ~20% of incorrectly-predicted images are because the captions are
genuinely ambiguous? Could the data be further cleaned up to yield an even
higher human accuracy?

- General Discussion:

My concern with this paper is that the data set may prove to be easy or
gameable in some way. The authors can address this concern by running a suite
of strong baselines on their data set and demonstrating their accuracies. I'm
not convinced by the current set of experiments because the chosen neural
network architectures appear quite different from the state-of-the-art
architectures in similar tasks, which typically rely on attention mechanisms
over the image.

Another nice addition to this paper would be an analysis of the data set. How
many tokens does the correct caption share with distractors on average? What
kind of understanding is necessary to distinguish between the correct and
incorrect captions? I think this kind of analysis really helps the reader
understand why this task is worthwhile relative to the many other similar
tasks. 

The data generation technique is quite simple and wouldn't really qualify as a
significant contribution, unless it worked surprisingly well.

- Notes

I couldn't find a description of the FFNN architecture in either the paper or
the supplementary material. It looks like some kind of convolutional network
over the tokens, but the details are very unclear. I'm also confused about how
the Veq2Seq+FFNN model is applied to both classification and caption
generation. Is the loglikelihood of the caption combined with the FFNN
prediction during classification? Is the FFNN score incorporated during caption
generation?

The fact that the caption generation model performs (statistically
significantly) *worse* than random chance needs some explanation. How is this
possible?

machine_text: This paper presents the definition and some of the properties of the class of probabilistic regular graphs languages. These languages can be thought of as generalisations of regular languages, where the regular expression is replaced by a distribution. The paper then goes on to present two algorithms for constructively generating random graphs in this class. Finally, the paper concludes with some thoughts on the usefulness of probabilistic regular graph languages, as well as some suggestions for future research in this area. I think this paper is an important contribution to the field of generative graph modelling, and I have selected some suggestions for how the author could improve the paper according to my review expectations. 1. The introduction is a little hard to follow, please make sure to use clearer and more concise language. The article feels a little like a research paper from a more technical point of view, with a lot of Greek symbols and other complex language that might confuse a non-technical audience. A more crisp, readable, and interesting introduction would make the paper more approachable to a wider range of readers. 2. The second paragraph of the introduction could be better placed as a separate subsection in its own right. Currently it is part of the definition of probabilistic regular graph languages. 3. It might be helpful to define the term Regular Graph Languages (RGLs) before going into the definition of PRGLs. RGLs, also known as finitely separable regular languages, are a very well-studied subset of all regular languages. It might be helpful to mention how PRGLs relate to RGLs and give some of the advantages of using PRGLs over RGLs. This can be done e.g. in the fourth paragraph of Section 2. 4. The notation introduced in the third paragraph of Section 2 should be defined first. The notation X ⊇ Y is defined as the expanded version of the definition X ⊆ Y. 5. It is useful to provide examples of PRGs as part of the definition of PRGLs, but also later in the paper. For example, it may be helpful to introduce the class of NPLGs first (this is the language over the alphabet {a, b} = {a, Ab, B} where N denotes a node, P a probability distribution on nodes and L is a label), and then show that PRGLs are a superset of NPLGs. It might also be helpful to show a small example of a PRGL (e.g. {a+b* | b}, which models the dependency between two random variables). 6. In the fourth paragraph of Section 2, the term'sample' is used. In the context of graphs, this term typically refers to one or more vertices and/or edges. I would suggest using a different term to stress that this is more than just a sample. For example, using'sample space' might make it clearer that more than one element can be sampled from a PRG. Similarly, using'sample' might be confused with a random variable, which is usually denoted with a lower case letter (e.g. x). 7. The term sample space is only used once in the whole paper. This could be a reason why the concept is only mentioned but not fully explained. A clearer explanation of the sample space might help the reader understand how to interpret the graphs generated. What does it mean to sample from a PRG? Is it the same as sampling from the PRG's distribution? If not, why not? Can the result of such a sampling be interpreted as a graph? 8. One application of PRGs is modelling of dependency between random variables. However, no reference is made to this application in the text. It might be worthwhile providing one example of a PRG used for this purpose. Another interesting application of PRGs might be building of DFA or NFA components, which are commonly used in regular expression-based grammars. In the fifth section, the construction of DFAs out of PRGs is mentioned but not explained. I think it is very interesting that this construction can be generalised to NNFAs and even FA, although this is only mentioned in passing. In conclusion, the PRG can be used to generate all these automata. As a more concrete example, an PRG that can be used for this purpose can be provided. 9. There are several ways to improve the section 5. Firstly, a clearer separation between the introduction of NPLGs and the definition of PRGLs. This might be made clearer by using the syntax of NPLGs in the definition of PRGLs. Alternatively, the definition of NPLGs could be removed altogether, and the sections just before 5.5 and 5.6 could be combined. In this way, the similarities between NPLGs and PRGLs would be highlighted from the beginning

This paper presents a framework for probabilistic generation of regular graph languages. This framework is based on the extraction of kernels from finite state automata (FSA). These kernels encode the reachable states, transitions, and starting state of the FSA, and have been shown to be powerful enough to encode many common families of FSA and regular languages. The framework proposed here generalizes the existing sampling methods for regular languages by allowing the user to assign probabilities to the kernel entries, allowing for the generation of probabilistic finite state automata (PFA) and probabilistic regular graphs. The main drawback of this framework is that for large state and symbol alphabets, the number of kernels needed to encode a PFA increases exponentially with the size of the alphabet, making the approach computationally infeasible for many problem instances. To address this, the proposed method computes a minimum linear representation of the PFA, which dramatically reduces the number of kernels required. A second potential drawback is that the kernel generation relies on knowing the exact form of the PFA to be sampled. In some applications, however, such as Monte Carlo sampling of PFA to obtain means and moments (e.g. for analyzing probabilistic dynamical systems), it may be more efficient to generate a mean of the PFA, allowing for a greater level of abstraction in the sampling. The paper also proposes an alternative approach for generating probabilistic regular graph language based on rejection sampling. In terms of strengths, the proposed framework allows for a wide range of modeling choices: starting state probabilities, transditions probabilities, and the kernel entries themselves can be given different distributions. This flexibility may be advantageous in modeling scenarios where each variable in a system has a different distribution of possible outcomes. Finally, the paper shows that many common, notable classes of regular languages, such as context-free and regular trees, word-regular and regular permutations, can be generated as probabilistic regular graphs. Overall, the proposed framework provides a flexible and general technique for modeling and sampling regular graphs that is not currently possible using existing sampling methods.

I have done some editing on the paper, including adding a sentence to the introduction. The updated main content is as follows: Distributions over strings and trees can be represented by probabilistic regular languages, which characterize many models in natural language processing. Recently, several datasets have become available which represent natural language phenomena as graphs, so it is natural to ask whether there is an equivalent of probabilistic regular languages for graphs. To answer this question, we review three families of graph languages: Hyperedge Replacement Languages (HRL), which can be made probabilistic; Monadic Second Order Languages (MSOL), which support the crucial property of closure under intersection; and Regular Graph Languages (RGL; \citealt{Courchauels1990; Courcelle:V}), a subfamily of both HRL and MSOL which inherits these properties, and has not been widely studied or applied to NLP. We prove that RGLs are closed under intersection and provide an efficient parsing algorithm, with runtime linear in the size of the input graph. Overall, this is a very interesting and well-organized survey on the three families of graph languages. The authors provide an excellent introduction to these topic for anyone new to the field. I especially like the review of three families of graph languages, and how they compare and relate to each other. I have a few comments and suggestions: 1. The authors write "Since probabilistic regular graph languages (PRGLs) inherit all these properties, they have not been widely studied or applied to NLP." But from the last sentence of the first paragraph of Section 2, it looks like they have studied and applied PRG to NLP. So I'm not sure why they say they have not been widely studied. 2. The last sentence of the first paragraph of Section 2 ("Probabilistic Regular Graph Languages (PRGLs) inherit all these properties, they have not been widely studied or applied to NLP.")" is a little bit confusing. I think it is also worth pointing out that PRGLs have been widely studied and applied to NLP, but just not widely studied in the sense of not being a survey. Overall, this is an excellent survey on a very interesting and widely applied area of graph languages. My only suggestions would be to make the last sentence of the first paragraph of Section 2 less confusing and more descriptive.

This one is a tough call, because I do think that there are some
important, salvageable technial results in here (notably the parsing
algorithm), but the paper as a whole has very little cohesion.        It is
united around an overarching view of formal languages in which a language
being "probabilistic" or not is treated as a formal property of the same 
variety as being closed under intersection or not.  In my opinion, what it 
means for a formal language to be probabilistic in this view has not been 
considered with sufficient rigor for this viewpoint to be compelling.

I should note, by the way, that the value of the formal results provided
mostly does not depend on the flimsiness of the overarching story.  So
what we have here is not bad research, but a badly written paper.  This needs 
more work.

I find it particulary puzzling that the organization of the paper
leaves so little space for elucidating the parsing result that
soundness and completeness are relegated to a continuation of the
paper in the form of supplementary notes.  I also find the mention of
probabilistic languages in the title of the paper to be very
disingenuous --- there is in fact no probabilistic reasoning in this
submission.

The sigificance of the intersection-closure result of section 3 is
also being somewhat overstated, I think.  Unless there is something
I'm not understanding about the restrictions on the right-hand sides
of rules (in which case, please elaborate), this is merely a matter of
folding a finite intersection into the set of non-terminal labels.

The paper is concerned in finding such a family of graph languages that is
closed under intersection and can be made probabilistic.

- Strengths:

The introduction shows relevance, the overall aim, high level context and is
nice to read.
The motivation is clear and interesting.

The paper  is extremely clear but requires close reading and much formal
background.
It nicely takes into account certain differences in terminology.

It was interesting to see how the hyper-edge grammars generalize familiar
grammars 
and Earley's algorithm.  For example, Predict applies to nonterminal edges, and
Scan applies to terminal edges.  

If the parsing vs. validation in NLP context is clarified, the paper is useful
because it is formally correct, nice contribution, instructive and can give new
ideas to other researchers.  

The described algorithm can be used in semantic parsing to rerank hypergraphs
that are produced by another parser.   In this restricted way, the method can
be part of the machinery what we in NLP use in natural language parsing and
thus relevant to the ACL.

- Weaknesses:

Reranking use is not mentioned in the introduction.

It would be a great news in NLP context if an Earley parser would run in linear
time for NLP grammars (unlike special kinds of formal language grammars). 
Unfortunately, this result involves deep assumptions about the grammar and the
kind of input. 

Linear complexity of parsing of an input graph seem right for a top-down
deterministic grammars but the paper does not recognise the fact that an input
string in NLP usually gives rise to an exponential number of graphs.  In other
words, the parsing complexity result must be interpreted in the context of
graph validation or where one wants to find out a derivation of the graph, for
example, for the purposes of graph transduction via synchronous derivations.

To me, the paper should be more clear in this as a random reader may miss the
difference between semantic parsing (from strings) and parsing of semantic
parses 
(the current work).

There does not seem to be any control of the linear order of 0-arity edges.  It
might be useful to mention that if the parser is extended to string inputs with
the aim to find the (best?) hypergraph for a given external nodes, then the
item representations of the subgraphs must also keep track of the covered
0-arity edges.                          This makes the string-parser variant
exponential.  

- Easily correctable typos or textual problems:

1)  Lines 102-106 is misleading.   While intersection and probs are true, "such
distribution" cannot refer to the discussion in the above.

2) line 173:  I think you should rather talk about validation or recognition
algorithms than parsing algorithms as "parsing" in NLP means usually completely
different thing that is much more challenging due to the lexical and structural
ambiguity.

3) lines 195-196 are unclear:  what are the elements of att_G; in what sense
they are pairwise distinct.  Compare Example 1 where ext_G and att_G(e_1) are
not disjoint sets.

4) l.206.  Move *rank* definition earlier and remove redundancy.

5) l. 267:  rather "immediately derives", perhaps.

6) 279: add "be"

7) l. 352:  give an example of a nontrivial internal path.

8) l. 472:   define a subgraph of a hypergraph

9) l. 417, l.418:  since there are two propositions, you may want to tell how
they contribute to what is quoted.

10) l. 458:  add "for"

Table:                          Axiom:              this is only place where this is
introduced as an
axiom.                    Link
to the text that says it is a trigger.

- General Discussion:

It might be useful to tell about MSOL graph languages and their yields, which
are
context-free string languages.                          

What happens if the grammar is ambiguous and not top-down deterministic? 
What if there are exponential number of parses even for the input graph due to
lexical ambiguity or some other reasons.  How would the parser behave then? 
Wouldn't the given Earley recogniser actually be strictly polynomial to m or k
?

Even a synchronous derivation of semantic graphs can miss some linguistic
phenomena where a semantic distinction is expressed by different linguistic
means.                    E.g. one language may add an affix to a verb when another
language may
express the same distinction by changing the object.  I am suggesting that
although AMR increases language independence in parses it may have such
cross-lingual
challenges.

I did not fully understand the role of the marker in subgraphs.  It was elided
later
and not really used.

at
this
point.

It seems that the normal order is not unique.  Can you confirm this?

It is nice that def 7, cond 1 introduces lexical anchors to predictions. 
Compare the anchors in lexicalized grammars.

l. 760.  Are you sure that non-crossing links do not occur when parsing

- Significant questions to the Authors:

Linear complexity of parsing of an input graph seem right for a top-down

What would you say about parsing complexity in the case the RGG is a

Although this question might seem like a confusion, it is relevant in the NLP

What prevents the RGGs to generate hypergraphs whose 0-arity edges (~words) are

  Is
the
linear order determined by the Earley paths (and normal order used in

There is no clear connection to (non)context-free string languages or sets of

to generate non-context-free languages.  Are these graph languages or string

machine_text: The paper is very well organized and clear. The authors present Tandem Anchoring, a novel approach to allow users to interactively select and refine a topic model. The approach, which is built on top of Topic Modeling via Likelihood Optimization (TMLO), consists of three major components: 1) Tandem Decay, which allows the model to converge on a solution even when alternating between different topics; 2) Cluster-wise Variance Reduction, which allows the model to find low-variance clusters in the model’s result; and 3) the Tandem Anchoring framework, which allows users to select and refine clusters in the model’s result. The authors evaluate the approach on two existing benchmarks and demonstrate that Tandem Anchoring outperforms the baseline and other state-of-the-art interactive approaches. I suggest accepting this review, as I believe this paper is an important contribution to the field of topic modeling and users will find this approach interesting and useful. My only suggestion is that the paper could be strengthened by including figures or live code for Tandem Anchoring. Additionally, while I think the paper is well-written, it may be helpful for the authors to more clearly define their terms such as Tandem Decay, Cluster-wise Variance Reduction, and Tandem Anchoring, as these are not intuitive concepts and it takes some effort to understand the paper in its current form. At the moment, it is also not clear how to set up a Tandem Anchoring environment.

In this paper Tandem Anchoring: a Multiword Anchor Approach for Interactive Topic Modeling, the authors present a method for topic modeling of long documents comprised of multiple noun phrases by proposing a Multiword Anchor approach. The approach consists of: 1) finding Multiword Anchors from the text, 2) applying Latent Dirichlet Allocation to the resulting set of Multiword Anchors, and 3) extracting topics from the resulting set of topics. The approach has two main strengths. First, it allows topic models to capture relationships between different topics, i.e. multiword anchors will reflect the same topic regardless of their position in the original document. Second, it is applicable to a broader range of topic models as it is based on local pattern matching, no separate dictionary or annotations are needed. The method is not without weaknesses. The authors need to set a reasonable threshold on the number of words per anchor, although a wide range of sensible values seems to work well in their experiments. A more serious potential weakness is the dependence on Latent Dirichlet Allocation, an unsupervised learning algorithm. Overall, I think this paper makes a valuable contribution to the field of topic modeling, and I recommend its publication in Computational Linguistics. Problem/Question Addressed: The authors introduce a method for topic modeling of long documents comprised of multiple noun phrases. Strength: The authors introduce a method for topic modeling of long documents comprised of multiple noun phrases. By using Multiword Anchors the method is able to capture relationships between different topics, i.e. multiword anchors will reflect the same topic regardless of their position in the original document. Weakness: The method has a dependency on Latent Dirichlet Allocation, an unsupervised learning algorithm. Overall, I think this paper makes a valuable contribution to the field of topic modeling, and I recommend its publication in Computational Linguistics.

The main content of Tandem Anchors: a Multiword Anchor Approach for Interactive Topic Modeling is good, and the idea is promising. However, there are several issues need to be further improved: 1. The synthetic investigation is only applied on single synthetic data, which can not truly reflected the performance of Tandem Anchors on real-world data sets. 2. The comparison with other approaches is only on a single interactive topic model, it's not the overall comparison. 3. There are not more detailed analysis of the implementation of Tandem Anchors. However, the author has done a good job in introducing Tandem Anchors and the future work needs to be worked on. metics Thanks for the feedback! I appreciate it and will work on making Tandem Anchors more practical for real-world data. First, I will expand the investigation to include analysis on real-world data. Secondly, I will compare against other anchor-based methods, such as BERT. And, I will share more details about the implementation. 2016 +1 Everything else Overall, Tandem Anchors: a Multiword Anchor Approach for Interactive Topic Modeling has a lot of potential, and the idea of using combinations of words as anchors is interesting. However, the current version is not yet ready for real-world applications. There are several issues that need to be improved before being used on real-world data sets, such as only using single synthetic data, only performing comparison on one interactive topic model, and not sharing more details about the implementation.

This paper discusses and solve the problem that sampling-based interactive topic modeling approaches, in terms of scale, lack the speed needed for interactive work but also have the lack of precision in identifying the inten- sitive topics. The idea is that single words, either alone or in combination, can be used as “anchors” to uniquely identify a topic, offering the speed needed for interactive work but with the semantics needed for user-facing applications. We begin with a synthetic investigation of this approach, using random topics and single words as anchors, then applying it to interactive topic modeling in a user study, comparing it to interac- tive and non-interactive approaches. Tan- dem anchors are faster and more intuitive than existing interactive approaches. 8.0 Speed The authors introduce a new anchor, combining words, Tan- dem Anchors, to improve the efficiency of interactive topic modeling. In the synthetic investigation, using random topics and single words as anchors, the combination of words anchor can uniquely identify the topics, offering the speed needed for interactive work. In the user study, using the Tan- dem Anchors approach to interactive topic modeling, we can achieve the speed of sampling-based interactive topic modeling approach, IPALM, without losing the semantics needed for user-facing applications. 9.1 Intuitive semantics Tan- dem Anchors are intuitive to use, offering a way to interact with large datasets that is both fast and semantics-based. 9.2 Novel approach to sampling-based interactive topic modeling The Tan- dem Anchors approach is a novel approach to sampling-based interactive topic modeling, offering a way to achieve the speed of IPALM while preserving the semantics needed for user-facing applications.
human_text:
- Strengths:

The paper offers a natural and useful extension to recent efforts in
interactive topic modeling, namely by allowing human annotators to provide
multiple "anchor words" to machine-induced topics. The paper is well-organized
and the combination of synthetic and user experiments make for a strong paper.

- Weaknesses:

The paper is fairly limited in scope in terms of the interactive topic model
approaches it compares against. I am willing to accept this, since they do make
reference to most of them and explain that these other approaches are not
necessarily fast enough for interactive experimentation or not conducive to the
types of interaction being considered with an "anchoring" interface. Some level
of empirical support for these claims would have been nice, though.

It would also have been nice to see experiments on more than one data set (20
newsgroups, which is now sort of beaten-to-death).

- General Discussion:

In general, this is a strong paper that appears to offer an incremental but
novel and practical contribution to interactive topic modeling. The authors
made the effort to vet several variants of the approach in simulated
experiments, and to conduct fairly exhaustive quantitative analyses of both
simulated and user experiments using a variety of metrics that measure
different facets of topic quality.

- Strengths:
Clear description of methods and evaluation
Successfully employs and interprets a variety of evaluations
Solid demonstration of practicality of technique in real-world interactive
topic modeling

- Weaknesses:
Missing related work on anchor words
Evaluation on 20 Newsgroups is not ideal
Theoretical contribution itself is small 

- General Discussion:
The authors propose a new method of interactive user specification of topics
called Tandem Anchors. The approach leverages the anchor words algorithm, a
matrix-factorization approach to learning topic models, by replacing the
individual anchors inferred from the Gram-Schmidt algorithm with constructed
anchor pseudowords created by combining the sparse vector representations of
multiple words that for a topic facet. The authors determine that the use of a
harmonic mean function to construct pseudowords is optimal by demonstrating
that classification accuracy of document-topic distribution vectors using these
anchors produces the most improvement over Gram-Schmidt. They also demonstrate
that their work is faster than existing interactive methods, allowing
interactive iteration, and show in a user study that the multiword anchors are
easier and more effective for users.

Generally, I like this contribution a lot: it is a straightforward modification
of an existing algorithm that actually produces a sizable benefit in an
interactive setting. I appreciated the authors’ efforts to evaluate their
method on a variety of scales. While I think the technical contribution in
itself is relatively small (a strategy to assemble pseudowords based on topic
facets) the thoroughness of the evaluation merited having it be a full paper
instead of a short paper. It would have been nice to see more ideas as to how
to build these facets in the absence of convenient sources like category titles
in 20 Newsgroups or when initializing a topic model for interactive learning.

One frustration I had with this paper is that I find evaluation on 20
Newsgroups to not be great for topic modeling: the documents are widely
different lengths, preprocessing matters a lot, users have trouble making sense
of many of the messages, and naive bag-of-words models beat topic models by a
substantial margin. Classification tasks are useful shorthand for how well a
topic model corresponds to meaningful distinctions in the text by topic; a task
like classifying news articles by section or reviews by the class of the
subject of the review might be more appropriate. It would also have been nice
to see a use case that better appealed to a common expressed application of
topic models, which is the exploration of a corpus.

There were a number of comparisons I think were missing, as the paper contains
little reference to work since the original proposal of the anchor word model.
In addition to comparing against standard Gram-Schmidt, it would have been good
to see the method from Lee et. al. (2014), “Low-dimensional Embeddings for
Interpretable Anchor-based Topic Inference”. I also would have liked to have
seen references to Nguyen et. al. (2013), “Evaluating Regularized Anchor
Words” and Nguyen et. al. (2015) “Is Your Anchor Going Up or Down? Fast and
Accurate Supervised Topic Models”, both of which provide useful insights into
the anchor selection process.

I had some smaller notes:
- 164: …entire dataset
- 164-166: I’m not quite sure what you mean here. I think you are claiming
that it takes too long to do one pass? My assumption would have been you would
use only a subset of the data to retrain the model instead of a full sweep, so
it would be good to clarify what you mean.
- 261&272: any reason you did not consider the and operator or element-wise
max? They seem to correspond to the ideas of union and intersection from the or
operator and element-wise min, and it wasn’t clear to me why the ones you
chose were better options.
- 337: Usenet should be capitalized
- 338-340: Why fewer than 100 (as that is a pretty aggressive boundary)? Also,
did you remove headers, footers, and/or quotes from the messages?
- 436-440: I would have liked to see a bit more explanation of what this tells
us about confusion.
- 692: using tandem anchors

Overall, I think this paper is a meaningful contribution to interactive topic
modeling that I would like to see available for people outside the machine
learning community to investigate, classify, and test hypotheses about their
corpora.

POST-RESPONSE: I appreciate the thoughtful responses of the authors to my
questions. I would maintain that for some of the complimentary related work
that it's useful to compare to non-interactive work, even if it does something
different.
