machine_text: Generally LSTMs are robust and capable models. The use of external knowledge to narrow down the search space will improve the model's accuracy. In this paper the authors apply hierarchical LSTMs to the problem of rare entity prediction and show that by incorporating knowledge from a large external dictionary, the model improves state-of-the-art results by 3.5%. A similar application of knowledge external to the training data set could be Featurization. Using the extra knowledge, the model can learn richer feature representations which will in turn improve accuracy. Earthquakes are a good example of a highly featurizable domain. If we were to use LSTMs, we can use SOS feature extraction to create additional input features that encapsulate the distance and direction information of the spatial coordinates of the earthquake. By incorporating this information, we can create a more robust model that can better predict if there will be an aftershock close to where the first earthquake occurred. Furthermore, by combining the power of hierarchical LSTMs and the external knowledge that is available in dictionaries, this model can also identify the rare entities in a document. For example, in Turkish, the model was able to identify 100% of the test set samples as rare entities even without being trained on any Turkish samples. The incorporation of external knowledge allows this model to achieve state-of-the-art results on a challenging and hard to reach application area of Rare Entity Prediction. Energy consumption of IT systems are an example of a highly featurizable domain. If we apply LSTMs we can use ASIC Latin Square testing to create additional features such as the days of the week and time of day that the energy was consumed. This creates a more robust model and improves the accuracy of predicting if the energy will be consumed. A well-trained LSTM model can also perform Named Entity recognition. In this example, a featurizable LSTM model can be used to determine if a name in a text is a person, organization, location, and more. Named entity recognition combined with featurization could create a powerful model that can perform personalized resource allocation and help optimize spend within an organization. **** Overall, this is an excellent paper. The application of Hierarchical LSTMs to the problem of Rare Entity Prediction has shown promising results. The incorporation of external knowledge helps further improve the model's accuracy.

The authors describe a framework for rare entity detection in clinical text that uses hierarchical LSTMs and external knowledge sources. The approach they take is interesting, and could be useful for other language use tasks with discrete latent classes. I think their treatment of rare entity classification as a multi-label classification problem is interesting, but I don’t think it works very well. The way they handle it is to use a one-vs-rest scheme, where for each label y_i, you train a separate model and look at the probability for y_i over all examples. Since this is a multiclass problem, each label is mutually exclusive, so the probability for each label is either 0 or 1, which is not a good way to combine these probabilities into a probability distribution over the entire set of labels. A better way would be to use a hierarchical softmax, which gives each label a soft probability across all labels, allowing each label to “carry” some of its probability over to other labels. Another potential weakness is the use of the BIO scheme to represent the labels. The BIO scheme is based on Shannon’s source coding theoretic optimal policy, which specifies that different labels should be separated to different numbers of bytes. In the case of rare entity classification, rare labels will tend to be similar, so BIO will encode them using fewer bytes than the non-BIO scheme. This might give an advantage to rare entity prediction over common entity predictions.

This paper addresses the problem of rare entity prediction: given a web document with several entities removed, models are tasked with predicting the correct missing entities conditioned on the document context and the lexical resources. This task is challenging due to the diversity of language styles and the extremely large number of rare entities. Our model using hierarchical LSTMs performs significantly better at rare entity prediction than those that do not. We introduce a new task and derive new models to drive progress towards this goal. The task of rare entity prediction: given a web document with several entities removed, models are tasked with predicting the correct missing entities conditioned on the document context and the lexical resources. This task is challenging due to the diversity of language styles and the extremely large number of rare entities. The main contribution of this work is the development of a new task and the presentation of a new, more difficult dataset, which we call Rare Entity Prediction (REP). We collected the corpus by crawling the Web and manually removing entities which are marked as rare in the large-scale lexical resources ELRA and Babel98. We then masked the corpus with common entity names like “€”, “ ”, ““” and “”” to increase the variety of text styles in the dataset. Additionally, to encourage models to consider lexical resources, we provide a parallel version of the corpus with entity names replaced by their entity descriptions from the corresponding resource. To illustrate the usefulness of external knowledge, our model using hierarchical LSTMs significantly outperformed the LSTM baseline as well as a model using distantly supervised text representation learning and information-integration baseline. Another interesting contribution of this work is the presentation of a new way of incorporating external knowledge into NLP models, which we hope will drive progress towards the broader goal of incorporating external knowledge in NLP research and development. The Rare Entity Prediction task and associated dataset could be used for training and testing similar methods. In sum, we present a new Rare Entity Prediction dataset and the Rare Entity Prediction (REP) challenge. Our hope is that this task will encourage the research community to incorporate external knowledge in NLP research and development. We hope the Rare Entity Challenge will be a valuable step towards this goal. We have organized a leaderboard to highlight leading teams and report progress towards the goal of incorporating external knowledge in NLP research and development. We also provide a parallel version of the dataset and entity descriptions for each entity name in the original corpus. Finally, we release our code and the dataset to the research community for evaluating the effectiveness of incorporating external knowledge into NLP systems.
human_text:
- Contents:
This paper proposes a new task, and provides a dataset. The task is to predict
blanked-out named entities from a text with the help of an external
definitional resource, in particular FreeBase. These named entities are
typically rare, that is, they do not appear often in the corpus, such that it
is not possible to train models specifically for each entity. The paper argues
convincingly that this is an important setting to explore. Along with multiple
baselines, two neural network models for the problem are presented that make
use of the external resource, one of which also accumulates evidence across
contexts in the same text. 

- Strengths:

The collection of desiderata for the task is well-chosen to advance the field:
predicting blanked-out named entities, a task that has already shown to be
interesting in the CNN/Daily Mail dataset, but in a way that makes the task
hard for language models; and the focus on rare entities should drive the field
towards more interesting models. 

The collection of baselines is well chosen to show that neither a NN model
without external knowledge nor a simple cosine similarity based model with
external knowledge can do the task well.

The two main models are chosen well.

The text is clear and well argued. 

- Weaknesses:

I was a bit puzzled by the fact that using larger contexts, beyond the
sentences with blanks in them, did not help the models. After all, you were in
a way using additional context in the HierEnc model, which accumulates
knowledge from other contexts. There are two possible explanations: Either the
sentences with blanks in them are across the board more informative for the
task than the sentences without. This is the explanation suggested in the
paper, but it seems a bit unintuitive that this should be the case. Another
possible explanation is that the way that you were using additional context in
HierEnc, using the temporal network, is much more useful than by enlarging
individual contexts C and feeding that larger C into the recurrent network.  Do
you think that that could be what is going on?

- General Discussion:

I particularly like the task and the data that this paper proposes. This setup
can really drive the field forward, I think. This in my mind is the main
contribution.

- General Discussion:

The paper deals with the task of predicting missing entities in a given context
using the Freebase definitions of those entities. The authors highlight the
importance of the problem, given that the entities come from a long-tailed
distribution. They use popular sequence encoders to encode the context and the
definitions of candidate entities, and score them based on their similarity
with the context. While it is clear that the task is indeed important, and the
dataset may be useful as a benchmark, the approach has some serious weaknesses
and the evaluation leaves some questions unanswered. 

- Strengths:

The proposed task requires encoding external knowledge, and the associated
dataset may serve as a good benchmark for evaluating hybrid NLU systems.

- Weaknesses:

1) All the models evaluated, except the best performing model (HIERENC), do not
have access to contextual information beyond a sentence. This does not seem
sufficient to predict a missing entity. It is unclear whether any attempts at
coreference and anaphora resolution have been made. It would generally help to
see how well humans perform at the same task.

2) The choice of predictors used in all models is unusual. It is unclear why
similarity between context embedding and the definition of the entity is a good
indicator of the goodness of the entity as a filler.

3) The description of HIERENC is unclear. From what I understand, each input
(h_i) to the temporal network is the average of the representations of all
instantiations of context filled by every possible entity in the vocabulary.
This does not seem to be a good idea since presumably only one of those
instantiations is correct. This would most likely introduce a lot of noise.

4) The results are not very informative. Given that this is a rare entity
prediction problem, it would help to look at type-level accuracies, and 
analyze how the accuracies of the proposed models vary with frequencies of
entities.

- Questions to the authors:

1) An important assumption being made is that d_e are good replacements for
entity embeddings. Was this assumption tested?

2) Have you tried building a classifier that just takes h_i^e as inputs?

I have read the authors' responses. I still think the task+dataset could
benefit from human evaluation. This task can potentially be a good benchmark
for NLU systems, if we know how difficult the task is. The results presented in
the paper are not indicative of this due to the reasons stated above. Hence, I
am not changing my scores.

- Strengths:
The paper empirically verifies that using external knowledge is a benefit.

- Weaknesses:
Real world NLP applications should utilize external knowledge for making better
predictions. The authors propose Rare Entity prediction task to demonstrate
this is the case. However, the motivation of the task is not fully justified.
Why is this task important? How would real world NLP applications benefit from
this task? The paper lacks a convincing argument for proposing a new task. For
current reading comprehension task, the evidence for a correct answer can be
found in a given text, thus we are interested in learning a model of the world
(i.e causality for example), or a basic reasoning model. Comparing to reading
comprehension, rare entity prediction is rather unrealistic as humans are
terrible with remembering name. The authors mentioned that the task is
difficult due to the large number of rare entities, however challenging tasks
with the same or even more difficult level exist, such as predicting correct
morphological form of a word in morphologically rich languages. Such tasks have
obvious applications in machine translation for example.

- General Discussion:
It would be helpful if the authors characterize the dataset in more details.
From figure 1 and table 4, it seems to me that overlapping entities is an
important feature. There is noway i can predict the **blank** in figure 1 if I
don't see the word London in Peter Ackoyd description. That's being said,
before brutalizing neural networks, it is essential to understand the
characteristic of the data and the cognitive process that searches for the
right answer.

Given the lack of characteristic of the dataset, I find that the baselines are
inappropriate. First of all, the CONTENC is a natural choice at the first sigh.
However as the authors mentioned that candidate entities are rare, the
embeddings of those entities are unrealizable. As a consequence, it is expected
that CONTENC doesn't work well. Would it is fairer if the embeddings are
initialized from pre-trained vectors on massive dataset? One would expect some
sort of similarity between Larnaca and Cyprus in the embedding space and
CONTENC would make a correct prediction in Table 4. What would be the
performance of TF-IDF+COS and AVGEMB+COS if only entities are used to compute
those vectors?

From modeling perspective, I appreciate that the authors chose a sigmoid
predictor that output a numerical score between (0,1). This would help avoiding
normalization over the list of candidates, which are rare and is difficult to
learn reliable weights for those. However, a sidestep technique does exist,
such as Pointer Network. A representation h_i for C_i (*blank* included) can be
computed by an LSTM or BiLSTM, then Pointer Network would give a probabilistic
interpretation p(e_k|C_i) \propto exp(dot(d_{e_k}, h_i)). In my opinion,
Pointer Network would be an appropriate baseline. Another related note: Does
the unbalanced set of negative/positive labels affect the training? During
training, the models make 1 positive prediction while number of negative
predictions is at least 4 times higher?

While I find the task of Rare Entity prediction is unrealistic, having the
dataset, it would be more interesting to learn about the reasoning process that
leads to the right answer such as which set of words the model attends to when
making prediction.

machine_text: The paper presents a framework for learning semantic parsers from weak supervision. Specifically, the paper leverages Freebase to create instances of relations for parser training. The author provides a high-level overview of the framework and presents empirical results on the PennTreebank and Freebase textual corpora. I recommend the paper for publication in the Springer journal International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR). This work is innovative and potentially highly impactful. Although traditional tree-based parsers handle edge cases relatively well, they are not designed to capture complex semantic relationships in free text. Neural Symbolic Machines has shown in the past few years of research that it is possible to train semantic parsers that capture complex semantic relationships from weak supervision. This is a highly useful advance for the Semantic Web, as it allows for rich semantic information to be annotated for large amounts of text in machine-readable form, and potentially lower the barrier of entry for downstream applications that use this knowledge. I have some suggestions for improvement of the current version of the paper. The first section of the paper (and the abstract) is quite vague and does not clearly convey the idea or contributions of the paper. The main idea could be made clearer, for example, by providing an example of what the setup exactly means. Additionally, it would be good to provide concrete examples of what kinds of Named Entity (NE) and semantic relationships are typically used in clinical NLP applications, and why these relationships cannot be hand-annotated (in terms of cost, expertise, or other constraints). The rest of the paper goes into more details about the setup and implementation, which is helpful for understanding the core contributions of the paper. However, the implementation is quite dense, and I was unable to parse it well in my reading. It might be helpful to provide a schematic overview of the overall system, as well as for each component, plus a reference implementation of that component. Additionally, it could be helpful to simplify the description of the main components, e.g. "the Neural Semantic Parser is a many-to-many framework that accepts both structured and unstructured inputs" - it is not very clear to me what the two forms mean in this context. I also have some concerns about the evaluation. In this work, the SRL parser, Relation Net, is trained on PennTreebank. However, it is evaluated on the PennTreebank paraphrasing corpus. I think it would be better to report the exact error rates on the PennTreebank test set, instead of the paraphrasing corpus. Also, the SRL parser in this work is only used for decoding (it is not utilized for scoring any generated parses). This means that any reported performances of the NSP are likely to be over-optimistic. Despite these comments, I think the research is interesting and well-motivated, and I recommend publishing this paper in the ICLR conference.

This paper introduces a new approach to semantic parsing in which the model is
equipped with a neural sequence to sequence (seq2seq) model (referred to as the
“programmer”) which encodes a natural language question and produces a
program. The programmer is also equipped with a ‘key variable’ memory
component which stores (a) entities in the questions (b) values of intermediate
variables formed during execution of intermediate programs. These variables are
referred to further build the program.                    The model is also equipped
with
certain
discrete operations (such as argmax or 'hop to next edges in a KB'). A separate
component ("interpreter/computer") executes these operations and stores
intermediate values (as explained before). Since the ‘programmer' is
inherently a seq2seq model, the "interpreter/computer” also acts as a
syntax/type checker only allowing the decoder to generate valid tokens. For
example, the second argument to the “hop” operation has to be a KB
predicate. Finally the model is trained with weak supervision and directly
optimizes the metric which is used to evaluate the performance (F score).
Because of the discrete operations and the non differentiable reward functions,
the model is trained with policy gradients (REINFORCE). Since gradients
obtained through REINFORCE have high variance, it is common to first pretrain
the model with a max-likelihood objective or find some good sequences of
actions trained through some auxiliary objective. This paper takes a latter
approach in which it finds good sequences via an iterative maximum likelihood
approach. The results and discussion sections are presented in a very nice way
and the model achieves SOTA results on the WebQuestions dataset when compared
to other weakly supervised model.

The paper is written clearly and is very easy to follow.

This paper presents a new and exciting direction and there is scope for a lot
of future research in this direction. I would definitely love to see this
presented in the conference.

Questions for the authors (important ones first)

1. Another alternative way of training the model would be to bootstrap the
parameters (\theta) from the iterative ML method instead of adding pseudo gold
programs in the beam (Line 510 would be deleted). Did you try that and if so
why do you think it didn’t work?
2. What was the baseline model in REINFORCE. Did you have a separate network
which predicts the value function. This must be discussed in the paper in
detail.
3. Were there programs which required multiple hop operations? Or were they
limited to single hops. If there were, can you provide an example? (I will
understand if you are bound by word limit of the response)
4. Can you give an example where the filter operation would be used?
5. I did not follow the motivation behind replacing the entities in the
question with special ENT symbol

This paper introduces Neural Symbolic Machines (NSMs) --- a deep neural model
equipped with discrete memory to facilitate symbolic execution. An NSM includes
three components: (1) a manager that provides weak supervision for learning,
(2) a differentiable programmer based on neural sequence to sequence model,
which encodes input instructions and predicts simplified Lisp programs using
partial execution results stored in external discrete memories. (3) a symbolic
computer that executes programs and provide code assistance to the programmer
to prune search space. The authors conduct experiments on a semantic parsing
task (WebQuestionsSP), and show that (1) NSM is able to model language
compositionality by saving and reusing intermediate execution results, (2)
Augmented REINFORCE is superior than vanilla REINFROCE for sequence prediction
problems, and (3) NSM trained end-to-end with weak supervision is able to
outperform existing sate-of-the-art method (STAGG).

- Strengths

* The idea of using discrete, symbolic memories for neural execution models is
novel.                    Although in implementation it may simply reduce to copying
previously
executed variable tokens from an extra buffer, this approach is still
impressive since it works well for a large-scale semantic parsing task.

* The proposed revised REINFORCE training schema using imperfect hypotheses
derived from maximum likelihood training is interesting and effective, and
could inspire future exploration in mixing ML/RL training for neural
sequence-to-sequence models.

* The scale of experiments is larger than any previous works in modeling neural
execution and program induction. The results are impressive.

* The paper is generally clear and well-written, although there are some points
which might require further clarification (e.g., how do the keys ($v_i$'s in
Fig. 2) of variable tokens involved in computing action probabilities?
Conflicting notations: $v$ is used to refer to variables in Tab. 1 and memory
keys in Fig 1.).

Overall, I like this paper and would like to see it in the conference.

* Weaknesses

* [Choice of Dataset] The authors use WebQuestionsSP as the testbed. Why not
using the most popular WebQuestions (Berant et al., 2013) benchmark set? Since
NSM only requires weak supervision, using WebQuestions would be more intuitive
and straightforward, plus it could facilitate direct comparison with
main-stream QA research.

* [Analysis of Compositionality] One of the contribution of this work is the
usage of symbolic intermediate execution results to facilitate modeling
language compositionality. One interesting question is how well questions with
various compositional depth are handled. Simple one-hop questions are the
easiest to solve, while complex multi-hop ones that require filtering and
superlative operations (argmax/min) would be highly non-trivial. The authors
should present detailed analysis regarding the performance on question sets
with different compositional depth.

* [Missing References] I find some relevant papers in this field missing. For
example, the authors should cite previous RL-based methods for knowledge-based
semantic parsing (e.g., Berant and Liang., 2015), the sequence level REINFORCE
training method of (Ranzato et al., 2016) which is closely related to augmented
REINFORCE, and the neural enquirer work (Yin et al., 2016) which uses
continuous differentiable memories for modeling neural execution.

* Misc.

machine_text: The paper "" is very interesting and well written. The authors identify paraphrases across a source and target language pair, and then use these paraphrases to cluster words into groups that represent similar meaning. The clusters then act as a substitution matrix for the source word in the paraphrase cluster, and the target word in the paraphrase cluster. The authors evaluate the effectiveness of this approach using both machine translation and human evaluation. I recommend accepting this for publication in its current form. One thing that is missing is a discussion of related work. The authors mention some related work in the introduction, but it would be good to cite other work in the introduction as well as in the conclusion. In particular, I would cite the recent work of @bernard2016 devil is in the detail, which used a very similar approach to analyze the differences between translations from human and machine translation. I also think it would be good to discuss how the proposed approach relates to recent work on zero-shot learning for word vectors, as word2vec and BERT have been shown to capture associations between words that are not readily apparent. Another comment is that in the case of machine translation, the human evaluation may not be a good metric of effectiveness. For example, the baseline for the human evaluation is to have a person translate the paraphrase cluster, which may not be a very good baseline since the person may have no idea how the paraphrase cluster relates to the source word. On the other hand, if the target word is in the paraphrase cluster, then a better performance metric would be BLEU@k, where k is the number of paraphrases in the source word. BLEU@k is computed using a precision-based approximation that trades off against the number of paraphrases used. In this sense, the proposed approach would perform very well on machine translation evaluations, as it is very hard to beat BLEU@1. I also have a few questions about the methodology. The authors mention that they use convolutional neural networks to build the paraphrase cluster mapping. Would it be better to use an autoencoder to compactly represent the mapping? In addition, if we treat each paraphrase as a unit, then each paraphrase cluster could be defined in terms of $K$ clusters. The authors report the results with $K=5$, but in general $K$ should not be a factor of $N$, where N is the total number of paraphrase clusters. What is the motivation for setting $K$ equal to 5, and can the method be improved by choosing a larger or smaller value of $K$? In summary, this is a very interesting paper that could be published in its current form, but I recommend a few modifications. First, I would cite the related work of Bernard et al., 2016. Second, I would include a discussion of zero-shot learning for word vectors, as this work shows that word2vec and BERT capture a lot of relationships between words that are not readily apparent. Third, I would discuss the optimization procedure for finding the best paraphrase cluster assignments, and there could be a method to select $K$ without a brute force search. Fourth, I would consider different values of $K$ and see if a smaller number of clusters captures as much information as a larger number of clusters. These changes could improve the paper and make it more widely applicable."

This paper presents a method for clustering paraphrases for substitutability. The authors propose to cluster paraphrases using two criteria: semantic similarity and lexical similarity. Semantic similarity is computed using an existing vector space model of the textual content of the paraphrases. Lexical similarity is computed using a MLN model which takes into account the parts of speech of the words in the original sentence and the paraphrase. The authors conduct experiments on two task: textual entailment and question answering and obtain interesting results. Here are some of the strengths of the paper: 1) The authors present a new method for clustering paraphrases which has not been proposed before; 2) The algorithm to compute the semantic similarity is based on a pre-trained model which makes it easy to expand the method to other languages; 3) The experiments on textual entailment and question answering are conducted and the results are convincing. Here are some of the limitations of the paper: 1) The method is purely syntactic, i.e., it doesn't take into account the semantics of the original sentence and the paraphrase; 2) The algorithm for computing the lexical similarity is based on aMLN model which might be unstable when the training data is not large; 3) The evaluation metric for the textual entailment task is not common. Some papers use verification accuracy while others useBLEU. despite the fact that the method presented in this paper addresses a relevant problem and is generally applicable, it could be improved in several aspects. First, the semantic similarity computation using a vector space model is only applicable to similar languages, since the authors only briefly mention how to extend the method to other languages. Second, the method for computing the lexical similarity is based on aMLN model which might be unstable when the training data is not large. Third, the method only considers the parts of speech of the words in the original sentence and the paraphrase, but it could also take into account other information such as the sentence position in the original and the paraphrase.

Hi, I have read the paper thoroughly and here are some constructive comments: The paper is well-organized and clear about the motivation and the problem statement. However, I would suggest to add some discussions on similar work and motivation behind choosing the specific dataset for the experiments. In the experiments, the authors use three baselines and two state of the art models. However, I think the authors should include another baseline which uses the language model. This will help to compare the improvement of the new method with other methods. I like the idea of using sense inventory for the sense filtering. However, the drawback here is that the sense inventory is not complete (as of now). The authors should compare the sense inventory with an existing WordNet to see if there are any sense which are not covered in sense inventory. In step 3 of the sense clustering, the authors have used very high dimensional embedding and Skip-Gram model. There could be other strategies/approaches which could also give better sense clustering. I also noticed that similar work has been done for NTM, but the author is using Neural network with long short term memory for the sense clustering. There is some mathematical formulation in the paper which is missing. For example, it is not clear how the sense distance metric is defined and how the sense clustering is done. In the concluding remarks, the authors should mention about the work in progress sense inventory, and improvements to the sense clustering etc. Overall, the article looks good and the idea of sense clustering for improving the substitution ranking is an interesting exploration, and will be of use to the NLP research community.

The paper Clustering Paraphrases for Substitutability addresses the question of improving existing models for lexical substitution by filtering the correct sense to the top of the rankings. The paper introduces a simple method for clustering paraphrases by sense with substitutability in mind. The sense clusters generated by the proposed method are broader and have more substitutable than existing sense inventories. The paper also describes a novel method for filtering the correct sense to the top of the rankings. The method results in broader sense clusters and outperforms existing sense inventories on a substitute breadth measure. The method proposed in the paper can be divided into three steps: 1) Build sense clusters by merging Word Sense Bases and word paraphrases in the Word Senses Clusters of the Sense-based Word Embedding Model (Sense-WCEM) using a criterion that reflects substitutability; 2) Filter substitutes in the sense clusters’ corresponding vector space based on a score computed using the Sense Stacked Matrix Factorization model; 3) Evaluate the substitutes in each sense cluster by ranking them according to existing substitutability-aware vector- and word embedding-based models and take the top sense of each cluster as substitutes. The method proposed in the paper has the following main advantages: 1) It can be applied to existing substitutability-agnostic ranking models, making it more broadly useful. 2) It can be applied to any sense-based word embedding model with sense clusters built by the Sense-WCEM model. 3) It can be applied to any substitutable word pairs in existing sense-based word embedding models. 4) The method can be applied to sense cluster-based ranking models (e.g. Sense Stacked MF). 5) The method can be applied to any substitutable word pairs. The Sense-WCEM model is used to build sense clusters and has the following main strengths: 1) It can be applied to any corpus that uses the Sense-WCEM model to generate word sense representations. 2) It can be applied to any corpus that uses the similarity joins method to generate word paraphrases from word similarity pairs. 3) It can be applied to a broader spectrum of text, both subtitled data and raw text from different sources. 4) The word sense inventory, Sense Stacked Matrix Factorization model, and Sense-WCEM model can all be easily customized for different applications. The paper presents an effective, broadly applicable method for filtering the correct sense to the top of the rankings that improves existing substitutability-agnostic ranking models. The Sense-WCEM model, the word sense inventory, and the Sense Stacked MF model build on existing, successful vector- and word embedding-based methods, making the approach broadly applicable. Sense-based word embedding models are applied to Sense-WCEM model to expand their application domain. The paper also describes a new substitute breadth measure. The substitute breadth can be applied to both cluster-based and pairwise models. The Sense-WCEM model improves Sense-based word embedding models by clustering word paraphrases by word sense with substitutability in mind and filtering the correct sense to the top of the rankings.
human_text:
This paper proposes integrating word sense inventories into existing approaches
for the lexical substitution task by using these inventories to filter
candidates. To do so, the authors first propose a metric to measure the mutual
substitutability of sense inventories with human judgments for the lexsub task,
and empirically measure the substitutability of inventories from various
sources such as WordNet and PPDB. Next, they propose clustering different
paraphrases of a word from PPDB using a multi-view clustering approach, to
automatically generate a sense inventory instead of using the aforementioned
inventories. Finally, they use these clusters with a naive (majority in top 5)
WSD technique to filter existing ranked list of substitution candidates.

- Strengths:

* The key idea of marrying vector space model based approaches and sense
inventories for the lexsub task is useful since these two techniques seem to
have complementary information, especially since the vector space models are
typically unaware of sense and polysemy.

* The oracle evaluation is interesting as it gives a clear indication of how
much gain can one expect in the best case, and while there is still a large gap
between the oracle and actual scores, we can still argue for the usefulness of
the proposed approach due to the large difference between the unfiltered GAP
and the oracle GAP.

- Weaknesses:

* I don't understand effectiveness of the multi-view clustering approach.
Almost all across the board, the paraphrase similarity view does significantly
better than other views and their combination. What, then, do we learn about
the usefulness of the other views? There is one empirical example of how the
different views help in clustering paraphrases of the word 'slip', but there is
no further analysis about how the different clustering techniques differ,
except on the task directly. Without a more detailed analysis of differences
and similarities between these views, it is hard to draw solid conclusions
about the different views.                                  

* The paper is not fully clear on a first read. Specifically, it is not
immediately clear how the sections connect to each other, reading more like
disjoint pieces of work. For instance, I did not understand the connections
between section 2.1 and section 4.3, so adding forward/backward pointer
references to sections should be useful in clearing up things. Relatedly, the
multi-view clustering section (3.1) needs editing, since the subsections seem
to be out of order, and citations seem to be missing (lines 392 and 393).

* The relatively poor performance on nouns makes me uneasy. While I can expect
TWSI to do really well due to its nature, the fact that the oracle GAP for
PPDBClus is higher than most clustering approaches is disconcerting, and I
would like to understand the gap better. This also directly contradicts the
claim that the clustering approach is generalizable to all parts of speech
(124-126), since the performance clearly isn't uniform.

- General Discussion:

The paper is mostly straightforward in terms of techniques used and
experiments. Even then, the authors show clear gains on the lexsub task by
their two-pronged approach, with potentially more to be gained by using
stronger WSD algorithms.

Some additional questions for the authors :

* Lines 221-222 : Why do you add hypernyms/hyponyms?
* Lines 367-368 : Why does X^{P} need to be symmetric?
* Lines 387-389 : The weighting scheme seems kind of arbitrary. Was this indeed
arbitrary or is this a principled choice?
* Is the high performance of SubstClus^{P} ascribable to the fact that the
number of clusters was tuned based on this view? Would tuning the number of
clusters based on other matrices affect the results and the conclusions?
* What other related tasks could this approach possibly generalize to? Or is it
only specific to lexsub?

Strengths:
The paper presents a new method that exploits word senses to improve the task
of lexical substitutability.  Results show improvements over prior methods.

Weaknesses:
As a reader of a ACL paper, I usually ask myself what important insight can I
take away from the paper, and from a big picture point of view, what does the
paper add to the fields of natural language processing and computational
linguistics.  How does the task of lexical substitutability in general and this
paper in particular help either in improving an NLP system or provide insight
about language?  I can't find a good answer answer to either question after
reading this paper.

As a practitioner who wants to improve natural language understanding system, I
am more focused on the first question -- does the lexical substitutability task
and the improved results compared to prior work presented here help any end
application?  Given the current state of high performing systems, any discrete
clustering of words (or longer utterances) often break down when compared to
continuous representations words (see all the papers that utilitize discrete
lexical semantics to achieve a task versus words' distributed representations
used as an input to the same task; e.g. machine translation, question
answering, sentiment analysis, text classification and so forth).  How do the
authors motivate work on lexical substitutability given that discrete lexical
semantic representations often don't work well?  The introduction cites a few
papers from several years back that are mostly set up in small data scenarios,
and given that this word is based on English, I don't see why one would use
this method for any task.  I would be eager to see the authors' responses to
this general question of mine.

As a minor point, to further motivate this, consider the substitutes presented
in Table 1.
1. Tasha snatched it from him to rip away the paper.
2. Tasha snatched it from him to rip away the sheet.

To me, these two sentences have varying meanings -- what if he was holding on
to a paper bag?  In that scenario, can the word "paper" be substituted by
"sheet"?  At least, in my understanding, it cannot.  Hence, there is so much
subjectivity in this task that lexical substitutes can completely alter the
semantics of the original sentence.

Minor point(s):
 - Citations in Section 3.1.4 are missing.

Addition: I have read the author response and I am sticking to my earlier
evaluation of the paper.

machine_text: The corpus presented is a useful tool for understanding the evolution of argumentative writing over time. As the title suggests, the papers in this corpus were selected for analysis because they were revised to present an argument against a position, in favor of an opposing position, or without modification. The paper provides a useful introduction to the topic, presenting an overview of argumentative writing and discussing the problems with using traditional evaluation methods. The paper then describes the development of the corpus and the methods for analyzing the changes made to the argument. The introduction is followed by a discussion of the corpus design and analysis. The analyses presented include details on the set up and the Corpus Toolbox queries used to sort and organize the data. The analyses discussed are useful and the presented corpus is a good start for researchers working with this type of data. As the corpus is still developing, I look forward to seeing future publications on the analyses of the data. The one drawback is that there is not much discussion of how to effectively search and find specific arguments. The search functionality is straightforward but to identify a specific argument, a much more advanced search and a description of how to formulate such a search would be beneficial. MY QUERIES AND ANALYSES After finalizing the corpus design, I ran a series of queries to separate the dataset into revisions with different functions. GUIDE FOR SEARCHING THE CORPUS Searching for specific arguments is currently the most difficult aspect of working with the corpus. The analysis described in the paper is technically sound, however, the analysis of search terms and argumentative relationships needs improvement. The paper does present a working framework for searching the corpus. In fact, Figure 1 from the paper shows the basic elements of the framework. Figure 2 from the paper is a screenshot of the "Keyword, Author, Date, Origin, Formulation, Restrictions" search.

The authors present a large annotated corpus of argumentative essays. The corpus has been annotated with multiple labels for propositional statements, factual statements, and logical forms. This is a very useful tool for practitioners interested in using deep learning techniques to tag propositional statements in argumentative essays. It would be very useful to have similar annotations for patterns of reasoning and informal fallacies. mems The authors present a large annotated corpus of argumentative essays. The corpus has been annotated with multiple labels for propositional statements, factual statements, and logical forms. This is a very useful tool for practitioners interested in using deep learning techniques to tag propositional statements in argumentative essays. It would be very useful to have similar annotations for patterns of reasoning and informal fallacies. One concern is that the corpus is very heavily biased towards American English. Only about a third of the documents are from other English-speaking countries. This is a major limitation given that much of the English-speaking world writes in non-American English. A second concern is that the corpus is heavily slanted towards conservative opinions. Only about half of the documents are from left-of-center viewpoints. This makes the corpus poorly suited for training supervised learning models that respect viewpoint diversity. Finally, the provided code for downloading and processing the corpus was very out of date. The code requires Python 3, which is no longer the most popular version of Python. Even if the code did work, the most up-to-date versions of some packages were required (such as scikit-learn). This makes it very difficult to adopt the techniques in the paper.

The author(s) present ArgRewrite, a corpus of revisions of argumentative essays. The paper also presents some preliminary studies using this corpus for performing comparison and revision analysis. The paper is well written and the topic is currently of high interest. However, I would suggest the author(s) to perform few more revision analyses using this corpus and report the results in the paper. Also, the comparison analysis using this corpus might require a larger sample size. In addition, the results of the revision purpose prediction analysis need to be discussed. I recommend including these studies in the later version of the paper. * The authors should definitely perform these studies. The corpus could be further improved by using more revisions from different writers/students; however, the analyses are still preliminary and require further studies to be performed on larger datasets. * The corpus revision analysis was conducted on a sample of 32 revisions from 16 different writers/students. The revision purpose was predicted for the sample, and the results are presented in the form of heat maps. The author should definitely include these results in the paper. * The corpus revision analysis was conducted on a sample of 32 revisions from 16 different writers/students. The revision purpose was not predicted with high accuracy, and the author should definitely discuss these results. * The authors analyzed a revision sample of 32 revisions from 16 different writers/students, using an analogous framework to the one used for predicting revision purposes in document authorship attribution, i.e. sentiment classification. The revision purpose was predicted for the sample, and the results are presented in the form of heat maps. The authors should definitely include these results and discuss their interpretation. * The authors analyzed a revision sample of 32 revisions from 16 different writers/students. The revision purpose was not predicted with high accuracy, and the authors should definitely discuss these results. In addition, the comparison analysis using this corpus seems to be performed on a sample of 32 revisions only. The author should definitely perform this analysis on a larger sample to demonstrate the effectiveness of the corpus and of the analysis. In conclusion, the paper is interesting, and the presented corpus and analyses have significant potential. The author(s) should definitely perform more revision analyses and discuss the results in the paper.
human_text:
This paper presents a corpus of annotated essay revisions. 

It includes two examples of application for the corpus:

1) Student Revision Behavior Analysis and 2) Automatic Revision Identification

The latter is essentially a text classification task using an SVM classifier
and a variety of features. The authors state that the corpus will be freely
available for research purposes.

The paper is well-written and clear. A detailed annotation scheme was used by
two
annotators to annotate the corpus which added value to it. I believe the
resource might be interesting to researcher working on writing process research
and related topics. I also liked that you provided two very clear usage
scenarios for the corpus. 

I have two major criticisms. The first could be easily corrected in case the
paper is accepted, but the second requires more work.

1) There are no statistics about the corpus in this paper. This is absolutely
paramount. When you describe a corpus, there are some information that should
be there. 

I am talking about number of documents (I assume the corpus has 180 documents
(60 essays x 3 drafts), is that correct?), number of tokens (around 400 words
each essay?), number of sentences, etc. 

I assume we are talking about 60 unique essays x 400 words, so about 24,000
words in total. Is that correct? If we take the 3 drafts we end up with about
72,000 words but probably with substantial overlap between drafts.

A table with this information should be included in the paper.

2) If the aforementioned figures are correct, we are talking about a very small
corpus. I understand the difficulty of producing hand-annotated data, and I
think this is one of the strengths of your work, but I am not sure about how
helpful this resource is for the NLP community as a whole. Perhaps such a
resource would be better presented in a specialised workshop such as BEA or a
specialised conference on language resources like LREC instead of a general NLP
conference like ACL.

You mentioned in the last paragraph that you would like to augment the corpus
with more annotation. Are you also willing to include more essays?

Comments/Minor:

- As you have essays by native and non-native speakers, one further potential
application of this corpus is native language identification (NLI).

- p. 7: "where the unigram feature was used as the baseline" - "word unigram".
Be more specific.

- p. 7: "and the SVM classifier was used as the classifier." - redundant.

machine_text: This paper presents a very nice application of deep reinforcement learning to solve the information access problem. This problem has been a long-standing challenge for dialogue agents that have to interface with users. The agent needs to be able to find the information it needs while keeping the user satisfied. The authors use a Monte Carlo Tree Search agent with a deep Q-learning algorithm. They present a number of experiments to evaluate the performance of their model. The model is able to achieve good performance on a novel, unobserved domain, showing that it has learned generic skills for information access. I do have some concerns about the application of deep Q-learning to this problem. As the authors note, the number of interaction steps required by the MCTS agent to perform a search is much higher than for a human. I wonder if a actor-critic architecture could alleviate this, by using a target network to evaluate the policy directly in parallel to the policy network. I also wonder if shared environment simulation could help reduce the environmental mismatch. Finally, another interesting observation was that the BLEU score of the generated responses was low. This could be because the model was optimizing a cheap surrogate task (finding the next item in the training distribution) instead of trying to generate realistic responses, for example by using a variational autoencoder. I think the approach in this paper could be very useful for developing agents that could perform information searches in a cost-efficient and scalable manner. I recommend this paper for publication with a few changes, as outlined below.

The paper Towards End-to-End Reinforcement Learning of Dialogue Agents for Information Access (Bi) addresses a very important problem in AI i.e. Dialogue Management. Most contemporary applications of AI in Dialogue Management focus on specific sub-problems, such as Open Information Extraction or Conversation Management, and lack the ability to coordinate the different sub-tasks through a high-level goal, which is typically some form of information gathering. This prevents the system from solving more complicated problems or realizing the full potential of the available technologies. In this paper, the authors propose a fully end-to-end trainable system that manages to jointly learn all sub-tasks required for successful dialogue management: Open Information Extraction, Information Gathering, Organizational Goal Arbitration and Natural Language Generation. The resulting model is able to deal with long-term dependencies, over-generalization problems and domain shift, and is able to achieve competitive performance on benchmark datasets. This work is a major step forward in applied AI in Dialogue Management and could have many important applications in e.g. Helpdesk or Technical Support. The authors accomplish their goal by using the latest technologies available in the field, such as Transformers for Open Information Extraction and Dialogue Management, Prioritized History-dependent Learning for Organizational Goal Arbitration and BERT for Natural Language Generation. The model is trained in an end-to-end fashion with simple loss functions, without the need for manually crafted features. The model is trained on the largest available dataset of Dialogue Management tasks. The main contribution of this work is the introduction of a new, more principled way of training interactive neural networks with the aim of coordinating the sub-tasks of Information Extraction, Organizational Goal Arbitration and Natural Language Generation. I strongly recommend this paper to researchers working in this field, and I look forward to new directions of this line of research.

This paper proposes KB-InfoBot - a multi-turn dialogue agent which helps users search Knowledge Bases (KBs) without composing complicated queries. Such goal-oriented dialogue agents typically need to interact with an external database to access real-world knowledge. Previous systems achieved this by issuing a symbolic query to the KB to retrieve entries based on their attributes. However, such symbolic operations break the differentiability of the system and prevent end-to-end training of neural dialogue agents. In this paper, we address this limitation by replacing symbolic queries with an induced soft retrieval process. Integrating the soft retrieval process with a reinforcement learner leads to higher task success rate and reward in both simulations and against real users. We also present a fully neural end-to-end agent, trained entirely from user feedback, and discuss its application towards personalized dialogue agents. 4 concerns I have about this paper: 1. Although the system could help users search knowledge bases without composing complicated queries, the paper only presented the dialogue process in simulations with a synthetic KB called MuQA, which is not real-world capable. We couldn't evaluate the paper's main claim which is that the proposed system helps users search KBs without composing complicated queries. 2. It would be more convincing if the system could also be applied to a real KB like Open Thinking Kleene (OTK) which contains more real-world meaning and has been used in commercial search engines. 3. In the system, the user would firstly encode her query to a numerical representation. Then the query is passed into a GAN-based approach to generate a posterior distribution over entities in the KB. Finally, the dialogue system selects the entity corresponding to the maximum of the posterior as the output response. Instead of calculating the softmax over all entities in the KB, we could only select the top k entities with high probabilities as the output. This method is more concise and efficient. 4. Figure 1 and 3 in the paper are similar, which makes it hard to understand the model structure and parameters in the paper.

Towards End-to-End Reinforcement Learning of Dialogue Agents for Information Access, directly end-to-end train a dialogue agent to search knowledge bases for users, which can answer the user's complex questions directly and efficiently without composing complicated queries, this is a good and meaningful work for the AI community and has great application prospects. The main strength of this work is that it solves the problems that previous symbolic-operation-based dialogue agents can not run, which can break the differentiability of the system and prevent end-to-end training of neural dialogue agents. The soft query method solves the problem that the dialogue agent is hard to train, and has a high application prospect in personalized dialogue agents. The main weakness of this work is that it only shows the soft retrieval process, without giving a concrete mechanism to get the soft information, so that the theory is not explained clearly. The usage of soft information in practice needs to combine with a probability density distillation algorithm, and the paper does not mention how to train a dialogue agent using the neural network architecture they designed. The combination of these two aspects will lead to more complex system structure, and the proof of the convergence requires more work. ty given The main strength of this work is that it solves the problems that previous symbolic-operation-based dialogue agents can not run, which can break the differentiability of the system and prevent end-to-end training of neural dialogue agents. human_text:
This paper presents a dialogue agent where the belief tracker and the dialogue
manager are jointly optimised using the reinforce algorithm. It learns from
interaction with a user simulator. There are two training phases. The first is
an imitation learning phase where the system is initialised using supervising
learning from a rule-based model. Then there is a reinforcement learning phase
where the system has jointly been optimised using the RL objective.

- Strengths: This paper presents a framework where a differentiable access to
the KB is integrated in the joint optimisation. This is the biggest
contribution of the paper. 

- Weaknesses: Firstly, this is not a truly end-to-end system considering the
response generation was handcrafted rather than learnt. Also, their E2E model
actually overfits to the simulator and performs poorly in human evaluation.
This begs the question whether the authors are actually selling the idea of E2E
learning or the soft-KB access. The soft-KB access actually brings consistent
improvement, however the idea of end-to-end learning not so much. The authors
tried to explain the merits of E2E in Figure 5 but I also fail to see the
difference. In addition, the authors didn't motivate the reason for using the
reinforce algorithm which is known to suffer from high variance problem. They
didn't attempt to improve it by using a baseline or perhaps considering the
natural actor-critic algorithm which is known to perform better.

- General Discussion: Apart from the mentioned weaknesses, I think the
experiments are solid and this is generally an acceptable paper. However, if
they crystallised the paper around the idea which actually improves the
performance (the soft KB access) but not the idea of E2E learning the paper
would be better.

machine_text: Authors: Yi Zhang, Hao Zhao, and Shiguang Shan Journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences Title: Fast and Accurate Sequence Labeling with Iterated Dilated Convolutions More thoughts: The paper presents a novel architecture named Iterated Dilated Convolutions (IDCN) for Sequence Labeling (LL), where each word in the sequence is associated with its corresponding label. The paper presents the results of applying this architecture on various public datasets and shows state of the art results. My main thoughts about this paper are: 1. The introduction could do with a bit of elaboration. the first sentence is a bit too short and gives a general idea of the paper but not enough to hold my attention. 2. The abstract is also not suitable for a short paper. Although it gives an idea of the main idea of the paper, the key takeaways are truncated. 3. The introduction provides the background for the problem and the state of the art. But the author should have highlighted the contribution of the paper in the latter part of the introduction. 4. The description of the system is very vague and does not allow me to visualize the system. What does each layer of the system do? How does it interact with the rest of the system? This is important for evaluation and replication purposes. 5. The model and implementation section is very dense and hard to follow. I couldn't understand how the parameters of the model are trained. A step by step procedure will help the reader to follow the process and hence will be less abstract. 6. The evaluation part is also very difficult to follow. It would be easier if the author could provide clear examples of inputs that should be given high or low score and then provide accuracy for that. 7. I also noticed a few Grammatical errors. For example, in the sentence "With an F1 measure of 91.5%, the IDCN model we proposed performs best on these datasets in this setting.". The word "this" is missing in the second sentence of this paragraph.

This paper presents a method for fast and accurate sequence labeling with Iterated Dilated Convolutions (IDC). The IDC module is an effective solution to the time warping problem in sequence labeling. However, the efficiency of IDC is limited by its diagonal approximation. In this paper, a novel iterative dilated convolution (iDconv) is proposed to overcome the diagonal approximation, leading to faster convergence and better performance. In addition, the iDconv can be incorporated with other efficient structures to further improve the performance. Finally, extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method on several widely used benchmarks. ice strengths: The method proposed in this paper can be readily extended to other structures such as the standard 1D convolution by merely replacing iDconv with DConv. The proposed iDconv has low computational cost, and can be readily deployed in both cloud and edge platforms. Moreover, the low computational cost allows it to be used in hardware-constrained devices such as mobile phones. Weaknesses: 1) The proposed iDconv is designed for fixed-size sequences, while in reality many tasks contain variable-length sequences such as text. To address this problem, one solution is to find a fixed-size period that covers the longest sequence, and apply the proposed method to this fixed-size period. 2) The proposed method uses $K$ datasets, and is sensitive to the choice of $K$. In the experiments, we provide methods for determining $K$ without consuming much additional cost.

Overall this paper presents a very compelling alternative to Bi-LSTM-CRF for solving sequence labeling tasks. The improvements are not only in terms of accuracy but also in terms of speed, especially over Bi-LSTM-CRF on extremely long sequences (e.g., hundreds of sentences). The proposed architecture is also simpler and easier to train. More importantly, the parallelism of the model makes it feasible to use for real-time applications. I highly recommend this paper to the readers. I have two main comments. The first is about the link to the model description, which is currently only applicable to the Bi-LSTM-CRF model. I think the readership of KDD will understand the difference between Bi-LSTM-CRF and IDCNN very well, but I would suggest making the IDCNN model available for evaluation on all three tasks. Second, in Table 2, you report the accuracy for SGD and RMSProp. In the section "A simple baseline for comparing against Bi-LSTM-CRF and IDCNN", you mention that the perplexity is not very different between SGD and RMSProp. But the corresponding accuracy column in the table seems to suggest that accuracy does decrease for the SGD setting. I think you meant to put RMSProp there instead. Also, you might want to add some references to related work, such as the fixed-context LSTM paper by van Noord (2015), as well as the sentence-level CNN model of Kim (2016).

Bi-directional LSTMs have emerged as a standard method for obtaining per-token vector representations serving as input to various token labeling tasks (whether followed by Viterbi prediction or independent classification). This paper proposes an alternative to Bi-LSTMs for this purpose: iterated dilated convolutional neural networks (ID-CNNs), which have better capacity than traditional CNNs for large context and structured prediction. We describe a distinct combination of network structure, parameter sharing and training procedures that is not only more accurate than Bi-LSTM-CRFs, but also 8x faster at test time on long sequences. Moreover, ID-CNNs with independent classification enable a dramatic 14x test-time speedup, while still attaining accuracy comparable to the Bi-LSTM-CRF. We further demonstrate the ability of ID-CNNs to combine evidence over long sequences by demonstrating their improved accuracy on whole-document (rather than per-sentence) inference. Unlike LSTMs whose sequential processing on sentences of length N requires O(N) time even in the face of parallelism, IDCNNs permit fixed-depth convolutions to run in parallel across entire documents. Today when many companies run basic NLP on the entire web and large-volume traffic, faster methods are paramount to saving time and energy costs. This work proposes to apply dilated convolutions for sequence tagging
(specifically, named entity recognition). It also introduces some novel ideas
(sharing the dilated convolution block, predicting the tags at each convolution
level), which I think will prove useful to the community. The paper performs
extensive ablation experiments to show the effectiveness of their approach.
I found the writing to be very clear, and the experiments were exceptionally
thorough.

Strengths:  
- Extensive experiments against various architectures (LSTM, LSTM + CRF)       
- Novel architectural/training ideas (sharing blocks)  

Weaknesses:  
- Only applied to English NER--this is a big concern since the title of the
paper seems to reference sequence-tagging directly.  
- Section 4.1 could be clearer. For example, I presume there is padding to make
sure the output resolution after each block is the same as the input
resolution.  Might be good to mention this.  
- I think an ablation study of number of layers vs perf might be interesting.

RESPONSE TO AUTHOR REBUTTAL:

Thank you very much for a thoughtful response. Given that the authors have
agreed to make the content be more specific to NER as opposed to
sequence-tagging, I have revised my score upward.

- Strengths:

The main strength promised by the paper is the speed advantage at the same
accuracy level.

- Weaknesses:

Presentation of the approach leaves a lot to be desired. Sections 3 and 4 need
to be much clearer, from concept definition to explaining the architecture and
parameterization. In particular Section 4.1 and the parameter tieing used need
to be crystal clear, since that is one of the main contributions of the paper.

More experiments supporting the vast speed improvements promised need to be
presented. The results in Table 2 are good but not great. A speed-up of 4-6X is
nothing all that transformative.

- General Discussion:

What exactly is "Viterbi prediction"? The term/concept is far from established;
the reader could guess but there must be a better way to phrase it.

Reference Weiss et al., 2015 has a typo.

I think the main suggestion you can make here is to clarify how you compare the response against the expected answer, as it is somewhat hidden in the middle of the paper. For example, you could move the table with your results next to the X and Y axes, so that a reader could see at a glance whether a response is a good or bad match to the expected answer. Also, as a point of style, it might be good to put a bit more explanation in the Abstract about what the test is designed to assess. empowered AI faces a critical dilemma: although the system is equipped with superb perception and intelligence, it lacks of communicative competence, i.e. the ability to engage in a effective discourse with humans. This paper addresses this challenge by proposing a novel Turing Test for assessing automated dialogue responses. Instead of judging the answer based on a human rater's opinion, we propose to evaluate the response against the ground truth response given by a human in a response set. The rationale is that automated response evaluation should not be influenced by social consideration or human aesthetic in contrast to human evaluation. We conduct the first public response evaluation based on a large-scale human annotated dialogue corpus, and further demonstrate the feasibility of the test by applying it to an automatic response generation system. The obtained results indicate that the proposed test is able to measure the competence gap between humans and systems in a more objective and fine-grained manner.

The learning to evaluate dialogue responses paper addresses an important problem in the field of natural language processing - automatic testing of conversational systems. Existing evaluation measures such asMeteor-1 and Romer-1 rely on the challenge/response paradigm where the system response is paired with an annotated ground-truth response. This not only requires specialized evaluation infrastructure (often in the form of a rendered response prompt on a mobile phone), but also limits evaluation to responses built during training. In contrast, evaluating on an open-domain test collection such as Ubuntu Dialogue Corpus requires the response to be classified into one of the predefined categories (8 in the case of Ubuntu Dialogue Corpus). However, it is difficult to apply human evaluations to these broad-brush measures. The paper takes a first step towards building an automatic testing paradigm that can evaluate dialogue systems on a more generic and fine-grained level. The proposed approach, Labeled Policy Variation (LPV), learns a model that can score responses according to a fine-grained task metric, such as task-specific sentiment score, based on a small number of automatically collected human feedback. LPV essentially combines supervised classification (since the response scores are valued according to a specific metric, the classification task is in fact partially supervised) with self-supervised learning (since the response is evaluated by simulating a dialogue interaction in an end-to-end system without requiring annotations of the response prompt). LPV can therefore be used to build an automatic testing paradigm that does not require specialized evaluation infrastructure, can be used to evaluate a wide range of response types (not only challenge/response dialogues but also chitchat scenarios), and is applicable to both domain-specific and open-domain test collections. One interesting aspect of LPV is that it is able to automatically generate examples of responses with high predicted scores which may not be part of the training dataset. Such out-of-domain examples can be used to further train the model by subjecting the model to "exposure to the environment" - in this case, generating high-scoring response examples that the model might not have encountered before (which is particularly useful for training on Ubuntu Dialogue Corpus where there are relatively fewer responses). As an example of the potential applications of this work, consider an autonomous car navigating to an unknown destination in an urban environment. For the vehicle to be useful, it has to be able to deal with the challenges the urban environment might pose to the autonomous driving algorithm (e.g. lack of a reliable GPS signal or traffic signals). While a human driver is able to cope with such situations by taking time to think through the problem, an autonomous driving algorithm has limited reasoning ability and if the situation is tricky, it could take the human driver much longer to find a solution. In this case, the automated testing paradigm can be used to evaluate the dialogue system's ability to solve the problem in such challenging situations. In this example, the response evaluation would be measured on a per-step basis (i.e. for each turn of a dialog, the model would learn the mapping from the system response to a score between 0-1), but the idea is the same: by having a model that can evaluate dialogue responses at multiple levels of granularity (e.g. response-level and turn-level), one could evaluate the system on scenarios that are both fine-grained (e.g. identify incorrect mapping of a particular response to a dialogue turn) and coarse-grained (e.g. overall system failure to solve the entire dialogue task). In conclusion, this paper presents a significant step forward in the direction of building an automatic testing paradigm that can evaluate dialogue systems on a fine-grained, open-endedly applicable level. One major drawback of the paper is that the model performance is evaluated using validation set and tested on the test set. Such “cross-validation” for model selection is necessary, but there is a potential for circularity in that the model is evaluated on the very same test set it is evaluated on. The paper attempts to alleviate this problem by breaking up the test set into small pieces and using a separate test-on-test method that randomly partitions the test set into disjoint pieces. However, given the small size of the training set, a substantial amount of stratified sampling has to be applied to create enough training instances for the model to learn an unbiased estimation of the model parameters, and such stratified sampling may not fully avoid the potential for bias. Another drawback of the paper is that the training procedure is not fully end-to-end. Two distinct components have to be trained separately and in parallel: the model for evaluating the responses and the model for picking the answer from the pool. Overall I find the work interesting and well-organized. however, I have some comments as below: 1.The method can be potentially useful, but at the current state it’s way too expensive to even try on a large scale system. In order to make it practically useful, the current “Collecting and Averaging” step should be removed. The model can just take in user utterances directly. 2.In the current “Collecting and Averaging” step, the author collect the human scores from a small set of human judges, which can’t reflect the real distribution of the scores. For example, for a high BLEU response, one may give a low score, while for a low BLEU but acceptable response, one may give a high score. The “averaging” step is actually the key here, but it should be more fine-grained, like giving more weights to some certain scores like “important for the success of the turn” / “useful for the follow up” etc. 3.Even though the final model does train on human judger scores, the model can still generalize to new domains. But there are many pairs of domains that have high human correlation but low model correlation (as shown in Table 2). For example, “book recommendation” vs “film recommendation” etc. I don’t think model can reach human level on such a large scale unstructured domain. I think the k532 data should be split into many smaller domains.

- Strengths:
This paper proposes an evaluation metric for automatically evaluating the
quality of dialogue responses in non-task-oriented dialogue. The metric
operates on continuous vector space representations obtained by using RNNs and
it comprises two components: one that compares the context and the given
response and the other that compares a reference response and the given
response. The comparisons are conducted by means of dot product after
projecting the response into corresponding context and reference response
spaces. These projection matrices are learned by minimizing the squared error
between the model predictions and human annotations.

I think this work gives a remarkable step forward towards the evaluation of
non-task-oriented dialogue systems. Different from previous works in this area,
where pure semantic similarity was pursued, the authors are going beyond pure
semantic similarity in a very elegant manner by learning projection matrices
that transform the response vector into both context and reference space
representations. I am very curious on how your projection matrices M and N
differ from the original identity initialization after training the models. I
think the paper will be more valuable if further discussion on this is
introduced, rather than focusing so much on resulting correlations. 

- Weaknesses:

The paper also leaves lots questions related to the implementation. For
instance, it is not clear whether the human scores used to train and evaluate
the system were single AMT annotations or the resulting average of few
annotations. Also, it is not clear how the dataset was split into
train/dev/test and whether n-fold cross validation was conducted or not. Also,
it would be nice to better explain why in table 2 correlation for ADEM related
scores are presented for the validation and test sets, while for the other
scores they are presented for the full dataset and test set. The section on
pre-training with VHRED is also very clumsy and confusing, probably it is
better to give less technical details but a better high level explanation of
the pre-training strategy and its advantages.

- General Discussion:

“There are many obvious cases where these metrics fail, as they are often
incapable of considering the semantic similarity between responses (see Figure
1).” Be careful with statements like this one. This is not a problem of
semantic similarity! Opposite to it, the problem is that completely different
semantic cues might constitute pragmatically valid responses. Then, semantic
similarity itself is not enough to evaluate a dialogue system response.
Dialogue system response evaluation must go beyond semantics (This is actually
what your M and N matrices are helping to do!!!) 

“an accurate model that can evaluate dialogue response quality automatically
— what could be considered an automatic Turing test —“ The original
intention of Turing test was to be a proxy to identify/define intelligent
behaviour. It actually proposes a test on intelligence based on an
“intelligent” machine capability to imitate human behaviour in such a way
that it would be difficult for a common human to distinguish between such a
machine responses and actual human responses. It is of course related to
dialogue system performance, but I think it is not correct to say that
automatically evaluating dialogue response quality is an automatic Turing test.
Actually, the title itself “Towards an Automatic Turing Test” is somehow
misleading!

“the simplifying assumption that a ‘good’ chatbot is one whose responses
are scored highly on appropriateness by human evaluators.” This is certainly
the correct angle to introduce the problem of non-task-oriented dialogue
systems, rather than “Turing Test”. Regarding this, there has been related
work you might like to take a look at, as well as to make reference to, in the
WOCHAT workshop series (see the shared task description and corresponding
annotation guidelines).

used”
