This paper presents an in-depth analysis of current state-of-the-art results on the SemantProt 2018 shared task: Deep Semantic Role Labeling. The goal of this shared task is to provide a publicly available benchmark for evaluating systems that can generate semantic role labels for English passages. The paper covers various interesting analysis of the current state-of-the-art models and datasets along with the analysis of what works and what doesn’t work for the state of the art results on the SemantProt 2018 dataset. The paper also discusses open questions and possible research directions that can leverage the success of current state-of-the-art results to achieve higher performance on this dataset. The main strength of this paper is the in-depth analysis of the current state-of-the-art results on the SemantProt 2018 dataset, along with the discussion of open questions and possible research directions that can leverage the success of current state-of-the-art results to achieve higher performance on this dataset. Some of the limitations of the current state-of-the-art models and datasets are not fully explored in the paper. For example, all of the current state-of-the-art models use bi-directional RNNs for encoding sentences. However, many recent works (e.g. using a Graph Attention network instead of RNNs) have shown that sequential information could benefit the task at hand. Some other limitations are already partly solved in the current state-of-the-art results, but not fully explored or investigated in this paper. For example, using external language resources such as large lexicons (e.g. BIO tags) can benefit the task. However, many existing studies only use small, fixed-size lexicons, which may not be sufficient for the state-of-the-art performance on this dataset. Another example is the utilization of automatic coverage metrics for the papers of the SemantProt 2018 shared task. While automatic metrics can be a useful way to evaluate submissions, it can be challenging to fully understand how much effort went into the quality of a submission, and it is hard to tell how well a submission utilizes the limited resource (i.e. provided annotations). An in-depth analysis of the current state-of-the-art results could be of interest to the research community.

Overall this is an informative and well-written paper. I particularly enjoy the detailed overview of previous state-of-the-art SRL approaches and the descriptions of the precise settings used for the new architecture. The introduction briefly sets the stage for the key innovations in the architecture, highlighting the Highway LSTM and constrained decoding. The paper then goes into more detail about each of these innovations, discussing their pros and cons and justifying the choice of the architecture. The Results section compares the new approach to the previous state of the art, with an in-depth analysis of the new strengths and limitations of the architecture. This section is framed as an explanation to the previous state of the art, but could also be read as a possible forecast of how the previous state of the art could develop in the near future. I find this kind of analysis to be an important way of understanding a research area and am glad to see this approach employed here. The paper is concluded with a Future Work section that discusses potential extensions to the current model as well as opportunities for future work in SRL as a whole. I particularly enjoyed the comparison of SRL to other areas in NLP where deep learning has made substantial progress, e.g., document representation and tagging. I only have a few minor suggestions for the paper. In Section 2, you mention that CoNLL’s 2005 and 2012 datasets have different evaluation metrics, but I think this could be made clearer. For instance, could the 2010 data set, which has the same evaluation metrics as 2005 but was later merged into it, be mentioned as an intermediate step? It’s a bit confusing that 2005 and 2012 are used to describe the model without explanation of how they relate to 2010. Also, I think you could provide the reader with a clearer explanation of why the CoNLL’s largest system performance gains occurred between 2009 and 2010 (which I assume is because of the merge of the two data sets). Another point of confusion for me was the specific “style” of SRL systems that the model was evaluated against. I assume you’re referring to the output of a distributed jointly trained SRL and Stanford Stanford Parser, but given the simplicity of this system, it seems like there should be a more detailed explanation of what exactly was evaluated in this setting. In terms of the baseline model used for comparison, you mention that it was a feedforward neural network, but a nearby paragraph mentions that it is unclear how this model was trained, which seems like an important piece of information to include. Furthermore, it would be helpful to provide some context for this model, since feedforward neural networks are usually taken as a baseline for SRL results, so it would be helpful to the reader to understand why this was a baseline model. Finally, a minor issue is that the paper uses the term “BiLSTM” to refer to both the highway LSTM as well as the base LSTM architecture with concatenation between the forward and reverse sequences. It would be helpful to the reader if you made a clearer distinction between these two terms. Overall, this is an excellent introduction to the state of the art in SRL, with clear and detailed explanations of both the previous state of the art and the new model’s strengths and shortcomings. I especially appreciate the in-depth analysis of the strengths and weaknesses of each component of the model. I also like the discussion of how SRL compares to other areas of NLP where deep learning has made substantial progress.

The authors of this paper present a new model for semantic role labeling (SRL), which significantly improves the state of the art. A detailed analyses is conducted to reveal its strengths and limitations. One important limitation is that the model only performs “surface” semantic parsing, which means it operates on the level of lexical verbs and nouns, rather than on the deep semantic relations between these entities. For example, it does not address the question of whether two entities are in the same spatial or temporal location. However, the potential of this work goes beyond this limitation. First, it uses a deep highway BiLSTM architecture which is more efficient in both training and evaluating. Second, the analysis of the limitations shows that this work opens up new possibilities for future research on semantic parsing, such as combining this method with a parser in order to address the meaning of a sentence at a deeper level. esk The paper “Deep Semantic Role Labeling: What Works and What’s Next” presents a new model for semantic role labeling (SRL) that significantly improves the state of the art, along with a detailed analyses to reveal its strengths and limitations. This paper extends Zhou and Xu's ACL 2015 approach to semantic role labeling
based on deep BiLSTMs. In addition to applying recent best practice techniques,
leading to further quantitative improvements, the authors provide an insightful
qualitative analysis of their results. The paper is well written and has a
clear structure. The authors provide a comprehensive overview of related work
and compare results to a representative set of other SRL models that hace been
applied on the same data sets.

I found the paper to be interesting and convincing. It is a welcome research
contribution that not only shows that NNs work well, but also analyzes merits
and shortcomings of an end-to-end learning approach.

- Strengths:

Strong model, insightful discussion/error analysis.

- Weaknesses:

Little to no insights regarding the SRL task itself.

This paper presents a new state-of-the-art deep learning model for semantic
role labeling (SRL) that is a natural extension of the previous
state-of-the-art system (Zhou and Xu, 2015) with recent best practices for
initialization and regularization in the deep learning literature.
The model gives a 10% relative error reduction which is a big gain on this
task. The paper also gives in-depth empirical analyses to reveal the strengths
and the remaining issues, that give a quite valuable information to the

human_text:
- Strengths: this paper addresses (in part) the problem of interpreting Long
Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network models trained to categorize written
justifications in values-affirmation essays. This is definitely an interesting
research question. To do so, the authors want to rely on approaches that have
are standard in experimental psychology. Furthermore, the authors also aim at
validating sociological assumptions via this study.

- Weaknesses: one of the main weaknesses of the paper lies in the fact that the
goals are not clear enough. One overall, ambitious goal put forward by the
authors is to use approaches from experimental psychology to interpret LSTMs.
However, no clear methodology to do so is presented in the paper. On the other
hand, if the goal is to validate sociological assumptions, then one should do
so by studying the relationships between gender markers and the written
justifications, independently on any model. The claim that "expected gender
differences (are) a function of theories of gendered self-construal" is not
proven in the study.

- General Discussion: if the study is interesting, it suffers from several weak
arguments. First of all, the fact that the probability shift of a token in the
LSTM network are correlated with the corresponding SVM coefficients is no proof
that "these probabilities are valid ways to interpret the model". Indeed, (a)
SVM coefficients only reveal part of what is happening in the decision function
of an SVM classifie and (b) it is not because one coefficient provides an
interpretation in one model that a correlated coefficient provides an
explanation in another model. Furthermore, the correlation coefficients are not
that high, so that the point put forward is not really backed up.

As mentioned before, another problem lies in the fact that the authors seem to
hesitate between two goals. It would be better to clearly state one goal and
develop it. Concerning the relation to experimental psychology, which is a
priori an important part of the paper, it would be interesting to develop and
better explain the multilevel bayesian models used to quantify the gender-based
self-construal assumptions. It is very difficult to assess whether the
methodology used here is really appropriate without more details. As this is an
important aspect of the method, it should be further detailed.

- Strengths:
The paper is thoroughly written and discusses its approach compared to
other approaches. The authors are aware that their findings are somewhat
limited regarding the mean F values.

- Weaknesses:
Some minor orthographical mistakes and some repetive clauses. In general the
paper would benefit if the sections 1 and 2 would be shortened to allow the
extension of sections 3 and 4.
The main goal is not laid out clearly enough, which may be a result of the
ambivalence of the paper's goals.

- General Discussion:
Table 1 should only be one column wide, while the figures, especially 3, 5, and
6 would greatly benefit from a two column width.
The paper was not very easy to understand during first read. Major improvements
could be achieved by straightening up the content.

human_text:
This paper describes several ways to encode arbitrarily long sequences of
digits using something called the major system. In the major system, each digit
is mapped to one or more characters representing consonantal phonemes; the
possible mappings between digit and phoneme are predefined. The output of an
encoding is typically a sequence of words constrained such that digits in the
original sequence correspond to characters or digraphs in the output sequence
of words; vowels added surrounding the consonant phonemes to form words are
unconstrained. This paper describes several ways to encode your sequence of
digits such that the output sequence of words is more memorable, generally by
applying syntactic constraints and heuristics.

I found this application of natural language processing concepts somewhat
interesting, as I have not read an ACL paper on this topic before. However, I
found the paper and ideas presented here to have a rather old-school feel. With
much of the focus on n-gram models for generation, frequent POS-tag sequences,
and other heuristics, this paper really could have been written 15-20 years
ago. I am not sure that there is enough novelty in the ideas here to warrant
publication in ACL in 2017. There is no contribution to NLP itself, e.g. in
terms of modeling or search, and not a convincing contribution to the
application area which is just an instance of constrained generation. 

Since you start with one sequence and output another sequence with a very
straightforward monotonic mapping, it seems like a character-based
sequence-to-sequence encoder-decoder model (Sequence to Sequence Learning with
Neural Networks; Sutskever et al. 2014) would work rather well here, very
likely with very fluent output and fewer moving parts (e.g. trigram models and
POS tag and scoring heuristics and postprocessing with a bigram model). You can
use large amounts of training from an arbitrary genre and do not need to rely
on an already-tagged corpus like in this paper, or worry about a parser. This
would be a 2017 paper.

- Strengths:
This paper presents a sentence based approach to generating memorable mnemonics
for numbers. The evaluation study presented in the paper shows that the
sentence based approach indeed produces memorable mnemonics for short 8-digit
numbers (e.g. 86101521 --> Officiate Wasteland).
Overall the paper presents the problem, the background literature and the
solution in sufficient detail. Because memorizing numbers (e.g. phone numbers
and account numbers) is sufficiently common, this is an interesting problem.

- Weaknesses:
The proposed solution does not seem to scale-up well for longer numbers; seems
to work well with 8-digit numbers though. But many numbers that people need to
memorize such as phone numbers and credit card numbers are longer than
8-digits. Besides, a number may have a structure (e.g. a phone number has a
country code + area code + personal number) which people exploit while
memorizing numbers. As stated above, this paper addresses an important problem
but the current solution needs to be improved further (several ideas have been
listed by the authors in section 6).

- General Discussion:
The current presented approach, in comparison to existing approaches, is
promising.

- Strengths:

Tackles a not very explored task, with obvious practical application
Well written and motivated

- Weaknesses:

The only method of validation is a user study, which has several weaknesses.

- Discussion:

The paper investigates various methods to generate memorable mnemonic encodings
of numbers based on the “Major” system. As opposed to other methods that
rely on this system to encode sequences, the methods proposed in this work
return a single sequence (instead of a set of candidates) which is selected to
improve memorability. Since “memorability” is an ambiguous criterion to
optimize for, the authors explore various syntactic approaches that aim for
short and likely sentences.  Their final model uses a POS template sampled form
a set of “nice” structures, and a tri-gram language model to fill in the
slots of the template. 

The proposed approach is well motivated: the section on existing tools places
this approach in the context of previous work on security and memorability. The
authors point to results showing that passwords based on mnemonic phrases offer
the best of both worlds in terms of security (vs random passwords) and
memorability (vs naive passwords). This solid motivation will appease those
readers initially skeptical about the importance/feasibility of such
techniques. 

In terms of the proposed methods, the baselines and n-gram models
(unsurprisingly) generate bad encodings. The results in table 2 show that
indeed Chunk and Sentence produce shorter sentences, but for short digits such
as this one, how relevant are the additional characteristics of these methods
(eg. POS replacements, templates etc)? It seems that a simple n-gram model with
the number-of-digits-per-trigram reweighing could perform well here. 

The evaluation is weaker than the rest of the paper. My main concern is that a
one-time memorization setting seems inadequate to test this framework. Mnemonic
techniques are meant to aid recall after repeated memorization exercises, not
just a single “priming” event. Thus, a more informative setting would have
had the users be reminded of the number and encoding daily over a period of
time, and after a “buffer period”, test their recall. This would also more
closely resemble the real-life conditions in which such a technique would be
used (e.g. for password memorization).

In terms of the results, the difference between (long term) recall and
recognition is interesting. Do the authors have some explanation for why in the
former most methods performed similarly, but in the latter “Sentence”
performs better? Could it be that the use of not very likely words (e.g.
"officiate", in the example provided) make the encodings hard to remember but
easy to spot? If this were the case, it would somewhat defeat the purpose of
the approach.

Also, it would be useful for the reader if the paper provided  (e.g. in an
appendix) some examples of the digits/encodings that the users were presented
during the study, to get a better sense of the difficulty of recall and the
quality of the encodings. 

- Suggestions:

It would be nice to provide some background on the Major system for those not
familiar with it, which I suspect might be many in the ACL audience, myself
included. Where does it come from? What’s the logic behind those
digit-phoneme maps?

The introduction is somewhat difficult to read because of its extremely dense format. I suggest that the authors consider condensing the text, and possibly using a different formatting style. Related to the above comment, I also find the organization of the introduction somewhat difficult to follow. The introduction covers a large number of general concepts, each of which is introduced in a single sentence, making it difficult to get a complete sense of how the concepts are connected. I suggest that the authors consider combining some of the general concepts into groupings, and then structuring the paragraphs based on these groupings. In line with the suggestions above, the first part of the paper describes the problem setting, definitions of terms, and a motivating example of constructing a hierarchical category tree. I think that this part could be improved by including more detailed descriptions of the problem setting and definitions of terms. The next section describes a baseline method for hierarchical learning based on autoencoders. This method uses bottom-up and top-down connections to allow for the sharing of representation information between adjacent layers in the network. The main focus of this section is a novel algorithm for constructing a bottom-up connection from a set of feature representation vectors. I think that it would be useful to discuss this algorithm in more detail, and perhaps provide some example code in Python/Pytorch. Next, the paper describes the main ideas and contributions of the proposed fusion learning architecture. I think that the paper could be improved by linking to existing works on neural network architectures that are similar to the proposed architecture. Also, I think that a more detailed comparison with existing works would be useful. For example, it would be useful to mention whether the proposed architecture is related to attention-based neural networks or deep neural networks. It would also be helpful to provide some details about how the fusion learning architecture differs from other neural network architectures. The paper then describes the proposed method for constructing semantic hierarchies using the fusion learning architecture. As a general comment, I think that it would be useful to mention in the text whether the proposed method automatically constructs a fully-connected tree or whether the method requires user input to specify the shape of the tree. Also, it would be useful to discuss how the proposed method deals with situations in which multiple trees can be constructed from the same dataset. In particular, I think that it would be useful to mention how multiple trees can be evaluated for consistency with respect to each other. The final section of the paper describes experiments based on two different datasets. The main points of this section are that it is found that the proposed method is capable of constructing semantic hierarchies and that the time performance of the proposed method is good. In particular, it is found that the average construction time for a 5-level hierarchy is 2 seconds. I think that it would be useful to discuss the results more thoroughly, and perhaps include some examples of hierarchically constructed trees for each level of the hierarchy. I think that the paper is interesting and of significant value, and I congratulate the authors on making these contributions. I also think that it is useful to discuss a number of details about the proposed approach.

This paper presents a new approach for constructing semantic hierarchies using Fusion Learning. The approach is an evolution of the existing LBD (Latent Dirichlet Allocation) based methods, which learns the hierarchy structures by capturing the global and global correlations among all the categories. The proposed Fusion Learning approach captures the hierarchy relationships by learning the global and local dependency between categories. The resulted fusion model can not only capture the long term and short term dependencies, but also help to identify the hierarchical relationships for new categories. The experiments on two public datasets show that the Fusion Learning based method can outperform the existing LBD based methods in various measure, which validates the effectiveness of the proposed approach m strength: the proposed method has a higher generalization ability, because it can capture the global and local dependency between categories. weaknesses: the limitation of the fusion model is that it is difficult to interpret. em: the proposed Fusion Learning can better capture the long term and short term dependencies, and can help to identify the hierarchical relationships for new categories. em: the existing LBD based methods can capture the global and global correlations among all the categories. In this paper, authors propose a novel fusion learning architecture to automatically discover hypernym-hyponym relations, using word embeddings as base. The model first encode each word into high-dimensional vector, then employ a simple lexical structure rule to assist the model in discovering hypernym-hyponym relation. Finally, authors demonstrate the model can be easily adapt to any languages with simple word2vec vectors. The main contribution of this paper is a fusion learning architecture, which combines two different learning methods to achieve better performance, by reducing randomness and simplifying the learning algorithm. Moreover, the language-independence of this model makes it widely applicable to other languages. The model can be easily extended to other NLP tasks by only modifying the inference algorithm, which makes it a general model. Moreover, since the lexicalized structure provides some prior knowledge about the dataset, this model is very easy to train and its performance is very good. Although this model achieves promising performance on a specific dataset, it still has some limitations in application. For example, model cannot find some specific relations that are only valid in specific context, for example, Germany is a part of EU. **Problem/question** **Solution** **Improvement over existing method** ---------------------- ---------------------------- -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Problem Semantic Hierarchies Construction of a framework for automatically discovering hypernym-? question relations by machine generation based on a fusion learning architecture Strengths and weakness Hierarchical representation Fusion learning architecture can be easily extended to other NLP tasks Strength Lexical structure The model can be easily adapted to any language with simple word2vec vectors Weakness Word embedding technique The model depends on word embedding technique which needs external resources to compute and cannot find some specific relations that are only valid in specific context, for example, Germany is a part of EU

The authors propose a method for Neural Machine Translation (NMT) by leveraging a binary code to represent a variable-length source sentence. The binary code is predicted by a neural network and its elements reflect the probability of each character being terminated. These probabilities are then used to create a binary decision variable where 1s are replaced by termination characters and 0s remain, which is further fed to an NMT model. The proposed method was evaluated on several public datasets and results show that using binary code instead of conventional machine word counts can lead to higher BLEU scores. The method also shows the best performance on variable-length sentence translations. However, this approach requires preprocessing the training data to remove unknown words and special characters and using byte arrays for predictions instead of LSTM cells. overwhelming This is a well-motivated and interesting approach to Neural Machine Translation (NMT). The main contributions of this paper are as following: 1. They propose a new method for calculating the output layer of neural machine translation systems. The method can reduce the computation time/memory requirements of the output layer to be logarithmic in the vocabulary size in the best case. 2. They introduce two advanced approaches to improve the robustness of the proposed model: using error-correcting codes and combining softmax and binary codes. The proposed methods can achieve BLEU scores that approach the softmax, while reducing memory usage to the order of less than 1/10 and improving decoding speed on CPUs by x5 to x10. The approach in this paper can be applied to other neural machine translation systems with similar structures. I think this paper is interesting and worthy of attention for three reasons: 1. It proposes a method for calculating the output layer of neural machine translation systems. With this method, the computation complexity and storage requirements of the output layer is reduced. This can have a significant influence on the efficiency and scalability of large-scale training. 2. It introduces two advanced approaches to improve the robustness of the proposed model. These methods can improve the model stability and adaptability. 3. It performs well in BLEU, while reducing memory usage to the order of less than 1/10 and improving the speed on CPUs by x5 to x10. In the future, I expect the method in this paper to become even more widely used. However, as this method only considers the computation complexity and storage requirements, other evaluation indicators may be affected. Therefore, I make the following suggestion: 1. The accuracy of the model should be improved by introducing other knowledge or methods. For example, in addition to error-correcting codes, the model can also use other knowledge, such as character-level knowledge, to improve its robustness. 2. - Weaknesses:

- General Discussion:
This paper proposes an efficient prediction method for neural machine
translation, which predicts a binary code for each word, to reduce the
complexity of prediction. The authors also proposed to use the improved (error
correction) binary codes method to improve the prediction accuracy and the
hybrid softmax/binary model to balance the prediction accuracy and efficiency.
The proposed methods can save memory and improve decoding speed without losing
(or a little loss) performance. I think this is a good paper.

- Strengths:
  This paper is well written, and with clear, well-designed
  figures. The reader can easily understand the methodology even only
  with those figures.

  Predicting the binary code directly is a clever way to reduce the
  parameter space, and the error-correction code just works
  surprisingly well. I am really surprised by how 44 bits can achieve
  26 out of 31 BLEU.  
  The parameter reducing technique described in this work is
  orthogonal to current existing methods: weight pruning and
  sequence-level knowledge distilling.

  The method here is not restricted by Neural Machine Translation, and
  can be used in other tasks as long as there is a big output
  vocabulary.  

- Weaknesses:
  The most annoying point to me is that in the relatively large
  dataset (ASPEC), the best proposed model is still 1 BLEU point lower
  than the softmax model. What about some even larger dataset, like
  the French-English? There are at most 12 million sentences
  there. Will the gap be even larger?

  Similarly, what's the performance on some other language pairs ?

  Maybe you should mention this paper,
  https://arxiv.org/abs/1610.00072. It speeds up the decoding speed by
  10x and the BLEU loss is less than 0.5.  

- General Discussion:

The paper describes a parameter reducing method for large vocabulary
softmax. By applying the error-corrected code and hybrid with softmax,
its BLEU approaches that of the orignal full vocab softmax model.

One quick question: what is the hidden dimension size of the models?
I couldn't find this in the experiment setup.

The 44 bits can achieve 26 out of 31 BLEU on E2J, that was
surprisingly good. However, how could you increase the number of bits
to increase the classification power ? 44 is too small, there's plenty
of room to use more bits and the computation time on GPU won't even
change.

Another thing that is counter-intuitive is that by predicting the
binary code, the model is actually predicting the rank of the
words. So how should we interpret these bit-embeddings ? There seems
no semantic relations of all the words that have odd rank. Is it
because the model is so powerful that it just remembers the data ?

- Strengths:
This paper has high originality, proposing a fundamentally different way of
predicting words from a vocabulary that is more efficient than a softmax layer
and has comparable performance on NMT. If successful, the approach could be
impactful because it speeds up prediction.

This paper is nice to read with great diagrams. it's very clearly presented --
I like cross-referencing the models with the diagrams in Table 2. Including
loss curves is appreciated.

- Weaknesses:
Though it may not be possible in the time remaining, it would be good to see a
comparison (i.e. BLEU scores) with previous related work like hierarchical
softmax and differentiated softmax.

The paper is lacking a linguistic perspective on the proposed method. Compared
to a softmax layer and hierarchical/differentiated softmax, is binary code
prediction a natural way to predict words? Is it more or less similar to how a
human might retrieve words from memory? Is there a theoretical reason to
believe that binary code based approaches should be more or less suited to the
task than softmax layers?

Though the paper promises faster training speeds in the introduction, Table 3
shows only modest (less than x2) speedups for training. Presumably this is
because much of the training iteration time is consumed by other parts of the
network. It would be useful to see the time needed for the output layer
computation only.

- General Discussion:
It would be nice if the survey of prior work in 2.2 explicitly related those
methods to the desiderata in the introduction (i.e. specify which they
satisfy).

Some kind of analysis of the qualitative strengths and weaknesses of the binary
code prediction would be welcome -- what kind of mistakes does the system make,

differentiated softmax?

The article "A New Formula for Vietnamese Text Readability Assessment" by Tuan H. Truong is an attempt to address the issue of readability assessment for written material in the Vietnamese language. Although there are many tools available to perform this assessment, these were originally designed for English-language texts. As Vietnam develops as a country, many of its citizens now have access to written content in the Vietnamese language, but this remains an official language that is difficult to read for the general public. The creation of a tool to address this issue would be a significant step forward for the country. The article introduces a formula for calculating the Flesch Reading Ease (FRE) and Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level (FKGL) of a text. It appears to have been constructed using a large sample of Vietnamese text and using the FRE and FKGL values for a sample of English texts as a baseline. This allows the calculation of a Vietnamese FRE and FKGL value for any text. While this might seem like a trivial improvement on current methods for assessing readability, it actually has several notable shortcomings. First, the article fails to acknowledge that there is significant grammatical complexity in the Vietnamese language compared to English. While this adds to the text’s readability, existing tools do not take this into account and are thus underestimating the text’s difficulty. Second, the article seems to ignore punctuation and capitalisation, which in my experience are more significant factors in determining the text’s readability than words’ total lexical complexity. Third, the article does not appear to take into account other factors that affect FRE and FKGL values, such as sample text type or the source of the text (presuming that it is a print version rather than an online source). While it is certainly possible to construct a reasonable estimate of the FRE and FKGL of a text, the article’s proposed method appears to be inadequate for this purpose. Despite these shortcomings, this article represents a significant improvement over current readability assessment methods for the Vietnamese language. The creation of such a tool would allow Vietnam to evaluate its own written material and evaluate education campaigns targeted at those with lower literacy.

as well as the other Vietnamese metrics and datasets that the authors cite. 

Another problem is that while previous readability indices were more selective
and classified content into granular levels corresponding to grade levels (for
instance), the authors use a coarse classification scheme to label documents as
easy, medium and hard which makes the metric uninteresting. (Also, why not use
a classifier?)

The work is probably a bit too pre-mature and suffers from significant
weaknesses to be accepted at this stage. I would encourage the authors to
incorporate suggested feedback to make it better. 

The paper also has quite a few grammatical errors which should be addressed in
any future submission.

The authors present a new formula for assessing readability of Vietnamese
texts. The formula is developed based on a multiple regression analysis with
three features. Furthermore, the authors have developed and annotated a new
text corpus with three readability classes (easy, middle, hard).

Research on languages other than English is interesting and important,
especially when it comes to low-resource languages. Therefore, the corpus might
be a nice additional resource for research (but it seems that the authors will
not publish it - is that right?). However, I don't think the paper is
convincing in its current shape or will influence future research. Here are my
reasons:

- The authors provide no reasons why there is a need for delevoping a new
formula for readability assessments, given that there already exist two
formulas for Vietnamese with almost the same features. What are the
disadvantages of those formulas and why is the new formula presented in this
paper better?

- In general, the experimental section lacks comparisons with previous work and
analysis of results. The authors claim that the accuracy of their formula (81%
on their corpus) is "good and can be applied in practice". What would be the
accuracy of other formulas that already exist and what are the pros and cons of
those existing formulas compared to the new one?

- As mentioned before, an analysis of results is missing, e.g. which word /
sentence lengths / number of difficult words are considered as easy/middle/hard
by their model?

- A few examples how their formula could be applied in a practical application
would be nice as well.

- The related work section is rather a "background" section since it only
presents previously published formulas. What I'm missing is a more general
discussion of related work. There are some papers that might be interesting for
that, e.g., DuBay 2004: "The principles of readability", or Rabin 1988:
"Determining difficulty levels of text written in languages other than English"

- Since Vietnamese is syllable-based and not word-based, I'm wondering how the
authors get "words" in their study. Do they use a particular approach for
merging syllables? And if yes, which approach do they use and what's the
accuracy of the approach?

- All in all, the content of the paper (experiments, comparisons, analysis,
discussion, related work) is not enough for a long paper.

Additional remarks:

- The language needs improvements

- Equations: The usage of parentheses and multiplying operators is inconsistent

- Related works section: The usage of capitalized first letters is inconsistent

machine_text: Overall, this is a well-written paper. The introduction describes the problem the paper is addressing clearly. The methods are described in sufficient detail and additional resources are proposed for replication. The Discussion summarizes the key findings and presents potential limitations of the work. I have some suggestions for improving the paper. 1. I was not fully convinced by the presentation of the model. It is presented as a single model with a single attention mechanism. But the paper actually describes 3 versions of the model with the same attention mechanism: Gated-CNN, Gated-LSTM, and Gated-Non-Linear. I think it would be useful to show how the different versions of the model can be compared. For example, the LSTM-gated model typically outperforms the Non-Linear-gated model, so it might make sense to compare the 2 models and see if the difference in gate types makes a difference in the model's performance. 2. It would be helpful to provide more information about the reader validation set. Are the validation results included in the Table 1? If so, I would change the order of the table and put the validation results in the last column. Alternatively, it might be helpful to show the reader validation results separately as a Table. This table could also be made part of the supplement. 3. The model predictions are provided as a probability. For low-resource languages like Turkish, these scores may not be very meaningful. It might be useful to compute the exact cutoff value using the estimated prediction scores. 4. The results for gated-LSTM are very mixed, with the model sometimes performing better and sometimes worse than the gated-non-linear version. One possible explanation is that the difference in the gate types makes the two models behave differently (e.g., one model might sometimes learn a trivial filter and then ignore important new words). It would be good to look at this difference more closely in the paper. The qualitative results for the gated-LSTM model seem promising. I would recommend using this model for future work rather than the gated-non-linear version. Overall, this is a very well-executed project! I look forward to seeing what the future brings!

The Gated-Attention Reader is a neural network architecture that can be used for text comprehension. The GAR can attend to and forget irrelevant parts of the input while preserving relevant aspects. The Gated-Attention Reader has shown to outperform other state-of-the-art methods on SQuAD, a widely used dataset for text comprehension. This paper makes several contributions. First, the paper presents several ways to initialize the Gated-Attention Reader and learns to parameterize them differently for different tasks. Second, the paper proposes to use several Gated-Attention Readers in parallel to retrieve relevant information from different aspects of the input at the same time. The paper shows that this approach often improves the performance on several tasks. Third, the paper applies the Gated-Attention Reader to different tasks. The paper shows that the model is applicable to different tasks if they can be described in the form of a table of sentences and questions. The paper shows that this is the case for summarization, abstract generation, and reading comprehension based on paragraph and longer essays. The strengths of this paper are that it covers several ways to initialize the Gated-Attention Reader and learns to parameterize it differently for different tasks. The paper also proposes to use several Gated-Attention Readers in parallel to retrieve relevant information from different aspects of the input at the same time. The paper is applicable to different tasks if they can be described in the form of a table of sentences and questions. The paper has some limitations as well. First, the paper uses SQuAD for evaluation. While SQuAD has become a de facto standard for evaluating text-comprehension systems, it has also been criticized for being biased towards systems that make progress on SQuAD itself. Second, the paper uses the Gated-Attention Reader only for the sake of demonstration. It does not explain how to use it for other tasks. Overall, this is a strong paper that makes several advances on the Gated-Attention Reader for different applications. The paper shows that it is also applicable to other tasks if they can be described in the form of a table of sentences and questions. This is a valuable addition to the Gated-Attention Reader family of models.

The paper of Gated-Attention Readers for Text Comprehension addresses the Cloze-style question answering over documents, which is an important problem in natural language understanding. The main content of this paper can be summarized as below: 1. They study the problem of answering Cloze-style questions over documents, which is to generate a response by filling in a word from the document given a cloze-style question. 2. The model named Gated-Attention Reader which integrates a multi-hop architecture with a novel attention mechanism, which is based on the query embedding and the intermediate states of a recurrent neural network document reader, can be applied to this task. 3. This reader can build query-specific representations of tokens in the document for accurate answer selection. 4. The Gated-Attention (GA) Reader obtains state-of-the-art results on three benchmarks for this task. 5. The effectiveness of multiplicative interaction is demonstrated by an ablation study, and by comparing to alternative compositional operators for implementing the gated-attention. The contribution of this paper is significant for this field, and the proposed model could be a good option for people work on this kind of tasks. I think this paper is a good candidate for a paper award in its current form. My only suggestion would be to clarify the distinction between two tasks the model was trained for and the new task for which the model was evaluated. I recommend to accept this paper for presentation at the Second Workshop on Reinforcement Learning in NLP (RLing 2019).

In this paper, the authors proposed the Gated-Attention (GA) Reader, which integrates a multi-hop architecture with a novel attention mechanism, to answer cloze-style questions over documents. The proposed GA Reader has the following strong points: 1) It uses a multi-hop architecture, which can capture long-range dependencies between context and query; 2) It uses a novel attention mechanism, which is based on multiplicative interactions between the query embedding and the intermediate states of a recurrent neural network (RNN) document reader, to enable the reader to build query-specific representations of tokens in the document. The GA Reader obtains state-of-the-art results on three benchmarks for this task, and is highly effective in building query-specific representations of the document content. Reviewer #1: This paper studies the problem of answering cloze-style questions over documents. The authors propose the Gated-Attention (GA) Reader, which integrates a multi-hop architecture with a novel attention mechanism, to answer cloze-style questions over documents. The paper is well-written with clearly explained experiments and findings. My only concern is that this paper studies the problem of answering cloze-style questions over documents and does not claim an improvement over previous methods. The latest C-Net and Gated-Attention Reader proposed by the authors of this paper also achieve state-of-the-art results on the same dataset, without claiming an improvement over previous models. I wonder if the authors tested other models and adapted in the paper, or whether the improvements are statistically significant. I believe the latter is the case since the improvements are significant in terms of hard CCG+ROT metrics, which is the standard for cloze-style question answering. I also wonder if there are any methods designed for this specific task of answering cloze-style questions over documents, such as generic reading comprehension. In general, generic reading comprehension aims to answer a question over a given document with a specified answer. I think this is a harder problem than the one studied in this paper, since it requires a reader to understand the content of the document to answer the question, while the studied approach only needs to answer the question given a document and a limited context from a query. Overall, I think this paper is a clear and rigorous study on a promising direction for cloze-style question answering, and I recommend this paper for submission to conferences or journals where it can be accepted for publication. This paper presents a gated attention mechanism for machine reading. 
A key idea is to extend Attention Sum Reader (Kadlec et al. 2016) to multi-hop
reasoning by fine-grained gated filter. 
It's interesting and intuitive for machine reading. 
I like the idea along with significant improvement on benchmark datasets, but
also have major concerns to get it published in ACL.

- The proposed GA mechanism looks promising, but not enough to convince the
importance of this technique over other state-of-the-art systems, because
engineering tricks presented 3.1.4 boost a lot on accuracy and are blended in
the result.

- Incomplete bibliography: Nearly all published work in reference section
refers arxiv preprint version. 
This makes me (and future readers) suspicious if this work thoroughly compares
with prior work. Please make them complete if the published version is
available. 

- Result from unpublished work (GA): GA baseline in table 1 and 3 is mentioned
as previous work that is unpublished preprint. 
I don't think this is necessary at all. Alternately, I would like the author to
replace it with vanilla GA (or variant of the proposed model for baseline). 
It doesn't make sense that result from the preprint which will end up being the
same as this ACL submission is presented in the same manuscript. 
For fair blind-review, I didn't search on arvix archive though.

- Conflict on table 1 and 2: GA-- (table 1) is the same as K=1(AS) in table 2,
and GA (fix L(w)) is for K=3 in table 2. 
Does this mean that GA-- is actually AS Reader? 
It's not clear that GA-- is re-implementation of AS. 
I assumed K=1 (AS) in table 2 uses also GloVe initialization and
token-attention, but it doesn't seem in GA--. 

- I wish the proposed method compared with prior work in related work section
(i.e. what's differ from related work).

- Fig 2 shows benefit of gated attention (which translates multi-hop
architecture), and it's very impressive. It would be great to see any

This paper presents an interesting model for reading comprehension, by
depicting the multiplicative interactions between the query and local
information around a word in a document, and the authors proposed a new
gated-attention strategy to characterize the relationship. The work is quite
solid, with almost state of art result on the whole four cloze-style datasets
achieved. Some of the further improvement can be helpful for the similar tasks.


Nevertheless, I have some concerns on the following aspect:

1. The authors have referred many papers from arXiv, but I think some really
related works are not included. Such as the works from Caiming Xiong, et al.
https://openreview.net/pdf?id=rJeKjwvclx and the work form Shuohang Wang, et
al. https://openreview.net/pdf?id=B1-q5Pqxl . Both of them concentrated on
enhancing the attention operation to modeling the interaction between documents
and queries. Although these works are not evaluated on the cloze-style corpus
but the SQuAD, an experimental or fundamental comparison may be necessary.

2. There have been some studies that adopts attention mechanism or its variants
specially designed for the Reading Comprehension tasks, and the work actually
share the similar ideas with this paper. My suggestion is to conduct some
comparisons with such work to enhance the experiments of this paper.

- Strengths:

* Paper is very well-written and every aspect of the model is well-motivated
and clearly explained.
* The authors have extensively covered the previous work in the area.
* The approach achieves state-of-the-art results across several text
comprehension data sets. In addition, the experimental evaluation is very
thorough.

- Weaknesses:

* Different variants of the model achieve state-of-the-art performance across
various data sets. However, the authors do provide an explanation for this
(i.e. size of data set and text anonymization patterns).

- General Discussion:

The paper describes an approach to text comprehension which uses gated
attention modules to achieve state-of-the-art performance. Compared to previous
attention mechanisms, the gated attention reader uses the query embedding and
makes multiple passes (multi-hop architecture) over the document and applies
multiplicative updates to the document token vectors before finally producing a
classification output regarding the answer. This technique somewhat mirrors how
humans solve text comprehension problems. Results show that the approach
performs well on large data sets such as CNN and Daily Mail. For the CBT data
set, some additional feature engineering is needed to achieve state-of-the-art
performance. 

Overall, the paper is very well-written and model is novel and well-motivated.
Furthermore, the approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on several data
sets. 

I had only minor issues with the evaluation. The experimental results section
does not mention whether the improvements (e.g. in Table 3) are statistically
significant and if so, which test was used and what was the p-value. Also I
couldn't find an explanation for the performance on CBT-CN data set where the
validation performance is superior to NSE but test performance is significantly
worse.

machine_text: This paper is an important step towards improving prepositional phrase (PPL) attachment recognition using distributed word representations. It leverages recent advances in distributed word representation models for improving the quality of prepositional phrases. On one hand, a contextualized word representation (AoA) model is used to obtain word representations for prepositions and their modifying words (e.g. the, of, to, with). On the other hand, a 300D GloVe word embedding is used to capture common words frequent in prepositional phrases, which leads to better representations of PPLs. The proposed model learns word representations from a large text corpus and assigns higher scores to those prepositional phrases that are more appropriate in the corpus. The paper also presents a new labeled corpus for PPLs that significantly enhances the accuracy of the model. The proposed model not only produces state-of-the-art results on standard datasets, but it is also able to achieve good results on a newly collected dataset, which contains hand-tagged PPLs and links them to relevant sentences in the corpus. The model also incorporates deep pre-trained contextualized word representation models into pre-trained word embeddings to improve the quality of the latter. The results show that the model improves upon the current state-of-the-art by a significant margin. The proposed model also has a strong generalization ability in that it can be used to enhance the performance of other NLP tasks, especially with respect to PPLs. Overall, the contributions of this paper are two-fold: (1) it proposes an approach for prepositional phrase attachment recognition that uses state-of-the-art pre-trained contextualized word representation models and publicly available word embeddings; and (2) it provides a labeled corpus for PPLs that can be used in other NLP tasks, and it improves the current state-of-the-art model for PPLs. Generally, this paper makes an important contribution to the NLP field. I have some questions and suggestions as follows. 1. In section 3.1, the authors present a general application example using the NER task, and they claim that the model can be easily generalized to other tasks. However, the model only outperforms the state-of-the-art on the PPLAT corpus, and they did not provide other independent datasets to test its generalization ability. Can the model really be applied to other tasks without further training? If not, how could the authors claim the general applicability of this model? 2. In the algorithm section, the authors presented a method to determine the semantic scores. However, this method is not described in sufficient detail, and I did not find this method in the literature. I would be very interested to see the derivation of this method and how the authors arrived at the specific formulas they used. 3. In the corpus generation section, the authors mentioned that they used publicly available pre-trained contextualized word representation models. However, in the model section, they only presented the GloVe word embedding. I could not find any information about the other two contextualized word representation models. 4. In Section 3.4, the authors performed an ablation study on different parts of the model. However, it would be good to do a more detailed analysis of different model components. For example, it would be interesting to see the performance of the model when using only the contextualized word representation model or only the Glove word embedding. This paper addresses the problem of computing embeddings for prepositional phrases (PPs) using multi-task learning with other NLP tasks. These embeddings should be sensitive to the semantic relationships between PPs and their arguments. This paper does a good job of describing the problem and motivation, but the author could be more rigorous in his explanation of the problem, and the relationship between the solution and the attachment task. The solution the author proposes is based on multi-task learning. He first solves another task (natural language inference) with a shared embedding matrix. He then performs separate tasks for each row of this matrix, to predict thedependency type of the token to the left and right of the dot. These two tasks are then combined using a linear layer to get the final prediction for the attachment task. The author justifies using the shared embedding matrix as a way to transfer knowledge between the prepositional phrase attachment task and the other tasks he is also solving. The proposed solution has some weaknesses, however. First, the author justifies the choice of using two tasks for each token, instead of using one big task with two sub-tasks, by the fact that the number of attachment types is fixed. But this means that you’re really only experimenting with two ways of combining the knowledge from the two attached tasks. Second, it would be interesting to experiment with using more than one shared embedding matrix, each dedicated to a layer in the model (e.g. one for the input layer, and one for the fully connected layer). In that case, the model would be solving a multi-layer version of the problem, which might be easier to solve than the one the author has designed. Overall, however, the author has designed an interesting multi-task solution to a challenging problem. I look forward to seeing other works on this topic, and extensions of this work!

I believe this work is interesting and has made significant contribution to the field of word embedding, I recommend to accept the paper, however, I have some suggestions that could be helpful to improve the quality of the paper: 1. In order to understand the characteristics of the prepared knowledge base, it is better to provide a detailed statistics, such as the number of tokens, the size of the vocabulary, etc. 3. In the attachment prediction task, since the POS is not used in the definition of the PP, I think the model can predict the PP attachment without POS tag information, if the model is trained on the data with POS tag information, such as ACE g retirement (AGR) and Noun phrase (NP) attachment, you can treat the POS as an extra feature of the model, it's better to use the multi-label classification algorithm to integrate these features. Based on the above suggestions, I believe the paper can be accepted with these modifications. Thanks for your valuable feedback, I appreciate your help! - Overview:

The paper proposes a new model for training sense embeddings grounded in a
lexical-semantic resource (in this case WordNet). There is no direct evaluation
that the learned sense vectors are meaningful; instead, the sense vectors are
combined back into word embeddings, which are evaluated in a downstream task:
PP attachment prediction.

- Strengths:

PP attachment results seem solid.

- Weaknesses:

Whether the sense embeddings are meaningful remains uninvestigated. 

The probabilistic model has some details that are hard to understand. Are the
\lambda_w_i hyperparameters or trained? Where does “rank” come from, is
this taken from the sense ranks in WordNet?

Related work: the idea of expressing embeddings of words as a convex
combination of sense embeddings has been proposed a number of times previously.
For instance, Johansson and Nieto Piña “Embedding a semantic network in a
word space” (NAACL, 2015) decomposed word embeddings into ontology-grounded

machine_text: Overall, this is a useful paper. Though the topic is relevant, the writing could use some improvement. Here are some suggestions for improvement: 1. Avoid jargon and long sentences. Tone and clarity can often be maintained by editing long sentences and obvious jargon out. 2. Capitalize on the importance of keyphrases in the rest of the paper. The introduction might benefit from clarifying why keyphrases are so important to the entire paper and the goal of keyphrase generation. 3. Use stronger examples. It could be more compelling how keyphrase generation can benefit the entire SEO industry. For instance, it could cite how keyphrase-dense articles outperform unkeyphrase articles in search results. 4. Provide a concrete example of a weak keyphrase and how the model performs poorly on it. The current example could be strengthened by showing a concrete example of a keyphrase that is too broad or too narrow. 5. Avoid repetitive or unnecessary examples. Currently, the author repeats the phrase "keyphrases can be generated for" several times. The examples could be consolidated into a more general "the examples provided can be..." statement. 6. Improve consistency. There are some spelling and formatting issues that should be fixed. For instance, in the abstract, "And per SEO best practice" and "And it's an SEO best practice" appear next to each other. In the conclusion, "are generated using a model that relies on a wide range of characteristics that are representative of the notion of a keyphrase (e.g., long, specific, meaningful, associated with a domain or URL)" appears alongside "keyphrase is generated for."

The paper “Deep Keyphrase Generation” by Denny Zhou addresses the problem of keyphrase extraction from documents. The keyphrase extraction process is often a crucial first step for many keyphrase-based text analysis tasks like search ranking or information retrieval, and current keyphrase extraction algorithms are often suboptimal. The paper describes a new approach to keyphrase extraction, which I believe is a significant improvement over existing methods. First, the authors introduce a new neural architecture for keyphrase extraction, which outperforms previous systems on several keyphrase extraction benchmarks. Second, the authors evaluate the keyphrase extraction capabilities of different parts of the architecture using an “Attention-Guided Dropout” technique. They show that the combination of the keyphrase extraction component and the separately-trained language model yields state-of-the-art performance on several keyphrase extraction benchmarks. The paper provides numerous insights into keyphrase extraction as an NLP problem and into how to build a more effective keyphrase extraction system. The paper also includes detailed experimental results and benchmarks. The author’s use pytorch for implementation, and source code is made available. The paper is well-written and would be of interest to anybody working on text analysis. Filed because this paper addresses an important problem in text analysis - keyphrase extraction. The author presents a novel neural architecture for keyphrase extraction and shows that it outperforms state of the art keyphrase extraction baselines. Furthermore, the author demonstrates that using separate keyphrase extraction component along with a deep learner such as BERT improves the keyphrase extraction performance.

Firstly, I would like to congratulations the authors for this great work. Deep Keyphrase Generation performs a very promising job on extracting keyphrases from a content which captures the semantic meaning behind the content. The performance of the model in finding keyphrases that appear in the content, and also find keyphrases that do not appear in the content, is very good. Here are my some comments and suggestion for the authors to consider in preparing the next version of the paper: 1. It would be better if the authors could give more explanation about the algorithm and how it works, especially in Section 3, where there is a long description on the encoder-decoder framework. Perhaps add a small explanation in the first paragraph of Section 3. 2. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/memray/seq2seq-keyphrase. It would be better if the authors can provide more details about the implementation details of the model, for example, how many epochs the model ran for, how big the batch size was, what kinds of optimizers are used etc. 3. As the paper presents, the model also can generate absent keyphrases. It would be better if the authors can also provide more explanation about the algorithm and how it works. In particular, it would be good to show examples of the model output for a given piece of content and a specific keyphrase that the model does not have.

Write a peer review by first describing what problem or question this paper addresses, then strengths and weaknesses, for the paper Deep Keyphrase Generation, its main content is as below: Keyphrase provides highly-summative information that can be effectively used for understanding, organizing and retrieving text content. Though previous studies have provided many workable solutions for automated keyphrase extraction, they commonly divided the to-be-summarized content into multiple text chunks, then ranked and selected the most meaningful ones. These approaches could neither identify keyphrases that do not appear in the text, nor capture the real semantic meaning behind the text. We propose a generative model for keyphrase prediction with an encoder-decoder framework, which can effectively overcome the above drawbacks. We name it as Deep Keyphrase Generation since it attempts to capture the deep semantic meaning of the content with a deep learning method. Empirical analysis on six datasets demonstrates that our proposed model not only achieves a significant performance boost on extracting keyphrases that appear in the source text, but also can generate absent keyphrases based on the semantic meaning of the text. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/memray/seq2seq-keyphrase. Problem Statement Automatic keyphrase extraction has recently become an important but challenging task in automated summarization. Current keyphrase extraction methods suffer from two shortcomings. First, they only identify a list of keyphrases that appear in the source text, but cannot identify keyphrases that do not appear in the text and do not reflect the semantic meaning of the text. Second, they cannot fully capture the real semantic meaning of the text. We name this more general problem as Deep Keyphrase Generation. Strength and Weaknesses Deep Keyphrase Generation can identify not only keyphrases that appear in the source text, but also those that do not appear in the text and those that do not reflect the semantic meaning of the text. The performance of Deep Keyphrase Generation on the benchmarked datasets are shown in the following table. The main reason that Deep Keyphrase Generation performs better than state-of-the-art keyphrase extraction approaches is that it captures the semantic meaning of the text with an encoder-decoder framework. The model consists of an encoder that encodes the input sequence to a fixed-length vector, and a decoder that generates the sequence from the encoded input and the previously generated tokens. Both the encoder and decoder are neural networks. The decoder generates one token at a time, and each token is generated by not only taking the previously generated token as an input, but also taking the input word embedding and the previously generated word vector from the encoder. The advantage of using an encoder-decoder framework is that it can capture not only the syntactic information of the text, but also the semantic meaning of the content. Deep Keyphrase Generation can capture keyphrases that not only appear in the source text, but also those that do not appear in the text and those that do not reflect the semantic meaning of the text.
human_text:
This paper proposes to use an encoder-decoder framework for keyphrase
generation. Experimental results show that the proposed model outperforms other
baselines if supervised data is available.

- Strengths:
The paper is well-organized and easy to follow (the intuition of the proposed
method is clear). It includes enough details to replicate experiments. Although
the application of an encoder-decoder (+ copy mechanism) is straightforward,
experimental results are reasonable and support the claim (generation of absent
keyphrases) presented in this paper.

- Weaknesses:
As said above, there is little surprise in the proposed approach. Also, as
described in Section 5.3, the trained model does not transfer well to new
domain (it goes below unsupervised models). One of the contribution of this
paper is to maintain training corpora in good quantity and quality, but it is
not (explicitly) stated.

- General Discussion:
I like to read the paper and would be pleased to see it accepted. I would like
to know how the training corpus (size and variation) affects the performance of
the proposed method. Also, it would be beneficial to see the actual values of
p_g and p_c (along with examples in Figure 1) in the CopyRNN model. From my
experience in running the CopyNet, the copying mechanism sometimes works
unexpectedly (not sure why this happens).

This paper divides the keyphrases into two types: (1) Absent key phrases (such
phrases do not match any contiguous subsequences of the source document) and
(2) Present key phrases (such key phrases fully match a part of the text). The
authors used RNN based generative models (discussed as RNN and Copy RNN) for
keyphrase prediction and copy mechanism in RNN to predict the already occurred
phrases. 

Strengths:

1. The formation and extraction of key phrases, which are absent in the current
document is an interesting idea of significant research interests. 

2. The paper is easily understandable.

3. The use of RNN and Copy RNN in the current context is a new idea. As, deep
recurrent neural networks are already used in keyphrase extraction (shows very
good performance also), so, it will be interesting to have a proper motivation
to justify the use of  RNN and Copy RNN over deep recurrent neural networks. 

Weaknesses:

1. Some discussions are required on the convergence of the proposed joint
learning process (for RNN and CopyRNN), so that readers can understand, how the
stable points in probabilistic metric space are obtained? Otherwise, it may be
tough to repeat the results.

2. The evaluation process shows that the current system (which extracts 1.
Present and 2. Absent both kinds of keyphrases) is evaluated against baselines
(which contains only "present" type of keyphrases). Here there is no direct
comparison of the performance of the current system w.r.t. other
state-of-the-arts/benchmark systems on only "present" type of key phrases. It
is important to note that local phrases (keyphrases) are also important for the
document. The experiment does not discuss it explicitly. It will be interesting
to see the impact of the RNN and Copy RNN based model on automatic extraction
of local or "present" type of key phrases.

3. The impact of document size in keyphrase extraction is also an important
point. It is found that the published results of [1], (see reference below)
performs better than (with a sufficiently high difference) the current system
on Inspec (Hulth, 2003) abstracts dataset. 

4. It is reported that current system uses 527,830 documents for training,
while 40,000 publications are held out for training baselines. Why are all
publications not used in training the baselines? Additionally,        The topical
details of the dataset (527,830 scientific documents) used in training RNN and
Copy RNN are also missing. This may affect the chances of repeating results.

5. As the current system captures the semantics through RNN based models. So,
it would be better to compare this system, which also captures semantics. Even,
Ref-[2] can be a strong baseline to compare the performance of the current
system.

Suggestions to improve:

1. As, per the example, given in the Figure-1, it seems that all the "absent"
type of key phrases are actually "Topical phrases". For example: "video
search", "video retrieval", "video indexing" and "relevance ranking", etc.
These all define the domain/sub-domain/topics of the document. So, In this
case, it will be interesting to see the results (or will be helpful in
evaluating "absent type" keyphrases): if we identify all the topical phrases of
the entire corpus by using tf-idf and relate the document to the high-ranked
extracted topical phrases (by using Normalized Google Distance, PMI, etc.). As
similar efforts are already applied in several query expansion techniques (with
the aim to relate the document with the query, if matching terms are absent in
document).

Reference:
1. Liu, Zhiyuan, Peng Li, Yabin Zheng, and Maosong Sun. 2009b. Clustering to
find exemplar terms for keyphrase extraction. In Proceedings of the 2009
Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, pages
257–266.

2. Zhang, Q., Wang, Y., Gong, Y., & Huang, X. (2016). Keyphrase extraction
using deep recurrent neural networks on Twitter. In Proceedings of the 2016
Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (pp. 836-845).

- Strengths:

Novel model.  I particularly like the ability to generate keyphrases not
present in the source text.

- Weaknesses:

 Needs to be explicit whether all evaluated models are trained and tested on
the same data sets.  Exposition of the copy mechanism not quite
clear/convincing.

- General Discussion:

This paper presents a supervised neural network approach for keyphrase
generation.  The model uses an encoder-decoder architecture that
first encodes input text with a RNN, then uses an attention mechanism to
generate keyphrases from
the hidden states.  There is also a more advanced variant of the
decoder which has an attention mechanism that conditions on the
keyphrase generated in the previous time step.

The model is interesting and novel. And I think the ability to
generate keyphrases not in the source text is particularly
appealing.  My main concern is with the evaluation:  Are all
evaluated models trained with the same amount of data and evaluated
on the same test sets?              It's not very clear.  For example, on the
NUS data set, Section 4.2 line 464 says that the supervised baselines
are evaluated with cross validation.

Other comments:

The paper is mostly clearly written and easy to follow.  However,
some parts are unclear:

- Absent keyphrases vs OOV.  I think there is a need to distinguish
  between the two, and the usage meaning of OOV should be consistent.  The RNN
models
  use the most frequent 50000 words as the vocabulary (Section 3.4
  line 372, Section 5.1 line 568), so I suppose OOV are words not in
  this 50K vocabulary.              In line 568, do you mean OOV or absent
  words/keyphrases?  Speaking of this, I'm wondering how many
  keyphrases fall outside of this 50K?              The use of "unknown words"
  in line 380 is also ambiguous.  I think it's probably clearer to say that
 the RNN models can generate words not present in the source text as long as
they appear
somewhere else in the corpus (and the 50K vocabulary)

- Exposition of the copy mechanism (section 3.4).  This mechanism has a
  more specific locality than the attention model in basic RNN model.
  However, I find the explanation of the intuition misleading.              If I
  understand correctly, the "copy mechanism" is conditioned on the
  source text locations that matches the keyphrase in the previous
  time step y_{t-1}.  So maybe it has a higher tendency to generate n-grams
seen source text (Figure 1).  I buy the argument that the more sophisticated
  attention model probably makes CopyRNN better than the RNN
  overall, but why is the former model particularly better for absent
  keyphrases?  It is as if both models perform equally well on present
keyphrases.

- How are the word embeddings initialized?
