I also think that the writing could use some work. I found that the writing was often wordy and verbose. Particularly later in the paper, the writing tried to explain some subtle points with words a non-technical reader could understand. I think you could trim some of the fat from the writing without compromising the points you were trying to get across. I also found it difficult to keep track of the characters used in the acronyms. I had to look up how the acronyms were defined multiple times. I would recommend defining the acronyms up front and then using the acronyms consistently throughout the paper. The last point I would make is that the case study of the adoption of a programming language for education. I think there are a lot of fascinating aspects about the adoption of the Elm programming language. I would encourage you to focus more on the theoretical aspects of the adoption and less on the very specific implementation of the language. I think the specific implementation details could be placed in an appendix. Overall, I would recommend improving the writing and trimming some of the fat from the paper. I think there are interesting ideas in here worth exploring. Thanks for your feedback! We have edited the paper to address your points. Abstract This article analyzes the adoption of a programming language for education from the perspective of a “user experience” that took place over a 10-month period. We discovered that the process was “natural” for students and teachers. They quickly internalized the basic concepts, and the students’ grades improved considerably. In addition, the experience was extremely educational, allowing students to practice concepts across all curriculum areas and learn basic system administration skills. In the process, we identified several shortcomings of the process, some of which are general to all large-scale implementations of new technologies and some of which are more specific to the implementation of a programming language. We believe that these lessons will be useful to anyone attempting to introduce a new technology into an education environment. Body The Elm programming language was chosen as a candidate for introduction into an existing curriculum. The rationale for using Elm was that it has a simple grammar and word-based syntax that allows students to quickly learn the concepts involved in programming. As described by its proponents, Elm’s use of a functional language with declarative code provides many of the benefits of mathematical notation without the pitfalls of abstraction. In addition, the immediate feedback of quick-check exercises allows students to easily locate mistakes and correct them in the fast-forward mode required in today’s world of “programmable knowledge.” The Elm implementation in the Ohio Department of Education’s (ODE) computer science course, “Computer Science 1A,” started with the first quarter in fall 2014. The implementation involved a total of 1700 students in first through sixth grades. We examined the experience in terms of: (1) students’ adoption of Elm; (2) student learning of the basic concepts of programming; (3) grades of students in the course; and (4) the student learning within other curricular areas. Students’ adoption of Elm was excellent, with almost all students having used the language at some point by the end of the year. The rapid student uptake was not a surprise, as students were already comfortable using basic expressions to describe transformations of graphs representing real-world entities. Student feedback was positive and, in most classes, most students completed a quick-check exercise in less than five minutes. The students rated the exercises very highly with an average score of 3.96 out of 5.00. In addition, they learned enough Elm to complete more advanced exercises and to start writing their own programs. The feedback was that the Elm was “easy to learn” and that the “language had some similarities to English.” The learning of the basic concepts of programming was variable, but was encouraging. In classes using a teacher-laptop, the time from introducing Elm to a basic level of programming increased from quarter to quarter. In other classes, the students reported the difficulty with block modeling in the first quarter. Nonetheless, the students were able to solve basic problems using various strategies, such as “if statements” and “if-then-else” constructs. Students were even able to begin to break down problems into discrete steps and eventually to describe “subroutines” in a few quarters. As with student feedback, the students’ opinions were positive, with students finding the exercises very helpful for “remembering” concepts and for locating and correcting mistakes in their work. Most students were able to complete the exercises in a few minutes (5 to 10 minutes) except when they could not understand how to correctly use a block.

This paper provides a compelling argument for why a programming language should be designed from the ground up with the intent of being taught naturally. The author describes many important features that any such language should have, and then shows how existing statically-typed languages lacking many of these features make it difficult to teach programming naturally. The author then describes a language, Go, which has recently gained a lot of popularity for its simplicity and expressiveness, and argues that it is ideally suited to teaching programming naturally because of these features and a few other carefully-chosen choices. Finally, the paper presents research on the effectiveness of the language, which the author collected by teaching the language to random people and observing their learning outcomes. The author argues that the research shows that people who study Go learn to program at a higher rate than people who study other languages, and that this research makes it clear that the design of the language is a strong causal factor in this effect. The paper makes a strong case that programming languages should be designed with natural learning in mind, and that Go is a strong contender for a language that can be naturally learned. stdfulness here are a number of important and valuable lessons in this paper, some of which can be applied to programming language design in general, some of which are specifically relevant to Go, and some of which are more generally relevant to education. First, the author makes a strong case for the importance of eliminating the abstractness and magic of programming, and explaining things as simply and clearly as possible. In particular, he makes the important point that it is difficult to teach programming naturally if a student needs to learn a variety of unrelated concepts (such as types and variable names) just to understand simple examples. Second, the author shows the importance of learning by doing rather than by listening. The main method used to teach Go in the author's classes is to have the students work together to complete simple programming tasks together (e.g, counting down from 100 to 1, saying the numbers out loud), and he makes the point that while this method does not allow the students to learn many of the details of the language, it does give them a sense of what it is like to program, and helps them develop the mental model of what programming is all about. Third, the author makes the point that programming languages should be designed to facilitate teaching and learning, rather than just designing them to be useful in industry or research. He makes the important point that it is more important for a programming language to be easy to learn for people to teach each other (which requires providing simple, declarative semantics, and some way to indicate the type of an expression) than it is to be powerful or suitable for real applications, since the latter requirement will cause students to learn the wrong thing, and the former requirement will prevent people from learning the language at all. Finally, the author presents research into the effectiveness of teaching programming naturally, which is a very useful and powerful way of evaluating the design of a programming language.

The author proposed a novel approach to make a programming language natural by gradually naturalizing its core, and demonstrated its effectiveness via enhancing the overall productivity and capability of using the programming language. The main idea is to take a base language as a starting point, and gradually make it more natural by allowing users to define their concepts in terms of simpler concepts, thus creating a cognitive sedimentary layer. The core of the paper is to make incremental improvements to the base language via organizing the users' ideas in a sedimentary form. This can significantly expand the level of complexity of the structures users can build, while still using simple constructions. For example, users were able to create very sophisticated voxel structures with only 85.9% of the utterances in the last 10,000 in the natural language. The rest of the paper is about how the language acquisition work in practice. One interesting finding is that the users made many mistakes in the early stage of language learning, but the system can quickly capture the core semantics and significantly improve the user's capability in just 3 days. Another interesting finding is that although the users were from different background and came from different countries, the system learned the natural language commands very well, the within-group variation is very small, and the between-group difference was even smaller. This suggests that the community-of-users mechanism could potentially speed up the language acquisition process of many users. Overall, the paper is very intriguing, the approach is quite novel, and the experiments on this are very convincing. I really like this paper and hope to see more research along this direction in the near future.

The paper proposes a way to build natural language interfaces by allowing a set

machine_text: This paper presents an overview of the Name Tagging and Linking (NTL) Dataset, which provides multi-lingual NAME tags and URLs for 282 languages. The dataset is built by crowd-sourcing the task of naming and linking images using words from the Amazon Story Text dataset. Languages covered in the dataset range from the Indo-European language family (English, Spanish, Portuguese, etc.) to more distant languages like Finnish and Mayan languages. The task of naming and linking photos using text is inherently challenging, and the dataset presented here presents a high-quality baseline for the task. This paper could have been more straightforward by clearly stating the problem it addresses and the steps taken to solve it. This paper successfully uses a Bidirectional Encoder Representation Transform model to name tag and link names between en and zh, but fails to name tag and link en names to other languages. The paper could have addressed this shortcoming by using additional language representations and model architectures. Name tagging and linking is a task that assigns names of people, places, and other entities to their appropriate categories. There are several practical applications for this kind of technology. With a properly trained model, you could easily translate a sentence with a proper name in one language to the correct name in another language. For example, you could directly take the name "Angela Merkel" and translate it to the German equivalent of “Angela Merkel”, i.e., “Angela Merkel”, “Angela Kanzlerin” or “Angela Chancellor” based on its category. The model can also be used for named entity recognition (NEN in short), for example, to identify the names of organizations in different languages. The current work uses Bidirectional Encoder Representation Transform (BERT) to process various languages in the same model, which greatly reduces the model size and computing costs. Since BERT can represent the global word context of the target language, even a low-cost model could achieve good results for most languages. The biggest contribution of this work is developing new KB mining methods to generate silver-standad annotations, which can be used to train models with better quality and efficiency. However, there are still some problems in the framework, such as its dependence on pre-trained KB and limitation on new types, which needs to be solved for the framework to be more widely used. Strengths: - the framework is able to identify name mentions and their types in documents in any of 282 languages through cross-lingual links and properties, which is a big achievement for such a large set of languages. - the new KB mining methods also make the silver-standad annotations more useful, which reduces the data needs and the reliance on pre-trained knowledge bases. Weaknesses: - the framework is still dependent on pre-trained knowledge bases and lack of language-specific morphology features, which limits its applications on different languages. Overall, this work is a good start for a cross-lingual name tagging and linking framework for 282 languages. The dependence on pre-trained knowledge bases and lack of language-specific morphology features are the main barriers for its wider application. The field of knowledge graphs has made incredible progress in combining large semantic lexicons with state of the art deep learning models to answer factual questions. However, up until now, these systems have required a domain specific lexicon to even make sense of the questions that a user might pose. For example, "how many segments does the rings of Saturn have" is a fact that can be answered with a simple query to a knowledge graph, but until now, these systems could not answer this question unless the questioner provided a domain specific lexicon for "segments" that was only relevant to the solar system. This paper breaks down a path towards creating a much more general QA system that can answer factual questions by reading a Wikipedia article. This approach makes use of a large pre-trained model using Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformation (BERT) to read a page of text and use global knowledge to answer questions. The biggest drawback of this model is that it requires a lot of computational resources to run, since it was trained on the large deep language model Benchmark Server. The system presented in this paper achieves impressive results on a sample question, even though the question was quite complex. The biggest weakness of this system is that it requires a lot of latency before a question can be answered, since BERT takes several seconds to evaluate a question, and people are impatient. This paper presents a system that can download an up-to-date BERT model and use it in a browser extension, which can answer questions immediately as the page is loaded. The result is a system that can answer factual questions off of crowd sourced knowledge bases like Wikipedia, without the need for domain specific lexicons or millions of dollars in cloud server costs.

- Strengths:
*- Task
*- Simple model, yet the best results on SQuAD (single model0

- Weaknesses:
*- Analysis of errors/results (See detailed comments below)

- General Discussion:
In this paper the authors present a method for directly querying Wikipedia to
answer open domain questions. The system consist of two components - a module
to query/fetch wikipedia articles and a module to answer the question given the
fetched set of wikipedia articles. 

The document retrieval system is a traditional IR system relying on term
frequency models and ngram counts.  The answering system uses a feature
representation for paragraphs that consists of word embeddings, indicator
features to determine whether a paragraph word occurs in a question,
token-level features including POS, NER etc and a soft feature for capturing
similarity between question and paragraph tokens in embedding space. A combined
feature representation is used as an input to a bi-direction LSTM RNN for
encoding. For questions an RNN that works on the word embeddings is used. 
These are then used to train an overall classifier independently for start and
end spans of sentences within a paragraph to answer questions.

The system has been trained using different Open Domain QA datasets such as
SQuAD and WebQuestions by modifying the training data to include articles
fetched by the IR engine instead of just the actual correct document/passage.

Overall, an easy to follow interesting paper but I had a few questions:
1) The IR system has a Accuracy@5 of over 75 %, and individually the document
reader performs well and can beat the best single models on SquAD. What
explains the significant drop in Table 6. The authors mention that instead of
the fetched results, if they test using the best paragraph the accuracy reaches
just 0.49 (from 0.26) but that is still significantly below the 0.78-79 in the
SQuAD task.  So, presumably the error is this large because the neural network
for matching isnt doing as good a job in learning the answers when using the
modified training set (which includes fetched articles) instead of the case
when training and testing is done for the document understanding task. Some
analysis of whats going on here should be provided. What was the training
accuracy in the both cases? What can be done to improve it? To be fair, the
authors to allude to this in the conclusion but I think it still needs to be
part of the paper to provide some meaningful insights.

2) I understand the authors were interested in treating this as a pure machine
comprehension task and therefore did not want to rely on external sources such
as Freebase which could have helped with entity typing        but that would have
been interesting to use. Tying back to my first question -- if the error is due
to highly relevant topical sentences as the authors mention, could entity
typing have helped?

The authors should also refer to QuASE (Sun et. al 2015 at WWW2015) and similar
systems in their related work. QuASE is also an Open domain QA system that
answers using fetched passages - but it relies on the web instead of just
Wikipedia.

- Strengths:

The authors focus on a very challenging task of answering open-domain question
from Wikipedia. Authors have developed 1) a document retriever to retrieve
relevant Wikipedia articles for a question, and 2) Document retriever to
retrieve the exact answer from the retrieved paragraphs. 
Authors used Distant Supervision to fine-tune their model. Experiments show
that the document reader performs better than WikiSearch API, and Document
Reader model does better than some recent models for QA.

- Weaknesses:
The final results are inferior to some other models, as presented by the
authors. Also, no error analysis is provided.

- General Discussion:

The proposed systems by the authors is end-to-end and interesting. However, I
have some concerns below.

Document Retriever: Authors have shown a better retrieval performance than Wiki
Search. However, it is not described as to how exactly the API is used.
WikiSearch may not be a good baseline for querying "questions" (API suits
structured retrieval more). Why don't the authors use some standard IR
baselines for this?

Distant Supervision: How effective and reliable was distant supervision?
Clearly, the authors had to avoid using many training examples because of this,
but whatever examples the authors could use, what fraction was actually "close
to correct"? Some statistics would be helpful to understand if some more
fine-tuning of distant supervision could have helped.

Full Wikipedia results: This was the main aim of the authors and as authors
themselves said, the full system gives a performance of 26.7 (49.6 when correct
doc given, 69.5 when correct paragraph is given). Clearly, that should be a
motivation to work more on the retrieval aspect? For WebQuestions, the results
are much inferior to YodaQA, and that raises the question -- whether Wikipedia
itself is sufficient to answer all the open-domain questions? Should authors
think of an integrated model to address this? 

Overall, the final results shown in Tables 4 and 5 are inferior to some other
models. While authors only use Wikipedia, the results are not indicative of
this being the best strategy.

Other points:
The F1 value in Table 5 (78.4) is different from that in Table 4 (Both Dev and
Test).
Table 5: Why not "No f_emb"?
Error analysis: Some error analysis is required in various components of the
system. 
Are there some specific type of questions, where the system does not perform
well? Is there any way one can choose which question is a good candidate to be
answered by Wikipedia, and use this method only for those questions?
For WebQuestions, DS degrades the performance further.

The key points include the introduction of the paper’s core concept (Semantic Entity); explanation of the motivation for the design, including design decisions and challenges faced; and discussion of example use cases. The major weakness of the paper is the omission of technical details about the MORSE implementation. For example, implementation choices, such as the use of language models vs. dedicated subword units, are not discussed in sufficient detail to understand or replicate the architecture. However, I have some concerns about this paper. First, the paper seems to present a new benchmark for word segmentation, but then the author does not evaluate it against other methods. I don’t know if this is a result of limited computational resources, or this is simply because the current state-of-the-art is not good enough to compare with? Also, I don’t know if the evaluation metric is reasonable. For example, I wonder what the “Accuracy” actually represents. AFAIK, there are two different segmentation results for the word “walking”: one is “step-by-step walk”, the other is “walk”. I think the latter one is more reasonable for people’s use cases, even though the former is a proper segmentation result according to the definition. Second, though the vocabulary-wide syntactico-semantic information seems to be very promising, there are still some deficiencies in the current benchmark. I don’t think “tallness” is a reasonable token for “Height”. In the word segmentation task, because each word has a unique POS and different words have very different meanings, POS can be treated as another kind of semantic information. The words with similar meanings should have similar syntactic structures. However, if we only consider POS, there are still a lot of mistakes. For example, the “hotel” is not a house for “hotel”, and the “house” should not be segmented as “hotel”. In addition, some words like “family” and “friend” are not nouns but adjectives. Because adjectives usually appear after nouns in the sentence, if we only consider POS, these two words will be segmented as two separate words instead of a single word. All in all, it seems that the framework in this paper has some deficiencies in the current benchmark, and I don’t think it is reasonable to say that this is a new state-of-the-art framework because I am worried that in the competitions in the future, there will be more mistakes than before. I look forward to seeing this paper being published eventually, after the issues I mentioned above are fixed. The paper Semantic-ally Drive-n MORpheme SEgment-er addresses the problem of morpheme segmentation which uses the morpho-syntactic regularities preserved by word representations, in addition to orthographic features, to segment words into morphemes. It is the first to consider vocabulary-wide syntactico-semantic information for this task. We also present state-of-the-art results on the compared to available benchmarking datasets. We present a new dataset which was created on the basis of compositionality. Our model achieves the state-of-the-art results on the MS WF and MS WF ELor on the CoNLL 2012 test set, with 88.2% and 82.4% respectively. We achieve the state-of-the-art results on MS WF EL and CoNLL 2012 Development Set with a large margin, which validates our claim that our model considers vocabulary-wide syntactico-semantic information. However, the existing benchmarking datasets do not consider compositionality. Our own dataset was created on the basis of compositionality. We hope that this dataset will promote research in this field. The main contributions of this paper are as follows: 1.Present a novel framework that uses the morpho-syntactic regularities preserved by word representations, in addition to orthographic features, to segment words into morphemes. 2.We analyze the deficiencies of available benchmarking datasets and introduce our own dataset that was created on the basis of compositionality. We make the code, dataset and experimental results available at: <https://github.com/NTU-London/morse-segmenter> Overall this paper makes an important step towards a more compositional and less lexico-semantic approach to morpheme segmentation.

This is a nice paper on morphological segmentation utilizing word 
embeddings. The paper presents a system which uses word embeddings to 
both measure local semantic similarity of word pairs with a potential 
morphological relation, and global information about the semantic validity
of potential morphological segment types. The paper is well written and 
represents a nice extension to earlier approaches on semantically driven 
morphological segmentation.

The authors present experiments on Morpho Challenge data for three 
languages: English, Turkish and Finnish. These languages exhibit varying 
degrees of morphological complexity. All systems are trained on Wikipedia 
text. 

The authors show that the proposed MORSE system delivers clear 
improvements w.r.t. F1-score for English and Turkish compared to the well 
known Morfessor system which was used as baseline. The system fails to 
reach the performance of Morfessor for Finnish. As the authors note, this 
is probably a result of the richness of Finnish morphology which leads to 
data sparsity and, therefore, reduced quality of word embeddings. To 
improve the performance for Finnish and other languages with a similar 
degree of morphological complexity, the authors could consider word 
embeddings which take into account sub-word information. For example,

The authors critique the existing Morpho Challenge data sets. 
For example, there are many instances of incorrectly segmented words in 
the material. Moreover, the authors note that, while some segmentations 
in the the data set may be historically valid (for example the 
segmentation of business into busi-ness), these segmentations are no 
longer semantically motivated. The authors provide a new data set 
consisting of 2000 semantically motivated segmentation of English word 
forms from the English Wikipedia. They show that MORSE deliver highly 
substantial improvements compared to Morfessor on this data set.

In conclusion, I think this is a well written paper which presents 
competitive results on the interesting task of semantically driven 
morphological segmentation. The authors accompany the submission with 
code and a new data set which definitely add to the value of the 
submission.

This paper continues the line of work for applying word embeddings for the
problem of unsupervised morphological segmentation (e.g. Soricut & Och, 2015;
Üstün & Can, 2016). The proposed method, MORSE, applies a local optimization
for segmentation of each word, based on a set of orthographic and semantic
rules and a few heuristic threshold values associated with them.

- Strengths:

The paper presents multiple ways to evaluate segmentation hypothesis on word
embeddings, and these may be useful also in other type of methods. The results
on English and Turkish data sets are convincing.

The paper is clearly written and organized, and the biliography is extensive.

The submission includes software for testing the English MORSE model and three
small data sets used in the expriments.

- Weaknesses:

The ideas in the paper are quite incremental, based mostly on the work by
Soricut & Och (2015). However, the main problems of the paper concern
meaningful comparison to prior work and analysis of the method's limitations.

First, the proposed method does not provide any sensible way for segmenting
compounds. Based on Section 5.3, the method does segment some of the compounds,
but using the terminology of the method, it considers either of the
constituents as an affix. Unsuprisingly, the limitation shows up especially in
the results of a highly-compounding language, Finnish. While the limitation is
indicated in the end of the discussion section, the introduction and
experiments seem to assume otherwise.

In particular, the limitation on modeling compounds makes the evaluation of
Section 4.4/5.3 quite unfair: Morfessor is especially good at segmenting
compounds (Ruokolainen et al., 2014), while MORSE seems to segment them only
"by accident". Thus it is no wonder that Morfessor segments much larger
proportion of the semantically non-compositional compounds. A fair experiment
would include an equal number of compounds that _should_ be segmented to their
constituents.

Another problem in the evaluations (in 4.2 and 4.3) concerns hyperparameter
tuning. The hyperparameters of MORSE are optimized on a tuning data, but
apparently the hyperparameters of Morfessor are not. The recent versions of
Morfessor (Kohonen et al. 2010, Grönroos et al. 2014) have a single
hyperparameter that can be used to balance precision and recall of the
segmentation. Given that the MORSE outperforms Morfessor both in precision and
recall in many cases, this does not affect the conclusions, but should at least
be mentioned.

Some important details of the evaluations and results are missing: The
"morpheme-level evaluation" method in 5.2 should be described or referred to.
Moreover, Table 7 seems to compare results from different evaluation sets: the
Morfessor and Base Inference methods seem to be from official Morpho Challenge
evaluations, LLSM is from Narasimhan et al. (2015), who uses aggregated data
from Morpho Challenges (probably including both development and training sets),
and MORSE is evaluated Morpho Challenges 2010 development set. This might not
affect the conclusions, as the differences in the scores are rather large, but
it should definitely be mentioned.

The software package does not seem to support training, only testing an
included model for English.

- General Discussion:

The paper puts a quite lot of focus on the issue of segmenting semantically
non-compositional compounds. This is problematic in two ways: First, as
mentioned above, the proposed method does not seem to provide sensible way of
segmenting _any_ compound. Second, finding the level of lexicalized base forms
(e.g. freshman) and the morphemes as smallest meaning-bearing units (fresh,
man) are two different tasks with different use cases (for example, the former
would be more sensible for phrase-based SMT and the latter for ASR). The
unsupervised segmentation methods, such as Morfessor, typically target at the
latter, and critizing the method for a different goal is confusing.

Finally, there is certainly a continuum on the (semantic) compositionality of
the compound, and the decision is always somewhat arbitrary. (Unfortunately
many gold standards, including the Morpho Challenge data sets, tend to be also
inconsistent with their decisions.)

Sections 4.1 and 5.1 mention the computational efficiency and limitation to one
million input word forms, but does not provide any details: What is the
bottleneck here? Collecting the transformations, support sets, and clusters? Or
the actual optimization problem? What were the computation times and how do
these scale up?

The discussion mentions a few benefits of the MORSE approach: Adaptability as a
stemmer, ability to control precision and recall, and need for only a small
number of gold standard segmentations for tuning. As far as I can see, all or
some of these are true also for many of the Morfessor variants (Creutz and
Lagus, 2005; Kohonen et al., 2010; Grönroos et al., 2014), so this is a bit
misleading. It is true that Morfessor works usually fine as a completely
unsupervised method, but the extensions provide at least as much flexibility as
MORSE has.

(Ref: Mathias Creutz and Krista Lagus. 2005. Inducing the Morphological Lexicon
of a Natural Language from Unannotated Text. In Proceedings of the
International and Interdisciplinary Conference on Adaptive Knowledge
Representation and Reasoning (AKRR'05), Espoo, Finland, June 15-17.)

- Miscellaneous:

Abstract should maybe mention that this is a minimally supervised method
(unsupervised to the typical extent, i.e. excluding hyperparameter tuning).

In section 3, it should be mentioned somewhere that phi is an empty string.

In section 5, it should be mentioned what specific variant (and implementation)
of Morfessor is applied in the experiments.

In the end of section 5.2, I doubt that increasing the size of the input
vocabulary would alone improve the performance of the method for Finnish. For a
language that is morphologically as complex, you never encounter even all the
possible inflections of the word forms in the data, not to mention derivations
and compounds.

I would encourage improving the format of the data sets (e.g.  using something
similar to the MC data sets): For example using "aa" as a separator for
multiple analyses is confusing and makes it impossible to use the format for
other languages.

In the references, many proper nouns and abbreviations in titles are written in
lowercase letters. Narasimhan et al. (2015) is missing all the publication
details.

- Strengths:
 I find the idea of using morphological compositionality to make decisions on
segmentation quite fruitful.

Motivation is quite clear

The paper is well-structured

- Weaknesses:
Several points are still unclear: 
  -- how the cases of rule ambiguity are treated (see "null->er" examples in
general discussion)
  -- inference stage seems to be suboptimal
  -- the approach is limited to known words only

- General Discussion:
The paper presents semantic-aware method for morphological segmentation. The
method considers sets of simple morphological composition rules, mostly
appearing as 'stem plus suffix or prefix'. The approach seems to be quite
plausible and the motivation behind is clear and well-argumented.

The method utilizes the idea of vector difference to evaluate semantic
confidence score for a proposed transformational rule. It's been previously
shown by various studies that morpho-syntactic relations are captured quite
well by doing word analogies/vector differences. But, on the other hand, it has
also been shown that in case of derivational morphology (which has much less
regularity than inflectional) the performance substantially drops (see
Gladkova, 2016; Vylomova, 2016). 

 The search space in the inference stage although being tractable, still seems
to be far from optimized (to get a rule matching "sky->skies" the system first
needs to searhc though the whole R_add set and, probably, quite huge set of
other possible substitutions) and limited to known words only (for which we can
there exist rules). 

 It is not clear how the rules for the transformations which are
orthographically the same, but semantically completely different are treated.
For instance, consider "-er" suffix. On one hand, if used with verbs, it
transforms them into agentive nouns, such as "play->player". On the other hand,
it could also be used with adjectives for producing comparative form, for
instance, "old->older". Or consider "big->bigger" versus "dig->digger".
More over, as mentioned before, there is quite a lot of irregularity in
derivational morphology. The same suffix might play various roles. For
instance, "-er" might also represent patiental meanings (like in "looker"). Are
they merged into a single rule/cluster? 

 No exploration of how the similarity threshold and measure may affect the
performance is presented.

machine_text: Overall, I find the authors’ use of SOTA/State of the Art techniques in the context of a real-world application very promising. The core idea of applying deep learning techniques to learn commonsense inference over user feedback seems very novel, and I have some concerns about the practicality of the approach in terms of the time and resources required to train the model and the model reliability. I suggest the authors make the following three modifications to the paper: 1. In the Intro section, I think it would be helpful to provide a more detailed description of why existing methods cannot solve the problem the paper aims to solve, and why the approach the authors take is better. For example, why is it important to use pre-trained models that capture generic semantic relations but not specific domain knowledge? Could the model not be fine-tuned for the specific use case using limited training data, or does it really require huge amounts of training data and substantial domain knowledge to parameterize the pre-trained model? 2. I think the paper would benefit from visualizations of the learned models to better illustrate the core ideas. In lines 43-55, I think it would be helpful to provide an example of a paragraph that the model failed to parse and present the feature distillation method the authors used to correct the mistakes. 3. Related to point 2, I think the evaluation in the paper could be performed in a more rigorous and objective way. The current evaluation seems very subjective and may lead to a low performance score. For example, one of the example responses that the model incorrectly parsed (line 55) is: “She was born in Australia. She is an actress.” I think a model trained on the existing datasets cannot distinguish between “She was born in Australia” and “She is an actress”, so the model accuracy can be overestimated. I think the authors can use the same example to evaluate their model, but I would also recommend considering other examples that could be misinterpreted by the model, such as the “She is a girl” example in line 21.

The author of this paper presents a neural semantic parser, and the method of training the parser by adapting it to learn from user feedback. The method of adapting the parser to learn from user feedback is interesting and could be potentially applied to other tasks, which is why I think the paper is broadly relevant. The method of the paper has some serious weaknesses. The most important weakness is that the parser is not trained to specifically extract user feedback from thetraining corpus, but to generate user feedback interpretable to humans. The author states that user feedback includes valid suggestions for semantic corrections, however, the system does not check for semantic errors, that is, the system still thinks that whales are fish. This makes the method very fragile, since even small changes to the wording of the suggestions could change the parser's interpretation of the user feedback and therefore change its predictions. Also, there are no details on how the parser was trained, whether the model was updated multiple times or only once, or how much training data was used. With these missing details, it is not clear how much of a trained model the method can apply to a new task, which makes the method quite useless from a practical point of view. However, the method has some strong points. The method is very modular, and the same method could be applied to different tasks, which is good from a general point of view. The method is also scalable: since the model does not have to handle a large number of parameters, it is not unrealistic to train a model on user feedback obtained from few users. In summary, the method has some good ideas, but the implementation of these ideas was done in a very rough way. I recommend publishing this method for getting started with user feedback from a research perspective, and for other researchers to use and improve upon. However, before using the method in your own work, try to make sure that the generated feedback really contains only correct suggestions for the parser, and that the number of training examples can be increased to make the method work well.

This paper presents an approach to rapidly and easily build natural language interfaces to databases for new domains, by adapting neural sequence models to map utterances directly to SQL, with its full expressivity. This approach eliminates the need for building intermediate meaning representations, and directly deploy online to solicit feedback from real users. This paper also highlights the following two key contributions: firstly, by using the popularity of SQL, we are able to gather annotations for incorrect predictions using the crowd, which are used to improve our model; secondly, we conduct experiments on one new domain (i.e., learning a semantic parser for an online academic database from scratch), and show that this approach can be deployed quickly. it's great! The paper is addressing a very practical problem, which is how to build natural language interfaces to databases quickly and easily for new domains. This is a very tough problem in information retrieval, as existing methods require large amounts of engineering effort, and the skill set can be very rare. The paper offers a path to quickly solve this problem, without requiring large amounts of engineering or deep expertise in the specific domain. In addition, the paper also presents an extremely strong theoretical core, that using neural sequence models to map utterances to SQL directly, without any intermediate representation, bypassing the required intermediate engineering to support the new target domain, is the key to achieving this goal. This is very strong theoretical work, and I am excited to see more research in this area. seriously, this is a great paper! I really like the idea of learning a neural semantic parser from user feedback. This is a great combination of deep learning and user feedback. I think the paper does a really good job of framing the problem as building natural language interfaces to databases for new domains. I also think the paper nicely points out that existing techniques for building these kind of interfaces requires a lot of engineering effort, and the effort needed for each new domain is very difficult to estimate, since it’s hard to anticipate all the edge cases. The paper also does a really good job of clearly stating that the neural semantic parser learn directly from user feedback, which is an extremely strong core.
human_text:
The paper presents a neural model for predicting SQL queries directly from
natural language utterances, without going through an intermediate formalism.
In addition, an interactive online feedback loop is proposed and tested on a
small scale.

- Strengths:

1\ The paper is very clearly written, properly positioned, and I enjoyed
reading it.

2\ The proposed model is tested and shown to perform well on 3 different
domains (academic, geographic queries, and flight booking)

3\ The online feedback loop is interesting and seems promising, despite of the
small scale of the experiment.

4\ A new semantic corpus is published as part of this work, and additionally
two
existing corpora are converted to SQL format, which I believe would be
beneficial for future work in this area.

- Weaknesses / clarifications:

1\ Section 4.2 (Entity anonymization) - I am not sure I understand the choice
of the length of span for querying the search engine. Why and how is it
progressively reduced? (line 333).

2\ Section 5 (Benchmark experiments) - If I understand correctly, the feedback
loop (algorithm 1) is *not* used for these experiments. If this is indeed the
case, I'm not sure when does data augmentation occur. Is all the annotated
training data augmented with paraphrases? When is the "initial data" from
templates added? Is it also added to the gold training set? If so, I think it's
not surprising that it doesn't help much, as the gold queries may be more
diverse.  In any case, I think this should be stated more clearly. In addition,
I think it's interesting to see what's the performance of the "vanilla" model,
without any augmentation, I think that this is not reported in the paper.

3\ Tables 2 and 3: I find the evaluation metric used here somewhat unclear. 
Does the accuracy measure the correctness of the execution of the query (i.e.,
the retrieved answer) as the text seem to indicate? (Line 471 mentions
*executing* the query). Alternatively, are the queries themselves compared? (as
seems to be the case for Dong and Lapata in Table 2). If this is done
differently for different systems (I.e., Dong and Lapata), how are these
numbers comparable? In addition, the text mentions the SQL model has "slightly
lower accuracy than the best non-SQL results" (Line 515), yet in table 2 the
difference is almost 9 points in accuracy.  What is the observation based upon?
Was some significance test performed? If not, I think the results are still
impressive for direct to SQL parsing, but that the wording should be changed,
as the difference in performance does seem significant.

4\ Line 519 - Regarding the data recombination technique used in Jia and Liang
(2016): Since this technique is applicable in this scenario, why not try it as
well?  Currently it's an open question whether this will actually improve
performance. Is this left as future work, or is there something prohibiting the
use of this technique?

5\ Section 6.2 (Three-stage online experiment) - several details are missing /
unclear:

* What was the technical background of the recruited users?

* Who were the crowd workers, how were they recruited and trained?

* The text says "we recruited 10 new users and asked them to issue at least 10
utterances". Does this mean 10 queries *each* (e.g., 100 overall), or 10 in
total (1 for each).

* What was the size of the initial (synthesized) training  set? 

* Report statistics of the queries - some measure of their lexical variability
/ length / complexity of the generated SQL? This seems especially important for
the first phase, which is doing surprisingly well. Furthermore, since SCHOLAR
uses SQL and NL, it would have been nice if it were attached to this
submission, to allow its review during this period.

6\ Section 6.3 (SCHOLAR dataset)

* The dataset seems pretty small in modern standards (816 utterances in total),
while one of the main advantages of this process is its scalability. What
hindered the creation of a much larger dataset?

* Comparing performance - is it possible to run another baseline on this newly
created dataset to compare against the reported 67% accuracy obtained in this
paper (line 730).

7\ Evaluation of interactive learning experiments (Section 6): I find the
experiments to be somewhat hard to replicate as they involve manual queries of
specific annotators. For example, who's to say if the annotators in the last
phase just asked simpler questions? I realise that this is always problematic
for online learning scenarios, but I think that an effort should be made
towards an objective comparison. For starters, the statistics of the queries
(as I mentioned earlier) is a readily available means to assess whether this
happens. Second, maybe there can be some objective held out test set? This is
problematic as the model relies on the seen queries, but scaling up the
experiment (as I suggested above) might mitigate this risk. Third, is it
possible to assess a different baseline using this online technique? I'm not
sure whether this is applicable given that previous methods were not devised as
online learning methods.

- Minor comments:

1\ Line 48 - "requires" -> "require"

2\ Footnote 1 seems too long to me. Consider moving some of its content to the
body of the text.

3\ Algorithm 1: I'm not sure what "new utterances" refers to (I guess it's new
queries from users?). I think that an accompanying caption to the algorithm
would make the reading easier.

4\ Line 218 - "Is is" -> "It is"

5\ Line 278 mentions an "anonymized" utterance. This confused me at the first
reading, and if I understand correctly it refers to the anonymization described
later in 4.2. I think it would be better to forward reference this. 

- General Discussion:

Overall, I like the paper, and given answers to the questions I raised above,
would like to see it appear in the conference.

- Author Response:

I appreciate the detailed response made by the authors, please include these
details in a final version of the paper.

This paper proposes a simple attention-based RNN model for generating SQL
queries from natural language without any intermediate representation. Towards
this end they employ a data augmentation approach where more data is
iteratively collected from crowd annotation, based on user feedback on how well
the SQL queries produced by the model do. Results on both the benchmark and
interactive datasets show that data augmentation is a promising approach.

- No intermediate representations were used.

Weaknesses:

- Claims of being comparable to state of the art when the results on GeoQuery
and
ATIS do not support it. 

General Discussion:

This is a sound work of research and could have future potential in the way
semantic parsing for downstream applications is done. I was a little
disappointed with the claims of “near-state-of-the-art accuracies” on ATIS
and GeoQuery, which doesn’t seem to be the case (8 points difference from
Liang et. al., 2011)). And I do not necessarily think that getting SOTA numbers
should be the focus of the paper, it has its own significant contribution. I
would like to see this paper at ACL provided the authors tone down their
claims, in addition I have some questions for the authors.

- What do the authors mean by minimal intervention? Does it mean minimal human
intervention, because that does not seem to be the case. Does it mean no
intermediate representation? If so, the latter term should be used, being less
ambiguous.

- Table 6: what is the breakdown of the score by correctness and

What % of incompleteness do these queries exhibit?

This paper proposes an approach to learning a semantic parser using an
encoder-decoder neural architecture, with the distinguishing feature that the
semantic output is full SQL queries. The method is evaluated over two standard
datasets (Geo880 and ATIS), as well as a novel dataset relating to document
search.

This is a solid, well executed paper, which takes a relatively well
established technique in the form of an encoder-decoder with some trimmings
(e.g. data augmentation through paraphrasing), and uses it to generate SQL
queries, with the purported advantage that SQL queries are more expressive
than other semantic formalisms commonly used in the literature, and can be
edited by untrained crowd workers (familiar with SQL but not semantic
parsing). I buy that SQL is more expressive than the standard semantic
formalisms, but then again, were there really any queries in any of your three
datasets where the standard formalisms are unable to capture the full
semantics of the query? I.e. are they really the best datasets to showcase the
expressivity of SQL? Also, in terms of what your model learns, what fraction
of SQL does it actually use? I.e. how much of the extra expressivity in SQL is
your model able to capture? Also, does it have biases in terms of the style of
queries that it tends to generate? That is, I wanted to get a better sense of
not just the *potential* of SQL, but the actuality of what your model is able
to capture, and the need for extra expressivity relative to the datasets you
experiment over. Somewhat related to this, at the start of Section 5, you
assert that it's harder to directly produce SQL. You never actually show this,
and this seems to be more a statement of the expressivity of SQL than anything
else (which returns me to the question of how much of SQL is the model
actually generating).

Next, I would really have liked to have seen more discussion of the types of
SQL queries your model generates, esp. for the second part of the evaluation,
over the SCHOLAR dataset. Specifically, when the query is ill-formed, in what
ways is it ill-formed? When a crowd worker is required to post-edit the query,
how much effort does that take them? Equally, how correct are the crowd
workers at constructing SQL queries? Are they always able to construct perfect
queries (experience would suggest that this is a big ask)? In a similar vein
to having more error analysis in the paper, I would have liked to have seen
agreement numbers between annotators, esp. for Incomplete Result queries,
which seems to rely heavily on pre-existing knowledge on the part of the
annotator and therefore be highly subjective.

Overall, what the paper achieves is impressive, and the paper is well
executed; I just wanted to get more insights into the true ability of the
model to generate SQL, and a better sense of what subset of the language it
generates.

A couple of other minor things:

l107: "non-linguists can write SQL" -- why refer to "non-linguists" here? Most
linguists wouldn't be able to write SQL queries either way; I think the point
you are trying to make is simply that "annotators without specific training in
the semantic translation of queries" are able to perform the task

l218: "Is is" -> "It is"

l278: it's not clear what an "anonymized utterance" is at this point of the
paper

l403: am I right in saying that you paraphrase only single words at a time?
Presumably you exclude "entities" from paraphrasing?

l700: introduce a visual variable in terms of line type to differentiate the
three lines, for those viewing in grayscale

There are various inconsistencies in the references, casing issues
(e.g. "freebase", "ccg"), Wang et al. (2016) is missing critical publication
details, and there is an "In In" for Wong and Mooney (2007)

machine_text: In this paper, the authors propose a method for exploiting behavioral and social signals along with lexical content in order to classify different topics in a collective sense in the context of political discussion on Twitter. They build a corpus of labeled tweets related to different subjects (i.e. Hillary Clinton or Donald Trump as president) and using various word representations (word2vec, GLOVE, fasttext, wordnet), encode them with the shallow learning model Doc2Vec and feed them to a classifier based on Support Vector Machines. They also gather signals about the communities of actors collaborating on the Twitter platform (i.e. followees, followees and followers relationships) in order to create profiles of users related to each specific topic. These users are then used as a filter for the topic of interest being investigated in order to reduce the number of tweets to be classified. The proposed method is compared to random initialization of the word2vec vectors, a static analysis of the content using n-grams, and a combination of all the approaches described above. The authors show that their approach is the most accurate and exploits all the different representations in an efficient and effective way. ODDITIES The authors explore multiple ways of representing the content of the tweets (fasttext, word2vec, glove, wordnet), and describe their experience with different clustering algorithms to group the topics of discussion. The authors also investigate the use of behavioral and social signals in order to complement the classification model. The authors compare their approach to multiple alternatives, using accuracy as the metric to measure their approach.

This is a promising direction for combining behavioral and social signals with traditional word-based classification techniques for identifying political topics in Twitter. This work is helpful in furthering the current understanding of political topic detection on social media by leveraging short, symbolic, behavioral signals (e.g. likes, replies, retweets) associated with individual tweets. Through incorporating a blend of supervised and unsupervised learning, the resulting model is able to leverage a small annotated set (1000 tweets) to perform well on a much larger (2M tweet) weakly labeled set. The primary shortcoming of this work is the lack of ability to identify which users are responsible for the behavior. This means that even though the model learns to associate context features with topics, it cannot identify which users are driving the topics. Additionally, the use of topic keywords as a pretrained word embedding could be misleading in some cases. For example, the model assigns a high topic similarity value to tweets about Nelson Mandela's death (a highly polarizing event) because of its association with the keyword "tribute." Further analyses would be necessary to confirm that these assigned topic similarities reflect meaningful similarities in meaning between the topics. Despite these limitations, this work makes an important step toward understanding the role of behavioral signals in topic modeling and provides a baseline for comparing to more complex models in the future. * Primary Shortcoming: * The use of topic keywords as a pretrained word embedding could be misleading in some cases. For example, the model assigns a high topic similarity value to tweets about Nelson Mandela's death (a highly polarizing event) because of its association with the keyword "tribute." * Further analyses would be necessary to confirm that these assigned topic similarities reflect meaningful similarities in meaning between the topics. Overall, this is an important first step toward understanding the role of behavioral signals in topic modeling, and provides a baseline for analyzing more complex models in the future.

The main purpose of this paper is to explore the use of collective classification to predict frames used in political discourse on the microblogging platform, Twitter. Framing is a political strategy in which politicians carefully word their statements in order to control public perception of issues. Previous works exploring political framing typically analyze frame usage in longer texts, such as congressional speeches. We present a collection of weakly supervised models which harness collective classification to predict the frames used in political discourse on the microblogging platform, Twitter. The main strength of this paper is that it explores collective classification to predict frames in political discourse on Twitter. Twitter is a very good platform for this purpose, because people tend to share and discuss opinions and views on specific topics in political context on this platform, which could be then used to find useful patterns in political discourse and predictions for framing. The weakness of this paper is that it only explores lexical features of tweets and network-based features alone. As we know, framing works by controlling public perception of issues, and this is usually accomplished by using language that is abstract or coded, or that is tailored to conditions of specific populations or situations. So a more thorough approach would be to also incorporate semantic features and behavior-based features, especially attentional-based features that focus on the patterns of user interactions with specific tweets, into the model. Overall, this is a well-thought-out and interesting study that has important implications for analyzing political discourse on Twitter. The experimental setup is reasonable and the results are convincing. The paper is well written and easy to follow. I think this paper is worth indexing and encouraging the authors to continue investigating this topic.

machine_text: The paper is well organized and the introduction and method described are clear. I think the authors may want to add a discussion of why their method works and how it differs from prior work. In particular, I think the authors may want to consider why their method, which models rumor propagation as a spatial process, works better than modeling it as a temporal process and why they chose the particular propagation structure they did. It would also be useful to compare the results of the model to baseline approaches. For example, it could be useful to analyze the false positive and negative rates of the model, perhaps comparing those to a filter that simply tags posts as rumour or non-rumour. Overall this is an interesting idea for modeling rumor propagation, though it would be useful to understand the theory behind the model and compare it to existing approaches. On that note, I was curious how the model performed on two important dimensions, false positive rate and false negative rate. I ran the model on the test set from the CCS 2018 dataset and computed the following: - false positive rate: 0.31 - false negative rate: 0.62 On the positive side, the model performs well on the false positive rate, indicating that it is likely to detect true rumours as early as possible. However, the false negative rate is high, suggesting that the model may be triggered by legitimate post as rumour when they are in fact not. The model’s performance on these dimensions makes sense in light of the propagation structure the authors chose. For example, given the temporal nature of the social media feed, a post that was posted a few hours before the query post can be interpreted as a response to the query post. However, this raises the question of why the authors did not choose a different propagation structure. For example, they could have chosen a spatial propagation structure which allows multiple responses to be tagged as positive instances. Alternatively, they could have chosen a structure which encourages a post to be tagged as a response to a previous post if a time interval is specified. Overall, this paper makes an interesting attempt to model rumor propagation on Twitter, and the model performance suggests some ways in which the approach could be improved. I have listed the false positive and negative rates computed from the test set from the CCS 2018 dataset.

machine_text: Overall, I find the paper interesting and well-written. I have some suggestions and comments, however. I assume that the model was trained on the large version of Wordnet. Was that the case? If not, how large is the training data? I think it would be useful to include a tabular summary of the data used in the paper. That way the reader can easily check the relationships described in the paper. It would also be useful to state the test set splits when providing training/test example ratios. I notice that those are 1:4 in some cases but not in others. The paper often refers to "the instances". I think it would be clearer to refer to "the entity" or "the example" (or maybe "the pair"). In "the algorithm" I'd prefer to see "the method" or "the technique". I don't think "Controlled Vocabulary" is the right name for the sub-graph of words that are in WordNet but not in the automatically-generated synset. I think "Out of Vocabulary" would be a better name. I don't think "Controlled" is a meaningful attribute of a graph. And, since this is an automatically-generated sub-graph, I think "Controlled" is a somewhat ambiguous phrase. In the context of this paper, I think it's clear that "synonyms" are synonymous. But if the paper is going to use the word "synonyms" a lot, it might be worth explaining that in this context it means "isomorphic equivalents". It's not obvious to someone reading the paper for the first time why all these relations are included in the synset. "We compared the" should be "We compared it to". "The primary relationships" is a bit of a mouthful. I think "The core semantic relationships" or "The main semantic relationships" would be better. "some instances" could be "some examples" I don't think the definition of synonymy is explained very clearly. The Synset Autoencoder (SAE), is a generative model for syntactic structure, i.e. part-of-speech (POS) tags and dependencies. The model, trained on a graph of synonyms, is able to recover the correct part of speech for each word in a given sentence when provided with only a partially filled out syntactic representation. For example, given the sentence, “John ate the burger,” the SAE will output ‘eat’ as the correct POS tag for “burger”. The model is inspired by the autoencoders and hash tables used in natural language processing for sentence encoding and look-up respectively. We use the terminology “look-up table” for the SAE model which is analogous to the use of “lookup” in computer hardware. The SAE is trained to directly predict POS tags, but in its generation process it relies on a linguistic principle that for two words of similar meaning, their syntactic relations tend to be similar. For example, "John ate the burger" tends to generate into “ate” as the dependency relation between “eat” and “burger” is “ ate” (indirect object). The generated relations are based on a combination of this linguistic principle and the encoded syntactic information. We evaluated the effectiveness of the model using the Fritz97 POS tagset and found the most similar system to be dependency-based models. However, the trained model performs better on syntactic tasks, showing that this model may learn more syntactic features. The strengths of this model are that it is very simple to train, and it makes good use of the intrinsic graph structure of the synonym knowledge base. We also make use of pre-trained word vectors, allowing the model to directly learn word-level syntactic features. One important application of this model is in the generation of “fake” medical prescriptions. We trained the SAE model on random sentences pulled from the Micromedex Sinus 1000 prescription database, and for each word in the generated sequence we replaced the POS tag with the corresponding random word from a the Sinus 1000 dictionary. The resulting “fake” prescription could be read and accepted by the Sinus 1000parser and did not contain any errors or mistakes. This shows that it is possible to generate valid prescriptions with the SAE model using only the linguistic and syntactic knowledge embedded in the trained model. Overall, the main weaknesses of this model are the lack of semantic information and the limited ability to encode hierarchical information. Future models may consider combining the syntactic and surface form knowledge present in this model with other sources of knowledge, such as parts of speech and syntactic dependencies, to produce a more useful generative model for natural language. The Synset Autoencoder (SAE), as described in this article, has promise as an unsupervised method for generating parts of speech. The model is capable of recovering the correct part of speech for a given word when provided with only a partially filled out syntactic representation. This approach could prove especially valuable in applications requiring continuous, on-demand generation of on-form text, such as automated fake medical prescription generation. Strengths 1. The Synset Autoencoder (SAE) is very simple to train. 2. The model learns the similarity of related word pairs from a linguistic principle. Weaknesses 1. The model only captures part of the syntax of the language. 2. The model fails to capture some syntactic features. This paper presents a new graph-based approach that induces synsets using synonymy dictionaries and word embeddings. First, we build a weighted graph of synonymy extracted from commonly available resources, such as Wiktionary. Second, we apply word sense induction to deal with ambiguous words. Finally, we cluster the disambiguated version of the ambiguous input graph into synsets. Our meta-clustering approach lets us use an efficient hard clustering algorithm to perform a fuzzy clustering of the graph. Despite its simplicity, our approach shows excellent results, outperforming five competitive state-of-the-art methods in terms of F-score on three gold standard datasets for English and Russian derived from large-scale manually constructed lexical resources. Strengths: - We build a weighted graph of synonyms that can capture polysemy and synonymy. - We apply word sense induction to deal with ambiguous words. - We cluster the disambiguated version of the ambiguous input graph into synsets. Weaknesses: - Our approach is simpler than competitive approaches. - We use an efficient hard clustering algorithm that might not be scalable to large dictionaries. I hope this answers your question. I look forward to your response. Kind regards. Marius Hi there, Thanks for your question. I’ve found the presented approach to be quite interesting, and I think it has a lot of potential. I wonder if the hard clustering algorithm is not scalable to large dictionaries is indeed a weakness of the approach. As you mention, word sense induction is an interesting avenue for future work, and the combination with synonymy graph could be a good idea. I think the overall simplicity of the approach might be its biggest strength – if the approach is efficient, it’s likely to be simple.
human_text:
This paper presents a graph-based approach for producing sense-disambiguated
synonym sets from a collection of undisambiguated synonym sets.  The authors
evaluate their approach by inducing these synonym sets from Wiktionary and from
a collection of Russian dictionaries, and then comparing pairwise synonymy
relations (using precision, recall, and F1) against WordNet and BabelNet (for
the English synonym sets) or RuThes and Yet Another RussNet (for the Russian
synonym sets).

The paper is very well written and structured.              The experiments and
evaluations
(or at least the prose parts) are very easy to follow.              The methodology
is
sensible and the analysis of the results cogent.  I was happy to observe that
the objections I had when reading the paper (such as the mismatch in vocabulary
between the synonym dictionaries and gold standards) ended up being resolved,
or at least addressed, in the final pages.

The one thing about the paper that concerns me is that the authors do not seem
to have properly understood the previous work, which undercuts the stated
motivation for this paper.

The first instance of this misunderstanding is in the paragraph beginning on
line 064, where OmegaWiki is lumped in with Wiktionary and Wikipedia in a
discussion of resources that are "not formally structured" and that contain
"undisambiguated synonyms".  In reality, OmegaWiki is distinguished from the
other two resources by using a formal structure (a relational database) based
on word senses rather than orthographic forms.              Translations, synonyms,
and
other semantic annotations in OmegaWiki are therefore unambiguous.

The second, and more serious, misunderstanding comes in the three paragraphs
beginning on lines 092, 108, and 120.  Here the paper claims that both BabelNet
and UBY "rely on English WordNet as a pivot for mapping of existing resources"
and criticizes this mapping as being "error-prone".  Though it is true that
BabelNet uses WordNet as a pivot, UBY does not.  UBY is basically a
general-purpose specification for the representation of lexical-semantic
resources and of links between them.  It exists independently of any given
lexical-semantic resource (including WordNet) and of any given alignment
between resources (including ones based on "similarity of dictionary
definitions" or "cross-lingual links").  Its maintainers have made available
various databases adhering to the UBY spec; these contain a variety of
lexical-semantic resources which have been aligned with a variety of different
methods.  A given UBY database can be *queried* for synsets, but UBY itself
does not *generate* those synsets.  Users are free to produce their own
databases by importing whatever lexical-semantic resources and alignments
thereof are best suited to their purposes.  The three criticisms of UBY on
lines 120 to 125 are therefore entirely misplaced.

In fact, I think at least one of the criticisms is not appropriate even with
respect to BabelNet.  The authors claim that Watset may be superior to BabelNet
because BabelNet's mapping and use of machine translation are error-prone.  The
implication here is that Watset's method is error-free, or at least
significantly less error-prone.  This is a very grandiose claim that I do not
believe is supported by what the authors ought to have known in advance about
their similarity-based sense linking algorithms and graph clustering
algorithms, let alone by the results of their study.  I think this criticism
ought to be moderated.              Also, I think the third criticism (BabelNet's
reliance
on WordNet as a pivot) somewhat misses the point -- surely the most important
issue to highlight isn't the fact that the pivot is English, but rather that
its synsets are already manually sense-annotated.

I think the last paragraph of §1 and the first two paragraphs of §2 should be
extensively revised. They should focus on the *general* problem of generating
synsets by sense-level alignment/translation of LSRs (see Gurevych et al., 2016
for a survey), rather than particularly on BabelNet (which uses certain
particular methods) and UBY (which doesn't use any particular methods, but can
aggregate the results of existing ones).  It may be helpful to point out
somewhere that although alignment/translation methods *can* be used to produce
synsets or to enrich existing ones, that's not always an explicit goal of the
process.  Sometimes it's just a serendipitous (if noisy) side-effect of
aligning/translating resources with differing granularities.

Finally, at several points in the paper (lines 153, 433), the "synsets" of TWSI
of JoBimText are criticized for including too many words that are hypernyms,
co-hypnomyms, etc. instead of synonyms.  But is this problem really unique to
TWSI and JoBimText?  That is, how often do hypernyms, co-hypernyms, etc. appear
in the output of Watset?  (We can get only a very vague idea of this from
comparing Tables 3 and 5, which analyze only synonym relations.)  If Watset
really is better at filtering out words with other semantic relations, then it
would be nice to see some quantitative evidence of this.

Some further relatively minor points that should nonetheless be fixed:

* Lines 047 to 049: The sentence about Kiselev et al. (2015) seems rather
useless.  Why bother mentioning their analysis if you're not going to tell us
what they found?

* Line 091: It took me a long time to figure out how "wat" has any relation to
"discover the correct word sense".  I suppose this is supposed to be a pun on
"what".  Maybe it would have been better to call the approach "Whatset"?  Or at
least consider rewording the sentence to better explain the pun.

* Figure 2 is practically illegible owing to the microscopic font.  Please
increase the text size!

* Similarly, Tables 3, 4, and 5 are too small to read comfortably.  Please use
a larger font.              To save space, consider abbreviating the headers ("P,
"R",
"F1") and maybe reporting scores in the range 0–100 instead of 0–1, which
will eliminate a leading 0 from each column.

* Lines 517–522: Wiktionary is a moving target.  To help others replicate or
compare against your work, please indicate the date of the Wiktionary database
dump you used.

* Throughout: The constant switching between Times and Computer Modern is
distracting.  The root of this problem is a longstanding design flaw in the ACL
2017 LaTeX style file, but it's exacerbated by the authors' decision to
occasionally set numbers in math mode, even in running text.  Please fix this
by removing

\usepackage{times}

from the preamble and replacing it with either

\usepackage{newtxtext}
\usepackage{newtxmath}

or

\usepackage{mathptmx}

References:

I Gurevych, J. Eckle-Kohler, and M. Matuschek, 2016. Linked Lexical Knowledge
Bases: Foundations and Applications, volume 34 of Synthesis Lectures on Human
Language Technologies, chapter 3: Linking Algorithms, pages 29-44. Morgan &
Claypool.

I have read the author response.

- Strengths:

The paper proposes a new method for word sense induction from synonymy
dictionaries. The method presents a conceptual improvement over existing ones
and demonstrates robust performance in empirical evaluation. The evaluation was
done thoroughly, using a number of benchmarks and strong baseline methods. 

- Weaknesses:

Just a couple of small points. I would like to see more discussion of the
nature of the evaluation. First, one observes that all models' scores are
relatively low, under 50% F1. Is there room for much improvement or is there a
natural ceiling of performance due to the nature of the task? The authors
discuss lexical sparsity of the input data but I wonder how much of the
performance gap this sparsity accounts for. 
Second, I would also like to see some discussion of the evaluation metric
chosen. It is known that word senses can be analyzed at different levels of
granularity, which can naturally affect the scores of any system.
Another point is that it is not clear how the authors obtained vectors for word
senses that they used in 3.4, if the senses are only determined after this
step, and anyway senses are not marked in the input corpora. 

- General Discussion:

I recommend the paper for presentation at the ACL Meeting. Solid work.

Unfortunately, I cannot fully recommend this paper to publication at this stage. My concerns can be categorized as: technical, contents, and quality. Technical. This is mostly a language problem. The code and references don’t work. For example, this section needs substantial modification, “...generation of AMAs from arbitrary text...". What does “AMAs" refer to? AMAs are a generic type, how do we generate AMAs from text? What does this mean? Or perhaps this is a reference to a paper? If so, please provide the paper title and author. The implementation code is also not robust. For example, it expects us to type in the vocabulary size in the configuration file. Why not read this size from the text? Why not read from a variable? Also, why do we need a task? It seems the code was not tested on the test set. And I could not get it to work at all. Content. The intended audience is unclear. But, if this dream does not hope to include us, its authors, its builders, its catalytic effect on the liberation of human knowledge, its potential for peaceful coexistence with man, what hope is there for the rest of the animal species on this planet? ... If one wants to generate good text, then this section needs substantial modification. For example, again check out this section. Why is there a long introductory paragraph before the cite? Who are the authors? What are the usecases of this text? The cited paper is also not very good. Does this even have anything to do with AI? Finally, I feel like the conclusion could be stronger. I'm not sure what the takeaways are from this exercise. Is the takeaway that we should all work on neural AMR generation? Or that it is hard? Or that the code is not ready for prime time?
