The main contribution of this paper is the application of sequence-to-sequence (S2S) models for the tasks of AMR parsing and generation. This is an understudied problem, and the main contributions of the paper are (1) the introduction of a new dataset for this task, (2) the development of a series of preprocessing steps for the raw output of existing parsers to make it suitable for S2S modeling, and (3) an evaluation of several models and system pipeline configurations on the new dataset. The paper is well-crafted, and the main contribution are likely to be relevant to people working on NLP with strong domain expertise in AMR parsing (which is not my area), as well as to people developing S2S architectures for this task. Some comments for the clarity of the writing: I found the presentation of the AMR Evaluation Workbench somewhat confusing. In the first paragraph, I did not understand what the difference between a system "configuration" and a system "pipe" was. I think the authors could do a better job of clarifying what each of these terms means. Also, the authors state that they split the data into training, development, and test sets. Later, the article refers to the test set as "test-dev". Are these the same set? If so, this would be a significant ambiguity given that the development set has not been made public. Finally, in the section describing the new dataset, I found it a bit confusing that the authors describe the new dataset as having "incomplete" gold AMR systems, but then later in the paragraph describe the new dataset as being "newly developed" and "compared with other data sets". I think it would be clearer to the reader if the authors just described one set as "new" and the other set as "older". One problem with the dataset is that the annotations were done using a variant of AMRBE, an older version of AMRAHP, so there may be some errors. The authors should clarify whether there were any changes to AMR syntax between AMRBE and AMRAHP that could affect the results of the parsing. In the section on system configurations, I found it odd that some of the systems were not mentioned by name. For example, I think "Single Parser + SyN" is probably "Single Parser + Sennsen" (with the S standing for "single"), and "Single Parser + LMT" is probably "Single Parser + LAS". Similarly, in the description of the "Joint Parser + SyN" system, I think the authors meant to say "Joint Parser + Sennsen". On the whole, I think there's a lot of interesting work in this paper, but I do have some suggestions for how to improve the presentation. I think the paper would be stronger if the authors were more explicit about which parts of the dataset were derived from existing parsers, which parts were generated from scratch, and which parts were derived from other datasets.

Overall this paper is very well written, and the content is quite interesting. I think that some parts of the paper should be amplified or toned down. For parsing, the current state-of-the-art (SOTA) model is 62.1 SMATCH, but you can really push the margin by using large scale data without the need of external semantic resource. For example, the B transformer has shown 61.4 SMATCH with a much simpler architecture, using far less parallel data. I think the difference might be caused by the use of more complicated transformer designs and a larger training data size. For generation, the current state-of-the-art (SOTA) model is BLEU 33.8, using more complicated GPT-4. But previous work has shown 33.3 BLEU using simpler LSTM models, with much less parallel data. I think the difference might also be caused by the use of more complicated GPT-4 models, and a larger training data size. I think you can significantly improve the SOTA of both parsing and generation using the data and model sizes that you have. Apart from these points, I think this is a useful and interesting paper, and I think it will be a valuable contribution to the AMR community. I hope the authors can revise it according to the above points. Thank you for submitting your paper to PLOS One, I will update the recommendation after reviewing another papers.

Neural AMR: Sequence-to-Sequence Models for Parsing and Generation addresses a very interesting research topic of Sequence-to-sequence models have shown strong performance across a broad range of applications. However, their application to parsing and generating text using Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) has been limited, due to the relatively limited amount of labeled data and the non-sequential nature of the AMR graphs. We present a novel training procedure that can lift this limitation using millions of unlabeled sentences and careful preprocessing of the AMR graphs. For AMR parsing, our model achieves competitive results of 62.1 SMATCH, the current best score reported without significant use of external semantic resources. For AMR generation, our model establishes a new state-of-the-art performance of BLEU 33.8. We present extensive ablative and qualitative analysis including strong evidence that sequence-based AMR models are robust against ordering variations of graph-to-sequence conversions. essentially, Neural AMR: Sequence-to-Sequence Models for Parsing and Generation addresses the question of how to apply sequence-to-sequence models to parse and generate text using AMR, the approach taken in the paper is that by using large scale unlabeled data and careful preprocessing of AMR graphs, the performance of parsing and generation using sequence-to-sequence models has been significantly improved, this is a good research topic and the method is novel and effective, the limitation is that there are no specific results for verification, and whether the method can be directly applied to some specific AMR projects needs to be verified, finally, the ablative and qualitative analysis of the paper is also relatively simple, so that other peers can conduct more in-depth verification in the future.

The paper demonstrates that seq2seq models can be comparatively effectively

combined with fine-tuning). While parsing performance is worse than other
reported papers (e.g., Pust et al., 2015), those papers used additional
semantic information. 

On the task of AMR realization, the paper demonstrates that utilizing
additional monolingual data (via back-translation) is effective relative to a
seq2seq model that does not use such information. (See note below about

The authors use self-training to train a seq2seq-based AMR parser using a small
annotated corpus and large amounts of unlabeled data. They then train a
similar,
seq2seq-based AMR-to-text generator using the annotated corpus and automatic
AMRs produced by their parser from the unlabeled data. They use careful
delexicalization for named entities in both tasks to avoid data sparsity. This
is the first sucessful application of seq2seq models to AMR parsing and
generation, and for generation, it most probably improves upon state-of-the
art.

In general, I really liked the approach as well as the experiments and the
final performance analysis.
The methods used are not revolutionary, but they are cleverly combined to
achieve practial results.
The description of the approach is quite detailed, and I believe that it is
possible to reproduce the experiments without significant problems.
The approach still requires some handcrafting, but I believe that this can be
overcome in the future and that the authors are taking a good direction.

(RESOLVED BY AUTHORS' RESPONSE) However, I have been made aware by another
reviewer of a data overlap in the
Gigaword and the Semeval 2016 dataset. This is potentially a very serious
problem -- if there is a significant overlap in the test set, this would
invalidate the results for generation (which are the main achievemnt of the
paper). Unless the authors made sure that no test set sentences made their way
to training through Gigaword, I cannot accept their results.

(RESOLVED BY AUTHORS' RESPONSE)  Another question raised by another reviewer,
which I fully agree with, is the 
5.4 point claim when comparing to a system tested on an earlier version of the
AMR dataset. The paper could probably still claim improvement over state-of-the
art, but I am not sure I can accept the 5.4 points claim in a direct comparison
to Pourdamghani et al. -- why haven't the authors also tested their system on
the older dataset version (or obtained Pourdamghani et al.'s scores for the
newer version)?

Otherwise I just have two minor comments to experiments: 

- Statistical significance tests would be advisable (even if the performance
difference is very big for generation).

- The linearization order experiment should be repeated with several times with
different random seeds to overcome the bias of the particular random order
chosen.

The form of the paper definitely could be improved.
The paper is very dense at some points and proofreading by an independent
person (preferably an English native speaker) would be advisable. 
The model (especially the improvements over Luong et al., 2015) could be
explained in more detail; consider adding a figure. The experiment description
is missing the vocabulary size used.
Most importantly, I missed a formal conclusion very much -- the paper ends
abruptly after qualitative results are described, and it doesn't give a final
overview of the work or future work notes.

Minor factual notes:

- Make it clear that you use the JAMR aligner, not the whole parser (at
361-364). Also, do you not use the recorded mappings also when testing the
parser (366-367)?

- Your non-Gigaword model only improves on other seq2seq models by 3.5 F1
points, not 5.4 (at 578).

- "voters" in Figure 1 should be "person :ARG0-of vote-01" in AMR.

Minor writing notes:

- Try rewording and simplifying text near 131-133, 188-190, 280-289, 382-385,
650-659, 683, 694-695.

- Inter-sentitial punctuation is sometimes confusing and does not correspond to
my experience with English syntax. There are lots of excessive as well as
missing commas.

- There are a few typos (e.g., 375, 615), some footnotes are missing full
stops.

- The linearization description is redundant at 429-433 and could just refer to
Sect. 3.3.

- When refering to the algorithm or figures (e.g., near 529, 538, 621-623),
enclose the references in brackets rather than commas.

- I think it would be nice to provide a reference for AMR itself and for the
multi-BLEU script.

- Also mention that you remove AMR variables in Footnote 3.

- Consider renaming Sect. 7 to "Linearization Evaluation".

- The order in Tables 1 and 2 seems a bit confusing to me, especially when your
systems are not explicitly marked (I would expect your systems at the bottom).
Also, Table 1 apparently lists development set scores even though its
description says otherwise.

- The labels in Table 3 are a bit confusing (when you read the table before
reading the text).

- In Figure 2, it's not entirely visible that you distinguish month names from
month numbers, as you state at 376.

- Bibliography lacks proper capitalization in paper titles, abbreviations and
proper names should be capitalized (use curly braces to prevent BibTeX from
lowercasing everything).

- The "Peng and Xue, 2017" citation is listed improperly, there are actually
four authors.

***
Summary:

The paper presents first competitive results for neural AMR parsing and
probably new state-of-the-art for AMR generation, using seq2seq models with
clever
preprocessing and exploiting large a unlabelled corpus. Even though revisions
to the text are advisable, I liked the paper and would like to see it at the
conference. 

(RESOLVED BY AUTHORS' RESPONSE) However, I am not sure if the comparison with
previous
state-of-the-art on generation is entirely sound, and most importantly, whether
the good results are not actually caused by data overlap of Gigaword
(additional training set) with the test set.

***
Comments after the authors' response:

I thank the authors for addressing both of the major problems I had with the
paper. I am happy with their explanation, and I raised my scores assuming that
the authors will reflect our discussion in the final paper.

The authors develop a method for jointly modeling content and discourse relations in dialogues. The content relations refer to the co-reference between two mentions in the same sentence, e.g. the patient-proxy conflict in the following two utterances: Alice: I want the patient to have the disease Bob: The patient has the disease The discourse relations refer to the relationships between two mentions in different sentences, e.g. the raise-question and answer in the following two utterances: Alice: Is the patient allergic to penicillin? Bob: No, the patient is not allergic to penicillin The authors first encode each sentence with its corresponding unique identifier, and then build a co-reference network and a triple network. A connection in the co-reference network between two mentions is established if they co-reference in at least one context. Similarly, a connection in the triple network between two mentions is established if they co-reference and discourse relation holds between them in at least one context. The authors then introduce a tensor to model the connections in both the co-reference network and the triple network. They further apply gradient descent to minimize the total loss, which is a combination of a binary mask loss and a Laplacian loss. The authors carry out extensive experiments on a widely-used clinical dialogue corpus and a user study to demonstrate the effectiveness of the method. The authors have introduced a novel technique to jointly model content and discourse relations in dialogues. This work can be regarded as an evolution of the works on dialogue relation extraction (DREE). The main contributions of this paper are as follows: 1. The co-reference network and the triple network are built for different purposes. In contrast to conventional co-reference networks that are used for cross-sentence grounding of co-referents, the triple network is used to capture the interaction between different discourse relation types. 2. The authors introduce a tensor to model the co-reference network, triple network and their interactions. They further apply gradient descent to train the model with both the co-reference network and the triple network. 3. The authors carry out extensive experiments on a widely-used clinical dialogue corpus and a user study to demonstrate the effectiveness of the method. The authors conducted a user study to evaluate the performance of the model on simulated patient-practitioner conversations. The overall F1 measure of the model was 0.79 on the clinical dialogue corpus, which was significantly higher than the F1 of 0.61 of a baseline system without the proposed model. The proposed model achieved significantly higher F1 scores than the state-of-the-art system on multiple subtasks, including providing medical advice, making suggestions for medical equipment, and communicating management requirements.

The paper is interesting and seems to have a good potential to further the research on meeting content selection and discourse relations, however, there are several issues that needs to be addressed before being accepted to thesig- ml list: 1. The paper only describes the results of the model for tasks of content selection and discourse relation prediction, but not for tasks of meeting summarization or dialogue act prediction, which are two main tasks of interest for Meeting OS. A model that can perform meeting summarization as well as both content selection and discourse relation prediction would be of significant more value. 2. The method proposed in this paper is a variation of a model that has been published previously, and the new part is that it also includes latent variables for discourse relations. Therefore, some readers may feel it is incremental, and not welcome to the community. Please note that at least for the machine summarization task, the incremental improvement has been shown to be significant. 3. As to the inconsistent team member understanding of meeting decisions, it is usually caused by a few dominate individuals who always have different opinion with the rest of the team, and the model will not capture this kind of diversity. For the case of small teams, you may want to introduce some additional variable to model the individual difference in terms of, for example, capacity to deliberate, opinion volatility etc., so that the inconsistent understanding can be modeled as well. Overall, I think the paper is worth being accepted to thesig- ml, but the focus on just one pair of content selection and discourse relation prediction and no machine summarization or dialogue act prediction is a concern, and the model may not be able to capture some of the individual differences in team members' understanding of meeting decisions.

The paper Joint Modeling of Content and Discourse Relations in Dialogues, its main content is as below: We present a joint modeling approach to identify salient discussion points in spoken meetings as well as to label the discourse relations between speaker turns. A variation of our model is also discussed when discourse relations are treated as latent variables. Experimental results on two popular meeting corpora show that our joint model can outperform state-of-the-art approaches for both phrase-based content selection and discourse relation prediction tasks. We also evaluate our model on predicting the consistency among team members' understanding of their group decisions. Classifiers trained with features constructed from our model achieve significant better predictive performance than the state-of-the-art. We believe this is an important step towards a better understanding of the challenges of task-oriented dialogues, and our model can be a useful addition to a dialog management tool. We start our discussion by introducing some related work on different problems discussed in the paper. Then we discuss some potential directions for future work. Related work Recent advances in computer vision have made it possible to detect and track a wide array of entities in video. Content-based dialogue systems often rely on the detected entities to assist the system in understanding the content of the user request and the correspond responses. For instance, in Asasey [1], the authors use MIT Lobe program to identify a large number of informable concepts in the dialogue, and this information is used to enrich the response with slot-value pairs that are relevant to the user request. Baumgartner [2] also presents a means of identifying informable concepts in the user request and responding using linguistic heuristics based on the syntax of the response. Ren [3] uses a two-stage process to identify key topics in the dialogue and present them to the system user as top-ranked responses. Other researchers have exploited a large body of resources to help the system detect and respond to informable concepts in the user request [4, 5]. However, most of these works focus on identifying individual concepts in a dialogue, rather than identifying the broader structure and/or content of a team discussion. In this work, we consider the content of a dialogue as the output of a team of writers who were tasked with describing a single, common topic. For example, as part of the development of a drug to treat epilepsy, the discussion may have looked like this: | Person | Topic | |-------- | ----- | | Todd | epilepsy | | Alice | seizure | | Bob | mode of action | | Cliff | effect on brain | | Paula | safety | In this example, Alice and Bob both mention “seizure,” which is a term that may be used to describe a person with epilepsy. In this case, Bob has incorrectly used the word “mode” (as in “mode of action”), and Alice points this out. In another example, Todd and Cliff have different opinions on the best way to describe the effects of the drug on brain structure. In this case, Todd believes that the word “brain” is sufficient, while Cliff believes that the discussion would be strengthened by using the word “effect” instead of “on.” In this work, we propose a joint model to identify salient discussion points in a team discussion, and predict discourse relations between subsequent speaker turns in the same team. In this example, Alice mentions “seizure” in her talk, and Bob replies with “mode of action.” In this example, Alice and Bob are involved in an *evidential disagreement* over the meaning of “mode of action.” The model should be able to determine that Alice is supporting her claim with “seizure” (which was mentioned by her a few seconds before), and Bob is contradicting his statement with “mode of action” (which was not mentioned by Alice). In this case, the model predicts that Bob opposes the statement made by Alice that “mode” should be changed to “mode of action.” This type of joint model of content and discourse relations has not been previously addressed by the literature on single-query document retrieval. An advantage of this approach is that it gives a global view of multiple stakeholders’ contributions to a discussion, as opposed to the more fine-grained identification of individual facts. For example, the model may identify that Alice, Bob, and Cliff are discussing the “mode” of action, while failing to identify that Alice and Bob disagree about the use of “mode” in the first place. machine_text: The paper addresses a very good problem of training an model to skim text by initially training the model to identify the important sentences. This is achieved by using the hard attention model which is trained with masked language model objective. The model is then trained to identify important sentences from the previously trained model. The model achieved significant improvement in BLEU score of 9.8% over the previous state of the art. which has some good points but also some limitations that could be addressed in the future works. The major issue is the use of hard attention mask which limits the generalizability of the model to new sentences. One possible solution to this issue is to use dynamic hard attention mask which is learned during training on new sentences. Another issue is the use of BLEU score which is a text matching metric and does not give importance to some of the aspects that an human annotator would give like 'clarity of the summary' and 'appropriateness of the summary for the context'. model should be tested on generated summary sentences to see if they achieve human standard of being a good summary. Overall this is an excellent work which makes a very good beginning in this space and approaches standardize measurement on new summaries generated by the model. ity! respective! DIRECTED ATTENTION FOR SKIMMING VMware proposes to develop learning to skim text (L2ST) model, which is a sequence-to-sequence (Seq2Seq) model pre-trained on machine translation (MT) tasks, such that the model can learn to identify important sentences in a given piece of text. The model is first pre-trained on masked language model (MLM) task to identify the sentences that are not vital for the the original text. After pre-training, the model is fine-tuned on LM task with the selected sentences for identifying important sentences. The model achieved significant improvement in BLEU score of 9.8% over the previous state of the art.

The authors propose a novel Neural Module Networks architecture for document-level click classification. The model is trained by first generating abstractive sentence proposals, and then predicting the relevance and the discrete categories of the documents in which each sentence appears. The model is evaluated on several public datasets and compared with the state of the art. The paper provides a nice introduction to NMT and GANs, and I really like the idea of sentence-level relevance prediction. The proposed NMT-DR model has some interesting extensions: first, the authors can apply a different NMT model to each document to generate diverse outputs; second, the model can be further extended to directly generate document-level relevance scores; third, instead of word-level relevance annotations, the authors can also use character-level attribute embedding to better model the semantic relevance between sentences. These interesting ideas could be worth pursuing in the future work. The paper “Learning to Skim Text” by Zhengdong Zhang, Ryan Scott, Richard Miron, Andrey Kutsov, Panos Mouratidis, Alan Liu, Thomas Debetz, Ruslan Salakhudinov, and Tyler Sengupta addresses the problem of improving the performance of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) by enabling them to skip irrelevant text. This is because RNNs, while extremely powerful, read text word by word which is slow for long documents. The solution proposed in the paper, a modified LSTM architecture called a Jumping LSTM, that enables RNNs to learn to skip text, has shown promising results on number prediction, sentiment analysis, news article classification and automatic Q&A. The main strength of this work is the development of a novel Jumping LSTM architecture that learns to skip text without human annotations. The paper also presents numerical evidence that the jumping LSTM is 6 times faster than a standard LSTM and can process text at a rate similar to that of a human reader. human_text:
The paper proposes a recurrent neural architecture that can skip irrelevant
input units. This is achieved by specifying R (# of words to read at each
"skim"), K (max jump size), and N (max # of jumps allowed). An LSTM processes R
words, predicts the jump size k in {0, 1...K} (0 signals stop), skips the next
k-1 words and continues until either the number of jumps reaches N or the model
reaches the last word. While the model is not differentiable, it can be trained
by standard policy gradient. The work seems to have been heavily influenced by
Shen et al. (2016) who apply a similar reinforcement learning approach
(including the same variance stabilization) to multi-pass machine reading. 

- Strengths:

The work simulates an intuitive "skimming" behavior of a reader, mirroring Shen
et al. who simulate (self-terminated) repeated reading. A major attribute of
this work is its simplicity. Despite the simplicity, the approach yields
favorable results. In particular, the authors show through a well-designed
synthetic experiment that the model is indeed able to learn to skip when given
oracle jump signals. In text classification using real-world datasets, the
model is able to perform competitively with the non-skimming model while being
clearly faster. 

The proposed model can potentially have meaningful practical implications: for
tasks in which skimming suffices (e.g., sentiment classification), it suggests
that we can obtain equivalent results without consuming all data in a
completely automated fashion. To my knowledge this is a novel finding. 

- Weaknesses:

It's a bit mysterious on what basis the model determines its jumping behavior
so effectively (other than the synthetic dataset). I'm thinking of a case where
the last part of the given sentence is a crucial evidence, for instance: 

"The movie was so so and boring to the last minute but then its ending blew me
away." 

In this example, the model may decide to skip the rest of the sentence after
reading "so so and boring". But by doing so it'll miss the turning point
"ending blew me away" and mislabel the instance as negative. For such cases a
solution can be running the skimming model in both directions as the authors
suggest as future work. But in general the model may require more sophisticated
architecture for controlling skimming.

It seems one can achieve improved skimming by combining it with multi-pass
reading (presumably in reverse directions). That's how humans read to
understand text that can't be digested in one skim; indeed, that's how I read
this draft. 

Overall, the work raises an interesting problem and provides an effective but
intuitive solution.

machine_text: The paper "Learning Symmetric Collaborative Dialogue Agents with Dynamic Knowledge Graph Embeddings" introduces a knowledge graph (KG) integration method for training dialogue managers. Dialogue Managers are an end-to-end system for multi-party conversation. It enables the system to engage in natural conversations with human-like communication skills. Most prior work uses hand-crafted rules or template-based systems to build such dialogue managers. However, manually constructing such rules is labor-intensive and hard to scale. Knowledge graph embedding techniques have recently achieved promising results on numerous NLP tasks, and we adopt this technique to facilitate knowledge graph embedding of dialogue manager rules. In particular, the proposed model lets each rule contain both an easy-to-domain sub-rule and a hard-to-domain sub-rule. The easy-to-domain sub-rule defines a node and a relation in the KG to which the rule applies. The hard-to-domain sub-rule defines another node and another relation, and requires more complex predicates and relations to describe. The proposed model optimizes both the cross-entropy loss and the regularization loss to train the model. We evaluate the proposed model on two public datasets and the results show the effectiveness of the proposed model. Overall, the paper introduces a novel knowledge graph integration method for training dialogue managers. The method significantly reduces the effort for manual rule construction. Additionally, the proposed model is capable of learning to generate both easy-to-domain and hard-to-domain rules for each rule category. I think this is a useful and novel method for building dialogue managers, and the paper presents the method in an accurately and clearly. I recommend it be accepted with only minor revisions. Please find my comments below: 1. Abstract: The paper introduces a novel knowledge graph integration method for training dialogue managers. The method significantly reduces the effort for manual rule construction. I don't think the method itself introduces new skills for rule construction, and it may not reduce the effort. The paper could present more in this part about the related work, and how this method is different from the baselines. 2. Introduction: There are two scenarios to introduce this method: 1) Dialogue managers often require rules to be mapped to predefined templates. These rules are hard to be maintained as new customer requirements arise. 2) Dialogue managers often require more complex rules to model relations between entities. For example, in the domain of customer service, the rule "If the customer places an order, the agent should recommend some related products" is more complex than "If the customer places an order, the agent should ask some questions about the order". I agree that knowledge graph embedding techniques have achieved promising results recently, and I think this method would be more suitable for the first case. 3. The detail of the method: The method optimizes both cross-entropy loss and the regularization loss. I think a simple cross-entropy loss would be enough to train the model. 4. The conclusion of the method: This method is effective and can be applied to different dialogue manager domains. I think this could be concluded based on the experimental results, and the paper could summarize the conclusion in the last part of the paper. 5. Table 1: I suggest giving more explanations for the columns in the table. For example, the last column "E(")" explains what "E()" stands for. 6. Fig 1: The icons used in the example could be clearer. I suggest providing clearer examples and the icons. Overall, this is a useful and novel method for building dialogue managers, and the paper presents the method in an accurately and clearly. I recommend it be accepted with only minor revisions. Sincerely Ling Ling is a freelance writer based in China with extensive writing experience on China cloud, data and AI. His work has been published in domestic and international media, such as The National Post, The Journal of Future Computing, Databricks, Gigaom andByte yeast.

Paper Title: Learning Symmetric Collaborative Dialogue Agents with Dynamic Knowledge Graph Embeddings This paper addresses the problem of learning collaborative dialogue agents that can communicate in a cooperative manner, even when the knowledge available to them is dynamically changing. The authors propose using a knowledge graph embedding to capture semantic similarities between entities, and a neural thread network to encode user and system replies to each message in the knowledge graph. The authors present two approaches to learning the knowledge embedding parameters using an asynchronous parallel parameter server, and a synchronous parameter averaging method. The experiments conducted on the DSTC8 and DSTC10 datasets show that the proposed model is able to generalize to previously unseen knowledge graphs and learn from dialogue datasets with limited amounts of annotated data. The paper also demonstrates that the proposed model is able to generalize to different message domains and user populations. The main strength of this paper is the introduction of a new approach to knowledge graph embedding using neural thread networks. The authors show that using a neural network to compute semantic similarities between entities provides a large margin of improvement over using a matrix to represent knowledge embeddings. Another strength of this paper is the introduction of an asynchronous parallel version of the knowledge graph embedding method, that can scale to large datasets and large numbers of training parameters, while still being able to converge in a reasonable amount of time. The weakness of this approach is that the convergence is not guaranteed, and it is not possible to control for the amount of knowledge graph evolution that is allowed for the model to learn. Overall, this is an exciting step towards building knowledge-rich dialog agents that can reason about new knowledge and generalize to different domains.

Thanks for sharing this work! The paper is nicely written and highlights an important research problem. My major concern is that the empirical evaluations are based on a small number of human-human dialogues. I worry that the results may not generalize to the real world where one may interact with an automated system. The model can appear effective because the evaluation metric is based on a binary success/fail output, which masks the fact that the model could have either easily achieved the goal or would have failed in a more nuanced way. For example, the system might not be very convincing or human-like, or might be overwhelming the user with too many options/options that are inconsistent with each other. In order for the paper to be more convincing, I recommend either extending the dataset with human-human conversations or using a different evaluation metric that measures the model's effectiveness in the real world. technology is evolving quickly, and we should expect that what works well in one setting will not necessarily work well in another setting. As such, the authors might want to consider including a set of real-world evaluations to see if the model shows promise in the real world. The authors might also consider using BLEU or another metric that is less biased towards binary success/fail outcomes. rebook Thanks for the comment! I agree that real-world evaluations are important to show the model's effectiveness in the real world. The model can still be successful even if the real-world evaluation does not perform as well as the binary success/fail evaluation, as long as the model is more effective than a simple rule-based model. For example, the model might generate a set of suggestions that are more consistent with the context, which could be more effective than a rule-based model. We have added an extra section to describe these real-world evaluations and report new metrics as well as results.

This paper Learning Symmetric Collaborative Dialogue Agents with Dynamic Knowledge Graph Embeddings addresses a novel open-ended dialogue state evaluation metric. They build a dynamic knowledge graph embedding model to explore the open-ended dialogue state representation and evaluate this model on both automatic evaluation and human evaluation. The paper is worth reading and might be of interest to you. exercise To evaluate a dialogue system on open-endedness, we suggest using the Shannon entropy of the system’s response candidates, which is calculated as follows: $$H=-\sum_{i=1}^{N}p(i)\log p(i),$$ where p(i) is the probability of the i-th most likely response among the system’s response candidates, and N is the number of all response candidates. A lower Shannon entropy indicates the system’s responses are more open-ended. The model with dynamic knowledge graph embeddings that evolves as the dialogue progresses makes better use of the dialogue history and makes more accurate predictions for the system’s responses. In the dialogue state (03), the system’s response “I don’t know” is more likely given that the user said “I don’t know” in the dialogue state (01) and “yes” in the dialogue state (02). The dynamic knowledge graph embedding model encodes this and other implicit semantic information into low-dimensional vectors that summarize the dialogue state. This dynamic knowledge graph embedding model is applied to dialogue state (03) and obtains the following entropy: Dialogue State: (03) System Response: “I don’t know” Shannon Entropy: 0.485 Model Response: “I don’t know” Shannon Entropy: 0.426 We can see the model response is less open-ended than the system response, and we can explain this by the following dialogue context: the model generates the response by analyzing the previous two system responses “yes” and “no”, while the system responds “I don’t know” based only on the previous dialogue state. This dynamic knowledge graph embedding model also obtains lower entropy in the automatic evaluation than the baseline models, which means it captures more implicit semantic information.

This paper presents a novel framework for modelling symmetric collaborative
dialogue agents by dynamically extending knowledge graphs embeddings. The task
is rather simple: two dialogue agents (bot-bot, human-human or human-bot) talk
about their mutual friends. There is an underlying knowledge base for each
party in the dialogue and an associated knowledge graph. Items in the knowledge
graph have embeddings that are dynamically updated during the conversation and
used to generate the answers.

- Strengths: This model is very novel for both goal-directed and open ended
dialogue. The presented evaluation metrics show clear advantage for the
presented model.

- Weaknesses: In terms of the presentation, mathematical details of how the
embeddings are computed are not sufficiently clear. While the authors have done
an extensive evaluation, they haven't actually compared the system with an
RL-based dialogue manager which is current state-of-the-art in goal-oriented
systems. Finally, it is not clear how this approach scales to more complex
problems. The authors say that the KB is 3K, but actually what the agent
operates is about 10 (judging from Table 6).

- General Discussion: Overall, I think this is a good paper. Had the
theoretical aspects of the paper been better presented I would give this paper
an accept.

machine_text: This paper presents a geometric contextual model (GCM) for identifying unseen metaphors. The GCM builds a metaphors-space in which each metaphor is a point. The context, which is represented as a vector in the same space, is represented as a vector originating from the metaphor point or pointing to it. The distances between these points reflect the similarity between metaphors. To identify metaphors in new contexts, their distances to any metaphors in the history of metaphors are calculated. The metaphors with significant changes in distances are considered as new metaphors. The GCM is evaluated on two metaphor datasets with gold standard metaphors and evaluation results show that the method can identify unseen high-probability metaphors. 80211 strously interesting idea, and a very good try at implementing it. Unfortunately, however, I am not sure this model can identify unseen metaphors. The reason is that, to calculate the distances, it seems to me that the model only considers the difference between the new context and each past context one by one, which would result in the situation that two similar but different contexts would both produce the same distance to any past metaphor. For example, for the contexts "A stroke of genius" and "AHA moment", according to the model, they would both produce the same distance to the past metaphor "A bolt of lightning". This seems incorrect to me. I think the model should either consider the differences between all past contexts and the new context at once, which may cause it to misjudge many similar contexts as different, or only consider some past contexts and ignore others, which may lose some subtle difference that make the past contexts similar to each other but different from the new context. I think the best that the model could do is to find out the past contexts that are similar to the new context and then judge if the new context belongs to the same category as these past contexts. Although I'm not sure if it can identify unseen metaphors, I think this type of metric is necessary for this type of model, since otherwise it seems like there could be many cases that this metric could not identify, in which case the model is not even useful for preventing humans from doing this type of analysis for identifying unseen metaphors.

The paper addresses the problem of identifying unseen metaphors. In the given dataset, there are two parts - train and test. The train dataset consists of sentences with words that could potentially be used to form a metaphor, while the test dataset contains a subset of these metaphors that have not appeared in the training data. The objective is to develop a model which can classify a new metaphor from the test dataset as metaphor or non-metaphor. The model created uses word embeddings along with various semantic and syntactic similarities to perform the classification. A geometric approach is used to find the closest matching metaphors in the training data. The paper does not cover all possible use cases for this problem but is generalizable to other related applications. The evaluation shows that the proposed method achieves an accuracy of 83% on the test dataset. esk The paper considers the problem of identifying unseen metaphors. This paper proposes an approach for classifying literal and metaphoric
adjective-noun pairs. The authors create a word-context matrix for adjectives
and nouns where each element of the matrix is the PMI score. They then use
different methods for selecting dimensions of this matrix to represent each
noun/adjective as a vector. The geometric properties of average, nouns, and
adjective vectors and their normalized versions are used as features in
training a regression model for classifying the pairs to literal or metaphor
expressions. Their approach performs similarly to previous work that learns a
vector representation for each adjective.

Supervision and zero-shot learning. The authors argue that their approach
requires less supervision (compared to previous work)  and can do zero-shot
learning. I don’t think this is quite right and given that it seems to be one
of the main points of the paper, I think it is worth clarifying. The approach
proposed in the paper is a supervised classification task: The authors form
vector representations from co-occurrence statistics, and then use the
properties of these representations and the gold-standard labels of each pair
to train a classifier. The model (similarly to any other supervised classifier)
can be tested on words that did not occur in the training data; but, the model
does not learn from such examples. Moreover, those words are not really
“unseen” because the model needs to have a vector representation of those
words.

Interpretation of the results. The authors provide a good overview of the
previous related work on metaphors. However, I am not sure what the intuition
about their approach is (that is, using the geometric properties such as vector
length in identifying metaphors). For example, why are the normalized vectors
considered? It seems that they don’t contribute to a better performance.
Moreover, the most predictive feature is the noun vector; the authors explain
that this is a side effect of the data which is collected such that each
adjective occurs in both metaphoric and literal expressions. (As a result, the
adjective vector is less predictive.) It seems that the proposed approach might
be only suitable for the given data. This shortcoming is two-fold: (a) From the
theoretical perspective (and especially since the paper is submitted to the
cognitive track), it is not clear what we learn about theories of metaphor
processing. (b) From the NLP applications standpoint, I am not sure how
generalizable this approach is compared to the compositional models.

Novelty. The proposed approach for representing noun/adjective vectors is very
similar to that of Agres et al. It seems that the main contribution of the
paper is that they use the geometric properties to classify the vectors.

machine_text: In this paper, the authors proposed to model topic modeling as a matrix factorization problem and to use a notion of topic similarity to predict inter-topic preferences. I agree with the paper except the following: 1. In my opinion, it is not a good idea to model topic modeling as a matrix factorization problem. For example, it is difficult to solve the corresponding optimization problem and the result may be not easy to interpret. I would recommend the authors to apply probabilistic topic models to generate topics and to use these topic texts to compute inter-topic similarities. 2. As for the modeling of inter-topic preferences, it is better to consider the similarities among topics instead of users directly. For example, it is possible to represent each topic as a $d$-dimensional vector, where $d$ is the number of dimensions of the vocabulary. Then the authors can compute the cosine similarity between each two topics and obtain the inter-topic preferences matrix. In this way, the model can be interpreted and some nice relations between topics can be analyzed. 3. The best dataset to test the model is microtexts. A microtext is generated based on a Twitter thread. It combines the responses of Twitter users to a root issue. The dataset is published by a group at Stanford. The authors could take this dataset as a test case to compare their model with other state of the art models. I hope you enjoy the read and the author give you permission to share this feedback.

In this paper, the authors try to predict the relation between two topics based on the presence of tweets mentioning both topics. The authors use two datasets, one with Twitter posts and another with published news articles. The news articles have a category (e.g. Politics, Science etc.) and each article is associated with a number of categories it belongs to. Similarly, the Twitter posts are also associated with categories, but the authors manually annotate a sample of posts to create a training and testing set. The authors represent each tweet as a 400 dimension vector, where each dimension represents the frequency of a particular word in the tweet. Using this tweet representation along with the categories mentioned in the news articles, the authors train a supervised machine learning model for the problem of topic prediction. The authors also compare their approach with the Latent Dirichlet Allocation model and show that their approach performs better in predicting the relations between topics. This paper can be useful for someone working in the field of information retrieval, who is trying to improve the relevance of news articles with respect to a particular topic. The method used in this paper might also be useful for someone who is trying to build a model that can detect association between people/accounts based on the presence of Tweet and/or post text. The authors should have clearly stated the problem they tried to solve in the introduction. The sub-section "Similar to other research works...", has a better introduction to the problem. Another issue the authors encountered was that the document frequency for many of the words were very low. Using a TF-IDF was not a good approach, as the authors used it only to normalize the matrix dimensions. The implementation of the algorithm, they used has many other steps that could have been done differently or better explained.

This paper presents a method for modeling inter-topic preferences on Twitter. The main idea is to use a topic modeling approach to get topics and then represent user preferences as a matrix which encodes the affinity between topics and users. The model then factorizes this matrix into a product of matrices which represent the topic affinity matrix and the user affinity matrix. The main contributions of this paper are: (1) extracting user preferences from linguistic patterns, (2) representing user preferences with a matrix which encodes the affinity between topics and users, and (3) presenting the model that factorizes this matrix. The experiment results show that the model can achieve good performance in prediction. reely, your paper is very good, especially the part about topic modeling. In your model, you use a matrix to represent the affinity between topics and users, and factorize this matrix. My suggestion is to use a graph to represent the affinity between topics and users, and use a tensor to represent the affinity. In this way, you can calculate the affinity between any two topics and users, not only two specific topics or users. ivated Thanks for your feedback. We agree that the affinity between topics and users could be modeled as a graph and use a tensor to represent the affinity. We have considered this extension in our revised version. adapter To answer your first question, we use a graph to model the affinity between topics and users. There are several existing work about topic models based on graphs. We can calculate the relationship between two topics/users as the affinity in the graph. For example, according to the weighted trust graph, the affinity between topics can be computed as the average trust values of corresponding nodes in the topic model.

In this paper, the authors model inter-topic preferences of Twitter users as a task of predicting users' preferences on statements agreeing and disagreeing with various topics. The paper presents a novel approach of extracting preferences from tweets through linguistic patterns of agreement and disagreement. The authors then model the task of predicting missing preferences as a matrix factorization problem. Finally, the paper conducts experiments on a task of predicting users' missing preferences and show that their approach of modeling inter-topic preferences is successful. The paper has several strengths. First, the authors present an innovative approach to modeling inter-topic preferences, i.e., tweets. Second, the authors demonstrate its effectiveness through experiments. Finally, the authors present a novel aspect of modeling inter-topic preferences as a subtask of missing preferences prediction. The paper also faces some limitations. First, the authors use only a single data source, i.e., Twitter, to model inter-topic preferences. Second, the authors evaluate their approach on a task of predicting missing preferences. An extension to an approach for a different task is not straightforward. Overall, the paper presents a novel and promising approach for modeling inter-topic preferences and shows its effectiveness through several experiments. Some of the presented linguistic patterns are complex. For example, “A is completely wrong” is a pattern that is complex to extract. The author should introduce an index to refer to similar patterns. There are many topics not included in the training set and there might be some topics that are not suitable for people to express agreement and disagreement on. An evaluation on a large number of topics is needed before using the presented model in practice. Some of the presented patterns are too generic and have low precision. For example, the authors define an item “A is completely wrong” as a pattern to express agreement. In practice, however, many users agree about some topics but do not use such a pattern. For example, “A is completely wrong” is only 10% accurate when users’ agreement is considered. To improve the accuracy of prediction, a more sophisticated definition of patterns and some mechanisms to enhance their coverage in practice are needed. The paper presents two directions for future work. The first is to apply this model on a larger set of topics. Second, the paper presents an approach for predicting missing preferences. The authors should also consider another task of predicting the top K topics that users prefer. These limitations and future directions of research suggest that the presented approach is useful and could be applied in a number of areas. However, it is not guaranteed to be successful in all cases. The strengths of this paper are its innovative approach to modeling inter-topic preferences, i.e., the linguistic patterns of agreement and disagreement, and its effectiveness through experiments. The paper presents the first approach that can predict users' preferences on statements agreeing and disagreeing with various topics based on linguistic patterns of agreement and agreement. The linguistic patterns presented in the paper are simple and some users do not express agreement using such patterns. The presented model can be applied to a number of areas, such as public opinion survey, electoral prediction, electoral campaigns, and online debates. It is useful but not guaranteed to be successful in all cases.

- Strengths:

The deviation between "vocal" users and "average users" is an interesting
discovery that could be applied as a way to identify different types of users.

- Weaknesses:

I see it as an initial work on a new topic that should be expanded in the
future. A possible comparison between matrix factorization and similar topics 
in distributional semantics (e.g. latent semantic analysis) would be useful. 

- General Discussion:

In this paper, the authors describe an approach for modeling the
stance/sentiment of Twitter users about topics. In particular, they address the
task of inter-topic preferences modeling. This task consists of measuring the
degree to which the stances about different topics are mutually related.This
work is claimed to advance state of the art in this task, since previous works
were case studies, while the proposed one is about unlimited topics on
real-world data.The adopted approach consists of the following steps: A set of
linguistic patterns was manually created and, through them, a large number of
tweets expressing stance towards various topics was collected. Next, the texts
were expressed as triples containing user, topic, and evaluation. The
relationships represented by the tuples were arranged as a sparse matrix. After
matrix factorization, a low-rank approximation was performed. The optimal rank
was identified as 100. The definition of cosine similarity is used to measure
the similarity between topics and, thus, detect latent preferences not
represented in the original sparse matrix. Finally, cosine similarity is also
used to detect inter-topic preferences.A preliminary empirical evaluation shows
that the model predicts missing topics preferences. Moreover, predicted
inter-topic preferences moderately correlate with the corresponding values from
a crowdsourced gold-standard collection of preferences. 
According to the overview discussed in the related work section, there are no
previous systems to be compared in the latter task (i.e. prediction of
inter-topic preferences) and, for this reason, it is promising.

machine_text: This paper presents a teacher-student framework for zero-resource neural machine translation (NMT). The main idea is to use student model to capture the "teacher's domain knowledge" and then use that knowledge to guide the generation of target sentence. In particular, we design a teacher-student framework based on teacher model with additional classification loss and student model with classification loss only. Such framework allows the student model to borrow strengths from the teacher model while avoid the negative effects from the excessive reliance on the features extracted by the teacher model. We perform experiments on Chinese-English and English-French translation and the results show that the proposed teacher-student framework can effectively guide the generation of target text with many accurate aspects, especially in terms of geographical expressions. This paper is strongly related to [1]. The framework in [1] is different from the current paper in two aspects. First, [1] use Gumbel noise to guide the update of student model, which is different from directly using classification loss to guide the update of student model. In addition, in [1] the target sentence is always paired with a source sentence, while in this paper the target sentence only receives a corresponding source sentence from a batch, which means the former one is supervised learning while the later one is unsupervised learning. The proposed teacher-student framework could also be interpreted as an example of "unexpected outcome of joint training" [2]. In the teacher-student framework, the teacher model has the same architecture as the student model except that the latter has zero parameters. During the training, the teacher model can guide the optimization of the student model by only giving the classification loss. The trained student model can borrow the strength from the successful parameter setting of the teacher model, such as good encoder/decoder structure and good language features. But at the same time, the student model can also avoid the over-fitting to the parameters of the teacher model, such as bad encoder/decoder structure and bad language features. In summary, this framework can effectively transfer the successful parameter setting from the teacher model to the student model while avoid the parameters which will make the student model worse but still use this framework to train. Besides providing the classification accuracy, the performance of the student model can also reflect the effectiveness of the framework. In this paper, two versions of student models are introduced, one uses classification loss only, the other uses classification loss plus additional regression loss. The classification loss only student model corresponds to the framework in [1], which means it transfers the good encoder/decoder structure from the teacher model to the student model. While the classification loss plus additional regression loss student model corresponds to the framework in [2], which means it makes the student model take advantage of the good language features from the teacher model without giving the parameter setting for the bad features to the student model. The classification accuracy of the classification loss only student model is 95.83% for Chinese-English and 98.67% for English-French, which is close to the classification accuracy (96.00% for Chinese-English and 98.33% for English-French) of the teacher model that we actually copy. The classification accuracy of the classification loss plus additional regression loss student model is 97.35% for Chinese-English and 98.67% for English-French, which shows that the student model can also take advantage of the good language features without having the parameter sharing between the good and bad features. Overall, the paper makes a good effort on solving the problem of zero-resource NMT by using the teacher-student framework with good prediction ability and little parameter sharing. This paper proposes a teacher-student framework for zero-resource neural machine translation (ZRNAMT). Unlike existing ZRL methods that translate in a one-to-one fashion, the student in the teacher-student framework focuses on the specific structural requirements of the task at hand. The teacher first generates translations based on a priori knowledge, and the student refines these translations based on a human proofreader. The student can then be used to produce high-quality translations quickly. We conduct experiments on two ZRL tasks and the results show that the student model yields better translations than the one-to-one model. We also apply the student model to a high volume translation scenario and show that the student model performs better than the one-to-one model under this scenario as well. swung ZRNAMT is a challenging task because training data is usually scarce for this task, especially for low-resource languages. A teacher-student framework is proposed to leverage prior knowledge and a human proofreader to facilitate low-resource ZRL. In particular, teacher first translates a given sentence based on a priori knowledge and human proofreader is used to correct the translation. Then, student learn from the teacher's mistake to produce better translations. Experiments on two ZRL tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of the student model. The student also shows higher efficiency than the one-to-one model when applying to a high-volume translation scenario. 67%? That’s impressive! Even though we only trained the student on a small amount of data (less than a tenth of the size of the training set for low-resource ZRL), the student still outperforms the one-to-one model. This shows the value of the student model — it’s able to leverage the teacher’s a priori knowledge and achieve a better generalization performance. The student model also shows better flexibility. Compared with the one-to-one model, the student has a better performance under low-resource scenarios but also show higher efficiency under a high-volume scenario.

The paper of A Teacher-Student Framework for Zero-Resource Neural Machine Translation presents a teacher-student method for training NMT model with 0 parallel corpus, the main content of the paper is as below: While end-to-end neural machine translation (NMT) has made remarkable progress recently, it still suffers from the data scarcity problem for low-resource language pairs and domains. In this paper, we propose a method for zero-resource NMT by assuming that parallel sentences have close probabilities of generating a sentence in a third language. The proposed method is able to train a source-to-target NMT model (``student'') without parallel corpora available guided by an existing pivot-to-target NMT model (``teacher'') on a source-pivot parallel corpus. Experimental results show that the proposed method significantly improves over a baseline pivot-based model by +3.0 BLEU points across various language pairs. This paper is worth of publication. Q1. Is this method suitable for low-resource language pairs? A1. This method works well for low-resource language pairs, but it still requires a small amount of parallel data for the target language. In addition, when the number of parallel sentences is small, the proposed method can also benefit from pre-training a source-specific model to obtain better initialization for the student model. Q2. Is this method suitable for low-resource domains? A2. The method is domain-independent and can be applied to low-resource domains by using domain information. However, in some low-resource domain pairs, the source and target domains have less relevance, such as in parody or interlingual humor. In this case, the proposed method may not be effective. We suggest the author uses self-supervised learning on the source-pivot corpus to pre-train the source-specific model and uses multi-domain learning on the target-pivot corpus to pre-train the teacher model, and then uses the student model to translate from the source language to the target language. Q3. What is the optimal size of the target-pivot corpus? A3. We recommend using at least 20 times the size of the source-pivot corpus. We simulate the cost of computing the gradient of the target-pivot corpus for different sizes of the corpus, and the result is as below: Size of target-pivot corpus | Computational cost 1x | 19.1 ms 10x | 38.2 ms 20x | 76.3 ms 50x | 76.3 ms 100x | 76.3 ms We think it's too expensive to calculate the target-pivot corpus for small sizes (1x) of the corpus, the cost will increase quickly as the size increases. Q4. Does the proposed method learn domain-specific knowledge? A4. The method assumes that the parallel sentences have close probabilities of generating a sentence in the third language, which is a general assumption for low-resource language pairs. In addition, the method also allows the student model to learn domain-specific knowledge from the teacher model. We know that teacher model pre-trained with low-resource domain usually hasDomain-specific knowledge encoded in the model. With the assumption that the parallel sentences have close probabilities of generating a sentence in the third language, the student model can also learn Domain-specific knowledge from the teacher model through the teacher model's representation. Q5. Can the teacher model help the student model to obtain better initialization? A5. Yes, with a pre-trained teacher model, the student model can get better initialization from the teacher model. We also tested this method and found that the student model with the initialized model from the teacher model performed better than the model initialized with the previously mentioned method. Q6. What is the relationship between the size of the target-pivot corpus and the performance of the student model? A6. The performance of the student model is related to the size of the target-pivot corpus, the bigger the size is, the better the performance is. However, for a large size, the cost of calculating the gradient of the target-pivot corpus will also increase, and the parameter in the student model will change too much to converge. In summary, the size of the target-pivot corpus is a trade-off between the performance and cost. For Chinese to English, 20x of the size is a good size; For English to Chinese, Chinese cannot translate to English, so 1x of the size is sufficient. We suggest the author experiment with different target-pivot corpus sizes and choose the size that meets the cost and evaluation requirements

human_text:
This paper proposes a novel strategy for zero-resource translation where
(source, pivot) and (pivot, target) parallel corpora are available. A teacher
model for p(target|pivot) is first trained on the (pivot, target) corpus, then
a student model for p(target|source) is trained to minimize relative entropy
with respect to the teacher on the (source, pivot) corpus. When using
word-level relative entropy over samples from the teacher, this approach is
shown to outperform previous variants on standard pivoting, as well as other
zero-resource strategies.

This is a good contribution: a novel idea, clearly explained, and with
convincing empirical support. Unlike some previous work, it makes fairly
minimal assumptions about the nature of the NMT systems involved, and hence
should be widely applicable.

I have only a few suggestions for further experiments. First, it would be
interesting to see how robust this approach is to more dissimilar source and
pivot languages, where intuitively the true p(target|source) and
p(target|pivot) will be further apart. Second, given the success of introducing
word-based diversity, it was surprising not to see a sentence n-best or
sentence-sampling experiment. This would be more costly, but not much more so
since you’re already doing beam search with the teacher. Finally, related to
the previous, it might be interesting to explore transition from word-based
diversity to sentence-based as the student converges and no longer needs the
signal from low-probability words.

Some further comments:

line 241: Despite its simplicity -> Due to its simplicity

277: target sentence y -> target word y

442: I assume that K=1 and K=5 mean that you compare probabilities of the most
probable and 5 most probable words in the current context. If so, how is the
current context determined - greedily or with a beam?

Section 4.2. The comparison with an essentially uniform distribution doesn’t
seem very informative here: it would be extremely surprising if p(y|z) were not
significantly closer to p(y|x) than to uniform. It would be more interesting to
know to what extent p(y|z) still provides a useful signal as p(y|x) gets
better. This would be easy to measure by comparing p(y|z) to models for p(y|x)
trained on different amounts of data or for different numbers of iterations.
Another useful thing to explore in this section would be the effect of the mode
approximation compared to n-best for sentence-level scores.

555: It’s odd that word beam does worse than word greedy, since word beam
should be closer to word sampling. Do you have an explanation for this?

582: The claimed advantage of sent-beam here looks like it may just be noise,
given the high variance of these curves.

In this paper the authors present a method for training a zero-resource NMT
system by using training data from a pivot language. Unlike other approaches
(mostly inspired in SMT), the author’s approach doesn’t do two-step
decoding. Instead, they use a teacher/student framework, where the teacher
network is trained using the pivot-target language pairs, and the student
network is trained using the source-pivot data and the teacher network
predictions of the target language.

- Strengths:

The results the authors present, show that their idea is promising. Also, the
authors present several sets of results that validate their assumptions.

- Weaknesses:

However, there are many points that need to be address before this paper is
ready for publication.

1)            Crucial information is missing

Can you flesh out more clearly how training and decoding happen in your
training framework? I found out that the equations do not completely describe
the approach. It might be useful to use a couple of examples to make your
approach clearer.

Also, how is the montecarlo sampling done? 

2)            Organization
The paper is not very well organized. For example, results are broken into
several subsections, while they’d better be presented together.  The
organization of the tables is very confusing. Table 7 is referred before table
6. This made it difficult to read the results.

3)            Inconclusive results:
After reading the results section, it’s difficult to draw conclusions when,
as the authors point out in their comparisons, this can be explained by the
total size of the corpus involved in their methods (621  ). 

4)            Not so useful information:
While I appreciate the fleshing out of the assumptions, I find that dedicating
a whole section of the paper plus experimental results is a lot of space. 

- General Discussion:

- Strengths:

- Weaknesses:
There were many sentences in the abstract and in other places in the paper
where the authors stuff too much information into a single sentence. This could

There could have been a section where the actual method used could be explained
in a more detailed. This explanation is glossed over in the paper. It's

During test time, you need the source-pivot corpus as well. This is a major

The model achieves state of the art performance on DBPEDIA, a dataset the authors created, through a novel combination of a self-supervised pre-training step and a few simple additions to a standard ranking loss. While the self-supervised pre-training step is interesting, it could be made more widely applicable and potentially further improved by using an authentic student sample instead of generated sentences. The paper itself is a bit rough around the edges, with some grammar and spelling errors and an overall feeling of the author being a first-time author, which could be slightly alleviated by providing more detail on how to code different parts of the model and how the model was trained. Overall, the paper provides an interesting model for knowledge base completion that could have wide applicability in the field. I recommend acceptance with some minor revisions. Minor revisions: - The manuscript would benefit from a technical reviewer. - It would be helpful to have more detail on how to code different parts of the model. Modifications recommended by reviewer: - Page 4, second paragraph: Replace "currently, little work has been done to try and apply knowledge distillation to KBC" with "to the best of our knowledge, little work has been done to try and apply knowledge distillation to KBC." - Page 5, first paragraph: Replace "against the strong Baseline model, which uses the Semanticbee dataset for knowledge distillation," with "against the strong Baseline model, which uses the Semanticbee dataset and linguistic features for knowledge distillation." - Page 7, first paragraph: Replace "uses" with "is based on" - Page 10, first paragraph: Replace "dataset of generated sentences" with "dataset of randomly generated sentences" - Page 14, first paragraph: Replace "Because we don't have an actual student training dataset," with "Because we don't have an actual student training dataset, we use the dataset of randomly generated sentences." - Page 14, first paragraph: Replace "a pre-trained model that performs well on a held-out testset," with "a pre-trained model that performs well on a held-out testset, and that we'll refer to as "Baseline"." - Page 16, last paragraph: In the second sentence of the second paragraph, replace "knowledge distillation" with " student dataset". The paper entitled An Interpretable Knowledge Transfer Model for Knowledge Base Completion introduces an approach, called ILT, for knowledge base completion where the model transfers knowledge from a larger, more reliable knowledge base to a smaller target knowledge base. The ILT model is motivated by the observation that humans often learn new concepts by referring to existing knowledge. The model transfers knowledge by finding similar concepts in the source knowledge base and transferring the most frequent knowledge about those similar concepts. The model is interpretable, in that it can be explained with natural language statements, and has been shown in experiments to transfer knowledge between smaller and smaller knowledge bases. The model has limitations. The number of nearest neighbors for a concept in the source knowledge base has to be specified. The paper does not explore the effectiveness of multiple values of this hyperparameter, nor does it explore the case where the number of nearest neighbors is larger than one. The model is also limited to transferring knowledge between concepts of the same general type (i.e., the source and target knowledge bases have to share the same namespace). However, the model is flexible, efficient, and has achieved success transferring knowledge between knowledge bases with large differences in size, and between knowledge bases with incomplete namespaces. The paper presents a strong baseline for future work. Overall, this is an important and interesting paper that could have a significant impact on the field of knowledge transfer. I recommend it be accepted with some minor revisions. * Strengths: The paper describes an approach to knowledge transfer that is broadly applicable and makes a strong baseline for future work. The transfer function is modular and natural language can be used to express rules for knowledge transfer. The paper explores transfer between knowledge bases with large differences in size and between knowledge bases with incomplete namespaces. The model provides an indication of which parts of the knowledge base are most important, so that only these are transferred. * Weaknesses: The model is limited to transferring knowledge between concepts of the same general type. The paper does not explore the effectiveness of multiple values of the number of nearest neighbors for a concept. The transfer function is not differentiable, so quantitative analysis of the transfer function is not possible. * Recommendations for future work: Exploring the effects of multiple values for the number of nearest neighbors for a concept and quantitative analysis of the transfer function would be useful. The paper does not mention an evaluation of the proposed method for transfer between knowledge bases with small differences in size or with large differences in size but with incomplete namespaces. In these cases, the transferred knowledge may not be relevant or applicable. These are significant limitations of the current work, but significant improvements could still make the model strong a baseline for future work. I recommend that the paper be accepted with these issues noted as major issues for the next iteration of the paper.

Overall this paper makes some important contributions. First, it proposes a novel Knowledge Transfer model named ITransF that can transfer statistical strength through the sharing of concepts. Second, the learned associations between relations and concepts, which are represented by sparse attention vectors, can be interpreted easily. Third, they evaluate ITransF on two benchmark datasets---WN18 and FB15k and achieves state-of-the-art performances on both the mean rank and Hits@10 metrics. However, there are some points that can be improved: 1- The organization of this paper is a little bit confusing, there are some duplicate paragraphs in different sections that should be combined or removed. 2- In the second paragraph of the introduction, the authors said that knowledge bases suffer from incompleteness, but then in the third paragraph they said that knowledge bases are complete. 3- In the fourth paragraph, "relation type" is a new abbreviation, which should be explained in the beginning of the paragraph. 4- In the fifth paragraph, there are some typos: "we would like to point" should be "we suggest" 5- In the sixth paragraph, the word "interpretability" should be replaced by "visualization". 6- In the seventh paragraph, the abbreviation "M+1" is not defined anywhere. 7- In the eighth paragraph, "formula" is used instead of "sentence" 8- In the ninth paragraph, "key concepts" should be replaced by "key terms". 9- In the tenth paragraph, "interpretation" should be replaced by "visualization". 10- In the last paragraph, some typos were left.
