human_text:
This paper considers the problem of KB completion and proposes ITransF for this
purpose. Unlike STransE that assigns each relation an independent matrix, this
paper proposes to share the parameters between different relations. A model is
proposed where a tensor D is constructed that contains various relational
matrices as its slices and a selectional vector \alpha is used to select a
subset of relevant relational matrix for composing a particular semantic
relation. The paper then discuss a technique to make \alpha sparse.
Experimental results on two standard benchmark datasets shows the superiority
of ITransF over prior proposals.

The paper is overall well written and the experimental results are good.
However, I have several concerns regarding this work that I hope the authors
will answer in their response.

1. Just by arranging relational matrices in a tensor and selecting (or more
appropriately considering a linearly weighted sum of the relational matrices)
does not ensure any information sharing between different relational matrices.
This would have been the case if you had performed some of a tensor
decomposition and projected the different slices (relational matrices) into
some common lower-dimensional core tensor. It is not clear why this approach
was not taken despite the motivation to share information between different
relational matrices.
2. The two requirements (a) to share information across different relational
matrices and (b) make the attention vectors sparse are some what contradictory.
If the attention vector is truly sparse and has many zeros then information
will not flow into those slices during optimisation. 
3. The authors spend a lot of space discussing techniques for computing sparse
attention vectors. The authors mention in page 3 that \ell_1 regularisation did
not work in their preliminary experiments. However, no experimental results are
shown for \ell_1 regularisation nor they explain why \ell_1 is not suitable for
this task. To this reviewer, it appears as an obvious baseline to try,
especially given the ease of optimisation. You use \ell_0 instead and get into
NP hard optimisations because of it. Then you propose a technique and a rather
crude approximation in the end to solve it. All that trouble could be spared if
\ell_1 was used.
4. The vector \alpha is performing a selection or a weighing over the slices of
D. It is slightly misleading to call this as “attention” as it is a term
used in NLP for a more different type of models (see attention model used in
machine translation).
5. It is not clear why you need to initialise the optimisation by pre-trained
embeddings from TransE. Why cannot you simply randomly initialise the
embeddings as done in TransE and then update them? It is not fair to compare
against TransE if you use TransE as your initial point.

Learning the association between semantic relations is an idea that has been
used in related problems in NLP such as relational similarity measurement
[Turney JAIR 2012] and relation adaptation [Bollegala et al. IJCAI 2011]. It
would be good to put the current work with respect to such prior proposals in
NLP for modelling inter-relational correlation/similarity.

Thanks for providing feedback. I have read it.

The LSTM model of LSTMEmbed: a Lexical and SemanTic Model of Embeddings allows for a more comprehensive understanding of the document from both a semantic and morphological perspective. This model has been developed and tested on the Chinese restaurant franchise task, and it significantly outperformed the previously published state-of-the-art. The model has been developed with a bidirectional LSTM, which encodes and analyzes the sequence of tokens in the given text from both a forward and backward perspective, making it possible to capture the directionality of the relationship between the words. The model obtains a score for the probability distribution over the vocabulary for each token given the context. Given the distributional hypothesis that related terms would appear near to one another in the word embedding space, the model assigns a score for each token based on the probability distribution of all the other words in the vocabulary. This approach takes into consideration not only the immediate neighbors of the tokens, which are the words adjacent to them in the sentence, but also the global semantics of the document. The model considers the order of the words in the sentence, which significantly improves the performance of the model. The model uses pre-trained embedding obtained from a large corpus, which reduces the risk of overfitting. The model also considers the order of the words in the sentence when calculating the vector representation of the words in the sentence. Using this aspect of the model, the model can be extended to more general applications such as text classification and question answering. In this paper we leverage a bidirectional LSTM while at the same time taking advantage of other semantic resources in order to create a vector space model for words and senses that outperforms most popular algorithms for learning embeddings. We evaluate our approach on the most well-known benchmarks on vector space representations. The main strength of the paper is the approach that combines various semantic resources and a bidirectional LSTM in order to produce superior word vector representations. The combination of different resources should be beneficial for this task. We believe that the model and its evaluation is not competitive over more recent and more powerful neural network based architectures for word2vec. The main weakness of the paper is that it does not address a serious shortcoming of LSTM, i.e. a limited ability to capture long range dependencies. Such dependencies are very important for lexical and semantic analysis. The difference in performance between the proposed model and the models based on simpler RNNs indicates the extent to which LSTM is able to capture long range dependencies. Overall, the proposed LSTM architecture represents an important step forward for word vector representations, however, further work is required in order to incorporate long range dependencies into such models.

machine_text: Overall, I find the paper interesting and well-written. However, I have some major concerns regarding the choice of using the L1 distance as the similarity metric for sequence pairs. The main drawback of using the L1 distance is that it does not make any assumptions about the nature of the underlying distributions of the compared sequences. This is a serious shortcoming when considering a number of applications that use distribution-based similarity measures (e.g., Luo’s edit distance). I strongly recommend the authors to investigate distribution-based similarity measures for their future work. My other major concern relates to the choice of the contextual window size w for calculating the L1 distance. As the authors note, a small value of w would assign very different probabilities to two sequences that contain exactly the same words in a long sequence, which would result in an erroneous similarity score. On the other hand, a large value of w would assign similar probabilities to these two sequences, but this would lead to understating the similarity between them. As such, the authors settle for using w = 7 for the current version of the TextFlow similarity measure. I strongly recommend the authors to perform a thorough sensitivity analysis of the contextual window size and to report the best performing version of TextFlow in their paper. Finally, I would like to encourage the authors to consider publishing the source code of TextFlow together with its reference implementation. Currently, the paper only describes a new method for calculating the similarity between two sequence of integers, but the code for this method is not available to the research community.

This paper presents a novel text similarity measure inspired from a common representation in DNA sequence alignment algorithms. The new measure, called TextFlow, represents input text pairs as continuous curves and uses both the actual position of the words and sequence matching to compute the similarity value. Our experiments on 8 different datasets show very encouraging results in paraphrase detection, textual entailment recognition and ranking relevance. One key strength of the TextFlow measure is that it can naturally model local similarities, that is, similarities between words that may occur in distinct n-grams but still are semantically related. This is because TextFlow compares the relative positions of these n-grams rather than individual n-grams themselves. Another strength of TextFlow is that it can capture global similarities, that is, similarities between the sequences themselves. For example, it is able to capture the fact that two similar sounding phrases may represent different entities when the order of the words differs. In contrast to most existing similarity measures that only use distinct n-grams and slices of the input text, TextFlow captures such global similarities. One potential disadvantage of the proposed measure is that it is not straightforward to transform it into a distance measure. For example, the identity-based normalization is not easily extendable to a measure of distance and as such a normalization factor has to be estimated. TextFlow captures both local and global similarities in a single measure and as such could be a useful addition to other similarity measures. At the same time, it is very easy to apply and thus well suited for use in applications that involve deep learning models. Overall I find this paper very well written, with excellent explanations of the proposed TextFlow measure and its applications. The potential of the proposed measure has good applications in many areas that involve text similarity/distance measure. The measure itself is very simple and straightforward to apply and as such could be a useful addition to the current collection of similarity measures.

In this paper, we present an approach to infer relative physical knowledge of actions and objects along five dimensions (e.g., size, weight, and strength) from unstructured natural language text. We frame knowledge acquisition as joint inference over two closely related problems: learning (1) relative physical knowledge of object pairs and (2) physical implications of actions when applied to those object pairs. Empirical results demonstrate that it is possible to extract knowledge of actions and objects from language and that joint inference over different types of knowledge sharpen performance. Learning commonsense knowledge from natural language text is nontrivial due to reporting bias: people rarely state the obvious, e.g., “My house is bigger than me. I am, after all, bigger than any object in my house.” However, while rarely stated explicitly, this trivial everyday knowledge does influence the way people talk about the world, which provides indirect clues to reason about the world. For example, a statement like, “Tyler entered his house” implies that his house is bigger than Tyler. In this paper, we present an approach to infer relative physical knowledge of actions and objects along five dimensions (e.g., size, weight, and strength) from unstructured natural language text. We frame knowledge acquisition as joint inference over two closely related problems: learning (1) relative physical knowledge of object pairs and (2) physical implications of actions when applied to those object pairs. The key to our approach is identifying a common prior over knowledge on an elementary level. For example, everyone is aware that people are typically bigger than cats and that objects are typically heavier than their owners. Based on such knowledge, joint inference over different types of knowledge is possible. For example, knowing that Tyler is bigger than his house and that Tyler entered his house, we can conclude that his house is bigger than Tyler. Joint inference allows us to gain more precise and fine-grained knowledge that goes beyond coarsely quantized values such as “larger” or “smaller” and “heavier” or “lighter”. For example, knowing that Tyler is bigger than his house and that Tyler entered his house, we can conclude that Tyler’s strength is at least as high as the strength of his house. We present an incremental approach to inferring physical implications of any object actions along the same five dimensions. The intuition is that object names and the verbs that describe actions over them are of a syntactic nature and they should at least implicitly encode the five dimensions. First, we construct a rich knowledge base of object pairs, where each object pair has the same two objects with different annotations for the five dimensions. Second, we collect a large amount of data by crowd-sourcing in which a worker translates natural language text to the physical implication (e.g., “The medicine makes Mary feel better.” implies that Mary’s strength is higher than the strength of the medicine). The knowledge in the knowledge base and the translation pairs are integrated in a translation approach to jointly infer knowledge of physical implications over a large set of object pairs. We experiment with the inferred knowledge, and show that it significantly outperforms a strong baseline approach on a set of examples.

Inferring physical knowledge of actions and objects (e.g., size, weight, and strength) from natural language text is a difficult task due to reporting bias. Most people don’t explicitly mention the trivial everyday knowledge, for example, “My house is bigger than me.” However, this trivial everyday knowledge can be indirectly inferred from people’s natural talk about the world. For example, a statement like, “Tyler entered his house” implies that his house is bigger than Tyler. In this paper, we present an approach to infer physical knowledge of actions and objects by jointly learning knowledge of objects pairs and their physical implications. We find that it is possible to infer knowledge of actions and objects from language and that joint inference improves performance. generally, this paper studies the problem of inferring physical knowledge from natural language text. This is a challenging task because people don’t explicitly mention trivial knowledge, for example, “My house is bigger than me.” The paper first introduces the methodology to jointly learn knowledge of object pairs and their physical implications. The framework extends previous work on modeling physical implications of actions by considering the case where actions might apply to multiple objects in the pair. Experiments with real and simulated data show that the method can infer physical knowledge from natural language text. 2. The proposed method jointly learns knowledge of object pairs and their physical implications. It first defines a dataset of object pairs and a set of relations which hold between them. It then defines a training objective that encodes the joint probability of these objects and their relations, and a neural network that predicts relations given the representation of the objects and their syntactic configuration. The method is evaluated on a held-out test set, and we find that the model can correctly identify the physical implications of the actions present in the training set. 3. The method could be extended to learn more complicated relations between objects, for example the physical force acting between two objects, the relations between the velocities of objects, or the direction of the gravitational force between objects. This method can also be applied to new data. It can generate knowledge about relations between objects that are not present in the training data. 4. The method assumes a coarse-grained knowledge of the world. For example, it does not know that Tyler’s house is two stories, and it infers that Tyler’s house is bigger than him. However, this method can be extended to learn more fine-grained knowledge by taking into account additional constraints that apply to a particular type of object or relation. 5. This method does not perform knowledge anchoring, for example, the inferred knowledge that the dog is less than the cat, is invalid because this relation does not hold in the real world. The method for inferring the knowledge that “the object X is smaller than the object Y” should be supplemented with knowledge anchoring using examples in the training data.

machine_text: Overall, I found this paper to be well-crafted and theoretically rigorous. The modeling paradigm seems appropriate for the domain, and the results are intriguing. My primary concern is about the applicability of the model to code generation. The model consists of a decoders followed by a small number of generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). The performance benefit of such a reduced model comes at the cost of generalizability: The system seems extremely dependent on the small number of specific examples that were used during training. It would be difficult to use the model without also training on similar examples. One approach to this challenge might be to collect a larger code corpus from the domain and then use transfer learning to apply the model to new code. Another approach would be to add more training examples during generation, by leveraging the dependency of the model and training examples on each other. In either case, I think there would be a stronger claim that this model could be used to generate code without also needing to be trained on the source code to which it should generalize. Finally, there is a concern about the external validity of the results, given the use of datasets from an information retrieval domain. There is nothing to suggest that the results will generalize beyond these datasets. Overall, this is an interesting paper with potential, but I think there is considerable work to do before it can be widely used. I look forward to seeing where this work goes! This paper presents a syntactic neural model for general-purpose code generation. This model is a fully differentiable translation model that maps a program statement to its AST and another map from AST to a valid C program. The model is end-to-end trainable and does not require intermediate control structures or other mechanics apart from decision nodes. In contrast to existing tree-based models, the neural model is able to encode long-range dependency between tokens, e.g., the influence of a preceding token to a following one. By showing that it outperforms the existing model on two code generation tasks, the symbolic model shows its feasibility for code generation. umetrics, strengths and weaknesses of the paper A Syntactic Neural Model for General-purpose Code Generation Pairing Problem: Does the Syntactic Neural Model Outperform the Tree-based Model? The syntactic neural model outperforms the tree-based model on two code generation tasks. First, the former can express long-range dependency between two adjacent tokens, such as the influence of one token to the next. Second, the former doesn’t need any intermediate control structures or other mechanics except decision nodes. This is not only fast but also easy to be implemented and understood. On the other hand, the syntactic model requires two additional and necessary modules, i.e., the code generation based on visitation and the beam search over the generated code. The beam search procedure increases the model complexity and the cost of generation. Additionally, the visitation mechanism provides direct access to the code generation results, which might facilitate the code refactoring or other edits. Overall, the syntactic neural model shows its feasibility for code generation and exhibits some advantages over the tree-based model.

The paper "A Syntactic Neural Model for General-Purpose Code Generation" by Zhang et al. describes the use of a neural model to parse natural language descriptions of code into valid code in a general-purpose language. The model uses a graph-based transition system to connect keywords and their derivatives, which are each associated with a transition function, to form a production rule set. The model is trained using reinforcement learning to generate valid code for a given input description. This is done by treating code generation as a reinforcement learning problem: the model is provided with an initial state and a goal state and generates actions that move the state between the initial and goal states in such a way as to maximize the number of steps taken before the state reaches a stopping condition. The stopping condition in this case is that a valid statement is generated, at which point the model terminates and produces the generated statement as its solution. Experiments show that this approach is effective for code generation from natural language, producing high-quality solutions that outperform previous data-driven code generation approaches. Paper Main Content: We consider the problem of parsing natural language descriptions into source code written in a general-purpose programming language like Python. Existing data-driven methods treat this problem as a language generation task without considering the underlying syntax of the target programming language. Informed by previous work in semantic parsing, in this paper we propose a novel neural architecture powered by a grammar model to explicitly capture the target syntax as prior knowledge. Our model uses a graph-based transition system to connect keywords and their derivatives, which are each associated with a transition function, to form a production rule set. The model is trained using reinforcement learning to generate valid code for a given input description. The model initially operates in the surface form of the input and uses the prior grammar knowledge to first convert to underlying syntax. The stopping condition in this case is that a valid statement is generated, at which point the model terminates and produces the generated statement as its solution. Experiments show that this approach is effective for code generation from natural language, producing high-quality solutions that outperform previous data-driven code generation approaches. The main contribution of this paper is using syntax as prior knowledge to code generation for the first time. This allows the model to generate high-level code at an abstract syntax level and still be able to properly formulate complex expressions and handle programmer-specific coding idioms. Note that this is still a relatively new field with more research needs to be done on this aspect. For example, better search capabilities and error handling needs to be added to make this a fully functional tool. Reinforcement Learning is used for exploration, which is a work in progress. In the future, this could be expanded to using deep Q-learning or other techniques to further improve the efficiency of the code generator.

This paper considers the problem of parsing natural language descriptions into source code written in a general-purpose programming language like Python. Existing data-driven methods treat this problem as a language generation task without considering the underlying syntax of the target programming language. Informed by previous work in semantic parsing, in this paper we propose a novel neural architecture powered by a grammar model to explicitly capture the target syntax as prior knowledge. Experiments find this an effective way to scale up to generation of complex programs from natural language descriptions, achieving state-of-the-art results that well outperform previous code generation and semantic parsing approaches. The major contributions of this work are as follows: 1. This paper is the first work to apply syntactic parsing to code generation. 2. This paper proposes a neural architecture to generate programs with explicit syntax modeling. 3. This paper applies a large-scale code grammar to syntax modeling, which is a practical and effective method for code generation. Overall, this is an important and exciting step towards solving the challenging code generation problem from natural language descriptions, and we hope this work will attract more research interest to this area. strengths and weaknesses This paper is the first work to apply syntactic parsing to code generation. Summary: The paper proposes a neural model for predicting Python syntax trees
from text descriptions. Guided by the actual Python grammar, the model
generates tree nodes sequentially in a depth-first fashion. Key ideas include
injecting the information from the parent node as part of the LSTM input, a
pointer network for copying the terminals, and unary closure which collapses
chains of unary productions to reduce the tree size. The model is evaluated on
three datasets from different domains and outperforms almost all previous work.

Strengths:

The paper is overall very well-written. The explanation of system is clear, and
the analysis is thorough.

The system itself is a natural extension of various ideas. The most similar
work include tree-based generation with parent feeding (Dong and Lapata, 2016)
and various RNN-based semantic parsing with copy mechanism (Jia and
Liang, 2016; Ling et al., 2016). [The guidance of parsing based on grammar is
also explored in Chen Liang et al., 2016 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.00020)
where a code-assist system is used to ensure that the code
is valid.] Nevertheless, the model is this paper stands out as it is able to
generate much longer and more complex programs than most previous work
mentioned. 

Weaknesses:

The evaluation is done on code accuracy (exact match) and BLEU score. These
metrics (especially BLEU) might not be the best metrics for evaluating the
correctness of programs. For instance, the first example in Table 5 shows that
while the first two lines in boxes A and B are different, they have the same
semantics. Another example is that variable names can be different. Evaluation
based on what the code does (e.g., using test cases or static code analysis)
would be more convincing.

Another point about evaluation: other systems (e.g., NMT baseline) may generate
code with syntactic error. Would it be possible to include the result on the
highest-scoring well-formed code (e.g., using beam search) that these baseline
systems generate? This would give a fairer comparison since these system can
choose to prune malformed code.

General Discussion:

* Lines 120-121: some approaches that use domain-specific languages were also
guided by a grammar. One example is Berant and Liang, 2014, which uses a pretty
limited grammar for logical forms (Table 1). In addition to comparing to that
line of work, emphasizing that the grammar in this paper is much larger than
most previous work would make this work stronger.

* Lines 389-397: For the parent feeding mechanism, is the child index being
used? In other words, is p_t different when generating a first child versus a
second child? In Seq2Tree (Dong and Lapata, 2016) the two non-terminals would
have different hidden states.

* Line 373: Are the possible tokens embedded? Is it assumed that the set of
possible tokens is known beforehand?

* The examples in the appendix are nice.

---

generation in general-purpose programming langauge, i.e., Python.

The authors introduce PositionRank, an approach to keyphrase extraction from scholarly documents that provides both topic and position information. The approach is motivated by the observation that keyphrases occur in documents not merely as words but also in positions in the text. A keyphrases enrichment method called Shift-Con operator is introduced to measure the strength of associations between keyphrases, and a ranking function is introduced to find documents that encode the association between keyphrases and their positions. Strength: The PositionRank approach can encode positional information of keyphrases, which has been shown to be important for keyphrases extraction, and as such it is a strong general approach to keyphrases extraction. The large and growing amounts of online scholarly data present both challenges and opportunities to enhance knowledge discovery. One such challenge is to automatically extract a small set of keyphrases from a document that can accurately describe the document's content and can facilitate fast information processing. In this paper, we propose PositionRank, an unsupervised model for keyphrase extraction from scholarly documents that incorporates information from all positions of a word's occurrences into a biased PageRank. Our model obtains remarkable improvements in performance over PageRank models that do not take into account word positions as well as over strong baselines for this task. human_text:
- Summary: 

The paper introduces a new dataset for a sarcasm interpretation task
and a system (called Sarcasm SIGN) based on machine translation framework
Moses. The new dataset was collected from 3000 sarcastic tweets (with hashtag
`#sarcasm) and 5 interpretations for each from humans. The Sarcasm SIGN is
built
based on Moses by replacing sentimental words by their corresponding clusters
on the source side (sarcasm) and then de-cluster their translations on the
target side (non-sarcasm). Sarcasm SIGN performs on par with Moses on the MT
evaluation metrics, but outperforms Moses in terms of fluency and adequacy. 

- Strengths:

the paper is well written

the dataset is collected in a proper manner

the experiments are carefully done and the analysis is sound.

- Weaknesses:

lack statistics of the datsets (e.g. average length, vocabulary size)

the baseline (Moses) is not proper because of the small size of the dataset

the assumption "sarcastic tweets often differ from their non sarcastic
interpretations in as little as one sentiment word" is not supported by the
data. 

- General Discussion: This discussion gives more details about the weaknesses
of the paper. 

Half of the paper is about the new dataset for sarcasm interpretation.
However, the paper doesn't show important information about the dataset such as
average length, vocabulary size. More importantly, the paper doesn't show any
statistical evidence to support their method of focusing on sentimental words. 

Because the dataset is small (only 3000 tweets), I guess that many words are
rare. Therefore, Moses alone is not a proper baseline. A proper baseline should
be a MT system that can handle rare words very well. In fact, using
clustering and declustering (as in Sarcasm SIGN) is a way to handle rare words.

Sarcasm SIGN is built based on the assumption that "sarcastic tweets often
differ from their non sarcastic interpretations in as little as one sentiment
word". Table 1 however strongly disagrees with this assumption: the human
interpretations are often different from the tweets at not only sentimental
words. I thus strongly suggest the authors to give statistical evidence from
the dataset that supports their assumption. Otherwise, the whole idea of
Sarcasm SIGN is just a hack.

--------------------------------------------------------------

I have read the authors' response. I don't change my decision because of the
following reasons: 

- the authors wrote that "the Fiverr workers might not take this strategy": to
me it is not the spirit of corpus-based NLP. A model must be built to fit given
data, not that the data must follow some assumption that the model is built on.

- the authors wrote that "the BLEU scores of Moses and SIGN are above 60, which
is generally considered decent in the MT literature": to me the number 60
doesn't 
show anything at all because the sentences in the dataset are very short. And
that,
if we look at table 6, %changed of Moses is only 42%, meaning that even more
than half of the time translation is simply copying, the BLUE score is more
than 60.

- "While higher scores might be achieved with MT systems that explicitly
address rare words, these systems don't focus on sentiment words": it's true,
but I was wondering whether sentiment words are rare in the corpus. If they
are, those MT systems should obviously handle them (in addition to other rare
words).

- Strengths:

(1) A new dataset would be useful for other researchers in this area

(2) An algorithm with sentiment words based machine translation is proposed to
interpret sarcasm tweets.

- Weaknesses:

(1) Do not provide detailed statistics of constructed dataset.

(2) Integrating sentiment word clustering with machine translation techniques
only is simple and straightforward, novelty may be a challenging issue. 

- General Discussion:

Overall, this paper is well written. The experiments are conducted carefully
and the analysis is reasonable. 

I offer some comments as follows.
(1) According to data collection process, each tweet should be annotated
five times. How to determine which one is regarded as gold standard for measure
performance?

(2) The MT technique (Moses) is well known, but it may not be a good
baseline. Another MT technique (RNN) should be put together for comparison.   

(3) Differ from most work focuses on sarcasm detection. The research topic
is interesting. It attempts to interpret sarcasm for reflecting semantics.

This paper focuses on interpreting sarcasm written in Twitter identifying
sentiment words and then using a machine translation engine to find an
equivalent not sarcastic tweet.

We have developed an automated Japanese short-answer scoring and support machine for new National Center written test exams. 2. This paper describes a system to assist written test scoring.

- Strengths:
The paper represents an application of an interesting NLP problem --
recognizing textual entailment -- to an important task -- written test scoring.

- Weaknesses:
There isn't anything novel in the paper. It consist of an application of an
existing technology to a known problem.

The approach described in the paper is not autonomous -- it still needs a human
to do the actual scoring. The paper lacks any quantitative or qualitative
evaluation of how useful such system is. That is, is it making the job of the
scorer easier? Is the scorer more effective as compared to not having automatic
score?

The system contains multiple components and it is unclear how the quality of
each one of them contributes to the overall experience.

The paper needs more work with the writing. Language and style is rough in
several places.

The paper also contains several detailed examples, which don't necessarily add
a lot of value to the discussion.

 For the evaluation of classification, what is the baseline of predicting the
most frequent class?

- General Discussion:
I find this paper not very inspiring. I don't see the message in the paper
apart from announcing having build such a system

- Strengths:

This paper tries to tackle a very practical problem: automated short answer
scoring (SAS), in particular for Japanese which hasn't gotten as much attention
as, say, English-language SAS.

- Weaknesses:

The paper simply reads like a system description, and is light on experiments
or insights. The authors show a lack of familiarity with more recent related
work (aimed at English SAS), both in terms of methodology and evaluation. Here
are a couple:

https://www.aclweb.org/anthology/W/W15/W15-06.pdf#page=97
https://www.aclweb.org/anthology/N/N15/N15-1111.pdf

There was also a recent Kaggle competition that generated several
methodologies:

https://www.kaggle.com/c/asap-sas

- General Discussion:

To meet ACL standards, I would have preferred to see more experiments (feature
ablation studies, algorithm comparisons) that motivated the final system
design, as well as some sort of qualitative evaluation with a user study of how
the mixed-initiative user interface features led to improved scores. As it is,
it feels like a work in progress without any actionable new methods or
insights.

Also, Pearson/Spearman correlation and kappa scores are considered more
appropriate than accuracy for these sorts of ordinal human scores.

This paper presents a text classification method based on pre-training
technique using both labeled and unlabeled data. The authors reported
experimental results with several benchmark data sets including TREC data, and
showed that the method improved overall performance compared to other
comparative methods.

I think the approach using pre-training and fine-tuning itself is not a novel
one, but the originality is the use of both labeled and unlabeled data in the
pre-training step. 
The authors compare their results against three baselines, i.e. without
pre-training and a deep learning with unsupervised pre-training using deep
autoencoders, but I think that I would be interesting to compare the method
against other methods presented in the introduction section.

The core assumption in this framework is that a word belongs to one and only one category or cluster in the embedding space. This is a very strong restriction and the validity of this assumption must be examined in practice. The approach taken to validate this assumption is to perform clustering on a large number of permutations of the same dataset and use some metric to show that the formed clusters are similar to the actual clusters. Once this assumption is shown to be valid, the rest of the framework to quantify gains can be applied. The paper shows a strong connection between the gains and the improvement in hit rate/Precision metric, used in the domain, when the given embedding space is used in the domain. The methodology to establish this connection is through a theoretical derivation and it would be useful to see how the achieved gains compared to the theoretical gains calculated. The strength of the paper is that it brings together a novel theoretical approach to quantify gains from using word embedding methods and the authors perform all the computation on the real world data and show how the gains are related to the Hit Rate metric. Another positive about the paper is that the same dataset is used for testing the framework on, to ensure the results are not idiosyncratic to the data used, and the authors validate this by showing how the gains vary when a different dataset is used for testing. A weakness of the paper is that the validation of the assumption that a word belongs to one and only one cluster in the embedding space is only qualitative. The validation is done by clustering the permuted versions of the dataset, but there is no measure to show the validity of the obtained clusters.

machine_text: Overall, the paper is well organized and written. However, I have some suggestions and questions as follow: 1. How does the model trained on Group A benefit for Group B? The model trained on Group A could be easily overfit to the data in Group A, such as erroneous synonyms and corrupted phrases. To evaluate if the knowledge learned from Group A also benefit Group B, how about using Group B as a validation set to monitor the training process? 2. The introduction of BERT as a baseline is a bit misleading. As far as I know, BERT is a neural machine translation model. Why is it treated as a NLP model here? And why don't you also try a transformer-based model like XLNet and GPT-4 in this case? BERT is a pre-trained deep bidirectional representation for language, which can be applied in many NLP tasks. If the model is a transformer-based one, such as XLNet and GPT-4, why didn't you also apply it here? It could generate better results than previous methods as a pioneering work. 3. In the "Warm-up-free training" section, the MT ground truth is collected before and after each epoch, and the gradient difference is used as a "proxy" for how well the model is trained. This method may trigger a concern that the accuracy of model checkpoint is not trustworthy because it may include non-epoch-related factors. How do you ensure that the accuracy is not inflated? To ensure that the accuracy is not inflated, we can double check that the loss curves on the validation set are stable. We can also calculate the accuracy on the validation set at the end of each epoch. If the accuracy on the validation set doesn't increase significantly, we can consider the model is well trained. 4. Is there a way to reduce the influence of synonyms and corrupted phrases on the accuracy of model? As the answer to the question 1, how to design a better validation set? Synonym/corrupted phrases extraction algorithm could be a possible solution. 5. The hyperparameter tuning is done on Group A, and the final model is evaluated on Group B. The model performance on Group B is actually never evaluated on the validation set during the hyperparameter optimization, which may lead to overfitting. How do you ensure the model performance on Group B is not overfitting? To avoid overfitting, we can always early stop the training if the model performance on Group B is not improving during the training. 6. There are some error samples in the evaluation results (Like extra spaces and extra commas). How do you guarantee the correctness of these results? I can't guarantee the correctness of all the results. I just manually checked some of the incorrect results and confirmed that they are incorrect. 7. In the ablation study, the best setting for each component is selected based on the performance on the validation set, and the model performance on the test set will not be affected. However, the selected parameter settings are all based on the results of validation set, which might cause overfitting. How to ensure the model performance on the test set isn't affected by overfitting? To avoid overfitting, we can use the weight importance calculated by Differentiable LR (DLR) to select the optimal parameter settings.

The paper "Adversarial Multi-task Learning for Text Classification" by Heng Wang et al. (https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.11760) addresses the important problem of how to effectively train a single model to perform multiple related tasks, in this case text classification, simultaneously. The key insight is to treat the related tasks as related samples of the same dataset and the problem as one of multi-task learning. The authors propose a novel method, adversarial multi-task learning, for solving this problem. The approach is based on co-training and adversarial training. The authors first introduce a generator network and a discriminator network. The generator network generates fake samples that look like real samples from the same class for the related tasks, and the discriminator network can tell the samples generated by the generator network from the real samples. The authors then use the fake samples generated by the generator network and the true samples from the related tasks to train the multi-task learning model. The generator network plays an important role in this paper, and a carefully designed generator network can help the model learn useful sample representations for the related tasks. The paper provides empirical evidence that the proposed method can effectively and efficiently train a single model to perform multiple related tasks. The paper has some limitations. First, the model architecture is not well defined. We need more details about the generator network and the cost function. Second, the method is only validated on the sentiment classification task. How does it perform on other tasks? Can the method scale to other datasets? Third, the paper does not provide much implementation information. We need to know how the authors train the model, which datasets the model was trained on and which model architectures were used.

This paper makes the following notable contributions: 1. It proposes an adversarial multi-task learning framework to learn common and private feature spaces. 2. It introduces auxiliary task to alleviate private feature space from interfering with each other. 3. The shared knowledge learned by the proposed approach can be regarded as off-the-shelf knowledge and easily transferred to new tasks. 4. It conducts extensive experiments on 16 different text classification tasks and demonstrates the effectiveness of the approach. This paper introduces new configurations and training objectives for neural
sequence models in a multi-task setting. As the authors describe well, the
multi-task setting is important because some tasks have shared information
and in some scenarios learning many tasks can improve overall performance.

The methods section is relatively clear and logical, and I like where it ended
up, though it could be slightly better organized. The organization that I
realized after reading is that there are two problems: 1) shared features end
up in the private feature space, and 2) private features end up in the 
shared space. There is one novel method for each problem. That organization up
front would make the methods more cohesive. In any case, they introduce one 
method that keeps task-specific features out of shared representation
(adversarial
loss) and another to keep shared features out of task-specific representations
(orthogonality constraints). My only point of confusion is the adversarial
system.
After LSTM output there is another layer, D(s^k_T, \theta_D), relying on
parameters
U and b. This output is considered a probability distribution which is compared
against the actual. This means it is possible it will just learn U and b that
effectively mask task-specific information from  the LSTM outputs, and doesn't 
seem like it can guarantee task-specific information is removed.

Before I read the evaluation section I wrote down what I hoped the experiments
would look like and it did most of it. This is an interesting idea and there
are 
a lot more experiments one can imagine but I think here they have the basics
to show the validity of their methods. It would be helpful to have best known
results on these tasks.

My primary concern with this paper is the lack of deeper motivation for the 
approach. I think it is easy to understand that in a totally shared model
there will be problems due to conflicts in feature space. The extension to 
partially shared features seems like a reaction to that issue -- one would 
expect that the useful shared information is in the shared latent space and 
each task-specific space would learn features for that space. Maybe this works
and maybe it doesn't, but the logic is clear to me. In contrast, the authors
seem to start from the assumption that this "shared-private" model has this
issue. I expected the argument flow to be 1) Fully-shared obviously has this
problem; 2) shared-private seems to address this; 3) in practice shared-private
does not fully address this issue for reasons a,b,c.; 4) we introduce a method
that more effectively constrains the spaces.
Table 4 helped me to partially understand what's going wrong with
shared-private
and what your methods do; some terms are _usually_ one connotation
or another, and that general trend can probably get them into the shared
feature
space. This simple explanation, an example, and a more logical argument flow
would help the introduction and make this a really nice reading paper.

Finally, I think this research ties into some other uncited MTL work [1],
which does deep hierarchical MTL - supervised POS tagging at a lower level,
chunking
at the next level up, ccg tagging higher, etc. They then discuss at the end
some of the qualities that make MTL possible and conclude that MTL only works
"when tasks are sufficiently similar." The ASP-MTL paper made me think of this
previous work because potentially this model could learn what sufficiently
similar is -- i.e., if two tasks are not sufficiently similar the shared model
would learn nothing and it would fall back to learning two independent systems,
as compared to a shared-private model baseline that might overfit and perform
poorly.

# Paper summary

This paper presents a method for learning well-partitioned shared and
task-specific feature spaces for LSTM text classifiers. Multiclass adversarial
training encourages shared space representations from which a discriminative
classifier cannot identify the task source (and are thus generic). The models
evaluates are a fully-shared, shared-private and adversarial shared-private --
the lattermost ASP model is one of the main contributions. They also use
orthogonality constraints to help reward shared and private spaces that are
distinct. The ASP model has lower error rate than single-task and other
multi-task neural models. They also experiment with a task-level cross
validation to explore whether the shared representation can transfer across
tasks, and it seems to favourably. Finally, there is some analysis of shared
layer activations suggesting that the ASP model is not being misled by strong
weights learned on a specific (inappropriate) task.

# Review summary

Good ideas, well expressed and tested. Some minor comments.

# Strengths

* This is a nice set of ideas working well together. I particularly like the
focus on explicitly trying to create useful shared representations. These have
been quite successful in the CV community, but it appears that one needs to
work quite hard to create them for NLP.
* Sections 2, 3 and 4 are very clearly expressed.
* The task-level cross-validation in Section 5.5 is a good way to evaluate the
transfer.
* There is an implementation and data.

# Weaknesses

* There are a few minor typographic and phrasing errors. Individually, these
are fine, but there are enough of them to warrant fixing:
** l:84 the “infantile cart” is slightly odd -- was this a real example
from the data?
** l:233 “are different in” -> “differ in”
** l:341 “working adversarially towards” -> “working against” or
“competing with”?
** l:434 “two matrics” -> “two matrices”
** l:445 “are hyperparameter” -> “are hyperparameters”
** Section 6 has a number of number agreement errors
(l:745/746/765/766/767/770/784) and should be closely re-edited.
** The shading on the final row of Tables 2 and 3 prints strangely…
* There is mention of unlabelled data in Table 1 and semi-supervised learning
in Section 4.2, but I didn’t see any results on these experiments. Were they
omitted, or have I misunderstood?
* The error rate differences are promising in Tables 2 and 3, but statistical
significance testing would help make them really convincing. Especially between
SP-MLT and ASP-MTL results to highlight the benefit of adversarial training. It
should be pretty straightforward to adapt the non-parametric approximate
randomisation test (see
http://www.lr.pi.titech.ac.jp/~takamura/pubs/randtest.pdf for promising notes a
reference to the Chinchor paper) to produce these.
* The colours are inconsistent in the caption of Figure 5 (b). In 5 (a), blue
is used for “Ours”, but this seems to have swapped for 5 (b). This is worth
checking, or I may have misunderstood the caption.

# General Discussion

* I wonder if there’s some connection with regularisation here, as the effect
of the adversarial training with orthogonal training is to help limit the
shared feature space. It might be worth drawing that connection to other
regularisation literature.

machine_text: Dear Author, The paper presents Sequential Matching Network, a new architecture for multi-turn response selection in retrieval-based chatbots. Synthetic datasets and your implementation of the LM-CNN model are used for evaluation. The biggest problem with chatbots is lack of human-level conversation ability. This paper adds new element to the state-of-the-art memory-centric chatbot LM-CNN, which is effective at question answering but lacks adequate conversational ability to support natural language conversation. The proposed approach has three key ideas. First, it makes conversation using a slot-filling system. That is, the model recommends a response from a response memory based on the conversation history and the input keyword. Second, it introduces novel attention mechanisms to the decoder. By using the state of the response selection, the model can focus on a specific portion of the response and generate natural language. Third, it expands the response memory from 1000 to 10000 entries. Because there is more space for exploration, the model has more opportunities to find appropriate responses. The model achieves 32.48% token accuracy on the WoZ 2.0 dev set, which is a new state-of-the-art result. The implementation and experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the model. Thank you for your hard work! I look forward to your future works. кboy! My sincerest gratitude for your detailed and constructive comments. We have taken your comments into careful consideration and revised the paper as followings: 1. We provide analysis on why the previous state-of-the-art memory-centric model doesn’t work well on the task of multi-turn response selection. 2. We add slot-filling system and investigate the effects of the proposed approach on the conversation ability of the model. 3. We extend the experiment dataset to WoZ 2.0 to demonstrate the effectiveness of the model.

The paper describes Sequential Matching Network (SMN), a new architecture for multi-turn response selection in retrieval-based chatbots. This is an important problem as current response selection methods are limited in their ability to generate responses that are both semantically related to the question and also syntactically valid. SMN addresses this problem by using Seq2Seq models with attention over a large LMs corpus to generate responses in the form of a sequence of sentences, where each sentence is dynamically selected from a large pre-defined grammar based on the input question. The effectiveness of the approach is demonstrated on several large scale KV pair datasets as well as a user study using movie questions. год features particularly interesting aspects of the paper, including: - Seq2Seam architectures allow for end-to-end training of the response selection component, allowing for generation of responses in a structured, variable length format - The use of a large pre-defined language model (LM) to allow the generation of responses in syntactically valid formats - The evaluation of the approach on several KV dataset pairs as well as a user study using movie questions esk Features the paper has difficulty addressing, or aspects that could be further explored in future work: - The limitation of using a single Seq2Seq model to generate all responses from a predefined set. The use of multiple models with differing context or domain specific parameters could potentially improve the robustness of the approach Overall, a useful contribution to the response selection field in retrieval-based chatbots

The authors of Sequential Matching Network: A New Architecture for Multi-turn Response Selection in Retrieval-Based Chatbots make some interesting points around response selection for multi-turn conversation in retrieval-based chatbots. First, they argue that existing work that selects a response based on matching a response to a highly abstracted context representation has lost information in the context. Instead, they introduce SMN which matches a response with each utterance in the context on multiple levels of granularity and then uses RNNs to model chronological relationships among the utterances and select a response. The approach is quite interesting and has the potential to help response selection for multi-turn conversation in retrieval-based chatbots. I think the paper could benefit from a few revisions. First, it would be helpful to the reader if the authors could provide a bit more detail about how to get a SMN model for a specific domain (e.g., using human-provided examples). For example, is this supervised training on a set of example responses and corresponding example contexts? Or is this a domain-specific, unsupervised training approach? If the former, a description of the dataset and approach would help the reader to understand if the SMN model can be applied to new domains. If the latter, does the authors think this would be a problem, and if so, how can the SMN be adapted for use in new domains? Also, it would be helpful to the reader to know more about the values of the hyper-parameters used in the experiments. For example, it would be helpful to know if changing the values of these parameters affected the performance of the SMN model. I recommend providing the full set of parameters for each model along with the results from the hyper-parameter search. Finally, it would be useful to know more about the type of chatbots the SMN model was tested on. For example, I wonder if this model was tested on a seq2seq model? If so, what decoder architecture is used? If not, it would be good to know what aspects of the chatbot design the SMN doesn’t apply to. I recommend accepting this review as is, and the authors can address the points above if they choose.

The main contribution of this paper is the introduction of a new model to solve the problem of response selection for multi-turn conversation in retrieval-based chatbots, which can address the problems of lost relationship between responses and inaccurate matching scores generated by the existing methods. The proposed model is developed based on the sequential matching network (SMN), which first matches each response to each utterance in the context on multiple levels of granularity, and then distills important matching information from each pair and compiles it into a vector, which is then used to model the relationship among the utterances in the sequential order. The method is tested on two public data sets and the results show that the proposed model can significantly outperform the state-of-the-art methods. Some possible improvements for the method can be listed as below: 1. The results in the paper are obtained from the response with the highest matching score. It is unclear how the matching result for each response would affect the final matching score of the entire conversation. It would be better to optimize the matching score for each response, so that the final matching score is improved as well. 2. The method can benefit more from the user feedback, if the chatbot shows one response and asks the user to review it one by one. It would be good to implement an autoreviewer for such chatbots, which can automatically screen the responses based on some predefined criteria, e.g. based on the length of the response. 3. Response selection is an important part for response-based chatbots. To provide a better chat experience for users, it is better to include other features like topic modeling and recommendation in the matching network model. Overall, this is a useful paper for response selection in retrieval-based chatbots, and the proposed model can be a good baseline for future improvements.

This paper proposes a new, simple, yet effective framework, named phrasal RNN networks for phrase representation. Phrasal RNN networks do not model a sentence as surface word sequences. Instead, they model all candidate phrases with arbitrary lengths. To represent phrases as fix-length real-valued vectors, we build the RNN pyramid, which is composed of shifted parallel RNN sequences. To utilize potential phrases, we employ the attention mechanism to compare and combine them. We test our model on language model and machine translation tasks. Our model leads to an improvement of over 10 points in perplexity both on standard Penn Treebank and FBIS English data set over a state-of-the-art LSTM language modeling baseline. It outperforms both the Moses (phrase-based statistical model) and a strong sequence-to-sequence baseline in the Chinese-English machine translation task. tutorial addresses the problem of language modeling (LM), which aims to predict the next word given a sequence of words, or more generally, a sequence of symbols. Prior research on word-based LMs relied on the use of sizable dictionaries to represent words and phrases. Phrase-based LMs alleviate this by using phrases as units of phrase instead of words. For example, "sky is blue" is a phrase but "blue" is a word. To use phrases in a phrase-based LM, a representation of phrases needs to be defined. Previously, this was done using static RNNs which model a sentence as a surface word sequence. This is inadequate as phrases can vary in length. We introduce a new, simple, yet effective framework called pRNNs which model phrases in an end-to-end fashion. pRNNs model all candidate phrases with arbitrary length and build an RNN pyramid to represent phrases. We test our model on the Penn language modeling benchmark and show that our model outperforms state-of-the-art phrase-based LMs. Our model also outperforms a phrase-based machine translation system on the Chinese-English task.

In this paper the authors describe an approach to obtaining referential word meanings from visual and distributional information. The approach taken looks at a word and finds similar images and the frequencies of these images across a large data set and tries to link these similar images to their referents. The approach is not fully explained in the paper but it seems to use an algorithm called DistilBERT to find these similar images and based on these images build a model that is used to find the most likely referent for the word. This is an interesting approach that could prove useful in combination with existing techniques forsemantic understanding such as image annotation or sense screening. It may be that by combining this approach with these other techniques we could achieve even greater results. There are a number of weaknesses of the approach. It does not explain how the DistilBERT algorithm works and so the model cannot be easily understood or inspected. Despite these issues this paper represents an interesting approach to the problem of word meaning that could prove useful for some applications.

Object naming is a sub-task of referring expression generation on real-world images. To date, most methods for addressing this problem use object recognition to obtain a large number of potential names and then apply some form of clustering or clustering-like approach to group names into sets that have similar meaning. These name sets are then given as candidate answers to the query image. However, this procedure can fail because: 1) it assumes that names are mutually exclusive, which is not true for many common terms, like “table” and “desk” 2) it relies on learning a mapping from visual features to a set of mutually exclusive names, which is very difficult to do well, especially when the number of names is large (e.g. many types of items in an office) or when the set of possible names is large (e.g. when a general name like “computer” is used to refer to many different devices). Instead of using semantic clustering to group names, some alternative attempts have focused on using distributional information to find concepts related to words that are then used in place of names (e.g. using WordNet to find common subtypes of visual objects, using part-of-speech tagging to find semantic concepts that describe parts of a visual object, or using a word2vec model to find the most similar word when given a visual word). We investigate models of referring expression generation that link visual to lexical information which we assume to be given through distributional word embeddings. We present a model that learns individual predictors for object names that link visual and distributional aspects of word meaning that we assume to be given through distributional word embeddings. We show that this is particularly beneficial for zero-shot learning, as compared to projecting visual objects directly into the distributional space. In a standard object naming task, we find that different ways of combining lexical and visual information achieve very similar performance, though experiments on model combination suggests that they capture complementary aspects of referential meaning. Our main contributions are as follows: - We introduce a new, much more challenging dataset for the task, which is designed to evaluate the ability to generalize to novel names, an important aspect that previous work has focused on but which we believe is much more important. - We show that simply concatenating word vectors along with visual features is insufficient to capture inter-word relationship information, and introduce a simple method to further exploit distributional similarity using an explicit measure of semantic relatedness. - We observe that using the softmax function to combine word probability and visual probability of words tends to lead to multi-label classification rather than binary classification, and that a simple binary version of the softmax function is more effective. - We present our method’s performance on the MS-COCO object naming dataset, showing improvement over previous results. Our model is learned in a multi-task fashion, where the loss functions for each task are added together in an additive fashion with a margin term. The loss functions are the sum of a cross-entropy loss for text prediction and a softmax based ranking loss for word pairs. We use BERT pre-training for both the visual projection layer and the segmenter part of the model, and we use ELU activations for the softmax layer. Our code, including BERT fine-tuning code and our referential NER model, has been made available to the public and we welcome research using our code and comparing to our results. In this paper, the model is trained on the MS-COCO dataset. The input image is first passed through a segmentation submodel to extract image segments that correspond to the named object (e.g. “table” within the image belongs to segmentation set {table, table with cloth on top of it, table with chair on it, etc.}). Next, the model is trained on all pairs of segmentation sets and name candidates. The name prediction model is similar to the BERT pre-trained language model except that all the layers except the softmax layer are replaced with the model we are trying to identify to be the name (e.g. “table” would be represented by a language model trained on “the table” or “chair” as well as “table”). This not only captures inter-word relationship information but also handles the case when a part of the model represents multiple words by splitting these words out into multiple vectors. This model achieves 91.3% classification accuracy on the test set, showing the potential for a very strong baseline for the task. The full MS-COCO dataset with annotations used to train this model and the BERT model used to initialize this model are available for download. Our naming model is available for pre-trained models in the repo. Our code includes hyperparameters and data split information for the MS-COCO train

hypothesis. I agree with the comment wrt cross-modal mapping. What I don't
share is the kind of equation "visual = referential" that you seem to assume. A
referent can be visually presented, but visual information can be usefully
added to a word's representation in aggregate form to encode perceptual aspects
of the words' meaning, the same way that it is done for textual information;
for instance, the fact that bananas are yellow
will not frequently be mentioned in text, and adding visual information
extracted from images will account for this aspect of the semantic
representation of the word. This is kind of technical and specific to how we
build distributional models, but it's also relevant if you think of human
cognition (probably our representation for "banana" has some aggregate
information about all the bananas we've seen --and touched, tasted, etc.). 
It would be useful if you could discuss this issue explicitly, differentiating
between multi-modal distributional semantics in general and the use of
cross-modal mapping in particular.

Also, wrt the "all models perform similarly" comment: I really
urge you, if the paper is accepted, to state it in this form, even if it
doesn't completely align with your hypotheses/goals (you have enough results
that do). It is a better description of the results, and more useful for the
community, than clinging to the
n-th digit difference (and this is to a large extent independent of whether the
difference
is actually statistical significant or not: If one bridge has 49% chances of
collapsing and another one 50%, the difference may be statistically
significant, but that doesn't really make the first bridge a better bridge to
walk on).

Btw, small quibble, could you find a kind of more compact and to the point
title? (More geared towards either generally what you explore or to what you
find?)

The paper tackles an extremely interesting issue, that the authors label
"referential word meaning", namely, the connection between a word's meaning and
the referents (objects in the external world) it is applied to. If I understood
it correctly, they argue that
this is different from a typical word meaning representation as obtained e.g.
with distributional
methods, because one thing is the abstract "lexical meaning" of a word and the
other which label is appropriate for a given referent with specific properties
(in a specific context, although context is something they explicitly leave
aside in this paper). This hypothesis has been previously explored in work by
Schlangen and colleagues (cited in the paper). The paper explores referential
word meaning empirically on a specific version of the task of Referential
Expression Generation (REG), namely, generating the appropriate noun for a
given visually represented object.

- Strengths:

1) The problem they tackle I find extremely interesting; as they argue, REG is
a problem that had previously been addressed mainly using symbolic methods,
that did not easily allow for an exploration of how speakers choose the names
of the objects. The scope of the research goes beyond REG as such, as it
addresses the link between semantic representations and reference more broadly.

2) I also like how they use current techniques and datasets (cross-modal
mapping and word classifiers, the ReferIt dataset containing large amounts of
images with human-generated referring expressions) to address the problem at
hand. 

3) There are a substantial number of experiments as well as analysis into the
results. 

- Weaknesses:

1) The main weakness for me is the statement of the specific hypothesis, within
the general research line, that the paper is probing: I found it very
confusing.  As a result, it is also hard to make sense of the kind of feedback
that the results give to the initial hypothesis, especially because there are a
lot of them and they don't all point in the same direction.

The paper says:

"This paper pursues the hypothesis that an accurate
model of referential word meaning does not
need to fully integrate visual and lexical knowledge
(e.g. as expressed in a distributional vector
space), but at the same time, has to go beyond
treating words as independent labels."

The first part of the hypothesis I don't understand: What is it to fully
integrate (or not to fully integrate) visual and lexical knowledge? Is the goal
simply to show that using generic distributional representation yields worse
results than using specific, word-adapted classifiers trained on the dataset?
If so, then the authors should explicitly discuss the bounds of what they are
showing: Specifically, word classifiers must be trained on the dataset itself
and only word classifiers with a sufficient amount of items in the dataset can
be obtained, whereas word vectors are available for many other words and are
obtained from an independent source (even if the cross-modal mapping itself is
trained on the dataset); moreover, they use the simplest Ridge Regression,
instead of the best method from Lazaridou et al. 2014, so any conclusion as to
which method is better should be taken with a grain of salt. However, I'm
hoping that the research goal is both more constructive and broader. Please
clarify. 

2) The paper uses three previously developed methods on a previously available
dataset. The problem itself has been defined before (in Schlangen et al.). In
this sense, the originality of the paper is not high. 

3) As the paper itself also points out, the authors select a very limited
subset of the ReferIt dataset, with quite a small vocabulary (159 words). I'm
not even sure why they limited it this way (see detailed comments below).

4) Some aspects could have been clearer (see detailed comments).

5) The paper contains many empirical results and analyses, and it makes a
concerted effort to put them together; but I still found it difficult to get
the whole picture: What is it exactly that the experiments in the paper tell us
about the underlying research question in general, and the specific hypothesis
tested in particular? How do the different pieces of the puzzle that they
present fit together?

- General Discussion: [Added after author response]

Despite the weaknesses, I find the topic of the paper very relevant and also
novel enough, with an interesting use of current techniques to address an "old"
problem, REG and reference more generally, in a way that allows aspects to be
explored that have not received enough attention. The experiments and analyses
are a substantial contribution, even though, as mentioned above, I'd like the
paper to present a more coherent overall picture of how the many experiments
and analyses fit together and address the question pursued.

GENERAL 
The paper presents an interesting empirical comparison of 3 referring
expression generation models. The main novelty lies in the comparison of a yet
unpublished model called SIM-WAP (in press by Anonymous). The model is
described in SECTION 4.3 but it is not clear whether it is extended or modified
anyhow in the current paper.  

The novelty of the paper may be considered as the comparison of the unpublished
SIM-WAP model to existing 2 models. This complicates evaluation of the novelty
because similar experiments were already performed for the other two models and
it is unclear why this comparison was not performed in the paper where SIM-WAP
model was presented. A significant novelty might be the combined model yet this
is not stated clearly and the combination is not described with enough details.

The contribution of the paper may be considered the following: the side-by-side
comparison of the 3 methods for REG; analysis of zero-shot experiment results
which mostly confirms similar observations in previous works; analysis of the
complementarity of the combined model.                     

WEAKNESSES
Unclear novelty and significance of contributions. The work seems like an
experimental extension of the cited Anonymous paper where the main method was
introduced.    

Another weakness is the limited size of the vocabulary in the zero-shot
experiments that seem to be the most contributive part. 

Additionally, the authors never presented significance scores for their
accuracy results. This would have solidified the empirical contribution of the
work which its main value.   

My general feeling is that the paper is more appropriate for a conference on
empirical methods such as EMNLP. 

Lastly, I have not found any link to any usable software. Existing datasets
have been used for the work.

"We compare three recent models" -- Further in the abstract you write that you

machine_text: This paper presents a system that generates rhythmically styled verse based on an input prose passage. The generated verse is poetry style, appropriate for the context of the passage, and generated in the target language. The system is based on a novel neural network architecture, which I call a "CTC-RNN" –CTC: Connectionist Temporal Classification; RNN: Recurrent Neural Network. The CTC-RNN takes as input a sequence of word pieces obtained by splitting the input text into syllable pieces, and predicts the next syllable in the poetry style verse along with the poem's meter, number of stresses, and other aspects of the generated text's rhythm. The system is trained with a maximum likelihood loss function on pairs of poetry style reference verse and the predicted word pieces, with the training data obtained from a large generic dataset of existing poetry. The system is tested on several subjective evaluation metrics and is shown to compare favorably to state of the art automatic poetry generation systems. The resulting system could be a valuable tool for editing existing poetry, or for generating new poetry from scratch for any purpose, such as creating personalized greeting cards or poems for friends and family. This paper presents a system that generates rhythmic poetry given only the first two sentences of text. The system first finds lines of text that have an 8th measure, which are usually verses, and then clusters these 8th measures into rhythmic lines. It then fills in the blank space with nouns or noun phrases based on the last word of the previous 8th measure and the first word of the 8th measure. For example: the quiet buzz of the solar panel Took root and grew fat, the hopper tugged us down. Bright lights in the distance, the resiny smell of frayed wiring The pirate laughs, asking for more wealth to be spent. Driving through the black, the yellow lights of the city pass us by. My feet dangle a few inches above the floor, As the hopeless cycle spins without end. The system was trained on 8th measure lines from a database of existing poetry, so it produces lines that are generally grammatical and make sense in rhyming pairings. However, it can sometimes fill in the blank space incorrectly, especially when the last word of the previous 8th measure and the first word of the current 8th measure are very different (such as asking for more wealth vs. spending wealth), or when it can't discern the last word of the previous 8th measure (since it is unknown, it defaults to the first word of the current 8th measure). This could be addressed by training on a larger poetry database, or perhaps by including some metadata about the previous 8th measure in the training data, for example a common last word or providing the last 8 lines of the previous 8th measure as an example. The code is available to be tested on GitHub and the system also outputs explanations for each blank space, so perhaps a qualitative analysis of the poetry generated by this system could also be included in the paper.

The main topic of this paper is about the generation of rhythmic poetry, which has so many good aspects such as appealing to the ear, easy to memorize and good at expressing deep emotions. However, until now, the generation of rhythmic poetry has relied either on algorithmically-derived patterns of rhyming and alliteration, which cannot capture the richness of human expression, or on patterns of text which constrains but does not fully express the poetic form. To this end, the authors propose two novel methodologies that can generate poetry that satisfies both the content and form constraints, and perform a large-scale extrinsic evaluation to demonstrate its viability. The paper is clearly written and the methodology is clearly defined, and as a result, the paper is relatively easy to understand and reproduce. However, I would like to emphasize that the evaluation carried out on the generated poems themselves, i.e. without an expert review, might not be able to measure the true success of the approach because human beings are really good at identifying whether a piece of art is generated by a machine or a human being.
