This paper presents a method to measure topic quality using Word Buckets. Word buckets are essentially sets of word vectors where each vector represents a different concept. The context of a sentence determines which concepts are activated. The premise of this method is that good topics will have high correlation with certain concepts in word buckets. The technique the paper uses is a topic modelling technique called Latent Dirichlet Allocation. They generate a topic model on a large corpus of documents and assign topics to individual words. They then assign a vector to each topic. The angle between these topics represents how well defined the topics are. A well defined topic will have a small angle. This is a good signal that the topic is well characterised by the selected words. This method would work well for certain topics. For example, if you are measuring the quality of news articles, then topics like “President Trump” or “Protests” would work well. The method would fail for topics like “Technology” or “Politics” because these topics have a low correlation with a specific subset of concepts in the word bucket vocabulary. The paper mentions that this technique works well for topics with a high response variance (the extent to which different people see different things in a topic). One strength of this paper is that it provides methods to define and calculate a large number of topics. The process of generating topics is manual and human validated. As a weakness, the authors do not clearly demonstrate why this method is better than existing alternatives. For example, why couldn’t they use a similar technique to calculate the quality of a book? The paper measures topic quality using Enron corpus. The topics that the paper is able to calculate the quality of are topics like “President Trump” and “Protests”. The paper does not show that the correlation between these topics and a specific subset of concepts in the word bucket vocabulary is low. This means that the method would also work for a topic like “Politics” which may not be well defined by the selected words.

Overall, I like the paper and think it has significant potential. However, I recommend performing the following revisions: 1- The paper could benefit from more description about the process of clustering. How the number of clusters is determined? How many iterations are there? How theSilhouette score is computed? Can you share the code and the hyperparameters? 2- The paper could benefit from a more detailed result of the clustering approach (i.e. using the Silhouette score). What is the difference between the Silhouette score of 0.3 and the Silhouette score of 0.8? 3- The term bucket is used several times without further explaining what is a bucket. Please define bucket in the paper. 4- Related to previous point, why not to use a single bucket per document? It seems like you loose very interesting piece of information - that some words are frequently used in a subset of documents and their general contribution to the topic is low 5- Related to previous point, can you explain why using SVD on the original word-by-document matrices instead of using SVD on the word-bucket-by-document matrices would help to improve the results? 6- In the section "SVD with reorganization", the authors calculate standard deviations of row norms of different matrices. I did not see results of this calculation or relate it to the topic coherence. Can you provide some examples? On the positive side, I think the idea of TBuckets is interesting. It will be interesting for users to be able to browse TBuckets based on some criteria (e.g. hot words, top contributing words etc.) I have implemented TBuckets, please see attachment below. It is a open source at Github.com Best regards Antti (0) The bucket words that are similar in meaning to the original word, will likely get grouped together (1) The bucket words that are strongly related, but not identical, to the original word, will also likely get grouped together (2) The bucket words that are weakly similar to the original word, will likely not get grouped together. Example: consider a bucket TBuckets1 formed of close variants of the original word 'buckets', 'bucket'. TBuckets1 is a cluster of related words, but not identical to the original word. Buckets also have an obvious mapping to the number of threads in SVD. The first bucket is related to the most general topic of the whole corpus, usually 'WhiteAlbum'. The proposed TBuckets approach for measuring topic quality addresses the problem of measuring topic quality of LDA-based topics. It addresses this problem by first clustering topic words using their word embeddings, then creating buckets of words using the clustering results. The clustering method, the singular value decomposition (SVD), is used to create buckets using the concept of word embeddings as a means to find clusters of semantically related words, and finally a reorganization method is used to reduce the number of buckets. The proposed approach is evaluated on three publicly available text datasets and the results show that the proposed approach outperforms the state-of-the-art techniques for measuring topic quality. Moreover, we show that the bucket structure and the relation between the topics can be used for other tasks, such as weakly supervised text classification. * The main problem that the paper tries to address is the following: measuring topic quality is essential for scoring the learned topics and their subsequent use in information retrieval and text classification. * The proposed TBuckets approach is an effective method for measuring topic quality. It first clusters topic words using their word embeddings, then creates buckets of words using the clustering results. The clustering method, the singular value decomposition (SVD), is used to create buckets using the concept of word embeddings. * Three different techniques for creating bucket groups - i) clustering based, ii) using singular value decomposition (SVD) and iii) SVD with reorganization. * The proposed approach is evaluated on three publicly available text datasets and the results show that the proposed approach outperforms the state-of-the-art techniques. * Further, we show that the bucket structure and the relation between the topics can be used for other tasks, such as weakly supervised text classification.
human_text:
This paper proposes a method for evaluating topic quality based on using word
embeddings to calculate similarity (either directly or indirectly via matrix
factorisation), achieving impressive results over standard datasets.

The proposed method represents a natural but important next step in the
evolutionary path of research on topic evaluation. The thing that troubled me
most with the results was that, while you achieve state-of-the-art results for
all three datasets, there are large inconsistencies in which methods perform
and which methods perform less well (below the state of the art). In practice,
none of the proposed methods consistently beats the state of the art, and the
SVD-based methods perform notably badly over the genomics dataset. For someone
who wants to take your method off the shelf and use it over any arbitrary
dataset, this is a considerable worry. I suspect that the lower results for
SVD over genomics relate to the proportion of OOV terms (see comment below),
and that it may be possible to automatically predict which method will perform
best based on vocab match with GloVe etc., but there is no such discussion in
the paper.

Other issues:

- the proposed method has strong similarities with methods proposed in the
  lexical chaining literature, which I would encourage the authors to read up
  on and include in any future version of the paper

- you emphasis that your method has no parameters, but the word embedding
  methods have a large number of parameters, which are implicit in your
  method. Not a huge deal, but worth acknowledging

- how does your method deal with OOV terms, e.g. in the genomics dataset
  (i.e. terms not present in the pretrained GloVe embeddings)? Are they simply
  ignored? What impact does this have on the method?

Low-level issues:

- in your description of word embeddings in Section 2.1, you implicitly assume
  that the length of the vector is unimportant (in saying that cosine
  similarity can be used to measure the similarity between two vectors). If
  the vectors are unit length, this is unproblematic, but word2vec actually
  doesn't return unit-length vectors (the pre-trained vectors have been
  normalised post hoc, and if you run word2vec yourself, the vector length is
  certainly not uniform). A small detail, but important.

- the graphs in Figure 1 are too small to be readable

This paper proposes a new method for the evaluation of topic models that
partitions the top n words of each topic into clusters or "buckets" based on
cosine similarity of their associated word embeddings. In the simplest setup,
the words are considered one by one, and each is either put into an existing
"bucket" â if its cosine similarity to the other words in the bucket is below
a certain threshold â or a new bucket is created for the word. Two more
complicated methods based on eigenvectors and reorganisation are also
suggested. The method is evaluated on three standard data sets and in a  weakly
supervised text classification setting. It outperforms or is en par with the
state of the art (RÃ¶der et al., 2015).

The basic idea behind the paper is rather simple and has a certain ad
hoc-flavour. The authors do not offer any new explanations for why topic
quality should be measurable in terms of wordâword similarity. It is not
obvious to me why this should be so, given that topics and word embeddings are
defined with respect to two rather different notions of context (document vs.
sequential context). At the same time, the proposed method seems to work quite
well. (I would like to see some significance tests for Table 1 though.)

Overall the paper is clearly written, even though there are some language
issues. Also, I found the description of the techniques in Section 3 a bit hard
to follow; I believe that this is mostly due to the authors using passive voice
("the threshold is computed as") in places were they were actually making a
design choice. I find that the authors should try to explain the different
methods more clearly, with one subsection per method. There seems to be some
space for that: The authors did not completely fill the 8 pages of content, and
they could easily downsize the rather uninformative "trace" of the method on
page 3.

One question that I had was how sensitive the proposed technique was to

This paper discusses coreference resolution in the Wikidata community edited version of the Wikipedia database. The paper has a broad scope, covering main concepts as well as proper names. The approach is to encode Stanford Open Coreference ELMo model neural network outputs as RDF graph fragments. This enables mapping the inference queries that a human analyst might run, as well as algorithms for coreference resolution. The article does have some weaknesses. For example, there is no consideration of performance in the case of multiple coreferent mentions in the same sentence, or of resolution of popular hybrid Coreference phenomena such as pronoun shifts. Another weakness is that some of the examples shown are not fully correct with respect to the Stanford NER or Coreference models, and so generate incorrect assumptions in the reader. Overall, however, I think this is a valuable contribution to the community edit version of Wikipedia, and the techniques could be readily applied to other large datasets with similar composition. cleavage The paper describes a technique for mapping the inference queries that a human analyst might run, as well as algorithms for coreference resolution. In this work, we revisit a seldom studied task which consists in identifying in a Wikipedia article all the mentions of the main concept being described. We show that by exploiting the Wikipedia markup of a document, as well as links to external knowledge bases such as Freebase, we can acquire useful information on entities that helps to classify mentions as coreferent or not. We designed a classifier that drastically outperforms fair baselines built on top of state-of-the-art coreference resolution systems. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our classifier on a dataset of 80k documents from the Ubuntu website and show that it significantly improves a full coreference resolution pipeline applied to Wikipedia texts. Our main contributions can be summarized as follows: - we analyze and design a Wikipedia coreference resolution system that exploits both page markup and links to Freebase; - we build a large dataset of documents related to Ubuntu released between 2005 and 2015 and use it to train, evaluate, and compare our approach; - we design a classifier that, to the best of our knowledge, is the first to be applied to this dataset and shows significant improvement over fair baselines; - we make our dataset and the code for the proposed approach publicly available. We hope our results can motivate further research on adapting coreference resolution to Wikipedia and on using this type of data in NLP. Paper link: https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.08043 Thank you for your attention. Jing Wan (Minsuk Yeo is the first author) 2022 ---------------------- Deep learning-based coreference resolution for Wikipedia arXiv:1911.08043 Minsuk Yeo, Jie Zhang, Xin Xie, and Qian Zhang Fudan University 2018 https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.12651 November 30, 2018 [ PDF] ---------------------- Extracting Knowledge from Unannotated Web Data Minsuk Yeo1, Xin Xie1, Jie Zhang2, and Qian Zhang2 Fudan University Abstract—With the ubiquity of Web search engines and the proliferation of online social media, a large amount of unannotated Web data is available for many novice NLP applications. However, current techniques to exploit such unannotated data are limited in two ways: First, many existing unannotated data collection approaches do not perform well at identifying the right regions of interest, which are often either long or partially overlap with the ground truth, leading to lots of false alarms. Second, most existing approaches that do identify the right regions of interest do not use the extra data for effective learning, which also leads to lots of false alarms. In this paper, we first conduct a user study to evaluate and identify the most informative types of unannotated Web data. In particular, we find that those types that identify the right region of interest and consider surrounding content usually lead to the most accurate predictions. We also perform a case study to evaluate and compare the effectiveness of different types of unannotated data for the task of named entity recognition (NER) on the widely used IMDB movie review dataset. We find that user feedback on similar cases is one of the most effective ways to train an NER model on the IMDB dataset using unannotated Web data. We further develop an open-source system capable of learning to recognize entities from unannotated Web data without using any manual labels. We perform an extensive empirical evaluation on three real-world datasets, and the results show that our system achieves statistically significant improvements over the state-of-the-art in entity recognition on unannotated Web data. As the first work to automatically and effectively recognize entities from unannotated Web data without using any manual labels, our work has the potential to open up more possibilities for using unannotated Web data in downstream NLP applications. Wikipedia is a great resource for NLP tasks but has not been explored in the area of coreference resolution, where the main challenge is to identify in a given document which mentions are referring to the same real-world entity. In this work we present a novel approach to this problem which exploits the Wikipedia markup of a document as well as links to external knowledge bases in Freebase. Our approach is to use a main concept identifier to identify the main topic of an article and use this to classify mentions into coreferent and non-coreferent. We develop a model that improves over the state of the art on a gold-standard test set with a large margin and show that the improvements from using this model are significant when applying it to a full coreference resolution pipeline. human_text:
The authors present a new version of the coreference task tailored to
Wikipedia. The task is to identify the coreference chain specifically
corresponding to the entity that the Wikipedia article is about.  The authors
annotate 30 documents with all coreference chains, of which roughly 25% of the
mentions refer to the "main concept" of the article. They then describe some
simple baselines and a basic classifier which outperforms these. Moreover, they
integrate their classifier into the Stanford (rule-based) coreference system
and see substantial benefit over all state-of-the-art systems on Wikipedia.

I think this paper proposes an interesting twist on coreference that makes good
sense from an information extraction perspective, has the potential to somewhat
revitalize and shake up coreference research, and might bridge the gap in an
interesting way between coreference literature and entity linking literature. 
I am sometimes unimpressed by papers that dredge up a new task that standard
systems perform poorly on and then propose a tweak so that their system does
better. However, in this case, the actual task itself is quite motivating to me
and rather than the authors fishing for a new domain to run things in, it
really does feel like "hey, wait, these standard systems perform poorly in a
setting that's actually pretty important."

THE TASK: Main concept resolution is an intriguing task from an IE perspective.
 I can imagine many times where documents revolve primarily around a particular
entity (biographical documents, dossiers or briefings about a person or event,
clinical records, etc.) and where the information we care about extracting is
specific to that entity. The standard coreference task has always had the issue
of large numbers of mentions that would seemingly be pretty irrelevant for most
IE problems (like generic mentions), and this task is unquestionably composed
of mentions that actually do matter.

From a methodology standpoint, the notion of a "main concept" provides a bit of
a discourse anchor that is useful for coreference, but there appears to still
be substantial overhead to improve beyond the baselines, particularly on
non-pronominal mentions. Doing coreference directly on Wikipedia also opens the
doors for more interesting use of knowledge, which the authors illustrate here.
So I think this domain is likely to be an interesting testbed for ideas which
would improve coreference overall, but which in the general setting would be
more difficult to get robust improvements with and which would be dwarfed by
the amount of work dealing with other aspects of the problem.

Moreover, unlike past work which has carved off a slice of coreference (e.g.
the Winograd schema work), this paper makes a big impact on the metrics of the
*overall* coreference problem on a domain (Wikipedia) that many in the ACL
community are pretty interested in.

THE TECHNIQUES: Overall, the techniques are not the strong point of this paper,
though they do seem to be effective. The features seem pretty sensible, but it
seems like additional conjunctions of these may help (and it's unclear whether
the authors did any experimentation in this vein).  The authors should also
state earlier in the work that their primary MC resolution system is a binary
classifier; this is not explicitly stated early enough and the model is left
undefined throughout the description of featurization.

MINOR DETAILS:

Organization: I would perhaps introduce the dataset immediately after "Related
Works" (i.e. have it be the new Section 3) so that concrete results can be
given in "Baselines", further motivating "Approach".

When Section 4 refers to Dcoref and Scoref, you should cite the Stanford papers
or make it clear that it's the Stanford coreference system (many will be
unfamiliar with the Dcoref/Scoref names).

The use of the term "candidate list" was unclear, especially in the following:

"We leverage the hyperlink structure of the article in order to enrich the list
of mentions with shallow semantic attributes. For each link found within the
article under consideration, we look through the candidate list for all
mentions that match the surface string of the link."

Please make it clear that the "candidate list" is the set of mentions in the
article that are possible candidates for being coreferent with the MC.        I think
most readers will understand that this module is supposed to import semantic
information from the link structure of Wikipedia (e.g. if a mention is
hyperlinked to an article that is female in Freebase, that mention is female),
so try to keep the terminology clear.

Section 6.1 says "we consider the union of WCR mentions and all mentions
predicted by the method described in (Raghunathan et al., 2010)." However,
Section 4.1 implies that these are the same? I'm missing where additional WCR
mentions would be extracted.

machine_text: Overall, I enjoyed this paper. I found the topic to be important and useful. The experimental design and findings were clearly articulated, and I think the findings are plausible and actionable. My main concerns relate to the empirical validation of the proposed approach. I think the experiments could be more rigorous and provide stronger evidence for the generalization of the proposed approach. I also have some reservations about the relevance of the methodology to POS tagging. I think the methodology might work better for Named Entity Recognition (NER) than Part of Speech (POS) tagging. Named entities usually have clear entity types and are usually locally distinct from other text. Thus, it may be easier to identify clean training and test datasets, and the confusion between supervision and guidance may not arise. I think the methodology could be more generally applied and validated through experimentation, and I think the discussion of the limitations could be expanded. MY STARES FOR DISCUSSION I really enjoyed this paper and found it to be both interesting and useful. I think the proposed approach is general and could be applied to other NLP tasks. However, I would recommend explicitly stating how the methodology can be applied to other NLP tasks. For example, I think this methodology might be better applied to Named Entity Recognition (NER) than Part of Speech (POS) tagging. Named entities usually have clear entity types (e.g, person, location, organization) and are usually locally distinct from other text. Thus, it might be easier to identify clean training and test datasets, and the confusion between supervision and guidance may not arise. I think the methodology could be more generally applied and validated through experimentation. I also have some reservations about the relevance of the methodology to POS tagging. I think the methodology might work better for Named Entity Typing (NIT) than Part of Speech (POS) tagging. Part of speech tagging often relies on local contexts, whereas Named entity typing might require more global considerations. For example, in the approach, the model assumes that the local entity types (e.g, person, location, organization) are globally consistent (e.g, all people should reside in a location), and this consistency should be inferred from data. I think this assumption might not hold in practice and the validity of the approach should be tested on another NLP task.

Thank you for this interesting paper! The paper addresses a challenging problem – supervised learning on a resource-intensive task when there is only weakly-supervised data. The main idea is to transfer information from a related, high-resource task and use a bi-LSTM based model to project representations of documents from a low-resource language to the high-resource one and learn a tagger from the transferred knowledge. The main advantage of the approach is that the taggers get trained on a much larger dataset, thus being more robust to the limited amount of training data for the low-resource language. The approach is evaluated on POS tagging of Vietnamese and good results are reported, with the system being much more robust to the amount of training data. The main weakness of the approach is the need for closely-related languages for transfer, which limits the applicability of the approach. However, this is a very interesting problem and the approach presented here could be a good starting point for future work in this area. {#section-1.unnumbered} The paper Learning when to trust distant supervision: An application to low-resource POS tagging using cross-lingual projection addresses the problem of supervised learning on a resource-intensive task when there is only weakly-supervised data. The authors describe an approach to solving this problem based on transferring information from a related, high-resource task and using a bi-LSTM-based model to project representations of documents from a low-resource language to the high-resource one and learn a tagger from the transferred knowledge. The approach is evaluated on POS tagging of Vietnamese and good results are reported, with the system being much more robust to the amount of training data. The approach is nice but has some weaknesses. The main weakness is the need for closely-related languages for transfer, which limits the applicability of the approach. {#section-2.unnumbered} The paper has several strengths. The approach is general and can be used in various applications where weakly supervised learning is needed but not enough data is available. The authors present a clear, step-by-step approach to transferring knowledge between similar tasks using cross-lingual word/character embedding projection and Bidirectional LSTM with CRF output. The description of the approach is well-targeted to a layman. The authors present state-of-the-art results on the Vietnamese POS tag dataset. The experiments are well described and the code is available. The paper could be more specific in discussing limitations of the approach. The authors present the approach in a general manner, but it seems that the approach would be most effective for low resource languages for which there is a close language with high resource. For example, it would not work for languages that are related but have too many differences (e.g. Latin, Italian, Spanish). Another example is related to the use of transfer learning. In the case of close language, it may not be necessary to have an annotated resource language to transfer knowledge to the low resource one. It would be possible to use transfer learning in some form, but the low resource language will not be able to benefit from all the progress in NLP. I think this could be mentioned as a limitation. {#section-3.unnumbered} Overall, this is an interesting and promising approach to the problem, and the experiments show that the approach works well in practice. There are also some limitations that the paper doesn't address. The main limitation of the approach is the need for closely-related languages for transfer, which limits the applicability of the approach. I think it would be interesting to mention in the paper that the approach can be used for pairs of closely-related languages, but not for pairs of less closely-related languages. Another important limitation is that the transfer has to be one-way. That is, you can only transfer knowledge from a close language to a low resource one, but not vice-versa. {#section-4.unnumbered} I have read this submission agree to make this submission public? Yamada Kenta University of Tsukuba, Japan **[Abstract]{}**: Many natural language processing (NLP) tasks have been studied with the aid of supervised learning, but the amount of data for such tasks is often not large enough. For example, there are many languages in the world but supervised learning for NLP for every language has not been achieved for various reasons. We take POS tagging as an example; although many languages have had their POS tags annotated in various ways, there are many low-resource languages for which no POS tagger has been trained with such high-quality data. In this paper, we present a method that can train POS taggers for low-resource languages with weak supervision, that is, POS tags for many words are tagged but not for all words. The method makes use of

Generally, the paper makes some good practices on low-resource NLP tasks. In addition, the authors present a new approach that leverages the assumption that similar languages share similar semantic representations and further utilizes this assumption to deal with the problem of scarce annotation in low-resource language pairs. The main contributions of the paper are valuable and has the potential to impact the real-world low-resource NLP tasks. However, I have some concerns about the evaluation of the model, which I summarized as below: The evaluation metric is not suitable for the low-resource NLP task. The assumption that similar languages share similar semantic representation is true only when the lengths of their typing romes are very similar or equal. However, in the paper, there are two low-resource languages Malagasy and Kinyarwanda that have very different romes from English (the high-resource language). Thus, the performance on the Malagasy or Kinyarwanda low-resource language could be adversely affected by the error in projected tags from English to the corresponding low-resource language. The paper only evaluates the proposed model on two real low-resource languages Malagasy and Kinyarwanda, but not other low-resource languages. The low-resource languages such as Malagasy and Kinyarwanda share very similar romes, however, it does not necessarily hold for other low-resource languages. The paper uses the low-resource word segmentation tool Judei to get the projected tags of English. However, the quality of the projected tags is related to the quality of Judei. In the low-resource NLP area, many toolswave for low-resource NLP. Why not use those tools to generate Judei-like tags instead of using Judei itself which may suffer from high error rate? It would be better if the authors can further validate their model on some related low-resource tasks. Since the projected tags are related to the low-resource language, the actual low-resource language, Malagasy, also can be used as the projected language for Judei to generate more Judei-like tags, which could be used for evaluating the model on another low-resource task such as POS tagging.

The main contribution of this paper is designing a debiasing layer to clean up the errors from cross-lingual projection, which is a novel and effective approach for sequence labeling. The paper is built upon the great work of Habel et al. (NAACL’18), who introduced the grommet framework and showed that cross-lingual projection could be applied to sequence labeling. However, the de facto system for low-resource POS tagging only achieved mageScore of 53.3% on newstest2015, much lower than the memory-efficient convolutional neural networks (CRNN) that achieved 73.9%. Thus this paper is quite promising. However, I have several concerns about this paper. First, the error analysis on the grommet paper is not available. Instead of the former claims, it’s more likely that the cross-lingual mapping from WMT’18 was noisy and buggy, as other WMT systems such as WMT17 were already very close to BBT’17 with only one-tenth of the parallel data. The new model might have learned to fit the data and “fixed” some bugs in the system. We can only hope that the improvement is from the true generalization power of neural networks, instead of overfitting to the noise. Second, in the paper, the grommet code is not available. Without seeing how the debiasing layer is implemented, it’s hard to evaluate the effectiveness of the paper. The grommet paper was already open source, but with watermarked versions, the assumption is that the authors want to prevent the code from being misused. The paper did not mention any open source repository or the source code of the debiasing layer. By now, I believe that the author has already published the grommet code, but without any updates since. In summary, I strongly encourage the authors to share their grommet code, and share the related errors on the WMT’18 data, or a public test server so that the research community can test the generalization power of the debiasing model.
human_text:
I reviewed this paper earlier, when it was an ACL 2016 short paper draft. At
that point, it had a flaw in the experiment setup, which is now corrected.

Since back then I suggested I'd be willing to accept the draft for another *ACL
event provided that the flaw is corrected, I now see no obstacles in doing so.

Another reviewer did point out that the setup of the paper is somewhat
artificial if we focus on real low-resource languages, relating to the costs of
*finding* vs. *paying* the annotators. I believe this should be exposed in the
writeup not to oversell the method.

There are relevant lines of work in annotation projection for extremely
low-resource languages, e.g., Johannsen et al. (2016, ACL) and Agic et al.
(2015, ACL). It would be nice to reflect on those in the related work
discussion for completeness.

In summary, I think this is a nice contribution, and I vote accept.

It should be indicated whether the data is made available. I evaluate those
parts in good faith now, presuming public availability of research.

The paper describes a modification to the output layer of recurrent neural
network models which enables learning the model parameters from both gold and
projected annotations in a low-resource language. The traditional softmax
output layer which defines a distribution over possible labels is further
multiplied by a fully connected layer which models the noise generation
process, resulting in another output layer representing the distribution over
noisy labels. 

Overall, this is a strong submission. The proposed method is apt, simple and
elegant. The paper reports good results on POS tagging for eight simulated
low-resource languages and two truly low-resource languages, making use of a
small set of gold annotations and a large set of cross-lingually projected
annotations for training. The method is modular enough that researchers working
on different NLP problems in low-resource scenarios are likely to use it.

From a practical standpoint, the experimental setup is unusual. While I can
think of some circumstances where one needs to build a POS tagger with as
little as 1000 token annotations (e.g., evaluations in some DARPA-sponsored
research projects), it is fairly rare. A better empirical validation of the
proposed method would have been to plot the tagging accuracy of the proposed
method (and baselines) while varying the size of gold annotations. This plot
would help answer questions such as: Does it hurt the performance on a target
language if we use this method while having plenty of gold annotations? What is
the amount of gold annotations, approximately, below which this method is
beneficial? Does the answer depend on the target language?

Beyond cross-lingual projections, noisy labels could potentially be obtained
from other sources (e.g., crowd sourcing) and in different tag sets than gold
annotations. Although the additional potential impact is exciting, the paper
only shows results with cross-lingual projections with the same tag set. 

It is surprising that the proposed training objective gives equal weights to
gold vs. noisy labels. Since the setup assumes the availability of a small gold
annotated corpus, it would have been informative to report whether it is
beneficial to tune the contribution of the two terms in the objective function.


In line 357, the paper describes the projected data as pairs of word tokens
(x_t) and their vector representations \tilde{y}, but does not explicitly
mention what the vector representation looks like (e.g., a distribution over
cross-lingually projected POS tags for this word type). A natural question to
ask here is whether the approach still works if we construct \tilde{y} using
the projected POS tags at the token level (rather than aggregating all
predictions for the same word type). Also, since only one-to-one word
alignments are preserved, it is not clear how to construct \tilde{y} for words
which are never aligned.

This paper is interesting, and some good ideas are explored. Here are some suggestions for improvement: 1. The contrast between traditional features and cognitive features does not seem well defined. The introduction mentions four levels of sentiment subtleties, but doesn't offer much analysis of why those are relevant to cognitive features. The feature description itself is also not very clear. For example, the contrast between lexical and contextual features is not very clear. I assume the purpose of these features is to capture the meaning of words based on the surrounding words (semantic relations). For example, the meaning of the word "cat" in "the cat sat on the mat" is different from that in "the cat chased the mouse". In terms of lexical features, there are number of different aspects that could be captured. The choice of which features to use is interesting. For example, is the word order relevant? E.g. in "the mouse sat on the mat" the cat is causing the affect of the sentiment, whereas in "the cat sat on the mat" the mouse is causing the affect. As another example, adjectives are often used to describe nouns (e.g. "the cat sat on a round mat"). Are such syntactic features useful? In general, it would be good to better motivate the choice of features and provide examples of how each feature is relevant to cognitive features. 2. The feature analysis and significance test is performed on a held-out dataset. However, the classification results on the held-out dataset are not reported. This is a common problem in machine learning, where pre-test performance on a test dataset may not reflect the true performance on a target dataset. A proper validation approach is to split the data into training and test sets, and report both the classification results on the test set, as well as the generalization errors (i.e. the difference between the results on the test set and the results on the target set). 3. The "Cognitive Sentiment Analyzer" sounds very promising, but there is no clear description of how to actually use this analyzer. The CSA only returns the classification result. Without the actual sentiment polarities, we cannot evaluate the CSA's performance. A deeper analysis of what cognitive features actually reveal is also lacking. What were the most useful features? What is the classification accuracy on negative and positive examples? What is the difference between cognitive features and conventional feature-based machine learning models?

In this paper, the authors use cognitive features derived from the eye-movement patterns of readers to enhance traditional features used for sentiment analysis. The enhanced features improve the performance of sentiment analysis on two public datasets. The main problem addressed in this paper is: Sentiments expressed in user-generated short text and sentences are nuanced by subtleties at lexical, syntactic, semantic and pragmatic levels. To address this, we propose to augment traditional features used for sentiment analysis and sarcasm detection, with cognitive features derived from the eye-movement patterns of readers. Statistical classification using our enhanced feature set improves the performance (F-score) of polarity detection by a maximum of 3.7% and 9.3% on two datasets, over the systems that use only traditional features. We perform feature significance analysis, and experiment on a held-out dataset, showing that cognitive features indeed empower sentiment analyzers to handle complex constructs. However, the paper Leveraging Cognitive Features for Sentiment Analysis might encounter some potential problems as below: 1. Sentiment analysis and sarcasm detection are very close domains and there might be overlaps in the techniques and/or features used by both domains. In this case, it might be difficult to clearly separate these domains and identify which one this paper is addressing. 2. The impact of cognitive features on sentiment analysis might not be that significant. Although the paper mentioned that by using cognitive features the performance of sentiment analysis improved by 3.7% and 9.3%, there might be other features or methods that could achieve the same results at lower costs. 3. The application of cognitive features in sentiment analysis might seem cool in the sentiment analysis community but might be not that novel and interesting to readers outside of this community. Overall, this is an interesting idea of fusing cognitive features with traditional features for sentiment analysis and the results are quite positive. However, to make this paper more widely applicable, the potential weaknesses above should be considered and maybe expanded in the future revision. Strengths: 1. This paper fuses two domains, sentiment analysis and sarcasm detection, which might help to separate the two domains. 2. The authors proposed a general framework of fusing cognitive features with other traditional features for sentiment analysis, which could be applied to different datasets and have a potential to be more widely adopted. 3. The cognitive features might help to improve the performance of sentiment analysis on some complex issues, for example, parsing subtle sentiment under sarcasm. Weaknesses: 1. The impact of cognitive features on sentiment analysis might not be that significant. Although the paper mentioned that by using cognitive features the performance of sentiment analysis improved by 3.7% and 9.3%, there might be other features or methods that could achieve the same results at lower costs. 2. The application of cognitive features in sentiment analysis might seem cool in the sentiment analysis community but might be not that novel and interesting to readers outside of this community. For the potential weakness 1, the authors can perform more experiments on some key situations, for example, on different levels of sarcasm. It might help to justify the significant results of cognitive features. For the potential weakness 2, the authors can include comments or notes to readers that the application of cognitive features might not be very novel and also explain why in the case of sentiment analysis. Finally, although this paper is still worth reading and the author did a good job to explain the potential weakness 1, the potential weakness 2 might limit the general use of the cognitive features for sentiment analysis. The authors might also think about the potential ways to highlight the cognitive features without giving the whole idea of cognitive features.

This paper proposed a very interesting idea of using cognitive features for
sentiment analysis and sarcasm detection. More specifically, the eye-movement
patterns of human annotators are recorded to derive a new set of features. The
authors claim that this is the first work to include cognitive features into
the NLP community. 

Strength: 
1. The paper is generally well written and easy to follow
2. Very interesting idea which may inspire research in other NLP tasks.

Weakness:
1. The motivation of using cognitive features for sentiment analysis is not
very well justified. I can imagine these features may help reflect the reading
ease, but I don't see why they are helpful in detecting sentiment polarities.
2. The improvement is marginal after considering cognitive features by
comparing Sn+Sr+Gz with Sn+Sr.
3. Although the authors discussed about the feasibility of the approach in
Section 7, but I'm not convinced, especially about the example given in section
7.2, I don't see why this technique is helpful in such a scenario.

This paper is about introducing eye-tracking features for sentiment analysis as
a type of cognitive feature.  I think that the idea of introducing eye-tracking
features as a proxy for cognitive load for sentiment analysis is an interesting
one.  

I think the discussion on the features and comparison of feature sets is clear
and very helpful.  I also like that the feasibility of the approach is
addressed in section 7.

I wonder if it would help the evaluation if the datasets didn't conflate
different domains, e.g., the movie review corpus and the tweet corpus.             
For one
it might improve the prediction of movie review (resp. tweets) if the tweets
(resp. movie reviews) weren't in the training.              It would also make the
results
easier to interpret.  The results in Table 2 would seem rather low compared to
state-of-the art results for the Pang and Lee data, but look much better if
compared to results for Twitter data.

In Section 3.3, there are no overlapping snippets in the training data and
testing data of datasets 1 and 2, right?  Even if they come from the same
sources (e.g., Pang & Lee and Sentiment 140).

Minor: some of the extra use of bold is distracting (or maybe it's just me);

This paper addresses the problem of training deep neural networks for domain translation with a small amount of labeled data. The idea is that you can exploit the large amount of unlabeled data to learn a general representation, which you can then adapt to a specific domain using only a small amount of labeled data. The idea is evaluated on the task of domain translation between web content, with existing state-of-the-art results, but the techniques can be applied to other domain adaptation problems. The main idea is to let the translation network propose a set of translations, and the discriminator is responsible for selecting the correct one. The generator tries to mimic the discriminative model, but uses the small amount of labeled data to update the parameters. Using this idea, the model is trained in a semi-supervised way, and can be applied to small amounts of labeled data. The paper describes an implementation of the model, and experiments on several public datasets show that the method works well for the task of translation adaptation with a small amount of labeled data. The main idea is to let the translation network propose a set of translations, and the discriminator is responsible for selecting the correct one. The generator tries to mimic the discriminative model, but uses the small amount of labeled data to update the parameters. Using this idea, the model is trained in a semi-supervised way, and can be applied to small amounts of labeled data. The paper describes an implementation of the model, and experiments on several public datasets show that the method works well for the task of translation adaptation with a small amount of labeled data. The model is based on the fully convolutional framework, so it can be applied to images, sequences, and word segments with a moderate computation cost. A very interesting result is the ability to apply the proposed technique to small datasets, e.g., less than 1000 samples. The main drawback of the approach is that the results are not as good as when using a very large amount of labeled data, but it still represents a very good solution in many scenarios.

The paper you have cited addresses an important problem, namely how to train machine translation systems with tiny amounts of in-domain data. Using semi-supervised convolutions, the authors are able to learn an in-domain analog model which predicts domain relevance for all the sentences in the general-domain data set. The sentence pairs with top scores are then used to train the system. The authors perform experiments on 4 language directions with three test domains and show that their approach significantly improves the performance over strong baselines. The method's success is likely due to its ability to transfer knowledge from the in-domain analog model to the general-domain model. actress tbl. 1: Compared with strong baseline systems trained with large amounts of data, the method proposed in this paper can improve the performance up to 3.1 BLEU. As shown in the experiments, even with only tiny in-domain data (e.g. as small as 100 sentences), the learned selection model can still provide effective transfer knowledge to the general-domain model. However, if the selected sentences for the general-domain model are highly biased to the specific in-domain data, the knowledge learned from the selection model will not be able to help the general-domain model to better generalize to the broader domain. Therefore, we assume that a good way to reduce the bias in selection model is to combine it with the training data that contains both in-domain and some out-of-domain data, which is, in fact, the idea of semi-supervised learning. However, we find that simply using a combination of in-domain data and a small amount of general-domain data cannot improve the model's generalization ability very much. As a result, although our approach works very well on small amounts of in-domain data, it cannot handle larger scale data-scarce domain adaptation tasks. In this paper, we first show that simply using a combination of in-domain data and a small amount of general-domain data cannot improve the model's generalization ability very much. As a result, although our approach works very well on small amounts of in-domain data, it cannot handle larger scale data-scarce domain adaptation tasks. Then, we propose to use a framework of semi-supervised deep clustering to address this problem. The idea is that, instead of directly using the general-domain data for model training, we use the general-domain data to learn clusters, and then use the in-domain data to search and select the most relevant clusters to improve model generalization. By carefully designing the loss function to take care of the in-domain-general domain balance, we can use a small amount of in-domain data and a large number of general-domain data to train a very effective model. In the in-domain-general domain balance term, we use a pairwise ranking loss similar to most previous works. In the cluster-based generalization term, we adopt a simple but effective triplet filtering strategy, in which the anchor and positive samples are from the same cluster, while the negative samples are from other clusters. Compared with previous works, our method can work well for much smaller in-domain data (e.g. as small as 100 samples). We also conduct extensive experiments on all 4 language directions with 3 different test domains, and the results show that our method significantly improves the performance over strong baselines. In addition, our method is also quite easy to implement, since we use off-the-shelf word2vec and classification models to train the cluster models.

human_text:
The paper describes an MT training data selection approach that scores and
ranks general-domain sentences using a CNN classifier. Comparison to prior work
using continuous or n-gram based language models is well done, even though  it
is not clear of the paper also compared against bilingual data selection (e.g.
sum of difference of cross-entropies).
The motivation to use a CNN instead of an RNN/LSTM was first unclear to me, but
it is a strength of the paper to argue that certain sections of a text/sentence
are more important than others and this is achieved by a CNN. However, the
paper does not experimentally show whether a BOW or SEQ (or the combination of
both( representation is more important and why.
The textual description of the CNN (one-hot or semi-supervised using
pre-trained embeddings) 
is clear, detailed, and points out the important aspects. However, a picture of
the layers showing how inputs are combined would be worth a thousand words.

The paper is overall well written, but some parentheses for citations are not
necessary (\citet vs. \citep) (e.g line 385).

Experiments and evaluation support the claims of the paper, but I am a little
bit concerned about the method of determining the number of selected in-domain
sentences (line 443) based on a separate validation set:
- What validation data is used here? It is also not clear on what data
hyperparameters of the CNN models are chosen. How sensitive are the models to
this?
- Table 2 should really compare scores of different approaches with the same
number of sentences selected. As Figure 1 shows, the approach of the paper
still seems to outperform the baselines in this case. 

Other comments:
- I would be interested in an experiment that compares the technique of the
paper against baselines when more in-domain data is available, not just the
development set.
- The results or discussion section could feature some example sentences
selected by the different methods to support the claims made in section 5.4.
- In regards to the argument of abstracting away from surface forms in 5.4:
Another baseline to compare against could have been the work of Axelrod, 2015,
who replace some words with POS tags to reduce LM data sparsity to see whether
the word2vec embeddings provide an additional advantage over this.
- Using the sum of source and target classification scores is very similar to
source & target Lewis-Moore LM data selection: sum of difference of
cross-entropies. A reference to this work around line 435 would be reasonable.

Finally, I wonder if you could learn weights for the sum of both source &
target classification scores by extending the CNN model to the
bilingual/parallel setting.

The paper describes a method for in-domain data selection for SMT with a
convolutional neural network classifier, applying the same framework as Johnson
and Zhang, 2015. The method performs about 0.5 BLEU points better than language
model based data selection, and, unlike the other methods, is robust even if
only a very small in-domain data set is provided. 

The paper claims improvements of 3.1 BLEU points. However, from the results we
see that improvements of this magnitude are only achieved if there are
in-domain data in the training set - training only on the in-domain data
already produces +2.8 BLEU. It might be interesting to also compare this to a
system which interpolates separate in- and out-domain models. 

The more impressive result, in my opinion, comes from the second experiment,
which demonstrates that the CNN classifier is still effective if there is very
little in-domain data. However, the second experiment is only run on the zh2en
task which includes actual in-domain data in the training set, possibly making
selection easier. Would the result also hold for the other tasks, where there
is no in-domain data in the training set? The results for the en2es and en2zh
task already point in this direction, since the development sets only contain a
few hundred sentence pairs. I think the claim would be better supported if
results were reported for all tasks when only 100 sentence pairs are used for
training.  

When translating social media text one often has to face very different
problems from other domains, the most striking being a high OOV rate due to
non-conventional spelling (for Latin scripts, at least). The texts can also
contain special character sequences such as usernames, hashtags or emoticons.
Was there any special preprocessing or filtering step applied to the data?  
Since data selection cannot address the OOV problem, it would be interesting to
know in more detail what kinds of improvements are made through adaptation via
data selection, maybe by providing examples.   

The following remarks concern specific sections:

Section 3.2:
- It could be made clearer how the different vectors (word embeddings, segment
vectors and one-hot vectors) are combined in the model. An illustration of the
architecture would be very helpful. 
- What was the "designated loss function"?

Section 5.2:
For completeness' sake, it could be mentioned how the system weights were
tuned.

We have checked the equations and made the necessary changes. Abstract Similar to most NLP tasks, topic modeling is also applied to large corpus, e.g. document representation. The traditional topic models, like LDA, use the word-level top keywords to represent a sentence, while there is no correlation between the topic and words. To this end, one potential solution is word representation via word2vec, which maps each word to a vector, and then a document is a aggregated vector of all words. Thus, we can get more semantic information from the word level to the document level. This aggregation procedure is called bag of words (BoW). However, this approach is still limited in representation, because the semantic information in each word is lost. To address this issue, this paper introduces a novel method to combine the advantages of both word2vec and topic models. Specifically, we generate a lexicon from the topic model according to the semantic information, and then propose to use both the words with corresponding IDs (word level) and their corresponding vectors (topic level) to represent a sentence. Experiments on two public datasets show the effectiveness of the proposed method. This paper presents a method to generate a lexicon from the topic model to improve the representation ability of the traditional topic models. It improves the LDA model by using the combination of word2vec and the traditional topic model. The main contributions of this paper are as following: 1.The method uses the combination of word2vec and the traditional topic model to generate a lexicon which makes the topic model to improve the representation ability of the lexicon. 2.The method shows the limitation of the traditional topic model and the advantage of combining with word2vec. 3.The method uses a fine-grained classification algorithm to generate the lexicon, which is simple, effective and efficient. In conclusion, the proposed method can be used to improve the representation ability of traditional topic models and shows the limitation of traditional topic models. We have added the detailed description of the method in the "Method" section. ## Paper Introduction Similar to most NLP tasks, topic modeling is also applied to large corpus, e.g. document representation. The traditional topic models, like LDA, use the word-level top keywords to represent a sentence, while there is no correlation between the topic and words. To this end, one potential solution is word representation via word2vec, which maps each word to a vector, and then a document is a aggregated vector of all words. Thus, we can get more semantic information from the word level to the document level. This aggregation procedure is called bag of words (BoW). However, this approach is still limited in representation, because the semantic information in each word is lost. To address this issue, this paper introduces a novel method to combine the advantages of both word2vec and topic models. Specifically, we generate a lexicon from the topic model according to the semantic information, and then propose to use

The paper addresses the problem of topic modeling for large corpus of documents using LDA. The LDA model has been popular for a long time, but for large documents (millions of words) and large corpus (tens of thousands of documents), the LDA model could take several days to train. The current techniques to address this problem involves parameter sharding and hardware accelerators, both of which have limitations. The authors presents a method to efficiently train LDA model using vector word embedding. It reduces the training from days to minutes. The authors also presents a way to extend the model to a generative model called DTM. The combination of LDA and word embedding technique can be used to improve most of the NLP tasks where large amount of training data is not available. One can use LDA model to get semantic concept of the corpus and then use the word embedding to generate new text similar to the corpus. The embedding based LDA model could be used for Machine Translation, text summary, etc The paper has few limitations. First, the authors uses sub-word unit (like GoogleDictionary emoji) to generate the word embedding. The sub-word unit is still a WIP and the resulting word vector may not be well defined. The second limitation is the embedding generated by this method could not capture semantic similarity. For example, the authors generates the embedding for the sentence "I like mushrooms" and "Mushrooms are good for you". The generated vector is same for these two sentences. However, these two sentences have different semantic meaning and the words "like" and "good" have low weight. The third limitation is also related to the first limitation. The authors use very simple hashing function to generate the vocabulary for the embedding, which results in many duplicate vectors (same for different but valid words). Despite these limitations, the authors makes an interesting observation that with a large corpus of documents, the LDA model can be used to generate the embedding for most of the words in the vocabulary. This opens up new application for these generated embedding and removes the need for these word in the training data. The applications could be text summary, machine translation, etc. I like mushrooms | Mushrooms are good for you The current paper also tries to address the problem of topic modeling using word embedding. LDA is a topic model that work by sampling the probability of a document being about a particular topic. The current popular approaches to improve this sampling based method uses sampling correction. The main assumption is that the most likely next word of a sequence of word is related to the previous word. The current approach use collapsing threshold to reduce the number of multiplication, but the effect is not very effective. The current paper also use word embedding but in a different approach. Instead of using the embedding to reduce the sampling errors, it use the embedding to represent the co-occurrence relationship in the corpus. For example, the authors show that the sentence “Mushrooms are good for you” and “I like mushrooms” gets two different embedding, but they are similar. The current paper has few interesting observation. First, the authors found that the number of parameters in the model double when using embedding instead of word embedding. The model also take longer to train. However, with large corpus of documents, the performance gain due to embedding is very significant. Second, the authors find that the word embedding model is not fully Bayesian, but it can be used as a approximation of Bayesian model. The good news is the authors have developed the new training algorithm that efficiently train the model using Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method. Overall, the current paper has interesting idea to blend LDA and embedding model to reduce sampling errors and increase the model capacity. The idea has some limitations but the good news is the algorithm to solve the problem is very effective. The current paper has good foundation to build a new generation of topic model for large corpus and also many NLP application that requires large corpus but not have enough training data.

Overall this is an interesting approach to combining distributed word representations with topic modeling to get a document representation, although I have a few comments and concerns. First, the neural network architecture is not fully fleshed out - e.g., how are the word vectors initialized? What type of distributed word representation is this? And how is the dimensionality reduction performed on the resulting vector? In addition, this is a very new area, and I wonder if there are some basic hyperparameters that could be explored to see how they affect the results. For example, could this method be used to find a sparse set of topics in a given text? I did a search but couldn't find a previous publication that compared against LDA, so I'm not sure how it could be applied to a given text to reduce the number of topics. I also wonder if this method could also be applied to large bodies of text with little or no human labeling to automatically derive new dictionaries of vectorized words. I think these are reasonable questions, but I think this method is interesting and worth exploring in more detail. Overall this is an interesting approach to mixing word embeddings and topic modeling to get a document representation. First, I would like to point out that this is an "unsupervised" method - I'm not sure if this is really unsupervised, since one of the steps in the training is classification of the topics, but I would be more confident in this if the author specified that this is unsupervised. Second, I think the paper does a good job of laying out the problem and motivation for the paper, but I was a bit confused by the model and network architecture. More details, such as how the word vectors are initialized and what type of distributed word representation this is, would help me evaluate the paper. In addition, in the densify piple and below, they mention that topics can be interpreted as "semantic themes," but they don't explain how this is done. Similarly, in the filtering piple they mention evaluating the topics for scientific use cases, but the details are again lacking. As a result, I'm not sure if this method is fully fleshed out, or if I'm missing some steps. Sorry about that, yes this is unsupervised. We chose to call it semi-supervised, since we are using class-specific embeddings for classification, but no labels during training. I think this method could also be used to derive new dictionaries of vectorized words, for example to automatically derive new words for a given word list. I think this would be an important area for future work. I would also be interested in applications that generate new dictionaries, especially if a method for selecting the most useful topics could be provided. This would allow this method to be applied to large bodies of text with little or no human labeling to automatically derive new dictionaries of vectorized words. I'm not sure how that would work, or if this method is the right tool for that task. In our method, there is no mechanism for selecting the most useful topics. This is an interesting open area for research, and we're not aware of any good solutions in that space, but we haven't explored that idea in this paper.

paper addresses the problem of how to efficiently compute document embeddings by first learning word embeddings and then factoring them into a product. Instead of directly optimizing the learned document vectors against a joint loss function, lda2vec first learns word vectors and then factorizes the product of these and learned vectors into a sum of a non-negative variables, each of which corresponds to a unique document. The non-negative variables are then learned by solving a convex optimization problem. The use of a simplex constraint to perform quantization keeps the variables sparse, allowing for efficient updates during training. We demonstrate that the resulting document embeddings encode useful semantic and syntactic regularities that are hard-to-capture by other document representations. We also show that l2vec is effective at capturing linear relationships between word vectors, which were not part of the original goal of the paper's authors. The lda2vec model can be trained in a supervised or unsupervised manner, the former of which we demonstrate is faster and requires less data. The learned document representations are also relevant for supervised tasks, as shown by experiments on document classification and similarity. Our paper is the first to show that it is possible to perform continuous variable optimization over a product of two numeric arrays, and that this approach can be more efficient than learning each variable individually. We also provide the first algorithm for computing sparse non-negative approximations to numeric arrays, which is of independent interest. In summary, the main contributions of our work are as follows: - We present a general framework for learning both word vectors and document representations by first factoring them into a product, which captures how tokens interact with one another as well as the document. - We introduce a novel non-obvious method for performing continuous optimization over a product of two numeric arrays, and introduce an algorithm for performing sparse non-negative approximations to numeric arrays. - Our method outperforms other published methods on several document representation tasks, including classification and similarity.

This paper proposes a neural-styled topic model, extending the objective of
word2vec to also learn document embeddings, which it then constrains through
sparsification, hence mimicking the output of a topic model.

I really liked the model that the authors proposed, and found the examples
presented by the authors to be highly promising. What was really missing from
the paper, however, was any empirical evaluation of the model -- evaluation
entirely falls back on tables of examples, without any indication of how
representative the examples are, or any attempt to directly compare with
standard or neural topic models. Without empirical evaluation, it is
impossible to get a sense of the true worth of the model, making it very hard
to accept the paper. Some ideas of how the authors could have achieved this:
(1) use the topic representation of each document in a supervised document
categorisation setup to compare against a topic model with the same topic
cardinality (i.e. as an indirect evaluation of the quality of the
representation); or (2) through direct evaluation over a dataset with document
similarity annotations (based on pairwise comparison over topic vectors).

It's fantastic that you are releasing code, but you have compromised anonymity
in publishing the github link in the submitted version of the paper (strictly
speaking, this is sufficient for the paper to be rejected outright, but I
leave that up to the PCs)

Other issues:

- how did you select the examples in Figures 3-6? presenting a subset of the
  actual topics etc. potentially reeks of cherry picking.

- in Section 2.2.1 you discuss the possibility of calculating word

  pre-trained embeddings (which include only small numbers of multiword

  in the paper you appear to train the model over the entire document
  collection so it perhaps isn't an immediate problem, but there will be
  contexts where you want to apply the trained model to novel documents, in
  which case the updating of the word2vec token embeddings is going to mean

  embeddings are not going to be directly comparable to the tuned embeddings.

machine_text: In this paper, the authors describe a method to detect non-compositional phrases by finding n-grams that appear in both a training set of texts with known non-compositional phrases removed and a second set of texts hypothesized to contain non-compositional phrases. The proposed approach was tested on the same manually annotated data that was used to train the CharFix Maximum Entropy model and found to improve the F1 score of the model from 86.6% to 89.0%. This method has some clear advantages over the prior state of the art of hand tagging large data sets with human reviewers. The proposed method is highly scalable, needing only a single pass through the training data. It also requires no global markov chain model, which is difficult to build and maintain, and is often a limiting factor in the scale at which text analysis can be done. The weaknesses of the proposed approach are also clearly stated. The set of n-grams used to identify non-compositional phrases was extracted from English text in the Persian language and may not be suitable for other text. This raises the question of whether there are similarly poor performing n-grams for other language pairs or even for English. The exact method of identifying n-grams that appear in both the training and test data but not in the null model is also not described. Finally, there is a danger of over-fitting the training data. A leave one out cross-validation on the manually annotated training set shows that the performance of the model on this data is 79% for the precision metric, which means that 19% of the text is labeled as non-compositional when in fact it is not. Despite these concerns, this is a well-written paper that describes an approach to improve the state of the art in the automatic detection of non-compositional phrases.

I am not sure if this paper is the greatest leap forward in the field of Computer Science since print was invented, but it is an interesting application of new technologies to an old problem and certainly worthy of attention. The problem the paper addresses is the classification of non-compositional phrases, i.e. phrases that do not fit into a simple classification scheme of verbs, nouns, and adjectives. Examples of phrases that are non-compositional include sentences, such as "We are all ears", or "He argued that...". In these cases, there is no inherent relationship between the noun (ears) or adjective (that...) and the verb (We are all, He argued). This lack of relationship can render such phrases as unsuspicious, but are in fact very indicative of fraud. The paper uses two innovative methods to solve this problem, one being a new algorithm for the Coherence Scoring method which they dub FastText, the other being the application of recent techniques in Natural Language Processing to the problem. With the FastText algorithm, a new model of word representation is created that captures syntactic and semantic relationships of words. This algorithm is compared to more traditional word embeddings like GLOBAL (Global Syntactic Word2Vec) or Glove in terms of their ability to classify non-compositional phrases. The second method uses a type of deep learning model, known as a neural network, to examine the combination of words in a phrase. This method is particularly interesting as it incorporates external knowledge that very few phrases are truly compositional, and that many of these phrases are related. In this way, the model may assign a high score to a phrase such as "He argued that the war was unwinnable" but a low score to a similar but less useful phrase such as "He argued that the Iraq war was unwinnable." The first approach has the weakness of using new and not fully understood technologies, but it appears to have clear advantages over Glove in terms of computational efficiency and success in classifying phrases. The second method has the advantage of using methods from deep learning to analyze phrases but has the challenge of only being able to analyze phrases in their raw form and without easy application to already developed models. It is still an exciting approach that may have far reaching applications in other areas of NLP. In conclusion, this is an interesting paper that explores two innovative methods for the same old problem, while also providing a useful comparison between well-known word embedding methods and an algorithm from a more cutting edge research field. It is an interesting read for anyone interested in Natural Language Processing, NLP, or Natural Language Inference, NLI.

This paper has an interesting topic but it falls short in several ways. The main claim of this paper is that compositionality detection provides a good testbed for compositional methods, but this is not really shown. In fact, this paper does not even describe what is meant by compositionality. Does it mean the semantics of phrases is compositional up to an intermediate representation? If so, then this is a strong claim that should be supported with evidence. If not, then this is very weak claim that should be avoided. The authors of the paper do study both compositional and non-compositional phrases, but in the process give us a number of examples of non-compositional phrases that according to the authors should have been detected as compositional. The authors use very strong composition operations (e.g. addition, multiplication, exponentiation) to demonstrate the weakness of the compositional approach. It is certainly the case that these strong composition operations are not well supported by current compositional methods, but then it seems likely that a simple distributional model might not support these operations either. A more appropriate comparison would be to the current non-compositional approach of applying neural embedding functions to calculate distances, rather than using the well-supported composition operations. The experiments also raise the question of the effects of data. The gold compositionality annotations were for examples taken from the WEBSPORTS section of the P1754 dataset. However, because of the way this data was extracted, it contains only 5 instances of weak compositionality. P1754 also has over 200,000 weakly compositional and non-compositional examples. The results on this large set of data is not particularly encouraging.

machine_text: The paper explores prediction uncertainty in machine translation quality estimation. In this respect, the paper brings awareness to an issue that has largely been ignored in the field so far. The existing practice of relying only on the P(Soft Det.) metric in MT quality estimation can be improved by considering other available evidence, such as P(Oracle). The authors present a quantitative approach to assessing prediction uncertainty and report results of experiments showing that incorporating prediction uncertainty in quality estimation improves the correlation with human ratings. Significance: The work highlights the importance of considering prediction uncertainty when making quality estimation decisions that have consequences for individuals and organizations. Such decision-making will increasingly be part of the mission of ML-based automation systems. We present a quantitative approach to assessing prediction uncertainty and report results of experiments showing that incorporating prediction uncertainty in quality estimation improves the correlation with human ratings. Significance: The work highlights the importance of considering prediction uncertainty when making quality estimation decisions that have consequences for individuals and organizations. Such decision-making will increasingly be part of the mission of ML-based automation systems. Potential Issues: * The results of the experiments reported in the paper depend on the specific way prediction uncertainty is measured. The paper presents a first step towards a quantitative assessment of prediction uncertainty, which will be useful to the research community. * The results presented in the paper are correlational.
