Paper Exploring Prediction Uncertainty in Machine Translation Quality Estimation describes how to calculate predictive uncertainty estimates for MT quality estimation tasks. The authors propose an approach that first identifies the most and least reliable MT systems available for a given language pair, then use machine learning to predict the output of the unreliable MT systems and use them to estimate the uncertainty of the main translation result. Using this new uncertainty measure, the paper shows that MT systems predictions are often overly confident and leaves much room for improvement. edition describes how to calculate predictive uncertainty estimates for MT quality estimation tasks. The authors propose an approach that first identifies the most and least reliable MT systems available for a given language pair, then use machine learning to predict the output of the unreliable MT systems and use them to estimate the uncertainty of the main translation result. Using this new uncertainty measure, the paper shows that MT systems predictions are often overly confident and leaves much room for improvement. One of the paper’s major contribution is to identify the unreliable MT systems. For this, the authors build on two sources of information: (1) the METEOR metrics which are widely used in the MT community to measure the correlation between two similar translations for the same sentence, and (2) the CSLT metric which is designed to capture the divergence of two translations for the same sentence. To estimate the uncertainty of the unreliable MT systems, the authors train a machine learning model to predict the METEOR and CSLT scores for the unreliable MT systems.

In the paper, the authors explore a method for predicting translation quality that is accompanied by a measure of uncertainty. They evaluate the method in terms of the full posterior predictive distribution, and also in an asymmetric risk scenario, which captures typical situations in translation workflows. I think this is an interesting and useful exploration of an under-explored problem in the field, and the paper is well-written with good explanations. My only suggestion would be to clarify the final section, where the authors introduce a new asymmetric risk scenario, as it’s not immediately clear to me what this is or how it relates to the rest of the work. Specifically, the new scenario is introduced to tackle a specific scenario that has “often been a challenge in the quality estimation community”, where one would like to minimize false negatives (high-quality, predicted as low-quality) but also minimize false positives (low-quality, predicted as low-quality). We should note that, although the paper mentions using uncertainty estimates in this asymmetric risk scenario, it does not introduce it as an application of the method they evaluate. I believe this final section could benefit from an introductory sentence to situate the new risk scenario within the overall body of the paper and clarify how it differs from the other scenarios. My suggestion is to first introduce the Bayesian formulation of the problem, explaining that point estimates are derived from the prior, whereas the full posterior is the distribution of interest. The main part of the paper focuses on two scenarios where posterior inference is challenging (related to the earlier comment about evaluation of the posterior). The new risk scenario then proceeds to describe two challenges with using the posterior: (1) calculating appropriate confidence/credible intervals is non-trivial, and (2) the solution is asymmetric — the full posterior provides a more appropriate measure of uncertainty compared to the point estimate based on a sample estimate. The authors make a good case for using the full posterior and introduce the new asymmetric risk scenario. The final section ends with a brief mention that the approach could be used in “asymmetric scenarios such as the one described above”. The final section is well-conceived, as it’s an extension of the idea of using the full posterior predictive distribution to evaluate the approach. I think the introduction could also be slightly tweaked to emphasize how the asymmetric risk scenario focuses on “one of the main shortcoming of using point estimates only” (and how this new risk scenario can alleviate this shortcoming). Overall, the method of using the full posterior predictive distribution and an asymmetric risk scenario could prove very useful in evaluating models for translation quality estimation, and the authors explore an under-explored problem in this field. I believe this approach could prove very useful in understanding model uncertainty in a more accurate and well-calibrated way.

This paper is explores the methodology of predicting translation quality based on machine learning models. The authors build on work by Kloth et al., who introduce neural networks as a method of machine translation quality estimation, however the question they then focus on is which properties of a neural network should be specified to implement quality estimation? Their answer is estimation of prediction uncertainty, which they evaluate in terms of point estimates (mean, median, and 95% credible interval) as well as a full posterior predictive distribution. The conclusion from the evaluation is that using predictive distributions for estimation provides a more faithful representation of uncertainty compared to point estimates, and this improvement can be used to better manage asymmetries in translation risk. There are some notable strengths of this paper. The research question is useful for understanding how to implement a machine translation quality model, and the evaluation is appropriate for this purpose. More generally, probabilistic methods for machine translation quality modeling have not been well-studied, so this is an interesting look at a promising direction. There are also some potential limitations. The evaluation methodology can be problematic. The point estimates are computed from the mean, median, and 95% CI from the posterior, but the evaluation does not describe how this sampling was performed. How does the procedure for estimating posterior predictive distributions compare to other methods for estimating prediction uncertainty? Moreover, the evaluation only evaluates the effectiveness of prediction uncertainty for capturing asymmetrical risk, which is just one use case. In general, this paper is a useful exploration of machine translation quality modeling from a new perspective of prediction uncertainty, but it could be strengthened by addressing the limitations noted above and further exploring the potential of this methodology for machine translation quality modeling more generally.
human_text:
The paper explores the use of probabilistic models (gaussian processes) to
regress on the target variable of post-editing time/rates for quality
estimation of MT output.
The paper is well structured with a clear introduction that highlights the
problem of QE point estimates in real-world applications. I especially liked
the description of the different asymmetric risk scenarios and how they entail
different estimators.
For readers familiar with GPs the paper spends quite some space to reflect
them, but I think it is worth the effort to introduce these concepts to the
reader.
The GP approach and the choices for kernels and using warping are explained
very clearly and are easy to follow. In general the research questions that are
to be answered by this paper are interesting and well phrased.

However, I do have some questions/suggestions about the Results and Discussion
sections for Intrinsic Uncertainty Evaluation:
- Why were post-editing rates chosen over prediction (H)TER? TER is a common
value to predict in QE research and it would have been nice to justify the
choice made in the paper.
- Section 3.2: I don't understand the first paragraph at all: What exactly is
the trend you see for fr-en & en-de that you do not see for en-es? NLL and NLPD
'drastically' decrease with warped GPs for all three datasets.
- The paper indeed states that it does not want to advance state-of-the-art
(given that they use only the standard 17 baseline features), but it would have
been nice to show another point estimate model from existing work in the result
tables, to get a sense of the overall quality of the models.
- Related to this, it is hard to interpret NLL and NLPD values, so one is
always tempted to look at MAE in the tables to get a sense of 'how different
the predictions are'. Since the whole point of the paper is to say that this is
not the right thing to do, it would be great provide some notion of what is a
drastic reduce in NLL/NLPD worth: A qualitative analysis with actual examples.

Section 4 is very nicely written and explains results very intuitively!

Overall, I like the paper since it points out the problematic use of point
estimates in QE. A difficult task in general where additional information such
as confidence arguably are very important. The submission does not advance
state-of-the-art and does not provide a lot of novelty in terms of modeling
(since GPs have been used before), but its research questions and goals are
clearly stated and nicely executed.

Minor problems:
- Section 4: "over and underestimates" -> "over- and underestimates"
- Figure 1 caption: Lines are actually blue and green, not blue and red as
stated in the caption.
- If a certain toolkit was used for GP modeling, it would be great to refer to
this in the final paper.

machine_text: Overall, the paper is well-written and the idea is novel. I have some suggestions for improvement. The authors compare three different word embedding methods on three types of massively multilingual corpora. For the Reddit and Yelp datasets, the authors use the subreddit and city name as the sentences for their dataset. However, I don’t think those subreddit and city names are proper sentences. For the Twitter dataset, the authors use the geolocated tweets as sentences. It is likely that some of the Reddit and Yelp sentences are not well-written English, and some of the geolocated Twitter sentences are not proper sentences. On the Reddit dataset, the authors calculate the correlation between the word embeddings and the self-assessment score of the Reddit users. The correlation between the self-assessment score and the word embeddings of the negative words, however, is much lower than that between the self-assessment score and the word embeddings of the positive words. The reason could be that the negative words are less important for people. For the Twitter dataset, the authors use the Stanford NLP TTS system to synthesize the comments. I think it is better to compare the machine translation quality instead of using the human evaluation to evaluate the quality of the word embeddings. I have some other suggestions that might be useful for the paper. One way to improve the performance of the word embeddings is to use the unsupervised word embedding method such as word2vec or GloVe. The authors can combine the labeled data with the unlabeled data to generate labeled corpus, and use the unsupervised word embedding method to generate word embeddings for the unlabeled data.

The paper "Massively Multilingual Word Embeddings" by Parita and colleagues is an excellent addition to the multilingual NLP community. It presents state-of-the-art methods to create multilingual word embeddings that can represent polysemous words and sentences across multiple languages. The authors explore two approaches: one based on multilingual neural networks and the other on bilingual dictionaries. The paper is clearly written and presents state-of-the-art results in the field. We believe this work will be instrumental in future work with multilingual NLP models. Strengths: The paper covers both neural network based multilingual word embeddings and bilingual dictionary based multilingual word embeddings. This is an increasingly important area of research given the need to build systems that can process texts in multiple languages. The state-of-the-art results are very promising and can be used by the NLP research community. The authors present a very good explanation of the different methods for constructing multilingual word embeddings. Even though the explanation is specific to neural network based methods for constructing multilingual word embeddings, it would be very easy for readers to understand this technique since it is based on a very intuitive concept - sharing parameters. The authors also present the evaluation methodology used for the many language pairs they tested (total of 7 pairs) and how they measure the quality of the multilingual embeddings. The authors explore the different dimensions of the parameter sharing method, which allowed them to obtain results that are very promising for some language pairs and less successful for other pairs. The exploration of the dimensions of parameter sharing was very interesting. For example, the authors show that the choice of the bilingual dictionary and the method for choosing the most similar word have an important impact on the quality of the result. Strengths: The exploration of these aspects to find the best configuration for the parameter sharing method was very interesting. Also, the results on the English-Spanish, English-French, and English-German language pairs were very interesting and could be very promising for the NLP community to build systems that process texts in multiple languages. The comparison of the performance of several NLP models on the German to English and the English to German language pair with the monolingual German model is an interesting perspective for the authors. It would be good to see if the multilingual embeddings would improve the NLP models performance on these language pairs. The authors also provide several visualizations of the multimodal aspect of these embeddings which can be very useful for the NLP community. Weaknesses: One aspect that can be improved is the validation procedure. For the English to Spanish, English to French, and English to German, the authors only evaluated the systems on the development set, which may have impacted the validation results. It would be interesting to evaluate the systems on the development set and also on the test set to be able to confirm the validity of the results. Strengths: The authors provide extensive references to the different works that have been conducted on the construction of multilingual embeddings and also to the NLP tools that can be used with these embeddings. It would be good to see the evolution of this field and to see where we can go in the near future. Overall, this paper represents an excellent addition to the multilingual NLP community. It presents state-of-the-art results on the two approaches to building multilingual word embeddings. It also provides a detailed explanation of both approaches and presents state-of-the-art evaluation methodology. We believe this work will be of great interest to the NLP community. This paper presents methods for estimating and evaluating embeddings of words in more than fifty languages in a shared embedding space. One of its main contributions is the development of multiCluster and multiCCA that make it possible to estimate embedding for words in more than fifty languages using dictionaries and monolingual data. The evaluation method presented in this paper multiQVECCCA is shown to correlate better than previous ones with two downstream tasks (text categorization and parsing). One of the strengths of this paper is the development of a web portal for evaluation that will facilitate further research in this area, along with open-source releases of all our methods. One of the weaknesses of this paper is the lack of comparison with methods that explicitly learn the mapping from one embedding space to another (instead of using word embeddings as starting point and simply performing fine-tuning). Finally, this paper neglects the problem of external resources like dictionaries being translated over time, which would result in the need to re-train the model every few years. Overall, this is a very nice paper that solves an important problem in the field of word embeddings, but its effects on downstream tasks (text categorization, parsing and more) need to be evaluated in subsequent papers. Finally, it would be very interesting to perform a comparison of this paper against previous state of the art on the task of learning word embeddings (word2vec and Glove), considering the set of languages jointly.
human_text:
This paper describes four methods of obtaining multilingual word embeddings and
a modified QVEC metric for evaluating the efficacy of these embeddings. The
embedding methods are: 

(1) multiCluster : Uses a dictionary to map words to multilingual clusters.
Cluster embeddings are then obtained which serve as embeddings for the words
that reside in each cluster. 

(2) multiCCA : Extends the approach presented by Faruqui and Dyer (2014) for
embedding bilingual words, to multilingual words by using English embeddings as
the anchor space. Bilingual dictionaries (other_language -> English) are then
used to obtain projections from other monolingual embeddings for words in other
languages to the anchor space. 

(3) multiSkip : Extends the approach presented by Luong et al. (2015b) for
embedding using source and target context (via alignment), to the multilingual
case by extending the objective function to include components for all
available parallel corpora. 

(4) Translation invariance : Uses a low rank decomposition of the word PMI
matrix with an objective with includes bilingual alignment frequency
components. May only work for  bilingual embeddings. 

The evaluation method uses CCA to maximize the correlation between the word
embeddings and possibly hand crafted linguistic data. Basis vectors are
obtained for the aligned dimensions which produce a score which is invariant to
rotation and linear transformations. The proposed method also extends this to
multilingual evaluations. 

In general, the paper is well written and describes the work clearly. A few
major issues:

(1) What is the new contribution with respect to the translation invariance
embedding approach of Gardner et al.? If it is the extension to multilingual
embeddings, a few lines explaining the novelty would help. 

(2) The use of super-sense annotations across multiple languages is a problem.
The number of features in the intersection of multiple languages may become
really small. How do the authors propose to address this problem (beyond
footnote 9)?

(3) How much does coverage affect the score in table 2? For example, for
dependency parsing, multi cluster and multiCCA have significantly different
coverage numbers with scores that are close. 

(4) In general, the results in table 3 do not tell a consistent story. Mainly,
for most of the intrinsic metrics, the multilingual embedding techniques do not
seem to perform the best.  Given that one of the primary goals of this paper
was to create embeddings that perform well under the word translation metric
(intra-language), it is disappointing that the method that performs best (by
far) is the invariance approach. It is also strange that the multi-cluster
approach, which discards inter-cluster (word and language) semantic information
performs the best with respect to the extrinsic metrics.

Other questions for the authors:

(1) What is the loss in performance by fixing the word embeddings in the
dependency parsing task? What was the gain by simply using these embeddings as
alternatives to the random embeddings in the LSTM stack parser? 

(2) Is table 1 an average over the 17 embeddings described in section 5.1? 

(3) Are there any advantages of using the multi-Skip approach instead of
learning bilingual embeddings and performing multi-CCA to learning projections
across the distinct spaces?

(4) The dictionary extraction approach (from parallel corpora via alignments or
from google translate) may not reflect the challenges of using real lexicons.
Did you explore the use of any real multi-lingual dictionaries?

This paper proposes two dictionary-based methods for estimating multilingual
word embeddings, one motivated in clustering (MultiCluster) and another in
canonical correlation analysis (MultiCCA).
In addition, a supersense similarity measure is proposed that improves on QVEC
by substituting its correlation component with CCA, and by taking into account
multilingual evaluation.
 The evaluation is performed on a wide range of tasks using the web portal
developed by the authors; it is shown that in some cases the proposed
representation methods outperform two other baselines.

I think the paper is very well written, and represents a substantial amount of
work done. The presented representation-learning and evaluation methods are
certainly timely. I also applaud the authors for the meticulous documentation.

My general feel about this paper, however, is that it goes (perhaps) in too
much breadth at the expense of some depth. I'd prefer to see a thorougher
discussion of results (e.g. regarding the conflicting outcome for MultiCluster
between 59- and 12-language set-up; regarding the effect of estimation
parameters and decisions in MultiCluster/CCA). So, while I think the paper is
of high practical value to me and the research community (improved QVEC
measure, web portal), I frankly haven't learned that much from reading it, i.e.
in terms of research questions addressed and answered.

Below are some more concrete remarks.

It would make sense to include the correlation results (Table 1) for
monolingual QVEC and QVEC-CCA as well. After all, it is stated in l.326--328
that the proposed QVEC-CCA is an improvement over QVEC.

Minor:
l. 304: "a combination of several cross-lingual word similarity datasets" ->
this sounds as though they are of different nature, whereas they are really of
the same kind, just different languages, right?

p. 3: two equations exceed the column margin

Lines 121 and 147 only mention Coulmance et al and Guo et al when referring to
the MultiSkip baseline, but section 2.3 then only mentions Luong et al. So,
what's the correspondence between these works?

While I think the paper does reasonable justice in citing the related works,
there are more that are relevant and could be included:

Multilingual embeddings and clustering:
Chandar A P, S., Lauly, S., Larochelle, H., Khapra, M. M., Ravindran, B.,

bilingual word representations. In NIPS.

similarity with neural machine translation. arXiv preprint arXiv:1412.6448.
Lu, A., Wang, W., Bansal, M., Gimpel, K., & Livescu, K. (2015). Deep
multilingual correlation for improved word embeddings. In NAACL.
Faruqui, M., & Dyer, C. (2013). An Information Theoretic Approach to Bilingual
Word Clustering. In ACL.

Multilingual training of embeddings for the sake of better source-language
embeddings:
Suster, S., Titov, I., and van Noord, G. (2016). Bilingual learning of
multi-sense embeddings with discrete autoencoders. In NAACL-HLT.
Guo, J., Che, W., Wang, H., and Liu, T. (2014). Learning sense-specific word
embeddings by exploiting bilingual resources. In COLING.

More broadly, translational context has been explored e.g. in
Diab, M., & Resnik, P. (2002). An unsupervised method for word sense tagging
using parallel corpora. In ACL.

machine_text: The paper is interesting and presents an interesting perspective on POS tagging. I have a few comments and suggestions on how to further strengthen the paper. 1) The part of speech tags provided by Merriam-Webster are very coarse and they lack information for many tokens. For example, they mark each word as noun or noun phrase, but there are many noun phrases that are not composed of just nouns. For example, the paper describes the tag np-> 'the heart' and n-> 'of Boston'. In my opinion, this kind of part of speech information should be included in the Merriam-Webster POS tags, so that the tags can be more specific. 2) On page 6, the paper claims that the model achieved an accuracy of 96% on the development set. I am not sure how the accuracy is calculated. It should be noted that the model is not perfect and it might be overfitting to the training data. Therefore, the 96% accuracy might not be realistic. Overall, this is a nice try of redefining POS classes with semantic models. Personally, I would like to see more examples of the predicted POS tags in the paper. I also want to understand better how the POS tagging is calculated in the model. But this is only a minor issue. I strongly believe this approach could be useful for POS tagging, and this paper makes an important first step in this direction. I recommend this paper for the ACL 2018 conference.

The author attempts to define part-of-speech (POS) classes through distributional semantic models. The approach is novel and could be a very effective one, because existing part-of-speech dictionaries often contain many outdated or incorrect entries. By using large quantity of data, pre-trained distributed representations can capture rich semantic information and define new POS classes. The author defines 9 new POS classes, including adverbial, article,articles, auxiliary, compound,determiner, infinitive, noun, and pronoun. He shows that these new classes improve state-of-the-art performance on Part of Speech (PoS) tagging task on both CoNLL 2013 and 2014 datasets. The approach has some limitations. First, the performance on many coarse-grained POS classes is still inadequate, for example, the performance on adverb is only 44.1% compared with gold standard. Second, the author simply treats each POS class as a single tag, while in fact many of these classes are actually polysemous. For example, articles can be used with a head noun to create a new noun phrase, or be used as a complement of a preposition. By simply defining them as a single tag, the authors fail to capture this important information. dernification and limitations The author attempts to define part-of-speech (POS) classes through distributional semantic models. The approach is novel and could be a very effective one, because existing part-of-speech dictionaries often contain many outdated or incorrect entries. By using large quantity of data, pre-trained distributed representations can capture rich semantic information and define new POS classes. The author defines 9 new POS classes, including adverbial, article, articles, auxiliary, compound, determinizer, infinitive, noun, and pronoun. He shows that these new classes improve state-of-the-art performance on Part of Speech (PoS) tagging task on both CoNLL 2013 and 2014 datasets. The approach has some limitations. First, the performance on many coarse-grained POS classes is still inadequate, for example, the performance on adverb is only 44.1% compared with gold standard. Second, the author simply treats each POS class as a single tag, while in fact many of these classes are actually polysemous. For example, articles can be used with a head noun to create a new noun phrase, or be used as a complement of a preposition. By simply defining them as a single tag, the authors fail to capture this important information.

This paper is interesting and worth publishing in the proceedings of Linguistic Models conference series. The motivation of this paper is very practical, which is to use word embedding trained on the British National Corpus to predict PoS. This is a natural consequence of the observation that PoS is a strong indicator of meaning and the contexts of words are often related to PoS. The starting point of the paper is a good idea, but it runs into difficulty when experimental results don’t show expected result. There are several potential problems that may lead to the negative results. First, the way that the paper constructs word vectors may not be able to capture enough information. Distributional semantic model is the basic assumption that a word’s meaning is determined by the sum of its context words. The assumption is based on the fact that word vectors are similar to the originals of word that they are belonging to, however it does not explain why two words with the same vector are similar. This motivates a deep learning model that uses multiple layers to generate high-quality word vectors. Another weakness of the assumption is it cannot capture some word relations that are not based on co-occurrence of words in sentences, for example, related words in the same sentence. Last but not the least, the golden rule for building POS tagger is to keep the annotation consistency. In real-world use, different annotators may assign different PoS to the same word. Training a strong tagger with too few samples may be easily affected by such a weak annotated data.

This paper addresses the problem of unsupervised part of speech (PoS) recognition with the help of word embeddings trained on the British National Corpus (BNC). The main contribution of this work is a discovery of hidden inconsistencies of the annotation process or guidelines and of `soft' or `graded' part of speech affiliations. The results show that the information about PoS affiliation contained in the distributional vectors allows us to discover groups of words with distributional patterns that differ from other words of the same part of speech. At the same time, it supports the notion of `soft' or `graded' part of speech affiliations. Finally, we show that information about PoS is distributed among dozens of vector components, not limited to only one or two features. We also test the hypotheses that particular PoS tags or combinations of them were assigned to similar sets of words due to certain communication or annotation purposes. For example, the `c' tag was over-represented on adverbs and particle verbs; the `n' and `u' tags were over-represented on proper nouns and personal names, respectively. We also tested whether the numbers of such pairs are higher than the expected numbers and our results showed that they are. This implies that the `c', `n', and `u' tags were in fact grouped in the proposed labels for such groups of words. The same was found for parts of speech pairs that have opposite polarities (e.g. `n' vs `u' and `a' vs `o') and for the pairs containing marginal amounts of words (e.g. `er' vs `est' and `ize' vs `asize'). Based on these findings, we suggest a revised classification of several PoS tags. We also suggest an extension of some of the existing pairs of PoS tags to allow them to have non-binary classifications (i.e. to allow for graded part of speech affiliations). The rest of the paper is organized as follows. We first describe related work in (soft) unsupervised PoS tagging. We then introduce the methodology, which consists of two parts: training the part of speech classifier with the BBC Parliament corpus and a new OOV detection method. In our experiments, we chose Universal PoS as our reference classification. We show the effectiveness of the new method by comparing the results with the ones obtained from the Universal PoS in two scenario: fulltext and token-level and mention-level annotations. We then explore the results of the OPRA 2017 Part-of-speech Tagging Shared Task which was based on Universal PoS and provide evidence that some of the PoS tags in our revised classification were discovered by the participants of this challenge.
human_text:
The aim of this paper is to show that distributional information stored in word
vector models contain information about POS labels. They use a version of the
BNC annotated with UD POS and in which words have been replaced by lemmas. They
train word embeddings on this corpus, then use the resulting vectors to train a
logistic classifier to predict the word POS. Evaluations are performed on the
same corpus (using cross-validation) as well as on other corpora. Results are
clearly presented and discussed and analyzed at length.

The paper is clear and well-written. The main issue with this paper is that it
does not contain anything new in terms of NLP or ML. It describe a set of
straightforward experiments without any new NLP or ML ideas or methods. Results
are interesting indeed, in so far that they provide an empirical grounding to
the notion of POS. In that regard, it is certainly worth being published in a
(quantitative/emprirical) linguistic venue.

On another note, the literature on POS tagging and POS induction using word
embeddings should be cited more extensively (cf. for instance Lin, Ammar, Duer
and Levin 2015; Ling et al. 2015 [EMNLP]; Plank, SÃ¸gaard and Goldberg
2016...).

## General comments:
This paper presents an exploration of the connection between part-of-speech
tags and word embeddings. Specifically the authors use word embeddings to draw
some interesting (if not somewhat straightforward) conclusions about the
consistency of PoS tags and the clear connection of word vector representations
to PoS. The detailed error analysis (outliers of classification) is definitely
a strong point of this paper.

However, the paper seems to have missing one critical main point: the reason
that corpora such as the BNC were PoS tagged in the first place. Unlike a
purely linguistic exploration of morphosyntactic categories (which are
underlined by a semantic prototype theory - e.g. see Croft, 1991), these
corpora were created and tagged to facilitate further NLP tasks, mostly
parsing. The whole discussion could then be reframed as whether the
distinctions made by the distributional vectors are more beneficial to parsing
as compared to the original tags (or UPOS for that matter). 

Also, this paper is missing a lot of related work in the context of
distributional PoS induction. I recommend starting with the review
Christodoulopoulos et al. 2010 and adding some more recent non-DNN work
including Blunsom and Cohn (2011), Yatbaz et al. (2012), etc. In light of this
body of work, the results of section 5 are barely novel (there are systems with
more restrictions in terms of their external knowledge that achieve comparable
results).

## Specific issues
In the abstract one of the contributed results is that "distributional vectors
do contain information about PoS affiliation". Unless I'm misunderstanding the
sentence, this is hardly a new result, especially for English: every
distributionally-based PoS induction system in the past 15 years that presents
"many-to-one" or "cluster purity" numbers shows the same result.

The assertion in lines 79-80 ("relations between... vectors... are mostly
semantic") is not correct: the <MIKOLOV or COLOBERT> paper (and subsequent
work) shows that there is a lot of syntactic information in these vectors. Also
see previous comment about cluster purity scores. In fact you revert that
statement in the beginning of section 2 (lines 107-108).

Why move to UPOS? Surely the fine-grained distinctions of the original tagset
are more interesting.

I do not understand footnote 3. Were these failed attempts performed by you or
other works? Under what criteria did they fail? What about Brown cluster
vectors? They almost perfectly align with UPOS tags.

Is the observation that "proper nouns are not much similar to common nouns"
(lines 331-332) that interesting? Doesn't the existence of "the" (the most
frequent function word) almost singlehandedly explain this difference?

While I understand the practical reasons for analysing the most frequent
word/tag pairs, it would be interesting to see what happens in the tail, both
in terms of the vectors and also for the types of errors the classifier makes.
You could then try to imagine alternatives to pure distributional (and
morphological - since you're lemmatizing) features that would allow better
generalizations of the PoS tags to these low-frequency words.

## Minor issues
Change the sentential references to \newcite{}: e.g. "Mikolov et al. (2013b)
showed"

machine_text: The paper presents a method to discover correspondences between languages which can be used to perform cross-language mapping between sentences encoded in different languages in a computer-understandable format. Using such correspondences, the method can perform sentence mapping between languages which lack a dictionary, and can also perform semantic mapping between sentences with different meanings but related contexts. The method is validated using cross-language sentence analogy data, and shows state-of-the-art performance for this task. The method can be used online and without linguistic expertise. The code and data to perform the cross-language mapping for any pairs of languages can be accessed at <link to website>. Comedy: The method can perform sentence mapping between languages which lack a dictionary. For example, it can map between English and Finnish, which lack a mapping for the sentence "Give a mouse a exactly similar mouse", by discovering a correspondence between the word "mouse" in English and German as they both refer to a similar-looking small rodent, and mapping "Give a mouse a exactly similar mouse" in English to "Geben Sie einen Maschinen eine genauere Behausung" in German. The method can also perform semantic mapping between sentences with different meanings but related contexts, for example mapping "The dog is on the table" in English to "Die Hunde ist auf der Tabelle" in German, despite the different meanings of dog and table in the two languages. -- The method can perform sentence mapping between languages which lack a dictionary, and can also perform semantic mapping between sentences with different meanings but related contexts.

The paper by Batzofin et al. ("Discovering Correspondences between Multiple Languages") addresses the problem of mapping strings between multiple languages, and their corresponding concepts in a knowledge base. The authors use a variant of the maximum entropy framework that has previously been used for word sense disambiguation. They also design a deep neural network that is able to both encode the input semantic parses and project them into a low-dimensional space suitable for searching. They apply the framework to map verbs between English and Spanish, and demonstrate that their method can perform better than the state of the art on a held-out validation set. This paper has several strengths. The authors' extension of the maximum entropy framework has not previously been applied to this problem, and their technique offers excellent empirical results. They also perform a complete evaluation of the impact of different parameters on the final performance. In particular, the performance improvement over the current state of the art shows that this approach can be a competitive technique for mapping verbs between languages. However, this paper also has several weaknesses. The authors only perform the mapping between English and Spanish, and do not demonstrate that the approach is robust to mapping between more closely related languages. The data needed for this problem is not available, so the authors instead perform some automated parts of the mapping, which limits the effectiveness of the approach. The mapping from English to Spanish is also compared to the current state of the art, but the performance of mapping from Spanish to English is not tested. The evaluation also does not cover cases where the source and target words are synonymous or where the mapping does not make sense. Word2Vec and many other similar models are presented as a mapping from words to concepts, but the target space is not explicitly defined. The authors perform no evaluation of the quality of the generated mappings, and there is no indication of how the generated correspondences would be used or how the model would be improved in any way.

Hi friends! Please write a review for this paper of Discovering Correspondences between Multiple Languages by MDL, its main content is as below: How can we automatically discover the most important correspondences between words from two or more languages? How can we do so allowing for correspondences between any subset of languages, without drowning in redundant results, and at the same time maintaining control over the level of detail? These are exactly the questions we answer in this paper. I think this is an interesting paper with challenging problems, and the approach taken here is quite elegant. The main idea is to use the Minimum Description Length principle to automatically discover the most important correspondences between words from two or more languages. This approach allows us to not only discover non-trivial correspondences but also control the level of detail. I have a few questions about the paper. 1. How is the correspondence learning problem defined? In this paper, the correspondence is defined as the mapping from one word to the corresponding word in the other language. So for example, the correspondence from word “apple” in English to its corresponding word in Chinese is “Apple”. Is this correspondence one-to-one? Can there be more than one correspondence between any two words? 2. What types of correspondences are considered? The correspondence between words is generally one-to-one, and for example there is one correspondence between the English word “apple” and its Chinese translation “Apple”. But what if two words in different languages have the same pronunciation? In this case, the correspondence from “apple” to “Apple” is not one-to-one but many-to-one. 3. How does the correspondence learning algorithm work? The correspondence learning algorithm first builds a co-occurrence matrix for all the possible word pairs in the two given languages. Then it finds the correspondence with the largest Jensen Shannon Divergence between the co-occurrence matrix and a Bernoulli distribution. In the paper, the Jensen Shannon Divergence is defined as follows: where P is the probability distribution of the co-occurring words in the language pairs. The Jensen Shannon D is said to correspond to the probability of each co-occurring word and is a maximum value between 0 and 1. It reflects how well the co-occurring word distribution follows a Bernoulli distribution. So the correspondence learning algorithm learns the most important correspondences between the co-occurring words in the two languages. It is worth noting that this approach also allows for correspondence learning between any subset of languages, without drowning in redundant results, and at the same time maintaining control over the level of detail. Overall, this is an interesting and creative work on correspondence learning between languages. There are some improvements that can be made, but the approach is quite promising. I hope this work can be published in the outstanding venue. Regards!

How can we automatically discover the most important correspondences between words from two or more languages? How can we do so allowing for correspondences between any subset of languages, without drowning in redundant results, and at the same time maintaining control over the level of detail? These are exactly the questions we answer in this paper. We approach the problem with the Minimum Description Length principle, and give an efficient algorithm for discovering statistically important correspondences. We test the efficacy of our method against a set of Slavic languages. The experiments show our method automatically discovers non-trivial associations, allowing for both quantitative and qualitative analysis of multiple languages. The main contribution of the paper is the answer to the above questions. In particular, we give an efficient algorithm for discovering statistically important correspondences. We also test the efficacy of our method against a set of Slavic languages. The experiments show our method automatically discovers non-trivial associations, allowing for both quantitative and qualitative analysis of multiple languages. I also want to point out that the question of how to statistically measure the importance of correspondences is also interesting, and a lot of existing work in the NLP community still revolves around finding ways to determine which correspondences are statistically significant. The approach taken in this paper is very different from existing work. One interesting future direction is to extend the algorithm to allow for weighted correspondences. This is particularly interesting when paired with techniques from graphical model based automatic discovery of dependencies between multiple variables. Finally, I want to mention that while this is a theoretical computer science paper, with lots of jargon, it is not difficult to read and it is still very applicable to NLP problems. For example, one interesting use of the method in this paper is for mapping unknown languages to close existing language families, through discovery of statistically significant correspondences between the unknown language and the languages of a known family.
human_text:
This paper proposes a method for discovering correspondences between languages
based on MDL. The author model correspondences between words sharing the same
meaning in a number of Slavic languages. They develop codes for rules that
match substrings in two or more languages and formulate an MDL objective that
balances the description of the model and the data given the model. 
The model is trained with EM and tested on a set of 13 Slavic languages. The
results are shown by several distance measures, a phylogenetic tree, and
example of found correspondences. 

The motivation and formulation of the approach makes sense. MDL seems like a
reasonable tool to attack the problem and the motivation for employing EM is
presented nicely. I must admit, though, that some of the derivations were not
entirely clear to me.
The authors point out the resemblance of the MDL objective to Bayesian
inference, and one thinks of the application of Bayesian inference in
(biological) phylogenetic inference, e.g. using the MrBayes tool. An empirical
comparison here could be insightful.  

Related work: 
- Lacking comparison to methods for borrowing and cognate detection or other
computational methods for historical linguistics. For example, the studies by
Alexandre Bouchard-Cote, Tandy Warnow, Luay Nakhleh and Andrew Kitchen. Some
may not have available tools to apply in the given dataset, but one can mention
List and Moran (2013). There are also relevant tools for biological phylogeny
inference that can be applied (paup, MrBayes, etc.). 

Approach and methodology
- Alignment procedure: the memory/runtime bottleneck appears to be a major
drawback, allowing the comparison of only 5 languages at most. As long as
multiple languages are involved, and phylogenetic trees, it would be
interesting to see more languages. I'm curious what ideas the authors have for
dealing with this issue. 
- Phylogenetic tree: using neighbor joining for creating phylogenetic trees is
known to have disadvantages (like having to specify the root manually). How
about more sophisticated methods?  
- Do you run EM until convergence or have some other stopping criterion? 

Data
- Two datasets are mixed, one of cognates and one not necessarily (the Swadesh
lists). Have you considered how this might impact the results? 
- The data is in orthographic form, which might hide many correspondences. This
is especially apparent in languages with different scripts. Therefore the
learned rules might indicate change of script more than real linguistic
correspondences. This seems like a shortcoming that could be avoided by working
on the level of phonetic transcriptions.

Unclear points
- What is the "optimal unigram for symbol usages in all rules"? (line 286)
- The merging done in the maximization step was not entirely clear to me. 

Minor issue
- "focus in on" -> "focus on" (line 440)

Refs
Johann-Mattis List, Steven Moran. 2013. An Open Source Toolkit for Quantitative
Historical Linguistics. Proceedings of the 51st Annual Meeting of the
Association for Computational Linguistics: System Demonstrations, pages
13â18, Sofia, Bulgaria. Association for Computational Linguistics.
http://www.aclweb.org/anthology/P13-4003.  
Andrew Kitchen, Christopher Ehret, Shiferaw Assefa and Connie J. Mulligan.
2009. Bayesian phylogenetic analysis of Semitic languages identifies an Early
Bronze Age origin of Semitic in the Near East

machine_text: Overall, this is a very good paper for the special issue. The problem of Named Entity Recognition (NER) is still an open problem in computational linguistics, and this paper provides a very good introduction on this topic. There are some points that could be improved. First, what does "NER across languages" mean? It seems like the authors tried to NER in one language and got itswiki version in another language. But how can one NER help establish the correlation between these two languages? For example, if I am trying to NER "Paul" in English, and there is no entity "Paul" in Chinese, how can I establish the correlation between these two names? Maybe this is the problem of language normalization? But the introduction of this paper doesn't mention normalization. Second, the introduction of the dual-language PEU identifies the pairs of source and target languages in the paper. However, later in the paper, the dual-language PEU is replaced by a monolingual PEU to establish the correlation between source and target languages. I think in this case, the dual-language PEU is still important. The source and target languages may have same POS and constituency, but the syntactic and semantic structures are different. So using the same language model for source and target sides may lead to mistakes. However, despite the above concerns, I still feel that this is an interesting and useful paper for NER in multilingual settings. It would be good if the author can discuss more on how to apply the dual-language PEU in more practical scenarios.

This paper addresses the problem of cross-lingual named entity recognition (NER). Named entities, especially proper names, have been shown to be quite useful in many natural language processing tasks. However, traditional NER systems, which typically rely on machine-readable gazetteers that often miss concepts in certain languages, often fail in cross-lingual NER setting. To tackle this problem, this paper proposes to use a crowdsourced Wikipedia table for contextual word representation, and applies multi-instance learning on the table representation to get region- and tag-specific entity representations. The paper shows that this simple approach achieves significant improvements over strong baseline systems and a bi-directional language model on both English to French and French to English datasets. strangely, the paper does not answer the question of how its method works, and does not describe its baseline or other evaluation metrics. These are important topics for any scientific publication. actors The paper tries to solve the problem of cross-lingual Named Entity Recognition (NER) via Wikification. It describes an algorithm that uses a crowdsourced Wikipedia table to compute region- and tag-specific representations of entities. These region-specific entity representations are then used in a multi-instance learning framework to do cross-lingual NER. displayed outcomes The approach in the paper achieves significant improvements over strong baselines and a bi-directional language model on both English to French and French to English datasets. fallow its method section, the paper first describes what problem or question this paper addresses, then strengths and weaknesses, for the paper Cross-Lingual Named Entity Recognition via Wikification

The paper is interesting, and the authors applied cross-lingual wikification to NER, which is novel and effective. The only concern is that the paper only shows results on 9 languages, but there are many other languages in wikipedia. However, the paper is useful for expanding NER research to lower resource language pairs, especially those that share no parallel data with the target language. Overall, this is a useful and well-written paper. We will give this paper an overall score of 90%. Points for improvement: - The evaluation settings need more details, such as dataset, type of results required and so on. We use the CoNLL09 dataset for Spanish, German and Dutch andthe OntoNotes 5.0 dataset for Turkish, Tagalog, Yoruba, Bengali and Tamil. The types of results required from NER systems in this setting are ELRA labeling for German and Spanish, respectively, and types from the DK ROOT dataset for Dutch and Turkish. We evaluate the method on standard NER metrics: Recall at 20, Mic, F 1 and Riep. For Spanish, German and Dutch, the model achieves a Mic of 80.31%, a F 1 of 81.05% and a Riep of 82.33%. For Turkish, Tagalog, Yoruba, Bengali and Tamil, we report the Mic, F 1 and Riep scores on the target language and on the translated side. For the German and Spanish evaluation, we also report the Mic, F 1 and Riep on the original side. These results are summarized in the following table: |LANGUAGE| Mic| F 1| Riep| SCORE | ES| 81.05| 80.31| 82.33| 81.05/90 = 90% | DE| 81.05| 80.31| 82.33| 81.05/90 = 90% | TR| 71.58| 71.58| 71.58| 71.58/90 = 77% | TL| 71.58| 71.58| 71.58| 71.58/90 = 77% | BG| 86.47| 86.47| 86.47| 86.47/90 = 92% | TH| 86.47| 86.47| 86.47| 86.47/90 = 92% | IN| 75| 75| 75| 75/90 = 83% Overall, we achieve an overall score of 90% for this paper. - Lu Yang, Jun Zhu,Yi Zhang, Hui Zhou, Songfang Cheng, Yan Zhao, Fengmeng Zhang. Cross-Lingual Named Entity Recognition via Wikification. CoRR, abs/1905.10725, arXiv, 2019.

Named Entity Recognition (NER) models for language L are typically trained using annotated data in that language. We study cross-lingual NER, where a model for NER in L is trained on another, source, language (or multiple source languages). We introduce a language independent method for NER, building on cross-lingual wikification, a technique that grounds words and phrases in non-English text into English Wikipedia entries. Thus, mentions in any language can be described using a set of categories and FreeBase types, yielding, as we show, strong language-independent features. With this insight, we propose an NER model that can be applied to all languages in Wikipedia. When trained on English, our model outperforms comparable approaches on the standard CoNLL datasets (Spanish, German, and Dutch) and also performs very well on low-resource languages (e.g., Turkish, Tagalog, Yoruba, Bengali, and Tamil) that have significantly smaller Wikipedia. Moreover, our method allows us to train on multiple source languages, typically improving NER results on the target languages. Finally, we show that our language-independent features can be used also to enhance monolingual NER systems, yielding improved results for all 9 languages. Strength 1. Cross-Lingual NER via wikification yields consistent features and generalizes well to low-resource languages. Weakness 1. NER performance on low-resource languages is not as good as on highresource languages. 2. On some languages, it was difficult to find a good mapping between English Wikipedia entities and the entities in the language in question. 3. NER performance can vary a lot for different instances of the same word or name in the same language. For example, we evaluate on Turkish, but the mapping of Turkish names to Freebase types is not as straightforward as that of, say, German. 4. Another problem is that the NER performance can vary a lot for different instances of the same word or name in the same language. For example, for the name “Erdoğan,” two different pronunciations yield two different NER labels. 5. Turkish names are sometimes similar but have different meanings in Turkish, e.g., “Emre” (nickname ofErdoğan) and “Atilla” (a surname). 6. The NER system is not aware of the existence of languagespecific dictionaries, which would include rule-based dictionaries for Turkish.
human_text:
This paper proposes an approach for multi-lingual named entity recognition
using features from Wikipedia. By relying on a cross-lingual Wikifier, it
identifies English Wikipedia articles for phrases in a target language and uses
features based on the wikipedia entry. Experiments show that this new feature
helps not only in the monolingual case, but also in the more interesting direct
transfer setting, where the English model is tested on a target language.

I liked this paper. It proposes a new feature for named entity recognition and
conducts a fairly thorough set of experiments to show the utility of the
feature. The analysis on low resource and the non-latin languages are
particularly interesting.

But what about named entities that are not on Wikipedia? In addition to the
results in the paper, it would be interesting to see results on how these
entities are affected by the proposed method. 

The proposed method is strongly dependent on the success of the cross-lingual
wikifier. With this additional step in the pipeline, how often do we get errors
in the prediction because of errors in the wikifier?

Given the poor performance of direct transfer on Tamil and Bengali when lexical
features are added, I wonder if it is possible to regularize the various
feature classes differently, so that the model does not become over-reliant on
the lexical features.

This paper is concerned with cross-lingual direct transfer of NER models using
a very recent cross-lingual wikification model. In general, the key idea is not
highly innovative and creative, as it does not really propose any core new
technology. The contribution is mostly incremental, and marries the two
research paths: (1) direct transfer for downstream NLP tasks (such as NER,
parsing, or POS tagging), and (2) very recent developments in the cross-lingual
wikification technology. However, I pretty much liked the paper, as it is built
on a coherent and clear story with enough experiments and empirical evidence to
support its claims, with convincing results. I still have several comments
concerning the presentation of the work.

Related work: a more detailed description in related work on how this paper
relates to work of Kazama and Torisawa (2007) is needed. It is also required to
state a clear difference with other related NER system that in one way or
another relied on the encyclopaedic Wikipedia knowledge. The differences are
indeed given in the text, but they have to be further stressed to facilitate
reading and placing the work in context. 

Although the authors argue why they decided to leave out POS tags as features,
it would still be interesting to report experiments with POS tags features
similar to Tackstrom et al.: the reader might get an overview supported by
empirical evidence regarding the usefulness (or its lack) of such features for
different languages (i.e., for the languages for which universal POS are
available at least). 

Section 3.3 could contribute from a running example, as I am still not exactly
sure how the edited model from Tsai and Roth works now (i.e., the given
description is not entirely clear).

Since the authors mention several times that the approaches from Tackstrom et
al. (2012) and Nothman et al. (2012) are orthogonal to theirs and that they can
be combined with the proposed approach, it would be beneficial if they simply
reported some preliminary results on a selection of languages using the
combination of the models. It will add more flavour to the discussion. Along
the same line, although I do acknowledge that this is also orthogonal approach,
why not comparing with a strong projection baseline, again to put the results
into more even more context, and show the usefulness (or limitations) of
wikification-based approaches.

Why is Dutch the best training language for Spanish, and Spanish the best
language for Yoruba? Only a statistical coincidence or something more
interesting is going on there? A paragraph or two discussing these results in
more depth would be quite interesting.

Although the idea is sound, the results from Table 4 are not that convincing
with only small improvements detected (and not in all scenarios). A statistical
significance test reported for the results from Table 4 could help support the
claims.

Minor comments:

- Sect. 2.1: Projection can also be performed via methods that do not require
parallel data, which makes such models more widely applicable (even for
languages that do not have any parallel resources): e.g., see the work of
Peirsman and Pado (NAACL 2009) or Vulic and Moens (EMNLP 2013) which exploit
bilingual semantic spaces instead of direct alignment links to perform the
transfer.

- Several typos detected in the text, so the paper should gain quite a bit from
a more careful proofreading (e.g., first sentence of Section 3: "as a the base
model"; This sentence is not 'parsable', Page 3: "They avoid the traditional
pipeline of NER then EL by...", "to disambiguate every n-grams" on Page 8)

machine_text: Overall, the author has done a good job of bringing together several strands of work on sentence pair scoring. However, I have some reservations about the need for a universal framework. While there is value in comparison across tasks, such a framework should also be able to capture the richness of different tasks. The author rightly points out that a standard metric like lexical diversity cannot capture the nuances of tasks like SPaG and that a paradigm-specific metric would also fail to capture such nuances. He then argues for a unified framework that can compute a metric for any task using features like functional similarity, semantic similarity, and paraphrase/contraste classes. While these features might form the basis of a generic framework, it remains to be seen how easily such a framework could be integrated with paradigms that have been built on automatic scoring (like SPaG) or on other features like part of speech tagging. Another point to note is that the author has categorized text complexity as syntactic and semantic. However, language understanding involves a wider range of complexities like dialogue act and emotional text. A unified framework should be able to capture these and the author could potentially expand the framework to include features like dialogue act and emotional text in the future. I would be interested to know the author's thoughts on the above points. Some of the key takeaways from the review: Overall, the author has done a good job of bringing together several strands of work on sentence pair scoring. While there is value in comparison across tasks, such a framework should also be able to capture the richness of different tasks. The author points out that a standard metric like lexical diversity cannot capture the nuances of tasks like SPaG and that a paradigm-specific metric would also fail to capture such nuances. I agree that a universal framework could benefit from comparing to a task-specific framework (although that is not universally true -- see section 3). However, there is also a role for a paradigm-specific framework to explain how a particular task can be improved. For example, I've found that the SPat GAder for Comprehension (SPAGGIC) framework is useful to understand the nuances of different text genres. For example, I've found that X Speech tends to generate more factual text (because X Speech simulates doctors discussing medical conditions), whereas Texts from Techno tends to generate more creative writing (because many of the prompts focused on subjective assessments). Text-to-Text generation might also be improved by using SPat GAder for Comprehension-inspired approaches to LSTMSeq generation (see, e.g, this SPat GAder for LSTMSeq model for Hospital Compare scenario generation). Some of the key questions that the universal framework could help answer include: 1. What is the relative merits of different SPaG systems (for example, could new unsupervised methods outperform the supervised learning-based approach shown in the paper?) 2. How do different SPaG systems compare across different tasks? For example, how does Diverse Late Parsing perform compared to classic SPaG? 3. How does the SPaG framework compare to other existing frameworks like template fill? I would be interested to see how the framework can be used to inform other Text Comprehension challenges like CoAuth and Leading AI. The framework could potentially be used to inform other Text Comprehension challenges like CoAuth and Leading AI. For example, the Functional Similarity feature could be used to compute a metric for the similarity of the answers provided by different participants in a round of CoAuth. The paraphrase classes could potentially be used to evaluate whether different answers are near-paraphrases or not. The emotional text could be used to inform computational empathy models, although this might be more of a stretch. I'm not sure if the framework can be easily adapted to other evaluation tasks. machine_text: Overall, this is an interesting and well-written paper. The contributions of this work are meaningful and well-discussed in the paper. The limitations of the current approach and some suggestions for future work are also discussed. My suggestion is to present and evaluate the performance on a wider range of data sets. First, the current approach can only parse subject and object of sentences. It would be also interesting to evaluate the parsing results by comparison to other parsers for predicate, modifier, and other relations. Second, it would be interesting to present parsing results on a wider range of data sets, such as those in the Parsing Fortress competition. The data sets in Parsing Fortress are designed for testing PPDP parsers and have complex syntactic structures. Although the current approach can parse data sets in different formats, there are some limitations in the evaluation metrics. The BLEU score is computed over the results returned by the parser, but it does not consider the ordering and overlapping of predicted sentence fragments. For example, if a sentence contains multiple entities and the predicted fragments are overlapping, the overlapping parts might be regarded as a higher BLEU score. Another example is when two sentence fragments are semantically and syntactically related but their ordering is incorrect. It is difficult for a human to judge the correctness of such ordering. Therefore, it would be more difficult to evaluate the performance of this approach compared with other parsers if other evaluation metrics are not used.

The authors present a novel approach to semantic parsing, transition-based model that covers a broader range of parsing tasks compared to previous models. The authors also add some additional new components to further advance the model such as hybrid transition system and temperature trick. The model achieves new state-of-the-art results on three widely-used semantic parsing tasks. One drawback of the model is that the latency is too slow because of using the Thompson sampling to approximate the difficult silence distribution. This paper presents a transition-based graph parser able to cope with the rich
representations of a semantico-cognitive annotation scheme, instantiated in the
UCCA corpora. The authors start first by exposing what, according to them,
should cover a semantic-based annotation scheme: (i) being graph-based
(possibility for a token/node of having multiple governors) (2) having
non-terminal nodes (representing complex structures â syntactic -: coordinate
phrases, lexical: multiword expression) and (3) allowing discontinuous elements
(eg. Verbs+particules). Interestingly, none of these principles is tied to a
semantic framework, they could also work for syntax or other representation
layers. The authors quickly position their work by first introducing the larger
context of broad-coverage semantic parsing then their annotation scheme of
choice (UCCA).              They then present 3 sets of parsing experiments: (i) one
devoted to phrase-based parsing using the Stanford parser and an UCCA to
constituency conversion, (ii) one devoted to dependency parsing using an UCCA
to dependency conversion and finally (iii) the core of their proposal, a  set
of experiments showing that their transition-based graph parser is suitable for
direct parsing of UCCA graphs.

I found this work interesting but before considering a publication, I have
several concerns with regards to the methodology and the empirical
justifications:

The authors claimed that there are the first to propose a parser for a
semantically-oriented scheme such as theirs. Of course, they are. But with all
due respect to the work behind this scheme, it is made of graphs with a various
level of under-specified structural arguments and semantically oriented label
(Process, state) and nothing in their transition sets treats the specificities
of such a graph. Even the transitions related to the remote edges could have
been handled by the other ones assuming a difference in the label set itself
(like adding an affix for example). If we restrict the problem to graph
parsing, many works post the 2014-2015 semeval shared tasks (Almeda and
Martins, 2014,2015 ; Ribeyre et al, 2014-2015) proposed an extension to
transition-based graph parser or an adaptation of a higher-model one, and
nothing precludes their use on this data set.  Itâs mostly the use of a
specific feature template that anchors this model to this scheme (even though
itâs less influencial than the count features and the unigram one). Anyway,
because the above-mentioned graph-parsers are available [1,2] I donât
understand why they couldnât be used as a baseline or source of comparisons.
Regarding the phrase-based  experiments using uparse, it could have been also
validated by another parser from Fernandez-Gonzales and Martins (2015) which
can produce LCFRS-like parsing as good as Uparse (ref missing when you first
introduced uparse).  

Because this scheme supports a more abstract view of syntaxico-semantic
structures than most of the SDP treebanks, it would have been important to use
the same metrics as in the related shared task. At this point in the field,
many systems, models and data set are competing and I think that the lack of
comparison points with other models and parsers is detrimental to this work as
whole. Yet I found it interesting and because weâre at crossing time in term
of where to go next, I think that this paper should be discussed at a
conference such as ConLL.

Note in random order
-         please introduce the âgrounded semanticâ before page 2, you use
that phrase before
-         why havenât you try to stick to constituent-tree with rich node
labels and propagater traces and then train/parse with the Berkeley parser? It
could have been a good baseline. 
-         The conversion to surface dependency trees is in my mind useless: you
loose too many information, here a  richer conversion such as the one from
âSchluter et al, 2014, Semeval SDP) should have been used.
-         Can you expand on âUCCA graphs may contains implicit unit that have
no correspondent in the textâ  or provide a ref or an example.
-         You mentioned other representations such as MRS and DRT, this raises
the fact that your scheme doesnât seem to allow for a modelling of quantifier
scope information. Itâs thus fully comparable to other more syntax-oriented
scheme. Itâs indeed more abstract than DM for example and probably more
underspecified than the semantic level of the PCEDT but how much? How really
informative is this scheme and how really âparsableâ is it? According to
your scores, it seems âharderâ but an  error analysis would have been

- As I said before, the 3 principles you devised could apply to a lot of

The paper presents the first broad-coverage semantic parsers for UCCA, one
specific approach to graph-based semantic representations. Unlike CoNLL
semantic dependency graphs, UCCA graphs can contain "nonterminal" nodes which
do not represent words in the string. Unlike AMRs, UCCA graphs are "grounded",
which the authors take to mean that the text tokens appear as nodes in the
semantic representation. The authors present a number of parsing methods,
including a transition-based parser that directly constructs UCCA parses, and
evaluate them.

Given that UCCA and UCCA-annotated data exist, it seems reasonable to develop a
semantic parser for UCCA. However, the introduction and background section hit
a wrong note to my ear, in that they seem to argue that UCCA is the _only_
graph-based semantic representation (SR) formalism that makes sense to be
studied. This doesn't work for me, and also seems unnecessary -- a good UCCA
parser could be a nice contribution by itself.

I do not entirely agree with the three criteria for semantic representation
formalisms the authors lay out in the introduction. For instance, it is not
clear to me that "nonterminal nodes" contribute any expressive capacity. Sure,
it can be inconvenient to have to decide which word is the head of a
coordinated structure, but exactly what information is it that could only be
represented with a nonterminal and not e.g. with more informative edge labels?
Also, the question of discontinuity does not even arise in SRs that are not
"grounded". The advantages of "grounded" representations over AMR-style ones
did not become clear to me. I also think that the word "grounded" has been used
for enough different concepts in semantics in the past ten years, and would
encourage the authors to find a different one ("anchored"? "lexicalized"?).
Thus I feel that the entire introductory part of the paper should be phrased
and argued much more carefully.

The parser itself seems fine, although I did not check the details. However, I
did not find the evaluation results very impressive. On the "primary" edges,
even a straightforward MaltParser outperforms the BSP parser presented here,
and the f-scores on the "remote" edges (which a dependency-tree parser like
Malt cannot compute directly) are not very high either. Furthermore, the
conversion of dependency graphs to dependency trees has been studied quite a
bit under the name "tree approximations" in the context of the CoNLL 2014 and
2015 shared tasks on semantic dependency parsing (albeit without "nonterminal"
nodes). Several authors have proposed methods for reconstructing the edges that
were deleted in the graph-to-tree conversion; for instance, Agic et al. (2015),
"Semantic dependency graph parsing using tree approximations" discuss the
issues involved in this reconstruction in detail. By incorporating such
methods, it is likely that the f-score of the MaltParser (and the LSTM-based
MaltParser!) could be improved further, and the strength of the BSP parser
becomes even less clear to me.

I recommend this paper for publication in the conference. ================================================================= TEXT: C. Northcote Parkinson 2020発売40周年 冒険の思cesarek 第5章．「不死鳥の果実 」 ================================================================= [5. The flyers fought hard. The result? ― C. Northcote Parkinson (4.23.2023) The result? They won, the flyers fought hard. ― so I heard, though I wasn’t there.] “They won, the flyers fought hard,” said Parkinson, “is a grammatical, though not a very exciting, sentence. What makes it interesting is that it contains two independent clauses connected by acoordinating conjunction, but not by a semicolon. The first clause has a finite verb ‘they won’ and a noun adjunct ‘the flyers fought hard’. The second clause contains a noun phrase ‘they won’ and an adverbial participle ‘how I heard, though I wasn’t there.’ Unlike many other languages, English doesn’t have any special symbols to connect independent clauses. Most people writing English simply split the second clause into two sentences using a semicolon. But some people dislike semicolons and write in a similar fashion, though not always with the coordination conjunction, e.g. “I heard, though I wasn’t there, they won.” Because the coordination conjunction in this sentence is far away from the two subjects and verbs, many parsers consider it as a hard parse error. But the stack LSTM parses it easily. The authors describe a novel approach to joint syntactic and semantic parsing by using a greedy approach and stacked LSTMs. The authors demonstrate improvements over previous state-of-the-art results on the Wall Street Journal (WSJ) corpus. The main contribution of this paper is the use of a stacked LSTM architecture, which makes the model able to encode long-range dependencies in the input sequence. In addition, they use a greedy approach to find a balance between accuracy and speed during training. Finally, the authors show that their approach is not limited to syntactic parsing and can also be used to perform semantic parsing. 's strengths This paper is innovative because it uses a greedy approach and stacked LSTMs to perform joint syntactic and semantic parsing. In addition, it shows that their approach is not limited to syntactic parsing and can also be used to perform semantic parsing. I also think that it is a strong demonstration of the effectiveness of using a greedy approach in conjunction with the stacked LSTM architecture to achieve state-of-the-art performance. Another strength of this paper is the use of a carefully constructed and richly annotated dataset for learning syntax and semantics together. Finally, the authors conducted an ablation study to show that the key component of their model is the use of a stacked LSTM, without which the model would not perform as well. super weaknesses The proposed dataset is heavily restricted, in that the corpus is written only for evaluating the joint syntactic and semantic parsing task. As a result, the dataset cannot capture some of the nuances of real-world text. For example, the authors note that the model performs worse on the dataset because the model has to learn to parse words (such as "Company" and "Firm") that appear at the beginning of a sentence, but do not denote semantic constituents. In practice, real-world datasets would contain such examples of extraneous words, because the details of documents are often omitted by authors during submission to conferences and journals. The proposed model is based on a joint representation, which consists of a tuple (syntax, semantics, alignment). I would suggest duplicating this annotation for each of the values in the tuple. For example, the syntax and semantics can be annotated separately for each word in the sentence, as done in the Treebank task, and then we could have multiple alignments between the two sequences of parsed trees.

I think this is an interesting paper, however I have some comments. First, I think the proposed model can be improved by using attention mechanism, which can capture more global contextual information in the input sequence. Second, the model is not efficiently computable, as it uses the CRF layer to conditionalize the LSTM layer. I think it is better to remove this CRF layer. Third, the code is not well organized, making it hard to follow. act: I agree that attention mechanism can help the model to better learn the global contextual information and thus better perform the task. And I think the model can be further improved by reducing the loop between the LSTM and the CRF layer, as it would help the model to learn more global information. And I think the code can be more organized by using Keras API. arroll Thanks for your comments.
