human_text:
This paper presents a Stack LSTM parser based on the work of Henderson et al.
(2008, 2013) on joint syntactic/semantic transition-based parsing and Dyer et
al. (2015) on stack LSTM syntactic parsing. The use of the transition system
from the former and the stack LSTM from the latter shows interesting results
compared to the joint systems on the CoNLL 2008 and 2009 shared tasks.

I like this paper a lot because it is well-written, well-explained, the related
work is good and the results are very interesting. The methodology is sound
(with a minor concern regarding the Chinese embeddings, leading me to believe
than very good embeddings can be more informative than a very clever model...).

Moreover, the description of the system is clear, the hyperparameters are
justified and the discussion is interesting.

The only thing I would say is that the proposed system lacks originality in the
sense that the work of Henderson et al. puts the basis of semi-synchronised
joint syntax-semantic transition-based parsing several years ago and Dyer et
al. came up with the stack LSTM last year, so it is not a new method, per say.
But in my opinion, we were waiting for such a parser to be designed and so I'm
glad it was done here.

General comments
================

The paper presents a joint syntactic and semantic transition-based dependency
parser,
inspired from the joint parser of Henderson et al. (2008).
The authors claim two main differences:
- vectorial representations are used for the whole parser's state, instead of
the top elements of the stack / the last parser's configurations
- the algorithm is a plain greedy search

The key idea is to take advantage of stack LSTMs so that the vector
representing the state of the parser
keeps memory of potentially large scoped syntactic features, which
are known to be decisive features for semantic role labeling
(such as the path between the predicate and the candidate role filler head).

The system is tested on the CoNLL 2008 data set (English) and on the
multilingual CoNLL 2009 data set.
The authors compare their system's performance to previously reported
performances,
showing their system does well compared to the 2008 / 2009 systems, 
but less compared to more recent proposals (cf. bottom of table 3).
They emphasized though that the proposed system does not require any hand-craft
features,
and is fast due to the simple greedy algorithm.

The paper is well written and describes a substantial amount of work,
building on the recently popular LSTMs, applied to the Henderson et al.
algorithm
which appears now to have been somewhat visionary.

I have reservations concerning the choice of the simple greedy algorithm:
it renders results not comparable to some of the cited works.
It would not have been too much additional work nor space to provide for
instance beam-searched performance.

More detailed comments / questions
==================================

Section 2:

A comment on the presence of both A1 and C-A1 links would help understanding
better the target task of the paper.

A summary of the differences between the set of transitions used in this work
and that of Henderson et al. should be provided. In its current form, it is
difficult to 
tell what is directly reused from Henderson et al. and what is new / slightly
modified.

Section 3.3

Why do you need representations concatenating the word predicate and its
disambiguated sense,
this seems redundant since the disambiguated sense are specific to a predicate
?

Section 4

The organization if the 4.1 / 4.2 sections is confusing concerning
multilinguality.
Conll 2008 focused on English, and CoNLL 2009 shared task extended it to a few
other languages.

This paper performs an overdue circling-back to the problem of joint semantic
and syntactic dependency parsing, applying the recent insights from neural
network models. Joint models are one of the most promising things about the
success of transition-based neural network parsers.

There are two contributions here. First, the authors present a new transition
system, that seems better than the Hendersen (2008) system it is based on. The
other contribution is to show that the neural network succeeds on this problem,
where linear models had previously struggled. The authors attribute this
success to the ability of the neural network to automatically learn which
features to extract. However, I think there's another advantage to the neural
network here, that might be worth mentioning. In a linear model, you need to
learn a weight for each feature/class pair. This means that if you jointly
learn two problems, you have to learn many more parameters. The neural network
is much more economical in this respect.

I suspect the transition-system would work just as well with a variety of other
neural network models, e.g. the global beam-search model of Andor (2016). There
are many other orthogonal improvements that could be made. I expect extensions
to the authors' method to produce state-of-the-art results.

It would be nice to see an attempt to derive a dynamic
oracle for this transition system, even if it's only in an appendix or in
follow-up work. At first glance, it seems similar to the
arc-eager oracle. The M-S action excludes all semantic arcs between the word at
the start of the buffer and the words on the semantic stack, and the M-D action
excludes all semantic arcs between the word at the top of the stack and the
words in the buffer. The L and R actions seem to each exclude the reverse arc,
and no other.

machine_text: The paper is well-written and logical in its approach. I do, however, have a few concerns. First, this is a distributed lock-in system. Can you provide some assurance that all parties will be using the same space, i.e., not linkable? Second, it only captures a single view of the world. How do you ensure that all views will converge? Third, will this system be susceptible to "winner's curse" and not be able to escape from its local optimum? Mills' peer review comments are in-line with the above comments and some others. For the distributed lock-in system, we apply fully-gossip-based algorithm to ensure all parties in the system are using the same space (and thus are linkable). We also apply consistent hashing to ensure all views would converge. As for the winner's curse, we will also apply normalization trick to reduce the possibility. We will put the implementation details in the paper. We believe these are very reasonable concerns and the system will achieve the goal of building a single unified semantic space for linkable, but random PPMI-enabled data. describe this system as "linkable", but not "linkable linkable". What does this mean? It means that the data is semantically homogeneous, but the connection between the data is not explicit or abstract, which means you can't get from one to the other, and the two groups of data cannot be "linked". For example, the space is "linkable" but not "gender-linkable" because a person's gender can be inferred by the name, but in the generated space, two names with the same "inference" are actually totally different. Another example is the movie rating data. A user may rate a movie with 4 stars and 4 stars are "linkable" to each other, but "linkable" does not mean that rating 1 and rating 2 actually represent the same movie, they can represent totally different movies. In fact, this is a key feature of the generated space, because if two totally different and random data point the same place, they will get aggregated and compress the data in that area, thus making the model stronger.

This paper is about constructing a semantic space of random projections based on the distribution of positive examples only. This is a challenging problem because the number of negative examples is often much larger than that of positive examples, and random projections have been shown to be positive-only. The authors present a novel approach, PPMI-enabled incremental semantically relevant negative sampling (SNS), that leverages user feedback to progressively adapt the random projection and solves the problem with very limited (one-time) human effort. The paper is both theoretical and empirically effective. The key idea is interesting and new. The implementation is straightforward and easy to adopt. The experiments on two real-world data sets show that the proposed method significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art baselines. This paper addresses a hard problem of constructing a semantic space of random projections based on the distribution of positive examples only. This is challenging because the number of negative examples is often much larger than that of positive examples. The proposed PPMI-enabled SNS brings a new approach that makes use of user feedback to progressively adapt the random projection space and solve the problem. The main idea is very interesting and new. The implementation is straightforward and easy to adopt. The empirical evaluation shows that the proposed method outperforms the state-of-the-art baselines. The main idea is interesting and new. The proposed PPMI-enabled SNS brings a new approach that makes use of user feedback to progressively adapt the random projection space and solve the problem. The main idea is very interesting and new. The implementation is straightforward and easy to adopt. The empirical evaluation shows that the proposed method outperforms the state-of-the-art baselines. One key idea in the proposed PPMI-enabled SNS is to use the projection matrix to encode the local structural information of the positive examples. This method is very effective in practice. However, as the authors also point out, the effectiveness of this approach heavily depends on the quality of the projection matrix. For example, if the projection matrix is noisy, the proposed method may still suffer from the negative impact of noise. To address this issue, the authors introduce a new scheme, triangle discrimination, to further improve the effectiveness of the projection. The empirical results show that the proposed method outperforms the state-of-the-art methods significantly.

The paper of Random Positive-Only Projections: PPMI-Enabled Incremental Semantic Space Construction is a novel method to construct semantic spaces which is based on random projections. This method uses random projections which the expected value of 0 (i.e., E(R)=0), thus it is highly scalable and computationally efficient. In contrast to the previous methods that used random projection matrices R with the expected value of 0, the proposed method uses R with E(R)>0. The Kendall's tau_b distance is used to compute vector similarities in the resulting non-Gaussian spaces. Furthermore, this paper also points out that by using the proposed method and PPMI, a highly efficient transfer method for embeddings learned by the proposed method to other spaces that are more discriminative for similarity assessments can be achieved. The proposed method is evaluated on the MEN benchmark and achieves an average score of 0.75. Issues In my opinion, the main contribution of this paper is the introduction of a new method to construct semantic spaces, which is based on random projections. As you can see from the proses above, the method used by this paper is different from other methods in three aspects. First, it uses random projections with the expected value of 0, thus it is highly scalable and computationally efficient. Second, it can be applied to any existing space, which makes it very useful in real applications. Third, it can be transferred to other spaces through PPMI, which makes it more applicable. I have several suggestions to this paper: First, in order to make the paper more appealing to a wider range of potential readers, I recommend making the introduction a bit clearer, particularly the description of the existing methods and how the proposed method differs from them. Second, the paper lacks some empirical results about the construction of the semantic space. As I mentioned before, the proposed method is very useful. By using this method, can we construct a space which is highly scalable and computationally efficient? What's more, can we transfer the embedding model to other spaces through PPMI? Third, it's good that this paper mentions that this method is different from other methods in using random projections with the expected value of 0. But is there any simulation result to prove it can be highly scalable and computationally efficient? I think it is important to provide simulation results to support the paper's claims.

This paper describes a novel method for constructing semantic spaces using only positive random projections, rather than the commonly used Gaussian random projections. The main benefit of the proposed method is that it is highly scalable and computationally efficient, especially when applied to large scale training data. The paper also provides an empirical evaluation of the proposed method, showing that it can achieve competitive results on several benchmark semantic similarity datasets. The weaknesses of the proposed method are that the projection directions are learned offline and the learned projections are static. spect Positive-only projection (PoP) is a novel and useful technique for constructing semantic spaces. The method is highly scalable and computationally efficient, especially for large-scale training data. Empirical evaluations on several benchmark datasets show that PoP can achieve competitive performance compared to the state of the art. The weakness of the current method is that the projection directions are offline determined and the learned projections are static. framework Problem: A scalable and efficient way to train a semantic similarity model on large-scale training data. I am buying some of the motivation: the proposed method is much faster to train
than it is to train a neural network. Also, it keeps some properties of the
distribution when going to lower dimensionality. 

However, I am not convinced why it is so important for vectors to be
transformable with PPMI.

Most importantly, there is no direct comparison to related work.

Detailed comments:

- p.3: The definition of Kendall's tau that the authors use is strange. This is
NOT the original formula; I am not sure what it is and where it comes from.

- p.3: Why not use Spearman correlation as is standard in semantic tasks (and
as teh authors do at evaluation time)?

- The datasets chosen for evaluation are not the standard ones for measuring
semantic relatedness that the NLP community prefers. It is nice to try other
sets, but I would recommend to also include results on the standard ones.

- I can only see two lines on Figure 1. Where is the third line?

- There is no direct comparison to related work, just a statement that 

Some typos:

- large extend -- extent

The paper presents a positive-only projection (PoP) word embedding method. This
is a random projection method with a random projection matrix whose expected
value is positive. The authors argue that this enables the application of PPMI
which is not possible with an expected value of 0 and that being a random
projection method, their computation is efficient.

My main reservation about this paper has to do with its clarity. Particularly:

1. I could not understand the core difference between the method proposed in
the paper and previous random projection methods. Hence, I could not understand
how (and whether) the advantages the authors argue to achieve hold.

2. It was hard to follow the arguments of the paper starting from the
introduction. 

3. Some of the arguments of the paper are not supported: 

- Line 114: Sentence starts with "in addition"

- Line 137: Sentence starts with "Since"

- Line 154: Sentence starts with "thus"

4. While I have worked on vector space modeling (who hasn't ?), I am not an
expert to random projections and have not used them in my research. It was hard
for me to understand the logic behind this research avenue from the paper. I
believe that a paper should be self contained and possible to follow by people
with some experience in the field.

5. The paper has lots of English mistakes (86: "To a large extend", 142: "such
PPMI").

In addition, I cannot see why the paper is evaluating only on MEN. There are a
couple of standard benchmarks (MEN, WordSeim, SimLex and a couple of others) -
if you present a new method, I feel that it is insufficient to evaluate only on
one dataset unless you provide a good justification.

I recommend that the authors will substantially improve the presentation in the
paper and will resubmit to another conference.

The paper App2Check and Tweet2Check: machine learning-based tools for Sentiment Analysis of Apps Reviews and Tweets by Zhaojun Wang, Liang Wang, Weihao Hu, Chengqing Chen, Ruirui Liu, Ming Song, and Guodong Zhou provides a tool that can analyze the sentiment of reviews or tweets about mobile applications. The tool uses deep learning to classify the sentiment using an architecture that combines a word embedding layer, a Bidirectional LSTM layer, and a Softmax layer. The data used to train the tool were obtained from theApp Store (App2Apps) and the Twitter Application Programming Interface (Tweet2Tweets). The tool achieves a macro F1-score of 0.86 for reviews and 0.89 for tweets, indicating that it can be used for commercial applications. However, because the datasets used for training the tool were collected from online sources that have commercial purposes, there may be concerns about privacy. The tool also only addresses the sentiment of reviews and tweets about mobile applications, and does not consider other factors that could influence sentiment, such as objective features, such as the popularity and function of the application. App2Check and Tweet2Check: machine learning-based tools for Sentiment Analysis of Apps Reviews and Tweets is a good paper about Sentiment Analysis. The paper describes a research performed on two benchmarks: apps reviews and tweets. The reviews and tweets have been processed using state-of-the-art NLP techniques in order to extract the sentiment expressed in each text. Two different tools have been developed and compared against the state-of-the-art research tools. The results show that the tools developed are the best approach both for apps reviews and for tweets. The main weakness of the paper is that the methodology is not clear enough. The experiment does not have an external validation. It is not clear how the users were selected and how they were trained on the same benchmark used to test the tools. In addition, the machine learning models have not been tested on the same datasets. The authors explain that the two tools developed have been tested using three different algorithms, but it is not clear how. Also, the list of the tools and their parameters used for the comparison is not provided. It is important to know this information because the comparison with the other tools is usually done using a configuration file that must be shared between the tool provider and the authors. The information about this file is missing. It would be interesting to know how the tools were trained on the datasets and on which parameters they were run. Some details about the processing of apps reviews and tweets are not provided, for example, the stop word list used to filter the text. Despite these weaknesses, the paper represents an important step forward for the development of better tools for Sentiment Analysis. The results shown are very promising. The software and the data used to develop the tools are available so other researchers can repeat the experiments using different approaches. The paper is well written and the information is clear. I believe that this paper can interest also researchers and developers working in the field of Sentiment Analysis. machine_text: This paper presents a compression approach for neural machine translation (NMT) models. The proposed approach enables selective execution of some operations in the decoder only, without hurting translation performance. It first identifies the operations that are harmful to performance, such as pointer alignment and updates, with an observation that these operations are typically executed on common sequences in the test set. Then it introduces a second training phase that only executes the identified harmful operations. The effectiveness of the approach is validated on large scale neural machine translation models, where up to 21.5% model size reduction can be obtained on NMT-64, and 9.2% on NMT-large. In addition, the proposed approach can also be applied to other neural models, such as RNN-based sequence to sequence models, and stochastic counterparts like OpenAI GPT. Dr. Young-Han Kim, Slava Gerusevicius, Bo Wang, Hajar Abdelkader Dr. Kim, Slavi Gerusevicius, and Bo Wang: thank you for taking the time to provide your reviews. We appreciate the comments and look forward to your continued feedback. Dr. Kim: thanks for the very encouraging comment. We agree that compression is always a concern for machine translation, and in this work, we focus on identifying and reducing the operations that are not helpful to translation but consume computation resources, such as pointer alignment and updates. We also clarify that the approach is applicable to other neural machine translation models beyond NMT-64 and NMT-large in this version. Dr. Gerusevicius: thanks for the suggestions on future work. We have considered your comments and have updated the version accordingly. Bo Wang: thanks for the positive review. We agree that it is very encouraging and the feedback is valuable. The authors propose a method to compress large neural machine translation models by eliminating learnable parameters, in a distillation scheme, based on local reasoning. The approach was validated on themt machine translation model and shown to achieve state of the art results on the IWSLT’19 test set. The proposed method is motivated by the observation that many machine translation models capture local reasoning, that is, the ability to translate word j under assumptions about word i, e.g, using a translation of i in a similar domain, or a paraphrase of i. The proposed method exploits this by training a small model to imitate this local behavior, and freezing the distillation bottoms weights, thus saving some compute but at the same time also reducing parameters. The method is evaluated on the official themt corpus, showing around 6% relative reduction in the model size while retaining similar performance. The approach is also shown to generalize well to more recent models, achieving 8.2% relative reduction in model size on the WMT’19 test set. The proposed method is simple and effective, and shows promise as a general approach to reduce model size while retaining performance. This is a well-defined question and the paper clearly lays out the problem and motivation. The paper describes the approach clearly, and highlights the reduction in model size and the test set performance. While this is not as good as the full model, the approach could be useful in scenarios where mobile or compute time is a concern. I have a couple of suggestions for the paper. The first is that it would be interesting to see the effect of the method on the decoder instead of the encoder, so that the method could be more generally useful. Second, it would be interesting to see some analysis of why the proposed method reduces the size of the model, or tries to argue for a connection between local reasoning and model size.

Neural Machine Translation (NMT), like many other deep learning domains, typically suffers from over-parameterization, resulting in large storage sizes. This paper examines three simple magnitude-based pruning schemes to compress NMT models, namely class-blind, class-uniform and class-distribution, which differ in terms of how pruning thresholds are computed for the different classes of weights in the NMT architecture. We demonstrate the efficacy of weight pruning as a compression technique for a state-of-the-art NMT system. We show that an NMT model with over 200 million parameters can be pruned by 40% with very little performance loss as measured on the WMT'14 English-German translation task. This sheds light on the distribution of redundancy in the NMT architecture. Our main result is that with with retraining, we can recover and even surpass the original performance with an 80%-pruned model. Weights in NMT are typically organized in layers, each layer corresponding to one specific task of the model. The first layer processes the input data, typically consisting of multiple sentences, and is typically composed of up to several hundreds of thousands of weights. Subsequent layers downsample the output, with some specific layers sharing the weights across different downsampled layers. The final layers correspond to the output layer, mapping the output downsampled layers to probabilities over the space of translation sentences. This form of sharing weights across layers turns out to be extremely wasteful and one of the major contributors to over-parameterization. Weight pruning can be used to address this issue by eliminating unimportant parameters, i.e. by slimming down the model. We demonstrate that by using class-based pruning, one can achieve significant compression while still keeping enough parameters to maintain acceptable performance. Weight pruning is tested on the widely-used WMT14 English-German translation task, which has become a standard benchmark. We focus on a state-of-the-art large low-resource NMT system which has millions of parameters. For this model, we explore three variants of magnitude-based pruning, and demonstrate that it is possible to reduce the model weight by 40% without too much performance drop. More interestingly, by retraining the pruned model with different starting temperatures, we are able to even surpass the original performance with an 80% weight reduction. Overall, we show that weight pruning can be a viable approach to address over-parameterization in NMT, and it is particularly effective when class-based metrics are used. The authors’ published their paper on the WMT'14 English-German translation task on arXiv. We provide the link: https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.6980
human_text:
This paper investigates three simple weight-pruning techniques for NMT, and
shows that pruning weights based on magnitude works best, and that retraining
after pruning can recover original performance, even with fairly severe
pruning.

The main strength of paper is that the technique is very straightforward and
the results are good. Itâs also clearly written and does a nice job covering
previous work.

A weakness is that the work isnât very novel, being just an application of a
known technique to a new kind of neural net and application (namely NMT), with
results that arenât very surprising. 

Itâs not clear to me what practical significance these results have, since to
take advantage of them you would need sparse matrix representations, which are
trickier to get working fast on a GPU - and after all, speed is the main
problem with NMT, not space. (There may be new work that changes this picture,
since the field is evolving fast, but if so you need to describe it, and
generally do a better job explaining why we should care about pruning.)

A suggestion for dealing with the above weakness would be to use the pruning
results to inform architecture changes. For instance, figure 3 suggests that
you might be able to reduce the number of hidden layers to two, and also
potentially reduce the dimension of source and target embeddings.

Another suggestion is that you try to make a link between pruning+retraining
and dropout (eg âA Theoretically Grounded Application of Dropout in Recurrent
Neural Networksâ, Gal, arXiv 2016).

Detailed comments:

Line 111: âsoftmax weightsâ - âoutput embeddingsâ may be a preferable
term

S3.2: Itâs misleading to call n the âdimensionâ of the network, and
specify all parameter sizes as integer multiples of this number as if this were
a logical constraint.

Line 319: You should cite Bahdanau et al here for the attention idea, rather
than Luong for their use of it.

S3.3: Class-uniform and class-distribution seem very similar (and naturally get
very similar results); consider dropping one or the other.

Figure 3 suggestion that you could hybridize pruning: use class-blind for most
classes, but class-uniform for the embeddings.

Figure 4 should show perplexity too.

What pruning is used in section 4.2 & figure 6?

Figure 7: does loss pertain to training or test corpora?

Figure 8: This seems to be missing softmax weights. I found this diagram
somewhat hard to interpret; it might be better to give relevant statistics,
such as the proportion of each class that is removed by class-blind pruning at
various levels.

Line 762: You might want to cite Le et al, âA Simple Way to Initialize
Recurrent Networks of Rectified Linear Unitsâ, arXiv 2015.

This paper applies the idea of translation model pruning to neural MT. The
authors explore three simple threshold and histogram pruning schemes, two of
which are applied separately to each weight class, while the third is applied
to the entire model. The authors also show that retraining the models produces
performance equal to the full model, even when 90% of the weights are pruned.
An extensive analysis explains the superiority of the class-blind pruning
scheme, as well as the performance boost through retraining. 

While the main idea of the paper is simple, it seems quite useful for
memory-restricted applications of NMT. I particularly liked the analysis
section which gives further insight into the model components that are usually
treated like black boxes. While these insights are interesting by themselves,
the paper's main motivation is model compression. This argument would be
stronger if the paper included some numbers on actual memory consumption of the
compressed model in comparison to the uncompressed model.     

Some minor remarks:
- There is a substantial amount of work on pruning translation models in
phrase-based SMT, which could be referenced in related work, e.g. 
Johnson, J., Martin, J., Foster, G. and Kuhn, R.: Improving Translation Quality
by Discarding Most of the Phrasetable. EMNLP 07 or
Zens, R., Stanton, D. and Peng X.: A Systematic Comparison of Phrase Table
Pruning Techniques. EMNLP 12

- It took me a while to understand Figure 5. I would find it more informative
to add an additional barplot under figure 4 showing highest discarded weight
magnitude by class. This would also allow a comparison across all pruning
methods.

The paper Delexicalized and Minimally Supervised Parsing on Universal Dependencies addresses the problem of Building high performance parsers using very little supervision. The authors present a system which does not require any existing supervised data to train a state-of-the-art dependency parser. The system utilizes a large amount of unsupervised data to guide the system’s semantic alignment. Additionally, the system is able to utilize very little amounts of labeled data for development and evaluation. The authors also present a novel framework for incrementally adapting the system’s performance on a small labeled data set. I recommend this paper for publication in the IEEE Transactions on Computational Natural Language Learning The paper is interesting and innovative. The proposed system is able to achieve state of the art performance on UD upon the very small quantity of labeled data that the authors provide for development and evaluation. I feel that the strengths of this work are that the problem the paper addresses is very real and the system has the potential to be easily deployed in practice. I also think that this work is an important contribution to the field of unsupervised learning. Few years ago, a similar work was proposed by Dulay et al., which showed that it was possible to build competitive syntactic parsers using large amounts of unsupervised data, but this required the use of complex encoder-decoder networks. The proposed work represents a simpler and more straight-forward approach for solving this problem. The main limitation of this paper is that it is only concerned with dependency parsing. While the method proposed in this work could in principle be applied to other dependency languages (e.g., Object Pascal, SQL) it is unclear whether the gains will be similar. Overall, I think that this is a relevant paper that should be published in IEEE Transactions on Computational Natural Language Learning.

This paper compares delexicalized transfer and minimally supervised parsing techniques on 32 different languages from Universal Dependencies treebank collection. The minimal supervision is in adding handcrafted universal grammatical rules for POS tags. The rules are incorporated into the unsupervised dependency parser in forms of external prior probabilities. We also experiment with this approach for learning the probabilities from other treebanks. The paper has following strengths: 1. It compares delexicalized transfer and minimally supervised parsing techniques on many different languages. 2. It is also suitable for those, for which the treebanks often do not exist by adding external prior probabilities from handcrafted rules. 3. The attachment score of our parser is slightly lower than delexicalized transfer parser, however, it performs better for languages from less resourced language families (non-Indo-European) and is therefore suitable for those. The weaknesses: 1. It does not compare these techniques on high resource language like English. 2. It only evaluates attachment score. The quality of parse is also important. I hope this helps! With best regards Alexander PS: The attachment score of our parser is slightly lower than delexicalized transfer parser, however, it performs better for languages from less resourced language families (non-Indo-European) and is therefore suitable for those. This part is not clear to me, does it mean that the delexicalized parser performs worse for high resource languages and hence is not suitable for less resourceful ones? If so, how can we explain the reason? For high resource language like English, the attachment score is the most important metric and the learnability from handcrafted rules is not as important as it is for low resource languages. And in my opinion, the reason is that in order to achieve a high attachment score, the delexicalized parser must make many constraints which are not easy to satisfy for the high resource language. If this is not clear, I can explain in more details. The attachment score is based on two ideas. The first is the so-called "frequency-based" which counts the number of times a relationship is observed in the labeled data. The second is the "smoothing" which puts a probability distribution on the formation of the attachment. For high resource languages, the attachment rules are often simple and the "frequency-based" metric is easy to achieve. For example, in English, the classifier can decide whether the preposition comes before or after the head noun according to whether the preposition is singular or plural. The "smoothing" metric depends on the probability distribution over the attachment rules. For example, if the classifier is allowed to use singular rule when the count of the count of the noun is greater than 10 and plural otherwise, then the attachment score is high. However, it is not straightforward to calculate the probability and the "smoothing" metric is often easier to achieve the attachment score. As you can see, the delexicalized technique requires the classifier to satisfy several complex constraints which is hard for the high resource language. For low resource languages, the attachment score may not matter as much. In this case, de-lexicalized parser can be chosen as the first preference. Another weakness of the paper is that the authors only evaluate attachment score. The quality of parse is also important. The attachment score is the metric used to compare different approaches of transfer parsing. However, because of the limitations of the hand-crafted attachment rules, the transfer parsing can not achieve the same level of quality as supervised parsing. If the attachment rules are simple and easily achieved high attachment score, then it indicates the attachment rules do not affect the attachment score that much. But if the attachment rules play an important role in the model, then the attachment score will decrease. For example, in the universal dependencies parser, the most common transfer parsing approach, there are hand-crafted dependency parsing rules which are used for attachment matching. Some of the rules are rules such as: if the head word is a function word like 'a' 'an' then the preposition must be before the head word. This rule does not relate to the attachment score but it is very important for dependency parsing. When the transfer parser meets such dependency parsing rule, it will not achieve an attachment score which is very difficult to achieve. Similar is true for many other hand-crafted attachment rules. The attachment rules are like a sieve to the transfer parsing. This is why I think the attachment score is not the best metric to measure the transfer parsing, other than the attachment rules are very simple. This paper presents results on the UD treebanks to test delexicalized transfer
parsers and an unsupervised parser which is enriched with external
probabilities.

The paper is interesting, but I think it could be improved further.

(5.2) "McDonald et al. (2011) presented 61.7% of averaged accuracy over 8
languages. On the same languages, our transfer parser on UD reached 70.1%."
Mcdonald et al could not use the UD treebanks since they were not available,
you should definitely state that this is the case here.

In footnote 9 you say: "We used the Malt parser with its default feature set.
Tuning in this specific delexicalized task would probably bring a
bit better results." You are using MaltParser with default settings, why don't
you use MaltOptimizer? Optimizing one model would be very easy. 
In the same way MSTParser could be optimized further.
In the same line, why don't you use more recent parsers that produce better
results? These parsers have been already applied to universal dependencies with
the leave one out setup (see references below). For instance, the authors say
that  the unsupervised parser "performs better for languages from less
resourced language families (non-Indo-European)", it would be interesting to
see whether this holds with more recent (and cross lingual) parsers.

Probabilities: Why do you use this probabilities? it seems like a random
decision (Tables 3-4) (esp 3), at least we need more details or a set of
experiments to see whether they make sense or not.

There are some papers that the authors should take into account.

1. Cross-Lingual Dependency Parsing with Universal Dependencies and Predicted
PoS Labels
J Tiedemann
2. One model, two languages: training bilingual parsers with harmonized
treebanks
D Vilares, MA Alonso, C GÃ³mez-RodrÃ­guez  (it presents results with
MaltParser)

And for results with more recent parsers (and also delexicalized parsers):
1. Crosslingual dependency parsing based on distributed representations. 
Jiang Guo, Wanxiang Che, David
Yarowsky, Haifeng Wang, and Ting Liu. 2015.  In Proc. of ACL

2. Many languages, one parser
W Ammar, G Mulcaire, M Ballesteros, C Dyer, NA Smith

-Minor points:
 I don't think we need Table 1 and Table 2, this could be solved with a
footnote to the UD website. Perhaps Table 2 should be included due to the
probabilities, but Table 1 definitely not.

This paper evaluates a minimally supervised dependency parser -- a version of
the DMV model with manually set prior probabilities -- on (most of) the
treebanks from Universal Dependencies, v1.2. It reports results that are on
average slightly lower than a couple of delexicalized transfer parsers but
(sometimes substantially) better on a few non-Indo-European languages.

The idea of biasing an otherwise unsupervised parser with some basic
"universal" rules have been used a number of times before in the literature, so
the main value of the present paper is an empirical evaluation of this approach
on the new UD treebanks. However, the approach and evaluation leaves some 
questions unanswered.

First of all, I want to know why only unlabeled parsing is considered. This may
have been appropriate (or at least necessary) before dependency labels were
standardised, but the whole point of UD is to give a uniform analysis in terms
of typed dependencies, and any parsing approach that does not take this into
account seems misguided. And since the approach is based on manually defined
universal rules, it would have been easy enough to formulate rules for labeled
dependencies.

Second, I would like to know more about how the prior probabilities were set
or, in other words, what universal grammar they are meant to encode and how.
Were alternatives tested and, if so, how were they evaluated? In the present
version of the paper, we are just presented with a bunch of numbers without any
explanation or justification except that they are âbased on UD annotation
styleâ.

Third, one of the main claims of the paper is that the unsupervised system
works better for non-Indo-European languages. This seems to be supported by the
raw numbers, but what exactly is going on here? What types of dependencies are
handled better by the unsupervised system? Even though a full error analysis
would be out of scope in a short paper, an analysis of a small sample could be
really interesting.

Finally, the comparison to the delexicalized transfer parsers seems to be
biased by a number of factors. Restricting it to unlabeled dependencies is one
such thing, since the delexicalized parser could easily have produced labeled
dependencies. Another thing is the amount of training data, which was
arbitrarily restricted to 10,000 tokens per treebank. Finally, it seems that
the delexicalized parsers were not properly tuned. Just replacing word forms
and lemmas by underscores without revising the feature models is not likely to
produce optimal results.

machine_text: The paper uses a state of the art deep learning model to determine the temporal orientation of a word sense. The model is built on Common Crawl data which has a lot of bias given the source of data. It will be useful to have a model that is generic and not limited to senses from a particular corpus. I have some suggestions to improve the paper. 1. Use a fairer corpus like PGNet. 2. Provide us with some example of misclassified examples so that I can understand how the model fails. 3. Try different metric to measure the similarity between word senses and see if that improve the model's accuracy. Overall, this is a good initial attempt and I recommend the paper to be accepted. I look forward to your response. Kind regards Prasenjit Kargap - Assistant Professor, University of Connecticut ----- The authors present a method for determining the temporal orientation of word senses by applying state-of-the-art deep learning techniques to a large lexicalized corpus. The authors present the need for a system that can reliably determine the temporal orientation of word senses in order to accurately process temporal discourse. The system presented in the paper uses deep learning techniques to evaluate a large corpus of word senses to determine the temporal orientation, which can then be used to derive the temporal orientation of word senses in new contexts. This paper presents an approach to tag word senses with temporal information
(past, present, future or atemporal). They model the problem using a
graph-based semi-supervised classification algorithm that allows to combine
item specific information - such as the presence of some temporal indicators in
the glosses - and the structure of Wordnet - that is semantic relations between
synsets â, and to take into account unlabeled data. They perform a full
annotation of Wordnet, based on a set of training data labeled in a previous
work and using the rest of Wordnet as unlabeled data. Specifically, they take
advantage of the structure of the label set by breaking the task into a binary
formulation (temporal vs atemporal), then using the data labeled as temporal to
perform a finer grained tagging (past, present or future). In order to
intrinsically evaluate their approach, they annotate a subset of synsets in
Wordnet using crowd-sourcing. They compare their system to the results obtained
by a state-of-the-art time tagger (Stanford's SUTime) using an heuristic as a
backup strategy, and to previous works. They obtain improvements around 11% in
accuracy, and show that their approach allows performance higher than previous
systems using only 400 labeled data. Finally, they perform an evaluation of
their resource on an existing task (TempEval-3) and show improvements of about
10% in F1 on 4 labels.

This paper is well-constructed and generally clear, the approach seems sound
and well justified. This work led to the development of a resource with fine
grained temporal information at the word sense level that would be made
available and could be used to improve various NLP tasks. I have a few remarks,
especially concerning the settings of the experiments.

I think that more information should be given on the task performed in the
extrinsic evaluation section. An example could be useful to understand what the
system is trying to predict (the features describe âentity pairsâ but it
has not been made clear before what are these pairs) and what are the features
(especially, what are the entity attributes? What is the POS for a pair, is it
one dimension or two? Are the lemmas obtained automatically?). The sentence
describing the labels used is confusing, I'm not sure to understand what
âevent to document creation timeâ and âevent to same sentence eventâ
means, are they the kind of pairs considered? Are they relations (as they are
described as relation at the beginning of p.8)? I find unclear the footnote
about the 14 relations: why the other relations have to be ignored, what makes
a mapping too âcomplexâ? Also, are the scores macro or micro averaged?
Finally, the ablation study seems to indicate a possible redundancy between
Lexica and Entity with quite close scores, any clue about this behavior?

I have also some questions about the use of the SVM.  For the extrinsic
evaluation, the authors say that they optimized the parameters of the
algorithm: what are these parameters?  And since a SVM is also used within the
MinCut framework, is it optimized and how? Finally, if it's the LibSVM library
that is used (Weka wrapper), I think a reference to LibSVM should be included. 

Other remarks:
- It would be interesting to have the number of examples per label in the gold
data, the figures are given for coarse grained labels (127 temporal vs 271
atemporal), but not for the finer grained.
- It would also be nice to have an idea of the number of words that are
ambiguous at the temporal level, words like âpresentâ.
- It is said in the caption of the table 3 that the results presented are
âsignificantly betterâ but no significancy test is indicated, neither any
p-value.

Minor remarks:
- Related work: what kind of task was performed in (Filannino and Nenadic,
2014)?
- Related work: ârequires a post-calibration procedureâ, needs a reference
(and p.4 in 3.3 footnote it would be clearer to explain calibration)
- Related work: âtheir model differ from oursâ, in what?
- Table 3 is really too small: maybe, remove the parenthesis, put the
â(p,r,f1)â in the caption and give only two scores, e.g. prec and f1. The
caption should also be reduced.
- Information in table 4 would be better represented using a graph.
- Beginning of p.7: 1064 â 1264
- TempEval-3: reference ?
- table 6: would be made clearer by ordering the scores for one column
- p.5, paragraph 3: atemporal) â atemporal

The authors present a method for event linking by first performing sentence extraction on new text using a Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory Network (BLSTMP) and then using sequence of word vectors to relate the extracted sentences to a knowledge base of event definitions. The paper is well written and presents its findings through multiple examples using previously developed event datasets. The main strength of this approach is that it allows for a very large number of potential event types, expressed through different combinations of words, to be considered without the need for hand-engineered features or careful feature selection. The authors demonstrate that similar results can be obtained using just features derived from the word vectors alone. One weakness of this method is that it requires that the knowledge base be provided with event definitions in terms of sequences of word vectors. This means that the method is not easily scalable to new event types that cannot be represented using sequences of words. It may also be challenging to use this method to link together events that involve entities not already included in the word vector index. textrm{Problem: Handling new event types requires hand-engineered features or careful feature selection. human_text:
This paper models event linking using CNNs. Given event mentions, the authors
generate vector representations based on word embeddings passed through a CNN
and followed by max-pooling. They also concatenate the resulting
representations with several word embeddings around the mention. Together with
certain pairwise features, they produce a vector of similarities using a
single-layer neural network, and compute a coreference score. 
The model is tested on an ACE dataset and an expanded version with performance
comparable to previous feature-rich systems.
The main contribution of the paper, in my opinion, is in developing a neural
approach for entity linking that combines word embeddings with several
linguistic features. It is interesting to find out that just using the word
embeddings is not sufficient for good performance. Fortunately, the linguistic
features used are limited and do not require manually-crafted external
resources.  

Experimental setting
- It appears that gold trigger words are used rather than predicted ones. The
authors make an argument why this is reasonable, although I still would have
liked to see performance with predicted triggers. This is especially
problematic as one of the competitor systems used predicted triggers, so the
comparison isn't fair. 
- The fact that different papers use different train/test splits is worrisome.
I would encourage the authors to stick to previous splits as much as possible. 

Unclear points
- The numbers indicating that cross-sentential information is needed are
convincing. However, the last statement in the second paragraph (lines 65-70)
was not clear to me.
- Embeddings for positions are said to be generaties "in a way similar to word
embeddings". How exactly? Are they randomly initialized? Are they lexicalized?
It is not clear to me why a relative position next to one word should have the
same embedding as a relative position next to a different word.
- How exactly are left vs right neighbors used to create the representation
(lines 307-311)? Does this only affect the max-pooling operation?
- The word embeddings of one word before and one word after the trigger words
are appended to it. This seems a bit arbitrary. Why one word before and after
and not some other choice?  
- It is not clear how the event-mention representation v_e (line 330) is used?
In the following sections only v_{sent+lex} appear to be used, not v_e.
- How are pairwise features used in section 3.2? Most features are binary, so I
assume they are encoded as a binary vector, but what about the distance feature
for example? And, are these kept fixed during training?

Other issues and suggestions
- Can the approach be applied to entity coreference resolution as well? This
would allow comparing with more previous work and popular datasets like
OntoNotes. 
- The use of a square function as nonlinearity is interesting. Is it novel? Do
you think it has applicability in other tasks?
- Datasets: one dataset is publicly available, but results are also presented
with ACE++, which is not. Do you have plans to release it? It would help other
researchers compare new methods. At least, it would have been good to see a
comparison to the feature-rich systems also on this dataset.
- Results: some of the numbers reported in the results are quite close.
Significance testing would help substantiating the comparisons.
- Related work: among the work on (entity) coreference resolution, one might
mention the neural network approach by Wiseman et al. (2015)  

Minor issues
- line 143, "that" is redundant. 
- One of the baselines is referred to as "same type" in table 6, but "same
event" in the text (line 670).        

Refs
- Learning Anaphoricity and Antecedent Ranking Features for Coreference
Resolution. Sam Wiseman, Alexander M. Rush, Jason Weston, and Stuart M.
Shieber. ACL 2015.

This paper presents a model for the task of event entity linking, where they
propose to use sentential features from CNNs in place of external knowledge
sources which earlier methods have used. They train a two-part model: the first
part learns an event mention representation, and the second part learns to
calculate a coreference score given two event entity mentions.

The paper is well-written, well-presented and is easy to follow. I rather like
the analysis done on the ACE corpus regarding the argument sharing between
event coreferences. Furthermore, the analysis on the size impact of the
dataset is a great motivation for creating their ACE++ dataset. However, there
are a few
major issues that need to be addressed:

- The authors fail to motivate and analyze the pros and cons of using CNN for
generating mention representations. It is not discussed why they chose CNN and
there are no comparisons to the other models (e.g., straightforwardly an RNN).
Given that the improvement their model makes according various metrics against
the
state-of-the-art is only 2 or 3 points on F1 score, there needs to be more
evidence that this architecture is indeed superior.

- It is not clear what is novel about the idea of tackling event linking with
sentential features, given that using CNN in this fashion for a classification
task is not new. The authors could explicitly point out and mainly compare to
any existing continuous space methods for event linking. The choice of methods
in Table 3 is not thorough enough.

- There is no information regarding how the ACE++ dataset is collected. A major
issue with the ACE dataset is its limited number of event types, making it too
constrained and biased. It is important to know what event types ACE++ covers.
This can also help support the claim in Section 5.1 that 'other approaches are
strongly tied to the domain where these semantic features are availableâ¦our
approach does not depend on resources with restrictedâ¦', you need to show
that those earlier methods fail on some dataset that you succeed on. Also,
for enabling any meaningful comparison in future, the authors should think
about making this dataset publicly available.

Some minor issues:
- I would have liked to see the performance of your model without gold
references in Table 3 as well.

- It would be nice to explore how this model can or cannot be augmented with a
vanilla coreference resolution system. For the specific example in line 687,
the off-the-shelf CoreNLP system readily links 'It' to 'bombing', which can be
somehow leveraged in an event entity linking baseline.

- Given the relatively small size of the ACE dataset, I think having a
compelling model requires testing on the other available resources as well.
This further motivates working on entity and event coreference simultaneously.
I also believe that testing on EventCorefBank in parallel with ACE is
essential. 

- Table 5 shows that the pairwise features have been quite effective, which
signals that feature engineering may still be crucial for having a competitive
model (at least on the scale of the ACE dataset). One would wonder which
features were the most effective, and why not report how the current set was
chosen and what else was tried.

machine_text: The paper has interesting ideas and makes some good points, but I have a few concerns that would need to be addressed before I can recommend it for publication. First, the Abstract begins by explaining that a key barrier to the use of dependency parsing for low-resource languages is the need to train new models for each new language. The authors solve this problem by proposing to use a shared low-resource parser as a "facilitator" to adapt other language specific parsers to new languages. However, this approach can only work if the shared parser is already a good "facilitator" for the new languages, which means it must have been trained on data from at least one of those languages. But the paper doesn't explain how the shared parser was trained, so it's not clear if it has the same problems when trying to adapt to a new language that a new model would have. Second, the authors use byte-level accuracy as the evaluation metric for the adapted parsers. But this metric doesn't provide much information about how well the adapted model actually works in practice. A model with good byte-level accuracy might not be able to convert the parsed structures to a desired meaning, e.g. a syntactic constituent might have an incorrect argument labels. Third, the paper provides no evidence that using the Shared Sudo Parsing model as a "facilitator" would actually be feasible in practice. In particular, it doesn't say anything about how much data the shared model would need in order to generate good adapted models, nor does it explain how the adapted models would be evaluated. Overall, I don't think this paper has addressed the challenges of adapting dependency parsing to new languages in a rigorous or practical way. I think it might be possible to get something working, but the method might not be generalizable to other low-resource languages or to related applications, and there are likely to be a lot of questions and uncertainties that would need to be addressed before attempting to use this method in practice.

The authors show a method to parse given untrained text to UD structures. The method is based on character-level MLC models, which they trained on a large multilingual dataset. They apply the pre-trained model on new documents and show that it is possible to recover UD trees for the documents even though the pre-trained model was not trained on the new domain. The method shows promise, but it has some limitations. First, it requires very long processing time - the authors show that pre-trained model converges after about 11k iterations, but in their experiments it took about 70k iterations for the pre-trained model to converge on their dataset. Second, the method is not fully unsupervised - in order to apply the pre-trained model to new documents, some amount of handcrafted features are still needed. Despite these limitations, the method shows that it is possible to recover UD structures for untrained language models, and it is likely that significant further improvements could be made by improving the efficiency of using the MLC model and reducing the amount of required handcrafted features. Strengths: The authors introduced a new approach to using pre-trained models for unsupervised parsing. They created a new large multilingual dataset and showed that it is possible to use the MLC model to recover UD trees for the documents in the new dataset even though the MLC model was not trained on the new domain. The results are quite impressive. This is likely the first fully unsupervised approach to UD parsing, without requiring any annotated data for the new domain. Weaknesses: The method is not fully unsupervised. It is still requires some amount of handcrafted features in order to apply the model to new documents. In addition, it takes about 70k iterations for the pre-trained model to converge on their dataset, which could be a concern for application in production systems. The paper shows that it is possible to recover UD trees for untrained model, and it will be very useful to the researchers and developers who are working on unsupervised parsing. Interesting. The main idea is not novel, previous work has also proposed a similar algorithm. For example, the serial of UD parse algorithm (sUDP) paper has similar motivation and implementation, and the differences and improvement over sUDP will be discussed later. The work is well suited to the description of the problem and the goals, although the choice of headline metrics is a mystery to me. For example, it is unclear how well the parser can generalize to unseen cases. The main contribution of this work is the implementation of an unsupervised parser for Universal Dependencies. It seems more interesting to me if the performance was compared to a strong supervised model (delexicalized transfer parser) on a large benchmark. It would also be interesting to see how well the parser generalizes to new languages, for example comparisons with a parser for Russian. Overall, it seems like a step forward to automatically build parsers for UD without explicit supervision. This is a very useful capability for NLP research. However, the implementation contains some bugs that prevent it from being useful for research. For example, the parser fails to load in cases when the headline includes non-ASCII letters, and it returns <unk> for some headlines. The underlying implementation is also not well documented. The user guide for the parser is a source file for the parser, which is not useful. A standalone tool to evaluate the parser using examples from the UD 2017 coreference test set is also not well documented. The result files include a link to the source file for the evaluation code, which is not helpful. On the whole, this is a useful contribution, but I recommend that the authors improve the quality of the implementation and document their model in more detail. However, the implementation is much better than the original model in the paper. In particular, the previous work cannot load arbitrary headlines (only those composed exclusively of ASCII letters). This is a very significant improvement. Finally, the parsing algorithm only uses a small set of specific dependency rules. This might allow the model to generalise better to unseen cases, but it is not general. This is a significant weakness of the model. In summary, this is an interesting contribution that improves upon a previous model in some important ways. I have the following suggestions for the authors: - The implementation is mostly fine, but the documentation could be improved. - The model is significantly improved over the previous model. However, it still only uses a small subset of rules from the UD format, which is a significant limitation. - The headline evaluation code and model needs to be improved. - The headline validation method is unclear. The paper describes that it is based on the headwords containing at least three characters and the first character being a letter, but it does not explain how these rules were arrived at. It would be interesting to evaluate the model on other languages, for example Russian. This would demonstrate that the model can generalize to new languages. It would also be interesting to show that the model performs worse on headlines that do not satisfy the validation rules. In summary, this is an interesting contribution that improves upon a previous model. However, it still has some significant limitations, and it will not work well on headlines that do not satisfy the validation rules. I recommend that the authors: - Implement validation for other languages. - Document the headline validation method. - Investigate more general parsing rules. On the whole, this is a useful contribution to NLP research. --- I realize this is an old paper, but I ran into it while reading the list of recently published papers. I think the issues listed here might still be relevant, so I'm posting this as a comment rather than an edit to the paper. Hi, this is Pranab Shenoy, a contributing writer for UD, RNNLP, and parser developer at Faiss. I understand that you are evaluating a new parser without any training, using a subset of UD rules called Dependency labels. This is an interesting idea, but there are some limitations to this approach. First, the dependency labels are designed for humans to read, not machines. The standard labels (e.g., directed edge, neutral edge, etc.) only provide a rough guide. When applied to different contexts, these labels can be extremely misleading, especially when the labels only describe part of the relation. For example, "ing" can be a neutral edge in one context, but a depend relation in another. The parser does not use a Machine Learning approach, which is not able to capture the full range of possible dependencies. Second, the validation of the dependency labels depends on the headline's first character being a letter. headlines with non-ASCII letters do not validate

The paper Parsing for Universal Dependencies without training, its main content is as below: We present UDP, an unsupervised parsing algorithm for Universal Dependencies (UD) based on PageRank and a small set of specific dependency head rules. The parser requires no training, and it is competitive with a delexicalized transfer system. UDP offers a linguistically sound unsupervised alternative to cross-lingual UD parsing. It is distinctly robust to domain change across languages. Advantages: - The parsing algorithm is competitive with a delexicalized transfer system, which means it can be trained on a small amount of data. - UDP offers a linguistically sound unsupervised alternative to cross-lingual UD parsing. - It is distinctly robust to domain change across languages. Limitations: - The parsing algorithm is evaluated on the widely used CoNLL03 shared task, but it can be applied to other UD versions. - The resulting parses are not fully delexicalized, but this can be remedied with a delexicalized transfer system. - It remains to be seen whether the achieved precision can be further improved, and how well it compares with supervised parsers on large data sets. Conclusion and Future Work: This is a novel and interesting paper that provides an unsupervised approach to parsing and offers a competitive alternative to transfer-based systems. The paper covers a lot of important ideas and intuitions underlying the design of the parsing algorithm and how it relates to the unsupervised learning framework. The parser is evaluated on the widely used CoNLL03 dataset and achieves competitive results, and as the paper shows, the ideas in the paper can be adapted to other UD versions and also to other languages. This is very useful contribution that opens up many new possibilities for future work, both in terms of improving the evaluation setting (delexicalized setting would be very interesting to test the parser on) and in terms of applying this approach to other languages, which as the authors also indicate in the paper is an open problem.
human_text:
This paper describes a new deterministic dependency parsing algorithm and
analyses its behaviour across a range of languages.
The core of the algorithm is a set of rules defining permitted dependencies
based on POS tags.
The algorithm starts by ranking words using a slightly biased PageRank over a
graph with edges defined by the permitted dependencies.
Stepping through the ranking, each word is linked to the closest word that will
maintain a tree and is permitted by the head rules and a directionality
constraint.

Overall, the paper is interesting and clearly presented, though seems to differ
only slightly from Sogaard (2012), "Unsupervised Dependency Parsing without
Training".
I have a few questions and suggestions:

Head Rules (Table 1) - It would be good to have some analysis of these rules in
relation to the corpus.
For example, in section 3.1 the fact that they do not always lead to a
connected graph is mentioned, but not how frequently it occurs, or how large
the components typically are.

I was surprised that head direction was chosen using the test data rather than
training or development data.
Given how fast the decision converges (10-15 sentences), this is not a major
issue, but a surprising choice.

How does tie-breaking for words with the same PageRank score work?
Does it impact performance significantly, or are ties rare enough that it
doesn't have an impact?

The various types of constraints (head rules, directionality, distance) will
lead to upper bounds on possible performance of the system.
It would be informative to include oracle results for each constraint, to show
how much they hurt the maximum possible score.
That would be particularly helpful for guiding future work in terms of where to
try to modify this system.

Minor:

- 4.1, "we obtain [the] rank"

- Table 5 and Table 7 have columns in different orders. I found the Table 7
arrangement clearer.

- 6.1, "isolate the [contribution] of both"

The authors proposed an unsupervised algorithm for Universal Dependencies that
does not require training. The tagging is based on PageRank for the words and a
small amount of hard-coded rules.
The article is well written, very detailed and the intuition behind all prior
information being added to the model is explained clearly.
I think that the contribution is substantial to the field of unsupervised
parsing, and the possibilities for future work presented by the authors give
rise to additional research.

This paper presents a way to parse trees (namely the universal dependency
treebanks) by relying only on POS and by using a modified version of the
PageRank to give more way to some meaningful words (as opposed to stop words).

This idea is interesting though very closed to what was done in SÃ¸gaard
(2012)'s paper. The personalization factor giving more weight to the main
predicate is nice but it would have been better to take it to the next level.
As far as I can tell, the personalization is solely used for the main predicate
and its weight of 5 seems arbitrary.

Regarding the evaluation and the detailed analyses, some charts would have been
beneficial, because it is sometimes hard to get the gist out of the tables.
Finally, it would have been interesting to get the scores of the POS tagging in
the prediction mode to be able to see if the degradation in parsing performance
is heavily correlated to the degradation in tagging performance (which is what
we expect).

All in all, the paper is interesting but the increment over the work of
SÃ¸gaard (2012) is small.

machine_text: Overall this is an interesting theoretical paper. I have some concerns about the main conceptual point of the paper though. The paper introduces a general form of non-differentiable function called Neural Program. This program is a mapping from some input to some output. When this mapping is represented as a neural network, the general form of program can be thought of as a function that takes a function as an input. The main advantage of this general form is that it allows the program to represent nonlinear mappings which otherwise would have been expressed as a nonlinear function. The paper defines program in the more general sense such that any differentiable function can be a program. Although I do find this definition quite general, I do not find it very exciting. I think the main idea behind Neural Program Architecture can be achieved through other methods without having to define a generic program structure. For example, if the goal is to encode any function that can generate sequences of numbers as a program, one way to do that is to use a looping network. This approach does not involve a generic program structure and can be directly applied to many problems that involve programs. I think the main limitation of the paper is the claim that having a generic program structure will allow the Neural Program Architecture to generalize better. I am not sure if this is the case, and in fact I think having a generic program structure might lead to overfitting to the input domain. For example, a Neural Program with a looping structure is equivalent to a standard neural network with many layers and many units. The looping structure is not useful except for the task of generating sequences. I think the point about generic programs being easier to generalize is also related to the first point. If a program contains many functions as a sub-programs, the overall function becomes too complex to understand.

The authors tackle the problem of generalization in neural programing by using recursion to introduce temporal structure into the programs being generated. They do this by using a differentiable neural programing transducer to convert the source expression into a nested fixed point, a technique they refer to as syntactic castling. This solves the problem of generalization by restricting the search space of the neural program generator. Although their approach shows promising results on a toy example and on a zero-queried benchmark, I do not see how it would perform on more complex, real world queries. The technique of syntactic castling was not invented recently. There are other more efficient ways to achieve the same goal, for example by using tree-based methods at the meta-program level, using graph rewriting systems, or other combinatory methods. arrification The paper Make Neural Programing Architectures Generalize addresses a problem that has been extensively studied in the field of symbolic program development, namely generalization. The authors propose a new method for achieving generalization through the use of recursion. They show that this approach leads to a method for program generation that is more stable and easier to adapt to changing goals. The approach presented has some clear advantages over the state of the art, however I don't believe it's effective enough to generate high-quality code for more complex applications. ally castling. The authors castle in time, through the use of a differentiable NPT, a technique that lets them introduce a temporal structure into the programs being generated. This addresses the issue of generalization by restricting the search space. They use a nested fixed point representation to compute the fixed points, which is achieved through the introduction of a virtual input that forces all variables to have a fixed value. They show that this approach is more general than previous techniques that only use a single fixed point. This approach is not new, previous research has used similar ideas to castle in time to perform hypervisor generation (Chand et al. 2020). The authors argue that their approach is more efficient because it eliminates the search for the optimal number of iterations and it uses less space to store the fixed point value. However, this efficiency comes at a cost. The method is more complicated. In fact, for each operator in the source language that is used to specify the program, they need to define a new reduction operator for the target language. In addition, the fixed point representation makes the generation process much more time consuming. Also, the introduction of a virtual input and the calculation of its fixed point complicates the recurrence relation, and thus the algorithm. This makes the approach inapplicable to cases where the target program is too large for the computation to finish before the timeout. Despite these drawbacks, the authors show that their approach leads to a more stable program generation process. They provide a counter example that shows how in some cases the classical iterative generation fails to generalize, whereas their approach can generate a valid program.

Neural networks that attempt to learn programs from data have exhibited poor generalizability, and it has been difficult to reason about the behavior of these models beyond a certain level of input complexity. In order to address these issues, we propose augmenting neural architectures with a key abstraction: recursion. As an example, we implement recursion in the Neural Programmer-Interpreter framework on four tasks: grade-school addition, bubble sort, topological sort, and quicksort. We demonstrate superior generalizability and interpretability with small amounts of training data. Recursion drastically reduces the domain of each neural network component, making it tractable to prove guarantees about the overall system’s behavior. Our experience suggests that in order for neural architectures to robustly learn program semantics, it is necessary to incorporate a concept like recursion. Reference + [1] Harrison, P.
