It's interesting to see that by purely using predictions over the differences between measurements for future step(s) and the presented step, the learning performance could surpass A3C and DSR in Doom. I have the following questions:

(1) In Figure 1, why there is a "Target f" drawn to the right of "Prediction P"? Though this makes the model looks more end-to-end, I guess the "Expectation" component and "Action" component are updating their parameters according to their own regression losses, instead of back-propagating through a unified end. 

(2) The reward formulation in this work is similar to Monte-Carlo methods. In this work, the cumulative reward is represented by summing up the outputs of expectation stream and action stream *over each time steps*. If only those over the last time step is considered, it will become almost same as Monte-Carlo. However, the presented work accumulates the difference over multiple future steps. Based on the proposed form of *f* (in Section 3), the reward collected by near-future steps are weighted more. Or we could see the weight to be interpreted as linearly decaying based on the time distance from the future step to the current step. If this is the case, re-formulating the proposed approach with linearly discounted Monte-Carlo could be possible. You may also compare such Monte-Carlo as a compelling baseline. Also, it's better to put more discussion over your reward formulation, since it contributes a lot to the performance improvement and it's better to let people understand why it works well. 

(3) I don't quite understand what is the meaning of *goal*. In Section 3, *g* is proposed to be of the same dimension as  *f*. The maximization is over g^T*f, but what the architecture try to regress is over f, and g is designed as part of inputs to the deep neural network. And action-selection is over the maximum of summed E and A over all future steps. We used a very small replay buffer (2,500 frames per actor thread, 20,000 frames in total), and have not observed any significant changes in results when making it smaller or larger. We are interested in sensorimotor control in immersive environments and chose Doom for this reason. We are looking forward to testing and further developing the approach in other simulators that are becoming available, such as DeepMind's new Lab.

Deep RL (using deep neural networks for function approximators in RL algorithms) have had a number of successes solving RL in large state spaces. Notably, this algorithm was the winner of the Visual Doom AI competition.

The key idea of their algorithm is to use additional low-dimensional observations (such as ammo or health which is provided by the game engine) as a supervised target for prediction. Importantly, this prediction is conditioned on a goal vector (which is given, not learned) and the current action. Once trained the optimal action for the current state can be chosen as the action that maximises the predicted outcome according the goal. Unlike in successor feature representations, learning is supervised and there is no TD relationship between the predictions of the current state and the next state.

There have been a number of prior works both in predicting future states as part of RL and goal driven function approximators which the authors review in section 2. The key contributions of this work are the focus on Monte Carlo estimation (rather than TD), the use of low-dimensional ‘measurements’ for prediction, the parametrized goals and, perhaps most importantly, the empirical comparison to relevant prior work.

In addition to the comparison with Visual Doom AI, the authors show that their algorithm is able to learn generalizable policies which can respond, without further training, to limited changes in the goal.

The paper is well-communicated and the empirical results compelling and will be of significant interest.

There is an approximation in the supervised training as it is making an on-policy assumption but it learns from a replay buffer (with the Monte Carlo regression the expectation of the remainder of the trajectory is assumed to follow the current policy, but is being sampled from episodes generated by prior versions of the policy). This should be discussed.
The algorithm uses additional metadata (the information about which parts of the sensory input are worth predicting) that the compared algorithms do not. I think this, and the limitations of this approach (e.g. it may not work well in a sensory environment if such measurements are not provided) should be mentioned more clearly.

I think that the paper is quite interesting and useful.

Interesting paper, definitely provides value to the community by discussing why large batch gradient descent does not work too well

I think that this is a great empirical exploration of long-held folk wisdom in the Deep Learning community - that using larger minibatches makes generalization error worse.  

The paper does a good of explaining why phenomenon occurs, by analyzing the "sharpness" of the loss function for large-batch and small-batch trained models.  

Some other connections that I think would be interesting to explore: 
  -If you use very small minibatches, does generalization get even better (perhaps at the expense of very slow training).  
  -Can other forms of noise injection compensate for the use of a larger minibatch?  For example, if I inject increasing amounts of noise into the gradients or the parameters with larger batches, does this close the gap with small-batch training?  
  -The motivation for using smaller minibatches here seems closely related to the motivation for adversarial examples (ensuring that loss is relatively flat in a large region around data points).

The paper is an empirical study to justify that: 1. SGD with smaller batch sizes converges to flatter minima, 2. flatter minima have better generalization ability. 

Pros and Cons:
Although there is little novelty in the paper, I think the work is of great value in shedding light into some interesting questions around generalization of deep networks. 

Significance:
I think such results may have impact on both theory and practice, respectively by suggesting what assumptions are legitimate for real scenarios for building new theories, or be used heuristically to develop new algorithms with generalization by smart manipulation of mini-batch sizes.

The paper presents a new algorithm, Amortised MAP Inference (AmMAP) for super-resolution. The work is motivated by the observation that a large number of previous super-resolution algorithms can be divided into two parts, an acquisition model and a redelivery model. The acquisition model specifies the distribution over possible high resolution ( HR) images that could have produced a low resolution (LR) observation, and the redelivery model specifies the distribution over possible LR images that could have produced the HR observation. The work presents an algorithm that optimises the acquisition model by solving an MAP problem with the joint distribution over HR and LR images. In the process the work develops a fast approximation algorithm for this problem, Amortised MAP Inference. The algorithm is compared to previous super-resolution algorithms on the BDD-Video dataset and demonstrates state-of-the-art performance. performed. Strengths: This work presents a general method for super-resolution using a redelivery model, applicable to a wide variety of models. It is robust to image degradation that alters the high frequency content but preserves overall image structure. The method also provides a natural way of regularising the solution using a l1 penalty. This helps reduce the risk of overfitting to the training set. The paper provides convergence proof and a practical way of speeding up the algorithm. The algorithm is evaluated on the BDD-Video dataset, which includes both studio and outdoor scenes, showing it is able to generalise to different datasets. The code and dataset are made publicly available. A limitation of the algorithm is that it can only generate high resolution images in the color space of the input image. This limits the type of super-resolution it can perform. Another limitation is that the algorithm is slower than previous super-resolution algorithms, although this may be offset by it's wider applicability.

This paper presents amortised MAP inference for image super-resolution (SR). Most current single image SR methods use empirical risk minimisation, often with a pixel-wise mean squared error (MSE) loss. However, the outputs from such methods tend to be blurry, over-smoothed and generally appear implausible. A more desirable approach would employ maximum a posteriori (MAP) inference, preferring solutions that always have a high probability under the image prior, and thus appear more plausible. Direct MAP estimation for SR is non-trivial, as it requires us to build a model for the image prior from samples. This paper introduces new methods for amortised MAP inference whereby we calculate the MAP estimate directly using a convolutional neural network. It also discusses experiments showing that the GAN based approach performs best on real image data. \section{Introduction} MAP inference, also known as inference under the Maximum a Posteriori (MAP) loss, has recently gained increasing attention from the computer vision and machine learning communities. MAP estimation was originally developed in the field of statistical physics and information theory, and has found important applications in data modelling and machine learning. In particular, MAP learning provides a unified framework for a large variety of density estimation problems, including generative modelling, label estimation, clustering and classification. Conventional MAP learning methods, e.g. expectation propagation and sampling-based methods such as Variational Auto-Encoders, often suffer from a slow convergence rate and lack of strong theoretical justifications. On the other hand, Maximum pseudolikelihood (MPL) estimation, provided by the EM algorithm, always converges to the global optimum. However, the problem with the EM algorithm is that it is hard to train and requires careful initialization. Recently, generative Adversarial nets (or GANs) have shown promising results in addressing both the convergence problem and the training difficulty. Amortised MAP Inference for Image Super-resolution (SR) Recently, Bayesian methods for image super-resolution (SR) have received much attention, with evidence lower bound (ELBO) methods proving especially promising. The main idea of ELBO methods is to express the intractable posterior distribution over high-resolution images given a low-resolution image, as an evidence lower bound (ELBO) in the form of a differentiable penalty function. This penalty function must be minimised, leading to a bilevel optimization problem which can be addressed by iterative refinement. Most recent approaches follow this idea, but use empirical risk minimisation (ERM) to estimate the high resolution image. This approach works well in practice, but suffers from a number of shortcomings: the solutions obtained are often blurry, over-smoothed and generally implausible. Although Maximum a Posteriori (MAP) inference would ideally produce more plausible results, it has been shown to be intractable to compute directly. In this work, we address the problem of solving the MAP inference problem for image super-resolution. The main contribution of this work is the introduction of a novel network architecture, that performs a projection to the affine subspace of valid solutions ensuring that the high resolution output is always consistent with the low resolution input. We show that, using this architecture, the MAP inference problem can be transformed into a denoising problem. We then propose three methods to solve this problem: generative adversarial networks (GANs), denoiser-guided SR, and a baseline method using maximum-likelihood training. I just wanted to comment that I found this to be a really great paper. There's a lot of new ideas, and the writing and experiments are extremely well executed.

The paper presents a new framework to solve the SR problem - amortized MAP inference and adopts a pre-learned affine projection layer to ensure the output is consistent with LR. Also, it proposes three different methods to solve the problem of minimizing cross-entropy. Generally, it is a great paper. However, I still have several comments:

1) The proposed amortized MAP inference is novel and different from the previous SR methods. Combined with GAN, this framework can obtain plausible and good results. Compared with another GAN-based SR methods - Photo-Realistic Single Image Super-Resolution Using a Generative Adversarial Network, question may arise as to what this new formulation adds to the latest state-of-the-art.

2) Using an affine projection architecture as a constraint, the model do not need any corresponding {HR, LR} image pairs for training. However, when training the affine projection layer, we still need the {HR, LR} image pairs. Does it mean that we merely transfer this training procedure to the training of affine projection?

3) The paper presents many results of the framework, including the results of natural images from ImageNet. Can the author also provide the results of Set5, Set14 or BSD100, which are conventional test dataset for SR, so that we can perform a fair comparison with previous work.

4) I see that the size of the results of nature images presented in this paper are limited to 128*128. Can this framework perform well on images with larger size? Because SR will encounter input with arbitrary size.

5) A normal GAN will have a noise term as a latent space, so that it can be better illustrated as learning a distribution. Do the author try the noise vector?

Overall, this paper provides a new framework for SR with solid theoretical analysis. The idea is novel and the author explore many methods. Though there still exist questions like the necessity and more experiments are needed. I think this work will will provide good inspiration to the community.

machine_text: Overall, the author has done an excellent job of laying out the problem and motivation for the paper. The introduction clearly describes the challenge and motivation to auto-encode state transitions for complex systems. The subsequent sections discussing related work and the proposed approach are also well described. I have some suggestions for the clarity in describing the proposed approach and for future work. The proposed approach is to use variational calculus to estimate the effect of each states on the next. Although the paper describes the method to use a neural network to approximate the variational form, it might be helpful to describe the motivation and some of the key contributions of this work. The first contribution is to apply variational calculus to physical systems that have states and dynamics. Previously, the application of variational calculus to physical systems has been done in the field of robotics (see the work ofurable for example). The second contribution is to use a neural network to approximate the variational form. This means that the proposed approach could potentially be applied to systems with an infinite number of states. I think the paper is generally well-written and clear. I have some suggestions for improving the clarity of the description of the proposed approach and for clarifying the description of the future work. I have enjoyed reviewing this paper. Thank you for the suggestion to use variational calculus to estimate the effect of states on transitions. I have taken your suggestion to write the motivation and first contribution in the introduction and also for writing the second contribution in the discussion.

This paper presents a new method for unsupervised learning of state transitions using only state observation trajectories. The main idea is to train a transition model using a maximum likelihood estimation loss, and then use the model to compute a likelihood over new observations. The algorithm is tested on 3 simulated tasks and on the Pennturn model, and results show that the method is able to recover the correct state transition model, even in the presence of grossly incorrect initial conditions. This is a significant contribution, as traditional autoencoders and GANs require access to full states to train, whereas the method presented in this paper only requires access to state observation trajectories. This greatly simplifies the learning problem, and could be of interest to practitioners in the field. However, the method is preliminary and has some drawbacks. First, the loss function used is a maximum likelihood estimation loss, which assumes a Gaussian distribution of state transitions. This is not necessarily true, and results may be suboptimal when this is not the case. Second, the model assumes that the initial state has an a priori probability of 0.5, which may not be true in many systems. These issues could be addressed in future work by replacing the MLE loss with a more robust loss function that assumes a known distribution over state transitions, or by changing the model to allow for different a priori probabilities for each initial state. In summary, this paper makes an important contribution by presenting a method for unsupervised state transition learning using only observation trajectories. The method is tested on 3 simulated tasks, and promising results are shown with reasonable assumptions. The contribution and shortcomings of this method will be of interest to practitioners in the state transition learning community.

Firstly, the GGT-NN architecture is derived from Gated Graph Neural Networks (GGNNs) introduced in (Li et al., 2016). The GGNNs generate a sequence of graphs from the given sequence of input data samples. In this way, the GGG-NNs model temporal information from data samples. Secondly, the paper does not mention what the input data is. However, it is not clear whether the input data is graph structured. On the contrary, the input data may be a sequence of samples with each sample being a vector. In this case, the model is a Graph Sequence Neural Network (GSNN). For example, in the original bAbI tasks, the input is a time-series of sensory signals from a robot interacting with the world. If the model is a GGNN, then it should understand the temporal relationship between samples. If the model is a GSNN, then it should be able to understand the sample relationships. In this work, the model was shown to be capable of solving almost all of the bAbI tasks, which indicates the model could understand the relationship between samples. However, if the model is a GSNN, then it could be possible to solve the bAbI tasks using the same approach. To apply the GGSNN to GGT-NN, the GGG-NNs transform the input data from graph structured representation to the original representation. However, there are some shortcomings. On the one hand, the model needs to know which nodes are nodes of interest (hot node representation), and which nodes are background nodes. For example, in Figure 1, the top three nodes are background nodes. In contrast, the bottom node is a hot node. If the model only consider the relationship between nodes, then it cannot distinguish the top three nodes from the bottom node. To solve this problem, one idea is to design a force function that makes the bottom node inactive at first, and make the model learn the representation of the hot nodes. Then, according to a certain probability, the force function causes the bottom node to wake up and acquire new nodes. At last, the model can generate a graph structure for the input data. The key to this approach is the design of the force function. One possible approach is a Hebbian rule. If the bottom node has more connections to the other nodes than the other way around, and they have not been learned, then the force function takes effect to learn the representation of the hot nodes. However, there are two shortcomings in this approach. On the one hand, when only one hot node is involved, the Hebbian rule will give way to strong selection bias that the only hot node will be learned to completion. Therefore, even when the hot node is the only useful node in the whole graph, the GSNN cannot generate the original input because it only focuses on the hot node. On the other hand, when a hot node is involved in a chain relationship with other nodes, and the nodes have not been learned, the Hebbian rule will keep focusing on one node and forget the chain relationship. For example, in Figure 1, the input data is time-series sensory signals. However, in Figure 2, all nodes are related to each other but the GGG-NN can only learn one node. In summary, using the GGG-NN to GGT-NN approach to apply GGS-NN on GGT-NN has following shortcomings. Firstly, the model is very complex and difficult to interpret.

The paper “Learning Graphical State Transitions” by Yunzhe Li et al. describes the Gated Graph Transformer Neural Network (GGT-NN), an extension of GGS-NNs that uses graph-structured data as an intermediate representation. The model can learn to construct and modify graphs in sophisticated ways based on textual input, and also to use the graphs to produce a variety of outputs. For example, the model successfully learns to solve almost all of the bAbI tasks (Weston et al., 2016), and also discovers the rules governing graphical formulations of a simple cellular automaton and a family of Turing machines. I introduce the Gated Graph Sequece Neural Network (GGS-NN), an application of Sequece Learning to Graph-structured Data, which can be viewed as a preliminary study of this work. The GGS-NN model can be viewed as a state-space model, with a state space represented by a graph and a observation space represented by a sequence of nodes and connections. The GGS-NN uses the Transformer network architecture (Vaswani, Shazeer, & Gebauer, 2012), which is widely used for sequence processing, for mapping inputs to a sequence. In GGS-NN the input is a graph, and the Transformer is used to map the graph into a sequence of node ids. The main idea of the GGS-NN is that a state space is represented as a graph. First, a state space is defined using a general-purpose modeling language, such as RuleML (Guenter et al., 2001) or Lego NPCS (Davila & Davila, 2014). The modeling language provides high-level primitives for describing simple state transition rules and state diagrams, and an external tools package, Lego NPS, can convert these into Statecharts (Harel, 1991), a representation with a strong mathematical foundation. Statecharts are then manually translated into a GraphQL (Pentico & Abrial, 1994) representation, a simple but effective format for describing graphs. Finally, the model is trained on this representation. One can think of each state as a state node, and each transition as a connection. An example is shown below: The GGS-NN uses the Gated Graph Sequece (GGS) algorithm (Zhao et al., 2017). The model first initializes a graph G0 to be the initial state, and computes expected output sequences {<S1, E1, S2, E2,...>} from an initial state S1. The computation uses the graph G0 to determine the state at each time step, and uses the sequence of events (E) to determine the output at each time step. The model then updates the state graph, by finding the set of edges that can be added to the existing graph to make it consistent with the expected sequence. This change is referred to as the action. If the change is a valid state transition, i.e., it satisfies the state transition rule, the action is accepted; otherwise, it is not. In the second step of this process the model computes the likelihood of the sequence given the action, and then repeats the first step using the new graph. The model can perform one kind of task, which is transcribing the rules of a simple cellular automaton (CAs) to the graphical form of the automaton. The states and transitions of the CA are specified in terms of black and white pixels. The result is an alternating sequence of black and white squares, which can be converted to text. The model is not explicitly told that this pattern is a simple CA; it is not required to learn the CA dynamics. It can discover this on its own. The model can also learn to perform two complex tasks, solving a Sudoku puzzle and writing Sudoku puzzles. In this instance, the state is a Sudoku puzzle, and the events are clues. The model is not given the full solution, but is instead presented with a sequence of clues and is expected to solve the puzzle. This work extends and improves upon the original GGS-NN paper (2016). The biggest change is the addition of a second state-space, allowing it to perform two complex tasks. The model learns to write Sudoku puzzles and to solve Sudoku puzzles. It is also able to learn how to transform state spaces, by discovering the rules of a simple cellular automaton from a sequence of black and white pixels. The GGS-NN model is based on a single algorithm, GGS, so a model trained on one problem domain often shows limited generalizability. The model was not designed for Sudoku puzzles, so its development is not expected to be fast. The model is not given the full solution, but is instead presented with a sequence of clues

Section 4.1 Supervision mentioned that the proposed method requires additional supervision by providing the correct graph at each timestep. 

I have some questions about whether this is practical: 

1. In some applications, human may or may not be able to provide the "correct graph" at each timestep. What if the human supervisor can only provide suboptimal graphs during training? How would that affect the results?

2. What was the result of not providing such intermediate supervision? Was the result slightly worse than the current result, or significantly different?

3. Such additional supervision would also require more "work" by the human. How can the amount of work be quantified, so the reader understands the implications of having to provide additional supervision?

4. I would appreciate if the need of such strong supervision was mentioned earlier in the paper, perhaps during the introduction or literature review, to give the reader some "warning". Some literature review/comparison of other approaches that require strong supervision would also be appreciated.

The main contribution of this paper seems to be an introduction of a set of differential graph transformations which will allow you to learn graph->graph classification tasks using gradient descent. This maps naturally to a task of learning a cellular automaton represented as sequence of graphs. In that task, the graph of nodes grows at each iteration, with nodes pointing to neighbors and special nodes 0/1 representing the values. Proposed architecture allows one to learn this sequence of graphs, although in the experiment, this task (Rule 30) was far from solved.

This idea is combined with ideas from previous papers (GGS-NN) to allow the model to produce textual output rather than graph output, and use graphs as intermediate representation, which allows it to beat state of the art on BaBi tasks.

This paper proposes learning on the fly to represent a dialog as a graph (which acts as the memory), and is first demonstrated on the bAbI tasks. Graph learning is part of the inference process, though there is long term representation learning to learn graph transformation parameters and the encoding of sentences as input to the graph. This seems to be the first implementation of a differentiable memory as graph: it is much more complex than previous approaches like memory networks without significant gain in performance in bAbI tasks, but it is still very preliminary work, and the representation of memory as a graph seems much more powerful than a stack. Clarity is a major issue, but from an initial version that was constructive and better read by a computer than a human, the author proposed a hugely improved later version. This original, technically accurate (within what I understood) and thought provoking paper is worth publishing.

The underlying idea is to propose a method that will be able build/modify a graph-structure as an internal representation for solving a problem, and particularly for solving question-answering problems in this paper. machine_text: The paper is commendable. It presents an novel way to approach the problem of insufficient data for training. The problem of small training datasets often limits the effectiveness of modern Machine Learning models such as Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN). In this work, the authors propose a simple yet powerful approach that significantly improves the performance of the CNN by training it on another, larger, dataset in a "reference" setting, and then, transferring the learned knowledge to the "test" setting. In the "test" setting, the knowledge is then applied by fine-tuning a subset of the original test dataset. The suggested approach has been tested on the "Segmentation of Stationary Environments (SASE1)" real-world dataset and the authors claim to have achieved 5.8% absolute gain in terms of Top-1 validation accuracy, which could potentially have a significant impact on the performance of the models trained on this data, and thus, on the applications relying on this dataset. The approach is relatively simple and has a high potential for improvement in many real-world scenarios where the datasets are scarce. The main drawback of the approach is the need for two independent sets - the "training" and the "reference" - which limits its applicability. * In this work, the authors suggest using another dataset, called "reference", to train the model and then apply the knowledge learned to the "test" setting. The suggested approach has a relatively low potential for improvement in comparison to the method where the model would be trained directly on the "test" setting. * It is not always possible or convenient to have two independent sets - the "training" and the "reference" - for several model training scenarios. In such cases, this approach would not be applicable.

This paper addresses a very important problem in the field of deep learning: the lack of generalizable success in applying deep neural networks to new tasks when trained on one dataset. For example, let us consider the task of image classification. If we use a large image classification dataset such as ImageNet, and we use a CNN architecture such as VGG, then switching the image background from black to white results in a large decrease in accuracy of the model. This is because the ImageNet model was not trained on this particular transformation, so it has no knowledge of how to process this information. This problem is called catastrophic forgetting. One way to overcome this problem is to retrain the weights of the model on the new data, but this often leads to overfitting to the new data, making the model useless on previously unseen data. This is called transferrable knowledge. Instead of retraining the weights of the network, this paper presents a method to retarget only the attention of the network to the new data, and not the content of the learned feature maps, thereby not losing knowledge of the first data set. The method uses a pretrained model in the author's own repository, and transfers the attention of the VGG model to the new data set, and this strategy allows the model to perform well on the new data, with minimal retraining of the weights of the network. structure This paper presents a method to retarget only the attention of the network to the new data, and not the content of the learned feature maps, thereby not losing knowledge of the first data set. The method uses a pretrained model in the author's own repository, and transfers the attention of the VGG model to the new data set, and this strategy allows the model to perform well on the new data, with minimal retraining of the weights of the network. The method described here is based on a similarity measurement between the data set to be transformed and the first data set that the model was trained on. The authors suggest using a combination of distance functions, including dice similarity, L2 distance and L1 distance. The attention maps for the first model are first transformed into a new size and pad in the four directions with zeroes. The similarity between the original and transformed data set is then calculated between each other after padding and then applying the same transformation to the attention map of the first data set. Finally, the authors suggest optimizing the attention map of the first data set by gradient descent on the similarity. There are two advantages to this method. Firstly, it can be applied to a very wide range of neural network architectures, and so may be more widely usable. Secondly, because it only retargets the attention of the network, it does not change the content of the feature maps, so there is no chance of overfitting to the new data set. In contrast, if only the weights of the network are retrained, the overfitting problem is still present. The authors' claim that they can achieve 50% top-1 accuracy on a 50% validation split on CIFAR-10, using only a small portion of the compute time of the model on CIFAR-100, is quite good. The transfer of attention does not seem to be able to be applied for images that do not share significant overlap with the first image set. This raises the interesting question of what types of similarity can be used in this method, and how far this approach can be applied to other types of data.

First of all, thank the authors for sharing this very interesting work. I think the main content of this work is worthwhile and interesting, which uses attention for convolutional neural networks to improve the performance. However, I have some questions for the authors to consider: 1.Why not use the latest residual learning architecture to design the student network? This could make the student network more similar to the teacher network and make it more likely to adopt the teacher's attention-related characteristics. 2.In order to find out the important regions of the image and pay more attention to them, the student network needs to have good initialisation of the parameters. However, this paper does not provide any methods to help the student network to get good initialisation of the parameters. male 1.We choose the CapsNet as the student network architecture for several reasons, the first of which is that CapsNets have been previously demonstrated to work very well in the context of knowledge transfer tasks, so we thought they would be a good starting point for this type of approach. Additionally, CapsNets are also very simple in terms of the number of trainable parameters, so that we can start by constraining the student network to be as similar to the teacher as possible while still maintaining a good performance. 2.As for getting good initialisation of the parameters, we guess this is the most difficult part of the approach. Although our method can transfer some of the knowledge from the teacher to the student network, it’s still not able to get good initialisation of the parameters. To overcome this, we set up an attention-based teacher-student learning framework, which is designed to train the student network in a way that makes it mimic the attention-based characteristics of the teacher network. I think these are the most important points we would need to address. Thank you again for your time.

This paper aims to answer the question of whether or not attention is explicitly allowed in the training of a convolutional neural network, and, if so, whether or not attention transferred from a teacher network can be a viable alternative to the normal training procedure. To do so, a novel approach to defining and training attention for a student network is presented. The main idea is to first define the appropriate type of attention for the task at hand (in this case, locational attention), and then learn how to estimate the quality of this attention. Once this estimation of attention quality is learned, the attention is then used in the final training phase. The paper shows this to be an effective approach, improving the performance of a student network on various tasks and datasets, while still being significantly less resource-intensive than other approaches to similar problems. absorption In this paper the authors propose a method of transferring attention from a teacher model to a student model, improving the performance of the student model. The key idea is to first define the type of attention that needs to be transferred (in this case, locational attention), and then estimate the quality of this transferred attention. The quality estimate is then used to update the student model parameters. The paper shows that this approach is effective and achieves significant improvements over the baseline student model. material This paper presents a method of transferring attention from a teacher model to a student model, improving the performance of the student model. The key idea is to first define the type of attention that needs to be transferred (in this case, locational attention), and then estimate the quality of this transferred attention. The quality estimate is then used to update the student model parameters. The paper shows that this approach is effective and achieves significant improvements over the baseline student model. The paper is novel in that it introduces a novel approach to defining and training attention for CNNs. First, attention is defined in a way that makes sense for the particular task at hand. Next, attention is estimated from a teacher model. Then, these two steps are tied together with a loss that encourages the student model to follow the attention of the teacher model. The paper shows that this approach works well on a variety of datasets and network architectures, with the Attention Transfer Framework achieving significant improvements over the baseline student model.

I like the idea of transferring attention maps instead of activations.

The paper presented a modified knowledge distillation framework that minimizes the difference of the sum of statistics across the a feature map between the teacher and the student network. The authors empirically demonstrated the proposed methods outperform the fitnet style distillation baseline. 

Pros:
+ The author evaluated the proposed methods on various computer vision dataset 
+ The paper is in general well-written

Cons:  
- The method seems to be limited to the convolutional architecture
- The attention terminology is misleading in the paper. The proposed method really just try to distill the summed squared(or other statistics e.g. summed lp norm) of  activations in a hidden feature map.
- The gradient-based attention transfer seems out-of-place. The proposed gradient-based methods are never compared directly to nor are used jointly with the "attention-based" transfer. It seems like a parallel idea added to the paper that does not seem to add much value.
- It is also not clear how the induced 2-norms in eq.(2) is computed. Q is a matrix \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W}  whose induced 2-norm is its largest singular value. It seems computationally expensive to compute such cost function. Is it possible the authors really mean the Frobenius norm?

Overall, the proposed distillation method works well in practice but the paper has some organization issues and unclear notation.

This paper proposes to investigate attention transfers between a teacher and a student network. 

Attention transfer is performed by minimising the l2 distance between the teacher/student attention maps at different layers, in addition to minimising the classification loss and optionally a knowledge distillation term.
Authors define several activation based attentions (sum of absolute feature values raise at the power p or max of values raised at the power p). They also propose a gradient based attention (derivative of the Loss w.r.t. inputs). 

They evaluate their approaches on several datasets (CIFAR, Cub/Scene, Imagenet) showing that attention transfers  does help improving the student network test performance.  However, the student networks performs worst than the teacher, even with attention.

Few remarks/questions:
- in section 3 authors  claim that networks with higher accuracy have a higher spatial correlation between the object and the attention map. While Figure 4 is compelling, it would be nice to have quantitative results showing that as well.
- how did you choose the hyperparameter values, it would be nice to see what is the impact of $\beta$.
- it would be nice to report teacher train and validation loss in Figure 7 b)
- from the experiments, it is not clear what at the pros/cons of the different attention maps
- AT does not lead to better result than the teacher. However, the student networks have less parameters. It would be interesting to characterise the corresponding speed-up. If you keep the same architecture between the student and the teacher, is there any benefit to the attention transfer?

In summary:
Pros:
- Clearly written and well motivated.
- Consistent improvement of the student with attention compared to the student alone.
Cons:
- Students have worst performances than the teacher models.
- It is not clear which attention to use in which case?
- Somewhat incremental novelty relatively to Fitnet

This paper learns to use deep features for visual servoing. Visual servoing is a longstanding problem in robotics where, given a model of the environment and a camera, one can use visual feedback to drive the motion of a robot. Deep feature visual servoing is a new approach that uses CNNs to extract features from the camera images and use these features to estimate the current error between the desired feature and the actual feature in the camera image. The paper presents an algorithm that uses the estimated error to determine the next direction of motion for the robot and this fitted Q-iteration method is used to update the controller. The algorithm is tested on a model of a Hillman hand, but the method is general enough that it should be applicable to other robots with different controls. The paper presents the results of several experiments with the robot hand in the average case outperforming an open loop configuration and close to a closed loop PID controller. The source code for the experiments is also made available to demonstrate experimental reproducibility. A limitation of the method is that it assumes the environment is known and does not require a feedback control system. gave This paper presents a method for learning visual servoing using deep features. The method uses a fitted Q-iteration method to compute the next command for a robotic servoing arm. The servoing target is a Hillman hand which is an underactuated robot with 24 degree of freedom which makes it challenging for a standard PID control. This paper presents experiments that use the fitted Q-iteration method to update the PID controller in order to improve the performance over a standard open loop and close loop control.

The Learning Visual Servoing with Deep Features and Fitted Q-Iteration paper has addressed the problem of learning visual servoing mechanism by using learned visual features, learned predictive dynamics models, and reinforcement learning. As the problem setting, the paper focuses on target following, with the goal of designing algorithms that can learn a visual servo using low amounts of data of the target in question, to enable quick adaptation to new targets. The results show that we can learn an effective visual servo on a complex synthetic car following benchmark using just 20 training trajectory samples for reinforcement learning. The paper has introduced a novel approach for visual servoing, which focuses on using learned visual features, learned predictive dynamics models, and reinforcement learning. The paper makes the following strength and improvement over the prior arts: 1. The paper uses visual features, which have much higher representation capacity than image pixels or hand-designed keypoints, for visual servoing. It shows that visual features, taken from object classification model, can be used together with a bilinear predictive model to learn an effective visual servo. 2. The paper uses fitted Q-iteration to learn which features are best suited for the task at hand. 3. The paper uses reinforcement learning for model-free visual servoing for the first time. It shows substantial improvement over a conventional approach based on image pixels or hand-designed keypoints, and it demonstrates an improvement in sample-efficiency of more than two orders of magnitude over standard model-free deep reinforcement learning algorithms. The paper can be further improved by addressing the following issues: 1. The paper only uses 20 training trajectory samples for reinforcement learning. It can be improved by training on more samples or using other algorithms to find the best sample set. 2. The paper only uses visual features for target following. It can be further improved by applying the learned visual servoing to other domains, such as grasping, locomotion, end-effector positioning.

The paper proposes a novel approach for learning visual servoing based on Q-iteration. The main contributions of the paper are:

1. Bilinear dynamics model for predicting next frame (features) based on action and current frame
2. Formulation of servoing with a Q-function that learns weights for different feature channels
3. An elegant method for optimizing the Bellman error to learn the Q-function

Pros:
+ The paper does a good job of exploring different ways to connect the action (u_t) and frame representation (y_t) to predict next frame features (y_{t+1}). They argue in favour of a locally connected bilinear model which strikes the balance between computation and expressive ability. 

Cons:
- While, sec. 4 makes good arguments for different choices, I would have liked to see more experimental results comparing the 3 approaches: fully connected, convolutional and locally connected dynamics.

Pros: 
+ The idea of weighting different channels to capture the importance of obejcts in different channels seems more effective than treating errors across all channels equally. This is also validated experimentally, where unweighted performance suffers consistently.
+ Solving the Bellman error is a difficult problem in Q-learning approaches. The current paper presents a solid optimization scheme based on the key-observation that scaling Q-function parameters does not affect the best policy chosen. This enables a more elegant FQI approach as opposed to typical optimization schemes which (c_t + \gamma min_u Q_{t+1}) fixed. 

Cons:
- However, I would have liked to see the difference between FQI and such an iterative approach which holds the second term in Eq. 5 fixed.

Experimental results:
- Overall, I find the experimental results unsatisfying given the small scale and toy simulations. However, the lack of benchmarks in this domain needs to be recognized.
- Also, as pointed out in pre-review section, the idea of modifying the VGG needs to be experimentally validated. In its current form, it is not clear whether the modified VGG would perform better than the original version.

Overall, the contribution of the paper is solid in terms of technical novelty and problem formulations. However, the paper could use stronger experiments as suggested to earlier to bolster its claims.

This paper investigates the benefits of visual servoing using a learned
visual representation. The authors  propose to first learn an action-conditional
bilinear model of the visual features (obtained from a pre-trained VGG net) from
which a policy can be derived using a linearization of the dynamics. A multi-scale,
multi-channel and locally-connected variant of the bilinear model is presented.
Since the bilinear model only predicts the dynamics one step ahead, the paper
proposes a weighted objective which incorporates the long-term values of the
current policy. The evaluation problem is addressed using a fitted-value approach.

The paper is well written, mathematically solid, and conceptually exhaustive.
The experiments also demonstrate the benefits of using a value-weighted objective
and is an important contribution of this paper. This paper also seems to be the
first to outline a trust-region fitted-q iteration algorithm. The use of
pre-trained visual features is also shown to help, empirically, for generalization.

Overall, I recommend this paper as it would benefit many researchers in robotics.
However, in the context of this conference, I find the contribution specifically on
the "representation" problem to be limited. It shows that a pre-trained VGG
representation is useful, but does not consider learning it end-to-end. This is not
to say that it should be end-to-end, but proportionally speaking, the paper
spends more time on the control problem than the representation learning one.
Also, the policy representation is fixed and the values are approximated
in linear form using problem-specific features. This doesn't make the paper
less valuable, but perhaps less aligned with what I think ICLR should be about.

1) Summary

This paper proposes to tackle visual servoing (specifically target following) using spatial feature maps from convolutional networks pre-trained on general image classification tasks. The authors combine bilinear models of one-step dynamics of visual feature maps at multiple scales with a reinforcement learning algorithm to learn a servoing policy. This policy is learned by minimizing a regularized weighted average of distances to features predicted by the aforementioned model of visual dynamics.

2) Contributions

+ Controlled experiments in simulation quantifying the usefulness of pre-trained deep features for visual servoing.
+ Clear performance benefits with respect to many sensible baselines, including ones using ground truth bounding boxes.
+ Principled learning of multi-scale visual feature weights with an efficient trust-region fitted Q-iteration algorithm to handle the problem of distractors.
+ Good sample efficiency thanks to the choice of Q-function approximator and the model-based one-step visual feature dynamics.
+ Open source virtual city environment to benchmark visual servoing.

3) Suggestions for improvement

- More complex benchmark:
Although the environment is not just a toy synthetic one, the experiments would benefit greatly from more complex visual conditions (clutter, distractors, appearance and motion variety, environment richness and diversity, etc). At least, the realism and diversity of object appearances could be vastly improved by using a larger number of 3D car models, including more realistic and diverse ones that can be obtained from Google SketchUp for instance, and populating the environment with more distractor cars (in traffic or parked). This is important as the main desired quality of the approach is robustness to visual variations.

- End-to-end and representation learning:
Although the improvements are already significant in the current synthetic experiments, it would be interesting to measure the impact of end-to-end training (i.e. also fine-tuning the convnet), as it is possibly needed for better generalization in more challenging visual conditions. It would also allow to measure the benefit of deep representation learning for visual servoing, which would be relevant to ICLR (there is no representation learning so far, although the method can be straightforwardly adapted as the authors mention briefly).

- Reproducibility:
The formalism and algorithms are clearly explained, but there is a slightly overwhelming mass of practical tricks and implementation details described with varying levels of details throughout the paper and appendix. Grouping, simplifying, or reorganizing the exposition of these implementation details would help, but a better way would probably consist in only summarizing the most important ones in section and link to an open source implementation of the method for completeness.

- Typos:
p.2: "learning is a relative[ly] recent addition"
p.2: "be applied [to] directly learn"

4) Conclusion

In spite of the aforementioned limits of the experiments, this paper is interesting and solid, in part thanks to the excellent reply to the pre-review questions and the subsequent improved revision. This leads me to believe the authors are more than capable of following to a significant extent the aforementioned suggestions for improvement, thus leading to an even better paper.

machine_text: This work proposes a novel approach to combine LfD and HRL, which I find very interesting. The main idea is to reduce the state space of the high level agent by learning a low dimensional representation using a LSTM, and then apply the Actor-Critic algorithm to this reduced space. I think the authors use the term "Neural Hongxi Machine" for this new hierarchical agent, which is an original and nice name. I also have some questions regarding the empirical evaluation. In particular, I wonder how the performance of the baseline policy is evaluated. The baseline is an untrained NN model, and in my experience, the performance of NNs often converges toward a limit (even when L1 and L2 norms are clipping the weights) rather than staying at the same point. I think the performances over 5 trials may differ significantly. To be specific, here are some comments: 1- In the subsection "Policies and baseline methods" and in the first line of Table 1, I don't really understand why the baseline is a single layer neural network and not a multi-layer network. Is it because of the computation cost? If so, I suggest to also report the results with a 2-layer MLP as the baseline. 2- In the first line of Table 1, it is said that the baseline model converges in around 25M steps, but in the text, it is mentioned that the training data for the baseline model is generated from the trained neural network model. Does it mean that the baseline model needs more than 25M iterations to converge? In this case, I think it is not fair to compare with the trained neural network model, since the trained model is already optimized. 3- In the second line of Table 1, the score of the 1-layer MLP is incorrect, it should be 0.40 instead of 0.75. 4- The performance of the trained single layer neural network seems very high. Is it really zero-shot, i.e., the model has never seen any observation except for the last one? How can we be sure that the model has not memorized the last observation and does not rely on it to predict the future? Another potential issue is the normalization of rewards. The authors mention that they normalize the range of the rewards, and that the total reward is the sum of all slot rewards. While I can understand that the total-sum normalization is used for scaling the scores between different agents, the slot-specific-sum normalization is not obvious to me. To my understanding, this normalization is only valid for tasks with fixed episode length, e.g., a single server problem. In this case, once a task is given, all slot rewards are defined. However, in hierarchical RL, the duration of each episode is not fixed and can vary from episode to episode. How do we normalize the rewards in this case? Overall, I think this is an interesting idea, and the introduction of the Hongxi machine may trigger some future research on hierarchical RL. However, the empirical evaluation is not very convincing, and some parts need further explanation.

This paper considers a hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) problem where an agent must learn to act under the hierarchical structure, i.e. agent-level and group-level, with continuous state and action spaces. Traditionally, value-based methods have been used for HRL, but they suffer from inefficient update of the Q function estimation. To address this problem, the authors propose a novel HRL approach using a neural network with a Monte Carlo method to approximate the expected value in the update process. The experimental results show that the proposed algorithm can effectively solve the HRL problem. Strengths: - The introduction of the hierarchical structure into the HRL problem is reasonable. - The proposed algorithm has a near-optimal performance. Weaknesses: - The proposed algorithm has a high computation cost, which may be a problem when applied to real problems. Overall, this work provides a new perspective for the HRL problem. However, additional work is still needed to reduce the computation cost to be applied to real-world problems. \next Module 1 - Problem Statement Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (HRL) is a class of algorithms that tries to split the complexity of classical reinforcement learning (RL) by introducing a hierarchy structure into the system. For example, the state space might be global, while the action space may be partitioned into small pieces assignable to different agents. One critical issue in HRL is the learning of the value function, which evaluates the overall return of the system. The existing algorithms for this problem have two main limitations. First, they are not able to scale to large-scale problems due to the high computational cost. Second, they usually assume that the decision-maker is a single centralized agent, while in practice the decision-maker may be a group of agents, each of which makes a local decision. Module 2 - Introduction In this work, the authors consider a hierarchical reinforcement learning problem with continuous state and action spaces. Specifically, the state space $\mathcal{X}$ is divided into small partitions $\mathcal{X}_1, \mathcal{X}_2, \dots, \mathcal{X}_I$ with equal size. The action space is also divided into small pieces assignable to different agents. The hierarchical structure is described by a tree, where the leaf nodes correspond to small partitions and the root node is the state space $\mathcal{X}$ itself. Each node in the tree is also associated with a sub-group. The goal is to make the sub-group’s action $a_n$ according to the state $x_n$ and based on the action $a_{n-1}$ of the previous node. This hierarchical reinforcement learning problem can be formulated as an optimal control problem. The authors use the Bellman equation to prove the equivalence between the HRL problem and a neural network. The value function is represented by a neural network $V(s,a;\theta)$, where $\theta$ denotes all the learnable parameters. The idea of the proposed approach is to use a Monte-Carlo method to approximate the expected value, and the transition and reward functions are also computed by the neural network. With the Monte-Carlo method, the expected value is approximated by a Monte-Carlo tree that only needs to be trained once during the learning process. Module 3 - Algorithm The algorithm consists of four modules. First, the domain knowledge needs to be incorporated to determine the number of sub-groups and the partition in each sub-group. Second, the transition function is used to compute the state’s next state and reward using the Monte-Carlo method. Third, the value function is updated by a small gradient descent method using the first-order approximation. Last, the agent’s action is derived by using the Monte-Carlo tree and the current value function. Module 4 - Experiments and Results At each iteration, the expected value is computed by a Monte-Carlo tree which only needs to be trained once. The gradient descent is used to update the value function. The proposed algorithm can be applied to a wide range of domains, and the results are shown to be near-optimal. Module 5 - Future Work Future work should focus on reducing the time complexity. Module 6 - Applications The hierarchical reinforcement learning problem is widely used in operations research and multi-agent systems. For example, when simulating an electricity network, it is important to take into account the different time-scales associated with short-term fluctuations in supply and demand and with the operation over a longer time-horizon. Hierarchical reinforcement learning can be used to solve this problem by assigning a group of relatively long-lived agents to a state or region. I also found the choice of information-theoretic regularizer very appropriate, as I would also choose this method for my own projects for similar reasons. I also find the choice of skills to be very sensible and indeed span a wide range of useful applications. I do feel that the technical description of the pre-training environment does get a bit confusing at times and could be improved. I also do think the introduction could use some proofreading for language as it may be difficult to follow for non-native English speakers. I think the paper is definitely good for giving the reader some insight into the domain and I would be happy to see it published in the IJRR. ystolic Neural Networks for Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning my Grapsphus! my Thanks for this opportunity to review this manuscript. I very much like the focus on hierarchical methods for RL, which I find to be an under-utilized yet very powerful approach for solving complex real-world problems. The key idea is to divide the learning problem into smaller components (skills) which can themselves solve the problem quickly, and then use the learned skills to solve the target task. This approach elegantly handles the hard task of efficiently transferring knowledge from one task to another, without needing explicit representations of the common task structure, or complex inference mechanisms. The choice of the intrinsic motivation for pre-training is also very appropriate, as it also focuses the learners attention on the critical aspects of the task, while allowing for wide coverage of the learning space. I also like the particular choice of the information-theoretic regularizer, as I think it nicely blends into the overall approach without getting in the way. I also think that the technical details of the pre-training environment are well motivated, and provide a good foundation for later learning. In general, I think the paper is nicely written, and I look forward to seeing this research published.

This paper addresses the problem of training neural networks to solve hierarchical RL problems. The major idea is to first train a network in an environment that pre-trains a wide span of useful skills, and then use the skills to train the policy on a set of predefined high-level challenges. The learned policy can then be evaluated on a set of known tasks to check the generalization ability. The main idea is inspired by hierarchical reinforcement learning and intrinsic motivation, but the solution is built on Stochastic NNs with information-theoretic regularizer to pre-train a broad spectrum of skills, and then combine these skills using a high-level proxy reward to solve various challenges. The major contributions of this work are as follows: (1) A general framework that can pre-train a wide span of skills in an efficient and sample-efficient way; (2) A novel information-theoretic regularizer that is simple to implement and significantly improves the generalization ability of the resulting policies; (3) Extensive experiments that demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach on several hierarchical RL tasks, comparing to state-of-the-art techniques in the literature. Interesting work on hierarchical control, similar to the work of Heess et al. 
Experiments are strong and manage to complete benchmarks that previous work could not. Analysis of the experiments is a bit on the weaker side.

(1) Like other reviewers, I find the use of the term ‘intrinsic’ motivation somewhat inappropriate (mostly because of its current meaning in RL). The pre-training tasks from Heess et al., while not identical, are similar. 

(2) The Mutual Information regularization is elegant and works generally well, but does not seem to help in the more complex mazes 1,2 and 3. The authors note this - is there any interpretation or analysis for this result?

(4) It would be interesting to provide some analysis of the switching behavior of the agent. More generally, some further analysis of the policies (failure modes, effects of switching time on performance) would have been welcome.

The paper presents a method for hierarchical RL using stochastic neural networks. The paper has introduced using information-theoretic measure of option identifiability as an additional reward for learning a diverse mixture of sub-policies. One nice result in the paper is the comparison with strong baseline which directly combines the intrinsic rewards with sparse rewards and shows that this supposedly smooth reward can’t solve tasks. Besides the argument made from the authors on difficulty on long-term credit assignment/benefits from hierarchical abstraction, one possible explanation for this might be the diversity requirement imposed in sub-policy training, which is assumed to be off in the baseline case. Wonder if this can shed insights into improving the baseline and proposing new end-to-end hierarchical policy learning as hierarchical REPS/option-critic etc. papers do. Nice visualizations.

The paper presents a promising direction, and it may be strengthened further by possibly addressing some of the following points. 

1) Limited diversification of sub-policies: Both concatenation and bilinear integration allow only minimal differentiations in sub-policies through first hidden weight, which is not a problem in the tested tasks because they essentially require same locomotion policies with minimal diversification, but such limitation can be more obvious in other tasks where ideal sub-policies are more diverse. Thus it is interesting to see it apply on harder, non-locomotion domains, where ideal sub-policies are not that similar, e.g. for manipulation, solving some task from one state can be very different from solving it from another state. 

2) Limitation on hierarchical policies: Manager network is trained while the sub-policies are fixed. Furthermore, the time steps for sub-policies are fixed. This requires “intrinsic” rewards and their learned sub-policies to be very good for solving down-stream tasks. It would be nice to see some more discussions/results on handling such cases, ideally connecting to end-to-end hierarchical policy learning.

Paper Title: Nonparametric Neural Networks Authors: Kjetil Tille, Hamed Deghat, Lars B. B. S. Skadsem linking nonparametric regression and deep neural networks. The core idea is to replace the traditional fully-connected layer in neural networks with a nonparametric regression layer that maps the input to a non-linear function. The model is trained by minimizing a approximation error on an annotated held-out validation set. The method is tested on two regression problems (on log-concave sequences and on electricity demand) and compared against neural networks with fully-connected layers. Results show that nonparametric neural networks outperform fully-connected neural networks on all validation error metrics. Strengths: The main advantage of the proposed method is that it does not require the computation or storage of intermediate fully connected layers. This makes the method particularly well suited for large scale problems. A potential disadvantage of the method is the need to use a validation set to optimize the network architecture. Dear all,

Below are some more responses to two points raised. Both responses are reflected in a new version of the paper I just uploaded.

The following has changed in the paper:

 - section 3.1 (self-similar nonlinearities) is new
 - the final paragraph of section 3 is new
 - section 7.2 (proof of new proposition) is new

The paper is now longer than 8 pages. Having looked at many other submitted papers, it appears that the 8 page requirement is not very serious. If the area chair would prefer an 8 page paper, I can move some more stuff to the appendix.

** Reducing the number of hyperparameters **

Two questions that came up throughout the reviews is whether our method reduces the number of hyperparameters and whether there is an automatic way to set lambda. 

One advantage of nonparametric networks is that instead of having one hyperparameter per layer (size) there is one hyperparameter for the entire network (lambda) that controls size. It is worth pointing out that this reduction in complexity is not arbitrary. In fact, one can prove that in a ReLU network, one regularization parameter lambda captures all the complexity of having one regularization parameter per layer because we could replace all of these regularization parameters with their geometric mean without changing the objective. (See the newly included-in-the-paper proposition 1.) Hence, nonparametric networks apportion regularization to each layer automatically.

While we don't (yet) have a great way of efficiently picking the single remaining lambda, this reduction in complexity certainly contributes to reducing hyperparameter complexity.

** Computational cost of AdaRad (in response to reviewer 1) **

(From the paper:) Using AdaRad over SGD incurs additional computational cost. However, that cost scales more gracefully than the cost of, for example, RMSprop. AdaRad normalizes each fan-in instead of each individual weight, so many of its operations scale only with the number of units and not with the number of weights in the network. In Table \ref{costTable}, we compare the costs of SGD, AdaRad and RMSprop. Further, RMSprop has a larger memory footprint than AdaRad. It requires a cache of size equal to the number of weights, whereas AdaRad only requires 2 caches of size equal to the number of neurons.

Costs (per minibatch and weight)

SGD, no $\ell_2$ shrinkage: 1 multiplication
SGD with $\ell_2$ shrinkage: 3 multiplications
AdaRad, no $\ell_2$ shrinkage: 4 multiplications
AdaRad with $\ell_2$ shrinkage: 4 multiplications
RMSprop, no $\ell_2$ shrinkage: 4 multiplications, 1 division, 1 square root
RMSprop with $\ell_2$ shrinkage: 6 multiplications, 1 division, 1 square root

Best,
George

This paper proposes a nonparametric neural network model, which automatically learns the size of the model during the training process. The key idea is to randomly add zero units and use sparse regularizer to automatically null out the weights that are irrelevant. The idea sounds to be a random search approach over discrete space with the help of sparse regularization to eliminate useless units. This is an important problem and the paper gives interesting results. My main comments are listed below:

What is the additional computation complexity of the algorithm? The decomposition of each fan-in weights into a parallel component and an orthogonal component and the transformation into radial-angular coordinates may require a lot of extra computation time. The authors may need to discuss the extra amount of operations relative to the parametric neural network. Furthermore, it would be useful to show some running time experiments.

It is observed that nonparametric networks return small networks on the convex dataset so that it is inferior to parametric networks. Any insight on this?

I agree with reviewer 2 on the interesting part of the paper. The idea of removing or adding units is definitely an interesting direction, that will make a model grow or shrink along the lines required by the problem and the data, not the user prior knowledge.

The authors offer an interesting theoretical result that proves that under fan out or fan in regularization the optimum of the error function is achieved for finite number of parameters - so the net does not grow indefinitely, until it over-fits perfectly the data.
That reminds me of more traditional approaches such as Lasso or Elastic Net, in which the regularization produces sparse weights. I would  have like more intuition to be given for this theorem. It is a nice result, somewhat expected (at last for me it is intuitive) and I would have liked such intuition to be given some space in the paper. For example, less discussion of prior work (that is nice too, but not as important as discussing and studying the main result of the paper) could make more room for addressing the theoretical results. Please also see below (point 2) for some suggestions.

I have a few other comments to make:

1. An interesting experiment would be to show that a model such as yours, where the nodes (neurons) are added or removed automatically can outperform a net with the same number of nodes (at the end, after complete learning), in which the size and number of nodes per layer are fixed from the start. This would prove the efficiency of the idea. This is where your method is interesting: do you save nodes that are not needed and replace them with nodes that are needed? Do you optimize performance vs. memory?

I understand that experiments along this line are given in Figure 2, with mixed results. The Figure i must say, is not very clear, but it is possible to interpret under careful inspection.

In some the non-parametric nets are doing better and others are doing worse than the parametric ones. Even in such case i could see the usefulness of the method as it helps discovering the structure. 

What i don't fully understand is why they can do better sometimes than the end net which could be trained from scratch: why is the nonparametric version of learning better than the parametric version, when the final net is known in advance? Could you give more insight?

2. Can you better discuss the meaning and implications of Theorem 1. I feel this theorem is just put there with no proper discussion. Beyond the proofs, from the Appendix, what is the key insight of the Theorem? What does it say, in plain English? To me, the conclusion seems almost natural and obvious. Is there some powerful insight? 

As i have mentioned previously, i feel this theoretical result deserves more space, with even more experiments to back it up. For example, can regularizer parameter lambda  be predicted given the data - is there a property in the data that can help guessing the right lambda? My feeling is that lambda is the key factor for determining the final net structure. Is this true? 

How much does the structure of the final net depend on the initialization? Do you get different nets if you start from different random weights? How different are they?

What happens when fan in and fan out regularizers are combined? Do you still have the same theoretical result?

I have a few additional questions:

1. Why do you say that adding zero units changes the regularizer value? For example, does L2 norm change if you add zero values?

2. Zero units are defined as having either the fan in or the fan out weights being zero. I think that what you meant is that both fan in and fan out weights are zero, otherwise you cannot remove the unit and keep the same output f. This should be clarified better I think.

I changed my rating to 7, while hoping that the authors will address my comments above.

This paper addresses the problem of allowing networks to change the number of units that are used during training.  This is done in a simple but elegant and well-motivated way.  Units with zero input or output weights are added or removed during training, while a group sparsity norm for regularization is used to encourage unit weights to go to zero.  The main theoretical contribution is to show that with proper regularization, the loss is minimized by a network with a finite number of units.  In practice, this result does not guarantee that the resulting network will not over- or under-fit the training data, but some initial experiments show that this does not seem to be the case.

One potential advantage of approaches that learn the number of units to use in a network is to ease the burden of tuning hyperparameters.   One disadvantage of this approach (and maybe any such approach) is that it does not really solve this problem.  The network still has several hyperparameters that implicitly control the number of units that will emerge, including parameters that control how often new units are added and how rapidly weights may decay to zero.  It is not clear whether these hyperparameters will be easier or harder to tune than the ones in standard approaches.  In fairness, the authors do not claim that they have made training easier, but it is a little disappointing that this does not seem to be the case.

The authors do emphasize that they are able to train networks that use fewer units to achieve comparable performance to networks trained parametrically.  This is potentially important, because smaller networks can reduce run-time at testing, and power consumption and memory footprint, which is important on mobile devices in particular.  However, the authors do not compare experimentally to existing approaches that attempt to reduce the size of parametrically trained networks (eg., by pruning trained networks) so it is not clear whether this approach is really competitive with the best current approaches to reducing the size of trained networks.

Another potential disadvantage of the proposed approach is that the same hyperparameters control both the number of units that will appear in the network and the training time.  Therefore, training might potentially be much slower for this approach than for a parametric approach with fixed hyperparameters. In practice, many parametric approaches require methods like grid search to choose hyperparameters, which can be very slow, but in many other cases experience with similar problems can make the choice of hyperparameters relatively easy.  This means that the cost of grid search is not always paid, but the slowness of the authors’ approach may be endemic.  The authors do not discuss how this issue will scale as much larger networks are trained.  It is a concern that this approach may not be practical for large-scale networks, because training will be very slow.

In general, the experiments are helpful and encouraging, but not comprehensive or totally convincing.  I would want to see experiments on much larger problems before I was convinced that this approach can really be practical or widely useful.  

Overall, I found this to be an interesting and clearly written paper that makes a potentially useful point.  The overall vision of building networks that can grow and adapt through life-long learning is inspiring, and this type of work might be needed to realize such a vision.  But the current results remain pretty speculative.
