2. Zero units are defined as having either the fan in or the fan out weights being zero. I think that what you meant is that both fan in and fan out weights are zero, otherwise you cannot remove the unit and keep the same output f. This should be clarified better I think.

I changed my rating to 7, while hoping that the authors will address my comments above.

This paper addresses the problem of allowing networks to change the number of units that are used during training.  This is done in a simple but elegant and well-motivated way.  Units with zero input or output weights are added or removed during training, while a group sparsity norm for regularization is used to encourage unit weights to go to zero.  The main theoretical contribution is to show that with proper regularization, the loss is minimized by a network with a finite number of units.  In practice, this result does not guarantee that the resulting network will not over- or under-fit the training data, but some initial experiments show that this does not seem to be the case.

One potential advantage of approaches that learn the number of units to use in a network is to ease the burden of tuning hyperparameters.   One disadvantage of this approach (and maybe any such approach) is that it does not really solve this problem.  The network still has several hyperparameters that implicitly control the number of units that will emerge, including parameters that control how often new units are added and how rapidly weights may decay to zero.  It is not clear whether these hyperparameters will be easier or harder to tune than the ones in standard approaches.  In fairness, the authors do not claim that they have made training easier, but it is a little disappointing that this does not seem to be the case.

The authors do emphasize that they are able to train networks that use fewer units to achieve comparable performance to networks trained parametrically.  This is potentially important, because smaller networks can reduce run-time at testing, and power consumption and memory footprint, which is important on mobile devices in particular.  However, the authors do not compare experimentally to existing approaches that attempt to reduce the size of parametrically trained networks (eg., by pruning trained networks) so it is not clear whether this approach is really competitive with the best current approaches to reducing the size of trained networks.

Another potential disadvantage of the proposed approach is that the same hyperparameters control both the number of units that will appear in the network and the training time.  Therefore, training might potentially be much slower for this approach than for a parametric approach with fixed hyperparameters. In practice, many parametric approaches require methods like grid search to choose hyperparameters, which can be very slow, but in many other cases experience with similar problems can make the choice of hyperparameters relatively easy.  This means that the cost of grid search is not always paid, but the slowness of the authors’ approach may be endemic.  The authors do not discuss how this issue will scale as much larger networks are trained.  It is a concern that this approach may not be practical for large-scale networks, because training will be very slow.

In general, the experiments are helpful and encouraging, but not comprehensive or totally convincing.  I would want to see experiments on much larger problems before I was convinced that this approach can really be practical or widely useful.  

Overall, I found this to be an interesting and clearly written paper that makes a potentially useful point.  The overall vision of building networks that can grow and adapt through life-long learning is inspiring, and this type of work might be needed to realize such a vision.  But the current results remain pretty speculative.

Extra points for clarity of the description and good pictures. Even more extra points for actually specifying what spaces are which layers are mapping into which (\mathbb symbol - two thumbs up!).

Overall, I liked the paper.

This paper prunes entire groups of filters in CNN so that they reduce computational cost and at the same time do not result in sparse connectivity. This result is important to speed up and compress neural networks while being able to use standard fully-connected linear algebra routines. 
The results are a 10% improvements in ResNet-like and ImageNet, which may be also achieved with better design of networks. New networks should have been also compared, but this we know it is time-consuming.
A good paper with some useful results.

This paper proposes a simple method for pruning filters in two types of architecture to decrease the time for execution.

Pros:
- Impressively retains accuracy on popular models on ImageNet and Cifar10

Cons:
- There is no justification for for low L1 or L2 norm being a good selection criteria. There are two easy critical missing baselines of 1) randomly pruning filters, 2) pruning filters with low activation pattern norms on training set.
- There is no direct comparison to the multitude of other pruning and speedup methods.
- While FLOPs are reported, it is not clear what empirical speedup this method gives, which is what people interested in these methods care about. Wall-clock speedup is trivial to report, so the lack of wall-clock speedup is suspect.

This paper proposes a very simple idea (prune low-weight filters from ConvNets) in order to reduce FLOPs and memory consumption. The proposed method is experimented on with VGG-16 and ResNets on CIFAR10 and ImageNet.

Pros:
- Creates *structured* sparsity, which automatically improves performance without changing the underlying convolution implementation
- Very simple to implement

Cons:
- No evaluation of how pruning impacts transfer learning

I'm generally positive about this work. While the main idea is almost trivial, I am not aware of any other papers that propose exactly the same idea and show a good set of experimental results. Therefore I'm inclined to accept it. The only major downside is that the paper does not evaluate the impact of filter pruning on transfer learning. For example, there is not much interest in the tasks of CIFAR10 or even ImageNet. Instead, the main interest in both academia and industry is the value of the learned representation for transferring to other tasks. One might expect filter pruning (or any other kind of pruning) to harm transfer learning. It's possible that the while the main task has about the same performance, transfer learning is strongly hurt. This paper has missed an opportunity to explore that direction.

This paper Improves Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) by incorporating the idea of Denoising Feature Matching (DFM) into the GAN training process. In the context of image generation, this allows the GAN to generate high quality images without over-fitting to the training data. One major challenge in training GANs is the need for a substantial amount of carefully generated training data. In many real world scenarios, this is not possible or costly to obtain. In such cases, over-fitting to the training data is of significant concern. The DFM algorithm allows the GAN to identify and match essential features between the generated image and the original sample in the training dataset. By incorporating this information into the GAN training, the generator learns to produce not just high-fidelity images but also representations that are invariant to small noise variations. The GAN model is trained on the Imagenet dataset, it is evaluated the perceptual quality of the images generated. In summary, the DFM improves the generalisation capability of the GAN model to new samples and reduces the need for expensive super-sets of the training dataset. Strength:The main strength of this paper is that it provides an easy way to improve GANs in an effective way without overfitting to the training data. The method is generic and can be applied to many GAN variants. Weakness:The proposed model is tested on the Imagenet dataset and it is unclear how it generalises to other GAN variants or other types of datasets. Overall, the DFM is a promising way to improve GAN models without the need for additional training data. The method is generic and can be applied to many GAN variants. This is evidenced by its success on the DC-GAN model. It would be interesting to further evaluate the method on other GANs and other types of datasets. Overall, this is a well-written paper. However, it would score higher if it was more detailed in its evaluation of other GAN variants and other types of datasets.

Overall, I find the paper interesting, but I have a few major points to make. The main idea of this paper is to improve the quality of generated images by using denoising auto-encoder to model the distribution of discriminator features and use it to guide the generator. In the beginning, the author conducts some experiments with CIFAR and FashionMNIST and it seems to work pretty well. Then the author apply this idea to UNMASK Generator, and the result is really good. However, I think this idea could be very general and apply to other GAN model. For example, if I just apply this idea to improve LARS-GAN, the quality of generated images will still be bad. I think the main problem is that the generated images by LARS-GAN still lack of high-level structure, like face masks in this example. The paper only focus on this specific case, but I think this general idea can be used to improve the quality of other type of GAN models. Secondly, I think the way of matching the distribution of features could be more flexible. For example, in the beginning of the paper, the author first tried to use Gaussian mixture model to model the distribution of features, but it didn't work very well. I think if we know the property of features and their distribution, we can design a better model to guide the generator. Thirdly, I think the way of adding the new loss is not the best way. In the beginning of the paper, the author uses CIFAR to determine the number of clusters of features. I think this is a very manual process, and it's not generalizable. In summary, I think this is an interesting paper with good result, but the method could be more general, and the way of adding the new loss should be more generalizable.

This paper Improving Generative Adversarial Networks with Denoising Feature Matching addresses some shortcomings of the original by proposing a denoising feature matching (DFM) training procedure for GANs. The framework estimates and tracks the distribution of discriminator features and uses it to propose high-level targets for the generator. The new loss with the original is evaluated on the task of unsupervised image synthesis from datasets comprising a diverse set of visual categories, noting a qualitative and quantitative improvement in the ``objectness'' of the resulting samples. We propose a more principled method to train GANs by learning feature matching in the spirit of denoising auto-encoders. Like in DANN but unlike in current GANs, we train a denoising feature matching network to find an encoding of the data that is equivalent to the encoded version of the training data. We use the encoding to synthesize new samples by simulating the original training procedure, but using the encoding as a good guess for the right feature representation. This procedure is inspired by recent work on solving ill-posed inverse problems using generative models. We apply it to train GANs using both the discriminator and generator as encoders, as well as separate encoders for each. The main contributions of this paper can be summarized as: - proposing a denoising feature matching procedure for training generative adversarial networks - applying the denoising feature matching procedure to train GANs with separate encoders for the generator and discriminator, as well as one encoder for both - combining the original GAN objective and the proposed denoising feature matching objective in different ways to address different shortcomings of the original - applying the proposed methods to unsupervised image synthesis from a diverse set of visual categories Overall, this is an interesting approach to training GANs, although I would suggest you specifically address the following points in the paper: - clarify the difference between DFM and the method proposed in DANN - explain how your method differs from the standard GAN setup - discuss the impact of combining DFM with the standard GAN setup Overall, your paper is a well-organized and presented piece that could find a good home in a specialized image processing journal. I have listed some suggestions for improvement in the points above. I look forward to reading new work on this topic and believe this paper will be an excellent foundation to future work in this area."
human_text:
The authors present a way to complement the Gerative Adversarial Network traning procedure with an additional term based on denoising autoencoders. The use of denoising autoencoders is motivated by the observation that they implicitly capture the distribution of the data they were trained on. While sampling methods based denoising autoencoders alone don't amount to very interesting generative models (at least no-one could demonstrate otherwise), this paper shows that it can be combined successfully with generative adversarial networks.

My overall assessment of this paper is that it is well written, well reasoned, and presents a good idea motivated from first principles. I feel that the idea presented here is not revolutionary or a very radical departure from what has been done before, I would have liked a slightly more structured experiments section which focusses on and provides insights into the relative merits of different choices one could make (see pre-review questions for details), rather than focussing just on demonstrating that a chosen variant works.

In addition to this general review, I have already posted specific questions and criticism in the pre-review questions - thanks for the authors' responses. Based on those responses the area I am most uncomfortable about is whether the (Alain & Bengio, 2014) intuition about the denoising autoencoders is valid if it all happens in a nonlinear featurespace. If the denoiser function's behaviour ends up depending on the Jacobian of the nonlinear transformation Phi, another question is whether this dependence is exploitable by the optimization scheme.

The idea of using a denoising autoencoder on features of the discriminator is sensible, and explored and described well here. The qualitative results are pretty good, but it would be nice to try some of the more recent likelihood-based methods for quantitative evaluation, as the inception score is not very satisfying. Also it would be interesting to see if this additional term helps in scaling up to larger images.

A revision has been posted, addressing several textual concerns, correcting an error in equation 5, and including discussion of the effect of the feature space Phi on the score function learned by the DAE. A further update will follow later this week if any of the additional experiments bear fruit. Apologies again for the delay.

This paper is well written, and well presented. This method is using denoise autoencoder to learn an implicit probability distribution helps reduce training difficulty, which is neat. In my view, joint training with an auto-encoder is providing extra auxiliary gradient information to improve generator. Providing auxiliary information may be a methodology to improve GAN.  
 
Extra comment:
Please add more discussion with EBGAN in next version.

This paper is about using denoising autoencoders to improve performance in GANs. In particular, the features as determined by the discriminator, of images generated by the generator, are fed into a denoising AE and we try to have these be reconstructed well. I think it's an interesting idea to use this "extra information" -- namely the feature representations learned by the discriminator. It seems very much in the spirit of ICLR! My main concern, though, is that I'm not wholly convinced on the nature of the improvement. This method achieves higher inception scores than other methods in some cases, but I have a hard time interpreting these scores and thus a hard time getting excited by the results. In particular, the authors have not convinced me that the benefits outweigh the required additional sophistication both conceptually and implementation-wise (speaking of which, will code be released?). One thing I'd be curious to know is, how hard is it to get this thing to actually work? 

Also, I view GANs as a means to an end -- while I'm not particularly excited about generating realistic images (especially in 32x32), I'm very excited about the future potential of GAN-based systems. So it would have been nice to see these improvements in inception score translate into improvements in a more useful task. But this criticism could probably apply to many GAN papers and so perhaps isn't fair here. 

I do think the idea of exploiting "extra information" (like discriminator features) is interesting both inside and outside the context of this paper.

|| C(phi(x)) - r(C(phi(x))) ||  rather than  || phi(x) - r(C(phi(x))) ||

2) This approach involves training 3 networks. It would be interesting to know what kind of training scheme was used? Whether, D,G and r networks are trained for one iteration each, or if some networks are trained for more iterations before updating the next network? 

3) It would also be interesting to know whether parameters l_denoise and l_adv are fixed or adjusted during training?

The authors present a way to complement the Gerative Adversarial Network traning procedure with an additional term based on denoising autoencoders. The use of denoising autoencoders is motivated by the observation that they implicitly capture the distribution of the data they were trained on. While sampling methods based denoising autoencoders alone don't amount to very interesting generative models (at least no-one could demonstrate otherwise), this paper shows that it can be combined successfully with generative adversarial networks.

My overall assessment of this paper is that it is well written, well reasoned, and presents a good idea motivated from first principles. I feel that the idea presented here is not revolutionary or a very radical departure from what has been done before, I would have liked a slightly more structured experiments section which focusses on and provides insights into the relative merits of different choices one could make (see pre-review questions for details), rather than focussing just on demonstrating that a chosen variant works.

In addition to this general review, I have already posted specific questions and criticism in the pre-review questions - thanks for the authors' responses. Based on those responses the area I am most uncomfortable about is whether the (Alain & Bengio, 2014) intuition about the denoising autoencoders is valid if it all happens in a nonlinear featurespace. If the denoiser function's behaviour ends up depending on the Jacobian of the nonlinear transformation Phi, another question is whether this dependence is exploitable by the optimization scheme.

The idea of using a denoising autoencoder on features of the discriminator is sensible, and explored and described well here. The qualitative results are pretty good, but it would be nice to try some of the more recent likelihood-based methods for quantitative evaluation, as the inception score is not very satisfying. Also it would be interesting to see if this additional term helps in scaling up to larger images.

A revision has been posted, addressing several textual concerns, correcting an error in equation 5, and including discussion of the effect of the feature space Phi on the score function learned by the DAE. A further update will follow later this week if any of the additional experiments bear fruit. Apologies again for the delay.

This paper is well written, and well presented. This method is using denoise autoencoder to learn an implicit probability distribution helps reduce training difficulty, which is neat. In my view, joint training with an auto-encoder is providing extra auxiliary gradient information to improve generator. Providing auxiliary information may be a methodology to improve GAN.  
 
Extra comment:
Please add more discussion with EBGAN in next version.

This paper is about using denoising autoencoders to improve performance in GANs. In particular, the features as determined by the discriminator, of images generated by the generator, are fed into a denoising AE and we try to have these be reconstructed well. I think it's an interesting idea to use this "extra information" -- namely the feature representations learned by the discriminator. It seems very much in the spirit of ICLR! My main concern, though, is that I'm not wholly convinced on the nature of the improvement. This method achieves higher inception scores than other methods in some cases, but I have a hard time interpreting these scores and thus a hard time getting excited by the results. In particular, the authors have not convinced me that the benefits outweigh the required additional sophistication both conceptually and implementation-wise (speaking of which, will code be released?). One thing I'd be curious to know is, how hard is it to get this thing to actually work? 

Also, I view GANs as a means to an end -- while I'm not particularly excited about generating realistic images (especially in 32x32), I'm very excited about the future potential of GAN-based systems. So it would have been nice to see these improvements in inception score translate into improvements in a more useful task. But this criticism could probably apply to many GAN papers and so perhaps isn't fair here. 

I do think the idea of exploiting "extra information" (like discriminator features) is interesting both inside and outside the context of this paper.

machine_text: This is a very nice contribution to the growing body of work in using deep neural networks to solve control problems. The authors present a framework for using a CNN trained on simulation to control a system in the physical domain. The framework they describe uses policy gradients with a function approximation in the Policy networks and a CSH DNN as the value function. In experiments they show that the framework can be trained to control different systems such as a pendulum and a simulated jetpack. The value function CSH DNN is trained using a replay buffer that maintains a separate log of both sim and real time data. This is an interesting approach to the need for simulation-real training data pairs and the authors do an admirable job of showing how to apply the framework to a system for which there is no simulation. The authors also implement a variation of the framework using a MobileNetv2 and demonstrate that this reduces the number of training iterations required. Overall this is an excellent paper that describes a valuable framework for using deep learning to solve control problems. The framework has the capability of learning good policies for a variety of problems but also requires simulation data for training the value function. The simulation requirements make this a framework that is best used in settings where there is access to a simulation platform that allows running the system of interest at simulated speeds. Citation: Jain, Rahul, Bhushan Shroff, and Wei Liu. "Learning Invariant Feature Spaces to Transfer Skills with Reinforcement Learning." Autonomous Agents and Multi-Agent Systems, 2019. Citing this paper: Rahul Jain, Bhushan Shroff, and Wei Liu. "Learning Invariant Feature Space to Transfer Skills with Reinforcement Learning." 2019. AI Technical Report. Preprint: https://github.com/Paddy4Courses/RL_TSS MAKS-2019 REVIEWS All three reviewers gave this paper very positive feedback. The consensus was that the framework described in the paper could have broad applicability to a wide range of RL problems. The framework could also be made easier to use by removing the need for separate networks for the value function and the policy network. However, all three reviewers also agreed that the initial implementation of the framework using a MobileNx and a separate replay buffer to maintain real and simulated data was more than necessary and would detract from use of the framework by others. The first reviewer recommended addressing this by using a single large dataset that contains both real and simulated data. The second reviewer suggested using a single convolutional neural network to replace the separate networks for the real and simulated data. The third reviewer recommended combining the real and simulated data into a single training dataset and using a single network for the policy and value function, but recommended validating the resulting controller using a separate dataset of real data. Overall, all three reviewers found the work interesting and they had positive things to say about the framework described. The framework could potentially be useful to a wide range of users. However, the need for a separate network to handle the data that comes from the simulation makes it more complicated to use than it needs to be, and this may deter users from the work. Paper title is Learning Invariant Feature Spaces to Transfer Skills with Reinforcement Learning. The paper describes how to transfer skills between simulators using Feature Space Augmentation and Reinforcement Learning. The model uses three different component: Skill Base Network, Feature Space Augmentation and the Actor-Critic algorithm. The main strength of the paper is that it solves the problem of non-unique features in Sim to Sim transfer. As the name implies, the paper shows how to identify a set of invariant features across different simulator domains and uses these features to train the Skill Base Network. Another strength of the paper is that it applies the Feature Space Augmentation technique to solve the problem of insufficient sample efficiency of reinforcement learning. This is because the Feature Space Augmentation method generates an auxiliary task that is equivalent to the original task but easier to complete for the agent, thus incentivizing the agent to explore the environment more. Lastly, the paper also shows how to reduce the problem of poor generalization of the model to new simulators. This is achieved by using a multi-task actor-critic algorithm that can train multi-task networks for skill transfer. I hope this answers your question. Here are the strengths and weaknesses of the paper: Strength 1. The paper shows how to identify a set of invariant features across different simulator domains and uses these features to train the Skill Base Network. 2. The paper also shows how to reduce the problem of poor generalization of the model to new simulators. This is achieved by using a multi-task actor-critic algorithm that can train multi-task networks for skill transfer. Weakness 1. The lack of mathematical induction in some parts of the paper make the result hard to verify. In particular, at the end of the Section 3.3 (Page 8), the authors argue that the system "distill the transferable skill" from a large set of samples of the auxiliary task, but unfortunately, the basis for this argument is not fully articulated. 2. Secondly, the model in this paper may not work well on complex high-dimensional control tasks. Here, "high-dimensional" means the action space is too large to conveniently define a set of invariant features. For example, how to find a set of features to describe the position and angle of a telescope? 3. The long training time of the model is another weakness. The paper used PPO to train the model, which needs to run for 150 hours to train a trained model. In the real world, if we need to transfer between simulators, how can we let the model train for so long?

Generally this is a interesting problem and the approach is also reasonable. In this paper, the main idea is to use the skill learned from one agent to train a model to transform features in other agent, and then use the model to transform features to make sure they can be recognized by the other model. The main idea of this paper is sound, and also the experiments on different robot structures show that the approach can be applied to different types of robot with different structures. The main issue of this paper is that the experiments only works for two similar robots, and it will not work if the two robots have very different structures. In summary, the paper still has significant practical value, and the author can make it more attractive by performing experiments on more similar robot models. aly Thanks for the comprehensive review, we have followed your suggestion and performed additional experiments with more similar robots. Please see our updated version at https://github.com/sjhl/rl4robotics/blob/master/docs/publication_guidelines.md#revise-the-paper. The results show that our approach is more effective when the two robots have similar structures. We also thank the reviewers for their comments. Based on your comments, we made some adjustments to the model and the experiments, which you can find at https://github.com/sjhl/rl4robotics/blob/master/docs/publication_guidelines.md#revise-the-paper. We also implemented a model that can transfer between more similar robots, which you can find at https://github.com/sjhl/rl4robotics/blob/master/docs/publication_guidelines.md#Transfer-between-similar-robots. We think these additions make the paper more attractive and useful.

This paper is about transferring skills between agents with different morphologies. human_text:
The paper considers the problem of transferring skills between robots with different morphologies, in the context of agents that have to perform several tasks.  A core component of the proposed approach is to use a task-invariant future space, which can be shared between tasks & between agents.

Compared to previous work (Ammar et al. 2015), it seems the main contribution here is to “assume that good correspondences in episodic tasks can be extracted through time alignment” (Sec. 2).  This is an interesting hypothesis. There is also similarity to work by Raimalwala et al (2016), but the authors argue their method is better equipped to handle non-linear dynamics. These are two interesting hypotheses, however I don’t see that they have been verified in the presented empirical results.  In particular, the question of the pairing correspondence seems crucial. What happens when the time alignment is not suitable. Is it possible to use dynamic time warping (or similar method) to achieve reasonable results?  Robustness to misspecification of the pairing correspondence P seems a major concern.

In general, more comparison to other transfer methods, including those listed in Sec.2, would be very valuable.  The addition of Sec.5.1 is definitely a right step in this direction, but represents a small portion of the recent work on transfer learning.  I appreciate that other methods transfer other pieces of information (e.g. the policy), but still if the end goal is better performance, what is worth transferring (in addition to how to do the transfer) should be a reasonable question to explore.

Overall, the paper tackles an important problem, but this is a very active area of research, and further comparison to other methods would be worthwhile.  The method proposed of transferring the representation is well motivated, cleanly described, and conceptually sound.  The assumption that time alignment can be used for the state pairing seems problematic, and should be further validated.

Dear Reviewers and Area Chair,
The reviewers for the paper provided a positive evaluation, with suggestions for additional experiments providing comparisons with several prior methods, some clarifications, and brought up the important problem of addressing time-based correspondence alignment. We have edited the paper to include additional experiments that address these issues, and therefore believe that the reviewer concerns about the work have been addressed. We discuss the specifics below.

AnonReviewer 1 Comments: 
“Compared to previous work (Ammar et al. 2015)”
- Performed this comparison and added the results into the Figures 5 and 8. We found that our method performed significantly better than this prior work. 
“Is it possible to use dynamic time warping (or similar method) to achieve reasonable results?  Robustness to misspecification of the pairing correspondence P seems a major concern.”
- We introduced an EM style algorithm which removes this assumption. Description of this method are in Section 3.3.2, and results in Figures 5 and 8. 
“more comparison to other transfer methods, including those listed in Sec.2, would be very valuable”
- We have implemented several more baselines: KCCA, Unsupervised Manifold Alignment as suggested by Bou Ammar et al, Direct mappings, random projections, CCA in Figures 5 and 8.

AnonReviewer3 Comments: 
“preferable to see comparisons for something more current and up to date, such as manifold alignment or kernel CCA”, “comparisons to related approaches is not very up to date” 
-Performed comparisons to Kernel CCA and Manifold Alignment using Unsupervised Manifold Alignment (Wang and Mahadevan, Bou Ammar et al) and added to our experiments in Figures 5 and 8. 

AnonReviewer4 Comments: 
“A limitation of the paper is that the authors suppose that time alignment is trivial [...] could be dealt with through subsampling, dynamic time warping, or learning a matching function” 
-We introduce a new EM style algorithm alternating between feature learning and dynamic time warping. Description is in Section 3.3.2 and results in Figures 5 and 8. 
“Another baseline (worse than CCA) would be to just have the random projections for "f" and "g"”
-We added this comparison in Figures 5 and 8.
“at least a much bigger sample budget should be tested [...] control for the fact that the embeddings were trained with more iterations in the case of doing transfer” 
- We ran the baseline with a significantly higher sample budget as shown in Table 1. The poor performance is likely due to not enough guided exploration happening without good reward shaping for the baseline. 
“problem of learning invariant feature spaces is also linked to metric learning [...] no parallel is drawn with Multi-Task learning in ML ”
-The additional references suggested have been added in the Related Work (Section 2).

Dear reviewers,

We have addressed the concerns presented in the reviews, including comparisons to several prior methods and a method for automatically determining alignment, as detailed in the individual reviewer responses. If you have suggestions for additional comparisons, we would be happy to add them in the final version. As such, we hope you will consider adjusting your reviews accordingly. 

Regards
Abhishek, Coline, Yuxuan, Pieter, Sergey

We thank the reviewers for their comments. Most comments asked for additional comparisons and learned state correspondences. 
In response to reviewer comments, we have added the following to our paper:

1. Learning state correspondences by using an alternating optimization to jointly assign the state pairs in P and learn the embedding functions f and g. This significantly relaxes the assumption that states can be paired by time-step and provides better performance in experiment 1. See section 3.3.2 for a description of this method and figures 5 and 7a for results.

2. All of the comparisons suggested by the reviewers: kernel-CCA, unsupervised manifold alignment (Ammar et al. 2015), and random projections. Results are in Figures 5 and 7a.

3. Connections to metric learning and multitask learning in Section 2.

The comparisons have been run on experiments 1 and 2 and will be added to experiment 3 for the final version.

This paper presents an approach for skills transfer from one task to another in a control setting (trained by RL) by forcing the embeddings learned on two different tasks to be close (L2 penalty). The experiments are conducted in MuJoCo, with a set of experiments being from the state of the joints/links (5.2/5.3) and a set of experiments on the pixels (5.4). They exhibit transfer from arms with different number of links, and from a torque-driven arm to a tendon-driven arm.

One limitation of the paper is that the authors suppose that time alignment is trivial, because the tasks are all episodic and in the same domain. Time alignment is one form of domain adaptation / transfer that is not dealt with in the paper, that could be dealt with through subsampling, dynamic time warping, or learning a matching function (e.g. neural network).

General remarks: The approach is compared to CCA, which is a relevant baseline. However, as the paper is purely experimental, another baseline (worse than CCA) would be to just have the random projections for "f" and "g" (the embedding functions on the two domains), to check that the bad performance of the "no transfer" version of the model is due to over-specialisation of these embeddings. I would also add (for information) that the problem of learning invariant feature spaces is also linked to metric learning (e.g. [Xing et al. 2002]). More generally, no parallel is drawn with multi-task learning in ML. In the case of knowledge transfer (4.1.1), it may make sense to anneal \alpha.

The experiments feel a bit rushed. In particular, the performance of the baseline being always 0 (no transfer at all) is uninformative, at least a much bigger sample budget should be tested. Also, why does Figure 7.b contain no "CCA" nor "direct mapping" results? Another concern that I have with the experiments: (if/how) did the author control for the fact that the embeddings were trained with more iterations in the case of doing transfer?

Overall, the study of transfer is most welcomed in RL. The experiments in this paper are interesting enough for publication, but the paper could have been more thorough.

This paper explores transfer in reinforcement learning between agents that may be morphologically distinct. The key idea is for the source and target agent to have learned a shared skill, and then to use this to construct abstract feature spaces to enable the transfer of a new unshared skill in the source agent to the target agent. The paper is related to much other work on transfer that uses shared latent spaces, such as CCA and its variants, including manifold alignment and kernel CCA. 


The paper reports on experiments using a simple physics simulator between robot arms consisting of three vs. four links. For comparison, a simple CCA based approach is shown, although it would have been preferable to see comparisons for something more current and up to date, such as manifold alignment or kernel CCA. A three layer neural net is used to construct the latent feature spaces. 

The problem of transfer in RL is extremely important, and receives less attention than it should. This work uses an interesting hypothesis of trying to construct transfer based on shared skills between source and target agent. This is a promising approach. However, the comparisons to related approaches is not very up to date, and the domains are fairly simplistic. There is little by way of theoretical development of the ideas using MDP theory.

The paper considers the problem of transferring skills between robots with different morphologies, in the context of agents that have to perform several tasks.  A core component of the proposed approach is to use a task-invariant future space, which can be shared between tasks & between agents.

Compared to previous work (Ammar et al. 2015), it seems the main contribution here is to “assume that good correspondences in episodic tasks can be extracted through time alignment” (Sec. 2).  This is an interesting hypothesis. There is also similarity to work by Raimalwala et al (2016), but the authors argue their method is better equipped to handle non-linear dynamics. These are two interesting hypotheses, however I don’t see that they have been verified in the presented empirical results.  In particular, the question of the pairing correspondence seems crucial. What happens when the time alignment is not suitable. Is it possible to use dynamic time warping (or similar method) to achieve reasonable results?  Robustness to misspecification of the pairing correspondence P seems a major concern.

In general, more comparison to other transfer methods, including those listed in Sec.2, would be very valuable.  The addition of Sec.5.1 is definitely a right step in this direction, but represents a small portion of the recent work on transfer learning.  I appreciate that other methods transfer other pieces of information (e.g. the policy), but still if the end goal is better performance, what is worth transferring (in addition to how to do the transfer) should be a reasonable question to explore.

Overall, the paper tackles an important problem, but this is a very active area of research, and further comparison to other methods would be worthwhile.  The method proposed of transferring the representation is well motivated, cleanly described, and conceptually sound.  The assumption that time alignment can be used for the state pairing seems problematic, and should be further validated.

-We added comparisons of our method to directly predicting the target states from the source states (see Figures 5, 8a)
-We have clarified the description of P in Sec 4.1
-We have added two previous approaches to the related work section.

We thank the reviewers for their comments. Most comments asked for additional comparisons and learned state correspondences. 
In response to reviewer comments, we have added the following to our paper:

1. Learning state correspondences by using an alternating optimization to jointly assign the state pairs in P and learn the embedding functions f and g. This significantly relaxes the assumption that states can be paired by time-step and provides better performance in experiment 1. See section 3.3.2 for a description of this method and figures 5 and 7a for results.

2. All of the comparisons suggested by the reviewers: kernel-CCA, unsupervised manifold alignment (Ammar et al. 2015), and random projections. Results are in Figures 5 and 7a.

3. Connections to metric learning and multitask learning in Section 2.

The comparisons have been run on experiments 1 and 2 and will be added to experiment 3 for the final version.

This paper presents an approach for skills transfer from one task to another in a control setting (trained by RL) by forcing the embeddings learned on two different tasks to be close (L2 penalty). The experiments are conducted in MuJoCo, with a set of experiments being from the state of the joints/links (5.2/5.3) and a set of experiments on the pixels (5.4). They exhibit transfer from arms with different number of links, and from a torque-driven arm to a tendon-driven arm.

One limitation of the paper is that the authors suppose that time alignment is trivial, because the tasks are all episodic and in the same domain. Time alignment is one form of domain adaptation / transfer that is not dealt with in the paper, that could be dealt with through subsampling, dynamic time warping, or learning a matching function (e.g. neural network).

General remarks: The approach is compared to CCA, which is a relevant baseline. However, as the paper is purely experimental, another baseline (worse than CCA) would be to just have the random projections for "f" and "g" (the embedding functions on the two domains), to check that the bad performance of the "no transfer" version of the model is due to over-specialisation of these embeddings. I would also add (for information) that the problem of learning invariant feature spaces is also linked to metric learning (e.g. [Xing et al. 2002]). More generally, no parallel is drawn with multi-task learning in ML. In the case of knowledge transfer (4.1.1), it may make sense to anneal \alpha.

The experiments feel a bit rushed. In particular, the performance of the baseline being always 0 (no transfer at all) is uninformative, at least a much bigger sample budget should be tested. Also, why does Figure 7.b contain no "CCA" nor "direct mapping" results? Another concern that I have with the experiments: (if/how) did the author control for the fact that the embeddings were trained with more iterations in the case of doing transfer?

Overall, the study of transfer is most welcomed in RL. The experiments in this paper are interesting enough for publication, but the paper could have been more thorough.

This paper explores transfer in reinforcement learning between agents that may be morphologically distinct. The key idea is for the source and target agent to have learned a shared skill, and then to use this to construct abstract feature spaces to enable the transfer of a new unshared skill in the source agent to the target agent. The paper is related to much other work on transfer that uses shared latent spaces, such as CCA and its variants, including manifold alignment and kernel CCA. 


The paper reports on experiments using a simple physics simulator between robot arms consisting of three vs. four links. For comparison, a simple CCA based approach is shown, although it would have been preferable to see comparisons for something more current and up to date, such as manifold alignment or kernel CCA. A three layer neural net is used to construct the latent feature spaces. 

The problem of transfer in RL is extremely important, and receives less attention than it should. This work uses an interesting hypothesis of trying to construct transfer based on shared skills between source and target agent. This is a promising approach. However, the comparisons to related approaches is not very up to date, and the domains are fairly simplistic. There is little by way of theoretical development of the ideas using MDP theory.

The paper considers the problem of transferring skills between robots with different morphologies, in the context of agents that have to perform several tasks.  A core component of the proposed approach is to use a task-invariant future space, which can be shared between tasks & between agents.

Compared to previous work (Ammar et al. 2015), it seems the main contribution here is to “assume that good correspondences in episodic tasks can be extracted through time alignment” (Sec. 2).  This is an interesting hypothesis. There is also similarity to work by Raimalwala et al (2016), but the authors argue their method is better equipped to handle non-linear dynamics. These are two interesting hypotheses, however I don’t see that they have been verified in the presented empirical results.  In particular, the question of the pairing correspondence seems crucial. What happens when the time alignment is not suitable. Is it possible to use dynamic time warping (or similar method) to achieve reasonable results?  Robustness to misspecification of the pairing correspondence P seems a major concern.

In general, more comparison to other transfer methods, including those listed in Sec.2, would be very valuable.  The addition of Sec.5.1 is definitely a right step in this direction, but represents a small portion of the recent work on transfer learning.  I appreciate that other methods transfer other pieces of information (e.g. the policy), but still if the end goal is better performance, what is worth transferring (in addition to how to do the transfer) should be a reasonable question to explore.

Overall, the paper tackles an important problem, but this is a very active area of research, and further comparison to other methods would be worthwhile.  The method proposed of transferring the representation is well motivated, cleanly described, and conceptually sound.  The assumption that time alignment can be used for the state pairing seems problematic, and should be further validated.

To address the reviewers’ questions, we have made the following changes:
-We added comparisons of our method to using canonical correlation analysis to find the embedding functions F and G (see Figures 5 and 8a)
-We added comparisons of our method to directly predicting the target states from the source states (see Figures 5, 8a)
-We have clarified the description of P in Sec 4.1
-We have added two previous approaches to the related work section.

The key idea is to find the optimal transport plan that aligns thelearned view-manifold representation with the target view-point, such that the viewpoint and category predictions are made with respect to the transported subspace. Experiments show that the proposed method can transfer knowledge from a large-scale object classification task to novel object retrieval, and outperform several state-of-the-art methods on the challenging Covertype and Oxford-five databases. 008 Though this is an interesting problem, there are many aspects that need to be clarified before I can provide an authentic review. 1. The paper is only related to object classification, but not object detection. Object detection is an essential step in many vision tasks, such as autonomous driving and robotics. Without object detection, the derived viewpoint classification is useless. 2. There are several existing methods that can perform object detection in novel viewpoints. The method proposed in this paper can only perform baseline comparison with other methods, but cannot outperform them. 3. The model proposed in the paper was tested on two large-scale datasets, Oxford-five and Covertype. However, no information is provided about the implementation details of these datasets. We need to know the number of categories, training images and objects, which are important factors that can affect the result of viewpoint classification. These three issues require further research to be resolved before I can provide an authentic review.

Paper: Transfer of View-manifold Learning to Similarity Perception of Novel Objects Problem: Previous methods of learning deep similarity metrics from sim- pair source views, such as Multi-View CNN (MVC), learn global similarity metrics, but do not take into account different local details that can still be important for similarity assessment. One such example is viewing a dog as similar to a dog, but not similar to a automobile. This paper improves upon previous approaches of view-manifold learning and applies it to learning local similarity for novel object recognition. First, the paper describes the process of aligning a query view to a source view and using a Procrustes analysis to determine an optimal alignment (Orthogonal Procrustes Analysis, OPA). The process of OPA allows for local differences between views of the same object to be preserved while still ensuring that similar regions across views are aligned. Next, a deep convolutional network is used to learn the similarity metrics across the projected source views. The network takes as input the result of the projection through an OPA matrix and outputs similarity values for all pairings of target and source views. The pairing can be between a query and a single source view or between all pairs of source views and the result is a metric that can be used to order the similarity of all pairs of novel objects. This approach is effective in capturing local similarity while still accounting for different local features of objects. The learned metrics have been shown to improve performance on several classification tasks of object similarity.

The paper proposes a novel framework of view-manifold learning that can transfer to similar objects in both trained and untrained categories as well as to completely novel artificial synthetic objects. The idea of view-manifold learning was first proposed in the previous version of this paper and achieved state-of-the-art results on the CAD-120 dataset. In this version, the paper further develops the framework and presents several improvements. Firstly, it provides a more detailed discussion of the motivation and underlying theory of view-manifold learning. Then, it discusses in more details the modifications made in the previous version. In addition, the paper presents more results, including the comparison with the previous state-of-the-art and qualitative analyses of the learned transformation. Finally, it presents a qualitative analysis of the view-manifold transformation learned for novel objects as well as a quantitative evaluation on the artificially synthesized novel objects. ing highlights: 1. New analysis on the underlying theory of view-manifold learning 2. more details on the modifications made in the previous version 3. more experiments and more results 4. more qualitative and quantitative evaluations on the view-manifold transformation for both trained and untrained categories as well as novel objects Economics of Learning The model is trained in a supervised fashion and assumes a fixed set of views available at test time. Under this setting, our first contribution is to relax the assumption of fixed views during test time. We consider a more practical setting where the model can also query a limited number of new views for a new object for which it has no training data. This can be useful, for example, when showing the model new objects encountered in the wild. This new setting leads to a more flexible model that generalizes better than previous methods, as illustrated in Fig. 1. Our results also show that effective transfer is possible even without any view training data for the new objects. In this case, the model is only exposed to a limited number of artificial views of the object during training, which becomes sufficient for the target task. To achieve this view synthesis, the paper further develops a novel loss function that considers the problem of view synthesis and metric learning in one framework, as opposed to treating them in isolation. This enables our model to synthesize new views that are perceptually similar to the original input and at the same time learn a useful distance metric for the views of the same object. In summary, our main contributions are the following: 1. New analysis on the underlying theory of view-manifold learning 2. more details on the modifications made in the previous version 3. more experiments and more results 4. qualitative and quantitative evaluations on the view-manifold transformation for both trained and untrained categories as well as novel objects Overall, this is an exciting and novel approach to transfer deep models from one task to another, without requiring extra training data for the target task. The method can be easily applied to a number of applications where it may be difficult or costly to obtain annotated views of new objects, or where we need to handle a large number of new objects without retraining the model. Our code and dataset are made publicly available. Fig. 1. Test set accuracy of our model and several baselines with and without synthetic views. Abstract View-manifolds refer to a collection of views of the same object seen from different viewpoints. They form a manifold locally around a specific view of the object. To abstract away from the specific views, the view-manifolds across different objects may be overlapping. View-manifolds have been used to capture the illusion of object persistence and continuity in our visual experience, which are two important elements in our development of perception of similar objects. This paper proposes a view-manifold learning method to abstract away from the specific view representations. The method learns to re-train the deep convolutional neural network (DCNN) using only the view-invariant features to capture view-manifolds of object representations. It provides a unified view-manifolding method and distance metric learning method in one framework, by optimizing the view-manifold and distance metric under the constraint of same object persistence. View-manifold learning is further demonstrated to have potential in solving similar tasks of other tasks by learning view-invariant representations. View-manifolds also are further applied to solve the similar yet new object classification task. The paper demonstrates that with the same training process, view-manifold learning can also be applied to similar but new objects in both trained and untrained categories. The learned view-manifold transformation can help the trained and similar objects to be classified correctly, while new categories of objects or even completely novel artificial synthetic objects can be discriminated and recognized. View-manifolds are able to represent the abstraction from the specific input views and thus can be easily applied to many tasks which require processing of similar objects, where a limited number of viewpoints

The main contribution of this paper is the view-manifold learning and distance metric learning under object persistence constraints, which have not been jointly considered before, to similarity perception of novel objects. First, this paper develops a 3D object model that captures the notion of object persistence and continuity in our visual experience. Given a collection of 3D objects, the 3D object model contains multiple views of each object, each of which presents a unique aspect of the object’s appearance. The persistence of the 3D objects is achieved by factorizing the 3D object model into multiple “objects in scene” which persist through different views, and “view” which only depend on a single view of the 3D objects. The object persistence is modeled via distance metric learning in the view-manifold. The proposed view-manifold learning generalizes the traditional mean-shift clustering to the projection onto the associated view-manifold, which clusters the object representations based on their distances in the view-manifold. The distance metric is learned under the constraint of view persistence, so the representations of objects in the same 3D object model but with different views remain close to each other, while the representations of objects in different 3D object models far away in the distance. This view-manifold learning with distance metric learning under view persistence constraints can flexibly capture the view-realities and generate natural view-dependent similarities between objects. Second, the proposed similarity learning method is applied to similarity judgments of novel 3D objects and found to achieve more effective and general representations for novel object similarity perception. The proposed model is also evaluated against state-of-the-art methods on the ModelNet dataset.

This paper proposes a model to learn across different views of objects.  The key insight is to use a triplet loss that encourages two different views of the same object to be closer than an image of a different object.  The approach is evaluated on object instance and category retrieval and compared against baseline CNNs (untrained AlexNet and AlexNet fine-tuned for category classification) using fc7 features with cosine distance.  Furthermore, a comparison against human perception on the "Tenenbaum objects” is shown.

Positives: Leveraging a triplet loss for this problem may have some novelty (although it may be somewhat limited given some concurrent work; see below).  The paper is reasonably written.

Negatives: The paper is missing relevant references of related work in this space and should compare against an existing approach.

machine_text: The authors present a novel model for learning to sample from a foveal region in visual scenes. The model consists of two components: a salience map that determines which regions of a scene are relevant, and a location map that stores the foveal regions selected by the salience map. Initially, the model randomly samples foveal regions from a set of possible regions distributed over the entire visual scene. The model then updates the salience and location maps based on visual cues. The salience map becomes more refined over time, and eventually selects a small region of the visual scene as the foveal region. The model was tested on a database of images, which had been previously rated for visual attentional focus. The model was trained to sample from the region of the scene that the database indicated as the attentional focus. The model learned to sample from the foveal region with high accuracy, and also learned to distribute its gaze over the scene with high accuracy. The model can also be modified to sample from the scene instead of from a region within the scene, and in this case the model learns to sample from a region that has high contrast with the rest of the scene. The model therefore learns to focus its attention, and also learns to distribute its attention over the scene. The authors test the hypothesis that the model's ability to focus its attention is learned, and not hard-wired, by showing that the model still learns to focus its attention even when the salience map is periodically reset to a uniformly-distributed distribution.

The authors describe a model that learns to sample from where the eyes should look in a visual scene based on learned filters. The model first computes the center of mass for each object in the image and then searches in a sampling window around the expected location for each object. Compared to prior work on attentional sampling, the model in this work learns to attend to interesting regions of the visual scene rather than just the center. The authors evaluate the model on a video game challenge dataset and the model learns to pick the correct location to inspect about 65% of the time on average. The model also shows increased performance on other tasks that require attentional sampling such as visual search and dynamic scene segmentation. asty The authors describe a model that learns to sample from where the eyes should look in a visual scene based on learned filters. The model searches in a sampling window around the expected location for each object. Compared to prior work on attentional sampling, the model in this work learns to attend to interesting regions of the visual scene rather than just the center.

Overall, I find the work interesting and well presented, with some limitations. The main limitation I found is that the model is trained on a visual search task requiring the classification of an object embedded in a visual scene amidst background distractors using the smallest number of fixations. As a result, the model's trained retinal sampling lattice exhibits tiling properties that are optimized for such a task, rather than being biologically plausible. For example, it includes a high resolution foveal region and a low resolution periphery. Therefore, I recommend modifying the model's task to be more biologically plausible. Specifically, I recommend modifying the model's task to be visual search in natural images, rather than images from a single dataset with clearly demarcated edges (boundaries) such as Oxford Street. In this way, the trained retinal sampling lattice will include regions of high and low resolution that are learned from natural scenes, rather than having a static foveal region and a periphery with independent regions of high and low resolution. Other comments: P5L1: The authors frequently use the word 'tiling' in the paper, which is a commonly used term in computer science to describe the arrangement of a set of equal-sized squares in a square grid. I think the paper would be easier to read and follow if the authors would define 'tiling' and the tiling properties they are studying here when first needed, rather than repeatedly using the word 'tiling'. I would also suggest to replace 'tiling' with'similarity mapping' or'sampling' throughout the paper. 'Tiling' is a commonly used word in computer science, and therefore the reader might easily get lost in a labyrinth of acronyms and initialisms if used without an introduction. Furthermore, the tiling properties of the retinal sampling lattice are only one of the main findings of the work, and the title already claims to found the emergence of foveal image sampling from learning to attend in visual scenes. Therefore, it seems to me that introducing the tiling properties first, and explaining them in more detail later in the paper is more efficient and useful. For example, in the first paragraph of the subsection "The Retinal Sampling Lattice and its Tiling Properties", the authors first mention the tiling properties of the retinal sampling lattice and their function. After that, they also introduce the function of the tiling properties as a clue to the learning mechanism of the model. This introduction is not really necessary, because the reader who is already familiar with the tiling property might not understand the need for such an introduction. Moreover, I do not think this introduction adds anything to the understanding of the paper for the non-expert reader. Therefore, I suggest avoiding the introduction of the tiling properties until first needed, and explaining them in more detail only when necessary. P17L4: Instead of using the terms'motion streaks' and 'double humps', I think it would be more helpful to the reader if the authors would introduce and explain the term 'phase clustering'. This is a widely used term in the imaging sciences and closely describes what the authors are trying to explain here with the term'motion streaks' and 'double humps'. P18L11: 'Sampling' would be a better term than 'tiling' to describe the tiling properties of the retinal sampling lattice. P21L14: 'Phase clustering' would be a better term than 'tiling' to describe the tiling properties of the retinal sampling lattice. P23L23: 'Relative orientation' would be a better term than 'tiling' to describe the tiling properties of the retinal sampling lattice. P26L30: 'The foveal image sampling was emergent from the learning of scene attention' would be a better title, because the function of the tiling properties seems to be a significant finding of the work. P28L34:'sampling' would be a better term than 'tiling' to describe the tiling properties of the retinal sampling lattice. P30L41: 'function' would be a better term than 'purpose' to describe the tiling properties of the retinal sampling lattice. The paper “Emergence of foveal image sampling from learning to attend in visual scenes” by Tara T. Q. Lê et al. (https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.08144) describes a neural attention model with a learnable retinal sampling lattice. The model is trained on a visual search task requiring the classification of an object embedded in a visual scene amidst background distractors using the smallest number of fixations. We explore the tiling properties that emerge in the model’s retinal sampling lattice after training. Specifically, we show that this lattice resembles the eccentricity dependent sampling lattice of the primate retina, with a high resolution region in the fovea surrounded by a low resolution periphery. We also find conditions where these emergent properties are amplified or eliminated providing clues to their function. This work is interesting because it presents a biologically plausible model for foveal viewing that leveraging recent advances in Deep Learning for the attention mechanism. Strengths: The paper presents biological plausible model of foveal viewing that incorporates recent advances in Deep Learning for the attention mechanism. The paper is well-motivated and carefully designed to explain the emergence of tiling properties in the model’s retinal sampling lattice. The tiling properties are interpreted and explained from several aspects (e.g. eccentricity dependent sampling, high resolution region in the fovea). The tiling properties have potential implications for the function of the retina. The paper has clear and complete descriptions of the model and results. The paper presents a baseline for future work in the area. The paper was written in an accessible and concise manner. Weaknesses: The main weakness is that the tiling property is only partially present in the model. The figure showing the tiling property only shows part of the sampling lattice and has many black borders. More figures showing more parts of the sampling lattice would better demonstrate the tiling property. Some figures are difficult to read because the contrast is either too high or too low. Adjusting contrast and making edges clearer would greatly improve the readability of the paper. The model is only tested on a visual search task that requires the classification of an object embedded in a visual scene amidst background distractors. The model’s tiling ability needs to be validated by eye-tracking experiment. Conclusion: This paper presents a novel approach for the development of a foveal image sampling mechanism and its implications for the structure and function of the primate retina. The model of the proposed attention mechanism effectively learns to attend to the location of an object of interest by only foveating a small region of the scene. This work is interesting for several reasons. First, it shows that an artificial system can be designed that not only learns to attend to specific regions of the visual field, but also learns to tile this region of the visual field in a way that is similar to that of the primate retina. Second, this paper is among the first to propose and investigate the function of the tiling property in the fovea. The analysis of the tiling property can serve as a useful model system to help understand how the fovea and its surrounding periphery interface with human behavior. Overall, this paper presents the novel idea that the tiling property can be used to explain the functionality of the fovea. The paper has identified a possible direction for future research on this topic by presenting a baseline model and providing an interpretation of the obtained results. I think the paper makes a significant contribution to the field of computational neuroscience. The Tiling property in the fovea with low resolution in the periphery may provide clues to understanding foveal suppression. The tiling property presented in this paper has significant implications for several fields of cognitive neuroscience, especially vision science. The tiling property means that the image of the whole visual field is divided into smaller and more regular pieces, and these pieces are represented in a more organized fashion in the brain. If attention is an optimizing search process, the tiling property implies that the cortex is able to resolve smaller and more regular pieces of information. If this is the case, this property may facilitate various forms of prediction, and improve the efficiency of various tasks that need to be performed with the visual information, such as the control of action, planning, and reasoning. The model presented in this paper can help us understand the coding efficiency of the image in the cortex. The tiling property suggests that the image is broken up into smaller and more regular pieces, allowing the cortex to process the image more efficiently. The tiling property can also help us understand the purpose of foveal suppression. The tiling property provides a foundation for foveal suppression. If the images are broken up into smaller and more regular pieces, then foveal suppression can be easily accomplished

This paper proposed a neural attention model which has a learnable and differentiable sampling lattice. The work is well motivated as few previous work focus on learning the sampling lattice but with a fixed lattice. This work is quite similar to Spatial Transformer Networks (Jaderberg 2015), but the sampling lattice is learned by the model. The experiments showed that the model can learn a meaning lattice to the visual search task where the sampling lattice looks similar to human being's. 

The main concern of the paper is that experiments are not sufficient. The paper only reports the results on a modified clustered MNIST dataset. It would be more interesting if the authors could conduct  the model on real datasets, such as Toronto Face dataset, CUB bird dataset and SVHN. For example, for the Face dataset, it would be nice if the model can learn to attend different parts of the face for expression recognition, or attend different part of birds for fine-grained classification. Since the authors replied in the pre-review question that the model can learn meaningful lattice on MSCOCO dataset, I think it would be better to add that results into the paper.

Another drawback of the model is that the paper only compare with different variants of itselves. I suggest that this paper should compare with  Spatial Transformer Networks, DRAW, etc., on the same dataset to show the advantage of the learned sampling lattice.

This was a borderline case. All reviewers and the AC appeared to find the paper interesting, while having some reservations. Given the originality of the work, the PCs decided to lean toward acceptance. We do encourage however the authors to revise their paper based on reviewer feedback as much as possible, to increase its potential for impact.

This paper presents a succinct argument that the principle of optimizing receptive field location and size in a simulated eye that can make saccades with respect to a classification error of images of data whose labels depend on variable-size and variable-location subimages, explains the existence of a foveal area in e.g. the primate retina.

The argument could be improved by using more-realistic image data and drawing more direct correspondence with the number, receptive field sizes and eccentricities of retinal cells in e.g. the macaque, but the authors would then face the challenge of identifying a loss function that is both biologically plausible and supportive of their claim.

The argument could also be improved by commenting on the timescales involved. Presumably the density of the foveal center depends on the number of of saccades allowed by the inference process, as well as the size of the target sub-images, and also has an impact on the overall classification accuracy.

Why does the classification error rate of dataset 2 remain stubbornly at 24%? This seems so high that the model may not be working the way we’d like it to. It seems that the overall argument of the paper pre-supposes that the model can be trained to be a good classifier. If there are other training strategies or other models that work better and differently, then it raises the question of why do our eyes and visual cortex not work more like *those ones* if evolutionary pressures are applying the same pressure as our training objective.

Why does the model with zooming powers out-do the translation-only model on dataset 1 (where all target images are the same size) and tie the translation-only model dataset 2 (where the target images have different sizes, for which the zooming model should be tailor-made?). Between this strange tie and the high classification rate on Dataset 2, I wonder if maybe one or both models isn’t being trained to its potential, which would undermine the overall claim.

Comparing this model to other attention models (e.g. spatial transformer networks, DRAW) would be irrelevant to what I take to be the main point of the paper, but it would address the potential concerns above that training just didn’t go very well, or there was some problem with the model parameterization that could be easily fixed.

The paper presented an extension to the current visual attention model that learns a deformable sampling lattice.  Comparing to the fixed sampling lattice from previous works, the proposed method shows different sampling strategy can emerge depending on the visual classification tasks. The authors empirically demonstrated the learnt sampling lattice outperforms the fixed strategies. More interestingly, when the attention mechanism is constrained  to be translation only, the proposed model learns a sampling lattice resembles the retina found in the primate retina.  


Pros:
+ The paper is generally well organized and written 
+ The qualitative analysis in the experimental section is very comprehensive.

Cons:
-  The paper could benefit substantially from additional experiments on different datasets.
-  It is not clear from the tables the proposed learnt sampling  lattice offer any computation benefit when comparing to  a fixed sampling strategy with zooming capability, e.g. the one used in DRAW model.

Overall, I really like the paper. I think the experimental section can be improved by additional experiments and more quantitative analysis with other baselines. Because the current revision of the paper only shows experiments on digit dataset with black background, it is hard to generalize the finding or even to verify the claims in the paper, e.g.  linear relationship
between eccentricity and sampling interval leads to the primate retina, from the results on a single dataset.

machine_text: The work presents an information-theoretic framework for fast and robust unsupervised learning via neural population infomax. The framework utilizes an approximate message passing scheme to learn latent representation for data, while the information-theoretic property of the scheme allows for automatic determination of the number of clusters based on the learnt representation. The model and algorithm are tested on both synthetic and real-world data and shown to outperform other competing schemes both in clustering validity and learning efficiency. actress Overall this paper presents an interesting information-theoretic unsupervised learning framework. I think the key contributions of the framework, learning automatic number of clusters as well as fast learning, might be useful to other researchers. I also think the framework is general and might be applied to other data types beyond images and the simulations used in the paper. I suggest the authors to add more comparisons with other state-of-the-art unsupervised learning methods and more applications of the framework to other data types. As a general suggestion, the paper would benefit from being condensed; currently the text is mostly a description of the theoretical framework and its application to a few specific examples, and the mathematical derivation and equations are hidden in the middle of the text. performed Overall this paper presents an interesting information-theoretic unsupervised learning framework.
