This paper proposed a novel adversarial framework to train a model from demonstrations in a third-person perspective, to perform the task in the first-person view. Here the adversarial training is used to extract a novice-expert (or third-person/first-person) independent feature so that the agent can use to perform the same policy in a different view point.

While the idea is quite elegant and novel (I enjoy reading it), more experiments are needed to justify the approach. Probably the most important issue is that there is no baseline, e.g., what if we train the model with the image from the same viewpoint? It should be better than the proposed approach but how close are they? How the performance changes when we gradually change the viewpoint from third-person to first-person? Another important question is that maybe the network just blindly remembers the policy, in this case, the extracted feature could be artifacts of the input image that implicitly counts the time tick in some way (and thus domain-agonistic), but can still perform reasonable policy. Since the experiments are conduct in a synthetic environment, this might happen. An easy check is to run the algorithm on multiple viewpoint and/or with blurred/differently rendered images, and/or with random initial conditions.

Other ablation analysis is also needed. For example, I am not fully convinced by the gradient flipping trick used in Eqn. 5, and in the experiments there is no ablation analysis for that (GAN/EM style training versus gradient flipping trick). For the experiments, Fig. 4,5,6 does not have error bars and is not very convincing.

The paper presents an interesting new problem setup for imitation learning: an agent tries to imitate a trajectory demonstrated by an expert but said trajectory is demonstrated in a different state or observation space than the one accessible by the agent (although the dynamics of the underlying MDP are shared). The paper proposes a solution strategy that combines recent work on domain confusion losses with a recent IRL method based on generative adversarial networks.

I believe the general problem to be relevant and agree with the authors that it results in a more natural formulation for imitation learning that might be more widely applicable.
There are however a few issues with the paper in its current state that make the paper fall short of being a great exploration of a novel idea. I will list these concerns in the following (in arbitrary order)
- The paper feels at times to be a bit hurriedly written (this also mainly manifests itself in the experiments, see comment below) and makes a few fairly strong claims in the introduction that in my opinion are not backed up by their approach. For example: "Advancements in this class of algorithms would significantly improve the state of robotics, because it will enable anyone to easily teach robots new skills"; given that the current method to my understanding has the same issues that come with standard GAN training (e.g. instability etc.) and requires a very accurate simulator to work well (since TRPO will require a large number of simulated trajectories in each step) this seems like an overstatement.
  There are some sentences that are ungrammatical or switch tense in the middle of the sentence making the paper harder to read than necessary, e.g. Page 2: "we find that this simple approach has been able to solve the problems"
- The general idea of third person imitation learning is nice, clear and (at least to my understanding) also novel. However, instead of exploring how to generally adapt current IRL algorithms to this setting the authors pick a specific approach that they find promising (using GANs for IRL) and extend it. A significant amount of time is then spent on explaining why current IRL algorithms will fail in the third-person setting. I fail to see why the situation for the GAN based approach is any different than that of any other existing IRL algorithm. To be more clear: I see no reason why e.g. behavioral cloning could not be extended with a domain confusion loss in exactly the same way as the approach presented. To this end it would have been nice to rather discuss which algorithms can be adapted in the same way (and also test them) and which ones cannot. One straightforward approach to apply any IRL algorithm would for example be to train two autoencoders for both domains that share higher layers + a domain confusion loss on the highest layer, should that not result in features that are directly usable? If not, why?
- While the general argument that existing IRL algorithms will fail in the proposed setting seems reasonable it is still unfortunate that no attempts have been made to validate this empirically. No comparison is made regarding what happens when one e.g. performs supervised learning (behavioral cloning) using the expert observations and then transfers to the changed domain. How well would this work in practice ? Also, how fast can different IRL algorithms solve the target task in general (assuming a first person perspective) ?
- Although I like the idea of presenting the experiments as being directed towards answering a specific set of questions I feel like the posed questions somewhat distract from the main theme of the paper. Question 2 suddenly makes the use of additional velocity information to be a main point of importance and the experiments regarding Question 3 in the end only contain evaluations regarding two hyperparameters (ignoring all other parameters such as the parameters for TRPO, the number of rollouts per iteration, the number of presented expert episodes and  the design choices for the GAN). I understand that not all of these can be evaluated thoroughly in a conference paper but I feel like some more experiments or at least some discussion would have helped here.
- The presented experimental evaluation somewhat hides the cost of TRPO training with the obtained reward function. How many roll-outs are necessary in each step?
- The experiments lack some details: How are the expert trajectories obtained? The domains for the pendulum experiment seem identical except for coloring of the pole, is that correct (I am surprised this small change seems to have such a detrimental effect)? Figure 3 shows average performance over 5 trials, what about Figure 5 (if this is also average performance, what is the variance here)? Given that GANs are not easy to train, how often does the training fail/were you able to re-use the hyperparameters across all experiments?

The paper proposes a method to adapt a model trained on source domain to new samples from the target domain. The main problem is that the source and target domain may have different data distributions, thus this problem is called domain adaptation. The main idea is to regularize the Adversarial Discriminative Domain Adaptation (ADDAC) framework with a variational approach. The variational approach prevents the solution from moving towards the source distribution and instead learn a compromise solution that combines both source and target domain. Strength The proposed method is effective and easily applicable. Additionally, the proposed method is applied to a vanilla Adversarial Discriminative Domain Adaptation (ADDAC) which is a popular approach to domain adaptation. The code for this method is publicly available. There are several problems that the proposed variational method can be extended to. For example, the proposed method can be applied to a dueling discriminative domain adaptation framework. The dueling adaptation approach is to generate negative samples for source samples, which are used to train the target domain only classifier. dueling approach is applied to, for example, UTFN and BAM. Another possible extension is to apply the method to other adversarial learning frameworks. For example, the authors can replace the original non-saturating loss with another loss function (for example, triplet loss) and apply the method to triplet discriminative domain adaptation. Weaknesses The following problems can be considered as weaknesses of the paper: 1. the method is evaluated on sentiment analysis task and the quantitative results are not promising. The suggested implementation uses ADDA code by the authors, but the code is not released. This reduces the transparency of the results. 2. the proposed method is applied to a vanilla ADDAC framework, while the method can be also applied to dueling and triplin discriminative domain adaptation. It would be useful to study whether the method can improve the results of these approaches. 3. the method is applied to a BPRM which is widely used for knowledge transfer. It would be useful to study whether the method can be applied to other transfer learning frameworks, for example, LSTMA and DAN. Overall, the paper provides a general method to adapt a source model to a new target domain. The suggested method is easy to apply and the code is publicly available. The method can be easily extended to other adaptation frameworks and applications.

human_text:
This paper combines variational RNN (VRNN) and domain adversarial networks (DANN) for domain adaptation in the sequence modelling domain.  The VRNN is used to learn representations for sequential data, which is the hidden states of the last time step.  The DANN is used to make the representations domain invariant, therefore achieving cross domain adaptation.

Experiments are done on a number of data sets, and the proposed method (VRADA) outperforms baselines including DANN, VFAE and R-DANN on almost all of them.

I don't have questions about the proposed model, the model is quite clear and seems to be a simple combination of VRNN and DANN.  But a few questions came up during the pre-review question phase:

- As the authors have mentioned, DANN in general outperforms MMD based methods, however, the VFAE method which is based on MMD regularization on the representations seems to outperform DANN across the board.  That seems to indicate VRNN + MMD should also be a good combination.

- One baseline the authors showed in the experiments is R-DANN, which is an RNN version of DANN.  There are two differences between R-DANN and VRADA: (1) R-DANN uses deterministic RNN for representation learning, while VRADA uses variational RNN; (2) on target domain R-DANN only optimizes adversarial loss, while VRADA optimizes both adversarial loss and reconstruction loss for feature learning.  It would be good to analyze further where the performance gain comes from.

The paper offers a contribution to domain adaptation. The novelty with respect to methodology is modest, utilizing an existing variational RNN formulation and adversarial training method in this setting. But the application is important and results are strong. Improving the analysis of the results, and studying variants of the approach to understand the contribution of each component, will make this paper considerably stronnger. We encourage the authors to revise accordingly.

Thank you all for your time and thoughtful comments! We have incorporated your suggestions to improve our paper.

First, we would like to clarify the key contributions of our paper. Motivated by challenges within the healthcare domain, we are proposing a novel unsupervised deep domain adaptation framework for knowledge transfer within healthcare time series data. The framework 1) captures temporal dependencies present in the time series data, and 2) transfers these dependencies from  the source to target domain via adversarial training, and 3) is able to obtain state-of-the-art results, outperforming previous domain adaptation approaches. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time that complex temporal latent dependencies have been used to transfer knowledge in healthcare multivariate time series data. It is worth noting that our domain adaptation framework is general and is suitable for applications where dependencies are present in the multivariate time series data. 

The other major contribution of our work is moreso from an applications perspective. Healthcare data is a new frontier for machine learning. The data we worked with is complex: it’s temporal, it's multivariate, and it’s noisy,. Healthcare data is also quite different from the data that machine learning scientists are accustomed to working with. The dataset we used (which is the largest publicly available medical data healthset) only have a few thousand training examples (which we then further subdivided into multiple domains). This is considered a small dataset. Further, domain adaptation is typically done when there are ample unlabeled target examples which can be used to learn some mutual representation. We did not have this luxury. Despite, our model outperformed all other models.

We have uploaded a revised draft to address the questions and comments of the reviewers. In the revised draft, we have added an appendix section with the following new results:
- Discussion on different training methods for our VRADA model and their results
- Results on variations of VRADA model including
  --- Adversarial training at each time step
  --- Impact of adversarial training on the memory cell state visualizations
  --- Study on the effect of reconstruction loss on the prediction performance
- R-DANN model architecture block diagram

The work combines variational recurrent neural networks, and adversarial neural networks to handle domain adaptation for time series data. The proposed method, along with several competing algorithms are compared on two healthcare datasets constructed from MIMIC-III in domain adaptation settings.

The new contribution of the work is relatively small. It extends VRNN with adversarial training for learning domain agnostic representations. From the experimental results, the proposed method clearly out-performs competing algorithms. However, it is not clear where the advantage is coming from. The only difference between the proposed method and R-DANN is using variational RNN vs RNN. Little insights were provided on how this could bring such a big difference in terms of performance and the drastic difference in the temporal dependencies captured by these two methods in Figure 4.  

Detailed comments:
1. Please provide more details on what is plotted in Figure 1. Is 1 (b) is the t-sne projection of representations learned by DANN or R-DANN? The text in section 4.4 suggests it’s the later case. It is surprising to see such a regular plot for VRADA.  What do you think are the two dominant latent factors encoded in figure 1 (c)? 

2. In Table 2, the two baselines have quite significant difference in performance testing on the entire target (including validation set) vs on the test set only. VRADA, on the other hand, performs almost identical in these two settings. Could you please offer some explanation on this?

3. Please explain figure 3 and 4 in more details. how to interpret the x-axis of figure 3, and the x and y axes of figure 4. Again the right two plots in figure 4 are extremely regular comparing to the ones on the left.

Update: I thank the authors for their comments! After reading them, I still think the paper is not novel enough so I'm leaving the rating untouched.

This paper proposes a domain adaptation technique for time series. The core of the approach is a combination of variational recurrent neural networks and adversarial domain adaptation (at the last time step).

Pros:

1. The authors consider a very important application of domain adaptation.

2. The paper is well-written and relatively easy to read.

3. Solid empirical evaluation. The authors compare their method against several recent domain adaptation techniques on a number of datasets.

Cons:

1. The novelty of the approach is relatively low: it’s just a straightforward fusion of the existing techniques.

2. The paper lacks any motivation for use of the particular combination (VRNN and RevGrad). I still believe comparable results can be obtained by polishing R-DANN (e.g. carefully penalizing domain discrepancy at every step)

Additional comments:

1. I’m not convinced by the discussion presented in Section 4.4. I don’t think the visualization of firing patterns can be used to support the efficiency of the proposed method.

2. Figure 1(c) looks very suspicious. I can hardly believe t-SNE could produce this _very_ regular structure for non-degenerate (non-synthetic, real-world) data.

Overall, it’s a solid paper but I’m not sure if it is up to the ICLR standard.

2. Figure 1(c) looks very suspicious. I can hardly believe t-SNE could produce this _very_ regular structure for non-degenerate (non-synthetic, real-world) data.

Overall, it’s a solid paper but I’m not sure if it is up to the ICLR standard.

This paper combines variational RNN (VRNN) and domain adversarial networks (DANN) for domain adaptation in the sequence modelling domain.  The VRNN is used to learn representations for sequential data, which is the hidden states of the last time step.  The DANN is used to make the representations domain invariant, therefore achieving cross domain adaptation.

Experiments are done on a number of data sets, and the proposed method (VRADA) outperforms baselines including DANN, VFAE and R-DANN on almost all of them.

I don't have questions about the proposed model, the model is quite clear and seems to be a simple combination of VRNN and DANN.  But a few questions came up during the pre-review question phase:

- As the authors have mentioned, DANN in general outperforms MMD based methods, however, the VFAE method which is based on MMD regularization on the representations seems to outperform DANN across the board.  That seems to indicate VRNN + MMD should also be a good combination.

- One baseline the authors showed in the experiments is R-DANN, which is an RNN version of DANN.  There are two differences between R-DANN and VRADA: (1) R-DANN uses deterministic RNN for representation learning, while VRADA uses variational RNN; (2) on target domain R-DANN only optimizes adversarial loss, while VRADA optimizes both adversarial loss and reconstruction loss for feature learning.  It would be good to analyze further where the performance gain comes from.

The authors present a new program synthesis approach for building large programs from small programs, where the small programs are derived from data. The method uses an attention-based program decoder and a conditional random field (CRF) to perform efficient hierarchical program synthesis. The approach can be used to generate programs from any source of variable-length data sequences, with or without associated task tags. The authors demonstrate the approach on program synthesis from clinical notes, but the general approach could be applied to program synthesis from any source of variable-length data. The main weakness of the approach is that it performs program synthesis from the bottom up, and there is no way to control which programs to synthesize, which could result in unstable solutions and infinite loops. To resolve this, the authors suggest that the program decoder should use an LSTM-based sequence model rather than a simple CNN. In summary, this is a promising approach for program synthesis, with potential to be applied to a wide range of problems. There is much room for improvement in the approach to make it more flexible and stable, and to evaluate which programs to synthesize and when. elly highlights a weakness of the approach that the program decoder should use an LSTM-based sequence model rather than a simple CNN. The suggestion could be adopted and the approach could be made more stable and better at solving the problem. ssessment Overall, this is a promising approach for program synthesis, with potential to be applied to a wide range of problems. There is much room for improvement in the approach to make it more flexible and stable, and to evaluate which programs to synthesize and how. To resolve this, the authors suggest that the program decoder should use an LSTM-based sequence model rather than a simple CNN.

This paper proposes a method for program synthesis for character level language modeling. First the model is parameterized by a program from a DSL, allowing the expression of non-trivial data dependencies. Second, we synthesize a program from the DSL to a program for character level language modeling. Finally, we learn the model parameters from the training data using counting, making the process fast and simple. The synthesized program can be manually inspected, understood and updated. The model is a good fit for both English text and program source code, with comparable precision to neural networks. I think this is an interesting idea and the results are quite good. I have some suggestions for improvement: 1.The paper only considers synthesizing programs for character level language modeling. To make the model more generally applicable, it would be interesting to also cover word level language modeling and generic program generation. 2.A more detailed discussion of how the model learns program parameters from the training data is needed. In particular, how to update the program parameters when new training data becomes available needs to be explained. Overall I think the results are interesting and the model design and the proof-of-concept for program synthesis for character level language modeling are well executed. I look forward to future work in this direction. I welcome you to submit a revised version of this paper that addresses the above points and that I can review again. Best, Will -- Will Pazzek, PhD Co-Founder Program Synthesis for AI www.prosynthesis.ai ## The Program Synthesis for Language Modeling is Compared with Neural Network and N-gram Model on Dataset of English Text Date: 2018-10-09 10:00:00 By Will Pazzek, PhD The Program Synthesis for Language Modeling is compared with Neural Network and N-gram Model on Dataset of English Text. The past few years have seen a resurgence in research into statistical language modeling approaches that use general-purpose probabilistic modeling techniques rather than Neural Networks. The advantage of these approaches is that they are typically much faster to train and can be applied to language modeling in a variety of scenarios, not just those where the underlying data corresponds directly as input features to a Neural Network architecture. In this work, I present results comparing a new Character-Level Language Model (called Program Synthesized Language Model - PSSLM) with Neural Networks and n-gram models on the Penn Treebank language modeling benchmark for the first time. PSSLM synthesis is based on the idea of program synthesis: using an appropriate programming DSL we can encode much of the complex dependencies present in most real world data sources into a series of computable functions and relations. By learning the program that encodes the language model in this way, we can leverage the efficiency of C/C++-based program synthesis in combination with well-known techniques from the field of statistics to generate efficient, accurate language models. It is immediately clear from the results that PSSLM performance is on a par with Neural Networks on this task, with a resulting complexity reduction of between 1.5 and 2 orders of magnitude (or more) that makes the method suitable for many real world applications. The remainder of the paper shows how we can use PSSLM to translate character-level language modeling tasks into easier problems on very large datasets, making it possible to use this approach for the first time to obtain state-of-the-art results on this very challenging task. Dating back to the end of the 19th century, language modeling approaches have been based on the assumption that the order in which words occur in a sample of text is of limited importance to the understanding of the message. In the language modeling task, we are typically given a training data sample containing a large number of sentences and for each sentence, a list of the words in that sentence. This task is then to produce a probability distribution for each word in the vocabulary, indicating how likely it is that that word is used in a given sentence. In recent years, however, a number of language modeling tasks have relied on datasets that include syntactic dependencies between words, either as a result of parsing the underlying data using a Penn Treebank or some other parsing technique or through the use of a deep parsing neural network that uses the structure of the text to learn word dependencies from the input features. In contrast to many NLP tasks such as part-of-speech tagging and parsing or coreference resolution, there are no corresponding existing large annotated datasets for training the language modeling component of these tasks. This means that the key assumption of this field, which is that word order is largely irrelevant to the meaning of a message, must either be encoded in the code of the language model itself or learned using some external means. However, in our experiments, we show that it

Proposed Statistical Model for Program Synthesis, is a good fit for both, program source code and English text. The model is parameterized by a program from a domain-specific language (DSL) that allows expressing non-trivial data dependencies. Learning is done in two phases: (i) we synthesize a program from the DSL, essentially learning a good representation for the data, and (ii) we learn parameters from the training data - the process is done via counting, as in simple language models such as n-gram. Our experiments show that the precision of our model is comparable to that of neural networks while sharing a number of advantages with n-gram models such as fast query time and the capability to quickly add and remove training data samples. Further, the model is parameterized by a program that can be manually inspected, understood and updated, addressing a major problem of neural networks. Finally, we believe that our model also has the advantage that it can be applied to any DSL - we provide the example of program synthesis for source code, but our method is in principle applicable to any DSL for data representation Our paper is briefly introduced via the example of program synthesis for source code, but our method is in principle applicable to any DSL for data representation, such as data tables, JSON and CSV. We begin by expressing the data dependencies using an assignment of a variable from the input to some constant expression in the program. To be precise, for every variable that might receive a value in the program, we define a (possibly empty) sequence of assignment expressions. To obtain a well-defined data dependency, it is required that each expression in the sequence is defined for a purpose, that is, expresses some value. For example, <program> a = b; c = d; </program> requires a definition of either b or d for a purpose, either as a read or as a write, because there is no other read of a or any writes of c occurring after this point in the program. An assignment expression is divided into three parts: * a : source expression that defines a variable * := : assignment operator * a’ : new value for the defined variable This model can be easily extended to handle global dependencies between data in the sense that all variables used in the expression for a particular purpose must be bound before the expression for that purpose can be evaluated, but it may become more complex to understand. As a last general point, our model is easily extensible to allow for complex dependencies that require a nesting of program elements. Our model is learned from a program synthesis viewpoint by first computing an abstract syntax tree (AST) from the DSL, and then translating it to a program representation. To account for the possibility of multiple correct answers, we define a probabilistic model and compute a probabilistic tree, from which we can sample multiple programs. The program synthesis can be performed during training if there are multiple programs for a given data set. The program is first divided into syntax modules, which only affect the top-level structure, such as statements, declarations, etc. Each syntax module is associated with a multinomial distribution, and the program is expressed as a product of these distributions. Each variable is assigned to a program segment, where the segment specifies its scope and purpose. Next, we estimate distributions for expressions using a generalized assignment probability distribution. For this we define the probability of read, write and no-read and for each assignment expression. Finally, we use these distributions to sample programs, using a tree model similar to decision trees. This program synthesis approach is performed once, during training, but it is robust to noise as it is an Expectation Maximization (EM) algorithm. To perform program synthesis during prediction, we compute a chain structure of assignment expressions, and then evaluate the expression by repeatedly selecting the next assignment expression based on its probability. This chain structure can also be used to limit the space of possible programs that can be evaluated. In order to compute the chain structure, we maintain a finite set of programs for the current program step, and only consider the next assignment expression if the current assignment expression and program are the same as the last program in the chain. This approach is also efficient, as the chain can be computed incrementally. Note that Program Synthesis can also generate programs that execute in infinite time - for example, the following Python program is computed by the model as a possible expression for b: b = (input('Give me something: ')).lower() The approach is efficient and well-suited to program synthesis for language modeling. We evaluate the model on two datasets, one from the field of automated synthesis of user interfaces, the other from the field of Web search.
human_text:
This paper introduces a novel method for language modeling which is suitable for both modeling programming language as well as natural language. The approach uses a program synthesis algorithm to search over program space and uses count-based estimation of the weights of the program. This is a departure from neural network-based approaches which rely on gradient descent, and thus are extremely slow to estimate. Count-based method such as regular n-gram models suffer because of their simplicity, i.e. not being able to model large context, and scaling badly as context increases. The proposed approach synthesizes programs using MCMC which learn context-sensitive probabilities using count-based estimation, and thus is both fast and able to model long-range context.

Experiments on a programming language datasets, the linux kernel corpus, show that this method is vastly better than both LSTM and n-gram language models. Experiments on the Wikipedia corpus show that the method is competitive, but not better, to SOTA models. Both estimation and query time are significantly better than LSTM LMs, and competitive to n-gram LMs.

It's debatable whether this paper is suitable for ICLR, due to ICLR's focus on neural network-based approaches. However, in the interest of diversity and novelty, such "outside" papers should be accepted to ICLR. This paper is likely to inspire more research into fusion of program synthesis and machine learning methods, which was a popular theme at NIPS 2016.

*Pros*
1. Novel approach.
2. Good results.

*Cons*
1. Some significant algorithmic details are not included in the paper. They should at least be included in an appendix for comprehensiveness.

*Comments*
1. Please include n-gram results in the table for Wikipedia results.

This work was a very controversial submission, with two strong accepts and one initial strong reject. There was significant discussion about the replicability of the paper, although all reviewers seem interested in the methods. 
 
 Pro:
 - There is strong originality to this work. One of the few submissions in the area not just using RNNs for LM.
 - The paper shows strong empirical results on PL language modeling, comparative results in natural language modeling, fast lookup compared to neural models, and presents a significantly different approach then the currently accepted NN methods. 
 
 
 Cons:
 - The original draft has clarity issues. In particular the MCMC approach is very difficult to follow and lacks clear explanation for this community, the interpretability of the method is not demonstrated, and too much of the work is devoted to laying out the language itself. (Note The authors have gone out of their way to include an appendix which caused one reviewer to go from recommending strong rejection to weak rejection, but also requires a much larger submission size. While two reviewers do like the work, their reviews are mainly based on the empirical sucess at program language modeling.)
 
 Overall, the PCs have determined that this work deserves to appear at the conference.

Generally reviewers seem quite willing to consider a paper like this for ICLR, particularly due to the experimental results, but are concerned that there is very-little-to-zero details given about the synthesis approach. This makes the details of the paper hard to check and unreplicable. 

If you feel like there is something you can do to sway them on this point, now would be a great time to respond.

This paper proposes an approach to character language modeling (CLMs) based on developing a domain specific language to represent CLMs. The experiments show mixed performance versus neural CLM approaches to modeling linux kernel data and wikipedia text, however the proposed DSL models are slightly more compact and fast to query as compared with neural CLMs. The proposed approach is difficult to understand overall and perhaps is aimed towards the sub-community already working on this sort of approach but lacks sufficient explanation for the ICLR audience. Critically the paper glosses over the major issues of demonstrating the proposed DSL is a valid probabilistic model and how training is performed to fit the model to data (there is clearly not a gradient-based training approach used). FInally the experiments feel incomplete without showing samples drawn from the generative model or analyzing the learned model to determine what it has learned. Overall I feel this paper does not describe the approach in enough depth for readers to understand or re-implement it.

Almost all of the model section is devoted to exposition of the DSL without specifying how probabilities are computed using this model and how training is performed. How are probabilities actually encoded? The DSL description seems to have only discrete decisions rather than probabilities.

Training is perhaps covered in previous papers but there needs to be some discussion of how it works here. Section 2.5 does not do enough to explain how training works or how any measure of optimality is achieved.

Given this model is quite a different hypothesis space from neural models or n-grams, looking and samples drawn from the model seems critical. The current experiments show it can score utterances relatively well but it would be very interesting if the model can sample more structured samples than neural approaches (for example long-range syntax constraints like brackets)

The authors propose a method for language modeling by first generating a program from a DSL, then learning the count-based parameters of that program. Pros include: The proposed method is innovative and highly different from standard LSTM-based approaches of late. The model should also be much quicker to apply at query time. Strong empirical results are obtained on modeling code, though there is some gap between the synthesis method and neural methods on the Hutter task. A detailed description of the language syntax is provided.

Cons/suggestions:
- The synthesis procedure using MCMC is left very vague, even though being able to make this procedure efficient is one of the key questions.
- The work builds on work from the PL literature; surely the related work could also be expanded and this work better put in context.
- More compact/convincing examples of human interpretability would be helpful.

Other comments
- Training time evaluation in Table 1 should give basic information such as whether training was done on GPU/CPU, CPU specs, etc.

machine_text: This is an interesting and thorough look at how to apply Deep Reinforcement Learning to the classic StarCraft micromanagement task. The use of ETDPPO (Epiestic Thinking for Deep Policy Planning) is a novel approach, and the results are quite impressive. The findings are a good inspiration for other players to start work on similar problems, and will be of interest to the larger Starcraft community as well. myself +1 for the creative direction, and +1 for the thorough explanation of the ETDPPO approach. I have some minor comments and suggestions for improvement, however: 1. The paper didn't mention what version of Starcraft this was tested on. This is important for two reasons: (1) The versions released after this release do not include the API needed to run this code, so this may not be very easily replicable by others; (2) This API only worked with the original StarCraft version (Starcraft version 1), not the more recent versions (Starcraft version 2, 3, etc.). I was only able to test this on the original StarCraft, not the more recent versions. This may have distorted the results, since the original StarCraft micromanagement version is more challenging than the newer ones. 2. The "agent" in the title is actually a Naive Bayes Classifier. This should be made clear in the title, and also in the text, so that readers know what to expect from this system. The ETDPPO algorithm is definitely cool, but this might be a source of confusion for some readers. 3. This is a very interesting paper, and the topic is clearly very interesting to the author. However, as a non-expert, I could only really appreciate a few of the key ideas and results. I would suggest improving the presentation to make the main ideas and results more clear to a general reader. 4. There are some cool ideas in this paper, but I was not able to figure out how they fit together, or to understand how to apply them to other domains. There are a number of inter-related ideas that are not clear in the paper. For example, the author presents a small fragment of the ETDPPO algorithm, and suggests that the rest of the algorithm could be applied to other tasks. But what does this even mean? What other kinds of tasks is this general approach applicable to? What other kinds of tasks does this ETDPPO algorithm actually solve? And how does one apply this to other problems? These kinds of connections between different ideas in the paper would be very helpful if the author is willing to make them. Overall, this is an interesting paper that might be very interesting to some readers. There is some good preliminary work here for future exploration in the area of StarCraft micromanagement, which was a very difficult AI challenge for years until recently. The authors presented an effective approach for Deep Deterministic Policy Search (D4) to learn an effective micromanagement policy for StarCraft. The D4 algorithm was originally developed for Atari 2600 games and has been successfully adapted to the real-time strategy (RTS) game StarCraft. The authors modified the algorithm to optimize for the micromanagement use case and showed that a well-trained D4 agent can achieve high-level strategy tasks better than a random agent. The main advantage of using D4 for micromanagement is that the policy is represented as a Markov decision process (MDP). This allows the search algorithm to efficiently evaluate a large number of options by cycling through discrete states, and to effectively learn policy changes by directly evaluating the policy improvement in the search. The authors evaluate the quality of the trained policy using the same game simulator as the search algorithm, without any additional hardware. This makes it practical to apply D4 to real-time strategy games, which have high compute costs for simulation. However, this comes at the cost of limiting the algorithm to problems that can be solved with simulated games. This paper has two major limitations. The first is that the search algorithm, D4, is designed to optimize for maximum reward. As a result, it is sensitive to hyper-parameter choices that control the time horizon of the learning. Since this paper does not present a systematic search for hyper-parameters, it is possible that the default settings of the D4 algorithm do not lead to good micromanagement policies. The second limitation is that the learned policies are not directly usable for a human player. A human player can make finer-grained decisions than the D4 agent, due to the use of different controller hardware. In addition, because the authors only use simulation for evaluating the policy, the learned policies have not been validated in the real world. This paper is a significant extension of an earlier version that presented an analysis of D4 and the development of a derivative method, D4-GP, that is more parameter-efficient. The updated version of the algorithm is well-motivated, and the main claim that a well-trained D4 agent can achieve high-level strategy tasks better than a random agent is supported by the validation results. The paper still has two major limitations, however, and should be viewed as a starting point for developing a practical approach to D4-based micromanagement.

This paper studies StarCraft micromanagement, that is, the low level control of team members in the real time strategy game StarCraft. The action space is very large and there is no obvious feature representation for the value functions. We describe our approach to tackle the scenarios with deep neural network controllers from raw state features. We also present a heuristic reinforcement learning algorithm that combines both direct exploration in the policy space and backpropagation. This algorithm can successfully learn non-trivial strategies for scenarios with armies of up to 15 agents, where both Q-learning and REINFORCE struggled. The main idea of the heuristic reinforcement learning algorithm is to combine direct exploration in the policy space and backpropagation. It collects traces for learning using deterministic policies, which appears much more efficient than e.g., ε-greedy exploration. The rest of this paper is structured as follows. Section II describes related work. Section III introduces the StarCraft micromanagement scenarios. Section IV describes the Heuristic Reinforcement Learning algorithm. Section V describes the Deep Deterministic Policy methodology. Section VI presents the evaluation methodology. Section VII describes the neural network architecture. Section VIII presents the algorithm hyperparameters. Section IX presents the results. Section X presents the discussion. Section XI presents the conclusion and future work. II. RELATED WORK The problem of StarCraft micromanagement has been approached using methods from different research fields, such as reinforcement learning, continuous dynamics, and artificial neural networks. First, related work exists in reinforcement learning, which has studied micromanagement in video games using different algorithm flavors, such as Q-learning [3], REINFORCE [12], and actor-critic [18]. These works face similar challenges to the one addressed in this paper, that is, the lack of a useful feature representation to describe the state of the game [3]. To overcome this, they map the state of the game into a continuous state-action space [12, 18], which provides a better representation of the state of the game. Nevertheless, these approaches still have to solve very large state-action spaces, which do not provide a clear separation between different actions. As a result, the use of function approximation is common [3, 12, 18]. Recent works in reinforcement learning use deep neural network architectures to learn control policies directly from raw state features [16, 17]. These works use two streams, one that learns a state representation from raw state features and another that produces a control policy from the state representation. For example, [16] uses a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to do state representation, and a fully connected network to produce control actions. [17] uses a fully convolutional network to represent the state and a dense network to map it to actions. [17] additionally employs attention mechanisms to the state representation to focus on specific parts of the state. Both of these works address the micromanagement problem, but only from the reinforcement learning perspective, with no relationship to the game dynamics or behavior. Deep Reinforcement Learning for Video Games (DRL4VG) is the first work that applied deep reinforcement learning in the domain of video games [7]. DRL4VG [7] uses a neural network architecture which takes the game image as input, but it assumes a simple 2D game board, not a 3D environment, as in StarCraft. [7] also uses end-to-end training, where both the policy and the value function are trained simultaneously. They demonstrate the feasibility of using a deep Q network to solve the game of Connect 4. Reinforcement Learning with Raw State Information for StarCraft (RSI-SSI) is the first work that proposed to tackle the micromanagement problem by incorporating knowledge from the game dynamics and behavior into the reinforcement learning process. This approach is similar to our work, but they use explicit state-action representation instead of a function approximation. RSI-SSI [10] performs a discretization of the continuous action space in different abstract actions, which are further combined in macro actions. The state-action space is explored using ε-greedy exploration, instead of an approach that directly uses a raw representation of the game state. Using Deep Neural Networks for Micromanagement is the second work that proposed to tackle the micromanagement problem using deep learning. They apply deep reinforcement learning to a very small micro-game in Starcraft, in which a virtual agent controls another agent. The micro-game does not try to model the full complexity of the real game, it uses a simplified map and a simplified interaction between the controlled and the controlled agent. DeepXDE [15] uses a two-stream architecture similar to [16], but here the state representation is done by a Deep Neural Network (DNN) with two hidden layers,

These tasks are difficult for recent DeepRL methods due to high-dimensional, variable action spaces (the action space is the task of each unit, the number of units may vary). The paper presents an approach to structured exploration in StarCraft micromanagement policies (essentially small tasks in the game). From an application standpoint, this is a notable advance, since the authors are tackling a challenging domain and in doing so develop a novel exploration algorithm that seems to work quite well here.
 
 The main downside of the paper is that the proposed algorithm does seem fairly ad-hoc: certain approximations in the algorithm, like ignoring the argmax term in computing the backprop, are not really justified except in that it "seems to work well in practice" (a quote from the paper), so it's really unclear whether these represent general techniques or just a method that happens to work well on the target domain for poorly understood reasons.
 
 Despite this, however, I think the strength of the application is sufficient here. Deep learning has been alternatively pushed forward by more algorithmic/mathematical advances and more applied advances, with many of the major breakthroughs coming from seemingly ad-hoc strategies applied to challenging problems. This paper falls in that later category: the ZO algorithm may or may not lead to something slightly more disciplined in the future, but for now the compelling results on StarCraft are I believe enough to warrant accepting the paper.
 
 Pros:
 + Substantial performance improvement (over basic techniques like Q-learning) on a challenging task
 + Nice intuitive justification of a new exploration approach
 
 Cons:
 - Proposed algorithm seems rather ad-hoc, making some (admittedly not theoretically justified) approximations simply because they seem to work well in practice

The paper presents a learning algorithm for micromanagement of battle scenarios in real-time strategy games. It focuses on a complex sub-problem of the full RTS problem. The assumptions and restrictions made (greedy MDP, distance-based action encoding, etc.) are clear and make sense for this problem.

The main contribution of this paper is the zero-order optimization algorithm and how it is used for structured exploration. This is a nice new application of zero-order optimization meets deep learning for RL, quite well-motivated using similar arguments as DPG. The results show clear wins over vanilla Q-learning and REINFORCE, which is not hard to believe. Although RTS is a very interesting and challenging domain (certainly worthy as a domain of focused research!), it would have been nice to see results on other domains, mainly because it seems that this algorithm could be more generally applicable than just RTS games. Also, evaluation on such a complex domain makes it difficult to predict what other kinds of domains would benefit from this zero-order approach. Maybe the authors could add some text to clarify/motivate this.

There are a few seemingly arbitrary choices that are justified only by "it worked in practice". For example, using only the sign of w / Psi_{theta}(s^k, a^k). Again later: "Also we neglected the argmax operation that chooses the actions". I suppose this and dividing by t could keep things nicely within or close to [-1,1] ? It might make sense to try truncating/normalizing w/Psi; it seems that much information must be lost when only taking the sign. Also lines such as "We did not extensively experiment with the structure of the network, but we found the maxpooling and tanh nonlinearity to be particularly important" and claiming the importance of adagrad over RMSprop without elaboration or providing any details feels somewhat unsatisfactory and leaves the reader wondering why.. e.g. could these only be true in the RTS setup in this paper?

The presentation of the paper can be improved, as some ideas are presented without any context making it unnecessarily confusing. For example, when defining f(\tilde{s}, c) at the top of page 5, the w vector is not explained at all, so the reader is left wondering where it comes from or what its use is. This is explained later, of course, but one sentence on its role here would help contextualize its purpose (maybe refer later to the section where it is described fully). Also page 7: "because we neglected that a single u is sampled for an entire episode"; actually, no, you did mention this in the text above and it's clear from the pseudo-code too.

This is a very interesting and timely paper, with multiple contributions. 
- it proposes a setup for dealing with combinatorial perception and action-spaces that generalizes to an arbitrary number of units and opponent units,
- it establishes some deep RL baseline results on a collection of Starcraft subdomains,
- it proposes a new algorithm that is a hybrid between black-box optimization REINFORCE, and which facilitates consistent exploration.


As mentioned in an earlier comment, I don’t see why the “gradient of the average cumulative reward” is a reasonable choice, as compared to just the average reward? This over-weights late rewards at the expense of early ones, so the updates are not matching the measured objective. The authors state that they “did not observe a large difference in preliminary experiments” -- so if that is the case, then why not choose the correct objective?

DPQ is characterized incorrectly: despite its name, it does not “collect traces by following deterministic policies”, instead it follows a stochastic behavior policy and learns off-policy about the deterministic policy. Please revise this.

The authors present a method of neural network compression called soft weight-sharing. The method compresses an already trained network by splitting the layers into groups, creating new groups that are copies of the original groups but with parameters shared between the groups. The shared parameters are adjusted during training on a held-out validation set to maximize the correlation between the groups. The groups then replace the corresponding original layers. Interesting, also, that there seems to be a regime where the empirical prior helps improving upon pretrained results (often very significantly). Thank you very much for the carefully crafted reviews. We agree with most points you are making. We would like to comment on them and give an outlook of future efforts.
 
VGG: We ran our algorithm that was successful for MNIST on ImageNet using the pretrained VGG network. However, due to some implementation inefficiencies we were only able to run it for a few epochs. This paper proposes to use an empirical Bayesian approach to learn the parameters of a neural network, and their priors.
A mixture model prior over the weights leads to a clustering effect in the weight posterior distributions (which are approximated with delta peaks). 
This clustering effect can exploited for parameter quantisation and compression of the network parameters.
The authors show that this leads to compression rates and predictive accuracy comparable to related approaches. 

Earlier work [Han et al. 2015] is based on a three-stage process of pruning small magnitude weights, clustering the remaining ones, and updating the cluster centres to optimise performance. The current work provides a more principled approach that does not have such an ad-hoc multi-stage structure, but a single iterative optimisation process.

A first experiment, described in section 6.1 shows that an empirical Bayes’ approach, without the use of hyper priors, already leads to a pronounced clustering effect and to setting many weights to zero. 
In particular a compression rate of 64.2 is obtained on the LeNet300-100 model.
In section 6.1 the text refers to figure C, I suppose this should be figure 1.

Section 6.2 describes an experiment where hyper-priors are used, and the parameters of these distributions, as well as other hyper-parameters such as the learning rates, are being optimised using Spearmint (Snoek et al., 2012). Figure 2 shows the performance of the  different points in the hyper-parameter space that have been evaluated (each trained network gives an accuracy-compressionrate point in the graph). The text claims that best results lie on a line, this seems a little opportunistic interpretation given the limited data. Moreover, it would be useful to add a small discussion on whether such a linear relationship would be expected or not. Currently the results of this experiment lack interpretation.

Section 6.3 describes results obtained for both CNN models and compares results to the recent results of (Han et al., 2015) and (Guo et al., 2016).
Comparable results are obtained in terms of compression rate and accuracy. 
The authors state that their current algorithm is too slow to be useful for larger models such as VGG-19, but they do briefly report some results obtained for this model (but do not compare to related work). It would be useful here to explain what slows the training down with respect to standard training without the weight clustering approach, and how the proposed algorithm scales in terms of the relevant quantities of the data and the model.

The contribution of this paper is mostly experimental, leveraging fairly standard ideas from empirical Bayesian learning to introduce weight clustering effects in CNN training.
This being said, it is an interesting result that such a relatively straightforward approach leads to results that are on par with state-of-the-art, but more ad-hoc, network compression techniques.
The paper could be improved by clearly describing the algorithm used for training, and how it scales to large networks and datasets.
Another point that would deserve further discussion is how the hyper-parameter search is performed ( not using test data I assume), and how the compared methods dealt with the search over hyper-parameters to determine the accuracy-compression tradeoff. Ideally, I think, methods should be evaluated across different points on this trade-off.

machine_text: This paper proposes a novel CNN architecture, called steerable CNN, that can generate orientation specific filters. The steerable CNN architecture is simple and can be efficiently implemented in hardware. The proposed architecture has a differentiable module which allows end users to train the steerable CNN from scratch or adapt an exiting pre-trained network for a new use case by adjusting the network’s parameters according to the users’ needs. Two adaptation scenarios are discussed in this paper, namely, single-image super-resolution and depth estimation from a single image. The steerable CNN is evaluated and compared against five state-of-the-art CNNs on the above two tasks and the results show that the proposed model can achieve promising results while saving significant parameters and computations. here are some suggestions for the paper: - The paper only focuses on the application of the steerable CNN architecture on super-resolution and depth estimation. However, the architecture of the steerable CNN can be easily extended to other tasks such as image classification and object detection. - The paper only discusses two adaptation scenarios of the steerable CNN, i.e., single-image super-resolution and depth estimation from a single image. The extension to other scenarios should be considered in the future work. - In the paper, the steerable CNN is parameterized by the steerable CNN’s layer. As such, the authors did not give any discussion on how to determine the parameters of the steerable CNN, i.e., the filter parameters. In practice, the parameters of the steerable CNN can be easily tuned by clustering the pre-trained CNNs’ filters. One can use the filter clusters of the base CNN to initialize the filter parameters of the steerable CNN. In this case, the steerable CNN is actually a variant of the Canonical-Network. With the filter cluster strategy, the steerable CNN can be trained in a fully end-to-end manner. - The paper only demonstrates the steerable CNN using two-dimensional filters. One can generalize the steerable CNN to three-dimensional filters by replacing the g(z) with a 3x3x3 3D kernel and training the network with the corresponding loss function. However, it is more difficult to tune the parameters of the 3D kernel. As such, the authors’ choice to use 2D filters is a practical and effective way to reduce the implementation complexity.

The main content of this paper is Steerable Convolutional Neural Networks, it has achieved state of the art results on the CIFAR image classification benchmark. The paper builds upon the work of F.G. Scholkopf who first proposed steerable filters to be used in Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). The main idea of this algorithm is that the representational capacity of a layer in a neural network should be restricted to the types of representations that are most useful in solving the specific classification problem at hand. They introduce steerable filters to effectively exploit the symmetry of natural images, which allows a steerable filter to be parameterized by a small number of learnable parameters. This small number of parameters implies that steerable filters can be efficiently trained and their learned representations can be easily transferred to new images. This general approach of using structural information about the signals being represented to design specialized filters is known as structural Risk Minimization (SRM). They design several layers of steerable filters to build a network with multiple layers of SRM units. They evaluate their method on the CIFAR 10 and CIFAR 100 datasets, and achieve better or comparable performance to other state of the art techniques. This paper is interesting because it applies this idea of SRM to the deep learning architecture of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to improve their performance. Steerable Convolutional Neural Networks build multiple layers of SRM units using steerable filters. This allows it to have fewer parameters and still achieve competitive performance to competing methods on CIFAR. The fact that it is a parameter-efficient deep neural network which can be trained using less training data is especially appealing. This research is also significant because it unifies a large body of earlier work on steerable representations. They build upon the work of Scholzkopf who proposed steerable filters to be used in Convolutional Neural Networks. They introduce steerable filters to effectively exploit the symmetry of natural images, and build multiple layers of SRM to achieve a competitive performance to other methods on CIFAR. The fact that it's parameter-efficient deep neural network which can be trained using less data is especially interesting. This paper is technically sound and the research question it asks is significant. The idea of applying structural knowledge about the signals being represented to the design of specialized filters is of interest to the deep learning community. The main problem I see with this paper is that although it has achieved state of the art performance on CIFAR, there is no work on the question of why this approach works, which means this is an empirical study and is less theoretical. Theories and evidence are important in explaining and justifying experimental results. Another related point is that because this is an empirical study, rather than building upon a strong theory, there are fewer restrictions on the design of steerable filters. More importantly, the types of steerable representations that can be achieved are not fully explored. We see that they achieve good performance by using multiple layers of SRM. However, it's not clear why this approach of adding layers of SRM is effective. There could be many other combinations of steerable filters and SRM that can also be effective. It's not clear if a principled way to search through all these possibilities has not been considered. Although the main idea of applying structural knowledge about the signals being represented to the design of specialized filters is interesting, the application of this idea in this paper does not achieve the full potential of this idea. Therefore, the paper is only a partial exploration of this idea. Overall, this paper is an interesting exploration of an under-explored application of a strong idea, and I think it would be an interesting future work to fully exploit the potential of this idea.
human_text: This paper essentially presents a new inductive bias in the architecture of (convolutional) neural networks (CNN). The mathematical motivations/derivations of the proposed architecture are detailed and rigorous. The proposed architecture promises to produce equivariant representations with steerable features using fewer parameters than traditional CNNs, which is particularly useful in small data regimes. Interesting and novel connections are presented between steerable filters and so called “steerable fibers”. The architecture is strongly inspired by the author’s previous work, as well as that of “capsules” (Hinton, 2011). The proposed architecture is compared on CIFAR10 against state-of-the-art inspired architectures (ResNets), and is shown to be superior particularly in the small data regime. The lack of empirical comparison on large scale dataset, such as ImageNet or COCO makes this largely a theoretical contribution. I would have also liked to see more empirical evaluation of the equivariance properties. It is not intuitively clear exactly why this architecture performs better on CIFAR10 as it is not clear that capturing equivariances helps to classify different instances of object categories. Wouldn’t action-recognition in videos, for example, not be a better illustrative dataset?

The AC fully agrees with reviewer #4 that the paper contains a bit of an overkill in formalism: A lot of maths whose justification is not, in the end, very clear. The paper probably has an important contribution, but the AC would suggest reorganizing and restructuring, lessening the excess in formalism. 

As for the PCs, while we believe extending the experiments would further support the claims made in the paper, overall we still believe this paper deserves to appear at the conference as a poster.

This paper presents a theoretical treatment of transformation groups applied to convnets, and presents some empirical results showing more efficient usage of network parameters.

The basic idea of steerability makes huge sense and seems like a very important idea to develop.  It is also a very old idea in image processing and goes back to Simoncelli, Freeman, Adelson, as well as Perona/Greenspan and others in the early 1990s.  This paper approaches it through a formal treatment of group theory.  But at the end of the day the idea seems pretty simple - the feature representation of a transformed image should be equivalent to a transformed feature representation of the original image.  Given that the authors are limiting their analysis to discrete groups - for example rotations of 0, 90, 180, and 270 deg. - the formalities brought in from the group theoretic analysis seem a bit overkill.  I'm not sure what this buys us in the end.  it seems the real challenge lies in implementing continuous transformations, so if the theory could guide us in that direction it would be immensely helpful.

Also the description of the experiments is fairly opaque.  I would have a hard time replicating what exactly the authors did here in terms of implementing capsules or transformation groups.

The authors propose a parameterization of CNNs that guarantees equivariance wrt a large family of geometric transformations.

The mathematical analysis is rigorous and the material is very interesting and novel. The paper overall reads well; there is a real effort to explain the math accessibly, though some small improvements could be made.

The theory is general enough to include continuous transformations, although the experiments are restricted to discrete ones. While this could be seen as a negative point, it is justified by the experiments, which show that this set of transformations is powerful enough to yield very good results on CIFAR.

Another form of intertwiner has been studied recently by Lenc & Vedaldi [1]; they have studied equivariance empirically in CNNs, which offers an orthogonal view.

In addition to the recent references on scale/rotation deep networks suggested below, geometric equivariance has been studied extensively in the 2000's; mentioning at least one work would be appropriate. The one that probably comes closest to the proposed method is the work by Reisert [2], who studied steerable filters for invariance and equivariance, using Lie group theory. The difference, of course, is that the focus at the time was on kernel machines rather than CNNs, but many of the tools and theorems are relatable.


Some of the notation could be simplified, to make the formulas easier to grasp on a first read:

Working over a lattice Z^d is unnecessarily abstract -- since the inputs are always images, Z^2 would make much of the later math easier to parse. Generalization is straightforward, so I don't think the results lose anything by it; and the authors go back to 2D latices later anyway.

It could be more natural to do away with the layer index l which appears throughout the paper, and have notation for current/next layer instead (e.g. pi and pi'; K and D instead of K_{l+1} and K_l).

In any case I leave it up to the authors to decide whether to include these suggestions on notation, but I urge them to consider them (or other ways to unburden notation).


A few minor issues: Some statements would be better supported with an accompanying reference (e.g. "Explicit formulas exist" on page 5, the introduction of intertwiners on page 3). Finally, there is a tiny mistake in the Balduzzi & Ghifary reference (some extra information was included as an author name).

[1] Lenc & Vedaldi, "Understanding image representations by measuring their equivariance and equivalence", 2015
[2] Reisert, "Group integration techniques in pattern analysis: a kernel view", 2008

The model is trained using a large corpus of human queries followed by human answers on manual vetted ambiguous texts. The model is then tested on new queries drawn from real human conversation and found to be able to answer related questions on ambiguous text from real human questions much better than a strong baseline. Overall, this is a thoughtful and engaging paper. The authors present an interesting new RL problem type - Query, Reason, and Answer Queries - that combines both interactive dialog and natural language understanding, all in the context of a machine learning challenge. The contributions of this paper are three-fold: (1) they define a novel RL task type, (2) they explore multiple methods of solving this task, and (3) they characterize how this task type scales along multiple dimensions. I have a few comments about each of these three points. First, I think the paper under-utilizes the "query" part of Query, Reason, and Answer Queries. The RL agent must decide, on the basis of previous conversations, what questions to ask the user. In particular, the user has just given the agent a story - the agent must decide to query some, none, or all of the elements of that story. The authors explore different methods for determining which queries to ask, but a stronger signal from the user could help the agent make better decisions. Second, I think the authors underplay the significance of the "reason" part of Query, Reason, and Answer Queries. This is the part of the problem that requires the agent to use its accumulated knowledge to answer the user's challenge question. In many RL settings, agents are expected to "justifications" for their actions - why did I do X? - but here there is no guarantee that the user's challenge question is actually answerable with the knowledge that the agent has already accumulated. The authors don't evaluate the extent to which different methods of reacting to the challenge question impact the performance of the agent, but I think this is an important piece of the puzzle. Third, I think the authors underplay the difficulty of scaling this problem type along multiple dimensions. The problem instance difficulty (and thus the value of the final reward) is determined by the user's story, the agent's initial state, and the dimensions along which it is being scaled. I think these dimensions, along with the quality of the user's description, should be the focus of the evaluation. For example, to what extent does the agent's ability to scale along these dimensions improve as a function of training time? Overall, I think this is an interesting paper that provides a unique and fun new RL problem type. The task is defined clearly, and some clever ideas have been proposed for determining the user's desired queries and the agent's responses to the challenge question. I think the next step would be to make stronger use of the "query" and "reason" parts of the problem definition, and to evaluate the effectiveness of these strategies in the more difficult settings.

The paper "Learning to Query, Reason, and Answer Questions On Ambiguous Texts" addresses a key problem in conversational AI systems: training an agent to help a user by performing task-specific tasks on structured and unstructured data. The key challenge here is that human conversation is often ambiguous, incomplete, and does not accurately communicate the messages the intent of the author. This creates ambiguity in the task that the agent is trying to accomplish by understanding what was explicitly conveyed and reasoning in the presence of missing or unclear information. The authors present a new synthetic domain, QRAQ (Query, Reason, Answer Questions) which tests a system's ability to ask the right questions to help resolve the ambiguity. The authors present four variations of the QRAQ problem designed to test the reasoning and interaction capabilities of a learning-based agent in a setting that requires multiple turns. They also present standard and improved reinforcement learning based memory-network architectures and evaluate them on four versions of the QRAQ dataset. The paper presents both standard RL techniques and an improved method to determine the best questions to ask based on supervised signals. The main takeaway here is that RL approaches are effective in solving this problem even in the more complex setting with less supervision, where each problem presents a new combination of ambiguity characteristics and complexity dimensions. This is an important problem that impacts a lot of current and future NLU work, and this paper presents a strong baseline approach to the problem. I especially like the introduction of the Query-Answer-Reason Question (QARQ) paradigm which defines each question asked as a sequence of queries. This provides a good way to understand the problem and define a metric to evaluate answers. The evaluation metric also seems to account for the ability to ask the right follow-up questions. I think the domain is suitable for a number of NLP tasks including but not limited to: 1) Paraphrasing: the questions can be used to find the right synonyms and phrases for sentence cloning 2) Synonym expansion: the questions can be used to find a list of related words for a search query 3) Opinion mining: the questions can be used to identify the key facts in a statement and important conflicting opinions 4) Quotation identification: the questions can be used to find the most relevant quotes in a document. There are also a number of improvements to the basic QA setting that could be made to make it even more challenging, such as: 1) Ambiguity resolution: instead of having a single correct answer, there could be multiple answers, with each answer corresponding to a different correct interpretation of the ambiguous input 2) Nested queries: instead of a single question with a single answer, there could be a series of questions that depend on the answer to the previous question 3) Intermediate questions: instead of asking a yes/no question, there could be a series of intermediate questions about different aspects of the answer This is a very helpful paper for several NLP research areas. I think the QA problem setting itself is an important area of research that has not been explored very much in recent years. Some minor comments/suggestions: 1) I was not sure what “crack” was in the domain name, but from the introduction it seems to be some form of bug or adversarial virus. This is not made very clear in the domain name and I think this could be better explained in the paper. 2) Instead of describing the problem with how the instructor talks to the student, perhaps it would be more helpful to provide some background on the background of the domain and how it was created. These are good points. We tried to find "crack" in the introduction, but wasn't able to. We will try to clarify this point in the introduction. We agree that more explanation of the domain and how it was created could be helpful. We have added some additional background in the introduction. Overall, I think this is a strong paper that presents an important problem and provides a good starting point for future work. A few responses to your last set of comments/questions:

To Reviewer 3:

We definitely agree that because of the limited vocabulary and grammar, this is more about reasoning than language.  As you point out, the interaction in these problems  boils down to repeated variable queries until the Agent decides it has enough info.  We decided on the term "interaction" to differentiate our problems from the bAbI problems, which are 1 shot question answering, and to emphasize the idea that, although simplified, this has the same structure as a dialogue interaction with the Agent (for example a tech support agent) asking clarifying questions of the User until being able to answer the User's question. We can try to think of a better term -- perhaps "multi-turn"?

To Reviewer 2:

(1) how does the model extend to the case with multiple variables in a single sentence?

Currently we leverage the fact that there is just one variable per sentence to save on parameters and avoid a linear transformation before the softmax in the query network.  To support more than one variable per sentence would just require adding a linear transformation on the output before softmax, making the query network have the same structure as the answer network.

(2) If the answer is out of vocabulary, how would the model handle it?

Out of vocabulary words are in general a problem for networks which do a softmax over a fixed vocabulary.  One potential way to address this would be to use something like the Pointer Networks of Vinyals, Fortunato, and Jaitly(

I think the baselines the authors use to test the tasks are appropriate. This paper investigates a set of tasks that augment the basic bAbI problems. In particular, some of the people and objects in the scenarios are replaced with unknown variables. Some of these variables must be known to solve the question, thus the agent must learn to query for the values of these variables. Interestingly, one can now measure both the performance of the agent in correctly answering the question, and its efficiency in asking for the values of the correct unknown variables (and not variables that are unnecessary to answer the question). This inferring of unknown variables goes beyond what is required for the vanilla version of the bAbI tasks, which are now more or less solved.

The paper is well-written, and the contributions are clear. Due to the very limited vocabulary and structure of the bAbI problems in general, I think these tasks (and variants on them) should be viewed more as basic reasoning tasks than natural language understanding. I’m not convinced by the claim of the paper that this really tests the ‘interaction’ capabilities of agents – while the task is phrased as a kind of interaction, I think it’s more aptly described by simply ‘inferring important unknown variables’, which (while important) is more related to reasoning. I’m not sure whether the connection of this ability to ‘interaction’ is more a superficial one.

That being said, it is certainly true that conversational agents will need basic reasoning abilities to converse meaningfully with humans. I sympathise with the general goal of the bAbI tasks, which is to test these reasoning abilities in synthetic environments, that are just complicated enough (but not more) to drive the construction of interesting models. I am convinced by the authors that their extension to these tasks are interesting and worthy of future investigation, and thus I recommend the acceptance of the paper.
