For example, the effect of diet on weight is typically non-linear, so drawing conclusions about relative energy contributions by looking at a single point in time is problematic. The authors should perform a Principal Components Analysis on the energy contributions, and compare the first two components to the diet groups. I think a stronger case can be made that the findings are not due to differences in energy contribution if the first two components are similar between groups. Along the same lines, the authors also seem to make a conclusion about calorie partitioning based on Principal Components Analysis of gene expression data. The authors should provide support for this claim as well, by showing which genes are loading heavily on each of the principal components. layer I agree that stronger conclusions about diet-related effects on metabolism could be made if the authors supported their conclusions with analysis of additional datasets. The authors claim that the first two components capture most of the variation in the data and correspond with the high- and low-diet groups. The high-loading genes on each component are sulfotransferase 2B1, cytochrome P450, family 4, subfamily a, polypeptide 5, solute carrier family 22, member 1, and hydroxysteroid 17-beta dehydrogenase 3. I agree that these genes might be interesting targets for follow-up experiments, but the authors should also show which genes were loading highly on the first two components, to show that the same genes are both highly loaded and clearly separated by the first two components.

Dudack, Ian Wilson, Andrew P. McInerny, David M. Roitman, and Philipp A. Scheet Introduction Dietary patterns are known to affect human health. Although there are multiple studies focusing on how specific dietary components affect human health, the relation between different diets and the molecular mechanisms behind this relation remain largely unknown. In this work, we use genomic data to identify differences in the blood plasma proteomes of mice consuming different diets. To do this, we use a supervised machine learning algorithm to classify different diets as "treatments" and compare the plasma proteomes of mice consuming the same diet but in different cages to identify "subtle differences" associated with each different diet. We find that several modules of interacting proteins (protein complexes) can be identified across different diets, some of which are unique to only a subset of the diets we tested. Furthermore, through a functional analysis of the genes associated with each module, we find that some of these modules are enriched with genes which contribute to distinct biological functions, such as Immune System Processes, Translation, and Oxidation-Reduction. The high-level outline of the approach followed in this paper is as follows: 1) we use a supervised machine learning algorithm to learn a function that can be used to predict diets based on the expression level of proteins in the blood plasma 2) we use this function to predict diets for samples not used during model training and evaluate the accuracy of this prediction 3) we identify differences in the expression of proteins between mice consuming the same diet but in different cages 4) we use protein interaction network analysis to partition the proteins identified in (3) into modules of interacting proteins and determine the relevance of these modules to diets What problem or question does this paper address? The authors use proteomic data to characterize how changes in diet affect the expression levels of proteins in the blood plasma of mice. They utilize a machine learning algorithm to train a function that can be used to predict diets based on the expression levels of proteins in the blood plasma. They then use this function to predict diets for samples not used during model training and evaluate the accuracy of this prediction. What is the main strength of this paper? The authors utilize a state-of-the-art machine learning algorithm to perform this prediction. What is the main weakness of this paper? The authors only show results for a small number of diets, which limits the generalizability of their findings. This is particularly true given that they have shown that different diets can lead to differential expression of proteins in the blood plasma. Given this result, it is likely that different diets will lead to different protein expression in different tissues and thus potentially affect the robustness of this model. Are there any other important weaknesses? The authors only use data from one type of mass spectrometry -- proteomics. It is likely that a different machine learning algorithm would perform better on RNA-seq data or quantitative PCR data, which would be more appropriate for transcriptomic analysis.

The paper "Diet Networks: Thin Parameters for Fat Genomics" presents a deep neural network architecture for population stratification based on Diet, with the main purpose to reduce the number of parameters. The idea is to first learn distributed representation for each input feature (e.g. for each position in the genome where variations are observed in data), and then learn how to map a feature's distributed representation to the vector of parameters specific to that feature in the classifier neural network. To the best of my knowledge, this is the first work to do so. The paper is well written with an intuitive explanation of the idea. The experiments on the population stratification task are also convincing. My one concern is that the presented solution is not a general purpose solution. In the case where distributed representation for input features is not available (e.g. 1D convolution), the approach will fail. I also wonder how the effectiveness of this solution scales to larger number of input features. Nevertheless, this is a novel idea and the proof of concept has been shown with excellent results. I strongly encourage the authors to submit this to a high impact journal for evaluation in the future research. The paper can be found at: Diet Networks: Thin Parameters for Fat Genomics Kazuki Yoshida, Kiyoshi Uehara, Masayuki Okuda, Shuji Takagi, Eiichi Mita, Shigeo Shimosaka Learning tasks such as those involving genomic data often poses a serious challenge: the number of input features can be orders of magnitude larger than the number of training examples, making it difficult to avoid overfitting, even when using the known regularization techniques. We focus here on tasks in which the input is a description of the genetic variation specific to a patient, the single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), yielding millions of ternary inputs. Improving the ability of deep learning to handle such datasets could have an important impact in medical research, more specifically in precision medicine, where high-dimensional data regarding a particular patient is used to make predictions of interest. Even though the amount of data for such tasks is increasing, this mismatch between the number of examples and the number of inputs remains a concern. Naive implementations of classifier neural networks involve a huge number of free parameters in their first layer (number of input features times number of hidden units): each input feature is associated with as many parameters as there are hidden units. We propose a novel neural network parametrization which considerably reduces the number of free parameters. It is based on the idea that we can first learn or provide a distributed representation for each input feature (e.g. for each position in the genome where variations are observed in data), and then learn (with another neural network called the parameter prediction network) how to map a feature's distributed representation (based on the feature's identity not its value) to the vector of parameters specific to that feature in the classifier neural network (the weights which link the value of the feature to each of the hidden units). This approach views the problem of producing the parameters associated with each feature as a multi-task learning problem. We show experimentally on a population stratification task of interest to medical studies that the proposed approach can significantly reduce both the number of parameters and the error rate of the classifier. This approach can be viewed as a kind of trans-differentiation: from the features distributed representation to the parameters. In other words, learning how to map distributed representation of each feature to the vector of parameters specific to that feature. However, I have some major concerns that should be addressed before this paper is considered for publication in NIPS. 1. I couldn't understand the motivation behind designing this model. As per the paper, the main aim is to generate natural images. I think the design choice of using a generative model for this purpose is questionable. The main reason for using a generative model is to capture the distribution of the data, and yet the paper uses a deterministic downsampling scheme to ensure that the samples from the model match the dimensions of the natural images. Please explain the thinking behind this design choice. 2. The model suffers from mode collapse. I already mentioned this in my comments on GitHub. The code is also available there. The mode collapse is further exacerbated by the downsampling operation. Please fix this problem by employing some variation of the Wasserstein barycenters framework to generate diverse images. 3. Regarding the fact that the code is available on Github, I would need the authors to provide some test images and examples of the generated images. 4. Paper: PixelVAE: A Latent Variable Model for Natural Images Author: Ali Eslami, Bhiksha Raj, Volker Morik, Kurtul Ulus fistfkin E-mail: nofistfkin@gmail.com Link: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/download/open-access/pixelvae-naeive-pixel-vael-paper/ Short Summary: This paper presents PixelVAE, a latent variable model for image generation. The proposed model is based on pixel level generative adversarial networks (PixelGAN). PixelVAE uses conditional PixelGANs to generate images at different scale and aspect ratios. The model can be trained from scratch or using snapshot version of pre-trained generator from Pix2Pix. Experiments on classical and conditional test sets of BigGAN show that PixelVAE can generate images with similar quality to that of the supervised model. The paper also provides interpretation of the loss functions used in the model. Strengths: The proposed model is based on pixel level generative adversarial networks (PixelGAN). PixelVAE uses conditional PixelGANs to generate images at different scale and aspect ratios. The model can be trained from scratch or using snapshot version of pre-trained generator from Pix2Pix. It also provides interpretation of the loss functions used in the model. Weaknesses: The proposed model takes a lot of time to train compared to previous work. Overall, I recommend this paper for readers to understand the concept and design of the model, especially for those who are new to this area.

Overall this paper is interesting and worth publishing in the top journal, e.g. IJCNN. The main idea is very good, especially using PixelCNN as the encoder part of the model, which makes the model capable of capturing global structures. However, there are also some weaknesses, for example, the author claims that the model has very few autoregressive layers, but in fact, the forth one is the decoder part, which will make the training more difficult and not good for general use. Also, the image generation results is not very clear, especially for the global patterns. Last but not least, the L1 and L2 weight regularizations are not clearly presented in the main content, it will need the auxiliary file to check the corresponding parameters and formulas. Natural image modeling is a landmark challenge of unsupervised learning. Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) learn a useful latent representation and model global structure well but have difficulty capturing small details. PixelCNN models details very well, but lacks a latent code and is difficult to scale for capturing large structures. We present PixelVAE, a VAE model with an autoregressive decoder based on PixelCNN. Our model requires very few expensive autoregressive layers compared to PixelCNN and learns latent codes that are more compressed than a standard VAE while still capturing most non-trivial structure. Finally, we extend our model to a hierarchy of latent variables at different scales. Our model learns hierarchical structures by using a series of invertible, affine layers to model short and long-range structure in the latent space. Our model achieves state-of-the-art performance on binarized MNIST, competitive performance on 64 × 64 ImageNet, and high-quality samples on the LSUN bedrooms dataset. # Problem statement - Does not capture small details - Requires very few expensive autoregressive layers compared to PixelCNN - But still needs to learn latent codes that are more compressed than a standard VAE # Main ideas - Use autoregressive decoder based on PixelCNN - Use a series of invertible, affine layers to model short and long-range structure in the latent space # Summary - Use PixelCNN as the encoder to encourage the decoder to produce accurate local structures - Use an autoregressive decoder to encourage the latent codes to be more compressed than a standard VAE # Details - Invertible, affine layers to model short and long-range structure in the latent space - Use PixelCNN as the encoder to encourage the decoder to produce accurate local structures - Encode images into a 1D vector - Decode using an autoregressive model with an affine transform and activation function # References - PixelVAE: A Latent Variable Model for Natural Images - https://github.com/shawnning/PixelVAEv2 - https://github.com/phillipiollmer/pixelcnnljs - https://github.com/phillipiollmer/pixelcnnljs/tree/master/contrib/PixelVAE - https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.11922 # Overall evaluation - Compatible with different local structure loss functions - Can scale to complicated images such as 64 x 64 images - Latent codes are more compressed than a standard VAE, good for downstream tasks - Autoencoder learning paradigm simplifies the model architecture - Easy to implement and fast to train # Limitations - Does not capture local structures beyond simple shapes - Not suitable for problems where long dependencies are needed - Latent codes are still dense, it is not possible to determine which part of the image each code corresponds to # Opportunities - Can use the decoder as a generative model for images - Use autoregressive decoder to encourage the latent codes to be more compact - No need to design expensive objective functions # Extensions - Can extend to a hierarchical model to capture even more complex structure - Can use PixelCNN encoding as an initialization - Can use PixelCNN to construct an initial state for the decoder - Can use more sophisticated invertible, affine layer for more complex specifications of local structure # Connections to existing models - PixelCNN is based on Pixel RL-CD algorithm, whose encoder is a type of autoencoder - PixelCNN has an invertible, affine layer to model local structure - PixelVAE also has invertible, affine layers to model local structure # Future work - Develop a stronger hierarchical model that captures even more complex structure # Datasets - binarized MNIST - 64x64 ImageNet - LSUN bedrooms dataset # Model architecture ![model architecture](model.png) # Model learning ![model training process](model_training.png) # Acknowledgement - Inspired by the Pixel RL-CD algorithm - Implementation based on: - Original PixelCNN implementation - PixelVAE encoder based on the original VariantVAE code - Modified the PixelCNN encoders to be invertible, and use these in the invertible, affine layer - Many thanks to the NVIDIA development community for help with optimizing the training process - Many thanks to Tom Browning for providing suggestions and feedback - Authors: Shawn Ng, Phillip Ying (From PhD supervisor of Shawn Ng) # Contact Please use the Metadata tab to provide details about the model. This paper combines the recent progress in variational autoencoder and autoregressive density modeling in the proposed PixelVAE model. The paper shows that it can match the NLL performance of a PixelCNN with a PixelVAE that has a much shallower PixelCNN decoder.
I think the idea of capturing the global structure with a VAE and modeling the local structure with a PixelCNN decoder makes a lot of sense and can prevent the blurry reconstruction/samples of VAE. I specially like the hierarchical image generation experiments.

I have the following suggestions/concerns about the paper:

1) Is there any experiment showing that using the PixelCNN as the decoder of VAE will result in better disentangling of high-level factors of variations in the hidden code? For example, the authors can train a PixelVAE and VAE on MNIST with 2D hidden code and visualize the 2D hidden code for test images and color code each hidden code based on the digit and show that the digits have a better separation in the PixelVAE representation. A semi-supervised classification comparison between VAE and the PixelVAE will also significantly improve the quality of the paper.

2) A similar idea is also presented in a concurrent ICLR submission "Variational Lossy Autoencoder". It would be interesting to have a discussion included in the paper and compare these works.

3) The answer to the pre-review questions made the architecture details of the paper much more clear, but I still ask the authors to include the exact architecture details of all the experiments in the paper and/or open source the code. The clarity of the presentation is not satisfying and the experiments are difficult to reproduce.

4) As pointed out in my pre-review question, it would be great to include two sets of MNIST samples maybe in an appendix section. One with PixelCNN and the other with PixelVAE with the same pixelcnn depth to illustrate the hidden code in PixelVAE actually captures the global structure.

I will gladly raise the score if the authors address my concerns.
The paper provides a solution that combines best of latent variable models and auto-regressive models. The concept is executed well and will make a positive contribution to the conference.

The paper combines a hierarchical Variational Autoencoder with PixelCNNs to model the distribution of natural images. 
They report good (although not state of the art) likelihoods on natural images and briefly start to explore what information is encoded by the latent representations in the hierarchical VAE.

I believe that combining the PixelCNN with a VAE, as was already suggested in the PixelCNN paper, is an important and interesting contribution. 
The encoding of high-, mid- and low-level variations at the different latent stages is interesting but seems not terribly surprising, since the size of the image regions the latent variables model is also at the corresponding scale. Showing that the PixelCNN improves the latent representation of the VAE with regard to some interesting task would be a much stronger result. 
Also, while the paper claims, that combining the PixelCNN with the VAE reduces the number of computationally expensive autoregressive layers, it remains unclear how much more efficient their whole model is than an PixelCNN with comparable likelihood.

In general, I find the clarity of the presentation wanting. For example, I agree with reviewer1 that the exact structure of their model remains unclear from the paper and would be difficult to reproduce.

All in all this is a nice paper.

I think the model is quite clever, attempting to get the best of latent variable models and auto-regressive models. The implementation and specific architecture choices (as discussed in the pre-review) also seem reasonable.
On the experimental side, I would have liked to see something more than NLL measurements and samples - maybe show this is useful for other tasks such as classification?

Though I don't think this is a huge leap forward this is certainly a nice paper and I recoemmend acceptance.

This is a very interesting paper. It combines the best of both world: PixelCNN and VAE. State-of-the-art LL and visually appealing images.

Below are some comments and suggestions.

1. In van dern Oord et al. 2016b they use an auto-encoder architecture with conditional PixelCNN as the decoder. It is not a variational one, though. It would be interesting to give a comparison between the model in this paper and their model. Are there any other differences, besides the KLD loss on latent variables and the (optional) hierarchical extension?

2. The introduction of latent varibles z definitely helps modeling global structure, however it also breaks the chain rule so the exact likelihood cannnot be derived.

3. How is the quality of representations learned by the encoder? Will the PixelCNN decoder help the encoder learn better representations, compared to Kingma et. al., "Semi-supervised learning with deep generative models"?

3. Also, it would be great if you can show some reconstruction results, in addition to generated samples.

But overall I like this paper very much.

Paper presents a concept called Snapshot Ensembles, where you pre-train a model using a base model and add info about what percentage of the data is in each snapshot. You can add as many snapshot ensembles as you want and use them all for prediction. The paper shows that this simple approach improves robustness and converges much faster compared to training from scratch. Paper also presents methodology for automatically determining percentages for each snapshot. One of the weak points of the approach is that it doesn’t provide an explanation why this approach works, which could be a limitation of the used explanation method. A snapshot ensemble is a pre-trained model where a different percentage of data points for each snapshot is used for training. The paper presents several techniques for determining the percentages of data points for each snapshot. Each ensemble consists of at least 3 snapshots. In order to evaluate the effectiveness of snapshot ensembles, the paper compares them to a model trained from scratch and to models that were finetuned from a pre-trained model. The performance of each model was evaluated on 2 metrics: RMSE and mean absolute error (MAB). The results show that snapshot ensembles converge significantly faster compared to training from scratch and finetuning from pre-trained models. Also, snapshot ensembles are more resistant to hyperparameter changes and noise in the data, as they are trained on a diverse set of data points. Grid search was used to find the optimal values of the following hyperparameters for the Cifar-10 dataset: learning rate, weight decay, number of epochs, batch size, momentum, and l2 regularization. For the ResNet18 model, the following hyperparameters were found using the same approach: number of epochs and l2 regularization. The paper shows that snapshot ensembles are more resistant to noise in the data.

This paper presents a new technique to improve the robustness and accuracy of deep neural networks, called snapshot ensembling. The key idea is to train a single model, but periodically snapshot it and save the model parameters for later rapid convergence. The model is trained using modern optimization techniques that use periodic changes in the learning rate to converge to a solution. Since the learning rate is constant in each snapshot, the approach is equivalent to ensembling many snapshots. The snapshot ensembling technique is very simple, yet it yields fast and repeated convergence to a good solution. We demonstrate the effectiveness of snapshot ensembling in a variety of tasks and network architectures, and show that it yields models with the same or lower error rates at no additional cost over learning from scratch. Paper link: https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.06732 # Snapshot Ensembles - Convergence Rate: Fast and repeated - No additional cost over learning from scratch - Models with lower error rates than state-of-the-art single models Paper Author: Yangyang Wang, Qingkai Yu, |hltz| Kingman Cheung ## Introduction Neural networks have been shown to be very effective at learning representations from large datasets, and have been the go-to tool for many challenging tasks in machine learning and data science, including image classification, language modeling, and music generation. However, neural networks are known to be brittle, or dependent on fine details of the data and the training procedure, for the task at hand. Averaging models the outputs of individual models, and has been a longstanding approach to building robust and stable models. Over time, many techniques for averaging models have been proposed, and they can be broadly classified into model averaging and cost/training curve analysis. * Model averaging includes: (1) early hybrids of model averaging and trial-and-error in history books. (2) Statistical model checking approaches, such as random forests and support vector machines. (3) Sample ensembling, which is the most common method today and can be viewed as a special case of Bayes optimal strategy when all models are biased toward the correct answer. (4) recent advances in deep learning, which use model averaging in multiple layers of a deep network, also known as deep averaging. * Cost/Training Curve Analysis includes: (1) Cost Averaging, which computes the mean per-parameter cost for a model and the simple addition of multiple models, resulting in a more stable model. (2) Bayesian optimization, which uses the surrogate objective, which converts the non-differentiable loss function into a black-box optimization problem to optimize the parameters, into a probabilistic model, which can be learned by Bayesian methods and used to perform hyperparameter search. Both model averaging and cost/training curve analysis have strengths and weaknesses, with each being more suitable for different problems. Cost/training curve analysis is the most sample efficient, i.e., it can be data-driven in the number of examples, but at the cost of training all models from scratch, which can be slow or non-convergent, especially for resource-constrained and asynchronous hardware such as mobile phones and IoT devices. Model averaging is more sample-inefficient, but provides strong robustness by averaging multiple models that may each be close to a local minimum. However, model averaging requires a central controller, such as a cooling schedule or random shuffling, or some sort of communication and coordination between the averaging models, to ensure that they converge to the same solution. Snapshot Ensembles combines the benefits of both model averaging and cost/training curve analysis. It reduces the cost of model averaging, since model averaging does not require updating parameters, and can be achieved simply by saving the model parameters at periodic snapshot intervals. The snapshot ensembling approach also builds in strong model averaging, by combining multiple different converging models. Each snapshot converges to a different local minima, and their combinations converge to a global minimum. The model snapshotting process is fully automated, with no extra cost over learning from scratch. The method also allows for more efficient model averaging than cost/training curve analysis, because it can be performed on existing well-trained models, which are more likely to be close to the global optimum. The snapshot ensemble method yields an alternative approach to model averaging, that provides strong robustness, efficient model averaging, and requires no central coordination. We evaluate snapshot ensembles on three tasks and demonstrate that snapshot ensembling outperforms strong baselines including model averaging and late fusion on these tasks. Addresses the question of how to train a neural network to obtain model averaging benefits without additional training cost. The main strength of the approach is that it is straightforward and very effective. The paper is also very easy to understand with very few proprietary optimization techniques. NoAdditionalTrainingCost is the strongest claim in the paper. Unfortunately, the paper lacks proof for most of the claims. The only benchmarked model is DenseNet and the results are limited to 4.4% error rate. The error rate is also very close to the state-of-the-art at that time (2016). It is unlikely that the technique can still compete with modern models years later. Finally, the code is not made available so it is not possible to reproduce the results. Overall, the paper provides a interesting approach to train neural networks, but lacks significant empirical evidence to validate its claims. *The main content of the paper is incorrect and the claims are highly questionable. Instead of addressing model averaging benefits without additional cost, the paper only claims that the model can achieve 3.4% CIFAR-10 error rate with no additional cost. The error rate is actually achieved with a very expensive method (Cyclic Learning Rate Schedules). The cost of the method is overshined by the claimed model performance. Additionally, the paper doesn't show the code and there are several other papers that already achieve similar results with much cheaper method. It is unlikely that this method would have been overlooked by the scientific community. In addition to the incorrect claims, the paper also lacks empirical evidence to validate the basic premise. No other models are tested and the results on CIFAR-100 are very limited. In summary, although the method claims to train neural networks with no additional cost, the result seems very unlikely and it is highly questionable. The claims should be justified by empirical evidence and the basic premise should be checked by testing other models.* As a side note, the paper references 1 and 2 in the introduction and shows some similarity to them. However, there are many significant differences: 1. Model averaging is concerned while in those papers, model weighting is concerned; 2. the proposed method saves the model parameters while in the paper 1, the models are pre-trained and only the parameters are saved; 3. The proposed method trains multiple local models while in the paper 1, only a single model is trained. In fact, the paper 1 also shows good result with much cheaper method (full training with cyclic learning rate) while the paper 2 only mentions it without presenting the results. In summary, although the idea is similar, the papers are very different and it is unlikely that the idea can lead to such results in the paper 2. *The referenced papers are: - 1: [Learning without Forgetting: periodically cyclic learning rates for efficient training of deep neural networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/1510.08463) - 2: [Learning without Measuring: periodically cyclic learning rates for efficient training of deep neural networks](https://www.ece.ucsb.edu/mailgly/ announcements/EM58-1@ece.ucsb.edu--Learning-without-Measuring.pdf) Furthermore, the authors first introduce the basic concept and then build up the whole model with no clear explanation and no comparison with other methods. The work presented in this paper proposes a method to get an ensemble of neural networks at no extra training cost (i.e., at the cost of training a single network), by saving snapshots of the network during training. Network is trained using a cyclic (cosine) learning rate schedule; the snapshots are obtained when the learning rate is at the lowest points of the cycles. Using these snapshot ensembles, they show gains in performance over a single network on the image classification task on a variety of datasets.


Positives:

1. The work should be easy to adopt and re-produce, given the simple techinque and the experimental details in the paper.
2. Well written paper, with clear description of the method and thorough experiments.


Suggestions for improvement / other comments:

1. While it is fair to compare against other techniques assuming a fixed computational budget, for a clear perspective, thorough comaprisons with "true ensembles" (i.e., ensembles of networks trained independently) should be provided.
Specificially, Table 4 should be augmented with results from "true ensembles".

2. Comparison with true ensembles is only provided for DenseNet-40 on CIFAR100 in Figure 4. The proposed snapshot ensemble achieves approximately 66% of the improvement of "true ensemble" over the single baseline model. This is not reflected accurately in the authors' claim in the abstract: "[snapshot ensembles] **almost match[es]** the results of far more expensive independently trained [true ensembles]."

3. As mentioned before: to understand the diversity of snapshot ensembles, it would help to the diversity against different ensembling technique, e.g. (1) "true ensembles", (2) ensembles from dropout as described by Gal et. al, 2016 (Dropout as a Bayesian Approximation).
Significant problem, interesting and simple solution, broad evaluation, authors highly responsive in incorporating feedback, all reviewers recommend acceptance. I agree.

After reading the paper, it appears to have a fatal flaw. In addition, it seems to me to make very disingenuous claims about its own experimental results.

As far as I can tell, this is how the authors train their snapshot ensemble:

(1) initialize the model
(2) train for a short period (e.g. 50 epochs for DenseNet) with a cosine schedule
(3) take a snapshot
(4) continue training with a "new" cosine schedule for another short period
(5) take a snapshot
(6) repeat steps 4 and 5 a few times
(7) ensemble the snapshots

Call this strategy A

Then the authors also discuss another strategy they call "full ensembling", which they compare to in Figure 4:

(1) initialize the model
(2) train for a long period (e.g. 300 epochs) with a "traditional" schedule
(3) take a snapshot
(4) re-initialize the model randomly
(5) train for a long period (e.g. 300 epochs) with a "traditional" schedule
(6) take a snapshot
(7) repeat steps (4) through (6) a few times
(8) ensemble the snapshots

Call this strategy B

However, consider the following strategy C:

(1) initialize the model
(2) train for a short period (e.g. 50 epochs in Figure 2) with a cosine schedule
(3) take a snapshot
(4) re-initialize the model randomly
(5) train for a short period (e.g. 50 epochs in Figure 2) with a cosine schedule
(6) take a snapshot
(7) repeat steps (4) through (6) a few times
(8) ensemble the snapshots

Strategy C is likely superior to strategy A, and this seems to invalidates the entire claim of the paper that it we should build ensembles by taking snapshots along the training path. It is likely better to train many independent models each with the cosine schedule for a short period instead of taking snapshots. Therefore, the paper appears to be a de-novation compared to full ensembling, not an innovation. This is obscured by the fact that the authors only compare to strategy B, which is a very weak baseline. Of course, if I want to train an ensemble quickly, it seems suboptimal to train any individual model for a very long time, which strategy B does.

The work presented in this paper proposes a method to get an ensemble of neural networks at no extra training cost (i.e., at the cost of training a single network), by saving snapshots of the network during training. Network is trained using a cyclic (cosine) learning rate schedule; the snapshots are obtained when the learning rate is at the lowest points of the cycles. Using these snapshot ensembles, they show gains in performance over a single network on the image classification task on a variety of datasets.

machine_text: Natural videos contain both smooth motion and detailed content, and disentangling them is a highly desirable property for video prediction. In this work, Chen et al. successfully decompose motion and content by defining them as two separated streams in a 3-channel video representation. In the separated streams, the content stream can be predicted using the motion stream and the paired content, and the motion stream can be further refined using the cross-stream relation with the content stream and the paired motion. By explicitly modeling the cross-stream relation, the proposed method obtains more coherent motion stream and thus better prediction for the content stream. The separated representation is also convenient for coplanar rotations and other transformations. The empirical evaluation on large scale video datasets shows that the proposed method significantly outperforms the state of the art. I have read the paper carefully and feel qualified to review it. I feel that the separation of motion and content is a useful idea and the model in the paper has good flexibility to handle various transformations. However, as the author admits, the current solution only addresses coplanar rotation. The extension to other transformations, such as background substitution, is missing. I suggest the following approach to improve the current solution. First, build separate sub-networks for different transformations. Then, apply the proposed method to each sub-network to get the final prediction. This way, the method can be applied to arbitrary transformations. Another point that should be considered in the future work is the application of the proposed method to video classification and semi-supervised learning. Currently, the method is purely unsupervised.

Strongly Related Work Decomposing Motion from content is difficult to process, especially for unconstrained videos. Motion estimation is an essential step in video processing. In the process of doing motion estimation, one could separate the motion information from the content information. However, content has a strong correlation with motion; therefore separating the motion from the content is really separating luminance from color. In the past few years, methods based on deep learning have achieved remarkable performance in video processing. For example, one of the earliest works proposed a two-stream network based on CNNs for separating motion and content. Later, some other networks based on 3D ConvNets and Generative Adversarial Nets were proposed for similar purposes. All these methods achieve state-of-the-art results on benchmark datasets. However, they cannot decompose motion and content on the fly during video streaming. Video viewers have to wait until the whole video is downloaded before the video content can be analyzed. By analyzing the problem, this paper focuses on natural video sequence prediction. Unlike previous video processing tasks, natural video is captured under unconstrained and evolving environments. Therefore, separating motion from content within natural videos is more complicated than analyzing a still image. In this context, the proposed two-stream network can learn the motion and content representation from the same input by comparing it against a memory buffer. Also, the two-stream network can be trained in an end-to-end fashion. Thus, the motion and content representation can be computed and deployed during video streaming. To the best of my knowledge, this is the first work that addresses this problem. Proposed Algorithm The proposed model is based on the two-stream network. The first stream is a motion stream, which encodes motion information from a global motion vector. The second stream is a content stream, which encodes content information from the decoded frames in the current time step. The two streams are combined by element-wise multiplying them. The product represents the similarity between the current time step and the past reconstructed frames. Since there is a huge difference between the current time step and reconstructed frames in the past, the similarity is very small. In contrast, if the two streams contain similar information, then the similarity is large. In other words, the similarity measures the temporal coherence between the current frame and the reconstructed ones. The similarity is further used to predict the next frame, based on the state machine. There are three loss functions in the proposed method. The first one is a reconstruction loss, which measures the temporal coherence between the current time step and the reconstructed frames. The second one is a KL divergence to measure the similarity between prior distributions. It is based on variational Autoencoders. The last one is a supervised loss, which is used to force the extracted content and motion features to be separable. In summary, the proposed model consists of three components: (1) a temporal prior, which models temporal coherence with a long-term memory buffer; (2) an encoder, which includes a multi-layer perceptron for encoding input videos; and (3) a decoder, which includes a KL divergence to measure the similarity between prior distributions. Model Architecture The whole network architecture is based on the VGG16 architecture. The video sequence is divided into non-overlapping frames of size N x N. The first three fully connected layers are removed. A new FC layer is added to output the size of N x 1 for each frame. Additionally, a time step size of 1 is added to each frame to give the size of N x 1 x T. At last, softplus is used to scale the outputs to ensure that they are non-negative. The frame representation is calculated by passing the input frame through a Convolutional layer with filter size 3 x 3 and a stride of 2. The outputs of the convolutional layer are then max pooled. Video Decoding The model is trained by a lossy reconstruction of the current frame, and the generated samples will be used in the next frame prediction. First, we decode the output of the last frame, then we use that to generate the previous two frames according to the current state machine. If the input sequence is p = (x_1,..., x_N), then the output is [y_1, y_2,..., y_n], where n = N - 1, and y_i = x_i + p_i, where p_i is the prediction of x_i from the model. It is worth mentioning that the presented approach works for many generation tasks, e.g., natural video synthesis, which provides another method to visualize the motion in natural videos. Thank you again for the feedback.

The proposed deep neural network for the prediction of future frames in natural video sequences has shown to achieve state-of-the-art performance on human activity videos. The key idea is to separate the motion and content information, which is the basic dynamic characteristics of an image or sequence. To achieve this, we use the Encoder-Decoder architecture with ConvLSTM. The model is trained end-to-end to decompose the motion and content information in the input sequence. The results show that modeling the motion and content independently is an effective way to reduce the complexity of dynamic prediction. Our model is trained on large human activity datasets, and shows state-of-the-art performance. The proposed model can be directly applied to other sequence prediction tasks, such as sports highlights prediction and automation, high-speed photography, etc. Our main contribution is a new end-to-end trainable model with motion and content separation for natural video prediction. Weaknesses: The model is evaluated on synthetic dataset and lack of real world dataset for benchmarking. In addition, the model can be further improved in terms of efficiency and accuracy. Strength: The proposed model is the first end-to-end trainable network architecture with separate modeling of motion and content for dynamic prediction in natural videos. The model can be applied to other sequence prediction tasks. Overall, the proposed model shows promise for dynamic prediction in natural videos, and could be applied to other sequence prediction tasks in different scenarios.
human_text:
1) Summary

This paper investigates the usefulness of decoupling appearance and motion information for the problem of future frame prediction in natural videos. The method introduces a novel two-stream encoder-decoder architecture, MCNet, consisting of two separate encoders -- a convnet on single frames and a convnet+LSTM on sequences of temporal differences -- followed by combination layers (stacking + convolutions) and a deconvolutional network decoder leveraging also residual connections from the two encoders. The architecture is trained end-to-end using the objective and adversarial training strategy of Mathieu et al.

2) Contributions

+ The architecture seems novel and is well motivated. It is also somewhat related to the two-stream networks of Simonyan & Zisserman, which are very effective for real-world action recognition.
+ The qualitative results are numerous, insightful, and very convincing (including quantitatively) on KTH & Weizmann, showing the benefits of decoupling content and motion for simple scenes with periodic motions, as well as the need for residual connections.

3) Suggestions for improvement

Static dataset bias:
In response to the pre-review concerns about the observed static nature of the qualitative results, the authors added a simple baseline consisting in copying the pixels of the last observed frame. On the one hand, the updated experiments on KTH confirm the good results of the method in these conditions. On the other hand, the fact that this baseline is better than all other methods (not just the authors's) on UCF101 casts some doubts on whether reporting average statistics on UCF101 is insightful enough. Although the authors provide some qualitative analysis pertaining to the quantity of motion, further quantitative analysis seems necessary to validate the performance of this and other methods on future frame prediction. At least, the results on UCF101 should be disambiguated with respect to the type of scene, for instance by measuring the overall quantity of motion (e.g., l2 norm of time differences) and reporting PSNR and SSIM per quartile / decile. Ideally, other realistic datasets than UCF101 should be considered in complement. For instance, the Hollywood 2 dataset of Marszalek et al would be a good candidate, as it focuses on movies and often contains complex actor, camera, and background motions that would make the "pixel-copying" baseline very poor. Experiments on video datasets beyond actions, like the KITTI tracking benchmark, would also greatly improve the paper.

Additional recognition experiments:
As mentioned in pre-review questions, further UCF-101 experiments on action recognition tasks by fine-tuning would also greatly improve the paper. Classifying videos indeed requires learning both appearance and motion features, and the two-stream encoder + combination layers of the MCNet+Res architecture seem particularly adapted, if they indeed allowed for unsupervised pre-trainining of content and motion representations, as postulated by the authors. These experiments would also contribute to dispelling the aforementioned concerns about the static nature of the learned representations.

4) Conclusion

Overall, this paper proposes an interesting architecture for an important problem, but requires additional experiments to substantiate the claims made by the authors. If the authors make the aforementioned additional experiments and the results are convincing, then this paper would be clearly relevant for ICLR.

5) Post-rebuttal final decision

The authors did a significant amount of additional work, following the suggestions made by the reviewers, and providing additional compelling experimental evidence. This makes this one of the most experimentally thorough ones for this problem. I, therefore, increase my rating, and suggest to accept this paper. Good job!

1) Summary

This paper investigates the usefulness of decoupling appearance and motion information for the problem of future frame prediction in natural videos. The method introduces a novel two-stream encoder-decoder architecture, MCNet, consisting of two separate encoders -- a convnet on single frames and a convnet+LSTM on sequences of temporal differences -- followed by combination layers (stacking + convolutions) and a deconvolutional network decoder leveraging also residual connections from the two encoders. The architecture is trained end-to-end using the objective and adversarial training strategy of Mathieu et al.

2) Contributions

+ The architecture seems novel and is well motivated. It is also somewhat related to the two-stream networks of Simonyan & Zisserman, which are very effective for real-world action recognition.
+ The qualitative results are numerous, insightful, and very convincing (including quantitatively) on KTH & Weizmann, showing the benefits of decoupling content and motion for simple scenes with periodic motions, as well as the need for residual connections.

3) Suggestions for improvement

Static dataset bias:
In response to the pre-review concerns about the observed static nature of the qualitative results, the authors added a simple baseline consisting in copying the pixels of the last observed frame. On the one hand, the updated experiments on KTH confirm the good results of the method in these conditions. On the other hand, the fact that this baseline is better than all other methods (not just the authors's) on UCF101 casts some doubts on whether reporting average statistics on UCF101 is insightful enough. Although the authors provide some qualitative analysis pertaining to the quantity of motion, further quantitative analysis seems necessary to validate the performance of this and other methods on future frame prediction. At least, the results on UCF101 should be disambiguated with respect to the type of scene, for instance by measuring the overall quantity of motion (e.g., l2 norm of time differences) and reporting PSNR and SSIM per quartile / decile. Ideally, other realistic datasets than UCF101 should be considered in complement. For instance, the Hollywood 2 dataset of Marszalek et al would be a good candidate, as it focuses on movies and often contains complex actor, camera, and background motions that would make the "pixel-copying" baseline very poor. Experiments on video datasets beyond actions, like the KITTI tracking benchmark, would also greatly improve the paper.

Additional recognition experiments:
As mentioned in pre-review questions, further UCF-101 experiments on action recognition tasks by fine-tuning would also greatly improve the paper. Classifying videos indeed requires learning both appearance and motion features, and the two-stream encoder + combination layers of the MCNet+Res architecture seem particularly adapted, if they indeed allowed for unsupervised pre-trainining of content and motion representations, as postulated by the authors. These experiments would also contribute to dispelling the aforementioned concerns about the static nature of the learned representations.

4) Conclusion

Overall, this paper proposes an interesting architecture for an important problem, but requires additional experiments to substantiate the claims made by the authors. If the authors make the aforementioned additional experiments and the results are convincing, then this paper would be clearly relevant for ICLR.

5) Post-rebuttal final decision

The authors did a significant amount of additional work, following the suggestions made by the reviewers, and providing additional compelling experimental evidence. This makes this one of the most experimentally thorough ones for this problem. I, therefore, increase my rating, and suggest to accept this paper. Good job!

machine_text: In your paper "Generalizing Skills with Semi-Supervised Reinforcement Learning", you propose a framework for semi-supervised generalizing skills, where you show that with access to few labeled samples from the target task, we can still learn to perform well on it by transferring from unlabeled samples. While the theoretical analysis is valuable, and the empirical results are satisfying, there are two potential problems in the current setup. First, the agent you are training in the tan-gboard could actually solve the target task by trial and error, which may not be generalizable. In order to evaluate if the learned skills are generalizable, you can either make the policy evaluation assumptions more flexible, or introduce a distillation mechanism to check the task-specificity of the policy. The first option may be harder in practice, but the second option may yield optimistic evaluation, because even if the policy is task-specific, the distillation could learn a trivial mapping from the actions to the targets. A stronger evaluation would be to use unsupervised recognition networks to check if the state feature extractor in the agent is capturing the discriminative information. The second potential problem is that the agent you trained may not be able to find the correct action when put in new states not seen during training. One possible solution is to add a new task-specific supervisor to the training set, which would evaluate the agent after seeing the new states, and force it to take the correct action. Gravity is an effective approach to mitigating cyclic behavior in the Atari game sandbox. However, this approach requires collecting human rewards, which are both time consuming and labor intensive. In this work, you present a method to train a single Q-network to play both end-to-end and independently of any reward signal. Extensive experiments on several sandbox games demonstrate that the method is effective in avoiding mode collapse and improving sample efficiency.

In this paper, the author addresses the problem of generalizing skills, which is a longstanding issue in reinforcement learning. The author proposes a solution that uses semi-supervised reinforcement learning, where a proxy task is used to help learn a general purpose policy. The proxy task is a board game, Chainmail, which provides a somewhat random aspect to the actions, making it a suitable training ground for a general purpose agent. The paper is well-written, and the proposal has promise, but there are some significant challenges in actually implementing this approach. One significant challenge is that Chainmail has a large number of states and actions, which means that for most tasks the agent would have to rely on observed information about the current state. This means that there would not be much learn from exploration, and the agent would need to depend on the initial state, which is already known to the agent. In addition, Chainmail does not have a clear objective, which means that the agent would not be learning to optimize a meaningful reward signal. -- Problem: Generalizing skills is a challenging problem in reinforcement learning, and the conventional solution is to use a specific task to train the agent. This approach has two major problems. First, it requires a lot of manual effort to design a task that captures the desired behavior, and even with that careful design, there may be significant variability between tasks, which makes it difficult to generalize the learned policy. Second, even with a well-designed task, there may be significant randomness in the environment, which makes it difficult to generalize the policy. Solution: The author of this paper describes a solution that uses semi-supervised reinforcement learning to train a general purpose agent. The proposed approach uses a proxy task, Chainmail, which provides a somewhat random aspect to the state. This allows the agent to generalize to new tasks by using a technique called experience replay. The author demonstrates that Chainmail is a good proxy task by comparing the resulting policy to human players. -- The paper Generalizing Skills with Semi-Supervised Reinforcement Learning describes a solution to the problem of generalizing skills using semi-supervised reinforcement learning. The author describes a proxy task, Chainmail, that provides some level of randomness in the state space, which is intended to allow the agent to generalize to new tasks. The Chainmail game is played on a grid where markers represent combatants and boxes represent terrain. At the start of the game, two generators choose two boxes and swap their positions. The generators are initially chosen by the agent, and the generators follow a random walk. The action space for Chainmail is very large, and even with experience replay, the algorithm is not able to converge to a good policy. The author describes an alternate strategy that reduces the state space, which allows the algorithm to achieve better performance. The author also describes experiments using the learned policy to play other unrelated games, which the author attributes to the increased generalization of the policy.

The main content of the paper is fairly interesting and has the potential to be very useful in practice. I have some suggestions to improve the paper. First, a more detailed background of RL and how it relates to the paper would be helpful. I am not an expert in both fields, and having a simple explanation of the differences in these two approaches could help others better understand the paper. Second, I think the terminology used in this paper could be better. E.g. in the first paragraph, the terms “supervisor” and “label” are used without an explanation. Third, it would be helpful to have a simple table that compares this work to related approaches, both in terms of what aspects are addressed and what benefits are achieved. Finally, I am concerned that the control tasks used in this work may be very difficult for the model to learn because the observations are images, which do not carry useful primitive values that could be extracted by the model. For example, the robot may not be able to tell the difference between a red floor and a green floor (this would not be useful information for the RL agent to learn). A simple control task that is easier to solve with a model would help validate the paper’s approach. Overall, I think this paper is technically sound and has the potential to be useful in practice, but it could be strengthened by describing its relation to existing work in the field and focusing more on control tasks that are more easily solved by a learned model.

In this paper, we propose a method to generalize deep reinforcement learning (RL) policies through experience that is not labeled. We call this method semi-supervised reinforcement learning (SSRL). We formulate SSRL as semi-supervised learning (SSL), where we train an algorithm to perform inference on the task objective in the unlabeled MDP and generalizes the agent’s behavior using the demonstrations by acting according to the inferred task objective. SSRL is closely related to prior work on reward function abstraction and generalization, but we make the important observation that we do not need to estimate the entire transfer function between states and actions; we can get a good approximation with only the demonstrations of the labeled MDPs. We develop a new algorithm that first learns an expressive but simple approximation of the task objective, and then performs planning and operation directly in the latent space. Our experiments in continuous control tasks show that SSRL can significantly outperform prior methods that only use supervised training from the labeled MDPs. implementation details of SSRL In our experiments, SSRL consists of two steps. First, an algorithm is trained to perform inference on the task objective in the unlabeled MDP. Then, based on the inferred task objective, the agent performs planning and operation in a latent space. We introduce a differentiable actor-critic algorithm, that first learns an approximation of the task objective and then performs online learning and execution. During training, we use the demonstrations of the labeled MDPs to refine the approximation of the objective, similar to inverse RL. Unlike previous work, we are not assuming access to the true task objective during execution.
human_text:
The paper proposes to study the problem of semi-supervised RL where one has to distinguish between labelled MDPs that provide rewards, and unlabelled MDPs that are not associated with any reward signal. The underlying is very simple since it aims at simultaneously learning a policy based on the REINFORCE+entropy regularization technique, and also a model of the reward that will be used (as in inverse reinforcement learning) as a feedback over unlabelled MDPs. The experiments are made on different continous domains and show interesting results

The paper is well written, and easy to understand. It is based on a simple but efficient idea of simultaneously learning the policy and a model of the reward and the resulting algorithm exhibit interesting properties. The proposed idea is quite obvious, but the authors are the first ones to propose to test such a model. The experiments could be made stronger by mixing continuous and discrete problems but are convincing.

This paper provides an interesting framework for handling semi-supervised RL problems, settings were one can interact with many MDPs drawn from some class, but where only a few have observable rewards; the agent then uses a policy derived from the labeled MDPs to estimate a reward function for the unlabeled MDPs. The approach is straightforward, and one reviewer raises the reasonable concern that this seems to be a fairly narrow definition and approach to the universe of things that could be thought of as semi-supervised reinforcement learning (elements like Laplacian value functions, e.g. proto value functions, for instance, present a very different take on could what also be considered semi-supervised RL).
 
 Overall, however, the main benefit of this paper is that the overall idea here is quite compelling. Even if it's a narrow view on semisupervised RL, it nonetheless is clearly thinking more broadly about skill and data efficiency than what is common in many current RL papers. Given this impressive scope, plus good performance (if only on a relatively small set of benchmarks), it seems like this paper is certainly above bar for acceptance.
 
 Pros:
 + Nice introduction of a new/modified semisupervised reinforce setting
 + Results on benchmarks look compelling (if still fairly small scale)
 
 Cons:
 - Rather limited view of the space of all possible semisupervised Rl
 - Results on hardest task (half-cheetah) aren't _that_ much better than much simpler approaches

In supervised learning, a significant advance occurred when the framework of semi-supervised learning was  adopted, which used the weaker approach of unsupervised learning to infer some property, such as a distance measure or a smoothness regularizer, which could then be used with a small number of labeled examples. The approach rested on the assumption of smoothness on the manifold, typically. 

This paper attempts to stretch this analogy to reinforcement learning, although the analogy is somewhat incoherent. Labels are not equivalent to reward functions, and positive or negative rewards do not mean the same as positive and negative labels. Still, the paper makes a worthwhile attempt to explore this notion of semi-supervised RL, which is clearly an important area that deserves more attention. The authors use the term "labeled MDP" to mean the typical MDP framework where the reward function is unknown. They use the confusing term "unlabeled MDP" to mean the situation where the reward is unknown, which is technically not an MDP (but a controlled Markov process). 

In the classical RL transfer learning setup, the agent is attempting to transfer learning from a source "labeled" MDP to a target "labeled" MDP (where both reward functions are known, but the learned policy is known only in the source MDP). In the semi-supervised RL setting, the target is an "unlabeled" CMP, and the source is both a "labeled" MDP and an "unlabeled" CMP. The basic approach is to use inverse RL to infer the unknown "labels" and then attempt to construct transfer. A further restriction is made to linearly solvable MDPs for technical reasons. Experiments are reported using three relatively complex domains using the Mujoco physics simulator. 

The work is interesting, but in the opinion of this reviewer, the work fails to provide a simple sufficiently general notion of semi-supervised RL that will be of sufficiently wide interest to the RL community. That remains to be done by a future paper, but in the interim, the work here is sufficiently interesting and the problem is certainly a worthwhile one to study.

This paper formalizes the problem setting of having only a subset of available MDPs for which one has access to a reward. The authors name this setting "semi-supervised reinforcement learning" (SSRL), as a reference to semi-supervised learning (where one only has access to labels for a subset of the dataset). They provide an approach for solving SSRL named semi-supervised skill generalization (S3G), which builds on the framework of maximum entropy control. The whole approach is straightforward and amounts to an EM algorithm with partial labels (: they alternate iteratively between estimating a reward function (parametrized) and fitting a control policy using this reward function. They provide experiments on 4 tasks (obstacle, 2-link reacher, 2-link reacher with vision, half-cheetah) in MuJoCo.

The paper is well-written, and is overall clear. The appendix provides some more context, I think a few implementation details are missing to be able to fully reproduce the experiments from the paper, but they will provide the code.

The link to inverse reinforcement learning seems to be done correctly. However, there is no reference to off-policy policy learning, and, for instance, it seems to me that the \tau \in D_{samp} term of equation (3) could benefit from variance reduction as in e.g. TB(\lambda) [Precup et al. 2000] or Retrace(\lambda) [Munos et al. 2016].

The experimental section is convincing, but I would appreciate a precision (and small discussion) of this sentence "To extensively test the generalization capabilities of the policies learned with each method, we measure performance on a wide range of settings that is a superset of the unlabeled and labeled MDPs" with numbers for the different scenarios (or the replacement of superset by "union" if this is the case). It may explain better the poor results of "oracle" on "obstacle" and "2-link reacher", and reinforce* the further sentences "In the obstacle task, the true reward function is not sufficiently shaped for learning in the unlabeled MDPs. Hence, the reward regression and oracle methods perform poorly".

Correction on page 4: "5-tuple M_i = (S, A, T, R)" is a 4-tuple.

Overall, I think that this is a good and sound paper. I am personally unsure as to if all the parallels and/or references to previous work are complete, thus my confidence score of 3.

It is based on a simple but efficient idea of simultaneously learning the policy and a model of the reward and the resulting algorithm exhibit interesting properties. The proposed idea is quite obvious, but the authors are the first ones to propose to test such a model. This paper provides an interesting framework for handling semi-supervised RL problems, settings were one can interact with many MDPs drawn from some class, but where only a few have observable rewards; the agent then uses a policy derived from the labeled MDPs to estimate a reward function for the unlabeled MDPs. The approach is straightforward, and one reviewer raises the reasonable concern that this seems to be a fairly narrow definition and approach to the universe of things that could be thought of as semi-supervised reinforcement learning (elements like Laplacian value functions, e.g. proto value functions, for instance, present a very different take on could what also be considered semi-supervised RL).
 
 Overall, however, the main benefit of this paper is that the overall idea here is quite compelling. Even if it's a narrow view on semisupervised RL, it nonetheless is clearly thinking more broadly about skill and data efficiency than what is common in many current RL papers. Given this impressive scope, plus good performance (if only on a relatively small set of benchmarks), it seems like this paper is certainly above bar for acceptance.

 + Nice introduction of a new/modified semisupervised reinforce setting
 + Results on benchmarks look compelling (if still fairly small scale)
 
 Cons:
 - Rather limited view of the space of all possible semisupervised Rl

In supervised learning, a significant advance occurred when the framework of semi-supervised learning was  adopted, which used the weaker approach of unsupervised learning to infer some property, such as a distance measure or a smoothness regularizer, which could then be used with a small number of labeled examples. The approach rested on the assumption of smoothness on the manifold, typically. 

This paper attempts to stretch this analogy to reinforcement learning, although the analogy is somewhat incoherent. Labels are not equivalent to reward functions, and positive or negative rewards do not mean the same as positive and negative labels. Still, the paper makes a worthwhile attempt to explore this notion of semi-supervised RL, which is clearly an important area that deserves more attention. The authors use the term "labeled MDP" to mean the typical MDP framework where the reward function is unknown. They use the confusing term "unlabeled MDP" to mean the situation where the reward is unknown, which is technically not an MDP (but a controlled Markov process). 

In the classical RL transfer learning setup, the agent is attempting to transfer learning from a source "labeled" MDP to a target "labeled" MDP (where both reward functions are known, but the learned policy is known only in the source MDP). In the semi-supervised RL setting, the target is an "unlabeled" CMP, and the source is both a "labeled" MDP and an "unlabeled" CMP. The basic approach is to use inverse RL to infer the unknown "labels" and then attempt to construct transfer. A further restriction is made to linearly solvable MDPs for technical reasons. Experiments are reported using three relatively complex domains using the Mujoco physics simulator. 

The work is interesting, but in the opinion of this reviewer, the work fails to provide a simple sufficiently general notion of semi-supervised RL that will be of sufficiently wide interest to the RL community. That remains to be done by a future paper, but in the interim, the work here is sufficiently interesting and the problem is certainly a worthwhile one to study.

This paper formalizes the problem setting of having only a subset of available MDPs for which one has access to a reward. The authors name this setting "semi-supervised reinforcement learning" (SSRL), as a reference to semi-supervised learning (where one only has access to labels for a subset of the dataset). They provide an approach for solving SSRL named semi-supervised skill generalization (S3G), which builds on the framework of maximum entropy control. The whole approach is straightforward and amounts to an EM algorithm with partial labels (: they alternate iteratively between estimating a reward function (parametrized) and fitting a control policy using this reward function. They provide experiments on 4 tasks (obstacle, 2-link reacher, 2-link reacher with vision, half-cheetah) in MuJoCo.

The paper is well-written, and is overall clear. The appendix provides some more context, I think a few implementation details are missing to be able to fully reproduce the experiments from the paper, but they will provide the code.

The link to inverse reinforcement learning seems to be done correctly. However, there is no reference to off-policy policy learning, and, for instance, it seems to me that the \tau \in D_{samp} term of equation (3) could benefit from variance reduction as in e.g. TB(\lambda) [Precup et al. 2000] or Retrace(\lambda) [Munos et al. 2016].

The experimental section is convincing, but I would appreciate a precision (and small discussion) of this sentence "To extensively test the generalization capabilities of the policies learned with each method, we measure performance on a wide range of settings that is a superset of the unlabeled and labeled MDPs" with numbers for the different scenarios (or the replacement of superset by "union" if this is the case). Hence, the reward regression and oracle methods perform poorly".

Overall, I think that this is a good and sound paper. I am personally unsure as to if all the parallels and/or references to previous work are complete, thus my confidence score of 3.
