human_text:
This paper proposes a new Bayesian neural network architecture for predicting the values of learning curves during the training of machine learning models. This is an exploratory paper, in that the ultimate goal is to use this method in a Bayesian optimization system, but for now the experiments are limited to assessing the quality of the predictions. This builds on previous work in Domhan, 2015, however in this work the model incorporates information from all tested hyperparameter settings rather than just extrapolating from a single learning curve. This paper also explores two MCMC methods for inference: SGLD and SGHMC, but I couldn’t tell if either of these were tested in Domhan, 2015 as well.

The performance seems overall positive, particularly in the initial phase of each curve where there is very little information. In this case, as expected, sharing knowledge across curves helps. One regime which did not seem to be tested, but might be very informative, is when some curves in the training set have been mostly, or fully observed. This might be a case where sharing information really helps.

Something that concerns me about this approach is the timing. The authors stated that to train the network takes about 20-60 seconds. In the worst case, with 100 epochs, this results in a little over 1.5 hours spent training the Bayesian network. This is a non-trivial fraction of the several hours it takes to train the model being tuned.

The Bayesian network makes many separate predictions, as shown in Figure 2. It would be interesting to see how accurate some of these individual pieces are. For example, did you bound the asymptotic value of the learning curve, since you mostly predicted accuracy? If not, did the value tend to lie in [0,1]?

Below are some minor questions/comments.

Figure 1 axes should read “validation accuracy”
Figure 6 can you describe LastSeenValue (although it seems self-explanatory, it’s good to be explicit) in the bottom left figure, and why isn’t it used anywhere else as a baseline?
Figure 7 and Table 1 are you predicting just the final value of the curves? Or every value along each curve, conditioned on the previous values?
Why do you only use 5 basis functions? Does this sufficiently capture all of the flexibility of these learning curves? Would more basis functions help or hurt?

The reviewers agreed that this is a good paper that proposes an interesting approach to modeling training curves. The approach is well motivated in terms of surrogate based (e.g. Bayesian) optimization. They are convinced that a great model of training curves could be used to extrapolate in the future, greatly expediting hyperparameter search methods through early stopping. None of the reviewers championed the paper, however. They all stated that the paper just did not go far enough in showing that the method is really useful in practice. While the authors seem to have added some interesting additional results to this effect, it was a little too late for the reviewers to take into account. 
 
 It seems like this paper would benefit from some added experiments as per the authors' suggestions. Incorporating this within a Bayesian optimization methodology is certainly non-trivial (e.g. may require rethinking the modeling and acquisition function) but could be very impactful. The overall pros and cons are as follows:
 
 Pros:
 - Proposes a neat model for extrapolating training curves
 - Experiments show that the model can extrapolate quite well
 - It addresses a strong limitation of current hyperparameter optimization techniques
 
 Cons
 - The reviewers were underwhelmed with the experimental analysis
 - The paper did not push the ideas far enough to demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach

Overall, the PCs have established that, despite some of its weaknesses, this paper deserved to appear at the conference.

The paper addresses the problem of predicting learning curves. The key difference from prior work is that (1) the authors learn a neural network that generalizes across hyperparameter settings and (2) the authors use a Bayesian neural network with SGHMC. 
The authors demonstrate that the proposed approach is effective on extrapolating partially observed curves as well as predicting unobserved learning curves on various architectures (FC, CNN, LR and VAE). This seems very promising for Bayesian optimization, I'd love to see an experiment that evaluates the relative advantage of this proposed method :)

Have you thought about ways to handle learning rate decays? Perhaps you could run the algorithm on a random subset of data and extrapolate from that?

I was thinking of other evaluation measures in addition to MSE and LL. In practice, we care about the most promising run. Would it make sense to evaluate how accurately each method identified the best run?

Minor comments:

Fonts are too small and almost illegible on my hard copy. Please increase the font size for legends and axes in the figures.

Fig 6: not all figures seem to have six lines. Are the lines overlapping in some cases?

This paper is about using Bayesian neural networks to model learning curves (that arise from training ML algorithms). The application is hyper-parameter optimization: if we can model the learning curve, we can terminate bad runs early and save time. The paper builds on existing work that used parametric learning curves. Here, the parameters of these learning curves form the last layer of a Bayesian neural network. This seems like a totally sensible idea. 

I think the main strength of this paper is that it addresses an actual need. Based on my personal experience, there is high demand for a working system to do early termination in hyperparameter optimization. What I'd like to know, which I wish I'd asked during pre-review questions, is whether the authors plan to release their code. Do you? I sincerely hope so, because I think the code would be a significant part of the paper's contribution, since the nature of the paper is more practical than conceptual.

The experiments in the paper seem thorough but the results are a bit underwhelming. I'm less interested in the part about whether the learning curves are actually modeled well, and more interested in the impact on hyperparameter optimization. I was hoping to see BIG speedups as a result of using this method, but I am left feeling unsure how big the speedup really is. Instead of "objective function vs. iterations" I would be more interested in the inverse plot: number of iterations needed to get to a fixed objective function value. Since what I'm really interested in is how much time I can save. Ideally there would also be some mention of real time as sometimes these hyperparameter optimization methods are themselves so slow that they end up being unusable. 

Finally, one figure that I feel is missing is a histogram of termination times over different runs. This would provide me with more intuition than all the other figures. Because it would tell me, what fraction of runs are being terminated early. And, how early? Right now I have no sense of this, except that at least *some* runs are clearly being terminated early, since this is neccessary for the proposed method to outperform other methods.

Overall, I think this paper merits acceptance because it is a solid effort on an interesting problem. The progress is fairly incremental but I can live with that.

The paper Learning to Optimize, its main content is as below: Algorithm design is a laborious process and often requires many iterations of ideation and validation. In this paper, we explore automating algorithm design and present a method to learn an optimization algorithm. We approach this problem from a reinforcement learning perspective and represent any particular optimization algorithm as a policy. We learn an optimization algorithm using guided policy search and demonstrate that the resulting algorithm outperforms existing hand-engineered algorithms in terms of convergence speed and/or the final objective value. This paper has several interesting ideas. First, it considers algorithm design as a continuous control problem, which is very common in machine learning. Many previous works only consider offline algorithm design, i.e., the design is performed before the actual function is known. In contrast, online algorithm design allows the designer to learn from experience as the function is made available. Second, the authors adopt reinforcement learning, which is proven effective in diverse areas. It would be natural to combine the insights from different fields to tackle a challenging problem. Third, this paper provides a very extensive comparison with other baselines, which is rarely seen in other papers in this field.  Pros:

There is a series of somewhat-related papers on learning to optimize for sparse coding and other L1/L2 optimization problems.
Inference in sparse coding is often performed with the Iterative Shrinkage and Thresholding Algorithm (ISTA). 
ISTA can be viewed as a kind of recurrent net in which the matrices and non-linearities are specified by the reconstruction matrix.
The main idea is to train the matrices in this recurrent net to produce an approximate solution faster than ISTA.

Here are two examples:
[Gregor & LeCun, ICML 2010]

This papers adds to the literature on learning optimizers/algorithms that has gained popularity recently. The authors choose to use the framework of guided policy search at the meta-level to train the optimizers. They also opt to train on random objectives and assess transfer to a few simple tasks.

As pointed below, this is a useful addition.

However, the argument of using RL vs gradients at the meta-level that appears below is not clear or convincing. I urge the authors to run an experiment comparing the two approaches and to present comparative results. This is a very important question, and the scalability of this approach could very well hinge on this fact. Indeed, demonstrating both scaling to large domains and transfer to those domains is the key challenge in this domain.

In summary, the idea is a good one, but the experiments are weak.

This paper proposes an approach to learning a custom optimizer for a given class optimization problems. I think in the case of training machine learning algorithms, a class would represent a model like “logistic regression”. The authors cleverly cast this as a reinforcement learning problem and use guided policy search to train a neural network to map the current location and history onto a step direction/magnitude. Overall I think this is a great idea and a very nice contribution to the fast growing meta-learning literature. However, I think that there are some aspects that could be touched on to make this a stronger paper.

My first thought is that the authors claim to train the method to learn the regularities of an entire class of optimization problems, rather than learning to exploit regularities in a given set of tasks. The distinction here is not terribly clear to me. For example, in learning an optimizer for logistic regression, the authors seem to claim that learning on a randomly sampled set of logistic regression problems will allow the model to learn about logistic regression itself. I am not convinced of this, because there is bias in the randomly sampled data itself. From the paper in this case, “The instances are drawn randomly from two multivariate Gaussians with random means and covariances, with half drawn from each.” It seems the optimizer is then trained to optimize instances of logistic regression *given this specific family of training inputs* and not logistic regression problems in general. A simple experiment to prove the method works more generally would be to repeat the existing experiments, but where the test instances are drawn from a completely different distribution. It would be even more interesting to see how this changes as the test distribution deviates further from the training distribution.

Can the authors comment on the choice of architecture used here? Why one layer with 50 hidden units and softplus activations specifically? Why not e.g., 100 units, 2 layers and ReLUs?
Presumably this is to prevent overfitting, but given the limited capacity of the network, how do these results look when the dimensionality of the input space increases beyond 2 or 3?

I would love to see what kind of policy the network learns on e.g., a 2D function using a contour plot. What do the steps look like on a random problem instance when compared to other hand-engineered optimizers?

Overall I think this a really interesting paper with a great methodological contribution. My main concern is that the results may be oversold as the problems are still relatively simple and constrained. However, if the authors can demonstrate that this approach produces robust policies for a very general set of problems then that would be truly spectacular.

Minor notes below.

Section 3.1 should you be using \pi_T^* to denote the optimal policy? You use \pi_t^* and \pi^* currently.

Are the problems here considered noiseless? That is, is the state transition given an action deterministic? It would be very interesting to see this on noisy problems.

This work appeared on arxiv just before we were able to release our learning to learn by gradient descent by gradient descent paper. 
In our case, we were motivated by neural art and a desire to replace the lBFGS optimizer with a neural Turing machine (both have the same equation forms - see appendix of our arxiv version). In the end, we settled on an LSTM optimizer that is also learned by SGD. 

This paper, on the other hand, uses guided policy search to choose the parameter updates (policy). Importantly, this paper also emphasizes the importance of transfer of optimizers to novel tasks.

This is undoubtedly a timely, good contribution to the learning to learn literature, which has gained great popularity in recent months.

I have some questions about the details of your experiments and algorithm. The paper presents a method using Guided Policy Search (GPS) techniques for learning optimization algorithm (\pi). Since the contribution is mainly empirical, convincing experimental analysis is expected. Currently, all of three experiments were conducted on toy datasets. The number of parameters to be optimized is so small (only no more than 10). I suggest you evaluate your method on some standard datasets on middle or large scale network structures. Besides, other popular optimization algorithms, such as Adam, RMSprop, etc. should be compared. 
 
Another point I was wondering is whether your method is suitable for practical use. Both the value and the gradient of the objective function at the most recent H steps (H=25 in the paper) are encoded as state space. Suppose that the dimension of the parameters to be optimized is N, the dimension of the state space would be (1+N)*H. Then they are fed to a one layer network with 50 hidden units to model the policy (\pi), yielding N outputs to update parameters. But in practical scenario, the computational complexity and memory used for optimization algorithm should better not exceed the complexity of the training algorithm. Your policy network takes the gradients of all the parameters as input, which means policy network itself has more parameters to learn than the parameters of the problem of interest.

machine_text: Overall, the idea of the proposed method is very novel. I would like to point out some limitations of the proposed method from a practical perspective. 1) Does the proposed method work for fully-convolutional networks? Yes, the proposed method can be applied to fully-convolutional networks. We only need to compute the first term of the Lagrangian, i.e., Q[params], outside the neural network as a spatial kernel. 2) The code and model will be provided upon request. Could you please share the code and model? Yes, please let me know if you have any questions. The code and model will be shared upon request. 3) How to select the trade off parameters C and \lambda. This is a tricky question. The recommended way to select the parameters is to search for a balance point in the validation set. Generally, C is around 1 and \lambda is around 10^-6. brainsci performed a great service by publishing this, this is the first paper that explores the idea of training fully connected layers as sparsely coded parameterizations of more complex functions. I have some comments and suggestions about the paper 1) I think the density-diversity term could be better motivated/introduced. I would start by saying that I understand this as a training method for approximations of shifted Laplace distributions. In addition, the choice of shifted Laplace is odd, because we do not know anything about the location of the optimum parametrization, which we might know from, e.g., shift normal distribution if we assume you want the learnt parameters to be in the stable regime. This is not necessarily the case, so making the distribution shift-invariant is not a necessary restriction and it is potentially confusing. 2) To understand the relation of this to other work, it would be good to explicitly consider a "hard" sparsity-inducing norm (e.g., L1) and compare to other approaches. I would also like to see a theoretic comparison of the performance against to other approaches, say, normalized compression, where the L1 norm is used in combination with Newton's method to solve a large number of small linear systems. 3) Maybe add an additional column to the top-right of the table with the optimal value of lambda discovered in the last column, to get a better visual of how this value changes through different methods. 4) Is there any comment on how these methods perform on weight sharing structures that are popular in ml like mnist-perm?

This paper addresses the issue of training very large fully-connected networks (i.e. containing many millions of parameters). Fully-connected networks have connectivity between every pair of units, which increases the expressiveness of the network, but also increases the amount of training data required, and the memory requirements for storage of the network weights. The paper proposes a simple technique for training such large fully-connected networks, by combining techniques from sparse regularization, distributed computation, and distillation. Sparse regularization is used to reduce the memory requirements of the network by reducing the total number of parameters. Distributed computation allows the network to be trained with a small number of machines, by splitting the computation across multiple machines. Finally, distillation is used to efficiently train the network during initialization, by training with a small number of examples (known as hard labels). The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated on large, deep fully-connected networks, and on networks with multiple branches, allowing the learning of multiple tasks simultaneously. particularly addressed how to train very large fully connected networks. This paper brings together techniques from sparse regularization, distributed computation, and distillation to efficiently train these large fully-connected networks. The authors show that they can train these networks on large datasets, and also train these networks with low storage requirements. The loss function was then made a combination of the sparse regularizer, distillation with hard labels and distributed computation to train the network. This allowed the paper to successfully train these networks with a very small memory foot print. The main downside to this method is that it is not clear how to extend this to networks with multiple branches, which are a very common architecture for learning multiple tasks at the same time. This would require additional training with hard labels, but as this would require multiple copies of the network to be trained with different labels, this would substantially increase the required amount of hard labels.

The paper is interesting and noteworthy. I recommend acceptance after the following points are addressed. 1. Although the work makes an interesting observation that DDP reduces the number of parameters and distinct values, the experiments and analysis are lack of rigor. For example, the quantitative analysis on the number of parameters and distinct values are based on random sampling without biological validation. The paper should be more focus on the theoretical/empirical analysis, e.g., how many parameters can be pruned while keeping 95% accuracy. 2. The paper only compares with baselines, but does not show the merits over other state-of-the-art methods, e.g., Tungstun’s threshold, dynamic splicing. 3. The motivation for DDP is to “let the model learn more sparsity by searching the global optimum”, which is arguable. The authors should give more insights about the global optimum searched by the model for the density-diversity penalty. 4. More comparisons to other model compression techniques, e.g., pruning, quantization, shall be included to convince the readers that DDP is not only a good technology for model compression, but also better than other model compression techniques. Otherwise, the work is worthy of acceptance with its current state. I have carefully read the paper and provided my feedback. Generally, the idea of imposing a penalty on the number of distinct values is interesting. However, there are not good parameterizations that lead to high distinct values (as the distinctness requirement is in turn hard to meet in a directly parameterizable way). The authors should present more discussion on the indirect form of the proposed penalty that can lead to high distinct values, such as the $\ell_1$ penalty on the magnitude of the parameters. Also, the authors claim that DDP can significantly reduce the number of distinct values without loss in performance. However, a more comprehensive set of experiments (e.g., involving multiple models and tasks) is needed to confirm this. Although I am not an expert on the applications of the training-on-constrained-devices, the proposed DDP can be potentially be applied to many such devices (e.g., smartphone, smartwatch, Internet-of-Things). I believe the authors should discuss more about the potential benefits of using DDP instead of compressing models in general. I believe the paper is potentially suitable for the publication in your journal. However, before making a decision, the journal should consider the above comments.

This paper effectively solves the problem of optimizing fully-connected layers of neural networks with a huge number of parameters. The regularizer they proposed has very good performance while being much more efficient in computation and storage, which means it can be applied to a wider range of scenarios. layer description Density-Diversity (D2D) regularizer is proposed to reduce the number of parameters andINSTEAD of increasing model capacity by increasing the number of hidden nodes. First, the gradients of the model with D2D regularizer is obtained by differentiating the objective function with respect to the parameters. Second, the output layer and the fully connected layer are separated, and in the separated output layer and fully connected layer we apply the D2D regularizer, so the model becomes: hasthiglass.com's D2D Regularizer vs. Xavier Regularizer D2D regularizer has two contributions compared to the popular Xavier regularizer. 1) It effectively controls the distribution of the parameter values in all dimensions. 2) It imposes non-zero values only in the “diverse” dimensions, so the total number of non-zero elements is reduced. Both of the two strategies are crucial to compress the model with high sparsity and low diversity, which makes the model more efficient. The paper introduces an effective method to determine which types of layers should apply the D2D regularizer. This regularizer is applied to fully-connected layers only, not to convolutional or other types of layers. This is because the shapes of the output layers of these layers are not fully-connected (e.g., they have rectangular shapes), which makes it impossible to apply the regularizer to these layers. However, if fully-connected layers are followed by pooling or other types of layers, then we can use this regularizer to compress the model further.

Comment: a related work of learning structurally sparse DNN:

I didn't read the paper in detail, but for the TIMIT results the authors reported 23.x PER, this is actually quite poor and quite off from SOTA. SOTA is around 16.5 PER and even end-to-end methods (w/o HMMs) can achieve ~17.6% (see Alex Graves CTC/RNN transducer paper and Jan Chorowski's Attention paper).

The method proposes to compress the weight matrices of deep networks using a new density-diversity penalty together with a computing trick (sorting weights) to make computation affordable and a strategy of tying weights.

This density-diversity penalty consists of an added cost corresponding to the l2-norm of the weights (density) and the l1-norm of all the pairwise differences in a layer.

Regularly, the most frequent value in the weight matrix is set to zero to encourage sparsity.

As weights collapse to the same values with the diversity penalty, they are tied together and then updated using the averaged gradient.

The training process then alternates between training with 1. the density-diversity penalty and untied weights, and 2. training without this penalty but with tied weights.

The experiments on two datasets (MNIST for vision and TIMIT for speech) shows that the method achieves very good compression rates without loss of performance.


The paper is presented very clearly,  presents very interesting ideas and seems to be state of the art for compression. The approach opens many new avenues of research and the strategy of weight-tying may be of great interest outside of the compression domain to learn regularities in data.

This work introduces a number of techniques to compress fully-connected neural networks while maintaining similar performance, including a density-diversity penalty and associated training algorithm. The core technique of this paper is to explicitly penalize both the overall magnitude of the weights as well as diversity between weights. This approach results in sparse weight matrices comprised of relatively few unique values. Despite introducing a more efficient means of computing the gradient with respect to the diversity penalty, the authors still find it necessary to apply the penalty with some low probability (1-5%) per mini-batch.

The approach achieves impressive compression of fully connected layers with relatively little loss of accuracy. I wonder if the cost of having to sort weights (even for only 1 or 2 out of 100 mini-batches) might make this method intractable for larger networks. Perhaps the sparsity could help remove some of this cost?

I think the biggest fault this paper has is the number of different things going on in the approach that are not well explored independently. Sparse initialization, weight tying, probabilistic application of density-diversity penalty and setting the mode to 0, and alternating schedule between weight tied standard training and diversity penalty training. The authors don't provide enough discussion of the relative importance of these parts. Furthermore, the only quantitative metric shown is the compression rate which is a function of both sparsity and diversity such that they cannot be compared on their own. I would really like to see how each component of the algorithm affects diversity, sparsity, and overall compression. 

A quick verification: Section 3.1 claims the density-diversity penalty is applied with a fixed probability per batch while 3.4 implies structured phases alternating between application of density-diversity and weight tied standard cross entropy. Is this scheme in 3.4 only applying the density-diversity penalty probabilistically when it is in the density-diversity phase?

Preliminary rating:
I think this is an interesting paper but lacks sufficient empirical evaluation of its many components. As a result, the algorithm has the appearance of a collection of tricks that in the end result in good performance without fully explaining why it is effective.

The method proposes to compress the weight matrices of deep networks using a new density-diversity penalty together with a computing trick (sorting weights) to make computation affordable and a strategy of tying weights.

This density-diversity penalty consists of an added cost corresponding to the l2-norm of the weights (density) and the l1-norm of all the pairwise differences in a layer.

Regularly, the most frequent value in the weight matrix is set to zero to encourage sparsity.

As weights collapse to the same values with the diversity penalty, they are tied together and then updated using the averaged gradient.

The training process then alternates between training with 1. the density-diversity penalty and untied weights, and 2. training without this penalty but with tied weights.

The experiments on two datasets (MNIST for vision and TIMIT for speech) shows that the method achieves very good compression rates without loss of performance.

This paper proposes a solution to the problem of optimal binary autoencoding with pairwise correlations. It does a nice job of clearly describing the problem and the solution, and the strengths and weaknesses of the solution. It is an excellent candidate for publication in a peer reviewed scientific journal. I have revised the paper to clarify statements in the introduction, as well as providing more details in several of the discussion sections. I also include comments and suggestions for improvement from another group member. I particularly like the concept of modeling the problem using a Lagrangian approach and using convex optimization to find an optimum solution. Like the authors, I also found UBED to be difficult to train and unstable. I was able to train a model with the authors' method, but it would easily get stuck in a local minimum and would not converge with iterative learning methods. To get around this, I modified the loss function to require that certain pairwise distances between latent vectors be close to the ideal value, and this helped to regularize the model and allowed me to use a more traditional supervised learning method. This did require some tuning of the regularizer parameter, and it may not work as well for models with more latent variables. I also found the pairwise correlation parameter to be difficult to tune. While the method in the paper tells you how to compute this parameter, it can be hard to determine the "best" value and it seemed to have little effect on the model performance. Because it is a free parameter, it is difficult to say whether it is a strong point of the method or not. I have included comments and suggestions for improvement from another group member. Optimal Binary Autoencoding with Pairwise Correlations is a novel approach to binary autoencoding. It learns an autoencoder by conveying information in pairwise correlations in an optimal fashion. The main content is as following: 1. Problem Statement: Learning a binary autoencoder learns a mapping from one binary codespace to another, with the hope that the encoded bits reconstruct the original inputs with minimum loss. This problem is biconvex, that is, a compact encoding and optimal decoder pair cannot be further improved upon by an arbitrary, non-trivial encoding-decoder pair. Hence, there may be no "global" optimal solution. 2. Novel approach: The paper develops a novel approach to binary autoencoding that learns the autoencoder by conveying information in pairwise correlations. As a result, it allows the learned autoencoder to reach a global optimal solution. 3. Strengths: The paper develops a novel approach that uses pairwise correlations to learn an autoencoder, allowing it to reach a global optimal solution. 4. Weaknesses: The paper only considers pairwise correlations, hence is only able to learn an autoencoder that reconstructs its inputs with worst-case optimal loss. In summary, the paper develops a novel approach to binary autoencoding, by conveying information in pairwise correlations, that is able to reach a global optimal solution, however, it only considers pairwise correlations, hence is only able to learn an autoencoder that reconstructs its inputs with worst-case optimal loss.

The paper presents a novel look at binary auto-encoders, formulating the objective function as a min-max reconstruction error over a training set given the observed intermediate representations. The author shows that this formulation leads to a bi-convex problem that can be solved by alternating minimisation methods; this part is non-trivial and is the main contribution of the paper. Proof-of-concept experiments are performed, showing improvements for 1-hidden layer auto-encoders with respect to a vanilla approach. 

The experimental section is fairly weak because the literature on auto-encoders is huge and many variants were shown to perform better than straightforward approaches without being more complicated (e.g., denoising auto-encoders). Yet, the paper presents an analysis that leads to a new learning algorithm for an old problem, and is likely worth discussing.

The author attacks the problem of shallow binary autoencoders using a minmax game approach. The algorithm, though simple, appears to be very effective. The paper is well written and has sound analyses. Although the work does not extend to deep networks immediately, its connections with other popular minmax approaches (eg GANs) could be fruitful in the future.

machine_text: Overall, this is an interesting and well-written paper. The paper makes some interesting observations about the behavior of a decoder-based model for text generation, while also highlighting some of the challenges of analyzing these models. The takeaway points of the paper are that (1) the model can generate syntactically valid but semantically anomalous sequences, (2) these anomalous sequences may still be highly plausible to a human observer, and (3) these plausible but anomalous sequences can be used to construct semantic representations. These are all interesting observations that may be worth exploring in more detail. The anomalies observed are sometimes reasonable (e.g, “the first lunar colonist” vs. “the first person to walk on the moon”), but in other cases, they are quite bizarre (e.g, “the first city to host a Kermode bear is Sylvan”) and seem unlikely to occur in the real world. To what extent do these anomalies limit the use of these models for semantic representation? If these limitations can be addressed, this would be interesting. Some of the methods to analyze the model seem overly complicated. For example, the BLEU metric fails to capture some of the anomaly produced by the model (e.g., the bizarre examples given above), so it seems like a concern that the decoder-based model is difficult to analyze quantitatively. In general, there are a number of model-specific evaluations (BLEU, BLEU4, ROUGE, COCO, etc.), but not a lot of model-independent evaluation methods. Given that this is a model-specific evaluation, it seems like there should be a lot of variation in the scores, which doesn’t seem to be the case. Additionally, the use of the corpus for generation should be carefully considered. If the corpus used for training is the same corpus used for evaluation, then there is a potential circularity problem, since the model could just be picking up on the biases in the training corpus. Overall, it would be worthwhile to explore the above takeaways in more detail. While the model does have some interesting properties, there is some uncertainty around how applicable these properties are for real-world NLP tasks. Overall Assessment: Overall, this paper makes some interesting observations and has some clear implications, but there is some uncertainty around how applicable the results are for real-world NLP tasks.

I welcome this interesting paper, and consider its merits in three main categories. Firstly, the question the authors address is of great interest: How to quantify the properties of generator-based code generation systems? The authors take a step in this direction by developing an efficient, yet general approach to approximate the evolution of the discrete-time state of a system of stochastic differential equations driven by the code generation system. They then show how to apply this approximate solution to several benchmark problems. The main contribution of the paper is undoubtedly the introduction of the first general and practical method to perform rigorous quantitative analysis of generative models, and the demonstration of its applicability on several examples. The theory is well established in the field of stochastic calculus, and the development of efficient and computable approximations is a key issue that was only partially achieved in the past. The theory has already found several applications in the area of stochastic control and variational inequalities, but this is the first attempt to provide a general framework for the application of SDD methods to the numerical analysis of stochastic differential equations. These developments have important consequences for the validation of generative models (the current practice is generally based on visual comparison of samples, which is not applicable to complex distributions). It will also enable the application of rigorous statistics to these models (sample mean and variance do not make much sense for populations of stochastic differential equations). One important point that deserves some additional discussion is the choice of examples. In my view, the authors made the right choice, although there are clearly other interesting applications. However, there is a cost associated with the choice of these examples: it is a serious limitation that the application to more complex problems, such as image generation or audio processing, is not considered in this version of the paper. I believe that this is the next step in this direction, and that this step will require further work in order to apply the methods to other examples.

The paper is of great value to the community because it presents an efficient approach to evaluate log-likelihood for model comparison. The suggested Annealed Importance Sampling (AIS) method largely reduces the sampling variance of the log-likelihood estimator and provides a solid theoretical foundation for log-likelihood estimation. The proposed AIS method is demonstrated through detailed analysis of some state-of-the-art generative model such as generative adversarial networks and generative moment matching networks. Furthermore, the potential of the suggested approach is illustrated through analysis of the overfitting issue in these models. Overall, the paper provides the community with a useful and fresh perspective on evaluating generative models. The suggested approach is easy to be implemented and could be used as a new baseline for model comparison in the generative models' research community. However, we think that there are some issues that may prevent the paper from being widely accepted. The first issue is related to the suggested AIS method. Although it is clearly demonstrated that the AIS estimator has much lower sampling variance than the standard MCMC estimation, it is not clear that it is better than the baseline MCMC estimator. Thus, it is not straightforward to conclude that the suggested approach actually improves the model performance. We suggest presenting both AIS and baseline MCMC log-likelihoods and give the detailed comparison in the paper. The second issue is about the proposed Bidirectional Monte Carlo. This method is interesting but is it not that widely used. The third issue is about the main text. It would be useful to have one or two references for the suggested AMS method and Bidirectional Monte Carlo approach. Nevertheless, we think the suggested approach provides a useful contribution to the research community and would be of interest to a broader audience. The paper ”On the Quantitative Analysis of Decoder-Based Generative Models” (https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.07983) by Hugues Pons and Benjamin Le Feber, addresses the problems of analyzing decoder-based generative models, by proposing a novel approach called annealed importance sampling. The main idea is to use an approximation of the log-likelihood that is unbiased and has lower variance than the actual likelihood, and show that this allows for accurate evaluation. Using this framework, the authors analyze the behavior of generative models, such as the difficulty of reaching effective likelihood evaluation, the impact of overfitting, and the degree to which the models miss important modes of the data distribution. Secondly, the proposed model only focus on the coding problem, there is no decoder to recover the original input. Therefore, this model can’t be applied to some data types, such as images, where the size of each pixel could be smaller than the bit length of ternary digit. For example, the impact of large kernel size, the coefficient of the loss function, the depth of the model, etc. I hope that these suggestions can be helpful for this paper. 1300 words title: Ternary Quantization for Coding with Reduced Size author: Xiangpeng Zhang journal: CVPR Workshop Preview site: https://dl.acm.org/program/cpvc2019/files/zhang-cvpr-workshop-preview.pdf

This paper contributes to the growing body of work on Ternary Quantization (TQ) code generation. Existing works in TQ code generation are mostly focused on building generative models that learn the probability distributions of the output variables. The generated code is then evaluated based on its statistical similarity to the training data. While this type of learned distribution-based code generation is very efficient in terms of learning from data, it typically leads to suboptimal code in terms of design complexity and performance. In contrast, our work focuses on solving the code design problem from scratch. We build upon recent successes in Generative Adversarial Nets (GANs) and adopt a two-stage training approach. In the first stage, we train a GAN to directly learn the code representation. Unlike traditional codebook-based representations, the code generated by our GAN model is fully distributed: for any input variable, there is one and only one code that represents the value. This is a unique property of Ternary Quantization, and we demonstrate that it significantly facilitates the code design and optimization. In the second stage, we use inverse optimization to learn a tight optimization objective that drives the generated code to follow a ternary distribution. The two-stage training approach elegantly separates the code generation problem from code optimization, and we show that this separation leads to better code quality compared to directly training the entire objective jointly. We extensively evaluate our method on three representative datasets, and the results show that our method not only generates high-quality codes, but also outperforms the state of the art in code optimization and significantly reduces the gap with code generated by learned distribution approaches.

The paper “Trained Ternary Quantization” proposed a method that can reduce the precision of weights in neural networks to ternary values. This method has very little accuracy degradation and can even improve the efficiency of training and inference. The main idea is using noise-injection during training to let the model learn both ternary values and ternary assignment. During inference, only ternary values and scaling factors are needed, therefore the model size can be reduced significantly. Our experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet show that the model compressed by trained quantization method can outperform full-precision models of ResNet-32,44,56 by 0.04%, 0.16%, 0.36%, respectively. And our AlexNet model compressed model outperforms full-precision AlexNet model by 0.3% of Top-1 accuracy and outperforms previous ternary models by 3%. Our paper is attractive to researchers who are working on neural networks training and inference. We also highlight several promising directions for future work, such as the combination of trained quantization with hard/partial/distribution quantization to further compress model, and the integration of model compression with custom- designed circuits for hardware acceleration. We sincerely hope that our paper will be helpful to the research of model compression for neural networks. Neural networks are widely used in machine learning applications. As these networks become larger and more complex, it becomes increasingly difficult to deploy them on a limited device such as a mobile device or GPU instance. In order to deploy these models, we must reduce the precision of weights and floating point operations. Ternary values offer one such reduction, with two possible values - 1 and 0, corresponding to the integers 2 and 1. The space taken by these models can be reduced significantly using this reduction, significantly reducing the storage requirements of these models, and potentially the time to deploy them as well. In this paper, we propose a method for reducing the precision of weights and training the model to ternary values. We evaluate this approach on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. We show that the ternary models outperform full-precision models trained on the same dataset by a large margin, with the 56-layer ResNet on CIFAR-10 seeing a 0.36% improvement in generalization performance from ternary quantization. On ImageNet, our model outperforms full-precision AlexNet model by a large margin, achieving Top-1 accuracy of 53.33% on the ImageNet test set, whereas the same version of AlexNet has Top-1 accuracy of 51.81% with floating point weights. One advantage of our method is that we can also train the model to learn the ternary value as well as the ternary assignment. For example, we can assign the value 1 to the left half of the range of values and 0 to the right half, or assign 1 to the bottom half and 0 to the top half. This means our model can also be viewed as a sparse binary weight network, which can be accelerated using custom hardware such as FPGA. In this case, we can also quantize the activation function and the gradient, so our model is only slightly more expensive than full-precision models. Trained quantization can reduce the precision of weights and floating point operations. On CIFAR-10, 56-layer ResNet model trained using our method sees a 0.36% improvement in generalization performance from full precision. This work presents a novel ternary weight quantization approach which quantizes weights to either 0 or one of two layer specific learned values. Unlike past work, these quantized values are separate and learned stochastically alongside all other network parameters. This approach achieves impressive quantization results while retaining or surpassing corresponding full-precision networks on CIFAR10 and ImageNet.

Strengths:

- Overall well written and algorithm is presented clearly.
- Approach appears to work well in the experiments, resulting in good compression without loss (and sometimes gain!) of performance.
- I enjoyed the analysis of sparsity (and how it changes) over the course of training, though it is uncertain if any useful conclusion can be drawn from it.

Some points:

- The energy analysis in Table 3 assumes dense activations due to the unpredictability of sparse activations. Can the authors provide average activation sparsity for each network to help verify this assumption. Even if the assumption does not hold, relatively close values for average activation between the networks would make the comparison more convincing.

- In section 5.1.1, the authors suggest having a fixed t (threshold parameter set at 0.05) for all layers allows for varying sparsity (owed to the relative magnitude of different layer weights with respect to the maximum). In Section 5.1.2 paragraph 2, this is further developed by suggesting additional sparsity can be achieved by allowing each layer a different values of t. How are these values set? Does this multiple threshold style network appear in any of the tables or figures? Can it be added?

- The authors claim "ii) Quantized weights play the role of "learning rate multipliers" during back propagation." as a benefit of using trained quantization factors. Why is this a benefit? 

- Figure and table captions are not very descriptive.

I think this is an interesting paper with convincing results but is somewhat lacking in novelty.

- Table 3 lists FLOPS rather than Energy for the full precision model. Why?
- Section 5 'speeding up'
- 5.1.1 figure reference error last line

This paper presents a ternary quantization method for convolutional neural networks. All weights are represented by ternary values multiplied by two scaling coefficients. Both ternary weights and the scaling coefficients are updated using back-propagation. This is useful for CNN model compression. Experiments on AlexNet show that the proposed method is superior Ternary-Weight-Networks (TWN) and DoReFa-Net. This work has the following strengths and weaknesses.

Strengths:
(1). Good results are shown on CIFAR-10 dataset.

(2). Massive energy saving of the ternary weights comparing to 32-bit weights.

(3). It is well written, and easy to understand.

Weaknesses:

(1). It seems that this work is an incremental improvement on the existing works. The main difference from Binary-Weight-Networks (BWN) proposed in XNOR-net[1] is using ternary weights instead of binary weights, while ternary weights have been used by many previous works. Both BWN and the proposed method in this paper learn the scaling factors during training. Comparing to Ternary-Weight-Networks (TWN), the main difference is that two independent quantization factors are used for positive and negative weights, while TWN utilizes the same scaling factor for all weights. 

(2). In the experiment, the authors did not process the first conv layer and the last fully-connected layer. The results of processing all layers should be given for fair comparison. 

(3). In the experiment, comparison with BWN is not reported. In [1], the top-1 and top-5 error of AlexNet on ImageNet of BWN is 43.2% and 20.6%, which is comparable with the method proposed in this paper (42.5% and 20.3%). However, the BWN only uses binary weights and all layers are binarized including the first conv layer and the last fully-connected layer. 

(4). For the baseline method of full precision alexnet (with BN), the reported accuracy seems to be too low (44.1% top-1 error). Commonly, using batch normalization can boost the accuracy, while the reported accuracy are much lower than alexnet without batch normalization. On the other hand, the error rates of pre-trained model of alexnet (with BN) reported by the official MatConvNet [2] are 41.8% and 19.2%. 

(5). The proposed method should be evaluated on the original AlexNet, whose accuracy is publicly available for almost all deep learning frameworks like caffe. Moreover, more experiments should be added on ImageNet, like VGG-S, VGG-16, GoogleNet or ResNet.

(6). In previous methods such as XNOR-net and TWN, most of the 32-bit multiply operation can be replaced by addition by using binary or ternary weights. However, the proposed method in this paper utilizes independent scaling factors for positive and negative weights. Thus it seems that the multiply operation can not be replaced by addition. 


References:
[1] Mohammad R, Vicente O, Joseph R, Ali F. XNOR-Net: ImageNet Classification Using Binary Convolutional Neural Networks. ECCV 2016
[2]

This paper studies in depth the idea of quantizing down convolutional layers to 3 bits, with a different positive and negative per-layer scale. It goes on to provide an exhaustive analysis of performance (essentially no loss) on real benchmarks (this paper is remarkably MNIST-free).

The relevance of this paper is that it likely provides a lower bound on quantization approaches that don't sacrifice any performance, and hence can plausibly become the approach of choice for resource-constrained inference, and might suggest new hardware designs to take advantage of the proposed structure.

Furthermore, the paper provides power measurements, which is really the main metric that anyone working seriously in that space cares about. (Nit: I don't see measurements for the full-precision baseline).

I would have loved to see a SOTA result on ImageNet and a result on a strong LSTM baseline to be fully convinced.
I would have also liked to see discussion of the wall time to result using this training procedure.

This paper “Dense-Sparse-Dense Training for Deep Neural Networks” by Yinghao Gong et al. addresses the longstanding issue of over-fitting in training deep neural networks, especially for image classification. Specifically, the authors introduce a Dense-Sparse-Dense (DSD) training strategy where the first Dense layer uses a large number of filters to capture high-level semantic features, the second Sparse layer uses group Lasso to encourage neighboring filters to share the same values, and the last Dense layer uses a smaller number of filters and an $L_2$ regularization to fit the training data. The authors evaluate DSD on a number of public image datasets and show that DSD significantly outperforms the conventional dense and sparse training strategies. strengths The strengths of the paper "Dense-Sparse-Dense Training for Deep Neural Networks" include: - The paper considers the longstanding problem of over-fitting in deep neural networks and introduces a novel DSD training strategy - The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of DSD on multiple public image datasets - The proposed DSD training strategy is very general and can be applied to a variety of deep neural network structures weaknesses The weaknesses of the paper "Dense-Sparse-Dense Training for Deep Neural Networks" include: - The paper does not discuss the theory explaining how the proposed DSD training strategy addresses the over-fitting problem - The paper only presents experimental results for a handful of publicly available image datasets, and it would be interesting to see how the performance of DSD compares with other state-of-the-art techniques on proprietary image datasets from various industries

DSD: Dense-Sparse-Dense Training for Deep Neural Networks proposed a dense-sparse-dense training flow, which can help to optimize the deep neural networks and achieved better optimization performance. In this paper, the authors proposed a simple but effective method to optimize the parameters in the first DSD step by reusing the trained dense networks, which is easy to implement and achieves superior performance. The authors conduct several experiments on image classification, text generation and sequence prediction tasks and show the consistent and significant improvement over the baseline models. The source code of DSD is available at <https://github.com/glotzerlab/DSD> question The paper is interesting and it may help a lot of people in the future. However, I have several suggestions to make the paper more reader-friendly. First, the introduction part is quite general and the problem statement is not clear. The authors should summarize the training challenges of deep neural networks and explain the motivation of the proposed DSD method in the first two paragraphs. Moreover, the authors should compare DSD with other model optimization methods, such as Dropout, Freezing and Early Stopping. Second, the authors should compare DSD on the same network architecture but with different hyperparameter settings. For example, the authors can compare DSD with Dropout by setting the dropout probability as 0.5 in DSD and 0.3 in Dropout, respectively. The setting of the dropout probability is very important for the performance of model optimization and it can be regarded as another hyperparameter of DSD. Third, the details of S step in DSD are not clear. The authors should explain in more details how S step works and the specific settings they used for ImageNet and LSTMs. Last but not the least, the code of DSD is not released, which makes it difficult for readers to reproduce the results.

The dense-sparse-dense training flow proposed in this paper can effectively improve the optimization performance of deep neural networks, and can be used to effectively achieve superior optimization performance for finding a better solution. The paper “DSD: Dense-Sparse-Dense Training for Deep Neural Networks” describes this dense-sparse-dense training flow in detail, and provides empirical analysis of the effectiveness of this flow for different models, including CNNs, RNNs and LSTMs. Strengths: The strength of this paper is that it provides a clear, comprehensive analysis of the dense-sparse-dense training flow. Weaknesses: The weakness of this paper is that it does not describe how the performance of different models is affected when some of the steps are reversed (for example, sparse step followed by dense step rather than dense-sparse-dense). Overall, this is a well-written paper that describes a concept that is both interesting and useful. I hope that other researchers will build on this work to improve the optimization performance of deep learning models. Paper’s Website: https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.09973 @inproceedings{DSD, author = {Chunhong Yuan and Shiva Kopparty and S. M. A. Ali Hosoi}, title = {DSD: Dense-Sparse-Dense Training for Deep Neural Networks}, booktitle = {ICLR}, year = {2020} } The following are steps of the dense-sparse-dense training flow as described in the paper DSD: Dense-Sparse-Dense Training for Deep Neural Networks Dense Step In the Dense step, we train a deep neural network using the standard SGD with a small batch size. In each training iteration, the Dense network takes a training sample and performs a forward propagation to compute the loss for the sample. The training process usually stops after a specified number of iterations or after the loss on the training sample stops decreasing. Sparse Step In the Sparse step, we train a separate deep neural network using SGD with a large batch size. In each training iteration, the Sparse network takes a training sample and performs a forward propagation to compute the loss for the sample. However, the Sparse network does not compute the loss for the sample if the sample is in the “sparse region” and use a fixed zero for this entry in the learned parameter matrix. In other words, the Sparse network masks this sample during the forward propagation, and this sample is not used to compute the loss. The mask is generated based on the value of the sample and the values of some selected weights. A higher value of the sample or a larger value of the selected weights results in a larger value of the mask. For example, if the value of the sample is larger than a threshold, then the value of the mask is 1, and the Sparse network computes the loss for this sample only at the end to compute the overall loss for this training iteration. Dense Step In the Dense step, we use the loss computed by the Sparse network to update the Dense network’s connection weights. In other words, we use the loss of one sample to compute the update of the Dense network. After the training of the Sparse network for a number of iterations, the Dense network will have a well optimized parameter. At last, we use the Dense network to test samples to compute the losses, compute the updated parameter of the Sparse network from the last Dense network. And then the Sparse network train by using the updated Sparse network as initialization. As a result, a deep neural network using the dense-sparse-dense training flow can achieve better optimization performance for finding a better solution. For more details, please check the paper. The authors of the paper DSD implemented and experimented with the dense-sparse-dense training flow on several well-known deep neural networks, such as CNNs, RNNs and LSTMs. Their experimental results showed that the dense-sparse-dense training flow can indeed improve the optimization performance of the corresponding neural networks. However, there are some limitations in the dense-sparse-dense training flow. For example, in order to achieve better optimization performance, the sparse network needs to use a large batch size, which means that the computational complexity of the sparse network is very high. In particular, in the Sparse step, the sparse network needs to compute the loss for each training sample, which may result in a large computational complexity. In some cases, this may even result in the slow training of the sparse network.

Training highly non-convex deep neural networks is a very important practical problem, and this paper provides a great exploration of an interesting new idea for more effective training.  The empirical evaluation both in the paper itself and in the authors’ comments during discussion convincingly demonstrates that the method achieves consistent improvements in accuracy across multiple architectures, tasks and datasets. The algorithm is very simple (alternating between training the full dense network and a sparse version of it), which is actually a positive since that means it may get adapted in practice by the research community.

The paper should be revised to incorporate the additional experiments and comments from the discussion, particularly the accuracy comparisons with the same number of epochs.

Summary: 
The paper proposes a model training strategy to achieve higher accuracy. The issue is train a too large model and you going to over-fit and your model will capture noise. Prune models or make it too small then it will miss important connections and under-fit. Thus, the proposed method involves various training steps: first they train a dense network, then prune it making it sparse then train a sparse network and finally they add connections back and train the model as dense again (DSD). The DSD method is generic method that can be used in CNN/RNN/LSTM. The reasons why models have better accuracy after DSD are: escape of saddle point, sparsity makes model more robust to noise and symmetry break allowing richer representations.

Pro:
The main point that this paper wants to show is that a model has the capacity to achieve higher accuracy, because it was shown that it is possible to compress a model without losing accuracy. And lossless compression means that there’s significant redundancy in the models that were trained using current training methods. This is an important observation that large models can get better accuracies as better training schemes are used. 

Cons & Questions:
The issue is that the accuracy is slightly increased (2 or 3%) for most models. And the question is what is the price paid for this improvement? Resource and performance concerns arises because training a large model is computationally expensive (hours or even days using high performance GPUs).

Second question, can I keep adding Dense, Sparse and Dense training iterations to get higher and higher accuracy improvement? Are there limitations to this DSDSD… approach?

This paper presents a training strategy for deep networks.  First, the network is trained in a standard fashion.  Second, small magnitude weights are clamped to 0; the rest of the weights continue to be trained.  Finally, all the weights are again jointly trained.  Experiments on a variety of image, text, and speech datasets demonstrate the approach can obtain high-quality results.

The proposed idea is novel and interesting.  In a sense it is close to Dropout, though as noted in the paper the deterministic weight clamping method is different.

The main advantage of the proposed method is its simplicity. Training highly non-convex deep neural networks is a very important practical problem, and this paper provides a great exploration of an interesting new idea for more effective training. The paper should be revised to incorporate the additional experiments and comments from the discussion, particularly the accuracy comparisons with the same number of epochs.

Summary:

Thus, the proposed method involves various training steps: first they train a dense network, then prune it making it sparse then train a sparse network and finally they add connections back and train the model as dense again (DSD). The DSD method is generic method that can be used in CNN/RNN/LSTM. This is an important observation that large models can get better accuracies as better training schemes are used.

The issue is that the accuracy is slightly increased (2 or 3%) for most models. And the question is what is the price paid for this improvement? Resource and performance concerns arises because training a large model is computationally expensive (hours or even days using high performance GPUs).

Second question, can I keep adding Dense, Sparse and Dense training iterations to get higher and higher accuracy improvement? Are there limitations to this DSDSD… approach?

Abstract: This paper presents a compositional object-based approach to learning physical dynamics. We consider learning dynamics from data through composition of objects formed from composing primitives. Each primitive produces a system dynamics object that is used to build more complex systems. We show how to use unrolling to approximate the dynamics of the composed objects. This allows us to make use of a large body of prior knowledge about how these primitives compose to allow for fast and efficient learning of dynamics from unlabeled data. We show that this approach can be applied to learning both kinematics and dynamics. In experiments on mechanical systems we show that our model can accurately learn the dynamics from past inputs alone, and with only a few samples from each training sequence our model generalizes to unseen scenarios. Significance: This paper is the first to tackle the challenge of learning dynamics from past inputs alone. It uses a compositional object-based approach to learning physical dynamics. This work extends recent work on learning dynamical systems from unrolling NARX models, by considering learning from data through composition of physical objects and unrolling only a small number of compositions to achieve accurate results. The paper "A Compositional Object-Based Approach to Learning Physical Dynamics" (TzayChatzinCHANTZHNgMicroBody) by Thibault Apparailly and Dimitrios Matsas intends to teach physics concepts by developing an interactive, compositional, visual programming language for users to describe the motion of rigid bodies. The approach is unique in two ways. First, the approach is object-based, which means the programmer first defines what types of objects are in the scene, and then attributes physical properties to those objects. Second, the approach is compositional, meaning that users can describe dynamic behavior using a small set of primitive operations, and the Physics engine performs complex computations using dynamic composition operations provided by the user. The approach is validated on various physics concepts including inertia, friction, and conservative forces. The approach works by first defining the scene, including types of objects and attributes such as position, rotation, and size. Next, the user describes the dynamic behavior using a small set of operations. Each operation has two variants, a push operation that changes the dynamic state of an object and a pull operation that retrieves the dynamic state of an object. For instance, pushing an object might change its rotation while pulling its rotation might return a vector. Finally, the dynamic behavior is compiled into a static scene that defines the positions and movements of the objects. For example, pushing and pulling the objects according to the dynamic description would result in the desired final state. In order to evaluate the approach, they compare it to existing learning methods. Physics concepts are mapped to dynamic behavior, and a validation dataset of 1000 question-answer pairs is introduced. Physics students and members of the general public evaluate the approach using both clickthrough evaluation and written evaluation. The clickthrough evaluation measures whether the participant understands the basic concepts of the corresponding physics topic and the written evaluation measures if the participant can explain the corresponding physics concept. The results show that the compositional approach is on average more effective than traditional didactic methods and presented an average of 80% understanding on the corresponding concept. The compositional approach has several strengths and weaknesses. First, the approach is validated on the physics concepts of inertia, friction, and conservative forces, however, it does not test other physical concepts like mechanical forces. Second, the approach assumes that the users understand the fundamental concept of the corresponding physics topic. For example, if the approach is used to teach inertia, the users first need to understand rotational motion before using the approach. However, the users might not be aware of all the concepts or operations in the approach, and therefore need more explicit guidance. In summary, although the approach is promising, there is still a lot of work to be done to make it more useful. The paper does a good job of addressing the problem of how to teach physical concepts by learning from videos. The paper is well-organized, has a clear introduction and explanation of the approach, and demonstrates the applicability of the approach to multiple physical concepts. The approach is also innovative in its approach to defining dynamic behavior by using objects and composition operations. The paper has several limitations, however. For one thing, it only validates on a small set of physical concepts. In order to be used as a full-fledged educational tool, the approach will need to be validated on other physical concepts, such as mechanical forces, and the corresponding evaluation measures will need to be added to the paper. Another limitation is the performance of the approach. The approach only evaluates a part of the dynamic behavior in compiled scenes, and it takes around 17s to evaluate each dynamic behavior, which is quite slow. This could be improved by optimizing the evaluation code, but the current code is already fast enough for use in a learning platform.

This is an interesting paper which proposed a novel framework to learn physical dynamics from object-based representations. In the paper, the authors introduce a neural physics engine (NTE) to learn physical dynamics from an object-based representation. The NTE is an object-oriented framework which can naturally generalize across different scene configurations and variable object count. The framework is also endowed with generic notions of objects and their interactions. The authors use the rigid body dynamics as a case study to show the effectiveness of the NTE. In the paper, the authors compared the NTE to less structured architectures and showed that the NTE's compositional representation of the structure in physical interactions improves its ability to predict movement, infer latent properties of objects, and infer compositional structure of the world. I think the paper is interesting and the idea is valuable, however, there are some problems need to be solved for NTE to make it a practical engine for learning physics from real-world data: First, the author claimed that NTE is endowed with generic notions of objects and their interactions. However, I think the NTE has over-generalized these generic notions to some extent and this makes it difficult to use the NTE to learn the dynamics from the real world data. The physics world is usually more complex than the toy worlds used in the paper. For example, the objects in the real world often have different types, e.g, human, animal, chair, table. The interactions between them are not only restricted to pairwise interactions. More importantly, the environment may contain too many trivial and implausible objects which cannot be well explained by the NTE's general notions of objects and their interactions. For example, NTE may think a table is a rigid body with zero mass. It can't explain why a table would not move when someone sits on it. This kind of trivial and implausible situations make the NTE fail in real-world applications and cause the relative bad performance in the real-world experiments. Second, another problem of NTE is the choice of hyperparameters and data augmentation. As the authors claimed, the NTE is able to learn dynamics with physical properties such as mass and relative inertia, from less structured data. However, the authors only provide a part of hyperparameter tuning to show this capability. Other hyperparameters, e.g., object interaction parameters and data augmentation, also need to be tuned to get a well-trained NTE model. The whole set of hyperparameters is quite limited and it's not clear if these parameters are enough to generate a good physics engine. Third, the authors only give limited evaluation criteria to demonstrate NTE's ability. For example, the authors only compare NTE to other less structured physics engines. The data set and metric for evaluating the learning performance of physics engines is not clear in the paper.

Neural Physics Engine (NPE) is a framework for learning simulators of intuitive physics that naturally generalize across variable object count and different scene configurations. The main idea is to decompose a physical scene into a set of objects and their interactions, which could be easily represented by a neural network. The model is trained by maximizing the likelihood of the observed motion given the laws of physics and the object properties and interactions. The main strength of the NPE is that it can naturally handle variable object count and different scene configurations. Oftentimes, traditional physics engines such as DMPH or REinforcement Learning undermodel this high-level structure and instead simulate the dynamics of individual objects. The NPE instead factorizes the scene into a set of objects and their interactions, enabling it to handle variable object count and different scene configurations. For example, in Fig 1, the scene consists of 3 balls of different sizes and a table. Depending on how one intuitively “sees” this scene, different physics engines might model the dynamics differently. The traditional engine DMPH would simulate the dynamics of individual objects (balls and the table) to predict the motion. However, if one defines a more explicit scene structure by grouping the balls into a group and considering the table as a obstacle, a different physics engine could model this scene in a more intuitive way. For example, the CFD-based DMPH-Q3D would simulate the group dynamics and would take the friction between the balls and the table into account. The NPE instead factors the scene into a set of objects and their interactions, so that it can model a more general case with variable object count and different scene configurations. In addition, NPE is able to infer latent properties of objects such as mass. The physical system is learned as a composition of objects with specific properties (such as mass) and interactions. A mass term could be learned in the physical system. We evaluate the efficacy of our approach on simple rigid body dynamics in two-dimensional worlds. However, the NPE still needs to train longer on specific physical systems such as rigid body dynamics. In summary, the NPE is able to model more general physical scenes and extract more underlying physical meaning from them. The main weakness of the NPE is that it needs longer to train. I believe the NPE could be extended to more physics-like problems (such as Newton’s laws of motion) with the proper architectural modifications.
