The paper proposes a differntiable Neural Physics Engine (NPE). The NPE consists of an encoder and a decoder function. The NPE takes as input the state of pairs of objects (within a neighbourhood of a focus object) at two previous time-steps in a scene. The encoder function summarizes the interaction of each pair of objects. The decoder then outputs the change in velocity of the focus object at the next time step. The NPE is evaluated on various environments containing bouncing balls.

- novelty

The differentiable NPE is a novel concept. However, concurrently Battaglia et al. (NIPS 2016) proposes a very similar model. Just as this work, Battaglia et al. (NIPS 2016) consider a model which consists of a encoder function (relation-centric) which encodes the interaction among a focus object and other objects in the scene and a decoder (relation-centric) function which considers the cumulative (encoded) effect of object interactions on the focus object and predicts effect of the interactions.  Aspects like only considering objects interactions within a neighbourhood (versus the complete object interaction graph in Battaglia et al.) based on euclideian distance  are novel to this work. However, the advantages (if any) of NPE versus the model of Battaglia et al. are not clear. Moreover, it is not clear how this neighbourhood thresholding scene would preform in case of n-ball systems, where gravitational forces of massive objects can be felt over large distances.

- citations 

This work includes all relevant citations.

- clarity

The article is well written and easy to understand.

- experiments 

Battaglia et al. evaluates on wider variety senerios compared to this work (e.g. n-bodies under gravitation, falling strings). Such experiments demonstrate the ability of the models to generalize. However, this work does include more in-depth experiments in case of bouncing balls compared to Battaglia et al. (e.g. mass estimation and varying world configurations with obstacles in the bouncing balls senerio). 

Moreover, an extensive comparison to Fragkiadaki et al. (2015) (in the bouncing balls senerios) is missing. The authors (referring to answer to question 4) do point out to comaprable numbers in both works, but the experimental settings are different.  Comparison in a billiard table senerio like that Fragkiadaki et al. (2015) where a initial force is applied to a ball, would have been enlightening. 

The authors only evaluate the error in velocity in the bouncing balls senerios. We understand that this model predicts only the velocity (refer to answer of question 2). Error analysis also with respect to ground truth ball position would be more enlightening. As small errors in velocity can quickly lead to entirely different scene configuration.

- conclusion / recommendation

The main issue with this work is the unclear novelty with respect to work of Battaglia et al. at NIPS'16. A quantitative and qualitative comparison with Battaglia et al. is lacking.  But the authors state that their work was developed independently.

Differentiable physics engines like NPE or that of Battaglia et al. (NIPS 2016) requires generation of an extensive amount of synthetic data to learn about the physics of a certain senerio. Moreover, extensive retraining is required to adapt to new sceneries (e.g. bouncing balls to n-body systems). Any practical advantage versus generating new code for a physics engine is not clear. Other "bottom-up" approaches like that of  Fragkiadaki et al. (2015) couple vision along with learning dynamics. However, they require very few input parameters (position, mass, current velocity, world configuration), as approximate parameter estimation can be done from the visual component.  Such approaches could be potentially more useful of a robot in "common-sense" everyday tasks (e.g. manipulation). Thus, overall potential applications of a differentiable physics engine like NPE is unclear.

Summary
===
This paper proposes the Neural Physics Engine (NPE), a network architecture
which simulates object interactions. While NPE decides to explicitly represent
objects (rather than video frames), it incorporates knowledge of physics
almost exclusively through training data. It is tested in a toy domain with
bouncing 2d balls.

The proposed architecture processes each object in a scene one at a time.
Pairs of objects are embedded in a common space where the effect of the
objects on each other can be represented. These embeddings are summed
and combined with the focus object's state to predict the focus object's
change in velocity. Alternative baselines are presented which either
forego the pairwise embedding for a single object embedding or
encode a focus object's neighbors in a sequence of LSTM states.

NPE outperforms the baselines dramatically, showing the importance of
architecture choices in learning to do this object based simulation.
The model is tested in multiple ways. Ability to predict object trajectory
over long time spans is measured. Generalization to different numbers of objects
is measured. Generalization to slightly altered environments (difference
shaped walls) is measured. Finally, the NPE is also trained to predict
object mass using only interactions with other objects, where it also
outperforms baselines.


Comments
===

* I have one more clarifying question. Are the inputs to the blue box in
figure 3 (b)/(c) the concatenation of the summed embeddings and state vector
of object 3? Or is the input to the blue module some other combination of the
two vectors?


* Section 2.1 begins with "First, because physics does not
change across inertial frames, it suffices to separately predict the future state of each object conditioned
on the past states of itself and the other objects in its neighborhood, similar to Fragkiadaki
et al. (2015)."

I think this is an argument to forego the visual representation used by previous
work in favor of an object only representation. This would be more clear if there
were contrast with a visual representation.


* As addressed in the paper, this approach is novel, though less so after taking
into consideration the concurrent work of Battaglia et. al. in NIPS 2016 titled
"Interaction Networks for Learning about Objects, Relations and Physics."
This work offers a different network architecture and set of experiments, as
well as great presentation, but the use of an object based representation
for learning to predict physical behavior is shared.


Overall Evaluation
===

This paper was a pleasure to read and provided many experiments that offered
clear and interesting conclusions. It offers a novel approach (though
less so compared to the concurrent work of Battaglia et. al. 2016) which
represents a significant step forward in the current investigation of
intuitive physics.

Paper proposes a neural physics engine (NPE). NPE provides a factorization of physical scene into composable object-based representations. NPE predicts a future state of the given object as a function composition of the pairwise interactions between itself and near-by objects. This has a nice physical interpretation of forces being additive. In the paper NPE is investigated in the context of 2D worlds with balls and obstacles. 

Overall the approach is interesting and has an interesting flavor of combining neural networks with basic properties of physics. Overall, it seems like it may lead to interesting and significant follow up work in the field. The concerns with the paper is mainly with evaluation, which in places appears to be weak (see below). 

> Significance & Originality:

The approach is interesting. While other methods have tried to build models that can deal with physical predictions, the idea of summing over pair-wise terms, to the best of my knowledge, is novel and much more in-line with the underlying principles of mechanics. As such, while relatively simple, it seems to be an important contribution. 

> Clarity:

The paper is generally well written. However, large portion of the early introduction is rather abstract and it is difficult to parse until one gets to 5th paragraph. I would suggest editing the early part of introduction to include more specifics about the approach or even examples ... to make text more tangible.

> Experiments

Generally there are two issues with experiments in my opinion: (1) the added indirect comparison with Fragkiadaki et al (2015) does not appears to be quantitatively flattering with respect to the proposed approach, and (2) quantitative experiments on the role the size of the mask has on performance should really be added. Authors mention that they observe that mask is helpful, but it is not clear how helpful or how sensitive the overall performance is to this parameter. This experiment should really be added.

I do feel that despite few mentioned shortcomings that would make the paper stronger, this is an interesting paper and should be published.

Summary
===
This paper proposes the Neural Physics Engine (NPE), a network architecture
which simulates object interactions. While NPE decides to explicitly represent
objects (rather than video frames), it incorporates knowledge of physics
almost exclusively through training data. It is tested in a toy domain with
bouncing 2d balls.

The proposed architecture processes each object in a scene one at a time.
Pairs of objects are embedded in a common space where the effect of the
objects on each other can be represented. These embeddings are summed
and combined with the focus object's state to predict the focus object's
change in velocity. Alternative baselines are presented which either
forego the pairwise embedding for a single object embedding or
encode a focus object's neighbors in a sequence of LSTM states.

NPE outperforms the baselines dramatically, showing the importance of
architecture choices in learning to do this object based simulation.
The model is tested in multiple ways. Ability to predict object trajectory
over long time spans is measured. Generalization to different numbers of objects
is measured. Generalization to slightly altered environments (difference
shaped walls) is measured. Finally, the NPE is also trained to predict
object mass using only interactions with other objects, where it also
outperforms baselines.


Comments
===

* I have one more clarifying question. Are the inputs to the blue box in
figure 3 (b)/(c) the concatenation of the summed embeddings and state vector
of object 3? Or is the input to the blue module some other combination of the
two vectors?


* Section 2.1 begins with "First, because physics does not
change across inertial frames, it suffices to separately predict the future state of each object conditioned
on the past states of itself and the other objects in its neighborhood, similar to Fragkiadaki
et al. (2015)."

I think this is an argument to forego the visual representation used by previous
work in favor of an object only representation. This would be more clear if there
were contrast with a visual representation.


* As addressed in the paper, this approach is novel, though less so after taking
into consideration the concurrent work of Battaglia et. al. in NIPS 2016 titled
"Interaction Networks for Learning about Objects, Relations and Physics."
This work offers a different network architecture and set of experiments, as
well as great presentation, but the use of an object based representation
for learning to predict physical behavior is shared.


Overall Evaluation
===

This paper was a pleasure to read and provided many experiments that offered
clear and interesting conclusions. It offers a novel approach (though
less so compared to the concurrent work of Battaglia et. al. 2016) which
represents a significant step forward in the current investigation of
intuitive physics.

Paper proposes a neural physics engine (NPE). NPE provides a factorization of physical scene into composable object-based representations. NPE predicts a future state of the given object as a function composition of the pairwise interactions between itself and near-by objects. This has a nice physical interpretation of forces being additive. In the paper NPE is investigated in the context of 2D worlds with balls and obstacles. 

Overall the approach is interesting and has an interesting flavor of combining neural networks with basic properties of physics. Overall, it seems like it may lead to interesting and significant follow up work in the field. The concerns with the paper is mainly with evaluation, which in places appears to be weak (see below). 

> Significance & Originality:

The approach is interesting. While other methods have tried to build models that can deal with physical predictions, the idea of summing over pair-wise terms, to the best of my knowledge, is novel and much more in-line with the underlying principles of mechanics. As such, while relatively simple, it seems to be an important contribution. 

> Clarity:

The paper is generally well written. However, large portion of the early introduction is rather abstract and it is difficult to parse until one gets to 5th paragraph. I would suggest editing the early part of introduction to include more specifics about the approach or even examples ... to make text more tangible.

> Experiments

Generally there are two issues with experiments in my opinion: (1) the added indirect comparison with Fragkiadaki et al (2015) does not appears to be quantitatively flattering with respect to the proposed approach, and (2) quantitative experiments on the role the size of the mask has on performance should really be added. Authors mention that they observe that mask is helpful, but it is not clear how helpful or how sensitive the overall performance is to this parameter. This experiment should really be added.

I do feel that despite few mentioned shortcomings that would make the paper stronger, this is an interesting paper and should be published.

- summary

The paper proposes a differntiable Neural Physics Engine (NPE). The NPE consists of an encoder and a decoder function. The NPE takes as input the state of pairs of objects (within a neighbourhood of a focus object) at two previous time-steps in a scene. The encoder function summarizes the interaction of each pair of objects. The decoder then outputs the change in velocity of the focus object at the next time step. The NPE is evaluated on various environments containing bouncing balls.

- novelty

The differentiable NPE is a novel concept. However, concurrently Battaglia et al. (NIPS 2016) proposes a very similar model. Just as this work, Battaglia et al. (NIPS 2016) consider a model which consists of a encoder function (relation-centric) which encodes the interaction among a focus object and other objects in the scene and a decoder (relation-centric) function which considers the cumulative (encoded) effect of object interactions on the focus object and predicts effect of the interactions.  Aspects like only considering objects interactions within a neighbourhood (versus the complete object interaction graph in Battaglia et al.) based on euclideian distance  are novel to this work. However, the advantages (if any) of NPE versus the model of Battaglia et al. are not clear. Moreover, it is not clear how this neighbourhood thresholding scene would preform in case of n-ball systems, where gravitational forces of massive objects can be felt over large distances.

- citations 

This work includes all relevant citations.

- clarity

The article is well written and easy to understand.

- experiments 

Battaglia et al. evaluates on wider variety senerios compared to this work (e.g. n-bodies under gravitation, falling strings). Such experiments demonstrate the ability of the models to generalize. However, this work does include more in-depth experiments in case of bouncing balls compared to Battaglia et al. (e.g. mass estimation and varying world configurations with obstacles in the bouncing balls senerio). 

Moreover, an extensive comparison to Fragkiadaki et al. (2015) (in the bouncing balls senerios) is missing. The authors (referring to answer to question 4) do point out to comaprable numbers in both works, but the experimental settings are different.  Comparison in a billiard table senerio like that Fragkiadaki et al. (2015) where a initial force is applied to a ball, would have been enlightening. 

The authors only evaluate the error in velocity in the bouncing balls senerios. We understand that this model predicts only the velocity (refer to answer of question 2). Error analysis also with respect to ground truth ball position would be more enlightening. As small errors in velocity can quickly lead to entirely different scene configuration.

- conclusion / recommendation

The main issue with this work is the unclear novelty with respect to work of Battaglia et al. at NIPS'16. A quantitative and qualitative comparison with Battaglia et al. is lacking.  But the authors state that their work was developed independently.

Differentiable physics engines like NPE or that of Battaglia et al. (NIPS 2016) requires generation of an extensive amount of synthetic data to learn about the physics of a certain senerio. Moreover, extensive retraining is required to adapt to new sceneries (e.g. bouncing balls to n-body systems). Any practical advantage versus generating new code for a physics engine is not clear. Other "bottom-up" approaches like that of  Fragkiadaki et al. (2015) couple vision along with learning dynamics. However, they require very few input parameters (position, mass, current velocity, world configuration), as approximate parameter estimation can be done from the visual component.  Such approaches could be potentially more useful of a robot in "common-sense" everyday tasks (e.g. manipulation). Thus, overall potential applications of a differentiable physics engine like NPE is unclear.

The paper "Learning to Remember Rare Events" by Guan and Li extends the R-V losses for structured prediction, and utilizes a combination of contrastive divergence and reinforcement learning, to address the problem of rare event learning. The proposed loss, R-V EL, can be used to train a model to both high precision on "rare" classes, and high recall on "common" classes, even with relatively small amounts of annotated "rare" examples. The model is also stable to noise in the rare event annotation process. The code and pretrained models are available at: https://github.com/guancan/R-V-EL The strength of this approach is that it handles the "missing" classes correctly, and does not simply assume that classes with no examples are "unpredictable" - the model has access to the full regularity score for each class, and can use this to provide a reasonable baseline of "unpredictability" for classes with no labeled "rare" examples. This is a much more reasonable approach than simply throwing away these classes, or assigning them a default regularization weight of zero. The model does need to be trained on a lot of "rare" examples, since it requires a significant amount of low entropy "pseudo-label" training examples - this is the source of the model's high recall on common classes. The authors show that, if less than 40% of the training examples are "rare", the model will still perform well on "common" classes, with recall above 60% (measured on a held-out validation set with 20% "rare" examples). The authors also show that it is possible to use a model with high recall on common classes for novel "rare" example generation, by sampling classes based on the predicted regularization score for each class. The resulting novel examples have significantly less entropy than the "true" rare events, and can be verified using a second, "reference" example, to ensure that the generated example is actually rare. The second examples are generated in the same way, by sampling from the regular classes, using the predicted regularization score for each class to ensure that sufficiently many "rare" examples are included. Overall this is an important contribution to the field of rare event learning, and the approach has potential to scale to larger and more relevant datasets, without requiring manual "rare" event annotation. The paper has several limitations. The model is only weakly optimized on the "rare" examples - it requires many "rare" examples, but only requires a few "rare" labels. The training set size required for this approach is likely to be very data-dependent. The "pseudo-label" approach to rare event detection also means that the model is not directly estimating the probability of each class being a "rare" event, and may fail to detect "rare" events that occur with low frequency, or which have a very high regular class probability (e.g. air conditioning). The authors describe these types of errors as "false positive" and "false negative" events, and indicate that post-processing using regular example substitution may be used to produce "true positive" and "true negative" rare event examples. This post-processing step may also significantly reduce the model's recall on common classes, since not all rare event examples are going to be classified as rare by the model, and not all rare events have a sufficiently high regular class probability to be detectable with confidence. The paper uses the term "rare" event to describe examples where only a few labeled "rare" examples are available. This is problematic, because there is no precise, agreed definition of what a "rare" event is, and the assumption that classes with few labeled "rare" examples are "rare" is not necessarily true. In some cases, the definition of a "rare" class may require only a few examples in the wild, but the distribution of these events is not "rare" (i.e. is not sparse or heavy-tailed), and it's not clear how many examples would be needed to estimate this distribution accurately. We present a large-scale life-long memory module for use in deep learning. The module exploits fast nearest-neighbor algorithms for efficiency and thus scales to large memory sizes. One-shot learning has been widely used in computer vision and machine learning in the last decade. It uses a small amount of training data for learning a model that can perform well on new, unseen data. Traditionally, if new data occurs, then the entire model has to be trained again from scratch, which is inefficient. One-shot learning aims to break the requirement for model rebuilding by using small amount of data, for example, one image, for training a model. There are two categories of one-shot learning. In one-shot recognition, the model is first trained on many similar examples, for example, a large set of similar images from ImageNet, and then tested on a query from a different but related dataset, for example, CIFAR-10. In one-shot optimization, the model is trained on one example but tested on many similar examples, for example, CIFAR-10. There are different approaches to one-shot learning, depending on the way the training example is transformed. We present a novel differentiable one-shot memory module for one-shot learning in deep neural networks. It has the following properties: 1) It can be added to any existing network. 2) It does not destroy the capability of the original network to produce output. 3) It is able to remember training examples shown many thousands of steps in the past and is able to generalize from them. 4) It is also able to do one-shot learning, with only a small amount of training data. 5) It is very easy to use. We apply the one-shot memory module to image classification and text translation, and set new state-of-the-art performance on Omniglot and few-shot classification, and new state-of-the-art performance on one-shot transfer and few-shot classification on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet.

Paper Title: Transfer Learning for Sequence Tagging with Hierarchical Recurrent Networks This paper proposes a Transfer Learning approach for Sequence Tagging (also known as Seq2Seq). The authors propose to first pre-train a tagger using a large corpus of unlabeled data, and then fine-tune this pre-trained model on a smaller labeled data set. The main benefit of this approach is that it uses the unlabeled data to pre-train the tagger to account for shift in distribution between the unlabeled and labeled data. The proposed model uses a hierarchical recurrent network which is similar to previous works on neural Seq2Seq model, but the use of attention mechanism gives better performance. The main drawback of this approach is the need to hand-pick the pre-trained model on the larger corpus. This is tedious and error-prone. A better approach would be to use hyperparameter search to automatically search for the best pre-trained model. Overall this is an interesting paper that extends recent advances in neural sequence tagging by incorporating transfer learning from a related task. The main results presented in the paper are statistically significant and show that the proposed approach leads to improvements over the current state of the art on several standard benchmarks. The main limitation of the paper is the lack of applicability to new tasks/domains/languages. The results have been obtained only for POS tagging of microblogs and transfer learning to POS tagging of Penn Treebank. The architectures and training procedures are fixed and cannot be applied to other tasks with different architectures and training procedures. The other limitation is related to the choice of the source task. The experiments show that using a related but a different task from the target task helps but there is a limit on the type of task that can be used. In the paper the source task is selected based on availability (i.e. POS tagging of Penn Treebank) and relatedness to the target task (i.e. POS tags of microblog posts). It would be useful to know whether similar results could be obtained by using a much easier source task (e.g. POS tagging of the New York Times). The last issue is the evaluation. In the paper the proposed model is compared with the one with the full supervised setting (i.e. using the gold tags for training the model). However, without the additional data it is not possible to know how the proposed transfer learning method would perform without using any labels during training. This should be tested to gauge the true impact of the method. In spite of these limitations, the paper presents an interesting approach to address the problem of limited training data and may serve as a baseline for future work on this topic.

This paper studies the problem of transfer learning for neural sequence taggers. In recent years, neural networks have achieved excellent results on many sequence tagging tasks. One appealing aspect of these systems is their generality, as they do not require task-specific feature engineering. However, one major limitation of these models is that they are typically developed and optimized on data of one specific task. It is unclear if these models can be applied to domains with limited training data. In this paper, we study the transfer learning for neural sequence taggers. Specifically, we explore the application of transfer learning across domains, applications and languages. Experiments show that with limited annotated data, we can still obtain considerable improvements by training on annotations of a similar task. These improvements lead to improvements over the current state-of-the-art on several well-studied tasks. This paper is useful for practitioners who are interested in applying neural sequence taggers to domains with limited annotated data. It also provides insights into the problems of domain adaptation and domain adaptation for neural sequence taggers. Although the proposed approach yields state-of-the-art performance on several sequence tagging tasks, it is an exploratory method and still needs to be improved to generalize to other tasks. For example, similar to most deep learning systems, the proposed framework relies on expensive compute resources (such as GPUs) and is not easily scalable. Some related works: - Knowledge transfer in deep neural network taggers, - Multi-task learning for sequence tagging with aspect-specific neural net supervision, - Self-supervised learning of hierarchical recurrent neural networks for sequence labeling, - Transfer learning for neural sequence taggers, - Tasks and Transfer Learning for Joint Sentence Parsing and NER, - Transfer learning for Neural Machine Translation, - Zero-shot learning for text sequence labeling, - Knowledge transfer for zero-shot language understanding, This work is also related to the general fields of transfer learning and domain adaptation. Some limitations of this work are also discussed. For example, the proposed approach can only be applied to sequence labeling tasks. Some future work includes more extensive experiments on different sequence labeling tasks and the exploration of more transfer learning schemes, such as simultaneously transfering knowledge across multiple related but different tasks.

This paper proposes a hierarchical framework of transfer learning for sequence tagging, which is expected to help the target task with the source task, by sharing as many levels of representation as possible. It is a general framework for various neural models. The paper has extensive and solid experiments, and the performance is competitive with the state of the art on multiple benchmark datasets. The framework is clear by itself, except that more details about training procedure, i.e. sec-3.3, need to be added. 

The experimental results show that for some task pairs {s,t}, this framework can help low-resource target task t, and the improvement increases with more levels of representations can be shared. Firstly, I suggest that the terms *source* and *target* should be more precisely defined in the current framework, because, due to Sec-3.3, the s and t in each pair are sort of interchangeable. That is, either of them can be the *source* or *target* task, especially when p(X=s)=p(X=t)=0.5 is used in the task sampling. The difference is: one is low-resourced and the other is not. Thus it could be thought of as multi-tasking between tasks with imbalanced resource. So one question is: does this framework simultaneously help both tasks in the pair, by learning more generalizable representations for different domains/applications/languages? Or is it mostly likely to only help the low-resourced one? Does it come with sacrifice on the high-resourced side? 

Secondly, as the paper shows that the low-resourced tasks are improved for the selected task pairs, it would also be interesting and helpful to know how often this could happen. That is, when the tasks are randomly paired (one chosen from a low-resource pool and the other from a high resource pool), how often could this framework help the low-resourced one?

Moreover, the choice of T-A/T-B/T-C lies intuitively in how many levels of representation *could* be shared as possible. This implicitly assumes share more, help more. Although I tend to believe so, it would be interesting to have some empirical comparison. For example, one could perhaps select some cross-domain pair, and see if T-A > T-B > T-C on such pairs, as mentioned in the author’s answer to the pre-review question. 

In general, I think this is a solid paper, and more exploration could be done in this direction. So I tend to accept this paper.

machine_text: Overall, this is an interesting idea for a paper. The core idea of the model and how it works is clear: in general, questions about content refer to a general area of knowledge, and a specific fact in that area of knowledge gets searched for and returned by the model. The model uses the search query and question pairs to learn which concepts are important for answering the question. I have some suggestions for improvement on how to try and improve the model’s accuracy and also suggestions for how to potentially combine this model with other models to further improve accuracy. I think the model has the potential to be very accurate, especially if the inference error from the single model is reduced, but there are many steps to take to make this model useful in real-life applications. model’s accuracy and also suggestions for how to potentially combine this model with other models to further improve accuracy. I think the model has the potential to be very accurate, especially if the inference error from the single model is reduced, but there are many steps to take to make this model useful in real-life applications. One way to further improve accuracy would be to increase the model’s ability to understand when more than one word or character is required to answer the question. Right now, if the question is “how many words are in the sentence?” the answer is “5”, but if the question is “what is the length of the sentence?” the answer is “41”. This model could be trained to consider the length of the answer, but a simpler approach would be to allow it to select both “5” and “41” as valid answers. This might involve additional trainable parameters, but I believe the performance gain from this additional complexity might be worth the additional parameter cost.

I agree with the goal of this paper which is to build a fine-grained gating mechanism for reading comprehension. Problem and question: It is unclear how the model achieves the new level of granularity and how it scales up to longer passages and more questions. The solution seems simple on the surface, but there are also some obvious drawbacks to this approach: 1) the model is tailored for a specific reading comprehension question, so it cannot be easily generalized to other scenarios, 2) there are too many hyperparameters and it is not clear how the model is tuned, 3) generating "enough" cells for rare words is computationally expensive. Overall, these are early days for this approach to reading comprehension, and although the idea is interesting, there are many open questions to be addressed before this approach can be considered practical for commercial deployment. Strength and weakness: In the introduction, the authors list many previous attempts at solving the reading comprehension problem, and while most of them were not tailored to a specific problem, there are some recent solutions that could be worth mentioning: T5'sQA module which is trained end-to-end for reading comprehension on large amounts of synthetic data, NovWriter which uses a Seq2Seq model to write questions that can be used to generate prompts for human writers, and DRAW which uses a template-based approach to generating prompt sentences. The problems that the current approach solves are the fine-grained analysis of a reading comprehension question and the generation of diverse prompt sentences, but we are still left with many open questions. Overall, I would give this paper a complementary rather than dominant signal, due to the many open questions and the lack of extensive evaluation.

Overall I am very satisfied with the content of the paper, the logic is clear and the topic is interesting. The experimental results also validate the effectiveness of the method, the model shows good performance on the Children's Book Test and Who Did What datasets, and even better performance on the social media tag prediction task. However, as the paper mainly focuses on the design of the gating method, there are some parts that can be further improved. For example, the choice of baselines and comparison with previous works is not very comprehensive, and some detailed parameter settings are not shown. Also, except for some simple tasks like social tag prediction, most existing datasets for reading comprehension are not analyzed in this paper. I think this is mainly because the differences among these datasets make it difficult to compare them with each other. Finally, I also think the paper title is a little misleading, as the core of the method is to use words or characters to gate the vector representation of questions and paragraphs, which means the content of the words or characters will determine whether a passage should be shown. If a question refers to something that is never mentioned in the passage, the corresponding passage will not be shown in any way. I think the best way to describe this would be to use the words 'only' or 'never', because if a passage does not contain something, then the model will never learn anything from that passage. However, as this is very common sense, I do not think the model will perform this poorly. In fact, I think with a lot of data, when the model encounters a passage that does not contain something, I do not think it can give much consideration to this, because this information is already contained in the fact that this passage is never mentioned in any question. I assume there must be a better way to ensure that all information in the passage is not lost, but I do not know what this better is.

This paper adds a gating mechanism to dynamically combine word-level and character-level representations to improve reading comprehension. The paper is interesting because it solves a long-standing problem in this area – using concatenation or scalar weighting, which are suboptimal for high-level tasks like reading comprehension, to integrate word-level and character-level representations. The idea of dynamic gating is also innovative and could be applied to a wider range of NLP tasks. The main content of the paper is as below: Both word-level and character-level representations have been widely used in reading comprehension, but previous works either use concatenation or scalar weighting to integrate the two kinds of representation, which is suboptimal. We present a dynamic gating mechanism to dynamically combine the two kinds of representation by properties of the words. Furthermore, the dynamic gating mechanism is also applicable to modeling the interaction between questions and paragraphs for reading comprehension. We conduct experiments on the Children's Book Test and Who Did What datasets, and our approach improves the performance on these two benchmarks, achieving new state-of-the-art results. We also apply our model to a social media tag prediction task, and the experiment results show that our model outperforms the strong baseline by a significant margin. The paper also analyzes the parameter settings and other implementation details, which is very helpful for practitioners to adopt the model or reproduce the results. Finally, we make the code and data available so that the model could be applied to new tasks easily.

The consensus amongst reviewers is that this paper's proposal for combining character level information with word-level information is sound, well presented, and well evaluated. The main negative sentiment was that the approach was perhaps a little increment, although the conceptual size of the increment was sufficient to warrant publication, and will be relevant to the interests of ICLR attendees working on the intersection of deep learning and NLP. After a cursory reading of the paper, I see no reason to disagree, and recommend acceptance.

This paper proposes a new gating mechanism to combine word and character representations. The proposed model sets a new state-of-the-art on the CBT dataset; the new gating mechanism also improves over scalar gates without linguistic features on SQuAD and a twitter classification task. 

Intuitively, the vector-based gate working better than the scalar gate is unsurprising, as it is more similar to LSTM and GRU gates. The real contribution of the paper for me is that using features such as POS tags and NER help learn better gates. The visualization in Figure 3 and examples in Table 4 effectively confirm the utility of these features, very nice! 

In sum, while the proposed gate is nothing technically groundbreaking, the paper presents a very focused contribution that I think will be useful to the NLP community. Thus, I hope it is accepted.

I think the problem here is well motivated, the approach is insightful and intuitive, and the results are convincing of the approach (although lacking in variety of applications). I like the fact that the authors use POS and NER in terms of an intermediate signal for the decision. Also they compare against a sufficient range of baselines to show the effectiveness of the proposed model.

I am also convinced by the authors' answers to my question, I think there is sufficient evidence provided in the results to show the effectiveness of the inductive bias introduced by the fine-grained gating model.

SUMMARY.

The paper proposes a gating mechanism to combine word embeddings with character-level word representations.
The gating mechanism uses features associated to a word to decided which word representation is the most useful.
The fine-grain gating is applied as part of systems which seek to solve the task of cloze-style reading comprehension question answering, and Twitter hashtag prediction.
For the question answering task, a fine-grained reformulation of gated attention for combining document words and questions is proposed.
In both tasks the fine-grain gating helps to get better accuracy, outperforming state-of-the-art methods on the CBT dataset and performing on-par with state-of-the-art approach on the SQuAD dataset.


----------

OVERALL JUDGMENT

This paper proposes a clever fine-grained extension of a scalar gate for combining word representation.
It is clear and well written. It covers all the necessary prior work and compares the proposed method with previous similar models.

I liked the ablation study that shows quite clearly the impact of individual contributions.
And I also liked the fact that some (shallow) linguistic prior knowledge e.g., pos tags ner tags, frequency etc. has been used in a clever way. 
It would be interesting to see if syntactic features can be helpful.

This paper considers the effect of varying the size of the recurrent layer in a recurrent neural network on the network’s training speed and final performance. The intuition is that, by making the recurrent layer smaller, you reduce the amount of computation needed at each step, thus allowing for faster training, but at the cost of lower accuracy. The authors compare the effect of using a smaller and a fixed-sized recurrent layer on the training speed and final performance. human_text:
The authors investigate a variety of existing and two new RNN architectures to obtain more insight about the effectiveness at which these models can store task information in their parameters and activations.

The experimental setups look sound. To generalize comparisons between different architectures it’s necessary to consider multiple tasks and control for the effect of the hyperparameters. This work uses multiple tasks of varying complexities, principled hyperparameter tuning methodology and a number of tuning iterations that can currently only be achieved by the computational resources of some of the larger industrial research groups. 

The descriptions of the models and the objective where very clear to me. The descriptions of the experiments and presentation of the results were not always clear to me at times, even with the additional details in the appendix available. Most of these issues can easily be resolved by editing the text. For example, in the memory task the scaling of the inputs (and hence also outputs) is not provided so it’s hard to interpret the squared error scores in Figure 2c. It’s not clear to me what the term ‘unrollings’ refers to in Figure 2b. Is this a time lag with additional hidden state updates between the presentation of the input sequence and the generation of the output? Since the perceptron capacity task is somewhat central to the paper, I think a slightly more precise description of how and when the predictions are computed would be helpful. Due to the large number of graphs, it can be somewhat hard to find the most relevant results. Perhaps some of the more obvious findings (like Figure 1(b-d) given Figure 1a) could move to the appendix to make space for more detailed task descriptions.

Novelty is not really the aim of this paper since it mostly investigates existing architectures. To use the mutual information to obtain bits per parameter scores in highly non-linear parameterized functions is new to me. The paper also proposed to new architectures that seem to have practical value. The paper adds to the currently still somewhat neglected research effort to employ the larger computational resources we currently have towards a better understanding of architectures which were designed when such resources were not yet available. I’d argue that the paper is original enough for that reason alone.

The paper provides some interesting new insights into the properties of RNNs. While observed before, it is interesting to see the importance of gated units for maintaining trainability of networks with many layers. It is also interesting to see a potential new use for vanilla RNNs for simpler tasks where a high capacity per parameter may be required due to hardware constraints. The proposed +RNN may turn out to have practical value as well and the hyperparameter robustness results shed some light on the popularity of certain architectures when limited time for HP tuning is available. The large body of results and hyperparameter analysis should be useful to many researchers who want to use RNNs in the future. All in all, I think this paper would make a valuable addition to the ICLR conference but would benefit from some improvements to the text.

Pros:
* Thorough analysis.
* Seemingly proper experiments.
* The way of quantifying capacity in neural networks adds to the novelty of the paper.
* The results have some practical value and suggest similar analysis of other architectures.
* The results provide useful insights into the relative merits of different RNN architectures.

Cons:
* It’s hard to isolate the most important findings (some plots seem redundant).
* Some relevant experimental details are missing.

The reviewers all agreed that this paper should appear at the conference. The experiments seem to confirm interesting intuition about the capacity of recurrent nets and how difficult they are to train, and the reviewers appreciated the experimental rigor. This is certainly of interest and useful to the ICLR community and will lead to fruitful discussion. The reviewers did request more fine details related to the experiments for reproducibility (thank you for adding more detail to the appendix). The authors are recommended to steer clear of making any strong but unsubstantiated references to neuroscience.

We have just uploaded the newest version of our paper. Based on the reviewers' helpful comments, the changes include:

- Minimal Gated Unit for Recurrent Neural Networks citation
- Improved descriptions of training tasks in Appendix (added missing details, such as time steps unrolled before computing loss)
- Added range of perceptron capacity HP b and plot showing that optimal dataset size selected by the HP tuner is only slightly more than mutual information calculated (Figure 1 of Appendix)
- Small text changes to emphasize that our results indicate the promise of the UGRNN and +RNN, but of course much more extensive testing is needed to declare that they are comparable to well-known, tried and true architectures
- Welch’s t-test statistics to test the significance of differences between architecture losses as a result of randomly selected hyperparameters (the experiment shown in Figure 5 and Table 1, and test statistics are reported in Table 2 of Appendix)

We are also in the process of releasing a dataset of the HPs and associated losses for all experiments described in the paper. While we can not be positive how long the release process will take, we plan to have the HP dataset publicly available by February 2017!

This paper performs a very important service: exploring in a clear and systematic way the performance and trainability characteristics of a set of neural network architectures -- in particular, the basic RNN motifs that have recently been popular.   

Pros:

* This paper addresses an important question I and many others would have liked to know the answer to but didn't have the computational resources to thoroughly attack it.   This is a nice use of Google's resources to help the community. 

* The work appears to have been done carefully so that the results can be believed.

* The basic answer arrived at (that, in the "typical training environment" LSTMs are reliable but basically GRUs are the answer) seems fairly decisive and practically useful.   Of course the real answer is more complicated than my little summary here, but the subtleties are discussed nicely in the paper.

* The insistence on a strong distinction between capacity and trainability helps nicely clear up a misconception about the reasons why gated architectures work.  In sum, they're much more easily trainable but somewhat lower capacity than vanilla RNNs, and in hard tasks, the benefits of better trainability far outweigh the costs of mildly lower capacity.

* The point about the near-equivalence of capacity at equal numbers of parameters is very useful.   

* The paper makes it clear the importance of HP tuning, something that has sometimes gotten lost in the vast flow of papers about new architectures.

* The idea of quantifying the fraction of infeasible parameters (e.g. those that diverge) is nice, because it's a practical problem that everyone working with these networks has but often isn't addressed. 

* The paper text is very clearly written.

Cons:

* The work on the UGRNNs and the +RNNs seems a bit preliminary.  I don't think that the authors have clearly shown that the +RNN should be "recommended" with the same generality as the GRU.   I'd at the least want some better statistics on the significance of differences between +RNN and GRU performances quantifying the results in Figure 4 (8-layer panel).   In a way the high standards for declaring an architecture useful that are set in the paper make the UGRNNs and +RNN contributions seem less important.   I don't really mind having them in the paper though.   I guess the point of this paper is not really to be novel in the first place -- which is totally fine with me, though I don't know what the ICLR area chairs will think. 

* The paper gives short shrift to the details of the HP algorithm itself.  They do say: 

     "Our setting of the tuner’s internal parameters was such that it uses Batched GP Bandits with an expected improvement acquisition function and a   
     Matern 5/2 Kernel with feature scaling and automatic relevance determination performed by optimizing over kernel HPs"  

and give some good references, but I expect that actually trying to replicate this involves a lot of missing details.   

* I found some of the figures a bit hard to read at first, esp. Fig 4, mostly due to the panels being small, having a lot of details, and bad choices for visual cleanliness.   

* The neuroscience reference ("4.7 bits per synapse") seems a little bit of a throw-away to me, because the connection between these results and the experimental neuroscience is very tenuous, or at any rate, not well explained.  I guess it's just in the discussion, but it seems gratuitous.   Maybe it should couched in slightly less strong terms (nothing is really strongly shown to be "in agreement" here between computational architectures and neuroscience, but perhaps they could say something like -- "We wonder if it is anything other than coincidence that our 5 bits result is numerically similar to the 4.7 bits measurement from neuroscience.")

CONTRIBUTIONS
Large-scale experiments are used to measure the capacity and trainability of different RNN architectures. Capacity experiments suggest that across all architectures, RNNs can store between three and six bits of information per parameter, with ungated RNNs having the highest per-parameter capacity. All architectures are able to store approximately one floating point number per hidden unit. Trainability experiments show that ungated architectures (RNN, IRNN) are much harder to train than gated architectures (GRU, LSTM, UGRNN, +RNN). The paper also proposes two novel RNN architectures (UGRNN and +RNN); experiments suggest that the UGRNN has similar per-parameter capacity as the ungated RNN but is much easier to train, and that deep (8-layer) +RNN models are easier to train than existing architectures.

CLARITY
The paper is well-written and easy to follow.

NOVELTY
This paper is the first to my knowledge to empirically measure the number of bits of information that can be stored per learnable parameter. The idea of measuring network capacity by finding the dataset size and other hyperparameters that maximizes mutual information is a particularly novel experimental setup.

The proposed UGRNN is similar but not identical to the minimal gated unit proposed by Zhou et al, “Minimal Gated Unit for Recurrent Neural Networks”, International Journal of Automation and Computing, 2016.

SIGNIFICANCE
I have mixed feelings about the significance of this paper. I found the experiments interesting, but I don’t feel that they reveal anything particularly surprising or unexpected about recurrent networks; it is hard to see how any of the experimental results will change the way either that I think about RNNs, or the way that I will use them in my own future work. On the other hand it is valuable to see intuitive results about RNNs confirmed by rigorous experiments, especially since few researchers have the computational resources to perform such large-scale experiments.

The capacity experiments (both per-parameter capacity and per-unit capacity) essentially force the network to model random data. For most applications of RNNs, however, we do not expect them to work with random data; instead when applied in machine translation or language modeling or image captioning or any number of real-world tasks, we hope that RNNs can learn to model data that is anything but random. It is not clear to me that an architecture’s ability to model random data should be beneficial in modeling real-world data; indeed, the experiments in Section 2.1 show that architectures vary in their capacity to model random data, but the text8 experiments in Section 3 show that these same architectures do not significantly vary in their capacity to model real-world data.

I do not think that the experimental results in the paper are sufficient to prove the significance of the proposed UGRNN and +RNN architectures. It is interesting that the UGRNN can achieve comparable bits per parameter as the ungated RNN and that the deep +RNNs are more easily trainable than other architectures, but the only experiments on a real-world task (language modeling on text8) do not show these architectures to be significantly better than GRU or LSTM.

SUMMARY
I wish that the experiments had revealed more surprising insights about RNNs, though there is certainly value in experimentally verifying intuitive results. The proposed UGRNN and +RNN architectures show some promising results on synthetic tasks, but I wish that they showed more convincing performance on real-world tasks. Overall I think that the good outweighs the bad, and that the ideas of this paper are of value to the community.

PROS
- The paper is the first of my knowledge to explicitly measure the bits per parameter that RNNs can store
- The paper experimentally confirms several intuitive ideas about RNNs:
    - RNNs of any architecture can store about one number per hidden unit from the input
    - Different RNN architectures should be compared by their parameter count, not their hidden unit count
    - With very careful hyperparameter tuning, all RNN architectures perform about the same on text8 language modeling
    - Gated architectures are easier to train than non-gated RNNs

CONS
- Experiments do not reveal anything particularly surprising or unexpected
- The UGRNN and +RNN architectures do not feel well-motivated
- The utility of the UGRNN and +RNN architectures is not well-established

It is interesting that the UGRNN can achieve comparable bits per parameter as the ungated RNN and that the deep +RNNs are more easily trainable than other architectures, but the only experiments on a real-world task (language modeling on text8) do not show these architectures to be significantly better than GRU or LSTM.

SUMMARY
I wish that the experiments had revealed more surprising insights about RNNs, though there is certainly value in experimentally verifying intuitive results. The proposed UGRNN and +RNN architectures show some promising results on synthetic tasks, but I wish that they showed more convincing performance on real-world tasks. Overall I think that the good outweighs the bad, and that the ideas of this paper are of value to the community.

PROS
- The paper is the first of my knowledge to explicitly measure the bits per parameter that RNNs can store
- The paper experimentally confirms several intuitive ideas about RNNs:
    - RNNs of any architecture can store about one number per hidden unit from the input
    - Different RNN architectures should be compared by their parameter count, not their hidden unit count
    - With very careful hyperparameter tuning, all RNN architectures perform about the same on text8 language modeling
    - Gated architectures are easier to train than non-gated RNNs

CONS
- Experiments do not reveal anything particularly surprising or unexpected
- The UGRNN and +RNN architectures do not feel well-motivated
- The utility of the UGRNN and +RNN architectures is not well-established

The authors investigate a variety of existing and two new RNN architectures to obtain more insight about the effectiveness at which these models can store task information in their parameters and activations.

The experimental setups look sound. To generalize comparisons between different architectures it’s necessary to consider multiple tasks and control for the effect of the hyperparameters. This work uses multiple tasks of varying complexities, principled hyperparameter tuning methodology and a number of tuning iterations that can currently only be achieved by the computational resources of some of the larger industrial research groups. 

The descriptions of the models and the objective where very clear to me. The descriptions of the experiments and presentation of the results were not always clear to me at times, even with the additional details in the appendix available. Most of these issues can easily be resolved by editing the text. For example, in the memory task the scaling of the inputs (and hence also outputs) is not provided so it’s hard to interpret the squared error scores in Figure 2c. It’s not clear to me what the term ‘unrollings’ refers to in Figure 2b. Is this a time lag with additional hidden state updates between the presentation of the input sequence and the generation of the output? Since the perceptron capacity task is somewhat central to the paper, I think a slightly more precise description of how and when the predictions are computed would be helpful. Due to the large number of graphs, it can be somewhat hard to find the most relevant results. Perhaps some of the more obvious findings (like Figure 1(b-d) given Figure 1a) could move to the appendix to make space for more detailed task descriptions.

Novelty is not really the aim of this paper since it mostly investigates existing architectures. To use the mutual information to obtain bits per parameter scores in highly non-linear parameterized functions is new to me. The paper also proposed to new architectures that seem to have practical value. The paper adds to the currently still somewhat neglected research effort to employ the larger computational resources we currently have towards a better understanding of architectures which were designed when such resources were not yet available. I’d argue that the paper is original enough for that reason alone.

The paper provides some interesting new insights into the properties of RNNs. While observed before, it is interesting to see the importance of gated units for maintaining trainability of networks with many layers. It is also interesting to see a potential new use for vanilla RNNs for simpler tasks where a high capacity per parameter may be required due to hardware constraints. The proposed +RNN may turn out to have practical value as well and the hyperparameter robustness results shed some light on the popularity of certain architectures when limited time for HP tuning is available. The large body of results and hyperparameter analysis should be useful to many researchers who want to use RNNs in the future. All in all, I think this paper would make a valuable addition to the ICLR conference but would benefit from some improvements to the text.

* Thorough analysis.
* Seemingly proper experiments.
* The way of quantifying capacity in neural networks adds to the novelty of the paper.
* The results have some practical value and suggest similar analysis of other architectures.
* The results provide useful insights into the relative merits of different RNN architectures.

Cons:
* It’s hard to isolate the most important findings (some plots seem redundant).
* Some relevant experimental details are missing.

The authors describe a method of using dynamic computation graphs to speed up deep learning training. This approach is motivated by the observation that in deep neural networks there is typically much less variability in the computation performed at a node than there is variability in the input received at the node. The authors introduce a scheme for creating separate dynamic graphs for each layer of the network, with the layer's input nodes and output nodes linked by an edge that can be assigned a run-time computation. This approach allows later layers to depend on results from earlier layers without recomputing if the computation can be parameterized and assigned to the connected edge run-time computation. The approach also avoids statically constructing the graph during training, instead using during training to compute a sequence of computation graphs on the fly. In experiments using the Cifar-10 dataset the approach is shown to achieve higher accuracy than prior art in some cases, particularly when the number of parameterizable computation steps is limited. The approach is demonstrated to be practical for implementation on existing deep learning hardware architectures. ACTUAL COMMENTS While there are a number of good ideas in this paper, the approach has limitations and there are some implementation issues. The main idea is to break up the deep learning computation into a sequence of modularizable computation steps. In the example given the computation includes both weight updates and feedforward of the full state of a layer. The weight updates could be assigned to an edge in a dynamic graph along with a known input node and output node pair (for example weight updates for a particular filter in a layer). The feedforward computation can be assigned to run-time dependency edges between unknown input nodes and output nodes. While it is possible to assign parameterizable computation for weight updates, this is not generally possible for feedforward computation. This presents a problem because there are often many variations of feedforward computation that are of interest to improve performance, for example different data layouts, data augmentation rules, and transpose operations. The approach described in this paper does not provide a way to define or optimize for specific computation for feedforward steps. The approach also only allows one step of computation per dependency edge. That is, while it is possible to define computations that apply for many steps, only one computation is implemented on each edge. While this allows for efficient implementation by hardware accelerators this may not be efficient for the full range of deep learning computations.

The paper describes a novel technique to improve the efficiency of computation graphs in deep learning frameworks. An impressive speedup can be observed in their implementation within TensorFlow. The content is presented with sufficient clarity, although some more graphical illustrations could be useful. This work is relevant in order to achieve highest performance in neural network training.


Pros:

- significant speed improvements through dynamic batching
- source code provided


Cons:

- the effect on a large real-world (ASR, SMT) would allow the reader to put the improvements better into context
- presentation/vizualisation can be improved
Adds \iclrfinalcopy and a link to the github repo which is now live
All reviewers viewed the paper favorably as a nice/helpful contribution to the implementation of this important class of methods.

I've just uploaded a minor revision in response to reviewer comments, in particular clarifying the intent of sections 3 and 3.5.1 with new/revised initial paragraphs. This pushed us a bit over the page limit so I moved the code example from 3.4 into an appendix per AnonReviewer1's suggestion. Thanks again AnonReviewers for your time and attention, I think this version is certainly an improvement over the original draft.

Authors describe implementation of TensorFlow Fold which allows one to run various computations without modifying computation graph. They achieve this by creating a generic scheduler as a TensorFlow computation graph, which can accept graph description as input and execute it.

They show clear benefits to this approach for tasks where computation changes for each datapoint, such as the case with TreeRNN.

In the experiments, they compare against having static batch (same graph structure repeated many times) and batch size 1.

The reason my score is 7 and not higher is because they do not provide comparison to the main alternative of their method -- someone could create a new TensorFlow graph for each dynamic batch. In other words, instead of using their graph as the scheduling algorithm, one could explicitly create each non-uniform batch as a TensorFlow graph, and run that using standard TensorFlow.

The paper presents a novel strategy to deal with dynamic computation graphs. They arise, when the computation is dynamically influenced by the input data, such as in LSTMs. The authors propose an `unrolling' strategy over the operations done at every step, which allows a new kind of batching of inputs.

The presented idea is novel and the results clearly indicate the potential of the approach. For the sake of clarity of the presentation I would drop parts of Section 3 ("A combinator library for neural networks") which presents technical details that are in general interesting, but do not help the understanding of the core idea of the paper. The presented experimental results on the "Stanford Sentiment Treebank" are in my opinion not supporting the claim of the paper, which is towards speed, than a little bit confusing. It is important to point out that even though the presented ensemble "[...] variant sets a new state-of-the-art on both subtasks" [p. 8], this is not due to the framework, not even due to the model (comp. lines 4 and 2 of Tab. 2), but probably, and this can only be speculated about, due to the ensemble averaging. I would appreciate a clearer argumentation in this respect.

Update on Jan. 17th:
after the authors update for their newest revision, I increase my rating to 8 due to the again improved, now very clear argumentation.

For example, images need to be generated such that they follow a desired probability distribution, and music samples need to follow a predefined stylistic rules. While there have been some research addressing the problem of mode collapse in GANs by using the Wasserstein distance between the distribution of real and generated samples, it is hard to estimate the distance between arbitrary distributions. In this paper, we propose autoregressive energy-based GAN (AE-GAN), which uses an energy-based model to parameterize the distribution of generated samples. This allows us to estimate the distance between arbitrary distributions. We evaluate the performance of AE-GAN on two distribution matching tasks, image and music generations. We also study the relation between our approach and the recent progress in data-driven distribution alignment. We minimize the distance between the energy-based model and an expected energy model, which is also trained using energy-based generative models. This allows us to estimate the distance between arbitrary distributions, which is hard to estimate with other distribution matching approaches. The authors in this paper introduce a framework for training energy-based generative adversarial networks (EB-GANs) and show that it provides a high-fidelity approximation to the data distribution. The paper has a very strong introduction, explaining the motivations and background for this line of research. The authors provide both theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation of the framework. The major weakness of the framework is that it requires several hours to days to train for high-dimensional images, making it inefficient for real-time applications. enabled inference and generation of high-dimensional images? The framework is efficient for high-dimensional images, where the image resolution is large but the dimension (number of pixels) is large. In this case, instead of directly representing the images using a fixed length vector, the authors represent each image using a pixel color code. This dramatically reduces the number of dimensions and thus the model complexity, while enabling the model to still capture the image structure. For low-dimensional images, such as hand-drawn sketches, the model is inefficient and it can take days to train. enables inference and generation of high-dimensional images? Yes. The model is inefficient for low-dimensional images, such as hand-drawn sketches. Instead of directly representing the images using a fixed length vector, the authors represent each image using a pixel color code. This dramatically reduces the number of dimensions and thus the model complexity, while enabling the model to still capture the image structure. How does it compare to normal GANs? The model is more expensive to compute as it needs to compute the per-pixel colors. However, the efficiency of the model only depends on the image dimension but not the dimension of the vector space. Therefore, the inefficiency problem of GANs with per-pixel manipulation is also inherent to the normal GANs. How does it compare to surrogated GANs? The EB-GAN is similar to surrogated GANs, which also uses an energy function to train the generator. However, surrogated GANs uses unphysical equations to represent the generator and this leads to several problems. (1) The training is very unstable and tends to converge to a local minimum instead of global minimum. (2) The spectra of the fake samples is not guaranteed to be constant, which means that a white noise still remains in the sample spectrum. (3) The convergence of the model is slow, and the model cannot produce high-fidelity images in real-time. (4) The training of the model requires days which is too slow for practical usage. It would be interesting to compare the EB-GAN to existing surrogated GANs and analyze the limitations of this type of model. how does it compare to energy-based GANs? The EB-GAN is similar to energy-based GANs. The two models have the same unphysical equations and training process. However, the purpose of the two models is quite different. The energy-based GANs uses unphysical equations to represent the generator, and the objective of the model is to prove that the generator and the discriminator have the same statistical distributions. The two models fail to be reconciled because their objectives are different. The EB-GAN model uses unphysical equations to represent the generator, and the objective is to produce high-fidelity images. The two models can be reconciled by adding new constraints on the model. One possible solution is to assume that the discriminator has a low-fidelity representation of the image and then to minimize the difference between the low-fidelity representation and the generator. how does it compare to prior art? EB-GAN can produce high-fidelity images. The efficiency is still limited by the color representation method for high-dimensional images. The representation method for low-dimensional images is inefficient. how does it compare to state of the art? EB-GAN captures the pixel structures in images, which makes it very efficient for high-dimensional images. However, for low-dimensional images, such as sketches, it is inefficient. how would you optimize this framework? Incorporating efficient representation methods for both low-dimensional and high-dimensional images into the framework. how can this framework be applied to new problems? The framework is designed for images, but it can be easily applied to other types of data. The only constraint is that the data should be able to be represented using a low-dimensional or low-resolution encoding.

The main content of this paper is about energy-based GAN (EBGAN), which is a flexible adversarial training framework that enables generator to converge to the true data distribution and the discriminator can retain the density information. The authors derived the analytic form of the induced solution and analyzed the properties of this framework. Also, they proposed two effective approximation techniques, which makes this framework practical to train. The main contribution of this paper can be used to great extend various GAN frameworks, e.g. WGAN, improved GAN and so on. strongly The paper describes an effective approach to train Energy-based Generative Adversarial Networks. This is done by building upon the framework of WGAN, ensuring that the generator converges to the true data distribution and the discriminator retains the density information. The analysis of this framework is done by deriving the analytic solution. In addition, two effective approximation techniques are proposed to make the training feasible. overview The main idea is to relax the objection of theKL divergence in WGAN, by using the energy functions instead, thus it avoids vanishing gradients problem. Also, the gradient update rule is modified to guarantee the stability. The proposed framework includes two major parts: one is the energy function, which is calculated by the convolution between the generated samples and the normal distribution, and the other one is the regularizer, which can be viewed as a temperature to the KL divergence. The two are coupled by the assumption of fixed kernel. The framework is evaluated on UCI datasets, and the convergence and the corresponding characteristics are verified. The paper is well written and clear.

In this paper, we propose to equip Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN) with the ability to produce direct energy estimates for samples. This is an important first step towards allowing the GAN to recover the density information of data, and enable the discriminator to recover the energy of data distribution. The main contributions are three-fold: (1) We rigorously prove that our framework not only ensures the generator converges to the true data distribution, but also enables the discriminator to retain the density information at the global optimal.
