We tried to address the reviewer's concerns by adding a substantial amount of new results and discussion, mainly to the Appendix (notice that some experiments are still running, thus many figures will need to be updated). We highlighted the modifications in red. We did not finish making all the modifications: we mostly still need to improve the main text. However, we decided to send a first update to give the reviewers the time to digest the new material, and to make the remaining changes in the next few days.

Below we describe in some detail how we addressed the reviewer's comments.

1. Modification to model architecture.

To address the reviewer's concern about lack of comparison of different ways of incorporating the action, we added a section in the Appendix (Section B.1.3, Figures 19 and 20) that compares the architecture used in the main text (combining the action a_t-1 only with h_t-1 in a multiplicative way), with 8 alternatives, namely combining a_t-1 with the frame before encoding (ConvA), combining a_t-1 only with the encoded frame s_t-1, combining a_t-1 with both h_t-1 and s_t-1 in 4 possible ways, having a multiplicative/additive interaction of a_t-1 with h_t-1, and considering the action as an additional input. 
From the figures and videos it looks like combining the action with the frame (dark green lines) is a bad idea, and that there is no much difference in performance among the remaining approaches, although combining a_t-1 with both h_t-1 and s_t-1 (W^h h_{t-1}xW^s s_{t-1}x W^{a} a_{t-1)) seems to be overall a bit better (notice that this architecture results in a quite different core than the traditional LSTM core).
The experiments are still running -- the experiments with considering the action as an additional input (light green lines) are behind the other experiments.

We also modified the section in the Appendix describing the difference between our direct action influence and the indirect action influence as in Oh et al. (now at the end of Section B.1.3). We changed Fig. 12 in the previous version with Figure 21 to show the difference in the other games in addition to Seaquest (we need to add Riverraid for which we want to use 2 subsequences of length T=15). 
Direct action influence performs similarly to indirect action influence in games with lower prediction error, such as Bowling, Freeway and Pong, but better in games with higher prediction error. The most striking difference is with Seaquest, which is most evident when looking at the videos (is is difficult to judge the difference in performance by looking at the prediction error only, that's why we added randomly selected videos from which the types of errors in the prediction can be visually understood). These results are computed using the best training scheme for Seaquest. The videos show that, with indirect action influence, the simulator models the fish quite poorly, even though using a training scheme that more strongly encourages long-term accuracy enables the simulator to learn the appearance of the fish better than with the training scheme of Oh et al. Therefore, these videos clearly show that the training scheme alone is not sufficient, our architecture plays a crucial role in substantially improving the prediction. Having indirect action influence also makes it more difficult to correctly update the score in some games such as Seaquest and Fishing Derby. Therefore, whilst the training scheme is the major responsible for improving long-term prediction, it needs to be combined with an appropriate architecture in order to work. 

All together, the experiments in Section B.1.3 suggest that having a direct (as opposed to Oh at al.) and global (as opposed to ConvA) action influence on the state dynamics is much preferable. On the other hand, performance is less sensitive to different ways of imposing direct action influence. We need to improve the discussion in the paper about this point.


2. Exploring the idea of jumpy predictions.

To address the reviewer's concerns about lack of a detailed analysis, we added a new section in the Appendix (Section B.2, Figures 25 and 26), and modified Figure 5(b) to include all games (except Breakout for which the prediction error is uninformative -- see the discussion about this game in Section B.1.1). Section B.2 compares different architectures, sequence lengths and number of subsequences (we plan to add a few more experiments in the next few weeks). 
It is clear from the results that the jumpy simulator is much more sensitive to changes of structure, and therefore fragile, than the single-step simulator. However, we show that with the right training structure, the jumpy simulator can be accurate in many games. Having accurate and fast to use simulators is essential for model-based reinforcement learning. Thus, whilst the novelty might seems marginal, it is of extreme interest for the community to advance in this type of approaches. Furthermore, accurate jumpy approaches are very difficult to obtain -- we believe that we are the first ones showing some success for long-term prediction in large scale domains.

We do not understand the sentence 'However, it is again not clear whether the modification in the current model leads to this effect or it could be achieved by previous models like Oh et al.'. The model of Oh et al. cannot be modified to perform jumpy predictions as, when omitting intermediate frames, the corresponding actions do not have any influence (as they influence the hidden states indirectly through the frames). This is actually an important reason why a direct action influence is preferable.

We would like to comment on the sentence “While this observation is interesting, this effect has been previously explored in detail in other works like schedule sampling (Bengio et al.) and to some extent in Oh et al.?”
The schedule sampling work of Bengio et al. focuses on different applications, with discrete data and on shorter-term prediction (for example, the length of sequences in the Image Captioning example (Section 4.1) is 11 on average). In this applications, the 100% Pred. Frames training scheme (called Always Sampling) actually performs poorly. Thus, based on the results of Bengio et al., we would never use the 100% Pred. Frames. We show that, in simpler games, this is actually the scheme that performs best, and that, in more complex games, a scheme that is as close as possible to such a scheme is preferable. Our analysis (especially in the new material) shows in detail the characteristics of each scheme on both short-term and long-term prediction. Thus, we make a significant contribution in advancing the understanding of different training schemes in frame prediction.
Oh et al. used a mixed scheme without any explanation. Thus, it is totally unclear from their paper the importance of using a mixed scheme and what are the differences of different types of mixing. That's actually the reason that motivatesd us to perform a detailed analysis. 

To improve the understanding of the results, we have added a section in the Appendix (Section B.1.1) that discusses the characteristics and effects of different training schemes on each game.

In conclusion, we addressed the reviewer's concerns on the analysis by adding more results and discussion. Regarding the concern on little novelty, we strongly disagree that this should be a concern. We greatly improved on the performance of previous methods (it is enough to compare the videos in Oh at al. with ours to realize that there is an enormous difference). Even more importantly, we improved the understanding of these methods with a detailed analysis. We believe that papers like our paper are as important for the community as papers that provide completely novel architectures without much analysis. 

Finally, the reviewer should understand that providing a detailed analysis and understanding is extremely challenging and time consuming, due to both the large scale and the complexity of the problem. Ours, whilst not fully comprehensive (as this is not possible), represents an enormous effort in trying to provide an in depth analysis and advance the understanding on the problem of high dimensional frame prediction.

1. modification to model architecture (used in Oh et al.) by using action at time t-1 to directly predict hidden state at t
2. exploring the idea of jumpy predictions (predictions multiple frames in future without using intermediate frames)
3. exploring different training schemes (trade-off between observation and prediction frames for training LSTM)

1. modification to model architecture
+ The motivation seems good that in past work (Oh et al.) the action at t-1 influences x_t, but not the state h_t of the LSTM. This could be fixed by making the LSTM state h_t dependent on a_{t-1}
- However, this is of minor technical novelty. Also, as pointed in reviewer questions, a similar effect could be achieved by adding a_t-1 as an input to the LSTM at time t. This could be done without modifying the LSTM architecture as stated in the paper. While the authors claim that combining a_t-1 with h_t-1 and s_t-1 performs worse than the current method which combines a_t-1 only with h_t-1, I would have liked to see the empirical difference in combining a_t-1 only with s_t-1 or only with h_t-1. Also, a stronger motivation is required to support the current formulation.
- Further, the benefits of this change in architecture is not well analyzed in experiments. Fig. 5(a) provides the difference between Oh et al. (with traditional LSTM) and current method. However, the performance difference is composed of 2 components (difference in training scheme and architecture). This contribution of the architecture to the performance is not clear from this experiment. The authors did claim in the pre-review phase that Fig. 12 (a) shows the difference in performance only due to architecture for "Seaquest". However, from this plot it appears that the gain at 100-steps (~15)  is only a small fraction of the overall gain in Fig. 5 (a) (~90). It is difficult to judge the significance of the architecture modification from this result for one game.

2. Exploring the idea of jumpy predictions:
+ As stated by the authors, omitting the intermediate frames while predicting future frames could significantly sppedup simulations.
+ The results in Fig. 5(b) present some interesting observations that omitting intermediate frames does not lead to significant error-increase for at least a few games.
- However, it is again not clear whether the modification in the current model leads to this effect or it could be achieved by previous models like Oh et al.
- While, the observations themselves are interesting, it would have been better to provide a more detailed analysis for more games. Also, the novelty in dropping intermediate frames for speedup is marginal.

3. Exploring different training schemes
+ This is perhaps the most interesting observation presented in the paper. The authors present the difference in performance for different training schemes in Fig. 2(a). The training schemes are varied based on the fraction of training phase which only uses observation frames and the fraction that uses only prediction frames.
+ The results show that this change in training can significantly affect prediction results and is the biggest contributor to performance improvement compared to Oh et al.
- While this observation is interesting, this effect has been previously explored in detail in other works like schedule sampling (Bengio et al.) and to some extent in Oh et al.

Clarity of presentation:
- The exact experimental setup is not clearly stated for some of the results. For instance, the paper does not say that Fig. 2(a) uses the same architecture as Oh et al. However, this is stated in the response to reviewer questions.
- Fig. 4 is difficult to interpret. The qualitative difference between Oh et al. and current method could be highlighted explicitly. 
- Minor: The qualitative analysis section requires the reader to navigate to various video-links in order to understand the section. This leads to a discontinuity in reading and is particularly difficult while reading a printed-copy.

Overall, the paper presents some interesting experimental observations. However, the technical novelty and contribution of the proposed architecture and training scheme is not clear.

The paper presents an action-conditional recurrent network that can predict frames in video games hundreds of steps in the future. The paper claims three main contributions: 
1. modification to model architecture (used in Oh et al.) by using action at time t-1 to directly predict hidden state at t
2. exploring the idea of jumpy predictions (predictions multiple frames in future without using intermediate frames)
3. exploring different training schemes (trade-off between observation and prediction frames for training LSTM)

1. modification to model architecture
+ The motivation seems good that in past work (Oh et al.) the action at t-1 influences x_t, but not the state h_t of the LSTM. This could be fixed by making the LSTM state h_t dependent on a_{t-1}
- However, this is of minor technical novelty. Also, as pointed in reviewer questions, a similar effect could be achieved by adding a_t-1 as an input to the LSTM at time t. This could be done without modifying the LSTM architecture as stated in the paper. While the authors claim that combining a_t-1 with h_t-1 and s_t-1 performs worse than the current method which combines a_t-1 only with h_t-1, I would have liked to see the empirical difference in combining a_t-1 only with s_t-1 or only with h_t-1. Also, a stronger motivation is required to support the current formulation.
- Further, the benefits of this change in architecture is not well analyzed in experiments. Fig. 5(a) provides the difference between Oh et al. (with traditional LSTM) and current method. However, the performance difference is composed of 2 components (difference in training scheme and architecture). This contribution of the architecture to the performance is not clear from this experiment. The authors did claim in the pre-review phase that Fig. 12 (a) shows the difference in performance only due to architecture for "Seaquest". However, from this plot it appears that the gain at 100-steps (~15)  is only a small fraction of the overall gain in Fig. 5 (a) (~90). It is difficult to judge the significance of the architecture modification from this result for one game.

2. Exploring the idea of jumpy predictions:
+ As stated by the authors, omitting the intermediate frames while predicting future frames could significantly sppedup simulations.
+ The results in Fig. 5(b) present some interesting observations that omitting intermediate frames does not lead to significant error-increase for at least a few games.
- However, it is again not clear whether the modification in the current model leads to this effect or it could be achieved by previous models like Oh et al.
- While, the observations themselves are interesting, it would have been better to provide a more detailed analysis for more games. Also, the novelty in dropping intermediate frames for speedup is marginal.

3. Exploring different training schemes
+ This is perhaps the most interesting observation presented in the paper. The authors present the difference in performance for different training schemes in Fig. 2(a). The training schemes are varied based on the fraction of training phase which only uses observation frames and the fraction that uses only prediction frames.
+ The results show that this change in training can significantly affect prediction results and is the biggest contributor to performance improvement compared to Oh et al.
- While this observation is interesting, this effect has been previously explored in detail in other works like schedule sampling (Bengio et al.) and to some extent in Oh et al.

Clarity of presentation:
- The exact experimental setup is not clearly stated for some of the results. For instance, the paper does not say that Fig. 2(a) uses the same architecture as Oh et al. However, this is stated in the response to reviewer questions.
- Fig. 4 is difficult to interpret. The qualitative difference between Oh et al. and current method could be highlighted explicitly. 
- Minor: The qualitative analysis section requires the reader to navigate to various video-links in order to understand the section. This leads to a discontinuity in reading and is particularly difficult while reading a printed-copy.

Overall, the paper presents some interesting experimental observations. However, the technical novelty and contribution of the proposed architecture and training scheme is not clear.

The authors propose a recurrent neural network architecture that is able to output more accurate long-term predictions of several game environments than the current state-of-the-art.
The original network architecture was inspired by inability of previous methods to accurately predict many time-steps into the future,
and their inability to jump directly to a future prediction without iterating through all intermediate states.
The authors have provided an extensive experimental evaluation on several benchmarks with promising results.
In general the paper is well written and quite clear in its explanations.
Demonstrating that this kind of future state prediction is useful for 3D maze exploration is a plus.

In this work, the authors propose EPOpt, a method for learning robust neural network policies. The method uses model ensembling to improve a neural network's policy, which can deal with large variations in the environment. The method first tunes an existing high-performing neural network policy using an entropy regularization term. Then, it uses several variations of the original policy, each trained on a different subset of the training data, and picks the best one based on validation performance. The method was shown to be effective on MuJoCo benchmarks, and the resulting policies were able to generalize to new environments and were robust to catastrophic forgetting. The proposed EPOpt method has several useful features. First, it allows for efficient computation of robust policies. Using model ensembling, the authors are able to quickly produce a new policy by training on a small subset of the data. Second, the method is easy to implement. Most existing methods for robust neural network policies require modifications to the training procedure, or access to specialized hardware, which may not be suitable for resource-limited agents. The EPOpt method, on the other hand, only requires a standard neural network training procedure and general-purpose hardware. Finally, the method is theoretically sound. The authors provide a theoretical analysis to prove that the method does not suffer from the negative side effects, such as poor generalizability, that often accompany ensemble methods. Overall, the proposed method can be a useful tool for practitioners. It allows for easy implementation of model-based optimization, while having good generalization and theoretical guarantees.

This paper presents EPOpt, which uses an ensemble of simulated source domains and adversarial training to learn policies that are robust and generalize to a broad range of possible target domains. The model ensemble, which consists of a base model and multiple variants, is updated with data from the target domain to approximate the underlying probability distribution of the source domains. Thus, EPOpt provides the benefit of both robustness and learning. The main contributions of this work are as follows: 1. We present a new model ensemble method that learns a probability distribution over source domains instead of a single source domain. 2. We extend the Adversarial Upper-Bound framework to use the model ensemble. 3. We use approximate Bayesian inference to adapt the ensemble probabilities. 4. We provide an empirical evaluation of the EPOpt method on the robot motion simulation domain, where we compare EPOpt with a method that uses a single source domain. 5. We demonstrate the applicability of EPOpt to a reinforcement learning application in the ArcGIS Environment, where we demonstrate that EPOpt can learn policies that are robust to different versions of a source domain and different domains that differ from the source domain in ways that are not fully known to the learner. armac feedback: The authors have presented EPOpt, which uses an ensemble of simulated source domains and adversarial training to learn policies that are robust and generalize to a broad range of possible target domains. This paper addresses the following problem:sample complexity and safety are major challenges when learning policies with reinforcement learning for real-world tasks, especially when the policies are represented using rich function approximators like deep neural networks. Model-based methods where the real-world target domain is approximated using a simulated source domain provide an avenue to tackle the above challenges by augmenting real data with simulated data. However, discrepancies between the simulated source domain and the target domain pose a challenge for simulated training. We introduce the EPOpt algorithm, which uses an ensemble of simulated source domains and a form of adversarial training to learn policies that are robust and generalize to a broad range of possible target domains, including to unmodeled effects. The main strength of this method is that it makes use of an ensemble of source domains and adversarial training to learn a robust policy. This is especially effective in scenarios with high uncertainty such as with small sample size or when the simulator generates samples that are significantly different from the real world. One drawback of this method is that the ensemble is static and can't adapt to new unseen target domains. Another limitation of the paper is that it only considers the finite-sumgame context, and doesn't extend to Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). On the strength side, this method makes use of an ensemble of source domains and adversarial training to learn a robust policy. It also further extends the approach by using an additional discriminator to compute the similarity between the real and the simulated source domains. This allows the model to be more robust to model mismatch. Another positive point is that the generated target domains are not fed back to the discriminator, which guards against the mode collapse problem. On the weakness side, the model only considers the finite-sumgame scenario, and doesn't extend to Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). Another limitation of the paper is that it only considers the binary cross entropy loss for adversarial training, and doesn't consider other types of loss functions. Overall, this paper provides a novel method to tackle the problem of sample complexity in model-based RL. By considering a more realistic modeling framework where the policy is composed of a fixed number of MDPs, the method is able to solve the problem of model uncertainty without incurring an excessive computation cost. The paper is also innovative in proposing the use of adversarial training and model ensembles to improve model robustness.

The paper looks at the problem of transferring a policy learned in a simulator to  a target real-world system.  The proposed approach considers using an ensemble of simulated source domains, along with adversarial training, to learn a robust policy that is able to generalize to several target domains.

Overall, the paper tackles an interesting problem, and provides a reasonable solution.  The notion of adversarial training used here does not seem the same as other recent literature (e.g. on GANs).  It would be useful to add more details on a few components, as discussed in the question/response round.  I also encourage including the results with alternative policy gradient subroutines, even if they don’t perform well (e.g. Reinforce), as well as results with and without the baseline on the value function. Such results are very useful to other researchers.

The approach here looks at learning policies that are robust over a parameterized class of MDPs (in the sense the probability that the policy doesn't perform well is small over this class. The idea is fairly straightforward, but the algorithm seems novel and the results show that the approach does seem to provide substantial benefit. The reviewers were all in agreement that the paper is worth accepting.
 
 Pros:
 + Nice application of robust (really stochastic, since these are chance constraints) optimization to policy search
 + Compelling demonstration of the improved range of good performance over methods like vanilla TRPO
 
 Cons:
 - The question of how to parameterize a class of MDPs for real-world scenarios is still somewhat unclear
 - The description of the method as optimizing CVaR seems incorrect, since they appear to be using an actual chance constraint, whereas CVaR is essentially a convex relaxation ... this may be related to the work in (Tamar, 2015), but needs to be better explained if so.

machine_text: Overall, I find the paper to be very well written and presenting an approach that could be quite useful for the many applications that require transferring knowledge from a source to a target domain, with minimal labeled support. My main suggestion would be to better motivate why the authors chose to focus on deep architectures over more traditional machine learning approaches, such as ensemble methods or regularization methods. While I do understand that the proposed approach is motivated by the limitations of these traditional approaches, I do not believe that this comes through clearly in the paper, and thus readers without a background in machine learning may find it difficult to understand why this approach was thought to be promising. I also feel that the paper could be generally strengthened by including additional discussion of related work, both in terms of papers that had come before this paper in this space, as well as related work in related areas (such as computer vision, where deep transfer approaches for that domain have shown great success) could be helpful in providing more context and guiding the reader through the choice of the deep transfer approach. More generally, I feel that the combination of a clear statement of the problem, a clear statement of the contributions of this paper, and the choice of focus on a deep approach without overwhelming the reader with technical jargon, is well suited to helping the paper find a broader audience, and will be of great interest to readers in the NLP community looking for a way to apply deep transfer approaches to their domain. I look forward to seeing this paper published in a reputable venue. Overall positive comments.

This paper presents Attend, Adapt and Transfer: Attentive Deep Architecture for Adaptive Transfer from multiple sources in the same domain. The paper makes an interesting contribution to the field of machine learning by proposing a new method for deep neural network architecture that improves the effectiveness of transfer learning. The paper describes a new architecture that uses a contrastive loss function to allow the model to attend to individual samples from the source domain, and adapt to the new domain by learning a generalizable representation. The paper presents results on two supervised learning tasks: speaker recognition and image classification, using character recognition as the domain source domain and image classification as the new domain. The results show that the proposed model outperforms traditional transfer learning methods by a large margin, with improvements of 9.2% relative and 2.8% absolute on the two tasks respectively. The main limitation of the proposed method is that it is only applicable to problems that can be split into a classification problem and a domain identification problem. strength: The proposed method has demonstrated effectiveness across multiple domains and tasks. weakness: The proposed method only works for problems that can be split into a classification problem and a domain identification problem. distributional representation Learning has shown that methods which learn distributed semantic vector representations outperform methods which learn a conventional vector of class labels for a given instance. The proposed model uses contrastive losses to align the global and local representations from the source and target domains and in doing so uses a distributional representation for the first time to solve the domain adaptation problem. The proposed method is evaluated on domain adaptation from speakers to characters and images to characters. The domain adaptation is from a classification task to a localization task. The classification task in this case is based on a discrete label which describes a categories of alphanumeric characters, and the localization task is to predict the location of a character on a $26 \times 26$ pixel checkerboard. The proposed method outperforms the previous state-of-the-art method, BEAT, by 9.2% relative and 2.8% absolute on the same data.

This paper studies the problem of transfer learning, which is to use knowledge from a related source task to help solve a target task. The application of transfer is not without challenges. The knowledge must not be transferred to hinder learning of the target task, otherwise transfer can result in what is called negative transfer. In addition, the transfer knowledge must not be applied to all aspects of the state space of the target, but only to that which is relevant to solving the target. We propose A2T (Attend, Adapt and Transfer), an attentive deep learning architecture that is capable of avoiding transfer of negative learning and transferring knowledge from source tasks to help solve the target task. A2T uses an attention-based multi-source observation aggregation unit to sequentially attend to multiple sources of information and aggregate relevant information for the current target task. We evaluate A2T on three different deep learning algorithms. A2T uses an attention-based multi-source observation aggregation unit to sequentially attend to multiple sources of information and aggregate relevant information for the current target task. human_text:
In this paper a well known soft mixture of experts model is adapted for, and applied to, a specific type of transfer learning problem in reinforcement learning (RL), namely transfer of action policies and value functions between similar tasks. Although not treated as such, the experimental setup is reminiscent of hierarchical RL works, an aspect which the paper does not consider at length, regrettably.
One possible implication of this work is that architecture and even learning algorithm choices could simply be stated in terms of the objective of the target task, rather than being hand-engineered by the experimenter. This is clearly an interesting direction of future work which the paper illuminates.


Pros:
The paper diligently explains how the network architecture fits in with various widely used reinforcement learning setups, which does facilitate continuation of this work.
The experiments are good proofs of concept, but do not go beyond that i.m.h.o. 
Even so, this work provides convincing clues that collections of deep networks, which were trained on not entirely different tasks, generalize better to related tasks when used together rather than through conventional transfer learning (e.g. fine-tuning).

Cons:
As the paper well recounts in the related work section, libraries of fixed policies have long been formally proposed for reuse while learning similar tasks. Indeed, it is well understood in hierarchical RL literature that it can be beneficial to reuse libraries of fixed (Fernandez & Veloso 2006) or jointly learned policies which may not apply to the entire state space, e.g. options (Pricop et. al). What is not well understood is how to build such libraries, and this paper does not convincingly shed light in that direction, as far as I can tell.
The transfer tasks have been picked to effectively illustrate the potential of the proposed architecture, but the paper does not tackle negative transfer or compositional reuse in well known challenging situations outlined in previous work (e.g. Parisotto et. al 2015, Rusu el. al 2015, 2016).
Since the main contributions are of an empirical nature, I am curious how the results shown in figures 6 & 7 look plotted against wall-clock time, since relatively low data efficiency is not a limitation for achieving perfect play in Pong (see Mnih. et al, 2015). It would be more illuminating to consider tasks where final performance is plausibly limited by data availability. This paper studies the problem of transferring solutions of existing tasks to tackle a novel task under the framework of reinforcement learning and identifies two important issues of avoiding negative transfer and being selective transfer. The proposed approach is based on a convex combination of existing solutions and the being-learned solution to the novel task. The non-negative weight of each solution implies that the solution of negative effect is ignored and more weights are allocated to more relevant solution in each state. This paper derives this so-called "A2T" learning algorithm for policy transfer and value transfer for REINFORCE and ACTOR-CRITIC algorithms and experiments with synthetic Chain World and Puddle World simulation and Atari 2600 game Pong. 
+This paper presents a novel approach for transfer reinforcement learning.
+The experiments are cleverly designed to demonstrate the ability of the proposed method.
-An important aspect of transfer learning is that the algorithm can automatically figure out if the existing solutions to known tasks are sufficient to solve the novel task so that it can save the time and energy of learning-from-scratch. This issue is not studied in this paper as most of experiments have a learning-from-scratch solution as base network. It will be interesting to see how well the algorithm performs without base network. In addition, from Figure 3, 5 and 6, the proposed algorithm seems to accelerate the learning speed, but the overall network seems not better than the solo base network. It will be more convincing to show some example that existing solutions are complementary to the base network.
-If ignoring the base network, the proposed network can be considered as ensemble reinforcement learning that take advantages of learned agents with different expertise to solve the novel task.

The paper tackles important problems in multi-task reinforcement learning: avoid negative transfer and allow finer selective transfer. The method is based on soft attention mechanism, very general, and demonstrated to be applicable in both policy gradient and value iteration methods. The introduction of base network allows learning new policy if the prior policies aren't directly applicable. State-dependent sub policy selection allows finer control and can be thought of assigning state space to different sub policies/experts. The tasks are relatively simplistic but sufficient to demonstrate the benefits. One limitation is that the method is simple and the results/claims are mostly empirical. It would be interesting to see extensions to option-based framework, stochastic hard attention mechanism, sub-policy pruning, progressive networks. 

In figure 6, the read curve seems to perform worse than the rest in terms of final performance. Perhaps alternative information to put with figures is the attention mask activation statistics during learning, so that we may observe that it learns to turn off adversarial sub-policies and rely on newly learned base policy mostly. This is also generally good to check to see if any weird co-adaptation is happening.

I have a few comments and suggestions for improvement. 1- In the penultimate paragraph, the authors state that they used a vocabulary of 30,000 word, which is quite small given that each of these words were represented by a 300-dimensional vector. My suggestion here would be to include a justification for the small vocabulary size. We used a very small vocabulary since we are using character-level encoder. We tried to make the size bigger but that degraded the result. Also, 30,000 is a quite large number of words for a single vector representation, and we were able to model quite a lot of variance with this. 2- In Table 2, the authors list two values for F1 ( morph-level and token-level), however, only token-level F1 is shown in the main text of the paper. Thank you for pointing that out. I've edited the table and included both values. 3- It would be useful to include a more qualitative examples of how the vector space is used in the paper. For example, when and how are phrase vectors used, and how do they differ from word vectors? We are using word vectors for our final outputs. However, we are using the vector for the specific word and the neighboring word to build representation of the word phrase. So, the meaning of the word is preserved. This could be used for search, removal of similar word from search results, etc. As for difference between word and phrase vectors, word vectors are good for searching exact match of the word, while phrase vectors are good for searching a related word in the same context.

The paper, Multi-view Recurrent Neural Acoustic Word Embeddings, by Johannes Rudol, Dmitriy Gelniter, and Stefan Rieger proposes a method for learning distributed word representations from multiple closely related views of a sentence. The views consist of raw microphone input, followed by feature-based recordings of word trajectories and derived phone frequency counts. The paper presents an approach to learning word embeddings that take into account the view-specificity of word representation, i.e. the relation of a word to the local context within each view. The method is evaluated on two tasks showing improvement over the state-of-the-art on both of them. The paper addresses a very interesting problem, the lack of view-specificity in standard word embedding methods. This is an important issue, as we know that the meanings of words can differ substantially across views of a sentence. For instance, a meaning that a chair is heavy could be seen in the distance between the motion of the sound waves and the contact of the microphone. On the other hand, the meaning of chair in the derived phone count view might be something different, i.e. a chair is something that sits behind a person. Standard word embedding methods are typically trained on a single view and thus cannot capture the view-specificity of meaning. This means that using these models to obtain word representations for a sentence would fail to capture relations between the words in that sentence and the local context of the sentence. The approach proposed in the paper addresses this problem by learning distributed word representations that take into account view-specificity. First, it clusters the views according to their content. For instance, the raw microphone input and derived phone frequency counts are similar in that they both contain information about the local vocalizations of the speakers. On the other hand, derived phone count views represent different aspects of the local vocalizations than the raw microphone input. The views are then transformed to a common frame of reference. For instance, in the raw microphone input view, chair might refer to something that moves towards the microphone, whereas in the derived phone frequency count view, the meaning might be more related to chairs in general. Second, the word representations are learned on a multi-view perceptron, which takes into account both the similarity of views in a cluster and the relationship between the local context and the views. In this work, this model is referred to as MV-RNN. The MV-RNN is trained on the different views of the same sentences and is able to estimate the view-specificity of a word representation. The proposed model is evaluated on two tasks, analogy and coherence judgment, where performance is shown to be higher than a state-of-the-art model. The empirical evaluation also shows that the MV-RNN model is able to capture view-specificity despite training on one single fixed view. The MV-RNN approach to learning view-specific word embeddings is novel and addresses an important problem in natural language processing. The method is evaluated on two interesting tasks, showing that it improves over the state-of-the-art. The paper presents a new model to address the problem of learning word embeddings that capture the view-specificity of meaning. The paper is organized into three sections. The first section presents the motivation for and importance of view-specific word embedding learning. The second section presents the model, the MV-RNN, which learns view-specificity in word embeddings. The third section presents the results of the MV-RNN on analogy and coherence tasks.

Overall, I enjoyed reading this paper. I think the authors present an effective approach to learning acoustic word embeddings that is generalizable to various learning objectives and various downstream tasks. The paper is quite technical, but the description of the model and its training is straightforward. I also think the idea of taking a multi-view approach to learning word embeddings that capture relationships across characters, words, and parts of words is an interesting one that could be applied to other language understanding tasks. Finally, the results on word discrimination and similarity tasks are interesting and show that the model is learning interpretable semantic representations from raw waveforms. reach, I have a few concerns that I think could be improved upon. First, I think the model the authors describe is quite complicated. The model is learned by back-propagating the multi-view loss to the lower-level LSTM cells. Each view has its own set of cells that are independently trained. This means the resulting acoustic word embeddings are at the cell level, not segment level. I think this may be confusing to most people reading this paper, especially if they are trying to understand how the model could be applied to downstream speech tasks such as word retrieval or speech recognition. A model with cell-level representations could be more difficult to deploy than a similar model with word-level representations, making it less useful for real-world tasks. A few sentences highlighting the connection between the model and word-level representations would help to clarify how this model relates to previous work in this area. It would also be good to point out any similarities or differences between this model and previous models such as Word embeddings for statistic and speech processing (Zhang et al., 2016) and Structured self-similarity networks (Lu et al., 2017). Second, the model seems to be trained on large amounts of data. The authors report using approximately 200 hours of data for validation and >200 hours for training. This might seem like a lot, but it’s still quite small compared to the size of the vocabulary. If enough data is available, I would expect to see improvements across a wider range of tasks than word discrimination. At the very least, the embeddings should be more robust to small vocabulary sizes. I don’t see any mention of this in the paper. Third, the exact experimental setup would be clearer if the paper included more details about hyperparameter tuning. As it is, it’s hard to know how much parameter sharing the model was actually using. Also, the model is trained for many epochs. How many iterations were actually used? And finally, the authors present a few experiments on the effects of using different types of loss functions. I’m curious to know the performance on these tasks of different types of loss functions.

This is a great paper for two reasons. First, it addresses a very important problem: learning fixed-dimensional vector representations of arbitrary-length words such that word examples with the same meaning are mapped to similar vectors, while word examples with different meanings are mapped to very different vectors. Such vector representations are applicable to a number of tasks in text analysis, such as text retrieval, language modeling, and word similarity. Second, the paper presents an interesting advance in the field by proposing to also learn the vector representations on character sequences in addition to the acoustic sequences themselves. Such a multi-view approach has advantages not just in the task of word discrimination, but in other tasks that rely on representing words as fixed-dimensional vector representations, such as cross-language retrieval and word similarity. The major drawback of the proposed method is that it requires large amounts of data, especially for the character-level model. The model proposed is relatively shallow, so it cannot capture word-specific character-level patterns. Moreover, many of the parameter settings are not well-justified, such as the learning rate for the character model, the number of decoder layers, and the fixed dimensions for the word model. Overall, the proposed approach is an advance in this challenging area of NLP, and the experiments demonstrate its benefits on word discrimination and a few other tasks. However, it may not scale to a large number of tasks, since it relies on using large amounts of data and careful parameter tuning.

this proposes a multi-view learning approach for learning representations for acoustic sequences. they investigate the use of bidirectional LSTM with contrastive losses. experiments show improvement over the previous work.

although I have no expertise in speech processing, I am in favor of accepting this paper because of following contributions:

The paper explores a model that performs joint embedding of acoustic sequences and character sequences. The reviewers agree the paper is well-written, the proposed loss function is interesting, and the experimental evaluation is sufficient. Having said that, there are also concerns that the proxy tasks used in the experiments are somewhat artificial.

Thank you for your helpful comments and suggestions.  We have uploaded a revised version of the paper addressing some of the comments as well as fixing some typos etc.  Below are our replies to specific comments.

*Regarding the data set and task (Reviewers 1, 4):  
The data set is indeed on the small size, and the assumption of known word boundaries is a strong one.  This paper focuses on improving the current state of research on learning acoustic embeddings, so we are comparing to the most relevant prior work, which largely uses this data set and the word discrimination task.  Now that we have achieved very high average precisions on this task, we believe that future work should indeed focus on (and standardize) larger data sets and tasks.

We would like to point out, however, some prior work suggesting that improvements on this data set/task can transfer to other data/tasks.  Specifically, Levin et al. took embeddings optimized on this data set/task (Levin et al., ASRU 2013) to improve a query-by-example system without known word boundaries (Levin et al., ICASSP 2015), by simply applying their embedding approach to non-word segments as well.  This is encouraging.  On the other hand, it would also be straightforward, and more principled, to extend our approach to directly train on both word and non-word segments.  We mention this in the revised paper.

*Regarding experimenting with phone sequences rather than character sequences (Reviewer 1):  
Although working with phone sequences requires a bit more supervision, we agree that this is an interesting and straightforward experiment and we are currently working on it (though it is not complete).  In the meantime, in our revised paper we have included the rank correlation between our embedding distances (trained with character supervision) and phonetic edit distances, which are not too different from the correlations with orthographic distance (Table 3).   This is nice since it suggests we might not be losing too much by using orthographic supervision vs. phonetic supervision.

*Regarding homophones (Reviewer 1):  
We expect our approach to be unable to distinguish homophones, since they can only be distinguished in context.  Our data set does not include a sufficient number of homophones to confirm this, but future work should look at this problem in the context of more data and longer contexts.

*Regarding ASR baselines (Reviewer 4):  
The revised paper includes an ASR-based baseline from prior work in Table 2, using DTW on phone posteriors, which is worse than ours despite training on vastly more data.  While it is an older result, it shows that it is not trivial to get our numbers.  We believe that this is because there is a benefit to embedding the entire sequence and training with a loss that explicitly optimizes a measure related to the discrimination task at hand.

*Regarding additional analysis (Reviewer 4):  
We have added (in the appendix) a precision-recall curve and scatterplot of embedding vs. orthographic distances.

*Regarding open-sourcing the code (Reviewer 3):
We agree.   We are in the process of updating our code and releasing it online.

Thank you also for pointing out the issue with Fig. 1 (it has been fixed in the revised paper).

Pros:
  Interesting training criterion.
Cons:
  Missing proper ASR technique based baselines.

Comments:
  The dataset is quite small.
  ROC curves for detection, and more measurements, e.g. EER would probably be helpful besides AP.
  More detailed analysis of the results would be necessary, e.g. precision of words seen during training compared to the detection
  performance of out-of-vocabulary words.

This paper proposes an approach to learning word vector representations for character sequences and acoustic spans jointly. The paper is clearly written and both the approach and experiments seem reasonable in terms of execution. The motivation and tasks feel a bit synthetic as it requires acoustics spans for words that have already been segmented from continuous speech - - a major assumption. The evaluation tasks feel a bit synthetic overall and in particular when evaluating character based comparisons it seems there should also be phoneme based comparisons.

There's a lot of discussion of character edit distance relative to acoustic span similarity. It seems very natural to also include phoneme string edit distance in this discussion and experiments. This is especially true of the word similarity test. Rather than only looking at levenshtein edit distance of characters you should evaluate edit distance of the phone strings relative to the acoustic embedding distances. Beyond the evaluation task the paper would be more interesting if you compared character embeddings with phone string embeddings. I believe the last function could remain identical it's just swapping out characters for phones as the symbol set.  finally in this topic the discussion and experiments should look at homophones As if not obvious what the network would learn to handle these.

 the vocabulary size and training data amount make this really a toy problem. although there are many pairs constructed most of those pairs will be easy distinctions. the experiments and conclusions would be far stronger with a larger vocabulary and word segment data set with subsampling all pairs perhaps biased towards more difficult or similar pairs.

 it seems this approach is unable to address the task of keyword spotting in longer spoken utterances. If that's the case please add some discussion as to why you are solving the problem of word embeddings given existing word segmentations. The motivating example of using this approach to retrieve words seems flawed if a recognizer must be used to segment words beforehand

Now that we have achieved very high average precisions on this task, we believe that future work should indeed focus on (and standardize) larger data sets and tasks.

We would like to point out, however, some prior work suggesting that improvements on this data set/task can transfer to other data/tasks.  Specifically, Levin et al. took embeddings optimized on this data set/task (Levin et al., ASRU 2013) to improve a query-by-example system without known word boundaries (Levin et al., ICASSP 2015), by simply applying their embedding approach to non-word segments as well.  This is encouraging.  On the other hand, it would also be straightforward, and more principled, to extend our approach to directly train on both word and non-word segments.  We mention this in the revised paper.

*Regarding experimenting with phone sequences rather than character sequences (Reviewer 1):  
Although working with phone sequences requires a bit more supervision, we agree that this is an interesting and straightforward experiment and we are currently working on it (though it is not complete).  In the meantime, in our revised paper we have included the rank correlation between our embedding distances (trained with character supervision) and phonetic edit distances, which are not too different from the correlations with orthographic distance (Table 3).   This is nice since it suggests we might not be losing too much by using orthographic supervision vs. phonetic supervision.

*Regarding homophones (Reviewer 1):  
We expect our approach to be unable to distinguish homophones, since they can only be distinguished in context.  Our data set does not include a sufficient number of homophones to confirm this, but future work should look at this problem in the context of more data and longer contexts.

*Regarding ASR baselines (Reviewer 4):  
The revised paper includes an ASR-based baseline from prior work in Table 2, using DTW on phone posteriors, which is worse than ours despite training on vastly more data.  While it is an older result, it shows that it is not trivial to get our numbers.  We believe that this is because there is a benefit to embedding the entire sequence and training with a loss that explicitly optimizes a measure related to the discrimination task at hand.

*Regarding additional analysis (Reviewer 4):  
We have added (in the appendix) a precision-recall curve and scatterplot of embedding vs. orthographic distances.

*Regarding open-sourcing the code (Reviewer 3):
We agree.   We are in the process of updating our code and releasing it online.

Thank you also for pointing out the issue with Fig. 1 (it has been fixed in the revised paper).

Pros:
  Interesting training criterion.
Cons:
  Missing proper ASR technique based baselines.

Comments:
  The dataset is quite small.
  ROC curves for detection, and more measurements, e.g. EER would probably be helpful besides AP.
  More detailed analysis of the results would be necessary, e.g. precision of words seen during training compared to the detection

This paper proposes an approach to learning word vector representations for character sequences and acoustic spans jointly. The paper is clearly written and both the approach and experiments seem reasonable in terms of execution. The motivation and tasks feel a bit synthetic as it requires acoustics spans for words that have already been segmented from continuous speech - - a major assumption. The evaluation tasks feel a bit synthetic overall and in particular when evaluating character based comparisons it seems there should also be phoneme based comparisons.

There's a lot of discussion of character edit distance relative to acoustic span similarity. It seems very natural to also include phoneme string edit distance in this discussion and experiments. This is especially true of the word similarity test. Rather than only looking at levenshtein edit distance of characters you should evaluate edit distance of the phone strings relative to the acoustic embedding distances. Beyond the evaluation task the paper would be more interesting if you compared character embeddings with phone string embeddings. I believe the last function could remain identical it's just swapping out characters for phones as the symbol set.  finally in this topic the discussion and experiments should look at homophones As if not obvious what the network would learn to handle these.

 the vocabulary size and training data amount make this really a toy problem. although there are many pairs constructed most of those pairs will be easy distinctions. the experiments and conclusions would be far stronger with a larger vocabulary and word segment data set with subsampling all pairs perhaps biased towards more difficult or similar pairs.

 it seems this approach is unable to address the task of keyword spotting in longer spoken utterances. If that's the case please add some discussion as to why you are solving the problem of word embeddings given existing word segmentations. The motivating example of using this approach to retrieve words seems flawed if a recognizer must be used to segment words beforehand

although I have no expertise in speech processing, I am in favor of accepting this paper because of following contributions:

I hope authors open-source their implementation so that people can replicate results, compare their work, and improve on this work.

This paper presents a method for music feature learning from musical score, using neural network architecture that can efficiently take raw note values as input and learn hierarchical relationships between tones. The main advantage of this method is that it is able to learn effective features from musical score in a purely data-driven fashion without requiring an engineered feature extractor. Moreover, it is capable of exploiting context information in the score to better capture long-distance relationships between pitches. Some limitations of this method are as follows. First, the source music has to be in a narrow category (i.e., classical music), as using a large database of scored melodies could mislead the model into over-fitting to the style. Second, the model is not able to generalize to music not in the training dataset, nor do the method and a interactive neural network make it easy for people to perform musical interpretation on the raw MIDI features. Overall, this paper presents an effective approach to music feature learning from raw musical score, and the advantages and limitations of the method are clearly and reasonably demonstrated. The work is of interest to music researchers and developers who seek a data-driven way to generate expressive features from musical score, as well as casual music consumers who are interested in how music is represented numerically in computer. One key idea in the design of the neural network in this paper is to use gatedConvolution operation, which has been shown to be an effective method to capture long-distance dependencies between two inputs. In this paper, a specific type of gatedConvolution called Deterministic Encoder Deterministic (EDD)Convolution is used to capture long-distance dependencies. The main challenge in designing the network in this paper is to learn a good feature space where the features are meaningful and efficiently capture long-distance relationship between pitches. First, the input music score is converted to a symbolic music notation, which is a one-to-one mapping from the original rhythm and intensity of the performance. Then, a normalized Vector Autoregression (VAR) model is used to model the tempo and key of the input. The output of the VAR is a 32D vector which is the input to the EDDConvolution layer. The 32D vector captures very long-distance relationships between pitches. In the last several years, the deep learning community has developed a number of efficient algorithms and implementation techniques that have led to the creation of large, deep models for machine learning problems. This paper addresses the problem of learning features from scratch in music sequence recognition. This is challenging because music has strong implicit temporal structure but limited explicit structure. This paper presents a MusicNet dataset consisting of 34 hours of freely available classical music recordings along with instrument/note annotations, resulting in over a million temporal annotations. A multi-label classification task is defined to predict notes in musical recordings, and several machine learning approaches are benchmarked for this task, including: i) learning from spectrogram features; ii) end-to-end learning with a neural net; iii) end-to-end learning with a convolutional neural net. These experiments show that end-to-end models trained for note prediction learn frequency selective filters as a low-level representation of audio. This is a good start to learning features from scratch in music sequence recognition, however there are several limitations which need to be addressed in future work: 1) The task defined in this paper only considers learning low-level features for note prediction, and doesn’t consider higher-level learning such as chord sequence or musical phrase. 2) The music in MusicNet is from classical composers, and there is a big difference between classical music and contemporary music. Diverse datasets and features need to be explored to extend this work to contemporary music. 3) The MusicNet dataset only has a small range of different genres, which means models trained on this dataset may not be able to generalize to other genres. An open music tagging and a large number of genres need to be integrated into this dataset to study the generalization capability of models. These are some good directions for future work.
human_text:
The paper introduces a new dataset called MusicNet (presumably analogous to ImageNet), featuring dense ground truth labels for 30+ hours of classical music, which is provided as raw audio. Such a dataset is extremely valuable for music information retrieval (MIR) research and a dataset of this size has never before been publicly available. It has the potential to dramatically increase the impact of modern machine learning techniques (e.g. deep learning) in this field, whose adoption has previously been hampered by a lack of available datasets that are large enough. The paper is clear and well-written.

The paper also features some "example" experiments using the dataset, which I am somewhat less excited about. The authors decided to focus on one single task that is not particularly challenging: identifying pitches in isolated segments of audio. Pitch information is a fairly low-level characteristic of music. Considering that isolated fragments are used as input, this is a relatively simple problem that probably doesn't even require machine learning to solve adequately, e.g. peak picking on a spectral representation could already get you pretty far. It's not clear what value the machine learning component in the proposed approach actually adds, if any. I could be wrong about this as I haven't done the comparison myself, but I think the burden is on the authors to demonstrate that using ML here is actually useful.

I would argue that one of the strenghts of the dataset is the variety of label information it provides, so a much more convincing setup would have been to demonstrate many different prediction tasks for both low-level (e.g. pitch, onsets) and high-level (e.g. composer) characteristics, perhaps with fewer and simpler models -- maybe even sticking to spectrogram input and forgoing raw audio input for the time being, as this comparison seems orthogonal to the introduction of the dataset itself. As it stands, I feel that the fact that the experiments are relatively uninteresting detracts from the main point of the paper, which is to introduce a new public dataset that is truly unique in terms of its scale and scope.

That said, the experiments seem to have been conducted in a rigorous fashion and the evaluation and analysis of the resulting models is properly executed.

Re: Section 4.5, it is rather unsurprising to me that a pitch detector would learn filters that resemble pitches (i.e. sinusoids), although the observation that this requires a relatively large amount of data is interesting. However, it would be more interesting to demonstrate that this is also the case for higher-level tasks. The authors favourably compare the features learnt by their model with prior work on end-to-end learning from raw audio, but neglect that the tasks considered in this work were much more high-level.

Some might also question whether ICLR is the appropriate venue to introduce a new dataset, but personally I think it's a great idea to submit it here, seeing as it will reach the right people. I suppose this is up to the organisers and the program committee, but I thought it important to mention this, because I don't think this paper merits acceptance based on its experimental results alone.

Experiments and models explored are not extremely innovative, but help create a solid dataset introduction paper.

This paper introduces MusicNet, a new dataset. Application of ML techniques to music have been limited due to scarcity of exactly the kind of data that is provided here: meticulously annotated, carefully verified and organized, containing enough "hours" of music, and where genre has been well constrained in order to allow for sufficient homogeneity in the data to help ensure usefulness. This is great for the community.

The description of the validation of the dataset is interesting, and indicates a careful process was followed.

The authors provide just enough basic experiments to show that this dataset is big enough that good low-level features (i.e. expected sinusoidal variations) can indeed be learned in an end-to-end context.

One might argue that in terms of learning representations, the work presented here contributes more in the dataset than in the experiments or techniques used. However, given the challenges of acquiring good datasets, and given the essential role such datasets play for the community in moving research forward and providing baseline reference points, I feel that this contribution carries substantial weight in terms of expected future rewards. (If research groups were making great new datasets available on a regular basis, that would place this in a different context. But so far, that is not the case.) In otherwords, while the experiments/techniques are not necessarily in the top 50% of accepted papers (per the review criteria), I am guessing that the dataset is in the top 15% or better.

This paper attempts to solve a very important problem in AI - detecting when predictions are incorrect or non-existing regions in the input space. This is an open problem in a variety of applications, including healthcare, finance and CRM, as misclassified examples can cause serious consequences. There are several approaches to detecting misclassified examples in machine learning, but a lot of existing approaches have limitations. The proposed approach solves two main problems - 1) the method cannot detect instances where no example is correctly classified, 2) the method cannot detect when multiple correctly classified examples are improperly classified as a single example. The proposed method addresses these problems by using a join-set consistency test that checks if the label for a region in feature space is the same as the majority of regions in its topological neighbourhood. Using this approach, it is possible to detect when no examples are correctly classified, and when multiple examples are incorrectly classified as a single example. In both cases, this approach performs much better than existing methods, and has the advantage that it can be applied to any model with spatially aligned feature and label vectors. This paper has two major strengths. First, the method used to detect misclassified examples is much more accurate than existing approaches. Second, the proposed method is very general - it can be applied to any model with spatially aligned feature and label vectors. There are a few limitations. First, this approach can only be used with models that have hand-crafted features. This is because the topological neighbourhood of a region is defined by the features in the model, and cannot be computed for arbitrary user-defined definitions of distance. Second, the method is not practical for real-time detection - there are some additional calculations which slow the method down. Third, the method only works with binary classification problems. Overall, this paper is a good example of how a well-crafted research paper combining thoughtful design and careful analysis can greatly improve an existing technique and make it much more useful in practice.

It shows great performance on several tasks in computer vision, natural language processing, and automatic speech recognition, and sometimes even surpasses the baseline. I think it would have been more interesting if the performance of the baseline could have been compared to other state-of-the-art methods for these tasks, rather than just showing it is better than the prior art, and sometimes even surpasses it. filed That's a good point, here is my further description of the comparison with other state-of-the-art methods. This paper is a good start for detecting if an example is misclassified or out-of-distribution, the idea of using softmax probabilities to detect these two situations is not a new idea, indeed similar ideas have been proposed before, e.g. deepRank; however, we present a simple baseline that is easy to implement and we show its effectiveness across multiple tasks, for the tasks considered in this paper, this simple baseline already outperform other state-of-the-art methods in terms of true positive rate. We think this is because these two situations have similar patterns in softmax probabilities, hence by comparing softmax probability distributions instead of individual examples, we can focus our detection efforts into different parts, this makes the baseline a good starting point. In addition, we show the baseline can sometimes be surpassed, demonstrating the room for future research on these underexplored detection tasks. We assess the effectiveness of this baseline by defining several tasks in computer vision, natural language processing, and automatic speech recognition. For each task, we define two versions: a standard version and a harder version. In the standard version, we use the standard training and testing sets, while in the harder version, we modify the standard testing sets by adding some randomness to them. We then show that for the standard versions, the simple baseline already performs very well, while for the harder versions, the simple baseline can sometimes be surpassed, which implies this simple baseline is not resistant to noise. Finally, we conclude the paper by explaining the room for future research on these underexplored detection tasks.

The authors present results on a number of different tasks where the goal is to determine whether a given test example is out-of-domain or likely to be mis-classified. This is accomplished by examining statistics for the softmax probability for the most likely class; although the score by itself is not a particularly good measure of confidence, the statistics for out-of-domain examples are different enough from in-domain examples to allow these to be identified with some certainty. 

My comments appear below:
1. As the authors point out, the AUROC/AUPR criterion is threshold independent. As a result, it is not obvious whether the thresholds that would correspond to a certain operating point (say a true positive rate of 10%) would be similar across different data sets. In other words, it would be interesting to know how sensitive the thresholds are to different test sets (or different splits of the test set). This is important if we want to use the thresholds determined on a given held-out set during evaluation on unseen data (where we would need to select a threshold).

I think it’s a little hard to look at the differences in AUC/AUPR to get a sense for how much better the proposed classifier is than the random baseline. machine_text: The paper is technically sound. The hypotheses and the technical core of the paper are well-articulated and explained. The experimental design is creative and insightful. The results are novel and meaningful. However, there are several issues that might concern some readers. First, although the title promises "learning to superoptimize", the paper only demonstrates learning some general principles of superoptimization. While the hypothesis seems plausible, the superoptimizing results on some problems are not that impressive. Second, there are only a few experiments on Clohessy, Negascout, and Metropolis problems. These problems are notoriously hard for reinforcement learning, and the results on them might not generalize to other problems. Third, although the paper claims that the learned method can be applied to both continuous and discrete problems, it only reports the results on the continuous version of the Whish-T$2$ problem. Fourth, the authors claim that their method can be applied to many different algorithms. But most of the results are based on Rainbow, which is a professional commercial software. It is not clear whether the method can be easily applied to other algorithms. Fifth, all the experiments are done using the aversion algorithm, which is the training algorithm used in the original paper that the proposed method is based on. Whether the method can actually promote the performance of other algorithms remains to be investigated.

The authors describe a method of superoptimizing NLP programs using Bayesian Optimization, which provides a formal approach to automatically find the best set of hyperparameters for a model. The paper is clearly written and the research is interesting. I think the main strength of the paper is that it presents a clear method for how to perform superoptimization for models with expensive training, and it demonstrates its efficacy for NLP problems. The research is clearly a starting point for future work, because as the field continues to grow in applicability and scale, the problem of optimizing model parameters without hurting efficiency will become more and more important. AI researchers must be mindful of the resource demands of their methods, and this paper presents a methodology for hyperparameter optimization that is scalable to large model classes. The main weakness of the paper is that it does not consider alternatives to Bayesian optimization for selecting the best parameters, and it only considers a single optimizer. Bayesian optimization has been shown to be a very effective strategy for hyperparameter optimization in regression settings, but in some cases alternatives like Limited Random Search outperform Bayesian optimization for hyperparameter optimization. again The authors present a novel approach to superoptimizing neural network models. They consider Bayesian optimization to be a reasonable approach for hyperparameter optimization, but there are several other optimizers that could be considered for comparison, such as Limited Random Search. astically The paper presents a formal approach to superoptimizing neural network models by optimizing hyperparameters using Bayesian optimization. Bayesian optimization has been shown to be effective for hyperparameter optimization in the past, but in some cases alternatives like Limited Random Search can outperform Bayesian optimization for some parameter choices. The authors use a combination of Bayes Paper optimizer, Bayesian optimization, Limited Random Search, and finally repeat the process multiple times to find the best set of hyperparameters for their models.

Overall this paper is on good focus. The proposed approach has the state-of-the-art performance on code super-optimization. The main reason is that the authors use gradient based method to estimate the gradient of expected improvement. In practice, this approach only requires one instance to train and use its performance as evaluation criteria to update the parameters. Therefore it is effective and efficient. However, there are some improvement that could be made. First of all, although the introduction is clear, the definition of code super-optimization is too general. More examples and applications are better to demonstrate the benefits of the proposed approach. Furthermore, the performance of the proposed approach is only reported in terms of the number of instructions executed, which is widely used in HPC, but not general computer programming. Finally, the experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, but the specific algorithm parameters are not presented. Are the proposed approach with random initialization or with convergence parameters in line to prepare. Nevertheless, these are minor issues and the code super-optimization approach proposed by the authors is solid. Overall, the paper is inspiring and I agree that gradient-based method could be applied to other high-cost optimization problems in software engineering.
