machine_text: Overall this is an excellent paper, which should be of interest to a broad audience in both the machine learning and the data science communities. The topic of the paper is also of great interest to me, and I have learned a lot by reading this paper. The abstract describes the key takeaways of the paper quite well. The paper presents a general model for interpreting the behavior of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs). The model is based on the corresponding DNNs’ parameter sensitivities with respect to the input. The resulting criteria for performance evaluation can be divided into three categories: separation, consistency, and efficiency. For each category, the paper proposes a performance model that is based on the corresponding DNNs’ parameter sensitivities. The paper also presents three applications of the model to benchmark DNNs on three tasks: object classification on the LSUN dataset, character recognition on the Universal Dataset, and question answering over Books & movies dataset. The results are presented in the form of scatter plots that show the predicted versus the actual performance scores. The paper includes several useful discussion points about the model and its applications. The paper nicely lays out the problem and the approach. My only comment is that the section “Neuron” is too long. It would be useful to present these results in tabular format. Here are some other comments: The consistency model is particularly useful for examining neural nets trained for multiple tasks. The separation and efficiency models also give some useful insights into how the models work, and they may be useful to experts in different areas of machine learning.

This paper presents a model for running deep neural networks on very large datasets made up of records of many features. The model is called Paleocaching and is based on the idea of cross-validation prediction latency hiding by asynchronous updating and aggregation of result curently used in GPU compute clusters. The key insight is that the training process resembles a cache fill, where the target labels for each observation are analogous to an inputbuffer in a CPU cache. When a batch of data is fetched from the training set by the model, this input buffer is filled with the new values. The filling of the buffer is asynchronous, so the latency of the network training is hidden by dividing up the input into chunks and filling in bits of the buffer as they become available. The fill rate on each chunk can be adjusted to find the optimal tradeoff between latency and wasted fill from overfilling one chunk and underfilling others. The final result is a very fast model with high compression on the training dataset. This model has many advantages over other model types in terms of memory and compute efficiency. However, it does require that the model being trained is a neural network with a latent layer that fills the input buffer. This model would be very useful in a setting where you have a huge training dataset and need to use machine learning models to analyze it, but you cannot fit the model into memory on a single machine. In such cases, you could use Paleocaching to partition the training dataset across multiple machines, decreasing the effective size of the training dataset without necessitating increases in memory or compute on each machine. The model also assumes that enough RAM is available to hold the input data in memory while the network is training. If this is not the case, the model does not provide any guidance on how to adjust the model parameters or data organization. This model also has very strong independence assumptions. For example, if you want to use it to train a model for neural network collaborative filtering, you should ensure that the training set is sufficiently large and diverse (i.e. it represents all possible combinations of users and items) and then split it into chunks that do not share any users or items. Finally, the algorithm is founded on the approximation that each input buffer takes on integral values. This assumption limits the types of models that can be applied to this setting, but because the Fill rate is tunable, this might be a way to get very good results with a wider range of models. Overall, this is a very exciting paper, and I think it has the potential to have a big impact on the world of large-scale machine learning. The main problem with this model is that it is not universally applicable. For example, it relies on the existence of a latent layer that fills an input buffer, and the method of dividing the input into chunks that asynchronously fill that buffer. Many models cannot fit these requirements, and even if they can, they cannot be optimized in the same way that a neural network can. In addition, the independence assumptions in the model also limit its applicability. For example, if the model is trained on data that is partitioned into users and items, then the model should not be able to predict items for users or users for items. The method cannot handle partial input dependencies. Finally, a large class of models are excluded by the requirement of a fillable input buffer. For example, recurrent neural networks and denoising autoencoders both have hidden states that must be initialized before the model can train, and these are not filled by the input buffer. Despite these limitations, I think that this paper is important because it identifies a very wide setting for this kind of model, and it identifies a very strong framework that can be used to optimize it. The main strength of this paper is that it presents a very strong optimization framework for a model that has not been widely used in practice. The results that can be obtained by this method are very good for the range of problems that this model can be applied to, and the algorithmic simplicity of the model makes it very attractive to practitioners. This paper is technically sound. It highlights well the strengths and weaknesses of the proposed simplified model.

In terms of impact, its novelty is limited, in the sense that the authors did seemingly the right thing and obtained the expected outcomes. The idea of modeling deep learning computation is not in itself particularly novel. As a companion paper to an open source release of the model, it would meet my bar of acceptance in the same vein as a paper describing a novel dataset, which might not provide groundbreaking insights, yet be generally useful to the community.

In the absence of released code, even if the authors promise to release it soon, I am more ambivalent, since that's where all the value lies. It would also be a different story if the authors had been able to use this framework to make novel architectural decisions that improved training scalability in some way, and incorporated such new insights in the paper.

UPDATED: code is now available. Revised review accordingly.

The reviewers were consistent in their praise of the paper. They asked for newer architectures, e.g. ResNet, DenseNet. The authors released an update with a Caffe converter which provides access to a wide range of CNNs and residual networks (ResNet-50 and DenseNet examples are provided). This seems like an incredibly useful tool and very glad it is open source. Paper is a clear accept.

We thank all the reviewers for reading and commenting on the paper!

This paper introduces an analytical performance model to estimate the training and evaluation time of a given network for different software, hardware and communication strategies. 
The paper is very clear.  The authors included many freedoms in the variables while calculating the run-time of a network such as the number of workers, bandwidth, platform, and parallelization strategy. Their results are consistent with the reported results from literature.
Furthermore, their code is open-source and the live demo is looking good. 
The authors mentioned in their comment that they will allow users to upload customized networks and model splits in the coming releases of the interface, then the tool can become very useful.
It would be interesting to see some newer network architectures with skip connections such as ResNet, and DenseNet.

In PALEO the authors propose a simple model of execution of deep neural networks. It turns out that even this simple model allows to quite accurately predict the computation time for image recognition networks both in single-machine and distributed settings.

The ability to predict network running time is very useful, and the paper shows that even a simple model does it reasonably, which is a strength. But the tests are only performed on a few networks of very similar type (AlexNet, Inception, NiN) and only in a few settings. Much broader experiments, including a variety of models (RNNs, fully connected, adversarial, etc.) in a variety of settings (different batch sizes, layer sizes, node placement on devices, etc.) would probably reveal weaknesses of the proposed very simplified model. This is why this reviewer considers this paper borderline -- it's a first step, but a very basic one and without sufficiently large experimental underpinning.

Please see our edited paragraph below: Some background on the Atari domain and the discrete action space, which is a mapping from states to actions, is necessary to understand the PGQL algorithm. Advantage functions and Q-learning are closely related. In particular, using theBellman equation, it can be shown that Q-learning estimates the exact Q function (i.e., the optimal Q function) given sufficient time and function approximation. One interpretation of this is that Q-learning "q-fits the reward" by minimizing the Bellman error. From an optimization perspective, Q-learning has a unique global optimal solution that can be found using an off-policy learning algorithm. However, a major challenge in practice is that Q-learning suffers from high sample complexity and computation cost, and is difficult to scale to larger problems. Policy gradient methods (like PGQL) rely on an effective approximation of the action-value function, referred to as the advantage function. The advantage function, along with a suitable exploration policy and discount factor, allows policy gradient methods to efficiently converge to a local minimum of the expected sum of future rewards. To train the policy, it is important to have a good baseline from which to contrast the learned behavior. The main challenge with policy gradient methods is that it is hard to obtain a good baseline because it requires a large amount of samples. PGQL has a good stability property, which means that the difference between the actual and the expected total rewards converges to zero with time. This is due to the use of the advantage function in place of the exact Q function. We have also included a paragraph to discuss the differences between Q-learning, advantage function, and policy iteration (or policy evaluation).

Policy gradient is an efficient technique for improving a policy in a reinforcement learning setting. However, vanilla online variants are on-policy only and not able to take advantage of off-policy data. In this paper we describe a new technique that combines policy gradient and Q-learning, drawing experience from a replay buffer. This is motivated by making a connection between the fixed points of the regularized policy gradient algorithm and the Q-values. This connection allows us to estimate the Q-values from the action preferences of the policy, to which we apply Q-learning updates. We refer to the new technique as ‘PGQL’, for policy gradient and Q-learning. We also establish an equivalency between action-value fitting techniques and actor-critic algorithms, showing that regularized policy gradient techniques can be interpreted as advantage function learning algorithms. We conclude with some numerical examples that demonstrate improved data efficiency and stability of PGQL. In particular, we tested PGQL on the full suite of Atari games and achieved performance exceeding that of both asynchronous advantage actor-critic (A3C) and Q-learning. The regularized policy gradient algorithm (also known as normalized iterativeppo-gradient, or NIPG), was proposed in @bu2008convergence and later on shown to have fixed points that coincide with Q-values in @liu2013connecting. The connection was made use of in @wang2016training to adapt the NIGP algorithm to the continuous action setting. We refer to @wang2016training’s method as ‘PG’. This paper improves upon the work of @wang2016training in several ways. First, they focus on the tabular case whereas we provide an analysis for the off-policy case; most importantly, they use on-policy updates whereas we use off-policy data for the Q-learning step. This gives rise to the new name ‘PGQL’. We establish that PGQL has the same generalization properties as A3C, namely, it converges to a local minimum of the expected loss. Empirically, we find that in addition to outperforming A3C and NIGP on the Atari domain, PGQL outperforms both A3C and NIGP on the MuJoCo continuous action domains.’’

This paper shows how policy gradient and Q-Learning may be combined together, improving learning as demonstrated in particular in the Atari Learning Environment. The core idea is to note that entropy-regularized policy gradient leads to a Boltzmann policy based on Q values, thus linking pi & Q together and allowing both policy gradient and Q-Learning updates to be applied.

I think this is a very interesting paper, not just for its results and the proposed algorithm (dubbed PGQ), but mostly because of the links it draws between several techniques, which I found quite insightful.

That being said, I also believe it could have done a better job at clearly exposing these links: I found it somewhat difficult to follow, and it took me a while to wrap my head around it, even though the underlying concepts are not that complex. In particular:
- The notation \tilde{Q}^pi is introduced in a way that is not very clear, as "an estimate of the Q-values" while eq. 5 is an exact equality (no estimation)
- It is not clear to me what section 3.2 is bringing exactly, I wonder if it could just be removed to expand some other sections with more explanations.
- The links to dueling networks (Wang et al, 2016) are in my opinion not explicit and detailed enough (in 3.3 & 4.1): as far as I can tell the proposed architecture ends up being very similar to such networks and thus it would be worth telling more about it (also in experiments my understanding is that the "variant of asynchronous deep Q-learning" being used is essentially such a dueling network, but it is not clearly stated). I also believe it should be mentioned that PGQ can also be seen as combining Q-Learning with n-step expected Sarsa using a dueling network: this kind of example helps better understand the links between methods
- Overall I wish section 3.3 was clearer, as it draws some very interesting links, but it is hard to see where this is all going when reading the paper for the first time. One confusing point is w.r.t. to the relationship with section 3.2, that assumes a critic outputting Q values while in 3.3 the critic outputs V. The "mu" distribution also comes somewhat out of nowhere.

I hope the authors can try and improve the readability of the paper in a final version, as well as clarify the points raised in pre-review questions (in particular related to experimental details, the derivation of eq. 4, and the issue of the discounted distribution of states).

Minor remarks:
- The function r(s, a) used in the Bellman equation in section 2 is not formally defined. It looks a bit weird because the expectation is on s' and b' but r(s, a) does not depend on them (so either it should be moved out of the expectation, or the expectation should also be over the reward, depending on how r is defined)
- The definition of the Boltzmann policy at end of 2.1 is a bit confusing since there is a sum over "a" of a quantity that does not depend (clearly) on "a"
- I believe 4.3 is for the tabular case but this is not clearly stated
- Any idea why in Fig. 1 the 3 algorithms do not all converge to the same policy? In such a simple toy setting I would expect it to be the case.

- "we refer to the classic text Sutton & Barto (1998)" => missing "by"?

- "the agent generates experience from interacting the environment" => with the environment
- in eq. 12 (first line) there is a comma to remove near the end, just before the dlog pi
- "allowing us the spread the influence of a reward" => to spread
- "in the off-policy case tabular case" => remove the first case
- "The green line is Q-learning where at the step an update is performed" => at each step
- In Fig. 2 it says A2C instead of A3C

Culture & Song of Real NVP Breathing Life into a Dead Language: Neural Architecture for Density Estimation Ofer Mell; Sebastian Ruder; Philipp Matzke; Kalyanmoy Deb; Lorenzo Soria; Maria Buiatti; Carsten Cerny Neural architecture for density estimation. One problem with neural nets is that they often “learn” to copy instead of truly learning the mapping from input to output. If this happens in the context of source code generation, this could mean that the software will only reproduce the exact input that resulted in the correct output during training. In the worst case, this could result in invalid, unstable or even malicious code. In this paper, we present a neural architecture that addresses this issue by using a variation-generator to add stochasticity to the input to the generator. This can also be viewed as a form of importance sampling that ensures that the density ratios computed by the net are well-behaved. This work builds on the RealNVP approach by @DBLP:journals/corr/abs-1808-10507 which uses a mixture of isomorphic models to approximate the true posterior distribution.

The paper Density estimation using Real NVP implements a model called Real NVP that uses neural nets to estimate probability densities. The density estimates can be used in a downstream classification task such as density-based clustering. The authors apply the Real NVP model to kernel density estimates computed from observed data, showing state of the art density estimates on several benchmark datasets. The main advantages of the Real NVP framework are the scalable density estimates and the end-to-end learning for the models. The main limitation of the Real NVP framework is that it learns the density only for a particular kernel. However, in many applications it is important to choose the kernel correctly. Another limitation is that the Real NVP model can not be applied to data with multiple dimensions, only to 2D data. In my opinion the Real NVP model offers a novel and interesting approach to the problem of kernel density estimation. I also like the application to density-based clustering, as this is an application that has not been seriously considered by previous authors. I have read the paper "Unsupervised Learning of Probabilistic Models" by Lipton et.al and have some concerns about its main content. As the paper focuses on the design of a new generative model using Real NVP, some related work could be discussed to put the work in perspective. In particular, an overview of invertible generative models could be useful to easily sample from the model and to avoid any confusion in the following parts of the paper. Some of the claims in the paper are not clear. For instance, in the first paragraph of the paper, it says that the log-likelihood is computed exactly, but this is not clearly stated anywhere in the paper. In fact, it is not even clear that the authors compute the true log-likelihood, since several assertions in the paper (e.g. exact latent variable evaluation, exact sampling) are not clearly proven. Furthermore, it would be useful to have an intuition on what kind of latent representations the model might output and how they could be qualitatively compared with those of other models. In summary, the paper has some unclear parts that require further clarification to evaluate the main claim of the paper, namely that the model can exactly compute the log-likelihood. However, it looks like the model might have some nice properties that could potentially be very useful in practice. I think that, even though it has some unclear aspects, the main idea of the model is worth exploring and it could be potentially very useful in practice. I, thus, propose to interpret the Real NVP as an interesting and potentially very useful architecture that, at the same time, might require further investigation to fully understand how it works. I really liked the idea of Real NVP and think it has potential. I see at least two interesting directions in which it could be further explored: the use of Real NVP in combination with other models and the understanding of Real NVP in itself. The use of Real NVP in combination with other models could be very interesting. Real NVP could be a very powerful prior that facilitates the training of other models. For example, by considering the Real NVP as a special kind of de-facto independence prior, one could interpret it as regularizing other models against non-invertible layers. The two components of the model, the non-volume preserving transformations and the Gaussian approximation, might also be parallelizable which could, in itself, be another appealing direction. The understanding of Real NVP in itself could also be interesting. For example, considering the Real NVP as a reparameterization or a reinterpretation of the variables of the model could shed new light on its working. There is definitely potential in continuing to explore Real NVP in itself and its applications.

This is an interesting paper which solves an important problem in unsupervised learning, namely the design of models with tractable learning, sampling, inference and evaluation. human_text:
Building on earlier work on a model called NICE, this paper presents an approach to constructing deep feed-forward generative models. The model is evaluated on several datasets. While it does not achieve state-of-the-art performance, it advances an interesting class of models. The paper is mostly well written and clear.

Given that inference and generation are both efficient and exact, and given that this represents a main advantage over other models, it would be great if the authors could provide some motivating example applications where this is needed/would be useful.

The authors claim that “unlike both variational autoencoders and GANs, our technique is able to learn a semantically meaningful latent space which is as high dimensional as the input space.” Where is the evidence for this claim? I didn’t see any analysis of the semantic meaningfulness of the latent space learned by real NVP. Stronger evidence that the learned representations are actually useful for downstream tasks would be nice.

I still think the author’s intuitions around the “fixed reconstruction cost of L2” are very vague. The factorial Gaussian assumption itself does not limit the generative model, it merely smoothes an otherwise arbitrary distribution, and to a degree which can be arbitrarily small, p(x) = \int p(z) N(x | f(z), \sigma^2) dz. How a lose lower bound plays into this is not clear from the paper.

This paper clearly lays out the recipe for a family of invertible density models, explores a few extensions, and demonstrates the overall power of the approach. The work is building closely on previous approaches, so it suffers a bit in terms of originality. However, I expect this overall approach to become a standard tool for model-building.
 
 The main weakness of this paper is that it did not explore the computational tradeoffs of this approach against related methods. However, the paper already had a lot of content.

This paper presents a clever way of training a generative model which allows for exact inference, sampling and log likelihood evaluation. The main idea here is to make the Jacobian that comes when using the change of variables formula (from data to latents) triangular - this makes the determinant easy to calculate and hence learning possible. 
The paper nicely presents this core idea and a way to achieve this - by choosing special "routings" between the latents and data such that part of the transformation is identity and part some complex function of the input (a deep net, for example) the resulting Jacobian has a tractable structure. This routing can be cascaded to achieve even more complex transformation. 

On the experimental side, the model is trained on several datasets and the results are quite convincing, both in sample quality and quantitive measures. 
I would be very happy to see if this model is useful with other types of tasks and if the resulting latent representation help with classification or inference such as image restoration.

In summary - the paper is nicely written, results are quite good and the model is interesting - I'm happy to recommend acceptance.

This paper proposes a new generative model that uses real-valued non-volume preserving transformations in order to achieve efficient and exact inference and sampling of data points.
The authors use the change-of-variable technique to obtain a model distribution of the data from a simple prior distribution on a latent variable. By carefully designing the bijective function used in the change-of-variable technique, they obtain a Jacobian that is triangular and allows for efficient computation.

Generative models with tractable inference and efficient sampling are an active research area and this paper definitely contributes to this field.

While not achieving state-of-the-art, they are not far behind. This doesn't change the fact that the proposed method is innovative and worth exploring as it tries to bridge the gap between auto-regressive models, variational autoencoders and generative adversarial networks.

The authors clearly mention the difference and similarities with other types of generative models that are being actively researched.
Compared to autoregressive models, the proposed approach offers fast sampling.
Compared to generative adversarial networks, Real NVP offers a tractable log-likelihood evaluation.
Compared to variational autoencoders, the inference is exact.
Compared to deep Boltzmann machines, the learning of the proposed method is tractable.
It is clear that Real NVP goal is to bridge the gap between existing and popular generative models.

The paper presents a lot of interesting experiments showing the capabilities of the proposed technique. Making the code available online will certainly contribute to the field. Is there any intention of releasing the code?

This paper addresses the problem of training deep neural networks with discrete/labeled data by using the representer theorem and using Recurrent Batch Normalization (RBN). The question/problem this paper addresses is whether RBN can be applied to standard/vanilla Deep Neural Networks (DNN) to make them work well on discrete/labeled data. The paper has some strengths. This paper builds on the idea of Recurrent Batch Normalization (RBN) first proposed in (Ilya Sekiya, Yuvraj Goliyan, Yann N. Shen, and Joao Tran, “Recurrent batch normalization,” arXiv preprint arXiv:1711.07477, November 2017). RBN applies Batch Normalization to the input-to-hidden transformation of RNNs but applies it consistently to the hidden-to-hidden transition. This allows RBN to reduce internal covariate shift between time steps. The main contribution of this paper is to demonstrate that it is also beneficial to batch-normalize the hidden-to-hidden transition. In contrast to the approach of Sekiya et al. where the authors had to copy all weight matrices and running statistics between each layer, we propose to use weight sharing and stateless batch normalization by deriving statistics from the mean and variance of the layer’s input. We evaluate our proposal on various sequential problems such as sequence classification, language modeling and question answering and observe consistent improvement over the baseline RNNs. We make our code and models available at: https://github.com/tensorlayer/RecurrentBN PROS: 1. Unlike Sekiya et al., the proposed approach does not need to copy all weight matrices and running statistics between each layer. Stateless Batch Normalization leads to smaller networks with faster training and better generalization. 2. In the experiments we observe consistent improvement over the baseline RNNs. CONS: 1. The proposed approach only applies to RNNs with the residual connection and the batch normalization layer after the last hidden layer. 2. More experiments are needed to evaluate the proposed approach on very long sequences such as paragraph or movie reviews.
human_text:
Contributions
The paper presents an adaptation of batch normalization for RNNs in the case of LSTMs, along the horizontal depth. Contrary to previous work from (Laurent 2015; Amodei 2016), the work demonstrates that batch-normalizing the hidden states of RNNs can improve optimization, and argues with quantitative experiments that the key factor to making this work is proper initialization of parameters, in particular gamma. Experiments show some gain in performance over vanilla LSTMs on Sequential MNIST, PTB, Text8 and CNN Question-Answering.

Novelty+Significance
Batch normalization has been key for training deeper and deeper networks (e.g. ResNets) and it seems natural that we would want to extend it to RNNs.  The paper shows that it is possible to do so with proper initialization of parameters, contrary to previous work from (Laurent 2015; Amodei 2016). Novelty comes from where to batch norm (i.e. not in the cell update) and in the per-time step statistics. 

Adding batch normalization to LSTMs incurs additional computational cost and bookkeeping; for training speed comparisons (e.g. Figure 2) the paper only compares LSTM and BN-LSTM by iteration count; given the additional complexity of the BN-LSTM I would have also liked to see a wall-clock comparison.

As RNNs are used across many tasks, this work is of interest to many.  However, the results gains are generally minor and require several tricks to work in practice. Also, this work doesn’t address a question about batch normalization that it seems natural that it helps with faster training, but why would it also improve generalization? 

Clarity
The paper is overall very clear and well-motivated. The model is well described and easy to understand, and the plots illustrate the points clearly.

Summary
Interesting though relatively incremental adaptation, but shows batch normalization to work for RNNs where previous works have not succeeded. Comprehensive set of experiments though it is questionable if the empirical gains are significant enough to justify the increased model complexity as well as computational overhead.

Pros
- Shows batch normalization to work for RNNs where previous works have not succeeded
- Good empirical analysis of hyper-parameter choices and of the activations
- Experiments on multiple tasks
- Clarity

Cons
- Relatively incremental
- Several ‘hacks’ for the method (per-time step statistics, adding noise for exploding variance, sequence-wise normalization)
- No mention of computational overhead
- Only character or pixel-level tasks, what about word-level?

The reviewers believe this paper is of significant interest to the ICLR community, as it demonstrates how to get the popular batch normalization method to work in the recurrent setting. The fact that it has already been cited a variety of times also speaks to its interest within the community. The extensive experiments are convincing that the method works. One common criticism is that the authors don't address enough the added computational cost of the method in the text or empirically. Plots showing loss as a function of wall-clock time instead of training iteration would be more informative to readers deciding whether to use batch norm. 
 
 Pros: 
 - Gets batch normalization to work on recurrent networks (which had been elusive to many)
 - The experiments are thorough and demonstrate the method reduces training time (as a function of training iterations)
 - The paper is well written and accessible
 
 Cons
 - The contribution is relatively incremental (several tweaks to an existing method)
 - The major disadvantage to the approach is the added computational cost, but this is conspicuously not addressed.

The paper shows that BN, which does not work out of the box for RNNs, can be used with LSTM when the operator is applied to the hidden-to-hidden and the input-to-hidden contribution separately. Experiments are conducted to show that it leads to improved generalisation error and faster convergence.

The paper is well written and the idea well presented. 

i) The data sets and consequently the statistical assumptions used are limited (e.g. no continuous data, only autoregressive generative modelling).
ii) The hyper parameters are nearly constant over the experiments. It is ruled out that they have not been picked in favor of one of the methods. E.g. just judging from the text, a different learning rate could have lead to equally fast convergence for vanilla LSTM. 

Concluding, the experiments are flawed and do not sufficiently support the claim. An exhaustive search of the hyper parameter space could rule that out.

This paper extends batch normalization successfully to RNNs where batch normalization has previously failed or done poorly. The experiments and datasets tackled show definitively the improvement that batch norm LSTMs provide over standard LSTMs. They also cover a variety of examples, including character level (PTB and Text8), word level (CNN question-answering task), and pixel level (MNIST and pMNIST). The supplied training curves also quite clearly show the potential improvements in training time which is an important metric for consideration.

The experiment on pMNIST also solidly shows the advantage of batch norm in the recurrent setting for establishing long term dependencies. I additionally also appreciated the gradient flow insight, specifically the impact of unit variance on tanh derivatives. Showing it not just for batch normalization but additionally the "toy task" (Figure 1b) was hugely useful.

Overall I find this paper a useful additional contribution to the usage of batch normalization and would be necessary information for successfully employing it in a recurrent setting.

ii) The hyper parameters are nearly constant over the experiments. It is ruled out that they have not been picked in favor of one of the methods. E.g. just judging from the text, a different learning rate could have lead to equally fast convergence for vanilla LSTM. 

Concluding, the experiments are flawed and do not sufficiently support the claim. An exhaustive search of the hyper parameter space could rule that out.

This paper extends batch normalization successfully to RNNs where batch normalization has previously failed or done poorly. The experiments and datasets tackled show definitively the improvement that batch norm LSTMs provide over standard LSTMs. They also cover a variety of examples, including character level (PTB and Text8), word level (CNN question-answering task), and pixel level (MNIST and pMNIST). The supplied training curves also quite clearly show the potential improvements in training time which is an important metric for consideration.

The experiment on pMNIST also solidly shows the advantage of batch norm in the recurrent setting for establishing long term dependencies. I additionally also appreciated the gradient flow insight, specifically the impact of unit variance on tanh derivatives. Showing it not just for batch normalization but additionally the "toy task" (Figure 1b) was hugely useful.

Overall I find this paper a useful additional contribution to the usage of batch normalization and would be necessary information for successfully employing it in a recurrent setting.

Contributions
The paper presents an adaptation of batch normalization for RNNs in the case of LSTMs, along the horizontal depth. Contrary to previous work from (Laurent 2015; Amodei 2016), the work demonstrates that batch-normalizing the hidden states of RNNs can improve optimization, and argues with quantitative experiments that the key factor to making this work is proper initialization of parameters, in particular gamma. Experiments show some gain in performance over vanilla LSTMs on Sequential MNIST, PTB, Text8 and CNN Question-Answering.

Novelty+Significance
Batch normalization has been key for training deeper and deeper networks (e.g. ResNets) and it seems natural that we would want to extend it to RNNs.  The paper shows that it is possible to do so with proper initialization of parameters, contrary to previous work from (Laurent 2015; Amodei 2016). Novelty comes from where to batch norm (i.e. not in the cell update) and in the per-time step statistics. 

Adding batch normalization to LSTMs incurs additional computational cost and bookkeeping; for training speed comparisons (e.g. Figure 2) the paper only compares LSTM and BN-LSTM by iteration count; given the additional complexity of the BN-LSTM I would have also liked to see a wall-clock comparison.

As RNNs are used across many tasks, this work is of interest to many.  However, the results gains are generally minor and require several tricks to work in practice. Also, this work doesn’t address a question about batch normalization that it seems natural that it helps with faster training, but why would it also improve generalization? 

Clarity
The paper is overall very clear and well-motivated. The model is well described and easy to understand, and the plots illustrate the points clearly.

Summary
Interesting though relatively incremental adaptation, but shows batch normalization to work for RNNs where previous works have not succeeded. Comprehensive set of experiments though it is questionable if the empirical gains are significant enough to justify the increased model complexity as well as computational overhead.

Pros
- Shows batch normalization to work for RNNs where previous works have not succeeded
- Good empirical analysis of hyper-parameter choices and of the activations
- Experiments on multiple tasks
- Clarity

Cons
- Relatively incremental
- Several ‘hacks’ for the method (per-time step statistics, adding noise for exploding variance, sequence-wise normalization)
- No mention of computational overhead
- Only character or pixel-level tasks, what about word-level?

Compared to regular SGD, warm restarts improve convergence by allowing SGD to "wake up"/"start over" itself periodically with previous, potentially less optimal, parameters. The main idea is to maintain a fixed number ofpast updates $M$, which is decreased periodically. The paper Stochastic Gradient Descent with Warm Restarts provides a novel approach to Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) by using Warm Restarts, a technique initially proposed for Staying Alive in Stubborn Solvable Problems. The paper makes the case that Stubborn Solvable Problems are really just finding local minima, so Stubborn Solvable Problems are not a limit of Stochastic Gradient Descent. The solution they found, Warm Restarts, works as follows: at the start of SGD, set a counter to 0. At each iteration, increase the counter by 1. If the iteration is a success, reset the counter to 0. When the counter reaches a large value, i.e. a warm restart, then reset the counter to 0 and return to the start of the line of descent. The paper demonstrates a significant speedup over Stochastic Gradient Descent with a baseline SGD using a regular warm restart. Here is a peer review for SGDR: Stochastic Gradient Descent with Warm Restarts: Restart techniques are common in gradient-free optimization to deal with multimodal functions. Partial warm restarts are also gaining popularity in gradient-based optimization to improve the rate of convergence in accelerated gradient schemes to deal with ill-conditioned functions. In this paper, we propose a simple warm restart technique for stochastic gradient descent to improve its anytime performance when training deep neural networks. We empirically study its performance on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets, where we demonstrate new state-of-the-art results at 3.14\% and 16.21\%, respectively. We also demonstrate its advantages on a dataset of EEG recordings and on a downsampled version of the ImageNet dataset. Our source code is available at https://github.com/UCLA-mLab/SGDR. The main contributions of this paper are: (1) We analyze the criticality of individual parameters and present a novel damping technique that improves convergence over standard fixed step size schemes. (2) We introduce the concept of ``warm restarts'' which warm up the values of the previous state and use it to initialize the next state in the same iteration thereby accelerating convergence. (3) We combine warm restarts with a novel monotonically decreasing step size rule and show its effectiveness even on harder non-convex problems such as EEG signals and downsampled versions of ImageNet dataset. (4) We empirically compare our results on standard classification datasets against state-of-the-art and demonstrate substantial improvement over them. I recommend to publish this work.

Several techniques are presented in a clear way and parameterized method is proposed and evaluated on the CIFAR task. The concept is easy to understand and the authors chose state-of-the-art models to show the performance of their algorithm. The relevance of these results goes beyond image classification.


Pros:

- Simple and effective method to improve convergence
- Good evaluation on well known database


Cons:

- Connection of introduction and topic of the paper is a bit unclear
- Fig 2, 4 and 5 are hard to read. Lines are out of bounds and maybe only the best setting for T_0 and T_mult would be clearer. The baseline also doesn't seem to converge

Remarks:
An loss surface for T_0 against T_mult would be very helpful. Also understanding the relationship of network depth and the performance of this method would add value to this analysis.

All reviewers viewed the paper favourably, with the only criticism being that seeing how the method complements other approaches (momentum, Adam) would make the paper more complete. We encourage the authors to include such a comparison in the camera ready version of their paper.

We thank all reviewers for their positive evaluation and their valuable comments. We've uploaded a revision to address the issues raised and briefly reply to the reviewers' concerns here.

Experiments on additional benchmarks 
==============================

In order to address the concerns of AnonReviewer4 about our method's generality, we added two more benchmarks to the main paper.

1. We had already included additional results for another domain in the appendix of the original submission. That domain is motor-control decoding based on EEG data, which, due to the large noise present in brain signals, is very different from visual object recognition in general, and CIFAR in particular. We realize that it was not the best decision to only mention those results in the supplementary material, and we have now moved them to the main paper (new Section 4.4). In fact, our work is in part motivated and funded by a project aimed at accelerating the processing of this sort of brain data (see acknowledgments).

2. We've now added a new experiment on a new downsampled version of the ImageNet dataset (new Section 4.5), which is much harder than the CIFAR benchmark because there are 1000 classes and because the target concept often only occupies a small part of the image. An interpretation of this might be that, while the initial learning rate seems to be very important, SGDR reduces the problem of improper learning rate selection by quickly annealing from the initial learning rate to 0.

This heuristic to improve gradient descent in image classification is simple and effective, but this looks to me more like a workshop track paper. Demonstration of the algorithm is limited to one task (CIFAR) and there is no theory to support it, so we do not know how it will generalize on other tasks

machine_text: This is an interesting paper. The authors introduce a framework that lets you use a neural network to parameterize a statistical relational model (SQRM), which can then be used to represent natural language queries. The learned SQRM is first evaluated on a simple question answering task and then used to train a natural language interface (NLI) model. The NLI model can answer natural language questions using a query representation based on the SQRM. The results are compared to an Elman RNN model as the state-of-the-art in this task. The NLI model trained using the SQRM parameterization is shown to perform better than the baseline model on a real-world dataset, as well as on a diverse set of evaluation metrics. I have a few concerns about the evaluation procedure and the claimed success for the SQRM model. First, the text description for the SQRM model is very generic and there is not much detail about how the SQRM is parameterized or what specific model is being used in this case. Second, the SQRM is only evaluated on a simple QA task using one dataset. The NLI model trained using the SQRM parameterization is then shown to perform better than the baseline model on a real-world dataset. However, this is only based on a single task and a single dataset. Can the SQRM model be applied to a wide range of NLI models and datasets to show its applicability to a broader range of tasks? Third, the NLI model trained using the SQRM is evaluated on both a real-world dataset and a synthetic dataset, while the baseline is only tested on the real-world dataset. In this case, the baseline is a stronger model and it is not fair to compare the SQRM model against the baseline using the same dataset. There are also some minor typos in the text. For example, in the first paragraph of the Results section, the formula (RLM + SQRM) is incorrectly written as (RLM + SQRM + LSTM). Similarly, in the third paragraph of the Discussion section, the formula RLM + SQRM + LSTM is incorrectly written as RLM + SQRM. Overall, the SQRM model represents a new direction for NLI and it would be useful to make more comparisons against other NLI models, such as LSTMs, and also investigate the learnability of the SQRM model to see if it can be specialized for a particular type of NLI model.

The learning a natural language interface with neural programmer (NLP-P) framework by @DBLP:journals/corr/abs-1901-07842 addresses the problem of building an end-to-end NLP system that can automatically generate high-quality text from an input prompt. The framework decomposes the task into two parts: a linguistic formatter that transforms the input prompt into a logical form, and a program generator based on a neural program generator. The framework learns the mapping between the input prompt and the logical form, and uses the program generator to generate the text from the generated logical form based on a set of knowledge and a set of training data. The framework uses two different types of neural networks as the program generator. The first type of network is a semantic program generator that uses the input prompt and the logical form to perform inference, and generates text by sampling from a simple distribution. The second type of network is a reinforcement program generator that uses an autoregressive decoder to generate a sequence of words, and rewards the program generator based on an RNN-based metric. The framework uses gradient reversal and adaptive moment estimation to update the parameters of the two types of network. The framework is evaluated on two datasets and experimental results show that the framework is able to outperform the state of the art by a significant margin. The framework has two main weaknesses. The first is that the program generator uses an autoregressive decoder that is susceptible to the choice of RNN cell architecture. Secondly, the program generator is trained with a simple reward signal, and it is not clear how the framework could be extended to use more complex reward signals. This framework demonstrates an important approach to NLP program generation, and the publication of this work has been followed by the development of open source code for the framework, which will allow its adoption and extension by the community. This work provides an important step towards the development of a NLP system that can generate natural language output, and we expect that in the future the framework will be improved in several directions. This is an excellent work that presents an important conceptual approach towards NLP program generation, and the paper is accompanied by a suite of code and a benchmark to allow the framework to be evaluated in the research community. The work clearly presents the challenges that remain to be addressed, and we expect that the framework will be significantly improved in the coming years.

Overall, the paper is pretty interesting, and makes a step further on program induction. However, I would like to suggest the following points for improvement. First, it is an empirical study and the mechanism how the PRG (neural program) works is not clearly explained. I believe it is better to have a conceptual explanation about how PRG works. As a programming language researcher, I think it is important to explain how the PRG is related to existing PL research such as higher-order programs, denotational semantics, static typing, program induction, and etc. Second, it would be good if the authors could compare with existing state-of-the-art methods. For example, Why cannot the PRG model achieve the same performance as Bizer et al. (2015) (27.6%)? How does the PRG+ ensemble compare with the state of the art? Third, the code of PRG model is not very readable. For example, Line 297-303: one or two spaces are missing between `expr` and `val`. Please check this kind of typos or coding mistakes. In summary, I think the PRG model has the potential to become a good option for programmers who want to write simple programs by using the corresponding natural language interface. However, it is still an open question whether PRG is a good programming paradigm in the same way that IF/THEN, PROLIF/THEN and function call are. The answer to this question can be found by comparing PRG with existing programming paradigms in the literature.

Neural Programmer is a new end-to-end neural network model that maps natural language questions to programs that can be executed to provide the desired response. To our knowledge, this is the first time a neural network model is trained end-to-end with only weakly labeled example questions and answers without requiring domain-specific grammars, rules, or annotations. The paper is interesting in the following aspects. First, this is the first paper applying Neural Programmer to natural language interface design. This is a challenging task that involves deep language understanding and multi-step reasoning. Neural Programmer is designed to perform this task with end-to-end training. Current solutions to this design challenge involve formulating the task as parsing a natural language statement into a logical form, which is then mapped to a program that can be executed. This is a two-step approach that requires a separate program mapping step which can be costly. Neural Programmer eliminates the parsing step and end-to-end trains a model to directly induce a program that can be executed. This is more efficient but more difficult. Second, the WikiTableQuestions dataset introduced in this paper is a challenging natural language interface design dataset. It is challenging because it requires understanding of multiple steps of reasoning including language understanding, word sense disambiguation, and common sense reasoning. This requires a model with strong general language understanding ability but also able to apply it to different use cases. This is often overlooked in NLP research. State-of-the-art models focus on solving one specific use case and lack the general language understanding ability and applicability. Neural Programmer also focuses on these two elements. It uses general NLP models (BERT) for language understanding and word sense disambiguation, and apply program induction to common sense reason and answer questions based on domain knowledge. Third, the effectiveness of Neural Programmer is demonstrated by comparing with previous end-to-end train models for this task. The baselines include DenseLSTM and BDL, both of which integrate the program induction step. Neural Programmer has more advanced program induction ability and therefore achieves better performance. However, a direct comparison with the parsing-based approach is also valuable. This is because Neural Programmer eliminates the need for the second step, which is program parsing. Answering a question with Neural Programmer is as simple as providing a program to execute. The paper isWeakly supervised, end-to-end Neural Programmer Learning a Natural Language Interface with Natural Language Interface Design task was defined as follows: Given a natural language question Q, predict the Program P such that S(P) == Q, where S() is a semantics function that translates the natural language to a logical form, and then the program is executed to get the answer. This is a challenging task because the semantic parse for the input query is only an intermediate representation for program induction. The generated program may not be executable, and the semantic parser may not be perfect. The Neural Programmer model for program induction is built with the Neural Programmer model. The Neural Programmer model includes a set of instructional rules, or a DSL, that can be used to perform arithmetic, comparison, selection, and iteration operations. This paper enhances the traditional Neural Programmer model by adding a parsing mechanism to Neural Programmer model. The code and models of the paper are available at the link below. https://github.com/NeuralProgrammer/

This paper proposes a weakly supervised, end-to-end neural network model for solving a challenging natural language understanding task. 
As an extension of the Neural Programmer, this work aims at overcoming the ambiguities imposed by natural language. 
By predefining a set of operations, the model is able to learn the interface between the language reasoning and answer composition using backpropagation. 
On the WikiTableQuestions dataset, it is able to achieve a slightly better performance than the traditional semantic parser methods. 

Overall, this is a very interesting and promising work as it involves a lot of real-world challenges about natural language understanding. 
The intuitions and design of the model are very clear, but the complication makes the paper a bit difficult to read, which means the model is also difficult to be reimplemented. I would expect to see more details about model ablation and it would help us figure out the prominent parts of the model design.

This paper presents an extension of the asynchronous advantage actor-critic (A3C) algorithm for solving reinforcement learning (RL) problems that are sensitive to timing. The method presented allows one to train RL agents on Reinforce, the popular open-source platform for training agents for RL, with speeds up to 20 times faster than competing methods. This is possible because the proposed method does not require repeated time-consuming bootstrapping phases and instead uses a small number of pre-trained models to initialize the learning process. The method also allows for efficient parallelization across many gpus. Finally, the paper also presents an extension to A3C that learns a natural action for coding up the policies found by the agent. Overall, this is an interesting paper that provides an interesting improvement to A3C. However, I have some concerns about the methodology used to arrive at the conclusions, particularly the use of small pre-trained models to initialize the training process and the use of the average policy distance as a metric to assess convergence. It would be helpful to perform crossvalidation on the small pre-trained models to ensure that they generalize to new problems. Additionally, although the improvement in speed is impressive, 20 times faster is still likely to be slower than most users would like to train models. Some justification is needed for the chosen speedup factor. Finally, although it is true that the paper does not require repeated bootstrapping phases, it is not clear why this is necessary or particularly problematic. The reason for this is likely to be in the implementation, but it would help the reader if the authors could elaborate further. Finally, in the comparison with TD(λ), it would be helpful to understand why the authors chose the particular values of λ and what difference this choice would make to the results obtained.

We introduce a system of queues and a dynamic scheduling strategy, potentially helpful for other asynchronous algorithms as well. 2. Exploring the combination of multiple GPUs and CPU cores could potentially achieve even better performance. 3. This paper only focuses on a single architecture, NVIDIA GPUs. There are other GPUs available in the market, such as AMD GPUs and Intel GPUs. Evaluating the performance of the proposed approach on different GPU types is also an interesting topic. This paper introduces a 'GPU-friendly' variant of A3C which relaxes some synchronicity constraints in the original A3C algorithm to make it more friendly to a high-throughput GPU device. The analysis of the effects of this added latency is thorough. The systems analysis of the algorithm is extensive. 

One caveat is that the performance figures in Table 3 are hard to compare since the protocols vary so much. I understand that DeepMind didn't provide reproducible code for A3C, but I gather from the comment that the authors have re-implemented vanilla A3C as well, in which case it would be good to show what this reimplementation of A3C achieves in the same setting used by DM, and in the setting of the experiment conducted using GA3C (1 day). It would be good to clarify in the text that the experimental protocol differed (top 5 out of 50 vs single run), and clarify why the discrepancy, even if the answer is that the authors didn't have time / resources to reproduce the same protocol. A bit more care would go a long way to establishing that indeed, there is no price to pay for the approximations that were made.

I applaud the authors for open-sourcing the code, especially since there is a relative shortage of properly tested open-source implementations in that general area, and getting these algorithms right is non-trivial.

A disclaimer: having never implemented A3C myself, I have a low confidence in my ability to appropriately assess of the algorithmic aspects of the work.

This paper suggests modifications to A3C - mainly by adding a system of queues to batch data - to obtain higher learning throughput on a GPU. The paper gives a solid systems analysis of the algorithm and performance. Although the method does not necessarily lead to higher Atari performance, it is a valuable and relevant contribution to the field, since it provides a stable, fast, open-source implementation of the currently best-performing deep RL algorithm.

This is now coherent with results reported in Figs. 6/7/8, where we achieve higher convergence rate by using a different learning rate.

Please also notice the code has been officially released on Github:

We first thank all the reviewers for the interesting comments they provided. All three reviewers agree on the potential importance of the proposed algorithm, but they also suggest that more experimental data are needed to demonstrate that GA3C achieves results in the same ballpark as the original A3C. This turns out to be particularly important in the light of the fact that the policy lag in GA3C can potentially introduce instabilities, as noted by Reviewer #1.

We have included a better description of this in Section 4.4 of the revised paper, as well as analyzed it in a newly added Section 5.3, while providing additional experiments to verify the game performance of GA3C and its stability. As pointed out by the reviewers and already highlighted in the paper, establishing a validation protocol that allows comparing the final scores achieved by GA3C with the scores achieved by other training algorithms is complex or even infeasible, as many implementation details are not shared, as well as validation protocols are poorly reproducible. Beyond that, the final score (still reported in Table 3) tells only part of the story, and therefore we espouse the idea shared by Reviewer #1 and #3 of reporting learning curves as a function of the time. The newly added Fig. 6 and 7 show the learning curves for GA3C and several games as a function of the time. The reader can easily compare these graphs with those reported in Mnih’s paper, as well as in other venues mentioned by the reviewers (e.g. github). The score vs. time curves show a similar dynamic for GA3C and A3C, although it is also important mentioning that curves reported in Mnih’s paper represent the average of the top 5 curves in a set of 50 with various learning rates, which we are unable to match due limitations in available computational resources. Since systems, system loads, environments and hyper-parameters are so widely varying, we also believe that releasing the GA3C code (which we plan to do in the next days) will allow other researchers to systematically evaluate the performances of GA3C and facilitate a fair comparison with new techniques.

Reviewer #1’s main concern is about instabilities introduced in GA3C. The training curves reported in the paper indeed show a few instabilities occurring in the training process, but these represent a common phenomenon in RL. Beyond analyzing in Section 4.4 how the policy lag in GA3C can generate these instabilities, we now show experimentally that such instabilities do not affect some games (e.g. Pong), while they can invalidate the learning process in other ones (e.g. Breakout), especially in the case of a large learning rate (Fig. 7 and 8). We found that properly tuning the algorithm hyper-parameters (and in particular the learning rate) dramatically limits the effect of instabilities on the learning process. GA3C would likely benefit from a thorough learning rate search as presented in Mnih’s paper over a set of 50 different learning rates for A3C. Beyond this, we also show how batching on training data (see the newly introduced Section 5.3, and Fig. 7 and 8 in particular) can be used to limit the effect of these instabilities, at the price of a slower convergence rate.

Specific answers to the individual reviewers follow.

===============================
Reviewer 1
===============================

We agree with the reviewer that instabilities may affect the learning process. This is indeed a commonly observed phenomenon in RL. Given the fact that GA3C and A3C are indeed (slightly) different algorithms (as now clearly explained in Section 4.4 of the paper), we followed the reviewer’s suggestion and performed a thorough evaluation of the instabilities of the learning process on several games. Experimental results are reported in Section 5.3 and in Fig. 7 and 8 in particular. These show that, for some games (e.g. Pong), the delayed computation of the gradient terms in GA3C (see Section 4.4) does not introduce convergence issues, that are however present in other games (e.g. Breakout). However, a proper selection of the algorithm hyper-parameters, and of the learning rate in particular, is sufficient to achieve results that are comparable to those achieved by A3C (see Table 3). Quite interestingly, the optimal learning rate for GA3C results to be smaller than the one reported in Mnih’s paper for A3C (as it can be seen in Fig. 6) - this somehow confirms that A3C and GA3C are indeed slightly different algorithms, and GA3C requires careful parameter tuning to obtain optimal results. We also demonstrated that batching of the training data can be used to limit the instabilities, at the price of a slower convergence rate.

===============================
Reviewer 2
===============================

Following the suggestion of the other two reviewers, and sharing the conviction that replicating the Deep Mind evaluation protocol is non-trivial, we now report in the paper more training curves for several games (Fig. 6) as a function of the training time. This allows the reader to perform a direct comparison between our training curves and the ones reported in Mnih’s paper, independently from the hardware system used for training. Although, the reader should be careful about this comparison since Mnih’s graphs show top 5 out of 50 runs which is hard to compare with the small number of runs considered in Fig. 6. These curves demonstrate that training time is comparable while achieving a similar training score. The analysis of the theoretical discrepancies between A3C and GA3C (Section 4.4) and its experimental evaluation in terms of instabilities (Section 5.3) should also serve to clarify that, once the hyper-parameters are properly set, GA3C is comparable to A3C in terms of performance.
As for the question about the protocol used for evaluation the score of our trained agents, we now better specify in the caption of table 3 and in the text that we are reporting the average score over 30 different runs for the best agent we trained with GA3C. A direct comparison using the protocol followed in Mnih’s paper is not feasible, as the authors did not share the “human start condition” for each game.

===============================
Reviewer 3
===============================

We agree with the reviewer that showing score vs. time plot would be more informative than reporting only the final score as in Table 3. Therefore, we added Fig. 6 to the paper, showing that, with the proper selection of the hyper-parameters, the dynamic of the learning curves of GA3C is similar to that shown in the original A3C paper by Mnih et al. We believe that other, more precise comparisons in terms of learning speed require an optimized implementation as well as a broad hyper-parameter search (in the style of the original A3C plot, showing top 5 results among a set of 50 learners trained with different learning rates), which is out of the scope for this paper. We also decided to keep Table 3 in the paper - although, as explicitly mentioned in the paper, this information is approximate, it gives an idea that GA3C and A3C achieves final score in the same ballpark.
We also suggest that the contribution of our paper is not limited to the implementation of GA3C, but it also includes the analysis of the computational aspects of GA3C and other RL algorithms that can be implemented through a similar architecture. This contribution stands independently from the potential stability issues for GA3C, while the proposed architecture (and the freely available code) can be modified or extended to address these issues, improve the convergence speed, or attack real world problems.

The paper gives a solid systems analysis of the algorithm and performance. Although the method does not necessarily lead to higher Atari performance, it is a valuable and relevant contribution to the field, since it provides a stable, fast, open-source implementation of the currently best-performing deep RL algorithm.

Please note we just updated the latest version of the paper with the latest version of Fig. 5.
This is now coherent with results reported in Figs. 6/7/8, where we achieve higher convergence rate by using a different learning rate.

Please also notice the code has been officially released on Github:

We first thank all the reviewers for the interesting comments they provided. All three reviewers agree on the potential importance of the proposed algorithm, but they also suggest that more experimental data are needed to demonstrate that GA3C achieves results in the same ballpark as the original A3C. This turns out to be particularly important in the light of the fact that the policy lag in GA3C can potentially introduce instabilities, as noted by Reviewer #1.

We have included a better description of this in Section 4.4 of the revised paper, as well as analyzed it in a newly added Section 5.3, while providing additional experiments to verify the game performance of GA3C and its stability. As pointed out by the reviewers and already highlighted in the paper, establishing a validation protocol that allows comparing the final scores achieved by GA3C with the scores achieved by other training algorithms is complex or even infeasible, as many implementation details are not shared, as well as validation protocols are poorly reproducible. Beyond that, the final score (still reported in Table 3) tells only part of the story, and therefore we espouse the idea shared by Reviewer #1 and #3 of reporting learning curves as a function of the time. The newly added Fig. 6 and 7 show the learning curves for GA3C and several games as a function of the time. The reader can easily compare these graphs with those reported in Mnih’s paper, as well as in other venues mentioned by the reviewers (e.g. github). The score vs. time curves show a similar dynamic for GA3C and A3C, although it is also important mentioning that curves reported in Mnih’s paper represent the average of the top 5 curves in a set of 50 with various learning rates, which we are unable to match due limitations in available computational resources. Since systems, system loads, environments and hyper-parameters are so widely varying, we also believe that releasing the GA3C code (which we plan to do in the next days) will allow other researchers to systematically evaluate the performances of GA3C and facilitate a fair comparison with new techniques.

Reviewer #1’s main concern is about instabilities introduced in GA3C. The training curves reported in the paper indeed show a few instabilities occurring in the training process, but these represent a common phenomenon in RL. Beyond analyzing in Section 4.4 how the policy lag in GA3C can generate these instabilities, we now show experimentally that such instabilities do not affect some games (e.g. Pong), while they can invalidate the learning process in other ones (e.g. Breakout), especially in the case of a large learning rate (Fig. 7 and 8). We found that properly tuning the algorithm hyper-parameters (and in particular the learning rate) dramatically limits the effect of instabilities on the learning process. GA3C would likely benefit from a thorough learning rate search as presented in Mnih’s paper over a set of 50 different learning rates for A3C. Beyond this, we also show how batching on training data (see the newly introduced Section 5.3, and Fig. 7 and 8 in particular) can be used to limit the effect of these instabilities, at the price of a slower convergence rate.

Specific answers to the individual reviewers follow.

===============================
Reviewer 1
===============================

We agree with the reviewer that instabilities may affect the learning process. This is indeed a commonly observed phenomenon in RL. Given the fact that GA3C and A3C are indeed (slightly) different algorithms (as now clearly explained in Section 4.4 of the paper), we followed the reviewer’s suggestion and performed a thorough evaluation of the instabilities of the learning process on several games. Experimental results are reported in Section 5.3 and in Fig. 7 and 8 in particular. These show that, for some games (e.g. Pong), the delayed computation of the gradient terms in GA3C (see Section 4.4) does not introduce convergence issues, that are however present in other games (e.g. Breakout). However, a proper selection of the algorithm hyper-parameters, and of the learning rate in particular, is sufficient to achieve results that are comparable to those achieved by A3C (see Table 3). Quite interestingly, the optimal learning rate for GA3C results to be smaller than the one reported in Mnih’s paper for A3C (as it can be seen in Fig. 6) - this somehow confirms that A3C and GA3C are indeed slightly different algorithms, and GA3C requires careful parameter tuning to obtain optimal results. We also demonstrated that batching of the training data can be used to limit the instabilities, at the price of a slower convergence rate.

===============================
Reviewer 2
===============================

Following the suggestion of the other two reviewers, and sharing the conviction that replicating the Deep Mind evaluation protocol is non-trivial, we now report in the paper more training curves for several games (Fig. 6) as a function of the training time. This allows the reader to perform a direct comparison between our training curves and the ones reported in Mnih’s paper, independently from the hardware system used for training. Although, the reader should be careful about this comparison since Mnih’s graphs show top 5 out of 50 runs which is hard to compare with the small number of runs considered in Fig. 6. These curves demonstrate that training time is comparable while achieving a similar training score. The analysis of the theoretical discrepancies between A3C and GA3C (Section 4.4) and its experimental evaluation in terms of instabilities (Section 5.3) should also serve to clarify that, once the hyper-parameters are properly set, GA3C is comparable to A3C in terms of performance.
As for the question about the protocol used for evaluation the score of our trained agents, we now better specify in the caption of table 3 and in the text that we are reporting the average score over 30 different runs for the best agent we trained with GA3C. A direct comparison using the protocol followed in Mnih’s paper is not feasible, as the authors did not share the “human start condition” for each game.

===============================
Reviewer 3
===============================

We agree with the reviewer that showing score vs. time plot would be more informative than reporting only the final score as in Table 3. Therefore, we added Fig. 6 to the paper, showing that, with the proper selection of the hyper-parameters, the dynamic of the learning curves of GA3C is similar to that shown in the original A3C paper by Mnih et al. We believe that other, more precise comparisons in terms of learning speed require an optimized implementation as well as a broad hyper-parameter search (in the style of the original A3C plot, showing top 5 results among a set of 50 learners trained with different learning rates), which is out of the scope for this paper. We also decided to keep Table 3 in the paper - although, as explicitly mentioned in the paper, this information is approximate, it gives an idea that GA3C and A3C achieves final score in the same ballpark.
We also suggest that the contribution of our paper is not limited to the implementation of GA3C, but it also includes the analysis of the computational aspects of GA3C and other RL algorithms that can be implemented through a similar architecture. This contribution stands independently from the potential stability issues for GA3C, while the proposed architecture (and the freely available code) can be modified or extended to address these issues, improve the convergence speed, or attack real world problems.

The paper introduces GA3C, a GPU-based implementation of the A3C algorithm, which was originally designed for multi-core CPUs. The main innovation is the introduction of a system of queues. The system is compared to the authors' own implementation of A3C as well as to published reference scores.

The paper introduces a very natural architecture for implementing A3C on GPUs. Batching requests for predictions and learning steps for multiple actors to maximize GPU occupancy seems like the right thing to do assuming that latency is not an issue. The automatic performance tuning strategy is also really nice to see.
