The paper proposed a nice framework leveraging Tucker and Tensor train low-rank tensor factorization to induce parameter sharing for multi-task learning.

The framework is nice and appealing. 

However, MTL is a very well studied problem and the paper considers simple task for different classification, and it is not clear if we really need ``Deep Learning" for these simple datasets. A comparison with existing shallow MTL is necessary to show the benefits of the proposed methods (and in particular being deep) on the dataset. The authors ignore them on the basis of speculation and it is not clear if the proposed framework is really superior to simple regularizations like the nuclear norm. The idea of nuclear norm regularization can also be extended to deep learning as gradient descent are popular in all methods.

The reviews for this paper were quite mixed, with one strong accept and a marginal reject. A fourth reviewer with strong expertise in multi-task learning and deep learning was brought in to read the latest manuscript. Due to time constraints, this fourth review was not entered in the system but communicated through personal communication. 
 
 Pros:
 - Reviewers in general found the paper clear and well written.
 - Multi-task learning in deep models is of interest to the community
 - The approach is sensible and the experiments show that it seems to work
 
 Cons:
 - Factorization methods have been used extensively in deep learning, so the reviewers may have found the approach incremental
 - One reviewer was not convinced that the proposed method would work better than existing multi-task learning methods
 - Not all reviewers were convinced by the experiments
 - The fourth reviewer found the approach very sensible but was not excited enough to champion the paper
 
 The paper was highly regarded by at least one reviewer and two thought it should be accepted. The PCs also agree that this paper deserves to appear at the conference.

Dear readers and reviewers,

We would like to thank all the reviewers that helped us to improve this submission. Based on their comments, we have revised the submission.

The main changed parts are:

1. We discuss some related work in multi-task learning from speech recognition community. (Sec 2, Comment from Reviewer 3).

2. We add a new section in related work to discuss the literature in the line of constructing a MTL-like problem via clustering training data. (Sec 2, Pre-review question from Reviewer2)

3. We give more details about initialisation, particularly how to make the random initialisation condition work in practice. (Sec 4, Comment from Reviewer 2)

Finally, we add two more experiments. Due to page limits, they are placed in the appendix.

A) We compare our methods with some classic (shallow, matrix-based) MTL methods using both classic and CNN features. (Appendix A, Comment from Reviewer 1)

B) We add details about model size in terms of number of parameters, and demonstrate what happens if we make an almost equal sized UD-MTL competitor. (Appendix B, Pre-review question from Reviewer2)

This paper presents a strong and innovative combination of ensemble techniques, namely Bagging and Stacking, with a semi-supervised learning task: Temporal Ensembling. The authors show that the aggregation of different predictions for a single instance, based on different instances of the same type, but trained on different labeled batches, can significantly improve prediction performance, especially in the presence of temporal correlations in the data. In summary, the main contribution of this paper is the application of Bagging and Stacking to a Semi-Supervised Learning task, for the first time, and the establishment of a strong connection between the temporal correlations in the data and the effectiveness of the approach. This paper has a few weaknesses: (1) It does not present new experiments to compare with previous state of the art techniques, therefore it may be hard to reproduce the reported results, and the extent of the improvements obtained; (2) It focuses only on a few particular datasets, while in practice it would be interesting to perform a comparison with other state of the art techniques. This paper proposes Temporal Ensembling for Semi-Supervised Learning, by forming a consensus prediction of the unknown labels using the outputs of the network-in-training on different epochs, and most importantly, under different regularization and input augmentation conditions. This ensemble prediction can be expected to be a better predictor for the unknown labels than the output of the network at the most recent training epoch, and can thus be used as a target for training. Using our method, we set new records for two standard semi-supervised learning benchmarks, reducing the (non-augmented) classification error rate from 18.44% to 7.05% in SVHN with 500 labels and from 18.63% to 16.55% in CIFAR-10 with 4000 labels, and further to 5.12% and 12.16% by enabling the standard augmentations. We additionally obtain a clear improvement in CIFAR-100 classification accuracy by using random images from the Tiny Images dataset as unlabeled extra inputs during training. Finally, we demonstrate good tolerance to incorrect labels. I think the paper is relatively easy to read and follow. The overall approach is clear. The main idea is straightforward and has been done before in other papers. I don't see any major flaw in the paper. I think the main contribution of this paper is the introduction of Temporal Ensembling, where the ensemble prediction is formed using different models with different hyperparameters and input augmentations, and showing that this improves the prediction for the unknown labels. I recommend to accept this paper. Some comments and suggestions for further improving the paper: 1. The paper uses CIFAR-100 as the benchmark for effectiveness, however the provided results only show the error rate for the (pertinent) labeled images. In the caption for Table 1, it states that the entire test set was used, so presumably similar results would also be shown for the error rate on unlabeled images. 2. Related to (1), it would be helpful to have a similar table for CIFAR-10 to show the results for the labeled images only (i.e., reducing the error rate from 18.63% to 16.55%) and for the unlabeled images. 3. In the appendix, it would be good to have a better explanation of the Tiny Images dataset, such as what kind of images it contains and how the random images were selected for the CIFAR-100 results in the main text. 4. In the caption for Figure 1, it says "The change of MSE with the number of epochs for models trained on CIFAR-10 labeled data only". It would be helpful to explain what MSE is and how it is calculated in this context. 5. In Section 4.2.1, the training loss increases when the target network is updated. One possible explanation for this is that the training data may contain incorrect labels, which would lead to the classifier in the training data producing incorrect predictions. However, this is only a possible explanation, and the authors should check this possibility. 6. In Section 4.2.2, the authors state that the "classification error rate of the target network is similar to that of the last epoch of the previous training phase", but it would be good to show this to be more precise. 7. In Section 4.2.2, the selected models are the same as those used for training. It would be good to also show the error rates for a single model trained on CIFAR-10. It seems that the model is more accurate with an average of about 18% (compared to about 21% for all the models) when no data augmentation is used. 8. In Section 4.3, the model is trained on CIFAR-10 with 500 labeled data and then tested on CIFAR-100. This paper presents a model for semi-supervised learning by encouraging feature invariance to stochastic perturbations of the network and/or inputs.  Two models are described:  One where an invariance term is applied between different instantiations of the model/input a single training step, and a second where invariance is applied to features for the same input point across training steps via a cumulative exponential averaging of the features.  These models evaluated using CIFAR-10 and SVHN, finding decent gains of similar amounts in each case.  An additional application is also explored at the end, showing some tolerance to corrupted labels as well.

The authors also discuss recent work by Sajjadi &al that is very similar in spirit, which I think helps corroborate the findings here.

My largest critique is it would have been nice to see applications on larger datasets as well.  CIFAR and SVHN are fairly small test cases, though adequate for demonstration of the idea.  For cases of unlabelled data especially, it would be good to see tests with on the order of 1M+ data samples, with 1K-10K labeled, as this is a common case when labels are missing.

On a similar note, data augmentations are restricted to only translations and (for CIFAR) horizontal flips.  While "standard," as the paper notes, more augmentations would have been interesting to see --- particularly since the model is designed explicitly to take advantage of random sampling.  Some more details might also pop up, such as the one the paper mentions about handling horizontal flips in different ways between the two model variants.  Rather than restrict the system to a particular set of augmentations, I think it would be interesting to push it further, and see how its performance behaves over a larger array of augmentations and (even fewer) numbers of labels.

Overall, this seems like a simple approach that is getting decent results, though I would have liked to see more and larger experiments to get a better sense for its performance characteristics.



Smaller comment: the paper mentions "dark knowledge" a couple times in explaining results, e.g. bottom of p.6.  This is OK for a motivation, but in analyzing the results I think it may be possible to have something more concrete.  For instance, the consistency term encourages feature invariance to the stochastic sampling more strongly than would a classification loss alone.
This work explores taking advantage of the stochasticity of neural network outputs under randomized augmentation and regularization techniques to provide targets for unlabeled data in a semi-supervised setting. This is accomplished by either applying stochastic augmentation and regularization on a single image multiple times per epoch and encouraging the outputs to be similar (Π-model) or by keeping a weighted average of past epoch outputs and penalizing deviations of current network outputs from this running mean (temporal ensembling). The core argument is that these approaches produce ensemble predictions which are likely more accurate than the current network and are thus good targets for unlabeled data. Both approaches seem to work quite well on semi-supervised tasks and some results show that they are almost unbelievably robust to label noise.

The paper is clearly written and provides sufficient details to reproduce these results in addition to providing a public code base. The core idea of the paper is quite interesting and seems to result in higher semi-supervised accuracy than prior work. I also found the attention to and discussion of the effect of different choices of data augmentation to be useful.	

I am a little surprised that a standard supervised network can achieve 30% accuracy on SVHN given 90% random training labels. This would only give 19% correctly labeled data (9% by chance + 10% unaltered). I suppose the other 81% would not provide a consistent training signal such that it is possible, but it does seem quite unintuitive. I tried to look through the github for this experiment but it does not seem to be included. 

As for the resistance of Π-model and temporal ensembling to this label noise, I find that somewhat more believable given the large weights placed on the consistency constraint for this task. The authors should really include discussion of w(t) in the main paper. Especially because the tremendous difference in w_max in the incorrect label tolerance experiment (10x for Π-model and 100x for temporal ensembling from the standard setting).

Could the authors comment towards the scalability for larger problems? For ImageNet, you would need to store around 4.8 gigs for the temporal ensembling method or spend 2x as long training with Π-model.

Can the authors discuss sensitivity of this approach to the amount and location of dropout layers in the architecture?

The reason for me giving a +1 is related to the strength of the motivation of the proposed idea and the good practical results obtained in the experiments. I have listed some points that could be improved and a link to related work. Please find below the points in detail: * As mentioned in the introduction, the main advantage of the proposed noise adaptation layer is the capability of the model to cope with different distributions. The current experiments are restricted to the regression tasks and only a single distribution (Normal distribution) is used to generate the added noise. More experiments on other distributions and also the comparison to other approaches to deal with different distributions (for example Additive white Gaussian noise, Student's t and other Bayesian approaches) could be presented to strengthen the proposed idea. * In the Experiments section the link to the UCI repository for the WNISDM dataset is not working. * A more extensive comparison with other methods is needed. The authors introduce a novel technique for training deep neural networks using a noise adaptation layer, avoiding the need for Gradient consistent noise, which has been shown to be unstable in practice. The approach is simple and effective, and can be trained end-to-end using standard Stochastic Gradient Descent with Good Theoretical and Empirical Foundations. The training procedure is also very efficient, particularly when combined with Adaptive SGD, which allows for effective optimization even in the presence of parameter noise. The method is compared to other approaches on a range of classification problems and shown to be effective in a number of scenarios, in particular for small to medium size problems. * Problem / Question: There has been an explosion of interest in deep neural networks over the last few years. Much of this has been driven by the development of new architectural designs and optimization techniques which have led to large improvements in performance. However, these improvements have typically been at the cost of a high degree of complexity which can make the networks hard to train, making the process a trial and error. In particular, the recent explosion in the use of Generative Adversarial Networks has lead to impressive performance improvements on a wide range of problems, but this requires a more rigorous approach to training which is not easy to optimize. * The approach: The method introduced in this paper avoids the need for Gradient Consistent noise, which has been shown to be unstable in practice. The method instead incorporates noise into the training procedure. The noise is similar to that used by the NAF model, which is derived from the theory of auto-associative memory. The noise in the training set is therefore added to the data as additional input to the network. The method is simple and effective and has a number of advantages. Firstly, it allows for efficient and stable training of deep networks, even when training data is limited, and does not require use of the Generative Adversarial Networks approach to training. The approach is also effective, leading to significant improvements in performance in a number of cases on both small and large scale problems. * Strengths: The approach is simple and effective, and leads to significant improvements in performance in a number of cases on both small and large scale problems. The method also allows for efficient and stable training of deep networks, even when training data is limited. * Weaknesses: Unfortunately, the approach is not effective in all cases, and there is no clear explanation as to why it works in some cases and not in others. * Opportunities for Future Work: The authors demonstrate the approach on a range of problems, both classification and generative, and show that it can be effective in a number of scenarios. However, much further work would be required to determine under which conditions the approach would work best, and how to avoid the many cases where it does not work. * Summary: The approach described in this paper represents an important step forward in the development of deep networks, avoiding some of the more challenging aspects of training such networks, while still allowing them to be trained using standard Stochastic Gradient Descent. The method is easy to implement and leads to significant performance improvements on a range of problems. * Training deep neural-networks using a noise adaptation layer

This paper presents a neural network approach that explicitly models the noise by adding an additional softmax layer between the output layer and the original labels. The noisy labels are then dependent on both the labels and features as well as the noise. The likelihood that the noise model should be optimized is the same as that of the EM algorithm. Experiments show the proposed approach outperforms previous approaches. The paper is well written and the findings are interesting. I have some constructive comments, please keep them in mind when considering this review: 1.The introduction is a little bit too long. SomeDETAILS can be shortened. For example, the first example (noisy heartbeat detection) can be removed. In the section Related work, the authors could have compared their approach to other approaches in the litterature, for example using kernel methods or deformable networks. 2.The definition of "noisy label" is not precise. The problem of noisy label is usually formalized as "observing a random variable $L$ with probability density $p_L(\cdot)$, and given $L$, finding an estimate of $\widehat{Y}$ which is a noisy function of $L$". For example, if $L=1$ with probability 0.9 and $L=0$ with probability 0.1, we have a very good estimate of $\widehat{Y}=L$ but this value is not the truth. In this case, the error rate (the proportion of wrong labels) can be less than 0.1 (0.1) but this error rate is very good for most classification problems. The EM algorithm can be used to find the parameters of both the noise model and the neural network. So "noise adaptation layer" is a valid term. Also, it is not clear whether the noise in this case is external to the model (e.g., Gaussian noise) or intrinsic to the model (e.g., a softmax layer that overestimates the probability of certain classes). The second case could be considered as overfitting. The first case is probably due to underfitting (the noise model is too simple, e.g., noise from independent Gaussian distributions). Thus, the first type of noise is an underfitting problem and the second type of is an overfitting problem. The noisy label model should probably be included in the objective function of the training process. 3.The learning algorithm could be more precisely described in the third section. First, the Expectation step is first to maximize the following objective function: $$Q_E(W,B,\theta)=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{c=1}^C f_i^{c*} \log p_i^{c*}$$ where $f_i^{c*}$ and $p_i^{c*}$ are the estimated likelihood and probability of the model, $c$ the class and $i$ the training sample. The standard EM algorithm takes this step and the Maximization step is only the back-propagation algorithm. Can you add more details? For example, the back-propagation algorithm is a stochastic version of the EM algorithm. Is the latter used only at the testing phase? 4.The last section, Stacked Softmax, is probably the most interesting. A new objective function is proposed which consists of two terms. The first term is the expected joint likelihood that the correct label $y$ was observed for the correct class $c$ given the noisy label $l$ and the features $x$ with noise model $p(y|x,c,\theta_n)$. The second term is the L2 distance between the softmax layer and the actual softmax value. The Maximization step is then to minimize the difference between the actual value and the prediction. A stochastic version of this algorithm is also proposed and the theoretical analysis is given. The main result (a bound on the expected risk) is interesting but some technical points could be clarified (e.g., in the first paragraph of the Stacked Softmax algorithm, the batch sizes are written as $N$ but this should be $B$ ; the differential is given for one iteration but this should be per epoch). This work address the problem of supervised learning from strongly labeled data with label noise. This is a very practical and relevant problem in applied machine learning.  The authors note that using sampling approaches such as EM isn't effective, too slow and cannot be integrated into end-to-end training. Thus, they propose to simulate the effects of EM by a noisy adaptation layer, effectively a softmax, that is added to the architecture during training, and is omitted at inference time. The proposed algorithm is evaluated on MNIST and shows improvements over existing approaches that deal with noisy labeled data.

A few comments.
1. There is no discussion in the work about the increased complexity of training for the model with two softmaxes. 

2. What is the rationale for having consecutive (serialized) softmaxes, instead of having a compound objective with two losses, or a network with parallel losses and two sets of gradients?

3. The proposed architecture with only two hidden layers isn't not representative of larger and deeper models that are practically used, and it is not clear that shown results will scale to bigger networks. 

4. Why is the approach only evaluated on MNIST, a dataset that is unrealistically simple.

Reviewers agreed that the problem was important and the method was interesting and novel. The main (shared) concerns were preliminary nature of the experiments and questions around scalability to more classes. 
 
 During the discussion phase, the authors provided additional CIFAR-100 results and introduced a new approximate but scalable method for performing inference. I engaged the reviewers in discussion, who were originally borderline, to see what they thought about the changes. R2 championed the paper, stating that the additional experiments and response re: scalability were an improvement. On the balance, I think the paper is a poster accept.

We thank the reviewers for the comments and suggestions

1) We uploaded a revised version that contains experiments on CIFAR-100 dataset. We results on the CIFAR-100 are consistent with results on other data set and show that the performance of our method is better than previous methods.   

2) In the uploaded revised version we also addressed the scalability issue of the method in case of many classes. In our approach we initialized the second soft-max layer using the confusion matrix of the baseline system. The confusion matrix is a good estimation of the label noise.  Assume the rows of the matrix correspond to the true labels and the matrix columns correspond to the noisy labels. The k largest elements in the i-th row are the most occurring noisy class values when the true class value is i.    We can thus connect  i-th elements in the first softmax layer only to its k most probable noisy class  candidates.  (Note that if we connect the i-label in the first softmax only to the i-label in the second softmax layer,  we obtain the standard baseline model.) Taking only k connections to the second softamx layer solves the scalability problem. In the revised version we show experiments on CIFAR-100  that show that by using this scalable approach there is no performance degradation.

This is a good paper where two main methods are proposed, the first one is a latent variable model and training would require the EM algorithm, alternating between estimating the true label and maximizing the parameters given a true label.

The second directly integrates out the true label and simply optimizes the p(z|x).

Pros: the paper examines a training scenario which is a real concern for big dataset which are not carefully annotated.
Cons: the results on mnist is all synthetic and it's hard to tell if this would translate to a win on real datasets.

Equation 11 should be expensive, what happens if you are training on imagenet with 1000 classes?
It would be nice to see how well you can recover the corrupting distribution parameter using either the EM or the integration method. 

Overall, this is an OK paper. However, the ideas are not novel as previous cited papers have tried to handle noise in the labels. I think the authors can make the paper better by either demonstrating state-of-the-art results on a dataset known to have label noise, or demonstrate that a method can reliably estimate the true label corrupting probabilities.

The paper addressed the erroneous label problem for supervised training. The problem is well formulated and the presented solution is novel. 

The experimental justification is limited. The effectiveness of the proposed method is hard to gauge, especially how to scale the proposed method to large number of classification targets and whether it is still effective.

For example, it would be interesting to see whether the proposed method is better than training with only less but high quality data. 

From Figure 2, it seems with more data, the proposed method tends to behave very well when the noise fraction is below a threshold and dramatically degrades once passing that threshold. Analysis and justification of this behavior whether it is just by chance or an expected one of the method would be very useful.

machine_text: Overall this is a very interesting and well-executed research, using reinforcement learning to learn how to compose sentences from words. I think the paper is well-written and adds interesting perspective on the use of reinforcement learning for language learning. Here are some points for improvement. 1) I wonder if the model could have learned to sequence the words differently, eg. by using a simple lookup table. This would allow the model to attend to different parts of the input sequence separately, and perhaps learn some higher-level sentence concepts. 2) I also think it would be interesting to try this model on other datasets besides MCTest. In particular, it would be interesting to try it on the LAMBADA dataset, which is much larger and has questions about a much broader range of linguistic phenomena. 3) I also wonder about applying this model to low-resource languages. It would be interesting to try this on a language with very little available training data, to see if the model can learn a reasonable level of competence. 4) Related to this, it would also be interesting to try this model on languages with different levels of complexity, for example languages with different degrees of morphosyntactic alignment. It would be interesting to see if the model requires a higher level of complexity in the language (as measured by the number of markers) to gain the ability to sequence the words into sentences. I hope these suggestions are helpful. Overall this is a very interesting and well-conceived research program, and I think the model shows promise for language acquisition in general. All the best, Jeff Date: 2022-05-01 Reviewer: Dr. Jorge Cham, Research Scientist General comments: This is an interesting and well written paper addressing a very timely topic: the use of reinforcement learning to teach low level tasks. This work combines a state-of-the-art sequence to sequence model with an effective reinforcement learning scheme to generate sequences of words that can be fed into a simple story-generation model. The model is trained on a simple benchmark dataset, the MCTest, and after one hundred and fifty hours of training the model is able to generate coherent sentences with a decent amount of specific details. The resulting model is evaluated on the LAMBADA dataset, which is much more challenging and is usually used to evaluate machine translation systems. The results show that the model generates decent but not yet perfect translations. However, the most interesting result is the positive reinforcement learning algorithm is able to generate grammatical sentences from the most basic form of instructions: a list of words. This is very surprising as most existing work on the topic focus on the automatic segmentation and generation of sentences from logical arguments, and the generation of complete, grammatical and syntactically correct sentences requires a compositional semantics and complex high-level syntactic structure. The results of the present model suggest that it is possible to teach a model a low-level task (composing sentences from words) without requiring high-level understanding of the syntax or semantic. This result is more than promising and can have many applications in areas such as education or text generation. In education, the model can be used to create textbooks for very specific topics, sentences from these texts can be provided to students as input and the students have to write down the sentences themselves. Alternatively, sentences generated by the model could be the output of a tutoring system and the student have to write the sentences based on the hints given by the system. In text generation, the sentences generated by the model can be used as input to an automatic summarization system or even a chatbot. For example, you can type in a sentence to Siri and you can train the system on how to respond to sentences that are fed to it as input. The present model can help the system generate a response that sound natural and that the user will consider appropriate. In this paper, the authors propose a new method to learn hierarchical representations of sentences, based on reinforcement learning. They propose to learn a neural shift-reduce parser, such that the induced tree structures lead to good performance on a downstream task. They use reinforcement learning (more specifically, the policy gradient method REINFORCE) to learn their model. The reward of the algorithm is the evaluation metric of the downstream task. The authors compare two settings, (1) no structure information is given (hence, the only supervision comes from the downstream task) and (2) actions from an external parser is used as supervision to train the policy network, in addition to the supervision from the downstream task. The proposed approach is evaluated on four tasks: sentiment analysis, semantic relatedness, textual entailment and sentence generation.

I like the idea of learning tree representations of text which are useful for a downstream task. The paper is clear and well written. However, I am not convinced by the experimental results presented in the paper. Indeed, on most tasks, the proposed model is far from state-of-the-art models:
 - sentiment analysis, 86.5 v.s. 89.7 (accuracy);
 - semantic relatedness, 0.32 v.s. 0.25 (MSE);
 - textual entailment, 80.5 v.s. 84.6 (accuracy).
From the results presented in the paper, it is hard to know if these results are due to the model, or because of the reinforcement learning algorithm.

PROS:
 - interesting idea: learning structures of sentences adapted for a downstream task.
 - well written paper.
CONS:
 - weak experimental results (do not really support the claim of the authors).

Minor comments:
In the second paragraph of the introduction, one might argue that bag-of-words is also a predominant approach to represent sentences.
Paragraph titles (e.g. in section 3.2) should have a period at the end.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
UPDATE

I am still not convinced by the results presented in the paper, and in particular by the fact that one must combine the words in a different way than left-to-right to obtain state of the art results.
However, I do agree that this is an interesting research direction, and that the results presented in the paper are promising. I am thus updating my score from 5 to 6.

All the reviewers agreed that the research direction is very interesting, and generally find the results promising. We could quibble a bit about the results not being really state-of-the-art and the choice of baselines, but I think the main claims are well supported by the experiments (i.e. the induce grammar appears to be useful for the problem in question, within the specific class of models). There are still clearly many issues unresolved, and we are yet to see if this class of methods (RL / implicit structure-based) can lead to state-of-the-art results on any important NLP problem. But it is too much to ask from a submission. I see the paper as a strong contribution to the conference.

I have not much to add to my pre-review comments.
It's a very well written paper with an interesting idea.
Lots of people currently want to combine RL with NLP. It is very en vogue.
Nobody has gotten that to work yet in any really groundbreaking or influential way that results in actually superior performance on any highly relevant or competitive NLP task.
Most people struggle with the fact that NLP requires very efficient methods on very large datasets and RL is super slow.
Hence, I believe this direction hasn't shown much promise yet and it's not yet clear it ever will due to the slowness of RL.
But many directions need to be explored and maybe eventually they will reach a point where they become relevant.

It is interesting to learn the obviously inherent grammatical structure in language though sadly again, the trees here do not yet capture much of what our intuitions are.

Regardless, it's an interesting exploration, worthy of being discussed at the conference.

The paper proposes to use reinforcement learning to learn how to compose the words in a sentence, i.e. parse tree, that can be helpful for the downstream tasks. To do that, the shift-reduce framework is employed and RL is used to learn the policy of the two actions SHIFT and REDUCE. The experiments on four datasets (SST, SICK, IMDB, and SNLI) show that the proposed approach outperformed the approach using predefined tree structures (e.g. left-to-right, right-to-left). 

The paper is well written and has two good points. Firstly, the idea of using RL to learn parse trees using downstream tasks is very interesting and novel. And employing the shift-reduce framework is a very smart choice because the set of actions is minimal (shift and reduce). Secondly, what shown in the paper somewhat confirms the need of parse trees. This is indeed interesting because of the current debate on whether syntax is helpful.

I have the following comments:
- it seems that the authors weren't aware of some recent work using RL to learn structures for composition, e.g. Andreas et al (2016).
- because different composition functions (e.g. LSTM, GRU, or classical recursive neural net) have different inductive biases, I was wondering if the tree structures found by the model would be independent from the composition function choice.
- because RNNs in theory are equivalent to Turing machines, I was wondering if restricting the expressiveness of the model (e.g. reducing the dimension) can help the model focus on discovering more helpful tree structures.

The work is very interesting and will have its place in the literature. The novelty of the work is the introduction of a framework to analyze transferability across models and attack methods. The main drawback is the introduction of several acronyms that could have been defined earlier in the text which makes it difficult to understand the main message of the introduction. However, the core of the paper is excellent and deserves to be published. Methods The manuscript describes a new adversary, called Adversarial Black-Box (or ABK) which is much more powerful than existing ones. The ABK requires the black-box model to make just one forward and one backward pass to be able to generate (or re-generate) an adversarial example. The construction of the ABK is novel and pretty clever. The ABK is tested on various black-box models (e.g., deepdream, faceNet, LIME) and on a wide range of attacks. The ABK works surprisingly well against all of them and is the most effective black-box adversary ever. The evaluation of the ABK is done in two ways. First, as a black-box attack: Adversarial examples found by the ABK are shown to be transferable across models and attacks. Second, as a defense, the ABK is used to generate defenses against existing attacks. The defense is excellent. Adversarial examples generated by the ABK on one model do not seem to be transferable to other models. That suggests that the defense based on the ABK has found a natural polymorphism. The performance of the ABK in black-box settings are impressive. The paper Delving into Transferable Adversarial Examples and Black-box Attacks addresses the transferability of adversarial examples among different architectures and its associated security implications. The paper provides an in-depth study of transferable adversarial examples both non-targeted and targeted. First, the paper explores the transferability of adversarial examples using a large scale dataset. They show that while transferable non-targeted adversarial examples are easy to find, targeted adversarial examples generated using existing approaches almost never transfer with their target labels. Therefore, they propose ensemble-based approaches to generating transferable adversarial examples. Using such approaches, they observe a large proportion of targeted adversarial examples that are able to transfer with their target labels for the first time. In addition, the authors study the transferability of adversarial examples in geometric terms and provide empirical evidences to demonstrate that adversarial examples can transfer even across different optimization methods and defense strategies. The proposed approaches and studies are important to help understanding the transferability of adversarial examples and their potential threat to security. Despite its interesting findings, this paper has some limitations. First, although the authors show that ensemble-based approaches are effective in generating transferable adversarial examples, the paper only provides empirical evidences for targeted transfer. It is not guaranteed that the same approach would also work for untargeted transfer. In addition, adversarial examples generated using ensemble-based approaches are subject to the randomness of random search. It is possible that with a large number of searches, the ensemble-based approach may fail to find an ensemble solution that generates good transferable adversarial examples. It is also unclear how to systematically search for an effective ensemble solution. Therefore, the effectiveness of ensemble-based approaches should be taken with a grain of salt. Overall, this is an important and interesting paper that explores the transferability of adversarial examples among different architectures and their associated security implications. The paper also provides insights into the effectiveness of ensemble-based approaches for generating transferable adversarial examples. Some Limitations: Although the paper shows that ensemble-based approaches are effective in generating transferable adversarial examples, the paper only provides empirical evidence for targeted transfer. It is not guaranteed that the same approach would also work for untargeted transfer. In addition, the effectiveness of ensemble-based approaches is subject to the randomness of the random search. It is possible that with a large number of searches, the ensemble-based approach may fail to find an ensemble solution that generates good transferable adversarial examples. It is also unclear how to systematically search for an effective ensemble solution.
human_text:
I reviewed the manuscript as of December 7th.

Summary:
The authors investigate the transferability of adversarial examples in deep networks. The authors confirm that transferability exists even in large models but demonstrate that it is difficult to manipulate the network to adversarially perturb an image into a specifically desired label. The authors additionally demonstrate real world attacks on a vision web service and explore the geometric properties of adversarial examples.

Major Comments:
1. The paper contains a list of many results and it is not clear what single message this paper provides. As mentioned in the comments, this paper is effectively 15 pages and 9 page of results in the Appendix heavily discussed throughout the main body of the paper. Although there is no strict page limit for this conference, I do feel this pushes the spirit of a conference publication. I do not rule out this paper for acceptance based on the length but I do hold it as a negative because clarity of presentation is an important quality. If this paper is ultimately accepted, I would suggest that the authors make some effort to cut down the length even further beyond the 13 pages posted elsewhere. I have marked some sections to highlight areas that may be trimmed.

2. The section of geometric understanding is similar to results of 'Adversarial Perturbations of Deep Neural Networks' in Warde-Farley and Goodfellow (2015). See Figure 1.2. I am not clear what the authors show above-and-beyond these results. If there are additional findings, the authors should emphasize them.

3. The authors expand on observations by Goodfellow et al (2014) and Szegedy et al (2013) demonstrating that large-scale models are susceptible to adversarial perturbations (see also Kurakin et al (2016)). The authors additionally demonstrate that attempting to perform adversarial manipulation to convert an image to a particular, desired label is more difficult.

4. The authors demonstrate that they can target a real-world vision API. These results are compelling but it is not clear what these results demonstrate above-and-beyond Papernot et al (2016). 

As far I can understand, I think that the most interesting result from this paper not previously described in the literature is to note about the unique difficulty about performing adversarial manipulation to convert an image to a particular, desired label. The rest of the results appear to expand on other results that have already appeared in the literature and the authors need to better explain what these makes these results unique above-and-beyond previous work.

Areas to Trim the Paper:
- Table 1 is not necessary. Just cite other results or write the Top-1 numbers in the text.
- Condense Section 2.2.1 and cite heavily.
- Figure 2 panels may be overlaid to highlight a comparison.

The paper is the first to demonstrate that it is possible for an adversary to change the label that a convolutional network predicts for an image to a specific value. Like Papernot et al., it presents a successful attack on Clarifai's image-recognition system. I encourage the authors to condense the paper to its key results (13 pages without / 24 pages with supplemental material is too long for a conference paper).

We have updated the paper with the following changes:

1) We shrink the paper in the following aspects:
   a) Sec 2.2 is condensed
   b) We remove the original Sec 2.3, which introduces transferability and black-box attack, since all materials have been covered in Sec 1
   c) The original Table 1 is moved to the appendix Table 7
   d) The original Table 2 and Table 4 are now merged as two panels of Table 1, so that only one caption needs be provided.
   e) The alternative approach to generate non-targeted adversarial images is moved to the appendix
   f) The paragraph discussing different models make the same mistake in original Sec 3.1 is moved to the appendix
   g) The paragraph discussing that adversarial images may come from multiple intervals along the gradient direction is moved to the appendix
   h) The results for random perturbation in original Sec 3.2 is moved to the appendix.
   i) We move the original Table 9 in Section 6 about cosine values between pairs of gradients to the appendix Table 33

2) We provide a contribution and organization paragraph in Section 1 to highlight the the main conclusions of this work and to facilitate readers to follow the arguments in the paper to support our conclusions.

3) In related work, we highlight the difference between our work and Papernot et al (2016ab) by explaining why our black-box attack is harder. Also, we discuss Fawzi et al (2016) at the beginning of Section 6.

4) We provide justification of why we choose three ResNet models in Section 2.3, and highlight the findings about the transferability between both homogeneous architectures (i.e., ResNet models) and heterogeneous architectures in various places (i.e., Section 3.1, Section 5 and Section 6).

We welcome new comments!

The paper presents an interesting and very detailed study of targeted and non-targeted adversarial examples in CNNs.

I’m on the fence about this paper but am leaning towards acceptance. Such detailed empirical explorations are difficult and time-consuming to construct yet can serve as important stepping stones for future work. I see the length of the paper as a strength since it allows for a very in-depth look into the effectiveness and transferability of different kinds of adversarial examples.  

There are, however, some concerns:

1) While the length of the paper is a strength in my mind, the key contributions should be made much more clear. As evidenced by my comment earlier, I got confused at some point between the ensemble/non-ensemble method, and about the contribution of the Clarifai evaluation and what I should be focusing on where. I’d strongly suggest a radical revision which more clearly focuses the story: 

- First, we demonstrate that non-targeted attacks are easy while targeted attacks are hard (evidenced by a key experiment comparing the two; we refer to appendix or later sections for the extensive exploration of e.g., current Section 3)

- Thus, we propose an ensemble method that is able to handle targeted attacks much better (evidenced by experiments focusing on the comparison between ensemble and non-ensemble method, both in a controlled setting and on Clarifai)

- Also, here are all the other details and explorations. 

2) Instead of using ResNet-152, Res-Net-101 and ResNet-50 as three of the five models, it would've been better to use one ResNet architecture and the other two, say, AlexNet and Network-in-Network. This would make the ensemble results a lot more compelling.

This paper present an experimental study of the robustness of state-of-the-art CNNs to different types of "attacks" in the context of image classication. Specifically, an attack aims to fool the classification system with a specially corrupted image, i.e. making it misclassify the image as (1) any wrong class (non-targeted attack) or (2) a target class, chosen in advance by the attacker (targeted attack). For instance, the attacker could corrupt an image of an ostrich in such a way that it would be classified as a megalith. Even though the attacker's agenda is not so clear in this example, it is still interesting to study the weaknesses of current systems in view of (1) improving them in general and (2) actual risks with e.g. autonomous vehicles.

The paper is mostly experimental. In short, it compares different strategies (already published in previous papers) for all popular networks  (VGG, GoogLeNet, ResNet-50/101/152) and the two aforementionned types of attacks. The experiments are well conducted and clearly exposed. A convincing point is that attacks are also conducted on "clarifai.com" which is a black-box classification system. Some analysis and insightful explanations are also provided to help understanding why CNNs are prone to such attacks (Section 6).

To sum up, the main findings are that non-targeted attacks are easy to perform, even on a black-box system. Non-targeted attacks are more difficult to realize with existing schemes, but the authors propose a new approach for that that vastly improves over existing attacks (even though it's still far from perfect: ~20% success rate on clarifai.com versus 2% with previous schemes).

Arguably, The paper still has some weaknesses:

 - The authors are treating the 3 ResNet-based networks as different, yet they are obviously clearly correlated. See Table 7 for instance. This is naturally expected because their architecture is similar (only their depth varies). Hence, it does not sound very fair to state that "One interesting finding is that [...] the first misclassified label (non-targeted) is the same for all models except VGG-16 and GoogLeNet.", i.e., the three ResNet-based networks.

 - A subjective measure is employed to evaluate the effectiveness of the attacks on the black box system. While this is for a good reason (clarifai.com returns image labels that are different from ImageNet), it is not certain that the reported numbers are fair (even though the qualitative results look convincing).

 - The novelty of the proposed approach (optimizing an ensemble of network instead of a single network) is limited. However, this was not really the point of the paper, and it is effective, so it seems ok overall.

 - The paper is quite long. This is expected because it is an extensive evaluation study, but still. I suggest the authors prune some near-duplicate content (e.g. Section 2.3 has a high overlap with Section 1, etc.).

 - The paper would benefit from additional discussions with the recent and related work of Fawzi et al (NIPS'16) in Section 6. Indeed the work of Fawzi et al. is mostly theoretical and well aligned with the experimental findings and observations (in particular in Section 6).


To conclude, I think that this paper is somewhat useful for the community and could help to further improve existing architectures, as well as better assess their flaws and weaknesses.

Summary:
The authors investigate the transferability of adversarial examples in deep networks. The authors confirm that transferability exists even in large models but demonstrate that it is difficult to manipulate the network to adversarially perturb an image into a specifically desired label. The authors additionally demonstrate real world attacks on a vision web service and explore the geometric properties of adversarial examples.

Major Comments:
1. The paper contains a list of many results and it is not clear what single message this paper provides. As mentioned in the comments, this paper is effectively 15 pages and 9 page of results in the Appendix heavily discussed throughout the main body of the paper. Although there is no strict page limit for this conference, I do feel this pushes the spirit of a conference publication. I do not rule out this paper for acceptance based on the length but I do hold it as a negative because clarity of presentation is an important quality. If this paper is ultimately accepted, I would suggest that the authors make some effort to cut down the length even further beyond the 13 pages posted elsewhere. I have marked some sections to highlight areas that may be trimmed.

2. The section of geometric understanding is similar to results of 'Adversarial Perturbations of Deep Neural Networks' in Warde-Farley and Goodfellow (2015). See Figure 1.2. I am not clear what the authors show above-and-beyond these results. If there are additional findings, the authors should emphasize them.

3. The authors expand on observations by Goodfellow et al (2014) and Szegedy et al (2013) demonstrating that large-scale models are susceptible to adversarial perturbations (see also Kurakin et al (2016)). The authors additionally demonstrate that attempting to perform adversarial manipulation to convert an image to a particular, desired label is more difficult.

4. The authors demonstrate that they can target a real-world vision API. These results are compelling but it is not clear what these results demonstrate above-and-beyond Papernot et al (2016).

The paper presents an interesting and very detailed study of targeted and non-targeted adversarial examples in CNNs.

I’m on the fence about this paper but am leaning towards acceptance. Such detailed empirical explorations are difficult and time-consuming to construct yet can serve as important stepping stones for future work. I see the length of the paper as a strength since it allows for a very in-depth look into the effectiveness and transferability of different kinds of adversarial examples.  

There are, however, some concerns:

1) While the length of the paper is a strength in my mind, the key contributions should be made much more clear. As evidenced by my comment earlier, I got confused at some point between the ensemble/non-ensemble method, and about the contribution of the Clarifai evaluation and what I should be focusing on where. I’d strongly suggest a radical revision which more clearly focuses the story: 

- First, we demonstrate that non-targeted attacks are easy while targeted attacks are hard (evidenced by a key experiment comparing the two; we refer to appendix or later sections for the extensive exploration of e.g., current Section 3)

- Thus, we propose an ensemble method that is able to handle targeted attacks much better (evidenced by experiments focusing on the comparison between ensemble and non-ensemble method, both in a controlled setting and on Clarifai)

- Also, here are all the other details and explorations. 

2) Instead of using ResNet-152, Res-Net-101 and ResNet-50 as three of the five models, it would've been better to use one ResNet architecture and the other two, say, AlexNet and Network-in-Network. This would make the ensemble results a lot more compelling.

This paper present an experimental study of the robustness of state-of-the-art CNNs to different types of "attacks" in the context of image classication. Specifically, an attack aims to fool the classification system with a specially corrupted image, i.e. making it misclassify the image as (1) any wrong class (non-targeted attack) or (2) a target class, chosen in advance by the attacker (targeted attack). For instance, the attacker could corrupt an image of an ostrich in such a way that it would be classified as a megalith. Even though the attacker's agenda is not so clear in this example, it is still interesting to study the weaknesses of current systems in view of (1) improving them in general and (2) actual risks with e.g. autonomous vehicles.

The paper is mostly experimental. In short, it compares different strategies (already published in previous papers) for all popular networks  (VGG, GoogLeNet, ResNet-50/101/152) and the two aforementionned types of attacks. The experiments are well conducted and clearly exposed. A convincing point is that attacks are also conducted on "clarifai.com" which is a black-box classification system. Some analysis and insightful explanations are also provided to help understanding why CNNs are prone to such attacks (Section 6).

To sum up, the main findings are that non-targeted attacks are easy to perform, even on a black-box system. Non-targeted attacks are more difficult to realize with existing schemes, but the authors propose a new approach for that that vastly improves over existing attacks (even though it's still far from perfect: ~20% success rate on clarifai.com versus 2% with previous schemes).

Arguably, The paper still has some weaknesses:

 - The authors are treating the 3 ResNet-based networks as different, yet they are obviously clearly correlated. See Table 7 for instance. This is naturally expected because their architecture is similar (only their depth varies). Hence, it does not sound very fair to state that "One interesting finding is that [...] the first misclassified label (non-targeted) is the same for all models except VGG-16 and GoogLeNet.", i.e., the three ResNet-based networks.

 - A subjective measure is employed to evaluate the effectiveness of the attacks on the black box system. While this is for a good reason (clarifai.com returns image labels that are different from ImageNet), it is not certain that the reported numbers are fair (even though the qualitative results look convincing).

 - The novelty of the proposed approach (optimizing an ensemble of network instead of a single network) is limited. However, this was not really the point of the paper, and it is effective, so it seems ok overall.

 - The paper is quite long. This is expected because it is an extensive evaluation study, but still. I suggest the authors prune some near-duplicate content (e.g. Section 2.3 has a high overlap with Section 1, etc.).

 - The paper would benefit from additional discussions with the recent and related work of Fawzi et al (NIPS'16) in Section 6. Indeed the work of Fawzi et al. is mostly theoretical and well aligned with the experimental findings and observations (in particular in Section 6).


To conclude, I think that this paper is somewhat useful for the community and could help to further improve existing architectures, as well as better assess their flaws and weaknesses.

In addition, I have some questions about the choices made in the implementation and evaluation of the system. For example, the authors use word embedding to represent the labels. I understand why word embedding is used but I would like to see what the performance would be if they used e.g. a a recurrent neural network (RNN) with long short-term memory (LSTM) cells. Furthermore, it would be good to see some independent verification that the system actually does what it is supposed to do. For example, can the authors provide a test set of known impostors along with the genuine samples and some measure of the performance of the system? This paper presents a framework for introducing a unique identity parameter in the deep learning training process. The paper then applies this framework to facial recognition, using a customizable approach to ensure fairness in identifying and representing different demographic groups in the dataset. The core idea is to introduce a new parameter which randomly switches between the standard neural network architecture and an identity-specific variation during training. The variations alter the loss calculation to discourage fitting to the specific identity instead of general model behavior. This approach has three key strengths. Firstly, it can add robustness to existing models by preventing extraction of explicit features which identify a specific individual. Secondly, it can be easily combined with other techniques to improve representation of sub-groups. Finally, it introduces minimal additional compute, making it suitable for deployment on existing models with minimal impact to performance. The paper provides several examples of how this framework can be applied to existing models and shows improvements over existing practice in identifying underrepresented demographics. details The authors introduce a framework that applies to facial recognition and customizable identity parameters to improve fairness and performance. The paper has three main strengths: 1) it reduces the risk of identifying explicit features that identify an individual; 2) it can be combined with other techniques to improve underrepresented demographic representation; and 3) it only requires a minimal computational cost, making it suitable for deployment on existing models. The paper also has weaknesses, which include the need to evaluate the impact on performance, and demonstrate its efficacy on existing models. benefit The authors introduce a framework that applies to facial recognition and customizable identity parameters to improve fairness and performance.

This paper puts the principle of identity parameterization on a more solid theoretical footing alongside further empirical progress. First, it gives a strikingly simple proof that arbitrarily deep linear residual networks have no spurious local optima. The same result for feed-forward networks in their standard parameterization is substantially more delicate. Second, it shows that residual networks with ReLu activations have universal finite-sample expressivity in the sense that the network can represent any function of its sample provided that the model has more parameters than the sample size. The same result for feed-forward networks in their standard parameterization is substantially more delicate. Independently, we experiment with a radically simple residual architecture consisting of only residual convolutional layers and ReLu activations, but no batch normalization, dropout, or max pool. Our model improves significantly on previous all-convolutional networks on the CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and ImageNet classification benchmarks. Overall, this paper is an excellent contribution to the rich tradition of rigorous design principles in machine learning. The ideas of identity representation and universal approximation by residual networks are already fascinating in their own right and this paper makes them intuitive and practically useful to practitioners. Some minor issues: - The first theorem in Section 2.1 could use a proof sketch. - The formulation of the universal approximation theorem (1) can be misleading since it implies that the representer theorem could in principle be applied to a non-linear problem. In fact, the representer theorem applies only to linear problems. A general method for constructing a universal approximation bound using the representer theorem without analyzing the problem family as a whole would be interesting. - Some of the English is a bit clumsy. Other than these minor issues, this is a very good paper. We have no strong objections to the paper as it stands. The only outstanding issue is the lack of experiments with the representer theorem. We would need to understand the approximation bounds that the theorem produces in order to properly evaluate the guarantees that it conveys. I would like to stress, though, that the representer theorem remains a very powerful and useful tool for proving upper bounds on the performance of learning algorithms, and this paper nicely demonstrates its wide applicability in the context of deep learning. Overall, we encourage the authors to submit the paper to a journal where these points can be adequately addressed. On the whole, very good paper! We look forward to seeing further progress in this very promising research direction! Best, The Gang of 88"

The paper begins by presenting a simple analysis for deep linear networks. This is more to demonstrate the intuitions behind their derivations, and does not have practical relevance. They then extend to non-linear resnets with ReLU units and demonstrate that they have finite sample expressivity. They formally establish these results. Inspired by their theory, they perform experiments using simpler architectures without any batch norm, dropout or other regularizations and fix the last layer and still attain competitive results. Indeed, they admit that data augmentation is a form of regularization and can replace other regularization schemes. 
 I think the paper meets the threshold to be accepted.

This paper provides some theoretical guarantees for the identity parameterization by showing that 1) arbitrarily deep linear residual networks have no spurious local optima; and 2) residual networks with ReLu activations have universal finite-sample expressivity. This paper is well written and studied a fundamental problem in deep neural network. I am very positive on this paper overall and feel that this result is quite significant by essentially showing the stability of auto-encoder, given the fact that it is hard to provide concrete theoretical guarantees for deep neural networks.

One of key questions is how to extent the result in this paper to the more general nonlinear actuation function case.

Dear colleague, I have carefully read your article, "Adversarial Feature Learning" and have a few points to share. First, I would like to ask, "What problem or question is this paper addressing?" The paper "Adversarial Feature Learning" by Zheng, Jun, et al. addresses whether feature learning from adversarial examples can benefit the feature learning task itself. The authors created "Attacker" and "Attacked" networks, where the Attacker network was trained to find the optimal inputs to a target network, which were classified as true. The Attacker network output features were then used to train a "Defender" network, which attempted to classify the Attacker output as true. The Attacker and Attacked networks were then combined to create the "Joint" network, which analyzed images to determine if they were true or not. Second, I would like to highlight "Strengths" of this paper. First, the attack and defense approach is innovative and has not been explored before. Second, the authors' usage of GANs to create the Defender network from scratch rather than finetuning from a pre-trained model was a new approach. The authors demonstrated this method on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets. Third, the authors performed an extensive evaluation of the Defender's performance and hyperparameter tuning. Finally, the authors created a toolkit of code and pretrained models for the Joint network, making the re-implementation of this research easy. Third, I would like to highlight "Weaknesses" of this paper. First, although the Joint network was shown to be very good at identifying adversarial examples, it did not perform as well on non-adversarial examples. The authors mentioned that the Defense approach was "challenging" in identifying non-adversarial inputs. This may be because the Defender was not optimized to classify non-adversarial inputs. Second, the authors also did not evaluate how much better the Joint network actually performed than the individual networks (Attacker, Attacker, and Attacker). Third, CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets are not domains where adversarial examples are common, which limited the Generalizability of this method. Overall, this paper has excellent ideas and a strong foundation for future work. However, the method of using an Attacker network to generate attacks for the Attacker to train a Defender network would likely need a larger dataset of adversarial examples and a longer training period to create a model with strong robustness. I recommend the authors try to generate attacks for the Defender network on a different dataset, such as CIFAR-10 or ImageNet, and evaluate the results. In addition, the CIFAR-10 dataset is too small for adversarial examples to be prevalent, so an evaluation of how well the Defender network identified non-adversarial inputs in the CIFAR-10 dataset would be beneficial. Overall, this is an excellent paper that addresses a problem that has not been explored before and provides a strong foundation for future work. I recommend the authors consider my comments when building on this work and submitting this paper to a journal.

The paper is providing a good approach to learn the feature representation based on Bidirectional Generative Adversarial Networks. The idea of learning the feature representation using GANs framework is interesting and motivate. However, in the paper, the authors only learn the mapping from latent space to data space. The paper only show the feature representation learned from the generated data can be used to accomplish the discrimination task in the data space. In order to make the feature representation learned from the GANs framework more useful, the authors should also be able to use it to accomplish discrimination task in the latent space. For example, the disambiguation of between different data points with the same (or similar) latent representation. The discriminator in the Bidirectional Generative Adversarial Networks may be trained to classify whether the input features come from the real data distribution or the generated distribution. In this case, the feature representation learned from the BiGANs can also be used to accomplish discrimination task in the latent space. I would suggest the authors to evaluate the learned feature representation from the BiGANs on this additional task. The evaluation on this additional task may give the authors more insights about the real usage of such feature representation in practice. overview of the Bidirectional Generative Adversarial Networks The BiGANs model consists of two GAN models, which work in opposite directions. The model learns to generate data from the data space to the latent space, and learns to generate latent from the latent space to the data space. Such two-way flow of information exchange allows the model to train each generator from the exactly opposite viewpoint, and results in the feature representation which can be used for both data space and latent space discrimination. In addition, the BiGANs model also includes a discriminator model, which takes in two sets of features from the two generators, and outputs the discrimination results. The discriminator model is trained to distinguish whether the two sets of features are from the same data distribution or different.

The authors extend GANs by an inference path from the data space to the latent space and a discriminator that operates on the joint latend/data space. They show that the theoretical properties of GANs still hold for BiGAN and evaluate the features learned unsupervised in the inference path with respect to performance on supervised tasks after retraining deeper layers.

I see one structural issue with this paper: Given that, as stated in the abstract, the main purpose of the paper is to learn unsupervised features (and not to improve GANs), the paper might spent too much space on detailing the relationship to GANs and all the theoretical properties. It is not clear whether they actually would help with the goal of learning good features. While reading the paper, I actually totally forgot about the unsupervised features until they reappeared on page 6. I think it would be helpful if the text of the paper would be more aligned with this main story.

Still, the BiGAN framework is an elegant and compelling extension to GANs. However, it is not obvious how much the theoretical properties help us as the model is clearly not fully converged. To me, especially Figure 4 seems to suggest that G(E(x)) might be doing not much more than some kind of nearest neighbour retrival (and indeed one criticism for GANs has always been that they might just memorize some samples). By the way, it would be very interesting to know how well the discriminator actually performs after training.

Coming back to the goal of learning powerful features: The method does not reach state-of-the-art performance on most evaluated tasks (Table 2 and 3) but performs competitive and it would be interesting to see how much this improves if the BiGAN training (and the convolutional architecture used) would be improved.

The paper is very well written and provides most necessary details, although some more details on the training (learning rates, initialization) would be helpful for reproducing the results.

Overall I think the paper provides a very interesting framework for further research, even though the results presented here are not too impressive both with respect to the feature evaluation (and the GAN learning).

Minor: It might be helpful to highlight the best performance numbers in Tables 2 and 3.

Note: the latest version includes significantly improved ImageNet classification results in Table 2 (up ~2% across the board compared to the previous version).  This is due to the fact that in previous versions, we evaluated using the predictions for a single (center) crop at test time, rather than averaging over 10 crops as we learned by correspondence was how the previous results from Noroozi & Favaro (2016) were obtained.  (Thanks to Mehdi for bringing this up!) There are also very slightly improved VOC classification results (Table 3) due to an unrelated minor bug.
All reviewers unanimously praised the novelty and quality of the paper. Minor revisions, following the reviewers' suggestions, will make the paper even better.

We thank all reviewers for their thoughtful comments and suggestions. We’ve uploaded a revision with an expanded introduction which clarifies the motivation for BiGAN and the theory in Section 3 in the context of feature learning.

Note that our theoretical arguments go beyond simply showing that BiGAN maintains the properties of the original GAN framework.  In particular, we show that the BiGAN objective is equivalent to that of an “L0 autoencoder”, encouraging the encoder and generator to invert one another (Theorem 3). If fully optimized, the encoder and generator are inverses of one another almost everywhere (Theorem 2).  We believe that these insights are quite important to understanding BiGAN’s behavior and its use as a model for feature learning.  We hope that the revised introduction explains this better.

With respect to the ImageNet visual feature learning evaluation, our results show BiGAN is state-of-the-art among purely unsupervised learning methods.  The methods that outperform BiGAN (e.g., Doersch et al.) are all based on “self-supervision,” requiring the design of a domain-specific supervised prediction task, and some (Agrawal et al. and Wang & Gupta) are “weakly supervised,” requiring auxiliary information (video, egomotion, or tracking) unavailable in images alone.  We’ve reorganized Table 3 to emphasize this point, and added discussion to Section 4.4 on the benefits of purely unsupervised approaches vs. self-supervised approaches.  (Following your suggestion, we’ve also bolded the best results of each group in Tables 2 and 3.)  We do agree, however, that our results are somewhat preliminary and likely to improve significantly with further model architecture search and improvements to the optimization.

Most optimization details (optimization algorithm, learning rate / step size, etc.) were included in Appendix C.  In the updated version, network initialization details are now included in Appendix C as well.  We’ll also be releasing the training code.

machine_text: Overall, this paper presents an excellent research topic. There are some parts that could be strengthened and the current form could be better. I highlight some of these points below. 1. The assumption that the network is rayleigh fading is a very common one and hence this should be stated as a prior. Additionally, the calculation of the alpha and beta should be provided for the case of Rayleigh fading. 2. The channel statistics are not explored deeply in this paper. The alpha and beta are calculated assuming the standard deviation of the channel is 0.5. If we want to calculate these for a different standard deviation, we can write a lookup table. However, there could be a plot that shows alpha and beta as a function of standard deviation and this would be more intuitive. 3. The derivation of the alpha and beta can be made more rigorous. First, we can find the average of a Gaussian random variable using the probability integral. Then, we need to calculate the sum of this random variable for a given alpha and beta. Using a proper transform, this sum can be expressed as the error function. 4. The application of this work could be extended to the orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) based 5G New Radio (NR). In 5G NR, the alpha and beta are usually calculated for two different cases: one for standalone and the other for mixed operation (standalone + LTE). If the standalone case is used as a prior, the values for alpha and beta can be used in this paper. Alternatively, the mixed case can be used, and the alpha and beta must be adjusted as needed. This work could be extended to the mixed case as well. 5. There are some typos and grammatical mistakes that should be fixed. Overall, this paper presents an excellent research topic. There are some parts that could be strengthened and the current form could be improved. I recommend the author to consider these comments and make the paper stronger.

The authors propose a low complexity algorithm for decoding high dimensional, over-parameterized linear neural networks. The model has a weight, and an activation function for each neuron in the network. The model can fit arbitrary non-linear functions. In this model, the authors focus on the case when the model has a very large number of parameters, e.g. one every bit is 1, so the model has a very large number of parameters itself. The question the paper tries to answer is whether it is possible to train such a very large model in a low complexity way, so the model can fit arbitrary functions. The authors show that it is possible to train such a model by optimizing a sequence of problems, each with a low-complexity, and each corresponding to a hard approximation of the previous problem in the sequence. The last step in the sequence, correspond to the desired arbitrary function. The main strength of this work is that it provides the first low-complexity algorithm for training very large neural networks. This is achieved by solving a sequence of low complexity approximation problems, where each approximation is good enough to ensure good generalization for the next problem in the sequence. The main limitation of this work is that it only provides a proof-of-concept for very high dimensional over-parameterized models, and it is not known if similar results can be shown for training neural networks with less than a thousand parameters. hui The main strength of this work is that it provides the first low-complexity algorithm for training very large neural networks. The main contributions of this paper are as follows: 1. The network quantization problem is studied. We show that the optimization of network quantization is equivalent to the entropy-constrained scalar quantization problem. Two numerical solution methods, uniform quantization and iterative solution, are proposed. 2. The proposed two solutions of network quantization can achieve compression ratios of 51.25, 22.17 and 40.65, for LeNet, 32-layer ResNet and AlexNet, respectively. 3. We evaluate the quantitative relation of quantization errors to the neural network loss function and identify that the Hessian-weighted distortion measure is locally the right objective function for the optimization of network quantization.
