This paper aims to investigate the question if shallow non-convolutional networks can be as affective as deep convolutional ones for image classification, given that both architectures use the same number of parameters. 
To this end the authors conducted a series of experiments on the CIFAR10 dataset.
They find that there is a significant performance gap between the two approaches, in favour of deep CNNs. 
The experiments are well designed and involve a distillation training approach, and the results are presented in a comprehensive manner.
They also observe (as others have before) that student models can be shallower than the teacher model from which they are trained for comparable performance.

My take on these results is that they suggest that using (deep) conv nets is more effective, since this model class encodes a form of a-prori or domain knowledge that images exhibit a certain degree of translation invariance in the way they should be processed for high-level recognition tasks. The results are therefore perhaps not quite surprising, but not completely obvious either.

An interesting point on which the authors comment only very briefly is that among the non-convolutional architectures the ones using 2 or 3 hidden layers outperform those with 1, 4 or 5 hidden layers. Do you have an interpretation / hypothesis of why this is the case? It  would be interesting to discuss the point a bit more in the paper.

It was not quite clear to me why were the experiments were limited to use  30M parameters at most. None of the experiments in Figure 1 seem to be saturated. Although the performance gap between CNN and MLP is large, I think it would be worthwhile to push the experiment further for the final version of the paper.

The authors state in the last paragraph that they expect shallow nets to be relatively worse in an ImageNet classification experiment. 
Could the authors argue why they think this to be the case? 
One could argue that the much larger training dataset size could compensate for shallow and/or non-convolutional choices of the architecture. 
Since MLPs are universal function approximators, one could understand architecture choices as expressions of certain priors over the function space, and in a large-data regimes such priors could be expected to be of lesser importance.
This issue could for example be examined on ImageNet when varying the amount of training data.
Also, the much higher resolution of ImageNet images might have a non-trivial impact on the CNN-MLP comparison as compared to the results established on the CIFAR10 dataset.

Experiments on a second data set would also help to corroborate the findings, demonstrating to what extent such findings are variable across datasets.

This paper describes a careful experimental study on the CIFAR-10 task that uses data augmentation and Bayesian hyperparameter optimization to train a large number of high-quality, deep convolutional network classification models from hard (0-1) targets.  An ensemble of the 16 best models is then used as a teacher model in the distillation framework, where student models are trained to match the averaged logits from the teacher ensemble.  Data augmentation and Bayesian hyperparameter optimization is also applied in the training of the student models.  Both non-convolutional (MLP) and convolutional student models of varying depths and parameter counts are trained.  Convolutional models with the same architecture and parameter count as some of the convolutional students are also trained using hard targets and cross-entropy loss.  The experimental results show that convolutional students with only one or two convolutional layers are unable to match the results of students having more convolutional layers under the constraint that the number of parameters in all students is kept constant.

Pros
+ This is a very thorough and well designed study that make use of the best existing tools to try to answer the question of whether or not deep convolutional models need both depth and convolution.
+ It builds nicely on the preliminary results in Ba & Caruana, 2014.

Cons
- It is difficult to prove a negative, as the authors admit.  That said, this study is as convincing as possible given current theory and practice in deep learning.

machine_text: This paper presents a novel architecture for language comprehension using memory augmented neural networks. The proposed model first encodes the given question and the paragraph which contains the answer into a distributed vector representation. The encoded question representation and the encoded paragraph representation are then embedded into a memory network. The paragraph representation is used to fill in the blank in the encoded question, and the memory network produces a response by reading information from both the question and the paragraph. The response and the encoded question are then read into a soft decoder to produce a more realistic response. The generated responses tend to be semantically and syntactically correct with respect to the given questions. The proposed model is evaluated on SQuAD 2.0 dataset and achieves performance improvements over the state-of-the-art methods. I would like to thank Tori Ha for reviewing this paper. I think the paper is very well organized and makes an interesting addition to the field of memory augmented neural networks for language understanding. I recommend accepting the paper with some minor revisions. One problem that I ran into is that the paper sometimes uses the terms interchangeably, which can make it difficult to follow. For example, the title of the first section of the paper describes a neural network which "Reads and remembers", whereas the description of the model basically says that it reads and generates. In another example, the sentence: "Rather than reading from a single memory slot, our model accesses the entire memory network to compose a response." I think the paper would benefit from a clarifying text which defines many of the used terms. The model description also lacks some crucial information. For example, the model is trained on SQuAD 2.0, but no information is given on how it was trained. I think it would be useful for the reader to know how the validation set was split between training and validation, and how the model was optimized. Additionally, the model's memory and knowledge is limited to a single paragraph. I think the model could be even more interesting if it was able to understand multiple paragraphs, or if it could retrieve information from external sources like the internet. I recommend accepting the paper with these minor revisions.

This paper is about a model called Memory Augmented Neural Networks (MANN) for language comprehension. MANN extends the encoder-decoder model with a memory module to help the model retain and re-use previously mentioned information. The model uses more factual statements than personalized statements, therefore it is easier to assess the relationship between two words in the factual statements than in the personalized statements. The model achieves state-of-the-art results on a span-based sentence question classification task on the Cambridge News dataset. MANN could be a good model to use for sentence question classification. The model uses a factual statement to help solve a easier task, which is determining if two words are related in the factual statement. In contrast, it is more difficult to evaluate if two words are related in a personally stated statement. The factual statements in the Cambridge News dataset are generic and easier to identify relationships in. The model does achieve state-of-the-art results on a dataset, but it is unclear if the results can be applied to real-world datasets with more personal statements. The model also uses a BERT-style encoder which has shown to be state-of-the-art on the language understanding task of Question Answering (QA). However, using a BERT-based encoder for the language representation for the input questions and memory makes the model more computationally expensive and less practical for application. The strengths of the MANN model are achieving state-of-the-art results on the Cambridge News dataset, which is a more widely used and more generic dataset than those used for training the original MANN model. The limitations of MANN model are that it is not practical, as it is slow and uses a lot of memory, making it less scalable and less applicable to real-world use.

In this paper, we introduce a computational hypothesis testing approach based on memory augmented neural networks. Our approach involves a hypothesis testing loop that reconsiders and progressively refines a previously formed hypothesis in order to generate new hypotheses to test. We apply the proposed approach to language comprehension task by using Neural Semantic Encoders (NSE). Our NSE models achieve the state-of-the-art results showing an absolute improvement of 1.2% to 2.6% accuracy over previous results obtained by single and ensemble systems on standard machine comprehension benchmarks such as the Children's Book Test (CBT) and Who-Did-What (WDW) news article datasets. Regression analysis and classification analysis are two commonly used hypothesis testing approaches. Neural networks can be used for both of them. In this paper, we focus on the regression hypothesis testing approach. The hypothesis we test in this paper can be described by a hypothesis function: h(x) = 0, where x is the input to the hypothesis function The hypothesis testing approach we use here is based on Monte Carlo approximation of the confidence interval of the function value at the optimal solution. Our hypothesis testing approach involves a hypothesis testing loop that reconsiders and progressively refines a previously formed hypothesis in order to generate new hypotheses to test. The hypothesis testing loop consists of: 1. Calculation of the function value h(x), where x is the input to the hypothesis function; 2. Estimate of the expectation (mean) of the function value h(x), E(h(x)); 3. Computation of the confidence interval of E(h(x)), ci; 4. Decision making: do we need to reject h(x) = 0 based on the result of ci? 5. If so, what is the reason for rejection? 6. New hypothesis testing: generate a new hypothesis by changing a portion of the input x to see if the result will change. If the result does not change, then the change to input is not critical to h(x). If the result changes, then we keep this new input x to the hypothesis function, and test it. This hypothesis testing approach, when used for regression problem, reduces to a form of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) algorithm where we re-compute the function value, the expectation and the confidence interval during each forward pass. We evaluate the proposed approach on two tasks: binary classification and 10-way multi-label classification. Our approach is shown to be capable of obtaining state-of-the-art results on both tasks. We also conduct ablation studies to better understand the proposed approach. For each baseline in the ablation study, we eliminate one step from the proposed approach. The ablation study results suggest that the proposed approach is an optimal algorithm for hypothesis testing with neural networks, in the sense that each step in the proposed approach is not absolutely necessary. Our approach can be easily extended to other machine learning models that have differentiable score functions, such as deep generative models (DGMs). Our approach is different from other existing hypothesis testing methods in many aspects. First, it’s Monte Carlo based, which yields high stability and robustness against test errors. Second, it performs multi-step updates, which extends the testing sample size and thus enhances the statistical efficiency. Third, it’s interpretable, as the decision-making procedure is performed in the form of sensitivity analysis, making it very easy to understand the limitations of the hypothesis test and the confidence of the conclusion. Finally, the hypothesis testing approach we use here is very general and flexible, as it doesn’t require any special assumptions on the testing function, such as monotonicity. We also evaluate our approach on classification tasks with continuous outputs. This extension is straight-forward, as we can transform the original binary classification problem to a regression problem with the same input and output. The regression hypothesis testing approach we use here can also be applied. A limitation of the current approach is that we use Monte Carlo approximation of the confidence interval to do hypothesis testing, which incurs some loss of accuracy. We are working hard to improve this, for example, by using Monte Carlo approximation of the percentile instead of the confidence interval. We also conduct a time-consuming pilot study to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach using real-world data. The test results demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly outperforms other baseline methods in terms of hypothesis testing accuracy. We believe that the proposed approach, although it is developed for classification problems, is also useful for regression problems. In the future, we will apply the proposed approach to other regression problems. This is a very interesting and novel work. The idea of applying Monte Carlo based confidence interval to hypothesis testing is interesting and seems to work well. There is potential to use Monte Carlo approximation

This paper proposed an iterative query updating mechanism for cloze-style QA. The approach is novel and interesting and while it is only verified in the paper for two Cloze-style tasks (CBT and WDW), the concept of read/compose/write operations seem to be more general and can be potentially applied to other reasoning tasks beyond Cloze-style QA. Another advantage of the proposed model is to learn when to terminate the iteration by the so-called adaptive computation model, such that it avoids the issue of treating the number of iterations as another hyper-parameter, which is a common practice of iterative models/multi-hop reasoning in previous papers.

There are a couple places that this paper can improve. First, I would like to see the results from CNN/Daily Mail as well to have a more comprehensive comparison. Secondly, it will be useful to visualize the entire M^q sequence over time t (not just z or the query gating) to help understand better the query regression and if it is human interpretable.

This paper proposes a memory-enhanced RNN in the vein of NTM, and a novel training method for this architecture of cloze-style QA. The results seem convincing, and the training method is decently novel according to reviewers, although the evaluation seemed somewhat incomplete according to reviewers and my own reading. For instance, it is questionable whether or not the advertised human performance on CNN/DM is accurate (based on 100 samples from a 300k+ dataset), so I'm not sure this warrants not evaluating or reporting performance on it. Overall this looks like an acceptable paper, although there is room for improvement.

First I would like to apologize for the delay in reviewing.

Summary : this work introduces a novel memory based artificial neural network for reading comprehension. Experiments show improvement on state of the art.
The originality of the approach seems to be on the implementation of an iterative procedure with a loop testing that the current answer is the correct one.

In order to get a better sense of the reason for improvement it would be interesting to have a complexity and/or a time analysis of the algorithm. I might be mistaken but I don't see you reporting anything on the actual number of loops necessary in the reported experiments.

The dataset description in section 2.2, should be moved to section 4 where the other datasets are described.

Thie paper proposed an iterative memory updating model for cloze-style question-answering task. The approach is interesting, and result is good. For the paper, I have some comments:

1. Actually the model in the paper is not single model, it proposed two models. One consists of "reading", "writing", "adaptive computation" and " Answer module 2", the other one is "reading", "composing", "writing", "gate querying" and "Answer module 1". Based on the method section and the experiment, it seems the "adaptive computation" model is simpler and performs better. And without two time memory update in single iteration and composing module, the model is similar to neural turing machine.

This paper proposed an iterative query updating mechanism for cloze-style QA. The approach is novel and interesting and while it is only verified in the paper for two Cloze-style tasks (CBT and WDW), the concept of read/compose/write operations seem to be more general and can be potentially applied to other reasoning tasks beyond Cloze-style QA. Another advantage of the proposed model is to learn when to terminate the iteration by the so-called adaptive computation model, such that it avoids the issue of treating the number of iterations as another hyper-parameter, which is a common practice of iterative models/multi-hop reasoning in previous papers.

Secondly, it will be useful to visualize the entire M^q sequence over time t (not just z or the query gating) to help understand better the query regression and if it is human interpretable.

machine_text: Overall, this is a interesting and well-motivated paper. The introduction covers a nice problem and goal, with a connection to related work and clear motivation. The subsequent sections describe the proposed approach and experiment. The findings are interesting and somewhat counter-intuitive, but I think the right context for the findings. I recommend the paper for publication after addressing some points. From a conceptual perspective, I was a little confused about the relationship between the proposed hierarchical model and the standard recurrent neural network model. The paper says that the former “uses the former’s latent representation to predict the latter’s future states” (page 4), but it’s not clear how these two models relate. Some additional explanation may be helpful for readers to understand the relationship between these models, and the implications of that relationship for the proposed hierarchical model. The experiments described in the paper are interesting. I wonder how representative they are of the proposed method. For example, the videos are short, so there’s not a lot of variety in the behaviors, or variety in the number of observations per behavior. More generally, it’s not clear how representative the data is of the types of patterns that would be found in a real world setting. The model performance seems to be good, given the difficulty of the task. The full model is good at explaining the current behavior in terms of what has happened before, but the transition from simple to complex behaviors seems to come as a surprise. I wonder if that happens because the transition is not well represented in the validation set (since it is much simpler than the training set), or if the proposed model makes some incorrect assumptions about how the behavior changes. Overall, I think the paper is well-motivated and conceptually clear, although some additional background on the relationship between the model proposed here and standard RNNs would be helpful to a broad readership. I have some suggestions for improving the presentation. It’s likely that the inclusion of more mathematical notation would make the paper more accessible to a broad readership, although I also think that some of the more novel parts of the paper would be better with more context, or at least with more intuitive explanations. For example, the derivation of the equations is helpful for understanding the ideas, but it would be helpful to see some sample values of the variables in this context.

The authors present a model for learning hierarchical representations of sequences of tasks. The model is a scalable hierarchical recurrent neural network that can be used to model sequences of tasks and hyper-parameters that achieve good performance on a range of evaluation tasks. The model can be used to create a generative model of task sequences, and can be used to perform semi-supervised and reinforcement learning on task sequences. The model is trained by back-propagating through time a sampled sequence of tasks and tasks parameters, while a measure of the model's capability to explain its previous behavior is aggregated across time. The model is tested on a range of evaluation tasks, and shown to perform competitively compared to state-of-the-art. The model is presented in a a standard neural network architecture, making it relatively easy to apply to new domains, and easy to implement and test on parallel devices. The model can be trained on small datasets, and given large datasets can be used to perform semi-supervised learning. The model can be used in a reinforcement learning setting, where it can be used to optimize a parameters space in parallel, and at an unlimited rate. The model is found to be effective in learning both long and short term dependencies, as demonstrated on the task of time series prediction. The model is also shown to perform well on a range of other evaluation tasks, including reinforcement learning tabular tasks, reinforcement learning tasks with a hierarchical task space, and tasks involving predicting the performance of tasks given their past. Finally, it is shown that the model can be used to design a cost-effective teacher-supervised system for semi-supervised learning, where it is shown to be effective at providing semi-supervised learning examples for new, hard task domains.

This paper presents a framework for detecting actions from motion sequences and modeling the sensory-motor relationship of animals. The main idea is to use a Generative Recurrent Neural Network, which can both predict the next frame of the input sequence and retain some information from past inputs to help predict the current output. The model is trained by jointly optimizing the labeling part and the generative part. We test our framework on two types of tracking data, fruit fly behavior and online handwriting. The results show that 1) the model is able to detect actions that are previously unseen during training, 2) the model is able to discover high level phenomena such as writer identity and fly gender, without supervision, and 3) the simulated motion trajectories, generated by treating motion prediction as input, have realistic structure and may be used to qualitatively evaluate the model’s ability in learning control rules. Actor-Critic Reinforcement Learning with a Closed Loop Policy Gradient for Active Behavior Modeling, ICRL-18-abs-0029, Qing Lan, Junhua Mao, Hao Sun Challenges in animal behavioral modeling: the need for action pattern detection; training robust models using limited data; transfer learning. The proposed model can address these challenges. The framework can be easily adapted to different tracking data by only changing the output layer. The model can also learn to detect actions from the unlabeled sequence, which makes it more general. The model can also learn complex relationships from the unlabeled data, as it can learn writer-dependent and fly-gender dependent phenomena.
human_text:
This paper proposes a recurrent architecture for simultaneously predicting motion and action states of agents.
The paper is well written, clear in its presentation and backed up by good experiments.
They demonstrate that by forcing the network to predict motion has beneficial consequences on the classification of actions states,
allowing more accurate classification with less training data.
They also show how the information learned by the network is interpretable and organised in a hierarchy.

Weaknesses:
- a critical discussion on the interplay between motion an behaviour that is needed to experience the benefits of their proposed model is missing from the paper.
- moreover, a discussion on how this approach could scale to more challenging scenarios "involving animals" and visual input for instance and more general "behaviours" is also missing;
The criticism here is pointed at the fact that the title/abstract claim general behaviour modelling, whilst the experiments are focused on two very specific and relatively simple scenarios,
making the original claim a little bit far fetched unless its backed up by additional evidence.
Using "Insects", or "fruit flies" would be more appropriate than "animals".

Originality and Significance:
  The paper develops a recurrently coupled discriminative / generative hierarchical model, as applied to fruit-fly behavior and online handwriting. Qualitative evaluation is provided by generating motions, in addition to quantitative results. Writer identity and fly gender are learned in an unsupervised fashion. While the individual components of the solution are not particularly novel, their combination together with the detailed experimental validation makes the method potentially interesting to a broad audience. Some reviewers have concerns about the broad claims that are implied by the title and abstract, and thus it is recommended that these be refined to be more specific about the method and the applications.
 
 Quality and Clarity:
  The paper is well written.
 
 Pros:
 - interesting problem and application domains; will be of broad interest
 - useful ideas and architecture: shows that forcing the network to predictions about motion leads to improved classification
 - well written paper backed up by good experiments
 
 Cons:
 - the individual architectural features have for the most part been proposed before

Dear reviewers,

Thank you all for your feedback and suggestions.

** We have added the following changes to the paper: 
- better explanation of figures 4 and 5 in their captions
- clearer definition a bout (Section 5.1, first paragraph)
- analogy between diagonal connections and skip connections added (Section 3.1, first paragraph)

** Regarding scaling to other data
In Section 4, paragraph 1, we describe how data should be represented to fit our framework, and we have added a discussion at the end of the paper about scaling to more complex scenarios (Section 6, paragraph 2).

** In response to modeling “behavior” being too strong of a claim and that it should be replaced with “spatiotemporal behavior” or “fruit fly behavior”:
1) We qualify our statement in the abstract, stating both that we focus on motion sequences (i.e. trajectories) and that we test it on fruit flies and handwriting, which we further elaborate on in the introduction.

2) I would argue that behavior is spatiotemporal.
People from different fields may think of behavior differently, ranging from generating to observing behavior. A roboticist may think of it in terms of moving joints, an animator in terms of moving vertices, and a computer vision researcher in terms of moving pixels.

As noted by Levitis et al. (

While my above review title is too verbose, it would be a more accurate title for the paper than the current one (an overall better title would probably be somewhere in between). 

The overall approach is interesting: all three of the key techniques (aux. tasks, skip/diagonal connections, and the use of internal labels for the kind of data available) make a lot of sense.

I found some of the results hard to understand/interpret. Some of the explanation in the discussion below has been helpful (e.g. see my earlier questions about Fig 4 and 5); the paper would benefit from including more such explanations. 

It may be worthwhile very briefly mentioning the relationship of "diagonal" connections to other emerging terms for similar ideas (e.g. skip connections, etc). "Skip" seems to me to be accurate regardless of how you draw the network, whereas "diagonal" only makes sense for certain visual layouts.

In response to comment in the discussion below: "leading to less over-segmentation of action bouts" (and corresponding discussion in section 5.1 of the paper): I would be like to have a bit more about this in the paper. I have assumed that "per-bout" refers to "per-action event", but now I am not certain that I have understood this correctly (i.e. can a "bout" last for a few minutes?): given the readership, I think it would not be inappropriate to define some of these things explicitly.

In response to comment about fly behaviours that last minutes vs milliseconds: This is interesting, and I would be curious to know how classification accuracy relates to the time-scale of the behaviour (e.g. are most of the mistakes on long-term behaviours? i realize that this would only tell part of the story, e.g. if you have a behaviour that has both a long-term duration, but that also has very different short-term characteristics than many other behaviours, it should be easy to classify accuractely despite being "long-term"). If easy to investigate this, I would add a comment about it; if this is hard to investigate, it's probably not worth it at this point, although it's something you might want to look at in future.

In response to comment about scaling to human behavior: I agree that in principle, adding conv layers directly above the sensory input would be the right thing to try, but seriously: there is usually a pretty big gap between what "should" work and what actually works, as I am sure the authors are aware. (Indeed, I am sure the authors have a much more experiential and detailed understanding of the limitations of their work than I do). What I see presented is a nice system that has been demonstrated to handle spatiotemporal trajectories. The claims made should correspond to this. 

I would consider adjusting my rating to a 7 depending on future revisions.

The paper presents a method for joint motion prediction and activity classification from sequences with two different applications: motion of fruit flies and online handwriting recognition.

The method uses a classical encoder-decoder pipeline, with skip connections allowing direct communication between the encoder and the decoder on respective levels of abstraction.
Motion is discretized and predicted using classification. The model is trained on classification loss combined with a loss on motion prediction. The goal is to leverage latter loss in a semi-supervised setting from parts of the data which do not contain action labels.

The idea of leveraging predictions to train feature representations for discrimination is not new. However, the paper presents a couple of interesting ideas, partially inspired from other work in other areas.

My biggest concern is with the experimental evaluation. The experimental section contains a large amount of figures, which visualize what the model has learned in a qualitative way. However, quantitative evaluation is rarer.

- On the fly application, the authors compare the classification performance with another method previously published by the first author.
- Again on the fly application, the performance gain on motion prediction in figure 5c looks small compared to the baseline. I am not sure it is significant.
- I did not see any recognition results on the handwriting application. Has this part not been evaluated?

Figure 5a is difficult to understand and to interpret. The term "BesNet" is used here without any introduction.

Figure 4 seems to tell multiple and different stories. I'd suggest splitting it into at least two different figures.

machine_text: Overall the paper is very well-written with clear and concise arguments. The ideas discussed in the paper are also interesting. However, I have a few concerns about the technical merits of the proposed methods. 1. The adversarial training procedure mentioned in the paper is conceptually similar to the adaptive moment estimation (Adam) algorithm. In fact, the introduction of the auxiliary classifier in the triplet loss formulation may be regarded as a variant of the Multitask Learning extension of Adam. It would be more clear if the authors could justify the need for an independent training procedure for the auxiliary classifier, and discuss the connections to other well-known triplet learning methods. 2. The authors mention that some of the data points can have more than one pair of positive/negative examples for balancing the positive/negative examples in the training set. Including multiple examples of the same data point in the training set may lead to overfitting of the model to this particular example, and might not generalise well to new data points with similar characteristics. Including multiple examples of the same data point in the training set may defeat the purpose of building a large dataset. It would be better to exclude such duplicated data points from the training set, or alternatively, design the model in a way that it is invariant to such variations. This also applies to the use of dropout as a regularizer. Including dropout on top of the auxiliary classifier and the classification layer may hurt the generalisation ability of the model. 3. In the triplet loss in Equation 3, the authors mention the use of hinge loss for the positive and negative examples. This may lead to inefficient usage of the negative examples. Instead, it may be better to use a loss that rewards the correct classification of the positive examples, such as the log loss or cross-entropy loss, while using a large negative sample radius to ensure that a significant proportion of the negative examples are used for computing the loss. 4. In the reported experimental results, the authors report the results on a per-epoch basis for the Adam and the proposed method. However, the reported per-epoch results cannot be directly compared since the total number of epochs required for convergence for the two methods could be different. It would be more direct to report the results on a per-trial basis and then compare these results. These minor points aside, the paper is well written and the ideas presented are interesting. I encourage the authors to improve the technical merits of the paper.

Problem: Adversarial machine learning (AML) is a challenging problem for both humans and machines to assess. It is difficult to train high-quality adversarial training datasets and tune hyperparameters. Even though modern machine learning frameworks provide built-in feature robustness, manually checking and adjusting them is extremely labor-intensive. Solution: The solution proposed in this paper uses aggregated logs from large number of training runs to train an ensemble of strong defendable classifiers with different feature sets. Each classifier covers different aspects of feature robustness, and can be easily customized and applied to different use cases. The ensemble can be tuned using only single-label classification loss, without the need of expensive adversarial training datasets or tuning high-dimensional adversarial attacks. This paper is the first one to apply adversarial training to large scale image datasets, which is quite important to scale up the attack success rate. In order to successfully scale up the training dataset and model size, the paper offers several important recommendations: 1) using feature quantization to reduce the model size and storage, 2) using short-cut connections to mimic the ResNet, 3) using warm-start to acceleration training process. The second contribution is the paper finds that single-step attack methods are more transferable than multi-step attack methods, which means it is easier to mount black-box attacks using single-step attack methods. The last but not the least, the paper finds that adversarially trained models perform better on adversarial examples than on clean examples, which means it is also easier to attack them using the similar black-box attacks. Adversarial Machine Learning at Scale is a thought-provoking and timely paper. Adversarial examples have been a thorn in the side of machine learning for some time, however up to now there has been no systematic method to train a model to be robust against them. The authors put forward the idea of adversarial training - the idea is to train a model to be robust against adversarial examples by including a dedicated adversarial training phase in the standard supervised learning process. The training data has benign examples that have been altered slightly to produce adversarial examples, the model is then trained to robust against the latter. The authors take on ImageNet, a large and complex dataset, and train a model on it using both standard and adversarial training. The results are very interesting - there is a tradeoff between achieving high accuracy on the training set and on the test set (for the standard model the test set accuracy is 89% vs 92% for the adversarial model) but the adversarial model has a much higher upper bound on the accuracy it can achieve on the test set. The authors put forward three interesting hypothesis why this might be so, and show that all of them are true in their experimental settings. This is an interesting paper, with implications for how we think about adversarial examples and training models. There is still a lot of hard work needed to bring this to real-world deployment - there is no reason a model would not be able to defend against adversarial examples if it has never seen them before.

This paper is a well written paper. This paper can be divided into 2 parts:
1.Adversary training on ImageNet 
2.Empirical study of label leak, single/multiple step attack, transferability and importance of model capacity

For part [1], I don’t think training without clean example will not make reasonable ImageNet level model. Ian’s experiment in “Explaining and Harnessing Adversarial Examples” didn't use BatchNorm, which may be important for training large scale model. This part looks like an extension to Ian’s work with Inception-V3 model. I suggest to add an experiment of training without clean samples.

For part [2], The experiments cover most variables in adversary training, yet lack technical depth.  The depth, model capacity experiments can be explained by regularizer effect of adv training;  Label leaking is novel; In transferability experiment with FGSM, if we do careful observe on some special MNIST FGSM example, we can find augmentation effect on numbers, which makes grey part on image to make the number look more like the other numbers. Although this effect is hard to be observed with complex data such as CIFAR-10 or ImageNet, they may be related to the authors' observation "FGSM examples are most transferable".  

In this part the authors raise many interesting problems or guess, but lack theoretical explanations. 

Overall I think these empirical observations are useful for future work.

This paper is an empirical study of adversarial training in a large-scale regime. 
 Its main contributions are to demonstrate that Imagenet models can be made robust to adversarial examples using relatively efficient constructions (so-called 'one-step' methods). Along the way, the authors also report the 'label leaking' effect, a flaw in previous adversarial constructions that limits the effectiveness of adversarial examples at regularizing training. 
 
 The reviewers were consensual that this contribution is useful to the field, and the label leaking phenomena is an important aspect that this paper helps address and mitigate. The authors responded promptly to reviewers questions. Despite limited novelty and lack of quantitative analysis, I recommend accept as a poster.

This paper has two main contributions: 
(1) Applying adversarial training to imagenet, a larger dataset than previously considered 
(2) Comparing different adversarial training approaches, focusing importantly on the transferability of different methods. The authors also uncover and explain the label leaking effect which is an important contribution.

This paper is clear, well written and does a good job of assessing and comparing adversarial training methods and understanding their relation to one another. A wide range of empirical results are shown which helps elucidate the adversarial training procedure. This paper makes an important contribution towards understand adversarial training and believe ICLR is an appropriate venue for this work.

This paper investigate the phenomenon of the adversarial examples and the adversarial training on the dataset of ImageNet. While the final conclusions are still vague, this paper raises several noteworthy finding from its experiments.
The paper is well written and easy to follow. Although I still have some concerns about the paper (see the comments below), this paper has good contributions and worth to publish.

Pros:
For the first time in the literature, this paper proposed the concept of ‘label leaking’. Although its effect only becomes significant when the dataset is large, it should be carefully handled in the future research works along this line.
Using the ratio of 'clean accuracy' over ‘adversarial accuracy’ as the measure of robust is more reasonable compared to the existing works in the literature. 

Cons:
Although the conclusions of the paper are based on the experiments on ImageNet, the title of the paper seems a little misleading. I consider Section 4 as the main contribution of the paper. Note that Section 4.3 and Section 4.4 are not specific to large-scale dataset, thus emphasizing the ‘large-scale’ in the title and in the introduction seems improper. 
Basically all the conclusions of the paper are made based on observing the experimental results. Further tests should have been performed to verify these hypotheses. Without that, the conclusions of the paper seems rushy. For example, one dataset of imageNet can not infer the conclusions for all large-scale datasets.

machine_text: The paper is really interesting and make an interesting addition to the Spatio-temporal visual attention field. The abstract over-interprets the main contribution, but it makes good points in the discussion. The main idea is to add a recurrent activation over the outputs of a mixture of Density Network, which is trained on multiple scales of image patch features. The resulting sequence of hidden states not only encode the density over space but also over time, which can focus on the most relevant spatial regions at each time step. The network is trained in a conditionalvanilla SR manner by minimizing the difference between generated sequence of hidden states and ground truth. I think the paper needs a clearer introduction and discussion. The introduction could give more examples of previous works using density techniques for attention and what problem it is trying to solve. Also, the definition of the density over time is missing. For example, what is the time step in the definition and how is it defined. The discussions about related work and the limitations are also not properly documented. It is not clear how related it is to other work and how it compares to them. Other than these minor issues, the rest of the paper is well written and make good points. I think it is well aligned to the space time visual attention direction and will be of interest to the community. This paper introduces a Recurrent Mixture Density Network (RMDN) for spatiotemporal visual attention. It addresses the problem of localizing visually attentive people in video by learning a dynamic mixture distribution over people locations. RMDN first generates low-dimensional representations for people in each frame, then models their motion using a first-order non-linear state space model. The model's state comprises both its location and dynamic states (e.g., out-of-plane rotations). The dynamic states allow RMDN to model both individual differences in people's body movements and longer-range changes in people's bodily appearance, such as clothing or facial expressions. RMDN uses these dynamic state distributions to model people's spatial dependencies without the need for strong spatial priors (i.e., RMDN does not need a grid of potential people locations). Rather, it directly models the dynamic states using a mixture of Gaussian distributions, each with a concentration parameter shared across locations. Learning this mixture is the key to RMDN's success. The learned distributions help RMDN to focus its visual attention on particular people without requiring spatial priors, and the shared mixture parameters encode the regularity in people's appearance and allow RMDN to track changes in people's bodily appearance over time. The paper shows that RMDN outperformed several existing methods for spatiotemporal visual attention and that it made fewer mistakes than humans in predicting which people in a frame were visually attentive. It also showed that RMDN's predictions of people's temporal appearances were highly coherent.

In this work, we present a mixture of Gaussian model to represent the probability distribution of saliency. The global video features and short-term video clips are used to guide the model to focus on the regions that humans are more likely to watch. The parameters of the model are learned using Maximum likelihood estimation on human fixation data. This model is tested on Hollywood2 and results show state-of-the-art performance on saliency prediction for video. This model can also be used to improve action classification accuracy on both Hollywood2 and UCF101. The main contributions of this paper are: 1) A mixture of Gaussian model to represent the probability distribution of saliency. 2) The model is trained using Maximum likelihood estimation on human fixation data. 3) The model is tested on Hollywood2 and state-of-the-art performance is shown on saliency prediction for video. 4) The proposed model can be used to improve action classification accuracy on both Hollywood2 and UCF101. Some preliminary results have been published in https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.07655. The current version of the code is available at: https://github.com/chenxiaolong/Mixture-of-Gaussian-for-Attention. paper link: https://www.ijirais.com/papers/2019-H2-SAN-A.html Some data description from UCF101 and Hollywood2: 1. UCF101 consists of 101actions from 10 different categories. It has 13 different viewpoints for each action. 2. Hollywood2 consists of 24 Action classes with 10 minutes long videos, each action class has 4 different viewpoints. Human fixation data collection: Human eye movement is the most natural way to collect visual attention data. Coded Eye-Tracking Devices can be used to record the viewing behavior of the participants. In this work, we use synthetic eye movement that is recorded using Coded Screen Mote, which can simulate the viewing behavior of human in an objective and accurate way. The Coded Screen Mote is an infrared emitter that is put on the screen of the participant. The infrared signal is then reflected and captured by the infrared camera, and simulates the viewing behavior of human based on the pixel values. Data annotation: Each video is divided into multiple small clips with a duration of 0.2 second, this unit is called clipped. Human fixations are then annotated for each clipped by a human expert. Model Architecture: The model parameters are estimated using L1-regularized Maximum Likelihood estimation. Given a video, its video-level deep-CNN feature is first computed. Then the spatial layer and the short-term temporal layer are constructed based on the deep- CNN feature and the global and local visual saliency map, respectively. The two layers are then fused by concatenation and passed through a fully connected layer to output the estimated parameters. In the paper, the following performance metrics is reported. The area under PR curve (AUC) is used for the discrimination accuracy, while the F1 is used for the classification accuracy. 1) Performance on Hollywood2: AUC: 0.88 F1: 0.79 2) Performance on UCF101: AUC: 0.88 F1: 0.83

In many computer vision tasks, the relevant information to solve the problem at hand is mixed to irrelevant, distracting information. This has motivated researchers to design attentional models that can dynamically focus on parts of images or videos that are salient, e.g., by down-weighting irrelevant pixels. In this work, we propose a spatiotemporal attentional model that learns where to look in a video directly from human fixation data. We model visual attention with a mixture of Gaussians at each frame. This distribution is used to express the probability of saliency for each pixel. Time consistency in videos is modeled hierarchically by: 1) deep 3D convolutional features to represent spatial and short-term time relations and 2) a long short-term memory network on top that aggregates the clip-level representation of sequential clips and therefore expands the temporal domain from few frames to seconds. The parameters of the proposed model are optimized via maximum likelihood estimation using human fixations as training data, without knowledge of the action in each video. Our experiments on Hollywood2 show state-of-the-art performance on saliency prediction for video. We also show that our attentional model trained on Hollywood2 generalizes well to UCF101 and it can be leveraged to improve action classification accuracy on both datasets. modified version of the paper: Recurrent Mixture Density Network for Spatial and Temporal Visual Attention Attention is closely related to human vision system. Humans can efficiently select information relevant to their tasks from complex surroundings by firstly being attracted by such information. Such knowledge can be defined as visual attention. With the development of deep convolutional neural networks, researchers begin to use deep neural networks to predict visual attention. However, the existing prediction methods mainly learn to predict the spatial distribution of visual attention, and ignore the temporal dynamics of visual attention, which limits their application in some applications such as action recognition. In this paper, we propose a spatiotemporal visual attention model which can not only predict the spatial distribution of visual attention but also model the temporal dynamics of visual attention by introducing the Long-Short-Term-Memory network. Firstly, we adopt Convolutional Neural Networks as the base network to extract deep visual features from the input image, such as fc7 of VGG-16. Secondly, a Long-Short-Term-Memory network is used to model the temporal dynamics of visual attention. Each layer of the Long-Short-Term-Memory network is connected to all the previous and following layers in the Memory part of the Long-Short-Term-Memory network. The response of the last layer of the Long-Short-Term-Memory network is used as the spatial distribution of visual attention. Our proposed model not only can predict the spatial distribution of visual attention but also can model the temporal dynamics of visual attention, which can be applied in action recognition. We evaluate the proposed model on Hollywood2 dataset, our model achieves state-of-the-art results on both saliency prediction and action classification. We also evaluate our model on two action recognition datasets, UCF101 and Hollywood2. Compared with other state-of-the-art methods, our model achieves the state-of-the-art result on UCF101, and can use Hollywood2 to improve the classification accuracy of action in UCF101, which proves that our model has good generalization ability.
human_text:
This paper proposes a new method for estimating visual attention in videos. The input clip is first processed by a convnet (in particular, C3D) to extract visual features. The visual features are then passed to LSTM. The hidden state at each time step in LSTM is used to generate the parameters in a Gaussian mixture model. Finally, the visual attention map is generated from the Gaussian mixture model.

Overall, the idea in this paper is reasonable and the paper is well written. RNN/LSTM has been used in lots of vision problem where the outputs are discrete sequences, there has not been much work on using RNN/LSTM for problems where the output is continuous like in this paper.

The experimental results have demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed approach. In particular, it outperforms other state-of-the-art on the saliency prediction task on the Hollywood2 datasets. It also shows improvement over baselines (e.g. C3D + SVM) on the action recognition task.

My only "gripe" of this paper is that this paper is missing some important baseline comparisons. In particular, it does not seem to show how the "recurrent" part help the overall performance. Although Table 2 shows RMDN outperforms other state-of-the-art, it might be due to the fact that it uses strong C3D features (while other methods in Table 2 use traditional handcrafted features). Since saliency prediction is essentially a dense image labeling problem (similar to semantic segmentation). For dense image labeling, there has been lots of methods proposed in the past two years, e.g. fully convolution neural network (FCN) or deconvnet. A straightforward baseline is to simply take FCN and apply it on each frame. If the proposed method still outperforms this baseline, we can know that the "recurrent" part really helps.

The paper describes a model for video saliency prediction using a combination of spatio-temporal ConvNet features and LSTM. The proposed method outperforms the state of the art on the saliency prediction task and is shown to improve the performance of a baseline action classification model.

The authors formulate a recurrent deep neural network to predict human fixation locations in videos as a mixture of Gaussians. They train the model using maximum likelihood with actual fixation data. Apart from evaluating how good the model performs at predicting fixations, they combine the saliency predictions with the C3D features for action recognition.

quality: I am missing a more thorough evaluation of the fixation prediction performance. The center bias performance in Table 1 differs significantly from the on in Table 2. All the state-of-the-art models reported in Table 2 have a performance worse than the center bias performance reported in Table 1. Is there really no other model better than the center bias? Additionally I am missing details on how central bias and human performance are modelled. Is human performance cross-validated?

You claim that your "results are very close to human performance (the difference is only 3.2%). This difference is actually larger than the difference between Central Bias and your model reported in Table 1. Apart from this, it is dangerous to compare AUC performance differences due to e.g. saturation issues.

clarity: the explanation for Table 3 is a bit confusing, also it is not clear why the CONV5 and the FC6 models differ in how the saliency map is used. At least one should also evaluate the CONV5 model when multiplying the input with the saliency map to see how much of the difference comes from the different ways to use the saliency map and how much from the different features.

Other issues:

You cite Kümmerer et. al 2015 as a model which "learns ... indirectly rather than from explicit information of where humans look", however the their model has been trained on fixation data using maximum-likelihood.

Apart from these issues, I think the paper make a very interesting contribution to spatio-temporal fixation prediction. If the evaluation issues given above are sorted out, I will happily improve my rating.

This work proposes to a spatiotemporal saliency network that is able to mimic human fixation patterns,
thus helping to prune irrelevant information from the video and improve action recognition.

The work is interesting and has shown state-of-the-art results on predicting human attention on action videos.
It has also shown promise for helping action clip classification.

The paper would benefit from a discussion on the role of context in attention.
For instance, if context is important, and people give attention to context, why is it not incorporated automatically in your model?

One weak point is the action recognition section, where the comparison between the two (1)(2) and (3) seems unfair.
The attention weighted feature maps in fact reduce the classification performance, and only improve performance when doubling the feature and associated model complexity by concatenating the weighted maps with the original features.

Is there a way to combine the context and attention without concatenation?
The rational for concatenating the features extracted from the original clip,
and the features extracted from the saliency weighted clip seems to contradict the initial hypothesis that `eliminating or down-weighting pixels that are not important' will improve performance.

The authors should also mention the current state-of-the-art results in Table 4, for comparison.

Overall, the idea in this paper is reasonable and the paper is well written. RNN/LSTM has been used in lots of vision problem where the outputs are discrete sequences, there has not been much work on using RNN/LSTM for problems where the output is continuous like in this paper.

The experimental results have demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed approach. In particular, it outperforms other state-of-the-art on the saliency prediction task on the Hollywood2 datasets. It also shows improvement over baselines (e.g. C3D + SVM) on the action recognition task.

My only "gripe" of this paper is that this paper is missing some important baseline comparisons. In particular, it does not seem to show how the "recurrent" part help the overall performance. Although Table 2 shows RMDN outperforms other state-of-the-art, it might be due to the fact that it uses strong C3D features (while other methods in Table 2 use traditional handcrafted features). Since saliency prediction is essentially a dense image labeling problem (similar to semantic segmentation). For dense image labeling, there has been lots of methods proposed in the past two years, e.g. fully convolution neural network (FCN) or deconvnet. A straightforward baseline is to simply take FCN and apply it on each frame. If the proposed method still outperforms this baseline, we can know that the "recurrent" part really helps.

The paper describes a model for video saliency prediction using a combination of spatio-temporal ConvNet features and LSTM. The proposed method outperforms the state of the art on the saliency prediction task and is shown to improve the performance of a baseline action classification model.

The authors formulate a recurrent deep neural network to predict human fixation locations in videos as a mixture of Gaussians. They train the model using maximum likelihood with actual fixation data. Apart from evaluating how good the model performs at predicting fixations, they combine the saliency predictions with the C3D features for action recognition.

quality: I am missing a more thorough evaluation of the fixation prediction performance. The center bias performance in Table 1 differs significantly from the on in Table 2. All the state-of-the-art models reported in Table 2 have a performance worse than the center bias performance reported in Table 1. Is there really no other model better than the center bias? Additionally I am missing details on how central bias and human performance are modelled. Is human performance cross-validated?

You claim that your "results are very close to human performance (the difference is only 3.2%). This difference is actually larger than the difference between Central Bias and your model reported in Table 1. Apart from this, it is dangerous to compare AUC performance differences due to e.g. saturation issues.

clarity: the explanation for Table 3 is a bit confusing, also it is not clear why the CONV5 and the FC6 models differ in how the saliency map is used. At least one should also evaluate the CONV5 model when multiplying the input with the saliency map to see how much of the difference comes from the different ways to use the saliency map and how much from the different features.

Other issues:

You cite Kümmerer et. al 2015 as a model which "learns ... indirectly rather than from explicit information of where humans look", however the their model has been trained on fixation data using maximum-likelihood.

Apart from these issues, I think the paper make a very interesting contribution to spatio-temporal fixation prediction. If the evaluation issues given above are sorted out, I will happily improve my rating.

This work proposes to a spatiotemporal saliency network that is able to mimic human fixation patterns,
thus helping to prune irrelevant information from the video and improve action recognition.

The work is interesting and has shown state-of-the-art results on predicting human attention on action videos.
It has also shown promise for helping action clip classification.

The paper would benefit from a discussion on the role of context in attention.
For instance, if context is important, and people give attention to context, why is it not incorporated automatically in your model?

One weak point is the action recognition section, where the comparison between the two (1)(2) and (3) seems unfair.
The attention weighted feature maps in fact reduce the classification performance, and only improve performance when doubling the feature and associated model complexity by concatenating the weighted maps with the original features.

Is there a way to combine the context and attention without concatenation?
The rational for concatenating the features extracted from the original clip,
and the features extracted from the saliency weighted clip seems to contradict the initial hypothesis that `eliminating or down-weighting pixels that are not important' will improve performance.

The authors should also mention the current state-of-the-art results in Table 4, for comparison.

This paper proposes an effective way to represent low-dimensional manifolds in high-dimensions using deep networks. The main idea is to map the original data into a space with higher dimensionalities using kernel functions, and then use deep networks to approximate the mapped data. The main challenge is to find a good mapping to reduce the dimensionality while keeping the data points useful for the task at hand. The proposed framework uses a Gaussian kernel to map the original data to a high dimensional space, and then uses multiple fully connected layers to approximate the mapped data. The main advantage of this approach is that the resulted representation is low-dimensional while preserving the locality of the data. In addition, the linear algebra based computation of the forward propagation makes this method computationally efficient. The main contributions of this paper are as follows: 1. The proposed method leverages the excellent properties of Gaussian Kernel functions, namely the locality and the simplicity of linear algebra, to achieve high-efficiency and low-dimensional representation for low-dimensional manifolds. 2. The proposed method uses multiple fully connected layers to get the approximation, instead of using one large fully connected layer which would require too much memory and computation. 3. The proposed method adds a regularization term to the loss function to control the complexity of the solution, which further improves the generalization of the method to unseen data. The effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated on both synthetic and real world data sets. The experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art on this problem, and the training of the proposed method is also much more efficient.

The ability of deep neural networks to represent data lying near a low-dimensional manifold is an important question in understanding how they work. In this paper, the authors consider this question for points on a special type of manifold, monotonic chains. The authors show that the first two layers of a deep neural network can exactly represent points lying on a monotonic chain in a high-dimensional space as a special type of low-dimensional Euclidean space. The authors start with a standard neural network with many layers and give it several initializations. SUMMARY 
This paper discusses how data from a special type of low dimensional structure (monotonic chain) can be efficiently represented in terms of neural networks with two hidden layers. 

PROS 
Interesting, easy to follow view on some of the capabilities of neural networks, highlighting the dimensionality reduction aspect, and pointing at possible directions for further investigation. 

CONS 
The paper presents a construction illustrating certain structures that can be captured by a network, but it does not address the learning problem (although it presents experiments where such structures do emerge, more or less). 

COMMENTS 
It would be interesting to study the ramifications of the presented observations for the case of deep(er) networks. 
Also, to study to what extent the proposed picture describes the totality of functions that are representable by the networks. 

MINOR COMMENTS 
- Figure 1 could be referenced first in the text.  
- ``Color coded'' where the color codes what? 
- Thank you for thinking about revising the points from my first questions. Note: Isometry on the manifold. 
- On page 5, mention how the orthogonal projection on S_k is realized in the network. 
- On page 6 ``divided into segments'' here `segments' is maybe not the best word. 
- On page 6 ``The mean relative error is 0.98'' what is the baseline here, or what does this number mean?

There is consensus among the reviewers that the paper presents an interesting and novel direction of study. Having said that, there also appears to be a sense that the proposed construction can be studied in more detail: in particular, (1) an average-case analysis is essential as the worst-case bounds appear extremely loose and (2) the learning problem needs to be addressed in more detail. Nevertheless, this paper deserves to appear at the conference.

The paper presents an analysis of the ability of deep networks with ReLU functions to represent particular types of low-dimensional manifolds. Specifically, the paper focuses on what the authors call "monotonic chains of linear segments", which are essentially sets of intersecting tangent planes. The paper presents a construction that efficiently models such manifolds in a deep net, and presents a basic error analysis of the resulting construction.

While the presented results are novel to the best of my knowledge, they are hardly surprising (1) given what we already know about the representational power of deep networks and (2) given that the study selects a deep network architecture and a data structure that are very "compatible". In particular, I have three main concerns with respect to the results presented in this paper:

(1) In the last decade, there has been quite a bit of work on learning data representations from sets of local tangent planes. Examples that spring to mind are local tangent space analysis of Zhang & Zha (2002), manifold charting by Brand (2002) and alignment of local models by Verbeek, Roweis, and Vlassis (2003). None of this work is referred to in related work, even though it seems highly relevant to the analysis presented here. For instance, it would be interesting to see how these old techniques compare to the deep network trained to produce the embedding of Figure 6. This may provide some insight into the inductive biases the deep net introduces: does it learn better representations that non-parametric techniques because it has better inductive biases, or does it learn worse representations because the loss being optimized is non-convex?

(2) It is difficult to see how the analysis generalizes to more complex data in which local linearity assumptions on the data manifold are vacuous given the sparsity of data in high-dimensional space, or how it generalizes to deep network architectures that are not pure ReLU networks. For instance, most modern networks use a variant of batch normalization; this already appears to break the presented analyses.

(3) The error bound presented in Section 4 appears vacuous for any practical setting, as the upper bound on the error is exponential in the total curvature (a quantity that will be quite large in most practical settings). This is underlined by the analysis of the Swiss roll dataset, of which the authors state that the "bound for this case is very loose". The fact that the bound is already so loose for this arguably very simple manifold makes that the error analysis may tell us very little about the representational power of deep nets.

I would encourage the authors to address issue (1) in the revision of the paper. Issue (2) and (3) may be harder to address, but is essential that they are addressed for the line of work pioneered by this paper to have an impact on our understanding of deep learning.


Minor comments: 

- In prior work, the authors only refer to fully supervised siamese network approaches. These approaches differ from that taken by the authors, as their approach is unsupervised. It should be noted that the authors are not the first to study unsupervised representation learners parametrized by deep networks: other important examples are deep autoencoders (Hinton & Salakhutdinov, 2006 and work on denoising autoencoders from Bengio's group) and parametric t-SNE (van der Maaten, 2009).
- What loss do the authors use in their experiments? Using "the difference between the ground truth distance ... and the distance computed by the network" seems odd, because it encourages the network to produce infinitely large distances (to get a loss of minus infinity). Is the difference squared?

Summary:
In this paper, the authors look at the ability of neural networks to represent low dimensional manifolds efficiently e.g. embed them into a lower dimensional Euclidian space. 
They define a class of manifolds, monotonic chains (affine spaces that intersect, with hyperplanes separating monotonic intervals of spaces) and give a construction to embed such a chain with a neural network with one hidden layer.

They also give a bound on the number of parameters required to do so, and examine what happens when the manifold is noisy. 

Experiments involve looking at embedding synthetic data from a monotonic chain using a distance preservation loss. This experiment supports the theoretical bound on number of parameters needed to embed the monotonic chain. Another experiment varies the elevation and azimuth of of faces, which are known to lie on a monotonic chain, on a regression loss.

Comments:

The direction of investigation in the paper (looking at what happens to manifolds in a neural network), is very compelling, and I strongly encourage the authors to continue exploring this direction.

However, the current version of the paper could use some more work:

The experiments are all with a regression loss and a shallow network, and as part of the reason for interest in this question is the very large, high dimensional datasets we use now, which require a deeper network, it seems important to address this case.

It also seems important to confirm that embedding works well when *classification* loss is used, instead of regression

The theory sections could do with being more clearly written -- I’m not as familiar with the literature in this area, and while the proof method used is relatively elementary, it was difficult to understand what exactly was being proved -- e.g. formally stating what could be expected of an embedding that “accurately and efficiently” preserves a monotonic chain, etc.

Thank you for your interest in this paper. I find the paper is both interesting and valuable. There are a few points that should be considered to improve the quality of the paper. First, the paper only focuses on the sparsely-connected network architecture. However, as the name suggests, the sparse connections only exist between a few neurons. Hence, the paper only considers the case of fully-connected networks with sparse connections. How to extend the proposed method to other types of networks, for example, convolutional neural networks, is still an open problem. Second, in order to further reduce the hardware cost, the paper uses linear-feedback shift registers (LFSR) to remap the connection weights from the weight space to the index space. However, a fully connected layer with a size of N*M has 2N*M non-zero entries, which means that the number of connections in the index space is far less than the size of the weight space. For this reason, the index space needs to have a higher resolution than the weight space. How to avoid this issue and reduce the hardware cost is an important open problem. Third, although the paper describes the design of the weight and state modules in the paper, the design of the intermediate node is not mentioned. The weight storage and calculation of the intermediate node are the keys to reducing the complexity of the network architecture and reducing the complexity of the hardware. How to design an appropriate number and type of intermediated nodes and the size of the corresponding connections are key to reducing the design complexity.

Recently, deep neural networks have received considerable attention due to their ability to extract and represent high-level abstractions in data sets. Deep neural networks such as fully-connected and convolutional neural networks have shown excellent performance on a wide range of recognition and classification tasks. However, their hardware implementations currently suffer from large silicon area and high power consumption due to the their high degree of complexity. The power/energy consumption of neural networks is dominated by memory accesses, the majority of which occur in fully-connected networks. In this paper, we propose sparsely-connected networks, by showing that the number of connections in fully-connected networks can be reduced by up to 90% while improving the accuracy performance on three popular datasets (MNIST, CIFAR10 and SVHN). We then propose an efficient hardware architecture based on linear-feedback shift registers to reduce the memory requirements of the proposed sparsely-connected networks. The proposed architecture can save up to 90% of memory compared to the conventional implementations of fully-connected neural networks. Moreover, implementation results show up to 84% reduction in the energy consumption of a single neuron of the proposed sparsely-connected networks compared to a single neuron of fully-connected networks. This paper presents several adversarial training methods for semi-supervised text classification. The problem of semi-supervised text classification is challenging as it requires both labeled and unlabeled data to train a model. Commonly used methods for semi-supervised text classification assume that the unlabeled data are labeled with noise variables, which is not the case for many real-world datasets. The author presents several techniques that improve the robustness of a text classification model to this kind of unlabeling attack. The author provides a comparative study of the effectiveness of these methods and shows that some of them lead to a significantly higher classification accuracy on some real-world datasets. USED PAPER TITLE Adversarial Training Methods for Semi-Supervised Text Classification StyleGAN for Labeled Noise Training, Deep Coherence, and Generative Adversarial Nets Give Unlabeled Data To One Model, Get Auxiliary Data For Another - StyleGAN for Labeled Noise Training - Deep Coherence - Generative Adversarial Nets Comparative Study Real-world datasets Effectiveness evaluation Robustness to unlabeling attack Future Work Conclusion Overall, this paper presents several effective and robust methods for unlabeling attack against semi-supervised text classification models. These methods can be easily integrated into current models with little change. A comparative study is conducted on several real-world datasets, and the effectiveness of these methods is proven. In the end, some potential directions for future work are also discussed, including white-box unlabeling attack and black-box unlabeling attack. Problem/question the paper addresses: Semi-supervised text classification is a challenging problem because it requires both labeled and unlabeled data to train a model. In practice, unlabeled data are often attacked with incorrectly labeled noise variables, which compromises the robustness of the model. The paper presents several effective and robust adversarial training methods to prevent this kind of unlabeling attack. Strengths: 1. The "StyleGAN for Labeled Noise Training" method uses generative models to generate more labeled data with the true label, which benefits model training and promotes the robustness of the model to unlabeling attack. 2. The "Deep Coherence" method uses the generative model to disperse the unlabeled data to generate more random noise, which diminishes the quality of the unlabeled data and reduces the effectiveness of the attack. 3. The "Generative Adversarial Nets" method uses the discriminator to detect unlabeled data and promotes the robustness of the model by limiting the number of labeled attacked. Weaknesses: 1. The paper only describes the unlabeling attack against one single model in a simple and basic framework, and the effectiveness of the methods in more complex scenarios remains to be further studied. 2. The paper only presents the attack method and does not give corresponding defense methods. As such, a strong adversary can still find an unlabeled data point in the generated labeled data and attack the model. Overall, the paper presents several effective and robust methods for unlabeling attack against semi-supervised text classification models. These methods can be easily integrated into current models with little change. A comparative study is conducted on several real-world datasets, and the effectiveness of these methods is proven. In the end, some potential directions for future work are also discussed, including white-box unlabeling attack and black-box unlabeling attack. Written by: Tengxiao Guo, MLS, Amazon Web Services
