machine_text: The presented work can be considered interesting and can be further developed into a practical application. However, there are some issues that need to be addressed before proceeding to the implementation section. - Since the discriminator serves a role of a regularizer, too much reliance on the discriminator can lead to over-fitting. How well the model generalizes to new samples, especially when the dataset is small, is yet to be seen. - The overall model relies on GANs to achieve the multi-view learning. It would be interesting to study the effect of the proposed model in the setting where only a single view is available for training. - The model is tested on a short video dataset. The generalization to the complicated real world problem would require the model to be tested on a much larger dataset. can you kindly suggest how to proceed with the above feedback to make the model more robust and generalizable? please write any further comments in the section below helps enables Disclaimer: I am not affiliated with HyperNetworks in any way. I just enjoy writing comments on papers like this one. modified comments Modified comments on the above comment: I think it is an interesting idea, however, I would expect it to work on a smaller dataset. In the modified section I have explained how to test the model on a larger dataset and make it more robust. Updated comments: I enjoyed reading about the concept of the model. One potential direction for improvement would be to use more sophisticated network architecture. Also, by using residual blocks would help in improving the efficiency of the model. Additionally, using an attention layer could help in processing different frames of the video as a group instead of independently. This would allow for temporal information to be captured. Additionally, an L2 normalization between the discriminator and generator could be introduced to improve the stability of training.

The paper HyperNetworks is about solving computer vision tasks using neural networks with a novel method called Hypergradation. The core idea of Hypergradation is to abstract away specific network details by replacing them with a single general parameterisation. This generalisation allows the method to apply to a broader class of neural networks and to reuse them for different tasks. The general network can be specialised by finding the best set of general parameters according to the task. HyperNetworks applies this method to train the last layer of a neural network. First the last layer is randomly initialised. Then the general parameters of the layer are updated by performining one gradient update per general parameter. This method works very well for many tasks but recently I have found a way to improve the method significantly. Instead of performing one update per general parameter, I propose to perform a batch of updates. Each batch comprises one update per general parameter and a specific learning rate for each parameter. The method is called HyperBatch and is easier to implement than Hypergradation. The code is available at https://github.com/HyperInteractive/HyperNetworks HyperNetworks answers the question “Can neural networks learn hyperparameters?” with an emphatic yes. The method is general and can be applied to many different types of neural networks. The key ingredient is to specialise the general network by learning the specific setting of its hyperparameters. The method works very well for many tasks and there are many current and forthcoming applications. My own work is an example of how the method can be applied to a different problem. My main criticism of the method is that it is unclear how to choose the best set of general parameters. While there is a lot of evidence that good general initialisations lead to better results, it is not clear how to find the best general parameters. The method uses SGD to find a good initialisation but it is unclear how to determine the learning rate for each parameter. I think a better method would be to initialise the general parameters by performing maximum likelihood learning on a validation set. There are many strengths of the method. The way that general parameters are specialised for a task makes it easy to apply to a broad class of neural networks and network architectures. The way that general parameters are specialised for a task also makes it easy to reuse generalised networks for related tasks. This is in contrast to conventional methods that often require significant retraining for small changes in the task. One weakness is that HyperNetworks does not provide a complete solution. The method only works for fine-tuning the last layer. To train the entire network, the method requires a method for initialising the earlier layers. This initialisation still depends on the last layer. This can be addressed by introducing feedback from earlier layers into the general parameter initialisation. Overall I think the method has significant potential and has already found many applications. It will be interesting to see what further developments occur in this field. My own work is a good example of how to apply the general method to a different problem. I am currently investigating how to apply HyperBatch to other parts of a network.

In this paper, the authors explore hypernetworks: an approach of using one network, also known as a hypernetwork, to generate the weights for another network. This work applies hypernetworks to generate adaptive weights for recurrent networks. The results show that hypernetworks can generate non-shared weights for LSTM and achieve state-of-the-art results on a variety of sequence modelling tasks including character-level language modelling, handwriting generation and neural machine translation. The main contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows: 1. We apply hypernetworks to recurrent networks. In this case, hypernetworks can be viewed as a relaxed form of weight-sharing across layers. 2. We introduce a HyperNetwork layer which uses a hypernetwork to generate weights for a given layer. 3. We apply the HyperNetwork layer to LSTM and achieve state-of-the-art results on character-level language modelling, handwriting generation, and neural machine translation. Overall, this paper makes the following novel contributions: 1. It explores hypernetworks, a relaxes weight-sharing paradigm. 2. It applies hypernetworks to LSTM, achieving state-of-the-art results on several sequence modelling tasks. Overall, this is an interesting paper and I recommend to be published in top tier conferences. There are some aspects that could be improved: 1. There is a typo in line 3, the last word should be \"accuracy\" instead of \"accuracies\". 2. Some parts of the text is too detailed, e.g. in lines 24-25, the authors could consider to remove some parts. Other aspects are excellent and this paper could have a wide general interest. Overall, I recommend to be accepted for publication, also considering the fact that I found it on arXiv. Best, Salvador.

This work applies this idea to generate adaptive weights for recurrent networks. The paper achieves state-of-the-art results on a variety of sequence modelling tasks. Here are the strengths of the paper: 1. The main concept of the paper is novel. The hypernetwork is a good way to name this idea, and this name has become a buzzword in the neural networks community. So the idea has received much attention. 2. The real-life application of this idea is very helpful to the future development of the research field. Hypernetworks has been successfully used in neural machine translation. This success has convinced the deep learning community that the idea can be generally useful. 3. The hypernetwork used in this work can be seen as a type of generative model, which is widely used in NLP. In recent years, great success in generative modelling has led to a new focus on the interrelated topics of networks and network architectures. This paper is a pioneering effort in this area, and the new directions it opens up are very exciting. Here are some potential avenues for future research: 1. The restriction that weights in hypernetworks be static seems very strong, and it will be good to explore relax this constraint. The paper also uses different types of layers as the base network, such as GRU and LSTM, it will be good to see how these differences influence the performance of hypernetworks. 2. The theory of hypernetworks still needs to be developed. Some questions such as the duality between weight-sharing and weight-concentration still need to be explored. 3. It would be good to conduct an ablation study to compare hypernetwork against other network architectures, including weight-sharing networks.
human_text:
*** Paper Summary ***

The paper proposes to a new neural network architecture. The layer weights of a classical network are computed as a function of a latent representation associated with the layer. Two instances are presented (i) a CNN where each layer weight is computed from a lower dimensional layer embedding vector; (ii) an RNN where each layer weight is computed from a secondary RNN state.

*** Review Summary ***

Pros: 
- I like the idea of bringing multiplicative RNNs and their predecessors back into the spotlight. 
- LM and MT results are excellent.

Cons:  
- The paper could be better written. It is too long for the conference format and need refocussing. 
- On related work, the relation with multiplicative RNN and their generic tensor product predecessor (Order 2 networks, wrt C. Lee Giles definition) should be mentioned in the related work section and the differences with earlier research need to be explained and motivated (by the way it is better to say that something is revisiting an old idea or training it at modern scale/on modern tasks than ommitting it).
- on focus, it is not clear if your goal is to achieve better performance or more compact networks. In the RNN section you lean toward the former, in the CNN section you seem to lean toward the latter.

I would suggest to make the paper shorter and clearer possibly leaving the CNN results for latter publication. The relation with multiplicative/order 2 networks and eventual differences need to be explained.

*** Detailed Review ***

Multiplicative networks are an extremely powerfull architecture and bringing them back into the spotlight is excellent. This paper has excellent results but suffer poor presentation, lack of a clear focus. It spends time on details and ommit important points. In its current form, it is much too long to long and his not self contained without the appendices.

Spending more time on multiplicative RNNs, order 2 networks at the begining of the paper would be excellent. This will let you highlight the difference between this paper and earlier work. It would also be necessary to spend a little time on why multiplicative RNN were less used than gated RNN: it seems that the optimization problem their training involve is tricker and it would be helpful to explain whether you had a harder time tweaking optimization parameters or whether you needed longer training sessions compared to LSTMs, regular CNN. On name, I am not sure that "hypernetwork" help the reader understand better what the proposed architecture compared to multiplicative interactions.

In section 3.2, you seem to imply that there are different settings of hypernetworks that allow to vary from an RNN to a CNN, this is not clear to me, maybe you could show how this would work on a simple temporal problem with equations. 

The work on CNN and RNN are rather disconnected to me: for CNN, you seem to be interested in a low rank structure of the weights, showing that similar performance can be achieved with less weights. It is not clear to me why to pursue that goal. Do you expect speedups? less memory for embedded applications? In that case you should compare with alternative strategies, e.g. model compression (Caruana et al 2006, aka Dark Knowledge, Hinton et al 2014) or hashed networks (Chen et al 2015). 

For RNN, you seem to target better perplexity/BLEU and model compactness is not a priority. Instead of making the weights have a simpler structure, you make them richer, i.e. dependent over time. It seems in that case models might be bigger and take longer to train. This paper makes an important first step towards an automatic Turing test. The paper describes a framework for training a model to automatically evaluate responses in a dialogue, given only a transcript and an answer selected by a human. The model is trained to discriminate between human and machine responses using a large database of human-human dialogs. The paper shows that the model is capable of making accurate score predictions for responses in that dataset. The paper also examines the model's response generation capability, showing that the model can be prevented from generating certain types of responses by requiring a minimum score. The strengths of the approach are primarily the use of a large existing dataset of human-human dialogs, and the evaluation of the model's response generation capability, however the paper only examines a small subset of responses and does not evaluate the model on new test responses generated by the model. The model is also restricted to scoring each response on a 0-1 scale. Although these scoring bins could represent certain dimensions (e.g., sentiment), there is no theoretical analysis of the signal in these bins, nor any metrics to compare against human evaluation. Further, it is not clear whether an algorithm with such restricted capabilities could be competitive against a human in responding to complex queries or building conversational queries. adhiscovering inherent structure in the data is an excellent strength of this approach. The paper uses state of the art techniques to train a supervised model on human-human conversation to distinguish between human and machine responses. Even though the model is tested on a very small subset of responses and scored on a 0-1 scale, the approach shows promising results for a first attempt at building an automatic Turing test. A limitation of the approach is the restricted scoring range (0-1) which could be problematic if the model was asked to score responses on multiple dimensions. The restricted set of responses examined could be a concern for generalization of the model to new domains or question types. Another limitation is that the model only examines a small subset of responses and does not evaluate the model on new test responses generated by the model. In addition, the theoretical analysis of the scoring bins is lacking. Without such an analysis, it is not clear whether the score can be effectively used to distinguish between human and machine responses. Overall, the model demonstrates the feasibility of training a model to evaluate dialogue responses on a large existing dataset of human-human dialogs.

In this paper, the author introduces a method to evaluate the response quality of dialogue system, which is an important but difficult problem. It first propose a new dataset, named Automatic Dialogue Evaluation metric (ADEM) that collect human responses and system responses along with human-evaluated response scores. Towards an automatic Turing test: Learning to evaluate dialogue responses, its main content is as below: Automatically evaluating the quality of dialogue responses for unstructured domains is a challenging problem. Unfortunately, existing automatic evaluation metrics are biased and correlate very poorly with human judgements of response quality (Liu et al., 2016). Yet having an accurate automatic evaluation procedure is crucial for dialogue research, as it allows rapid prototyping and testing of new models with fewer expensive human evaluations. In response to this challenge, we formulate automatic dialogue evaluation as a learning problem. We present an evaluation model (ADEM) that learns to predict human-like scores to input responses, using a new dataset of human response scores. We show that ADEM model's predictions correlate significantly, and at level much higher than word-overlap metrics such as BLEU, with human judgements at both the utterance and system-level. We also show that ADEM can generalize to evaluating dialogue models unseen during training, an important step for automatic dialogue evaluation. One drawback of ADEM is that it takes about a second per-response, which is too slow for systems. To address this, we also propose a fast version (FDEM) that predicts a response's scores at a sample-level, rather than individual-response, speed. We also present an ablation study on the effects of different model components in ADEM and FDEM. Another interesting direction for future work is to develop more scalable and less-biased automatic evaluation methods. We believe ADEM's strength is that it can be easily deployed on any system for which a response policy is available. We plan to make the code and evaluation data publicly available.

Noting the authors' concern about one of the reviewers, I read the paper myself and offer my own brief review.
 
 Evaluation is an extremely important question that does not get enough attention in the machine learning community, so the authors' effort is welcomed. The task that the authors are trying to evaluate is especially hard; in fact, it is not even clear to me how humans make these judgments. The low kappa scores on some of the non-"overall" dimensions, and only moderate agreement on "overall," are quite worrisome. What makes a good "chat" dialogue? The authors seem not to have qualitatively grappled with this key question, rather defining it empirically as "whatever our human judges think it is." This is, I think the deepest flaw of the work; the authors are rushing to automate evaluation without taking the time to ponder what good performance actually is. 
 
 That aside, I think the idea of automatic evaluation as a modeling problem is worth studying. The authors note that this has been done for other problems, such as machine translation. They give only a cursory discussion of this prior work, however, and miss the seminal reference, "Regression for sentence-level MT evaluation with pseudo references," Albrecht, Joshua, and Rebecca Hwa, ACL 2007.
 
 The paper would be much stronger with some robustness analysis; does the quality of the evaluation hold up if the design decisions are made differently, if less data are used to estimate the evaluation model, etc.? How does it hold up across datasets, and across different types of dialogue systems? As a methodological note, there are a lot of significance tests here and no mention of any attempt to correct for this (e.g., Bonferroni, FDR, etc.).

I do think that the ideas it presents should be hashed out in a public forum sooner rather than later, and therefore recommend it as one of a few papers to be presented at the workshop.

We are concerned about the quality of review provided by Reviewer #4. The only point of criticism offered by the reviewer is that "the proposed solution depends on a reasonably good dialogue model to begin with, which is not guaranteed, rendering the new metric possibly meaningless." We believe the review indicates that the reviewer did not thoroughly read or understand our paper, for several reasons:

This can be seen by simply looking at our main results table, where we have additional results using publicly available sentence embedding methods (i.e. tweet2vec). What our method does require is a sentence embedding method, but we believe this is hardly a limitation of the work. 

2) Several details in the reviewer's summary of our paper are incorrect (it is not simply an LSTM used to encode the context, but a hierarchical model; our evaluation method is not in itself a dialogue model, as explained to Reviewer #1), although we do not mention this in our rebuttal. 

3) As stated in the rebuttal, we show that our evaluation procedure works (is correlated with human judgements) on a dataset (Twitter) that has seen the significant use in the recent literature. It is obvious that our method works on this popular dataset (since we demonstrate it in our experiments); thus, the claim that our method is 'meaningless' is not accurate (it would be very useful even if it only worked for Twitter).

4) Finally, the domain in which the reviewer implies our method would be 'meaningless' (when there exists no sentence embedding method for that domain) is very small: it encompasses only domains that (a) have too little data to train an embedding method (and if this is the case, it likely has too little data to train a dialogue model anyway), and (b) are different enough from all existing domains such that transfer learning can't be used (i.e. one can't use a generic embedding method such as skip-thought). We would appreciate if this could be taken into consideration when deciding whether to accept or reject this paper.

The paper Gated Multimodal Units for Information Fusion presents a systematic approach to fuse information from different modalities, namely text, images and speech, using multimodal fusion with gates in a neural network architecture. The main contribution of the paper is the design of novel multimodal fusion gates which are inspired by biological inspirations, namely neurons in the auditory brainstem and midbrain and in the cortex. The efficacy of the proposed fusion gate architecture is demonstrated by performing information retrieval on a standard image retrieval dataset and on a popular spoken language understanding benchmark dataset. The experiments performed show that gating information from different modalities substantially improves the retrieval performance and significantly reduces the necessity of large amounts of annotated data for language understanding. elly presented a novel multimodal fusion gate based on the concepts of auditory brainstem and midbrain and cortex. The paper introduces Gated Multimodal Units GMUs, which use multiplicative weights to select the degree to which a hidden unit will consider different modalities in determining its activation.  The paper also introduces a new dataset, "Multimodal IMDb," consisting of over 25k movie summaries, with their posters, and labeled genres.

GMUs are related to "mixture of experts" in that different examples will be classified by different parts of the model, (but rather than routing/gating entire examples, individual hidden units are gated separately).  They are related to attention models in that different parts of the input are weighted differently; there the emphasis is on gating modalities of input.

The dataset is a very nice contribution, and there are many experiments varying text representation and single-modality vs two-modality.  What the paper is lacking is a careful discussion, experimentation and analysis in comparison to other multiplicative gate models---which is the core intellectual contribution of the paper.  For example, I could imagine that a mixture of experts or attention models or other gated models might perform very well, and at the very least provide interesting scientific comparative analysis.  I encourage the authors to continue the work, and submit a revised paper when ready.

As is, I consider the paper to be a good workshop paper, but not ready for a major conference.

This paper proposed The Gated Multimodal Unit (GMU) model for information fusion. The GMU learns to decide how modalities influence the activation of the unit using multiplicative gates. The paper collected a large genre dataset from IMDB and showed that GMU gets good performance.

The proposed approach seems quite interesting, and the audience may expect it can be used in general scenarios beyond movie genre prediction. So it is quite straightforward that the paper should test the algorithm in other applications, which was not done yet. That is the biggest shortcoming of this paper in my opinions.  

Another concern lies in how to evaluate the performance of information fusion. The abstract claims "The model improves the macro f-score performance of single-modality models by 30% and 4% with respect to visual and textual information respectively", however, such an improvement is off the key. If two modals are complementary to each other, the fusion results will always be higher. The key fact is how much better than baselines the proposed GMU is. There is a long list of techniques for fusions, so it is difficult to conduct an impressive comparison on only one real dataset. I think GMU did a nice work on movie dataset, but I would also expect other techniques, including fine-tuning, dropout, distillation may help too.  It would be nice if the author could compare these techniques. 

I also hope this paper could talk in more details the connection with mixture-of-expert (MoE) model. Both models are based on the nonlinear gated functions, while both method may suffer from local minimum for optimization on small datasets. I would like more in-depth discussion in their similarity and difference.

To gain more attention for GMU, I would encourage the author to open-source their code and try more datasets.

The main idea is to use an actor-critic architecture to train the actor to encode the state representation and the critic to provide the relative importance of each class. The actor-critic model is trained through an asynchronous progressive advantage actor-critic (APA) algorithm. Extensive experiments on the Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms several state-of-the-art unsupervised methods and non-learning baselines. rule; modification, until to be accepted you can find the paper in link: https://github.com/chenyc93/APA-Unsupervisailbe-Perceptual-Rewards repair; modification, until to be accepted The original paper "Asynchronous Progressed Advantage Actor-Critic algorithm with Off-policy data" by Chen et al. extends the classic actor-critic algorithm by allowing the critic to use data from the actor during training. By tracking the advantage during training, we can achieve improved sample efficiency and prevent the parameterization of readily-avoidable states. However, in this method, the advantage calculation requires all training samples in the dataset be kept in memory, which is not only inefficient but also limits the size of the dataset that can be used. To address this issue, we present an asynchronous version of the actor-critic algorithm that only requires the training data from the most recent time period to be kept in memory. We further show that asynchronous update rules allow the algorithm to scale to larger datasets. We term this asynchronous algorithm the asynchronous progressive advantage actor-critic (APA) algorithm.

The paper Unsupervised Perceptual Rewards for Imitation Learning addresses a problem that is of great interest in the Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning communities in general, and the Imitation Learning community in particular. Specifically, it addresses the problem of unsupervised setting, where the goal is to train a feature extractor (e.g, a CNN) in an environment, without labeled training data. The solution that the paper proposes uses an alternate, supervision-free approach, based on (1) predicting a baseline (a set of expected rewards) from the feature extractor, and (2) using the discrepancy between the predicted and actual rewards as the reward signal to the feature extractor. This approach has the benefit of not relying on any direct supervision for the training of the feature extractor, and potentially giving rise to a better overall estimate of the expected reward, compared to the typical direct supervision approach, as it avoids potential bias from the direct supervision. The approach, however, also has the potential disadvantage of requiring more data to estimate the expected baseline and reward signal reliably. The paper carefully examines the tradeoff between the bias-variance tradeoff in the baseline/reward estimate, and the sample complexity required to achieve the desired performance, and gives the optimal solution as a function of the desired level of performance. I believe that this work will have significant impact in the Imitation Learning field, and would be of interest to the readership of the Imitation Learning Conference and Journal.

human_text:
The paper explores a simple approach to learning reward functions for reinforcement learning from visual observations of expert trajectories for cases were only little training data is available. To obtain descriptive rewards even under such challenging conditions the method re-uses a pre-trained neural network as feature extractor (this is similar to a large body of work on task transfer with neural nets in the area of computer vision) and represents the reward function as a weighted distance to features for automatically extracted "key-frames" of the provided expert trajectories.

The paper is well written and explains all involved concepts clearly while also embedding the presented approach in the literature on inverse reinforcement learning (IRL). The resulting algorithm is appealing due to its simplicity and could prove useful for many real world robotic applications. I have three main issues with the paper in its current form, if these can be addressed I believe the paper would be significantly strengthened:
1) Although the recursive splitting approach for extracting the "key-frames" seems reasonable and the feature selection is well motivated I am missing two baselines in the experiments:
   - what happens if the feature selection is disabled and the distance between all features is used ? will this immediately break the procedure ? If not, what is the trade-off here ? 
   - an even simpler baseline than what is proposed in the paper would be the following procedure: simply use all frames of the recorded trajectories, calculate the distance to them in feature space and weights them according to their time as in the approach proposed in the paper. How well would that work ?
2) I understand the desire to combine the extracted reward function with a simple RL method but believe the used simple controller could potentially introduce a significant bias in the experiments since it requires initialization from an expert trajectory. As a direct consequence of this initialization the RL procedure is already started close to a good solution and the extracted reward function is potentially only queried in a small region around what was observed in the initial set of images (perhaps with the exception of the human demonstrations). Without an additional experiment it is thus unclear how well the presented approach will work in combination with other RL methods for training the controller.
3) I understand that the low number of available images excludes training a deep neural net directly for the task at hand but one has to wonder how other baselines would do. What happens if one uses a random projection of the images to form a feature vector? How well would a distance measure using raw images (e.g. L2 norm of image differences) or a distance measure based on the first principal components work? It seems that occlusions etc. would exclude them from working well but without empirical evidence it is hard to confirm this.

Minor issues:
- Page 1: "make use of ideas about imitation" reads a bit awkwardly
- Page 3: "We use the Inception network pre-trained ImageNet" -> pre-trained for ImageNet classification
- Page 4: the definition of the transition function for the stochastic case seems broken
- Page 6: "efficient enough to evaluate" a bit strangely written sentence

Additional comments rather than real issues:
- The paper is mainly of empirical nature, little actual learning is performed to obtain the reward function and no theoretical advances are needed. This is not necessarily bad but makes the empirical evaluation all the more important. 
- While I liked the clear exposition the approach -- in the end -- boils down to computing quadratic distances to features of pre-extracted "key-frames", it is nice that you make a connection to standard IRL approaches in Section 2.1 but one could argue that this derivation is not strictly necessary.

 The work is well motivated and clearly written -- no issues there.

 The idea is simple and well motivated, i.e., the learning of reward functions based on feature selection from identified subtasks in videos.
 
 pros:

 - the benefit with respect to other baselines for various choices, although the latest version does contain updated baselines
 - the influence of the initial controller on the results

 I am very much on the fence for this paper.
 It straddles a number of recent advances in video segmentation, robotics, and RL, which makes the specific technical contributions harder to identify. I do think that a robotics conference would be appreciative of the work, but better learning of reward functions is surely a bottleneck and therefore of interest to ICLR.

The paper tries to present a first step towards solving the difficult problem of "learning from limited number of demonstrations". The paper tries to present 3 contributions towards this effort:
1. unsupervised segmentation of videos to identify intermediate steps in a process
2. define reward function based on feature selection for each sub-task

Pros:
+ The paper is a first attempt to solve a very challenging problem, where a robot is taught real-world tasks with very few visual demonstrations and without further retraining.
+ The method is well motivated and tries to transfer the priors learned from object classification task (through deep network features) to address the problem of limited training examples.
+ As demonstrated in Fig. 3, the reward functions could be more interpretable and correlate with transitions between subtasks.
+ Breaking a video into subtasks helps a video demonstration-based method achieve comparable performance with a method which requires full instrumentation for complex real-world tasks like door opening.

Cons:
1. Unsupervised video segmentation can serve as a good starting point to identify subtasks. However, there are multiple prior works in this domain which need to be referenced and compared with. Particularly, video shot detection and shot segmentation works try to identify abrupt change in video to break it into visually diverse shots. These methods could be easily augmented with CNN-features.
(Note that there are multiple papers in this domain, eg. refer to survey in Yuan et al. Trans. on Circuits and Systems for video tech. 2007)

2. The authors claim that they did not find it necessary to identify commonalities across demonstrations. This limits the scope of the problem drastically and requires the demonstrations to follow very specific set of constraints. Again, it is to be noted that there is past literature (video co-segmentation, eg. Tang et al. ECCV'14) which uses these commonalities to perform unsupervised video segmentation.

3. The unsupervised temporal video segmentation approach in the paper is only compared to a very simple random baseline for a few sample videos. However, given the large amount of literature in this domain, it is difficult to judge the novelty and significance of the proposed approach from these experiments.

4. The authors hypothesize that "sparse independent features exists which can discriminate a wide range of unseen inputs" and encode this intuition through the feature selection strategy. Again, the validity of the hypothesis is not experimentally well demonstrated. For instance, comparison to a simple linear classifier for subtasks would have been useful.

Overall, the paper presents a simple approach based on the idea that recognizing sub-goals in an unsupervised fashion would help in learning from few visual demonstrations. This is well motivated as a first-step towards a difficult task. However, the methods and claims presented in the paper need to be analyzed and compared with better baselines.

This paper proposes a novel method to learn vision feature as intermediate rewards to guide the robot training in the real world. Since there are only a few sequences of human demonstrations, the paper first segments the sequences into fragments so that the features are roughly invariant on the corresponding fragments across sequences, then clusters and finds most discriminative features on those fragments, and uses them as the reward function. The features are from pre-trained deep models.

The idea is simple and seems quite effective in picking the right reward functions. Fig. 6 is a good comparison (although it could be better with error bars). However, some baselines are not strong, in particular vision related baselines. For example, the random reward ("simply outputs true or false") in Tbl. 2 seems quite arbitrary and may not serve as a good baseline (but its performance is still not that bad, surprisingly.). A better baseline would be to use random/simpler feature extraction on the image, e.g., binning features and simply picking the most frequent ones, which might not be as discriminative as the proposed feature. I wonder whether a simpler vision-based approach would lead to a similarly performed reward function. If so, then these delicate steps (segment, etc) altogether.

The paper is well written and explains all involved concepts clearly while also embedding the presented approach in the literature on inverse reinforcement learning (IRL). The resulting algorithm is appealing due to its simplicity and could prove useful for many real world robotic applications. I have three main issues with the paper in its current form, if these can be addressed I believe the paper would be significantly strengthened:
1) Although the recursive splitting approach for extracting the "key-frames" seems reasonable and the feature selection is well motivated I am missing two baselines in the experiments:
   - what happens if the feature selection is disabled and the distance between all features is used ? will this immediately break the procedure ? If not, what is the trade-off here ? 
   - an even simpler baseline than what is proposed in the paper would be the following procedure: simply use all frames of the recorded trajectories, calculate the distance to them in feature space and weights them according to their time as in the approach proposed in the paper. How well would that work ?
2) I understand the desire to combine the extracted reward function with a simple RL method but believe the used simple controller could potentially introduce a significant bias in the experiments since it requires initialization from an expert trajectory. As a direct consequence of this initialization the RL procedure is already started close to a good solution and the extracted reward function is potentially only queried in a small region around what was observed in the initial set of images (perhaps with the exception of the human demonstrations). Without an additional experiment it is thus unclear how well the presented approach will work in combination with other RL methods for training the controller.
3) I understand that the low number of available images excludes training a deep neural net directly for the task at hand but one has to wonder how other baselines would do. What happens if one uses a random projection of the images to form a feature vector? How well would a distance measure using raw images (e.g. L2 norm of image differences) or a distance measure based on the first principal components work? It seems that occlusions etc. would exclude them from working well but without empirical evidence it is hard to confirm this.

Minor issues:
- Page 1: "make use of ideas about imitation" reads a bit awkwardly
- Page 3: "We use the Inception network pre-trained ImageNet" -> pre-trained for ImageNet classification
- Page 4: the definition of the transition function for the stochastic case seems broken
- Page 6: "efficient enough to evaluate" a bit strangely written sentence

Additional comments rather than real issues:
- The paper is mainly of empirical nature, little actual learning is performed to obtain the reward function and no theoretical advances are needed. This is not necessarily bad but makes the empirical evaluation all the more important. 
- While I liked the clear exposition the approach -- in the end -- boils down to computing quadratic distances to features of pre-extracted "key-frames", it is nice that you make a connection to standard IRL approaches in Section 2.1 but one could argue that this derivation is not strictly necessary.

Quality, Clarity:
 
 The work is well motivated and clearly written -- no issues there.
 
 Originality, Significance:
 
 The idea is simple and well motivated, i.e., the learning of reward functions based on feature selection from identified subtasks in videos.
 
 pros:
 - the problem is difficult and relevant: good solutions would have impact
 
 cons:
 - the benefit with respect to other baselines for various choices, although the latest version does contain updated baselines
 - the influence of the initial controller on the results

 I am very much on the fence for this paper.
 It straddles a number of recent advances in video segmentation, robotics, and RL, which makes the specific technical contributions harder to identify. I do think that a robotics conference would be appreciative of the work, but better learning of reward functions is surely a bottleneck and therefore of interest to ICLR.
 Given the lukewarm support for this paper by reviewers, the PCs decided not to accept the paper, but invite the authors to present it in the workshop track.

The paper tries to present a first step towards solving the difficult problem of "learning from limited number of demonstrations". The paper tries to present 3 contributions towards this effort:
1. unsupervised segmentation of videos to identify intermediate steps in a process
2. define reward function based on feature selection for each sub-task

Pros:
+ The paper is a first attempt to solve a very challenging problem, where a robot is taught real-world tasks with very few visual demonstrations and without further retraining.
+ The method is well motivated and tries to transfer the priors learned from object classification task (through deep network features) to address the problem of limited training examples.
+ As demonstrated in Fig. 3, the reward functions could be more interpretable and correlate with transitions between subtasks.
+ Breaking a video into subtasks helps a video demonstration-based method achieve comparable performance with a method which requires full instrumentation for complex real-world tasks like door opening.

Cons:
1. Unsupervised video segmentation can serve as a good starting point to identify subtasks. However, there are multiple prior works in this domain which need to be referenced and compared with. Particularly, video shot detection and shot segmentation works try to identify abrupt change in video to break it into visually diverse shots. These methods could be easily augmented with CNN-features.
(Note that there are multiple papers in this domain, eg. refer to survey in Yuan et al. Trans. on Circuits and Systems for video tech. 2007)

2. The authors claim that they did not find it necessary to identify commonalities across demonstrations. This limits the scope of the problem drastically and requires the demonstrations to follow very specific set of constraints. Again, it is to be noted that there is past literature (video co-segmentation, eg. Tang et al. ECCV'14) which uses these commonalities to perform unsupervised video segmentation.

3. The unsupervised temporal video segmentation approach in the paper is only compared to a very simple random baseline for a few sample videos. However, given the large amount of literature in this domain, it is difficult to judge the novelty and significance of the proposed approach from these experiments.

4. The authors hypothesize that "sparse independent features exists which can discriminate a wide range of unseen inputs" and encode this intuition through the feature selection strategy. Again, the validity of the hypothesis is not experimentally well demonstrated. For instance, comparison to a simple linear classifier for subtasks would have been useful.

Overall, the paper presents a simple approach based on the idea that recognizing sub-goals in an unsupervised fashion would help in learning from few visual demonstrations. This is well motivated as a first-step towards a difficult task. However, the methods and claims presented in the paper need to be analyzed and compared with better baselines.

This paper proposes a novel method to learn vision feature as intermediate rewards to guide the robot training in the real world. Since there are only a few sequences of human demonstrations, the paper first segments the sequences into fragments so that the features are roughly invariant on the corresponding fragments across sequences, then clusters and finds most discriminative features on those fragments, and uses them as the reward function. The features are from pre-trained deep models.

The idea is simple and seems quite effective in picking the right reward functions. Fig. 6 is a good comparison (although it could be better with error bars). However, some baselines are not strong, in particular vision related baselines. For example, the random reward ("simply outputs true or false") in Tbl. 2 seems quite arbitrary and may not serve as a good baseline (but its performance is still not that bad, surprisingly.). A better baseline would be to use random/simpler feature extraction on the image, e.g., binning features and simply picking the most frequent ones, which might not be as discriminative as the proposed feature. I wonder whether a simpler vision-based approach would lead to a similarly performed reward function. If so, then these delicate steps (segment, etc) altogether.

This paper addresses the problem of automatically determining clusters or categories for the purpose of evaluating the effectiveness of distributed representations such as word vectors. The authors introduce the idea of correlating clusters from a parallel corpus with those that result from clustering a word vectors in a non-parametric manner using Jensen-Shannon Divergence, a method of determining cluster significance based on divergence from a mixture distribution. The paper has a few potential strengths. First, it is innovative in the sense that it introduces a new way of clustering word vectors using a non-parametric method. Second, it shows that the clusters resulting from this method have correlation with those determined by human annotators, which is a useful performance metric. Third, it shows that this method is computationally efficient, with results being available in a matter of minutes on a standard desktop computer. However, there are also a number of areas for future work. The choice of Jensen-Shannon Divergence as the measure of cluster significance is somewhat ad hoc, with the choice of distance measure not being particularly well motivated. In addition, the authors note that more work is needed on tuning parameters to make the method more scalable to large corpora. 1. Problem: Identify clusters for the purpose of evaluating distributed representations. 2. Strength: The method is non-parametric, making it efficient and easy to apply to large datasets. 3. Weakness: The choice of Jensen-Shannon divergence to measure cluster significance is arbitrary, and more work needs to be done on tuning parameters to make the method scalable to large datasets.

I have some constructive comments and concerns, please take them into consideration when you read this. 1. The introduction could be clearer what the proposed method actually does, how it differs from related work and why it is relevant for the task at hand. 2. The motivation for the particular choice of clusters and evaluation methodology should be explained in more detail. 3. It would be good to include a reference to the code that was used to create the gold-standard dataset, as well as a link to it on GitHub. 4. Would be good to have some qualitative evaluation as well, e.g. visualisations of clusters, or some samples of how the outliers looked like, in order to give the reader a better sense of what the outliers look like. 5. The claimed correlation between outlier detection and sentiment analysis might be too optimistic, as the proposed evaluation setup is fairly standardly used for evaluating word embeddings. So, I think it would be fair to say that performance on the outlier detection task might help to evaluate word embeddings, but it is certainly not a replacement for using the actual real-world data and correlation/regression analysis to evaluate sentiment analysis task. I think the proposed method might have some value as a general tool for the evaluation of distributed representations, but it is certainly not a replacement for other evaluation methodologies, which are usually more tailored to a specific task and datasets. Any other thoughts? I look forward to your responses. Thank you for your work. Best, Filippo Radicchi PS. Please let me know if you want me to make any changes to the paper based on these comments. This paper proposes a language-agnostic way of automatically generating sets of semantically similar clusters of entities along with sets of "outlier" elements, which can be used to perform an intrinsic evaluation of word embeddings in the outlier detection task. The authors use a network of distantly supervised entity pairs, with the hypothesis that if two entities are likely to be in the same cluster, their representations in the word2vec space are likely to be similar as well. To evaluate a set of clusters, the authors create a gold-standard dataset called WikiSem500, by considering a similarity measure for entity pairs and using a clustering algorithm to group similar entities together. The authors use four different evaluation datasets, which are different depending on the purpose of the models being evaluated: distantly-supervised, paraphrase, distant-clone and binary-classification. The results show that the proposed methodology is language-independent and can be applied to any evaluation dataset. This way, the intrinsic evaluation of word embeddings can be performed in a more automatic and scalable way, with the hope that new models are compared to a higher quality baseline. The main drawback of the proposed approach is that it requires a large set of aligned sentences, which are hard to obtain for languages other than English. This is the case because the authors use a logistic regression model to predict if two entities are likely to appear in the same document, which requires fixed chunks of text. To overcome this problem, the authors evaluate their approach on three other languages besides English, but it would be interesting to see how the approach would perform if evaluated on languages without such resources available. Another interesting point to mention is that the authors use the ROC-AUC metric to compare the results of different models, but this metric is not fully compatible with the distribution of the datasets that are being evaluated. It would be interesting to see how the approach performs if other evaluation metrics are used. Overall, this is an interesting approach to evaluate word embeddings, as it is a novel way to evaluate these models in an intrinsic way, without the need of any extra labeled data. The drawback of this method is that the aligned text needed for the logistic regression model is hard to come by for other languages. The results show that the approach is language-independent and can be applied to any evaluation dataset, so this is definitely a method that should be kept in mind for anyone working with NLP models. The dataset WikiSem500 contains clusters of entities with a score representing the level of semantic relatedness of the clusters, and "outlier" entities that may not be well represented by the cluster. The authors also provide precomputed clusters for over 200K entity pairs, which can be downloaded from the website. The dataset has two main uses. The first is as a baseline for intrinsic evaluation of semantic representations, which is achieved by training a model to predict if pairs of entities are similar according to some semantic metric. The model will typically underestimate the degree to which pairs of entities are similar, because it only takes into account the co-occurrence of the two entities in the text, without considering other factors such as the similarity of their semantics. A second use is to identify "outliers" (i.e. pairs of entities that are more similar than expected based on their co-occurrence in text). This can be important because many NLP tasks benefit from knowing if two entities are similar or not, but this property is often ignored by models. For example, we might want to identify entity pairs which are likely to be used in a paraphrase detection task, or pairs of entities that are likely to appear in the same document but have not been considered by the model during training. The main idea is that we want to find semantically similar, but unlike, entities to evaluate a set of models. One approach is to use a clustering algorithm to group similar entities together, and compute the average semantic relatedness of each cluster to the other entities in the set. We want to identify the "outlier" entities that are dissimilar to the clusters of similar entities. A naïve way of evaluating a model based on co-occurrence would assign the mean similarity to each entity. However, this does not account for the fact that similar entities are usually more similar than dissimilar entities. So if we compute the mean similarity over all entities, some entities which actually lie in the distinct cluster of dissimilar entities will now appear as similar as entities in the similar cluster of similar entities. Thus, it is also important to identify these outliers. The main contribution of this work is a model to predict if two entities are likely to appear in the same document (which is needed to compute the similarity score between entities using logistic regression), using a soft-clustering approach to account for noisy and unreliable labeled data. First, let me praise the authors for generating and releasing an NLP data set: a socially useful task.

The authors use an algorithm to generate a 500-cluster-per-language data set in semantic similarity. This brings up a few points.

1. If the point of using the algorithm is to be scalable, why release such a small data set? It's roughly the same order of magnitude as the data sets released in the SemEval tasks over the recent years. I would have expected something orders of magnitude larger.

2. The authors hand checked a small subset of the clusters: they found one where it was ambiguous, and should probably have been removed. Mechanical Turk can scale pretty well -- why not post-facto filter all of the clusters using MT? This is (in effect) how ImageNet was created, and it has millions of items.

3. Evaluating data set papers is an tricky issue. What makes a data set "good" or publishable? There are a number of medium-sized NLP data sets released every year (e.g., through SemEval). Those are designed to address tasks in NLP that people find interesting. I don't know of a data set that exactly addresses the task that the authors propose: the task is trying to address the idea of semantic similarity, which has had multiple data sets thrown at it since SemEval 2012. I wish that the paper had included comparisons to show that the particular task / data combination is better suited for analyzing semantic similarity than other existing data sets.

Two final notes:

A. This paper doesn't seem very well-suited to ICLR.  New NLP data sets may be indirectly useful for evaluating word embeddings (and hence representations). But, I didn't learn much from the paper: GloVe is empirically less good for semantic similarity than other embeddings? If true, why? That would be interesting.

B. The first proposal for the "put a word into a cluster and see if it stands out" task (in the context of human evaluation of topic models), is

Jonathan Chang, Jordan Boyd-Graber, Chong Wang, Sean Gerrish, and David M. Blei. Reading Tea Leaves: HowHumans Interpret Topic Models. Neural Information Processing Systems, 2009

which deserves a citation, I think.

The reviewers (and I) welcome new approaches to evaluation, and this work appears to be a sound contribution to that space. I suggest that, because the paper's incremental findings are of somewhat narrower interest, it is a good fit for a workshop, so that the ideas can be discussed at ICLR and further developed into a more mature publication.

This paper introduces a new dataset to evaluate word representations. The task considered in the paper, called outlier detection (also known as word intrusion), is to identify which word does not belong to a set of semantically related words. The task was proposed by Camacho-Collados & Navigli (2016) as an evaluation of word representations. The main contribution of this paper is to introduce a new dataset for this task, covering 5 languages. The dataset was generated automatically from the Wikidata hierarchy.
Entities which are instances of the same category are considered as belonging to the same cluster, and outliers are sampled at various distances in the tree. Several heuristics are then proposed to exclude uninteresting clusters from the dataset.

Developing good ressources to evaluate word representations is an important task. The new dataset introduced in this paper might be an interesting addition to the existing ones (however, it is hard to say by only reviewing the paper). I am a bit concerned by the lack of discussion and comparison with existing approaches (besides word similarity datasets). In particular, I believe it would be interesting to discuss the advantages of this evaluation/dataset, compared to existing ones such as word analogies. The proposed evaluation also seems highly related to entity typing, which is not discussed in the paper.

Overall, I believe that introducing ressources for evaluating word representations is very important for the community. However, I am a bit ambivalent about this submission. I am not entirely convinced that the proposed dataset have clear advantages over existing ressources. It also seems that existing tasks, such as entity typing, already capture similar properties of word representations. Finally, it might be more relevant to submit this paper to LREC than to ICLR.

This paper describes a new benchmark for word representations: spotting the “odd one out”. The authors build upon an idea recently presented at the RepEval workshop, but are able to collect a significantly larger amount of examples by relying on existing ontologies.

Although the innovation is relatively incremental, it is an important step in defining challenging benchmarks for general-purpose word representations. While humans are able to perform this task almost flawlessly (given adequate domain knowledge), the experiments in this paper show that current embeddings fall short. The technical contribution is thorough; the dataset construction appears logical, and the correlation analysis is convincing. I would like to see it accepted at ICLR.

machine_text: Overall, the authors have nicely presented an extension to the Shift-aggregate framework for order-preserving updates, and demonstrated its ability to improve the state of the art on several benchmark datasets. I have a few comments/questions regarding the implementation, which might be useful in future work. 1) The introduction of the notion of neighbourhood is a very interesting idea, and is generally applicable to many different modelling tasks. However, in this specific case, it seems quite restrictive, since the number of possible neighbours is fixed to the number of previous shifts. It would be interesting to see how the results would be affected when this restriction is lifted (or at least made clearer). 2) Similarly, in the description of the algorithm, it is mentioned that the order of the candidates for the next shift is not important. However, as far as I can see, the exact order does matter, since different neighbours in the function space correspond to different orderings of the dimensions. How about exploring that space of permutations in order to find the best candidate? 3) Another potentially more efficient approach would be to avoid calculating the update at all, and use only the average and variance of the neighbouring models, as done in the original Shift paper. It would be interesting to compare the current method, which involves updating the model explicitly, with one which uses only the sample mean and variance. 4) Finally, it seems possible to adapt the algorithm for situations where the functions are real-valued, rather than discrete. In that case, the term square distance would have to be modified, since the sum in the square distance loss should be replaced by an outer product. Beyond these general remarks, I think the paper is an interesting contribution to the field, and I recommend it for publication.

This paper addresses a question that has been identified as important to the ML community: how to train deep neural nets such that extracted features reflect the relevant structure of the data. The core technique the paper introduces, Shift Aggregate Extract (SAE), is an efficient way to train deep neural nets that capture spatial relationships in input data. The paper makes a case for SAE in two broad ways. First, SAE, by its nature, is a spatially-sensitive architecture; that is, it can only learn to encode spatial relationships between inputs. Second, the authors show that SAE has achieved state of the art results on image recognition tasks, thus providing a track record of success. However, the SAE architecture is relatively complex, so it is not intuitively obvious how to apply it to other tasks. The bulk of the examples are in the paper's Appendix, and while these examples provide insights into how to apply the SAE architecture, they do not fully explore its potential. More generally, this paper could have benefited from a more systematic treatment of SAE's properties and relation to the broader body of work on neural architecture design. Some related work is the 1997 works of Carlevaro et al. and Merkle and Hüllermeier. There are many other examples of modular neural architectures, each with their own strengths and weaknesses. An evaluation of SAE in comparison with these other architectures could have given the paper more insight into SAE's strengths and weaknesses.

For further validation, the algorithm can be tested on multiple dataset and result comparison with other state of the art algorithms would be good. 3. There are several parameters in the algorithm. I think there should be a study on the selection of these parameters. Overall, the algorithm has promising results and can be a state of the art for the problem of learning representations from social network data. I recommend to publish the paper in a good conference or journal. Best, D. Introduction ============ People and organizations interact with other people and organizations in social networks. To understand the content of these interactions, one can think of social networks as labeled graphs in which nodes are people or organizations and edges represent the interactions between people and organizations. For example, consider a friendship network between people. The nodes in this network can be people and the edges can be the friendships between them. In the similar way, consider a product-purchase network between organizations, where the nodes are the organizations and the edges represent the purchase of the products between them. In summary, in this work we consider both social networks and the data related to them as labeled graphs. With the labeled graph, one can apply machine learning techniques to learn a good representation for the nodes. The learned representation can be used to efficiently process the nodes, such as computing the neighbors of a node or generating fake nodes to mislead the machine learning model. There are several works on using deep learning to learn a good representation for the nodes in a labeled graph. However, most of these works construct a new labeled graph that is different from the original labeled graph. For example, for a social network, the nodes are the people and the edges represent the friendships between them. However, they first construct a new labeled graph in which the nodes are the friendships and the edges represent the people. By changing the original labeled graph, the new algorithm may not perform as well as the original algorithm on the initial model because of the differences in the constructed labeled graph and the domain gap between the new labeled graph and the domain of the initial model. Moreover, the new algorithm is usually more complex and it is difficult to explain and maintain. Hence, it would be good to have an algorithm that can learn a good representation for the nodes in the labeled graph. Vector representations of each object are learnt by applying'shift', 'aggregate' and 'extract' operations on the vector representations of its parts. The algorithm for domain compression takes advantage of symmetries in hierarchical decompositions to reduce the memory usage and speed up the algorithm. In this work, we consider networks of people. This has three major advantages: (1) The choice of human interaction data over any other type of data will likely be a deciding factor for adoption and commercial success. (2) It's an extremely relevant domain for many practical applications. (3) As a technical contribution, while the theory can be applied to any domain, we provide empirical validation on this domain. Contributions ------------- - We introduce the shift, aggregate and extract operations that can generate high level representation of the nodes in a graph. - We describe an algorithm that learns representations from a network of people through a series of three operations applied on the nodes of the network. - We demonstrate the effectiveness of shift aggregate extract network on benchmark dataset. - We demonstrate that SAEN can compute node representation using only a small part of the nodes in a network while preserving the correctness for the rest of the nodes. Some of the key details in this paper are very poorly explained or not even explained at all. The model sounds interesting and there may be something good here, but it should not be published in it's current form. 

Specific comments:

The description of the R_l,pi convolutions in Section 2.1 was unclear. Specifically, I wasn't confident that I understood what the labels pi represented.

The description of the SAEN structure in section 2.2 was worded poorly. My understanding, based on Equation 1, is that the 'shift' operation is simply a summation of the representations of the member objects, and that the 'aggregate' operation simply concatenates the representations from multiple relations.  In the 'shift' step, it seems more appropriate to average over the object's member's representations h_j, rather than sum over them.

The compression technique presented in Section 2.3 requires that multiple objects at a level have the same representation. Why would this ever occur, given that the representations are real valued and high-dimensional? The text is unintelligible: "two objects are equivalent if they are made by same sets of parts for all the pi-parameterizations of the R_l,pi decomposition relation." 

The 'ego graph patterns' in Figure 1 and 'Ego Graph  Neural Network' used in the experiments are never explained in the text, and no references are given. Because of this, I cannot comment on the quality of the experiments.

The authors present a novel architecture, called Shift Aggregate Extract Network (SAEN), for learning representations on social network data. SAEN decomposes input graphs into hierarchies made of multiple strata of objects. The proposed approach gives very promising experimental results on several real-world social network datasets. 
 
 The idea is novel and interesting. However, the exposition of the framework and the approach could be significantly improved. The authors clearly made an effort to revise the paper and improve the clarity. Yet, the paper would still certainly benefit from a major revision, to clarify the exposition and spell out all the details of the framework. 
 
 A extensive use of the space in the supplement could potentially help overcoming the space limitation in the main part of the paper which can make exposition of new frameworks challenging in general. This would allow an extensive explanation of the proposed framework and related concepts. 
 
 A major revision of the paper will generate a stronger submission, which we invite the authors to submit to the workshop track.

A) we rewrote section 2:
    A1) we generally improved the wording,
    A2) we added a figure in order to exemplify H-hierarchical decompositions,
    A3) we improved the explanation of the \pi labels (now called "membership types"),
    A4) we rewrote and clarified the assumptions under which domain compression works,
    A5) we added a footnote with the definition of r-neighborhood subgraphs/ego-graphs,
    A6) we introduced the term 'collapsibility' for the equivalence relation between objects in the same stratum.

The paper contributes to recent work investigating how neural networks can be used on graph-structured data. As far as I can tell, the proposed approach is the following:

  1. Construct a hierarchical set of "objects" within the graph. Each object consists of multiple "parts" from the set of objects in the level below. There are potentially different ways a part can be part of an object (the different \pi labels), which I would maybe call "membership types". In the experiments, the objects at the bottom level are vertices. At the next level they are radius 0 (just a vertex?) and radius 1 neighborhoods around each vertex, and the membership types here are either "root", or "element" (depending on whether a vertex is the center of the neighborhood or a neighbor). At the top level there is one object consisting of all of these neighborhoods, with membership types of "radius 0 neighborhood" (isn't this still just a vertex?) or "radius 1 neighborhood".

  2. Every object has a representation. Each vertex's representation is a one-hot encoding of its degree. To construct an object's representation at the next level, the following scheme is employed:

    a. For each object, sum the representation of all of its parts having the same membership type.
    b. Concatenate the sums obtained from different membership types.
    c. Pass this vector through a multi-layer neural net.

I've provided this summary mainly because the description in the paper itself is somewhat hard to follow, and relevant details are scattered throughout the text, so I'd like to verify that my understanding is correct.

Some additional questions I have that weren't clear from the text: how many layers and hidden units were used? What are the dimensionalities of the representations used at each layer? How is final classification performed? What is the motivation for the chosen "ego-graph" representation? 

The proposed approach is interesting and novel, the compression technique appears effective, and the results seem compelling. However, the clarity and structure of the writing is quite poor. It took me a while to figure out what was going on---the initial description is provided without any illustrative examples, and it required jumping around the paper to figure for example how the \pi labels are actually used. Important details around network architecture aren't provided, and very little in the way of motivation is given for many of the choices made. Were other choices of decomposition/object-part structures investigated, given the generality of the shift-aggregate-extract formulation? What motivated the choice of "ego-graphs"? Why one-hot degrees for the initial attributes?

Overall, I think the paper contains a useful contribution on a technical level, but the presentation needs to be significantly cleaned up before I can recommend acceptance.

CL-FTRL depends on using finite differences to compute gradients, which can be inefficient for real-world models. The authors should consider using automatic differentiation to compute the gradients in the experiments. 2. The paper only discusses the binary classification task. It would be nice to also discuss how CL-FTRL would scale to other tasks (e.g, multiclass classification or regression). 3. In the experiment section, for CIFAR-10, the model trained by CL-FTRL only has 22M parameters, while the baseline model NetTrain has 55M parameters. It would be nice to also mention the computational cost of CL-FTRL compared to NetTrain. 4. A lot of useful information are missing from the paper. For example, I'm not sure how well CL-FTRL performs compared to other approaches. Did the authors compare CL-FTRL with other DFI implementations? Did the authors study the effect of changing hyperparameters? etc. Overall, I think the paper is interesting, and it would be nice if the authors could address the above comments. The Differentiable Forth Interpreter (DFI) is implemented as a variant of the well-known DPP-Forth programming paradigm. Here is an explanation of the differentiable interpreter: The differentiable interpreter is designed to allow the behaviour of sketches to be optimized through gradient descent on user-specified objectives, as opposed to manual optimizations (e.g., constant folding) that are often only achievable by experts with full insight into the program structure. End-to-end gradient-based optimisation of the behaviour allows learning of complex tasks from a small number of program examples. The dual stack machine architecture underpins the Forth interpreter, which allows the incorporation of prior program structure into the model. A sketch can be implemented as a Forth program that uses slots for specifying the behaviour. These are filled with neural networks that implement the behaviour of the sketch. The Forth interpreter evaluates sketches that combine program fragments according to the Lisp syntax, passing the output to the corresponding functions of the slots. The main framework of the differentiable interpreter is as follows: The program is translated into Lisp by the P4interpreter, the front end of the Forth interpreter, which allows a simple and efficient evaluation of the program. The Forth interpreter simulates the execution of the Forth program in the back end. During the execution of the program, the API of the Forth interpreter is used by the user to capture the gradients of the objective function with respect to the behaviour of the sketch. Here are the key differences between the dual stack machine and other neural network-based machine learning approaches: Unlike the key-value memory of DNN, the dual stack machine is more efficient for Lisp-based programming languages because its programs consist of slots that can be filled by specific implementations. The programming languages for the dual stack machine include Lisp and Forth, but DNNs are usually only able to process strings. The third important characteristic of the dual stack machine for practical applications is the partial independence between the program and the model: the model only provides an implementation of the behaviour, but does not change the code of the program. This allows multiple sketches with the same API but different program contents to be incorporated into a model and shared by multiple applications. Besides the Forth interpreter and the Lisp interpreter, another key component of the differentiable interpreter is the API for capturing the gradients of the objective function with respect to the behaviour. Using this API, the behaviour can be updated in an end-to-end gradient-based manner, allowing for more complex and sophisticated sketches. Based on the Forth interpreter and the Lisp interpreter, the Forth interpeter can be viewed as an interpreter for the Lisp-based dual stack machine. The remainder of the paper focuses on the implementation of the Forth interpreter and provides the following implementation details: 1. The dual stack architecture of the Forth interpreter 2. The Forth interpreter tokenizer and virtual lexical system 3.
