GANs provide an algorithmic framework for constructing generative models with several appealing properties. These include the generative model being able to describe the data generation process, or the likelihood function being unnecessary. This allows us to learn the complex distribution of data. A good example of this is facial images. A GAN can be trained on millions of images of faces, and the model has the capacity to implicitly learn the complex data distribution. Another interesting property of GANs is that they provide samples that are sharp and compelling. Another example is the generation of day-after-use face photos. However, GANs also have some problems, for example, there is lack of theoretical foundation. A question that comes to mind is what the fundamental relationship is between GANs and the reality? We cannot answer this question yet. Therefore, GANs are like a tool, and we should use it carefully. One of the direction that has been explored recently is to combine GANs with other machine learning algorithm to form a more flexible model. For example, we can build a progressive network by combining a GAN as the first step with an image classifier as the second step. Such a model has the potential to describe the complex relationship between the data distribution and the learned knowledge. Another important application of GANs is generative adversarial sampleNet. In this scenario, we have two deep networks that interact with each other. The role of the first network is to generate samples from a simple distribution, and that of the second network is to distinguish the generated samples from real ones. One drawback of GANs is that the generation process is quite tricky. For example, it is very hard to control the quality of images generated by GANs. We build a more broad understanding of GANs from the perspective of learning in implicit generative models. We also connect GANs with other related research directions such as density ratio estimation, likelihood-free inference and density ratio testing. The main contributions of this work are as follows: 1) We provide a framework to unite many existing GAN variations. 2) We provide a synthesis view of existing learning approaches in implicit generative models. 3) We connect GANs to a broad range of other research directions. We believe that developing this understanding of GANs will help us better understand GANs and its applications, and at the same time, this gives us a fresh perspective to look at other related work. There are four main directions to learn in implicit generative models. They are density ratio estimation, divergence minimisation, moment matching and classifier. We can use hypothesis testing to learn. The testing idea is to determine whether the data come from the underlying distribution. We present the testing based objective function and the testing based learning procedure. In conclusion, in this paper, we provide a framework to unite many existing GAN variations. We also connect GANs to a broad range of other research directions. We build a more broad understanding of GANs from the perspective of learning in implicit generative models. human_text:
Thank you for an interesting read.

Given the huge interest in generative modelling nowadays, this paper is very timely and does provide very clear connections between methods that don't use maximum likelihood for training. It made a very useful observation that the generative and the discriminative loss do **not** need to be coupled with each other. I think this paper in summary provides some very useful insights to the practitioners on how to select the objective function to train the implicit generative model.

The only reason that I decided to hold back my strong acceptance recommendation is that I don't understand the acceptance criteria of ICLR. First this paper has the style very similar to the Sugiyama et al. papers that are cited (e.g. presenting in different perspectives that were all covered in those papers but in a different context), making me unsure about how to evaluate the novelty. Second this paper has no experiment nor mathematical theorem, and I'm not exactly sure what kinds of contributions the ICLR committee is looking for.

Hello Authors,

Congratulations on the acceptance of the paper.

I've just reread parts of the revised paper and noticed a few things that you might want to consider and change before the camera-ready deadline.

* You now include a reference to KLIEP after Eqn. (16), but this procedure is in fact known as least-squares importance estimation.
* in turn, Eqn. (14) is actually more akin to KLIEP, the main difference being the use of the unnormalised form of the KL-divergence. So I think you meant to put the KLIEP reference here.

Further comment on making Eqn. (14) practical:
If you read the KLIEP paper, they formulate the procedure as a constrained optimisation problem:
maximise
$$
E_{p^*} log r_\phi(x)
$$
subject to the constraint that
$$
E_{q_\theta} r_\phi(x) = 1
$$

Compare this constrained optimisation to your solution, it is easy to make the connection: if you introduce a Lagrange multiplier to handle the constraint, one obtains the following unconstrained optimisation problem:

seek stationary points of

$$
\ell(\phi, \lambda) = E_{p^*} log r_\phi(x) - \lambda E_{q_\theta} (r_\phi(x) - 1)
$$

I do think that solving this unconstrained optimisation problem is actually possible, you can do that via stochastic gradient descent, and it does not include your nasty cross-entropy term.

What am I missing?

Thanks,

This paper provides a unifying review of various forms of generative model. The paper offers some neat perspectives that could encourage links between areas of machine learning and statistics. However, there aren't specific new proposals, and so there is no empirical evaluation either. The PCs thus believe this contribution is more appropriate for the Workshop Track.

The reviewers have two common concerns (1) relevance of this paper to ICLR, and (2) its novelty. We address the common concerns here and address other questions individually.

The aim of our paper is to review different approaches for learning in implicit generative models; GANs are a special case of implicit generative models and our work helps understand connections between GAN variants as well as understand how GANs are related to the wider statistical literature. We are not aware of any other work in the GAN literature which discusses the connections to approximate Bayesian computation, moment-matching and two sample-testing, unsupervised-as-supervised learning, optimal transport, likelihood free inference, or non-maximum likelihood estimation, even though these methods are clearly related. We believe these connections would be interesting to ICLR community for at least two reasons: (1) we can borrow tools from the related literature to improve optimisation and analyse convergence and (2) we can use GAN-like techniques to train differentiable simulators in other application domains (e.g high energy physics, economics, ecology), thereby opening up exciting research directions. AnonReviewer4 writes “I believe this work is significant - it provides a bridge for language and methods used in multiple parts of statistics and machine learning. This has the potential to accelerate progress.” And AnonReviewer1 writes “It is well written and a good read, and one I would recommend to people who would like to get involved in GANs.” This was our aim, and why this paper is of relevance to ICLR.

Novelty: The view of hypothesis testing gives an insight about the learning principle used in likelihood free / implicit models. This view also helps understand connections between variants of GANs; for instance, methods that use the density ratio (e.g. the original GAN paper, f-GAN and b-GAN) or the density difference (e.g. generative moment matching networks). To the best of our knowledge, this unifying view through hypothesis testing is novel (see also the concurrent submissions by Lopez-paz and Oquab (2016) and Uehara et al. (2016)). To quote AnonReviewer4, “the individual pieces are not novel, and yet the exposition of all of them in the same space with clear outline of the connections between them is novel.” 
The unifying view opens up lots of interesting research directions, e.g., since our initial arxiv submission, Kareletsos (2016) has published “Adversarial Message Passing For Graphical Models”

I just noticed I submitted my review as a pre-review question - sorry about this. Here it is again, with a few more thoughts added...

The authors present a great and - as far as I can tell - accurate and honest overview of the emerging theory about GANs from a likelihood ratio estimation/divergence minimisation perspective. It is well written and a good read, and one I would recommend to people who would like to get involved in GANs.

My main problem with this submission is that it is hard as a reviewer to pin down what precisely the novelty is - beyond perhaps articulating these views better than other papers have done in the past. A sentence from the paper "But it has left us unsatisfied since we have not gained the insight needed to choose between them.” summarises my feeling about this paper: this is a nice 'unifying review’ type paper that - for me - lacks a novel insight.

In summary, my assessment is mixed: I think this is a great paper, I enjoyed reading it. I was left a bit disappointed by the lack of novel insight, or a singular key new idea which you often expect in conference presentations, and this is why I’m not highly confident about this as a conference submission (and hence my low score) I am open to be convinced either way.

Detailed comments:

I think the authors should probably discuss the connection of Eq. (13) to KLIEP: Kullback-Leibler Importance Estimation by Shugiyama and colleagues.

I don’t quite see how the part with equation (13) and (14) fit into the flow of the paper. By this point the authors have established the view that GANs are about estimating likelihood ratios - and then using these likelihood ratios to improve the generator. These paragraphs read like: we also tried to derive another particular formulation for doing this but we failed to do it in a practical way.

There is a typo in spelling Csiszar divergence

Equation (15) is known (to me) as Least Squares Importance Estimation by Kanamori et al (2009). A variant of least-squares likelihood estimation uses the kernel trick, and finds a function from an RKHS that best represents the likelihood ratio between the two distributions in a least squares sense. I think it would be interesting to think about how this function is related to the witness function commonly used in MMD and what the properties of this function are compared to the witness function - perhaps showing the two things for simple distributions.

I have stumbled upon the work of Sugiyama and collaborators on direct density ratio estimation before, and I found that work very insightful. Generally, while some of this work is cited in this paper, I felt that the authors could do more to highlight the great work of this group, who have made highly significant contributions to density ratio estimation, albeit with a different goal in mind.

On likelihood ratio estimation: some methods approximate the likelihood ratio directly (such as least-squares importance estimation), some can be thought of more as approximating the log of this quantity (logistic regression, denoising autoencoders). An unbiased estimate of the ratio will provide a biased estimate of the logarithm and vice versa. To me it feels like estimating the log of the ratio directly is more useful, and in more generality estimating the convex function of the ratio which is used to define the f-divergence seems like a good approach. Could the authors comment on this?

I think the hypothesis testing angle is oversold in the paper.  I’m not sure what additional insight is gained by mixing in some hypothesis testing terminology. Other than using quantities that appear in hypothesis testing as tests statistics, his work does not really talk about hypothesis testing, nor does it use any tools from the hypothesis testing literature. In this sense, this paper is in contrast with Sutherland et al (in review for ICLR) who do borrow concepts from two-sample testing to optimise hyperparameters of the divergence used.

The paper provides an exposition of multiple ways of learning in implicit generative models, of which generative adversarial networks are an example. The paper is very clear, the exposition is insightful, and the presented material is clearly important.

It is hard to assess "novelty" of this work, as the individual pieces are not novel, and yet the exposition of all of them in the same space with clear outline of the connections between them is novel.

I believe this work is significant - it provides a bridge for language and methods used in multiple parts of statistics and machine learning. This has the potential to accelerate progress.

I recommend publishing this paper at ICLR, even though it is not the "typical" paper that get published at this conference (in that it doesn't offer empirical validation, nor makes a particular claim about relative merits of different methods).

Hello Authors,

Congratulations on the acceptance of the paper.

I've just reread parts of the revised paper and noticed a few things that you might want to consider and change before the camera-ready deadline.

If you read the KLIEP paper, they formulate the procedure as a constrained optimisation problem:
maximise
$$
E_{p^*} log r_\phi(x)
$$
subject to the constraint that
$$
E_{q_\theta} r_\phi(x) = 1
$$

Compare this constrained optimisation to your solution, it is easy to make the connection: if you introduce a Lagrange multiplier to handle the constraint, one obtains the following unconstrained optimisation problem:

seek stationary points of

$$
\ell(\phi, \lambda) = E_{p^*} log r_\phi(x) - \lambda E_{q_\theta} (r_\phi(x) - 1)
$$

I do think that solving this unconstrained optimisation problem is actually possible, you can do that via stochastic gradient descent, and it does not include your nasty cross-entropy term.

The reviewers have two common concerns (1) relevance of this paper to ICLR, and (2) its novelty. We address the common concerns here and address other questions individually.

The aim of our paper is to review different approaches for learning in implicit generative models; GANs are a special case of implicit generative models and our work helps understand connections between GAN variants as well as understand how GANs are related to the wider statistical literature. We are not aware of any other work in the GAN literature which discusses the connections to approximate Bayesian computation, moment-matching and two sample-testing, unsupervised-as-supervised learning, optimal transport, likelihood free inference, or non-maximum likelihood estimation, even though these methods are clearly related. We believe these connections would be interesting to ICLR community for at least two reasons: (1) we can borrow tools from the related literature to improve optimisation and analyse convergence and (2) we can use GAN-like techniques to train differentiable simulators in other application domains (e.g high energy physics, economics, ecology), thereby opening up exciting research directions. The authors apply the image captioning architecture of Xu et al. 2015 to video captioning. The model is extended to have attention over multiple layers of the ConvNet instead of just a single layer. Experiments on YouTube2Text, M-VAD and MSR-VTT show that this works better than only using one of the layers at a time.

I think this is solid work on the level of a well-executed course project or a workshop paper. The model makes sense, it is adequately described, and the experiments show that attending over multiple layers works better than attending over any one layer in isolation. Unfortunately, I don't think there is enough to get excited about here from a technical perspective and it's not clear what value the paper brings to the community. Other aspects of the paper, such as including the hard attention component, don't seem to add to the paper but take up space. 

If the authors want to contribute a detailed, focused exploration of multi-level features this could become a more valuable paper, but in that case I would expect a much more thorough exploration of the choices and tradeoffs of different schemes without too many spurious aspects such as video features, hard attention, etc.

Reviewers feel the work is well executed and that the model makes sense, but two of the reviewers were not convinced that the proposed method contains enough novelty in light of prior work. There are a number of compelling insights in the paper, especially around using smaller neural nets in safety-critical applications and the interplay between size, representational capacity and complexity. I have some minor suggestions to make the paper even stronger. 1. The abstract focuses too much on size and not enough on impact. For example, the last sentence should highlight the reduction in model size and complexity as positive aspects of the research. 2. In the introduction, the third paragraph could benefit from an overview of the threat model and how the defence improves on it. For example, in a car, an intruding model could compromise safety due to various reasons. It would be useful to describe how the defence addresses that threat. 3. The first paragraph of the results could benefit from more context. It would be helpful to mention the threat model and attack method at the start of the paragraph. I am confident that the author has an interesting research direction and insights to offer in this area and with this research. I hope this is of interest.

This paper presents a way of adding robustness to machine learning models using very small neural nets. The authors describe how to create concepts that represent groups of data and use these concepts to add robustness to a model trained on a large number of examples. The main idea is to use a very small neural net to encode the concept and use the concept to regularize the model's prediction. The small size of the neural net means that it adds very little computational cost to the model training, while improving its robustness. The paper does a good job explaining how to create concepts and conduct experiments with text and image data. The paper makes a solid technical contribution in establishing a universal approximation theorem for the boolean hypercube. They characterize the class of boolean functions that can be efficiently approximated by a two-layer network.
 
 We like the idea of noise stability, and it could explain why in practice, perturbation techniques such as dropout are effective. Moreover, humans can identify images, despite corruptions, and hence, intuitively the concepts we aim to learn should be robust.
 
 However, the framework of the paper deviated from the networks and data structures that are the norm in practice. In practice, we rarely have boolean functions. And it is well known that boolean functions can behave quite differently from continuous functions. 
 
 We recommend that the authors widen the scope of their work, and attempt to connect their findings to practical networks and functions. Moreover, we recommend that they do a more thorough literature survey. For instance, the idea of robust concepts has appeared before

SUMMARY 
This paper presents a study of the number of hidden units and training examples needed to learn functions from a particular class. 
This class is defined as those Boolean functions with an upper bound on the variability of the outputs. 

PROS
The paper promotes interesting results from the theoretical computer science community to investigate the efficiency of representation of functions with limited variability in terms of shallow feedforward networks with linear threshold units. 

CONS 
The analysis is limited to shallow networks. The analysis is based on piecing together interesting results, however without contributing significant innovations. 
The presentation of the main results and conclusions is somewhat obscure, as the therein appearing terms/constants do not express a clear relation between increased robustness and decreasing number of required hidden units. 

COMMENTS 

- In the abstract one reads ``The universal approximation theorem for neural networks says that any reasonable function is well-approximated by a two-layer neural network with sigmoid gates but it does not provide good bounds on the number of hidden-layer nodes or the weights.'' 

In page 1 the paper points the reader to a review article. It could be a good idea to include also more recent references. 

Given the motivation presented in the abstract of the paper it would be a good idea to also comment of works discussing the classes of Boolean functions representable by linear threshold networks. 
For instance the paper [Hyperplane Arrangements Separating Arbitrary Vertex Classes in n-Cubes. Wenzel, Ay, Paseman] discusses various classes of functions that can be represented by shallow linear threshold networks and provides upper and lower bounds on the number of hidden units needed for representing various types of Boolean functions. In particular that paper also provides lower bounds on the number of hidden units needed to define a universal approximator. 

- It certainly would be a good idea to discuss the results on the learning complexity in terms of measures such as the VC-dimension. 

- Thank you for the explanations regarding the constants.  
So if the noise sensitivity is kept constant, larger values of epsilon are associated with a smaller value of delta and of 1/epsilon. 
Nonetheless, the description in Theorem 2 is in terms of poly(1/epsilon, 1/delta), which still could increase? 
Also, in Lemma 1 reducing the sensitivity at a constant noise increases the bound on k? 

- The fact that the descriptions are independent of n seems to be related to the definition of the noise sensitivity as an expectation over all inputs. This certainly deserves more discussion. One good start could be to discuss examples of functions with an upper bound on the noise sensitivity (aside from the linear threshold functions discussed in Lemma 2). 
Also, reverse statements to Lemma 1 would be interesting, describing the noise sensitivity of juntas specifically, even if only as simple examples. 

- On page 3 ``...variables is polynomial in the noise-sensitivity parameters'' should be inverse of?

MINOR COMMENTS

On page 5 Proposition 1 should be Lemma 1?

This work finds a connection between Bourgain's junta problem, the existing results in circuit complexity, and the approximation of a boolean function using two-layer neural net. I think that finding connections between different fields and applying the insights gained is a valid contribution. For this reason, I recommend acceptance.

But my current major concern is that this work is only constrained to the domain of boolean hypercube, which is far from what is done in practice (continuous domain). Indeed, the authors could argue that understanding the former is a first step, but if the connection is only suitable for this case and not adaptable to more general scenarios, then it probably would have limited interest.

The approximation capabilities of neural networks have been studied before for approximating different classes of functions. The goal of this paper is to provide an analog of the approximation theorem for the class of noise-stable functions. The class of functions that are noise-stable and their output does not significantly depend on an individual input seems an interesting class and therefore I find the problem definition interesting.  The paper is well-written and it is easy to follow the proofs and arguments. 

I have two major comments:

1- Presentation: The way I understand this arguments is that the noise-stability measures the "true" dimensionality of the data based on the dependence of the function on different dimensions. Therefore, it is possible to restate and prove an analog to the approximation theorems based on "true" dimensionality of data. It is also unclear when the stability based bounds are tighter than dimension based bounds as both of them grow exponentially. I find these discussions interesting but unfortunately, the authors present the result as some bound that does not depend on the dimension and a constant (!??) that grows exponentially with (1/eps). This is not entirely the right picture because the epsilon in the stability could itself depend on the dimension. I believe in most problems (1/epsilon) grows with the dimension. 

2- Contribution: Even though the connection is new and interesting, the contribution of the paper is not significant enough. The presented results are direct applications of previous works and most of the lemmas in the paper are restating the known results. I believe more discussions and results need to be added to make this a complete work.

The authors present an algorithm for learning continuous semantic representations of symbolic expressions using gradient descent. The proposed model, called Program2Plan, first maps a symbolic expression to a program in some semantic domain using an encoder. The program is then executed in an artificial neural network to yield a plan. The parameters of the neural network are updated by Back-Propagation through the program and plan layers. To train the Program2Plan model, the authors use a proxy objective, called the Loss of Control, that punishes accidental plan deviance. The proxy objective is trained by connecting the program and plan layers with two directed edges with a Lagrange multiplier in between. The training data for Program2Plan is generated by feeding in random programs from a large search space to a MechanicalTurk worker. The authors demonstrate that Program2Plan can plan successfully for novel tasks by showing it can learn to approximate the semantics of arbitrary symbolic expressions by the time it receives a trajectory execution instruction. The authors also find that Program2Plan can perform multiple tasks simultaneously by learning semantically meaningful decompositions of expressions via hierarchical program representation. Finally, the authors propose a Multi-Domain Program2Plan model that learns to map programs to semantic representations in multiple domains by sharing program-specific layers and having a multi-domain composite plan layer. The model is trained by connecting the program and plan layers with a loss of control objective that punishes accidental plan deviation. The parameters of the neural network are updated by back-propagation through the program and plan layers. Second, the authors develop a method for training the model using a proxy loss function that is punishes accidental plan deviation. This loss function is learned by connecting the program and plan layers with a loss of control objective that is computed using a learned surrogate trajectory execution model. Third, the authors propose a multi-domain extension of the model, which shares program-specific layers and has a multi-domain plan layer. The main shortcoming of the paper is the lack of a solid baseline to validate the effectiveness of the proposed loss function. The authors compare Program2Plan with a probabilistic encoder based program induction model and an LSTM based sequence-to-sequence model. This paper addresses the problem of learning continuous semantic representations of symbolic expressions, for more details please see the main content as below. The neural equivalence networks proposed in this work is a step in incorporating continuous and syntax-directed semantic reasoning into a broader framework of program induction. The main idea is to learn deep representations that capture semantic equivalence even of expressions that are syntactically very different. As a strong challenge towards this goal, the expressiveness of the underlying symbolic representation must be carefully managed. Semantic representations must be computed in a syntax-directed manner, because semantics is compositional, but at the same time, small changes in syntax can lead to very large changes in semantics, which can be difficult for continuous neural architectures. We perform an exhaustive evaluation on the task of checking equivalence on a highly diverse class of symbolic algebraic and boolean expression types, showing that our model significantly outperforms existing architectures. The proposed model is motivated in part by recent progress in structured neural networks, where several authors have introduced strategies for sharing computation in deep neural nets via sharing of lower-level compute entities such as op codes, intermediate representations, and data formats. This work has shown that useful computation can be carried out efficiently at run time by reusing pre-computed structures. We adapt this strategy to symbolic expressions, using a highly parameterized equation editor as the low-level compute entity, and sharing a set of neural equivalence network modules to compute on top of it. A key challenge of the approach is that semantic equivalence must be computed in a syntax-directed manner, because semantics is compositional, but at the same time, small changes in syntax can lead to very large changes in semantics, which can be difficult for continuous neural architectures. To address this, we introduce a dynamic composition strategy, in which we decompose a large expression into its component parts, compute a deep representation of each part, and then combine the parts in a concise but semantically expressive way. We perform an exhaustive evaluation on the task of checking equivalence on a highly diverse class of symbolic algebraic and boolean expression types, showing that our model significantly outperforms existing architectures. Overall, this is a step in the right direction towards incorporating continuous and syntax-directed semantic reasoning into a broader framework of program induction. The framework of program induction aims to learn a mapping from observations of examples of program execution to program parameters, and has recently shown impressive results for several classes of functions that are continuous or describe smooth curves or surfaces. However, these programs typically handle a very limited amount of data. Our work shows that improving upon this is crucial to achieve more general and flexible representation and reasoning ability. This work was presented at NeurIPS 18. Strengths: The proposed model is very large model that is capable of representing and reasoning on arbitrary symbolic expressions, including high-level algebra such as program composition and automatic differentiation. As a major advance over prior work, it represents the full extent of the symbolic expression in memory, not just a surface approximation. The proposed approach provides the basis for both exact inference, by choosing a formula in a metal to prove or disprove, and sampling-based learning. The model is trained by minimizing the energy function, which is efficiently computed using dynamic programming on a parse tree. The approach is highly scalable. As a major advance over prior work, it is able to represent and reason on arbitrary symbolic expressions of any complexity, not just very short expressions. The authors show that their model significantly outperforms existing approaches on a large evaluation task involving a diverse set of symbolic algebraic and boolean expression types. Weaknesses: As a major advance over prior work, the model is able to represent and reason on arbitrary symbolic expressions. The architecture relies on a small number of templates, each representing a fixed set of operations, and it is not clear how to generalize the approach to support a large number of different operators. This work proposes to compute embeddings of symbolic expressions (e.g., boolean expressions, or polynomials) such that semantically equivalent expressions are near each other in the embedded space.  The proposed model uses recursive neural networks where the architecture is made to match that of the parse tree of a given symbolic expression.  To train the model parameters, the authors create a dataset of expressions where semantic equivalence relationships are known and minimize a loss function so that equivalent expressions are closer to each other than non-equivalent expressions via a max-margin loss function.  The authors also use a “subexpression forcing” mechanism which, if I understand it correctly, encourages the embeddings to respect some kind of compositionality.

Results are shown on a few symbolic expression datasets created by the authors and the proposed method is demonstrated to outperform baselines pretty convincingly.  I especially like the PCA visualization where the action of negating an expression is shown to correspond roughly to negating the embedding in its vector space — it is a lot like the man - woman + queen = king type embeddings that we see in the word2vec and glove style papers.  

The weakest part of the paper is probably that the setting seems somewhat contrived — I can’t really think of a real setting where it is easy to have a training set of known semantic equivalences, but still more worth it to use a neural network to do predictions.   The authors have also punted on dealing with variable names, assuming that distinct variables refer to different entities in the domain.  This is understandable, as variable names add a whole new layer of complexity on an already difficult problem, but also seems high limiting.  For example, the proposed methods would not be useable in an “equation search engine” unless we were able to accurately canonicalize variable names in some way.

Other miscellaneous points:
* Regarding problem hardness, I believe that the problem of determining if two expressions are equivalent is actually undecidable — see the “word problem for Thue systems”.  Related to this, I was not able to figure out how the authors determine ground truth equivalence in their training sets.  They say that expressions are simplified into a canonical form and grouped, but this seems to not be possible in general, so one question is — is it possible that equivalent expressions in the training data would have been mapped to different canonical forms?  Would it have been easier/possible to construct and compare truth tables?
* The “COMBINE” operation uses what the authors describe as a residual-like connection.  Looking at the equations, the reason why this is not actually a residual connection is because of the weight matrix that is multiplied by the lower level l_0 features.  A true residual connection would have passed the features through unchanged (identity connection) and would have also been better at fighting gradient explosion…. so is there a reason why this was used rather than an identity connection?

None of these problems is particularly damning but it is slightly disappointing not to see these issues discussed in the review process.

Overall, the reviews, which I found superficial in comparison to the other papers I am chairing, found the method proposed here sound, although some details lacked explanation. The consensus was that the general problem being addressed is interesting and timely, given the attention the topics of program induction and interpretation have been receiving in the community recently. There was also consensus that the setting the model was evaluated on was far too simple and unnatural, and that there is need for a more complex, task involving symbolic interpretation to validate the model. It is hard to tell, given all the design decisions made (l2-normalisation vs layer norm, softmax not working), whether the end product is tailored to the task at hand, and whether it will tell us something useful about how this approach generalises. I am inclined, on the basis of the reviewer's opinions of the setting and my own concerns outlined above, to recommend redirection to the workshop track.

My main concern is the evaluation "score". It appears to be precision on a per query basis. I believe a more standard metric, precision-recall or roc would be more informative. The goal of this paper is to learn vector representation of boolean and polynomial expressions, such that equivalent expressions have similar representations.

The model proposed in the paper is based on recursive neural network, as introduced by Socher et al. (2012). Given the syntactic parse tree of a formula (either boolean or polynomial), the representation for a node is obtained by applying a MLP on the representation of the children. This process is applied recursively to obtain the representation of the full expression. Contrary to Socher et al. (2012), this paper proposes to use more than one layer (this is especially important to capture XOR operation, which is not surprising at all). The paper also introduces a reconstruction error (called SubexpForce), so that the expression of children can be recovered from the expression of the parent (if I understood correctly). The model is trained using a classification loss, where the label of a given expression corresponds to its equivalence class. The method is then evaluated on randomly generated data, and compared to baselines such as tf-idf, GRU RNN or standard recursive neural network.

While I do agree with the authors that learning good representation for symbolic expressions (and to capture compositionality) is an important task, I am not entirely convinced by the experimental setting proposed in this paper. Indeed, as stated in the paper, the task of deciding if two boolean expressions are equivalent is NP-hard, and I do not understand if the model can do better than implicitly computing the truth table of expressions. While sometimes a bit hard to follow, the paper is technically sound. In particular, the proposed model is well adapted to the problem and outperforms the baselines.

This work proposes to compute embeddings of symbolic expressions (e.g., boolean expressions, or polynomials) such that semantically equivalent expressions are near each other in the embedded space.  The proposed model uses recursive neural networks where the architecture is made to match that of the parse tree of a given symbolic expression.  To train the model parameters, the authors create a dataset of expressions where semantic equivalence relationships are known and minimize a loss function so that equivalent expressions are closer to each other than non-equivalent expressions via a max-margin loss function.  The authors also use a “subexpression forcing” mechanism which, if I understand it correctly, encourages the embeddings to respect some kind of compositionality.

Results are shown on a few symbolic expression datasets created by the authors and the proposed method is demonstrated to outperform baselines pretty convincingly.  I especially like the PCA visualization where the action of negating an expression is shown to correspond roughly to negating the embedding in its vector space — it is a lot like the man - woman + queen = king type embeddings that we see in the word2vec and glove style papers.  

The weakest part of the paper is probably that the setting seems somewhat contrived — I can’t really think of a real setting where it is easy to have a training set of known semantic equivalences, but still more worth it to use a neural network to do predictions.   The authors have also punted on dealing with variable names, assuming that distinct variables refer to different entities in the domain.  This is understandable, as variable names add a whole new layer of complexity on an already difficult problem, but also seems high limiting.  For example, the proposed methods would not be useable in an “equation search engine” unless we were able to accurately canonicalize variable names in some way.

Other miscellaneous points:
* Regarding problem hardness, I believe that the problem of determining if two expressions are equivalent is actually undecidable — see the “word problem for Thue systems”.  Related to this, I was not able to figure out how the authors determine ground truth equivalence in their training sets.  They say that expressions are simplified into a canonical form and grouped, but this seems to not be possible in general, so one question is — is it possible that equivalent expressions in the training data would have been mapped to different canonical forms?  Would it have been easier/possible to construct and compare truth tables?
* The “COMBINE” operation uses what the authors describe as a residual-like connection.  Looking at the equations, the reason why this is not actually a residual connection is because of the weight matrix that is multiplied by the lower level l_0 features.  A true residual connection would have passed the features through unchanged (identity connection) and would have also been better at fighting gradient explosion…. so is there a reason why this was used rather than an identity connection?

machine_text: Overall, the paper is well written. However, I have some concerns about the introduction and the proposed solution. 1- I didn't really understand what the problem is that the paper is trying to address. Maybe you can include a motivation and background. 2- In the "Background" section, you mentioned using dropout but I didn't really understand why you used dropout for training the net and then you applied pooling to the output of the last layer. I thought you use pooling because you want to reduce the number of parameters of the net. But if that is the case, you can simply apply dropout after the pooling layer. 3- The problem you are addressing can be framed as a regression problem. So maybe you can name the layers and the type of activation function used for each layer. This will help the reader to understand the approach that you are taking to address the problem. 4- in the "Model Architecture" section, you are using two separated ResNet blocks, but in the paper "Ensemble of ResNet for BCI-MI" (https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Xiaoxiang_Yang/publication/337565492_Ensemble_of_ResNet_for_BCI_MI/links/5707e8fce0cfcaae5000000.pdf) there is a combined ResNet architecture that achieves better performance than the two separate ResNet architecture. Can you elaborate on why you decided to use two separate ResNet blocks? 5- it would be nice if you could provide the exact configuration for each layer of the model (number of neurons, activation function,...) 6- In the "Training" section, you are using Adam as optimizer. I think you should use SGD as the optimizer because SGD is less prone to get stuck in a local minimum than Adam. 7- In the implementation, you use TensorFlow. I think you should use Keras. Keras is a high level API over TensorFlow that hides some of the complexity of using TensorFlow. The implementation is nice, but in some places, you repeat the same operation with different parameters (e.g. the dropout mask in the last layer). It would be nice if you could unify these two lines. 8- In the implementation, you do not use GPU. I think using a GPU is a must if you want to achieve good performance. I think for a problem of this nature, a GPU is required. Overall, it would be nice if you could address the above issues and maybe expand the section "Discussion" to provide a deeper analysis of the advantages and disadvantages of using your approach over other approaches. I have gone through the paper carefully. I am satisfied with the paper now, and I think it can be of interest for Peer Reviewers.

The authors presented a framework to modularize neural networks, such that each module can be easily swapped in and out for different tasks. Specifically, the authors trained a base network and several optimization layers on a fixed set of modules. They then presented a principled way to select a combination of modules, and a simple pre-processing function to allow fast deployment to a new task. The modules are pretrained on a generic dataset and the preprocessing function is a simple fine-tuning on the target task. The authors evaluated the framework on a toy task and small image classification tasks, and showed that the framework can scale to largeImageNet. The framework has several nice properties. First, it is easy to implement, and is very easy to scale to complex tasks. Each of the modules is a small network, which are easier to debug and maintain. Furthermore, the authors showed that different versions of the modules can be used together, by treating the selection of modules as a form of dropout. Finally, the combination of modules is determined by the optimization algorithm, which does not require the enumeration of all possible module combinations. The method achieved promising results, although the authors did not study the effect of each module, it is clear that the coarse initialization and the averaging pool are especially useful. The method may still be improved in several ways. First, it can be interesting to study what happens if the modules are trained for the same task, but in the authors' case, the modules are trained on different initialization, and therefore complement each other. Second, it would be interesting to try different methods for combining modules. The authors showed that random sampling works, but other choices might be more optimal. Finally, it will be interesting to study if the framework can be applied to other models and frameworks for constructing neural networks.

In this work we study the problem of network morphism, an effective learning scheme to morph a well-trained neural network to a new one with the network function completely preserved. Different from existing work where basic morphing types on the layer level were addressed, we target at the central problem of network morphism at a higher level, i.e., how a convolutional layer can be morphed into an arbitrary module of a neural network. To simplify the representation of a network, we abstract a module as a graph with blobs as vertices and convolutional layers as edges, based on which the morphing process is able to be formulated as a graph transformation problem. Two atomic morphing operations are introduced to compose the graphs, based on which modules are classified into two families, i.e., simple morphable modules and complex modules. We present practical morphing solutions for both of these two families, and prove that any reasonable module can be morphed from a single convolutional layer. Extensive experiments have been conducted based on the state-of-the-art ResNet on benchmark datasets, and the effectiveness of the proposed solution has been verified. steal https://arxiv.org/pdf/1905.01386.pdf for the paper. I sincerely thank the reviewer for the attention and time spent on this work. Best, AIoT London Modularized Morphing of Neural Networks Article Number: 1905.01386 Last updated: April 18, 2023 DOI: 10.18117/98. mmHg.1905.01386_submit Abstract The explosive growth of big data brings along the demand for distributed machine learning, where modules rather than whole networks are trained in parallel and assembled later to perform the task at hand. However, current network morphing techniques are often based on layer-level mapping rules and have the following drawbacks. (1) The granularity is too fine-grained and manual intervention is often needed. (2) The learned mapping is rigid and hard to apply to other tasks or network structures. (3) The applicability is limited to networks with the same composition of basic modules. (4) The search space is too large and efficient optimization is hard to achieve. To address these challenges, we propose modularized network morphing (MNM), which replaces the module-level mapping by a more general graph transformation that allows the network to be assembled from modules that may have different compositions and different mapping rules. The key to solving this more general problem is to identify two kinds of modules - simple and complex modules. We present two atomic module transformation rules that compose any graph into another. We then use these two kinds of rules and several other properties to solve the network-level transformation problem. We finally introduce several optimization strategies to make the search space manageable and efficient. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of MNM, both in terms of flexibility and efficiency. Scientific Background Recently, with the explosive growth of big data, distributed machine learning has become an effective solution to its large computation consumption. In particular, since many learning tasks can be formulated as network architectures, a promising approach is to divide the network into several sub-networks and train them independently in a parallel manner. After training, these sub-networks can be simply assembled to form the final network. Along this line of work, morphing networks has been emerged as a general module-based transformation technique to enable network assembling from existing ones. However, existing work on network morphing has several drawbacks. First, current techniques often need to know the module structure in advance, and a one-to-one mapping is often used between modules and networks, which results in heavy manual intervention for mapping. Second, the current mapping are often too rigid and hard to be applied to other task or network structures. Third, it is applicable to networks with the same module structure. Fourth, the search space is too large, and it is hard to obtain the optimal solution. To address these issues, we present a more general network morphing technique that allows network assembling from modules that may have different compositions and different module mapping rules. We name this general technique modularized network morphing (MNM). We design two atomic module transformation rules that compose any graph into another. We then use these two kinds of rules and several other properties to solve the network-level transformation problem. We also propose several optimization strategies to make the search space manageable and efficient. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of MNM, both in terms of flexibility and efficiency. human_text:
The paper presents an interesting incremental approach for exploring new convolutional network hierarchies in an incremental manner after a baseline network has reached a good recognition performance.

The experiments are presented for the CIFAR-100 and ImageNet benchmarks by morphing various ResNet models into better performing models with somewhat more computation.

Although the baselines are less strong than those presented in the literature, the paper claims significant error reduction for both ImageNet and CIFAR-100.

The main idea of the paper is to rewrite convolutions into multiple convolutions while expanding the number of filters. It is quite unexpected that this approach yields any improvements over the baseline model at all.

However, for some of the basic tenets of network morphing, experimental evidence is not given in the paper. Here are some fundamental questions raised by the paper:
- How does the quality of morphed networks compares to those with the same topology trained from scratch?
- How does the incremental training time after morphing relate to that of the network trained from scratch?
- Where is the extra computational cost of the morphed networks come from?
- Why is the quality of the baseline ResNet models lag behind those that are reported in the literature and github? (E.g. the github ResNet-101 model is supposed to have 6.1% top-5 recall vs 6.6 reported in the paper)
More evidence for the first three points would be necessary to evaluate the validity of the claims of the paper.

The paper is written reasonably well and can be understood quite well, but the missing evidence and weaker baselines make it looks somewhat less convincing. 
I would be inclined to revise up the score if a more experimental evidence were given for the main message of the paper (see the points above).

The paper investigates the problem of morphing one convolutional network into another with application to exploring the model space (starting from a pre-trained baseline model). The resulting morphed models perform better than the baseline, albeit at the cost of more parameters and training. Importantly, it has not been demonstrated that morphing leads to training time speed-up, which is an important factor to consider when exploring new architectures starting from pre-trained models. Still, the presented approach and the experiments would be of interest to the community, so I recommend the paper for workshop presentation.

- 5) One major advantage of this type of knowledge transfer (Net2Net, NetMorph) is to speedup training and model exploration. There seems to be no experiments demonstrate such advantage (possibly due to the lose initialization of BatchNorm). This is the major drawback of this paper.

In summary, this paper studies a novel problem of knowledge transfer in a macroscopic level. The method could be of interest to the ICLR community. The experiments should be improved (comment 5) to make the results more convincing and practically useful and I strongly encourage the authors to do so.

machine_text: This paper presents a method for learning a parameterized policy for the problem of reinforcement learning. The method is based on the concept of decomposing the overall learning problem into a series of multiple learning problems, each of which is simpler and easier to learn but still captures the essential feature of the overall learning objective. The method proposed in this paper can be categorized as modular multitask reinforcement learning. Specifically, it decomposes the overall learning problem into a series of M multiple learning problems, each of which is corresponding to a specific task. Each of the multiple learning problems is simpler than the overall learning problem in one aspect. A policy sketch is proposed to represent the parameters of the policy. The key idea of the method is to apply the Monte Carlo simulation to estimate the value of the multiple learning problems by averaging over multiple samples, and to apply the weighted cumulative averaging to estimate the value of the overall learning problem. The theoretical analysis shows that the estimated value will converge to the optimal value with the increase of the length of the simulation. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed method can converge to the optimal value and the number of policy sketches can be pruned according to the experience replay table. anning AI is still in an early stage. When people discuss the challenges of AI, generally they talk about the challenges of specialized AI, for example, imaging diagnosis, autonomous driving, and game AI, but not general AI, which means that the AI can easily lead to dysfunction or even collapse of a system. One of the reasons for this situation is that the AI algorithm designed by most people is relatively simple, such as a one-size-fits-all algorithm with a strong Supervising Teacher. This method of supervision not only causes the training data for each model to be insufficiently distinctive, but also leads to larger fluctuations in the generalization ability of the model, and these problems are especially obvious in large-scale learning. In this paper, we propose a novel and efficient method for learning a parameterized policy. The method can be applied to modular multitask reinforcement learning, so that different learning problems correspond to different tasks, and each learning problem is relatively simple and has a corresponding easy-to-overload teacher. This method not only solves the problem of weak generalization ability of the single-model learning algorithm, but also enables the model to achieve a high level of generalization ability after training. The method is effective, and can be widely used.

This paper addresses the problem of large scale multi-task reinforcement learning (RL) with continuous action space, and provides an effective solution using the multi-agent actor-critic method with decentralized action synchronization. Compared with single-task learning, multi-task learning could exploit the transferable knowledge across different tasks through simultaneous training, and has the advantage of scaling to a large number of tasks without losing efficiency. With the capability of deep neural networks, deep multitask RL has achieved great success in various domains, such as robotics manipulation, automatic driving, and dialogue management. However, most of the existing deep multitask methods are only suitable for low-dimensional action spaces, such as dallas revolution task. This limits their applications in real-world applications with high-dimensional and continuous actions, such as robotics and manufacturing. In this paper, the authors proposed to use modularly parameterized deep Q-learning to deal with large-scale multi-task learning with continuous action space. The main contributions of this work include: 1) the efficient solution of policy sketching for large-scale high-dimensional MDPs, and 2) the efficient and general method for combining the multitask and episodic tasks together. The paper has two main applications in robotics and manufacturing. The first is using the modular deep Q-learning with policy sketching to task-switching demand fulfillment warehouse scenarios. The paper presents an example of solving a warehouse problem with 36 independent jobs and explores the effects of different network sizes and scheduling steps. The second application is using the efficient combination of episodic tasks and multitask tasks to large-scale robotics training. In the experiment, the authors used three kinds of simulated robots with different scenarios. For the one-to-one mapping action space, the agent learned to assemble parts and to program joint angles for seven different robots. The results indicate that the proposed approach could obtain better or comparable performance than the baselines. The code and data are available at: https://github.com/SundeepK/MultiTaskRL The main limitation of the proposed approach is that the performance is not guaranteed if the parameter size of Q-function is too big. In this case, the standard backpropagation would not be effective. The author will further study the limitation and increase the robustness of the model in the future. The main strength of this work includes: 1) the efficient solution of policy sketching for large-scale high-dimensional MDPs, 2) the efficient and general method for combining the multitask and episodic tasks together. The policy sketching approach is a generic method for large-scale high-dimensional MDPs. The idea is that the learned model can be a good approximation of the target model when the number of latent variables are properly chosen. The authors also provided a method to search for the right latent variables. This approach can be applied to a large class of off-policy deep reinforcement learning algorithms. The authors also show that this method can be extended to samples from a mini-batch. The combination of episodic tasks and multitask tasks is also a novel idea. To our best knowledge, this is the first time to combine these two techniques for large-scale deep multitask learning. The authors showed that the combination is promising for learning efficiency and performance. Overall, this paper makes important progress in the field of large-scale high-dimensional MDPs. The method of policy sketching can be applied to a wide range of deep reinforcement learning problems. This method can also be applied to other high-dimensional MDPs, such as imaging diagnosis. The limitations of the method could be further improved. In the experiments, it is assumed that the agent has continuous control actions. If the action space is discrete, it would be more efficient to solve the problem using difference programming. If the parameter size of Q-function is too big, it could be further applied deep lifelong learning techniques to reduce the required computation budget.

In this paper, the authors propose a framework for multitask deep reinforcement learning guided by policy sketches. The main idea is to associate every subtask with its own modular subpolicy, and jointly optimizes over full task-specific policies by tying parameters across shared subpolicies. The effectiveness of this approach is evaluated on a maze navigation game and a 2-D Minecraft-inspired crafting game. The main contributions of this paper are as follows: 1. It formalizes the policy sketches and describes a framework for multitask deep reinforcement learning guided by policy sketches. 2. It clearly illustrates the main advantages of the proposed method over the state-of-the-art. 3. It shows the efficiency and effectiveness of the proposed approach for tasks with sparse rewards. Live long and PRCrawl on live long and PRCrawl on Novel Architectures for Scalable Robust Reinforcement Learning The past few years have seen a proliferation of methods for solving Reinforcement Learning (RL) problems with Deep Neural Networks (DNNs). While prior work has focused on distributed representations of the state and action spaces, a new trend is to embed the RL policy into a continuous vector space where the loss function is the derivative of the cumulative reward. At training time, one can compute the gradient efficiently via a function approximation method such as REINFORCE, while at test time, one can employ SGD to learn the optimal policy. Despite this progress, current DRL methods are not well-equipped to handle a broad spectrum of tasks for two reasons: (a) they require functions that map the state to the action and are therefore ill-equipped to handle state sparse MDPs, and (b) they require access to a large buffer to store data during off-policy training, making them poorly-suited for use in resource-constrained environments such as the natural language domain. To address these concerns, we introduce a new actor-critic algorithm that maintains a table of advantage samples instead of a trajectory buffer. Our method achieves state of the art performance on classic environments from the domain of hyperparameter tuning and finance, and an order of magnitude speedup on a challenging medical imaging dataset. While most of our approach is algorithmic, we also discuss how to evaluate a policy for hard AI tasks such as image recognition via human evaluation.

This paper addresses the problem of training a policy to complete multiple tasks, by first describing a framework for multitask reinforcement learning with policy sketches. In addition to describing the framework, the main content of this paper is as below: * The framework allows learning high-level structural relationships among tasks, but does not provide detailed guidance required by previous work on learning policy abstractions for RL (e.g. intermediate rewards, subtask completion signals, or intrinsic motivations). * The optimization is accomplished via a simple decoupled actor–critic training objective that facilitates learning common behaviors from diverse tasks. * The framework and decoupled actor-critic training objective are evaluated on maze navigation and a 2-D Minecraft-inspired crafting tasks. The results show that the approach can perform better than baseline methods that learn task-specific or shared monolithic policies. * Furthermore, our method naturally induces a library of primitive behaviors that can be recombined to rapidly acquire policies for new tasks. The framework and decoupled actor-critic training objective are new ideas, and the experiments on maze navigation and 2-D Minecraft-inspired crafting are also innovative. The policy sketch is an intuitive concept, which allows describing the structural relationships among tasks. However, the use of one big policy for all subtasks might cause bad performance. How to efficiently divide the subtasks to each policy and learn policy weights is an open problem. The decoupled actor-critic training objective makes the critic easy to optimize and encourage the common behavior, but how to design an appropriate reward function to make the actor learn such common behaviors is a big challenge. This work provides a good balance of theory and practice, and could be an important stepping stone for future research on multi-task reinforcement learning with policy sketches.
human_text:
The paper presents an approach to learning shared neural representations of temporal abstractions in hierarchical RL, based on actor-critic methods. The approach is illustrated in two tasks: gridworld with objects and a simplified Minecraft problem).  The idea of providing symbolic descriptions of tasks and learning corresponding "implementations" is potentially interesting and the empirical results are promising.  However, there are two main drawbacks of the current incarnation of this work.  First, the ideas presented in the paper have all been explored in other work (symbolic specifications, actor-critic, shared representations).  While related work is discussed, it is not really clear what is new here, and what is the main contribution of this work besides providing a new implementation of existing ideas in the context of deep learning. The main contribution if the work needs to be clearly spelled out.  Secondly, the approach presented relies crucially on curriculum learning (this is quite clear from the experiments).  While the authors argue that specifying tasks in simplified language is easy, designing a curriculum may in fact be pretty complicated, depending on the task at hand.  The examples provided are fairly small, and there is no hint of how curriculum can be designed for larger problems. Because the approach is sensitive to the curriculum, this limits the potential utility of the work. It is also unclear if there is a way to provide supervision automatically, instead of doing it based on prior domain knowledge.
More minor comments:
- The experiments are not described in enough detail in the paper. It's great to provide github code, but one needs to explain in the paper why certain choices were made in the task setup (were these optimized? What's this the first thing that worked?) Even with the code, the experiments as described are not reproducible
- The description of the approach is pretty tangled with the specific algorithmic choices. Can the authors step back and think more generally of how this approach can be formalized?  I think this would help relate it to the prior work more clearly as well.

As per all the reviews, the work is clearly promising, but is seen to need additional discussion / formalization / experimental comparison with related work, and stronger demonstrations of the application of this technique.
 Further back-and-forth with the reviewers would have been useful, but there should be enough to go on in terms of directions. This work would benefit from being part of the workshop track.

This paper studies the problem of abstract hierarchical multiagent RL with policy sketches, high level descriptions of abstract actions. The work is related to much previous work in hierarchical RL, and adds some new elements by using neural implementations of prior work on hierarchical learning and skill representations. 

Sketches are sequences of high level symbolic labels drawn from some fixed vocabulary, which initially are devoid of any meaning. Eventually the sketches get mapped into real policies and enable policy transfer and temporal abstraction. Learning occurs through a variant of the standard actor critic architecture. 

Experiments are provided through a standard game like domain (maze, minecraft etc.). 

The paper as written suffers from two problems. One, the idea of policy sketches is nice, but not sufficiently fleshed out to have any real impact. It would have been useful to see this spelled out in the context of abstract SMDP models to see what they bring to the table. What one gets here is some specialized invocation of this idea in the context of the specific approach proposed here. Second, the experiments are not thorough enough in terms of comparing with all the related work. For example, Ghavamzadeh et al. explored the use of MAXQ like abstractions in the context of mulitagent RL. It would be great to get a more detailed comparison to MAXQ based multiagent RL approaches, where the value function is explicitly decomposed.

The paper proposes a new RL architecture that aims at learning policies from sketches i.e sequence of high-level operations to execute for solving a particular task. The model relies on a hierarchical structure where the sub-policy is chosen depending on the current operation to execute in the sketch . The learning algorithm is based on an extension of the actor-critic model for that particular case, and also involves curriculum learning techniques when the task to solve is hard. Experimental results are provided on different learning problems and compared to baseline methods. 

The paper is well-written and very easy to follow. I am not really convinced by the impact of such a paper since the problem solved here can be seen as an option-learning problem with a richer supervision (i.e the sequence of option is given). It thus corresponds to an easier problem with a limited impact. Moreover, I do not really understand to which concrete application this setting corresponds. For example, learning from natural langage instructions is clearly more relevant. So since the model proposed in this article is not a major contribution and shares many common ideas with existing hierarchical reinforcement learning methods,  the paper lacks a strong motivation and/or concrete application. So, the paper only has a marginal interest for the RL community

@pros: 
* Original problem with well design experiments
* Simple adaptation of the actor-critic method to the problem of learning sub policies


@cons:
* Very simple task that can be seen as a simplification of more complex problems like options discovery, hierarchical RL or learning from instructions
* No strong underlying applications that could help to 'reinforce' the interest of the approach

The platform is based on Open Neural Network Exchange (ONNX), and it runs on standard JavaScript engines such as Node.js and web browsers. The application can conduct distributed training with a high degree of parallelism and low communication overhead. The source code of the platform is open and is compatible with the TensorFlow Distribute training framework. The performance of the application is tested on both a server with a GPU and multiple clients with CPUs. Training the large version of the Stanford Natural Language Processing (NLP) corpus with 77 GB of data takes the platform about 25 minutes on a server with a GPU and less than 10 minutes on four clients with CPUs. The platform developed in this paper can be a useful addition to the TensorFlow Distribute training framework and significantly enhances its ability to conduct distributed training of deep learning models with high throughput on a broad array of hardware. segment 1 The paper provides a JavaScript deep learning platform and application to conduct distributed deep learning training. The platform and application are built on ONNX, which is an open standard for representing deep learning models and exchanging their formats. The application allows for dividing the data and machines into different groups and running the training on theses groups in parallel. It also allows the machines communicating with each other without much communication overhead. The source code of the platform is also available, which can be extensible and easily be compiled for different types of hardware. segment 2 The platform and application have some strengths and some weaknesses. The main advantage of the application is that it enables conducting distributed training with a high degree of parallelism and low communication overhead. There are multiple versions of the platform, which can be useful for running the training on servers with GPUs and on a number of clients with CPUs. In terms of weaknesses, the application has some dependencies on third-party packages and ONNX, which can make the deployment a bit more complicated.

As a peer review for the paper of Development of JavaScript-based deep learning platform and application to distributed training, the author implements a matrix library and deep learning framework that uses JavaScript. It can run on web browsers operating on ordinary personal computers and smartphones. Using JavaScript, deep learning can be accomplished in widely diverse environments without the necessity for software installation. Using GPGPU from WebCL framework, the framework can train large scale convolutional neural networks such as VGGNet and ResNet. In the experiments, we demonstrate their practicality by training VGGNet in a distributed manner using web browsers as the client. From my point of view, this work makes some interesting exploration and has certain implication for wider use of deep learning. However, I have several concerns about the implementation and presentation. First, the implementation lacks documentation. The library includes many functions, and it’s not clear how to use them all, or how to use them together. Detailed explanation is expected. Second, implementation details are not shown. The paper only says that it trains VGGNet in a distributed manner. How does it work? What’s the error metric? What’s the protocol? It’s very important to understand for evaluating the correctness of implementation and applying it to other problems. Third, this work can be divided into two parts: library and framework. The library is the foundation, and the framework is the application built on the library. However, they are very tightly coupled. A change in one part will have an impact on the other. And it’s very hard to extract individual strength. I think they should be separated. Overall, the work makes an important exploration in a promising area, but the author should further clarify the implementation and presentation to make the work more suitable for wide adoption. Recommendation: this work makes an important exploration in a promising area, but the author should further clarify the implementation and presentation to make the work more suitable for wide adoption.

This paper develops a JavaScript-based deep learning platform and application that addresses the problem of training large scale deep neural networks on client machines with limited CPU and GPU resources, by using cloud resources in the form of heterogeneous parallel architectures. The framework allows neural networks to be trained in a distributed manner, and is developed to be able to perform operations such as matrix multiplications using the web browser's own GPGPU capabilities, thereby eliminating the need for the client machine to have its own special purpose hardware for performing these operations. The main content of the paper are as below: 1. Use JavaScript to develop a deep learning platform and application 2. Develop a GPGPU matrix library that uses WebCL for execution 3. Distribute training of VGGNet in a distributed manner using cloud resources 4. Experimental validation of the framework The main strength of this paper is that it develops a JavaScript deep learning platform and application that can be deployed to cloud resources and used to train large scale deep neural networks using distributed learning methods. The framework uses WebCL to enable the efficient performance of matrix operations, including matrix multiplications, in the client browser, eliminating the need for the client machine to have its own special purpose hardware. This is the first deep learning framework to be developed that can be deployed to cloud resources and used to train large scale deep neural networks, and is expected to be widely used. One of the main weaknesses of this paper is that it only demonstrates a single case for training VGGNet. It would be useful to include more examples of training different neural network architectures on this platform to validate the effectiveness of the approach.

I will start by describing what problem or question this paper addresses, then strengths and weaknesses. The paper Differentiable Physics Engine for Deep Learning in Robotics addresses the problem of how to train robotic systems on real-world physical systems that are often expensive or unsafe to obtain data from. To solve this problem, the paper describes a differentiable physics engine that can be used to perform expensive physics simulations in a cheap, differentiable way, while keeping the physical system’s continuous dynamics intact. This enables the resulting system to still train on the data from the physical system with no loss in accuracy. One major strength of the paper is that it solves a very common problem in robotics. Simulating the physical world is a critical component of training a robot. However, simulating the physical world is often prohibitive because simulators are often expensive and the data from simulators is often noisy and lacks the high-fidelity representations that are needed for the neural network to accurately learn. The paper describes a way of achieving this with a differentiable physics engine that can perform expensive physics simulations in a cheap, differentiable way. This would be useful for training on physical systems that are expensive or unsafe to obtain data from, such as high fidelity locomotion simulators. A weakness of this approach is that it only works for scenarios where the simulated physics is Gaussian. However, this is a very common application for learning from data, and Gaussian physics is a good baseline to have for simulation-based learning. The authors note that they are working to extend this technique to general physics engines. Overall, this is a useful approach that would be useful to a lot of practitioners in the field of robotics. Simulation is a critical part of training a robot, and this improves the accuracy and efficiency of physical simulation for use in training with deep learning.
