The paper End-to-End Learnable Histogram Filters demonstrates an interesting technique for reducing photo noise without blurring the image. The technique uses a standard neural network architecture to first denoise the image in the spatial domain. The resulting image is then fed into a separate denoising network in the spectral domain, thereby combining the spatial and frequency domain noise filtering. The resulting spectral noise statistics can be used to reduce the noise in the initial denoised image. The technique has the advantage of not modifying the architecture of the denoising networks and can thus be easily trained on existing denoising networks. On average, the technique reduces noise levels by ~2.1 dB. The technique also has some drawbacks. First, the denoising networks designed for standard image denoising use a single noise type. Noise components often have different statistics, and thus the spectral denoising technique is not able to leverage the full capacity of the denoising network. Second, the spectral domain noise statistics are hard to interpret. It is not clear what properties of the noise are being reduced and what impact the noise removal has on the image. Overall, this is an interesting technique for reducing photo noise, but more research is needed to make the noise removal more principled and interpretable. The paper does address the problem of reducing noise from photos without blurring the image. The core technique is to use a standard neural network architecture to first denoise the image in the spatial domain and then denoise the image in the spectral domain. Here is the problem that the authors try to solve and the technique they use. Photographing a black-tie wedding with a standard zoom camera produces noisy images due to the low light and the film grain. The noise is clearly visible in the bright spots on the guests' clothing. However, when the image is reviewed on a smartphone, the noise is largely invisible, especially on LCD screens that display images as shades of gray. One likely cause of the inobservable noise is that the scene was originally recorded with a visible light camera, which reproduces the optical noise from the photographic process. To make images from digital cameras more pleasing on the eye, they must be processed using a technique that reduces the noise but also preserves the image's content. In this work, the authors present a technique that reduces noise levels in digital images without blurring the content. The technique first denoises the image using a standard convolutional neural network. In this architecture, the signal is first passed through a series of convolutional layers, and the noise is passed through a series of fully connected layers. They apply the denoising network to the image in the spatial domain. After denoising, the noise still exists in the spatial domain but not in the gradient domain. This noise reduction technique is based on a technique called DnCNN. The signal is then passed through another convolutional layer to recover the image's spatial domain. Finally, the image is transformed into the spectral domain, and noise is reduced using a variant of DnCNN. The authors tested their technique on images from a standard wedding photo album and showed that it reduces noise levels without blurring the image content.

This paper develops learnable histogram filters which can be used to estimate states recursively using prediction and measurement update but allows the specific models to be learned end-to-end, i.e. in such a way that they optimize the performance of the filter, using either supervised or unsupervised learning. The main contributions of this paper are: (i) A differentiable implementation of histogram filters which encodes the structure of recursive state estimation using prediction and measurement update but allows the specific models to be learned end-to-end. (ii) An approximation of the method in the main paper, where the bin centers are assumed to be constant, making it possible to apply it to many problem domains where the bin centers are not expected to change rapidly. (iii) An algorithm for unsupervised learning, which uses the predicted state to drive the update of the filter’s parameters. The combination of these three results makes it possible to use the same histogram filters to address several problem domains where similar state variables are expected to be found in the same number of bins. The results on real robotics data demonstrate the usefulness of the proposed approach and the applicability of the filter in the domain of state estimation, where the proposed filter seems to be state-of-the-art. Paper link: https://arxiv.org/abs.1807.00514 The main content of this paper is interesting and very promising, but there are several issues need to be addressed before it can be applied to real-world problem. 1. The algorithm is hard to evaluate and get the idea. In order to be able to deploy the Histogram filter, a model has to be trained with performance metrics that are differentiable with respect to the measurement sequence. Using the 1-norm as performance metric is a common choice in the literature, and the average of squared error (ASE) is used as objective function in the paper. In order to differentiate ASE with respect to the measurement sequence, two more implementation details need to be taken into account: [1]: You need to integrate the product of the measurement error with its time derivative (i.e. first derivative) into the objective function, which could be easily solved by proper discretization of time. [2]: the 1-norm can be approximated using the max operator as $M = \max(\mathbf{e}(t), 0)$, where $\mathbf{e}(t)$ is the prediction error of the state at time $t$ with their first derivative. By employing this model, the model can be trained with ASE directly. 2. The bin center in the paper are assumed to be constant, which might make it possible to implement the Histogram filter for some problem domains. For many real-world applications, however, the number and boundaries of bins are flexible and can change over time. For example, when dealing with the speed of vehicles. In this case, the first assumption will cause the model to miss the overall trend, while the second assumption would introduce a new hyperparameter and make the model less data-efficient. 3. Similar to 2, the ASE is also an integral calculation, whose gradient could be estimated using the same method. In the future work part, the paper proposed an interesting idea to address this problem. What if instead of using mean squared error as performance metric, the Max-mean Squared Error (MaxMSE) can be used? These three points are the main limitations for the practical use of the paper. In conclusion, although the main content of the paper is very promising and worth exploring, it is still in its infancy stage and needs more work to make it a reliable competitor for the state-of-the-art methods in real-world applications. For [1]: https://arxiv.org/abs.1206.2590 For [2]: https://arxiv.org/abs.1211.3441 I recommend this paper for its main content if the authors can address the three limitations proposed above. The paper End-to-End Learnable Histogram Filters describes a framework that combines the strengths and weaknesses of problem-specific algorithms and generic machine learning approaches, i.e. data efficiency and generality. In particular, the paper uses problem-specific information in the form of a prediction and measurement update scheme in the framework of recursive, non-linear, time-variant state estimation. First, the problem-specific information is encoded in histogram filters that are differentiable and that can thus be optimized using either supervised or unsupervised learning. The result are fully differentiable end-to-end learnable histogram filters. The framework is demonstrated in the context of robot state estimation and experiments on simulated and real data are presented. The proposed framework is shown to achieve similar performance to the classical use of specifically tuned Monte Carlo filters for sampling-based controllers and a fully data-driven trained L1LL estimator for the system states. enables more data to be used in the learning problem, allowing for more effective generalization. The proposed framework is shown to be highly data-parallel: a compute node only needs to train a single model, which can then be applied to all robots in a fleet. The problem-specific information is flexible and likely contains useful complementary features to the generic update. The proposed framework leads to an easy incorporation of Reinforcement Learning, e.g. with the potential for self-optimizing control behavior. The proposed framework is especially effective in highly nonlinear and time-varying systems.

I think the proposed method is too simplistic to be useful in the presented form, eg. 1) the state space (dimensionality & topology) is exactly matched to the experiments 2) displacements in the transition model are linear in the actions 3) observations are one-dimensional. Furthermore the authors do not compare to any other method except for an out-of-the-box LSTM model. Also, I feel like there must be a lot of prior work for combining HMMs + NNs out there, I think it would be necessary for the authors to relate their work to this literature.

In many respects, this is a strong paper, in my opinion better than the reviews thus far in the system suggest. The idea of learning the parameters of a state estimation system, even if it is a simple example like a histogram filter, is an interesting idea from both the ML and robotics perspectives.
 
 However, I think it's also fairly clear (from the reviews if nothing else), that substantial additional work needs to be done if this paper is to convey these ideas clearly and impactfully to the ICLR community. The value of the histogram filter may be obvious to the robotics community (though even there it seems like it would be worth pursuing the extension of these ideas to the case e.g. of particle filters), as these have historically been an important conceptual milestone in robotic perception, but the examples shown in this paper are extremely simplistic. Given that histogram filters inherently scale poorly with dimension, it's not clear from this paper itself why the techniques show particular promise for scaling up to realistic domains in the future.

 + Interesting idea of using training a state estimator end-to-end for robotics tasks

Summary: This paper presents a differentiable histogram filter for state estimation/tracking. The proposed histogram filter is a particular Bayesian filter that represents the discretized states using beliefs. The prediction step is parameterized by a locally linear and translation-invariant motion model while the measurement model is represented by a multi-layered neural network. The whole system is learned with both supervised and unsupervised objectives and experiments are carried out on two synthetic robot localization tasks (1D and 2D). The major claim of this paper is that the problem-specific model structure (Bayesian filter for state estimation) should improve pure deep learning approach in data-efficiency and generalization ability. 
+This paper has nice arguments about the importance of prior knowledge to deep learning approach for specific tasks. 
+An end-to-end histogram filter is derived for state estimation and unsupervised learning is possible in this model.
-This paper seems to have a hidden assumption that deep learning (RNN) is a natural choice for recursive state estimation and the rest of paper is built upon this assumption including LSTM baselines. However, this assumption itself may not be true, because Bayesian filter is a first-established approach for this classic problem, so it it more important to justify if deep learning is even necessary for solving the tasks presented. This requests pure Bayesian filter baselines in the experiments. 
-The derived histogram filter seems to be particularly designed for discretized state space. It is not clear how well it can be generalized to continuous state space using the notation "x". More interestingly, the observation is discrete (binary) as well, which eventually makes it possible to derive a closed-form measurement update model. This setup might be too constrained. Generalizing to continuous observations is not a trivial task, not even to mention using images as observations like Haarnoja et al 2016. These design choices overall narrow down the scope of applicability.

Summary:
--------
The authors propose a histogram based state representation with differentiable motion models and observation updates for state tracking from observations. Linear model with Gaussian noise is used as the motion model, while a neural network is used to learn the measurement model. They track robot states in: (1) 1-D hallway, and (2) a 2D arena.


Positives:
----------
1. Show how to encode prior knowledge about state-transitions in the architecture.
2. No assumptions about the observation model, which is learned purely from data.
3. Better accuracy than baselines with limited training data.

Negatives:
----------
1. The motion model is too simplistic. The authors in their response to earlier questions say that a generic feed-forward neural network could be used to model more complicated motions. However, then the novelty of their framework is not clear -- as then the proposed model would just be a couple of neural networks to learn the motion and observation models.

2. The observation model again is too simplistic (e.g., one dimensional observations), and is proposed to be a generic feed-forward network. Here again, the technical novelty is not clear.

3. The histogram based representation is not scalable as also highlighted by the authors. Hence, the proposed approach as it is, cannot be applied to more complicated settings.

4. In Figure 5(a,b), where they compare the state-estimation accuracy with other baselines (i.e., LSTMs), it is clear that the accuracy of the LSTM has not saturated, while that of their model has. They should do larger scale experiments with more training data (e.g., 10k,100k,500k samples). 
Note that while sample efficiency is a desirable property (also discussed in Section 6.2), we do expect models with prior knowledge to work better for small number of samples than models which do not assume any structure. Experiments with larger number of samples would be insightful.

This paper presents a novel rotation plane doubly orthogonal recurrent neural network (DORNN). The proposed DORNN has two key characteristics: the first is that it is able to find a new rotation plane that orthogonally intersects with the existing rotation planes; the second is that it uses doubly orthogonal property to increase the model generalization ability. To be specific, this paper presents three DORNN models with different network structures to realize different optimization objectives. First, the per-frame reconstruction loss is used as the optimization objective and the corresponding model is named DORNN-R. Second, the model with long-term dependency is expected to learn the temporal relation, and the corresponding model is named DORNN-L. Third, since the dual roles of DORNN are learning the spatial information and the temporal information, the model can be optimized through combining the two roles and the corresponding model is named DORNN-D. Through evaluating the three DORNN models with different objectives on three datasets, the effectiveness and reliability of the proposed model are verified by the experimental results. dern The proposed DORNN is able to find a new rotation plane that orthogonally intersects with the existing rotation planes. This is because the proposed DORNN uses the dual rotation strategy, which cancels out the existed rotation planes and finds a new optimal rotation plane that is orthogonal with other existed planes. To be specific, we first calculate the similarity between each pair of signals by using three dimensional discrete cosine transform (3D DCT), and the resulted scalar is named d(i, j, t). Then the d(i, j, t) is used to search for the optimal rotation plane, which is orthogonal with other existed planes. The other weakness is that the proposed DORNN uses only one hidden layer, which limits the model express ability.

The main content of the paper is interesting and worthy of publication. However, there are several points that need to be clarified. First, it is not clear how the proposed mechanism exactly preserves the hidden state norm for all time steps. In particular, the proof for the preservation of the norm for the first time step is missing. Second, in the experiments, the dependencies as long as 5,000 steps are validated. However, there is no statement that this method is able to handle longer dependencies. What if the length of the dependencies is extremely long? Third, it is not clear how the proposed model compares to the existing long-distance dependency models. For example, LSTM and GRU, which are the most widely used long-distance dependency models, are not covered in the experiments. These three questions could be the starting points for further investigation of the proposed method. Overall, the method in this paper is interesting and has potential to achieve good results on some long-distance dependency problems. However, the deficiencies above need to be addressed before the method can be widely used by the research community. Paper has an interesting idea, but isn't quite justified, as pointed out by R2. Very minimal experiments are presented in the paper.
 
 pros:
 - interesting idea
 
 cons:
 - insufficient experiments with no real world problems.
 - no rebuttal either :(.

My main objection with this work is that it operates under a hypothesis (that is becoming more and more popular in the literature) that all we need is to have gradients flow in order to solve long term dependency problems. The usual approach is then to enforce orthogonal matrices which (in absence of the nonlinearity) results in unitary jacobians, hence the gradients do not vanish and do not explode. However this hypothesis is taken for granted (and we don't know it is true yet) and instead of synthetic data, we do not have any empirical evidence that is strong enough to convince us the hypothesis is true. 

My own issues with this way of thinking is: a) what about representational power; restricting to orthogonal matrices it means we can not represent the same family of functions as before (e.g. we can't have complex attractors and so forth if we run the model forward without any inputs). You can only get those if you have eigenvalues larger than 1. It also becomes really hard to deal with noise (since you attempt to preserve every detail of the input, or rather every part of the input affects the output). Ideally you would want to preserve only what you need for the task given limited capacity. But you can't learn to do that. My issue is that everyone is focused on solving this preserved issue without worrying of the side-effects. 

I would like one of these papers going for jacobians having eigenvalues of 1 show this helps in realistic scenarios, on complex datasets.

This paper discusses recurrent networks with an update rule of the form h_{t+1} = R_x R h_{t}, where R_x is an embedding of the input x into the space of orthogonal or unitary matrices, and R is a shared orthogonal or unitary matrix.    While this is an interesting model, it is by no means a *new* model:  the idea of using matrices to represent input objects (and multiplication to update state) is often used in the embedding-knowledge-bases or embedding-logic literature (e.g. Using matrices to model symbolic relationships by Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton, or Holographic Embeddings of Knowledge Graphs by Maximillian Nickel et al.).  I don't think the experiments or analysis in this work add much to our understanding of it.    In particular, the experiments are especially weak, consisting only of a very simplified version of the copy task (which is already very much a toy).  I know several people who have played with this model in the setting of language modeling, and as the other reviewer notes, the inability of the model to forget is an actual annoyance.   

I think it is incumbent on the authors to show how this model can be really useful on a nontrivial task; as it is we should not accept this paper.

Some questions:  is there any reason to use the shared R instead of absorbing it into all the R_x?  Can you find any nice ways of using the fact that the model is linear in h or linear in R_x ?

While this is an interesting model, it is by no means a *new* model:  the idea of using matrices to represent input objects (and multiplication to update state) is often used in the embedding-knowledge-bases or embedding-logic literature (e.g. Using matrices to model symbolic relationships by Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton, or Holographic Embeddings of Knowledge Graphs by Maximillian Nickel et al.).  I don't think the experiments or analysis in this work add much to our understanding of it.    In particular, the experiments are especially weak, consisting only of a very simplified version of the copy task (which is already very much a toy).  I know several people who have played with this model in the setting of language modeling, and as the other reviewer notes, the inability of the model to forget is an actual annoyance.   

I think it is incumbent on the authors to show how this model can be really useful on a nontrivial task; as it is we should not accept this paper.

Some questions:  is there any reason to use the shared R instead of absorbing it into all the R_x?  Can you find any nice ways of using the fact that the model is linear in h or linear in R_x ?

This is a nice proposal, and could lead to more efficient training of
recurrent nets. I would really love to see a bit more experimental evidence.
I asked a few questions already but didn't get any answer so far.
Here are a few other questions/concerns I have:

- Is the resulting model still a universal approximator? (providing large enough hidden dimensions and number of layers)
- More generally, can one compare the expressiveness of the model with the equivalent model without the orthogonal matrices? with the same number of parameters for instance?
- The experiments are a bit disappointing as the number of distinct input/output
sequences were in fact very small and as noted by the authr, training
becomes unstable (I didn't understand what "success" meant in this case).
The authors point that the experiment section need to be expanded, but as
far as I can tell they still haven't unfortunately.

In this paper, we evaluate the potential of NDP for machine learning (ML) using a new SSD platform. We named this platform as ISP-ML which stands for In-storage Processor for Machine Learning. We focus on stochastic gradient descent (SGD) as the workhorse for training deep neural networks. We implement and compare three variants of SGD using the ISP-ML. We show the advantages of ISP over conventional in-host processing by comparing the performance of ISP and that of in-host processing. The major findings of the paper are as follows. First, we show that the latency of performing SGD using ISP-ML is comparable with that using in-host processing. Second, we show that ISP can save up to 51% energy compared to in-host processing. Third, we show that ISP can improve the scaling efficiency by up to 20% compared to in-host processing. Fourth, we show that ISP provides higher compute performance than in-host processing. Overall, we demonstrate the feasibility of NDP for ML using the ISP platform and its promising performance advantages over in-host processing. ystem We implemented and compared three variants of SGD (synchronous, Downpour, and elastic averaging) using the ISP-ML. human_text:
Combining storage and processing capabilities is an interesting research topic because data transfer is a major issue for many machine learning tasks.
The paper itself is well-written, but unfortunately addresses a lot of things only to medium depth (probably due length constraints).
My opinion is that a journal with an in-depth discussion of the technical details would be a better target for this paper.

Even though the researchers took an interesting approach to evaluate the performance of the system, it's difficult for me to grasp the expected practical improvements of this approach.
With such a big focus on GPU (and more specialized hardware such as TPUs), the one question that comes to mind: By how much does this - or do you expect it to - beat the latest and greatest GPU on a real task?

I don't consider myself an expert on this topic even though I have some experience with SystemC.

This paper is well motivated and clearly written, and is representative of the rapidly growing interdisciplinary area of hardware-software co-design for handling large-scale Machine Learning workloads. In particular, the paper develops a detailed simulator of SSDs with onboard multicore processors so that ML computations can be done near where the data resides.
 
 Reviewers are however unanimously unconvinced about the potential impact of the simulator, and more broadly the relevance to ICLR. The empirical section of the paper is largely focused on benchmarking logistic regression models on MNIST, which reviewers find underwhelming. It is conceivable that the results reflect performance on real hardware, but the ICLR community would atleast expect to see realistic deep learning workloads on larger datasets such as Imagenet, where scalability challenges have been throughly studied. Without such results, the impact of the contribution is hard to evaluate and the claimed gains are bit of a leap of faith. 
 
 The authors make several good points in their response about the paper - that their method is expected to scale, that high quality simulations can given insights that can inform hardware manufacturing, and that their approach complements other hardware and algorithmic acceleration strategies. They are encouraged to resubmit the paper with a stronger empirical section, e.g., benchmarking training and inference of Inception-like models on ImageNet.

For more than a decade, near data processing has been a key requirement for large scale linear learning platforms, as the time to load the data exceeds the learning time, and this has justified the introduction of approaches such as Spark

Deep learning usually deals with the data that can be contained in a single machine and the bottleneck is often the CPU-GPU bus or the GPU-GPU-bus, so a method that overcomes this bottleneck could be relevant.

Unfortunately, this work is still very preliminary and limited to linear training algorithms, so of little interest yet to ICLR readership. I would recommend publication to a conference where it can reach the large-scale linear ML audience first, such as ICML. This paper is clear and well written in the present form and would probably mostly need a proper benchmark on a large scale linear task. Obviously, when the authors have convincing DNN learning simulations, they are welcome to target ICLR, but can the flash memory FPGA handle it?

For experiments, the choice of MNIST is somewhat bizarre: this task is small and performance is notoriously terrible when using linear approaches (the authors do not even report it)

machine_text: Overall, I found this paper to be well-written and organized. The introduction provides a clear overview of the subject matter, and the paper is adequately detailed, I did not find any redundant explanations. My main suggestions for improvement would be to add a few references to the references section and to be more explicit about the implemented hyperparameter settings in the appendix. Reference: 1. Y. LeCun, Y. Bengio, and G. Hinton. "Convolutional Neural Networks for Sentence Classification." In The Handbook of Natural Language Processing, 3rd ed., 769-786. New York: Springer, 2012. 2. D. D. Lewis and S. G. Cox. "Supervised Learning with Fisher Linear discriminant Analysis."Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence, IEEE Transactions, vol. 24, no. 7, pp. 1134-1141, July 2011. In the implementation section, it would be useful to list the hyperparameter settings you have explored and present the results of the best setting. The Table 1 in the main text appears to correspond to Table 2 in the appendix, since both summarize the best hyperparameter settings. Also, in the last sentence of the subsection "Experiments", replace the expression “41.3%” with “42.8%”." Finally, I noticed that there is no reference in the Abstract. Table 1. hyperparameter settings and corresponding classification accuracy on the Diabetes dataset. Rank Setting Classification accuracy 1 Linear kernel, default C, 10-fold cross validation 40.6% 2 Linear kernel, C = 1, 10-fold cross validation 41.3% 3 RBF kernel, C = 10, 10-fold cross validation 45.3% 4 RBF kernel, C = 100, 10-fold cross validation 45.5% 5 RBF kernel, C = 1000, 10-fold cross validation 45.8% This results in an overall classification accuracy of 42.8%." In the last paragraph of the section "Experiments", the authors mention that “According to the logistic function, the optimal classification threshold is 0.5”. It would be useful to add a reference for this statement. In Table 1, the classification accuracy for the RBF kernel with C = 10 is 45.3%. Since this result is significantly higher than the classification accuracy obtained with the default C and with C = 1, I assume that the authors tried out different values for the C parameter. However, the authors do not explain why they chose C = 10 over C = 100 or C = 1000. I would recommend explaining this in the last paragraph of the "Experiments" section. The classification model built with the RBF kernel and C = 10 sensitivity depends on the selected threshold (i.e., the logistic function is not fully flexible). To evaluate this model’s sensitivity, we can compute the mean sensitivity for a few selected thresholds: 0.48, 0.5, 0.52, 0.54, 0.56. The mean sensitivity is 0.52, and the standard deviation is 0.02. Thus, although the model is not fully flexible, the sensitivity is robust with respect to the selected threshold. The authors should add a reference for the statement about the sensitivity of the model. The logistic function’s optimal threshold is 0.5, but its sensitivity is not 1 for most of the studied thresholds. Thus, the conclusion that the sensitivity is robust with respect to the selected threshold should be revised." The authors could add Table 1 with all the hyperparameter settings, together with the corresponding classification accuracy. The code used for training the experiments is available at https://github.com/huggingface/transformers. I have already reviewed the paper “Exploring the Application of Deep Learning for Supervised Learning Problems”, https://github.com/huggingface/transformers All comments have been addressed, and the revised version is now ready for indexing.

The authors use publicly available datasets and a simple feed forward deep neural network to solve a few challenging machine learning problems. The strengths of this paper are the implementation and analysis of the standard classification datasets using standard deep learning architectures. The weakness of the paper are the limited use of ablation studies and the lack of application to the medical image analysis domain. The findings from this study can be easily translatable to other challenging machine learning problems. The use case and applicability to the medical imaging community is also limited. ools Addresses the following three learning problem using publicly available datasets and a simple feed forward deep neural network. 1. Learning to predict presence of cancer in biopsy images using CNNs with binary cross-entropy loss function 2. Learning to classify colon cancer into malignant or benign classes using CNNs with binary cross-entropy loss function 3. Mining radiomic features from imaging and vectorization of pixel intensities to characterize lung cancer. The paper uses the term validation set for internal validation and the term testing set for external evaluation. The final model selection is conducted on the combined testing set. The authors use ADAM for optimization with the default settings. The source code and pre-trained model are released. The classification accuracy on the testing set for the first two problems is 83% and 92% respectively. The features used are hand designed for the first problem and fully automated for the second problem. Some useful insights are: 1. The overfitting is not properly assessed using standard validation metrics (RMSE, MAE, R2) and simple techniques like monitoring loss on early stopping. 2. A simple L2 penalty does not perform well in L2 regularized problems. 3. Repeated experiments with different learning rates and kernel size show the model is not overfit to the particular choice of hyperparameters Some suggestions for improvement could be: 1. In the first problem, the authors could conduct an ablation study by comparing the model with early stopping and MLP with different numbers of layers. 2. In the second problem, the authors could use transfer learning with a pre-trained Resnet50 on ImageNet to speed up the model training. 3. In the third problem, it is not clear how the CNN is vectorized to the pixel intensities? The authors could provide more details on this part of the code Generally this paper is well executed with good performance on the problem stated.

The paper is interesting and innovative. The results are informative and helpful for people who are interested in applying deep learning to new application domains. The analysis methodology is rigorous and well-defined. The discovered insights are helpful and insightful. The conclusions are well-supported by the findings. The paper is technically sound. ding specific comments: General comment: I would encourage the authors to explore the application of more advanced techniques in this field. As an example, I think it would be very interesting to investigate the use of generative adversarial networks (GANs) in this setting. It would be especially useful to apply different GAN architectures and analyze their impact on performance. More detailed comments: I think the title is a bit misleading. The core of the work is not about using deep learning for supervised learning problems. The work has a much broader scope. In fact, the paper does not focus on analyzing the effectiveness of different layers of DNNs. The work is more about analyzing DNNs from many aspects and exploring their effect on performance. Although there is a part of this work that analyzes the effectiveness of different layers of DNNs, it is only a small part of the work. I suggest the authors changed the title to better describe the scope of the work. Figure 1 is useful to describe the main findings. Some additional items could be added to the Figure 1. For example, how the discovered insights relate to common DNN architectures. Also, it would be helpful to give some examples of the topologies that have been found in the study. For example, S, T, and R shape: these are three examples of topologies that have been found in the study. On the other hand, I don't think the interpretation of the found insights is very clear. In my opinion, the authors should provide a user guide or additional insights about how to apply the discovered insights in practice.

One of the main difficulties in applying deep neural nets (DNNs) to new domains is the need to explore multiple architectures in order to discover ones that perform well. We analyze a large set of DNNs across multiple domains and derive insights regarding their effectiveness. We also analyze the characteristics of various DNNs and the general effect they may have on performance. Finally, we explore the application of meta-learning to the problem of architecture ranking. We demonstrate that by using topological features and modeling the changes in its weights, biases and activation functions layers of the initial training steps, we are able to rank architectures based on their predicted performance. We consider this work to be a first step in the important and challenging direction of exploring the space of different neural network architectures. Our work has the following strengths: 1. We analyze a large set of DNNs across multiple domains and derive insights regarding their performance. 2. We also analyze the characteristics of various DNNs and the general effect they may have on performance. 3. We explore the application of meta-learning to the problem of architecture ranking. We demonstrate that by using topological features and modeling the changes in its weights, biases and activation functions layers of the initial training steps, we are able to rank architectures based on their predicted performance. Our work has the following weaknesses: 1. We only consider the application of meta-learning to the problem of architecture ranking. We should have discussed other applications of meta-learning, such as learning to learn. 2. We didn’t extensively explore the use of different types of features to represent the models. We only consider topological features. Other types of features, such as parameter-based features, could be used to represent the models. In conclusion, we consider this work to be a first step in the important and challenging direction of exploring the space of different neural network architectures.
human_text:
This paper presents an intriguing study of how one can pose architecture search as a meta learning problem. By collecting features from networks trained on various datasets and training a “ranking classifier” (the actual details of the classifier do not seem to be described in detail) one can potentially infer what a good architecture for a new problem could be by simply running the ranker on the extracted features for a new problem setup.

One notable comment from the paper is that the authors fix some important hyper-parameters for all the networks. I am of the opinion that optimizing the learning rate (and its decay schedule) is actually quite important. I hypothesize that a lot of the conclusions of this paper may change quite a bit if the authors did an actual search over the rates instead. I suspect that instead of training 11k nets, one can train 2k nets with 5 learning rates each and get a much better result that is actually compelling.

I am not convinced that the protocol for generating the various architectures is doing a good job at creating a diversity of architecture (simply because of the max depth of 8 layers and 14 components overall). I suspect that most of these generated architectures are actually almost identical performance-wise and that it’s a waste to train so many of them on so many tasks. Unless the authors are already doing this, they should define a pruning mechanism that filters out nets that are too similar to already existing ones.

The batch normalization experiments in Table 2 seem odd and under-explained. It is also well-known that the optimal learning rates when using batch norm vs. not using batch norm can differ by an order of magnitude so given the fixed learning rate throughout all experiments, I take these results with some grain of salt.

I am not sure we got many insights into the kinds of architectures that ended up being at the top. Either visualizations, or trends (or both), would be great.

This work seems to conflate the study of parallel vs. serial architectures with the study of meta learning, which are somewhat distinct issues. I take issue with the table that compares parallel vs. serial performance (table 2) simply because the right way would be to filter the architectures by the same number of parameters / capacity.

Ultimately the conclusion seems to be that when applying deep nets in a new domain, it is difficult to come up with a good architecture in advance. In that sense, it is hard to see the paper as a constructive result, because it’s conclusions are that while the ranker may do a good job often-times, it’s not that reliable. Thus I am not convinced that this particular result will be of practical use to folks who are intending to use deep nets for a new domain.
The reviewers unanimously recommend rejection.

The topic is very interesting, but the paper is not convincing. Specifically, the experiment part is weak. The study should include datasets that are familiar to the community as well as the ones "that are not often addressed by deep learning". The comparison to other approaches is not comprehensive.

This paper aims at attacking the problem of preselecting deep learning model structures for new domains. It reported a series of experiments on various small tasks and feed-forward DNNs. It claims that some ranking algorithm can be learned based on these results to guide the selection of model structures for new domains.

Although the goal is interesting I found their conclusion is neither convincing nor useful in practice for several reasons:

1. They only explored really simple networks (feed-forward DNNs). While this significantly limited the search space, it also limited the value of the experiments. In fact, the best model architecture is highly task (domain) dependent and the type of model (DNN vs CNN vs LSTM) is often much more important than size of the network itself.
2. Their experiments were conduced with some important hyper parameters (e.g., learning rate schedule) fixed. However, it is well known  that learning rate often is the most important hyper parameter during training. Without adjusting these important hyper parameters the conclusion on the best model architecture is not convincing.
3. Their experiments seem to indicate that the training data difference is not important. However, this is unlikely to be true as you would definitely want to use larger models (total number of parameters) when your training set is magnitude larger (i.e., log(datasize) can be an important feature). This is likely because they did not run experiments on large datasets.

In addition, I think the title of the paper does not accurately reflect what the paper is about and should be modified. Also, this paper cited Sainath et al. 2015 as the work that leads to breakthrough in speech recognition. However, the breakthrough in ASR happened much earlier. The first paper with all three key components was published in 2010:

Yu, D., Deng, L. and Dahl, G., 2010, December. Roles of pre-training and fine-tuning in context-dependent DBN-HMMs for real-world speech recognition. In Proc. NIPS Workshop on Deep Learning and Unsupervised Feature Learning.

and the more detailed paper was published in 2012

Dahl, G.E., Yu, D., Deng, L. and Acero, A., 2012. Context-dependent pre-trained deep neural networks for large-vocabulary speech recognition. IEEE Transactions on Audio, Speech, and Language Processing, 20(1), pp.30-42.

As a conclusion, this paper presented some very preliminary result. Although it's interesting it's not ready for publishing.

This paper presents an intriguing study of how one can pose architecture search as a meta learning problem. By collecting features from networks trained on various datasets and training a “ranking classifier” (the actual details of the classifier do not seem to be described in detail) one can potentially infer what a good architecture for a new problem could be by simply running the ranker on the extracted features for a new problem setup.

One notable comment from the paper is that the authors fix some important hyper-parameters for all the networks. I am of the opinion that optimizing the learning rate (and its decay schedule) is actually quite important. I hypothesize that a lot of the conclusions of this paper may change quite a bit if the authors did an actual search over the rates instead. I suspect that instead of training 11k nets, one can train 2k nets with 5 learning rates each and get a much better result that is actually compelling.

I am not convinced that the protocol for generating the various architectures is doing a good job at creating a diversity of architecture (simply because of the max depth of 8 layers and 14 components overall). I suspect that most of these generated architectures are actually almost identical performance-wise and that it’s a waste to train so many of them on so many tasks. Unless the authors are already doing this, they should define a pruning mechanism that filters out nets that are too similar to already existing ones.

The batch normalization experiments in Table 2 seem odd and under-explained. It is also well-known that the optimal learning rates when using batch norm vs. not using batch norm can differ by an order of magnitude so given the fixed learning rate throughout all experiments, I take these results with some grain of salt.

I am not sure we got many insights into the kinds of architectures that ended up being at the top. Either visualizations, or trends (or both), would be great.

This work seems to conflate the study of parallel vs. serial architectures with the study of meta learning, which are somewhat distinct issues. I take issue with the table that compares parallel vs. serial performance (table 2) simply because the right way would be to filter the architectures by the same number of parameters / capacity.

Ultimately the conclusion seems to be that when applying deep nets in a new domain, it is difficult to come up with a good architecture in advance. In that sense, it is hard to see the paper as a constructive result, because it’s conclusions are that while the ranker may do a good job often-times, it’s not that reliable. Thus I am not convinced that this particular result will be of practical use to folks who are intending to use deep nets for a new domain.

machine_text: Overall, I think this is an interesting exploration study for count-based exploration for deep reinforcement learning. However, I would like to see the followings: 1. Sample Complexity Analysis. How efficient the algorithm performance with different sample sizes? 2. Generalizability Analysis. How the algorithm perform on different domains? 3.parameter analysis. How robust the algorithm with different parameter settings? 4. Analysis of Exploration Heuristic. I find that the algorithm just focus on the exploration and not exploitation, which may cause under-utilization of the current system. Report Problems - There is no evaluation on different sample sizes. It may cause under-sample problem in some cases. - The algorithm only explore rather than exploit. It may cause under-utilization of the current system. Solution 1. Sample Complexity Analysis - As we known, a large sample size is preferred for Q-learning based algorithms, due to the fact that Q-learning algorithm needs to estimate the q-function, which requires sufficient data to train. In this work, the exploration is based on the count-based method, so the sample size doesn't play a role. However, we can still use episodes instead of time steps, since a episode means more than a single time step. In addition, we can also analyse the rollout number with Soft Q-Network (SQN), which is also Q-learning algorithm based on the sample size. The code is publicly available. 2. Generalizability Analysis - As the algorithm only explore instead of exploit, it may not cause over-fitting or under-fitting, since exploration and exploitation are two sides of the same coin. Implementation Details - For Soft Q-Network, we can use the following code as reference. The model architecture is similar to Arcade Learning Environment. ``` model = Sequential() model.add(Lambda(alpha):Linear(in_size=len(action_space), out_size=dim, bias=init_bias, metadata=len(action_space) + 1)) model.add(Dense(512, activation='relu')) model.add(Dense(256, activation='relu')) model.add(Dense(256, activation='relu')) model.add(Dense(num_actions)) model.add(Activation('softmax')) ``` The algorithm just improve the exploration by adding the count-based method, without changing the algorithm. The algorithm is more about how to compute the exploration count, instead of the algorithm itself. The exploration count is: $$c(s) = \frac{\mathrm{ Num \ of \ time \ step \ in \ s}}{\mathrm{Num \ of \ total \ time \ step \ in \ the \ episode}}$$ Note that the exploration count here is not based on the rollout number. It is the time step count in the state s. For better result, it is recommended to have enough states in the state space. Predefined hyper-parameters - batch_size = 32 - num_steps = 10000 - batch_chunk_size = 256 - action_candidate_size = 100 - exploration_count_threshold = 10 - exploration_window = 1 - exploration_min_interval = 1 - initial_exploration_count = 1 - exploration_count_coefficient = 2 Conclusion In this paper, we present a study on count-based exploration for Deep Reinforcement Learning. We show that count-based exploration has the potential to significantly speed up learning in a range of problems. We introduce a general algorithm framework, and conduct a series of numerical experiments to illustrate the effectiveness of the framework in practice.

The authors introduce Count-Based Exploration (CBE), a model-free algorithm for deep reinforcement learning, that scales to high-dimensional action spaces. CBE adjusts the exploration rate according to a count of the number of times the agent has performed a particular action. The authors discuss several properties that make CBE model-free: - Counting without a model simplifies learning the relationship between the action and the reward. - When multiple actions have the same count, the authors introduce a natural way to break a tie: the count itself can be interpreted as a popularity score. The authors perform experiments on the Dactyl plugin episode of the MuJoCo benchmarks, and show that CBE performs as well as or better than other state-of-the-art methods for model-free reinforcement learning. Overall, this is a well-written paper that describes a useful algorithm for model-free reinforcement learning. The authors present a rigorous analysis of CBE in the case of Dactyl, and present code for the Count-Based Exploration algorithm on OpenAI gym. Some potential areas for improvement include: - The Dactyl plugin is a contrived example. More challenging environments would help evaluate the effectiveness of CBE. - The authors’ definition of “good” and “bad” visits to a state differs from the standard. A more robust definition of “count” could significantly increase the applicability of CBE. One simple solution is to count only the last action and last time step. - In the paper and code, the authors compare CBE to “random” and “linearly incrementing”. It would be useful to know how CBE performs compared to other count-based exploration schemes, such as Upper-Bound Monte Carlo or Delta-Gamma. Despite these points for improvement, CBE is a promising algorithm for model-free reinforcement learning.

Write a peer review of #Exploration: A Study of Count-Based Exploration for Deep Reinforcement Learning This paper describes a simple general approach for exploration in deep reinforcement learning (RL). The approach is simple and based on hashing the states and counting their occcurrences in an experience replay buffer. A useful bonus is computed based on the original state and the corresponding hash code. The approach is evaluated on many continuous control tasks and Atari 2600 games and yields near state-of-the-art performance in some cases. The exploration strategy was originally motivated as a way to deal with high-dimensional continuous state space. The described method also works for high-dimensional discrete state spaces, an setting in which it was traditionally thought that count-based exploration doesn’t work. The main idea behind this approach is to use hashing to produce a low-dimensional representation of the state space that captures some aspects of the original state space while being low-dimensional. From the low-dimensional representation one can compute a count that can be used to compute a bonus that will be part of the reward signal in the MDP. The bonus is based on the idea that the agent should not only focus on the latest observed state A but also at states that were observed a lot in the recent past (A^r). The hashing function plays a crucial role in this approach. If the hashing function is too coarsely grained, then there is not enough structure in the state space and the bonus will not be high enough. If the function is too finely grained, then the bonus will be too high. The paper describes a simple scheme that is designed to find a good balance between these two extremes. The exploration approach was evaluated on many continuous control tasks and Atari 2600 games and performed well in many cases. The only other algorithm that was tested on most of the continuous control tasks and performed better is the LTD (Local TD) algorithm. The Local TD algorithm trains a separate copy of the agent for each element of the state space and therefore is better suited to control methods that depend on a global state space representation. The proposed exploration algorithm is not so strong in that aspect but it is easier to implement and more computationally efficient. On the Atari 2600 games the performance varies between the evaluated algorithms. The Locomotor and Montezuma’s Revenge are the two games that the exploration approach performed best on. However, there were also games that were very difficult for the exploration algorithm but were solved very easily by other algorithms. The most striking example is Missile Command, which is one of the hardest Atari 2600 games. Overall, the proposed approach to exploration in RL is a simple and general one that can be applied in a lot of different situations. The fact that it has shown to perform well on several continuous control tasks and Atari 2600 games could open new possibilities for applying it to new problems and simpler systems. Some aspects of the approach may be improved in the future. For example, it would be interesting to see whether combining the hashing approach with techniques used for high-dimensional reinforcement learning (such as using a Laplacian eigenmap to map states to a high-dimensional latent space) would improve the results further. It is also possible to further simplify the approach by only using a subset of the original state information to compute the bonus. For example, the bonus could be computed using only the most recent state and using the last few hashes of the state instead of the full history. This would probably allow one to apply the approach to more complex problems that currently seem to suffer from the high dimensionality of the state space. Overall, the proposed exploration approach to reinforcement learning is a simple and powerful one that could be useful for many applications. Significance: The exploration approach is general and does not assume a particular structure in the state space. It allows for efficient implementation and is computationally cheap. It performs well on several continuous control tasks and Atari 2600 games. weaknesses: The main shortcoming of the approach is that it requires the state space to be low-dimensional, where low-dimensional refers to the original state dimensions plus the hashing dimension. In some cases this may not be the case. For example, if the state space is high-dimensional but all changes of a particular state (such as a specific combination of parameters for a continuous control task) lead to the same next state, then the corresponding state dimensions are superfluous. The hashing function would be the same in all these cases and therefore doesn’t add any information to the state space. In this case the only way to achieve a good bonus would be to do something like using a limited version of past states which doesn’t use the full history. human_text:
This paper proposed to use a simple count-based exploration technique in high-dimensional RL application (e.g., Atari Games). The counting is based on state hash, which implicitly groups (quantizes) similar state together. The hash is computed either via hand-designed features or learned features (unsupervisedly with auto-encoder). The new state to be explored receives a bonus similar to UCB (to encourage further exploration).

Overall the paper is solid with quite extensive experiments. I wonder how it generalizes to more Atari games. Montezuma’s Revenge may be particularly suitable for approaches that implicitly/explicitly cluster states together (like the proposed one), as it has multiple distinct scenarios, each with small variations in terms of visual appearance, showing clustering structures. On the other hand, such approaches might not work as well if the state space is fully continuous (e.g. in RLLab experiments). 

The authors did not answer my question about why the hash code needs to be updated during training. I think it is mainly because the code still needs to be adaptive for a particular game (to achieve lower reconstruction error) in the first few iterations . After that stabilization is the most important. Sec. 2.3 (Learned embedding) is quite confusing (but very important). I hope that the authors could make it more clear (e.g., by writing an algorithm block) in the next version.

The paper proposes a simple approach to exploration that uses a hash of the current state within a exploration bonus approach (there are some modifications to learned hash codes, but this is the basic approach). The method achieves reasonable performance on Atari game tasks (sometimes outperformed by other approaches, but overall performing well), and it's simplicity is its main appeal (although the autoencoder-based learned hash seems substantially less simple, so actually loses some advantage there). 
 
 The paper is likely borderline, as the results are not fantastic: the approach is typically outperformed or similarly-performed by one of the comparison approaches (though it should be noted that no comparison approach performs well over all tasks, so this is not necessarily that bad). But overall, especially because so many of these methods have tunable hyperparameters it was difficult to get a clear understanding of just how these experimental results fit.
 
 Pros:
 + Simple method for exploration that seems to work reasonably well in practice
 + Would have the potential to be widely used because of its simplicity
 
 Cons:
 - Improvements over previous approaches are not always there, and it's not clear whether the algorithm has any "killer app" domain where it is just clearly the best approach
  
 Overall, this work in its current form is too borderline. The PCs encourage the authors to strengthen the empirical validation and resubmit.

We have updated the paper with the following changes

(1) The distinction between static hashing (e.g. LSH) and learned hashing is made clear. They are now discussed separately in sections 2.2 and 2.3. BASS is moved to the experimental part (section 3.2), since it is specific to Atari.

(2) The text in section 2.3 is improved to clarify details of training the autoencoder. A separate algorithm block (Algorithm 2) clarifies that the autoencoder is retrained periodically.

(3) Robustness of SimHash and and the comparison between state counting and state action counting are included in Appendix A.6.

This paper introduces a new way of extending the count based exploration approach to domains where counts are not readily available. The way in which the authors do it is through hash functions. Experiments are conducted on several domains including control and Atari. 

It is nice that the authors confirmed the results of Bellemare in that given the right "density" estimator, count based exploration can be effective. It is also great the observe that given the right features, we can crack games like Montezuma's revenge to some extend.

I, however, have several complaints:

First, by using hashing, the authors did not seem to be able to achieve significant improvements over past approaches. Without "feature engineering", the authors achieved only a fraction of the performance achieved in Bellemare et al. on Montezuma's Revenge. The proposed approaches In the control domains, the authors also does not outperform VIME. So experimentally, it is very hard to justify the approach. 

Second, hashing, although could be effective in the domains that the authors tested on, it may not be the best way of estimating densities going forward. As the environments get more complicated, some learning methods, are required for the understanding of the environments instead of blind hashing. The authors claim that the advantage of the proposed method over Bellemare et al. is that one does not have to design density estimators. But I would argue that density estimators have become readily available (PixelCNN, VAEs, Real NVP, GANs) that they can be as easily applied as can hashing. Training the density estimators is not difficult problem as more.

The paper proposes a new exploration scheme for reinforcement learning using locality-sensitive hashing states to build a table of visit counts which are then used to encourage exploration in the style of MBIE-EB of Strehl and Littman.

Several points are appealing about this approach: first, it is quite simple compared to the current alternatives (e.g. VIME, density estimation and pseudo-counts). Second, the paper presents results across several domains, including classic benchmarks, continuous control domains, and Atari 2600 games. In addition, there are results for comparison from several other algorithms (DQN variants), many of which are quite recent. The results indicate that the approach clearly improves over the baseline. The results against other exploration algorithms are not as clear (more dependent on the individual domain/game), but I think this is fine as the appeal of the technique is its simplicity. Third, the paper presents results on the sensitivity to the granularity of the abstraction.

I have only one main complaint, which is it seems there was some engineering involved to get this to work, and I do not have much confidence in the robustness of the conclusions. I am left uncertain as to how the story changes given slight perturbations over hyper-parameter values or enabling/disabling of certain choices. For example, how critical was using PixelCNN (or tying the weights?) or noisifying the output in the autoencoder, or what happens if you remove the custom additions to BASS? The granularity results show that the choice of resolution is sensitive, and even across games the story is not consistent.

The authors decide to use state-based counts instead of state-action based counts, deviating from the theory, which is odd because the reason to used LSH in the first place is to get closer to what MBIE-EB would advise via tabular counts. There are several explanations as to why state-based versus state-action based counts perform similarly in Atari; the authors do not offer any. Why?

It seems like the technique could be easily used in DQN as well, and many of the variants the authors compare to are DQN-based, so omitting DQN here again seems strange. The authors justify their choice of TRPO by saying it ensures safe policy improvement, though it is not clear that this is still true when adding these exploration bonuses.

The case study on Montezuma's revenge, while interesting, involves using domain knowledge and so does not really fit well with the rest of the paper.

So, in the end, simple and elegant idea to help with exploration tested in many domains, though I am not certain which of the many pieces are critical for the story to hold versus just slightly helpful, which could hurt the long-term impact of the paper.

This paper introduces a new way of extending the count based exploration approach to domains where counts are not readily available. The way in which the authors do it is through hash functions. Experiments are conducted on several domains including control and Atari. 

It is nice that the authors confirmed the results of Bellemare in that given the right "density" estimator, count based exploration can be effective. It is also great the observe that given the right features, we can crack games like Montezuma's revenge to some extend.

I, however, have several complaints:

First, by using hashing, the authors did not seem to be able to achieve significant improvements over past approaches. Without "feature engineering", the authors achieved only a fraction of the performance achieved in Bellemare et al. on Montezuma's Revenge. The proposed approaches In the control domains, the authors also does not outperform VIME. So experimentally, it is very hard to justify the approach. 

Second, hashing, although could be effective in the domains that the authors tested on, it may not be the best way of estimating densities going forward. As the environments get more complicated, some learning methods, are required for the understanding of the environments instead of blind hashing. The authors claim that the advantage of the proposed method over Bellemare et al. is that one does not have to design density estimators. But I would argue that density estimators have become readily available (PixelCNN, VAEs, Real NVP, GANs) that they can be as easily applied as can hashing. Training the density estimators is not difficult problem as more.

The paper proposes a new exploration scheme for reinforcement learning using locality-sensitive hashing states to build a table of visit counts which are then used to encourage exploration in the style of MBIE-EB of Strehl and Littman.

Several points are appealing about this approach: first, it is quite simple compared to the current alternatives (e.g. VIME, density estimation and pseudo-counts). Second, the paper presents results across several domains, including classic benchmarks, continuous control domains, and Atari 2600 games. In addition, there are results for comparison from several other algorithms (DQN variants), many of which are quite recent. The results indicate that the approach clearly improves over the baseline. The results against other exploration algorithms are not as clear (more dependent on the individual domain/game), but I think this is fine as the appeal of the technique is its simplicity. Third, the paper presents results on the sensitivity to the granularity of the abstraction.

I have only one main complaint, which is it seems there was some engineering involved to get this to work, and I do not have much confidence in the robustness of the conclusions. I am left uncertain as to how the story changes given slight perturbations over hyper-parameter values or enabling/disabling of certain choices. For example, how critical was using PixelCNN (or tying the weights?) or noisifying the output in the autoencoder, or what happens if you remove the custom additions to BASS? The granularity results show that the choice of resolution is sensitive, and even across games the story is not consistent.

The authors decide to use state-based counts instead of state-action based counts, deviating from the theory, which is odd because the reason to used LSH in the first place is to get closer to what MBIE-EB would advise via tabular counts. There are several explanations as to why state-based versus state-action based counts perform similarly in Atari; the authors do not offer any. Why?

It seems like the technique could be easily used in DQN as well, and many of the variants the authors compare to are DQN-based, so omitting DQN here again seems strange. The authors justify their choice of TRPO by saying it ensures safe policy improvement, though it is not clear that this is still true when adding these exploration bonuses.

The case study on Montezuma's revenge, while interesting, involves using domain knowledge and so does not really fit well with the rest of the paper.

So, in the end, simple and elegant idea to help with exploration tested in many domains, though I am not certain which of the many pieces are critical for the story to hold versus just slightly helpful, which could hurt the long-term impact of the paper.

AI BEFORE PROCEEDS Introduction Few-shot learning, or one-shot learning, as the literature often refers to it, is the task of classifying samples from a new class based on only a few examples, or one example. Such an emergency case of learning has important real-world applications, such as emergency calls where the caller only provides few details about the emergency and the service provider needs to respond accordingly. As a result, there is a growing interest in this field of machine learning, in recent years. A recent approach to few-shot learning called Matching Networks (Mnets) has shown that in addition to learning good distance measures between points, it is also important to maintain access to a support set (orgallery) which contains instances of each class. The network is first trained to find the shortest distance to points in the support set. During test time, the network outputs the class with which the closest point in the support set was labelled. This approach has demonstrated state-of-the-art performance for few-shot learning, but the complex fine-tuning and attention-based support set representation make it difficult to scale. In this work, we present Prototypical Networks, a simple solution to few-shot learning. We show that by maintaining a support set in memory, but using Euclidean distance to prototype representations of each class, our approach is competitive with state-of-the-art on standard few-shot learning tasks. Page 3, l. 21: Change ‘support set’ to ‘the support set’ {#section-1.unnumbered} We first present the few-shot learning task, and then describe our method for solving it, based on the Prototypical Network architecture. One-shot learning (or one-shot classification) is the task of classifying a sample from one of a set of known classes, based on only one example, or one-shot. Several approaches have been developed for performing one-shot learning. One approach is to transform the sample to a high-dimensional space, use clustering to find a good match in the archive, and then apply a similar dimensionality reduction to the new sample to find the corresponding cluster. This approach works well only if the differences between classes are observable in high dimensions. For example, if a dataset contains binary attributes (such as flowers and dogs have white hair), one-shot learning based on this method is very simple and effective. Another approach is related to metric learning. If a distance function can be found such that the points are close in this metric space if and only if they belong to the same class, then given only one example of one of these classes, we can use this metric learning approach to perform one-shot learning by only finding the distance to the support set of the current example. This approach is very general but the expensive cost of calculating the distance between all points in the support set and a new point makes it unsuitable for many applications. We propose a simple approach to one-shot learning that is faster and more scalable. Instead of calculating the distance between all points and a new point, we find the distance to a prototype representation of each point. The K-Means algorithm is used to find a set of centers that can be used as prototype representations. The K-Means algorithm is fast and the clustering inside the K-Means algorithm is such that a query point is close to a prototype representation of a cluster iff. it is close to that cluster’s prototype representation. We demonstrate that Prototypical Networks are as effective as the state-of-the-art for one-shot learning on standard datasets. We also show that by using the efficient SSD_k algorithm [DSSD] to perform a k-NN search in the metric space instead of the original Euclidean space, our approach is scalable to large datasets and even one-shot learning for new classes. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. We first define one-shot learning and the main approaches that have been used for it. Next, we present our simple approach to one-shot learning. *** Paper Summary ***

This paper simplify matching network by considering only a single prototype per class which is obtained as the average of the embedding of the training class samples. Empirical comparisons with matching networks are reported.

*** Review ***

The paper reads well and clearly motivate the work. This work of learning metric learning propose to simplify an earlier work (matching network) which is a great objective. The space of learning embeddings to optimize nearest neighbor classification has been explored before, but the idea of averaging the propotypes is interesting (as a non-linear extension of Mensink et al 2013). The paper is an extension of the matching networks by Vinyals et al. in NIPS2016. Instead of using all the examples in the support set during test, the method represents each class by the mean of its learned embeddings. The training procedure and experimental setting are very similar to the original matching networks. I am not completely sure about its advantages over the original matching networks. It seems to me when dealing with 1-shot case, these two methods are identical since there is only one example seen in this class, so the mean of the embedding is the embedding itself. When dealing with 5-shot case, original matching networks compute the weighted average of all examples, but it is at most 5x cost. The experimental results reported for prototypical nets are only slightly better than matching networks. I  think it is a simple, straightforward,  novel extension, but I am not fully convinced its advantages.

This paper proposes an improved version of matching networks, with better scalability properties with respect to the support set of a few-shot classifier. Instead of considering each support point individually, they learn an embedding function that aggregates over items of each class within the support set (eq. 1). This is combined with episodic few-shot training with randomly-sampled partitions of the training set classes, so that the training and testing scenarios match closely.

Although the idea is quite straightforward, and there are a great many prior works on zero-shot and few-shot learning, the proposed technique is novel to my knowledge, and achieves state-of-the-art results on several  benchmark datasets. One addition that I think would improve the paper is a clearer description of the training algorithm (perhaps pseudocode). In its current form the paper a bit vague about this.

The paper is an extension of the matching networks by Vinyals et al. in NIPS2016. Instead of using all the examples in the support set during test, the method represents each class by the mean of its learned embeddings. The experimental results reported for prototypical nets are only slightly better than matching networks. I  think it is a simple, straightforward,  novel extension, but I am not fully convinced its advantages.

This paper proposes an improved version of matching networks, with better scalability properties with respect to the support set of a few-shot classifier. Instead of considering each support point individually, they learn an embedding function that aggregates over items of each class within the support set (eq. 1). This is combined with episodic few-shot training with randomly-sampled partitions of the training set classes, so that the training and testing scenarios match closely.

Although the idea is quite straightforward, and there are a great many prior works on zero-shot and few-shot learning, the proposed technique is novel to my knowledge, and achieves state-of-the-art results on several  benchmark datasets. One addition that I think would improve the paper is a clearer description of the training algorithm (perhaps pseudocode). In its current form the paper a bit vague about this.

This paper explores the issue of optimization convergence, speed and gradient stability in training neural networks for tasks that exhibit long term dependencies. The authors find that hard constraints on orthogonality can negatively affect the speed of convergence and model performance. In particular, they propose to use a weight matrix factorization and parameterization to bound matrix norms and thereby control the degree of expansivity induced during backpropagation. Loss function: The authors apply several methods to encourage or enforce orthogonality during optimization, among which they find that hard constraints can negatively affect the speed of convergence and model performance. Instead, they propose to use soft constraints through parameterized weight matrix decompositions to bound matrix norms and thereby control the degree of expansivity induced during backpropagation. In particular, the authors apply two different approaches: 1) Weight matrix factorization: The first approach is to factorize the weight matrices as XTX, where T is an orthogonal matrix. This factorization encourages orthogonality and can be computed efficiently during backpropagation; however, the authors note that this can negatively affect the speed of convergence and model performance. 2) Weight parameterization: The second approach is to parameterize the matrices as Ue, where e is the VdEro parameter. This parameterization controls the degree of expansivity, and thereby the expansivity of the weight matrices during backpropagation. The VdEro parameter can be computed efficiently during backpropagation; however, the authors note that this method can also negatively affect the speed of convergence and model performance. The authors finally conclude that the balance between achieving orthogonality and avoiding negative impacts on convergence, speed and model performance is a very difficult problem that deserves further investigation, and they leave this exploration as an open question for future work.
