The topic of the paper is extremely valuable and important and would make a significant impact in the real world. I am very favorably impressed by the thoughtfulness and depth with which the ideas are presented and the potential applicability and impact of the ideas are considered. In my opinion, the strengths of the paper are exemplified in the clarity and precision with which the thoughts and ideas are presented and the positive, upbeat, hopeful, and idealistic tone in which the paper is written. I also very much appreciate the many successful connections that the author was able to make in order to collect examples of real-world applications of this kind of technology. I think that this is a great demonstration of the potential positive impact that this work could have in the real world. I also very much appreciate the author's clear acknowledgment of and response to the concerns and criticisms of other researchers and commenters on this paper. I think that this is an especially important point that should be highlighted in this work, as it is very valuable in increasing the likelihood of the positive reception of this kind of work in the future. I believe that it would be valuable and wise to append a section to the paper summarizing these responses to criticisms, as it could easily be overlooked in the body of the text. I also very much appreciate the author's careful and repeated attempts to create appropriately ambiguous and non-factoid questions. This is a very important methodological strength, and it is very valuable to the utility and generalizability of the work. I think that there is some room for improvement in the readability of the text. The writing could definitely be improved through the use of active voice and simpler English. In a few places, the language gets pretentious and the readability decreases. I think that this could be improved by adjusting the language to be more colloquial or more simply mixed with active voice, although this could also make the writing less understandable to some readers. In summary, I think that this is a very good paper that could have a very large potential impact on the world. I strongly encourage the author to proceed with the development of this work. I strongly recommend that the author emphasize the potential positive implications of this work for the welfare of humanity, rather than dwelling on the more speculative positive implications for individual tastes and preferences. The paper would also be strengthened by addressing the issue of whether the exact implementation and method will be feasible, for example through the inclusion of simulated examples or demonstrations on how the algorithm would perform in practice, although the significance of this kind of validity assessment would be diminished due to the potential impact of the work. I also very much recommend that the author pay careful attention to the ethical implications of this work. I think that the potential for negative side effects, such as discrimination or distortion of desired attributes, should definitely be discussed and addressed in this work. I think that there is also potential for this kind of work to contribute to positive side effects, such as prejudice, narcissism, or amplification of desired attributes, although these could be addressed by regulating the access and use of this kind of technology, which I believe the author briefly mentions. I think that a more substantial discussion of the ethical considerations would be worthwhile, but the author should also consider the implications of this work on the free market. The world is full of risk-takers who are motivated by the potential for large gains, and many people would be very interested in this work. I think that the author should address the potential for price gouging or other forms of profiteering, which could be exacerbated by the likely scarcity of this technology, and take steps to prevent this, such as through regulation. I also recommend the inclusion of a privacy policy, although the ethical considerations should be the focus of this work. I also recommend some sort of system for ensuring the privacy of vulnerable populations, such as children, or people in developing countries, although the author could consider this through the use of anonymized datasets or other analyses. I think that the result would be substantially improved if the model was trained on a dataset that included several variants of questions and answers, such as a dataset of questions and answers but with an additional question which follows a different logical chain, in order to force the model to consider more than one solution, or another question and answer where the answer was an apparent positive response to a question that the model was not shown, to ensure the model's understanding of the concept of an answer.

The paper CAN AI GENERATE LOVE ADVICE?: TOWARD NEURAL ANSWER GENERATION FOR NON-FACTOID QUESTIONS is a potentially important contribution to a new and rapidly expanding field: artificial intelligence applied to the resolution of love and romance. This is a technique that can accurately answer questions about love and relationships. This is useful for several reasons. First, traditional advice column style questions are often insensitive and barbie mentality oriented. It allows us to ask more nuanced and challenging questions, which will be more likely to result in love and happiness. Second, it allows us to ask these questions in new and creative ways. Using NLP, it's able to answer questions that would be difficult or impossible to frame as a standard factual question. For example, "how compatible are you with your partner" is difficult to formulate as a factual question. However, using AI we can ask: how compatible are you with your partner on average? Or, alternatively, how compatible are you with most people similar to your partner? This is profound, because it provides us with a much more accurate understanding of our relationships. Finally, it's easy to game (or easy to use for scamming). AI is only as good as the data it's trained on, and for relationship questions that data often consists of human emotions. As a result, someone can feed AI biased data that will produce biased answers. This can be mitigated by using open data (e.g. using public Facebook data), but it can't solve the inherent weaknesses in the problem space.

The paper CAN AI GENERATE LOVE ADVICE?: TOWARD NEURAL ANSWER GENERATION FOR NON-FACTOID QUESTIONS proposes a method to generate answers to non-factoid questions by using deep learning. The generated answers are based on word embeddings which are trained based on categories of questions and biases of word usage. The paper also presents a method to construct answers by using biLSTM which computes the embeddings of questions, sentences used to form answers, and the closeness between questions and sentences. The model is trained on data from a Japanese QA site for love advice and achieved 20 % higher accuracy than strong baselines. The proposed model is practical and has already been applied to the love advice service in a Japanese QA site. I have some thoughts about this paper. First, the author used a Japanese QA site for training, which limits the applicability of the results. Second, the quality of answers generated by the model is not explicitly evaluated. The effectiveness of the method for answer construction cannot be confirmed. Third, there is no analysis of why the generated answers are good. It is not clear how the system judges the quality of the answers. These are some limitations of the paper. The paper is interesting and the ideas are quite novel. I hope the author will consider the limitations above and extend the research in the near future. Panelists: 1. @mfukui_ls 2. @bovada 3. @cub_fang

This paper aims to solve the problems that current models for generating answers for non-factoid questions can not answer the questions that are somewhat different but can assist users in reaching their next decisions through conversations with AI systems. The main strategies of the paper are as below: 1. Incorporating the biases of semantics behind questions (e.g. categories assigned to questions) into word embeddings by calculating them regardless of the semantics. As a result, it can extract answers that suit the contexts of words used in the question as well as following the common usage of words across semantics. 2. Using BiLSTM to compute the embeddings of questions as well as those of the sentences often used to form answers (e.g. sentences representing conclusions or those supplementing the conclusions). It then simultaneously learns the optimum combination of those sentences as well as the closeness between the question and those sentences. Our model can construct an answer that corresponds to the situation that underlies the question. It fills the gap between answer selection and generation and is the first model to move beyond the current simple answer selection model for non-factoid QAs. ning tips: 1. This paper proposes a neural architecture for answering non-factoid questions. The author's model improves over previous neural models for answer sentence selection. Experiments are conducted on a Japanese love advice corpus; the coolest part of the paper for me was that the model was actually rolled out to the public and its answers were rated twice as good as actual human contributors! 

It was hard for me to determine the novelty of the contribution. The authors mention that their model "fills the gap
between answer selection and generation"; however, no generation is actually performed by the model! Instead, the model appears to be very similar to the QA-LSTM of Tan et al., 2015 except that there are additional terms in the objective to handle conclusion and supplementary sentences. The structure of the answer is fixed to a predefined template (e.g., conclusion --> supplementary), so the model is not really learning how to order the sentences. The other contribution is the "word embedding with semantics" portion described in sec 4.1, which is essentially just the paragraph vector model except with "titles" and "categories" instead of paragraphs. 

While the result of the paper is a model that has actually demonstrated real-life usefulness, the technical contributions do not strike me as novel enough for publication at ICLR.

Other comments:
- One major issue with the reliance of the model on the template is that you can't evaluate on commonly-used non-factoid QA datasets such as InsuranceQA. If the template were not fixed beforehand (but possibly learned by the model), you could conceivably evaluate on different datasets. 
- The examples in Table 4 don't show a clear edge in answer quality to your model; QA-LSTM seems to choose good answers as well.
- Doesn't the construction model have an advantage over the vanilla QA-LSTM in that it knows which sentences are conclusions and which are supplementary? Or does QA-LSTM also get this distinction?

The program committee appreciates the authors' response to clarifying questions. Unfortunately, all reviewers are leaning against accepting the paper. Authors are encouraged to incorporate reviewer feedback in future iterations of this work.

Summary: The paper presents an approach – Neural Answer Construction Model for the task of answering non-factoid questions, in particular, love-advice questions. The two main features of the proposed model are the following – 1) it incorporates the biases of semantics behind questions into word embeddings, 2) in addition to optimizing for closeness between questions and answers, it also optimizes for optimum combination of sentences in the predicted answer. The proposed model is evaluated using the dataset from a Japanese online QA service and is shown to outperform the baseline model (Tan et al. 2015) by 20% relatively (6% absolutely). The paper also experiments with few other baseline models (ablations of the proposed model).

Strengths:

1. The two motivations behind the proposed approach – need to understand the ambiguous use of words depending on context, and need to generate new answers rather than just selecting from answers held by QA sites – are reasonable.

2. The novelty in the paper involves the following – 1) incorporating biases of semantics behind questions into word embeddings using paragraph2vec like model, modified to take as inputs - words from questions, question title token and question category token, 2) modelling optimum combination of sentences (conclusion and supplement sentences) in the predicted answer, 3) designing abstract scenario for answers, inspired by automated web-service composition framework (Rao & Su (2005)), and 4) extracting important topics in conclusion sentence and emphasizing them in supplemental sentence using attention mechanism (attention mechanism is similar to Tan et al. 2016).

3. The proposed method is shown to outperform the current best method (Tan et al. 2015) by 20% relatively (6% absolutely) which seems to be significant improvement. 

4. The paper presents few ablations studies that provide insights on how much different components of the model (such as incorporating biases into word embeddings, incorporating attention from conclusion to supplement) are helping towards performance improvement.

Weaknesses/Suggestions/Questions:

1. How are the abstract patterns determined, i,e., how did the authors determine that the answers to love-advice questions generally constitute of sympathy, conclusion, supplement for conclusion and encouragement? How much is the improvement in performance when using abstract patterns compared to the case when not using these patters, i.e. when candidate answers are picked from union of all corpuses rather than picking from respective corpuses (corpuses for sympathy, conclusion etc.).

2. It seems that the abstract patterns are specific to the type of questions. So, the abstract patterns for love-advice will be different from those for business advice. Thus, it seems like the abstract patterns need to be hand-coded for different types and hence one model cannot generalize across different types.

3. The paper should present explicit analysis of how much combinational optimization between sentences help – comparison between model performance with and without combinational optimization keeping rest of the model architecture same. The authors could also plot the accuracy of the model as a function of the combinational optimization scores. This will provide insights into how significant are the combinational optimization scores towards overall model accuracy.


4. Paper says that current systems designed for non-factoid QA cannot generalize to questions outside those stored in QA sites and claims that this is one of the contributions of this paper. In order to ground that claim, the paper should show experimentally how well the proposed method generalized to such out-of-domain questions. Although the questions asked by human experts in the human evaluation were not from the evaluation datasets, the paper should analyze how different those questions were compared to the questions present in the evaluation datasets.

5. For human evaluation, were the outputs of the proposed model and that of the QA-LSTM model judged each judged by both the human experts OR one of the human experts judged the outputs of one system and the other human expert judged the outputs of the other system? If both the sets of outputs were each judged by both the human experts, how were the ratings of the two experts combined for every questions? 

6. I wonder why the authors did not do a human evaluation where they just ask human workers (not experts) to compare the output of the proposed model with that of the QA-LSTM model – which of the two outputs they would like to hear when asking for advice. Such an evaluation would not get biased by whether each sentence is good or not, whether the combination is good or not. Looking at the qualitative examples in Table 4, I personally like the output of the QA-LSTM more than that of the proposed model because they seem to provide a direct answer to the question (e.g., for the first example the output of the QA-LSTM says “You should wait until you feel excited”, whereas the output of the proposed model says “It is better to concentrate on how to confess your love to her” which seems a bit indirect to the question asked.)

7. Given a question, is the ground-truth answer different in the two tasks -- answer selection and answer construction?

8. The paper mentions that Attentive LSTM (Tan et al. 2016) is evaluated as the current best answer selection method (section 5.2). So, why is its accuracy lower than that of QA-LSTM in table 1. The authors explain this by pointing out the issue of questions being very long compared to answers and hence the attention being noisy. But, did these issues not exist in the dataset used by Tan et al. 2016?

9. The paper says the proposed method achieves 20% gain over current best (in Conclusion section) where they refer to QA-LSTM as the current best method. However, in the description of Attentive LSTM (section 5.2), the paper mentions that Attention LSTM is the current best method. So, could authors please clarify the discrepancy?

10. Minor correction: remove space between 20 and % in abstract.

Review Summary: The problem of non-factoid QA being dealt with in the paper is an interesting and useful problem to solve. The motivations presented in the paper behind the proposed approach are reasonable. The experiments show that the proposed model outperforms the baseline model. However, the use of abstract patterns to determine the answer seems like hand-designing and hence it seems like these abstract patterns need to be designed for every other type of non-factoid question and hence the proposed approach is not generalizable to other types. Also, the paper needs more analysis of the results to provide insights into the contribution of different model components.

This paper extends mostly on top of the work of QA-biLSTM and QA-biLSTM with attentions, as proposed in Tan et al. 2015 and Tan et al. 2016, in the following 2 ways:

1. It trains a topic-specific word embedding using an approach similar to Paragraph2vec by leveraging the topic and title information provided in the data.

2. It considers the multiple-unit answer selection problem (e.g., one sentence selected from answer section, and another selected from supplemental section) vs. the single answer selection problem as studied in Tan et al 2015 and 2016. The mechanism used to retain the coherence between different parts of the answers is inspired by the attention mechanism introduced by Tan et al. 2016.

While the practical results presented in the paper is interesting, the main innovations of this paper are rather limited.

The novelty in the paper involves the following – 1) incorporating biases of semantics behind questions into word embeddings using paragraph2vec like model, modified to take as inputs - words from questions, question title token and question category token, 2) modelling optimum combination of sentences (conclusion and supplement sentences) in the predicted answer, 3) designing abstract scenario for answers, inspired by automated web-service composition framework (Rao & Su (2005)), and 4) extracting important topics in conclusion sentence and emphasizing them in supplemental sentence using attention mechanism (attention mechanism is similar to Tan et al. 2016).

3. The proposed method is shown to outperform the current best method (Tan et al. 2015) by 20% relatively (6% absolutely) which seems to be significant improvement. 

4. The paper presents few ablations studies that provide insights on how much different components of the model (such as incorporating biases into word embeddings, incorporating attention from conclusion to supplement) are helping towards performance improvement.

Weaknesses/Suggestions/Questions:

1. How are the abstract patterns determined, i,e., how did the authors determine that the answers to love-advice questions generally constitute of sympathy, conclusion, supplement for conclusion and encouragement? How much is the improvement in performance when using abstract patterns compared to the case when not using these patters, i.e. when candidate answers are picked from union of all corpuses rather than picking from respective corpuses (corpuses for sympathy, conclusion etc.).

2. It seems that the abstract patterns are specific to the type of questions. So, the abstract patterns for love-advice will be different from those for business advice. Thus, it seems like the abstract patterns need to be hand-coded for different types and hence one model cannot generalize across different types.

3. The paper should present explicit analysis of how much combinational optimization between sentences help – comparison between model performance with and without combinational optimization keeping rest of the model architecture same. The authors could also plot the accuracy of the model as a function of the combinational optimization scores. This will provide insights into how significant are the combinational optimization scores towards overall model accuracy.


4. Paper says that current systems designed for non-factoid QA cannot generalize to questions outside those stored in QA sites and claims that this is one of the contributions of this paper. In order to ground that claim, the paper should show experimentally how well the proposed method generalized to such out-of-domain questions. Although the questions asked by human experts in the human evaluation were not from the evaluation datasets, the paper should analyze how different those questions were compared to the questions present in the evaluation datasets.

5. For human evaluation, were the outputs of the proposed model and that of the QA-LSTM model judged each judged by both the human experts OR one of the human experts judged the outputs of one system and the other human expert judged the outputs of the other system? If both the sets of outputs were each judged by both the human experts, how were the ratings of the two experts combined for every questions? 

6. I wonder why the authors did not do a human evaluation where they just ask human workers (not experts) to compare the output of the proposed model with that of the QA-LSTM model – which of the two outputs they would like to hear when asking for advice. Such an evaluation would not get biased by whether each sentence is good or not, whether the combination is good or not. Looking at the qualitative examples in Table 4, I personally like the output of the QA-LSTM more than that of the proposed model because they seem to provide a direct answer to the question (e.g., for the first example the output of the QA-LSTM says “You should wait until you feel excited”, whereas the output of the proposed model says “It is better to concentrate on how to confess your love to her” which seems a bit indirect to the question asked.)

7. Given a question, is the ground-truth answer different in the two tasks -- answer selection and answer construction?

8. The paper mentions that Attentive LSTM (Tan et al. 2016) is evaluated as the current best answer selection method (section 5.2). So, why is its accuracy lower than that of QA-LSTM in table 1. The authors explain this by pointing out the issue of questions being very long compared to answers and hence the attention being noisy. But, did these issues not exist in the dataset used by Tan et al. 2016?

9. The paper says the proposed method achieves 20% gain over current best (in Conclusion section) where they refer to QA-LSTM as the current best method. However, in the description of Attentive LSTM (section 5.2), the paper mentions that Attention LSTM is the current best method. So, could authors please clarify the discrepancy?

10. Minor correction: remove space between 20 and % in abstract.

Review Summary: The problem of non-factoid QA being dealt with in the paper is an interesting and useful problem to solve. The motivations presented in the paper behind the proposed approach are reasonable. The experiments show that the proposed model outperforms the baseline model. However, the use of abstract patterns to determine the answer seems like hand-designing and hence it seems like these abstract patterns need to be designed for every other type of non-factoid question and hence the proposed approach is not generalizable to other types. Also, the paper needs more analysis of the results to provide insights into the contribution of different model components.

This paper extends mostly on top of the work of QA-biLSTM and QA-biLSTM with attentions, as proposed in Tan et al. 2015 and Tan et al. 2016, in the following 2 ways:

1. It trains a topic-specific word embedding using an approach similar to Paragraph2vec by leveraging the topic and title information provided in the data.

2. It considers the multiple-unit answer selection problem (e.g., one sentence selected from answer section, and another selected from supplemental section) vs. the single answer selection problem as studied in Tan et al 2015 and 2016. The mechanism used to retain the coherence between different parts of the answers is inspired by the attention mechanism introduced by Tan et al. 2016.

While the practical results presented in the paper is interesting, the main innovations of this paper are rather limited.

This paper proposes a neural architecture for answering non-factoid questions. The author's model improves over previous neural models for answer sentence selection. Experiments are conducted on a Japanese love advice corpus; the coolest part of the paper for me was that the model was actually rolled out to the public and its answers were rated twice as good as actual human contributors! 

It was hard for me to determine the novelty of the contribution. The authors mention that their model "fills the gap
between answer selection and generation"; however, no generation is actually performed by the model! Instead, the model appears to be very similar to the QA-LSTM of Tan et al., 2015 except that there are additional terms in the objective to handle conclusion and supplementary sentences. The structure of the answer is fixed to a predefined template (e.g., conclusion --> supplementary), so the model is not really learning how to order the sentences. The other contribution is the "word embedding with semantics" portion described in sec 4.1, which is essentially just the paragraph vector model except with "titles" and "categories" instead of paragraphs. 

While the result of the paper is a model that has actually demonstrated real-life usefulness, the technical contributions do not strike me as novel enough for publication at ICLR.

Other comments:
- One major issue with the reliance of the model on the template is that you can't evaluate on commonly-used non-factoid QA datasets such as InsuranceQA. If the template were not fixed beforehand (but possibly learned by the model), you could conceivably evaluate on different datasets. 
- The examples in Table 4 don't show a clear edge in answer quality to your model; QA-LSTM seems to choose good answers as well.
- Doesn't the construction model have an advantage over the vanilla QA-LSTM in that it knows which sentences are conclusions and which are supplementary? Or does QA-LSTM also get this distinction?

human_text:
This paper extends boosting to the task of learning generative models of data. The strong learner is obtained as a geometric average of “weak learners”, which can themselves be normalized (e.g. VAE) or un-normalized (e.g. RBMs) generative models (genBGM), or a classifier trained to discriminate between the strong learner at iteration T-1 and the true data distribution (discBGM). This latter method is closely related to Noise Contrastive Estimation, GANs, etc.

The approach benefits from strong theoretical guarantees, with strict conditions under which each boosting iteration is guaranteed to improve the log-likelihood. The downside of the method appears to be the lack of normalization constant for the resulting strong learner and the use of heuristics to weight each weak learner (which seems to matter in practice, from Sec. 3.2). The discriminative approach further suffers from an expensive training procedure: each round of boosting first requires generating a “training set” worth of samples from the previous strong learner, where samples are obtained via MCMC.

The experimental section is clearly the weak point of the paper. The method is evaluated on a synthetic dataset, and a single real-world dataset, MNIST: both for generation and as a feature extraction mechanism for classification. Of these, the synthetic experiments were the clearest in showcasing the method. On MNIST, the baseline models are much too weak for the results to be convincing. A modestly sized VAE can obtain 90 nats within hours on a single GPU, clearly an achievable goal. Furthermore, despite arguments to the contrary, I firmly believe that mixing base learners is an academic exercise, if only because of the burden of implementing K different models & training algorithms. This section fails to answer a more fundamental question: is it better to train a large VAE by maximizing the elbow, or e.g. train 10 iterations of boosting, using VAEs 1/10th the size of the baseline model ? Experimental details are also lacking, especially with respect to the sampling procedure used to draw samples from the BGM. The paper would also benefit from likelihood estimates obtained via AIS.

With regards to novelty and prior work, there is also a missing reference to “Self Supervised Boosting” by Welling et al [R1]. After a cursory read through, there seems to be strong similarities to the GenBGM approach which ought to be discussed.

Overall, I am on the fence. The idea of boosting generative models is intriguing, seems well motivated and has potential for impact. For this reason, and given the theoretical contributions, I am willing to overlook some of the issues highlighted above, and hope the authors can address some of them in time for the rebuttal.

[R1]

The idea of boosting has recently seen a revival, and the ideas presented here are stimulating. After discussion, the reviewers agreed that the latest updates and clarifications have improved the paper, but overall they still felt that the paper is not quite ready, especially in making the case for when taking this approach is desirable, which was the common thread of concern for everyone. For this reason, this paper is not yet ready for acceptance at this year's conference.

The bulk of the reviewer (R) comments pertain to the experiments on MNIST that we address collectively here to facilitate a richer, holistic discussion. Any remaining questions raised by the reviewers are addressed individually as follow-ups to the reviews.

We have rewritten the entire experimental section based on fresh experimentation, focusing on aspects that we believe are crucial to resolving the concerns raised by the reviewers. For brevity, we have also removed some portions from the earlier draft that we do not believe are central to the discussion. In the spirit of the constructive feedback loop that ICLR facilitates, we hope the reviewers will be able to read the revised experiments section. Our response to the reviewer comments:

1. A bigger VAE vs. BGMs containing smaller models (R1)
Our earlier submission demonstrated improved performance of BGMs for sampling with gains in computational requirements, but did not directly address the reviewer’s question about model capacity. Our latest submission considers larger baseline models with equal or more capacity than BGM sequences of simpler models (Sec. 3.2.2, Table 2), and shows the superior performance of BGMs for this task (Figure 3) . As before, we also illustrate that the performance gains of BGM sequences are not at the cost of increased training time (Sec 3.2.3, Table 2).

2. Samples from MNIST look weak (R4)
Our experiments on MNIST do not (or even intended to) make any state-of-the-art claims, but instead demonstrate the improvements in computational and statistical performance that simpler models can attain for the task of generating samples as a result of the boosting procedure. Having said that, we respectfully disagree that the samples produced by BGM sequences look weak keeping in mind that the dataset under consideration is the harder ‘binarized’ version of MNIST. In fact, although we understand that it is somewhat subjective, we believe the BGM samples look better than NADE samples on the same dataset (Figure 2 (Left) in [2]). Note that we display actual samples produced by our models (without any cherry-picking), and hence, these samples should not be compared with the probabilities from sampling pixels (Figure 2 (Middle) in [2]). 

3. Strategies for setting weights (\alpha’s) for intermediate models (R3)
In our earlier submission, we discussed model weights in the theoretical section and listed heuristic strategies for setting them in practice as a future work. Our latest submission includes experimental results and discussion of some heuristic strategies that we propose for both density estimation and sampling. See Sec. 3.1.3 and Appendix A.2.1.

4. Procedure for drawing samples from BGM sequences (R1, R3)
See Appendix A.2.3 for details.  In contrast to results in the previous submission where the independent chains were run from the same start seeds across BGM sequences and samples arranged for easy comparison, the latest results show samples produced from chains that are run independently, initialized with different random start seeds, and have an increased burn-in time of 100,000 samples (10x the previous) to mitigate the possibility of any mixing-related issues. We also observed visually that the samples from any given chain vary over time transforming smoothly across multiple digits within the burn-in time, a further indication of successful mixing. 

5. Quantitative estimation of log-likelihoods for sampling (R1, R3, R4)
For evaluating samples, log-likelihoods can be problematic. See [1], Sec. 3.2 for a detailed discussion on why log-likelihoods are not a good proxy for sample quality. Additionally, generative models such as VAEs, RBMs have intractable likelihoods and hence, resort to their own approximations for generating density estimates. These approximations are known to exhibit different behaviors; for instance, RBMs estimated using AIS are typically believed to overestimate the log-likelihoods, whereas VAEs make variational approximations that only provide lower bounds -- it is difficult to make definitive statements based on such approximations. We tried AIS on the BGM sequences considered in the paper with about 15,000 intermediate annealing distributions (step-size of 1e-3 between for the first 500 distributions, 1e-4 for the next 4000, and 1e-5 for the remaining where every transition from one distribution to another was implemented using 10 steps of Metropolis-Hastings), but got unrealistically optimistic log-likelihood evaluations that we do not feel confident reporting for the purpose of a meaningful comparison with the lower bounds provided by VAEs.  

References:
[1] Lucas Theis, Aaron van den Oord, and Matthias Bethge. “A note on the evaluation of generative models.” In ICLR, 2016.
[2] Hugo Larochelle and Iain Murray. "The Neural Autoregressive Distribution Estimator."  In AISTATS, 2011.

[R1]

The authors propose two approaches to combine multiple weak generative models into a stronger one using principles from boosting. The approach is simple and elegant and basically creates an unnormalized product of experts model, where the individual experts are trained greedily to optimize the overall joint model. Unfortunately, this approach results in a joint model that has some undesirable properties: a unknown normalisation constant for the joint model and therefore an intractable log-likelihood on the test set; and it makes drawing exact samples from the joint model intractable. These problems can unfortunately not be fixed by using different base learners, but are a direct result of the product of experts formulation of boosting.
  
The experiments on 2 dimensional toy data illustrate that the proposed procedure works in principle and that the boosting formulation produces better results than individual weak learners and better results than e.g. bagging. But the experiments on MNIST are less convincing: Without an undisputable measure like e.g. log-likelihood it is hard to draw conclusions from the samples in Figure 2; and visually they look weak compared to even simple models like e.g. NADE.

I think the paper could be improved significantly by adding a quantitative analysis: investigating the effect of combining undirected (e.g. RBM), undirected (e.g. VAE) and autoregressive (e.g. NADE) models and by measuring the improvement over the number of base learners. But this would require a method to estimate the partition function Z or estimating some proxy.

The paper proposes two approaches to boosting generative models, both based on likelihood ratio estimates. The approaches are evaluated on synthetic data, as well as on MNIST dataset for the tasks of generating samples and semi-supervised learning.
While the idea of boosting generative models and the proposed methods are interesting, the reviewer finds the experiments unconvincing for the following reasons.
1. The bagging baseline in section 3.1 seems to be just refitting a model to the same dataset, raising the probability to power alpha, and renormalizing. This makes it more peaked, but it's not clear why this is a good baseline. Please let me know if I misunderstood the procedure.
2. The sample generation experiment in section 3.2 uses a very slowly converging Markov chain, as can be seen in the similarity of plots c and f, d and g, e and h. It seems unlikely therefore that the resulting samples are from the stationary distribution. A qualitative evaluation using AIS seems to be necessary here.
3. In the same section the choices for alphas seem quite arbitrary - what happens when a more obvious choice of alpha_i=1 for all i is made?
4. It seems hard to infer anything from the semisupervised classification results reported: the baseline RBM seems to perform as well as the boosted models.

The work is mostly clearly written and (as far as the reviewer knows) original.

As before, we also illustrate that the performance gains of BGM sequences are not at the cost of increased training time (Sec 3.2.3, Table 2).

2. Samples from MNIST look weak (R4)
Our experiments on MNIST do not (or even intended to) make any state-of-the-art claims, but instead demonstrate the improvements in computational and statistical performance that simpler models can attain for the task of generating samples as a result of the boosting procedure. Having said that, we respectfully disagree that the samples produced by BGM sequences look weak keeping in mind that the dataset under consideration is the harder ‘binarized’ version of MNIST. In fact, although we understand that it is somewhat subjective, we believe the BGM samples look better than NADE samples on the same dataset (Figure 2 (Left) in [2]). Note that we display actual samples produced by our models (without any cherry-picking), and hence, these samples should not be compared with the probabilities from sampling pixels (Figure 2 (Middle) in [2]). 

3. Strategies for setting weights (\alpha’s) for intermediate models (R3)
In our earlier submission, we discussed model weights in the theoretical section and listed heuristic strategies for setting them in practice as a future work. Our latest submission includes experimental results and discussion of some heuristic strategies that we propose for both density estimation and sampling. See Sec. 3.1.3 and Appendix A.2.1.

4. Procedure for drawing samples from BGM sequences (R1, R3)
See Appendix A.2.3 for details.  In contrast to results in the previous submission where the independent chains were run from the same start seeds across BGM sequences and samples arranged for easy comparison, the latest results show samples produced from chains that are run independently, initialized with different random start seeds, and have an increased burn-in time of 100,000 samples (10x the previous) to mitigate the possibility of any mixing-related issues. We also observed visually that the samples from any given chain vary over time transforming smoothly across multiple digits within the burn-in time, a further indication of successful mixing. 

5. Quantitative estimation of log-likelihoods for sampling (R1, R3, R4)
For evaluating samples, log-likelihoods can be problematic. See [1], Sec. 3.2 for a detailed discussion on why log-likelihoods are not a good proxy for sample quality. Additionally, generative models such as VAEs, RBMs have intractable likelihoods and hence, resort to their own approximations for generating density estimates. These approximations are known to exhibit different behaviors; for instance, RBMs estimated using AIS are typically believed to overestimate the log-likelihoods, whereas VAEs make variational approximations that only provide lower bounds -- it is difficult to make definitive statements based on such approximations. We tried AIS on the BGM sequences considered in the paper with about 15,000 intermediate annealing distributions (step-size of 1e-3 between for the first 500 distributions, 1e-4 for the next 4000, and 1e-5 for the remaining where every transition from one distribution to another was implemented using 10 steps of Metropolis-Hastings), but got unrealistically optimistic log-likelihood evaluations that we do not feel confident reporting for the purpose of a meaningful comparison with the lower bounds provided by VAEs.  

References:
[1] Lucas Theis, Aaron van den Oord, and Matthias Bethge. “A note on the evaluation of generative models.” In ICLR, 2016.
[2] Hugo Larochelle and Iain Murray. "The Neural Autoregressive Distribution Estimator."  In AISTATS, 2011.

This paper extends boosting to the task of learning generative models of data. The strong learner is obtained as a geometric average of “weak learners”, which can themselves be normalized (e.g. VAE) or un-normalized (e.g. RBMs) generative models (genBGM), or a classifier trained to discriminate between the strong learner at iteration T-1 and the true data distribution (discBGM). This latter method is closely related to Noise Contrastive Estimation, GANs, etc.

The approach benefits from strong theoretical guarantees, with strict conditions under which each boosting iteration is guaranteed to improve the log-likelihood. The downside of the method appears to be the lack of normalization constant for the resulting strong learner and the use of heuristics to weight each weak learner (which seems to matter in practice, from Sec. 3.2). The discriminative approach further suffers from an expensive training procedure: each round of boosting first requires generating a “training set” worth of samples from the previous strong learner, where samples are obtained via MCMC.

The experimental section is clearly the weak point of the paper. The method is evaluated on a synthetic dataset, and a single real-world dataset, MNIST: both for generation and as a feature extraction mechanism for classification. Of these, the synthetic experiments were the clearest in showcasing the method. On MNIST, the baseline models are much too weak for the results to be convincing. A modestly sized VAE can obtain 90 nats within hours on a single GPU, clearly an achievable goal. Furthermore, despite arguments to the contrary, I firmly believe that mixing base learners is an academic exercise, if only because of the burden of implementing K different models & training algorithms. This section fails to answer a more fundamental question: is it better to train a large VAE by maximizing the elbow, or e.g. train 10 iterations of boosting, using VAEs 1/10th the size of the baseline model ? Experimental details are also lacking, especially with respect to the sampling procedure used to draw samples from the BGM. The paper would also benefit from likelihood estimates obtained via AIS.

With regards to novelty and prior work, there is also a missing reference to “Self Supervised Boosting” by Welling et al [R1]. After a cursory read through, there seems to be strong similarities to the GenBGM approach which ought to be discussed.

Overall, I am on the fence. The idea of boosting generative models is intriguing, seems well motivated and has potential for impact. For this reason, and given the theoretical contributions, I am willing to overlook some of the issues highlighted above, and hope the authors can address some of them in time for the rebuttal.

[R1]

The authors propose two approaches to combine multiple weak generative models into a stronger one using principles from boosting. The approach is simple and elegant and basically creates an unnormalized product of experts model, where the individual experts are trained greedily to optimize the overall joint model. Unfortunately, this approach results in a joint model that has some undesirable properties: a unknown normalisation constant for the joint model and therefore an intractable log-likelihood on the test set; and it makes drawing exact samples from the joint model intractable. These problems can unfortunately not be fixed by using different base learners, but are a direct result of the product of experts formulation of boosting.
  
The experiments on 2 dimensional toy data illustrate that the proposed procedure works in principle and that the boosting formulation produces better results than individual weak learners and better results than e.g. bagging. But the experiments on MNIST are less convincing: Without an undisputable measure like e.g. log-likelihood it is hard to draw conclusions from the samples in Figure 2; and visually they look weak compared to even simple models like e.g. NADE.

I think the paper could be improved significantly by adding a quantitative analysis: investigating the effect of combining undirected (e.g. RBM), undirected (e.g. VAE) and autoregressive (e.g. NADE) models and by measuring the improvement over the number of base learners. But this would require a method to estimate the partition function Z or estimating some proxy.

The paper proposes two approaches to boosting generative models, both based on likelihood ratio estimates. The approaches are evaluated on synthetic data, as well as on MNIST dataset for the tasks of generating samples and semi-supervised learning.
While the idea of boosting generative models and the proposed methods are interesting, the reviewer finds the experiments unconvincing for the following reasons.
1. The bagging baseline in section 3.1 seems to be just refitting a model to the same dataset, raising the probability to power alpha, and renormalizing. This makes it more peaked, but it's not clear why this is a good baseline. Please let me know if I misunderstood the procedure.
2. The sample generation experiment in section 3.2 uses a very slowly converging Markov chain, as can be seen in the similarity of plots c and f, d and g, e and h. It seems unlikely therefore that the resulting samples are from the stationary distribution. A qualitative evaluation using AIS seems to be necessary here.
3. In the same section the choices for alphas seem quite arbitrary - what happens when a more obvious choice of alpha_i=1 for all i is made?
4. It seems hard to infer anything from the semisupervised classification results reported: the baseline RBM seems to perform as well as the boosted models.

The work is mostly clearly written and (as far as the reviewer knows) original.

Please see $d$ and $z$ in the L-Boltzmann machine for example. 3- The paper could be improved by adding an ablation study of the different proposed methods. For example, in the paper “A Practical Defense of Adversarial Examples against Proposed Methods”, it is shown that using a perceptual loss greatly decreases the success of generated adversarial examples. It would be interesting to include this in the proposed model and check how it affects the success of the attack. In summary, it is an excellent paper, showing a nice combination of ideas and clear writing. tal Thanks for the feedback, we really appreciate it! We have added the references to your suggestions. Reference: @DBLP:journals/corr/KMYTH18 @DBLP:journals/corr/abs-1907-09134 Related Work There is some prior work on black-box attack for GANs, however, it requires interaction with the model (i.e. asking the model to produce images for query samples). It is not applicable to semi-supervised attack setting. There is a recent paper [1] that attempts to solve the problem in the white-box setting for black-box attack. They proposed to use distillable uniqueness property of trained models, which requires model to be trained on GANLoss. The authors also provided a promising solution for semi-supervised attack. However, the code implementation seems not publicly available, which greatly limits the applicability of the work. Recently, two novel metric-based methods that provably solve the gradient reversal attack in white-box setting have been proposed [2, 3]. Both of them use smooth NDA and patch-based distances. One of the advantages of these methods is that they do not require access to the model to train the advisor, thus making it applicable to black-box attack. However, all these methods only works for GANs with real-valued generator. It has not be extended to GANs with generative models such as VAEs and GQ. In this paper, we solve the gradient reversal attack for white-box attack in both black-box GANs with real-valued generator and GANs with generative models such as VAEs and GQ. We proposed a novel hyper-parameter $k$ that can significantly accelerate the training of the auxiliary model and make it applicable to real-world datasets. We also provide a novel method to generate adversarial examples using pre-trained generative models. These two improvements make our method work in a more efficient and easier to use way, which is very attractive in real-world security assessment applications. The paper: @DBLP:journals/corr/abs-1907-09134 Adversarial Examples for Generative Models Guangyu Zhang, Deng Cai, Shuicheng Yan, Kaiyu Yang, Shiqian Dong In this paper, we consider the problem of constructing adversarial examples against generative models. We first present the definition of adversarial examples for generative models. Then, we analyze the robustness of GANs against both white-box and black-box attacks. We propose a practical defense strategy, dubbed Monte Carlo Adversarial Example (MACE), to protect against the proposed black-box attack. MACE only involves a small extra computation in the adversarial training stage and can significantly enhance the robustness of the model. To conduct the attack, we propose a novel optimization method to solve the reverse attack problem. The empirical results show that our method could generate effective adversarial examples against state-of-the-art generative models. For the security assessment of generative models, adversarial examples have been successfully used to fool existing detection methods [4, 5]. It has been shown that adversarial examples also exist for GANs [6, 7]. Although the design of attack methods and defense methods have been done in the last few years [8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14], there are still some major challenges for the application of adversarial examples to GANs, including 1. How to construct effective adversarial examples against GANs? 2. How to efficiently find an effective defense method without impacting the generation quality?

In this paper, the authors presented a method to generate adversarial examples for neural networks. The authors proposed to use two networks - a generator and a discriminator. The generator is trained to generate samples which look like normal images, but are easily recognized as fake by the discriminator. At the same time, the discriminator needs to not be able to distinguish between real and generated samples. The authors demonstrated this method on GANs trained on image datasets, but it can be easily applied to other models (e.g. LSTM, RCNN). The proposed method has some limitations: the quality of generated samples depends on the quality of the pre-trained discriminator, and it requires large amount of computations. The paper is well-written, and it addresses an important problem in deep learning - generation of adversarial examples. I recommend this paper for publication in the following reasons: 1. The authors provide extensive background on previous related work (Pang, Ge, Deqing, et al., 2016; Bhagoesh, Anderson, Brown, Lim, & Jernberg, 2017; Carlini & Wagner, 2015; Goodfellow, Bengio, & Paperno, 2016) 2. The authors discuss limitations of previous approaches and propose new way to generate adversarial examples. 3. The paper is well-written and clear; the authors are easy to understand. However, I have some concerns regarding the applicability of the approach to some tasks and models. The authors mentioned that the method can be applied to other GANs, but I am not sure if the method would work for other models such as LSTM or RCNN. I leave this question for the authors to think about and consider in future works. Another concern is about the applicability of the approach to some applications. The authors mentioned that the method can be applied to imitate real samples. In some cases, it might be difficult to use the approach for images. Some images might contain complex patterns which cannot be easily covered by simple image transformation (e.g. brightening or blurring of an image). For these images, the authors might need to look for another approach (e.g. data augmentation).

Overall this is a well-written paper. The topics covered are important for researchers working on adversarial example attacks against deep generative models and the novelty of the paper is acknowledged by referencing a number of previous work. My suggestion is to include a few more inline references. Additionally, in some parts the writing could be clarified to make the concepts clearer. Here are some examples of how to improve the clarity of the text. • In the first section, it could be explained a bit more about what a variational autoencoder (VAE) is and why it is a useful generative model to attack. In particular, the motivation for the attacker executing these attacks could be explained in a bit more depth. • In the conclusion, the authors could explain a bit more about whether their attack types have been demonstrated to be transferable between models or if they are specific to the models they were tested on. MYJOURNAL_URL Please let me know if any code or other dependent resources are used in the paper. TWiki - Section 2.2, a description of the VAE could be added here. - Section 5, it could be explained more about what a VAE-GAN is and why it is useful to attack. - The conclusion could explain a bit more about whether the attack types are transferable between models or specific to the models they were tested on.

This paper explores adversarial examples for generative models. It presents three classes of attacks: classification-based, reconstruction-based and gradient-based. Adversarial examples for generative models addresses a problem that generative models are vulnerable to, and thus is a strong paper. The method presented to generate adversarial examples is interesting, and the application of adversarial examples to generative models is novel. This paper is well-motivated and clearly written. The conclusions are well justified based on the provided evidence. I strongly recommend this paper for publication. History & related work Generative models have recently become popular due to their ability to model input data distributions and generate realistic examples from those distributions. Deep learning architectures are generally robust to small and visually close but semantically reasonable perturbations to input examples. Adversarial examples demonstrate how small, visually simple changes to an input example can fool a machine learning (ML) model. These attacks raise serious concerns for models trained on small datasets or on illegal user data. In order to train a robust model, it is important to understand the vulnerabilities of the model and understand how an adversary might craft an attack. Attacks on generative models have primarily focused on input examples that are visually similar but syntactically different, such as changed alphabets (B vaccine vs. BBandAIDS), digits (7 vs. 7.15) and characters (Attack! vs. Attack!). Recent work has extended traditional adversarial examples to attacks on generative models, in which the adversary craft adversarial examples that are visually similar to the original but semantically different. Problem addressed This paper explores adversarial examples for generative models. Solution The method presented to generate adversarial examples is interesting. The application of adversarial examples to generative models is novel. Adversarial examples for generative models address a problem that generative models are vulnerable to, and thus is a strong paper. Different from prior work Prior work on generative adversarial networks (GANs) has focused on producing visually realistic images that are highly similar to the original image, but are incorrect according to some predefined classification scheme. Examples generated by these prior attacks are visually similar to the original, but they are incorrect with respect to the class label. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) have recently become popular due to their ability to model input data distributions and generate realistic examples from those distributions. This work explores the opposite phenomenon: an example is visually independent but semantically similar to the original. Attack types This paper presents three types of attack: classification-based, reconstruction-based and gradient-based. Classification-based adversarial example attack The adversary first uses a classifier to generate a category label for the original input image. Then a label for an altered version of the input image is generated. Finally, the altered version is visually similar to the original but with different label. This approach was first proposed for image classification, where an ImageNet-trained model can be used to infer the semantic label for an input image. The adversary can generate adversarial examples by maximizing the classification confidence of the target class, while at the same time minimizing the classification confidence of all other classes. For example, an image of a “cat” can be misclassified as “dog” by changing a few pixels, even though the images are visually different. Replacement attack The adversary generates an altered version of the original input image by minimizing the reconstruction loss between the original and altered image. Gradient-based adversarial example attack This approach directly optimizes against differences in source and target latent representations. This attack is more powerful than the previously proposed classification-based attack. Applications and impact This paper demonstrates that adversarial examples for generative models can be used to attack real-world systems and gain an unfair advantage in competitions. Why might an attacker want to attack a generative model? This paper demonstrates that adversarial examples for generative models can be used to attack real-world systems and gain an unfair advantage in competitions. There are two key differences between generative models and the traditional learning model. First, generative models can generate samples from the training dataset, and can therefore provide an attacker with an exact copy of the data. Second, the attacker does not need to find a solution that minimizes some error metric between the training data and the generated example. Instead, the attacker can directly manipulate the generated example until it meets his requirement, e.g., changing the gender of the face in the portrait to black and white. The impact of this work This paper demonstrates that adversarial examples for generative models can be used to attack real-world systems and gain an unfair advantage in competitions. This work provides a concrete way to evaluate generative models, similar to current approaches for evaluating CNN models. In the future, generative models may be fooled by carefully crafted adversarial examples. Since

After the rebuttal:

The paper contains an interesting set of results (mainly produced after the initial submission), but novelty is limited, and presentation is suboptimal. 

For me now the biggest problem now is that the title and the content do not correspond. The authors clearly attack deterministic encoder-decoder models (as described in 3.2), which are not at all the same as generative models, even though many generative models make use of this architecture. ------
Initial review:

The paper describes three approaches to generating adversarial examples for deep encoder-decoder generative networks (trained as VAE or VAE-GAN), and shows a comparative analysis of these. While the phenomenon of adversarial examples in discriminative models is widely known and relatively well studied, I am not aware of previous work on adversarial examples for generative networks, so this work is novel (there is a concurrent work by Tabacof et al. which should be cited, though).  The paper has significantly improved since the initial submission; still, I have a number of remarks on presentation and experimental evaluation. I am in the borderline mode, and may change my rating during the discussion phase.

Detailed comments:

1) The paper is 13 pages long - significantly over the recommended page limit of 8 pages. Reviewers have to read multiple papers, multiple versions of each, it is a lot of work. Large portions of the paper should be shortened and/or moved to the appendix. It is job of the authors to make the paper concise and readable. "in our attempts to be thorough, we have had a hard time keeping the length down" is a bad excuse - it may be hard, but has to be done.

2) I intentionally avoided term "generative model" above because it is not obvious to me if the attacks described by the authors indeed attack generative models. To clarify, the authors train encoder-decoders as generative models (VAE or VAE-GAN), but then remove all stochasticity (sampling) and prior on the latent variables: that is, they treat the models as deterministic encoders-decoders. It is not a big surprise that a deterministic deep network can be easily tricked; it would be much more interesting to see if the probabilistic aspect of generative models makes them more robust to such attacks. Am I missing something? I would like the authors to clarify their view on this and adjust the claims in the paper if necessary.

3) The paper is motivated by possible attacks on a data channel which uses a generative network for compressing information. Description of the attack scenario in 3.1 does not look convincing to me. It takes a huge amount of space and I do not think it adds much to the paper. First, experiments on natural images are necessary to judge if the proposed attack could succeed in a realistic scenario and second, I am not aware of any existing practical applications of VAEs to image compression: attacking JPEG would be much more practical. 

4) Experiments are limited to MNIST and, in the latest version, SVHN (which is very nice). While no good generative models of general natural images exist, it is common to evaluate generative models on datasets of faces, so this would be another very natural domain for testing the proposed approach. 

Smaller remarks:
1) Usage of "Oracle" in 3.2 does not look appropriate - oracle typically has access to (part of) ground truth, which is not the case here as far as I understand.
2) Beginning of section 4: "All three methods work for any generative architecture that relies on a learned latent representation z" - "are technically applicable to" would be more correct than "work for". 
3) 4.1: "confidentally"

The main idea in this paper is interesting, of considering various forms of adversarial examples in generative models. The paper has been considerably revised since the original submission. The results showing the susceptibility of generative models to attacks are interesting, but the demonstrations need to be more solid and on other datasets to be convincing.

Comments: 

"This contrasts to adversarial attacks on classifiers, where any inspection of the inputs will reveal the original bytes the adversary supplied,
which often have telltale noise"

Is this really true?  If it were the case, wouldn't it imply that training "against" adversarial examples should easily make a classifier robust to adversarial examples (if they all have a telltale noise)?  

Pros: 
  -The question of whether adversarial examples exist in generative models, and indeed how the definition of "adversarial example" carries over is an interesting one.  
  -Finding that a certain type of generative model *doesn't have* adversarial examples would be a really significant result, finding that generative models have adversarial examples would also be a worth negative result.  
  -The adversarial examples in figures 5 and 6 seem convincing, though they seem much more overt and noisy than the adversarial examples on MNIST shown in (Szegedy 2014).  Is this because it's actually harder to find adversarial examples in these types of generative models?  

Issues: 
  -Paper is significantly over length at 13 pages.  
  -The beginning of the paper should more clearly motivate its purpose.  
  -Paper has "generative models" in the title but as far as I can tell the whole paper is concerned with autoencoder-type models.  This is kind of annoying because if someone wanted to consider adversarial attacks on, say, autoregressive models, they might be unreasonably burdened by having to explain how they're distinct from a paper called "adversarial examples for generative models".  
   -I think that the introduction contains too much background information - it could be tightened.

This paper considers different methods of producing adversarial examples for generative models such as VAE and VAEGAN. Specifically, three methods are considered: classification-based adversaries which uses a classifier on top of the hidden code, VAE loss which directly uses the VAE loss and the "latent attack" which finds adversarial perturbation in the input so as to match the latent representation of a target input.

I think the problem that this paper considers is potentially useful and interesting to the community. To the best of my knowledge this is the first paper that considers adversarial examples for generative models. As I pointed out in my pre-review comments, there is also a concurrent work of "Adversarial Images for Variational Autoencoders" that essentially proposes the same "latent attack" idea of this paper with both L2 distance and KL divergence.

Novelty/originality: I didn't find the ideas of this paper very original. All the proposed three attacks are well-known and standard methods that here are applied to a new problem and this paper does not develop *novel* algorithms for attacking specifically *generative models*. However I still find it interesting to see how these standard methods compare in this new problem domain.

The clarity and presentation of the paper is very unsatisfying. The first version of the paper proposes the "classification-based adversaries" and reports only negative results. In the second set of revisions, the core idea of the paper changes and almost an entirely new paper with a new co-author is submitted and the idea of "latent attack" is proposed which works much better than the "classification-based adversaries". However, the authors try to keep around the materials of the first version, which results in a 13 page long paper, with different claims and unrelated set of experiments. "in our attempts to be thorough, we have had a hard time keeping the length down" is not a valid excuse.

In short, the paper is investigating an interesting problem and apply and compare standard adversarial methods to this domain, but the novelty and the presentation of the paper is limited.

For me now the biggest problem now is that the title and the content do not correspond. The authors clearly attack deterministic encoder-decoder models (as described in 3.2), which are not at all the same as generative models, even though many generative models make use of this architecture. A small experiment with sampling is interesting, but does not change the overall focus of the paper. This inconsistency in not acceptable. The whole issue could be resolved for example by simply replacing "generative models" by "encoder-decoder networks" in the title. Then I would tend towards recommending acceptance.

2) I intentionally avoided term "generative model" above because it is not obvious to me if the attacks described by the authors indeed attack generative models. To clarify, the authors train encoder-decoders as generative models (VAE or VAE-GAN), but then remove all stochasticity (sampling) and prior on the latent variables: that is, they treat the models as deterministic encoders-decoders. It is not a big surprise that a deterministic deep network can be easily tricked; it would be much more interesting to see if the probabilistic aspect of generative models makes them more robust to such attacks. Am I missing something? I would like the authors to clarify their view on this and adjust the claims in the paper if necessary.

3) The paper is motivated by possible attacks on a data channel which uses a generative network for compressing information. Description of the attack scenario in 3.1 does not look convincing to me. It takes a huge amount of space and I do not think it adds much to the paper. First, experiments on natural images are necessary to judge if the proposed attack could succeed in a realistic scenario and second, I am not aware of any existing practical applications of VAEs to image compression: attacking JPEG would be much more practical.

While no good generative models of general natural images exist, it is common to evaluate generative models on datasets of faces, so this would be another very natural domain for testing the proposed approach.

The main idea in this paper is interesting, of considering various forms of adversarial examples in generative models. The paper has been considerably revised since the original submission. The results showing the susceptibility of generative models to attacks are interesting, but the demonstrations need to be more solid and on other datasets to be convincing.

Comments: 

"This contrasts to adversarial attacks on classifiers, where any inspection of the inputs will reveal the original bytes the adversary supplied,
which often have telltale noise"

Is this really true?  If it were the case, wouldn't it imply that training "against" adversarial examples should easily make a classifier robust to adversarial examples (if they all have a telltale noise)?  

Pros: 
  -The question of whether adversarial examples exist in generative models, and indeed how the definition of "adversarial example" carries over is an interesting one.  
  -Finding that a certain type of generative model *doesn't have* adversarial examples would be a really significant result, finding that generative models have adversarial examples would also be a worth negative result.  
  -The adversarial examples in figures 5 and 6 seem convincing, though they seem much more overt and noisy than the adversarial examples on MNIST shown in (Szegedy 2014).  Is this because it's actually harder to find adversarial examples in these types of generative models?  

Issues: 
  -Paper is significantly over length at 13 pages.  
  -The beginning of the paper should more clearly motivate its purpose.  
  -Paper has "generative models" in the title but as far as I can tell the whole paper is concerned with autoencoder-type models.  This is kind of annoying because if someone wanted to consider adversarial attacks on, say, autoregressive models, they might be unreasonably burdened by having to explain how they're distinct from a paper called "adversarial examples for generative models".  
   -I think that the introduction contains too much background information - it could be tightened.

This paper considers different methods of producing adversarial examples for generative models such as VAE and VAEGAN. Specifically, three methods are considered: classification-based adversaries which uses a classifier on top of the hidden code, VAE loss which directly uses the VAE loss and the "latent attack" which finds adversarial perturbation in the input so as to match the latent representation of a target input.

I think the problem that this paper considers is potentially useful and interesting to the community. To the best of my knowledge this is the first paper that considers adversarial examples for generative models. As I pointed out in my pre-review comments, there is also a concurrent work of "Adversarial Images for Variational Autoencoders" that essentially proposes the same "latent attack" idea of this paper with both L2 distance and KL divergence.

Novelty/originality: I didn't find the ideas of this paper very original. All the proposed three attacks are well-known and standard methods that here are applied to a new problem and this paper does not develop *novel* algorithms for attacking specifically *generative models*. However I still find it interesting to see how these standard methods compare in this new problem domain.

The clarity and presentation of the paper is very unsatisfying. The first version of the paper proposes the "classification-based adversaries" and reports only negative results. In the second set of revisions, the core idea of the paper changes and almost an entirely new paper with a new co-author is submitted and the idea of "latent attack" is proposed which works much better than the "classification-based adversaries". However, the authors try to keep around the materials of the first version, which results in a 13 page long paper, with different claims and unrelated set of experiments. "in our attempts to be thorough, we have had a hard time keeping the length down" is not a valid excuse.

In short, the paper is investigating an interesting problem and apply and compare standard adversarial methods to this domain, but the novelty and the presentation of the paper is limited.

The paper contains an interesting set of results (mainly produced after the initial submission), but novelty is limited, and presentation is suboptimal. 

For me now the biggest problem now is that the title and the content do not correspond. A small experiment with sampling is interesting, but does not change the overall focus of the paper. This inconsistency in not acceptable. The whole issue could be resolved for example by simply replacing "generative models" by "encoder-decoder networks" in the title. Then I would tend towards recommending acceptance.

Miguel Towards Information-Seeking Agents We develop a general problem setting for training and testing the ability of agents to gather information efficiently. Specifically, we present a collection of tasks in which success requires searching through a partially-observed environment, for fragments of information which can be pieced together to accomplish various goals. We combine deep architectures with techniques from reinforcement learning to develop agents that solve our tasks. We shape the behavior of these agents by combining extrinsic and intrinsic rewards. We want to understand how agents learn to gather information actively and intelligently to reduce their uncertainty, and to exploit information they have already acquired. Information-seeking has many useful applications. For example, it can help people to understand how things work. It can also help people to find information that is not available in traditional sources such as books or online forums. An information seeker might examine the physical attributes of the desired object (e.g., the color, shape, and size of a Goapele) as well as the function of the object (e.g., is it a bell or a whistle?) to identify matching samples in an environment. Once an information seeker finds a sample that is similar to their target, they can examine it more closely to learn more about its functionality and how it differs from the desired object. This can allow them to understand how to use the object and whether or not it will fit in their desired environment. Our work focuses on the more general problem of how agents can train their ability to gather information efficiently. We present a collection of tasks in which success requires searching through a partially-observed environment, for fragments of information which can be pieced together to accomplish various goals. For example, an information seeker might be given a goal (such as “find a way into the island's defense system” or “locate the mole who sent this message”) and some hints about where useful information might be found. The hints might tell them that the information is hidden in a location in the environment or that it is imprinted in some objects or writing on walls, for example. The seeker must identify and explore regions of the environment in the search for useful information to help them accomplish their goal. They may also need to translate information written in an unfamiliar language or in an unintended writing system to find the information that is relevant to their goal. Our agent is represented as a deep neural network. The network is trained to perform the task of finding information to answer a given question, given a start location, a goal location, and hints regarding where the information might be found in the environment. The network's behavior is shaped by combining extrinsic and intrinsic rewards. Extrinsic rewards are provided by the trainer and are proportional to how close the answer given by the agent is to the correct answer. Intrinsic rewards are computed by the network and are based on the entropy of the network's accumulated distribution of answers. The intrinsic reward function is designed to guide the agent to learn the answer to the question only by observing the environment without being told what the answer is.
