The paper Taming the waves: sine as activation function in deep neural networks develops a method of using the sine function as an activation function in deep neural networks. This work is very well suited for use in deep neural networks, as it is differentiable, stable and sensitive to differentiators. The sine function is not expressed through a probability distribution, thus allowing the model to avoid shift invariance problems. The sine function, however, can become very small, which can result in numerical issues for long chains. The paper describes an effective method of addressing this problem of vanishing gradients, using a dual damping scheme. The strengths of this paper are that it develops a highly useful activation function, which is appropriate for use in deep learning, and presents effective and straightforward methods of addressing long chain vanishing gradients. The weakness of this work is that it is model specific, and cannot be applied generally to all models. Additionally, the paper only addresses the issue of long chain vanishing gradients, which is just one cause of problems in using the sine function as an activation function. The sine function is a periodic function with a period of 2 pi, and is thus not expressible through a probability distribution. This allows the model to avoid shift invariance problems, which can occur when using the logistic or tanh functions as activation functions. Additionally, the sine function can be difficult to evaluate numerically, as it can become very small. The dual damping scheme presented in this paper addresses both long chain vanishing gradients and the issue of the sine function becoming very small, by introducing two damping factors, alpha and beta, that decay over time. The damping factors are determined by the global step and local step, and ensure that the activation function never becomes too small or negative. The paper Taming the waves: sine as activation function in deep neural networks formalizes the study of the limitations of using sine function in deep neural networks. Although sine function has been used with success in specific scenarios, the generalizability of these successes remains largely unproven. In addition, the theoretical foundations on why these methods are difficult to train are not provided. Therefore, this paper deserves further study with wider application before this kind of studies is generally accepted. Nevertheless, the theoretical foundations do provide a clear hint for future possible improvements. First, the use of non-monotonic activation functions is the first and necessary step towards the use of non-convex functions, which can achieve better optimization results in general. Theoretically, the local minimum problems of traditional functions can be resolved by using functions that are not only non-monotonic, but also quasiconvex. Second, the analysis in the paper reveals that the use of infinitely many local minima in the case of simple problems. It is very likely that the introduction of a random component in the function will make it impossible to solve the problem using a fixed network. In this regard, deep neural networks themselves can be seen as a type of random function, and the excellent performance achieved in specific situations is indeed highly unexpected. These hypotheses need to be confirmed by further experimentation. Nevertheless, the main points from the paper are interesting and require further study. For example, the introduction of randomness into quasiconvex functions to make local minima impenetrable is certainly a good approach to be further explored. Furthermore, although this paper only reveals the local minimum problem in the case of simple problems, it is likely that the local maximum problem also requires infinitely many solutions to be solved. It is likely that more research will be needed to find more effective activation functions than the sine function that can be used in deep neural networks.

The main contributions of this paper are as follows: 1. It formally characterizes why neural networks with a sinusoidal activation function are hard to train even for simple examples. 2. It explains good performance achieved on a typical classification task by the fact that the presence of infinitely many shallow local minima emerges from the architecture. 3. It shows that for some network architectures the presence of periodic cycles is ignored when the training is successful, and the learned functions only care about the long-term behaviors, which are not affected by the Sinusoidal activation functions. The reviewer strongly recommends avoiding this paper for publication due to the extremely narrow applicability of its main results, which are only valid for extremely simple scenarios. In particular, the paper shows that the bad training behavior for neural networks with sinusoidal activation functions can be linked to the infinitely many local minima, but the proofs also require extremely strong assumptions, such as infinitely many local minima and non-constant depth of the local minimum; Furthermore, none of the special structures employed in this paper are widely used in real-world applications. For example, the reviewer notes that while the CIFAR10 dataset is used in the paper, it is clear from looking at the CIFAR10 dataset that this is not a classification task that would be particularly difficult for a neural network with a sinusoidal activation function (the issue is not even raised in the paper, and it would be completely discarded by the good performance achieved on this dataset!). So the reviewer strongly recommends against publication of this paper in its present form. On the positive side, the reviewer appreciates the clear descriptions of the main results and the comparison of them to related work. In addition, the reviewer takes merit in the attempts to generalize the results to other scenarios, including CIFAR-10, using extremely strong assumptions (in particular infinitely many local minima). So the reviewer recommends minor revisions to the paper, for example by toning down the extremely strong assumptions, to make the results more broadly applicable, say, by removing the assumption of infinitely many local minima or the requirement of non-constant depth of local minimum. Overall the reviewer strongly recommends against the publication of this paper in its present form, because of its extremely limited applicability.

Thank you to all the reviewers for the helpful comments. Probably due to a lack of clarity of the paper, some details in the proposed summaries differ from the main points we tried to convey. Let us then attempt to clarify what the point of the paper is supposed to be, both here and in the manuscript.

The main point of the paper is to analyze the effect of sine as an activation function, how it affects the representation learned and what consequences it has on learning. 

The main contributions of the paper are:
O1 - a proof that confirms the claim that networks with sine might easily get stuck into local minima, obtained by analytically characterizing the loss surface.
O2 - evidence showing that when training is successful for typical datasets (as it's the case for most previous works using sine presented in Section 2) the network is actually not relying on the periodicity of the function. The network relies almost exclusively on the central part of the function, that is monotonic and similar to a tanh. Evidence for this is presented on MNIST and in the new version on Reuters too.
O3 - there might still be room for sine as activation function in certain artificial/algorithmic tasks where sine is intuitively beneficial, since there are at least two simple tasks (i.e. sum and diff) where sin can outperform a standard RNN baseline using tanh.

We are trying to make these points more clear and explicit in the paper.

Summary:
In this paper, the authors explore the advantages/disadvantages of using a sin activation function.
They first demonstrate that even with simple tasks, using sin activations can result in complex to optimize loss functions.
They then compare networks trained with different activations on the MNIST dataset, and discover that the periodicity of the sin activation is not necessary for learning the task well.
They then try different algorithmic tasks, where the periodicity of the functions is helpful.

Pros:
The closed form derivations of the loss surface were interesting to see, and the clarity of tone on the advantages *and* disadvantages was educational.

Cons: 
Seems like more of a preliminary investigation of the potential benefits of sin, and more evidence (to support or in contrary) is needed to conclude anything significant -- the results on MNIST seem to indicate truncated sin is just as good, and while it is interesting that tanh maybe uses more of the saturated part, the two seem relatively interchangeable. The toy algorithmic tasks are hard to conclude something concrete from.

Authors propose using periodic activation functions (sin) instead of tanh for gradient descent training of neural networks.
This change goes against common sense and there would need to be strong evidence to show that it's a good idea in practice. 
The experiments show slight improvement (98.0 -> 98.1) for some MNIST configurations. They show strong improvement (almost 100% higher accuracy after 1500 iterations) on a toy algorithmic task. It's not clear that this activation function is good for a broad class of algorithmic tasks or just for the two they present. Hence evidence shown is insufficient to be convincing that this is a good idea for practical tasks.

machine_text: This paper presents a model that uses data graph to improve the generalization of CNN. The main idea is to capture the high level semantics from the training data and include it in the model. This approach helps the model to see the global patterns in the data. The model proposed in this paper is generic and can be used on any model that contains layers. For model implementation, the paper uses CNN for digit recognition task. The model trained on the small dataset performs badly on the test set with unseen digits. The paper then introduces the data graph that captures the relationships between the images in the training data. This helps the model to learn better and generalizes better on the test data. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) have been a standard tool for image processing for several years now, with its success largely attributed to the efficacy of the convolution operation that uses the geometric properties of a low dimensional grid structure to efficiently compute high-level features. This research suggests a generalization of CNNs to a higher-level concept of data that not only utilizes an image's spatial relationships but also its graph-like connectivity. The authors propose a convolution framework that shares weights on all features, providing parameter efficiency while also allowing for much more flexible models (and thus harder to understand). They apply this framework to traditional image data (on the MNIST data set) as well as a molecular activity data set, and in doing so challenge the state-of-the-art on that dataset. The major contribution of this paper is the development of a new model and method for computer vision tasks using graph-based convolutions. The proposed method has the following benefits: - parameter efficiency: the model uses multi-layer perceptrons (MLP) with shared weights for all nodes in a layer, which allows the same computation to be performed on many graph edges simultaneously; - flexible model: the model allows arbitrary connectivity between nodes, beyond the limitations of regular grids used in convolution; - interpretable model: the computation in each layer is explicit, making it easier to analyze how the computations relate to the derived features. The major drawback of this work is that it is an initial foray into using graph convolutions and that there are many aspects that can be explored to improve the model and application. This includes using a more sophisticated method for learning the graph structure, e.g. using a graph neural network as an alternative to the straightforward method of performing a random walk. Also, the training is done onMNIST data, which is only small and relatively easy to evaluate on, so it's hard to know how the model will perform on more realistic data sets. human_text:
This work proposes a convolutional architecture for any graph-like input data (where the structure is example-dependent), or more generally, any data where the input dimensions that are related by a similarity matrix. If instead each input example is associated with a transition matrix, then a random walk algorithm is used generate a similarity matrix.

Developing convolutional or recurrent architectures for graph-like data is an important problem because we would like to develop neural networks that can handle inputs such as molecule structures or social networks. However, I don't think this work contributes anything significant to the work that has already been done in this area. 

The two main proposals I see in this paper are:
1) For data associated with a transition matrix, this paper proposes that the transition matrix be converted to a similarity matrix. This seems obvious.
2) For data associated with a similarity matrix, the k nearest neighbors of each node are computed and supply the context information for that node. This also seems obvious.

Perhaps I have misunderstood the contribution, but the presentation also lacks clarity, and I cannot recommend this paper for publication. 

Specific Comments:
1) On page 4: "An interesting attribute of this convolution, as compared to other convolutions on graphs is that, it preserves locality while still being applicable over different graphs with different structures."  This is false; the other proposed architectures can be applied to inputs with different structures (e.g. Duvenaud et. al., Lusci et. al. for NN architectures on molecules specifically).

This work studies the problem of generalizing a convolutional neural network to data lacking grid-structure. 
 
 The authors consider the Random Walk Normalized Laplacian and its finite powers to define a convolutional layer in a general graph. Experiments in Merck molecular discovery and mnist are reported. 
 
 The reviewers all agreed that this paper, while presenting an interesting and important problem, lacks novelty relative to existing approaches. In particular, the AC would like to point out that important references seem to be missing from the current version. 
 
 The proposed approach is closely related to 'Convolutional neural networks on graphs with fast localized spectral filtering', Defferrand et al. NIPS'16 , which considers Chevyshev polynomials of the Laplacian and learns the polynomial coefficients in an efficient manner. Since the Laplacian and the Random Walk Normalized Laplacian are similar operators (have same eigenvectors), the resulting model is essentially equivalent. Another related model that precedes all the cited works and is deeply related to the current submission is the Graph Neural Network from Scarselli et al.; see 'Geometric Deep Learning: going beyond Euclidean Data', Bronstein et al,

Previous literature uses data-derived adjacency matrix A to obtain neighbors to use as foundation of graph convolution. They propose extending the set of neighbors by additionally including nodes reachable by i<=k steps in this graph. This introduces an extra tunable parameter k, so it needs some justification over the previous k=1 solution. In one experiment provided (Merk), using k=1 worked better. They don't specify which k that used, just that it was big enough for their to be p=5 nodes obtained as neighbors. In the second experiment (MNIST), they used k=1 for their experiments, which is what previous work (Coats & Ng 2011) proposed as well. A compelling experiment would compare to k=1 and show that using k>1 gives improvement strong enough to justify an extra hyper-parameter.

Update: I thank the authors for their comments! After reading them, I decided to increase the rating.

This paper proposes a variant of the convolution operation suitable for a broad class of graph structures. For each node in the graph, a set of neighbours is devised by means of random walk (the neighbours are ordered by the expected number of visits). As a result, the graph is transformed into a feature matrix resembling MATLAB’s/Caffe’s im2col output. The convolution itself becomes a matrix multiplication. 

Although the proposed convolution variant seems reasonable, I’m not convinced by the empirical evaluation. The MNIST experiment looks especially suspicious. I don’t think that this dataset is appropriate for the demonstration purposes in this case. In order to make their method applicable to the data, the authors remove important structural information (relative locations of pixels) thus artificially increasing the difficulty of the task. At the same time, they are comparing their approach with regular CNNs and conclude that the former performs poorly (and does not even reach an acceptable accuracy for the particular dataset).

I guess, to justify the presence of MNIST (or similar datasets) in the experimental section, the authors should modify their method to incorporate additional graph structure (e.g. relative locations of nodes) in cases when the relation between nodes cannot be fully described by a similarity matrix.

I believe, in its current form, the paper is not yet ready for publication but may be later resubmitted to a workshop or another conference after the concern above is addressed.

This paper evaluates the robustness of defensive methods against multiple adversary models. The main contribution of this paper is that the adversarial retraining framework can defend most of the adversarial examples notably and consistently without adding additional vulnerabilities or performance penalty to the original model. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we provide related work. In Section 3, we describe the experiments. In Section 4, we present the evaluation results. We conclude in Section 5. Related Work ============ Adversarial Examples -------------------- Adversarial examples [@66804] are inputs purposely crafted to violate the strict requirements of a system. They were originally thought of as an effective countermeasure for machine learning (ML) systems, because they force the system to make incorrect decisions. Many recent studies have shown that many modern ML models are quite fragile against adversarial examples. For example, the large perturbation method is used to generate robust adversarial examples of imagenet classification models. Such robust adversarial examples can not be distinguished from original examples by the models with high confidence. Madry et al. [@madry2018towards] give a survey of the most relevant recent advances in crafting adversarial examples. In recent years, many adversarial attack algorithms have been proposed. Goodfellow et al. [@Goodfellow2015] proposed the fast facial aging (FGSM), which simply amplifies the smallest perceptible differences between the image and the target. Carlini and Wagner [@carlini2017towards] proposed the basic iterative method (BIM), known as one of the most efficient and flexible attacks. Ahn et al. [@Ahn2018CleverHunt] presented the first large-scale white-box adversarial attack on transfer learning, exploiting knowledge of both the source and the target domains. Malicious Insights -------------------- A malicious model is a model intentionally designed to behave poorly (violating business needs) or break all rules (security regulations). Breach of predictions or decisions may be the only signs of a malicious model. Malicious models can also cause more subtle problems that are more difficult to detect. For example, they might affect the output quality of the model, increase operating costs, or even cause legal liability. More and more malicious models emerge every day. Large tech companies have recently suffered from this problem, such as Waymo, a Google subsidiary, having their fleet of driverless vehicles attacked by maliciously modified android models. It is also an increasingly common phenomenon that traditional security products cannot detect all malicious models. Evaluation of Defensive Methods -------------------------------- Since the emergence of adversarial attack methods, many works have been done to propose effective defensive methods. He et al. [@he2016deep] proposed a straightforward approach usingDropout to improve the robustness of DNNs. In another work, Madry et al. [@Madry2017] showed that deep learning models were vulnerable to adversarial perturbations that were protected by robust optimization, which guaranteed accurate predictions for a large range of adversarial attacks. Gao et al. [@gao2019towards] applied several additional loss functions into DNNs to enhance the robustness. Among these methods, adversarial retraining is simple and easy to implement, which has achieved good results. Meng et al. [@meng2020network] showed that using a simple gradient-based algorithm with a small number of forward and backward passes could improve the robustness of DNNs. DeepXplain [@deepxplain] is a more flexible approach, using a generative model that can be retrained in a self-supervised fashion on uncorrupted versions of the input data. Li et al. [@li2020extending] and Zheng et al. [@zheng2020deep] both proposed adding adversarial examples into the training set as a part of the normal data to improve the robustness. Evaluation of Defensive Strategies ----------------------------------- Xiong et al. [@xiong2019double] adopted double- Deep neural network (DDN) to achieve robustness to multi-scale and obfuscated adversarial examples. Ge et al. [@ge2020revoke] used multiple reconstruction networks to detect and discard anomalous instances. On the other hand, B-model [@brown2019adversarial] proposed an adversarial retraining framework, which trained a model to predict the original label from the perturbed version of it. Their approach did not directly use the adversarial examples to defend the actual model, but instead generated adversarial examples to retune the adversarially trained model. --------------------------- -------------------------------------------------------------- Attack Model Basic Iterative Method (BIM) Defensive Method Adversarial Retraining Evaluation Metrics Retrain on Adversarial examples Adversary Model FGSM Attack Runtime (days) 11.5 White-box Attack Success 43%

I reviewed the manuscript as of December 6th.

The authors perform a systematic investigation of various retraining methods for making a classification network robust to adversarial examples. The authors achieve lower error rates using their RAD and IAEC methods perform better then previously introduced distillation methods for retraining networks to be robust to adversarial examples. This method suggests a promising direction for building a defense for adversarial examples.

Major Comments:
I find the paper to not be lacking in exposition and clarity. The paper has a laundry list of related results (page 2) but no clear message. I *think* one larger point is the superior performance of their retraining techniques but it is not clear how well these techniques perform compared to other retraining techniques, nor are the details of the retraining techniques clear. The paper requires more discussion and a clear exposition about the methods the authors introduced (i.e. RAD, IAEC). What follow are some more detailed comments along this theme of improving the exposition and clarity:

- The authors should provide more details about how they constructed the auto-encoder in the IAEC method (diagram?). The same needs to be said for the RAD method. The authors point to a previous workshop submission (

The paper investigates several retraining approached based upon adversarial data. While the experimental evaluation looks reasonable, the actual contribution of this paper is quite small. The approaches being evaluated, for the most part, are already proposed in the literature, with the one exception being the "improved autoencoder stacked with classifier" (IAEC), which is really just a minor modification to the existing AEC approach with an additional regularization term. The results are fairly thorough, and seem to suggest that the IAEC method performs best in some cases, but this is definitely not a novel enough contribution to warrant publication at ICLR.
 
 Pros:
 + Nice empirical evaluation of several adversarial retraining methods
 
 Cons:
 - Extremely minor algorithmic advances
 - Not clear what is the significant contribution of the paper

The main contribution of this paper is in extending causal discovery algorithms to account for the scenario where the underlying cause and effects are probabilistic, rather than deterministic. This is significant as current causal discovery algorithms rely on the independence of mechanisms assumption, which often does not hold in practice. The authors propose a new causal model that overcomes this limitation and demonstrate how to efficiently train and evaluate the model on both synthetic and real world data. yes and weaknesses The main limitation of this paper is that it only applies to problems that can be framed as a normal mean shift problem. This is because the algorithms developed by the authors rely on the implicit assumption that the underlying mechanism has a gaussian distribution, and so does not apply to problems such as video prediction or anomaly detection, where the underlying mechanism is more likely to be a max shift or an activation function. gain The paper is technically innovative in that it extends the traditional causal discovery algorithms to the probabilistic regime, where the underlying cause and effects are not deterministic, but probabilistic. The applicability of the algorithms is extended to problems that do not satisfy the independence of mechanisms assumption. win and strengths The main advantage of this paper is that it provides a scalable algorithm to train the model for probabilistic causal discovery. The algorithm is based on the implicit mean shift optimization framework, and can be extended to other probabilistic models as long as they can be framed as a normal mean shift problem. The model is also data-efficient as it uses several i.i.d. samples to approximate the conditional distribution of the effects given the causes.

The paper addresses the problem of causal relationship identification in electronic health records using deep neural networks. The main content of this paper includes using the causal regularizer to steer deep neural network architectures towards causally-interpretable solutions, and performing a large-scale analysis of electronic health records. We conducted a causal relationship between the given input and response variables using expert's judgment as the ground truth. We show that our causally-regularized algorithm outperforms its L1-regularized equivalence in both predictive performance as well as causal relevance. Finally, we show that the proposed causal regularizer can be used together with representation learning algorithms to yield up to 20% improvement in the causality score of the generated hypothesis. introduced an efficient method for solving the problem by using causal regularizer to steer deep neural network architectures towards causally-interpretable solutions. The main idea is that the deep network learns the most relevant factors by maximization of the log-probability, however, this could happen at the cost of disregarding the causal relationship between the input and response variables. To address this, we introduced the independence of mechanisms assumption and introduced the causal regularizer that constrained the outputs of the model independent of the inputs. We conducted a large-scale analysis of electronic health records, and showed that our causally-regularized algorithm outperformed its L1-regularized equivalent both in terms of predictive performance as well as causal relevance. We also showed that the proposed causal regularizer could be used together with representation learning algorithms to yield up to 20% improvement in the causality score of the generated hypotheses.
human_text:
The present submission discusses a "causal regularizer", which promotes the use of causal dependencies (X -> Y, where X is a feature of the learning problem, and Y is the target variable) in predictive models. Similarly, such causal regularizer penalizes the use of non-causal dependencies, which can arise due to reverse causation (Y -> X) or confounding (X <- Z -> Y, where Z is a hidden confounder).

+ Overall, this submission tackles one of the most important problems in machine learning, which is to build causal models. The paper discusses and addresses this issue effectively when applied to a dataset in heart disease. In their experiments, the authors correctly identify some of the common causes of heart disease by virtue of their causal regularizer.

- The authors do not discuss the robustness of their approach with respect to choice of hyper-parameters (both describing the neural network architecture and the generative model that synthesizes artificial causal data). This seems like a crucial issue, in particular when dealing with medical data.

- The conclusions of the experimental evaluation should be discussed in greater length. On the one hand, Figure 4.a shows that there are no differences between L1 and causal regularization in terms of predictive performance, but it is difficult to conclude if this result is statistically significant without access to error-bars. On the other hand, Table 3 describes the qualitative differences between L1 and causal regularization. However, this table is hard to read: How were the 30 rows selected? What does the red highlighting mean? Are these red rows some true causal features that were missed? If so, this is related to precision. What about recall? Did the causal regularization pick up many non-causal features as causal?

- Regarding causal classifiers, this paper should do a much better job at reviewing previous work. For instance, the paper "Towards a Learning Theory of Cause-Effect Inference" from Lopez-Paz et al. is missing from the references. However, this prior work studies many of the aspects that are hinted as novel in this submission. In particular, the prior work of Lopez-Paz 1) introduces the concept of Mother distribution (referred as Nature hyper-prior in this submission) which explicitly factorizes the distribution over causes and mechanisms, 2) circumvented intractable likelihoods by synthesizing and training on causal data, 3) tackled the confounding case (compare Figure 1 of this submission and Appendix C of Lopez-Paz), and 4) dealt with discrete data seamlessly (such as the ChaLearn data from Section 5.3 in Lopez-Paz).

On a positive note, this is a well-written paper that addresses the important, under-appreciated problem of incorporating causal reasoning into machine learning. On a negative note, the novelty of the technical contributions is modest and the qualitative evaluation of the results could be greatly extended. In short, I am leaning slightly towards acceptance.
The reviewers pointed out several issues with the paper, and all recommended rejection. The revision seems to not have been enough to change their minds.

We made a major revision to the paper.  Here is the summary of the main changes:

Experiments:
-- Providing **ground truth causality** evaluation (by hiring Robert Chen, a clinical expert). (Figure 1, Table 2) The results show a significant gain in causality discovery using the proposed method.
-- Including a new **publicly available dataset** (MIMIC III) to ensure reproducibility of the results. (Table 1 and Figure 4)
-- Adding standard deviation to the results.

Novel methodology:
-- Providing a neural network architecture that allows multivariate causal hypothesis generation, see Section 2.3 and Figure 2.b.
-- Providing the ground truth causality evaluation for the causal hypotheses generated by our algorithm. (Figure 5b)

Writeup:
-- Adding more discussion on the related works (Sections 2.1 and 2.2). 
---- In the introduction and Section 2.2 we clearly describe the novelty of this paper with respect to the papers listed by David Lopez-Paz and the reviewers.
-- Revising the background section 2.1 and making it both more accessible and more mathematically precise.
-- Adding new visualizations in Figure 2 and removing diagrams that didn’t help delivering the concepts.
-- Restructuring the methodology section. Now Section 2.2 only discusses the proposed causal regularizer and Section 2.3 describes its combination with neural networks.
-- Moving the experimental results on the causality detection (and other extra results) to Appendix A.1, to allow space for evaluation of the main results of the paper.
-- Finally, we revised the introduction accordingly.

This paper proposes to use a causality score to weight a sparsity regularizer.  In that way, selected variables trade off between being causal and discriminative.  The framework is primarily evaluated on a proprietary health dataset.  While the dataset does give a good motivation to the problem setting, the paper falls a bit short for ICLR due to the lack of additional controlled experiments, relatively straightforward methodology (given the approach of Chalupka et al., arXiv Preprint, 2016, which is a more interesting paper from a technical perspective), and paucity of theoretical motivation.

At the core of this paper, the approach is effectively to weight a sparsity regularizer so that "causal" variables (as determined by a separate objective) are more likely to be selected.  This is generally a good idea, but we do not get a proper validation of this from the experiments as ground truth is absent.  A theorem on identifiability of causal+discriminative variables from a data sample combined with adequate synthetic experiments would have probably been sufficient, for example, to push the paper towards accept from a technical perspective, but as it is, it is lacking in insight and reproducibility.

The authors extend their method of causal discovery (Chalupka et al 2016) to include assumptions about sparsity via regularization.  They apply this extension to an interesting private dataset from Sutter Health.  While an interesting direction, I found the presentation somewhat confused, the methodological novelty smaller than the bulk of ICLR works, and the central results (or perhaps data; see below) inadequate to address questions of causality.

First, I found the presentation somewhat unclear.  The paper at some points seems to be entirely focused on healthcare data, at other points it uses it as a motivating example, and at other points it is neglected.  Also, algorithm 1 seems unreferenced, and I'm not entirely sure why it is needed.  Figure 2 is not needed for this community.  The key methodological advance in this work appears in section 2.1 (Causal regularizer), but it is introduced amidst toy examples and without clear terminology or standard methodological assumptions/build-up.  In Section 3.1 (bottom of first paragraph), key data and results seem to be relegated to the appendices.  Thus overall the paper read rather haphazardly.  Finally, there seems to be an assumption throughout of fairly intimate familiarity with the Cholupka preprint, which i think should be avoided.  This paper should stand alone.

Second, while the technical contributions/novelty are not a focus of the paper's presentation, I am concerned by the lack of methodological advance.  Essentially a regularization objective is added to the previous method, which of itself is not a bad idea, but I can't point to a technical novelty in the paper that the community can not do without.

Third, fundamentally i don't see how the experiments address the central question of causality; they show regularization behaving as expected (or rather, influencing weights as expected), but I don't think we really have any meaningful quantitative evidence that causality has been learned.  This was briefly discussed (see "ground truth causality?" and the response below).  I appreciate the technical challenges/impossibility of having such a dataset, but if that's the case, then I think this work is premature, since there is no way to really validate.

Overall it's clearly a sincere effort, but I found it wanting in terms of a few critical areas.

Learning classifiers to distinguish between causal, anticausal, and confounded dependencies is not a novel idea. It was introduced in the competitions of Guyon [1,2], and later developed in the context of kernel machines [3,4], learning theory [4], and neural networks [5]. These classifiers were applied to discrete data [1,2,3,4,5,6], extend to multiple random variables [4 Appendix C, 6], generalize the additive noise model assumption [5,6], consider hidden confounding [1,2,4 Appendix C, 6], and make use of classifier soft-scores to measure predictive uncertainty [1,2,3,4,5,6].

The idea of causal regularization is not novel, either. It was proposed at least in [1 Page 181] and [2 Section 3]. Causal regularization is also at the heart of invariant prediction [7], and causal transfer [8,9].

None of these works are cited by this manuscript or by the companion manuscript (Chalupka et al., 2016). This omission undermines the novelty claims of the manuscript, and prevents the readers from easily seeing what the contribution is. The authors should therefore add a comprehensive discussion of the related works and a realistic discussion of the claimed novelty in this work.

This paper proposes to use a causality score to weight a sparsity regularizer.  In that way, selected variables trade off between being causal and discriminative.  The framework is primarily evaluated on a proprietary health dataset.  While the dataset does give a good motivation to the problem setting, the paper falls a bit short for ICLR due to the lack of additional controlled experiments, relatively straightforward methodology (given the approach of Chalupka et al., arXiv Preprint, 2016, which is a more interesting paper from a technical perspective), and paucity of theoretical motivation.

At the core of this paper, the approach is effectively to weight a sparsity regularizer so that "causal" variables (as determined by a separate objective) are more likely to be selected.  This is generally a good idea, but we do not get a proper validation of this from the experiments as ground truth is absent.  A theorem on identifiability of causal+discriminative variables from a data sample combined with adequate synthetic experiments would have probably been sufficient, for example, to push the paper towards accept from a technical perspective, but as it is, it is lacking in insight and reproducibility.

They apply this extension to an interesting private dataset from Sutter Health.  While an interesting direction, I found the presentation somewhat confused, the methodological novelty smaller than the bulk of ICLR works, and the central results (or perhaps data; see below) inadequate to address questions of causality.

machine_text: In this work, the L-SR1 method is proposed for training deep learning models. L-SR1 is an implementation of the SR1 optimization algorithm that has been modified to work for training neural networks. SR1 is an algorithm from the family of conditional gradient methods that has been shown to be able to find local minima for a variety of machine learning tasks. The work explores the use of second order information in the objective function in order to further improve the generalization capabilities of SR1. The proposed method is tested on multiple datasets and compared to other deep learning training methods. The results indicate that the proposed method outperforms other state of the art training methods in terms of generalization performance. author, date, and reference: [1] Huan Fang, Yuan Li, and Huiquan Wen, "L-SR1: A Second Order Optimization Method for Deep Learning," in IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems, vol. 35, no. 13, pp. 4647-4656, September 2018. challenge and motivation: Deep learning has shown state-of-the-art performance on a range of tasks including image classification, semantic segmentation, and domain adaptation. However, deep learning models have been shown to be vulnerable to adversarial examples, examples generated to look like normal inputs to the model but that trigger incorrect classification responses. This indicates that it is likely possible to generate examples that cause deep learning models to make incorrect decisions without these examples appearing to be particularly anomalous to a human observer. Additionally, it has been shown that even large networks have low capacity to capture all high-level and long-term relationships in the data, leading to the possibility that even state-of-the-art algorithms could be improved with better use of higher-order information. These two findings suggest that using local optimization techniques coupled with higher-order information might be a good approach to improving the generalization performance of deep learning models.

L-SR1: A Second Order Optimization Method for Deep Learning is a good and interesting paper. The paper presents an optimization method for training deep neural networks. The optimization method is an alternative to the popular Adam optimization method. The L-SR1 optimization method reformulates the optimization problem as a second order cone program (SOCP), and uses the Chubanov rotation method to solve the optimization problem. The paper presents the theoretical foundations of the optimization method. The theory of the method is correct. The paper also presents experiments using the optimization method to train several deep neural network architectures. The experiments are interesting. Here is my peer review for the paper of L-SR1: A Second Order Optimization Method for Deep Learning: The paper provides a practical second order method called L-SR1 for training deep neural networks. The major challenge in training deep neural networks is the optimization problem is non-convex and the local minimizers are not guaranteed to be global minimizers. A popular approach to addressing this issue is second order methods which have second order convergence in theory. Unfortunately, second order methods have not been successful in practice. Two reasons for this are saddle points and the condition of the hessian. L-SR1 overcomes both of these issues. First, it uses a momentum term to smoothly and quickly overcome saddle points. Second, it uses a contraction metric that avoids bad conditioning of the hessian. L-SR1 performs at least as well as Nesterov's Accelerated Gradient Descent on the MNIST and CIFAR10 dataset. L-SR1 is well suited for distributed training and gains competitive performance on CIFAR10 even on shallower networks like LeNet5 and even on deeper networks like residual networks. Finally, the experimental analysis of L-SR1 with respect to its hyper-parameters gains greater intuition for this method. This is worth pursuing as understanding these hyper-parameters is crucial to using this method in distributed training of deep networks. baytransparent Overall this is an interesting paper. It provides a practical second order method for training deep neural networks and shows that it performs at least as well as Nesterov's Accelerated Gradient Descent. The main drawback of L-SR1 is that it performs worse than Adam when used with GPUs.

L-SR1: A Second Order Optimization Method for Deep Learning describes a practical second order method that addresses the limitations of previous methods. The method, L-SR1, addresses two significant concerns when applying second order methods to training deep neural networks: 1) the presence of saddle points in the loss function, and 2) the condition of the Hessian. L-SR1 overcomes both of these concerns. In the case of saddle points, L-SR1 utilizes a diagonal Hessian update rather than a full factorization, allowing the method to scale to large datasets without sacrificing convergence. In the case of the condition of the Hessian, L-SR1 utilizes a complexity aware initialization scheme that preserves goodconditioning for distributed training on large datasets. We demonstrate the applicability of L-SR1 on two benchmark datasets, MNIST and CIFAR10. On the CIFAR10 dataset, we achieve competitive performance to Nesterov's Accelerated Gradient Descent. Furthermore, we provide experimental results showing that L-SR1 performs at least as well as Nesterov's Accelerated Gradient Descent on the MNIST dataset. mended version: L-SR1: A Second Order Optimization Method for Deep Learning explains a practical second order method that addresses the limitations of previous methods. The paper proposes an interesting approach, in that (unlike many second-order methods) SR1 updates can potentially take advantage of negative curvature in the Hessian. However, all reviewers had some significant concerns about the utility of the method. In particular, reviewers were concerned that the method does not show a significant gain over the Adam algorithm (which is simpler/cheaper and easier to implement). The public reviewer also points out that there are many existing quasi-Newton methods designed for DL, so it is up to the authors to compared to at least one of these. For these reasons I'm recommending rejection at this time.

The paper proposes a new second-order method L-SR1 to train deep neural networks. It is claimed that the method addresses two important optimization problems in this setting: poor conditioning of the Hessian and proliferation of saddle points. The method can be viewed as a concatenation of SR1 algorithm of Nocedal & Wright (2006) and limited-memory representations Byrd et al. (1994). First of all, I am missing a more formal, theoretical argument in this work (in general providing more intuition would be helpful too), which instead is provided in the works of Dauphin (2014) or Martens. The experimental section in not very convincing considering that the performance in terms of the wall-clock time is not reported and the advantage over some competitor methods is not very strong even in terms of epochs. I understand that the authors are optimizing their implementation still, but the question is: considering the experiments are not convincing, why would anybody bother to implement L-SR1 to train their deep models? The work is not ready to be published.

In this paper, the authors use adversarial imagination prior to do image inversion. The inversion is performed by retrieving imaginations from memory repositories when given an image. The retrieve can be done using a network with image and exemplar memory as input. The retrieval result is an imagination whose graph can be fed to a graphics-like rendering network to get the image rendering results. The key part of the method is using adversarial imagination prior to drive the inversion. The inversion procedure does not require paired data, using just an image and the memory of different scenes. The paper describes a network architecture for inverse problems in computer vision. Example inverse problems considered are image inpainting, computing intrinsic image decomposition and foreground/background separation.
The architecture is composed of (i) a generator that produces target (latent) output (such as foreground / background regions), 
(ii) renderer that composes that latent output back to the image that can be compared with the input to measure reconstruction error, 
and (iii) adversarial prior that ensures the target output (latent) image respects a certain image statistics.

Strong  points.
- The proposed architecture with memory database is interesting and appears to be novel. 

Weak points:
- Experimental results are only proof-of-concept in toy set-ups and do not clearly demonstrate benefits of the proposed architecture.
- It is unclear whether the memory retrieval engine that retrieves images based on L2 distance on pixel values is going generalize to other more realistic scenarios. 
- Clarity. The clarity of explanation can be also improved (see below).


Detailed evaluation.

Originality:
- The novelty of this work lies in the (iii) adversarial prior that places an adversarial loss between the generated latent output and a single image retrieved from a large unlabelled database of target output examples (called memory). The adversarial prior has a convolutional form matching local image statistics, rather than the entire image.  The particular form of network architecture with the memory-based fully convolutional adversarial loss appears to be novel and potentially interesting.

- Motivation for the Architecture. The weakest point of the proposed architecture is the "Memory retrieval engine" R (section 2.4),
where images are retrieved from the memory by measuring L2 distance on pixel intensities. While this maybe ok for simple problems considered in this work, it is unclear how this can generalize to other more complicated datasets and problems.  
This should be better discussed, better justified and ideally results in some more realistic set-up shown (see below).


Quality:
- Experiments. Results are shown for inpainting of MNIST digits, intrinsic image decomposition on the MIT intrinsic image database, and figure/ground layer extraction on the synthesized dataset of 3D chairs rendered onto background from real photographs.  
 The experimental validation of the model is not very strong and proof-of-concept only. All the experiments are performed in simplified toy set-ups. The MNIST digit inpainting is far from current state-of-the-art on image inpainting in real photographs (see e.g. Pathak et al., 2016). The foreground background separation is done on  only synthetically generated test data. Even for intrinsic image demposition problem there is now relatively large-scale dataset of (Bell et al., 2014), see the citation below.  

While this is probably ok for the ICLR paper, it diminishes the significance of the work. Is this model going to be useful in a real settings? One possibility to address this would be to focus on one of the problems and show results on a challenging state-of-the-art data. It would be great to see the benefits of the memory database.

This paper proposes a model that generates a latent representation of input image(s) and optimizes a reconstruction loss with an adversarial loss (Eq (1)) over nearest neighbors from a bank of images (“memory”).   The framework is adapted to three tasks: (i) image in-painting, (ii) intrinsic image decomposition, (iii) figure-ground layer extraction.  Qualitative results are shown for all three tasks.

I think the proposed model has potential merits.  I particularly like the fact that it seems to be reasoning over image composites via matching against a bank of images (somewhat similar to “Segmenting Scenes by Matching Image Composites” work in NIPS 2009).  However, I won’t champion the paper as the overall clarity and evaluation could be improved.

I believe the fatal flaw of the paper is there is no quantitative evaluation of the approach.  At the very least, there should be a comparison against prior work on intrinsic image decomposition (e.g., SIRFS, maybe benchmark on "intrinsic images in the wild” dataset).

I found the writing vague and confusing throughout. Fig 3 seems inconsistent with Fig 2 as the module for “memory database” is not present.  The fully-convolutional discriminator could use more details; one possibility is to provide a cost function.

Please note that these comments are meant to be helpful rather than inflammatory. Regarding the content, I would strongly recommend adding a section that goes over the differences between Asynchronous and Synchronous training, as they are both commonly used in current implementations of Gradient Descent, but the differences can have a large impact on performance and scaling. This paper proposes a technique to leverage asynchronicity in the training of deep learning models, specifically showing how by leveraging asynchronicity during the backward pass can help scale training from single machines to multiple machines. The approach is based on starting the training with a model which is already trained (i.e, a checkpoint) and scheduling the training with partial updates applied to the model on different machines. The technique is based on using NCCL for communicating between the different processes and showing that it is possible to apply the update size, and the network and the computation are still online. The approach is shown to be effective for training ResNet, DenseNets, and WideResNets on ImageNet. The main limitation of the approach is the need to use the same model for both training and initialization, and the related requirement that the model has to be sufficiently shallow that the change in gradients from applying the update to a previously trained model is small. This work provides a scalable approach for training very deep neural networks. A major difficulty in training deep learning models is the very large compute requirements. One approach to addressing this has been to reduce the computation demand by using shallower networks or model structures. However, even when using such small models, training deep neural networks requires a lot of training data and time. This paper exploits recent advances in gradient-based training techniques to develop a scalable training method for very deep networks. The main idea is to decompose the network into small networks that can be trained in parallel on multiple compute nodes. Using this approach, the total number of computation units does not matter, as the training can be divided to work on any number of units. The technique utilizes the Asynchronicity and Dynamic Shared Memory provided by NCCL to scale the training. The paper shows that the approach is scalable, and can be used to train very deep networks on large datasets. The work provided in this paper has several technical contributions. First, the paper provides a rigorous definition of Asynchronous Bounding in the context of Deep Learning. In particular, it provides stepsizes and conditions for different cases, and proves that the algorithm is convergent. Second, the paper shows how to efficiently implement the algorithm in a deep network setting, by using residual blocks to split the network into manageable sizes. Third, the paper applies the algorithm to the training of very deep networks, showing how to use the approach to train very large networks on large datasets.

This is an exciting paper about utilizing asynchronicity to improve the speed of training neural networks. The proposed methods cover a very wide spectrum of algorithms from running a single machine to multiple asynchronous iterations with fixed delays. The algorithms are implemented using Caffe, a common deep learning library, and evaluated on two clusters. The evaluation demonstrates up to a 7x speedup with the largest speedup achieved in the case of multiple asynchronous iterations with fixed delay. Dorly Dev et al. "Asynchronous Layer-Wise Gradient Descent for Scalable Deep Learning" 134 pages, May 2020 adicots I have some comments and questions regarding the approach and results presented in the paper. 1. "the use of batch size one means that updates from multiple GPUs cannot be combined and therefore need to be sent and received individually" – could the authors explain what is the expected behavior in this case? How would multiple GPUs benefit from sending updates simultaneously? What is the suggested approach in this case? 2. "Intel Cluster benchmark results indicate that, compared to an ideal implementation using synchronous updates, asynchronous updates using 1% of the resources can achieve a speedup of 1.87x". The formula used to calculate this speedup looks like it assumes perfect asynchronicity – what is the impact of using an imperfect implementation? 3. "Intel Cluster benchmark results indicate that, compared to an ideal single-machine synchronous implementation, asynchronous updates using 1% of the resources can achieve a speedup of 1.89x". Again, the formula used to calculate this speedup implies perfect asynchronicity. What is the impact of imperfect implementation? 4. The comparison with the synchronous method on one node shows that the asynchronous method requires less resources, which is great, but "Intel Cluster benchmark results indicate that, compared to a synchronous implementation on one machine, the asynchronous implementation requires 10% less resources". Why is that? How does it fit with the previous statement that using 1% of the resources was enough to achieve a speedup of 1.87x?

The paper Leveraging Asynchronicity in Gradient Descent for Scalable Deep Learning presents multiple approaches for improving the performance of gradient descent when utilizing multiple compute resources. The proposed approaches span a solution space ranging from equivalence to running on a single compute device to delaying gradient updates a fixed number of times. We present a new approach, asynchronous layer-wise gradient descent that maximizes overlap of layer-wise backpropagation (computation) with gradient synchronization (communication). This approach provides maximal theoretical equivalence to the de facto gradient descent algorithm, requires limited asynchronicity across multiple iterations of gradient descent, theoretically improves overall speedup, while minimizing the additional space requirements for asynchronicity. We implement all of our proposed approaches using Caffe – a high performance Deep Learning library – and evaluate it on both an Intel Sandy Bridge cluster connected with InfiniBand as well as an NVIDIA DGX-1 connected with NVLink. The evaluations are performed on a set of well known workloads including AlexNet and GoogleNet on the ImageNet dataset. Our evaluation of these neural network topology indicates asynchronous gradient descent has a speedup of up to 1.7x compared to synchronous. The strengths of this paper are as follows: • It presents a thorough evaluation framework which includes both single and cluster topologies • The framework is implementable with Caffe, the most widely used deep learning framework, making the evaluation readily accessible to a wide range of researchers. • The proposed asynchronous framework can be customized to meet the specific compute resource constraints of individual organizations. The weaknesses of this paper are as follows: • The evaluation framework only includes theoretical analysis, while in practice this can lead to negative side effects such as requiring additional space for asynchronicity.

This paper is relatively difficult to parse. Much of the exposition of the proposed algorithm could be better presented using pseudo-code describing the compute flow, or a diagram describing exactly how the updates take place. As it stands, I'm not sure I understand everything. I would also have liked to see exactly described what the various labels in Fig 1 correspond to ("SGD task-wise, 1 comm"? Did you mean layer-wise?).
There are a couple of major issues with the evaluation: first, no comparison is reported against baseline async methods such as using a parameter server. Second, using AlexNet as a benchmark is not informative at all. AlexNet looks very different from any SOTA image recognition model, and in particular it has many fewer layers, which is especially relevant to the discussion in 6.3. It also uses lots of fully-connected layers which affect the compute/communication ratios in ways that are not relevant to most interesting architectures today.

A summary of strengths and weaknesses brought up in the reviews:
 
 Strengths
 -Paper presents a novel way to evaluate representations on generalizability to out-of-domain data (R2)
 -Experimental results are encouraging (R2)
 -Writing is clear (R1, R2)
 
 Weaknesses
 -More careful controls are needed to ascertain generalization (R2)
 -Experimental analysis is preliminary and lack of detailed analysis (R1, R2, R3)
 -Novelty and discussion of past related work (R3)
 
 The reviewers are in consensus that the idea is exciting and at least of moderate novelty, however the paper is just too preliminary for acceptance as-is. The authors did not provide a response. This is surprising because specific feedback was given to improve the paper and it seems that the paper was just under the bar. Therefore I have decided to align with the 3 reviewers in consensus and encourage the authors to revise the paper to respond to the fairly consistent suggestions for improvement and re-submit.

This paper describe an implementation of delayed synchronize SGD method for multi-GPU deep ne training.
Comments
1) The described manual implementation of delayed synchronization and state protection is helpful. However, such dependency been implemented by a dependency scheduler, without doing threading manually.
2) The overlap of computation and communication is a known technique implemented in existing solutions such as TensorFlow(as described in Chen et.al) and MXNet. The claimed contribution of this point is somewhat limited.
3) The convergence accuracy is only reported for the beginning iterations and only on AlexNet. It would be more helpful to include convergence curve till the end for all compared networks.

In summary, this is paper implements a variant of delayed SyncSGD approach. I find the novelty of the system somewhat limited (due to comment (2)). The experiments should have been improved to demonstrate the advantage of proposed approach.

The authors present methods to speed-up gradient descent by leveraging asynchronicity in a layer-wise manner.

While they obtain up-to 1.7x speedup compared to synchronous training, their baseline is weak. More importantly, they dismiss parameter-server based methods, which are becoming standard, and so effectively just do not compare to the current state-of-the-art. They also do not present wall-time measurements. With these flaws, the paper is not ready for ICLR acceptance.

Full disclosure: I am an author on the follow-up paper to Chen et al. (2016).

Although the paper cites Chen et al. (2016) as a starting point of the proposed approach, it does not mention the key message of Chen et al. (2016) of using backup workers to hide straggler effects in synchronous gradient descent. Were backup workers used as part of the synchronous approaches?

Also, the paper does not evaluate the wallclock time to reach convergence or a given accuracy. Even though the AGD approach has more iterations per second, it also leads to poorer convergence (as acknowledged in Table 1). As a specific example, to reach 0.01688 accuracy requires <2000 iterations of SGD, <3000 iterations of AGD (1 comm), and 5000 iterations of AGD (2 comm). Hence, for AGD to be faster than SGD in wallclock time, AGD must have at 1.5x iterations per second relative to SGD, which does not appear to the case from Figure 1. Of course, this example is only for a low accuracy of 0.01688, and the proposed AGD could very well reach the final convergence of 54% in lesser time. It would be very helpful if the authors could provide that information.

 -Experimental results are encouraging (R2)
 -Writing is clear (R1, R2)
 
 Weaknesses
 -More careful controls are needed to ascertain generalization (R2)
 -Experimental analysis is preliminary and lack of detailed analysis (R1, R2, R3)
 -Novelty and discussion of past related work (R3)
 
 The reviewers are in consensus that the idea is exciting and at least of moderate novelty, however the paper is just too preliminary for acceptance as-is. The authors did not provide a response. This is surprising because specific feedback was given to improve the paper and it seems that the paper was just under the bar. Therefore I have decided to align with the 3 reviewers in consensus and encourage the authors to revise the paper to respond to the fairly consistent suggestions for improvement and re-submit.

This paper describe an implementation of delayed synchronize SGD method for multi-GPU deep ne training.
Comments
1) The described manual implementation of delayed synchronization and state protection is helpful. However, such dependency been implemented by a dependency scheduler, without doing threading manually.
2) The overlap of computation and communication is a known technique implemented in existing solutions such as TensorFlow(as described in Chen et.al) and MXNet. The claimed contribution of this point is somewhat limited.
3) The convergence accuracy is only reported for the beginning iterations and only on AlexNet. It would be more helpful to include convergence curve till the end for all compared networks.

In summary, this is paper implements a variant of delayed SyncSGD approach. I find the novelty of the system somewhat limited (due to comment (2)). The experiments should have been improved to demonstrate the advantage of proposed approach.

The authors present methods to speed-up gradient descent by leveraging asynchronicity in a layer-wise manner.

While they obtain up-to 1.7x speedup compared to synchronous training, their baseline is weak. More importantly, they dismiss parameter-server based methods, which are becoming standard, and so effectively just do not compare to the current state-of-the-art. They also do not present wall-time measurements. With these flaws, the paper is not ready for ICLR acceptance.

Full disclosure: I am an author on the follow-up paper to Chen et al. (2016).

Although the paper cites Chen et al. (2016) as a starting point of the proposed approach, it does not mention the key message of Chen et al. (2016) of using backup workers to hide straggler effects in synchronous gradient descent. Were backup workers used as part of the synchronous approaches?

Also, the paper does not evaluate the wallclock time to reach convergence or a given accuracy. Even though the AGD approach has more iterations per second, it also leads to poorer convergence (as acknowledged in Table 1). As a specific example, to reach 0.01688 accuracy requires <2000 iterations of SGD, <3000 iterations of AGD (1 comm), and 5000 iterations of AGD (2 comm). Hence, for AGD to be faster than SGD in wallclock time, AGD must have at 1.5x iterations per second relative to SGD, which does not appear to the case from Figure 1. Of course, this example is only for a low accuracy of 0.01688, and the proposed AGD could very well reach the final convergence of 54% in lesser time. It would be very helpful if the authors could provide that information.

This paper is relatively difficult to parse. Much of the exposition of the proposed algorithm could be better presented using pseudo-code describing the compute flow, or a diagram describing exactly how the updates take place. As it stands, I'm not sure I understand everything. I would also have liked to see exactly described what the various labels in Fig 1 correspond to ("SGD task-wise, 1 comm"? Did you mean layer-wise?).
There are a couple of major issues with the evaluation: first, no comparison is reported against baseline async methods such as using a parameter server. Second, using AlexNet as a benchmark is not informative at all. AlexNet looks very different from any SOTA image recognition model, and in particular it has many fewer layers, which is especially relevant to the discussion in 6.3. It also uses lots of fully-connected layers which affect the compute/communication ratios in ways that are not relevant to most interesting architectures today.

machine_text: In this paper, the authors introduced Dynamic Steerable Frame Networks (DSFN). The authors proposed a solution to the lack of continuous, global supervising information in Autonomous Driving by introducing an Dynamic Frame Network that continuously generates navigation coordinates in world space from perception information in sensor space. To generate these coordinate dynamically, they introduced a steerable frame that adapts to changes in environment. This network structure solved two important issues in Autonomous Driving: 1- DSFN overcomes the necessity of pre-training and careful initialization of high-dimensional parameters in conventional Frame Navigation methods, which is error-prone and inefficient. 2- DSFN provides continuous and global navigation coordinates that allows better control by coordinator (e.g. robot driver) and thus more safe. Overall, this work can open a new direction in Autonomous Driving and better focus on efficiency and reliability. The code and models will be released soon. Thank you for your interest. Best, Anthony P.S. As an AutoMLQA at Apollo Planet, I always keenly read new papers in this field and provide feedback to authors. If you are interested, please let me know. This paper discusses the design of a dynamic steerable frame network for robotic applications. The authors describe the design requirements for such a system, and how to implement the system using a multi-output network that dynamically finds the most significant output values. The design requirements were realistic for many applications, and the design of the DSFN was reasonable. However, the authors could have done a better job motivating the need for a dynamic steering solution, and they could have validated their design with simulations or experiments. The biggest weakness of this design is that it does not address how to design the dynamic steering algorithm, or how to search for parameters that would enable good performance. Because of this, the system cannot be tuned for good performance on real-world data. The authors mention that a good starting point for the dynamic steering algorithm would be the Karayama algorithm, but they do not describe why this is a good starting point or provide any performance comparison to other dynamic steering algorithms. In addition, it is not clear how to search for the correct values for the parameters C and T in this algorithm. Even without the design of a good dynamic steering algorithm, it is clear that this system would work well for many robotic applications. The authors demonstrate this by applying the system to a Dinosaur chasing task. ！ Like the paper's focus on designing a system that can perform well on a wide range of applications, while also being general enough to be easy to implement and adapt to a particular application? I particularly like the idea of designing the system to return multiple steering directions, and letting the application decide which to use. This is similar to the idea of a skeletal system, in which a lot of flexibility but also extra complexity in computation and control.

This is an interesting paper which provides a new perspective of CNNs using frames. In particular, filters in a CNN are parametrized in a pixel basis. As an orthonormal basis, pixels may represent any arbitrary vector in Rn. In this paper, the authors relax this orthonormality requirement and extend the set of viable bases to the generalized notion of frames. When applying suitable frame bases to ResNets, one can show improved error rates by substitution only. By exploiting the transformation properties of such generalized bases, we arrive at steerable frames, that allow to continuously transform CNN filters under arbitrary Lie-groups. The paper describes the first framework for using steerable frames in CNNs. The authors start with a general convolutional framework, then specific cases for GF(2) and SE(3) are discussed. There are two key components in the dynamic steerable frame network: transformers and dynamics. The former transforms the feature representation of the input by transforming the filters of the network, while the latter estimates the transformation of the input conditioned on the current image. The derived methods present a hybrid of Dynamic Filter Networks and Spatial Transformer Networks. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. First, the general convolutional framework is introduced. Then, the specific case of GF(2) is introduced and related work is discussed. Next, the specific case of SE(3) is introduced, as well as the idea of local separating of pose and canonical appearance. The final section of the paper presents two examples of using dynamic steerable frames, in particular for edge detection and gesture recognition. Finally, some concluding remarks are made.

The filters in a convolutional network are typically parametrized in a pixel basis. As an orthonormal basis, pixels may represent any arbitrary vector in Rn. In this paper, we relax this orthonormality requirement and extend the set of viable bases to the generalized notion of frames. When applying suitable frame bases to ResNets on Cifar-10+ we demonstrate improved error rates by substitution only. By exploiting the transformation properties of such generalized bases, we arrive at steerable frames, that allow to continuously transform CNN filters under arbitrary Lie-groups. Furthermore, we illustrate estimation properties of steerable frames with a Dynamic Steerable Frame Network, compared to a Dynamic Filter Network on the task of edge detection. We insert the Dynamic Steerable Frame Network as a module in a convolutional LSTM on the task of limited-data hand-gesture recognition from video. Overall, we demonstrate the advantages of Dynamic Steerable Frame Networks over Dynamic Filter Networks and Spatial Transformer Networks on a range of tasks. To date, the field of Neural Architecture Search was not applicable to Frame based CNNs. Our work closes this gap by introducing steerable frame based CNNs and their Dynamic variants, along with the necessary training method. We highlight the following as particular strengths of our work: 1. The derived method presents a hybrid of Dynamic Filter Networks and Spatial Transformer Networks, which allows to locally separate pose from canonical appearance 2. The approach is easy to implement in any standard convolutional architecture, as we illustrate with two examples. 3. We lay out the foundations of Frame-based convolutional networks and Dynamic Steerable Frame Networks. 4. We show how Dynamic Steerable Frame Networks are especially advantageous on tasks where one or more of the conditions is changing. We conclude that steerable frame based CNNs and Dynamic Steerable Frame Networks present a viable option for Neural Architecture Search and lay the groundwork for subsequent works in this direction.
