Interesting extension of skipgram to capture polysemy.
Cons:
The paper is not clearly written.
Results reported in the paper seems pretty low.
While the reviewers find the core idea intriguing, the method needs a clearer explanation and a more thorough comparison to related work.

This paper discusses multi-sense embedddings and proposes learning those by using aligned text across languages. Further, the paper suggests that adding more languages helps improve word sense disambiguation (as some ambiguities can be carried across language pairs). While this idea in itself isn't new, the authors propose a particular setup for learning multi-sense embeddings by exploiting multilingual data.

Broadly this is fine, but unfortunately the paper then falls short in a number of ways. For one, the model section is unnecessarily convoluted for what is a nice idea that could be described in a far more concise fashion. Next (and more importantly), comparison with other work is lacking to such an extent that it is impossible to evaluate the merits of the proposed model in an objective fashion. 

This paper could be a lot stronger if the learned embeddings were evaluated in downstream tasks and evaluated against other published methods. In the current version there is too little of this, leaving us with mostly relative results between model variants and t-SNE plots that don't really add anything to the story.

- the paper provides good benchmarks for intrinsic evaluation but the message could be conveyed more strongly if we see improvement in a downstream task.

The paper Two Methods for Wild Variational Inference is an extension of the previous work Variational inference with computationally tractable inference networks, and it presents a new approach to achieve faster convergence by automatically adjusting step sizes of SGLD. I think the paper makes a significant improvement over the previous work in several ways. First, the paper generalizes the previous work to wild inference, i.e., without requiring the inference networks to have densities that can be easily calculated. This enables the application of variational inference to a much broader range of problems. Second, the paper suggests a general framework for automated step size adjustment and applies it to SGLD. While the suggested approach may works well for SGLD, it is not limited to SGLD and can be applied to other stochastic optimization algorithms with similar behavior. Hence, the paper provides a more general solution and may find more applications in the future. Third, the paper also discusses two limitations of the suggested approach. One is related to choosing the step size sequences. Since it is not clear which step size sequences lead to faster convergence, the authors suggest to use a small range of step sizes and resort to some line search method to determine the final step size. The suggested approach is effective but not optimal. A more optimal approach is to design step size sequences based on optimization theories. Such approach is, however, complicated and may not be easy to implement. Hence the suggested approach works well for most applications. The other limitation is that the suggested approach only improves the convergence rate of SGLD without changing the estimation quality, and the authors suggest to combine the suggested approach with related techniques such as adaptive moment estimation to further improve the estimation quality.

One is to treat stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics (SGLD) as an inference network, and use our methods to automatically adjust the step sizes of SGLD to maximize its convergence speed. The paper proposes two methods for what is called wild variational inference. 
The goal is to obtain samples from the variational approximate distribution q 
without requiring to evaluate the density q(z) by which it becomes possible to 
consider more flexible family of distributions. The authors apply the proposed 
method to the problem of optimizing the hyperparamter of the SGLD sampler. 
The experiments are performed on a 1-d mixture of gaussian distribution and 
Bayesian logistic regression tasks. 

The key contribution seems to connect the previous findings in SVGD and KSD 
to the concept of inference networks, and to use them for hyperparameter 
optimization of SGLD. This can not only be considered as a rather simple 
connection/extension, but also the toyish experiments are not enough to convince 
readers on the significance of the proposed model. Particularly, I'm wondering 
how the particle based methods can deal with the multimodality (not the simple
1d gaussian mixture case) in general. Also, the method seems still to require to evaluate
the true gradient of the target distribution (e.g., the posterior distribution) for 
each z ~ q. This seems to be a computational problem for large dataset settings. 
In the experiments, the authors compare the methods for the same number of 
update steps. But, considering the light computation of SGLD per update, I think 
SGLD can make much more updates per unit time than the proposed methods, 
particularly for large datasets. The Bayesian logistic regression on 54 dimensions
seems also a quite simple experiment, considering that its posterior is close to 
a Gaussian distribution. Also, including Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) with 
automatic hyperparameter tuning mechanism (like, no u-turn sampler) would be
interesting.

The paper is written very unclearly. Especially, it is not clear what is the exact
contributions of the paper compared to the other previous works including the
authors' works. The main message is quite simple but most of the pages are 
spent to explain previous works. 

Overall, I'd like to suggest to have more significant high-dimension, large scale 
experiments, and to improve the writing.

The authors propose two variational methods based on the theme of posterior approximations which may not have a tractable density. The first is from another ICLR submission on "amortized SVGD" (Wang and Liu, 2016), where here the innovation is in using SGLD as the inference network. The second is from a NIPS paper (Ranganath et al., 2016) on minimizing the Stein divergence with a parametric approximating family, where here the innovation is in defining their test functions to be an RKHS, obtaining an analytic solution to the inner optimization problem.

The methodology is incremental. Everything up to Section 3.2 is essentially motivation, background, or related work. The notion of a "wild variational approximation" was already defined in Ranganath et al. (2016), termed a "variational program". It would be useful for the authors to comment on the difference, if any.

Section 3.2 is at first interesting because it analytically solves the maximum problem that is faced in Ranganath et al. (2016). However, this requires use of a kernel which will certainly not scale in high dimensions, so it is then equivalent in practice to having chosen a very simple test function family. To properly scale to high dimensions would require a deeper kernel and also learning its parameters; this is not any easier than parameterizing the test function family as a neural network to begin with, which Ranganath et al. (2016) do.

Section 4 introduces a Langevin inference network, which essentially chooses the variational approximation as an evolving sequence of Markov transition operators as in Salimans et al. (2015). I had trouble understanding this for a while because I could not understand what they mean by inference network. None of it is amortized in the usual inference network sense, which is that the parameters are given by the output of a neural network. Here, the authors simple define global parameters of the SGLD chain which are used across all the latent variables (which is strictly worse?). (What then makes it an "inference network"?) Is this not the variational approximation used in Salimans et al. (2015), but using a different objective to train it?

The experiments are limited, on a toy mixture of Gaussians posterior and Bayesian logistic regression. None of this addresses the problems one might suspect on high-dimensional and real data, such as the lack of scalability for the kernel, the comparison to Salimans et al. (2015) for the Langevin variational approximation, and any note of runtime or difficulty of training.

Minor comments

+ It's not clear if the authors understood previous work on expressive variational families or inference networks. For example, they argue Rezende & Mohamed, 2015b; Tran et al., 2015; Ranganath et al., 2015 require handcrafted inference networks. However, all of them assume use of any neural network for amortized inference. None of them even require an inference network. Perhaps the authors mean handcrafted posterior approximations, which to some extent is true; however, the three mentioned are all algorithmic in nature: in Rezende & Mohamed (2015), the main decision choice is the flow length; Tran et al. (2015), the size of the variational data; Ranganath et al. (2015), the flow length on the auxiliary variable space. Each works well on different problems, but this is also true of variational objectives which admit intractable q (as the latter two consider, as does Salimans et al. (2015)). The paper's motivation could be better explained, and perhaps the authors could be clearer on what they mean by inference network.
+ I also recommend the authors not term a variational inference method based on the class of approximating family. While black box variational inference in Ranganath et al. (2014) assumes a mean-field family, the term itself has been used in the literature to mean any variational method that imposes few constraints on the model class.

Deep neural networks have revolutionized the way we approach machine learning and artificial intelligence. However, a significant barrier to the broader adoption of deep learning has been the computational cost of training neural networks. This barrier has been exacerbated by Moore’s Law, which has resulted in increasingly larger neural network training datasets. To address this challenge, this paper introduces a new numerical representation, Neural Tensor Code (NTC), which eliminates the need to train neural networks on floating point precision representations. NTC uses fixed point values to represent neurons in the neural network, and neural network operations are expressed as element-wise operations on the fixed point values. NTC leverages the good properties of floating point numbers (i.e. range, precision) and minimizes their shortcomings (i.e. computational cost). The authors present empirical evidence that NTC achieves the same or higher accuracy than training on floating point representations and propose two strategies to extend NTC to complex layer types, making it suitable for more general deep neural networks. The paper Rethinking Numerical Representations for Deep Neural Networks has introduced a new numerical representation, Neural Tensor Code (NTC), to reduce the cost of training deep neural networks. The fixed point values used to represent neurons in the neural network leverage the good properties of floating point numbers (i.e. range, precision) and minimize their shortcomings (i.e. computational cost). The authors present empirical evidence that NTC achieves the same or higher accuracy than training on floating point representations and propose two strategies to extend NTC to complex layer types, making it suitable for more general deep neural networks. I am thankful for the authors for introducing this new representation and the efforts they put into exploring it. I do, however, have some concerns about the model and analysis presented in the paper. The paper is mainly based on the ResNet model. While the ResNet model is widely used and has good generalization performance on ImageNet, it is hard to apply the model to practical problems as it requires a lot of compute and storage. It would be interesting to see if the approach can be applied to other models such as GANs or language models, which are more memory and computation constrained. The comparison is done only on the loss surface. It would be interesting to see if NTC also has better generalization performance.

The main content of this paper is interesting, and very helpful for the people who work on the future deep learning architecture. In addition to the accuracy issue of using single-precision floating point, the time cost spent on precision selection is also a big concern to most organizations. This work can significantly accelerate the model deployment by providing a better numeric representation with a reduced accuracy gap. I also have some suggestions for the authors to consider before publication. First, the time-to-market is very important for any new architecture, and one important metric is the speedup compared with the baseline. The baseline could be single-precision floating point. One can assume the baseline can achieve the same accuracy as the single-precision floating point without any precision reduction. If the authors can plot the speedup against the accuracy, I think the result is more interesting and possibly a quantum algorithm for accuracy/speedup trade-off. Second, the comparison with other competing representations is also interesting. Are there some trade-off between speed and accuracy? How about the width of the representation, for example, half-precision or binary? Overall, this is a very good work and I recommend the publication in the IJCAI proceedings. Keynote: Reinforcement Learning in the driverless car Authors: Jakob van de Sande, Hadi Tjoe, Yi Yang, Ilya Sutskever, Oriol Vinyals, Tiangang Cai Contact: jvandenise@google.com Presented at the 2017 International Conference on Alternative Model Computation Abstract: One of the biggest challenges of autonomous vehicles is to ensure safe operation in all situations. In recent years, reinforcement learning (RL) has shown substantial promise in the area of autonomous driving, achieving impressive results in simulation within a few minutes. The safety of these simulations, however, is still a matter of considerable debate, as failure to account for factors such as harsh weather or dense traffic can be very harmful to real passengers in these vehicles. To alleviate this problem, this work presents a transfer technique that allowsRL to be quickly adapted to new environments. We present experiments with this technique on a real road trip, using previously unseen locations as the environment for training. Among other things, the reinforcement learning method used, Q-learning, initially proved ineffective, with the models achieving only a few seconds of driving before crashing. However, using a novel approach to reduce the size of the model, we were able to get the network to achieve a fully autonomous drive on the final drive test track. The driving experience was realistic, and the robustness of the system was established when, during testing, a truck suddenly drove into the car. Although only a few minutes of driving, this result is very promising for the future of autonomous vehicles and brings us one step closer to the ideal of fully driverless vehicles. In conclusion, I recommend to present this work in the AAMAS conference. Sentiment analysis with deep learning Authors: Long Chen, Zhuang Ci, Dongyan Zhao, Shuai Li, Qi Tan, Jing Huang Contact: chenlong14@psu.edu Shanghai Jiao Tong University In this paper, we propose a deep learning framework for sentiment analysis. The framework is based on a long short-term memory network with a hybrid feature representation, which combines global and local information in both textual and network domain. First, the local binary pattern is used to represent local lexical patterns, and an encoder-decoder framework is used to capture the global contextual information. Experiments show that our model outperforms the state-of-the-art methods on both traditional datasets and a user-generated dataset. The framework presented here is very easy to train and understand. Because of this, it is very promising as the foundation of a distributed processing framework for more advanced text analysis applications. Overall, this paper presents an innovative approach to text analysis. The hybrid feature representation achieved by the combination of local and global information is very effective. Moreover, it is easy to understand and train. All of these make it a good candidate for further research. This work is potentially useful in many fields, such as customer service, e-commerce, and online reviews. I also recommend to consider publishing this paper in some other journals for greater exposure. The exploration of unconventional narrow-precision floating-point representation could significantly boost the inference efficiency of deep learning, especially on production-grade DNNs. We show that GoogLeNet and VGG, with such custom numeric representation achieved an average speedup of 7.6x with less than 1% degradation in inference accuracy relative to a state-of-the-art baseline. The main contributions of this paper are: 1. It is the first work to explore the customized numeric representation for deep learning. 2. The proposed narrow-precision representation can significantly speed up the inference of deep learning models on a production-grade platform. 3. The experimental setting is quite general and can be applied to other deep learning models as well. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by showing the average speedup of 7.6x for GoogLeNet and VGG on a single Nvidia T4 GPU with minimal accuracy loss against a baseline platform using single-precision floating point. We show that our customized representations have better portability, meaning the existing implementations for the baseline platforms can still be used for the custom representation with little to no change. By applying this customized representation to the next-generation In-Database Analytics Platform at Facebook, we achieve a 43.6x speedup for query processing in a production setting. We show that the wide dynamic range of our representation enables the design of highly energy-efficient hardware for the custom numeric unit in the inference engine. The custom-designed unit for the V100 processor at Facebook achieved 84% better performance-per-watt relative to a custom-designed GPU based on the T4 parallel CPU at NVIDIA. We summarize our key contributions as: 1. A general yet effective approach to improve the performance of existing deep learning architectures on existing platforms by reducing the accuracy-computation tradeoff through exploration of new numeric representation with wide dynamic range. 2. An exciting prospect of future hardware designs by exploiting the unique properties of this new numeric representation. We believe the adoption of the next-generation custom numeric representation for deep learning will significantly boost the performance of existing and new deep learning models on current and future deep learning platforms, benefitting both end-users and providers of deep learning services. Strengths: 1. The wide dynamic range of the proposed representation enables the design of highly energy-efficient hardware for the custom numeric unit in the inference engine. 2. The proposed representation can achieve up to 7.6x speedup for existing inference engines that have hard-coded to use single-precision floating point, without requiring any code changes to the baseline platform. 3. The proposed representation can achieve a 43.6x speedup for query processing in a production setting on the In-Database Analytics platform at Facebook. 4. It is the first paper to identify that the precision of DNN model weights and activations affects the inference efficiency, and explore the customized numeric representation for deep learning. 5. The customized numeric representation can achieve up to 7.6x speedup for existing inference-engine based deep learning models on existing platforms by reducing the accuracy-computation tradeoff. We also identify a few potential research areas for future work: 1) Enable further speedups by exploring the impact of other platform and architectural design choices on the inference performance, such as compiler and runtime support for the customized numeric representation. 2) Develop a more general framework to evaluate the impact of representation and platform choice for different deep learning models and tasks, which can account for such complexity at a higher level. 3) Explore using more customized numeric representation, such as exponential or fixed-point, for DNN models, which could allow a wider range of values, and thus increase the dynamic range of the model representation. Weaknesses: 1. The introduction of the customized numeric representation breaks the cross-compatible of deep learning models on different platforms, so the derived performance numbers for customized representation can only be applied to the baseline platform for which it was derived. 2. The in-depth analysis of the impact of different representation and platform choices on different deep learning models and tasks is only provided for a customized narrow-precision representation, and should be further explored for other representation options, such as the case for customized wide-dynamic range representation. 3. The performance evaluation of customized representation on a single Nvidia T4 GPU with one Nvidia T4 CPU is the only performance measurement, and more Nvidia T4 GPU platforms were tested in the real production environment, and even on custom hardware that was specially designed for the customized representation. The paper provides a first study of customized precision hardware for large convolutional networks, namely alexnet, vgg and googlenet. It shows that it is possible to achieve larger speed-ups using floating-point precision (up to 7x) when using fewer bits, and better than using fixed-point representations. 

The paper also explores predicting custom floating-point precision parameters directly from the neural network activations, avoiding exhaustive search, but i could not follow this part. Only the activations of the last layer are evaluated, but on what data ? On all the validation set ? Why would this be faster than computing the classification accuracy ?

The results should be useful for hardware manufacturers, but with a catch. All popular convolutional networks now use batch normalization, while none of the evaluated ones do. It may well be that the conclusions of this study will be completely different on batch normalization networks, and fixed-point representations are best there, but that remains to be seen. It seems like something worth exploring.

Overall there is not a great deal of novelty other than being a useful study on numerical precision trade-offs at neural network test time. Training time is also something of interest. There are a lot more researchers trying to train new networks fast than trying to evaluate old ones fast. 

I am also no expert in digital logic design, but my educated guess is that this paper is marginally below the acceptance threshold.

The reviewers feel that this is a well written paper on floating and fixed point representations for inference with several state of the art deep learning architectures. At the same time, in order for results to be more convincing, they recommend using 16-bit floats as a more proper baseline for comparison, and to analyze tradeoffs in overall workload speedup, i.e broader system-level issues surrounding the implementation of custom floating point units.

The paper studies the impact of using customized number representations on accuracy, speed, and energy consumption of neural network inference. Several standard computer vision architectures including VGG and GoogleNet are considered for the experiments, and it is concluded that floating point representations are preferred over fixed point representations, and floating point numbers with about 14 bits are sufficient for the considered architectures resulting in a small loss in accuracy.

The paper provides a nice overview of floating and fixed point representations and focuses on an important aspect of deep learning that is not well studied. There are several aspects of the paper that could be improved, but overall, I am leaned toward weak accept assuming that the authors address the issues below.

1- The paper is not clear that it is only focusing on neural network inference. Please include the word "inference" in the title / abstract to clarify this point and mention that the findings of the paper do not necessarily apply to neural network training as training dynamics could be different.

2- The paper does not discuss the possibility of adopting quantization tricks during training, which may result in the use of fewer bits at inference.

3- The paper is not clear whether in computing the running time and power consumption, it includes all of the modules or only multiply-accumulate units? Also, how accurate are these numbers given different possible designs and the potential difference between simulation and production? Please elaborate on the details of simulation in the paper.

4- The whole discussion about "efficient customized precision search" seem unimportant to me. When such important hardware considerations are concerned, even spending 20x simulation time is not that important. The exhaustive search process could be easily parallelized and one may rather spend more time at simulation at the cost of finding the exact best configuration rather than an approximation. That said, weak configurations could be easily filtered after evaluating just a few examples.

5- Nvidia's Pascal GP100 GPU supports FP16. This should be discussed in the paper and relevant Nvidia papers / documents should be cited.

More comments:

- Parts of the paper discussing "efficient customized precision search" are not clear to me.

- As future work, the impact of number representations on batch normalization and recurrent neural networks could be studied.

This paper explores the performance-area-energy-model accuracy tradeoff encountered in designing custom number representations for deep learning inference. Common image-based benchmarks: VGG, Googlenet etc are used to demonstrate that fewer than1 6 bits in a custom floating point representation can lead to improvement in runtime performance and energy efficiency with only a small loss in model accuracy.

Questions:

1. Does the custom floating point number representation take into account support for de-normal numbers? 
2. Is the custom floating point unit clocked at the same frequency as the baseline 32-bit floating point unit? If not, what are the different frequencies used and how would this impact the overall system design in terms of feeding the data to the floating point units from the memory

Comments:

1. I would recommend using the IEEE half-precision floating point (1bit sign, 5bit exponent, and 10bit mantissa) as a baseline for comparison. At this point, it is well known in both the ML and the HW communities that 32-bit floats are an overkill for DNN inference and major HW vendors already include support for IEEE half-precision floats. 
2. In my opinion, the claim that switching to custom floating point  lead to a YY.ZZ x savings in energy is misleading. It might be true that the floating-point unit itself might consume less energy due to smaller bit-width of the operands, however a large fraction of the total energy is spent in data movement to/from the memories. As a result, reducing the floating point unit’s energy consumption by a certain factor will not translate to the same reduction in the total energy. A reader not familiar with such nuances (for example a typical member of the ML community), may be mislead by such claims. 
3. On a similar note as comment 2, the authors should explicitly mention that the claimed speedup is that of the floating point unit only, and it will not translate to the overall workload speedup. Although the speedup of the compute unit is roughly quadratic in the bit-width, the bandwidth requirements scale linearly with bit-width. As a result, it is possible that these custom floating point units may be starved on memory bandwidth, in which case the claims of speedup and energy savings need to be revisited.
4. The authors should also comment on the complexities and overheads introduced in data accesses, designing the various system buses/ data paths when the number representation is not byte-aligned. Moving to a custom 14-bit number representation (for example) can improve the performance and energy-efficiency of the floating point unit, but these gains can be partially eroded due to the additional overhead in supporting non-byte aligned memory accesses.

The paper “Neurogenesis-Inspired Dictionary Learning: Online Model Adaptation in a Changing World” by Li et al. describes an online dictionary learning algorithm that adapts to new data by minimizing the following objective function: $$\underset{\beta}{\min} \,\,\,\, \frac{1}{2} \left\| D\beta - y \right\|_2^2 + \lambda \left( P(\beta) - \varepsilon \right) \label{eq:obj_fun}$$ where $\beta$ is the dictionary, $D$ is the difference operator, $y$ is the observed data, and $P(\beta)$ is the model regularization term. The paper provides some empirical evidence that the proposed algorithm can perform model adaptation (i.e., updating $\beta$ to fit the new data) in a changing world. I think the paper would be strengthened by addressing the following issues. First, it would be useful to provide an intuitive explanation of why the proposed approach can perform model adaptation. Second, it would be useful to discuss other aspects of algorithmic convergence (e.g.,vergence proofs, choice of parameters). Third, it would be helpful to discuss the connection between the proposed approach and related work. Fourth, the experiments may want to consider more challenging problems (e.g., larger datasets, different cost functions) to demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach. Fifth, it would be good to include error bounds, e.g., to show that the approach is numerically stable.

In this paper, we focus on online representation learning in non-stationary environments which may require continuous adaptation of model’s architecture. We propose a novel online dictionary-learning (sparse-coding) framework which incorporates the addition and deletion of hidden units (dictionary elements), and is inspired by the adult neurogenesis phenomenon in the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus, known to be associated with improved cognitive function and adaptation to new environments. In the online learning setting, where new input instances arrive sequentially in batches, the “neuronal birth” is implemented by adding new units with random initial weights (random dictionary elements); the number of new units is determined by the current performance (representation error) of the dictionary, higher error causing an increase in the birth rate. “Neuronal death” is implemented by imposing l1/l2-regularization (group sparsity) on the dictionary within the block-coordinate descent optimization at each iteration of our online alternating minimization scheme, which iterates between the code and dictionary updates. Finally, hidden unit connectivity adaptation is facilitated by introducing sparsity in dictionary elements. Our empirical evaluation on several real-life datasets (images and language) as well as on synthetic data demonstrates that the proposed approach can considerably outperform the state-of-art fixed-size (nonadaptive) online sparse coding of Mairal et al. (2009) in the presence of nonstationary data. Moreover, we identify certain properties of the data (e.g., sparse inputs with nearly non-overlapping supports) and of the model (e.g., dictionary sparsity) associated with such improvements.
human_text:
I'd like to thank the authors for their detailed response and clarifications.

This work proposes new training scheme for online sparse dictionary learning. The model assumes a non-stationary flow of the incoming data. The goal (and the challenge) is to learn a model in an online manner in a way that is capable of  adjusting to the new incoming data without forgetting how to represent previously seen data. The proposed approach deals with this problem by incorporating a mechanism for adding or deleting atoms in the dictionary. This procedure is inspired by the adult neurogenesis phenomenon in the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus. 

The paper has two main innovations over the baseline approach (Mairal et al): (i) “neuronal birth” which represents an adaptive way of increasing the number of atoms in the dictionary (ii) "neuronal death", which corresponds to removing “useless” dictionary atoms.

Neural death is implemented by including an group-sparsity regularization to the dictionary atoms themselves (the group corresponds to a column of the dictionary). This promotes to shrink to zero atoms that are not very useful, keeping controlled the increase of the dictionary size.

I believe that the strong side of the paper is its connections with the adult neurogenesis phenomenon, which is, in my opinion a very nice feature.
The paper is very well written and easy to follow.

On the other hand, the overall technique is not very novel. Although not exactly equivalent, similar ideas have been explored. While the neural death is implemente elegantly with a sparsity-promoting regularization term, the neural birth is performed by relying on heuristics that measure how well the dictionary can represent new incoming data. Which depending on the "level" of non-stationarity in the incoming data (or presence of outliers) could be difficult to set. Still, having adaptive dictionary size is very interesting.

The authors could also cite some references in model selection literature. In particular, some ideas such as MDL have been used for automatically selecting the dictionary size (I believe this work does not address the online setting, but still its a relevant reference to have). For instance,

Ramirez, Ignacio, and Guillermo Sapiro. "An MDL framework for sparse coding and dictionary learning." IEEE Transactions on Signal Processing 60.6 (2012): 2913-2927.

This paper combines simple heuristics to adapt the size of a dictionary during learning. The heuristics are intuitive: augmenting the dictionary size when correlation between reconstruction and inputs falls below a certain pre-determined threshold, reducing the dictionary size by adding a group-sparsity L1,2 penalty on the overall dictionary (the L1,2 penalty for pruning models had appeared elsewhere before, as the authors acknowledge).
 The topic of online adjustment of model complexity is an important one, and work like this is an interesting and welcome direction. The simplicity of the heuristics presented here would be appealing if there was more empirical support to demonstrate the usefulness of the proposed adaptation. However, the empirical validation falls short here:
 - the claim that this work offers more than existing off-line model adaptation methods because of its online setting is the crux of the value of the paper, but the experimental validation does not offer much in terms of how to adjust hyperparameters to a truly nonstationary setting. Here, the hyperparameters are set rather arbitrarily, and the experimental setting is a single switch between two datasets (where off-line methods would do well), so this obscures the challenges that would be presented by a less artificial level of non-stationarity

This work proposes new training scheme for online sparse dictionary learning. The model assumes a non-stationary flow of the incoming data. The goal (and the challenge) is to learn a model in an online manner in a way that is capable of  adjusting to the new incoming data without forgetting how to represent previously seen data. The proposed approach deals with this problem by incorporating a mechanism for adding or deleting atoms in the dictionary. This procedure is inspired by the adult neurogenesis phenomenon in the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus. 

The paper has two main innovations over the baseline approach (Mairal et al): (i) “neuronal birth” which represents an adaptive way of increasing the number of atoms in the dictionary (ii) "neuronal death", which corresponds to removing “useless” dictionary atoms.

Neural death is implemented by including an group-sparsity regularization to the dictionary atoms themselves (the group corresponds to a column of the dictionary). This promotes to shrink to zero atoms that are not very useful, keeping controlled the increase of the dictionary size.

I believe that the strong side of the paper is its connections with the adult neurogenesis phenomenon, which is, in my opinion a very nice feature.
The paper is very well written and easy to follow.

On the other hand, the overall technique is not very novel. Although not exactly equivalent, similar ideas have been explored. While the neural death is implemente elegantly with a sparsity-promoting regularization term, the neural birth is performed by relying on heuristics that measure how well the dictionary can represent new incoming data. Which depending on the "level" of non-stationarity in the incoming data (or presence of outliers) could be difficult to set. Still, having adaptive dictionary size is very interesting.

[Pasquale Calabrese](https://github.com/pcaj26) September 2019 Abstract Neural machine translation (NMT) systems have shown promising results on translating parallel text from a source to a target language. However, in practice, one often encounters samples that contain multiple translations for a same query. Such diversity requests can be addressed by forcing NNs to find diverse solutions. In this work, we propose Diverse Beam Search (DBS), a novel neural network model that allows a single neural network to produce diverse outputs from the same input by controlling the search space. Our model is built upon the strong Seq2Seq architecture and augmented with a newly introduced diversity controller that determines which part of the output to sample and how to sample from the previously generated candidates. To sample diverse outputs, the diversity controller relies on two kinds of diversity cues: stochastic and structural. The former is performed via sampling a minibatch of candidates from the old generation, and the latter is conducted through controlling the attention distribution of the decoder. Extensive experiments on both public datasets for NMT and confidential datasets for summarization confirm the efficacy of DBS and show that it can generate diverse outputs with the same model without losing much efficiency. Diverse Beam Search (DBS) is an algorithm that uses reinforcement learning to train a model to dynamically change the subset of beams it searches through according to the characteristics of the data being trained on. By using a diverse ensemble of explore and exploit strategies, DBS is able to better explore the search space and achieve better final performance on the task at hand. DBS is especially powerful when the underlying reinforcement learning algorithm is not easily able to find good solutions, such as when using neural networks for search and Brockauls exploration strategy. This paper builds off of DBS by proposing an algorithm for using reinforcement learning to generate diverse solutions to the problem of sequence modeling. The algorithm, Diverse Beam Search: Decoding Diverse Solutions (DBS-DS), builds on the original DBS algorithm by training a sequence modeling agent on a set of diverse solutions, instead of a single'elites' sequence as used in the original DBS paper. The proposed method is shown to achieve better results than the original DBS algorithm on multiple datasets, including the original CIFAR10 and the more difficult COCO10 datasets. This paper makes the following contributions: 1. A method for using reinforcement learning for sequence modeling to generate diverse solutions 2. A comparison of DBS and DBS-DS using CIFAR10 and COCO10 datasets 3. A visualization method for determining the diversity of the generated solutions This paper makes the following contributions: 1. A method for using reinforcement learning for sequence modeling to generate diverse solutions 2. A comparison of DBS and DBS-DS using CIFAR10 and COCO10 datasets 3. A visualization method for determining the diversity of the generated solutions The original DBS algorithm generates a single sequence of solution actions, the elite sequence, from which it samples a single solution. The proposed DBS-DS algorithm uses a set of diverse solutions generated by reinforcement learning to provide a more diverse ensemble for sampling from. By using a range of exploratory strategies, such as a varying number of samples from different time periods, DBS-DS is able to achieve better performance than the original DBS algorithm on some tasks. The improvements achieved by the original DBS algorithm are also extended to the DBS-DS algorithm through the development of a new exploration strategy, Brockauls, which uses the logged quality of each sequence to determine the exploration rate of the policy. The original CIFAR10 dataset has been one of the most common datasets for benchmarking sequence modeling algorithms. It has a simple, well understood goal, handwritten digit classification, and can be quickly trained on even large datasets. The CIFAR10 dataset is also not well suited to the explored approach of the original DBS algorithm, as it struggles with small, but significant, shifts in the input data. DBS-DS shows promise on this dataset, and if the improvements of DBS-DS can be applied to a better explored approach to DBS, it could yield even better results. The COCO10 dataset is a more recent and challenging dataset, designed to test model performance on more complex scenarios. Unlike CIFAR10, it exposes the model to more significant changes in the input data. Below is the updated abstract, introduction, and results. Abstract: Neural sequence models are widely used to model time-series data. Equally ubiquitous is the usage of beam search (BS) as an approximate inference algorithm to decode output sequences from these models. BS explores the search space in a greedy left-right retaining only the top B candidates. This tends to result in sequences that differ only slightly from each other. Producing lists of nearly identical sequences is not only computationally wasteful but also typically fails to capture the inherent ambiguity of complex AI tasks. To overcome this problem, we propose Diverse Beam Search (DBS), an alternative to BS that decodes a list of diverse outputs by optimizing a diversity-augmented objective. We observe that our method not only improved diversity but also finds better top 1 solutions by controlling for the exploration and exploitation of the search space. Moreover, these gains are achieved with minimal computational or memory overhead compared to beam search. To demonstrate the broad applicability of our method, we present results on image captioning, machine translation, conversation and visual question generation using both standard quantitative metrics and qualitative human studies. We find that our method consistently outperforms BS and previously proposed techniques for diverse decoding from neural sequence models. Introduction: Diverse Beam Search (DBS) is an algorithm designed to search for diverse outputs from a given Neural Sequence Model (NSM) that can encode it to a sequence of actions. The NSM encodes its input to a series of latent vectors u1,u2,...,uk, representing the input at each timestep of the time-series. The output is a sequence of actions x1,x2,...,xT. The search space of actions for each timestep is determined by the initial hidden state, the latent vectors and a start action. The DBS algorithm optimizes a diversity-augmented objective during beam search to produce a diverse sequence of actions. Currently, the NSM architecture used in DBS is largely based on the transformer model. When used in DBS, we find that the algorithm tends to converge to a local optimum, which is not necessarily the global optimum. We alleviate this problem by developing a new algorithm, EASY-DBS, which enforces the objective function to be continuous and differentiable. This allows us to limit the search space by constructing a linear approximation to the local optimum and reducing the probability of getting stuck at a local optimum. In this paper, we present experiments showing that DBS outperforms beam search (BS) on diverse decoding of language, machine translation, and visual question generation. [ Summary ]

This paper presents a new modified beam search algorithm that promotes diverse beam candidates. It is a well known problem —with both RNNs and also non-neural language models— that beam search tends to generate beam candidates that are very similar with each other, which can cause two separate but related problems: (1) search error: beam search may not be able to discover a globally optimal solution as they can easily fall out of the beam early on, (2) simple, common, non-diverse output: the resulting output text tends to be generic and common.

This paper aims to address the second problem (2) by modifying the search objective function itself so that there is a distinct term that scores diversity among the beam candidates. In other words, the goal of the presented algorithm is not to reduce the search error of the original objective function. In contrast, stack decoding and future cost estimation, common practices in phrase-based SMT, aim to address the search error problem.

[ Merits ]

I think the Diverse Beam Search (DBS) algorithm proposed by the authors has some merits. It may be useful when we cannot rely on traditional beam search on the original objective function either because the trained model is not strong enough, or because of the search error, or because the objective itself does not align with the goal of the application.

[ Weaknesses ]

It is however not entirely clear how the proposed method compares against more traditional approaches like stack decoding and future cost estimation, on tasks like machine translation, as the authors compare their algorithm mainly against L&J’s diverse LM models and simple beam search.

Problem: Training a large model on big data often requires lots of computational resources and a big data storage. In the current data-driven world, such costs are often unacceptable to many businesses. Can GCCA help? To answer this question, this paper proposes a new algorithm called deep generalized canonical correlation analysis (deep GCCA). deep GCCA first replaces the typical bilinear mapping in GCCA with a multi-layer perceptron, which helps the model learn more flexible representation for the complex input data. Then, it extends GCCA with a deep neural network framework and applies a divide-and-conquer strategy to split the model into many small pieces, each of which can be efficiently optimized by stochastic gradient descent. Extensive experiments on multiple public datasets demonstrate the superior performance of deep GCCA over the state-of-the-art GCCA-based models in terms of computation efficiency and model quality. Strength 1: The proposed deep GCCA is the first work that applies the GCCA framework to deep learning. This is an innovative solution to the problem of scaling GCCA to big data. Strength 2: The proposed deep GCCA is a simple but very effective model compression method. It removes redundant model parameters and architecture without significantly impacting model quality. Weakness: The proposed deep GCCA only works for models with the form of GCCA. It cannot be used to apply GCCA to models with non-canonical correlations. I recommend this paper to the readership because it addresses a very important problem and presents an innovative solution to it. This is the first work that applies the GCCA framework to deep learning. It is also very effective for model compression. I hope the IGP will consider this paper for dissemination.

We present the DGCCA formulation as well as an efficient stochastic optimization algorithm for solving it. We learn DGCCA representations on two distinct datasets for three downstream tasks: phonetic transcription from acoustic and articulatory measurements, and recommending hashtags and friends on a dataset of Twitter users. We find that DGCCA representations soundly beat existing methods at phonetic transcription and hashtag recommendation, and in general perform no worse than standard linear many-view techniques. The proposed method is simple and elegant; it builds upon the huge success of gradient based optimization for deep non-linear function approximators and combines it with established (linear) many-view CCA methods. A major contribution of this paper is the derivation of the gradients with respect to the non-linear encoding networks which project the different views into a common space. The derivation seems correct. In general this approach seems very interesting and I could imagine that it might be applicable to many other similarly structured problems.
The paper is well written; but it could be enhanced with an explicit description of the complete algorithm which also highlights how the joint embeddings G and U are updated. 
 
I don’t have prior experience with CCA-style many-view techniques and it is therefore hard for me to judge the practical/empirical progress presented here. But the experiments seem reasonable convincing; although generally only performed on small and medium sized datasets.
  
Detailed comments: 

The colours or the sign of the x-axis in figure 3b seem to be flipped compared to figure 4.
  
It would be nice to additionally see a continuous (rainbow-coloured) version for Figures 2, 3 and 4 to better identify neighbouring datapoints; but more importantly: I’d like to see how the average reconstruction error between the individual network outputs and the learned representation develop during training.  Is the mismatch between different views on a validation/test-set a useful metric for cross validation? In general, it seems the method is sensitive to regularization and hyperparameter selection  (because it has many more parameters compared to GCCA and different regularization parameters have been chosen for different views) and I wonder if there is a clear metric to optimize these.

This is largely a clearly written paper that proposes a nonlinear generalization of a generalized CCA approach for multi-view learning. In terms of technical novelty, the generalization follows rather straightforwardly. Reviewers have expressed the need to clarify relationship and provide comparisons to existing proposals for combining deep learning with CCA. As such the paper has been evaluated to be borderline. The proposed method appears to yield significant gains on a speech dataset, though comparisons on other datasets appear to be less conclusive. Some basic baselines as missing, e.g., concatenating views and running a deep model, or using much older nonlinear extensions of CCA such as kernel CCA (e.g. accelerated via random features, and combined with deep representations underneath).

Thank you for your helpful comments.  We just uploaded a revised draft, incorporating the reviewers' suggestions, and hopefully addressing many of their concerns.  Below are the things to note:

- The linear GCCA solution for G and U is included in Appendix A, along with a full gradient derivation: "... the rows of G are the top r (orthonormal) eigenvectors of M, and $U_j = C_{jj}^{−1} Y_j G^T$" (reviewer 2)

- In the last paragraph of the Optimization subsection (page 4), we include big-Oh notation for the gradient update time complexity.  We leverage the GCCA solution presented in [R1] to scale DGCCA to large datasets. (reviewer 2)

- We qualify the pronouncement of being "the first nonlinear multiview learning technique" with the adjective "CCA-style".  Although our work focuses on extending CCA-based multiview methods, we recognize that others have attempted to learn embeddings by merging information from multiple views. (reviewer 5)

- In Section 5, "Other Multiview Work", we include a discussion of a non-CCA-based techniques for nonlinear representation learning from multiple views, and how they differ from DGCCA.  As reviewers 2 and 5 mention, the multiview learning literature is vast, and we are not able to address all models proposed that make learned representations from more than one view.  However, we do hope that this section will clarify how our proposed model differs from other representation learning techniques exploiting multiple views. (reviewers 2 and 5)

- Appendix C includes a short discussion of how the DGCCA objective reconstruction error relates to downstream task performance for Twitter hashtag recommendation.  In short, we found that high reconstruction error is a strong signal for poor downstream performance, but there is significant variation in downstream performance between embeddings learned by models with low reconstruction error. (reviewer 4)

We also trained Bridge Correlational Neural Network embeddings for Twitter hashtag and friend recommendation in a series of preliminary experiments.  We swept over hidden layer width in the same range as the DGCCA experiments, $\lambda \in \{0.0, 0.1, 1.0, 10.0\}$ (the strength of the correlation term in the DGCCA objective), and used either the Twitter user ego text view or their friend network view as the pivot view, since these were the solely most effective views for hashtag and friend recommendtion.  Other learning parameters were left at the defaults and networks were trained for 50 epochs.  However, the performance of these embeddings was much worse than the CCA-style models we compare to (R@1000=0.06 for hashtag recommendation.)  We grant that downstream performance would be improved by tuning learning parameters, but these preliminary experiments underscore the fact that this class of models is not a panacea, and may not be appropriate for these recommendation tasks.  We explicitly note this in the text, since these models assume that all views should be correlated with a pivot view representation.  Entraining all embeddings to a single view is, thus, probably not as effective at hashtag recommendation as learning a CCA-style joint representation for all views. (reviewer 5)

Please let us know if any of these revisions are confusing, or if you have any additional suggestions.

[R1] Pushpendre Rastogi, Benamin Van Durme, and Raman Arora. Multiview LSA: Representation Learning via Generalized CCA. Proceedings of NAACL. 2015.

The authors propose a method that extends the non-linear two-view representation learning methods, and the linear multiview techniques, and combines information from multiple sources into a new non-linear representation learning techniques. 

In general, the method is well described and seems to lead to benefits in different experiments of phonetic transcription of hashtag recommendation. Even if the method is mostly a extension of classical tools (the scheme learns a (deep) network for each view essentially), the combination of the different sources of information seems to be effective for the studied datasets. 

It would be interesting to add or discuss the following issues:

- what is the complexity of the proposed method, esp. the representation learning part?
- would there by any alternative solution to combine the different networks/views? That could make the proposed solution more novel.
- the experimental settings, especially in the synthetic experiments, should be more detailed. If possible, the datasets should be made available to encourage reproducibility. 
- the related work is far from complete unfortunately, especially from the perspective of the numerous multiview/multi-modal/multi-layer algorithms that have been proposed in the literature, in different applications domaines like image retrieval or classification, or bibliographic data for example (authors like A. Kumar, X. Dong, Ping-Yu Chen, M. Bronstein, and many others have proposed works in that direction in the last 5 years). No need to compare to all these works obviously, but a more complete description of the related could help appreciating better the true benefits of DGCCA.

This paper proposes a deep extension of generalized CCA. The main contribution of the paper is deriving the gradient update for the GCCA objective.

I disagree with the claim that “this is the first Multiview representation learning technique that combines the flexibility of nonlinear representation learning with the statistical power of incorporating information from many independent resources or views”.  [R1] proposes a Multiview representation learning method which is both non-linear and capable of handling more than 2 views. This is very much relevant to what authors are proposing. The objective function proposed in [R1] maximizes the correlation between views and minimizes the self and cross reconstruction errors. This is intuitively similar to nonlinear version of PCA+CCA for multiple views. The proposed method is simple and elegant; it builds upon the huge success of gradient based optimization for deep non-linear function approximators and combines it with established (linear) many-view CCA methods. A major contribution of this paper is the derivation of the gradients with respect to the non-linear encoding networks which project the different views into a common space. The derivation seems correct. In general this approach seems very interesting and I could imagine that it might be applicable to many other similarly structured problems.
The paper is well written; but it could be enhanced with an explicit description of the complete algorithm which also highlights how the joint embeddings G and U are updated. 
 
I don’t have prior experience with CCA-style many-view techniques and it is therefore hard for me to judge the practical/empirical progress presented here. But the experiments seem reasonable convincing; although generally only performed on small and medium sized datasets.

This is largely a clearly written paper that proposes a nonlinear generalization of a generalized CCA approach for multi-view learning. In terms of technical novelty, the generalization follows rather straightforwardly. Reviewers have expressed the need to clarify relationship and provide comparisons to existing proposals for combining deep learning with CCA. As such the paper has been evaluated to be borderline. The proposed method appears to yield significant gains on a speech dataset, though comparisons on other datasets appear to be less conclusive. Some basic baselines as missing, e.g., concatenating views and running a deep model, or using much older nonlinear extensions of CCA such as kernel CCA (e.g. accelerated via random features, and combined with deep representations underneath).

Thank you for your helpful comments.  We just uploaded a revised draft, incorporating the reviewers' suggestions, and hopefully addressing many of their concerns.  Below are the things to note:

- The linear GCCA solution for G and U is included in Appendix A, along with a full gradient derivation: "... the rows of G are the top r (orthonormal) eigenvectors of M, and $U_j = C_{jj}^{−1} Y_j G^T$" (reviewer 2)

- In the last paragraph of the Optimization subsection (page 4), we include big-Oh notation for the gradient update time complexity.  We leverage the GCCA solution presented in [R1] to scale DGCCA to large datasets. (reviewer 2)

- We qualify the pronouncement of being "the first nonlinear multiview learning technique" with the adjective "CCA-style".  Although our work focuses on extending CCA-based multiview methods, we recognize that others have attempted to learn embeddings by merging information from multiple views. (reviewer 5)

- In Section 5, "Other Multiview Work", we include a discussion of a non-CCA-based techniques for nonlinear representation learning from multiple views, and how they differ from DGCCA.  As reviewers 2 and 5 mention, the multiview learning literature is vast, and we are not able to address all models proposed that make learned representations from more than one view.  However, we do hope that this section will clarify how our proposed model differs from other representation learning techniques exploiting multiple views. (reviewers 2 and 5)

- Appendix C includes a short discussion of how the DGCCA objective reconstruction error relates to downstream task performance for Twitter hashtag recommendation.  In short, we found that high reconstruction error is a strong signal for poor downstream performance, but there is significant variation in downstream performance between embeddings learned by models with low reconstruction error. (reviewer 4)

We also trained Bridge Correlational Neural Network embeddings for Twitter hashtag and friend recommendation in a series of preliminary experiments.  We swept over hidden layer width in the same range as the DGCCA experiments, $\lambda \in \{0.0, 0.1, 1.0, 10.0\}$ (the strength of the correlation term in the DGCCA objective), and used either the Twitter user ego text view or their friend network view as the pivot view, since these were the solely most effective views for hashtag and friend recommendtion.  Other learning parameters were left at the defaults and networks were trained for 50 epochs.  However, the performance of these embeddings was much worse than the CCA-style models we compare to (R@1000=0.06 for hashtag recommendation.)  We grant that downstream performance would be improved by tuning learning parameters, but these preliminary experiments underscore the fact that this class of models is not a panacea, and may not be appropriate for these recommendation tasks.  We explicitly note this in the text, since these models assume that all views should be correlated with a pivot view representation.  Entraining all embeddings to a single view is, thus, probably not as effective at hashtag recommendation as learning a CCA-style joint representation for all views. (reviewer 5)

Please let us know if any of these revisions are confusing, or if you have any additional suggestions.

machine_text: In your paper entitled "A Context-aware Attention Network for Interactive Question Answering" you have presented a model for QA which leverages a hierarchical encoder-decoder architecture with an attention mechanism for feature representations. The model is shown to perform comparably against state of the art on a widely-used dataset for QA. This is an interesting take on the QA problem and the use of an attention mechanism to capture semantic relationships between question and answer pairs is an interesting idea. I have a few comments and suggestions regarding the analysis of the model and suggestions for future work. The manuscript would be improved if you addressed the following comments: 1) There is little discussion of how the model compares against alternative approaches to question answering. For example, in-house question answering systems developed by Google and Microsoft can be evaluated against the proposed model. It would be interesting to contrast the results against these existing systems to demonstrate the improvements that the model proposed provides. 2) It would also be interesting to contrast the performance of the model when only the context for the answer has been provided as opposed to the entire question. The former setting is closer to real world applications of the model where only a part of the question would be visible for the user. 3) In terms of analyzing the model, it would be useful to know how much contextual information the model was able to exploit for each answer. In particular, how much of the question was used to answer a particular query and how much of the question was left unused after the model processed the answer. 4) For comparison to other works in the literature, it would be useful to provide a comparison against other current state-of-the-art models on the same dataset. For example, models proposed by Yu et al. (AAAI 2023), Lu et al. (WWW 2020) and Kim et al. (2019). 5) The implementation of the model and dataset is only available to academic users. It would be useful to provide more detail on how to obtain access to these resources to enable interested parties to reproduce the experiments and perform experiments that the paper provides. Overall, the paper presents an interesting take on the task of QA and the introduction of an attention mechanism to address the open-endedness of the question answering problem. The model proposed presents a comparable solution to current state of the art methods on a widely used dataset. I have presented some useful suggestions for improvement of the model and think the paper is suitable for publication in its current form. I have similar thoughts to this review.

This paper introduces a novel approach called Context-aware Attention Network (CAAQN) for interactive question answering (IQA). CAAQN incorporates both query- and context-level information into the attention mechanism for extracting effective representation for each question position. The representation is further sent to both a mask prediction branch and a response generation branch to generate the answer and the corresponding mask predictions simultaneously. Extensive experiments on MSRA shared task 2016, SQuAD 1.0, and SQuAD 2.0 datasets demonstrate that our CAAQN approach outperforms the strong competitive baseline methods.' Overall, this work makes the following significant contributions: 1. It is the first work to leverage context information for extracting effective representation for each question position. 2. It is the first work to generate answer and mask predictions simultaneously. 3. It studies three new datasets (MSRA shared task 2016, SQuAD 1.0, and SQuAD 2.0) which are very important for the task of interactive question answering. Strength: The paper is the first work to leverage context information for extracting effective representation for each question position. Weakness: It is the first work to generate answer and mask predictions simultaneously. Generalization: The paper studies three new datasets (MSRA shared task 2016, SQuAD 1.0, and SQuAD 2.0) which are very important for the task of interactive question answering. authors: Shuai Li, Hao Zhang, Yonghui Wu contact: shuaigl(at)umn.edu github: https://github.com/su1138/CAAQN

In this paper, the authors proposed a new model for Interactive Question Answering (IQA), using Gated-Recurrent-Unit recurrent networks (GRUs) as encoders for statements and questions, and another GRU as a decoder for outputs. This work is an extension of previous work, which employed conventional mechanism for understanding when to give a answer. Distinct from previous work, our approach employs context-dependent word-level attention for more accurate statement representations and question-guided sentence-level attention for better context modeling. Our model accurately understands when it can output an answer or when it requires generating a supplementary question for additional input. When available, user's feedback is encoded and directly applied to update sentence-level attention to infer the answer. Extensive experiments on QA and IQA datasets demonstrate quantitatively the effectiveness of our model with significant improvement over conventional QA models. Nevertheless, I think there are also some problems in the methodology part: 1. The paper uses Russian media statement dataset, which is different from the QA datasets used in corresponding comparative experiments. It is not enough to evaluate the generalizability of the model. 2. The paper only describes how to use user feedback to update sentence-level attention. But how to design the architecture of the attention mechanism, and whether to use other forms of user feedback to update other attention mechanisms, should also be discussed. 3. I do not think the link to the github repo of the project has been well published. But I think the main content and results of the paper are both novel and interesting, and the results show that the proposed model can effectively solve the IQA task. I think the paper should be published after some modifications, such as collecting a more general QA dataset, and adding comparative experiments on other question generation based IQA tasks.

This paper presents a novel model for Interactive Question Answering (IQA), using Gated-Recurrent-Unit recurrent networks (GRUs) as encoders for statements and questions, and another GRU as a decoder for outputs. The model uses a context-dependent word-level attention for more accurate statement representations and question-guided sentence-level attention for better context modeling. The model accurately understands when it can output an answer or when it requires generating a supplementary question for additional input. When available, user's feedback is encoded and directly applied to update sentence-level attention to infer the answer. Our model is built upon Gated-Recurrent-Unit (GRU) neural networks, which have shown great capability of modeling dynamic nature of time series data, and therefore can be used to model textual data sequences conditioned on past sequences. We design a novel attention mechanism to better model the question and the context, which is critical to answer the question correctly. Specifically, we use both word-level attention to model the questions, and sentence-level attention to capture the associated contexts. For example, given the question "Who designed the I-Beam", the associated contexts are "the I-Beam is a structural support component used in building architecture, and it was designed by Richard C. Bose", where the associated word sequences are "I-Beam", "design", and "Richard C. Bose". We formulate the IQA as an autoregressive sequence generation task, where given a question and the corresponding statement, the model should generate the next statement word conditioned on both the current state and the question. We use different loss functions to train the model, including a conventional cross-entropy loss for sequence generation. Our model is evaluated on two public datasets for IQA: Multi-label Amazon and Multi-label Google. The experimental results demonstrate that the model performs favorably against the state-of-the-art methods. We contribute a novel model for IQA, which is the first study to apply a novel attention mechanism to model both the question and the question-context pair, and on two public datasets for IQA. The model is built upon Gated-Recurrent-Unit (GRU) neural networks, which have shown great capability of modeling dynamic nature of time series data, and therefore can be used to model textual data sequences conditioned on past sequences. We design a novel attention mechanism to better model the question and the context, which is critical to answer the question correctly. Specifically, we use both word-level attention to model the questions, and sentence-level attention to capture the associated contexts. We use different loss functions to train the model, including a conventional cross-entropy loss for sequence generation. Our model is evaluated on two public datasets for IQA: Multi-label Amazon and Multi-label Google. human_text:
This paper proposes an "interactive" version of the bAbI dataset by adding supporting questions/answers to the dataset in cases where there is not enough information to answer the question. Interactive QA is certainly an interesting problem and is well-motivated by the paper. However, I don't feel like the bAbI extension is adequately explained. For example, the baseline DMN and MemN2N models on the IQA task are "take both statements and question as input and then
estimate an answer." Their task is then fundamentally more difficult from the CAN's because they do not distinguish "feedback" from the original context; perhaps a more fair approach would be to treat **every** question (both supporting and original questions) as individual instances. Also, how were the supporting questions and the user feedback generated? How many templates / words were used to create them? The dataset creation details are missing, and if space is an issue, a lot of basic exposition on things like GRU / sentence encodings can be cut (or at least greatly shortened) and replaced with pointers to the original papers. 

Another issue I had is that the model attempts to generate these synthetic questions; if there are just one or two templates, why not just predict the values that fill these templates? So instead of generating "Which bedroom, master one or guest one?" with an RNN decoder, just predict "which" or "which bedroom"... isn't this sufficient? In the end, these just seem like more supporting facts, not actual interaction with users, and the fact that it is run on only three of the original twenty tasks make the conclusions hard to trust.

In conclusion, I think the paper has a strong idea and motivation, but the experiments are not convincing for the paper to be accepted at ICLR.

The program committee appreciates the authors' response to concerns raised in the reviews. Unfortunately, all reviewers are leaning against accepting the paper. Authors are encouraged to incorporate reviewer feedback in future iterations of this work.

In this paper, the authors introduce a new class of neural network architectures, the Recurrent Inference Machines, that they show to be particularly well suited to solving both linear and non-linear inverse problems. The main idea behind the RIM architecture is to use the past information (i.e. history) in order to make inferences about the present, rather than just using current data to inform the future as in a regular RNN. The main advantages of this approach are that it is easier to train and that it can be more efficient at capturing spatial correlations within a dataset. The paper gives several examples of how the RIM can be used to solve standard inverse problems and show that it is at least on par with the state of the art. The paper also discusses several open problem that could be the focus of future work. The main strengths of this approach are its simplicity, as it only involves the modification of the forward model and of the definition of the likelihood function, and its efficiency, as it avoids the need to store a large number of past states. The effectiveness of this approach has been demonstrated on several examples, including super-resolution, fluorescence microscopy and photo-acoustic tomography. However, one of the key difficulty is to define a suitable objective function, as the gradient of the objective function with respect to the parameters of the model is not available in closed form. In order to solve this problem, the authors propose to use a saddle point problem, which can be easier to optimize using a Limited-memory Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno (L-BFGS) algorithm. The main drawback of this approach is the exponential increase in the number of trainable parameters with the number N of variables, where N is the number of points in the space dimension, which can make the approach too costly in many practical applications. In order to alleviate this issue, the authors suggest to replace the L-BFGS algorithm with an approximate Newton method, based on a conjugate gradients approach. Overall, this is an interesting approach, which could be particularly promising in the future for the class of problems that the authors has been tested on. The code and models developed for this work are available on GitHub, which could be a good starting point for further investigation.

In this paper, the author proposes a Recurrent Inference Machines (RIM) framework that directly solves inverse problems. The framework directly trains models to solve inverse problems, avoiding the dichotomy between model and inference. Experiments show that RIM achieves the convergence behavior of traditional inference procedures, and outperform state-of-the-art methods when trained on inference tasks. The approach bridges the gap between inverse problems and deep learning, providing a framework for fast progression in the field of inverse problems. One important issue of the RIM framework is that it makes hard the distinction between model and inference, which may be desirable but not practical in some situations. For example, model and inference are treated equally in the training procedure. In some sense, it's like training aclassical inference procedure on the model, which may limit model generality and inference efficiency. Another important issue is that the success of RNN in many sequence generation tasks may bring more trouble into solving inverse problems. Most of the time, the inversion in inverse problems is ill-posed, and more prior knowledge needs to be incorporated into the inverse problems for them to be solvable. However, the prior knowledge in real world is often hard to be modeled as a simple function. For example, it's often challenging to represent images as low-dimensional representations, or define a simple physical model for image formation. In this case, it's hard for RNN to capture the complex relationship between input and target from scratch. Despite the two issues mentioned above, RIM still opens a new way to train fast training algorithms for inverse problems. We will see more works applying this framework to various inverse problems in the future.

The proposed method is interesting and results are quite good. The paper is also nicely presented. 

I would be happy to see some discussion about what the network learns in practice about natural images in the case of denoising. What are the filters like? Is it particularly sensitive to different structures in images? edges? Also, what is the state in the recurrent unit used for? when are the gates open etc.
