This paper presents a thorough analysis of different methods to do curriculum learning. The major issue I have with it is that the dataset used seems very specific and does not necessarily justified, as mentioned by AnonReviewer3. It would have been great to see experiments on more standard tasks. Also, I really can't understand how the performance of FFNN models can be so good, please elaborate on this (see last comment).
However, the paper is well written, the comparisons of the described methods are interesting and would probably apply to some other datasets as well.

The paper is way too long (18 pages!). Please reduce it or move some of the results to an appendix section.

The method described is extremely similar to the one described in Reinforcement learning neural turing machines (Zaremba et al., 2016,

This is an empirical paper which compares three different instantiations of a kind of incremental/curriculum learning for sequences.
 
 The reviews from R1 and R3 (which gave confidence scores of 4) were negative. The main concerns addressed by the reviewers:
 * Paper is too long -- 17 pages -- and length is due to experiments (e.g. transfer learning) which are tangential to the main message of the paper (R3, R1) 
 * Lack of novelty (R3)
 * Tests only on single, synthetic, small dataset and questioning the claim that this new synthetic dataset is helpful to the community (R3, R1)
 
 However, R3 and R1 both pointed out that they found the ablation studies interesting. R4 (who gave a confidence score of 3) was gave a more positive score but also expressed similar concerns with R1 & R3 (page length, similarity to existing work, dataset too specific and not necessarily justified).
 
 The author argued for the novelty of the paper, agreed to reduce the paper length and also argued that the data was indeed helpful (giving a specific case of another researcher who was extending the data). The author also provided a "twitter trail" countering the argument that the dataset was created for the sole purpose of showing that the method works.
 
 After engaging the reviewers in discussion, R4 admitted they were originally too generous with their score and downgraded to 5. The AC has decided that, while the paper has merits as acknowledged by the reviewers, it's not strong enough for acceptance in its present form. The AC encourages the author to work on an improved version (perhaps with experiments on an additional real dataset) and organize it with the audience in mind.

Two reviewers had questions about which problems the approach is expected to work for. I did not find the time to do further experiments, but I did in the mean time think about when the approach can be expected to confer benefit. When there are long range dependencies where it is necessary to learn relations with a substantial part of the history, it is to be expected that gradually growing the length of the history over which relations are learned can bring benefit. 
As noted, I am willing to reduce the paper to the suggested 8 pages, and use an appendix for remaining material.

First up, I want to point out that this paper is really long. Like 17 pages long -- without any supplementary material. While ICLR does not have an official page limit, it would be nice if authors put themselves in the reviewer's shoes and did not take undue advantage of this rule. Having 1 or 2 pages in addition to the conventional 8 page limit is ok, but more than doubling the pages is quite unfair. 

Now for the review: The paper proposes a new artificial dataset for sequence learning. I call it artificial because it was artificially generated from the original MNIST dataset which is a smallish dataset of real images of handwritten digits. In addition to the dataset, the authors propose to train recurrent networks using a schedule over the length of the sequence, which they call "incremental learning". The experiments show that their proposed schedule is better than not having any schedule on this data set. Furthermore, they also show that their proposed schedule is better than a few other intuitive schedules. The authors verify this by doing some ablation studies over the model on the proposed dataset. 

I have following issues with this paper: 

-- I did not find anything novel in this paper. The proposed incremental learning schedule is nothing new and is a natural thing to try when learning sequences. Similar idea have already been tried by a number of authors, including Bengio 2015, and Ranzato 2015. The only new piece of work is the ablation studies which the authors conduct to tease out and verify that indeed the improvement in performance is due to the curriculum used. 

-- Furthermore, the authors only test their hypothesis on a single dataset which they propose and is artificially generated. Why not use it on a real sequential dataset, such as, language modeling. Does the technique not work in that scenario? In fact I am quite positive that for language modeling where the vocabulary size is huge, the performance gains will be no where close to the 74% reported in the paper.

-- I'm not convinced about the value of having this artificial dataset. Already there are so many real world sequential dataset available, including in text, speech, finance and other areas. What exactly does this dataset bring to the table is not super clear to me. While having another dataset may not be a bad thing in itself, I almost felt that this dataset was created for the sole purpose of making the proposed ideas work. It would have been so much better had the authors shown experiments on other datasets. 

-- As I said, the paper is way too long. A significant part of the length of the paper is due to a collection of experiments which are completely un-related to the main message of the paper. For instance, the experiment in Section 6.2 is completely unrelated to the story of the paper. Same is true with the transfer learning experiments of Section 6.4.

The submitted paper proposes a new way of learning sequence predictors. In the lines of incremental learning and curriculum learning, easier samples are presented first and the complexity is increased during training. The particularity here is that the complexity is defined as the length of the sequences given for training, the premise being is that longer sequences are harder to learn, since they need a more complex internal representation.

The targeted application is sequence prediction from primed prefixes, tested on a single dataset, which the authors extract themselves from MNIST.

The idea in the paper is interesting and worth reading. There are also many interesting aspects of evaluation part, as the authors perform several ablation studies to rule out side-effects of the tests. The proposed learning strategy is compared to other strategies.

However, my biggest concern is still with evaluation. The authors tested the method on a single dataset, which is non standard and derived from MNIST. Given the general nature of the claim, in order to confirm the interest of the proposed algorithm, it need to be tested on other datasets, public datasets, and on a different application.

The paper is too long and should be trimmed significantly.

The transfer learning part (from prediction to classification) is a different story and I do not see a clear connection to the main contribution of the paper.

The presentation and organization of the paper could be improved. It is quite sequentially written and sometimes reads like a student's report.

machine_text: The paper is in principle an interesting and good initial exploration of the skip-gram model, but with some limitations that could limit the applicability of the model and the scope of the conclusions drawn. 1. The choice of the word analogy task for the evaluation is problematic, because it measures mostly the semantic similarity, and not the syntactic similarity. The two names can be similar in terms of meaning, but the two sentences, with the same meaning, may be very different in terms of grammaticality. For instance, the names Brad and Brian can be seen as an analogy because they both begin with a B. But the corresponding sentences "Brad is Brian" and "Brian is Brad" are syntactically very different. So the accuracy of the model on this evaluation metric should be considered with care and should not be used as a general measure of the quality of the generated text. 2. Another important metric to consider is the BLEU score. It is based on the same principle as the LLM based metrics, namely that a human expert would assign a higher score to outputs that generate outputs that are very similar to the ground-truth. But like LLM, BLEU does not take into account the syntax of the output text. Thus the two outputs "Brad is Brian" and "Brian is Brad" can have the same score on the BLEU metric even if they are very different from a linguistic point of view. For this reason, BLEU cannot be considered as a rigorous and objective evaluation metric. However, these two problems could be challenging to solve, because the metrics based on syntactic correctness (like the LLM) or based on similarity of meaning (like BLEU) do not exist yet. So the only way to evaluate the quality of the results is to generate new text and see how users evaluate this new text. In this case, I think the paper has a strong message since the name of the company is a very meaningful and well-known word, and the decoder correctly generated the word "skip". The author could decide to refine the model, for example by choosing a different evaluation metric and a more precise evaluation method to see if the results are still good from a linguistic point of view.

The paper has a very clear problem statement which is network data analysis using graph embeddings. The authors provide a detailed overview of the problem and also the use case of medical image graph analysis for healthcare. The authors then give an overview of theSkipGram model which is a neural network model that learns word embeddings and then show how to apply this to graph embeddings. They provide code to perform this training on a dataset of connected users (known as friends-of-friends) to test the model. The model was able to learn useful embeddings even from small training sets (as low as 500 data points) and generalises well to new data points (even on a graph that was not seen during training). The model performed best when using path embeddings which were created using the Louvre painting path embedding method. They then show how to apply the model to a more general use case of computational graph analysis. The model was then able to learn useful embeddings for nodes that were not part of the training set (i.e. new users). The model has a number of strengths: 1. The model is simple to train using standard machine learning libraries and does not require complex parameter tuning. 2. The embeddings preserve the local structure of the graph, so that nearby nodes are close in the embedded space (this is demonstrated by performing k-means on the embedded graph and then plotting the resulting clusters). 3. The model is easily extendible to new types of graph. The model also has some limitations: 1. The quality of the embeddings degrades as the training set size decreases. 2. The model can over-fit the training data if not applied carefully (e.g. by performing cross validation on a random subset of nodes) Overall, the model has many of the required properties for performing network data analysis using graph embeddings and this paper provides a useful baseline method for performing this task. The strengths of the model are the simple training and the preservation of local structure. The local structure allows for very fast nearest neighbour search. The local structure is also easy to understand for non-technical users. The disadvantages are the low quality of the embedding for small training sets and the over-fitting problem that can occur if the model is not applied carefully.

The paper makes an attempt to apply the deep learning technology to learning feature representation for graph-structured data, the approach is interesting and has good practicability. However, there are some shortcomings in the design of the experiment, for example: 1. The data and implementation setup: The paper conducts the experiment on some public data sets which are freely available, but the detailed data and implementation setup are not provided, such as the graph representation, the structure of the training data, the specific settings of the experiments, and the evaluation metric, making it hard for others to reproduce the experiment results. 2. The evaluation metric: Only some of the experiment results are presented and compared with other methods, and there is no clear explanation for choosing this specific comparison method and those specific results to show the effectiveness of the proposed approach, which will be a big barrier for adoption of the proposed approach in the real world. 3. The generalization ability of the model: The model is evaluated on some specific data sets, and the generalization ability to other data sets is unclear. 4. The parameters of the model: The parameters and application prospect of the proposed model need to be further studied and verified. The model proposed in the paper has good application prospects, but there are some shortcomings that need to be improved. I hope the authors can modify the paper according to these comments and do some experiments to verify the effectiveness of the model on more data sets. Some important issues that need to be considered when evaluating the model are as follows: 1. We cannot evaluate a model by only focusing on the accuracy of the test set. This metric may be invalid because the model has not been exposed to the test set information. It is only concerned with the model’s ability to accurately classify the test set. Therefore, at least three methods need to be applied, such as the area under the curve (AUC) of the receiver operating curve (AUROC), a receiver operating curve (ROC) and a Spearman rank correlation coefficient (rho) to evaluate the results. 2. The learned vector representation depends on the types of model and algorithm, the specific implementation and the application purpose of the model. The author only provides the source code and the type of implementation of the model, so the third party does not have many choices about implementing the same model in a different way to meet their own purposes. Some suggestions about the implementation of the model include: 1. Record the running time of the algorithm for various kinds of hardware. 2. Storing the graph representation of the solution and the parameters of the model. The article makes a good attempt to analyze the proposed model. I hope the author will pay more attention to the application prospect of the proposed model and the evaluation metric of the experiment results, and try to reproduce the experiment results on other data sets and achieve better results. ## Authors Zhao-Ping Huang, Xiaolin Li, Jing Zhang ## Acknowledgement This research was supported by National Natural Science Foundation of China (No.61876022) and Higher Education Commission of Pakistan. ## Reference 1. The paper “Skip-graph: Learning graph embeddings with an encoder-decoder model” studies a method for obtaining a generic feature representation for a graph using an unsupervised approach. The neural encoder-decoder model is a method that has been used in the natural language processing domain to learn feature representations of sentences. In our proposed approach, we train the encoder-decoder model to predict the random walk sequence of neighboring regions in a graph given a random walk along a particular region. The goal is to map subgraphs — as represented by their random walks — that are structurally and functionally similar to nearby locations in feature space. We evaluate the learned graph vectors using several real-world datasets on the graph classification task. The proposed model is able to achieve good results against state-of- the-art techniques. The main contributions of this paper are as follows: 1. The proposed model can be applied to any kind of graph, does not need task-specific parameters, and can also be extended to other graph representation learning tasks. 2. The model is capable of learning low-dimensional and semantic graph embeddings that retain high-level semantic meaning from the raw graph. 3. We introduce two techniques for addressing the zero-shot learning problem in the proposed model. Zero-shot learning is the capability to recognize graphs that are similar but with no known labels in a large collective dataset. 4. The proposed model can also be used to generate low-dimensional and semantic embeddings for graphs, and the learned embeddings can be utilized for various graph tasks. The paper provides a high-level overview of the proposed method and contains experiments showing that the proposed method is a useful tool for learning low-dimensional and semantic feature representation for graphs.
human_text:
The paper presents a method to learn graph embeddings in a unsupervised way using random walks. It is well written and the execution appears quite accurate. The area of learning whole graph representations does not seem to be very well explored in general, and the proposed approach enjoys having very few competitors.

In a nutshell, the idea is to linearize the graph using random walks and to compute the embedding of the central segment of each walk using the skip-thought criterion. Being not an expert in biology, I can not comment whether or not this makes sense, but the gains reported in Table 2 are quite significant. 

An anonymous public comment compared this work to a number of others in which the problem of learning representations of nodes is considered. While this is arguably a different goal, one natural baseline would be to pool these representations using mean- or max- pooling. It would very interesting to do such a comparison, especially given that the considered approach heavily relies on pooling (see Figure 3(c))

To sum up, I think it is a nice paper, and with more baselines I would be ready to further increase the numerical score.

The idea of applying skip-graphs to this graph domain to learn embeddings is good. The results demonstrate that this approach is competitive, but do not show a clear advantage. This is difficult, as the variety of approaches in this area is rapidly increasing. But comparisons to other methods could be improved, notably deep graph kernels.

Dear reviewers, thank you very much for all the insightful comments and suggestions. Please find below a summary of our response to each of the points that were raised. Please note that we have paraphrased some of the comments and combined similar ones.

Anonymous Reviewer 2:

Comment 1. Use the same classifier for all the compared methods.

We have updated the results in our paper to reflect the changes from using a common classifier for all the compared methods. The changes can be found in section 3.2.

Comment 2. Use mean- or max-pooling to aggregate the embeddings learned by methods such as DeepWalk or node2vec and include this as a baseline.

The paper has been updated to include results from Deepwalk which was added as an additional baseline. Changes were made to sections 3.2 and 3.3.

Anonymous Reviewer 3:

Comment 3. Provide more information about the exact values of the parameters that were used in the grid search.

The information have been added to the paper. This can be found in section 3.2.

Anonymous Reviewer 1:

Comment 4. Need more experiment to demonstrate the power of their feature extraction methods. (Clustering, Search, Prediction etc.). Only comparing the classification accuracy by using the proposed method is not enough.

We plan to extend the experiments by using the embedding for graph clustering and graph search tasks in future works/journal extension. Due to the suggested page limit of ICLR, it is not easy to add these additional experiments without deleting some existing results in the paper. In the existing results, we have demonstrated the power of the embedding through prediction tasks and visualization of the embedding.

Comment 5. Presentation of the paper is weak. There are lots of typos and unclear statements. 

The latest version of the paper has been proofread by several individuals and to the best of our knowledge we have removed the major typos and/or unclear statements. 

Comment 6. What is the difference from graph kernel methods? The comparison with graph kernel is missing. 

We agree that the problem studied in the deep graph kernel paper seems to be very similar, or even the same, to the one we are studying. However, the underlying approach is slightly different and we argue that that in itself is a good motivation for the work as there has not been too many work published in the area. We use an encoder-decoder model which has not been used, and for one we can identify functionally similar subgraphs. 

Regrettably, due to time constraints we are unable to add a comparison with Deep Graph Kernels. However, we have tested against methods that have been shown to achieve good results on the type of graphs we used (ECFP and NeuralFPS) and we have also tested against DeepWalk. The introduction section has been updated to include some discussion on this.

Anonymous Reviewer 4:

Comment 7. Comparisons with recent work like LINE and node2vec are missing. You can compare them easily by applying the same aggregation strategy to their node embeddings.

We have already addressed the comment of a previous reviewer and have included DeepWalk as a baseline. We did not add comparisons against node2vec and LINE as these, in general, belong to the same family of methods.

Comment 8. As the current datasets are small (e.g., the average number of nodes per graph is around 30), it would be great to explore larger graph datasets to further investigate the method. 

To compensate in a way, we tested the method on four different molecular graph datasets. Regrettably, we are unable to add experiments on more datasets at the moment.

Comment 9. The description about how to split the random walk sequence into 3 sub-sequences is missing. Also, the line “l_min >= (n_k - 1), … >= l_max” in section 2.2.2 is a mistake.

Section 2.2.2 has been updated to correct this. Thank you very much for pointing this out.

The paper Deep Character-Level Neural Machine Translation By Learning Morphology addresses the problem of translating sentences with characters as tokens, not words. It does this by first training a deep network on word pieces, then using the word piece outputs to identify the characters in the original sentence and using those character identities to lookup character-level translation tables, then finally re-encoding the translated sentence to word pieces. The character-level translation table is created by encoding the entire character set as a single character, then clustering the translations into groups. This means the model has to represent each translation as a separate character. This could be viewed as a weakness since the model must represent each translation as a different character, instead of word, which would be advantageous for describing longer concepts. It should also be noted that most character-level translation tools provide syntax translation, not semantic meaning. * Strength: the model creates translation tables based on character identities. This allows it to handle characters without lexical representation (no-Nul character, digits, etc..). * Weakness: the model must represent each translation as a separate character, instead of word, which would be advantageous for describing longer concepts. Also, most character-level translation tools provide syntax translation, not semantic meaning. Overall this is a well-crafted and clearly written paper. The potential benefit of the model is clearly explained, as is the weakness of the approach. I would recommend this paper for consideration for the ML category of the next System Simulation and Analysis Best Paper Awards.

Overall this is a nice paper. I have some comments and questions. In your model, you train the 6 characters in parallel. However, you evaluate it only on the token level, which may not be optimal. In fact, in terms of time complexity, character-level decoding is worse than word-level decoding, since the length of character is large (in your case, there are six of them). However, in terms of the BLEU score, character-level decoding may outperform word-level decoding, since you can find more neighbor words per input word by searching among the 6 candidates. In this regard, I would like to ask you how well does this model perform on the sentence-level evaluation? Another thing I noticed is that in order to prevent the large vocabulary problem, the authors use a very effective solution: after each position of the input word, an extra's' character is appended, which serves as a "placeholder" for the future decoding of that word. However, this method is not without issues. For example, in the sentence "Watching TV is always green", because there is no's' character at the end of the second word, the decoder will simply skip it, leading to incorrect translation "Watching TV is always green*" instead of "Watching TV is always green", where "*" represents the omitted word. To tackle this problem, another approach is to limit the number of's' characters that can be inserted. However, this can limit the model's capability to generate potential valid sequences. For example, in the sentence "Watching TV is always fun", when there are no valid words to fill in the blank, the decoder will simply replace it with a's' character, which in fact makes more sense in this sentence. What if we could make the model learn the valid and invalid words from the examples and properly weight them during training? These two problems can be solved by using the connection between character-level and word-level n-gram statistics, i.e, the former can help to reduce the latter. In other words, if we can get the word-level n-grams during training, it is then possible to do an n-gram look-up on the character level. Here is one example: the word "always" always follows a noun, and thus we can encode this prior knowledge into the word-level n-gram statistics, and then during the inference, as long as we see a noun in the n-gram, we can look up the character n-gram from the word-level n-gram. This method has been widely used in the field of morphology acquisition in previous decades. Finally, as for the implementation, although you achieve a score that is comparable to the existing state-of-the-art phrase-based systems, there are some techniques you can try to further reduce the training time. For example, instead of building a 6-layer model, you can start with a 4-layer model, and at the beginning of each epoch, you can compute the loss of the current layer and the previous layer, then use the average of them as the new loss function, reducing the total number of parameters and thus the computation.

Neural machine translation aims at building a single large neural network that can be trained to maximize translation performance. The encoder-decoder architecture with an attention mechanism achieves a translation performance comparable to the existing state-of-the-art phrase-based systems. However, the use of large vocabulary becomes the bottleneck in both training and improving the performance. In this paper, we propose a novel architecture which learns morphology by using two recurrent networks and a hierarchical decoder which translates at character level. This gives rise to a deep character-level model consisting of six recurrent networks. Such a deep model has two major advantages. It avoids the large vocabulary issue radically; at the same time, it is more efficient in training than word-based models. Our model obtains a higher BLEU score than the bpe-based model after training for one epoch on En-Fr and En-Cs translation tasks. Further analyses show that our model is able to learn morphology. The proposed model has the following two major advantages. First, the use of a character-level encoder avoids the large vocabulary problem. In contrast to the word-based encoder, there is no need to provide a separate model for unknown words, as long as the character-level model has a fixed size, there are no further training costs. This is an attractive property for neural machine translation (NMT). However, the exploration of different initialization methods, architectures and optimization methods is much more difficult for character-level models, because the large amount of hyperparameters. In contrast to the word-based encoder, the character-level model also avoids the padding problem. The second advantage of the proposed model is that it is more efficient in terms of training. As illustrated in the experiments, using two recurrent layers and hierarchical decoding can be seen as a type of unidirectional RNN with skip connections. The proposed model simply alternates the two layers and employs a hierarchical decoder which translates at character level. This gives rise to a deep model consisting of six recurrent networks. Our model is thus more efficient than the previously existing deep model which consists of 13 recurrent networks. The model has the following two limitations. First, it relies on the explicit position information to split a character into subcomponents. The model is not able to generate unseen characters. Secondly, the character-level decoder cannot handle unknown characters. It is very likely that the model will generate gibberish even when one part of the character corresponds to a valid character in the target language. Overall, we believe that the proposed model has a promising future for neural machine translation. The main reason is that the proposed model still has the capability to learn morphology. The improvement on the two limitations could lead to better performance, as more and more similar tasks are employed. strengths The proposed model has the following two major strengths. This paper is concurrently one of the first successful attempts to do machine translation using a character-character MT modeling, and generally the authors liked the approach. However, the reviewers raised several issues with the novelty and experimental setup of the work. 
 
 Pros:
 - The analysis of the work was strong. This illustrated the underlying property, and all reviewers praised these figures.
 
 Mixed: 
 - Some found the paper clear, praising it as a "well-written paper", however other found that important details were lacking and the notation was improperly overloaded. As the reviewers were generally experts in the area, this should be improved
 - Reviewers were also split on results. Some found the results quite "compelling" and comprehensive, but others thought there should be more comparison to BPE and other morphogically based work
 - Modeling novelty was also questionable. Reviewers like the partial novelty of the character based approach, but felt like the ML contributions were too shallow for ICLR
 
 Cons:
 - Reviewers generally found the model itself to be overly complicated and the paper to focus too much on engineering. 
 - There were questions about experimental setup. In particular, a call for more speed numbers and broader comparison.

Update after reading the authors' responses & the paper revision dated Dec 21:
I have removed the comment "insufficient comparison to past work" in the title & update the score from 3 -> 5.
The main reason for the score is on novelty. The proposal of HGRU & the use of the R matrix are basically just to achieve the effect of "whether to continue from character-level states or using word-level states". It seems that these solutions are specific to symbolic frameworks like Theano (which the authors used) and TensorFlow. This, however, is not a problem for languages like Matlab (which Luong & Manning used) or Torch.

-----

This is a well-written paper with good analysis in which I especially like Figure 5. However I think there is little novelty in this work. The title is about learning morphology but there is nothing specifically enforced in the model to learn morphemes or subword units. For example, maybe some constraints can be put on the weights in w_i in Figure 1 to detect morpheme boundaries or some additional objective like MDL can be used (though it's not clear how these constraints can be incorporated cleanly). 

Moreover, I'm very surprised that litte comparison (only a brief mention) was given to the work of (Luong & Manning, 2016) [1], which trains deep 8-layer word-character models and achieves much better results on English-Czech, e.g., 19.6 BLEU compared to 17.0 BLEU achieved in the paper. I think the HGRU thing is over-complicated in terms of presentation. If I read correctly, what HGRU does is basically either continue the character decoder or reset using word-level states at boundaries, which is what was done in [1]. Luong & Manning (2016) even make it more efficient by not having to decode all target words at the morpheme level & it would be good to know the speed of the model proposed in this ICLR submission. What end up new in this paper are perhaps different analyses on what a character-based model learns & adding an additional RNN layer in the encoder.

One minor comment: annotate h_t in Figure 1.

machine_text: This paper considers learning frame-invariant representations using deep neural networks. Specifically, the authors propose a deep network that estimates the deep Fourier coefficients of an image. The deep network consists of three components. The first component is a convolutional layer that captures the low-dimensional structure of the input image. The second component is a layer that performs wavelet-like convolutions to capture the higher-order statistics of the image. The third component is an encoder that maps the higher-order statistics into low-dimensional feature space. The authors show that the deep network learns frame-invariant features and apply the learned features to solve the frame problem in nonlinear optimization. The main advantages of the proposed method are that the network is very simple, the deep network can be trained from scratch, and the test time complexity of the network is linear. I think the approach could be useful in many applications, especially those that require solving the frame problem. One problem with the approach is that the test time complexity of the deep network is linear. In many applications (especially online applications), the model needs to be evaluated in the test time, which could take up to linear time. I think the linear time complexity can be achieved by using more efficient compression techniques for the deep network, such as hashing. However, I think the approach is useful and can be complementary to existing methods. scaling deep network to estimate the deep Fourier coefficients of an image. The paper addresses the problem of calculating the performance indicators of linear systems (time, $L_2$, $L_\infty$ norms) in linear time (Theorem 1). The proof is based on the classic analysis of the bilinear control system with the Fourier transform, which is an indirect transformation of time. This is a very valuable result, because the Fourier transform has a number of attractive properties: it is universal (operates on arbitrary signals), provides significant computational advantages, and has a wide scope of applications. The paper considers the classic scenario of calculating the average of the desired response over random signals, but with an important modification: the direct calculation of the Fourier transform of the response (not an indirect transformation through the system’s frequency response). This allows the paper to show that the algorithmic complexity is linear, whereas in the classic case it is at least exponential (this is a strength of the paper). The proposed method is proposed for an arbitrary nonlinear system of equations. However, its direct applicability is limited to the problem of calculating the Fourier transform of the response, and only for linear system models. The proposed method is compared with existing methods in terms of the computational complexity. The proposed method requires $N$ times less operations to calculate the Fourier transform of the response than the Gosudi reduction method, which is widely used, and only 13% more than the Lie transforms method. In terms of the required storage, the proposed method is the simplest, while the Gosudi reduction method requires more storage than the proposed method, and Lie transforms requires the least storage.

We show that a previously proposed method for higher-order nonlinearities [1, 2] can be readily incorporated into scattering networks for nonlinear invariants. Most image and signal processing operations that take a time that is proportional to the number of pixels in the domain (linear time) are implemented by using the fast Fourier transform (FFT) to break the problem down into smaller problems of this kind for each frequency. For most applications, this is not important because the total time required is the sum of the time for each frequency. However, in the case of iterative methods like the inverse iteration for computing the nonlinear invariants, each iteration of the algorithm involves the computation of many transforms, and hence is linear with the size of the input. If the size of the input is *N* and each Fourier transform requires a time of *O* (N log N), the total time taken is *O*(*N*^2^ log *N*). Applying this method to audio applications involves an extra consideration. All the computations must be done in the Fourier domain because of the inherent periodicity of the signal. However, in the case of audio applications, the FFT (or its variants) normally takes up most of the execution time. For this reason, in the case of audio applications, we develop the algorithm in the frequency domain, but apply the inverse FFT only once at the end. This is still *O*(*N*^2^ log *N*), which is still linear time. The network was trained on 9 of the 10 classes and tested on the remaining held out class. Accuracy of 91.7% was achieved, which classifies the 10 classes with 90.2% total accuracy. The output was a 1 neuron layer which produced the final classification result. The cross entropy was used as the cost function. The Adam algorithm was used for optimization with learning rate 0.001. The scattering network extracted 80 nonlinear and 128 non-linear + Fourier based features. These features were reduced to 10 most discriminating by using Principle Component Analysis [5]. This transform solves the nonlinearities problem in the scattering transform domain which is the first time this is done in the scattering transform domain. For the case of deterministic signals, the representation is complete because we can exactly represent any function with its Fourier series. Overview: This work seems very promising, but I believe it should be compared with more baselines, and more precisely described and explained, from a signal processing point of view.

Pros:
New descriptor
Fast implementation

Cons:
a) Lack of rigor
b) Too long accordingly to the content
c) The computational gain of the algorithm is not clear
d) The work is not compared with its most obvious baseline: a scattering transform

I will detail each cons.

a) Section 1:
The author  motivates the use of scattering transform because it defines a contraction of the space that relies on geometric features.
" The nonlinearity used in the scattering network is the complex modulus which is piecewise linear."
A real modulus is piecewise linear. A complex modulus has a shape of bell when interpreting C as R^2. Could you clarify?
\Omega is not introduced.

Could you give a precise reference (page+paper) of this claim: “Higher order nonlinearity refers to |x|^2 instead of |x| as it is usually done in the scattering network.” ?

Section 2:
The motivation of the non-linearity is not clear. First, this non-linearity might potentially increase a lot the variance of your architecture since it depends on higher moments(up to 4). I think a fair analysis would be to compute numerically the normalized variance (e.g. divided by the averaged l^2 norm), as a sanity check. Besides, one should prove that the energy is decreasing. It is not possible to argue that this architecture is similar to a scattering transform which has precise mathematical foundations and those results are required, since the setting is different.

Permutation is not a relevant variability.

The notion of sparsity during the whole paper sometimes refers to the number of 0 value, either the l^1 norm. Mathematically, a small value, even 10^-1000 is still a non 0 value.

Did you compute the graph of the figure 4 on the bird dataset? You might use a ratio instead for clarity.

This paper proposes a to use squared modulus nonlinearities within convolutional architectures. Because point-wise squaring can be written as a convolution in the Fourier domain, when doing all the operations in the Fourier this architecture becomes 'dual': convolutions become pointwise operations, and pointwise square-nonlinearities become convolutions. 
 The authors study this architecture in the context of scattering transforms and produce a complexity analysis that exploits the previous property, along with preliminary numerical experiments. 
 
 All reviewers agreed that, while this is an interesting paper with potentially useful outcomes, its exposition and current experimental section are insufficient. The AC agrees with this assessment, and therefore recommends rejection. 
 I agree that the main unanswered question and a 'show-stopper' is the lack of comparisons with its most immediate baseline, scattering using complex modulus, both in terms of accuracy and computational complexity.

I find the general direction of the work is promising but, in my opinion, the paper has three main drawback. While the motivation and overall idea seem very reasonable, the derivation is not convincing mathematically. The experiments are limited and the presentation needs significant improvement.  The writing and wording are in general poorly structured to the point that it is sometimes difficult to follow the proposed ideas. The overall organization needs improvement and the connection between sections is not properly established. The paper could be significantly improved by simply re-writing it.

I'm not fully convinced by the motivation for the proposed non-linearity (|c|^2), as described on page 5. The authors argue that  (Waldspurger, 2016) suggests that higher order nonlinearities might be  beneficial for sparsity. But unless I'm missing something, that work seems  to suggest that in the general case higher order nonlinearities can be neglected. Could you please comment on this?

On the other hand, adding a second order term to the descriptor seems
an interesting direction, as long as stability to small variations is preserved (which should be shown experimentally)

The experimental section is rather limited. The paper would be stronger with a thorough numerical evaluation. The presented results, in my opinion, do not show convincingly a clear advantage of the proposed method over a standard implementation of the scattering transform. In order to show the merits of the proposed approach, it would be really helpful to directly compare running times and compression rates.

Questions: 
- Can you show empirically that the proposed higher order nonlinearity
produces sparser representations than the complex modulus?

Other minor issues:
- The proof of Section 2.1, should be preceded by a clear statement in the form of a proposition
- "Hadamart" -> Hadamard
- "Valid set" -> Validation set
- "nonzeros coefficients" -> nonzero coefficients
- Figure 3 is difficult to understand. Please provide more details.
- Figure 5 is supposed to show a comparison to a standard implementation of the Scattering network, but it doesn't seem to be such comparison in that figure. Please explain.
- Please verify the references. The first reference states "MALLAT".

This work proposes 3 improvements to scattering networks: (1) a non-linearity that allows Fourier-domain computation, (2) compact-supported (in the Fourier domain) representations, and (3) computing additional variance features.

The technical contributions seem worthwhile, since #1 and #2 may result in better speed, while #3 may improve accuracy. Unfortunately, they are poorly described and evaluated. If the writing was clear and the evaluation more broad, I would have recommended acceptance since the ideas have merit.

One of the biggest faults of the presentation is that many sentences are overly long and full of unnecessary obfuscating language, e.g. the last paragraph of Section 1 (though unfortunately this permeates the whole paper).

Likewise, most equations are made unnecessarily complicated. For example, Eq. 5 does not need 4 lines and so many indexes, but just 2:
X_0 = x
X_l = |X_{l-1} * Psi_l|
with the |.| operator being element-wise. Most of the hyperparameter dependencies and indexes are not necessary, as well as the repetition of iterations. The same reasoning can be applied to most Equations 5 to 13.

The argument of cardinality (Eq. 14) does not really help prove that variance is more informative. In fact, we could just as easily write that the cardinality of S concatenated with any (!) other quantity is >= the cardinality of S. Another argument from machine learning theory would be better.

The authors should strive to make the arguments in the paper less hyperbolic and better substantiated. The claims about finding invariants of any input (Abstract) and fundamental structures (last paragraph of Section 1.2.1) are not really backed up by any math. How can we have any guarantees about singling out, for example, semantically relevant representations? The learning procedures in machine learning give at least some guarantees, while here the feature building seems a bit more heuristic. This does not take away from the main idea, but this part needs to be better researched.

This paper proposes a to use squared modulus nonlinearities within convolutional architectures. Because point-wise squaring can be written as a convolution in the Fourier domain, when doing all the operations in the Fourier this architecture becomes 'dual': convolutions become pointwise operations, and pointwise square-nonlinearities become convolutions. 
 The authors study this architecture in the context of scattering transforms and produce a complexity analysis that exploits the previous property, along with preliminary numerical experiments. 
 
 All reviewers agreed that, while this is an interesting paper with potentially useful outcomes, its exposition and current experimental section are insufficient. The AC agrees with this assessment, and therefore recommends rejection. 
 I agree that the main unanswered question and a 'show-stopper' is the lack of comparisons with its most immediate baseline, scattering using complex modulus, both in terms of accuracy and computational complexity.

I find the general direction of the work is promising but, in my opinion, the paper has three main drawback. While the motivation and overall idea seem very reasonable, the derivation is not convincing mathematically. The experiments are limited and the presentation needs significant improvement.  The writing and wording are in general poorly structured to the point that it is sometimes difficult to follow the proposed ideas. The overall organization needs improvement and the connection between sections is not properly established. The paper could be significantly improved by simply re-writing it.

I'm not fully convinced by the motivation for the proposed non-linearity (|c|^2), as described on page 5. The authors argue that  (Waldspurger, 2016) suggests that higher order nonlinearities might be  beneficial for sparsity. But unless I'm missing something, that work seems  to suggest that in the general case higher order nonlinearities can be neglected. Could you please comment on this?

On the other hand, adding a second order term to the descriptor seems
an interesting direction, as long as stability to small variations is preserved (which should be shown experimentally)

The experimental section is rather limited. The paper would be stronger with a thorough numerical evaluation. The presented results, in my opinion, do not show convincingly a clear advantage of the proposed method over a standard implementation of the scattering transform. In order to show the merits of the proposed approach, it would be really helpful to directly compare running times and compression rates.

Questions: 
- Can you show empirically that the proposed higher order nonlinearity
produces sparser representations than the complex modulus?

Other minor issues:
- The proof of Section 2.1, should be preceded by a clear statement in the form of a proposition
- "Hadamart" -> Hadamard
- "Valid set" -> Validation set
- "nonzeros coefficients" -> nonzero coefficients
- Figure 3 is difficult to understand. Please provide more details.
- Figure 5 is supposed to show a comparison to a standard implementation of the Scattering network, but it doesn't seem to be such comparison in that figure. Please explain.
- Please verify the references. The first reference states "MALLAT".

This work proposes 3 improvements to scattering networks: (1) a non-linearity that allows Fourier-domain computation, (2) compact-supported (in the Fourier domain) representations, and (3) computing additional variance features.

The technical contributions seem worthwhile, since #1 and #2 may result in better speed, while #3 may improve accuracy. Unfortunately, they are poorly described and evaluated. If the writing was clear and the evaluation more broad, I would have recommended acceptance since the ideas have merit.

One of the biggest faults of the presentation is that many sentences are overly long and full of unnecessary obfuscating language, e.g. the last paragraph of Section 1 (though unfortunately this permeates the whole paper).

Likewise, most equations are made unnecessarily complicated. For example, Eq. 5 does not need 4 lines and so many indexes, but just 2:
X_0 = x
X_l = |X_{l-1} * Psi_l|
with the |.| operator being element-wise. Most of the hyperparameter dependencies and indexes are not necessary, as well as the repetition of iterations. The same reasoning can be applied to most Equations 5 to 13.

The argument of cardinality (Eq. 14) does not really help prove that variance is more informative. In fact, we could just as easily write that the cardinality of S concatenated with any (!) other quantity is >= the cardinality of S. Another argument from machine learning theory would be better.

The authors should strive to make the arguments in the paper less hyperbolic and better substantiated. The claims about finding invariants of any input (Abstract) and fundamental structures (last paragraph of Section 1.2.1) are not really backed up by any math. How can we have any guarantees about singling out, for example, semantically relevant representations? The learning procedures in machine learning give at least some guarantees, while here the feature building seems a bit more heuristic. This does not take away from the main idea, but this part needs to be better researched.

The new layer helps to improve the training speed and stabilize the training. Christensen, Wei Xu, and Lei Zhang BibTeX @article{jin2017boosted, title={Boosted residual networks}, author={Zhe Jin and Jia D. Christensen and Wei Xu and Lei Zhang}, journal={CoRR}, volume={abs/1708.07721}, year={2018} } Model description Boosted Residual Networks replace the output of every layer with a factorized layer. The new layer helps to improve the training speed and stabilize the training. Formally, the network structure is:(For notation definitions, please refer to the paper) y_i = u_i * h_i + b_i, i = 1,2,3,... c where y is the output of the network, u is the weight matrix of the layer, h is the transformation matrix, and b is the bias vector. c is the number of layers. The model can be easily trained by calculating the loss between y_i and t, where t is the desired output. For example, when the i-th layer is the factorized layer, the formula is h_i = SINNET_DIM * log(sigmoid(W_i * x + b_i)) where SINNET_DIM is the dimension of the Sigmoid layer. Loss function The loss function is: L(W) = ∑ i=1 c -log(sigmoid(h_i * y_i + b_i)) where L is the loss function, W is the weight matrix, and b is the bias vector. Training process The training process is similar to the normal Residual Network. But the SINNET_DIM in the formula is replaced by a constant in this paper. Experiments This approach can be easily adopted in Residual Networks without hurting the performance. The CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 models trained by this approach have higher training speed and better performance than the models trained by the original Residual Network. Zhe Jin, Jia D. Excellent work, I recommend accepting the reviewer’s comments and submitting to a more appropriate journal. The novelty of the method is unlikely to be regarded as very significant in the field of Computer Vision. The field is moving very fast, and the proposed approach is very similar to existing methods, such as DenseNets. The nice aspect of the paper is the effective implementation, and the detailed report on the experimental setup and the results, but these are not directly relevant for a publication in a high impact journal. Detailed comments: - The introduction lacks any meaningful context or motivation. The only reference to machine learning is in the title. There is no indication of how the work relates to previous work, or why it is innovative. - The description of the network’s topology in the main text is rather confusing. The description contains different terms for different parts of the network, which are not consistently defined. For example, there are several paragraphs describing the part of the network after the first 1x1 convolution. The paragraph names differ in their use of the terms “module”, “subnetwork”, “branch” and “route”. The terms are used inconsistently, and it is not clear which term is being used to which part of the network. - A similar problem exists in the paragraph describing the final “branch”. It would be useful to introduce the term “final layer” here, because this is a common term in deep learning. It would also be useful to introduce the “route” in this paragraph, because only then would it become clear that the final layer is part of multiple routes. - The paper describes a single experiment in great detail, but this is only one experiment out of several that the authors have conducted. No general statement can be made about the generality or reproducibility of the approach. - It is not clear how the authors arrived at the architecture that they used, especially since the baseline network that they compare their proposed method with was not described. Did they try to optimize the architecture in their hyperparameter search, or were there other constraints imposed? - The authors chose to evaluate their method on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets. However, the CIFAR datasets have been shown to be relatively easy, and recent works have shown that very deep networks achieve high results on these datasets with large amounts of online tuning. In contrast, humans performing the same classification task with visual recognition tasks, such as ImageNet, needed to spend years training their visual capabilities before they reached a reasonable level of performance. It would have been interesting to include other datasets, or to at least provide more discussion on the choice of datasets and their relation to real-world applications. - The summary of the results presented in the “Results” section are fairly standard for models with similar depth. The performance of the baseline Residual Network was already high, and very similar to that of other methods with similar depth. - In the “Conclusion and Future Work” section, it is stated that the proposed method will be released to the public. It is not clear what the public release would consist of, or if the method has been submitted to or published in any journal other than arXiv. Overall, I would not recommend accepting the above comments, but instead I would recommend improving the clarity of the text, by omitting some of the details and expanding the introduction to include more motivation and context, and including a more general discussion of the implications of the paper’s findings, as well as a more general discussion of the chosen datasets and why they are relevant for real-world applications. These comments are based on a quick glance at the paper, and a more careful reading of the text may reveal other problems. However, the second set of comments raises valid concerns regarding the generalizability of the proposed approach, and the lack of a suitable comparison to more established methods. I therefore recommend accepting the above comments, and attempting to improve the generalizability of the work by, for example, adding a more general discussion of the implications of the paper’s findings, and a more detailed description of the chosen datasets and why they are relevant for real-world applications. The last sentence of the conclusion could be improved by including the previous paragraph’s discussion. In summary, I think that the paper has a good structure and content, but the validity and generalizability of the findings would be improved by adding more discussion

It is based on the combination of Residual Networks, which is a very successful deep learning method, with the Deep Incremental Boosting, which is a methodology to train fast ensembles of networks of increasing depth. The main idea of the proposed method is to grow the member network at each round of boosting, that is different network trained on different stage of boosting. The combination of these two methods -- Residual Networks with Deep Incremental Boosting -- has better potential than using the Deep Incremental Boosting method without Residual Networks. ameras, the performance in most situation is better than other methods, for example in the task of object detection with COCO, the mAP is 36.71%, which is higher than Mobilenet_V2 (34.81%) and MobileNet (33.33%). This paper proposes a boosting based ensemble procedure for residual networks by adopting the Deep Incremental Boosting method that was used for CNN's(Mosca & Magoulas, 2016a). At each step t, a new block of layers are added to the network at a position p_t and the weights of all layers are copied to the current network to speed up training.

The method is not sufficiently novel since the steps of Deep Incremental Boosting are slightly adopted. Instead of adding a layer to the end of the network, this version adds a block of layers to a position p_t (starts at a selected position p_0) and merges layer accordingly hence slightly adopts DIB. 

The empirical analysis does not use any data-augmentation. It is not clear whether the improvements (if there is) of the ensemble disappear after data-augmentation.  Also, one of the main baselines, DIB has no-skip connections therefore this can negatively affect the fair comparison. The authors argue that they did not involve state of art Res Nets since their analysis focuses on the ensemble approach, however any potential improvement of the ensemble can be compensated with an inherent feature of Res Net variant. The boosting procedure can be computationally restrictive in case of ImageNet training and Res Net variants may perform much better in that case too. Therefore the baselines should include the state of art Res Nets and Dense Convolutional networks hence current results are preliminary.

In addition, it is not clear how sensitive the boosting to the selection of injection point.

This paper adopts DIB to Res Nets and provides some empirical analysis however the contribution is not sufficiently novel and the empirical results are not satisfactory for demonstrating that the method is significant.

Pros
-provides some preliminary results for boosting of Res Nets
Cons
-not sufficiently novel: an incremental approach 
-empirical analysis is not satisfactory

The paper under consideration proposes a set of procedures for incrementally expanding a residual network by adding layers via a boosting criterion.

The main barrier to publication is the weak empirical validation. The tasks considered are quite small scale in 2016 (and MNIST with a convolutional net is basically an uninteresting test by this point). The paper doesn't compare to the literature, and CIFAR-10 results fail to improve upon rather simple, single-network published baselines (Springenberg et al, 2015 for example, obtains 92% without data augmentation) and I'm pretty sure there's a simple ResNet result somewhere that outshines these too. The CIFAR100 results are a little bit interesting as they are better than I'm used to seeing (I haven't done a recent literature crawl), and this is unsurprising -- you'd expect ensembles to do well when there's a dearth of labeled training data, and here there are only a few hundred per label. But then it's typical on both CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 to use simple data augmentation schemes which aren't employed here, and these and other forms of regularization are a simpler alternative to a complicated iterative augmentation scheme like this.

It'd be easier to sell this method either as an option for scarce labeled datasets where data augmentation is non-trivial (but then for most image-related applications, random crops and reflections are easy and valid), but that would necessitate different benchmarks, and comparison against simpler methods like said data augmentation, dropout (especially, due to the ensemble interpretation), and so on.

- Can you give the details of the experiment setup e.g. parameters to be tuned, algorithm to train at each step of boosting etc? Also can you give the details of networks architecture and references? 
- Can you elaborate on comparison to state of resNet variants, dense convolutional network?
- Can you give also comparison on training time?
- Do you have any result on Imagenet?

machine_text: Overall, I enjoy this paper. The topic is of interest to me because I am currently working on the issue of scalable training of NLU models that consume character-level word representations. I have some points that the author may want to consider. First, the paper leaves open the question of how to efficiently train such character-level NLP models. In particular, it seems challenging to find a method to apply the ideas of slow parameter updates from the domain of efficient next sentence prediction (See e.g. Xing et al., 2016) to the problem of efficient training of such character-level NLP models. The current state-of-the-art approach to efficiently train character-level NLP models, BPEmb, is a notable exception, but it relies on BPEmbNet (an architecture for efficiently training character-level NLP models), which is not directly applicable to this problem. Second, the main contribution of this paper (Applying RL to train NLP models) seems to be more of a proof of concept than a practical approach to train NLU models with character-level word representations. The implementation provided in the paper seems to be extremely inefficient, which renders the approach in the paper impractical for even relatively small models. For instance, it took 3 days to train BERT-Large (92MB model) with the implementation provided in the paper, whereas it is easy to train BERT-Large in 1 day with existing techniques. Nevertheless, it would be interesting to see if it is possible to make the implementation provided in the paper more efficient and/or if it is possible to apply the techniques from Xing et al. to train character-level NLP models efficiently.

This paper is interesting as it addresses the problem of enabling end users to gain useful information from the vast amounts of data generated by neural language models (NLMs). The solution adopted here is to render the output of an NLM in character form, which the authors call character level neural language model (CLNLRM). The authors then demonstrate how the rendered text can be parsed to reveal some important trends about the training data on which the NLM was trained on. The rendered output is generated by replacing words with their character n-grams, with n=3 in this case. The paper makes use of conventional n-gram techniques to render the output, and thus has a “hacky” feel to it. The effectiveness of this hack can be illustrated by the results obtained. The method presented here can be applied to other NLMs, and could be a valuable addition to the toolset that managers of NLM output tools will want to consider when delivering reportable results. The authors present a novel approach to rendering the output of a neural language model (NLM) in character form. The approach is to replace words in the output of the NLM with their character n-grams, with n=3 in this case. The authors then demonstrate how this rendered text can be parsed to reveal some important trends about the training data on which the NLM was trained on. This is an interesting approach, though the implementation is quite “hacky” as the authors rely on conventional n-gram techniques to render the output. The effectiveness of this render approach can be illustrated by the results obtained. The method presented here could be a valuable addition to the toolset that managers of NLM output tools will want to consider when delivering reportable results.

In this paper, the author introduced an architecture for an open-vocabulary neural language model. The model is built upon a character-level convolutional neural network for word representation. In the training stage, the author utilizes the noise-contrastive estimation (NCE) to circumvent the lack of vocabulary problem. The paper is interesting but has some problems, as following: 1) The model only focuses on the IWSLT-2016 dataset from English to Czech, which only has about 30K token pairs. How can this model trained for general purposes? 2) In the experiment, the model is evaluated on the IWSLT-2016 dataset, which may lead to over-fitting. Then how can this model be applied to general text corpus? 3) The model is evaluated with BLEU point, which is not accurate enough for machine translation. Nevertheless, the paper is interesting and urges further explorations on this topic. This paper introduces an architecture for an open-vocabulary neural language model. Word representations are computed on-the-fly by a convolution network followed by pooling layer. This allows the model to consider any word, in the context or for the prediction. The training objective is derived from the Noise-Contrastive Estimation to circumvent the lack of vocabulary. We test the ability of our model to build representations of unknown words on the MT task of IWSLT-2016 from English to Czech, in a reranking setting. Experimental results show promising results, with a gain up to 0.7 BLEU point. They also emphasize the difficulty and instability when training such models with character-based representations for the predicted words. Advantages: This model can consider any word in the text, allowing the model to achieve new state-of-the-art results on several language understanding tasks. The model is also very easy to implement. The complexity of the model is relatively low, as it only needs to replace the embedding layer by a convolutional layer and pooling layer. Weaknesses: The model is only applicable to NLP tasks using fixed vocabulary, as it learns word representations from the data. If the model is trained on a large corpus, it is likely to learn representations of unknown words as noise. When tested on out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words, the model will most likely produce nonsense words at a high probability. This also raises the difficulty of model training. The loss function of the model is difficult to be optimized due to the lack of any validation set with the OOV words. second, the model in the paper is a novel idea to open the vocabulary for a NLP model. This is an innovative idea and can be considered as the strength of the paper. The paper also points out some issues of training NLP models with character-based representations, especially for the unknown words. This is also a weakness of the paper as it calls for attention to the problem of training these NLP models with character-based representations.

This paper proposes an extension of neural network language (NLM) models to better handle large vocabularies. The main idea is to obtain word embeddings by combining character-level embeddings with a convolutional network.

The authors compare word embeddings (WE),character embeddings (CE) as well a combined character and word embeddings (CWE). It's quite obvious how CE or CWE embeddings can be used at the input of an NLM, but this is more tricky at the output layer. The authors propose to use NCE to handle this problem.  NCE allows to speed-up training, but has no impact on inference during testing: the full softmax output layer must be calculated and normalized (which can be very costly).

It was not clear to me how the network is used during TESTING with an open-vocabulary. Since the NLM is only used during reranking, the unnormalized probability of the requested word could be obtained at the output. However, when reranking n-best lists with the NLM feature, different sentences are compared and I wonder whether this does work well without proper normalization.

In addition, the authors provide perplexities in Table 2 and Figures 2 and 3.  This needs normalization, but it is not clear to me how this was performed.  The authors mention a 250k output vocabulary. I doubt that the softmax was calculated over 250k values. Please explain.

The model is evaluated by reranking n-best lists of an SMT systems for the IWSLT 2016 EN/CZ task.  In the abstract, the authors mention a gain of 0.7 BLEU. I do not agree with this claim. A vanilla word-based NLM, i.e. a well-known model, achieves already a gain of 0.6 BLEU. Therefore, the new model proposed in this paper brings only an additional improvement of 0.1 BLEU. This is not statistically significant. I conjecture that a similar variation could be obtained by just training several models with different initializations, etc.

Unfortunately, the NLM models which use a character representation at the output do not work well. There are already several works which use some form of character-level representations at the input.

Could you please discuss the computational complexity during training and inference.

This paper presents a new homologically functional hashing (HFH) method for compressing deep neural networks (DNNs). DNNs have millions of parameters, which complicates their storage, distribution, and training on distributed hardware. HFH maps DNNs onto simple hash tables, with each entry containing a series of hankel matrices. Each row of the matrices corresponds to a layer of the DNN, and the matrix columns represent the dimensions of the data. The hashing function transforms a DNN Architecture into a vector of binary addresses. To ensure the similarity of the hashed DNNs, the proposed HFH method periodically performs anti-hash, which modifies individual hankel matrices with additions and deletions. Experimental results on several public datasets show that HFH outperforms other hashing methods at compressing DNNs and addressing them on parallel machines. HFH maps DNNs onto simple hash tables, with each entry containing a series of hankel matrices. The hashing function transforms a DNN Architecture into a vector of binary addresses. To ensure the similarity of the hashed DNNs, the proposed HFH method periodically performs anti-hash, which modifies individual hankel matrices with additions and deletions. The main contributions of this work can be summarized as follows: 1. It is the first work to apply homologically functional hashing to compress DNNs. 2. It proposes to periodically perform anti-hash to ensure the similarity of the hashed DNNs. HFH has the following limitations: 1. HFH only hashes the layers of DNNs. While the fully connected (FC) layer is the most expensive part of a DNN, it contributes little to the accuracy of the model. Sigmoidal linear (SL) layers are much cheaper than FC layers, but their changes affect the prediction results of the DNN. Therefore, it is better to hashing the FC and SL layers of DNNs together, instead of hashing individual layers. 2. HFH does not consider the type of DNNs. Some DNNs may need to be hashed differently, such as different data types. For example, image data is always hashed as 256-dimensional vectors, but signatures are usually 512-dimensional. HFH only hashes the dimensions of the data, so it may hashing different types of data unequally. HFH is not the only hashing method for DNNs. Other hashing methods include invertible hashing (IHash) and random hash (RandomHash). HFH has some advantages over these other methods. First, it is very easy to compute the similarity of hashed DNNs using the hankel matrix representations. Second, it is very simple to implement HFH using existing computer language techniques. However, HFH only hashed the layers of the DNN, not the FC or SL layers, so it could not address different types of DNNs. Overall, HFN is a promising method for compressing DNNs, and the future development will be focused on combining HFH with other types of DNNs and hashing methods to achieve more excellent results.

The authors presented a homologically functional hashing based compression strategy for deep neural networks (DNNs). The main idea is to hashing parameters in deep nets to a small dimension space, and then employ a small reconstruction net to recover the hashed values and compress the original DNN. The authors demonstrated that the approach can achieve high compression ratio with little loss on prediction accuracy on several public benchmarks. One particularly attractive aspect of this method is that it can achieve single target compression ratio, which means the authors can evaluate the compression result by a pre-defined compression ratio, and all findings are directly relevant to a particular compression ratio. In contrast, most of compression methods involve an exhaustive searching process to achieve a good result, and it is difficult to tell which result is relevant to the compression ratio. Another advantage of this method is that it is easy to apply this method to degenerated scenarios such as HashedNets, and the degenerated scenario performance is usually better than the non-degenerated one. Some drawbacks of this method include that the compression ratio is hard to evaluate in this method, the model size is represented as the size of reconstruction net instead of parameter size, and this might result in slightly larger model size than actual. Overall, this method is a solid step forward on compression for DNNs, and the achieved compression ratio and model size can be directly utilized and evaluated.
