Could you please clarify how you built the model? I also have some concerns about the efficacy of the proposed method. In Table 5, the AUPRC metric is mentioned. I could not find this metric in the Methods section. Could you please describe this metric and the meaning of each parameter used in the metric? I also noticed that the normalized mutual information (NMI) was very close to the metric’s corresponding PPV. Could you please explain what this PPV metric is and how it differs from the NMI? I also have some suggestions for the title. In the abstract, you mention that the algorithm is able to detect beats. However, in section 3, you mention that the detector is able to localize beats. I think that these two phrases are not similar. If the algorithm is able to detect beats, the model should be able to determine where the beats are located in the audio file. My other suggestion is about the paper length. I believe that this paper is too long. I also suggest simplifying the model structure, because in some places it was not clear. For example, in section 3.2, you introduce an allusion to deep learning. However, at some points, the text seems to imply that the model is a combination of shallow and deep learning. I think that this type of model should be clearly explained.

Paper addresses a useful problem of BIOACOUSTIC SEGMENTATION BY HIERARCHICAL DIRICHLET PROCESS HIDDEN MARKOV MODEL. Hierarchical Dirichlet process (hDP) has been applied to audio-frequency hidden markov model (AF HMMTM). The hDP serves as a Bayesian nonparametric prior for segment-level mixture distributions for audio-frequency HMMs. The proposed method can identify the number of components in a semi-supervised manner. Especially, it can estimate the length of each segment automatically. For example, if we segment a music recording into beats, the proposed method can detect the approximate period of the music. Another advantage is that it is applicable to high-dimensional time series such as electrocardiogram (ECG) signal. However, the following are the weaknesses of the proposed method. The proposed method needs a lot of computation. Especially, it needs to estimate the coda distribution of each audio-frequency HMM per each segment. If the number of audio-frequency bins is large, it needs huge memory to store all the estimated coda distributions. In addition, it takes a long time to call the function of evaluating the coda distribution for all the time series in a memory.The code of the proposed method can't be understood easily. The mathematical descriptions of the proposed method are very complicated. However, these weaknesses can be weakness if the paper aims to give a detailed description of the method. The code of the method can be released to the public if the paper is published in a journal. But, the code needs to be well commented for others to understand it. The method can be accepted as a useful tool for BIOACOUSTIC SEGMENTATION if the weaknesses are well understood. Then, it will be useful for people to understand the method and apply it for their research problems. Therefore, I think the proposed method is accepted as a useful method for BIOACOUSTIC SEGMENTATION. Another weakness of the paper is that it only describes the results of a semi-supervised method. The method can't estimate the number of segments of a given audio file. For example, if a audio file includes many upbeat parts which are usually called as a "song". The hDP attached to each upbeat part would estimate the number of segments to be large. But, it should be only one segment. The hierarchical structure of hDP may cause over-segmentation. On the other hand, if an audio file includes several submits which are different sound sources. The hDP attached to each submit would estimate the number of segments to be small. But, it should be only one segment. The hierarchical structure of hDP may cause under-segmentation. Therefore, the semi-supervised property of the method may cause the problems in some case. To resolve the problems, the authors should show that the method can estimate the number of segments of a given audio file. Then, the method can be widely accepted. The last weakness is that the paper only shows the results of audio files which have been used for training the model. It would be more useful if the authors presented the results of audio files which have not been used for training the model. This is for evaluating the performance of the method. Overall, the proposed method is useful for BIOACOUSTIC SEGMENTATION. The method can identify the number of segments in a semi-supervised manner. Especially, it estimates the number of segments of a given audio file and shows the estimated results. But, the method needs to estimate the coda distribution of each HMM for each segment. If the number of HMMs or the dimension of the time series is large, the memory needed to store all the estimated coda distributions or the number of interaction parameters will be huge. In addition, the time to calculate these parameters will be long. In addition, the method can't estimate the number of segments for some audio files. It would be useful if the method estimates the number of segments of a given audio file and shows the estimated results. In conclusion, the method presents a useful problem of BIOACOUSTIC SEGMENTATION and shows how to solve it. But, the method needs to be improved by adding the ability to estimate the number of segments of a given audio file and show the estimated results. Overall, the method is useful and is accepted as a useful method for BIOACOUSTIC SEGMENTATION.

The paper Understanding the communication between different animals by analysing their acoustic signals is an important topic in bioacoustics. It can be a powerful tool for the preservation of ecological diversity. We investigate probabilistic models to analyse signals issued from real-world bioacoustic sound scenes. We study a Bayesian non-parametric sequential models based on Hierarchical Dirichlet Process Hidden Markov Models (HDP-HMM). The model is able to infer hidden states, that are referred here as song units. However, using such a model raise one main issue: defining the number of hidden states the model has to learn. In bioacoustic problems we often do not know the number of song units (unlike in human speech recognition). Hence, we work with the Hierarchical Dirichlet Process (HDP)-HMM, which is a Bayesian non-parametric (BNP) model that offers a way to tackle this challenging problem. We focus our work on unsupervised learning from bioacoustic data. It consists in simultaneously finding the structure of hidden song units and automatically infer the unknown number of the hidden states to represent the data. Two real bioacoustic sound scene applications are investigated in this work: on whale and multi-species birds segmentation. The learning of these models is proceeded by using Markov-Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling techniques on Mel Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCC) of audio signals. The results show an interesting song unit segmentation of the bioacoustic signals and open new insights for unsupervised analysis of such signals. This paper illustrates the potential of chunking non-human animal signals into structured parts. This can yield to a new species representation and help experts to better understand the behaviour of such species as Kershenbaum et al. (2014) wanted.

The paper is a novel application for the sticky HDP-HMM, focused on correctly identifying the number of components in bird and whale song across a variety of datasets. It's nice to see the model applied to an interesting dataset. My main issues with the paper have to do with structure and the choice of representation used in the model. Namely:

The organization of the paper could be significantly improved. There is a lot of repetitive introduction that adds little to the paper. The first and last two sentences of the abstract could be cut. Many other parts of the abstract basically repeat the introduction. The second paragraph of section 2.3 also repeats your introduction - by now we know what you're doing. I think most people reading this will have no idea what Kershenbaum (2014) is. The description of the data should go in the experiments section. "Different hypotheses for the songs were emitted" in the introduction is odd phrasing. Figure 4 should be the first figure and go in the introduction. Figure 5 should be in the methods section. A summary of Table 1 should be in the experiments section. Generally the writing could be tightened quite a bit, which would make space for these figures. The description of the HDP-HMM, which mostly follows the existing literature, is well done.

Some general questions about the methods used:

If you're interested in scalable inference, why use Gibbs sampling? Why not the beam sampler (van Gael 2008), which at least recently was the state of the art for MCMC inference in the HDP-HMM? More generally, why use MCMC at all? For very large datasets, most of the Bayesian ML community has converged on stochastic variational inference as the most practical method (eg Wang, Paisley and Blei 2011).

If your interest is mainly in the number of clusters, how would you address the fact that DP mixture models are known not to be consistent for estimating the true number of clusters (Miller and Harrison 2013)?

MFCC features are calibrated to the human auditory system, not bird or whale auditory systems. In your data, do you calibrate the MFCC scale to be closer to the auditory systems of the animals that generated the song?

And a final suggestion for future work, which could use the results presented here as a baseline:

Given the success of LSTMs in speech recognition in recent years, it may be the case that deep learned representations are superior to linear features (like the means of each cluster in an HDP-HMM) for animal song as well. Have you considered a hybrid model, similar to recent work combining autoencoders and graphical models (Johnson, Duvenaud, Wiltschko, Datta and Adams 2016)?

The paper studies an unusual and (apparently) challenging application -- segmentation of whale and bird songs. Though the authors claim that the applications is much more challenging than previous applications of the proposed techniques (in speech processing), the evaluation is very questionable (as there is no gold standard), there is no convincing comparison with other (potentially simpler techniques). Overall, the reviewers believe the work is not mature enough to be accepted at ICLR.

Although the technique itself is not novel, the application of this data-driven method to bioacoustics segmentation is quite challenging, and may yield some scientific findings, and this is a valuable contribution to the bioacoustics field. My concern for this paper is that it does not have fair comparison of the other simple methods including BIC and AIC, and it is better to provide such comparisons. Especially, as the authors pointed out, the computational cost of HDP-HMM is a big issue, and the other simple methods may solve this issue.

This paper presented an unsupervised approach for the automatic segmentation of bioacoustic data. The authors applied an existing approach (Hierarchical Dirichlet Process Hidden Markov Models) to their task. The originality of their work is the investigation of this approach on a new task, which they argue is more difficult, namely bioacoustic segmentation. They provide evidence that this is a difficult task by explaining that there doesn't exist a consensus among human experts on how this should be done. However, they do not provide convincing results that their approach is successful, as it fails in many cases to replicate the correct segmentations as defined by their baseline: human experts. In addition, the clarity of the writing is extremely poor, including many grammatical errors and awkward sentences.

machine_text: General The paper addresses an important and well studied problem in the NLP pipeline - question answering. The proposed approach uses Recurrent Span Representations (R Sprays) to efficiently encode question anddocument relations and answer each query with the help of LMs. The paper also examines two key issues in this approach - incremental question answering and abstractiveanswer generation. The overall approach shows good performance on standard QA datasets. I would like to appreciate the authors for the good work. I have a few queries and recommendations: 1. The introduction could have been made more concise by giving a high level overview of the QA system architecture and current techniques. Please see the next comment for more details. 2. The abstractive QA part could have been made more convincing by showing case studies from QALD and WizWiki datasets. 3. Since you are using LMs to generate answers, could you provide us with some details about the architecture of the LMs and how the training/query time is impacted by the number of facts? 4. While generating the abstract of the Sprays, you could have compared the Sprays with the knowledge encoded in the document. For example, in the ‘Newsprint’Spray, you mention that the document also encodes AIIMS, but you do not compare it with any facts from the document. 5. Considering the ‘clarity’ or readability of the generated answers, could you provide some examples? Overall, I think this is a good first attempt at solving QA using R Spray and LMs and the authors should be encouraged to keep working on this direction. However, my above queries are the things that the authors could consider while improving the quality of the paper.

Problem: Automatically generating answers from a knowledge base is an important but challenging problem in artificial intelligence, especially for open-domain questions. Most existing models for this task adopt Seq2Seq learning framework and explicitly define answer sequences in the decoder. While such a “slide-by-slide” annotation has shown to be effective for simple questions, it limits the model to generate answers according to a predefined template. For example, it cannot answer questions that require complex computations, or answer questions in different formats. Solution: In this work, we propose an extractive question answering (Q/A) model based on the task-specific restricted Boltzmann machine (TSRBM). It not only learns to generate answers from question tokens to open-domain questions, but also complex logical expressions in a compact code. We also propose two techniques to improve the model performance: 1) Separate training for question classification and answer extraction, so the model can answer questions without involving unnecessary answer templates; 2) Differentiable code recognition to simplify the answer extraction code. Our model significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art on a widely used Q/A dataset, Semanticuen 8.0, by 14.5% F1 score on hard examples.' indeed, this paper deals with the problem of automatically generating answers from a knowledge base in an open-domain question answering setting. The approach the authors take is through using a restricted Boltzmann machine, which is optimized with gradient descent to identify a code which can be treated as a layer of a deep neural network to answer the question. The model is able to answer questions that contain a mix of complex logical expressions and simple question keywords with high F1 scores. The paper also contains innovations such as training question classification and answer extraction separately and generating answer codes that are specific enough to the question, both of which are able to significantly improve the F1 score of the model.

The paper makes some good points about learning span representation for extractive question answering, which is currently an active research topic. The paper mainly focuses on the answer extraction task on SQuAD, a popular dataset for this task. The evaluation metric also needs to be taken into consideration. pei Generally speaking, this paper makes some interesting points about learning span representation for extractive question answering. The model is based on a sequence-to-sequence framework, which is able to map the representations of spans in an input document to the representations of spans in a hypothesized answer. The learned representations could effectively capture the relationship between spans in the document and the answer. A key point is that the extracted spans may contain certain noises, which need to be further dealt with. This paper Learning Recurrent Span Representations for Extractive Question Answering addresses the answer extraction task, which can be formalized as a multi-label classification problem, where for each span in the evidence document a label needs to be assigned. A simple baseline is to factor the prediction into separate predictions about words or start and end markers. A more recent model, presented in this paper, factors the prediction into a single prediction about explicit span representations. The model presented in this paper significantly improves upon the best published results of Wang & Jiang (2016) by 5% and decreases the error of Rajpurkar et al.’s baseline by > 50%. impact hand over what problem or question this paper addresses, then strengths and weaknesses, for the paper Learning Recurrent Span Representations for Extractive Question Answering, its main content is as below: Problem Definition & Motivation: Given a question, described as a sequence of tokens, and an evidence article, with each sentence potentially representing a document span, this paper addresses the problem of extracting a answer from the document span, which can be formalized as a multi-label classification problem. The model is required to score each of the spans in the document against each of the candidate answer span labels. Previous attempts at this problem have relied on answer selection, by pre-defining or via an NLP pipeline, a small number of answer spans. The SQUAD dataset (Rajpurkar et al., 2016) provides a new, more general, benchmark, with answers that can be arbitrary strings from the text. Although answer spans have been shown to be effective for previous generations of SQuAD, this new dataset warrants the design of new scoring methods. Strengths: - The proposed SpanKnowNet model is an efficient means of learning fixed length span representations - The span representation can be easily adapted to any answer selection task with span labels - The span representation improves the baseline by 5% on SQuAD 2.0 - The paper justifies the use of span representations via an ablation study - The code is available for others to reproduce experiments - The paper covers topics that other submissions to this conference have so far avoided, such as how to choose a network architecture and how to pre-train it - The model is straightforward and intuitive, with a single line of code needed to train a new model - The paper cites other recent papers that have the same concern, e.g. ELMAN & PAMEL, Akata et al., Girdhar et al., Ravi & Hassibi, et al. Weaknesses: - The limited range of experiments on the SQuAD 2.0 validation set may detract from the generalizability of the results. - The lack of investigation of effective ways of combining span representations with word representations or character level embeddings could also be considered a weakness.
human_text:
The authors proposed RASOR to address the problem of finding the best answer span according to a given question. The focus of the paper is mainly on how to model the relationship between question and the answer spans. The idea proposed by this paper is reasonable, but not ground breaking. The analysis is interesting and potentially useful. I would hope the authors can go extra miles to analyze different choices of boundary prediction models and make a more convincing case for the necessity of modeling the score of the span globally.

The main idea behind RASOR is to globally normalize and rank the scores of the possible answer spans. RASOR is able to achieve this by first modeling the hidden vectors of all words with LSTMs. Then, the representation of a text span is formed by concatenating the corresponding hidden vectors of the start and the end word of the corresponding chunk. The approach is reasonable, but not earth shattering. Also, the table 6 shows that the improvement over end-prediction point is not very large.

I appreciate the fact that authors conduct several analysis experiments as some of them are quite interesting. For example, it seems that question independent representation is also very import to the performance. In addition to the current analysis, I also want to get a clear idea on what makes the current model be better than the Match-LSTM. Is it hyper-parameter tuning? Or it is due to the use of the question independent representation?

Another good thing about the proposed model is that it is relatively simple, so there is a chance that the proposed techniques can be combined with other newly proposed ones.

The program committee appreciates the authors' response to concerns raised in the reviews. Unfortunately, most reviewers are not leaning sufficiently towards acceptance. In particular, it is unfortunate that authors can not evaluate their model on the leaderboard due to copyright issues. The role of standard datasets and benchmarks is to allow for meaningful comparisons. Evaluation on non-standard splits defeats this purpose. Fortunately, sounds like authors are working on getting their model evaluated on the leaderboard. Resolving that and incorporating reviewers' feedback will help make the paper stronger.

We thank all three reviewers for the valuable comments and suggestions. 

We agree with reviewer 1 that the lack of test results is not ideal and sadly we do not yet have a manner in which we can run on the hidden test set, as not all of our code is open-sourced. However, we hope that the significant dev set size of 10k items, along with the cross-validation results add some reassurance that our hyperparameter tuning scheme has not overfit the data.

Reviewer 3 points out that the results in this paper are no longer state of the art. It is true that there are other papers on the leaderboard that have now surpassed our results, largely through ensembling. However, we believe that our paper is the only work to specifically study the impact of different span representations and we agree with Reviewer 3 that our findings should be complementary to other recent work on this dataset. We have added some extra quantitative and qualitative analysis of the differences between the span classifier and the endpoints predictor to illustrate the manner in which the quality of endpoint predictions degrade for longer sentences, in particular showing the tendency of endpoint models to pick out endpoints from separate answer candidates.

Reviewer 2 points out that the difference in performance between our model and the Match-LSTM cannot be accounted for by the difference in label type alone, and asks for the other most salient differences between the two approaches. While there are many small differences between the two implementations, the ablations in Table 2.a. suggest that most of this gap is accounted for by the passage independent question representation that is missing in the Match-LSTM. We have added an analysis of this representation in a new Table 3 and we have updated our discussion of the Match LSTM to clarify the basis of our comparison.

This paper proposes RaSoR, a method to efficiently representing and scoring all possible spans in an extractive QA task. While the test set results on SQuAD have not been released, it looks likely that they are not going to be state-of-the-art; with that said, the idea of enumerating all possible spans proposed in this paper could potentially improve many architectures. The paper is very well-written and the analysis/ablations in the final sections are mostly interesting (especially Figure 2, which confirms what we would intuitively believe). Based on its potential to positively impact other researchers working on SQuAD, I recommend that the paper is accepted.

This paper presents an architecture for answer extraction task and evaluates on the SQUAD dataset. The proposed model builds fixed length representations of all spans in the answer document based on recurrent neural network. It outperforms a few baselines in exact match and F1 on SQUAD.

It is unfortunate that the blind test results are not obtained yet due to the copyright issue. There are quite a few other systems/submissions on the SQUAD leader board that were available for comparison.

Given that there's no result on the test set reported, the grid search for hyperparameters on the dev set directly is also a concern, even though the authors did cross validation experiments.

The authors proposed RASOR to address the problem of finding the best answer span according to a given question. The focus of the paper is mainly on how to model the relationship between question and the answer spans. The idea proposed by this paper is reasonable, but not ground breaking. The analysis is interesting and potentially useful. I would hope the authors can go extra miles to analyze different choices of boundary prediction models and make a more convincing case for the necessity of modeling the score of the span globally.

The main idea behind RASOR is to globally normalize and rank the scores of the possible answer spans. RASOR is able to achieve this by first modeling the hidden vectors of all words with LSTMs. Then, the representation of a text span is formed by concatenating the corresponding hidden vectors of the start and the end word of the corresponding chunk. The approach is reasonable, but not earth shattering. Also, the table 6 shows that the improvement over end-prediction point is not very large.

I appreciate the fact that authors conduct several analysis experiments as some of them are quite interesting. For example, it seems that question independent representation is also very import to the performance. In addition to the current analysis, I also want to get a clear idea on what makes the current model be better than the Match-LSTM. Is it hyper-parameter tuning? Or it is due to the use of the question independent representation?

Another good thing about the proposed model is that it is relatively simple, so there is a chance that the proposed techniques can be combined with other newly proposed ones.

The program committee appreciates the authors' response to concerns raised in the reviews. Unfortunately, most reviewers are not leaning sufficiently towards acceptance. The role of standard datasets and benchmarks is to allow for meaningful comparisons. Evaluation on non-standard splits defeats this purpose. Fortunately, sounds like authors are working on getting their model evaluated on the leaderboard. Resolving that and incorporating reviewers' feedback will help make the paper stronger.

We thank all three reviewers for the valuable comments and suggestions. 

We agree with reviewer 1 that the lack of test results is not ideal and sadly we do not yet have a manner in which we can run on the hidden test set, as not all of our code is open-sourced. However, we hope that the significant dev set size of 10k items, along with the cross-validation results add some reassurance that our hyperparameter tuning scheme has not overfit the data.

Reviewer 3 points out that the results in this paper are no longer state of the art. It is true that there are other papers on the leaderboard that have now surpassed our results, largely through ensembling. However, we believe that our paper is the only work to specifically study the impact of different span representations and we agree with Reviewer 3 that our findings should be complementary to other recent work on this dataset. We have added some extra quantitative and qualitative analysis of the differences between the span classifier and the endpoints predictor to illustrate the manner in which the quality of endpoint predictions degrade for longer sentences, in particular showing the tendency of endpoint models to pick out endpoints from separate answer candidates.

Reviewer 2 points out that the difference in performance between our model and the Match-LSTM cannot be accounted for by the difference in label type alone, and asks for the other most salient differences between the two approaches. While there are many small differences between the two implementations, the ablations in Table 2.a. suggest that most of this gap is accounted for by the passage independent question representation that is missing in the Match-LSTM. We have added an analysis of this representation in a new Table 3 and we have updated our discussion of the Match LSTM to clarify the basis of our comparison.

This paper proposes RaSoR, a method to efficiently representing and scoring all possible spans in an extractive QA task. While the test set results on SQuAD have not been released, it looks likely that they are not going to be state-of-the-art; with that said, the idea of enumerating all possible spans proposed in this paper could potentially improve many architectures. The paper is very well-written and the analysis/ablations in the final sections are mostly interesting (especially Figure 2, which confirms what we would intuitively believe). Based on its potential to positively impact other researchers working on SQuAD, I recommend that the paper is accepted.

The paper A Neural Stochastic Volatility Model, its main content is as below: In this paper, we show that the recent integration of statistical models with recurrent neural networks provides a new way of formulating volatility models that have been popular in time series analysis and prediction. The model comprises a pair of complementary stochastic recurrent neural networks: the generative network models the joint distribution of the stochastic volatility process; the inference network approximates the conditional distribution of the latent variables given the observable ones. Our focus in this paper is on the formulation of temporal dynamics of volatility over time under a stochastic recurrent neural network framework. Our derivations show that some popular volatility models are a special case of our proposed neural stochastic volatility model. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed model generates a smoother volatility estimation, and largely outperforms a widely used GARCH model on several metrics about the fitness of the volatility modelling and the accuracy of the prediction. It generates a smoother volatility estimation. And the inferred volatility sequence tends to be persistent. This is to say, the volatility is to a certain extent predictable. The model also shows larger efficiency than the GARCH model on several metrics about the fitness of the volatility modelling and the accuracy of the prediction. However, I have several suggestions for the paper. First, it would be interesting to apply the model to a more complex time series, such as a equity price series. I wonder if the model could fit well with some other benchmark models, for example, GARCH model with stochastic LaguerreGPL parameters. It would be more convincing if the model could also fit well the equity price series. It would be more convincing if the model could also capture the heavy tailed distribution of the returns, for example, using an Student's T-distribution instead of the normal distribution. A Student's T-distribution has a larger mean and variance than the normal distribution. I wonder if the proposed model could still work well with this kind of changing distribution. In addition, the performance on out-of-sample prediction would be more convincing. I think the idea of using a stochastic neural network to model the volatility is very interesting. This is because the underlying stochastic network can encode a lot of distributional assumptions about the volatility process. And the dynamics of the volatility is modeled by a simple autoregressive process. I also think this is a good attempt to increase the flexibility of the Vol model, especially for non-Gaussian data. I think the only problem with the approach is that it is difficult to tune the model's hyper-parameters, especially the `temperature' parameter `θ'. I think there are two approaches to deal with this issue. One approach is to apply approximate Bayesian methods, for example, slice sampling. The other approach is to minimize an approximation of the evidence lower bound. It is also possible to combine the two approaches. I think this would be a nice extension of the paper. I think the paper has the potential to contribute to the volatility modelling community. In my opinion, the model has two advantages. The first advantage is the stochastic network formulation makes the model very flexible. The model can be applied to various volatility models as a special case. For example, it is straightforward to add stochastic variance to GARCH model or to any other mean-reverting models. The second advantage of the proposed model is that it not only generates a smooth and stationary distribution, it also captures the structural change in volatility dynamic. The advantage is that, compared to models only based on ordinary differential equation (ODE) or random processes, it is more reasonable and easier to capture the change in the dynamics of the volatility. The proposed model has several appealing properties. First, the structural change in volatility is explicitly represented by the dynamic of the inference network. Second, it also has some inference network which can capture the heavy tailed distribution of the returns. This could help to further improve the model's efficiency. human_text:
Thank you for an interesting read.

I found the application of VRNN type generative model to financial data very promising. But since I don't have enough background knowledge to judge whether the performance gap is significant or not, I wouldn't recommend acceptance at this stage. 

To me, the biggest issue for this paper is that I'm not sure if the paper contains significant novelty. The RNN-VAE combination has been around for more than a year and this paper does not propose significant changes to it. Maybe this paper fits better to an application targeting conference, rather than ICLR. But I'm not exactly sure about ICLR's acceptance criteria, and maybe the committee actually prefer great performances and interesting applications?

This paper presents an interesting application of variational methods for time series, in particular VRNN-like approaches, for stochastic volatility. Applications such as these are clearly in the scope of the conference, which was a point that one of the reviewer brought up. That said, questions of context, especially with regards to relation to different approaches, especially smoothing are relevant. Also, the number of methods GRACH and stochastic volatility is immense and this makes assessing the impact of this very hard to do and is more is needed to address this point. This paper is certainly interesting, but given these concerns, the paper is not yet rady for acceptance at the conference.

The authors propose a recurrent variational neural network approach to modelling volatility in financial time series. This model consists of an application of Chung et al.’s (2015) VRNN model to volatility forecasting, wherein a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) structure is repeated at each time step of the series. 

The paper is well written and easy to follow (although this reviewer suggests applying a spelling checking, since the paper contains a number of harmless typos). 

The paper’s main technical contribution is to stack two levels of recurrence, one for the latent process and one for the observables. This appears to be a novel, if minor contribution. The larger contribution is methodological, in areas of time series modelling that are both of great practical importance and have hitherto been dominated by rigid functional forms. The demonstration of the applicability and usefulness of general-purpose non-linear models for volatility forecasting would be extremely impactful.

I have a few comments and reservations with the paper:
1) Although not  mentioned explicitly, the authors’ framework are couched in terms of carrying out one-timestep-ahead forecasts of volatility. However, many applications of volatility models, for instance for derivative pricing, require longer-horizon forecasts. It would be interesting to discuss how this model could be extended to forecast at longer horizons.
 
2) In Section 4.4, there’s a mention that a GARCH(1,1) is conditionally deterministic. This is true only when forecasting 1 time-step in the future. At longer horizons, the GARCH(1,1) volatility forecast is not deterministic. 

3) I was initially unhappy with the limitations of the experimental validation, limited to comparison with a baseline GARCH model. However, the authors provided more comparisons in the revision, which adds to the quality of the results, although the models compared against cannot be considered state of the art. It would be well advised to look into R packages such as `stochvol’ and ‘fGarch’ to get implementations of a variety of models that can serve as useful baselines, and provide convincing evidence that the modelled volatility is indeed substantially better than approaches currently entertained by the finance literature.

4) In Section 5.2, more details should be given on the network, e.g. number of hidden units, as well as the embedding dimension D_E (section 5.4)

5) In Section 5.3, more details should be given on the data generating process for the synthetic data experiments. 

6) Some results in the appendix are very puzzling: around jumps in the price series, which are places where the volatility should spike, the model reacts instead by huge drops in the volatility (Figure 4(b) and (c), respectively around time steps 1300 and 1600). This should be explained and discussed.

All in all, I think that the paper provides a nice contribution to the art of volatility modelling. In spite of some flaws, it provides a starting point for the broader impact of neural time series processing in the financial community.

The authors propose a recurrent neural network approach for constructing a
stochastic volatility model for financial time series. They introduce an
inference network based on a recurrent neural network that computes the
approximation to the posterior distribution for the latent variables given the
past data. This variational approximation is used to maximize the marginal
likelihood in order to learn the parameters of the model. The proposed method
is validated in experiments with synthetic and real-world time series, showing
to outperform parametric GARCH models and a Gaussian process volatility model.

Quality:

The method proposed seems technically correct, with the exception that in

machine_text: The paper entitled "Parametric Exponential Linear Unit for Deep Convolutional Neural Networks" by Heung-Yeung Shum and Simon Hayat presents a modification to the exponential linear unit (ELU) and shows improved performance on a range of tasks. Specifically, the proposed Parametric ELU (PELU) is able to model the velocity of changing outputs, and so can be used in dynamic settings. The PElu is constructed as a scaling, bias and parametric element, and the scaling parameter can be learned. The PElu is shown to improve performance across several different tasks and architectures. The work is sound and the conclusions are valid. There are, however, a few points that may help the reader better understand the work. First, it would be useful to know the detailed architecture of the ELU and PElu. For example, is the element used in each case the same? Or is there a different element used in the PElu? This would help interpret the differences in performance. The current text is unclear on this point, and might be confusing to some readers. A second area for improvement is in the choice of tasks. The work is presented for language and vision tasks, and it would be good to extend the work to other domains such as reinforcement learning and NLP. The paper could also be strengthened by using additional quantitative measures such as BLEU. These would provide stronger evidence of the effectiveness of the PElu over the ELU. These are minor points, and the work described is clearly an improvement over the ELU. However, the PElu might provide another useful tool for those working with deep learning, and this is an area where improvements are likely to continue.

This paper introduces the Parametric Exponential Linear Unit (PELU), an improved architecture for deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs). In this model, the matrix exponential is used to define a set of mathematical operations analogous to the Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) and PReLU. Unlike previous works that optimize the network structure, PELU expands the domain of the rectifier by allowing the exponential parameters to vary over the convolution filter. Thus, PELU can effectively improve the representational power of the shallow network and reduce the training burden of the deep network. PELU also helps to stabilize the training process by limiting the explode degrees of the parameters. Authors present a parameterized variant of ELU and show that the proposed function helps to deal with vanishing gradients in deep networks in a way better than existing non-linearities. They present both a theoretical analysis and practical validation for presented approach. 

Interesting observations on statistics of the PELU parameters are reported. Perhaps explanation for the observed evolution of parameters can help better understand the non-linearity. It is hard to evaluate the experimental validation presented given the difference in number of parameters compared to other approaches.

The paper describes a parametric version of the exponential linear unit (ELU) activation function. The novelty of the contribution is limited, and the experimental evaluation in its current form is not convincing.

The paper deals with a very important issue of vanishing gradients and the quest for a perfect activation function. Proposed is an approach of learning the activation functions during the training process. I find this research very interesting, but I am concerned that the paper is a bit premature.

There is a long experimental section, but I am not sure what the conclusion is. The authors appear to be somewhat confused themselves. The amount of "maybe" "could mean", "perhaps" etc. statements in the paper is exceptionally high. For this paper to be accepted it needs a bold statement about the performance, with a solid evidence. In my opinion, that is lacking as of now. This approach is either a breakthrough or a dud, and after reading the paper I am not convinced which case it is.

The theoretical section could be made a little clearer.

Finally, how is the performance affected. The huge advantage if ReLU is in the fact that the formula is so simple and thus not costly to evaluate. How do PELU-s compare.

This paper presents a new non-linear function for CNN and deep neural networks. 
The new non-linearity reports some gains on most datasets of interest, and can be used in production networks with minimal increase in computation.

This paper proposes a modification of the ELU activation function for neural networks, by parameterizing it with 2 trainable parameters per layer. This parameter is proposed to more effectively counter vanishing gradients. 

My main concern regarding this paper is related to the authors' claims about the effectiveness of PELU. The analysis in Sections 2 and 3 discusses how PELU might improve training by combating gradient propagation issues. This by itself does not imply that improved generalization will result, only that models may be easier to train. However, the experiments all seek to demonstrate improved generalization performance.
But this could in principle be due to a better inductive bias, and have nothing to do with the optimization analysis. None of the experiments are designed to directly support the stated theoretical advantage of PELU compared to ELU in optimizing models.

In the response to the pre-review question, the authors state that the claims in Section 2 and 3.3 are meant to apply to generalization performance. I fail to see how this is true for most claims, except the flexibility claim. As the authors agree, better training may or may not lead to better out-of-sample performance. I can only agree that having flexibility can sometimes help the network adapt its inductive bias to the problem (instead of overfitting), but this is a much weaker claim compared to the mathematical justifications for improved optimization.

On selection of learning hyperparameters:
The authors state in the discussion on OpenReview that the learning rates selected were favorable to ReLU, and not PELU. However, this does not guarantee that they were not unfavorable to ELU. It raises the question: can a regime be constructed where ELU has better performance than PELU? If so, how can we draw the conclusion that PELU is better?

Overall, I am not yet convinced by the experimental setup and the match between theory and experiments in this paper.

This paper describes an approach for unsupervised learning of state representation using robotic priors (RLSP). The main idea is to use a standard recurrent neural network architecture, but the fully-connected layers are replaced with layers that map from robot states to a common frame. The network is trained end-to-end using only the target state sequence as supervision. Performance is evaluated on two simulated robotic tasks, and the effectiveness of the robotic priors is demonstrated. The approach of using robot state encodings as prior knowledge for unsupervised learning has several advantages over previous work. First, RLSP is completely unsupervised, i.e. no labeled data about the state distribution is required. This makes the approach more generally applicable. Second, state representation is explicitly learned without supervision, which may be more general than previous work which required pre-defined structuring of state via hand-engineered feature vectors. Third, the approach is relatively simple and can be easily combined with other unsupervised approaches, further increasing the variety of knowledge that can be transferred from simulation to reality. The main drawbacks of RLSP are the resulting low resolution state representation (7DOF vs 29DOF for full state) and the limited scalability to higher-dimensional state spaces. These drawbacks are partially addressed in the paper through the use of residual connections and a hierarchical extension of the model. Despite these improvements, it remains difficult to directly apply the learned state representation to a new robot. One approach to alleviate this issue is to use the same model at test time but with different random initializations, a procedure which is shown to be effective at increasing the generalization performance.

The approach of this paper aims to reproduce this simplification process using a neural network to produce a simple low dimensional state representation of the world from images acquired by a robot. As proposed in Jonschkowski & Brock (2015), we train the neural network in an unsupervised way, using the "a priori" knowledge we have about the world as loss functions called "robotic priors" that we implemented through a siamese network. This approach has been used to learn a one dimension representation of a Baxter head position from raw images. The experiment resulted in a 97,7% correlation between the learned representation and the ground truth, and show that relevant visual features form the environment are learned. The core of this method is to use "robotic priors" to guide the neural network into a state where a simplified low-dimensional state representation of the world can be recovered. As J&B argue, this simplification is a side effect of our brain using this method to learn a low-dimensional state representation. The simplification process is valuable as it reveals the essence of the input to the system. For example, we can understand that a locust is really just moving legs and nothing more by simplifying its three-dimensional state to two dimensions. This simplified state representation can be widely used in many areas, such as automatic image retrieval, robotic control, and even natural language processing. This method have some appealing properties. First, the model is able to reduce the dimensionality of the state space, implicitly clustering similar states together. Second, the high correlation between the ground truth state and the reduced state representation shows that the network indeed has learned the essence of the state space. Third, the network is trained in an unsupervised manner, without requiring access to the reward function or relying on reinforcement learning algorithm to optimize the policy. As discussed in J&B, the core of the algorithm is to use the similarity between states during the training process, and the resulted structure of the state space can reflect the similarity between the different aspects of the state. This work presents a beautiful experiment that successfully reproduced the essence of the state with a similar result. There are two downsides of this method. First, the computation cost is expensive, which is caused by the need to calculate the kernel matrices in the objective function. The kernel matrices will increase rapidly with the increase of the state space dimension. For example, if a three-layer fully connected network is used as the discriminator, and we want to explore the state space with one-dimensional state, the kernel matrix size is 12, i.e., 6 * 2 (the number of input and output layers). This high computational cost greatly limits the usage of this method. Second, the current version of this method only supports a low-dimensional state space. Extrapolating this algorithm to high dimensional spaces is difficult as we need to find more powerful similarity metrics between the high-dimensional states. Although there is an inspiring discussion on transferring the knowledge from low- to high-dimensional state space (Tishby & Zaslavsky, 2010), the performance still needs to be evaluated. Overall, this is a promising method to perform unsupervised learning of a low-dimensional state representation. The limitation of dimensionality and the difficulty to extend to higher-dimensional state space must be solved by further exploration of the similarity metrics or finding more efficient training method. As human beings, we live in a world where we have a priori knowledge about the world we live in. For example, we know how the earth is shaped, and we understand its gravitational pull. These a priori knowledge provide a very intuitive way to simplify our perception of the world and our interaction with it. This paper aims to reproduce this simplification process using a neural network. As the name of the approach suggests, this is achieved by unsupervised learning, that is, the network is trained without directly providing it with the simplified state representation we are looking for. Instead, the network learns to reproduce the a priori knowledge in the form of a loss function, through a siamese network. This approach has been used to learn a one dimension representation of a Baxter head position, and the experiment resulted in a 97,7% correlation between the learned representation and the ground truth. The learned representation has also been shown to contain relevant visual features of the world. izar, the approach as described in the paper has several interesting ideas, but there are some aspects that need further clarification. For example, why siamese network? Why one dimension? Can the results be improved by using more dimensions? Mi observations) The siamese network is used to compare the two states of the network, that is, the current state and the next state of the network. The structure of the siamese network is designed in a way that let the network learn the similarity between two states based on the objective the network is trying to reach. In this case, the siamese network is used to compare the current state and the one dimensional state representation the network would like to learn. The loss function is designed to minimize the distance between these two state representations, that is, the negative log likelihood of the one dimensional representation calculated by the siamese network. As the name suggests, this method is an implementation of the unsupervised approach. The result has been shown to be able to learn a one-dimensional state representation of a Baxter head position, and the correlation between the learned representation and the ground truth is 97.7%.

This paper implements the method of Jonschkowski & Brock to learn a low-dimensional state representation represented as the last layer of a neural network. The experiments apply the method for learning a one-dimensional state representation of a simulated robot’s head position from synthetic images.

Learning state representations is an active and useful area of research for learning representations in interactive domains such as robotics. However, there seems to be no novelty in the method, over Jonschkowki & Brock. The primary contribution is the experimental evaluation performed on one task, where the paper evaluates the correlation between the learned state representation and the ideal state representation for the task (which is the robot’s head position).

As acknowledged by the authors, the experiments are very preliminary, only showing one simple task with a one-dimensional learned representation and a two-dimensional discrete action space. To make the experiments compelling, there need to be comparisons to prior methods such as Lange et al. ’12, Watter et al. NIPS ’15, and Finn et al. ICRA ’16 which also learn state representations from raw images. PCA on the images would also be a useful comparison, especially for simple tasks. Without these comparisons, it is impossible to evaluate the effectiveness of the method.

Lastly, as mentioned in the pre-review questions, the related work should include a discussion of other state representation learning methods such as Watter et al. NIPS ’15, Finn et al. ICRA ’16, and van Hoof et al. IROS ’16.

In summary, this paper lacks novelty and significance, as the paper implements an existing method and demonstrates results on only one simple task. Without comparisons, the results are impossible to interpret. More challenging tasks and experimental comparisons would significantly improve the paper. Additionally, this paper does not introduce any novel contributions to state representation learning for solving challenges in this domain. One pro is that the paper is generally written clearly.

With proper experiments, and if the method works in interesting realistic scenarios, this could become a good paper.

This paper proposed to use unsupervised learning to learn features in a reinforcement learning setting. It is unclear what "unsupervised" means here since the "causality prior" uses reward signals for training. This is reinforcement learning, not unsupervised learning.

The experiments are also very premature. The task is as simple as moving the head of the robot left or right. There is also no comparison to baselines.

In conclusions section, the authors claim the proposed method can be used for transfer learning without experiments to backup the claim.

Overall this paper is confusing and premature.

This paper addresses the problem of coarse pruning of convolutional neural networks (CNNs). They use a method they call random masks, which is actually a form of dropout, and prune a network by setting some of the layers’ weights to 0. The paper shows that by randomly setting a percentage of the weights in a layer to 0 and then training the network, you can reduce the size of the network without too much loss in performance. The method used by the paper to randomize the masks, which is crucial to getting good results, is to shift each mask by a random value before applying it. The method could be extended to other kinds of pruning, such as channel pruning. The paper also shows that by using a more complicated network architecture, called a bottleneck architecture, you can improve the performance of the network even when a large percentage (~50%) of the weights are randomized. This paper shows that it is possible to prune large portions of a deep network without hurting performance too much. This might allow for greater compression of deep networks without decreasing performance, which would be helpful for deploying them on mobile devices or other systems with limited capacity. The paper has some weaknesses. First, there is no attempt to analyze how much computing power the network uses, so it is unclear how much this method would reduce the cost of inference for the network. Second, it only demonstrates results for small CIFAR-100 datasets, so it is unclear whether the method would also be effective on larger datasets. Third, because the method is simply dropout in disguise, it might not be sufficiently statistical to get good results, and the paper includes a comparison with a baseline where a small subset of the randomly chosen masks are actually not dropped. Overall, this is a useful contribution for the field of network compression, and the method could be easily adopted by other researchers. Some of the ideas in this paper could be improved by analyzing how much each layer’s computation contributes to the overall network performance. At a high level, this could involve using guided dropout, but it would probably require collecting extensive data about how the loss changes as each weight is varied, which would take a lot of time and be subject to the usual trade-offs between running time and statistical precision. Another idea for improving this method would be to modify the architecture of the network to emphasize different parts of the dataset. For example, if you were trying to classify small CIFAR-100 images, you would want to use a network with many more layers than if you were trying to classify large ones. A possible solution would be to use a network architecture called a capsule network, in which each layer has a certain number of regions, or capsules, each capsule containing a connection to every neuron in that layer. A new mask could be generated for each capsule instead of for each individual weight. If you combined this kind of architecture with the knowledge about which part of the dataset a model is trying to classify, it might be possible to prune a network to much lower sizes without significant loss in performance. The sufficient number of random pruning masks to try depends on the pruning ratio, and is around 100 when 40% complexity reduction is needed. This paper addresses the issue of computational complexity of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs). The training of DNNs requires summing up the contribution of all the weights in the network, known as Forward Pass. The Forward Pass for an input x is a function f(x), and the complexity is roughly O(n) where n is the number of weights. However, during prediction, the evaluation of the Forward Pass is done for only one input example, known as a Forward Pass of a sample. Since the evaluation of the Forward Pass is performed for only one sample, the evaluation complexity reduces to O(1). However, the complexity of Forward Pass is same as that of the entire Training. Therefore, the complexity of Training and Prediction for DNNs is O(n+1). This paper proposes a solution to reduce the complexity of DNNs to O(n). The main idea is to select a subset of weights to be non-zero. The non-zero selected weights are realized using a structure like a sparse matrix, leading to reduced complexity. The paper describes a technique to find the best subset of weights based on a certain measure of complexity. The measure of complexity needed for finding the best subset is customized. The best subset is selected using a given range of complexity values. The process is repeated for different ranges of complexity values, and an optimal complexity is found. The proposed approach of reducing the complexity of DNNs works as follows. The Forward Pass is divided into multiple iterations, and each iteration is processed using a separate kernel. The kernel can be a sequence of fixed filters, or a trainable layer. The kernel operates on a fixed set of input features and a random subset of weights. The kernel has less number of weights as compared to the total number of weights in the network. The complexity of Forward Pass for a subset of weights is reduced, since the Forward Pass for each sample is performed only once, instead of n times for the full set of weights. The computational complexity is further reduced by using parallel processing in GPUs or CPUs for parallel evaluation of Kernels. The optimal complexity found is used for further reducing the complexity of the network. For instance, it is split into feature maps, and later into kernels. Since the number of kernels is smaller than the number of feature maps, the complexity is further reduced. The kernel pruning is performed on a feature map, using a similarity metric between filters. The feature map with similarity above a certain threshold is grouped into a cluster. Each cluster is assigned a representative filter. The representative filters have high similarity and hence low complexity. The threshold used for grouping the feature map is determined using a validation set. The kernel pruning mask is the binary representation of the cluster id. The complexity of the representative filter is low, and hence the complexity of the feature map is also low. The representative filter is replaced by the pruning mask. The representative filter is used for the Forward Pass for samples, to which the pruning mask is 0. The prediction for the samples for which the pruning mask is 0, is performed using the original weights for the representative filter. The prediction for the samples for which the pruning mask is 1, is performed using the randomly generated pruning masks for the representative filter. The prediction for the entire Forward Pass for a sample is done by combining the outputs of the representative filter and the outputs from the corresponding pruned feature map. The pruned feature map with original weights, and the representative filter with randomly selected pruning masks are the main contributions. The paper also provides the evaluation of the proposed approach on CIFAR-10, SVHN and MNIST datasets. The paper has the following limitations. The pruning of kernels is performed by using the similarity metric between features from a feature map. The representative filter is used for both the feature map and the kernel. Since the similarity metric is used to identify the representative filter, the performance may suffer due to the limitations in the similarity metric. Furthermore, the pruning of kernels results in empty kernel. The empty kernel will be a problem when the pruned network is used for evaluation. The evaluation of the pruned network on a subset of samples may not provide expected result, as there is some erroneous output from the empty kernel. The representative filter may be something like a filter with Zero-Bias, which passes the input directly to the next layer. A Filter with Zero-Bias would be a good representative. The pruned feature map is also not optimal, since it is selected using only a certain similarity metric. Other similarity metrics can be used for finding the representative. The paper also does not describe the architecture of the pruned network. The model architecture used for the baseline is not shared. The model validation is also not shown. Summary: There are many different pruning techniques to reduce memory footprint of CNN models, and those techniques have different granularities (layer, maps, kernel or intra kernel), pruning ratio and sparsity of representation. The work proposes a method to choose the best pruning masks out to many trials. Tested on CIFAR-10, SVHN and MNIST.

Pros:
Proposes a method to choose pruning mask out of N trials. 
Analysis on different pruning methods.

Cons & Questions:
“The proposed strategy selects the best pruned network through N random pruning trials. This approach enables one to select pruning mask in one shot and is simpler than the multi-step technique.” How can one get the best pruning mask in one shot if you ran N random pruning trials? (answered)
Missing tests of the approach with bigger CNN: like AlexNet, VGG, GoogLeNet or ResNet. (extended to VGG ok)
Since reducing model size for embedded systems is the final goal, then showing how much memory space in MB is saved with the proposed technique compared with other approaches like Han et al. (2015) would be good.

Misc:
Typo in figure 6 a) caption: “Featuer” (corrected)

Unfortunately this paper is not competitive enough for ICLR. The paper is focusing on efficiency where for the results to be credible it is of utmost importance to present experiments on large scale data and state-of-the-art models.
 I am afraid the reviewers were not able to take into account the latest drafts of the paper that were submitted in January, but those submissions came very late.

2) Lebedev, Vadim, and Victor Lempitsky. "Fast convnets using group-wise brain damage." Proceedings of the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2016.
3) Alvarez, Jose M., and Mathieu Salzmann. "Learning the Number of Neurons in Deep Networks." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems. 2016.

can you please take a look at the responses by the authors and add a comment indicating that you have taken them into consideration?

Thanks!

This paper proposes a simple randomized algorithm for selecting which weights in a ConvNet to prune in order to reduce theoretical FLOPs when evaluating a deep neural network. The paper provides a nice taxonomy or pruning granularity from coarse (layer-wise) to fine (intra-kernel). The pruning strategy is empirically driven and uses a validation set to select the best model from N randomly pruned models. Makes claims in the intro about this being "one shot" and "near optimal" that cannot be supported: it is "N-shot" in the sense that N networks are generated and tested and there is no evidence or theory that the found solution is "near optimal."

Pros:
- Nice taxonomy of pruning levels
- Comparison to the recent weight-sum pruning method

Cons:
- Experimental evaluation does not touch upon recent models (ResNets) and large scale datasets (ImageNet)
- Paper is somewhat hard to follow
- Feature map pruning can obviously accelerate computation without specialized sparse implementations of convolution, but this is not the case for finer grained sparsity; since this paper considers fine-grained sparsity it should provide some evidence that introducing that sparsity can yield performance improvements

Another experimental downside is that the paper does not evaluate the impact of filter pruning on transfer learning. For example, there is not much direct interest in the tasks of MNIST, CIFAR10, or even ImageNet. Instead, a main interest in both academia and industry is the value of the learned representation for transferring to other tasks. One might expect pruning to harm transfer learning. It's possible that the while the main task has about the same performance, transfer learning is strongly hurt. This paper has missed an opportunity to explore that direction.

In summary, the proposed method is simple, which is good, but the experimental evaluation is somewhat incomplete and does not cover recent models and larger scale datasets.

This paper proposes two pruning methods to reduce the computation of deep neural network. In particular, whole feature maps and the kernel connections can be removed with not much decrease of classification accuracy. 
However, this paper also has the following problems. 
1)	The method is somehow trivial, since the pruning masks are mainly chosen by simple random sampling. The novelty and scalability are both limited. 
2)	Experiment results are mainly focused on the classification rate and the ideal complexity. As a paper on improving computation efficiency, it should include results on practical time consumption. It is very common that reducing numbers of operations may not lead to reduced computational time on a highly parallel platform (e.g., GPU). 
3)	It is more important to improve the computational efficiency on large-scale models (e.g., ImageNet classification network) than on small models (e.g., MNIST, CIFAR network). However, results on large-scale network is missing.
4)	(*Logical validity of the proposed method*) For feature map pruning, what if just to train reduced-size network is trained from scratch without transfer any knowledge from the pretrained large network? Is it possible to get the same accuracy? If so, it will simply indicate the hyper-parameter is not optimal for the original network. Experimental results are necessary to clarify the necessity of feature map pruning. 
Note that I agree with that a smaller network may be more generalizable than a larger network. 

----------------------------------------------

Comments to the authors's response:

Thanks for replying to my comments. 

1) I still believe that the proposed methods are trivial.
2) It is nice to show GPU implementation. Compared to existing toolboxes (e.g., Torch, Caffe, TensorFlow), is the implementation of convolution efficient enough?
3) Experiments on Cifar-100 are helpful (better than cifar-10), but it is not really large-scale, where speed-up is not so critical. ImageNet and Places datasets are examples of large-scale datasets.
4) The author did not reply to the question wrt the validity of the proposed methods. This question is critical.

machine_text: In general, the paper is well written. It is a very good introduction to the ENet architecture, explaining the main ideas and design choices. However, I have some concerns about the evaluation, in particular about the use of the average intersection over union metric. I think this is a flawed metric to compare models, as it does not reflect the differences in the precision of the predictions. The average IoU only measures how many pixels are correctly classified, regardless of whether those pixels are in the correct objects. For example, if I predicted all the pixels as belonging to the pig, the average IoU would be 1, even if the pig is correctly classified only 90% of the time. I think the paper would improve if the authors switched to using the positive prediction accuracy (PPA) metric, which measures the accuracy at which pixels are correctly classified to specific objects. Here is a table with the average IoU and PPA for several models: Model average IoU PPA ResNet-50-FPN 0.903 0.903 DLA-38-64s 0.872 0.872 DLA-38-256s 0.849 0.849 DLA-50-64s 0.834 0.850 ENet-B5 0.825 0.845 ENet-B7 0.825 0.849 DenseNet-BC 0.825 0.850 I think the ENet-B5 model would have a much lower average PPA if it was compared with the ResNet-50-FPN model in the same paper, because in many cases the ENet-B5 incorrectly classifies background as table, whereas ResNet-50-FPN correctly predicts that most pixels are background. I think the PPA metric is more appropriate than the average IoU when evaluating models for real-world use cases, such as semantic segmentation. I agree that the average IoU can be a useful metric for comparing models in the same paper, for example when comparing ENet to another model such as ResNet-50-FPN. In summary, I think the PPA metric would be more appropriate than the average IoU for evaluating the ENet model, and I think the authors should consider using PPA instead of the average IoU when comparing models in the same paper or in public assessment campaigns such as Mask Pass AI.\

The ENet architecture is a novel, deep, fully convolutional neural network for real-time semantic image segmentation. The authors present an elegant solution to the often-encountered problem of limited GPU memory when training very deep CNNs. Instead of using a fully-convolutional layer, they split the fully-convolutional layer into several smaller, less-expensive, convolutional layers, reducing the total memory requirements of the network. The performance improvement is able to justify the complexity of the network architecture, with the accompanying visualization tools provide insights into how the network is extracting semantic information from the images. The code is also provided, so that others can reproduce the authors’ results and check their own findings. The ENet architecture provides a solution to the problem of limited GPU memory when training very deep networks. It is especially useful for very large, complex tasks, such as internet-of-things scene understanding, where the number of regions of interest can be extremely large but the amount of RAM in GPUs is much more limited. The trade-off of using this network architecture is a slight performance degradation, but the overall effectiveness of the network in segmenting individual regions of interest warrants the slight loss in performance. The code and data are available to ensure other researchers can reproduce the authors’ results and validate their own findings. Overall, this is a very well-written and presented paper that will be of interest to others working on similar problems to improve the efficiency and performance of very deep networks for semantic image segmentation. I’ve summarized the paper’s key contributions below. 1. The ENet architecture is a novel approach to segmenting individual regions of interest using very deep networks. The network architecture splits the fully-convolutional layer into several smaller, less-expensive, convolutional layers that reduce the total memory requirements without significant performance degradation. 2. The effectiveness of the architecture is demonstrated by the authors’ consistent performance improvement on the Cityscapes dataset. 3. The accompanying visualization tools provide clear insights into how the network is parsing the images to extract semantic information. 4. The code is made available to ensure others can reproduce the authors’ results and validate their own findings. Overall, this is a very well-designed and presented paper that will be of interest to researchers working on very deep networks for semantic image segmentation. Here are the paper’s key limitations. 1. There are many complex issues when using deep networks for semantic image segmentation, such as scaling to very large data sets. To the authors’ credit, this problem is mentioned as a significant limitation of the ENet architecture. 2. There is a very significant gap between the published and actual paper in terms of methodological detail. For example, there is no information about how the authors perform hyperparameter tuning, which is a very common step in the process of building a deep network. 3. There is no information about how the authors use data preprocessing to prepare the training data. This could be preprocessing the images to improve semantic segmentation, using more sophisticated data augmentation techniques, or both. 4. The paper introduces a lightweight network for semantic segmentation that combines several acceleration ideas.
As indicated in my preliminary question, the authors do not make the case about why any of the techniques they propose is beyond what we know already: factorizing filters into alternating 1-D convolutions, using low-rank kernels, or any of the newer inception network architectures.

I have had a hard time figuring out what is the take-home message of this paper. All of these ideas are known, and have proven their worth for detection. If a paper is going to be accepted for applying them to semantic segmentation, then in the next conference another paper should be accepted for applying them to normal estimation, another to saliency estimation and so on. 

As the authors mention in their preliminary review:
"I agree that most improvements from classification architectures are straightforward to apply to object segmentation, and that's exactly what we've done - our network is based on current state of the art models. Instead of repeating most of the discussion on factorizing filters, etc., that has been discussed in a lot of papers already, we have decided that it's much more valuable to describe in depth the choices that are related to segmentation only - these are the most important contributions of our paper."

I do not see however any in-depth discussion of certain choices - e.g. an analysis of how certain choices influence performance or speed. Instead all one gets are some statements "these gave a significant accuracy boost" "this helped a lot", "that did not help", "this turned out to work much better than that" . This is not informative - and is more like an informal chat rather than an in-depth discussion. 

If novelty is not that important, and it is only performance or speed that matter, I am still not convinced.
The authors only compare to [1,2] (SegNet) in terms of both accuracy and speed. I cannot see the reason why they do so, and they do not really justify it. According to the authors' evaluation, [1] requires ~1 sec. per frame,  while Deeplab v2, without the DenseCRF, runs at 5-8fps.
