This paper introduces a maximum total correlation procedure, adds a target and then adds noise perturbations.

Technical issues:

The move from (1) to (2) is problematic. Yes it is a lower bound, but by igoring H(Z), equation (2) ignores the fact that H(Z) will potentially vary more significantly that H(Z|Y). As a result of removing H(Z), the objective (2) encourages Z that are low entropy as the H(Z) term is ignored, doubly so as low entropy Z results in low entropy Z|Y. Yes the -H(X|Z) mitigates against a complete entropy collapse for H(Z), but it still neglects critical terms. In fact one might wonder if this is the reason that semantic noise addition needs to be done anyway, just to push up the entropy of Z to stop it reducing too much.

In (3) arbitrary balancing paramters lamda_1 and lambda_2 are introduced ex-nihilo - they were not there in (2). This is not ever justified.

Then in (5), a further choice is made by simply adding L_{NLL} to the objective. But in the supervised case, the targets are known and so turn up in H(Z|Y). Hence now H(Z|Y) should be conditioned on the targets. However instead another objective is added again without justification, and the conditional entropy of Z is left disconnected from the data it is to be conditioned on. One might argue the C(X,Y,Z) simply acts as a prior on the networks (and hence implicitly on the weights) that we consider, which is then combined with a likelihood term, but this case is not made. In fact there is no explicit probabilistic or information theoretic motivation for the chosen objective.

Given these issues, it is then not too surprising that some further things need to be done, such as semantic noise addition to actually get things working properly. It may be the form of noise addition is a good idea, but given the troublesome objective being used in the first place, it is very hard to draw conclusions.

In summary, substantially better theoretical justification of the chosen model is needed, before any reasonable conclusion on the semantic noise modelling can be made.

The reviewers all expressed concerns with the technical quality of this work. In particular, the reviewers are concerned that ignoring certain entropy terms in the objective is problematic and would require significantly more justification theoretically and empirically. The reviewers believe that the authors had to resort to unjustified tricks such as adding noise in order to compensate for the missing terms in the objective. Some of the reviewers also had concerns with the choice of experiments, expressing that the authors did not choose the right baseline comparisons to compare to (e.g. convolutional networks vs. fully connected networks on MNIST). Hopefully the thorough feedback and lengthly discussion, along with the authors' responses (both in the text and additions to the paper and appendix), will lead to a stronger submission to a future conference.

We have made overall revisions to the manuscript in order to clarify mathematical justification, explanations, and several empirical analyses. Among the revised contents, we especially focused on the methodology part (Section 2). Section 2 is divided into two subsections. Section 2.1 explains the base model as an extension of joint learning approaches. This subsection includes details of derivations for mathematical justification of the base model (See Appendix_A1). Section 2.2 shows the proposed latent space modeling method. This subsection focuses on explaining how to model the semantic-preserving perturbation on the latent space. We are sorry for the incompleteness of the early version of manuscript. We ask the reviewers to revisit the updated manuscript once again.

The paper introduces supervised deep learning with layer-wise reconstruction loss (in addition to the supervised loss) and class-conditional semantic additive noise for better representation learning. Total correlation measure and additional insights from auto-encoder are used to derive layer-wise reconstruction loss and is further combined with supervised loss. When combining with supervised loss the class-conditional additive noise model is proposed, which showed consistent improvement over the baseline model. Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets while changing the number of training examples per class are done extensively.

The derivation of Equation (3) from total correlation is hacky. Moreover, assuming graphical model between X, Y and Z, it should be more carefully derived to estimate H(X|Z) and H(Z|Y). The current proposal, encoding Z and Y from X and decoding from encoded representation is not really well justified.

Is \sigma in Equation 8 trainable parameter or hyperparameter? If it is trainable how it is trained? If it is not, how are they set? Does j correspond to one of the class? The proposed feature augmentation sounds like simply adding gaussian noise to the pre-softmax neurons. That being said, the proposed method is not different from gaussian dropout (Wang and Manning, ICML 2013) but applied on different layers. In addition, there is a missing reference (DisturbLabel: Regularizing CNN on the Loss Layer, CVPR 2016) that applied synthetic noise process on the loss layer.

Experiments should be done for multiple times with different random subsets and authors should provide mean and standard error. Overall, I believe the proposed method is not very well justified and has limited novelty.

The paper presents a new regularization technique for neural networks, which seeks to maximize correlation between input variables, latent variables and outputs. This is achieved by defining a measure of total correlation between these variables and decomposing it in terms of entropies and conditional entropies.

Authors explain that they do not actually maximize the total correlation, but a lower-bound of it that ignores simple entropy terms, and only considers conditional entropies. It is not clearly explained what is the rationale for discarding these entropy terms.

Entropies measures are applying to probability distributions (i.e. this implies that the variables in the model should be random). The link between the conditional entropy formulation and the reconstruction error is not made explicit. In order to link these two views, I would have expected, for example, a noise model for the units of the network.

Later in the paper, it is claimed that the original ladder network is not suitable for supervised learning with small samples, and some empirical results seek to demonstrate this. But a more theoretical explanation why it is the case would have been welcome.

The MNIST results are shown for a particular convolutional neural network architecture, however, most ladder network results for this dataset have been produced on standard fully-connected architectures. Results for such neural network architecture would have been desirable for more comparability with original ladder neural network results.
An updated version of the paper has been uploaded. This version includes more clear explanation of the base model, reflecting the issues raised by AnnoReviewer3.

machine_text: The paper is clearly written with good explanations. The strategies for selecting the most appropriate vocabulary for machine translation are tested and compared on 4 different datasets, using 4 different Neural Machine Translation models, and the results are shown to be promising. In my opinion, the most important part of this work is to test and compare the effectiveness of different strategies on different datasets. This makes the approach proposed in this paper more general and practical for everyone to apply it to other related tasks and datasets. Reid: A01 + BOS test sets Wu: CoNLL 2003 shared task dataset Mnih: 2007 dataset Shen: Penn 2030 dataset ininings The vocabulary selection strategies proposed in this work can be applied to other tasks that involve selecting a subset of vocabulary. I think the most straightforward application is sentence encoding, where a vocabulary index is created and assigned to each token in a sentence, then the word encoding will be a matrix with rows as sentences and columns as tokens. The same strategy can be applied to neural machine translation by saving the trained model into a file, then select a small subset of vocabulary to read in test data for evaluation. The paper is written in a good format with good explanations of the tested strategies and promising but not optimal results. I hope the results are improved on larger datasets in the future work. Overall, this is a good work that shows the potential of saving model performance by choosing the appropriate vocabulary for target task. I recommend this paper for publication in the ACL or anotherpeer reviewed journal. Some suggestions for improvement: 1. Vocabulary selection is likely a continuous task, where at each word a certain threshold can be chosen to determine if the word should be kept or not. Considering this, the vocabulary selection is more of an optimization problem and can be addressed by looking at the objective function, first-order derivative and second-order derivative. The author only performed gradient check for the selected words and didn't explore other directions. 2. It is a common method to perform n-grams derived from a corpus to build the vocabulary. In this work, the n-grams are not shared across different tasks, which limits the generalization of the proposed approach. 3. The performance improvement on small datasets may not be that significant, which may be caused by the randomness of the selected words. The method of rolling dice may be a good idea to make the selection more systematic. 4. The reported results on the testing set of different datasets are different. For the sentence encoding task, the result on the testing set of 2007 dataset is similar to the result on the BOS test set. Overall, this paper offers a good exploration of the vocabulary selection strategy, and some modification can improve the results in some cases. The more promising idea, such as optimizing the objective function with respect to the number of selected words, could be applied to other related tasks. This paper is well written and provides a good overview of vocabulary selection strategies for neural machine translation. The approach of comparing different strategies on different datasets can be a good method to find the best approach for a particular problem. I do have a few suggestions to improve this paper further. 1. The selected vocabulary on different datasets may not be optimal. For example, for the 2007 and CoNLL 2003 dataset, only one keyword is selected while for the BOS test set and Penn 2030 dataset, 5 keywords are selected. Therefore, it may be more effective to select a larger number of words to improve the overall performance. 2. The vocabulary selection strategies could also be applied to other tasks besides the translation task. For example, the sentence encoding task could benefit from such strategies. The same method could be applied to select different number of keywords for these tasks. In this way, the method can be more generally applicable. Overall, this paper presents a good overview of the vocabulary selection strategies. I recommend this paper for publication in the ACL or another peer-reviewed journal. Some suggestions for improvement: 1. The vocabulary selection could be a more systematic approach that also considers the optimization objectives with respect to the number of selected words. 2. The vocabulary selection strategies could be compared to other approaches to further improve the results. Overall, this is a good paper that highlights the importance of vocabulary selection for the NMT task. I recommend this paper for publication in the ACL or another peer-reviewed journal. Some suggestions for improvement: 1. The vocabulary selection strategies were only tested on four NMT models, so there may not be a significant performance difference. More studies on a larger number of NMT models can be performed to validate the approach. 2. The vocabulary selection strategies may not work for some other tasks besides machine translation. Paper makes an interesting attempt at solving the vocabulary selection problem in Neural Machine Translation (NMT). The authors propose to compute selection score for each token using several loss functions and train a separate predictor model to select the most promising ones. They show significant improvements over state-of-the-art systems on the described public dataset. However, I have a few concerns regarding the choice of the datasets and the evaluation metric. First of all, the used datasets are small in size and, as the paper points out, the selection procedure might not work as well on large scale training data. The same is also true for the chosen evaluation metric, BLEU, which only takes into account whether the system generated the correct word in the right place, but not how similar the generated sentence is to the reference one. For example, in the example from the paper, BLEU doesn’t indicate whether the generated sentence is similar to the reference one or just a bunch of randomly selected words. This makes it difficult to draw any general conclusions from the results. Despite these concerns, the approach proposed in the paper seems very promising and it would be good to see more rigorous evaluation in the future. Problem or question the paper addresses: The vocabulary selection problem in Neural Machine Translation Strength of the paper: Significant improvements over state-of-the-art systems on the described public dataset. Weakness of the paper: Small size of the used datasets and the chosen evaluation metric. Overall, I think the paper is very interesting and it would be good to see more rigorous evaluation in the future. First of all, I would like to thank the authors for sharing their work. I really enjoyed reading the introduction and the proposed solution to the vocabulary selection problem in Neural Machine Translation. On the other hand, I would like to mention a few problems with the used datasets and the chosen evaluation metric. The vocabulary selection problem as the authors described is about building the system that selects the most promising vocabulary to train a model. The problem is that small datasets make it hard to build a selection model that generalizes well. As the authors pointed out, the size of the vocabulary should not be greater than X parameters or so. However, in order to build such model, one needs a much bigger dataset. In the paper, the authors use the nmtparse tool to split the dataset and get the train/development/test split. The problem is that such split doesn’t follow the ratio of 1:1:1 like the number of words in the train and development are not the same. The nmtparser tool splits the train dataset in a way that the train contains about the same number of occurrences of each word in the vocabulary. The problem is that in the development and test set, some words may appear only a few times, thus it may not be possible to train a model that can generalize well. Also, the evaluation metric used by the nmtparser is BLEU, but in the way it’s used, it does not really make sense. BLEU makes sense when one wants to check whether the system generated the correct word in the right place, but it does not say anything about how similar the generated sentence is to the reference one. I have doubts about how the above-mentioned problems will have significant influence on the model performance, but in order to make any conclusions, it would be good to have a bigger dataset and a different way of splitting it. The overall idea of the proposed solution seems very good. Still, it would be nice to see some generalization to a bigger dataset and a more thorough evaluation. The problem this paper tries to solve is to reduce the decoding time of Neural Machine Translation (NMT) model, especially on single CPU platform, by reducing the search space of possible translations. In the past work on NMT, the selection of valid translation candidates is based on the inferrable from the source sentence alone, which is often a subset of actual valid translations. This limits the scalability and efficiency of NMT models. In this paper, the authors explore the use of contextual information to select valid translations, which speeds up NMT decoding while maintaining high accuracy. The effectiveness of this strategy is confirmed on WMT15 English-German and WMT16 English-Romanian tasks. The speed-accuracy trade-off is also investigated in more detail. volunteers The main idea of the paper is to adopt context to validate the translation candidates, to expand the search space and therefore speed up NMT decoding, while incurring only negligible accuracy drop. The authors explore this idea on WMT15 English-German and WMT16 English-Romanian tasks, and the results show that the proposed method can reduce the decoding time by 90% on CPUs, and the training time is also reduced by 25% at the cost of only a negligible accuracy drop. ice-summary The paper proposes a method to validate the output translation candidates of NMT model, by using contextual information to determine whether the candidate is valid or not. The results show that this method can bring significant speed improvement while incurring only negligible accuracy drop.
human_text:
This paper evaluates several strategies to reduce output vocabulary size in order to speed up NMT decoding and training. It could be quite useful to practitioners, although the main contributions of the paper seem somewhat orthogonal to representation learning and neural networks, and I am not sure ICLR is the ideal venue for this work.

- Do the reported decoding times take into account the vocabulary reduction step?
- Aside from machine translation, might there be applications to other settings such as language modeling, where large vocabulary is also a scalability challenge?
- The proposed methods are helpful because of the difficulties induced by using a word-level model. But (at least in my opinion) starting from a character or even lower-level abstraction seems to be the obvious solution to the huge vocabulary problem.
The reviewers agree that the method is exciting as practical contributions go, but the case for originality is not strong enough.

This paper conducts a comprehensive series of experiments on vocabulary selection strategies to reduce the computational cost of neural machine translation.

A range of techniques are investigated, ranging from very simple methods such as word co-occurences, to the relatively complex use of SVMs.

The experiments are solid, comprehensive and very useful in practical terms.  It is good to see that the best vocabulary selection method is very effective at achieving a very high proportion of the coverage of the full-vocabulary model (fig 3).  However, I feel that the experiments in section 4.3 (vocabulary selection during training) was rather limited in their scope - I would have liked to see more experiments here.

A major criticism I have with this paper is that there is little novelty here.  The techniques are mostly standard methods and rather simple, and in particular, there it seems that there is not much additional material beyond the work of Mi et al (2016).  So although the work is solid, the lack of originality lets it down.

Minor comments: in 2.1, the word co-occurence measure - was any smoothing used to make this measure more robust to low counts?

This paper compares several strategies for guessing a short list of vocabulary for the target language in neural machine translation. The primary findings are that word alignment dictionaries work better than a variety of other techniques.

My take on this paper is that to have a significant impact, it needs to make the case for why one might want vocabulary rather than characters or sub word units like BPE. I think there are likely many very good reasons to do this that could be argued for (synthesize morphology, deal with transliteration, etc), but most of these would suggest some particular models and experiments, which are of course not in this paper. As it is, I think this paper is a useful but minor contribution that shows that word alignment is a good way of getting short lists, but it does not strongly make the case that we should abandon work in other directions.

Minor comments:
In addition to the SVM approach for modeling vocabulary, the discriminative word lexicon of Mauser et al. (2009) and the neural version of Ha et al. (2014) are also worth mentioning.

It would be useful to know what the coverage rate of the actual full vocabulary would be (rather than the 100k “full vocabulary”). Since presumably this technique could be used to work with much larger vocabularies.

When reducing the vocabulary size for training, the Mi et al. (2016) technique of taking the union of all the vocabularies in a mini batch seems like a rather strange objective. If the vocabulary of a single sentence is used, the probabilistic semantics of the translation model can still be preserved since p(e | f, vocab(f)) = p(e | f) if p(vocab(f) | f) = 1, i.e., is deterministic, which it is here. Whereas the objective is no longer a sensible probability model in the mini batch vocabulary case. Thus, while it may be a bit more difficult to implement, it seems like it would at least be a sensible comparison to make.

In this paper, the authors present several strategies to select a small subset of target vocabulary to work with per source sentence, which results in significant speedup. The results are convincing and I think this paper offers practical values to general seq2seq approaches to language tasks. However, there is little novelty in this work: the authors further mostly extend the work of (Mi et al., 2016) with more vocabulary selection strategies and thorough experiments. This paper will fit better in an NLP venue.

The paper addresses the problem of how to reduce the cost of communication that is required for parallel training of a neural network. The state-of-the-art method, Bulk Synchronous Parallel Stochastic Gradient Descent (BSP-SGD), requires many collective communication operations, like broadcasts of parameters or reductions for sub-gradient aggregations, which for large messages quickly dominates overall execution time and limits parallel scalability. To address this problem, we develop a new technique for collective operations, referred to as Linear Pipelining (LP). It is tuned to the message sizes that arise in BSP-SGD, and works effectively on multi-GPU systems. Theoretically, the cost of LP is invariant to P, while the cost of more conventional Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) scales like O(log P). LP also demonstrate up to 2x faster bandwidth than Bidirectional Exchange (BE) techniques that are widely adopted by current MPI implementations. We apply these collectives to BSP-SGD, showing that the proposed implementations reduce communication bottlenecks in practice while preserving the attractive convergence properties of BSP-SGD. The proposed algorithms are evaluated on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets, showing that the proposed implementations reduce communication bottlenecks in practice while preserving the attractive convergence properties of BSP-SGD. We evaluate the communication efficiency of proposed methods against several state-of-the-art parallel training algorithms on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets. Our implementation is based on the PyGogo framework.

The primary point made by this paper is that given certain architectural characteristics of multi-GPU systems, namely the use of bi-directional PCI-E for communication and the integration of two independent DMA engines on recent GPU devices (providing support for simultaneous independent communications), and given the characteristics of the communications patterns required by synchronous SGD trainers for deep neural networks, namely that the messages are large, dense, and have a fixed length, it makes sense to design communication collectives such as broadcast, reduce, and allreduce specifically for the use case of synchronous SGD training on a multi-GPU system.  The paper describes the implementation of these three collectives (broadcast, reduce, and allreduce) using a linear pipelining (LP) scheme on a (logical) ring topology.  The paper compares the LP collectives to two alternatives:  collectives based on a minimal spanning tree (MST) topology and collectives based on bidirectional exchange (BE).  First, a theoretical comparison is made using a standard cost model used in the high performance computing community.  When assumptions based on multi-GPU system architecture (very low latency for messages) and on the communication characteristics of synchronous SGD training (very large messages) are integrated into the model, the paper finds that the LP collectives should be less costly than BE collectives by a factor of 2 and less costly than MST collectives by a factor of log(p), where p is the number of GPUs being used.  Second, an empirical comparison is performed in which (1) the time required to perform each of the different collectives on a 4-device (k40m) system is measured as a function of message size and (2) the time required to perform each of the different collectives with a 200 MB message length is measured as a function of the number of devices in the system.  These measurements show that the LP-based collectives are consistently the fastest.  Third, DNN training experiments with AlexNet and GoogLeNet are performed on a 4-device system using three different synchronous SGD algorithms with the different implementations of the collectives (a total of 6 different algorithms in all).  Measurements of the communication and computation costs show that the LP collectives reduce communication costs without affecting computation costs (as expected).  Measurements of the convergence of the training loss as a function of time for the two DNN architectures show that use of the LP collectives leads to faster training.

While the theory says that the costs of LP collectives should be invariant to the number of devices in a multi-GPU system, the empirical work shows that in practice this does not hold going from 4 to 5 devices (in the tested configuration) because in a 5-device system messages must traverse the QPI.  Are there other practical considerations that the authors are aware of that affect the scaling of the LP collectives?  If so, these should be mentioned in the paper.

In the sentence "Worringen (2003) proposed a pipeline collective model in shared memory environment for CPU data, but communications of different MPI processes sharing the same CPU memory bus within the same CPU socket." I really can't figure out what the words after "but communications of different MPI processes" are trying to convey.  This sentence is not comprehensible.

"Please note the latency term is log pα, which is the smallest among algorithms in Table.1. Therefore, MST only suits for high frequent short messages."  The claim that MST collectives are only suitable for high-frequency, short messages does not follow from the statement that MST collectives have the smallest latency term.  You also need to consider the way the cost scales with message size (the bandwidth term).  If the MST collectives had a better bandwidth term than the other collectives, then they would also be superior for large messages.

"Let’s take an appropriate block size b to ensure n/b ≪ α."  This looks wrong, since n > b.  Should it be b/n ≪ α?

"However, the parameters are not consistent after several iterations due to the precision issues of float multiplications in Gradient Update."  Are you sure the inconsistency in weight estimates across devices is due to multiplication?  I would expect that it would be due to gradients being accumulated in different orders; that is, because floating point addition is not commutative.

This paper presents a linear pipeline All-reduce approach for parallel neural networks on multiple GPU. The paper provides both theoretical analysis and experiments. Overall, the results presented in the paper are interesting, but the writing can be improved. 

Comments:

- The authors compare their proposed approach with several alternative approaches and demonstrate strong performance of the proposed approaches. But it is unclear if the improvement is from the proposed approach or from the implementation.  

- The paper is not easy to follow and the writing can be improved in many place (aside from typos and missing references). Specifically, the authors should provide more intuitions of the proposed approach in the introduction and in Section 3. 

- The proposition and the analysis in Section 3.2 do not suggest the communication cost of linear pipeline is approximately 2x and log p faster than BE and MST, respectively, as claimed in many places in the paper. Instead, it suggests LP *cannot* be faster than these methods by 2x and log p  times. More specifically, Eq (2) shows T_broadcase_BE/ T_broadcase_LP < 2. This does not provide an upper-bound of T_broadcase_LP and it can be arbitrary worse when comparing with T_broadcase_BE from this inequality. Therefore, instead of showing T_broadcase_BE/ T_broadcase_LP < 2, the authors should state T_broadcase_BE/ T_broadcase_LP > 1 when n approaches infinity. 

- It would be interesting to emphasize more on the differences between designing parallel algorithms on CPU v.s. on GPU to motivate the paper.

This paper analyzes the ring-based AllReduce approach for multi-GPU data parallel training of deep net.
Comments
1) The name linear pipeline is somewhat confusing to the readers, as the technique is usually referred as ring based approach in Allreduce literature. The author should use the standard name to make the connection easier. 
2) The cost analysis of ring-based Allreduce is already provided in the existing literature. This paper applied the analysis to the case of multi-GPU deep net training, and concluded that the scaling is invariant of number of GPUs.
3) The ring-based allreduce approach is already supported by NVidia’s NCCL library, although the authors claim that their implementation comes earlier than the NCCL implementation.
4) The overlap of communication of computation is an already applied technique in systems such as TensorFlow and MXNet. The schedule proposed by the authors exploits the overlap partially, doing backprop of t-1 while doing reduce.  Note that the dependency pattern can be further exploited; with the forward of layer t depend on update of parameter of layer t in last iteration. This can be done by a dependency scheduler.	
5) Since this paper is about analysis of Allreduce, it would be nice to include detailed analysis of tree-shape reduction, ring-based approach and all-to-all approach. The discussion of all-to-all approach is missing in the current paper. 
In summary, this is a paper discussed existing Allreduce techniques for data parallel multi-GPU training of deep net, with cost analysis based on existing results. While I personally find the claimed result not surprising as it follows from existing analysis of Allreduce, the analysis might help some other readers. I view this as a baseline paper. The analysis of Allreduce could also been improved (see comment 5).

This paper presents a linear pipeline All-reduce approach for parallel neural networks on multiple GPU. The paper provides both theoretical analysis and experiments. Overall, the results presented in the paper are interesting, but the writing can be improved. 

Comments:

- The authors compare their proposed approach with several alternative approaches and demonstrate strong performance of the proposed approaches. But it is unclear if the improvement is from the proposed approach or from the implementation.  

- The paper is not easy to follow and the writing can be improved in many place (aside from typos and missing references). Specifically, the authors should provide more intuitions of the proposed approach in the introduction and in Section 3. 

- The proposition and the analysis in Section 3.2 do not suggest the communication cost of linear pipeline is approximately 2x and log p faster than BE and MST, respectively, as claimed in many places in the paper. Instead, it suggests LP *cannot* be faster than these methods by 2x and log p  times. More specifically, Eq (2) shows T_broadcase_BE/ T_broadcase_LP < 2. - It would be interesting to emphasize more on the differences between designing parallel algorithms on CPU v.s. on GPU to motivate the paper.

This paper analyzes the ring-based AllReduce approach for multi-GPU data parallel training of deep net.
Comments
1) The name linear pipeline is somewhat confusing to the readers, as the technique is usually referred as ring based approach in Allreduce literature. The author should use the standard name to make the connection easier. 
2) The cost analysis of ring-based Allreduce is already provided in the existing literature. This paper applied the analysis to the case of multi-GPU deep net training, and concluded that the scaling is invariant of number of GPUs.
3) The ring-based allreduce approach is already supported by NVidia’s NCCL library, although the authors claim that their implementation comes earlier than the NCCL implementation.
4) The overlap of communication of computation is an already applied technique in systems such as TensorFlow and MXNet. The schedule proposed by the authors exploits the overlap partially, doing backprop of t-1 while doing reduce.  Note that the dependency pattern can be further exploited; with the forward of layer t depend on update of parameter of layer t in last iteration. This can be done by a dependency scheduler.	
5) Since this paper is about analysis of Allreduce, it would be nice to include detailed analysis of tree-shape reduction, ring-based approach and all-to-all approach. The discussion of all-to-all approach is missing in the current paper.

While I personally find the claimed result not surprising as it follows from existing analysis of Allreduce, the analysis might help some other readers. I view this as a baseline paper. The analysis of Allreduce could also been improved (see comment 5).

machine_text: The paper describes a method for predicting housing prices using time series data. The author uses artificial neural networks to create a forecasting model. The model appears to perform well, with R-squared values reaching as high as 0.8 for some periods. The main issue I have with the paper is that the method was created using data from Australia. Forecasting prices in different markets requires historical data from those markets. The model may have performed well because of its simplicity and lack of parameters, but I'm not sure that it will perform as well on data from other markets. I also have some questions about the approach the author took to data preprocessing. The author used hospital cleaning to remove weekend effects from the data. However, the cleaning procedure did not appear to be well documented and I'm not sure how valid the cleaning was. Also, the author used principal component analysis to reduce the number of explanatory variables in the model. Principal component analysis is a data transformation technique and cannot be used to determine the optimal number of variables that should be included in the model. Finally, the author excluded location from the model. It's not clear why the author decided to do this, but including location as an explanatory variable in the model was probably needed to predict price changes in different markets. Overall, I don't think this paper is suitable for it's intended purpose. A model that could accurately predict house prices in Australia would probably not perform as well on data from other markets. Also, the data preprocessing used in the model may not be appropriate for different markets. I can't recommend publishing this paper in its current form.

The problem this paper addresses is how to best represent temporal information in partition models. Temporal information is useful for many purposes, but it is particularly useful for conditional modeling, such as for predicting sales, services, or counts in the future based on observations from the past. Partition models are a powerful class of stochastic models that have the advantage of being able to represent time explicitly in the form of slices or periods. This paper proposes a method of optimizing the duration and timing of the slices in order to best represent time-dependent phenomena. The method includes maximizing the entropy of the partition model likelihood to find the optimal duration and timing of the slices. It also presents a way to sample the slice duration and timing that is expected to have nearly the same statistical properties as the optimal solution. — Strongly disagree. This paper does not address the problem it promises. The method presented is interesting but it is too resource intensive to be practically applicable. The method only considers a single problem, optimizing slice duration, and only for a single model, the Poisson-Gamma distribution. And even for this case, it presents no empirical results to demonstrate that the optimized solution yields better results than existing methods. The method presented could be used to optimize the slice duration, but the proposed maximization problem is not convex, and the proposed method only finds a local maximum. But the biggest problem is that this method does not address the problem it claims to address. There is no reason to think that optimizing the duration of slices will yield better results than simply not assuming that time dependence occurs. This method ignores a long tradition of people considering time to be exogenous. Time just jumps from one period to the next, and if you don't allow for jumps, you can just lump everything into one long period. This method also ignores the growing body of work that addresses non-Markovian effects, in which the change in behavior over time has dependencies that cannot be captured by the simple time-homogenous Poisson process used by this method. Rather than summing up expert votes as in products of experts, we employ for each variable the opinion of the most reliable expert. In this paper, we propose and investigate a novel memory architecture for neural networks called Hierarchical Attentive Memory (HAM). It is based on a binary tree with leaves corresponding to memory cells. This allows HAM to perform memory access in O(log n) complexity, which is a significant improvement over the standard attention mechanism that requires O(n) operations, where n is the size of the memory. We show that an LSTM network augmented with HAM can learn algorithms for problems like merging, sorting or binary searching from pure input-output examples. In particular, it learns to sort n numbers in time O(n log n) and generalizes well to input sequences much longer than the ones seen during the training. We also show that HAM can be trained to act like classic data structures: a stack, a FIFO queue and a priority queue. LSTM networks augmented with HAM achieved state-of-the-art results on benchmark problems. The authors introduce a new memory model which allows memory access in O(log n) time.

Pros:
* The paper is well written and everything is clear.
* It's a new model and I'm not aware of a similar model.
* It's clear that memory access time is an issue for longer sequences and it is clear how this model solves this problem.

Cons:
* The motivation for O(log n) access time is to be able to use the model on very long sequences. While it is clear from the definition that the computation time is low because of its design, it is not clear that the model will really generalize well to very long sequences.
* The model was also not tested on any real-world task.

I think such experiments should be added to show whether the model really works on long sequences and real-world tasks, otherwise it is not clear if this is a useful model.
All three reviewers point to significant deficiencies. No response or engagement from the authors (for the reviews). I see no basis for supporting this paper.

This paper introduces a novel hierarchical memory architecture for neural networks, based on a binary tree with leaves corresponding to memory cells.  This allows for O(log n) memory access, and experiments additionally demonstrate ability to solve more challenging tasks such as sorting from pure input-output examples and dealing with longer sequences.

The idea of the paper is novel and well-presented, and the memory structure seems reasonable to have advantages in practice. However, the main weakness of the paper is the experiments. There is no experimental comparison with other external memory-based approaches (e.g. those discussed in Related Work), or experimental analysis of computational efficiency given overhead costs (beyond just computational complexity) despite that being one of the main advantages. Furthermore, the experimental setups are relatively weak, all on artificial tasks with moderate increases in sequence length.  Improving on these would greatly strengthen the paper, as the core idea is interesting.

This paper proposes to use a hierarchical softmax to speed up attention based memory addressing in memory augmented network (e.g. NTM, memNN…).

The model build a hierarchical softmax on top of the input sequence then at each time step SEARCH for the most relevant input to predict the next output (this search is discrete), and use its corresponding embedding to update the state of an LSTM that will then produce the output. Finally the embedding of the used input is update by a WRITE function (an LSTM working that takes hidden state of the other LSTM as an input). The model has a discrete component (the SEARCH) and is thus trained with REINFORCE. In the experimental section they test their approach on several algorithmic tasks such as search, sort...

The main advantage of replacing the full softmax by a hierarchical softmax is that during inference, the complexity goes from O(N) to O(log(N)). It would be great to see if the gain in complexity allows to tackle problem which are a few orders of magnitude bigger than the one addressed with full softmax. However the authors only test on toy sequences up to 32 tokens, which is quite small. 

The model requires a relatively complex search mechanism that can only be trained with REINFORCE. While this seems to work on problems with relatively small and simple sequences, it would be great to see how performance changes with the size of the problem. 

Overall, while the idea of replacing the softmax in the attention mechanism by a hierachical softmax is appealing, this work is not quite convincing yet. Their approach is not very natural, may be hard to train and may not be that simple to scale. The experiment section is very weak.

This paper revisits the classic Distributed Synchronous SGD protocol with a peer-to-peer communication model. In the original paper, the authors adopt a point-to-point communication model, in which a worker needs to tell the trainer the global model parameter. This leads to a significant communication cost and low training efficiency. To address this, the author adopts a peer-to-peer communication model, in which workers help each other to update global model parameters. This approach greatly reduces the communication cost and leads to higher training efficiency. The author points out that the original paper only focuses on the case when all workers share the same model. In practice, different models need to be trained for different tasks. The assumption that all workers share the same model cannot be always met. The author extends the model to the scenario when each worker has its own model. The evaluation shows that the paper achieves better training efficiency and comparable performance compared with existing methods. strength This paper addresses a longstanding problem in the distributed training field, which is optimizing model parameters by relying on point-to-point communication. The original SGD requires a worker to send model parameter to the trainer one after another, which leads to high communication cost and low efficiency. The proposed model parameters are optimized by peers with low communication cost. The model is also extended to the scenario with different models for workers. weakness The model can be further improved in several aspects. First, the communication overhead in the model should be analyzed. The paper only considers the case when a worker needs to tell the trainer the global model parameters, while other models may share some model parameters. The analysis for the case with different model parameters is needed. Second, in the model, each worker only maintains a local model parameter, while in practice a worker may have more than one models. How to efficiently aggregate these local model parameters and how to ensure workers with the same model parameters are divided into appropriate clusters remain to be further studied.

If the efficiency of learners does not follow such distribution, I do not think that the proposed algorithm will work. So I suggest two revisions:

- provide more experiments to show the performance with different efficiency distributions of learners.
- assuming that all learners follow the same distribution of efficiency and show the expected idle time is minor by using the proposed algorithm.

The paper claim that, when supported by a number of backup workers, synchronized-SGD 
actually works better than async-SGD. The paper first analyze the problem of staled updates
in async-SGDs, and proposed the sync-SGD with backup workers. In the experiments, the 
authors shows the effectiveness of the proposed method in applications to Inception Net
and PixelCNN.

The idea is very simple, but in practice it can be quite useful in industry settings where 
adding some backup workders is not a big problem in cost. Nevertheless, I think the 
proposed solution is quite straightforward to come up with when we assume that 
each worker contains the full dataset and we have budge to add more workers. So, 
under this setting, it seems quite natural to have a better performance with the additional 
backup workers that avoid the staggering worker problem. And, with this assumtion I'm not 
sure if the proposed solution is solving difficult enough problem with novel enough idea. 

In the experiments, for fair comparison, I think the Async-SGD should also have a mechanism 
to cut off updates of too much staledness just as the proposed method ignores all the remaining 
updates after having N updates. For example, one can measure the average time spent to 
obtain N updates in sync-SGD setting and use that time as the cut-off threashold in Async-SGD 
so that Async-SGD does not perform so poorly.

Is this technique efficient? If you are using 5-10% extra resources (backup workers), do you get at least 5-10% speedup over sync SGD? Figure 8(a) does not have any sync results. It is well understood that async may sometimes never converge to the correct results.

The proposed technique of over-provisioning a few workers to improve the hardware efficiency of synchronous training gives a very welcome boost, as evidenced beautifully by Figure 6.

However, as I have discussed in private communication with the authors, the comparison with asynchronous methods leaves a few questions regarding tuning. 

Learning rate: 

The authors carefully describe the process of tuning the synchronous implementation. However no tuning is reported for the asynchronous implementation: the value is set to 0.045 for all configurations. Figure 7(a) shows that tuning the learning rate can cause a difference of almost a whole percentage point in test precision.
1. What other values of LR have the authors tried for asynchronous training?
2. Is 0.045 the best one for all configurations they report?
3. Is there any chance that the 0.5% difference in precision between sync and async is due to insufficient LR tuning (as suggested by Figure 7(a))?

machine_text: This paper presents a method for predicting potential human intention using supervised competitive learning. This method can be effectively applied to the control of human-machine collaborative systems, which need to be operated by human. However, there are two main challenges to implement this method. One is to design a supervised learning task to capture the intention of human. The other is to handle the asynchronous data collection from human and machine. The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows. 1. A task is designed to capture human intention based on the machine training data and human operation data. It can be seen as a sequence-to-sequence problem. 2. The asynchronous data collection from human and machine is handled by a clock-synchronized co-processing scheme. The machine gathers the training data with a fixed period, and human can provide feedback with another fixed period. 3. The proposed method is evaluated on three tasks. The results show that the method can achieve promising results for the prediction of potential human intention. ******************************************************************** PLEASE SUPPORT THIS ARTICLE BY CLICKING ON THE LINKS BELOW: 1. The paper PREDICTION OF POTENTIAL HUMAN INTENTION USING SUPERVISED COMPETITIVE LEARNING by Mäte Publishing House describes an approach to predict human intention using supervised competitive learning. The proposed method is evaluated on the IMDb dataset and compared with state-of-the-art models for intention prediction. The model achieved best result in predicting movie box office gross outcome using film characters' intention prediction as a starting point. The model shows significant improvement over previous state-of-the-art in several datasets, including IMDB. The paper provides clear explanations of the used data and research design. The research design could benefit from a more thorough analysis of the inter-rater reliability for the IMDb dataset. The current split-half validation is not enough to validate the model's performance. Furthermore, it would be good to have a deeper analysis of the external datasets the model was trained on. It would be interesting to see how the model's performance depends on the number of cross-validated training examples the model was trained on, and how sensitive the performance is to the model's hyperparameters (e.g., learning rate). The performance analysis of the baseline method would be interesting. Are the the F1-score and mAP metric undefined for the baseline method? How does the baseline method compare to the state of the art on the IMDb dataset? The code is not thoroughly explained. Currently, it is not possible to reproduce the experiments described in this paper. As a result, it is hard to understand the proposed approach and evaluate it properly.

We propose a method to quantify human intention using supervised learning. Our method applies competitive learning to human behavior prediction as supervised learning. In our approach, competitive learning generates several outputs that are then associated with several potential situations imagined by a human. We applied the proposed method to human driving behavior and will extract three potential driving patterns. Our results showed that the prediction error is reduced to 1/25 that of a conventional method. Furthermore, we found that competitive learning can distinguish valid data from disturbance data in order to train a model. Paper link: https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.04173 Interested readers can access the complete paper via the following link: https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.04173 I believe this method is innovative and has the potential to be widely used in many applications. However, I also believe that the authors might have overstated some of the results. For example, I don't think the method can distinguish valid data from disturbance data without using external knowledge such as the disturbances during the data collection. I also believe the sample size is too small. The method can probably achieve good results on similar datasets, but it won't outperform classical methods on real-world problems. For example, the authors claim that the prediction error is reduced to 1/25 that of a conventional method. I believe this result is misleading and misleading people to overestimate this method. In general, I think the paper requires major revisions to make it ready for publication in a good journal. For example, I think the introduction needs to be more detailed and I think the authors need to tone down their claims and show more acknowledgement of the challenges.

The paper PREDICTION OF POTENTIAL HUMAN INTENTUSING SUPERVISED COMPETITIVE LEARNING addresses the question of how to quantify human intention. It starts by explaining the general problem it tries to solve, then describes the method it uses, namely supervised competitive learning. It is demonstrated that by applying this method to human driving behavior, it is possible to predict with a low error rate the potential driving patterns of humans based on the imagined situation. Strength: The method uses competitive learning, which means that it is based on deep learning and therefore the method is more efficient and more accurate than other methods. The competitive learning can also distinguish valid data from disturbance data. Weakness: The article only addresses the question of how to quantify human intention. It does not explain why competitive learning works for this purpose, nor how it is possible to reduce the squared error from 1/25 to 1/200. Furthermore, it is not explained how the method was applied to human driving behavior. davided addresses the question of how to quantify human intention. human_text:
Authors propose a competitive learning architecture that learn different RNN predictors independently, akin to a committee of experts which are chosen with a hard switch at run-time. This work is applied to the task of predictive different driving behaviors from human drivers, and combines behaviors at test time, often switching behaviors within seconds. Prediction loss is lower than the similar but non-competitive architecture used as a baseline.
It is not very clear how to interpret the results, what is the real impact of the model. If behaviors switch very often, can this really be seen as choosing the best driving mode for a given situation? Maybe the motivation needs to be rephrased a little to be more convincing?
The competitive approach presented is interesting but not really novel, thus the impact of this paper for a conference such as ICLR may be limited.

The authors present a prediction framework that involves multiple 'competitive' RNNs, and they claim that they are predicting human intention. It is unclear if this method, which seems quite ad-hoc, is any different from a simple ensemble approach, and it is unclear that the model is predicting human intention. The experiments do not adequately demonstrate either.

This paper introduces a neural network architecture and training procedure for predicting the speed of a vehicle several seconds into the future based on video and vehicle state input. The architecture allows several RNNs to compete to make the best predictions, with only the best prediction receiving back propagation training at each time step. Preliminary experimental results show that this scheme can yield reduced prediction error.

 It is not clear how the best-performing RNN is chosen for each time point at test time. That is, how is the “integrated prediction” obtained in Fig. 7? Is the prediction the one with minimum error over all of the output layers? If so, this means the prediction cannot be made until you already know the value to be predicted.

It seems possible that a larger generic RNN might be able to generate accurate predictions. If I understand correctly, the competitive architectures have many more parameters than the baseline. Is the improved performance here due to the competitive scheme, or just a larger model? 

A large amount of additional work is required to sustain the claim that this scheme is successfully extracting driver ‘intentions’. It would be interesting to see if the scheme, suitably extended, can automatically infer the intention to stop at a stop sign vs slowing but not stopping due to a car in front, say, or to pass a car vs simply changing lanes. Adding labels to the dataset may enable this comparison more clearly.

More generally, the intention of the driver seems more related to the goals they are pursuing at the moment; there is a fair amount of work in inverse reinforcement learning that examines this problem (some of it in the context of driving style as well).

This paper proposes a neural network architecture for car state prediction while driving based on competitive learning. Competitive learning creates several duplicates of the baseline neural architecture and during training only updates the architecture with minimum loss. The experiments compare the competitive learning approach to a single baseline architecture on a driving benchmark task. The paper is understandable but could benefit from some copy editing. 

The competitive learning approach seems rather adhoc and this paper feels quite incomplete without significant discussion and comparisons to ensembling. Much recent work has shown that duplicating and ensembling neural architectures can produce gains, and it’s not clear why competitive learning is better than ensembling, it seems less theoretically sound to me.

There is a huge confound in the experiments due to the competitive learning architecture having many more free parameters than the baseline architecture. Again I think comparing to ensembling with the same number of architectures duplicated and perhaps comparing to a single baseline with larger hidden layers to make the total number of free parameters comparable is critical to validating the proposed approach.

The graphical model of the driving process depicted in figure 1 seems nonsensical. If e is observed then all variables are known given the dependencies shown. Further, it is at best very poor notation to say that the driving action d decided at time t affects the vehicle state s at that same time. It should be that s_t depends on d_(t-1). Also, according to this figure the driving decision d does not depend on the observed vehicle state x which also seems invalid.

Odd to have a paragraph break in abstract

Figure 1 caption should include a brief explanation of the variables shown

This paper presents a multi-label learning method with semantic embeddings to assign multiple labels to documents. The method uses document vectors, computed by Deep Semantic hashing, to perform hashing-based binary classification to produce a label-specific representation. Labels are then assigned to documents using these label-specific representations. The method can be used with a variety of prediction tasks, and the semantic embeddings can be transferred from a source domain to a target domain with minimal loss in performance. This paper has several strengths. First, it tackles the problem of multi-label learning in a new and different way from previous approaches. Second, it uses Deep Semantic Hashing to produce document vectors, which are simple to compute and can be used to perform a wide range of tasks. Third, the method can be used with a variety of prediction tasks, and the semantic embeddings can be transferred from a source domain to a target domain with minimal loss in performance. This paper also has some weaknesses. First, it only considers the Hamming loss for label assignment, even though other loss functions are sometimes better suited to particular problems. Second, it only considers the transfer of semantic embeddings between domains of the same class structure. In particular, it doesn’t consider the case where the source and target domains differ significantly in their class structure. Overall, this is a useful and interesting paper that fills an important gap in the field of multi-label learning. I have some comments and questions about the paper that I will now discuss. First, this paper considers only the Hamming loss for the problem of multi-label learning. However, in practice other loss functions are often more appropriate. For example, if one of the labels is ‘negative’ then it might be better to assign all positive labels to the document, rather than the Hamming loss. Second, this paper only considers the transfer of semantic embeddings between domains of the same class structure. In particular, it doesn’t consider the case where the source and target domains differ significantly in their class structure. In this situation, the class-based similarities that are required by the method might not be valid, and this could lead to poor performance of the method. For example, suppose that the source domain is document classification, and the target domain is question classification. Then the class structure is different, because questions often have topics that cross a number of categories, rather than being purely categorization of documents. These comments are only a few of the questions that I have about the paper. I’d be interested to know whether these comments represent a misunderstanding on my part, or whether the paper contains a solution to the problems that I have identified. I look forward to reading the replies, and to any future work on this topic. Sincerely, writeUPS

This is an interesting paper that addresses a very difficult problem, namely multi-label learning. The proposed approach is simple but effective, and I think it could potentially be very scalable to large data sets. This paper focuses on multi-label learning problem in the area of machine learning. It proposed a simple but effective neural net approach, the Semantic Embedding Model (SEM), that models the labels for an instance as draws from a multinomial distribution parametrized by nonlinear functions of the instance features. A Gauss-Siedel mini-batch adaptive gradient descent algorithm is used to fit the model. To handle extremely large label sets, we propose and experimentally validate the efficacy of fitting randomly chosen marginal label distributions. This paper compares the proposed model with several state-of-the-art methods and achieves the state-of-the-art performance. This is because the embedding layer can encode the semantic information between the labels, which is often non-linearly correlated. The proposed algorithm is easy to implement and efficiently scales to large label spaces. The key idea of this paper is valuable and worth to be promoted. I strongly recommend this paper be accepted for publication in the mentioned conferences and/or publication in a journal. However, I have some concerns about the assumptions, implementation and results of the proposed model. First, the paper assumes that the correlations between different label sets can be characterized by a global label embedding. In practice, this assumption may not hold for different label sets. For example, for product classification, the image/product categories and the product functions (e.g. scooter vs bicycle) are different. Such problems are difficult to solve in the paper. How to model the label correlation for different domains and applications is still an open problem. Second, the paper proposes a simple but effective algorithm. In fact, there are more effective methods to optimize the model parameters. For example, the Bayesian personalization approach (BPR) can be used for highly correlated binary labels. Besides, the local optima problem of the proposed algorithm is not discussed. Despite those concerns, the proposed model is simple and efficient. I recommend that the authors make the code and configuration settings publicly available. I recommend this paper be accepted for publication in the conference. This paper proposes SEM, a simple large-size multilabel learning algorithm which models the probability of each label as softmax(sigmoid(W^T X) + b), so a one-layer hidden network. This in and of itself is not novel, nor is the idea of optimizing this by adagrad. Though it's weird that the paper explicitly derives the gradient and suggests doing alternating adagrad steps instead of the more standard adagrad steps; it's unclear whether this matters at all for performance. The main trick responsible for increasing the efficiency of this model is the candidate label sampling, which is done in a relatively standard way by sampling labels proportionally to their frequency in the dataset.

Given that neither the model nor the training strategy is novel, it's surprising that the results are better than the state-of-the-art in quality and efficiency (though non-asymptotic efficiency claims are always questionable since implementation effort trades off fairly well against performance). I feel like this paper doesn't quite meet the bar.

This is largely a well written paper proposing a sensible approach for multilabel learning that is shown to be effective in practice. However, the main technical elements of this work: the model used and its connections to basic MLPs and related methods in the literature, the optimization strategy, and the speedup tricks are all familiar from prior work. Hence the reviewers are somewhat unanimous in their view that the novelty aspect of this paper is its main shortcomings. The authors are encouraged to revise the paper and clarify the precise contributions.

The paper proposes a semantic embedding based approach to multilabel classification. 
Conversely to previous proposals, SEM considers the underlying parameters determining the
observed labels are low-rank rather than that the observed label matrix is itself low-rank. 
However, It is not clear to what extent the difference between the two assumptions is significant

SEM models the labels for an instance as draws from a multinomial distribution
parametrized by nonlinear functions of the instance features. As such, it is a neural network.
The proposed training algorithm is slightly more complicated than vanilla backprop.  The significance of the results compared to NNML (in particular on large datasets Delicious and EUrlex) is not very clear. 

The paper is well written and the main idea is clearly presented. However, the experimental results are not significant enough to compensate the lack of conceptual novelty.

The paper presents the semantic embedding model for multi-label prediction.
In my questions, I pointed that the proposed approach assumes the number of labels to predict is known, and the authors said this was an orthogonal question, although I don't think it is!
I was trying to understand how different is SEM from a basic MLP with softmax output which would be trained with a two step approach instead of stochastic gradient descent. It seems reasonable given their similarity to compare to this very basic baseline.
Regarding the sampling strategy to estimate the posterior distribution, and the difference with Jean et al, I agree it is slightly different but I think you should definitely refer to it and point to the differences.
One last question: why is it called "semantic" embeddings? usually this term is used to show some semantic meaning between trained embeddings, but this doesn't seem to appear in this paper.

machine_text: Overall I find the proposed approach interesting and innovative. I have some comments and questions that I think could improve the quality of the paper. 1- Why did you choose MCMC and not CV for sampling from GANs? In my opinion, there is no need to use MCMC to improve the quality of sampling from GANs. The convergence problem of GANs could be easily solved by adding an orthogonal constraint to the latent code. As you can see in my previously suggested solution to this problem: https://medium.com/@adibabado/fixing-the-convergence-problem-of-autoencoders-by-adding-orthogonal-constraint-to-the-latent-code-cae318f6ac82, using orthogonal constraint to the latent code is a effective and simple solution to the convergence problem. 2- Can you please provide a more detailed pseudocode for MCMAS to make it easier to follow? 2- How did you choose the specific MCMAS algorithm that you used? You need to specify how the MCMAS algorithm was chosen, because this has a big impact on the effectiveness of the algorithm. In the Kaiming Discriminative Version of MCMAS paper, they applied first-order optimization algorithm such as SGD to find the update for the parameters. I think this choice is reasonable, because this method was originally proposed for using this method for learning the parameters of a probabilistic model, not for learning the parameters of a neural network. I think the algorithm can be improved by using an algorithm such as ADAM that is designed for finding the update for the parameters of a deep neural network. 3- How did you compare this approach with the state-of-the-art? In this approach, you used a standard GAN training process. For the standard GAN training, we can use the same standard GAN training process with an additional MCMAS update to improve the quality of the sampling from GANs. How did you compare this approach with the state-of-the-art? 4- What is the effect of the additional MCMAS update? In the Additional experiments section, you can see that the MCMAS update improves the quality of the sampling but also increases the average number of generated examples. What is the benefit of this increase? 5- What are some advantages of using this method over the state-of-the-art? This method has some advantages over the state-of-the-art for using MCMAS for improving the sampling from GANs. As you mentioned before, using an orthogonal constraint to the latent code is a simple and effective solution to the convergence problem of GANs. MCMAS is also a simple algorithm and does not require any additional training of the generator model. Using MCMAS for sampling from GANs does not change the generator and discriminator models. Using MCMAS is a promising approach to improve the sampling from GANs, which can simplify the training of GANs. 6- Could you please provide some examples of using this approach for some applications? 6- I understand that you applied this approach to GANs, but do you have any suggestions about using this approach for sampling from other generative models? I think this approach can be applied to other generative models. In the area of image processing, there are some effective and simple methods to solve the convergence problem of GANs. One of these methods is constraining the discriminator to accept the generated images as correct. We can use MCMAS to improve the sampling from GANs using this approach.

This paper addresses the problem of sampling from a Generative Autoencoder (GAE) using the Noise Contrast Estimation (MLE) algorithm. This is challenging because the standard sampling approach, dropout sampling, tends to over-regularize the GAE and results in poor samples. The MLE algorithm, on the other hand, uses statistics about the GAE’s encode distribution to produce samples that are both detailed and smoothly varying. The paper’s strength is in its simplicity, using a two-step MLE approach that makes it easy to implement and effective. One weakness is that, unlike the GAE, the samples produced have a lot of structural noise, which the authors address by adding noise to the samples and using a simple denoising autoencoder to regularize the samples. In summary, this is an effective approach for sampling from GAEs and should be easy to apply to other GAE variants. Problem: How to Sample from a Generative Autoencoder ======================================================= Autoencoders have been used successfully for generative modeling in a variety of settings. Autoencoders are commonly trained on large amounts of data, which leads to high capacity, but when presented with inputs other than the most common (samples from the training data), the autoencoder is forced to generalize and represent these inputs with a low number of output codes. This compression is based on having fewer representative output codes for more uncommon inputs. Sampling from an autoencoder without a specific, fixed number of samples is difficult, because it requires the selection of a particular number of samples. Because of the autoencoder’s large capacity, only a small number of inputs can be distinguished, and because of the large search space, the choice of samples cannot be guided by a specific heuristic, as it would be for sampling from a normal random variate. The Noise Contrast Estimation (MLE) algorithm is one method for sampling from an autoencoder that is particularly effective, as it overcomes this issue by using an approximation of the encode distribution to efficiently find samples. A Stochastic Solution: MLE ========================= The MLE algorithm is a family of algorithms for finding samples from an unknown distribution, “D,” when only a sample from that distribution is known, “S.” To use the MLE algorithm, S is first generated using a uniform sample from D. This sampled value, S, is then perturbed from its true value according to some noise level, λ. This perturbed value, S’ is then evaluated, and the result is stored in a list of output samples. This procedure is repeated for a large number of values of S, and for a variety of different values of the noise level. Averaging across all of the values of S and λ yields an estimate of the distribution, D, which may be used to sample from, and thus approximate S. The MLE algorithm is effective, because it uses the encode distribution of an autoencoder to efficiently find samples. Approximate sampling from a generative autoencoder ==================================================== The MLE algorithm is an effective approach for sampling from a generative model and is used to generate samples from a generative autoencoder. The samples produced have a high degree of realism, and have the property that even though a few samples might seem obviously absurd, they still appear to be plausible. The procedure, described in the paper, first generates a random sample using standard dropout sampling, and then samples from the autoencoder using MLE. The MLE generated sample is then used to initialize a MCMC procedure, which converges to a distribution similar to the GAE’s encode distribution, making it easy to generate further samples from this new distribution. Comparison with Dropout Sampling -------------------------------- The approach in this paper improves upon dropout sampling, which is commonly used to generate samples from generative models. Dropout sampling yields an approximation to a sampling procedure from the GAE’s encode distribution, with a high degree of realism. The samples produced by dropout sampling are smooth, but are often overly regularized. The samples from this approach are often very similar to each other and do not vary smoothly. The MLE sampling procedure does not have this problem. Improvements ------------ The MLE procedure has one weakness, in that the samples it produces have structural noise. These structural flaws are introduced by the MLE procedure’s use of noise to sample from the encode distribution. The noise applied to the first sampled value, S, is added to all subsequent values of S. A simple denoising autoencoder can be used to remove the structural flaws present in MLE samples, but it is not clear how to remove these flaws without first using the MLE procedure. In conclusion, the MLE approach can be applied to sampling from a GAE, and samples from this approach have a number of advantages

I find the proposed MCMC based approach very interesting. By iteratively decoding and encoding, we are able to sample from the learned latent distribution. Since, the generative model learns to map from the learned latent distribution, rather than the prior, we may use MCMC to improve the quality of samples drawn from the generative model, especially when the learned latent distribution is far from the prior. Using MCMC sampling, we are able to reveal previously unseen differences between generative autoencoders trained either with or without a denoising criterion. However, there are some limitations: 1) the encoding distribution has to be a symmetric distribution which is common for GANs (e.g. prior in GANs), while we may sample from much more general distributions with MCMC; 2) the proposal distribution needs to be fixed, which means we have to tune it for different applications. Thus, the solution proposed may not be very general. Nevertheless, this is a very interesting direction and I think this work may have significant impact in GANs. My suggestion for this work: 1) How about using random variable transformation (RVT), which is a general approach to generate from any distribution, to replace MCMC? It could be possible given that we have a GAN model which can be treated as a generative model and encode to learned latent distribution; 2) The assumption that the encoder is symmetric is critical for the validity of MCMC sampling. If we can prove that the prior is symmetric, then we may use RVT to generate from the whole sample space. Please let me know if there are any questions.

The main contribution of the paper is the MCMC scheme to improve the sampling from generative autoencoders. This is achieved by modifying the generative model so that it maps to the learned latent distribution, rather than the prior. This allows us to reveal previously unseen differences between generative autoencoders trained either with or without a denoising criterion. We evaluate our method on both continuous and discrete distributional benchmarks, and show that MCMC improves the sampling and can reveal characteristics of the generative models which cannot be observed when simply training the models without MCMC. ulating The main contribution of the paper is the MCMC scheme to improve the sampling from generative autoencoders. This is achieved by modifying the generative model so that it maps to the learned latent distribution, rather than the prior. This allows us to reveal previously unseen differences between generative autoencoders trained either with or without a denoising criterion. We evaluate our method on both continuous and discrete distributional benchmarks, and show that MCMC improves the sampling and can reveal characteristics of the generative models which cannot be observed when simply training the models without MCMC. The paper makes the following specific contributions: 1. A novel scheme to train a generative autoencoder using Markov chains, 2. The first to show that there are important differences between generative autoencoders trained either with or without a denoising criterion, 3. The first to show that a generative autoencoder can be trained to map from the learned latent distribution to the prior, rather than the learned latent distribution itself.
