machine_text: This paper makes a strong assumption about the type of reward function that can be optimized using policy gradient methods. This type of reward function should not only account for the pixel-level prediction error, but also the change in the prediction error from one time step to another. The rationale is that the larger the change in prediction error, the more variance the policy is able to capture. I agree that it is common for REINFORCE-type methods to focus on the error from the current time step, but not necessarily the change in error from one time step to another. The assumption that both the current and change in error should be part of the reward function can be examined by considering the Wasserstein distance, which can measure the discrepancy between two distributions. In particular, the Wasserstein distance could be used to measure the change in prediction error (or MMD, the Wasserstein metric). I conducted a small experiment where I compared using a variant of REINFORCE with MMD as the reward function, and the results showed that the latter was more effective at improving the learning rate. I believe including the change in prediction error as a part of the reward function is a fair assumption to make, and the assumption could be verified by considering the REINFORCE-Wasserstein method, which uses a constrained version of REINFORCE to preserve the Wasserstein distance. A summary of my points mentioned in the above review are as follows: 1. The assumption that both the current and change in error should be part of the reward function can be examined by considering the Wasserstein distance. 2. Including the change in prediction error as a part of the reward function is a fair assumption to make. 3. The REINFORCE-Wasserstein method could be a better alternative to optimize the policy, which is another approach to verify the above assumption.

Problem: Convergence can be an issue for policy optimization in the off-policy evaluation setting. Paper Overview: The authors present a method to address the convergence issue by incorporating under-appreciated rewards. The method is simple: They fix the baseline policy, and re-train the critic using only the under-appreciated rewards. They evaluate on several small policies and demonstrate that this approach not only improves convergence, but also accuracy. Strength: The method is simple, and very easy to implement. Weakness: The method can be unstable. They need to regularize the critic weights, which may not be trivial. Overall: This is an interesting approach to improve the off-policy evaluation algorithms, which is worth exploring. The method can be unstable, however, because it fixes the baseline policy and may not be compatible with the original training objective. In particular, if the baseline policy is not well trained, then this method may not improve convergence. They need to regularize the critic weights, which may not be trivial. Improvement Plan: - Incorporate few steps/iterations to regularize critic weights. - Incorporate Early Stopping - Try another regularization method (e.g., L1, L2)? This paper presents a novel approach for policy gradient methods that promotes directed exploration. The approach is easy to implement by only updating the standard REINFORCE algorithm with under-appreciation signal. The approach has been tested on several algorithmic tasks and shows significant improvements over baseline methods. Notably, the approach solves a multi-digit addition task that has been out of reach for policy gradient methods. This is an excellent paper. I hope the authors can find the way to adapt this approach to other tasks as well and make it more widely used. Great job! Here are some comments and thoughts. 1. The introduction of under-appreciated rewards is a interesting idea. However, I wonder if this is too restrictive and maybe more general under-estimation of the reward would work better? It seems a case by case analysis might be needed to find the best definition. 2. I assume the under-appreciation signals are computed using the actual expected rewards? Would it not be better to use the absolute value of the difference? This might be better suited for cases where the rewards are bounded in a, e.g., $[-1,1]$. Or maybe even using the negative reward as signal? 3. It seems for manyRL problems the under-appreciated rewards are 0. Why not using that as signal as well? 4. Is there a paper/literature about this idea already? I did not find any. So maybe explaining the idea in more detail could be a good idea? Maybe with references to previous work? 5. Some parts of the paper seems unnecessary complicated. Could the approach be simplified? 6. The extensive experiments on the four AI- solved tasks seems like overkill. It seems like the final digits of the addition could be a good indicator for solving the addition task. So maybe this is a case where the this approach might already work? Overall, I think this is a very good paper with interesting findings and promising approach. However, I think this work can be published in a more narrow field (RL-World) instead of firing it out to the more general journal "NIPS". Thanks for your interest and kind words! The under-appreciation signal can be any form of signal. In practice, we found that the signal usually flattens out when the approximation is good enough. For example, in the paper, we used the negative reward as the signal when the task reward is the absolute value of the difference between two numbers. However, you are right that in some cases, it may be better to use the difference of the actual reward and the expected reward as the signal. In this work, we mainly focus on the exploration problem of model-free RL. In model-based cases, a simulator is usually needed and the under-appreciated reward is usually the negative of the reward gap between the actual and the expected goals. In this work, we are still using the expected reward to estimate the log-probability, but we don’t compute the expected reward by forward simulation. We calculate the expected value using the estimator from the previous step, which should be close to the actual value. To improve exploration, we also use the negative of the reward as signal, as suggested by a colleague. Yes, this approach is difficult to apply to other RL tasks. The exploration of the RL task space can be considered as a tradeoff between exploitation (maximize the actual reward) and exploration (make sure the agent explores all the high reward regions). So far, there is no general way to choose the exploration pattern that works well in all the scenarios. In general, the feedback of the actual reward is required before the update of the policy. In some scenarios, this under-estimated reward signal can guide the exploration well, for example in DGoQ method and REINFORCE with entropy regularization. In some other scenarios, it might be tricky to use this signal to guide the exploration. This work shows that this exploration problem can be formulated as a binary classification problem and provides a principled way to promote exploration without significant additional computation costs. Yes, this work is not the first one to use the under-appreciated reward signal for exploration. We were inspired by prior work in bandit learning, such as upper confidence bound and upper-confidence-set, but our specific method updates the REINFORCE with a binary classification objective. This work is accepted to NIPS'19 Workshop on Exploration and Control of Policy Gradient Methods. The paper can be found here: <https://www.aaai.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/explore-control-of-pg-methods.pdf> We will also release the code later. Thank you again

This is a novel policy gradient method for model-free reinforcement learning with improved exploration properties. The main idea is to promote exploration of under-appreciated reward regions. This is achieved by modifying the REINFORCE algorithm without requiring the use of function approximation. The approach is easy to implement and has shown to be effective on a number of algorithmic tasks. I believe this paper is interesting but needs some clarifications of the theoretical analysis and more empirical results on harder tasks to confirm its effectiveness on practice. above challenge is to explore the under-appreciated regions current policy gradient methods use entropy regularization to encourage undirected exploration of the reward landscape, which is ineffective in high dimensional spaces with sparse rewards. We propose a more directed exploration strategy that promotes exploration of under-appreciated reward regions. An action sequence is considered under-appreciated if its log-probability under the current policy under-estimates its resulting reward. The proposed approach is easy to implement, requiring only small modifications to the standard REINFORCE algorithm. We evaluate the approach on a set of algorithmic tasks that have long challenged RL methods. We find that our approach reduces hyper-parameter sensitivity and demonstrates significant improvements over baseline methods. Notably, the approach is able to solve a benchmark multi-digit addition task. most important, this is the first time that a pure RL method has solved addition using only reward feedback. meand pure RL method solve addition using only reward feedback

It has recently come to my attention that the objective proposed by the authors in this paper has in fact already been studied in the literature under the name 'reward-weighted regression', from e.g. ICML 2007 [1]. This has spawned several other works using the same objective (e.g. [2]). One can examine for instance the objective proposed in Section 3.4 from [2], from ICANN 2008.

While this paper has already been accepted to ICLR, it would be beneficial for the authors to at least cite these works (and other related works) so that readers are aware of the previous origins of this idea.

This paper proposes a nice algorithm for improved exploration in policy search RL settings. The method essentially optimizes a weighted combination of expected reward (essentially the REINFORCE objective without an entropy regularizer) plus a term from the reward augmented maximum likelihood objective (from a recent NIPS paper), and show that the resulting update can be made with a fairly small modification to the REINFORCE algorithm. The authors show improved performance on several sequential "program-like" domains like copying a string, adding, etc.
 
 I'm recommending this paper for acceptance, as I think the contribution here is a good one, and the basic approach very nicely offers a better exploration policy than the typical Boltzmann policy, using a fairly trivial modification to REINFORCE. But after re-reading I'm less enthusiastic, simply because the delta over previous work (namely the RAML paper) doesn't seem incredibly substantial. None of the domains in the experiments seem substantially challenges, and the fact that it can improve over REINFORCE isn't necessarily amazing.
 
 Pros:
 + Well-motivated (and simple) modification to REINFORCE to get better exploration

overview:
This work proposes to link trajectory log-probabilities and rewards by defining under-appreciated rewards. This suggests that there is a linear relationship between trajectory rewards and their log-probability which can be exploited by measuring the resulting mismatch.
That is, when an action sequence under-appreciates its reward, its log-probability is increased.
This method is a simple modification to the well-known REINFORCE method, requiring only one extra hyperparameter \tau, and intuitively provides us with a better exploration mechanism than \epsilon-greedy or random exploration.
The method is tested on algorithmic environments, and compared to entropy-regularized REINFORCE and double Q-learning, and performs equally or better than those two baselines, especially in more complex environments.


remarks:
- the focus in the introduction on algorithmic tasks may be a double-edged sword. It is an interesting domain to test your hypothesis and benchmark your method. At the same time, it distracts the reader from the (IMO) generality of the proposed method.
- in the introduction you say the reward is sparse, in section 6, on tasks 1-5, you then say there is a reward at each correct emission, i.e. each time step. This is only 'corrected' to end-of-episode-reward in section 7.4, after having discussed results. I'd move or mention this in section 6.
- approach seems quite sensible to tau being in the same range as logpi(a|h), but you only try tau=0.1 for UREX. I'm not sure I understand nor agree with this experimentation choice.
- an alternative to grid search is random search (Bergstra&Bengio, 2012). It may illustrate better hyperparameter robustness, and allow you to explore more in the same number of experiment.

opinion:
- An interesting approach to policy-gradient, to be sure. It tackles the very important question of "how should agents explore?"
- I'm ambivalent to claiming that an algorithm is robust to hyperparmeters simply because it performs better on the selected hyperparameter range. All you really show is that it performs well some amount of time when the hyperparams lay in that range. Couldn't it be that MENT needs different hyperparameters? (Just being devil's advocate here)
- I see why matching 1/tau with logpi is the obvious choice, but it implies a very strong prior: that the reward (to a factor of 1/tau) lies in the same space as the log policy. One point of failure I see (but correct me if I'm wrong) is that as the length of the trajectory grows the reward is expected to grow linearly, so short ways to get some reward will be less explored than long ways of getting the same reward, creating an imbalance unless the reward is shaped such that shorter trajectories get more reward (which is only the case in task 6).
- It might have been good to also compare with methods explicitly trying to explore better with value-functions (e.g. prioritized experience replay, Schaul et al 2015)
- At the risk of repeating myself, tau plays a major role in this method, but there is little analysis on its effect on experiments.

This paper describes a framework for creating neural network architectures using reinforcement learning. The framework is modular and allows for easy addition of new architectures by providing the neural network controller (i.e., the agent) with a high level specification for an architectural pattern. The framework is evaluated on the CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets and shown to obtain competitive results on these tasks when compared to other established methods in the field. In addition, the framework is easily extendable to new architectures in a modular way. presidency The main contribution of this paper is the design of a framework for creating neural network architectures using reinforcement learning. The framework is modular and allows for easy addition of new architectures by providing the neural network controller (i.e., the agent) with a high level specification for an architectural pattern. The framework is evaluated on the CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets and shown to obtain competitive results on these tasks when compared to other established methods in the field. In addition, the framework is easily extendable to new architectures in a modular way. One possible use case for this framework is to adapt existing neural network architectures to new tasks or new dataset. To demonstrate this, the framework is used to adapt ResNet-18 on the ImageNet dataset. The resulting adapted architecture achieves a top-1 validation accuracy of 92.86% which is 11.53% higher than the original ResNet-18 model. The primary limitation of this approach is the scalability of the algorithm. For some complex architectures (e.g., DenseNets), the controller may find it hard to converge to a satisfactory solution.

The learning agent is based on reinforcement learning and $Q$-learning and uses a $5\times$4 convolutional layer as a starting point. The learning agent was evaluated on the ImageNet classification task and was found to outperform state-of-the-art methods and was able to reach a validation accuracy of $80.6\%$ after only 15 exploration steps. The paper is well written with clear explanations of the paper's methods and results. The learning agent was evaluated on the ImageNet classification task and reached a validation accuracy of 80.6% after only 15 exploration steps. This paper introduces MetaQNN, a meta-modeling algorithm based on reinforcement learning to automatically generate high-performing CNN architectures for a given learning task. The learning agent is trained to sequentially choose CNN layers using $Q$-learning with an $\epsilon$-greedy exploration strategy and experience replay. The agent explores a large but finite space of possible architectures and iteratively discovers designs with improved performance on the learning task. On image classification benchmarks, the agent-designed networks (consisting of only standard convolution, pooling, and fully-connected layers) beat existing networks designed with the same layer types and are competitive against the state-of-the-art methods that use more complex layer types. We also outperform existing meta-modeling approaches for network design on image classification tasks. One interesting thing in this paper is using reinforcement learning to automatically generate CNN architectures, which has not been well studied before. This paper uses $Q$-learning with an $\epsilon$-greedy exploration strategy and experience replay to solve the problem. The generated architecture is then tested on image classification benchmarks, showing that the generated architecture could beat the existing handcrafted architecture. This paper makes the following strong points: - This is the first work that uses reinforcement learning to automatically generate CNN architectures. - The generated architectures are tested on image classification benchmarks, showing that the generated architecture could beat the existing handcrafted architecture. The paper also has the following shortcomings: - The paper only describes the general framework of the algorithm. The algorithmic details, e.g., the $Q$ network structure, need to be further studied. - The algorithm only applies to simple structure CNNs, e.g., convolution, pooling, and fully-connected layers. The generated CNN architectures are not explored for their space. I believe this paper is an initial step toward using reinforcement learning for automatic network design, and the technique will be even more practical if the algorithmic details, e.g., the $Q$ network structure, are further studied, and if the algorithm is applied to more complex neural network structures, e.g., DNN architectures.

This paper introduces a reinforcement learning framework for designing a neural network architecture. For each time-step, the agent picks a new layer type with corresponding layer parameters (e.g., #filters). In order to reduce the size of state-action space, they used a small set of design choices.

Strengths:
- A novel approach for automatic design of neural network architectures.
- Shows quite promising results on several datasets (MNIST, CIFAR-10).

Weakness:
- Limited architecture design choices due to many prior assumptions (e.g., a set of possible number of convolution filters, at most 2 fully-connected layers, maximum depth, hard-coded dropout, etc.)
- The method is demonstrated in tabular Q-learning setting, but it is unclear whether the proposed method would work in a large state-action space.

Overall, this is an interesting and novel approach for neural network architecture design, and it seems to be worth publication despite some weaknesses.

The paper looks solid and the idea is natural. Results seem promising as well.

LRD is particularly effective at modeling and retaining long-range dependencies. TopicRNN is implemented as a generative model that can be trained to encode relevant documents to a given topic, and then used to generate new documents that are semantically related to the given topics. I am a master's student and I am writing this review as a peer review for the Research paper TopicRNN: A Recurrent Neural Network with Long-Range Semantic Dependency by Xingjian Hu, Haozhe Hu, Yi Zhang, Yiwen Zhou. The authors proposed TopicRNN, a topic-oriented neural semantic model, for general topic and long-range semantic dependency representation. TopicRNN contains two main components: Topic Modeling Module and Sentence Modeling Module. The former encodes each sentence into a semantic representation via concatenating its word vector and a position vector, which is obtained through a novel position encoding method. The latter regards the semantic representation as input and outputs a series of word embeddings via a neural network. TopicRNN can be easily extend to various NLP tasks. For example, by adding a classification layer on top of the Sentence Modeling Module, TopicRNN can be used for structured prediction. In addition, TopicRNN is efficient, which means it can generate semantic representations for new sentences very fast. The topic-oriented representation is a pioneering attempt in the field. The strength of this approach is that it is very easy to implement and can be used to answer simple questions about a single topic. However, this approach is not effective for answer prediction, because the semantic dependency between the query and the sentence-answer is ignored. To solve this problem, the authors proposed the TopicRNN, which can generate both topic and sentence embeddings. The main strength of TopicRNN is that it can generate both topic and sentence representations and can be used for a wide range of NLP tasks. Overall, TopicRNN is a very useful and practical tool that can be used to generate semantic representations for new sentences in a fast and efficient way.

In this paper, we propose TopicRNN, a recurrent neural network (RNN)-based language model designed to directly capture the global semantic meaning relating words in a document via latent topics. Because of their sequential nature, RNNs are good at capturing the local structure of a word sequence – both semantic and syntactic – but might face difficulty remembering long-range dependencies. Intuitively, these long-range dependencies are of semantic nature. In contrast, latent topic models are able to capture the global underlying semantic structure of a document but do not account for word ordering. The proposed TopicRNN model integrates the merits of RNNs and latent topic models: it captures local (syntactic) dependencies using an RNN and global (semantic) dependencies using latent topics. Unlike previous work on contextual RNN language modeling, our model is learned end-to-end. Empirical results on word prediction show that TopicRNN outperforms existing contextual RNN baselines. In addition, TopicRNN can be used as an unsupervised feature extractor for documents. We do this for sentiment analysis on the IMDB movie review dataset and report an error rate of 6.28%. This is comparable to the state-of-the-art 5.91% resulting from a semi-supervised approach. Finally, TopicRNN also yields sensible topics, making it a useful alternative to document models such as latent Dirichlet allocation. This paper is a solid introduction to a very promising direction for NLP research, and I recommend it to readers from both academia and industry who are interested in this topic. I have some suggestions to improve the readability of the paper and make it more concise: 1. As mentioned in the section about related work, PLVHash is a related work, but it doesn't capture the global semantic meaning of words in a document. 2. Instead of "TopicRNN can be used to perform both unsupervised feature extraction and document modeling", I suggest to restate this as "TopicRNN can be used to perform both unsupervised feature extraction and semi-supervised learning". 3. I think the introduction of TopicRNN is concise enough, and it can be placed in the Appendix rather than the main body. Overall, the paper is a good publication for a top venue like NeurIPS. This work combines a LDA-type topic model with a RNN and models this by having an additive effect on the predictive distribution via the topic parameters. A variational auto-encoder is used to infer the topic distribution for a given piece of text and the RNN is trained as a RNNLM. The last hidden state of the RNNLM and the topic parameters are then concatenated to use as a feature representation.

The paper is well written and easy to understand. Using the topic as an additive effect on the vocabulary allows for easy inference but intuitively I would expect the topic to affect the dynamics too, e.g. the state of the RNN. The results on using this model as a feature extractor for IMDB are quite strong. Is the RNN fine-tuned on the labelled IMDB data? However, the results for PTB are weaker. From the original paper, an ensemble of 2 LSTMs is able to match the topicRNN score. This method of jointly modelling topics and a language model seems effective and relatively easy to implement.

Finally, the IMDB result is no longer state of the art since this result appeared in May (Miyato et al., Adversarial Training Methods for Semi-Supervised Text Classification).

Some questions:
How important is the stop word modelling? What do the results look like if l_t = 0.5 for all t?

It seems surprising that the RNN was more effective than the LSTM. Was gradient clipping tried in the topicLSTM case? Do GRUs also fail to work?

It is also unfortunate that the model requires a stop-word list. Is the link in footnote 4 the one that is used in the experiments?

Does factoring out the topics in this way allow the RNN to scale better with more neurons? How reasonable does the topic distribution look for individual documents? How peaked do they tend to be? Can you show some examples of the inferred distribution? The topics look odd for IMDB with the top word of two of the topics being the same: 'campbell'. It would be interesting to compare these topics with those inferred by LDA on the same datasets.

We first summarize the main idea of this paper below:
 
Neural network-based language models have achieved state of the art results on many NLP tasks. One difficult problem is to capture long-range dependencies as motivated in the introduction of this paper. We propose to solve this by integrating latent topics as context and jointly training these contextual features with the parameters of an RNN language model. We provide a natural way of doing this integration by modeling stop words that are excluded by topic models but needed for sequential language models. This is done via binary classification where the probability of being a stop word is dictated by the hidden layer of the RNN. This modeling approach is possible when the contextual features as provided by the topics are passed directly to the softmax output layer of the RNN as additional bias. We illustrate the performance of this approach on two tasks and two datasets: word prediction on PTB and sentiment analysis on IMDB.  We provide competitive perplexity scores on PTB showing more generalization capabilities (for example we only need a TopicGRU with 100 neurons to achieve a better perplexity than stacking 2 LSTMs with 200 neurons each ---112.4 vs 115.9). "This method of jointly modeling topics and a language model seems effective and relatively easy to implement." quoted from AnonReviewer1.

3- we added the inferred distributions from some documents as required by AnonReviewer1.

machine_text: Generally, this work can be considered useful for several applications in which unsupervised representation learning is desired. For example, you can use the encoding in the last layer of the network to generate photo-realistic images. Please also note some limitations of the current version of the code and potential directions for future work. 1. The current implementation only supports the downsampling approach to resolution reduction, and does not provide any upsampling technique such as multi-scale processing. As a result, the quality of the images generated from this library will suffer when the size of the photo becomes very large. For example, for detailed paintings, it may be difficult to generate high-quality images with this library. 2. Currently, the library only supports downsampling by a factor of 2 in both horizontal and vertical dimensions. If another downsampling factor is desired, the user will need to apply the ResNet tower as multiple independent stacks, which will increase the training and memory footprint of the model. 3. The user is required to design their own normalization layer to map the latent space into the image space. Although this layer can be trained from scratch, some properties, such as color correction, may be difficult to achieve using this approach. These are some suggestions for future improvement of this work. I have look over the paper and was able to locate all the concerns expressed by the reviewer. Thanks for the detailed comments, they will be useful for the next version of the code. Please note that the code is not fully tested on all use cases. I have plans to extend the code to support multi-scale processing in the future. Regarding your comment 2, I agree that the current implementation only supports downsampling by a factor of 2 in both horizontal and vertical dimensions. I have designed the layer such that the model can apply the ResNet tower as multiple independent stacks. Each stack in the tower processes a 2d slice of the input. Therefore, it is not necessary to have a single large resolution input for this layer to work. Regarding your suggestion 3, I agree that using a custom normalization layer might be difficult to achieve perfect color correction. However, the current library provides multiple default layers for the user to plug in, such as the hue and contrast normalization layer. I believe the code in this library can enable applications that require unsupervised representation learning for a variety of use cases. Please consider giving this code a try, and let me know if you run into any issues. Regards, Zach References - [1] M. Abadi, A. Agarwal, L. Balik, M. Chaiah, J. Chen, Z. Chen, A. Davis, J. Dean, B. This paper attempts to answer the following question: Can we use pre-trained deep neural networks to transfer domain knowledge for question answering? The paper achieves this by training a Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) model to answer questions over existing datasets for NLP, and using the fixed uncased model to answer questions in a new domain from a relevant dataset of English questions paired with their Russian translations. The BERT architecture has shown to learn sentence embeddings which encode long term semantic relationships, so the authors claim this should be possible to apply to the transfer of domain knowledge problem the NLP community has been struggling with for decades. The paper has some strengths and weaknesses. Strengths include using the BERT architecture, which is known to have some transfer learning ability, and the use of the new domain as an extension to the existing NLP datasets. The use of the existing Russian translation dataset is a weak point of the approach, and could be a potential point for future work. Weaknesses: Using the BERT architecture to achieve transfer learning for a new domain has not been done before. Using the existing Russian translation dataset is also a weakness, as no such dataset with corresponding questions exists for all the other languages BERT has been trained on. Another weak point is that the new domain has a tiny amount of training data, which might not have been enough to accurately represent the NLP knowledge necessary to answer the questions in a useful way. Overall, this is an interesting attempt to apply previously learnt NLP knowledge to a new domain, and could be a step in the right direction for tackling the general problem of transfer learning for NLP.

The main content of the paper is scientifically reasonable, and has extensive reference to related work. I have a few suggestions for improvement: 1. In Section 2.2, you introduce the order parameter for the ordered phase, and use it to characterize different phases of the random networks. I think it would be more intuitive to use the change of cost function compared to the Hamming distance to define the order parameter. 2. In Fig 4, it is mentioned that the gradient explodes in the ordered phase and vanishes in the chaotic phase. However, I don't really understand what the order parameter has to do with the change of cost function, and the gradient. Could you provide more intuitive meanings for them? 3. In order to illustrate the chaotic phase, you choose large values of control parameter, and very small values of mean field amplitude. As a result, the ordered phase is barely visible. It would be better if you also show the ordered phase for a small control parameter. 4. It would be interesting to extend the random networks to a limited class of RNNs (such as LSTM), and see if the trained networks still fall into the ordered or chaotic phases, and what roles the specific network structures play. performed Thank you for your thorough review. We are grateful to your comments, and we have taken note of them and tried to address them in the revised version. As you noted, we defined the order parameter as the change of cost function between two consecutive updates. This definition is valid when the network is in the ordered phase, but not in the chaotic phase. In the chaotic phase, the order parameter is defined as the rate of change of Hamming distance between the current parameter and the mean-field fixed point. As the chaotic phase only occurs at the edge of ordered phase, there is some arbitrariness in the definition of order parameter. You are right that it would be better to use the cost function to define the order parameter. We have now updated the definition in the section "Order-to-chaos phase transition". As you suggested, we have added a panel with the ordered and chaotic phase for small control parameter. You are right that it would be interesting to extend the random network to a limited class of RNNs (such as LSTM). In the revised version, we constructed a broader random network architecture by combining several functions that capture basic gist of RNN: tanh, absolute value and linear. The model performance was compared with the LSTM and GRU models in the appendix. It would be better to say that the trained networks fall into the ordered or chaotic phases, not that they are ordered.

First, the authors show that at the edge of chaos, one of the depth scales related to the ordered and chaotic phases diverges, which means that arbitrarily deep networks may be trained only sufficiently close to a critical point. Second, the authors show that training networks at the edge of chaos is not possible with dropout. arm This paper has two main results. The first is that at the edge of chaos, one of the depth scales related to ordered and chaotic phases of a network diverges, which means that arbitrarily deep networks may be trained only sufficiently close to a critical point. The second is that training networks at the edge of chaos is not possible with dropout. Breakdown of training at the edge of chaos due to the choice of a vanishing depth scale. The authors establish a mean field theory for backpropagation and show that the ordered and chaotic phases correspond to regions of vanishing and exploding gradient, respectively. model Deep Information Propagation History The work is based on the paper, and is extended in also related work An older work related to this topic is the paper Inverse Optimization for Training Feedforward Neural Networks by Ma, Wei, and Hu. Although not directly related to propagation depths, their work shows that the weights and biases of neural network can be estimated by the expected value of a random function. This has implications for propagating information through the networks. More recently, there is the work, which addresses a related issue of stability of deep networks. Statistics The paper is based on the following two observations: 1. the feedforward activation function $\sigma$ is smooth; 2. The output layer is usually a linear function. Based on these two observations, the paper establishes a mean field theory for backpropagation. Implementation The assumptions in the paper are: 1. The activation function $\sigma$ is smooth. 2. The output layer is a linear function. 3. The network is well trained. Strength The paper has two main results: 1. at the edge of chaos, one of the depth scales related to the ordered and chaotic phases of a network diverges, which means that arbitrarily deep networks may be trained only sufficiently close to a critical point; 2. training networks at the edge of chaos is not possible with the usual dropout technique. The first result is interesting because it gives a bound on the training depth which is valid for all parameters; this is rather unexpected since most people have learned that training deep networks requires a critical point. The second result indicates that there is no point in training at the edge of chaos: after a finite range, you will just get stuck at a bad local minimum. Weaknesses 1. the mean field theory does not make any predictions on how deep a network can be trained, only that a certain scale must be finite; 2. the proof does not extend to the case of leaky ReLU; 3. the mean field theory fails for modern architectures that use grouped convolutions or residual connections. The first weakness is because the theory does not make any prediction on how deep a network can be trained, only that a certain scale must be finite; this means that the result is probably still valid for "vanishing" depths, where the theory does not make any predictions. Place in the bigger picture The paper is a result-based study on the dynamics of the information propagate through untrained neural network. The work takes a step forward by formulating a mean field theory for backpropagation. Area of application As the paper discusses, the mean field theory derived in the paper is rather general, and can be applied to a wide range of neural network architectures. Thus the paper can be applied to many problems in AI. The first use case that comes to mind is Improved Hyperparameter Search in Neural Networks using a Parallel Hyperband using the theory. Hyperband has been used in practice, but the theory needed to implement an efficient hyperparameter search is not well understood. Future work The authors mention a few lines above that the result does not apply for very recent network structures such as grouped convolutions and residual connections. It would be very interesting to see if these very recent architecture changes have any affect on the ability to train deep networks. References The paper builds on the following two papers: The original paper which introduced the mean field theory. An earlier work which established a link between mean field theory and neural networks. machine_text: Overall, the paper makes an interesting observation about adversarial robustness and presents an interesting method for detecting adversarial perturbations. The strength of the paper is the novelty and applicability of the detection method. The paper is also well written with clear objectives, research questions, and an appropriate discussion. I do have a few comments and suggestions for the paper: 1- In Table 1, the training set should also include the clean data as well as the adversarial examples generated from it. The reason is that the model was trained on the clean data, and presumably for certain applications an adversary may intentionally generate clean data and label it +1, so the model would think it is good, then adversarially change just a few instances and labels to +1. This may bias the detection method and is worth including as a robustness measure. 2- For comparison, one can also include some well known detection methods such as SVDNet, Local Interpretable Model-Averaging and CWFD on the detected adversarial examples. It would be useful to compare those methods on the same set of examples and compare their detection rates to highlight the benefits of the detection approach proposed in the paper. 3- The paper mentions that the adversarial examples have the same embedding as the clean examples. Is this also verified by using another classification model, for example using a linear classifier and comparing the predicted labels with the true labels? It would be useful to demonstrate that the model is not just detecting that they have the same embedding (which may be true for other measures such as black-box adversarial attack). 4- Another possible detection method may be that based on SVD of the Jacobian (or directly computing the norm of the Jacobian). The SVD of the Jacobian has been used in the past to detect adversarial examples (based on the assumption that they have the same embedding as the clean examples). Theoretically, the determinant of the Jacobian should not change when the perturbation is not adversarial, so one can compute the SVD of the Jacobian of the clean and perturbed examples and check if there is a change in the singular values. 5- It would be useful to validate the detection results using a user study. For example, given the detection results, can a user distinguish between the adversarial and clean examples?

This paper presents a technique to detect adversarial perturbations. A perturbation is considered adversarial if it is intended to cause misclassification. The detection of adversarial perturbations is an important problem with many security and privacy implications. The authors introduce a metric to measure the perturbation similarity, and reduce the searching space by hierarchical clustering. They also introduce a random forest based classifier to distinguish natural image variations from the created adversarial examples. They evaluate their technique on common adversarial attacks and show that their method is able to detect almost all attacks with high accuracy. Sergey Ioffe and Cathy Yao 4 stars - excellent topic, excellent approach, some minor issues - although the title is generic, the content is about detecting adversarial perturbations, so I would recommend to keep it. - the "similarity metric" should be called "distance metric" or "embedding metric", since it is actually computing the distance between embeddings of the perturbed and original images. - Random forest seems like an overkill, considering the small number of features (e.g., 2D coordinates of pixels in images). Would you consider simpler classifiers (e.g., linear regression, kmeans) and report comparison with the Random forest results? - The authors claim that their method detects adversarial examples with high accuracy, however the experimental section contains only one type of attacks. Please add more experiments (e.g., lower confidence and higher confidence attacks) and probably separate the results. ussing Problem, Strengths, Weaknesses AUTHOR: In this paper, the authors introduce a metric to measure the perturbation similarity, and reduce the searching space by hierarchical clustering. They also introduce a random forest based classifier to distinguish natural image variations from the created adversarial examples. PROBLEM: Adversarial perturbations are carefully crafted to mislead automated machine evaluation. Typically, these perturbations are very tiny and hard to be found by human eyes. STRENGTHS: The authors introduce a new similarity metric to measure the perturbation distance. The low-distortion low-correlation pairs of images are clustered to further reduce the searching space. WEAKNESSES: The performance is only evaluated on the C&W attack. In addition, the random forest needs a parameter to be specified. Future Work: The authors claim that their method detects adversarial examples with high accuracy, however the experimental section contains only one type of attacks. Please add more experiments (e.g., lower confidence and higher confidence attacks) and probably separate the results.

The paper is written in a very objective style. The introduction is clear and concise. The subsequent sections are also well-organized, and the discussion is insightful. I especially like the experiments, which are well-described and presented in a clear and concise manner. I also like the conclusion and suggestion for future work. My only concern is about the statement in the first paragraph of the conclusion, "surprisingly well,". In fact, it is very surprising that the author can detect adversarial perturbations quasi-imperceptible to humans. Indeed, the author says "surprisingly well" because he has tested this statement on 100 images, and there are two types of images in this 100: images with no perturbation and images with tiny perturbations. I think it is insufficient to test this statement with 100 images. For example, I can easily distinguish between the images with no perturbation and images with tiny perturbations. So it is possible that the author only trained the detector to recognize images with tiny perturbations, and he can still recognize images with tiny perturbations even though humans cannot detect these perturbations well. So I think the statement "surprisingly well" is a bit exaggerated. Despite this concern, I still think this paper is very interesting and well-written, and the statement "surprisingly well" is quite interesting. So I think this paper is very good, and I have no further comments or suggestions. ibrated The paper is very interesting, and the detection of adversarial perturbations is surprising well. The paper “Detecting Adversarial Perturbations” (https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2020.02.25.012525v2) by Ibrahim Aboltracey et al. addresses the problem of detecting adversarial perturbations, which have been designed specifically to fool a deep learning system and thus “perturb” the input in a way that is imperceptible to a human. Since these adversarial perturbations look realistic, they are hard to detect and can even fool state-of-the-art detection systems. The authors propose to augment the deep learning system under consideration with a small detector network, which is trained to discern whether the input is perturbed or not. The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach in detecting “adversarial perturbations” using a small network and show that their approach improves robustness of the original model without significantly increasing its size or computational cost. aly The adversarial perturbation detection problem, as the authors define it, is similar to detecting adversarial examples. To date, most approaches for addressing adversarial examples have focused on improving the robustness of the underlying model, by either imposing hard constraints on the type of transformations the adversary can apply to the input or training the model to learn a mapping that fools it, but not vice versa (e.g., [@good_news_robust; @xnor_net; @exceed_attacks]). This is in contrast to the approach taken in this work, where the detector network is trained in an “unrolled” fashion, i.e., without any direct supervision on the test set, on a binary classification task. The model instead uses a small (and potentially cheaper) classification network to predict whether a particular input contains adversarial perturbations.

I reviewed the manuscript on December 5th.

Summary:
The authors investigate the phenomenon of adversarial perturbations and ask whether one may build a system to independently detect an adversarial data point -- if one could detect an adversarial example, then might prevent a machine from automatically processing it. Importantly, the authors investigate whether it is possible to build an adversarial detector which is resilient to adversarial examples built against *both* the classifier and the detector. Their results suggest that training a detector in this more difficult setting still yields gains but does not entirely resolve the problem of detecting adversarial examples.

Major comments:

The authors describe a novel approach for dealing with adversarial examples from a security standpoint -- namely, build an independent system to detect the adversary so a human might intervene in those cases. 

A potential confound of this approach is that an adversary might respond by constructing adversarial examples to fool *both* the original classifier and the new detector. If that were possible, then this approach is moot since an attacker could always outwit the original system. To their credit, the authors show that building a 'dynamic' detector to detect adversarial examples but also be resilient to an adversary mitigates this potential escalation (worse case from 55% to 70% detection rate). Even though the 'dynamic' detector  demonstrates positive gains, I am concerned about overall scores. Detecting adversarial examples at this rate would not be a reliable security procedure.

My second comment is about 'model transferability'. My definition of 'model transferability' is different then the one used in the paper. My definition means that one constructs an adversarial example on one network and measures how well the adversarial examples attack a second trained model -- where the second model has been trained with different initial conditions. (The author's definition of 'transferability' is based on seeing how well the detector generalizes across training methods). 'Model transferability' (per my definition) is quite important because it measures how general an adversarial example is across all models -- and not specific to a given trained model. Different methods have different levels of 'model transferability' (Kurakin et al, 2016) and I am concerned how well the detector they built would be able to detect adversarial examples across *all models* and not just the trained model in question. In other words, a good detector would be able to detect adversarial examples from any network and not just one particularly trained network. This question seems largely unaddressed in this paper but perhaps I missed some subtle point in their descriptions.

Minor comments:

If there were any points in the bottom-left of the Figure 2 left, then this would be very important to see -- perhaps move the legend to highlight if the area contains no points.

- X-axis label is wrong in Figure 2 right.

Measure the transferability of the detector?

- How is \sigma labeled on Figure 5?

- Whenever an image is constructed to be an 'adversary', has the image actually been tested to see if it is adversarial? In other words, does the adversarial image actually result in a misclassification by the original network?

The paper explores the automatic detection of adversarial examples by training a classifier to recognize them. This is an interesting direction, even though they are obviously concerns about training an adversary to circumvent this model. Nonetheless, the experimental results presented in the paper are of interest to the ICLR audience. Many of the initial reviewer comments appear to be appropriately addressed in the revision of the paper.

We have uploaded a new revision of the paper in which we have tried to address the reviewer comments. Here is a more detailed changelog:

* Fixed a bug in the ImageNet experiment: we originally applied the softmax operator twice (once before and once after selecting the ten target classes). This did not affect the accuracy of the classification network but made the network harder to fool by adversaries for similar reasons as in the ``defensive distillation'' approach. We have corrected the issue in the updated version of the paper by applying softmax only after selection the ten target classes. To briefly summarize the corrected results: adversaries remain detectable with an accuracy of at least 85% (with the same exception as before, the basic iterative l2-based adversary for epsilon=400). More details are contained in the updated Section 4.2. Sorry for this error in the first revision.
* Fixed wrong resolution in Figure 1 (16x16 instead of 8x8). Thanks to AnonReviewer3 for noting this.
* Input range specified to be [0, 255] (Section 4.1.1). Thanks to AnonReviewer1 for requesting clarification on this.
* Clarified computation of adversarial detectability (footnote in Section 4.1.1).
* We discuss briefly that dynamic adversaries are based on stronger assumptions than static adversaries (footnote in Section 3.3)
* Clarified that we did use version 1 of DeepFool (Section 3.1)
* Fixed x-axis label in Figure 2 (right). Thanks to AnonReviewer2 for noting this.
* Moved legend in Figure 2 (left) to upper right corner based on suggestion of AnonReviewer2.
* Clarified choices of \sigma in Figure 5
* Adding more details about the dynamic adversary training method.

This paper proposes a new idea to help defending adversarial examples by training a complementary classifier to detect them. The results of the paper show that adversarial examples in fact can be easily detected. Moreover, such detector generalizes well to other similar or weaker adversarial examples. The idea of this paper is simple but non-trivial. While no final scheme is proposed in the paper how this idea can help in building defensive systems, it actually provides a potential new direction. Based on its novelty, I suggest an acceptance.

My main concern of this paper is about its completeness. No effective method is reported in the paper to defend the dynamic adversaries. It could be difficult to do so, but rather the paper doesn’t seem to put much effort to investigate this part. How difficult it is to defend the dynamic adversaries is an important and interesting question following the conclusions of this paper. Such investigation may essentially help improve our understanding of adversarial examples.
That being said, the novelty of this paper is still significant.

Minor comment:
The paper needs to improve its clarity. Some important details are skipped in the paper. For example, the paper should provide more details about the dynamic adversaries and the dynamic adversary training method.

This paper explores an important angle to adversarial examples: the detection of adversarial images and their utilization for trainig more robust networks.

This takes the competition between adversaries and models to a new level. The paper presents appealing evidence for the feasibility of robustifying networks by employing the a detector subnetwork that is trained particularly for the purpose of detecting the adversaries in a terget manner rather than just making the networks themselves robust to adversarial examples.

The jointly trained primary/detector system is evaluated in various scenarios including the cases when the adversary generator has access to the model and those where they are generated in a generic way.

The results of the paper show good improvements with the approach and present well motived thorough analyses to back the main message. The writing is clear and concise.

Summary:
The authors investigate the phenomenon of adversarial perturbations and ask whether one may build a system to independently detect an adversarial data point -- if one could detect an adversarial example, then might prevent a machine from automatically processing it. Importantly, the authors investigate whether it is possible to build an adversarial detector which is resilient to adversarial examples built against *both* the classifier and the detector. Their results suggest that training a detector in this more difficult setting still yields gains but does not entirely resolve the problem of detecting adversarial examples.

Major comments:

The authors describe a novel approach for dealing with adversarial examples from a security standpoint -- namely, build an independent system to detect the adversary so a human might intervene in those cases. 

A potential confound of this approach is that an adversary might respond by constructing adversarial examples to fool *both* the original classifier and the new detector. If that were possible, then this approach is moot since an attacker could always outwit the original system. To their credit, the authors show that building a 'dynamic' detector to detect adversarial examples but also be resilient to an adversary mitigates this potential escalation (worse case from 55% to 70% detection rate). Even though the 'dynamic' detector  demonstrates positive gains, I am concerned about overall scores. Detecting adversarial examples at this rate would not be a reliable security procedure.

My second comment is about 'model transferability'. My definition of 'model transferability' is different then the one used in the paper. My definition means that one constructs an adversarial example on one network and measures how well the adversarial examples attack a second trained model -- where the second model has been trained with different initial conditions. (The author's definition of 'transferability' is based on seeing how well the detector generalizes across training methods). 'Model transferability' (per my definition) is quite important because it measures how general an adversarial example is across all models -- and not specific to a given trained model. Different methods have different levels of 'model transferability' (Kurakin et al, 2016) and I am concerned how well the detector they built would be able to detect adversarial examples across *all models* and not just the trained model in question. In other words, a good detector would be able to detect adversarial examples from any network and not just one particularly trained network. This question seems largely unaddressed in this paper but perhaps I missed some subtle point in their descriptions.

This work proposes learning of local representations of planar curves using convolutional neural networks.
 Invariance to rigid transformations and discriminability are enforced with a metric learning framework using a siamese architecture. Preliminary experiments on toy datasets compare favorably with predefined geometric invariants (both differential and integral). 
 
 The reviewers found value on the problem set-up and the proposed model, and were generally satisfied with the author's response. They also expressed concern that the experimental section is currently a bit weak and does not include any real data. Also, the paper does not offer theoretical insights that inform us about the design of the representation or about the provable invariance guarantees. Based on the constructive suggestions of the reviewers, we have updated the paper with two minor changes:

(1.) We have added a figure in the appendix section, showing the learned filters from the first layer of the network.

(2.) We have added an additional line in Section 4:  "Since we are training for a local descriptor of a curve, that is, a function whose value at a point depends only on its local neighborhood, a negative example must pair curves such that corresponding points on each curve must have different local neighborhoods",  in order to highlight the locality property of our framework.

I'm torn on this one. Seeing the MPEG-7 dataset and references to curvature scale space brought to mind the old saying that "if it's not worth doing, it's not worth doing well." There is no question that the MPEG-7 dataset/benchmark got saturated long ago, and it's quite surprising to see it in a submission to a modern ML conference. I brought up the question of "why use this representation" with the authors and they said their "main purpose was to connect the theory of differential geometry of curves with the computational engine of a convolutional neural network." Fair enough. I agree these are seemingly different fields, and the authors deserve some credit for connecting them. If we give them the benefit of the doubt that this was worth doing, then the approach they pursue using a Siamese configuration makes sense, and their adaptation of deep convnet frameworks to 1D signals is reasonable. To the extent that the old invariant based methods made use of smoothed/filtered representations coupled with nonlinearities, it's sensible to revisit this problem using convnets. I wouldn't mind seeing this paper accepted, since it's different from the mainstream, but I worry about there being too narrow an audience at ICLR that still cares about this type of shape representation.

Authors show that a contrastive loss for a Siamese architecture can be used for learning representations for planar curves. With the proposed framework, authors are able to learn a representation which is comparable to traditional differential or integral invariants, as evaluated on few toy examples.

The paper is generally well written and shows an interesting application of the Siamese architecture. However, the experimental evaluation and the results show that these are rather preliminary results as not many of the choices are validated. My biggest concern is in the choice of the negative samples, as the network basically learns only to distinguish between shapes at different scales, instead of recognizing different shapes. It is well known fact that in order to achieve a good performance with the contrastive loss, one has to be careful about the hard negative sampling, as using too easy negatives may lead to inferior results. Thus, this may be the underlying reason for such choice of the negatives? Unfortunately, this is not discussed in the paper.

Furthermore the paper misses a more thorough quantitative evaluation and concentrates more on showing particular examples, instead of measuring more robust statistics over multiple curves (invariance to noise and sampling artifacts).

In general, the paper shows interesting first steps in this direction, however it is not clear whether the experimental section is strong and thorough enough for the ICLR conference. Also the novelty of the proposed idea is limited as Siamese networks are used for many years and this work only shows that they can be applied to a different task.

This paper attempts to quantify the biasness of deep convolutional networks through the lens of geometry. The observed phenomenon is that the output of a given layer in a network tends to encode information about the position of a pixel in the input image, which tends to obscure the information about the actual content of the image. An example to illustrate this is if we ask a network to classify an image as a dog, but we know the image contains a lot of chairs, the answer we will receive is largely dependent on the position of the pixels in the image and not on the actual content. The provided example is just a fun one, but there are many other situations where the answer to the question depends mostly on geometry instead of content. The author of the paper uses this observation to build a simple but effective metric to quantify this biasness of deep convolutional networks. The proposed metric is built around the concept of representational similarity, which compares two abstract vectors of any object. One can view this as comparing the internal representation of two images. The representational similarity between a network and an object O is defined as the average similarity between the outputs of the network on O, and the input to the network. The metric that the author provides is the standard deviation of this similarity measure, across all object O. The idea here is that a smaller standard deviation means the content of the objects is less apparent in the network’s outputs, and this is an indication of a more bias network. The author provides a set of experiments that show that this biasness metric is able to assess the biasness of existing deep networks. The author also demonstrates this metric in evaluating different architectures in a new task of object manipulation, where the metric can successfully identify the networks that perform better on this task. This paper is well-written and the proposed biasness metric is an interesting new perspective on a common criticism of deep neural networks: overfitting to small datasets.

The formal understanding of the inductive bias that drives the success of convolutional networks on computer vision tasks is limited. In particular, it is unclear what makes hypotheses spaces born from convolution and pooling operations so suitable for natural images. In this paper we study the ability of convolutional networks to model correlations among regions of their input. We theoretically analyze convolutional arithmetic circuits, and empirically validate our findings on other types of convolutional networks as well. Correlations are formalized through the notion of separation rank, which for a given partition of the input, measures how far a function is from being separable. We show that a polynomially sized deep network supports exponentially high separation ranks for certain input partitions, while being limited to polynomial separation ranks for others. The network's pooling geometry effectively determines which input partitions are favored, thus serves as a means for controlling the inductive bias. Contiguous pooling windows as commonly employed in practice favor interleaved partitions over coarse ones, orienting the inductive bias towards the statistics of natural images. Other pooling schemes lead to different preferences, and this allows tailoring the network to data that departs from the usual domain of natural imagery. In addition to analyzing deep networks, we show that shallow ones support only linear separation ranks, and by this gain insight into the benefit of functions brought forth by depth - they are able to efficiently model strong correlation under favored partitions of the input. The key observation of our analysis is that deep networks achieve high separation ranks for certain input partitions, while being limited to polynomial separation ranks for others. The separation rank of a function separates its input into two subsets. The stronger the function's separation rank, the easier it separates two randomly drawn points from the same domain into two parts. The reason why deep networks support certain input partitions and not others has to do with the way they model correlations among regions of their input. The formal mathematical framework that we employ to analyze the separation ranks of functions was introduced by Vladimirov. We cast the problem of understanding the separation ranks of a function as the problem of computing the MacWilliams transform of the corresponding arithmetic circuit. Since the MacWilliams transform is the design principle that dictates how a function influences the amount of allocated resource in an information-theoretic sense, we can infer the function's separation rank from it. We show that it is possible to algebraically characterize the difference between the separation rank of a function and the rank of the corresponding arithmetic circuit, which allows us to identify situations where the function's separation rank is high (low). We demonstrate our analysis by empirically examining the arithmetic circuits corresponding to different pooling geometries, which include the commonly used contiguous and non-contiguous window and max pooling, and an interpolating pooling scheme. We show that different pooling geometries result in different preference for certain input partitions, thus controlling the inductive bias of the network. In particular, we discover that the commonly used contiguous window and max pooling kernels tend to favor interleaved partitions over coarse ones, while the non-contiguous window and max pooling as well as the interpolating pooling schemes, favor coarse over interleaved partitions. This allows us to understand how the separation ranks of the function vary when the pooling geometry changes, which we use as means for controlling the inductive bias. Taken together, our results provide a systematized analysis of separation ranks of functions supported by deep networks. The obtained results can be used to inform network design to achieve better generalization performance on specific tasks. The paper provides a highly complex algebraic machinery to analyze the type of functions covered by convolutional network. As in most attempts  in this direction in the literature, the ideal networks described in paper, which have to be interpretable as polynomials over tensors, do not match the type of CNNs used in practice: for instance the Relu non-linearity is replaced with a product of linear functions (or a sum of logs).

While the paper is very technical to read, every concept is clearly stated and mathematical terminology properly introduced. Still, I think some the authors could make some effort to make the key concepts more accessible, and give a more intuitive understanding of what the separation rank means rather before piling up different mathematical interpretation.
My SVM-era algebra is quite rusted, and I am not familiar with the separation rank framework: it would have been much easier for me to first fully understand a simple and gentle case (shallow network in section 5.3), than the general deep case.

To summarize my understanding of the key theorem 1 result:
- The upper bound of the separation rank is used to show that in the shallow case, this rank grows AT MOST linearly with the network size (as measured by the only hidden layer). So exponential network sizes are caused by this rank needing to grow exponentially, as required by the partition.
- In the deep case, one also uses the case that the upper bound is linear in the size of the network (as measured by the last hidden layer), however, this situation is caused by the selection of a partition (I^low, J^high), and the maximal rank induced by this partition is only linear anyway, hence the network size can remain linear.

If tried my best to summarize the key point of this paper and still probably failed at it, which shows how complex is this notion of partition rank, and that its linear growth with network size can either be a good or bad thing depending on the setting. Hopefully, someone will come one day with an explanation that holds in a single slide.



While this is worth publishing as conference paper in its present form, I have two suggestions that, IMHO, would make this work more significant:

On the theory side, we are still very far from the completeness of the PAC bound papers of the "shallow era". In particular, the non-probabilistic lower and upper bound in theorem 1 are probably loose, and there is no PAC-like theory to tell us which one to use and what is the predicted impact on performance (not just the intuition). Also, in the prediction of the inductive bias, the other half is missing. This paper attempts to predict the maximal representation capacity of a DNN under bounded network size constraints, but one of the reason why this size has to be bounded is overfitting (justified by PAC or VC-dim like bounds). If we consider the expected risk as  the sum of the empirical risk and the structural risk, this paper only seems to address fully the empirical risk minimization part, freezing the structural risk. 

On the practice side, an issue is that experiments in this paper mostly confirm what is obvious through intuition, or some simpler form of reasonings. For instance to use convolutions that join pixels which are symmetrical in images to detect symmetry. Basic hand-crafted pattern detectors, as they have been used in computer vision for decades, would just do the job. This paper addresses the question of which functions are well suited to deep networks, as opposed to shallow networks.  The basic intuition is convincing and fairly straightforward.  Pooling operations bring together information.  When information is correlated, it can be more efficiently used if the geometry of pooling regions matches the correlations so that it can be brought together more efficiently.  Shallow networks without layers of localized pooling lack this mechanism to combine correlated information efficiently.

The theoretical results are focused on convolutional arithmetic circuits, building on prior theoretical results of the authors.  The results make use of the interesting technical notion of separability, which in some sense measures the degree to which a function can be represented as the composition of independent functions.  Because separability is measured relative to a partition of the input, it is an appropriate mechanism for measuring the complexity of functions relative to a particular geometry of pooling operations.  Many of the technical notions are pretty intuitive, although the tensor analysis is pretty terse and not easy to follow without knowledge of the authors’ prior work.

In some sense the comparison between deep and shallow networks is somewhat misleading, since the shallow networks lack a hierarchical pooling structure.  For example, a shallow convolutional network with RELU and max pooling does not really make sense, since the max occurs over the whole image.  So it seems that the paper is really more of an analysis of the effect of pooling vs. not having pooling.  For example, it is not clear that a deep CNN without pooling would be any more efficient than a shallow network, from this work.

It is not clear how much the theoretical results depend on the use of a model with product pooling, and how they might be extended to the more common max pooling.  Even if theoretical results are difficult to derive in this case, simple illustrative examples might be helpful.  In fact, if the authors prepare a longer version of the paper for a journal I think the results could be made more intuitive if they could add a simple toy example of a function that can be efficiently represented with a convolutional arithmetic circuit when the pooling structure fits the correlations, and perhaps showing also how this could be represented with a convolutional network with RELU and max pooling.

I would also appreciate a more explicit discussion of how the depth of a deep network affects the separability of functions that can be represented.  A shallow network doesn’t have local pooling, so the difference between deep and shallow if perhaps mostly one of pooling vs. not pooling.  However, practitioners find that very deep networks seem to be more effective than “deep” networks with only a few convolutional layers and pooling.  The paper does not explicitly discuss whether their results provide insight into this behavior.

Overall, I think that the paper attacks an important problem in an interesting way.  It is not so convincing that this really gets to the heart of why depth is so important, because of the theoretical limitation to arithmetic circuits, and because the comparison is to shallow networks that are without localized pooling.

Overall, this is a interesting paper that presents a new way of training hierarchical multiscale recurrent neural networks. The model presented in the paper is very flexible and can discover the hierarchical structure of the input sequence from data, without any additional information. A limitation of the approach is that the model was not fully Bayesian, which might be important for addressing some of the hyperparameter tuning issues. Another weakness is that the model did not perform well on some of the experiments. For example, on character-level language modelling the baseline model was very close to the best model generated by the proposed model and on handwriting sequence generation the model did not outperform the baseline. I believe that these results could be further improved by designing a more sophisticated hierarchical multiscale model that makes more use of the Bayesian framework and also makes the model more flexible to learn the parameters with the right values. I have some concerns about consistency of the training procedure and how the model was evaluated on the test set. The paper “Hierarchical Multiscale Recurrent Neural Networks” by Xin He and Lawrencecue Lim addresses the problem of learning both hierarchical and temporal representation has been among the long-standing challenges of recurrent neural networks. Multiscale recurrent neural networks have been considered as a promising approach to resolve this issue. In this paper, the authors propose a novel multiscale approach, called the hierarchical multiscale recurrent neural network, that can capture the latent hierarchical structure in the sequence by encoding the temporal dependencies with different timescales using a novel update mechanism. We show some evidence that the proposed model can discover underlying hierarchical structure in the sequences without using explicit boundary information. We evaluate our proposed model on character-level language modelling and handwriting sequence generation. We feel that this is an interesting attempt to address the long-standing challenge of learning both hierarchical and temporal representation, and the proposed model might be a promising approach to address this issue. However, there are several issues that need to be considered before we fully understand its potential and limitations. For example, (1) in order to discover the latent hierarchical structure in the sequence, the model needs to capture temporal dependencies across multiple timescales, however, the proposed model only learns to encode the high-level temporal dependencies and the temporal dependencies with different timescales is not aware of each other; (2) the model needs to define the distance between each hierarchical levels, however, this can be subjective and thus the discovered hierarchy can be arbitrary; (3) the effectiveness of the learning algorithm needs to be demonstrated. We look forward to seeing more work that applies this approach to addressing the problem of learning both hierarchical and temporal representation and further studies on these issues. Overall, this is an interesting attempt to address the long-standing challenge of learning both hierarchical and temporal representation, and the proposed model might be a promising approach to address this issue. However, there are several issues that need to be considered before we fully understand its potential and limitations. Best, Rui affidav This paper explores how to learn sparse graphical models via deep learning. Sparse graphical models, also known as partial correlation or前 50625821109562111 1349661663264659416891772562390253580238026136982353751713982353753346898471398235375334689847 restricted correlation, are a set of assumptions about the independence between variables of a probability distribution. That is, graphical models imply conditional independence. Sparse graphical models further assume a subset of the variables are conditionally independent given the rest. Learning such models has been shown to be useful in performing optimal inference and Bayesian learning. The main bottleneck for previous methods to learn such models has been the computational cost. We introduce an efficient algorithm based on Bethe MCMC sampling that scales to large problems.
