This paper describes modern deep learning approach to the problem of predicting the medications taken by a patient during a period of time based solely upon the sequence of ICD-9 codes assigned to the patient during that same time period. This problem is formulated as a multilabel sequence classification (in contrast to language modeling, which is multiclass classification). They propose to use standard LSTM and GRU architectures with embedding layers to handle the sparse categorical inputs, similar to that described in related work by Choi, et al. In experiments using a cohort of ~610K patient records, they find that RNN models outperform strong baselines including an MLP and a random forest, as well as a common sense baseline. The differences in performance between the recurrent models and the MLP appear to be large enough to be significant, given the size of the test set.

Strengths:
- Very important problem. As the authors point out, two the value propositions of EHRs -- which have been widely adopted throughout the US due to a combination of legislation and billions of dollars in incentives from the federal government -- included more accurate records and fewer medication mistakes. These two benefits have largely failed to materialize. This seems like a major opportunity for data mining and machine learning.
- Paper is well-written with lucid introduction and motivation, thorough discussion of related work, clear description of experiments and metrics, and interesting qualitative analysis of results.
- Empirical results are solid with a strong win for RNNs over convincing baselines. This is in contrast to some recent related papers, including Lipton & Kale et al, ICLR 2016, where the gap between the RNN and MLP was relatively small, and Choi et al, MLHC 2016, which omitted many obvious baselines.
- Discussion is thorough and thoughtful. The authors are right about the kidney code embedding results: this is a very promising result.

Weaknesses:
- The authors make several unintuitive decisions related to data preprocessing and experimental design, foremost among them the choice NOT to use full patient sequences but instead only truncated patient sequences that each ends at randomly chosen time point. This does not necessarily invalidate their results, but it is somewhat unnatural and the explanation is difficult to follow, reducing the paper's potential impact. It is also reduces the RNN's potential advantage.
- The chosen metrics seem appropriate, but non-experts may have trouble interpreting the absolute and relative performances (beyond the superficial, e.g., RNN score 0.01 more than NN!). The authors should invest some space in explaining (1) what level of performance -- for each metric -- would be necessary for the model to be useful in a real clinical setting and (2) whether the gaps between the various models are "significant" (even in an informal sense).
- The paper proposes nothing novel in terms of methods, which is a serious weakness for a methods conference like ICLR. I think it is strong enough empirically (and sufficiently interesting in application) to warrant acceptance regardless, but there may be things the authors can do to make it more competitive. For example, one potential hypothesis is that higher capacity models are more prone to overfitting noisy targets. Is there some way to investigate this, perhaps by looking at the kinds of errors each model makes?

I have a final comment: as a piece of clinical work, the paper has a huge weakness: the lack of ground truth labels for missing medications. Models are both trained and tested on data with noisy labels. For training, the authors are right that this shouldn't be a huge problem, provided the label noise is random (even class conditional isn't too big of a problem). For testing, though, this seems like it could skew metrics. Further, the assumption that the label noise is not systemic seems very unlikely given that these data are recorded by human clinicians. The cases shown in Appendix C lend some credence to this assertion: for Case 1, 7/26 actual medications received probabilities < 0.5. My hunch is that clinical reviewers would view the paper with great skepticism. The authors will need to get creative about evaluation -- or invest a lot of time/money in labeling data -- to really prove that this works.

For what it is worth, I hope that this paper is accepted as I think it will be of great interest to the ICLR community. However, I am borderline about whether I'd be willing to fight for its acceptance. If the authors can address the reviewers' critiques -- and in particular, dive into the question of overfitting the imperfect labels and provide some insights -- I might be willing to raise my score and lobby for acceptance.

This is a well-conducted and well-written study on the prediction of medication from diagnostic codes. The authors compared GRUs, LSTMs, feed-forward networks and random forests (making a case for why random forests should be used, instead of SVMs) and analysed the predictions and embeddings.

The authors also did address the questions of the reviewers.

My only negative point is that this work might be more relevant for a data science or medical venue rather than at ICLR.

This paper applies RNNs to predict medications from billing costs. While this paper does not have technical novelty, it is well done and well organized. It demonstrates a creative use of recent models in a very important domain, and I think many people in our community are interested and inspired by well-done applications that branch to socially important domains. Moreover, I think an advantage to accepting it at ICLR is that it gives our "expert" stamp of approval -- I see a lot of questionable / badly applied / antiquated machine learning methods in domain conferences, so I think it would be helpful for those domains to have examples of application papers that are considered sound.

This is a well written, organized, and presented paper that I enjoyed reading.  I commend the authors on their attention to the narrative and the explanations.  While it did not present any new methodology or architecture, it instead addressed an important application of predicting the medications a patient is using, given the record of billing codes.  The dataset they use is impressive and useful and, frankly, more interesting than the typical toy datasets in machine learning.  That said, the investigation of those results was not as deep as I thought it should have been in an empirical/applications paper.  Despite their focus on the application, I was encouraged to see the authors use cutting edge choices (eg Keras, adadelta, etc) in their architecture.  A few points of criticism:

-The numerical results are in my view too brief.  Fig 4 is anecdotal, Fig 5 is essentially a negative result (tSNE is only in some places interpretable), so that leaves Table 1.  I recognize there is only one dataset, but this does not offer a vast amount of empirical evidence and analysis that one might expect out of a paper with no major algorithmic/theoretical advances.  To be clear I don't think this is disqualifying or deeply concerning; I simply found it a bit underwhelming.

- To be constructive, re the results I would recommend removing Fig 5 and replacing that with some more meaningful analysis of performance.  I found Fig 5 to be mostly uninformative, other than as a negative result, which I think can be stated in a sentence rather than in a large figure.

- There is a bit of jargon used and expertise required that may not be familiar to the typical ICLR reader.  I saw that another reviewer suggested perhaps ICLR is not the right venue for this work.  While I certainly see the reviewer's point that a medical or healthcare venue may be more suitable, I do want to cast my vote of keeping this paper here... our community benefits from more thoughtful and in depth applications. Instead I think this can be addressed by tightening up those points of jargon and making the results more easy to evaluate by an ICLR reader (that is, as it stands now researchers without medical experience have to take your results after Table 1 on faith, rather than getting to apply their well-trained quantitative eye). 

Overall, a nice paper.

In light of the detailed author responses and further updates to the manuscript, I am raising my score to an 8 and reiterating my support for this paper. I think it will be among the strongest non-traditional applied deep learning work at ICLR and will receive a great deal of interest and attention from attendees.

This paper describes modern deep learning approach to the problem of predicting the medications taken by a patient during a period of time based solely upon the sequence of ICD-9 codes assigned to the patient during that same time period. This problem is formulated as a multilabel sequence classification (in contrast to language modeling, which is multiclass classification). They propose to use standard LSTM and GRU architectures with embedding layers to handle the sparse categorical inputs, similar to that described in related work by Choi, et al. In experiments using a cohort of ~610K patient records, they find that RNN models outperform strong baselines including an MLP and a random forest, as well as a common sense baseline. The differences in performance between the recurrent models and the MLP appear to be large enough to be significant, given the size of the test set.

Strengths:
- Very important problem. As the authors point out, two the value propositions of EHRs -- which have been widely adopted throughout the US due to a combination of legislation and billions of dollars in incentives from the federal government -- included more accurate records and fewer medication mistakes. These two benefits have largely failed to materialize. This seems like a major opportunity for data mining and machine learning.
- Paper is well-written with lucid introduction and motivation, thorough discussion of related work, clear description of experiments and metrics, and interesting qualitative analysis of results.
- Empirical results are solid with a strong win for RNNs over convincing baselines. This is in contrast to some recent related papers, including Lipton & Kale et al, ICLR 2016, where the gap between the RNN and MLP was relatively small, and Choi et al, MLHC 2016, which omitted many obvious baselines.
- Discussion is thorough and thoughtful. The authors are right about the kidney code embedding results: this is a very promising result.

Weaknesses:
- The authors make several unintuitive decisions related to data preprocessing and experimental design, foremost among them the choice NOT to use full patient sequences but instead only truncated patient sequences that each ends at randomly chosen time point. This does not necessarily invalidate their results, but it is somewhat unnatural and the explanation is difficult to follow, reducing the paper's potential impact. It is also reduces the RNN's potential advantage.
- The chosen metrics seem appropriate, but non-experts may have trouble interpreting the absolute and relative performances (beyond the superficial, e.g., RNN score 0.01 more than NN!). The authors should invest some space in explaining (1) what level of performance -- for each metric -- would be necessary for the model to be useful in a real clinical setting and (2) whether the gaps between the various models are "significant" (even in an informal sense).

This paper presents a novel framework for semi-supervised classification using graph convolutional networks. Specifically, the paper explores the use of side information that is naturally represented as a graph (such as clustering, tree structure, or any other type of derived graph), in order to promote clustering of instances into separate classes, and propose a method to exploit this information in the form of a graph convolutional network. The proposed method can be used in two modes: (1) an original mode in which the labeled and unlabeled instances both follow the input graph, and (2) a transductive mode in which the labeled instances follow the input graph but the unlabeled instances are assumed to be unlabeled during training. The proposed method is evaluated on several benchmark datasets, and state-of-the-art results are reported on several tasks, both in the original and the transductive modes. arrovement highlights First, the paper explores a new application of GCNs, which have been shown to be very effective in learning node representations, to graph-based data. This is an orthogonal approach to most current methods for semi-supervised learning with GNNs which rely on messages & talker identities. Secondly, the authors evaluate the proposed method on 3 standard tasks: classification, clustering, and node classification. The results show that the method yields state-of-the-art results on all 3 tasks. Third, the paper describes the potential applicability of the method to multiple modes, both the original and the transductive modes. Fourth, the paper describes in detail the design choices and the experiments conducted to validate those choices. Fifth, the paper includes an in-depth analysis of the method on several benchmark datasets. Sixth, the method is very easy to use, with source code provided and users from several domains, including Semantic Web, AI, and Statistics, showing promising results on their own datasets.

Therefore, this paper is an ideal reference for those who are interested in this field. Based on my knowledge, there are some minor errors in the following content: 1. The first sentence of the first paragraph of the Introduction may attract some readers who are not interested in the field of Graph Learning. Although it introduces the basic idea of graph convolution, it is not specific for this field. 2. On the second paragraph of the Introduction, "Note that the spatial domain can be regarded as a 1D graph" may not be an intuitive explanation for someone who has never heard of graph neural networks. "Spatial" here does not mean a 1D graph, but rather an abstract concept of a physical space in which "graphs" can represent relationships between different objects. For example, two people can be connected by an edge in an interaction graph. This paper only defines the concept of "graph structure" on a function approximation level rather than a deep learning framework level. 3. The first paragraph of the "Related Work" refers to a recent academic paper on this topic. The paper needs to be cited with the full name. The author may consider citing the paper [1] by Naman Agarwal et al. However, this paper only introduces the background and framework of graph neural networks. The above two papers [1, 2] are the most similar to this work. Therefore, I would like to recommend that the author updates this part based on the above two papers. 4. The last sentence of the first paragraph of the "Related Work" implies that this work is based on [2]. However, this work only takes into account of the local graph structure. In other words, it is a localized first-order approximation of spectral graph convolutions. 5. In the fifth paragraph of the "Why not use CNN for graph-structured data?" section, the sentence "This could help us to solve a large number of real-world problems" may give readers the wrong impression. Many researchers around the world have been attempting to use CNN to solve real-world problems. For example, Shakhnarovich has published more than 20 papers on various types of graphs or graph-based representation learning and mining, and his name has appeared in the academic papers related to many famous graph algorithms. This paragraph should be cited as a reference to better explain this point. 6. The second paragraph of the "Why not use the CNN for graph-structured data?" section does not discuss the disadvantages of the application of CNN to graph-structured data. As a matter of fact, the "overparameterization issue" is the biggest challenge to using a generic graph convolved approximation. 7. The last paragraph of the "Why not use the CNN for graph-structured data?" section uses "significantly" three times. Please simplify it. 8. The last sentence of the fifth paragraph of the "Why not use the CNN for graph-structured data?" section is confusing. Based on my limited understanding of [3], the maxout network is not a graph convolutional network. 9. In the fifth paragraph of the "A simple extension" section, the sentence "For each triplet (o, p, n) a learnable kernel *K* ~1~,..., *K* ~9~..." may confuse readers. I think this sentence has no technical meaning. For example, *K* ~1~ is a kernel? I think it is better to write "For each triplet (s, p, n), a kernel *K* ~1~,..., *K* ~9~...". 10. It may be better to write "The outputs of these nodes define the filtering degree of different areas." 11. In this paper, the author proposed a new architecture for graph convolutional networks which are based on first-order approximation of spectral graph convolutions. The model was tested and compared with related methods on different datasets, which showed that this approach performed better than the existing methods. The paper is interesting and well-presented, however, there are a few things that the author could have mentioned or elaborated more. For example, it is mentioned that the method was tested on citation networks and on a knowledge graph, but the type of the two datasets are not revealed, which are some details that the author could have mentioned more. Another thing that the author could have mentioned more is that this approach is a new version of GCN and this approach is based on first-order approximation of spectral graph convolutions. implementation details: The implementation details are also a part of the method, for example, the approach is tested on a 8layer graph convolutional network and the model is trained on a single GeForce GTX 1080 Ti GPU, it is hard to know whether the approach is efficient. refers Semi-Supervised Classification with Graph Convolutional Networks INGHERITANCE OF GRAPH CONV CONVOLUTIONS In this paper, we present a convolutional architecture for graph convolutional networks (GCNs) that are based on a localized first-order approximation of spectral graph convolutions. We show that this approach learns node representations which encode both local graph structure and features of nodes. As such, we introduce a new variant of GCN that we call graph conv convolutions (GCCNs) and apply it to a number of different tasks on various datasets. In particular, we demonstrate that our approach not only scales linearly in the number of graph edges, but also learns hidden layer representations that encode both local graph structure and features of nodes. As such, GCCNs represent a family of efficiently learnable, scalable and general graph neural networks.
human_text:
This paper proposes the graph convolutional networks, motivated from approximating graph convolutions.  In one propagation step, what the model does can be simplified as, first linearly transform the node representations for each node, and then multiply the transformed node representations with the normalized affinity matrix (with self-connections added), and then pass through nonlinearity.

This model is used for semi-supervised learning on graphs, and in the experiments it demonstrated quite impressive results compared to other baselines, outperforming them by a significant margin.  The evaluation of propagation model is also interesting, where different variants of the model and design decisions are evaluated and compared.

It is surprising that such a simple model works so much better than all the baselines.  Considering that the model used is just a two-layer model in most experiments, this is really surprising as a two-layer model is very local, and the output of a node can only be affected by nodes in a 2-hop neighborhood, and no longer range interactions can play any roles in this.  Since computation is quite efficient (sec. 6.3), I wonder if adding more layers helped anything or not.

Even though motivated from graph convolutions, when simplified as the paper suggests, the operations the model does are quite simple.  Compared to Duvenaud et al. 2015 and Li et al. 2016, the proposed method is simpler and does almost strictly less things.  So how would the proposed GCN compare against these methods?

Overall I think this model is simple, but the connection to graph convolutions is interesting, and the experiment results are quite good.  There are a few questions that still remain, but I feel this paper can be accepted.
The reviewers are in agreement that this paper is well written and constitutes a solid contribution to graph-based semi-supervised learning based on variants of CNNs.

Dear Reviewers,

Thanks a lot for reviewing our paper and for your valuable comments. 

To incorporate your feedback, we have uploaded a revision of our paper with the following changes:

1) We have added the Iterative Classification Algorithm (ICA) from Lu & Getoor (2003) as a baseline as suggested by Reviewer 2. Thanks a lot for pointing out the references on iterative classification. ICA is indeed a powerful baseline that we have not considered previously and it compares favorably against some of the other baselines. We have put the code to reproduce the ICA baseline experiments on Github:

The paper develops a simple and reasonable algorithm for graph node prediction/classification. The formulations are very intuitive and lead to a simple CNN based training and can easily leverage existing GPU speedups. 

Experiments are thorough and compare with many reasonable baselines on large and real benchmark datasets. Although, I am not quite aware of the literature on other methods and there may be similar alternatives as link and node prediction is an old problem. I still think the approach is quite simple and reasonably supported by good evaluations.

The paper introduces a method for semi-supervised learning in graphs that exploits the spectral structure of the graph in a convolutional NN implementation. The proposed algorithm has a limited complexity and it is shown to scale well on a large dataset. The comparison with baselines on different datasets show a clear jump of performance with the proposed method.

The paper is technically fine and clear, the algorithm seems to scale well, and the results on the different datasets compare very favorably with the different baselines. The algorithm is simple and training seems easy. Concerning the originality, the proposed algorithm is a simple adaptation of graph convolutional networks (ref Defferrard 2016 in the paper) to a semi-supervised transductive setting. This is clearly mentioned in the paper, but the authors could better highlight the differences and novelty wrt this reference paper. Also, there is no comparison with the family of iterative classifiers, which usually compare favorably, both in performance and training time, with regularization based approaches, although they are mostly used in inductive settings. Below are some references for this family of methods.

The authors mention that more complex filters could be learned by stacking layers but they limit their architecture to one hidden layer. They should comment on the interest of using more layers for graph classification.

863.

machine_text: Overall the paper is well-written, and the methodology makes sense. However, I have a few suggestions for the author to consider. The problem statement/title doesn't match the main hypothesis of the paper. The problem is stated as: "Dropout mitigates the problem of exploding gradients in deep learning, but with the observation that common practice of removing dropout after a few iterations may be too aggressive." However, in the rest of the paper, the author is trying to solve a more general problem of infilling the missing dropout locations in training data. It's not a problem with exploding gradients. In the problem statement, it's missing some important details. For example, it doesn't mention if the problem is specific to fully-connected layers or if it can also happen for other layers. It may be useful to include those details in the problem statement, and then the author can exclude them from the hypotheses. The rationale for expecting linear regularization is not clear. The author mentions "Because the expected value of a Gaussian random variable is 0, we expect the mean-field regularization to yield a solution with zero mean". I assume they mean the expected loss, but it needs to be clarified. Also, the conclusion is based on a toy example. It would be more solid if we can show this for a more complex model (e.g. denoising autoencoder). There are some typos in the equations of Section 3 and Figures 1, 2. Overall this is a good candidate for a paper for XXX conference.

This paper looks at the problem of how to effectively regularize a neural network that has a large number of parameters but only a few of which are relevant to the prediction task at hand. The authors propose an additional term in the objective function which depends on the expected value of the gradient of the loss function with respect to the parameters, times a penalty constant. They argue that this term promotes solutions with sparser parameter vectors when evaluated using the L1 norm. They provide several empirical results to demonstrate the efficacy of this approach on the standard CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets. They also discuss the relationship between their approach and other recent works on regularizing neural networks. implementation and contributions The main contribution of this paper is the development of an effective approach for regularizing neural networks that has sparse solutions. The authors propose to add an additional term to the objective function that rewards the sparser the solution, and at the same time does not significantly increase the computational cost of training the model. The additional term in the objective function is the penalty for having a large number of parameters in the network, times the expected value of the gradient of the loss function with respect to the parameters. The proposed method has been tested on the CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets and it is shown to be more effective at learning sparse models than state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, the proposed method can be combined with other regularization techniques to further reduce the number of parameters in the network.

This paper puts forward a not entirely new, but also not sufficiently understood interpretation of dropout regularization. The authors derive useful theorems that estimate or put bounds on key quantities that are of interest when analyzing dropout regularized networks from their perspective. They furthermore introduce an explicit regularization term that should have a well understood impact on these key quantities. In the experimental section they convincingly show that the proposed regularization indeed has the expected effect and that their perspective on dropout is therefore useful and meaningful.

Their proposed regularization also seems to have a positive impact on the models performance but they demonstrate this only on rel. small scale benchmark problems. I therefore don’t belief that this approach will have a large impact on how practitioner train models.  But their general perspective is well aligned with the recently proposed idea of “Dropout as a bayesian approximation” and the insights and theorems in this paper might enable future work in that direction.

This paper presents a theoretical underpinning of dropout, and uses this derivation to both characterize its properties and to extend the method. A solid contribution. I am surprised that none of the reviewers mentioned that this work is closely related to the uncited 2015 paper "Variational Dropout and the Local Reparameterization Trick" by Diederik P. Kingma, Tim Salimans, Max Welling.

We made the following revisions:

1. We switched the section 6.3 and 6.4 to make the paper more clear.

2. We added the definition of MC dropout on page 8.

3. We fixed all the typos in the three reviewers' comments.

summary

The paper explains dropout with a latent variable model where the dropout variable (0 or 1 depending on which units should be dropped) is not observed and is accordingly marginalised. Maximum likelihood under this model is not tractable but standard dropout then corresponds to a simple Monte Carlo approximation of ML for this model.

The paper then introduces a theoretical framework for analysing the discrepancy (called inference gap) between the model at training (model ensemble, or here the latent variable model), and the model at testing (where usually what should be an expectation over the activations over many models becomes the activation of one model with averaged weights).
This framework introduces several notions (e.g. expectation linearity) which allow the study of which transition functions (and more generally layers) can have a small inference gap. Theorem 3 gives a bound on the inference gap.

Finally a new regularisation term is introduced to account for minimisation of the inference gap during learning.

Experiments are performed on MNIST, CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 and show that the method has the potential to perform better than standard dropout and at the level of Monte Carlo Dropout (the standard method to compute the real dropout outputs consistently with the training assumption of an ensemble, of course quite expensive computationally)


The study gives a very interesting theoretical model for dropout as a latent variable model where standard dropout is then a monte carlo approximation. This is very probably widely applicable to further studies of dropout.

The framework for the study of the inference gap is interesting although maybe somewhat less widely applicable.

The proposed model is convincing although 1. it is tested on simple datasets 2. the gains are relatively small and 3. there is an increased computational cost during training because a new hyper-parameter is introduced.

machine_text: Generally, I quite like this paper. The problem it addresses is important and the content is presented in a clear and understandable format. I have a few suggestions for improvement though. 1) The learning procedure is often framed as learning how to draw samples from a distribution, which I think is overstating it. The real learning problem is actually learning to draw samples that approximate a distribution with a certain property (e.gв™ accurate samples from a multivariate normal distribution). The specific approximation used here is that the samples satisfy a set of linear constraints. 2) The authors use AIF as a surrogate objective, but the surrogate loss is never properly tied to the training procedure. In particular, the AIF approximation used at each iteration is never shown to be improving over time. It would be useful if this convergence proof were provided. 3) The authors note that even though this method works well on GANs with discrete latent variables, it could potentially over-parameterize the problem and hurt performance on generative models with continuous latents. Can the method be adapted to continuous latents? 4) It would be helpful if the code for the sample model were made available so that other researchers could easily try this approach on other models, or on other datasets. All in all, this is an excellent paper with a few minor comments. I strongly encourage the authors to accept this feedback and update the manuscript to incorporate these suggestions. I recommend for the first point to emphasize that you are only drawing samples that approximate a distribution with a set of linear constraints, and not the exact distribution. The second point makes it clear that the AIF approximation is improving over time. The third point can be addressed by changing the definition of the AIF approximation so that it is independent from the generator parameters (i.e., using sampling) The fourth point can be addressed by releasing code for the generator and the sample model (see footnote 1) The final comment about trying the approach on other datasets can also be addressed by releasing code for the sample model. The main takeaway is that this paper presents an important problem and demonstrates a useful approach to solving it, that can be readily applied to many other problems. I recommend publishing this work as is, with a few modifications mentioned above. Note 1 - With regards to the release of code, the sample model is learned on a per-batch basis, so for each model version, the code for one epoch of training on the validation set has to be made publicly available. The entire training dataset itself is not publicly available because it contains images that the model has never seen before, and that would be distressing for the model. But the code to generate a validation sample is public, and that is sufficient for any reproduction.

The paper titled Learning to Draw Samples: With Application to Amortized MLE for Generative Adversarial Learning describes a method of sampling data that can be used for a variety of applications. This method is a generalization of the DiscoverPattern algorithm, originally developed by the authors in a similar context but improved here by implementing an algorithm that allows for amortized optimization. The method is general and can be used to sample from a wide range of distributions, but for concreteness is applied to the problem of amortized Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) in Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). This is important because understanding MLE, even for simplified models like GANs, is an important step in using these models in practice and therefore this represents a useful contribution. The method is interesting because it allows for easy generation of new examples while maintaining the ability to estimate the true density of data in some sense, and the algorithm converges quickly to a good solution. The paper has a number of strengths. First, the authors establish some mathematical notation and describe the general idea in a clear and accessible way. This is important because it will be useful for others who may want to apply this to other problems. Second, they give an intuitive motivation for the algorithm and its major components. This makes it easy to understand what is going on and why. Third, they implement the algorithm and conduct experiments showing that it works well in practice. This is a strength because it provides evidence that this algorithm should be used with care, but also that it could be useful in practice. However, the paper also has some weaknesses. First, the context and motivation for the problem are not very clear. This is an abstract method and for it to be useful a clearer explanation is needed of what it is for and why it is difficult to achieve the goals by other methods. In particular, the connection to GANs and why this problem needs to be solved in general is not clear. In some way it appears that the problem is only related to GANs because that is the application of the MLE algorithm. In this case, it would be clearer to start with a broader set of applications and then specialize the method after applying it to that problem. Second, the convergence of the algorithm and empirical results are only sufficiently shown, without explanations of why they are good or bad. This limits the strength of the paper. Overall, this is a clear and useful contribution, but needs improvement to be more broadly applicable and convincing.

This paper is interesting and has a good potential to deliver. The proposed method is related to the amortized MLE which is a very interesting topic in its own right. The contribution is very significant as it is the first paper that attempts to optimize a neural sampler by an amortized MLE framework. The algorithm presented is practical in the sense that it only uses the normal output of the network as the training signal and in the experiments they show that it is possible to train a neural sampler using only one gradient calculation. The experiments also demonstrate the applicability of the method to image generation tasks. ing and concerns The main issue with this work is that the authors did not prove that the algorithm converges. The proof of convergence for their proposed algorithm is nontrivial and needs to be explored. The other issues relate to the choice of the proposed method as the paper only focuses on the application to image generation and the proposed method can also be used for other applications. For instance, a simple version of this method could be used for training variational autoencoder, where one can use the normal output of the autoencoder as the training signal. investigation First of all, I want to congratulate the authors for their impressive amout of work! The paper is very well written, and the method is very interesting. I have a couple of minor concerns about the paper. First, the authors only mentioned that the method is able to train a neural sampler using only one gradient calculation. But from my understanding, this is only possible because the MSE loss is used, which is the same as regularization. In fact, this implies that there is no exploration/exploitation problem during the training, and therefore there is no guarantee that the sampler can be trained to approximate the target distribution. The convergence of the method then becomes an open question. This analysis is based on my understanding from the description in the paper, and I may have misunderstood something. But I think there needs to be a discussion on the applicability of this method to others tasks, such as am MLE or guaranteeing the convergence of the method. To sum up, although the method proposed in this paper has its advantages in some application scenarios, I think the authors should address the following questions: 1. Can the authors show that the algorithm will converge? 2. What limitations does the proposed method have in terms of the application? My suggestion is to remove the statements that the method can be applied to any MLE problem and only focus on the application to the case of image generation for now. And the conclusion can be adjusted after addressing these concerns.

The Learning to Draw Samples: With Application to Amortized MLE for Generative Adversarial Learning answers the question how to train stochastic neural networks to draw samples from given targets. The method proposed in the paper is generally applicable for any black-box model, with strong performance in image generation. The paper has the following merits: (1) The method is general and easy to implement. It only requires a small change on the output layer, which is the most operation part of a neural network model. (2) The samples generated are realistic and could be printed on paper. (3) The theory behind the method is also detailed. In particular, the proof of convergence relies on Stein’s lemma, a powerful method to compute the gradient of divergence. The main limitation of this method is that it only handles discrete outputs. Meanwhile, the computational cost of this method is expensive because it needs to solve a dual problem. Overall, this method is generally applicable and gives state-of-the-art performance in image generation. The proposed method in this paper solves the following problem. Assume we have a neural network $f_\theta(\mathbf{x})$, where $\theta$ denotes the weight parameters, and the data is denoted as $\mathcal{D}$. We are given the target distribution $p_T(\mathbf{x})$, but we do not have the its normalizer. Thus, we can not directly compute the likelihood of the data. Instead, we can compute the cross entropy between the actual distribution and $p_T(\mathbf{x})$, which is related to the log-probability of the data. So our goal is to optimize the neural network so that the output changes along a direction to increase the likelihood of the data. This direction is the Stein variational gradient, which can be computed based on Stein’s lemma. The main steps are as follows. 1. Compute the unnormalized density of the target $p_T(x)$ and compute the cross entropy with the actual distribution. 2. Apply the ReWeight technique to transform the cross entropy into a normalized form. 3. Compute the Stein variational gradient based on Stein’s lemma. 4. Update the network parameters by minimizing the corresponding dual objective function. Overall, the theory behind this method is well motivated and the implementation is not difficult. Some questions arise from this method: (1) Is this method guaranteed to converge to a local minimum? (2) What kind of applications can this method be applied to? (3) Can this method be extended to continuous outputs case? These are interesting questions, and we leave it as a promising future work. Some examples of using this method for training deep energy models are provided in the paper. Theoretically, this method can be applied to train other neural networks for different tasks.
human_text:
This paper considers the energy-based model interpretation of GAN, where the discriminator is an unnormalized model for the likelihood of a generative model p(x|theta) and the generator is a directed model that approximates this distribution. The generator is used to draw approximate negative phase samples that are used in stochastic maximum likelihood / contrastive divergence learning of the EBM / discriminator.

The main idea in the paper is to fit the generator by following the Stein variational gradient. In practice this gradient consists of the usual gradient provided by the discriminator with an added term that provides a repulsive force between the sampled data points to increase sample diversity.

The idea of using a kernel to push apart the sampled points is interesting, and will work in low dimensions, but it is hard to see how it can work in full scale images. For high dimensional samples x, the proposed kernel is unlikely to provide a useful distance measure between points. There are no convincing experiments in the paper that show otherwise. Specifically:

- There is no experiment that compares between standard GAN and GAN + repulsion, using the same architecture. (please address this in the rebuttal)
- If the Stein variational idea is taken literally, the right thing to do would be to fully optimize the generator at every step, and then taking a single optimization step on the discriminator. Instead, each is updated in turn, and the learning rates of both steps are adjusted to keep the two "in line".
- The kernel used to fit the generator is defined in the auto-encoder space of the discriminator, and thus depends on the discriminator parameters. The objective that is used to fit the generator thus changes at every step, and the procedure can no longer be interpreted as stochastic gradient descent with respect to any single well defined objective.

The authors obtain good results: The generated images clearly look better than those generated by DCGAN. However, their approach has a number of changes compared to DCGAN, so it is not clear where the improvement comes from. In addition, by now the DCGAN is no longer a very strong baseline, as various other techniques have been proposed.

Note: The use of phi for both the "particle gradient direction" and energy function is confusing

This paper presents an idea with a sensible core (augmenting amortized inference with per-instance optimization) but with an overcomplicated and ad-hoc execution. The reviewers provided clear guidance for how this paper could be improved, and thus I invite the authors to submit this paper to the workshop track.

We highly appreciate the time and feedback from all the reviewers, all of which we will take into serious consideration in our revision. We will particularly strengthen and clarify the empirical experiments. Below we address some of the major points: 

[Testing Accuracy Score]
We agree with the reviewers' point on the "testing accuracy" score, but think that it still provides some valuable insight about the dataset. Its blindness to the background can be a good thing in that it captures more information about the "effective amount" of objects the dataset contains.  The problem is that it is very difficult to obtain a *perfect* score, and reporting more than one metrics (in an objective fashion) can help to gain more comprehensive understandings. 

[Repulsive Term in High Dimension]
Our repulsive force works due to two tricks: 1) scaling the bandwidth with the data diversity using the median trick, which alleviates the exponential decay of RBF kernel. 2) define kernel on the feature space instead of the raw pixels of the images, which allows us to respect the manifold structure of the images. The framework of SVGD allows us to use any positive definite kernels and change it adaptively during iterations, because the kernel only defines the "tangent space" for improvement. 

SteinGAN without kernel corresponds to Viterbi training of the energy model and we find it work well with careful tuning of parameters, but tend to converge to a small number of bad-looking images after running a large number of iterations; adding the kernel under the same setting helps prevent this problem. Our current results on CIFAR10 shows that SteinGAN without kernel gives an inception score of 6.34, while that SteinGAN with kernel gives 6.76. 

[Amortized is slower than non-amortized]
Although the amortized algorithm has the overhead of updating $\xi$, it stores the information in a generative network, and allows us to simulate as many images as we need. By using the one-step gradient update we proposed, the update of $\xi$ is the same as standard backpropagation except replacing the Dlogp with the SVGD gradient.

This paper proposes an amortized version of the Stein variational gradient descent (SVGD) method in which "a neural network is trained to mimic the SVGD dynamics". It applies the method to generative adversarial training to yield a training procedure where the discriminator is interpreted as an energy-based probabilistic model.

One criticism I have of the presentation is that a lot of time and energy is spent setting the table for a method which is claimed to be widely applicable, and the scope of the empirical evaluation is narrowed down to a single specific setting. In my view, either the paper falls short of its goal of showing how widely applicable the proposed method is, or it spends too much time setting the table for SteinGAN and not enough time evaluating it.

The consequence of this is that the empirical results are insufficient in justifying the approach proposed by the paper. As another reviewer pointed out, DCGAN is becoming outdated as a benchmark for comparison.

Qualitatively, SteinGAN samples don't look significantly better than DCGAN samples, except for the CelebA dataset. In that particular case, the DCGAN samples don't appear to be the ones presented in the original paper; where do they come from?

Quantitatively, DCGAN beats SteinGAN by a small margin for the ImageNet Inception Score and SteinGAN beats DCGAN by an even smaller margin for the CIFAR10 Inception Score. Also, in my opinion, the "testing accuracy" score is not a convincing evaluation metric: while it is true that it measures the amount of information captured in the simulated image sets, it is only sensitive to information useful for the discrimination task, not for the more general modeling task. For instance, this score is likely completely blind to information present in the background of the image.

Because of the reasons outlined above, I don't think the paper is ready for publication at ICLR.

The authors propose amortized SVGD, an amortized form of prior work on SVGD, which is a particle variational method that maximally decreases the KL divergence at each update. "amortized SVGD" is done by training a neural network to learn this dynamic. They then apply this idea to train energy-based models, which admit a tractable unnormalized density.

In SVGD, the main difference from just MAP is the addition of a "repulsive force" that prevents degeneracy by encouraging probability mass to be spread to locations outside the mode. How this is able to still act as a strong enough entropy-like term in high dimensions is curious. From my understanding of their previous work, this was not a problem as the only experiments were on toy and UCI data sets.

In the experimental results here, they apply the kernel on the hidden representation of an autoencoder, which seems key, similar to Li et al. (2015) where their kernel approach for MMD would not work as well otherwise. However, unlike Li et al. (2015) the autoencoder is part of the model itself and not fixed. This breaks much of the authors' proposed motivation and criticisms of prior work, if they must autoencode onto some low-dimensional space (putting most effort then on the autoencoder, which changes per iteration) before then applying their method.

Unlike previous literature which uses inference networks, their amortized SVGD approach seems in fact slower than the non-amortized approach. This is because they must make the actual update on xi before then regressing to perform the update on eta (in previous approaches, this would be like having to perform local inferences before then updating inference network parameters, or at least partially performing the local inference). This seems quite costly during training.

I recommend the paper be rejected, and that the authors provide more comprehensive experimental results, expecially around the influence of the autoencoder, the incremental updates versus full updates, and the training time of amortized vs non-amortized approaches. The current results are promising but unclear why given the many knobs that the authors are playing with.

The main idea in the paper is to fit the generator by following the Stein variational gradient. In practice this gradient consists of the usual gradient provided by the discriminator with an added term that provides a repulsive force between the sampled data points to increase sample diversity.

The idea of using a kernel to push apart the sampled points is interesting, and will work in low dimensions, but it is hard to see how it can work in full scale images. For high dimensional samples x, the proposed kernel is unlikely to provide a useful distance measure between points. There are no convincing experiments in the paper that show otherwise. Specifically:

- There is no experiment that compares between standard GAN and GAN + repulsion, using the same architecture. (please address this in the rebuttal)
- If the Stein variational idea is taken literally, the right thing to do would be to fully optimize the generator at every step, and then taking a single optimization step on the discriminator. Instead, each is updated in turn, and the learning rates of both steps are adjusted to keep the two "in line".
- The kernel used to fit the generator is defined in the auto-encoder space of the discriminator, and thus depends on the discriminator parameters. The objective that is used to fit the generator thus changes at every step, and the procedure can no longer be interpreted as stochastic gradient descent with respect to any single well defined objective.

The authors obtain good results: The generated images clearly look better than those generated by DCGAN. However, their approach has a number of changes compared to DCGAN, so it is not clear where the improvement comes from. In addition, by now the DCGAN is no longer a very strong baseline, as various other techniques have been proposed.

This paper presents an idea with a sensible core (augmenting amortized inference with per-instance optimization) but with an overcomplicated and ad-hoc execution. The reviewers provided clear guidance for how this paper could be improved, and thus I invite the authors to submit this paper to the workshop track.

We highly appreciate the time and feedback from all the reviewers, all of which we will take into serious consideration in our revision. We will particularly strengthen and clarify the empirical experiments. Below we address some of the major points: 

[Testing Accuracy Score]
We agree with the reviewers' point on the "testing accuracy" score, but think that it still provides some valuable insight about the dataset. Its blindness to the background can be a good thing in that it captures more information about the "effective amount" of objects the dataset contains.  The problem is that it is very difficult to obtain a *perfect* score, and reporting more than one metrics (in an objective fashion) can help to gain more comprehensive understandings. 

[Repulsive Term in High Dimension]
Our repulsive force works due to two tricks: 1) scaling the bandwidth with the data diversity using the median trick, which alleviates the exponential decay of RBF kernel. 2) define kernel on the feature space instead of the raw pixels of the images, which allows us to respect the manifold structure of the images. The framework of SVGD allows us to use any positive definite kernels and change it adaptively during iterations, because the kernel only defines the "tangent space" for improvement. 

SteinGAN without kernel corresponds to Viterbi training of the energy model and we find it work well with careful tuning of parameters, but tend to converge to a small number of bad-looking images after running a large number of iterations; adding the kernel under the same setting helps prevent this problem. Our current results on CIFAR10 shows that SteinGAN without kernel gives an inception score of 6.34, while that SteinGAN with kernel gives 6.76. 

[Amortized is slower than non-amortized]
Although the amortized algorithm has the overhead of updating $\xi$, it stores the information in a generative network, and allows us to simulate as many images as we need. By using the one-step gradient update we proposed, the update of $\xi$ is the same as standard backpropagation except replacing the Dlogp with the SVGD gradient.

This paper proposes an amortized version of the Stein variational gradient descent (SVGD) method in which "a neural network is trained to mimic the SVGD dynamics". It applies the method to generative adversarial training to yield a training procedure where the discriminator is interpreted as an energy-based probabilistic model.

One criticism I have of the presentation is that a lot of time and energy is spent setting the table for a method which is claimed to be widely applicable, and the scope of the empirical evaluation is narrowed down to a single specific setting. In my view, either the paper falls short of its goal of showing how widely applicable the proposed method is, or it spends too much time setting the table for SteinGAN and not enough time evaluating it.

The consequence of this is that the empirical results are insufficient in justifying the approach proposed by the paper. As another reviewer pointed out, DCGAN is becoming outdated as a benchmark for comparison.

Qualitatively, SteinGAN samples don't look significantly better than DCGAN samples, except for the CelebA dataset. In that particular case, the DCGAN samples don't appear to be the ones presented in the original paper; where do they come from?

Quantitatively, DCGAN beats SteinGAN by a small margin for the ImageNet Inception Score and SteinGAN beats DCGAN by an even smaller margin for the CIFAR10 Inception Score. Also, in my opinion, the "testing accuracy" score is not a convincing evaluation metric: while it is true that it measures the amount of information captured in the simulated image sets, it is only sensitive to information useful for the discrimination task, not for the more general modeling task. For instance, this score is likely completely blind to information present in the background of the image.

Because of the reasons outlined above, I don't think the paper is ready for publication at ICLR.

The authors propose amortized SVGD, an amortized form of prior work on SVGD, which is a particle variational method that maximally decreases the KL divergence at each update. "amortized SVGD" is done by training a neural network to learn this dynamic. They then apply this idea to train energy-based models, which admit a tractable unnormalized density.

In SVGD, the main difference from just MAP is the addition of a "repulsive force" that prevents degeneracy by encouraging probability mass to be spread to locations outside the mode. How this is able to still act as a strong enough entropy-like term in high dimensions is curious. From my understanding of their previous work, this was not a problem as the only experiments were on toy and UCI data sets.

In the experimental results here, they apply the kernel on the hidden representation of an autoencoder, which seems key, similar to Li et al. (2015) where their kernel approach for MMD would not work as well otherwise. However, unlike Li et al. (2015) the autoencoder is part of the model itself and not fixed. This breaks much of the authors' proposed motivation and criticisms of prior work, if they must autoencode onto some low-dimensional space (putting most effort then on the autoencoder, which changes per iteration) before then applying their method.

Unlike previous literature which uses inference networks, their amortized SVGD approach seems in fact slower than the non-amortized approach. This is because they must make the actual update on xi before then regressing to perform the update on eta (in previous approaches, this would be like having to perform local inferences before then updating inference network parameters, or at least partially performing the local inference). This seems quite costly during training.

I recommend the paper be rejected, and that the authors provide more comprehensive experimental results, expecially around the influence of the autoencoder, the incremental updates versus full updates, and the training time of amortized vs non-amortized approaches. The current results are promising but unclear why given the many knobs that the authors are playing with.

The authors describe an exploration of trace functions and recurrence in Deep Q-Networks (DQN). The exploration uses information from previously saved states in a trained DQN and uses this to determine likely causes of previously seen behavior and classify new observations. The work is interesting for a number of reasons. First, it provides an analysis that can potentially be applied to previously saved states in a trained DQN to help understand the cause of previously observed behavior. Second, it provides a definition of trace functions that may be of use in developing new representation for exploration of latent space in other DRL methods. The study is performed on a toy problem, but the theoretical basis and implementation are of interest to the RL community more generally. There are some limitations to the approach, for example the definition of traces is only applicable to the problem studied and the identification of likely causes is rather qualitative. Nevertheless, the paper is of interest to the broader community and the approach is amenable to extension and application to other problems in the future. Quantitative problem: determining likely causes of previously seen behavior Qualitative problem: identification of likely causes Theoretical basis: definition of traces Implementation: applied to a toy problem Limitations: identification of likely causes is rather qualitative, the approach can be applied to other problems but with some modification to the theoretical basis and implementation The authors address a valuable problem. The definition of recurrence and traces could be useful in furthering our understanding of how DRL agents learn and could provide an approach to addressing the qualitative problem of identifying likely causes of previously seen behavior.

Eligibility traces in reinforcement learning are used as a bias-variance trade-off and can often speed up training time by propagating knowledge back over time-steps in a single update. We illustrate the benefits of both recurrent nets and eligibility traces in some Atari games, and highlight also the importance of the optimization used in the training. Overall, this is an interesting study, showing the effectiveness of recurrent networks with eligibility traces in several Atari games, and the impact of the optimization technique. However, it is not always clearly explained how the optimization technique was different between training runs. It would be useful to describe in more detail the differences between the different experiments and how those differences impact the training. Also, it would be useful to mention in more details how the eligibility traces help the agent to play the games, for example by having a look at the updates of specific parameters during training or providing additional training images with the trace on or off. It would be useful to show the traces also in some of the training runs to give the reader an impression of how they evolve over time. Additionally, there are some grammar issues and typos that should be corrected before being published. Overall, this is an interesting study, showing the benefits of recurrent networks with eligibility traces in several Atari games, and the impact of the optimization technique. However, there are still some issues that could be improved to provide a more clear description of the results and how they were achieved. We gratefully acknowledge this work and all contributors. The main contribution of this paper is investigating the use of recurrent networks in addition to the standard Q-learning algorithm in the Atari domain. Instead of using a simple feed forward neural network, we use a gated recurrent unit (GRU) network to explore the benefits of using recurrent networks in this domain. We also discuss the importance of using optimal update rules for the recurrent networks, and how this can also speed up training time. One major problem with the Q-learning algorithm in the Atari domain is the slow time-step update, which is achieved by using an eligibility trace that propagates knowledge back over time-steps in a single update. We show that recurrent networks in combination with the standard Q-learning algorithm can achieve the same effect, without the need to use an eligibility trace. This simplifies the implementation and the training process. We also discuss the choice of recurrent architecture and optimization method. The most efficient recurrent architecture, the GRU, is not very different than a standard feed forward neural network. We also show that LSTM cells are needed to capture long term dependencies in the game. Using an asynchronous algorithm to update the recurrent network layers is crucial for efficiently training the network. Finally, we show the performance difference between standard Q-learning, and using the GRU and an asynchronous algorithm to update recurrent networks, in several Atari games. On some games the recurrent network with asynchronous updates clearly outperforms the standard Q-learning algorithm. On other games, the difference is smaller or not significant at all.
human_text:
This paper investigates the use of eligibility traces with recurrent DQN agents. As in other recent work on deep RL, the forward view of Sutton and Barto is used to make eligibility traces practical to use with neural networks. Experiments on the Atari games Pong and Tennis show that traces work better than standard Q-learning.

The paper is well written and the use of traces in deep RL is indeed underexplored, but the experiments in the paper are too limited and do not answer the most interesting questions.

As pointed out in the questions, n-step returns have been shown to work better than 1-step returns both in the classical RL literature and more recently with deep networks. [1] shows that using n-step returns in the forward view with neural networks leads to big improvements on both Atari and TORCS. Their n-step Q-learning method also combines returns of different length in expectation, while traces do this explicitly. This paper does not compare traces with n-step returns and simply shows that traces used in the forward view help on two Atari games. This is not a very significant result. It would be much more interesting to see whether traces improve on what is already known to work well with neural networks.

The other claimed contribution of the paper is showing the strong effect of optimization. As with traces, I find it hard to make any conclusions from experiments on two games with fixed hyperparameter settings. This has already been demonstrated with much more thorough experiments in other papers. One could argue that these experiments show that importance of hyperparameter values and not of the optimization algorithm itself. Without tuning the optimization hyperparameters it's hard to claim anything about the relative merits of the methods.

[1] "Asynchronous Methods for Deep Reinforcement Learning", ICML 2016.

The reviewers agree that the paper is clear and well-written, but all reviewers raised significant concerns about the novelty of the work, since the proposed algorithm is a combination of well-known techniques in reinforcement learning. It is worth noting that the use of eligibility traces is not very heavily explored in the deep reinforcement learning literature, but since the contribution is primarily empirical rather than conceptual and algorithmic, there is a high bar for the rigorousness of the experiments. The reviewers generally did not find the evaluation to be compelling enough in this regard. Based on this evaluation, the paper is not ready for publication.

This paper combines DRQN with eligibility traces, and also experiment with the Adam optimizer for optimizing the q-network. This direction is worth exploring, and the experiments demonstrate the benefit from using eligibility traces and Adam on two Atari games. The methods themselves are not novel. Thus, the primary contributions are (1) applying eligibility traces and Adam to DRQN and (2) the experimental evaluation. The paper is well-written and easy to understand.

The experiments provide quantitative results and detailed qualitative intuition for how and why the methods perform as they do. However, with only two Atari games in the results, it is difficult to tell how well it the method would perform more generally. Showing results on several more games and/or other domains would significantly improve the paper. Showing error bars from multiple random seeds would also improve the paper.

The paper presents a deep RL with eligibility traces. The authors combine DRQN with eligibility traces for improved training. The new algorithm is evaluated on a two problems, with a single set of hyper-parameters, and compared with DQN.

The topic is very interesting. Adding eligibility traces to RL updates is not novel, but this family of the algorithms have not been explored for deep RL. The paper is written clearly, and the related literature is well-covered. More experiments would make this promising paper much stronger. As this is an investigative, experimental paper, it is crucial for it to contain a wider range of problems, different hyper-parameter settings, and comparison with vanilla DRQN, Deepmind's DQN implementation, as well as other state of the art methods.

machine_text: Authors should provide explanations on how the L2 regularizer was applied to the norm of the weight matrix as well as the value of the regularizer coefficient, beyond a single constant regularizer coefficient. Authors should also include a more detailed explanation of the Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss surface. pter The paper presents an empirical analysis of the loss surfaces of deep networks trained for semantic segmentation on the Cityscapes dataset. The analysis is performed with the L2 regularizer applied to the norm of the weight matrix as well as with a single constant regularizer coefficient. The paper also reports on the MSE loss surface. ight! credit L2 regularizer was applied to the norm of the weight matrix as well as with a single constant regularizer coefficient mael L2 regularizer was applied to the norm of the weight matrix as well as with a single constant regularizer coefficient meantime, Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss was reported chair The MSE loss surface is affected by a local minimum at the origin and a second local minimum at a different location portion MSE loss is not suitable for measuring the distance between two pixel-wise related vectors, of which one is expected to be translated to the other (e.g. translated image: wrong label, wrong image: correct label). The paper suggests this distance is measured via a distance metric, e.g. the MSE loss. However, the MSE loss can be viewed as a basic approximation of the first order derivative of the Translation Error Functional. A good distance metric should be positive defined, symmetric, and should lead to the minimization of the Translation Error Functional. Therefore, the MSE loss is not the best distance metric to be used in the context of semantic segmentation.

This paper examines the loss surfaces of modern deep networks, and characterizes their stability and saddle points. The loss surfaces of neural networks are often perceived as challenging to analyze, but the analysis in this paper is quite elegant. The loss surfaces are characterized as consisting of local minima, saddle points, and global minima. The paper also introduces a practical procedure for avoiding saddle points. This is important because according to the second-order critical point theory, local minima are unstable, while saddles and global minima are stable. Thus, the practical impact of this work is that deep networks can be optimized by first-order methods without worrying about saddle points. layout Next, the paper examines the loss surfaces of two popular activation functions, ReLU and tanh. They prove that the second-order critical points of ReLU correspond to local minima. However, for tanh, it is not clear if the second-order critical points are local minima or saddles. To study this, they use analytical techniques from geometric optimization and study the Hessian of the second-order critical points of tanh. They show that the Hessian of the second-order critical points of tanh has one negative eigenvalue and two positive eigenvalues. Thus, the second-order critical points of tanh are saddle points with one negative and two positive eigenvalues. Next, the paper applies the same techniques to analyze the loss surfaces of ResNet and DenseNet. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion of the limitations of their technique and future work.

This paper provides an empirical analysis of loss surfaces for state-of-the-art neural networks. Specifically, the paper studies the loss functions for ResNet, DenseNet, and Wide & Deep Network. The main idea is to visualize the loss surfaces through different visualization methods and summarize the loss surface characteristics. The main results are as following. (1) Loss surfaces are complicated and irregular: most of the time the loss surface is not single-valley and there are many peaks and deep valleys. (2) The loss surfaces have many similar local minima, which makes the search for the global minimum difficult. (3) The number of oscillation is large. (4) The loss functions on the left side of a valley are much higher than that on the right side of a valley. The main contributions of this paper are: - It provides a new perspective to understand the loss surfaces of deep neural networks. - It summarizes the loss surface characteristics on ResNet, DenseNet, and Wide & Deep Networks. - It visualizes the loss surfaces using a polygon visualization method. This paper can be seen as a first step to better understand the loss surface of neural networks, and there are many interesting issues to be further studied. For example, the loss surface is correlated with the generalization performance of the model.
