Here are answers to some common questions the authors have been asked about the current work in the past by readers of the manuscript. We hope these will help clarify any other questions our reviewers/readers might have.

Q: Why doesn't the paper present numerical comparision to state-of-the-art/recent pruning techniques?

A: Under certain motivational assumptions, it is understandable to demand benchmarking comparisons against state-of-the-art methods, but this may be missing the fundamental purpose of the present research. Our investigation is intended less to propose a competing alternative to existing pruning techniques and more to shed light on the limitations of generally accepted approaches to pruning and the degree to which increased numbers of parameters affect learning representations in neural networks. The paper does talk about most, if not all popoular pruning techniques out there. In fact, we examined the literature for numerical methods to approximate the importance of network elements, and the widely-cited 1st & 2nd order techniques proposed by Mozer, LeCun, Hassibi, Stork, et al. provided our initial inspiration. This is the jumping off point for our research in terms of key insights.

Q: The idea of using Taylor series approximations seems interesting but not really effective.

A: It is not effective when used as a pruning technique but it is VERY effective to test out the effectiveness of existing pruning techniques, which is what we do here. We have mentioned it multiple times in the paper that the motivation behind this work is NOT to propose a new pruning technique that will outperform all other techniques out there but to tap into learning representations to see how effective our established techniques are when seen from the perspective of representations. The Taylor series approximations play an important role here. A lot of pruning techniques out there use 2nd Order error gradients and assume that using them is the most effective way to prune networks. We have conclusively proved using the Taylor series that this is very much not the case. Our results with the brute-force method show us that there is a much larger extent to which networks can be pruned. This makes for a great starting-off point for future research to find methods that can produce similar results.

Q: Why did you decide in favor of sigmoid activation functions instead of something more recent and more popular like ReLUs? 

A: As mentioned above, the main contribution of this work is to demonstrate the feasibility of pruning entire neurons from trained networks, and offer novel insight on learning representations. We use Taylor methods to approximate the results achieved by the brute-force method but this is not an ideal solution to the problem, as we discuss. The 2nd order approximation technique will not work for ReLU networks because ReLUs do not have a 2nd derivative, unless we use the soft-plus function as a continuous approximation. Furthermore, due to the fact that we are approximating the error surface of a network element with respect to the output using a parabola, if there is no useful parabola to approximate this relationship, then the method breaks down. The derivatives of the activation function are simply parameters of the Taylor series. It doesn’t cease to be a parabolic approximation or become more effective if we use a different doubly-differentiable activation function. 

Q: Why carry out your experiments on the MNIST dataset and not go for a larger and more practical image dataset?

A: All experiments were necessarily carried out on optimally trained networks (not counting Section 4.5, which specifically examines non-optimally trained networks), so there is no way to improve them. We derived the algorithm assuming the well-studied sigmoid activation function. Furthermore, the MNIST dataset is a de-facto standard for demonstrating the potential of new techniques. A different dataset, task, activation function, or network architecture will not change the trends we see in the results but could make the results less interpretable. 

Q: The best setting is Iterative Re-ranking with Brute Force removal which is too expensive.

A: The brute-force method is highly parallelizable, so time complexity is not necessarily a deal-breaker. Our focus is the proof of concept, and we intend to investigate potential speedups in future work. Also, since pruning is anyways a single step carried out after the training process is over (which usually takes orders of magnitude more time), this is potentially acceptable.

My main concern is that this is primarily a tool/IDE implementation paper and not a user experience paper. The user experience of playing an SNES game in the Retro Learning Environment (REL) is not well discussed or explored. The goal of this research was to demonstrate how an open-source emulator can be used in the REL to allow students to experience SNES games in the context of the REL. Although this is an interesting direction for future work, I think there is value in exploring the actual gameplay experience. How did the emulator perform? Did the students enjoy the experience? I really enjoyed this paper, which is about playing the Super Nintendo (SNES) in the Retro Learning Environment (REL). The SNES is a very iconic gaming system, and in this case, the REL is specifically tailored to host SNES games. This allows for a really authentic retro gaming experience, complete with sprites and other retro graphics. The REL is also an open source project, which I think is really interesting. It allows for the creation of new and exotic games, potentially even games exclusive to the SNES hardware! SNES games are also organized in unique binary formats. This is a huge problem if you are attempting to play obscure or rare games, as it’s very unlikely that you will have the appropriate software to load these files. The paper proposes a simple solution to this problem. First, it suggests that you use a decompression tool to convert the SNES.ZIP files to plain text files. Then, you can use regular text-based archive tools to browse the list of available games. The main downside of this solution is the computational cost of decompression and archive extraction. This will slow down the playing of the SNES, and this is particularly problematic on the Nintendo Switch, where modern applications are often given a higher priority than older games. accuplyning a high-performance computing environment on a single host to play games from the SNES library is not trivial. The SNES uses custom graphics hardware that is not readily ported to current generation hardware. The CPU was also not designed for gaming, and in fact, contains special instruction to speed up scrolling on certain screen updates. Finally, the SNES game cartridges are not compressed. Text-based archive tools are used to access the games, but decompressing the games and reading the raw ROM content is very slow.

Mastering a video game requires skill, tactics and strategy. While these attributes may be acquired naturally by human players, teaching them to a computer program is a far more challenging task. In recent years, extensive research was carriedout in the field of reinforcement learning and numerous algorithms were introduced, aiming to learn how to perform human tasks such as playing video games. As a result, the Arcade Learning Environment (ALE) (Bellemare et al., 2013) has become a commonly used benchmark environment allowing algorithms to train on various Atari 2600 games. In many games the state-of-the-art algorithms outperform humans. In this paper we introduce a new learning environment, the Retro Learning Environment — RLE, that can run games on the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES), Sega Genesis and several other gaming consoles. The environment is expandable, allowing for more video games and consoles to be easily added to the environment, while maintaining the same interface as ALE. Moreover, RLE is compatible with Python and Torch. SNES games pose a significant challenge to current algorithms due to their higher level of complexity and versatility. In this paper, a new SNES game, 'SNES Game Dev' by Te Papa museum is used as a running example. Firstly, the retro learning environment (RLE) is introduced. RLE is a framework which consists of several components. The first component is the Game Controller which defines the communication interface between the environment and the games. The second is the Game Repository which is a database of pre-defined games and the instructions on how to play them. The third is the Gameplay Bench which is a simulator which runs on the server and simulates the gameplay from a users' specified starting position. The players' interaction with the game is sent to the server and then replayed by the simulator. The last two components are the Gameplay Recorder and the Player Models which run the recording and the players, respectively. The recorded data is then analysed by the trainer model to generate the updates and provide the feedback to the player. RLE is compatible with Python and Torch. Torch is an open-source framework developed by the artificial intelligence group at Université de Montreal and has recently gained popularity for playing the game of Go. However, RLE is not limited to SNES games, it can be used to train players to any SNES games that have pre-defined instructions on how to play them. The RLE is evaluated by playing the 'SNES Game Dev'. The recorded gameplay is then analysed by the trainer model to generate the updates. The updates are sent to the players and then replayed by the player models. The algorithmic improvement is analysed by comparing the improvement of the players with different levels of skill. The paper presents a new environment, called Retro Learning Environment (RLE), for reinforcement learning. The authors focus on Super Nintendo but claim that the interface supports many others (including ALE). Benchmark results are given for standard algorithms in 5 new Super Nintendo games, and some results using a new "rivalry metric".

These environments (or, more generally, standardized evaluation methods like public data sets, competitions, etc.) have a long history of improving the quality of AI and machine learning research. One example in the past few years was the Atari Learning Environment (ALE) which has now turned into a standard benchmark for comparison of algorithms and results. In this sense, the RLE could be a worthy contribution to the field by encouraging new challenging domains for research.

That said, the main focus of this paper is presenting this new framework and showcasing the importance of new challenging domains. The results of experiments themselves are for existing algorithms. There are some new results that show reward shaping and policy shaping (having a bias toward going right in Super Mario) help during learning. And, yes, domain knowledge helps, but this is obvious. The rivalry training is an interesting idea, when training against a different opponent, the learner overfits to that opponent and forgets to play against the in-game AI; but then oddly, it gets evaluated on how well it does against the in-game AI! 

Also the part of the paper that describes the scientific results (especially the rivalry training) is less polished, so this is disappointing. In the end, I'm not very excited about this paper.

I was hoping for a more significant scientific contribution to accompany in this new environment. The authors present a new set of environments, similar to ALE but based on Super Nintendo rather than Atari. This paper introduces a new reinforcement learning environment called « The Retro Learning Environment”, that interfaces with the open-source LibRetro API to offer access to various emulators and associated games (i.e. similar to the Atari 2600 Arcade Learning Environment, but more generic). The first supported platform is the SNES, with 5 games (more consoles and games may be added later). Authors argue that SNES games pose more challenges than Atari’s (due to more complex graphics, AI and game mechanics). Several DQN variants are evaluated in experiments, and it is also proposed to compare learning algorihms by letting them compete against each other in multiplayer games.

I like the idea of going toward more complex games than those found on Atari 2600, and having an environment where new consoles and games can easily be added sounds promising. With OpenAI Universe and DeepMind Lab that just came out, though, I am not sure we really need another one right now. Especially since using ROMs of emulated games we do not own is technically illegal: it looks like this did not cause too much trouble for Atari but it might start raising eyebrows if the community moves to more advanced and recent games, especially some Nintendo still makes money from.

Besides the introduction of the environment, it is good to have DQN benchmarks on five games, but this does not add a lot of value. The authors also mention as contribution "A new benchmarking technique, allowing algorithms to compete against each other, rather than playing against the in-game AI", but this seems a bit exaggerated to me: the idea of pitting AIs against each other has been at the core of many AI competitions for decades, so it is hardly something new. The finding that reinforcement learning algorithms tend to specialize to their opponent is also not particular surprising.

Overall I believe this is an ok paper but I do not feel it brings enough to the table for a major conference. This does not mean, however, that this new environment won't find a spot in the (now somewhat crowded) space of game-playing frameworks.

Other small comments:
- There are lots of typos (way too many to mention them all)
- It is said that Infinite Mario "still serves as a benchmark platform", however as far as I know it had to be shutdown due to Nintendo not being too happy about it
- "RLE requires an emulator and a computer version of the console game (ROM file) upon initialization rather than a ROM file only. The emulators are provided with RLE" => how is that different from ALE that requires the emulator Stella which is also provided with ALE?
- Why is there no DQN / DDDQN result on Super Mario?
- It is not clear if Figure 2 displays the F-Zero results using reward shaping or not
- The Du et al reference seems incomplete

This paper presents a valuable new collection of video game benchmarks, in an extendable framework, and establishes initial baselines on a few of them.

Reward structures: for how many of the possible games have you implemented the means to extract scores and incremental reward structures? From the github repo it looks like about 10 -- do you plan to add more, and when?

“rivalry” training: this is one of the weaker components of the paper, and it should probably be emphasised less. On this topic, there is a vast body of (uncited) multi-agent literature, it is a well-studied problem setup (more so than RL itself). To avoid controversy, I would recommend not claiming any novel contribution on the topic (I don’t think that you really invented “a new method to train an agent by enabling it to train against several opponents” nor “a new benchmarking technique for agents evaluation, by enabling them to compete against each other, rather than playing against the in-game AI”). Instead, just explain that you have established single-agent and multi-agent baselines for your new benchmark suite.

Your definition of Q-function (“predicts the score at the end of the game given the current state and selected action”) is incorrect. It should read something like: it estimates the cumulative discounted reward that can be obtained from state s, starting with action a (and then following a certain policy).

Minor:
* Eq (1): the Q-net inside the max() is the target network, with different parameters theta’
* the Du et al. reference is missing the year
* some of the other references should point at the corresponding published papers instead of the arxiv versions

This paper addresses the problem of optimizing the objective function in a Riemannian manifold, in this case, the Space of Binary Matrices. The main contribution is the use of the Polak-Ribiere conjugate method for optimization on the manifold, which reduces the problem to one involving matrices. The authors formulate the optimization problem as minimizing the squared Euclidean distance between the predicted and target matrices, and establish the equivalence to a problem involving the log determinant of the matrix square. The latter is solved using the adjoint method, which yields the Polak-Ribiere update. The derived algorithm is applied to the L1 norm regularized optimization of the Skip-Gram Negative Sampling objective. The authors evaluate the method on three language modeling tasks: CoNLL 2003, WMT 2014, and TAC KBP 2017. The results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms the state of the art on these tasks. adem The main contribution of this paper is the application of the Polak-Ribiere conjugate method to optimize the L1 regularized L2-norm of the matrix square. The method is applied to the Negative Sampling objective in the Skip-Gram model for sequence modeling. The method outperforms the state of the art on the CoNLL 2003 and WMT 2014 tasks, and is comparable on the TAC KBP 2017 task. The main challenge in applying the method is the lack of first-order gradient information. To address this, the authors use the Stiefel Manifold and compute the first-order approximation by the Jacobian of the square of the matrix. Another challenge is the evaluation of the trace of the product of two matrices. To address this, the authors resort to the approximation given by the quadrature rule.

It can be shown that optimizing for SGNS objective can be viewed as an optimization problem of searching for a good matrix with the low-rank constraint. The most standard way to solve this type of problems is to apply Riemannian optimization framework to optimize the SGNS objective over the manifold of required low-rank matrices. The application of complex factorization method such as SVD to the word similarity calculation cost a lot of time. The SPP algorithm solved this problem efficiently, but it only works when the corpus is symmetric, so some scholars developed SPPMI to solve the problem that the corpus is not symmetric. In the process of solving, if the optimization process is stopped before reaching the local optimum, the obtained solution will lose some of the global optimal properties. In this paper, we propose a new way to solve the optimization of Skip-gram model by using Riemannian optimization, which can achieve both the objective optimization and the low rank constraint. The algorithm is compared with several baselines and experimental results show that the proposed method is the best on optimizing the SGNS objective on the word similarity dataset. The theoretical connection to Riemannian optimization is nice though, and it might be useful for understanding related methods in the future.
The paper is mostly clearly written. The observation made in the paper that word-embedding models based on optimizing skip-gram negative sampling objective function can be formulated as a low-rank matrix estimation problem, and solved using manifold optimization techniques, is sound. However, this observation by itself is not new and has come up in various other contexts such as matrix completion. As such the reviewers do not see sufficient novelty in the algorithmic aspects of the paper, and empirical evaluation on the specific problem of learning word embeddings does not show striking enough gains relative to standard SGD methods. The authors are encouraged to explore complimentary algorithmic angles and benefits that their approach provides for this specific class of applications.
The paper considers Grassmannian SGD to optimize the skip gram negative sampling (SGNS) objective for learning better word embeddings. It is not clear why the proposed optimization approach has any advantage over the existing vanilla SGD-based approach - neither approach comes with theoretical guarantees - the empirical comparisons show marginal improvements. Furthermore, the key idea here - that of projector splitting algorithm - has been applied on numerous occasions to machine learning problems - see references by Vandereycken on matrix completion and by Sepulchre on matrix factorization. 

The computational cost of the two approaches is not carefully discussed. For instance, how expensive is the SVD in (7)? One can always perform an efficient low-rank update to the SVD - therefore, a rank one update requires O(nd) operations. What is the computational cost of each iteration of the proposed approach?

You are claiming that your model outperforms previous approaches that directly optimizes over (W, C). But since the end result (the factors) is the same, can the authors provide some intuition and justification why the proposed method works better?

Did you try to multiply the factors W and C from other optimizers and then factorize the product using the method in section 2.3, and use the new W for your downstream tasks? I am not sure if this would cause much difference in the performance.

Overall, I think it is always interesting to apply advanced optimization techniques to machine learning problems. The current paper would be stronger from the machine learning perspective, if more thorough comparison and discussion (as mentioned above) are provided. On the other hand, my expertise is not in NLP and I leave it to other reviewers to decide the significance in experimental results.

machine_text: Dear reviewer, This is in-depth investigation on Classless Network Architecture (CNA), implemented using Neural Networks and used for domain specific applications like DDoS etc. The CNA is proven to be scalable, flexible and robust, addressing the scalability issues faced by previous proposed solutions. The performance evaluation conducted shows that CNA provides considerable improvement in terms of efficiency, storage overhead, execution time, distortion and network visibility. The analysis carried out in the paper is precise and well explained. The conclusion drawn in the paper is well suited to the content presented and the analysis is well justified. I recommend this paper for indexing in major conferences with similar scope. ings Pleased to submit my review for "Classless Association using Neural Networks". This paper is an analysis of CNA, a recently proposed solution to scale IPv4 ACLs, for use in application specific security protocols like DDoS. The analysis is presented through a rigorous technical discussion, supported by a comprehensive benchmarking conducted on real-world large scale network traces. The concluding remarks are well presented and motivate future work for application in the security space. The analysis performed in the paper is precise and well explained. I have a few suggestions for the paper to make it more solid. 1) Expanded discussion on limitations of using DDoS as a use case. DDoS is a popular choice for security evaluations and its wider use case and adoption by the ecosystem would provide a more comprehensive evaluation of the proposed solution. 2) The impact of aggregation, a design decision taken in CNA, has not been discussed. Considering the wide adoption of aggregation in network security solutions, the analysis should have taken its effect into account as well. 3) A few places the word "Classful" is used without explanation. "Classful" is a term associated withhistorical addressing schemes like IPv4 and this could be discussed to provide a wider perspective on the analysis conducted. All in all, I do think this is a well-written and interesting analysis of CNA and consider it for indexing in major conferences.

Classless ANNs can have many uses, but one place where this system shines is in security. This technique takes in inputs like hashes, certificates, and likely other things and outputs a trust score for how likely it is that a transaction should be valid. This is extremely valuable for decentralized applications, where there is no central authority to trust, and maintaining that trust is expensive and error prone. This system can save huge sums of money in these scenarios. The strength of this model is that it can learn patterns that humans cannot, such as differences between hash functions, that humans do not understand. Another way to say this is that this model can learn arbitrary 451 levels of understanding, versus 10 for humans. The weakness of this model is that it only works for single use cases, i.e. if you give this model a certificate it cannot learn that it is invalid, nor can it learn how to mix certificates together to invalidate all security analysis. Also, like all machine learning, this model can be fooled with sufficiently high volume and bad samples. This is a very important problem, and one that I don't believe has a good solution yet. Overall, I recommend this paper, because while the weakness is substantial, the model has applicability in other areas and could be modified to solve the broader problem of arbitrary trust certification. If nothing else, I'm glad they explored this approach, as it might inspire others to work on the harder problem of trustworthy machine learning in general.

The goal of this paper is to train a model based on the relation between two instances that represent the same unknown class. This scenario is inspired by the Symbol Grounding Problem and the association learning in infants. We propose a novel model called Classless Association. It has two parallel Multilayer Perceptrons (MLP) that uses one network as a target of the other network, and vice versa. In addition, the presented model is trained based on an EM-approach, in which the output vectors are matched against a statistical distribution. We generate four classless datasets based on MNIST, where the input is two different instances of the same digit. In addition, the digits have a uniform distribution. Our classless association model is evaluated against two scenarios: totally supervised and totally unsupervised. In the first scenario, our model reaches a good performance in terms of accuracy and the classless constraint. In the second scenario, our model reaches better results against two clustering algorithms. I think the presented model could be of interest to the community, given its potential in classless association. However, I recommend the authors to address the following limitations: 1- The presented model has some important hyperparameters that need to be tuned. For instance, the temperature in the te choice of t distribution is quite high. 2- The generated datasets have the limitation of having a small number of samples. 3- The evaluation has the limitation of using two simple clustering algorithms and not a more difficult clustering algorithm from the clustering community.

This paper attempts to solve the Symbol Grounding Problem using neural networks. This problem is inspired by the development of a baby's vision, where they learn to discriminate between different objects by observing patterns of pixels on a screen. The training procedure of this model called Classless Association uses an EM algorithm to match output vectors to a statistical distribution of the input values. The association between two input vectors is modeled by two parallel MLP's, in which one MLP acts as a target of the other MLP, and vice versa. The model was tested on two classes of digit data, MNIST, and the model performed well in both totally supervised and totally unsupervised scenarios. Here are the paper's main strengths: 1- The model was tested on two classes of digit data, MNIST, and the model performed well in both totally supervised and totally unsupervised scenarios. 2- The proposed model is simple and consists of a few lines of code. 3- The model is fast to train and have an acceptable convergence speed. Here are the paper's main weaknesses: 1- The model definition is not fully detailed. 2- The training dataset is generated based on uniform distributions, which are not realistic. 3- The model validation is performed against two comparison scenarios, which are not that diverse and complex. Overall, this model is an interesting approach to symbol grounding problem, but more studies and analysis is needed in order to bring this model to the industry.

The paper explores neural-network learning on pairs of samples that are labeled as either similar or dissimilar. The proposed model appears to be different from standard siamese architectures, but it is poorly motivated. The experimental evaluation of the proposed model is very limited.

We have updated our paper.  The changes are
* We have improved the clarity and motivation of our model
* We have evaluated our model to three more classless datasets (Rotated-90 MNIST, Inverted MNIST, and Random Rotation MNIST).
* We have updated Figure 4 and 5 for showing some random output classification samples instead of the mean of all images.
* We have added two more examples and demo as supplemental material

The paper presents an alternative way of supervising the training of neural network without explicitly using labels when only link/not-link information is available between pairs of examples. A pair of network is trained each of which is used to supervise the other one.


The presentation of the paper is not very clear, the writing can be improved.
Some design choice are not explained: Why is the power function used in the E-step for approximating the distribution (section 2.1)? Why do the authors only consider a uniform distribution? I understand that using a different prior breaks the assumption that nothing is known about the classes. However I do not see a practical situations where the proposed setting/work would be useful.  

Also, there exist a large body of work in semi-supervised learning with co-training based on a similar idea. 

Overall, I think this work should be clarified and improved to be a good fit for this venue.

The paper explores a new technique for classless association, a milder unsupervised learning where we do not know the class labels exactly, but we have a prior about the examples that belong to the same class. Authors proposed a two stream architecture with two neural networks, as streams process examples from the same class simultaneously. Both streams rely on the target (pseudo classes or cluster indices) of each other, and the outputs an intermediate representation z, which is forced to match with a statistical distribution (uniform in their case). The model is trained with EM where the E step obtains the current statistical distribution given output vectors z, and M step updates the weights of the architecture given z and pseudo-classes. Experimental results on re-organized MNIST exhibits better performance compared to classical clustering algorithms (in terms of association accuracy and purity). The authors further provide comparison against a supervised method, where proposed architecture expectedly performs worse but with promising results.

The basic motivation of the architecture apparently relies on unlabeled data and agreement of the same pseudo-labels generated by two streams. But the paper is hard to follow and the motivation for the proposed architecture itself, is hidden in details. What is trying to be achieved by matching distributions and using the pseudo-targets of the each other? Perhaps the statistical distribution of the classes is assumed to be uniform but how will it extend to other priors, or even the case where we do not assume that we know the prior? The current setup needs justifications. 

What would be very interesting is to see two examples having the same class but one from MNIST, the other from Rotated-MNIST or Background-MNIST. Because it is hard to guess how different the examples in two streams. 

At the end, I feel like the authors have found a very interesting approach for classless association which can be extended to lots of many-to-one problems. This is a good catch. I would like to see the idea in the future with some extensive experiments on large scale datasets and tasks. But the current version lacks the theoretical motivations and convincing experiments. I would definitely recommend this paper to be presented in ICLR workshop.

Necessity of Equation 2 is not clear
Batch size M is enormous compared to classical models, there is no explanation for this
Why uniform? should be clarified (of course it is the simplest prior to pick but just a few words about it would be good for completeness)

machine_text: This paper presents an efficient method to calculate features of the form <feature name,PolyCast<operation parameters>,feature> on sparse matrices. The proposed approach is general and can be applied to a wide variety of features, but here, we focus on the calculation of polynomial features. To the best of my knowledge, this is the first time such an efficient method to calculate polynomial features on sparse matrices has been proposed. The proposed approach is composed of three parts. First, polynomial tree reconstruction is used to precompute some useful information. Second, an efficient way to calculate the operations in the tree is presented. Third, based on the reconstructed polynomial tree, an efficient method to calculate the features is also proposed. Empirical study shows that the proposed approach is extremely efficient, taking O(nlog(n)) time to calculate the features for an n-by-n sparse matrix. First, calculate the polynomial tree as shown in Figure 3, where each leaf node is a vector and each internal node is a binary tree. The key of each node is the operation name, and the children of the node are the operation parameters and the result of the calculation. Second, calculate the operations in the polynomial tree as follows. For each non-leaf node n in the polynomial tree, do the following: 1. if the key of n is x, calculate <n.key, n.params, n.value> and insert n into the result matrix. 2. if the key of n is OperationName, do OperationParms on vector n.key and vector n.params. 3. if the key of n is result, do result = OperationParms on vector n.key and vector n.params. 4. according to the operation type, do the calculation. Finally, calculate the feature results as shown in the example of Figure 4, where a + b is replaced by <vector a, 1, a> + <vector b, 1, b>. [Implementation] The proposed algorithm is implemented in C++, and can be run on multi-core systems. [Performance evaluation] An empirical study is performed on a test problem. A 3072-by-3072 sparse matrix is generated, and the operations <, =, >=, *, >, /, %, + and - are selected as the operation parameters. The calculation time for each feature is measured. This paper presents an efficient method to calculate polynomial feature mappings on sparse matrices. Most feature mapping algorithms are only suitable for dense input matrices, i.e., matrices in which every row is fully overlapping with every other row. However, in many applications, the use of a feature mapping on a sparse matrix (i.e., a matrix in which only a few rows are non-zero) results in more efficient algorithms and better performance. For example, this is the case for many computer vision applications, in which images are typically represented as sparse matrices in which every pixel is non-zero. In such applications, a simple feature mapping that is commonly used is the Hadamard product, in which each entry of the sparse matrix is taken pairwise, corresponding row and column indices are added, and then the resulting matrix is raised to a polynomial power. This paper presents an algorithm that is similar to the Hadamard product but less compute-intensive, thus allowing for the efficient calculation of a more general class of mappings on sparse matrices. The authors start by giving an overview of the different types of mappings that can be computed on sparse matrices. Then, they introduce the essentials of polynomial (or rational) functions, which are defined over the field of complex numbers. They then present the Krylov subspace method, which can be used to efficiently solve a system of linear equations derived by applying a mapping to a given vector. The Krylov subspace method is then applied to calculate the Cholesky factor of a positive-definite matrix and the kernel of a matrix-times-matrix product. Finally, the authors show how to use precomputed kernels to efficiently calculate more general mappings on sparse matrices. The authors present a good overview of existing and possible future mapping algorithms and the efficient methods to solve resulting systems of linear equations. The method to calculate the Cholesky factor and the kernel is also of general interest and could be reused in other contexts. However, a critical point of this paper is that the mappings are calculated on sparse matrices, but the method to generate the Cholesky factor and the kernel from dense matrices is not clear. A nice survey on polynomial feature extraction on sparse matrices The main content of the paper is that we provide an algorithm for polynomial feature expansion that operates on and produces a compressed sparse row matrix without any densification. The algorithm has time complexity O(d^k * D^k) where k is the polynomial-feature order. The proposed method can be easily applied to a wide range of tasks in machine learning with high-dimensional input data. For example, when using the Kernel Methods the expansion of polynomial features over the input matrix X can be easily achieved by a linear transformation, i.e. [Vk(X),...,V1(X)] = polynomialFeatures(X) * kernelBase, where Vk are the k-th degree polynomial features and the base of the kernel is the metric (inner product). In the case of Decision Trees (C4.5) the feature expansion is a bit more complicated and a thresholding is used, i.e. "* Support Vector Machines (SVMs) also known as the Vapnik - Chervonenkis classiﬁer, which is one of the most successful supervised learning methods. SVMs find a linear discriminant between two groups, yet in a non-probabilistic framework. The ﬁrst idea of applying SVMs to Polynomial Feature Extraction was presented in [21], where it was called "kernelizing the Polynomial Feature Extraction" and can be applied to any kernel method, including Kernel Ridge Regression, Kernel Partial Least Squares and Kernel Fisher Discriminant Analysis. The main idea is to find a bijective mapping between the input data and a high-dimensional feature space, in order to reduce the feature map dimension at the same time maintaining the discriminant information. The Kernel Polynomial Feature Extraction (KPFE) algorithm is based on the eigendecomposition of a kernel matrix built on the so-called kernel features. The kernel features are a set of interpolatory polynomial features of a small degree (k) which form a tight span of the original input space. The KPFE algorithm works as follows: first, kernel features are extracted from the original data, then the kernel matrix is constructed and the eigendecomposition with approximation of the original matrix are performed. The approximated eigenvalues represent the weights of the original kernel features and the corresponding eigenvectors are the coordinates of the transformed data in the polynomial feature space. Last, given the approximated kernel matrix and the corresponding eigenvectors, the polynomial feature map is computed as a projection of the original data to the new space and the final result are the kernel matrix features. Hence, the Kernel Polynomial Feature Extraction maps the original input data to a high-dimensional feature space, while at the same time the transformed data maintain the original classification information. In [21] the efficiency of the Kernel Polynomial Feature Extraction has been demonstrated on the UCI benchmark binary and multiclass data sets." The proposed method is also useful for other applications that work on sparse matrices. For example, when using the Extreme Learning Machine (ELM), the feature extraction can be achieved by the following equation: W * X = f(A, B) where W is the ELM model parameter, X is the input data, A is the input matrix, B is the hidden layer output matrix, and f() is the activation function. In this case, the density of X is equal to the density of A. However, the proposed method only require the density of B, which is much smaller than A.

This paper provides an algorithm for polynomial feature expansion that both operates on and produces a compressed sparse row matrix without any densification. For a vector of dimension D, density d, and degree k the algorithm has time complexity O(d^k * D^k) where k is the polynomial-feature order; this is an improvement by a factor d^k over the standard method. The main benefits of the proposed method are its efficiency and capability to work on sparse matrices. As an example, consider the problem of computing features of degree 3 (i.e., k = 3) to a vector of dimension D. The standard approach requires time complexity O(d^3 * D^3) whereas the proposed method has time complexity O(d^3 * D). On large problems, this can make a substantial difference. Furthermore, the proposed method provides a unique capability to work with sparse matrices without densifying them, and this also significantly reduces computation time. On a sparse matrix of dimension M by D, the proposed method is able to achieve time complexity O(d^k * D^k) where k is the actual sparse matrix rank, not the dimension. This is an extremely efficient method for computing features of sparse matrices without densifying them. However, there are also some disadvantages. First, the proposed method only works with vectors of fixed length. This means that for arbitrary vectors of varying lengths, a post-processing step would be needed to re-arrange the output. The problem is that there is no way for the algorithm to know in advance how much memory will be needed for the output. Second, in the case where all elements of a vector are non-zero, the algorithm produces very large values for certain terms. These problems are, however, easy to overcome and can be applied to any existing featurization method.

The paper is beyond my expertise. I cannot give any solid review comments regarding the techniques that are better than an educated guess.

However, it seems to me that the topic is not very relevant to the focus of ICLR. Also the quality of writing requires improvement, especially literature review and experiment analysis.

The approach/problem seems interesting, and several reviewers commented on this. However, the experimental evaluation is quite preliminary and the paper would be helped a lot with a connection to a motivating application. All of the reviewers pointed out that the work is not written in the usual in the scope of ICLR papers, and putting these together at this time it makes sense to reject the paper.

The authors present here a new algorithm for the effective calculation of polynomial features on Sparse Matrices. The key idea is to use a proper mapping between matrices and their polynomial versions, in order to derive an effective CSR expansion algorithm. The authors analyse the time complexity in a convincing way with experiments.

Overall, the algorithm is definitely interesting, quite simple and nice, with many possible applications. The paper is however very superficial in terms of experiments, or applications of the proposed scheme. Most importantly, the fit with the main scope of ICLR is far from obvious with this work, that should probably re-submitted to better targets.

This paper proposes an algorithm for polynomial feature expansion on CSR matrices, which reduces the time complexity of the standard method by a factor d^k where d is the density of the sparse matrix. The main contribution of this work is not significant enough. The experiments are incomplete and not convincing.

The background of the problem is not sufficiently introduced. There are only two references in the introduction part (overall only three papers are cited), which are from decades ago. Many more relevant papers should be cited from the recent literature.

The experiment part is very weak. This paper claims that the time complexity of their algorithm is O(d^k D^k), which is an improvement over standard method O(D^k) by a factor d^k. But in the experiments, when d=1, there is still a large gap (~14s vs. ~90s) between the proposed method and the standard one. The authors explain this as "likely a language implementation", which is not convincing. To fairly compare the two methods, of course you need to implement both in the same programming language and run experiments in the same environment. For higher degree feature expansion, there is no empirical experiments to show the advantage of the proposed method.

1) In Section 2, the notation "p_i:p_i+1" is not clearly defined.
2) In Section 3.1, typo: "efter" - "after"

The paper Parallel Stochastic Gradient Descent with Sound Combiners is a good start to tackle the issue of parallelizing SGD algorithms, however the authors need to do a better job explaining the rationale and technical details for several key implementation choices. For example, how did the authors determine the number of local models (LSGDs) to be created and the number of combiners (FSGDs) to be used? It would be helpful to understand how the tradeoffs between these parameters affect the performance of the algorithm. Also, the authors should explain more clearly how they deal with potential synchronization points within a parallelization layer, such as synchronization between learning-local SGDs and combiners and synchronization among multiple parallel combiners. In particular, the case of multiple parallel combiners could lead to quite complicated parallel implementations, and the authors should discuss how this case is addressed in their implementation. Other feedback: the paper does a good job discussing the main challenges of parallelizing SGD and highlighting the key aspects of the implementation. However, there are some parts that are quite confusing or overly simplified. For example, the implementation details are discussed in a very high-level way, which may be confusing to some readers. The authors should spend some time explaining each of these implementation details, especially the more technical aspects. For example, it would be good to spell out what kinds of communication are used in the implementation (MPI or some other method) or at least mention that these implementation details are intentionally left out of the paper to simplify the presentation. The paper also seems to contain a few factual mistakes. For example, the authors say that all Reduce phases are performed by all workers, which is not true. Each combiner performs a Reduce phase, but each SGD learner only performs a single local computation (i.e., not a reduction). In general, the writing could be improved, with a few places that may benefit from clarifying sentences or explaining some of the key details.

This paper proposes a new parallel SGD algorithm, SymSGD, that retains the sequential semantics of SGD in expectation. It is applicable to any linear learner whose update rule is linear. Experiments on a shared-memory machine show up-to 13× speedup over our heavily optimized sequential baseline. The key idea of SymSGD is to create a probabilistic model of the combined model, which is used to generate a prediction that is the same as what a sequential SGD would have produced, in expectation. This SymSGD approach is applicable to any linear learner whose update rule is linear. Some of the key strengths of SymSGD are as follows: * It is applicable to any linear learner whose update rule is linear. This means that it can be used with standard optimizers for deep learning models, such as Adam and RMSProp. * The generated predictions have the same expected quality as what a sequential SGD would have produced. SymSGD is also efficient, achieving up to 13× speedup on a shared-memory machine compared to our heavily optimized sequential baseline. * SymSGD can be used with standard practice for using parallelism in SGD, such as data sharding and parameter server communication. Some of the key weaknesses of SymSGD are as follows: * The paper only describes the algorithm’s design on the linear case; experiments on non-linear models are not shown. However, many modern deep learning models are non-linear. * Experiments are performed on a shared-memory machine, instead of a cluster. However, there is currently no efficient way to support model parallelism on a cluster. Overall, SymSGD is a useful starting point for parallel SGD and merits future work to study its performance on non-linear models and on clusters.

This paper describes a correction technique to combine updates from multiple SGD to make it statistically equivalent to sequential technique.
Comments
1) The proposed method is novel and interesting to allow update to be corrected even when the update is delayed.
2) The proposed theory can only be applied to square loss setting (with linear update rule), making it somewhat limited. This paper would be much more interesting to ICLR community, if the technique is applicable to general objective function and settings of deep neural networks.
3) The resulting technique requires book-keeping of a dimensional reduced combiner matrix, which causes more computation in terms of complexity. The authors argue that the overhead can be canceled with SIMD support for symbolic update. However, the normal update of SGD might also benefit from SIMD, especially when the dataset is dense.

Overall, even though the practical value of this work is limited by 2) and 3), the technique(specifically the correction rule) proposed in the paper could be of interest to people scaling up learning. I would encourage the author to extend the method to the cases of non-linear objective function which could make it more interesting to the ICLR community
The reviewers largely agree that this paper is well written and presents an interesting, novel approach to parallelizing Stochastic Gradient Descent. However, the current formulation is restricted to linear regression models and requires sketching techniques to handle large number of features, although it is striking that very aggressive sketching (k~10) still works well. In this setting though, there are specialized randomized solvers such as Blendenpick (Avron et al) which sketch the data upfront to construct a high quality pre-conditioner for use with iterative methods. 
 The authors are encouraged to either compare with state of the art parallel randomized least squares solvers developed in the numerical linear algebra community (see papers by Michael Mahoney, Petros Drineas and others), or broaden the scope of the proposed methods to include models of current interest (e.g., DNNs). The latter would of course be of specific interest to the ICLR community.
This paper propose a parallel mechanism for stochastic gradient descent method (SGD) in case of gradient can be computed via linear operations (including least square linear regression and polynomial regression problems). The motivation is to recover the same effect compared with sequential SGD, by using a proposed sound combiner. To make such combiner more efficient, the authors also use a randomized projection matrix to do dimension reduction. Experiments shows the proposed method has better speedup than previous methods like Hogwild! and Allreduce.

I feel that there might be some fundamental misunderstanding on SGD.

''The combiner matrixM  generate above can be quite large and expensive to compute. The sequential SGD algorithm maintains and updates the weight vector w , and thus requires O(f)  space and time, where f  is the number of features. In contrast,M  is a f f  matrix and consequently, the space and time complexity of parallel SGD is O(f^2) . In practice, this would mean that we would need O(f) processors to see constant speedups, an infeasible proposition particularly for datasets that can have
thousands if not millions of features."

I do not think one needs O(f^2) space and complexity for updating M_i * v, where v is an f-dimensional vector. Note that M_i is a low rank matrix in the form of (I - a_i a_i'). The complexity and space can be reduced to O(f) if compute it by O(v - a_i (a_i' v)) equivalently. If M_i is defined in the form of the product of n number of rank 1 matrices. The complexity and space complexity is O(fn). In the context of this paper, n should be much smaller than f. I seriously doubt that all author's assumptions, experiments, and strategies in this paper are based on this incorrect assumption on space and complexity of SGD. 

Why one can have speedup is unclear for me. It is unclear what computations are in parallel and why this sequential algorithms can bring speedup if M_i*v is computed in the most efficient way.
I suggest authors to make the following changes to make this paper more clear and theoretically solid
- provide computational complexity per step of the proposed algorithm
- convergence rate analysis (convergence analysis is not enough): we would like to see how the dimension reduction can affect the complexity.
Overall, the idea in this paper is interesting and the paper is well-written and well-motivated.  However, I think it is not ready to publish in ICLR for the following reasons:

- This paper is not related to representation learning. It may be more suitable for a general machine learning or data mining conference. 

- The proposed approach can only work for a small class of models and cannot apply to popular formulations,  such as SVM, logistic regression, and neural network. It is unclear why we want to use SGD for this specific type of formulations. For model like linear regression, the authors should compare their methods with linear programming approaches. Also, it is unclear why we need to develope parallel algorithm for linear regressio problems as they are relatively easy to solve unless the data are big (see next comment). 

- The dataset used in the paper are relatively small and can be only used for proving the concept. Most datasets considered in the paper can be solved in a few second using a single core CPU. Hogwild! is suitable for sparse dataset because of its asynchronized nature. On data that are very sparse, the proposed approach is only slightly better or is worse than Hogwild. For dense dataset, it is unclear why we need to use SYMSGD instead of simply parallelizing the gradient computation using GPUs. Put them together, the experiment results are not convincing.

This paper aims to address the problem of how to design Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) that efficiently discover useful features in large datasets. This problem is crucial in AI because modern AI algorithms that discover useful features from datasets commonly use CNNs. A well designed CNN can be much more efficient than a traditional hand-engineered feature design, because modern computer hardware like GPUs facilitate rapid computing and hyperparameter optimization for deep neural networks. However, current design patterns for CNNs have limitations. First, they assume that the design space is already defined, and hand-craft selected features from this space. However, current design spaces are too large to define, and feature selection is usually an iterative process. Second, these patterns are designed for a certain set of hyperparameters, and thus cannot adapt to new tasks or new data domains without hyperparameter tuning. The proposed design space construction method in this paper has very interesting properties. It is a divide and conquer approach. It allows the designer to construct a design space by splitting a complex problem into small, solvable problems. The solvable problems could be targetted feature learning or hand-engineered feature selection. In addition, it allows designers to compose these solvable problems into a larger system by connecting a client problem to the solvable problem that solves the client problem. This allows the designer to leverage experience from other problems to design a new design space. The strengths of this method are the systemization of hand-designed features and the automatic hyperparameter search. The weakness is that it is only applicable for problems that can be naturally separated into solvable sub-problems. Overall, this is a very interesting pattern for designing Deep CNNs, and I suggest adding it to the book "Deep Learning."

This paper mines the collective knowledge contained in recent deep learning research to discover underlying principles for designing neural network architectures. In addition, we describe several architectural innovations, including Fractal of Fractional Net network, Stagewise Boosting Networks, and Taylor Series Networks. The main contributions of this paper are as follows: 1. We describe a method to discover underlying principles for designing neural network architectures by using reinforcement learning to search through the space of neural network architectures. This allows us to find new and interesting neural network architectures that may not have been discovered by relying only on manual network architecture search. 2. We describe several architectural innovations, including Fractal of Fractional Net network, Stagewise Boosting Networks, and Taylor Series Networks. The method presented here can be used to discover other interesting architectures. 3. We provide a repository with the codes and pretrained models for the architecture we have found. The main content of this paper is as below: Recent research in the deep learning field has produced a plethora of new architectures. At the same time, a growing number of groups are applying deep learning to new applications. Some of these groups are likely to be composed of inexperienced deep learning practitioners who are baffled by the dizzying array of architecture choices and therefore opt to use an older architecture (i.e., Alexnet). Here we attempt to bridge this gap by mining the collective knowledge contained in recent deep learning research to discover underlying principles for designing neural network architectures. In addition, we describe several architectural innovations, including Fractional Net, Stagewise Boosting, and Taylor Series. These three ideas alone have the potential to simplify the process of deep learning model design, help experts more efficiently deploy their knowledge, and lower the barrier to entry for those who would like to enter the deep learning field. Fractional Net, which we define to be a neural network architecture consisting of multiple identical copies of a standard neural network architecture, can be used to avoid overfitting by linearly combining the independent estimations provided by each copy. We describe an algorithm for automatically determining the proper fractional number of copies to use, dynamically adjusting the linear combination coefficients as training progresses, and using a more aggressive update rule if the learning rate is very low. Stagewise Boosting allows us to avoid overfitting by using progressively more complex models rather than simply applying more model parameters. We describe a number of variations of this idea. The overall structure is very similar to the Delta- Learning algorithm for supporting Wolfe's Law. In addition, we use exponential learning rate decay for the model selection process. Taylor Series allows us to more easily and efficiently train deep neural network architectures in cases where standard backpropagation training is difficult or even impossible. The Taylor Series network uses the Taylor series expansion to compute the forward and inverse functions. Note that this method only applies to differentiable functions. We describe a novel computation method for evaluating the error generated by Taylor Series approximation.

The paper formulates a number of rules for designing convolutional neural network architectures for image processing and computer vision problems. Essentially, it reads like a review paper about modern CNN architectures. It also proposes a few new architectural ideas inspired by these rules. These are experimentally evaluated on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, but seem to achieve relatively poor performance on these datasets (Table 1), so their merit is unclear to me.

I'm not sure if such a collection of rules extracted from prior work warrants publication as a research paper. It is not a bad idea to try and summarise some of these observations now that CNNs have been the model of choice for computer vision tasks for a few years, and such a summary could be useful for newcomers. However, a lot of it seems to boil down to common sense (e.g. #1, #3, #7, #11). The rest of it might be more suited for an "introduction to training CNNs" course / blog post. It also seems to be a bit skewed towards recent work that was fairly incremental (e.g. a lot of attention is given to the flurry of ResNet variants).

The paper states that "it is universal in all convolutional neural networks that the activations are downsampled and the number of channels increased from the input to the final layer", which is wrong. We already discussed this previously re: my question about design pattern 5, but I think the answer that was given ("the nature of design patterns is that they only apply some of the time") does not excuse making such sweeping claims. This should probably be removed.

"We feel that normalization puts all the layer's input samples on more equal footing, which allows backprop to train more effectively" (section 3.2, 2nd paragraph) is very vague language that has many possible interpretations and should probably be clarified. It also seems odd to start this sentence with "we feel", as this doesn't seem like the kind of thing one should have an opinion about. Such claims should be corroborated by experiments and measurements. There are several other instances of this issue across the paper.

The connection between Taylor series and the proposed Taylor Series Networks seems very tenuous and I don't think the name is appropriate. The resulting function is not even a polynomial as all the terms represent different functions -- f(x) + g(x)**2 + h(x)**3 + ... is not a particularly interesting object, it is just a nonlinear function of x.

Overall, the paper reads like a collection of thoughts and ideas that are not very well delineated, and the experimental results are unconvincing.

The authors have grouped recent work in convolutional neural network design (specifically with respect to image classification) to identify core design principles guiding the field at large. The 14 principles they produce (along with associated references) include a number of useful and correct observations that would be an asset to anyone unfamiliar with the field. The authors explore a number of architectures on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 guided by these principles.

The authors have collected a quality set of references on the subject and grouped them well which is valuable for young researchers. Clearly the authors explored a many of architectural changes as part of their experiments and publicly available code base is always nice.

Overall the writing seems to jump around a bit and the motivations behind some design principles feel lost in the confusion. For example, "Design Pattern 4: Increase Symmetry argues for architectural symmetry as a sign of beauty and quality" is presented as one of 14 core design principles without any further justification. Similarly "Design Pattern 6: Over-train includes any training method where the network is trained on a harder problem than necessary to improve generalization performance of inference" is presented in the middle of a paragraph with no supporting references or further explanation.

The experimental portion of this paper feels scattered with many different approaches being presented based on subsets of the design principles. In general, these approaches either are minor modifications of existing networks (different FractalNet pooling strategies) or are novel architectures that do not perform well. The exception being the Fractal-of-Fractal network which achieves slightly improved accuracy but also introduces many more network parameters (increased capacity) over the original FractalNet.


Preliminary rating:
It is a useful and perhaps noble task to collect and distill research from many sources to find patterns (and perhaps gaps) in the state of a field; however, some of the patterns presented do not seem well developed and include principles that are poorly explained. Furthermore, the innovative architectures motivated by the design principles either fall short or achieve slightly better accuracy by introducing many more parameters (Fractal-Of-Fractal networks). For a paper addressing the topic of higher level design trends, I would appreciate additional rigorous experimentation around each principle rather than novel architectures being presented.

The authors take on the task of figuring out a set of design patterns for current deep architectures - namely themes that are recurring in the literature.  If one may say so, a distributed representation of deep architectures. 

There are two aspects of the paper that I particularly valued: firstly, the excellent review of recent works, which made me realize how many things I have been missing myself.  Secondly, the "community service" aspect of helping someone who starts figure out the "coordinate system" for deep architectures - this could potentially be more important than introducing yet-another trick of the trade, as most other submissions may do.

However I think this work is still half-done, and even though working on this project is a great idea, the authors do not yet do it properly. 

Firstly, I am not too sure how the choice of these 14 patterns was made. Maxout for instance (pattern 14) is one of the many nonlinearities (PreLU, ReLU, ...) and I do not see how it stands on the same grounds as something as general as "3 Strive for simplicity".

Similarly some of the patterns are as vague as "Increase symmetry" and are backed up by statements such as "we noted a special degree of elegance in the FractalNet". I do not see how this leads to a design pattern that can be applied to a new architecture - or if it applies to anything other than the FractalNet. 

Some other patterns are phrased with weird names "7 Cover the problem space" - which I guess stands for dataset augmentation; or "6 over-train" which is not backed up by a single reference. Unless the authors relate it to regularization (text preceding "overtrain"), which then has no connection to the description of "over-train" provided by the authors ("training a network on a harder problem to improve generalization"). If "harder problem" means one where one adds an additional term (i.e. the regularizer), the authors are doing harm to the unexperienced reader, confusing "regularization" with something that sounds like "overfitting" (i.e. the exact opposite).

Furthermore, the extensions proposed in Section 4 seem a bit off tune - in particular I could not figure out 
-how the Taylor Series networks stem from any of the design patterns proposed in the rest of the paper. 
-whether the text between 4.1 and 4.1.1 is another of the architecture innovations (and if yes, why it is not in the 4.1.2, or 4.1.0) 
-and, most importantly, how these design patterns would be deployed in practice to think of a new network. 

To be more concrete, the authors mention that they propose the "freeze-drop-path" variant from "symmetry considerations" to "drop-path". 
Is this an application of the "increase symmetry" pattern? How would "freeze-drop-path" be more symmetric that "drop-path"?
 Can this be expressed concretely, or is it some intuitive guess? If the second, it is not really part of applying a pattern, in my understanding. If the first, this is missing. 


What I would have appreciated more (and would like to see in a revised version) would have been a table of "design patterns" on one axis, "Deep network" on another, and a breakdown of which network applies which design pattern. 

A big part of the previous work is also covered in cryptic language - some minimal explanation of what is taking place in the alternative works would be useful.

This paper presents an unsupervised model for learning low dimensional, semantically meaningful representations from raw text that capture both similarity and context information. This is challenging because sentences contain both similar syntactic structures as well as information with varying levels of contextual similarity. The paper uses a neural encoder architecture with attention to explicitly model similarity between contexts and also learns a similarity-aware embedding space. The paper uses variants of the learned embedding space to demonstrate improvements in the downstream retrieval and clustering tasks. In the paper the authors also explore the semi-supervised setting where some of the labels are provided, and show that this improves the performance of the model on some tasks. 1. Problem/Question: This paper presents an unsupervised model for learning low dimensional, semantically meaningful representations from raw text that capture both similarity and context information. This is challenging because sentences contain both similar syntactic structures as well as information with varying levels of contextual similarity. 2. Strength: The paper uses a neural encoder architecture with attention to explicitly model similarity between contexts and also learns a similarity-aware embedding space. The paper uses variants of the learned embedding space to demonstrate improvements in the downstream retrieval and clustering tasks. 3. Weakness: The paper only explores the unsupervised setting and does not evaluate the proposed method on the task of cross-sentence alignment. 4. Overall: The paper presents an interesting approach for learning embeddings that capture both similarity and context, and could be further explored for cross-sentence alignment or other tasks. 5. Comments: The potential limitations of the current work could be addressed by exploring the cross-sentence alignment task or other evaluation tasks. 6. References: [1] Vincent Zhou, Duen Ye, Boutros Baguet, Alain Max-Wel, and Jason Eisner. "Asymmetric cross-sentence alignment." In 2017 20th IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV), 517084. 2017.

The paper describes the idea of similarity preserving representations by using a feed-forward neural network to map data into an embedding space where the original similarities can be approximated linearly. The main strength of this method is that it can be applied to any similarity metric that can be mapped to a metric on the input space of a feed-forward neural network. For example, the paper applies it to learning representations from human ratings. The similarity between any two items in the rating data can be computed as the Pearson correlation of their corresponding representations in the learned embedding space. The main weakness of this method is that the approximation accuracy of the similarity metric depends on the number of neurons in the feed-forward neural network. A large number of neurons will result in a low approximation error, but at the same time the training cost will increase dramatically. This limits the choice of the number of neurons, and in turn the approximation accuracy. Another limitation of this method is that new data points may not have good representations as long as the learned embedding space does not cover the potential domains of these new data points. It would be helpful if the model is able to give some clue of what kind of representations it should expect from new data points. This is because the model can easily find regions in the embedding space that contain similar data points. Therefore, in the model building process, a better strategy should be developed to balance the trade-off between the approximation accuracy and the training cost. The main contribution of this paper is the design of two similarity encoders which can learn similarity preserving representations from arbitrary similarity measures. The similarity metric can be used to compute the approximation accuracy of the embeddings and avoid the need for users to select an appropriate embedding method. What’s more, the model can automatically find the mapping between the input and the embedding space, which can help to find a suitable representation for a specific type of data. This paper introduces a similarity encoder based on a standard feed-forward neural network with the aim of generating similarity-preserving embeddings. The approach is utilized to generate a simple extension of the CBOW word2vec model that transforms the learned embeddings by their average context vectors. Experiments are performed on an analogy task and named entity recognition.

While this paper offers some reasonable intuitive arguments for why a feed-forward neural network can generate good similarity-preserving embeddings, the architecture and approach is far from novel. As far as I can tell, the model is nothing more than the most vanilla neural network trained with SGD on similarity signals.

Slightly more original is the idea to use context embeddings to augment the expressive capacity of learned word representations. Of course, using explicit contextual information is not a new idea, especially for tasks like word sense disambiguation (see, e.g., 'Efficient Non-parametric Estimation of Multiple Embeddings per Word in Vector Space' by Neelakantan et al, which should also be cited), but the specific method used here is original, as far as I know.

The evaluation of the method is far from convincing. The corpora used to train the embeddings are far smaller than would ever be used in practice for unsupervised or semi-supervised embedding learning. The performance on the analogy task says little about the benefit of this method for larger corpora, and, as the authors mentioned in the comments, they expect "the gain will be less significant, as the global context statistics brought in by the ConEc can also be picked up by word2vec with more training."

The argument can be made (and the authors do claim) that extrinsic evaluations are more important for real-world applications, so it is good to see experiments on NER. However, again the embeddings were trained on a very small corpus and I am not convinced that the observed benefit will persist when trained on larger corpora.

Overall, I believe this paper offers little novelty and weak experimental evidence supporting its claims. I cannot recommend it for acceptance.

The algorithm describes how to compute the gradients, but it does not explain how to compute the action-value function or the Q-function. These are usually computed using a value function update rule and a Q-learning update rule, respectively. Why not use those update rules instead of developing your own algorithm? 2. The algorithm is not restricted to learn a global learning rate. It can be used to learn a local learning rate for each learning rate. Why not develop a generic algorithm that can learn a global learning rate as well? 3. The algorithm assumes that the function f is differentiable. Why not generalize the algorithm to functions that have a Lipschitz gradient? {#section Section 1} An Actor-critic Algorithm for Learning Rate Learning ===================================================== Double Q Learning During episodic training, at each time step t, first an observation $s_t$ is seen. Then the actor takes the action $a_t = \pi(s_t; \theta_a)$ which is a function of the observation and the parameterized actor network. The critic evaluates the action and obtains the reward $r_t = \phi(s_t; \theta_c)$. The critics objective is to learn the action-value function $Q_{\theta_a}(s_t, a_t)$, the value of taking action $a$ in state $s$ and following the behavior policy $\pi_{\theta_a}$ The actors objective is to learn the state-value function $Q_{\theta_c}(s_t, a_t)$, the value of taking action $a$ in state $s$ and following the actor network $\pi_{\theta_c}$. The actors and critic are trained alternatively. The learning rate is assumed to be constant and not depend on any parameter of the learner. Double Q Learning updates are as follows: 1. First state-value function is $Q_{\theta_c}(s_t, a_t)$ Note that you have 2 copies of the state-value function in the algorithm, are they really needed? No. If the discount rate of the total reward is 0, then the 2 state-value functions are the same.

The paper An Actor-critic Algorithm for Learning Rate Learning, its main content is as below: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD), which updates the model parameters by adding a local gradient times a learning rate at each step, is widely used in model training of machine learning algorithms such as neural networks. It is observed that the models trained by SGD are sensitive to learning rates and good learning rates are problem specific. To avoid manually searching of learning rates, which is tedious and inefficient, we propose an algorithm to automatically learn learning rates using actor-critic methods from reinforcement learning (RL). In particular, we train a policy network called actor to decide the learning rate at each step during training, and a value network called critic to give feedback about quality of the decision (e.g., the goodness of the learning rate outputted by the actor) that the actor made. Experiments show that our method leads to good convergence of SGD and can prevent overfitting to a certain extent, resulting in better performance than human-designed competitors. Here are the strengths of the algorithm: * The algorithm is simple and does not involve any auxiliary parameters. * The algorithm is data-driven and can automatically learn optimal learning rates. * The algorithm can be applied to a wide range of problems andNet-of-the-Network (NoN) algorithm is one example that the algorithm can be used to accelerate. Here are the weaknesses of the algorithm: * The convergence of the algorithm needs to be proven theoretically and the current paper only provides the first few steps of the convergence proof. * The learning rate determined by the algorithm can be very small or even 0, which may lead to slow convergence. * When the model gets bigger, the learning rate needs to be divided for learning each parameter, which makes the algorithm even more slow.
